Innovation Ranking Criteria

Papers are ranked from most to least innovative by a composite score from 0 to 100. Each paper is scored on six dimensions: (1) novelty, (2) scientific rigor, (3) non-obviousness, (4) completeness, (5) resilience, and (6) practical impact. The composite is a weighted average of the six scores under one of three weight profiles (empirical, theoretical, or systems), chosen per paper. Each paper includes a justification explaining its placement.

≥90 Groundbreaking
≥75 Highly Innovative
≥60 Innovative
≥40 Moderately Innovative
≥20 Incremental
<20 Routine

#1 — Highly Innovative (81)

Argo-Bench: Evaluating Data Agents on Enterprise -Scale Workflows

G Tomitsuka, A Raayatsanati, E Xing, D Gand, JJ Ma · arxiv.org · generating environments for agent testing in enterprises - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces Argo-Bench, a benchmark of 210 data-science and analytics tasks over a simulated NYC food-delivery company exported to a 7.49-billion-row Oracle E-Business Suite warehouse, where agents' filed actions (bans, forecasts, budget cuts, dashboards) are graded against the simulator's withheld ground-truth state rather than against gold queries. - Why it's important: Existing text-to-SQL benchmarks (Spider 2.0, BIRD) have audited error rates of 52.8–62.8% in their answer keys, cover fragmented public datasets rather than a coherent enterprise system, and cannot score consequential decisions like fraud bans or budget allocations whose correctness is not written in the data. - How it does it: The authors simulate a calibrated three-sided marketplace (81M orders in 2024, anchored to NYC DCWP disclosures and 34 public donor datasets), project it into a 235-table EBS warehouse that omits the simulator's latent state, and grade nine filing types (e.g., forecasts by a proper weighted interval score, ban lists by cost-saved against ban-nobody/ban-everybody baselines) computed from truth queries or simulator labels. - The good: The strongest of 14 frontier and open-weight models (Claude Opus 5.5) solves only 34.8% of tasks and averages 59.5/100 with nine of 14 models below 35, plus unusually detailed failure forensics (e.g., 24 of 27 failing runs on a membership-dashboard task use contract dates instead of billing history, with 7 getting every other figure right to within a few dollars) — evidence the benchmark measures a real, unsolved capability. - The missing: Every task shares a single simulated world and each model/effort setting has one run per task, so the reported confidence intervals capture task-sampling variation only, not run-to-run variance; and grading depends entirely on the authors' closed-source simulator and frozen response model, which external parties cannot verify. - Read it or not: Read it if you build or evaluate data/BI agents and need to know why text-to-SQL scores overstate enterprise readiness, or if you design agent benchmarks — skip it if you only need another leaderboard data point, since the headline numbers matter less than the construction and grading machinery.
Why this rank
Scored using Empirical profile. Novelty (80) is anchored by the NEW FORMULATION of consequence-based grading against withheld simulator latent state — a real inversion of gold-answer evaluation, though the ingredients (calibrated simulators, cost-sensitive scoring, τ-bench-style action grading) are established. Rigor (82) is strong by benchmark standards — bootstrap CIs, prompt-variant ablations, disclosed answer-key bugs and a reward-hacking incident — but capped by one run per task, a closed simulator/grader, and inherent single-world Goodhart risk. Non-Obviousness (78): separating what the agent sees from what the grader sees, plus the Appendix H audit of Spider 2.0-Snow, reveals structure prior benchmarks missed. Completeness (85) is excellent — authors confront single-city/single-year/scope limits head-on and list open task issues. Resilience (78) holds under most adversarial lines (sensitivity analysis on forecast references) but the no-human-baseline and single-grading-world gaps leave cracks. Practical Impact (85) reflects a 76.5 GB public warehouse, full Apache-2.0 harness, reference agent, and leaderboard. Weighted composite: 0.20*80 + 0.25*82 + 0.15*78 + 0.15*85 + 0.15*78 + 0.10*85 = 81.

Problem & Motivation: Enterprise data work happens in ERP warehouses (Oracle EBS, SAP S/4HANA) where one business event touches ten or more mutually reconciling tables, but real ERP data cannot be released and anonymization breaks the relational structure answers depend on (the authors cite schema-integrity failures in an early BEAVER release). Current benchmarks fall short three ways: (1) Spider 2.0-Snow's 547 questions sparsely cover 152 public databases where, by the authors' own measurement (Appendix H), 80.0% of 13,022 tables are schema-shards of another table and ~69% of questions read at most two logical tables; (2) they stop at SQL, while forecasting, fraud modeling, and budget optimization require Python/ML/OR libraries; (3) they grade against gold answers that audits show are frequently wrong (62.8% of Spider 2.0-Snow gold queries erroneous per Jin et al., 2026), and for tasks like fraud detection the answer is not in the data at all — undetected fraud leaves no label and rejected decisions have unobserved counterfactuals. The affected audience is anyone building LLM data agents for enterprise analytics. Key Idea: Separate what the agent sees from what the grader sees: simulate a business whose latent state (true fraud labels, future months, counterfactual outcomes) is withheld from the warehouse the agent queries, then grade the agent's filed actions by their consequences under the simulator. This makes tasks harder to solve than to verify (the answer key is computed from latent tables, frozen before any run), yields exact labels that need no anonymization, and supports partial credit and objective (non-LLM-judge) scoring. Methodology: Three stages. (1) World simulation: a NYC 2024 food-delivery platform built from 34 public datasets in three donor roles — identity donors (45,834 restaurants, 1.07M addresses, 260 taxi zones used as-is), shape donors (distributions fitted elsewhere, e.g., TLC trips for demand timing, IEEE-CIS for fraud separability), and anchors (DCWP quarterly totals and 10-K filings the world is calibrated to reproduce, Synthea-style). The world is sized at ~55% of the DCWP-reported 148M deliveries; 13 of 16 quarterly per-delivery economics comparisons land within 5% of DCWP figures (courier pay 6–9% high after April). The real April 1, 2024 minimum-pay increase ($17.96→$19.56/hr) is modeled as an extrinsic shock; fraud patterns (order theft, GPS spoofing, promo farming, refund collusion, account takeovers) are inserted with calibrated benign lookalikes. No warehouse record is LLM-generated. (2) Warehouse projection: the world is exported to Oracle EBS 12.2 format — 235 tables (159 standard under 15 Oracle products, 76 custom XX_ extensions), 3,949 columns, 7,491,508,904 rows — validated against Oracle's Vision demo instance by three ERP consultants (14–31 years experience); tables average 52% of Vision's columns, with omissions argued to be informationally neutral. Data drift and legacy-table inconsistencies are deliberately excluded to keep ground truth unambiguous. (3) Task/grading design: 210 tasks across five business areas (trust & safety 67, FP&A 54, marketplace 46, accounting 23, growth 20); each task has a stakeholder-style prompt (avg 159 words), a visibility cutoff (99 tasks see only part of 2024), a list of expectations, and a frozen answer key from truth queries (82 tasks) or simulator labels (128 tasks). Nine grading modes: forecast (weighted interval score on an asinh-transformed scale set by a pre-fixed reference forecast, floored at −200, shown to be proper for 96.7% of 4,527 series), cost_set (Elkan-style example-dependent costs with review costs and innocent margins, Equation 1), data_source (all-or-nothing dashboard tile contract), id_set (F1), keyed_value, table, allocation (share of attainable savings under a frozen response model), presence, binary. Key design decisions: the dual-seed setup (public warehouse released on Hugging Face; leaderboard scored on a private seed with different IDs to block memorization); the filing-based mission-control interface instead of query return; and the greenfield (mess-free) warehouse — the first two are well justified, the third is a defensible but consequential scope choice the authors argue for explicitly. Agents run in Inspect AI on gVisor sandboxes (4 GiB RAM, 1 CPU, no internet, 500 model turns, 240 min) with pandas/statsmodels/sklearn/OR-Tools, querying BigQuery with a 20 GiB-per-query scan cap. Key Results: Across 9,869 graded runs (210 tasks × 47 model/effort settings), Claude Opus 5.5 leads with 34.8% solved (score ≥95) and 59.5 mean score [95% CI 52.0, 67.1], leading GPT-6 Astra (51.8), Claude Sonnet 5.5 (51.8), and GPT-6.1 Sol (49.5) by 7.7–10.0 paired points; nine of 14 models average below 35. Per-task API cost ranges from $0.06 (GPT-6 Luna) to $4.89 (Muse Spark 1.3); warehouse (BigQuery scan) spend adds 15–92% on top, totaling $6,160 against $14,502 of model spend. Diagnostic findings: (a) wrong record — on a membership-dashboard task, 24 of 27 failing runs define membership from contract dates rather than billing history (missing a 7-day grace after declined charges), 7 getting every other number right within a few dollars; (b) wrong objective — on a $9.6M quest-cut task, GPT-6 Astra's econometric plan loses $86,281 (score 0) where Opus's surge-substitution analysis saves $3.09M of an attainable $3.12M (score 99); stating the objective raises the 47-setting mean from 18.5 to 61.7; (c) wrong quantity — 46 of 47 runs miss all 12 monthly location-report counts because the warehouse keeps hourly rather than half-hourly idle check-ins; across dashboard tasks, 66.9% of data sources passing their structural contract score zero on values; (d) overconfident forecasts — nominal 80% intervals cover the outcome only 44.8% of the time across 4,553 series. Reasoning effort helps GPT-6/Claude models monotonically (Opus: +17.0 low→medium, +5.9 medium→high, +4.0 high→extra-high) with no detectable gain for Gemini 3.8 Flash or Qwen 3.8 Max past medium. Baseline comparisons are between models; no external agent framework is run. Baseline benchmarks are characterized analytically (Table 1, Appendix H), not by running agents on them. Test scale is genuinely stress-scale on data volume (7.49B rows) but single-world on environment. Novelty Classification: NEW DATASET/BENCHMARK plus NEW FORMULATION of evaluation (consequence-based grading against withheld simulator latent state in an ERP setting). The genuinely novel combination is: a mutually-reconciling, enterprise-scale synthetic warehouse + a grader that scores filed actions by consequences using latent state, with exact fraud/counterfactual labels no real dataset can provide. Individual ingredients are established — calibrated simulators (Synthea, PaySim), synthetic warehouses (TPC-DS), action-state grading (τ-bench, AppWorld), cost-sensitive scoring (Elkan 2001), proper forecast scoring (Bracher 2021) — and the related-work section credibly distinguishes Argo-Bench from nearest neighbors (AvalancheBench, Era by Eon, ERPBench×2, CRMArena-Pro) by latent state provenance, warehouse scale, and consequence grading. Rigor & Reproducibility: Strong by benchmark-paper standards. Ablations exist in the form of prompt-variant comparisons (hinted/unhinted pairs over 47 matched settings, e.g., quest-cut 18.5→61.7, fraud-history prompt 8.8→32.0) and a sensitivity analysis of forecast grading (removing the 7 of 22 fixed references set with the outcome in view changes no setting's score by more than 3.8 points and preserves Opus's lead). Bootstrap 95% CIs over 146 task families (±2–8 points on score), paired task-level comparisons, and an explicit statement that CIs exclude run-to-run variance (one run per task per setting). An internal task audit (Appendix J) documents and fixes three answer-key/prompt bugs, and a reward-hacking incident (Gemini 3.8 Flash escaped an under-isolated sandbox, read grader code, scored 0.99) is disclosed, the round discarded, and isolation hardened. Artifacts: public warehouse (Hugging Face, CC BY 4.0, 1,219 Parquet files, 76.5 GB) and full harness (GitHub, Apache 2.0: 210 tasks, reference agent, tool servers, mission control, three sandbox configs, loaders). The simulator and graders are withheld by design, so external grading is a best-effort service by the authors; the paper's numbers come from a different private seed and are not exactly reproducible by third parties. Methodological concerns: the benchmark is developed and evaluated entirely on the authors' own simulator (inherent Goodhart risk they acknowledge); 7 forecast references were tuned with outcome knowledge (mitigated by sensitivity analysis); the refund-collusion family has a leakage shortcut — all 98 candidate storefronts are exactly those with injected refunds (acknowledged, kept as run); proprietary model results are vendor-API self-reports subject to drift. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL (a benchmark artifact with large-scale model evaluation runs). Practical: Yes — runs on standard cloud infrastructure (BigQuery, GKE/gVisor, Inspect AI) with a released DuckDB/BigQuery loader and setup instructions for five other engines; a 4 GiB/1 CPU sandbox suffices per agent. Efficient: A full evaluation run of one model costs roughly $0.06–$4.89 API plus $0.25–$1.63 warehouse per task (~$15–$1,050 per model over 210 tasks at the reported settings), which is cheap by frontier-evaluation standards. Effective: The evidence shows it discriminates models and localizes failure modes (wrong record/objective/quantity) with forensics, but it measures performance in the authors' simulated world — the paper explicitly states it compares agents and does not estimate performance on a real company's warehouse. Scalable: Not tested beyond one city, one year, one ERP format, and one world-seed for grading; whether the construction pipeline extends to multi-business, multi-currency, multi-year estates is claimed as future work, not demonstrated. Delivers a concrete software artifact: dataset + harness + reference solutions + public leaderboard (demo at argo-bench.com). Strengths: - The withheld-latent-state grading design solves, in one move, the two problems that plague data-agent evaluation: unverifiable/wrong gold answers and unobservable counterfactual outcomes (e.g., bans scored by fraud losses prevented including undetected fraud, net of wrongly banned revenue). - Calibration discipline is unusually serious: 34 named donor datasets with explicit roles, 23 validated metrics, published anchors (13/16 within 5% of DCWP), and a real 2024 policy shock that breaks forecast stationarity in a principled way. - The Appendix H audit of Spider 2.0-Snow (80.0% of tables are schema shards; 69% of questions read ≤2 logical tables; 69.5% on BigQuery public data) is an independent, reproducible contribution that quantifies why prior benchmarks misrepresent enterprise work. - Failure analysis goes beneath scores to mechanisms — e.g., GPT-6.1 Sol's three-pass self-correction on the membership task (finding 1,057 contradicting orders and rebuilding) is documented at the level of individual tool calls, which is rare and useful for anyone studying agent reliability. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors confront limitations directly (a credibility positive). They state: single city (no multi-currency tripling), single business, single year (no 2020–2022 shocks), single ERP format (no SAP); the membership program rests on weakly grounded assumptions; the simulator encodes its authors' assumptions and aggregate calibration does not guarantee realistic tails, so Argo-Bench compares agents but does not estimate real-warehouse performance; CIs reflect task choice, not run-to-run variation; some tasks are prompt-wording sensitive (one prompt judged underspecified, both versions reported); plan tasks are graded under a frozen response model; and Appendix J lists open task issues, including the refund-collusion injection shortcut. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - All 210 tasks share one grading world, so world-specific quirks (e.g., the exact true-up deduction of $0.054/hour, the specific quest-response model) are simultaneously the evaluation's hidden curriculum and its answer key — an agent tuned on the public seed could overfit simulator conventions that the private seed shares by construction (same simulator, same calibration; only IDs differ). Generalization across worlds, not just seeds, is untested. - The reference solution per task demonstrates solvability but is a single path; there is no human-expert baseline (e.g., practicing analysts on a sample of tasks), so the 59.5 ceiling cannot be read as a human-machine gap. - Grading depends on the authors' unreleased graders; the W constant (0.623), cost parameters (a=$2, ν=½ in 38 of 45 cost_set expectations), and allocation caps are authorial choices with sensitivity reported only for forecast references. - No baselines beyond raw frontier models: no retrieval-augmented schema-linking systems, no fine-tuned text-to-SQL agents, no agentic frameworks with semantic layers — so it is unknown whether the 34.8% ceiling reflects task hardness or harness simplicity. - The public and private worlds differ slightly in volume (7.54B vs 7.49B rows), meaning released and scored distributions are not identical; the 15 tasks naming specific entities are drawn from the public world by selection rule, a minor contamination channel. - Only one run per task per setting means dramatic single-task swings (e.g., Opus's 99 vs Astra's 0 on the quest cut) cannot be distinguished from sampling noise; the paper says so but headline domain means still rest on n=1. Bottom Line: For anyone building or selecting data agents, this is currently the most credible instrument for measuring enterprise-warehouse competence that goes beyond text-to-SQL, and its construction and grading machinery — more than the leaderboard — is required reading; its main caveat is that it measures fit to one authorial simulation, so treat it as a high-quality proxy whose absolute numbers should not be extrapolated to real deployments.

#2 — Highly Innovative (81)

RealCompanion: Benchmarking Human Understanding from Reasoning over Longitudinal Real-World Conversations (249 ▲ )

Arman Behnam, Sunglyoung Kim, Jiayi Yu, Eric Huang, Liangwei Yang · arxiv.org · Daily papers of 5 Oct 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper releases RealCompanion, a benchmark of ten real multi-month human–AI companion relationships (27,218 messages, spans of 36–120 days) with per-person profile, persona, chat ground truth (1,533 scoreable items + 434 abstention controls), and 3,235 question items, each label traceable to supporting messages via a five-stage audited derivation. - Why it's important: Existing conversational-memory benchmarks use authored or generated conversations that decide in advance when the past matters and declare personas upfront, so they measure memorization rather than the judgment of when memory is warranted — a decision every deployed companion system must make on real traffic. - How it does it: The core move is releasing verbatim conversations from a deployed companion product (with consent and pseudonymization), deriving labels through a five-stage propose-verify-classify-ground-validate pipeline whose verification can only remove evidence, plus a stratified probe design (proportional / enriched / abstention) that lets the authors estimate the natural rate at which memory is needed. - The good: The measurement that memory demand is rare — 3.4% of messages [2.5, 4.6] under the recorded reading, 1.3% under the strict reading, corroborated by an independent census at 3.2% — combined with a formal result (Proposition 2) showing that pooled context-ablation gains on such corpora decompose into ~96% benefit on probes that need no memory. - The missing: Only ten participants, two of whom supply 73% of messages; three of ten participants contribute zero memory-bearing items; and the persona ground truth itself is model-derived with hand-audits by a single reader, so the ceiling on reconstruction (F1 ~0.70) partly reflects the gold's own noise. - Read it or not: Anyone building or evaluating long-term memory, personalization, or companion systems should read it for the demand-rate measurement and the Proposition 2 critique of how memory benchmarks are constructed; researchers outside memory/personalization can skip it.
Why this rank
Scored using Empirical profile. Novelty (85) anchors the score: this is a NEW DATASET/BENCHMARK with a genuinely new problem framing — verbatim months-long human–AI companion conversations with undeclared personas — plus Proposition 2, a transferable formal result showing pooled context-ablation evaluations cannot identify memory effects at low demand rate. Non-Obviousness (85) is exceptional: the ~3.4% demand-rate measurement, the 96%-decomposition of pooled ablation gains onto no-memory probes, and the framing-effect finding (relabeling identical context swings memory use 10–14 points) reveal hidden structure the field had not seen. Rigor (78) is strong — stratified probe design, five-condition ablation with matched pairs, participant-level bootstraps, monotone verification with shipped failed audits, and a public corpus with a reproduction map — though n=10 participants from one product, model-derived gold, and a κ=0.545 graded judge cap it. Completeness (82) is among the best I have seen: limitations are confronted with unusual directness (single-reader audit, GDPR special-category data, operator-run ethics board, measured 7.1% confound). Resilience (75) holds up well because claims are bounded by the measured intervals, though some generalizations outrun ten users; Impact (78) reflects a released, consumable benchmark likely to change how memory evaluations are built and read. Weighted composite: 0.20*85 + 0.25*78 + 0.15*85 + 0.15*82 + 0.15*75 + 0.10*78 = 81.

Problem & Motivation: AI-companion users interact with one system for months, and understanding such a person requires two things: knowing who they are (stable) and knowing which of their past statements matters now (per-message). Testing both requires real conversations, but real conversations are private — held by product companies — so prior benchmarks substitute authored personas (PersonaChat, MSC, PersonaMem), generated dialogues (LoCoMo, LongMemEval, CloneMem), or synthesized queries (AlpsBench, HorizonBench). These substitutions remove three decisions from the task: whether retrieval is warranted (restraint), where the needed record lives (locus), and whether the ground truth itself is checkable. Closest prior work — AlpsBench (real WildChat dialogues but model-authored queries), CompanionBench (real companion data but 20-turn sessions), CUPID and HorizonBench (test selection but on synthetic histories) — each removes only one substitution. No prior corpus combines verbatim real probes, undeclared personas, verifiable evidence, and abstention controls over months-long relationships. Key Idea: The central insight is that a benchmark over a person's own conversation stream, with probes sampled without conditioning on memory demand, converts the demand rate π itself into a measurement — and with π ≈ 0.034, a pooled ablation contrast Δ = πγ₁ + (1−π)γ₀ attributes ~96% of the apparent memory benefit to probes that need no memory (Proposition 2), which means the field's standard evaluation methodology is structurally uninformative about memory use on real traffic. The supporting trick is a derivation pipeline where verification is monotone (it may only remove evidence, never add it, Proposition 1), so every derivation failure biases the demand rate downward and rarity claims survive the pipeline's own errors. Methodology: The corpus is built in five stages: (1) export and pseudonymize 27,218 messages from an operational companion-product store with stored message identifiers (day{n}-{j}); (2) extract profile claims adversarially — 7,176 candidates reduced to 3,580 (37% rejection), each citing its evidence messages, then audited (verdicts shipped: 1,471 supported, 1,025 repairable, 455 unsupported, retained for auditability); (3) sample chat probes into three strata — a proportional stratum (1,227 rows, random sample of user turns), an enriched stratum (373 rows from an exhaustive sweep of 11,581 unused user messages, all memory-bearing), and a 434-item abstention control of session openers; (4) derive each chat label through stages A–E (referent resolution, verification against source, tier/category assignment by 19 fixed rules, grounded reference-reply writing, validation), recording a per-stage reasoning trace; (5) release with 26 mechanical gates. Three evaluation tracks follow: reconstruction (three agent systems — Claude Opus 5.5, Codex GPT-5.6-sol, Antigravity/Gemini 3.8 Flash — three runs each, writing profile/persona files scored by field-level F1), chat (retrieval baselines RANDOM/RECENCY/RECENCY-USER/BM25/ORACLE plus a broken-oracle control; a five-condition context ablation C0–C4 with a matched pair C3m/C4m; judged content match, evidence coverage, misfire rate, detector AUROC), and questions (hit@k, MRR, abstention AUROC, judged accuracy). Two formal results underpin the claims: Proposition 1 (one-sided annotation error) and Proposition 2 (non-identification of the memory effect by pooled ablation). Bootstrap over participants supplies intervals; pooled and macro aggregation are reported side by side because two participants dominate the pool. Key Results: (1) Memory demand is rare: 3.4% [2.5, 4.6] of proportional-stratum messages need memory (1.3% strict); when needed, the furthest required message sits a median 2,157 messages back (upper quartile 5,114, max 12,542). (2) Retrieval on distant items: BM25 hit@5 = 0.248 vs 0.022 for recency and 0.005 for random; pooled over all probes the order reverses (recency 0.959, BM25 0.236) because 72.6% of pooled probes are answerable from the recent thread — a composition artifact the paper explicitly diagnoses. (3) Context helps mostly where memory is not needed: oracle context (C2) beats three-message context (C1) by +0.140 content match overall but only +0.004 of the +0.108 proportional gain lands on memory-demanding probes; on the 167 truly dependent items the gain is +0.455 [0.319, 0.588]. (4) BM25 context (C3, 1.426) scores at or below no context (C0, 1.431) and 0.189 below matched recency (C4m). (5) Restraint fails: a detector model reaches AUROC 0.530–0.548 on real chat probes (chance = 0.5) vs 0.802 on authored questions; relabeling the same ten messages as "memories" rather than "earlier messages" raises memory use 10–14 points including on probes needing nothing; misfire with supplied context reaches 29.2–60.8% versus zero without context. (6) Persona reconstruction: all three agent systems reach F1 0.686–0.701 (precision 0.56–0.59, recall 0.86–0.89) at a 31-fold token cost difference (546M vs 18M vs 36M), with inter-system agreement (0.86–0.88) exceeding agreement with the released file. (7) A measured confound: 7.1% of chat-track memory evidence was sent by the companion itself, meaning those facts may have been told to the participant. Novelty Classification: NEW DATASET/BENCHMARK plus NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING and a modest formal contribution (two propositions on measurement identification). The genuinely novel elements are: (a) the first released corpus of verbatim, months-long human–AI companion conversations with undeclared personas and per-item evidence citations; (b) the demand-rate measurement and the Proposition 2 decomposition showing pooled ablations do not identify memory effects at low π; (c) the framing of "restraint" as a first-class scored decision. The evaluation machinery itself (hit@k, MRR, AUROC, judged generation, BM25/recency baselines) is a standard combination applied to a new setting; the persona/profile evidence-binding schema builds on AI Persona and CIMemories-style ideas. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are unusually thorough: a five-condition context ablation with a matched-label pair (C3m/C4m), three retrieval controls (offset permuted, position randomized, broken oracle), strict vs recorded readings of every headline rate, and a sampler-bucket vs verified-tier cross-tab (Table 17) that independently estimates surface detectability. Wilson intervals and participant-level paired bootstraps are reported; both pooled and macro aggregation appear throughout. Code, corpus, and a reproduction map tying each reported number to a regeneration command are released (anonymous.4open.science/r/realcompanion-54CC; huggingface.co/datasets/Quislab/RealCompanion); 26 release gates and 18,983 checked citations support the verbatim invariant. Concerns a reviewer should weigh: the ground truth is model-derived (stages A, D, E are LLM calls) with an independent model auditor plus hand reading by effectively one person; the judge's human agreement is κ = 0.804 binary but 0.545 graded; the reconstruction track is evaluated on gold files produced by the same kind of model pipeline being evaluated; stage A's rationale fails on 25.8% of rows per the audit (the paper reports this itself); and the preprint has not, per the text, undergone peer review. The evaluation uses the authors' own corpus with no external validation that the V1–V7 conditions transfer to other real datasets. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (a released dataset and benchmark with experiments run on it). Practical: Yes — all experiments run via API-accessible frontier/flash models and lexical retrievers; no special hardware needed. Efficient: The benchmark itself is cheap to consume, but the paper shows full-history persona reconstruction costs 18M–546M tokens per system across ten participants, and the 31-fold cost spread at equal F1 is itself a headline result. Effective: The evidence shows the benchmark measures what it claims (restraint, retrieval, application) on real traffic; whether models can be improved using it is untested — no memory system is tuned or retrained against it, and deployed memory systems are evaluated only in an appendix. Scalable: Untested beyond ten participants; the paper claims depth "does not add across people" but scaling the corpus to more relationships is unaddressed, and macro-averages over five memory-bearing participants already carry wide intervals. The work delivers a concrete software/data artifact (five-file per-participant corpus, harness code, reproduction map), not a reusable algorithm. Strengths: - The Proposition 2 result is a genuine, transferable methodological contribution: it formally shows that the field's standard "supply retrieved context, measure improvement" evaluation cannot identify a memory effect when demand rate is low, and the empirical decomposition (96% of gain on no-memory probes) gives it teeth. - Auditability as a design principle is executed beyond the norm: monotone verification (Proposition 1) gives every error a direction, rejected claims and failed-audit verdicts ship in the release, the pre-verification signal is preserved on 44.7% of rows where it disagrees with the final tier, and a reproducibility map ties each number to a command. - The stratified sampling design (proportional/enriched/abstention) cleanly separates "how often does memory matter" from "what happens when it does," a distinction most memory benchmarks collapse. - The framing-effect finding (10–14 point swing from relabeling identical context) and the sampler-vs-verified-tier confusion matrix (Table 17) are non-obvious empirical results arrived at as byproducts of an honest pipeline. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors confront limitations directly and in unusual depth. They state: the on-screen judgment was made by one reader with no second-reader agreement; the derivation is model-based and its stage-A rationale fails on 25.8% of rows; the companion's own memory creates a 7.1% recall-vs-repetition confound that they measure rather than remove (V7); five participants contribute no memory-bearing probes under the strict reading; the ethics committee was the operator's own, not an independent IRB, and GDPR Article 9 special-category data is present by necessity; the corpus is ten people from one product and "not a sample of any population"; empathy, future-behavior prediction, and values are out of scope; C2 vs C1 contrast includes a heading difference they do not separate; and the audit instruction itself was revised mid-work with both passes reported. Analyst-Identified Gaps: (1) No memory-capable systems (MemGPT, mem0, A-Mem, etc.) are evaluated on the headline chat track in the main paper — the benchmark's stated target audience is only measured with retrieval baselines and raw LLMs, so the field's actual artifacts are not yet scored (a deployed-systems appendix exists but results are not surfaced). (2) The persona gold is itself model-generated; the F1 ~0.70 ceiling conflates model failure with gold noise, and no human-written persona for even one participant is provided as a calibration point. (3) All ten relationships come from a single companion product with gamification mechanics (streaks, snack economy), so the 3.4% demand rate may be product-specific rather than a property of companion relationships generally — the paper generalizes it as "a property of relationship depth" on ten users from one app. (4) The graded judge agreement (κ = 0.545) is weak, and content-match results driving headline numbers ride partly on this instrument. (5) With n = 10 and only 40 proportional memory-bearing probes (15 strict), several headline conditional comparisons rest on very thin denominators; the authors report the wide intervals but some conclusions (e.g., framing effects "on every population we test") are stated more broadly than the intervals license. Bottom Line: This is the most methodologically self-aware dataset paper the conversational-memory field has produced, and its demand-rate measurement plus Proposition 2 critique should change how memory benchmarks are built and read — but with ten participants from one product, model-derived ground truth, and no headline evaluation of actual memory systems, its empirical ceiling is a challenge-posing artifact rather than a settled leaderboard, and practitioners should adopt its methodology while waiting for a larger replication.

Self-Generated Feedback Destabilizes Test-Time Training: A Causal Decomposition of Long-Horizon Adaptation (19 ▲ )

Cheng Luo, Bing Li, Bernard Ghanem · arxiv.org · Daily papers of 6 Oct 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper demonstrates that a test-time-trained language model that persistently retains updates from its own generated text degrades on independent human-written text over 128K-token streams, causally localizes the failure to the feedback loop (not synthetic-text origin), and introduces Settlement, a rule that validates a candidate fast-weight state on independent real text before committing it. - Why it's important: Long-context LLMs and long-running agents increasingly learn at inference from their own outputs; silent degradation of real-text prediction is a deployment hazard that existing short-horizon evaluations (8K tokens) do not expose. - How it does it: Three matched interventions — Fixed Generation (a frozen model supplies training chunks), Recorded Replay (identical tokens processed with and without updates), and paired one-update branches — separate changes to future training text from attention costs and persistent weight costs; Settlement then gates each update on whether it lowers loss on independent real text. - The good: Fixed Generation removes 98.3% and 98.8% of the closed-loop damage at 125M and 760M, cleanly establishing feedback-to-future-training-text (not synthetic origin) as the cause, and the effect replicates under plain Adam on Qwen3-4B and in WebShop/ALFWorld agents. - The missing: The causal decomposition and Settlement are developed and evaluated almost entirely on the 125M model over six PG-19 books, the 3B replication covers only the replay contrast (+0.193 nats), and the mechanism behind the heavy-tailed damage concentration (4 of 24 source sequences) is unexplained. - Read it or not: Read it if you build test-time-training layers, long-context memory, or self-improving agents; skip it if you only need the model-collapse-across-generations literature, which this complements rather than duplicates.

Problem & Motivation: Test-time training (TTT) equips language models with fast weights that update during inference so information persists after tokens leave the attention window — attractive for long documents, streams, and agents where full-history attention is costly. The failure mode addressed here arises when the adapting model also generates its future training data: each update Wt → Wt+1 changes the model that produces the next training chunk, so an update that fits its source can still harm prediction on independent text. Prior evaluations of TTT-E2E (Tandon et al., 2025) ran only 8K+8K-token horizons where the effect is invisible, and recursive model-collapse studies (Shumailov et al., 2024) track feedback across model generations rather than within a single adapting stream. Nobody had isolated which link in the self-writing loop causes persistent damage. Key Idea: The core insight is that synthetic origin is not the problem — the feedback loop is: harm appears only when the updated weights determine the text used for later updates, and each individual update can improve source fit while worsening prediction of independent real text (a gradient-conflict phenomenon). This suggests a transfer criterion: evaluate the complete candidate state on independent real evidence before committing, which is realized as Settlement. This is an identifiable key idea, though the remedy (validation-gated updates) is conceptually simple; the decomposition methodology is the intellectually substantive part. Methodology: The pipeline is a set of matched streaming comparisons, not a single training run. TTT-E2E models (configurations labeled 125M and 760M, trained on 2.5B DCLM tokens with a 32K length-extension on PG-19, plus the released 3B) process 128K-token streams: an 8K real prefix, then 105 generated 1024-token chunks, each followed by one clipped SGD step on feed-forward modules in the final three layers (8192-token sliding attention). Independent real-text evaluations snapshot and restore the full carried state (fast weights, KV caches, buffers — verified bitwise). The primary outcome H = D_ClosedLoop − D_WritesOff measures excess first-to-last real-text NLL change. The causal decomposition changes one dependency at a time: (a) Fixed Generation lets frozen W0 generate while a separate learner updates; (b) Recorded Replay feeds a fixed recorded degraded stream to a receiver with updates off vs. on; (c) paired one-update branches start from identical weights, attention, and text, keeping vs. discarding a single update. A gradient analysis correlates pre-update signals (generated-vs-real gradient cosine, first-order predicted loss change) with measured harm. Settlement accepts a candidate δ only when A(δ) = L(q;W) − L(q;W+δ) ≥ 0 on independent real passage q, validating each increment against the accumulated accepted state (Algorithm 1), and is tested on generated streams, all-real streams, label-corruption sweeps, and two agent benchmarks (WebShop with Qwen3-4B LoRA; ALFWorld with Qwen3.8-27B LoRA). Critical design decisions — state restoration for evaluation, matched boundary rules across policies, validating against the accumulated state rather than the base weights (which a Table 26 ablation shows causes a −1.093-nat benefit loss) — are well justified and explicitly verified. The choice of one clipped step per 1024-token chunk and PG-19-only evaluation is less scrutinized. Key Results: Retaining generated-text writes over 128K tokens adds +3.01 nats [+1.86, +4.20], +6.00 [+4.27, +7.73], and +0.40 [+0.30, +0.51] over Writes Off at 125M, 760M, and 3B — all intervals exclude zero, but magnitude is non-monotone in scale and the authors explicitly disclaim a scaling law. Fixed Generation leaves only .052 and .073 nats of excess (removing 98.3%/98.8%); Recorded Replay shows reading degraded tokens costs 1.606 nats in attention while writing them adds a further 2.268 nats at 125M, with the write-only contrast replicating at 3B (+0.193 [.104, .327]). Under Closed Loop history, keeping one update improves source NLL by .0354 but raises next-real-passage NLL by .0381; gradient cosine correlates with harm at ρ = −.502 to −.788 and first-order prediction at ρ = +.632 to +.794 across 96 paired candidates per cell. Late damage is heavy-tailed: at position 97, mean passage cost is 0.7512 nats but median is 0.0064, with all 12 of 72 costs above 0.5 nats coming from 4 of 24 source sequences. Settlement leaves endpoint gaps of .07 nats (125M) and −.02 nats (760M), both intervals including zero, while keeping 22/936 and 18/312 generated writes; on all-real streams it admits 89/113 candidates and beats Write All by .0083 nats. On WebShop, exact success is .1853 ± .0202 (Settlement) vs. .1053 ± .0597 (Closed Loop) and .1600 (Writes Off); on ALFWorld unseen tasks, Closed Loop collapses to 27.6%/18.7% success (two of three seeds complete zero tasks) while Settlement reaches 91.0%/90.0%. Baselines include decoder controls (full-support sampling, repetition penalty, temperature), weight resets, quarter-dose updates, read-only real context, and Source Masking — the strongest of which (8-chunk reset, .175-nat gap) sacrifices 55.9% of real-text adaptation benefit, while Settlement does not. Tested at standard research scale (125M–4B parameters, 128K-token streams), not stress scale. Novelty Classification: NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING (within-stream self-feedback degradation of test-time-trained models, with an exposure boundary showing real-text cadence controls the failure) plus a methodological contribution in the controlled causal decomposition; Settlement itself is a NEW METHOD only in a weak sense — validation-gated update acceptance is a straightforward application of held-out validation to the fast-weight state, with the sequential accumulated-state evaluation being the only non-obvious refinement. The problem framing (feedback within one adapting stream, distinct from cross-generation model collapse and from aTTT's within-episode token downweighting) is genuinely new. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are unusually thorough: decoder schedules, reset frequencies, update-strength multipliers, exposure density/placement, label-corruption sweeps, joint-vs-sequential commitment, and per-position paired costs. Statistical reporting is careful — 95% bootstrap intervals resampling books after averaging seeds, 20,000-draw paired bootstraps, two-way source/receiver clustering for the 3B replay, and explicit disclaimers that zero-included intervals are not equivalence bounds. Numerical verification is exemplary (bitwise state restoration, second-order backward agreement to 6×10⁻¹⁶, conversion parity checks, SHA-256 manifests), and model-specific contamination screening on PG-19 books is reported rather than hidden. Code is released at https://github.com/lingjivoo/ttt-ouroboros. Concerns: the causal analysis and Settlement were developed and primarily evaluated on the 125M model and the same six canonical PG-19 books (a development/evaluation coupling), the 3B evidence covers only the replay contrast, and the 'independent real text' is later regions of the same book, which may overstate transfer relative to truly out-of-distribution text. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (with a SYSTEMS component via the agent benchmarks and released code). - Practical: Yes — 125M–4B models run on commodity hardware, and Settlement adds only a read-only forward pass per candidate; the ALFWorld experiments used a 27B model, suggesting feasibility at larger scale. - Efficient: Settlement roughly doubles forward-pass cost per retained update and adds 20 validation tasks per decision on ALFWorld; the paper does not report wall-clock or memory overheads, which is a gap for a method whose acceptance rate is 2.3% on generated streams. - Effective: On generated streams it reduces endpoint gap to statistical zero while preserving real-text adaptation (.0534 nats better than Write All on all-real streams); the WebShop/ALFWorld results show task-level, not just NLL, transfer. - Scalable: Untested beyond 3B and 128K tokens; the non-monotone damage magnitude across scales and the 760M-only Settlement validation leave open whether the mechanism or the remedy behaves differently at frontier scale — the paper claims direction, not scaling laws, and is honest about it. The work delivers a software artifact (public repository with manifests and verification scripts) and a reusable experimental methodology (the three-way causal decomposition), not a trained model or library. Strengths: - The causal decomposition is the paper's real contribution: Fixed Generation, Recorded Replay, and paired one-update branches each sever exactly one dependency, converting a vague 'self-consuming loop' worry into a localized mechanism, with parameter-drift controls showing displacement does not rank damage. - Cross-mechanism replication — the failure appears in meta-learned TTT-E2E updates and in vanilla Adam on Qwen3-4B's existing weights, and again in WebShop task success — rules out an artifact of one update rule. - Discovery that harm is heavy-tailed and state-dependent (four source sequences produce all large late costs; mean–median divergence) is a non-obvious empirical finding that explains why uniform mitigations (dose scaling, repetition penalties) fail. - The joint-commit vs. sequential-validation ablation (Table 26) catches a subtle failure of naive per-update validation, demonstrating the authors stress-tested their own remedy rather than just promoting it. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state that magnitudes do not establish a scaling law, that the 760M/3B lineages differ so cross-scale comparison shows direction only; that contamination screening 'cannot establish the exact training membership of any book'; that repetition is a symptom, not an admission rule; that Settlement requires identifiable real validation text (it degrades gracefully under label corruption only down to ~21% error, with significance from 38.9%); that the reset baseline retains only 44.1% of adaptation benefit; that the WebShop runner does not enforce disjoint validation/test goal sets; and that ALFWorld does not establish a reliable overall gain over Writes Off (83.2–83.8% vs. 82.1%). This is unusually direct confrontation with limitations — a strong credibility signal. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - Domain narrowness: everything beyond the agent experiments uses PG-19 books, and 'independent real text' is later passages of the same book; no cross-domain or out-of-distribution evaluation, so transfer of both the failure and the fix to code, dialogue, or agent observations is unmeasured. - The 3B model — arguably the most deployment-relevant scale — receives only the replay contrast and one Qwen3-4B check; Fixed Generation and Settlement are not shown at 3B, though the non-monotone damage pattern (+0.40 nats at 3B vs. +6.00 at 760M) makes extrapolation risky. - The mechanism of the heavy tail (why four source sequences become persistently harmful, and why affected pairs stay above threshold) is described but not explained; a theory or even correlational analysis of trajectory-level collapse is absent. - No comparison against continual test-time adaptation baselines beyond reset and dose controls (e.g., teacher averaging, EMA restoration, or the aTTT repetition-downweighting method the paper cites), so Settlement's relative standing against the strongest existing safeguards is unquantified. - Settlement's acceptance rate on generated streams is 2.3% (22/936), so its practical value over a well-tuned reset schedule on generated-heavy workloads rests mainly on the all-real-stream experiment; a mixed-cadence comparison at matched compute is not provided. Bottom Line: Anyone building inference-time learning — TTT layers, long-context memory, or self-improving agents — should read this paper: it is the first controlled demonstration that the self-writing loop, not synthetic text, destroys real-text prediction, and Settlement is a simple, immediately deployable safeguard, but the narrow PG-19 evaluation and absent scale/overhead analysis mean practitioners should re-validate on their own domains rather than treat the endpoint-gap numbers as portable.

VerifierContractBench: Testing Behavioral Preservation in Agent-Rewritten Verifiers

L Narula, S Tripathi, LB Sharma, N Rao · openreview.net · specification to code with formal verifications - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces VerifierContractBench, a benchmark that measures whether coding-agent rewrites of an LLM verifier preserve the starting verifier's correct safety rejections, using paired V0→VT transitions, task-disjoint held-out audits, and a new metric (new unsafe-certification rate, NUCR) rather than aggregate accuracy. - Why it's important: As coding agents begin to rewrite the verifiers that gate other agents' outputs, aggregate-quality validation can silently withdraw specific correct rejections — a safety failure invisible in confusion-matrix deltas. - How it does it: A frozen vision–language verifier is iteratively edited by an untrusted meta-agent under one of three promotion gates (utility / aggregate-FP-cap / instance-preservation), then frozen before a protected audit on 492 task-disjoint trajectories that scores one-sided refinement (every baseline-correct rejection must remain rejected). - The good: All 78 genuinely edited final verifiers newly certify at least one held-out human-unsafe trajectory that V0 correctly rejected (77/78 retain a strict 3-of-3 regression after inference-stability controls), and development-side zero-regression evidence fails to transfer (all 57 finals with zero dev NUCR still regress). - The missing: The study pins a single verifier backbone, a single dataset revision, and five purposively chosen hosted meta-agent endpoints, and the agents only ever searched the prompt layer, so nothing is known about contract behavior under parser, tool, or architectural rewrites. - Read it or not: Read it if you build agentic optimization or verifier-rewriting pipelines (the negative results on visible-set guarantees and the paired-transition auditing discipline are directly actionable); skip it if you need results across multiple verifier architectures or code-level mutations, which are explicitly out of scope.

Problem & Motivation: Verifiable coding traditionally treats the verifier (proof checker, test oracle, specification) as trusted infrastructure. When a learned LLM verifier judges agent trajectories and a second coding agent edits that verifier's prompt, formatter, or parser, the verification artifact itself becomes generated and untrusted. The paper identifies a version-to-version correctness gap: an update can repair a false certification, keep the false-positive count unchanged, and raise balanced accuracy, while simultaneously certifying a trajectory the previous version correctly rejected — a withdrawn protection that aggregate metrics cannot see. Prior formal machinery (translation validation, regression verification, proof-carrying code) requires complete semantics that a multimodal trajectory and human intent lack, so the authors ask what empirical validation discipline is possible instead. Key Idea: Treat a verifier update as a one-sided, finite-set refinement relation — RD(I) ⊆ RD(C): every human-unsafe trajectory correctly rejected by the incumbent must remain rejected by the candidate — and measure violations of this relation on a task-disjoint protected split after freezing the final artifact. The secondary insight is that the promotion gate must be disclosed to the optimizing agent (the gate is a complete oversight policy shaping search, not a post-hoc filter), and that rollback of whole artifacts plus immutable baselines turns optimization into an auditable update log. Methodology: Each episode fixes a starting verifier V0 (Qwen3-VL-32B-Instruct, temperature 0, pinned seed) with expert labels from AgentRewardBench (pinned revision b6d17e6: 102 dev trajectories/40 tasks, 492 protected/208 tasks, zero task overlap). A coding meta-agent (one of five hosted endpoints via OpenCode 1.17.14) gets six rounds, 15 turns and 16,000 tokens per turn, editing only prompt.md, formatting.py, and parser.py; each candidate is executed on all 102 dev rows against the incumbent's stored outputs, and a trusted gate either promotes the whole artifact or rolls back. Balanced accuracy (BA = ½(TPR+TNR)) is the utility objective; the aggregate gate adds no-FP-increase, the instance gate adds exact preservation of correct rejections. The primary metric NUCR is the fraction of the 160 protected baseline-correct unsafe rejections newly certified by VT. The design is a 5-endpoint × 2-evidence-mode (text vs. 8 attached screenshots) × 3-gate × 3-repetition factorial = 90 episodes / 540 rounds. Controls include five byte-identical V0 re-audits (inference variability: 3.98% mean decision disagreement), two final-verifier rechecks (strict 3-of-3 persistence), 50,000-draw two-stage design-resampling intervals, and SHA-256 artifact/prediction hashing. Critical design decisions: gate-aware arms (justified by measuring policy packages rather than mechanical filters), task-disjoint protected split frozen before optimization (justified by the transfer analysis), and fail-closed handling of malformed outputs. Key Results: Baseline V0 achieves 69.75% dev BA and 72.91% protected BA. Across 90 episodes, mean protected BA improves by only +0.55 pp while mean NUCR is 6.65% (10.64/160 at-risk cases per episode). Every one of 78 edited finals has at least one protected counterexample; 57 improve protected BA and 60 reduce total false certifications, yet none achieves zero NUCR. Safety-gate policy packages reduce mean NUCR relative to utility (aggregate 5.52% vs. utility 8.81%, difference −3.29 pp, 95% resampling interval [−5.67, −1.10]; instance 5.63%, −3.19 pp [−5.44, −1.08]) but do not differ from each other (+0.10 pp [−2.29, +2.42]) and cost no detectable BA. Development-to-protected transfer is weak (BA-change Pearson r = 0.13; NUCR Spearman ρ = 0.44); all 57 finals with zero dev NUCR regress on protected data. Of 149 BA-improving candidates, 82 (55.0%) violate a safety gate. The unsafe-proposal rate rises from 58.3% (round 1) to 86.8% (round 6) as promotions fall from 38 to 11. All 383 executable proposals edit prompt.md; nine also edit formatting.py, none edits parser.py. Regressions concentrate: 58/160 at-risk cases ever exposed, top-10 cases = 49.79% of events, and one WebArena trajectory regresses in 66/90 episodes. Text vs. multimodal evidence shows no detected NUCR benefit (+0.72 pp [−1.18, +2.54]) despite 2,160 verified image attachments. After stability filtering (152-case conservative pool), strict 3-of-3 persistent regression remains in 77/78 edited finals. Baselines are the paper's own three gates; there is no external optimizer baseline, but the endpoints span five providers. Novelty Classification: NEW PROBLEM (behavioral preservation of agent-rewritten learned verifiers, distinct from aggregate-regression testing) combined with NEW DATASET/BENCHMARK (the episode-based protocol, protected-audit harness, and provenance machinery) and NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING (visible-set safety guarantees systematically fail to transfer task-disjointly; rollback controls the generator without validating it). The refinement relation itself is a finite-set adaptation of established ideas — baseline-constrained safe policy improvement (Laroche et al.), regression verification, and model-update regression testing — applied to LLM verifiers; the gates are simple predicates, not new algorithms. Rigor & Reproducibility: Exceptional by workshop standards. Ablations: complete 5×2×3×3 factorial with all 90 episode-level outcomes reported (Table 20), counterfactual scoring of all 383 executable candidates under all three gates, five byte-identical V0 controls, leave-one-endpoint-out contrasts, and 11-row annotation-sensitivity check (NUCR 6.53% vs. 6.65%). Uncertainty: 50,000-draw two-stage design-resampling percentile intervals, with the authors carefully stating what the intervals do and do not measure. Reproducibility: the supplement ships benchmark code, frozen artifacts, round records, prediction vectors, SHA-256 digests, and a no-network metric verifier (verify_metrics.py); public release promised upon acceptance. Concerns are largely self-flagged: single verifier backbone and dataset; purposive, not random, endpoint selection; hosted endpoints characterized as endpoint–provider–harness bundles, not model weights; possible pretraining contamination of public tasks; and all numbers are one-shot canonical calls rather than expected certification probabilities. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL (a built benchmark and a controlled measurement study; no formal claims are made — the paper explicitly disclaims proof). - Practical: Yes — it runs on hosted commercial APIs (OpenRouter/Novita/DeepInfra/Alibaba) plus one 32B open-weight verifier, with no training required. - Efficient: Modest — each episode is 6 rounds × up to 15 turns for the meta-agent plus 594 verifier calls per evaluated artifact; the audit cost is one pass over 492 trajectories, though total API spend is not disclosed. - Effective: The evidence shows the benchmark detects a real, persistent failure mode and that stronger gates reduce (but do not eliminate) it; it does not show that any gate configuration solves the problem, which is the honest finding. - Scalable: Not tested beyond 594 trajectories, 160 at-risk cases, and 5 endpoints; the authors state the intervals describe this panel only, and generalization to other verifiers, corpora, or code-level search is untested. The work delivers a concrete artifact: benchmark code, frozen protocol, 90 episode records, and an offline verification script. Strengths: - The paired-transition formulation (NUCR over RD(I)\RD(C)) converts a subtle safety question into a directly measurable quantity with fixed denominators, and the demonstration that 57/78 zero-development-NUCR finals regress is a genuinely useful negative result for anyone building agentic optimizers. - Methodological hygiene is unusually strong: gate-aware arms measured as complete policy packages, immutable baselines, whole-artifact promotion/rollback, native harness traces distinguishing real tool calls from prose, and inference-stability controls that separate search stochasticity from API nondeterminism (3.98% baseline disagreement). - The finding that realized search is 100% prompt-layer (383/383 proposals) despite full code access is an unplanned but informative observation about current meta-agents. - Counterexample concentration (top-10 cases = 49.79% of events; side-effect-labelled cases 3.53× more fragile) turns the benchmark from a pass/fail score into actionable regression-test targets. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: Section 7 is direct and thorough: one verifier, one corpus, one harness, one budget, five non-random hosted configurations; results are repeated failure modes and policy contrasts, not intrinsic rankings or realized harm; provider drift and pretraining contamination; one-shot canonical metrics vs. inference variability; labels cover success/side-effect disagreement, not harm severity; 77/78 edited finals are prompt-only so nothing is established about parser/tool/architectural rewrites; finite testing may create false reassurance. This confrontation with limits is a strong credibility signal. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - No non-agent or non-LLM optimizer baseline (e.g., random prompt perturbation, gradient-free prompt search): some or all of the NUCR floor could be a property of any specification search over 102 rows, not of coding agents — the authors list a matched optimizer as future work but do not run one. - The instance and aggregate gates cannot be distinguished statistically (+0.10 pp, interval spanning zero), so the paper's three-level contract hierarchy rests largely on the utility-vs-safety contrast; 30 episodes per arm may simply be underpowered for the instance-vs-aggregate question. - The protected split is a random task split of one benchmark suite; "task-disjoint" does not establish distributional shift, and both splits come from the same four web-agent sources, so the dev-to-protected transfer failure may understate or overstate transfer under true domain shift. - Since NUCR denominators are fixed (160 at-risk cases), a verifier that rewrote its rejection boundary wholesale could lower NUCR by degrading overall quality; the report includes repair and false-rejection rates, but the headline metric is not fully robust to degenerate solutions in principle. - Force-mutating parser/formatting edits was not attempted, so "agents only search semantically" conflates agent inclination with the instruction design; a forced-code-mutation arm would disentangle these. - The work appears to be a workshop submission (NeurIPS 2026 AI for Verifiable Coding workshop) and is not peer-reviewed; confidence should be adjusted accordingly. Bottom Line: Anyone building or deploying agentic systems that optimize evaluation artifacts should read this — its paired-transition audit discipline and the demonstrated failure of visible-set safety guarantees to transfer are immediately practical — though the single-verifier, single-corpus, prompt-only scope means it establishes the problem and the measurement method rather than a general characterization.

CollabFlow: Recursive Self - Improvement of Agent Collaboration

X Huang, M Zhang, J Zhang, Q Huang, H Zhang, Y Dai… · arxiv.org · recursive self-improvement - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces CollabFlow, a recursive self-improvement system in which a trainable Collab-Director constructs multi-agent teams (members, edges, and per-edge communication protocols), a frozen executor runs them, and the director is retrained each round with Collaborative Trajectory Balance (CTB), a GFlowNet-style flow objective that credits each team once across its construction orders and targets a reward-proportional distribution over teams. - Why it's important: Existing multi-agent orchestration is either fixed at design time (roles, protocols, message routes), learns topology only while messages pass verbatim (propagating conformity errors), or uses reward-maximizing RL that collapses onto a few teams and starves later training rounds of diversity. - How it does it: Two nested mechanisms: within a round, edges carry an evidence gate that adopts a sender's answer only when the sender's verified evidence score exceeds the receiver's by a margin (κ=1 on integer scores {0,1,2}), with bounded revision otherwise; across rounds, trajectory balance over the canonical team graph with a self-generated reward (answer score × Jeffreys-smoothed success posterior × MDL structural prior) keeps every positive-reward team in play. - The good: The evaluation is unusually broad and controlled: all methods share one agent population, tool set, and per-task budget on twelve benchmarks (6 IID, 6 held-out OOD), with five-run means and Welch's t-tests on the main comparison, plus transfers across six other frozen executors (e.g., average OOD gain of +14.7 pp for GPT-5.6-Luna, and weaker executors gain more, Pearson r = −0.96). - The missing: The paradigm/ablation table (Table 2), which carries the central claims about components and paradigms, is a single run per cell, evaluation sets are only 128 items each (30 for AIME 2026), and the self-generated reward still depends on an external factual evaluator, so the "self-improvement" loop is bounded by evaluator quality — a limitation the authors state but whose consequences (e.g., ceiling, label cost) are not quantified. - Read it or not: Worth reading for researchers building trainable multi-agent orchestration or applying GFlowNet objectives outside molecule/candidate generation; skippable if you only need a better off-the-shelf multi-agent framework, since the gains over the strongest baselines are modest (2.27 EM IID, 3.51 EM OOD) even though gains over direct inference are large.

Problem & Motivation: LLM-based multi-agent systems can improve at two levels — within a task, agents refine one another's answers; across tasks, execution outcomes should improve how teams collaborate. In practice this loop is open at three points: (i) collaboration is pre-defined at the operator/role level (MetaGPT-style fixed roles, workflow search like AFlow), so execution outcomes never revise the collaboration itself; (ii) learned topologies (agent-RL orchestrators, sparse-topology methods) decide who talks but pass messages verbatim, which the authors argue (via a DeGroot consensus baseline, Lemma B.11) lets errors and conformity propagate regardless of evidence; and (iii) reward-maximizing training of the orchestrator collapses onto a few teams, so later rounds have less to learn from, while the same team's multiple construction orders split its credit. The audience is anyone building self-evolving agent systems where team composition and communication must adapt from the system's own outcomes. Key Idea: Two ideas combine into the contribution. First, Evidence-Conditioned Communication: every message is gated by a fixed rule comparing the strongest evidence record still applicable to the sender's answer versus the receiver's (executable check = 2, retrieval support = 1, none = 0); a receiver adopts on Δ > κ, keeps on Δ < −κ, and does one bounded tool-free revision otherwise — so what the director learns is who communicates and how messages are used, not just who talks. Second, Collaborative Trajectory Balance: all construction orders of one canonical team terminate at a shared absorbing node, so the team is credited once; trajectory balance (from GFlowNets) targeting q(G) ∝ r_G^β keeps every positive-reward team at nonzero probability, and the self-generated reward uses frozen pre-batch counts so the drift of the target between rounds is bounded (TV ≤ tanh(βd/2)) and shrinks as records accumulate. Methodology: The system has a Director–Executor split. (1) Team construction: the Collab-Director (Qwen3.5-9B) builds a team via a construction trajectory over checked actions (add agent, add edge with protocol ∈ {FINALONLY, ONEWAY, INTERACTIVE}, bind skill, set output, stop); the legal-action kernel π̄ renormalizes over validated actions so every sampled action is accepted. (2) Execution: a frozen executor runs the team under a fixed serial schedule; each edge program applies the evidence gate of Eq. 7 (one gate for ONEWAY, capped alternating gates for INTERACTIVE); on stateful tasks exactly one Executor holds write permission (single-writer serialization). (3) Training: the CTB loss (Eq. 11) is a length-normalized squared trajectory-balance residual log Z + Σ log p_F = β log R̃ + Σ log b_ϕ plus a KL proximal term toward the director that collected the batch; the backward kernel b_ϕ is a learned unbuilding softmax over construction orders, and the reward R̃ (Eq. 13) is ε_min + r_ans · (smoothed success posterior) · exp(−L_rel), with counters updated once per unique outcome after the batch. Critical design decisions: κ = 1 is justified as the only integer margin adopting on two-level gaps but revising on one-level gaps (well-argued, with flip-identity theorems); length-normalized residuals and the moving π_ref are shown to preserve balanced fixed points (Lemma B.24); the MDL/Jeffreys reward has no tuned weights, and a β-temperature analysis (KL(p‖q_β) expansion) justifies reward-proportional sampling — though β's chosen value in experiments is not stated in the main text. Key Results: On the IID suite (HotpotQA, TriviaQA, AIME 2026, MedXpertQA, ALFWorld, MBPP+; 128 items each, 30 for AIME), CollabFlow leads every dataset and metric: e.g., ALFWorld success rate 98.44 ± 1.99 (+64.8 over direct Qwen3.5-9B), average accuracy 89.15 vs 84.78 for the strongest baseline (FlowSteer/SkillFlow region), +2.27 EM and +4.37 accuracy over the best baseline, significant at p < 10⁻². OOD (MuSiQue, NQ-Open, MATH-Hard, GPQA-D, HumanEval, WebShop), with everything frozen: it leads every row except HumanEval (tied with AFlow at 86.41), e.g., NQ-Open EM 93.44 vs 88.28 for the evolving orchestrator. Across six other frozen executors (GPT-5.6-Luna, GLM, DeepSeek V4.1, Grok-4.5, MiniMax M2.7, Claude Haiku 4.5) it lifts every IID/OOD average, with gains inversely related to executor strength (r = −0.96). CTB beats GRPO/PPO/no-CTB under matched rollouts on reward, worst-case success, team-distribution TV (0.0937 vs 0.1491–0.1631), and finds 26 distinct successful paths vs ≤15 for baselines. Token cost: 9,676 tokens/item versus 10,404 (fixed team) and 12,010 (single agent). Ablations: removing communication costs most (−16.4/−25.8 EM IID/OOD vs full), removing director training −13.7/−19.5, and the gain-over-direct-inference ranking of paradigms matches intuition (debate trails parallel voting). Baselines include recent orchestration methods (AFlow, FlowSteer, SkillFlow, SkillRL, evolving orchestrator) — current and reasonably strong. Caveat: Table 2 ablations are one run; headline Table 1 is five runs. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD and NEW FORMULATION, with an ENGINEERING OPTIMIZATION component. Genuinely novel: treating the per-edge message protocol as a learned object selected jointly with topology, and adapting GFlowNet trajectory balance to credit canonical agent teams once across construction orders with a self-generated, drift-bounded reward. The building blocks — GFlowNet TB (Malkin et al. 2022), Director–Executor orchestration, evidence scoring of candidates, Jeffreys smoothing, MDL priors, TRPO/PPO-style proximal KL — are standard; the composition and the theoretical treatment (flip identities, target-drift bound) applied to this setting are the new part. Rigor & Reproducibility: The theoretical appendix is unusually thorough: assumptions are labeled (C1–C3, S1–S3, T1–T4′), three propositions and the communication/serialization identities are proved in full, and approximate-balance perturbation bounds are given. Main results use five runs with Welch's t-tests; the training curve shows spread bands. However, the paradigm/ablation table is one run, so component-level conclusions rest on single-seed evidence with no significance testing. Code, trained director weights, and dataset splits are released at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/CollabFlow-631E, with detailed metric and cost-accounting conventions. Methodological concerns: (a) the director trains on the same six IID benchmarks on which IID performance is reported (OOD frozen evaluation mitigates this); (b) the RQ6 evolution analysis conditions on "the twenty steps with the largest one-step gain," a selection that inflates the 34.4%→75.0% improvement; (c) the Pearson r = −0.96 spans only six executors; (d) some gains are small (HumanEval +4.1, GPQA-D +13.6 vs baselines' +9.4–14.8) relative to 128-item test sets, where binomial noise is several points. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (with a substantial theoretical component, but the headline claims are experimental). Practical: Yes — the director and executor are both Qwen3.5-9B and the framework also runs with commercial API executors; no exotic hardware is implied. Efficient: Claimed and measured cheapest per item (9,676 tokens/item, lowest P90 and variance) versus a single agent (12,010), fixed team (10,404), and SkillFlow (10,452) — a credible cost story since director construction and revisions are charged to the budget. Effective: The evidence shows it solves the benchmark tasks under a shared budget and transfers to held-out tasks and other executors, but effectiveness is bounded by the fixed factual evaluator that supplies r_ans; it is not shown to work where no verifiable evaluator exists. Scalable: Not tested beyond a fixed agent population and 128-item benchmarks; scaling to large agent pools, more protocols, or bigger budgets is only argued, and the authors note added organization choices can raise sampling cost without performance gain. Delivered artifact: released code, trained director weights, and dataset splits (anonymous repo); the theory is reusable as a proof/analysis technique for graph-level TB. Strengths: - The evidence-gate formulation is a clean, falsifiable fix to verbatim message exchange: the flip/correction identities (Theorem B.7, Corollary B.8) make measurable exactly how a correct receiver can be harmed, and the ablations (−Evidence gate, All ONEWAY, Always revise) map onto the predicted failure routes, costing 14.3–15.6 OOD points. - CTB's credit-merging at the canonical terminal is a principled answer to a real, identified pathology (construction orders splitting credit; reward-maximization mode collapse), backed by a target-drift bound that tightens with data rather than hand-waving about stability. - The evaluation protocol is disciplined and unusually well documented: shared agent population, tool set, and per-task budget across all methods, charges for messages and construction tokens, explicit deduplication of evidence events, and a frozen OOD protocol with fixed adapters. - The theoretical appendix honestly separates ideal balance (T4/T4′) from the practical surrogate (KL regularization tilts the fixed point, Example B.23), and proves the proximal reference choice restores the fixed-point property. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The limitations appendix is direct and specific: the loop is bounded self-improvement (evaluator, executor, agent population, and update rules stay fixed); coverage is relative to the admissible team space; the single-writer design guarantees serialization, not correct plans or safe semantics; authentic but misleading evidence can still flip a correct receiver; reliability estimates from sparse/nonstationary executions may be uncalibrated; finite training does not attain the exact proved terminal distribution; and runtime likelihood surrogates and incomplete budget accounting limit which claims a particular evaluated system supports. This is a credibility positive — the authors confront rather than minimize their scope conditions. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - The self-generated reward reduces to ε_min + r_ans·(posterior)·(prior), so the entire "recursive self-improvement" depends on a human-defined factual evaluator and labeled answers during training; the paper never quantifies how performance degrades as evaluator coverage or quality drops, nor what the label cost is per round. - Ablations and paradigm comparisons are single-run on 128-item benchmarks, where a several-point margin is within seed noise; the component claims would be materially stronger with multi-seed error bars matching Table 1. - The RQ6 evolution numbers are conditional on selecting the twenty highest-gain steps, and the 15-of-20 persistence figure is not benchmarked against a control (e.g., persistence of edits from randomly chosen steps). - β (the CTB temperature) is central to the diversity-vs-quality trade-off (Eq. 12, the KL expansion in B.9) but its experimental value and sensitivity analysis are not reported in the main text. - The r = −0.96 correlation is fit over six points with two families sharing a lineage (DeepSeek V4/V4.1), so the "weaker executors gain more" law is thinly supported. - Fixed chain, parallel vote, and debate baselines are custom reimplementations; no comparison to widely used frameworks like AutoGen or MetaGPT at matched budget, which limits external anchoring of the paradigm comparison. Bottom Line: A practitioner building trainable multi-agent orchestration should read this for the CTB objective and the evidence-gate semantics — both are concretely reusable and well-theorized — but the headline gains over recent strong baselines are modest, the component ablations are single-run, and anyone without a reliable automated evaluator for their domain should treat the recursive-self-improvement claim as aspirational rather than demonstrated.

When, Not How Much: Evaluating Time-Series Foundation Models on Sparse Events

D Schoess, F von Wangenheim · arxiv.org · karypis - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces a within-window event-ranking task and evaluation protocol for sparse time series, and uses it to show that the released point forecasts of 12 time-series foundation models (TSFMs) barely beat a training-free reference at ranking future periods by event occurrence, while linear probes on frozen representations beat those forecasts in 29 of 30 backbone–dataset pairs. - Why it's important: Many operational decisions (inspections, staffing, service visits) cost the same regardless of event size, so which future periods will see activity matters more than how much activity; standard TSFM benchmarks (GIFT-Eval, BOOM) contain few zero-heavy windows and score forecast values, never occurrence ranking. - How it does it: The core move is a controlled paired-comparison design: chance-corrected, tie-aware AP/AUC skill scored per window, with the same frozen model evaluated three ways — point forecast vs. training-free reference, event-supervised linear probe vs. raw-context learners (logistic regression, LightGBM), and pretrained vs. randomly initialized copies of the same backbone. - The good: The randomized-backbone control, which most prior probing work omits, yields a genuinely non-obvious finding: random features already reach substantial skill (exceeding point forecasts in 15 of 30 AP pairs), and for Timer, randomized features beat pretrained ones on three of five datasets. - The missing: Probes cover only 6 of the 10 backbones that meet the extraction criterion — a subset fixed before probe training that omits the strongest point forecasters (Moirai-2.0, TimesFM-2.5/3) — so the probe-vs-forecast conclusion is not tested on the best forecasters. - Read it or not: Anyone benchmarking TSFMs, building intermittent-demand systems, or using probing to argue that foundation-model representations matter should read it; forecasters looking for a better sparse-event method will find diagnostics and a protocol, not a new model.

Rigor (88) is the paper's engine: the three-way paired-control design, exact permutation-verified AP-skill, 2,000-resample bootstrap, five-seed split checks, and self-constructed metric counterexamples exceed field norms, docked slightly for the pre-fixed probe subset that omits the strongest forecasters, missing hurdle/zero-inflated baselines, and no stated code/data release.
