Problem & Motivation: Sparse, mostly-zero time series — item-level retail sales, rare-condition case counts, peripheral transit pickups, niche web pages — appear across retail, operations, and web analytics. When an event triggers a fixed-cost action, the decision depends only on whether a future period contains activity, not on its magnitude. Since E[y|x] = P(y>0|x)·E[y|y>0,x], a point forecast ranks by expected amount, conflating the two factors; worse, seven of the evaluated TSFMs release a median, which is zero whenever event probability is below 50%, making a 1%-event position indistinguishable from a 49%-event one. Standard TSFM benchmarks do not cover this: the authors audit GIFT-Eval and BOOM and find only 24% and 1.6% of forecast windows contain ≥40% zeros, and their per-step metrics score values, not within-window ordering. The gap: no task, dataset, or protocol exists for judging pretrained forecasters on occurrence ranking. Key Idea: The key idea is not an algorithm but an evaluation design: score event ranking per window with skill scores corrected for chance (SAP = (AP − AP0)/(1 − AP0), with AP0 the exact permutation expectation under the window's tie structure; SAUC = 2·AUROC − 1), and answer every question with paired contrasts under matched supervision — including a randomized-backbone control that separates what the frozen representation contributes from what any trained probe extracts from any features. A secondary insight is that the reduction of the forecast distribution to a point (median vs. quantile average) materially changes ranking quality. Methodology: Three paired questions (Q1–Q3) on five curated sparse datasets built from public sources (Amazon purchases, Favorita, M5, NYC taxi, Wikipedia web traffic), with ≥40% zero positions required per series; windows pair a 364-day (or 336-hour) context with a 64-step horizon, tiled with non-overlapping targets, scored only on mixed-label targets. Q1 ranks the point forecasts of 12 TSFMs (Chronos-2, Chronos-Bolt, Moirai-1.1/2.0/MoE, Sundial, TimeMoE, Timer, TimesFM-2.5/3, TiRex, Toto-2.0) against a validation-selected training-free reference (seasonal event-rate/mean profile or horizon ramp). Q2 trains linear probes on frozen forecast-aligned representations of six backbones with event labels, against the backbone's own point forecast, same-family logistic regression on the raw context, and per-position LightGBM. Q3 retrains the same probe on randomly initialized copies of each backbone (default source-code initialization, same extraction path and seed). Uncertainty uses 2,000-resample paired bootstrap over series; five seeded series-disjoint splits (taxi split by year) give sign-stability counts; a 100k-window training cap is verified insensitive (≤0.0054 AP-skill change for two checked backbones). Critical design decisions: per-window scoring rather than pooling (justified by an explicit counterexample showing pooling rewards between-window activity); threshold AP with ties entering at shared thresholds; fixing the probe subset before any training (justified as pre-registration, though it excludes the strongest forecasters). The closed form for AP0 is verified by enumeration against all 2,604 mixed labelings for n ≤ 6. Key Results: (1) Q1: no TSFM point forecast exceeds the training-free reference by more than 0.031 AP skill on any dataset, and under AUC skill the median TSFM falls below the reference on all five datasets; on web traffic under equal-series weighting every TSFM trails the reference by up to 0.064 AUC skill. Averaging quantiles instead of taking the median raises the best gain over the reference from 0.031 to 0.057 AP skill (Chronos-2 on NYC taxi). (2) Q2: linear probes beat their backbone's point forecast in 29 of 30 backbone–dataset pairs (both metrics; e.g., median +0.082 AP skill on Favorita) and beat raw-context logistic regression in 22 of 30; comparison with raw LightGBM is dataset-dependent — probes lead on Amazon, M5 (by 0.007–0.012 AP skill), and NYC taxi, but on web traffic all six probes trail LightGBM by a median of 0.115 AP skill even with a GBM readout. (3) Q3: pretrained beats randomized features in 26 of 30 AP comparisons, with large variance (Chronos-2 +0.113 vs. Toto-2.0 +0.026 on Favorita); Timer reverses on Favorita (0.172 randomized vs. 0.135 pretrained), M5, and web traffic. Randomized probes alone exceed point forecasts in 15 of 30 AP pairs. Amazon is nearly uninformative for all methods (<0.014 AP skill). Baselines are current (2024–2026 checkpoints) and the controls are unusually strong; tested scale is standard (321,747 evaluated windows on Favorita down to 19,207 on taxi). Novelty Classification: NEW PROBLEM (within-window event ranking for sparse series as a TSFM evaluation task), NEW DATASET/BENCHMARK (five curated sparse datasets plus chance-corrected, tie-aware skill protocol), and NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING (released point forecasts add little over training-free references for occurrence; pretrained-feature advantage is backbone-dependent, with Timer reversing). The individual techniques — linear probing, LightGBM, randomized-feature controls from NLP probing (Hewitt & Liang; Zhang & Bowman), Croston-style sparse forecasting literature — are standard; the novelty is their assembly into a rigorously controlled paired protocol and the resulting findings, which is a genuine but primarily evaluative contribution. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations and sensitivity analyses are extensive: equal-window vs. equal-series weighting (including a documented sign reversal on web traffic traced to 145 windows), exclusion of low-zero windows, missing-value subsets for web traffic, training-size sensitivity for two backbones, a GBM probe variant, supervised readouts of model outputs, and a per-pair pretraining-overlap classification (median pretrained-minus-randomized gap of 0.019 AP skill in 12 disclosed-exclusion pairs vs. 0.035 in 13 disclosed-overlap pairs). Uncertainty: 2,000-resample paired bootstrap intervals, five-seed split sign counts (169 of 192 contrasts agree in all five splits). Honestly flagged: intervals are pointwise and uncorrected for multiplicity; NYC taxi has one fitted run per procedure. Code or data release is not stated in the provided text. Methodological concerns: the probe subset was fixed before training but omits the four strongest point forecasters; each representation is read at a single extraction point; the AP-skill construction can yield positive skill under equal marginal event probabilities (the authors prove a counterexample themselves — commendable, but it complicates AP-only interpretation); evaluation is entirely on the authors' own five datasets, though these are curated from public sources with audited filters. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL (benchmark, probes, and learners actually run; no new system deployed). Practical: Yes — all components (frozen TSFM inference, linear probes, LightGBM) run on commodity hardware; probes are a single linear map from ≤2,048 dimensions to 64 scores. Efficient: Probe training is capped at 100,000 windows and is cheap relative to running the backbones; the comparison itself costs one forward pass per window for ten of twelve TSFMs. Effective: The evidence supports the stated conclusion — point forecasts are weak occurrence rankers and event-supervised probes improve on them — but absolute skill is low outside Favorita/M5/taxi, and near-oracle performance is far off (best methods place ~3.0–5.0 events in the top 8 positions vs. an oracle 7.0–7.6). Scalable: Not tested at larger scale; the training cap is only spot-checked for two backbones, and 100× window counts or longer horizons are unexamined. Deliverable: a protocol and five curated evaluation datasets in paper form; no software artifact, trained model, or repository URL is mentioned in the provided text. Strengths: - The three-way control structure (output vs. reference, probe vs. raw-context, pretrained vs. randomized) is the paper's real intellectual contribution; the randomized-backbone control, imported from NLP probing but absent from prior TSFM probing work, overturns what a naive probe-only reading would conclude. - Metric engineering is unusually careful: exact permutation expectation of tie-aware AP (verified by enumeration), a constructed counterexample showing pooling across windows inflates skill, and an explicit construction where AP skill is positive under equal marginal event probabilities — the authors stress-test their own metrics. - Honest negative and null results are reported at the same level as positives: the web-traffic LightGBM dominance, the Timer reversal, and the near-zero Amazon skill are all foregrounded, and pretraining-data contamination is quantified rather than ignored. - The audit of GIFT-Eval and BOOM zero-heavy coverage (24% and 1.6% of windows ≥40% zeros; 0.28% of GIFT-Eval target mass in ≥80%-zero windows) convincingly establishes that existing benchmarks cannot answer this question. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state that conclusions cover five datasets, target-only inputs, a 64-step horizon, and mixed-label targets only (fully inactive horizons are not assessed); zeros may be missing records (68% of web-traffic zero labels) or stockouts; daily splits share calendar time; disclosed pretraining overlap could favor pretrained features (they report the overlap-stratified gaps); probes cover six of ten eligible backbones at one extraction point; event-supervised fine-tuning is out of scope; LightGBM may not bound all direct learners; intervals are uncorrected for multiplicity; and the metrics assess ranking, not calibration or downstream decision value. This is direct, non-minimizing limitation reporting — a strong credibility signal. Analyst-Identified Gaps: Beyond the acknowledged issues: (1) the probe subset excludes exactly the models with the strongest point forecasts (Moirai-2.0, TimesFM-2.5/3), so the headline "probes beat forecasts" claim is untested where it would be hardest; (2) the M5 probes that beat raw LightGBM all come from backbones disclosing M5 exclusion, but exclusion is self-reported by vendors and unverifiable, so contamination of the one clean probe-beats-trees result cannot be ruled out; (3) no dedicated occurrence/count baselines (Croston, TSB are dismissed on a technicality — constant-across-horizon forecasts score zero within-window — but hurdle or zero-inflated event models, which the related-work section cites, are never run); (4) Amazon, where every method scores below 0.014 AP skill, contributes ~19% of evaluated windows while carrying essentially no signal about method differences; (5) the Timer reversal analysis stops at correlation (pattern-readout R² tracks the gap at ρ = 0.69) without a causal test; (6) no repository or data release is stated, which for a paper whose main deliverable is a protocol and datasets limits immediate reuse. Bottom Line: This is the most methodologically careful evaluation of TSFMs on a task they were never built for, and its paired-comparison protocol plus the randomized-feature finding should become standard practice in TSFM benchmarking — but it delivers a mirror, not a method, and practitioners needing better sparse-event forecasts should look to it for the evaluation recipe and the quantile-averaging trick rather than for a deployable model.

TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces PhantomEnvironments, rule-generated fictional-world multi-turn RL environments (built on PhantomWiki, with Prolog-verified rewards and no LLMs or humans in the generation pipeline) and shows that LLM agents RL-trained in them transfer to real-world multi-hop search benchmarks. - Why it's important: RL training of LLM agents is bottlenecked by environment curation — human-curated data is expensive and goes stale, and LLM-synthesized environments risk hallucinated rewards, contamination, API cost, and the generator's capability ceiling; a zero-marginal-cost, exactly verifiable alternative changes the economics of agent training. - How it does it: It converts template-generated fictional wikis and CFG-generated multi-hop questions (grounded in random social graphs) into a searchable corpus with GRPO fine-tuning and F1-based outcome reward, so any transfer must come from procedural search skills (decompose → retrieve → compose) rather than factual memorization. - The good: The head-to-head against real Wikipedia training is the strongest evidence — real data wins only in-domain (56.7 vs 52.2 avg F1, Qwen2.5-3B, on Wikipedia-2018 benchmarks) while synthetic wins out-of-domain (32.1 vs 28.4), and the SynthWorlds Knowledge-Advantage gap (8% → 11% with real training) closes to 0% with synthetic training, cleanly demonstrating that fictional environments teach search skill rather than memorization shortcuts. - The missing: There is no comparison against LLM-synthesized environment baselines (e.g., ZeroSearch, ASearcher), so the claim that rule-generated environments are a competitive third data source rests only on comparison with human-curated data; evaluation is also confined to 3B/7B models and small curated corpora rather than open-web settings. - Read it or not: Read it if you build or budget for RL environments for LLM agents — the transfer results, the search-scaling observation, and the constraint-shortcut ablation are directly actionable; skip it if you only care about open-web deep-research agents, which the authors explicitly do not evaluate.

Problem & Motivation: Teams training LLM search agents with RL need environments that provide long multi-turn trajectories, verifiable terminal rewards, and cheap regeneration at scale. Human-curated corpora (NQ, HotpotQA) are expensive, fixed to a Wikipedia snapshot, and invite memorization shortcuts; LLM-generated environments (ZeroSearch, ASearcher, WebDancer, KARL, etc.) introduce hallucinated or LLM-judged rewards, API cost, contamination risk, and a capability ceiling set by the generator. The paper asks where verifiable, interactive, long-horizon training environments should come from, and whether an environment that shares zero facts, entities, or document distribution with the real world can teach transferable agentic search — an outcome that, a priori, has no reason to hold. Key Idea: Strip the environment down to pure relational structure: sample a random social graph, render it as templated articles, generate multi-hop questions via context-free grammars whose answers are computed by an attached Prolog query, and index the corpus for dense retrieval. Because rewards are exactly verifiable by construction and generation cost is zero, the environment becomes a controllable experimental variable — difficulty, universe size, and question type are knobs — forcing the agent to learn procedural search (decompose the question, issue queries, compose across turns) with no factual content to memorize. Methodology: The pipeline has three stages: (1) environment generation — PhantomWiki universes (training universe: 1,000 people, 100 family trees, up to 7-hop questions), extended with bidirectional anchor sampling to remove positional bias in answer placement, and extended generators for comparison questions (paired chains + comparison predicate) and constraint questions (up to 3 attribute filters); (2) RL fine-tuning — GRPO (group-normalized advantages, token-level clipped surrogate, environment tokens in <information> masked from the loss, KL penalty removed, ratio clip-higher at 2.0) on ~55K questions, F1 reward after SQuAD normalization, Search-R1-style <search>/<answer> tag protocol, full fine-tuning of four models (Qwen2.5-3B/7B-Instruct, Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct, Phi-4-mini-instruct) for 1 epoch × 2 seeds on 2× B200 in ~2 days via SkyRL/vLLM/FSDP2; (3) evaluation — six real-world multi-hop benchmarks with per-benchmark corpora, using a stronger evaluation retriever (Qwen3-Embedding-4B, 20 turns, 32K context) than training (e5-base-v2, 10 turns, 8K context). Critical design decisions: masking environment tokens in GRPO (standard, justified by Search-R1 precedent); evaluating with a deliberately superior retriever setup (justified via an ablation, Tables 4–5); balancing question difficulty strata via cell-balanced sampling (justified as preventing hop-count stratification from dominating the mixture). One notable deviation: on entropy-spike training degeneration in some runs, they report the best held-out checkpoint — reasonable but a soft form of model selection. Key Results: Training in PhantomEnvironments improves F1 over base models on all six benchmarks and all four LLMs: Qwen2.5-7B rises from 44.2→64.1 on HotpotQA, 29.1→66.7 on 2WikiMultihopQA, 15.6→40.6 on SynthWorlds-SM, 16.2→35.4 on FRAMES; Llama-3.2-3B improves 7.1× on SynthWorlds-SM (3.8→27.0). Averages: 1.7× gains on Wikipedia-2018 benchmarks (HotpotQA, 2Wiki, MuSiQue) and 2.2× on newer benchmarks (SynthWorlds-RM/SM, FRAMES). Against real NQ+HotpotQA training at matched 55K data budget, real data wins in-domain (56.7 vs 52.2 avg F1, Qwen2.5-3B) but synthetic wins out-of-domain (32.1 vs 28.4) and fully closes the SynthWorlds Knowledge-Advantage gap to 0% for Qwen models while real training widens it (8→11%). Qwen models exhibit emergent "search scaling" — number of search calls grows roughly linearly with question hop count — absent in Phi-4-mini and partial in Llama-3.2-3B. Agents generalize to unseen fictional universes (1K and 10K people) with parallel F1 and scaling behavior. Pooled noisy corpus testing degrades performance only slightly (−1.6 to −1.9 avg F1). Constraint-augmented environments (Hops+Constraints) hurt transfer (39.6 vs 42.1 avg F1 for Hops on Qwen2.5-3B) by rewarding verbatim monolithic queries that skip decomposition — a diagnosed and illustrated failure mode. Benchmarks are standard, 500–824 questions each; no comparison against LLM-synthesized environments is run. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD (first rule-generated, LLM-free, multi-turn RL search environment with exact Prolog verifiability, extending PhantomWiki from an evaluation dataset to an interactive training environment) plus NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING (fictional-only environments transfer to real-world agentic search and can outperform real training data on out-of-domain benchmarks; emergent per-model search scaling). The RL recipe (GRPO + Search-R1 format), the retriever stack (e5/FAISS), and the benchmark suite are standard combinations; the genuinely new element is the environment-as-design-surface demonstration and the complexity-axis ablation, not the training algorithm. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are present and informative: retriever configuration (Tables 4–5), search-corpus pooling (Tables 3, 6–7), environment complexity axes (Figures 5–6, 11), and parametric-knowledge retention (PopQA/MMLU/Wiki-18 perplexity, Table 8). Two training seeds with mean ± standard error throughout, per-category decomposition of gains, and verbatim trajectory analysis of the constraint shortcut raise confidence. Code is open-sourced at github.com/kilian-group/phantom-envs with generator configurations released. Concerns: (1) only two seeds and occasional best-checkpoint selection after training degeneration; (2) evaluation uses a strictly stronger retriever/turn budget than training — favorably handled via ablation, but it still means headline numbers are not achievable under the training configuration; (3) evaluation sets are small (500 questions for most benchmarks); (4) the strongest head-to-head (SynthWorlds KA gap) uses a benchmark suite from a related evaluation line (SynthWorlds) that shares motivation with the paper's thesis; (5) no LLM-synthesized-environment baseline despite the motivation centering on the three-way comparison. This is a preprint and has not, to the reviewer's knowledge, completed peer review. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (method run and measured by the authors). - Practical: Yes — training fits on 2× NVIDIA B200 GPUs in ~2 days per run, and the environment generator is CPU-scale Python with Prolog; the compute footprint is unusually low for RL agent work. - Efficient: Environment generation has zero marginal cost by construction, dominating both human curation and LLM-synthesis on cost; the RL run itself is standard-cost for 3–7B models. - Effective: The evidence shows it solves the stated problem — teaching transferable search procedure — on curated multi-hop QA corpora; whether it solves open-web search (the realistic deployment target) is untested, a proxy-level gap the authors concede. - Scalable: Only partially tested — unseen universes up to 10K people and pooled 6-benchmark corpora are the ceiling; 10–100× scale (larger universes, longer hop counts, 70B-class models, live web) is claimed as future work, not demonstrated. The work delivers a software artifact (open-source environment generator and training code); no trained model weights are mentioned as released. Strengths: (1) The controlled real-vs-synthetic comparison at matched data budget, with the SynthWorlds real/synthetic-mirror pair acting as a memorization probe, is a clean experimental design that isolates procedural skill from factual recall — the KA-gap closure from 8–11% to 0% is the paper's most convincing single result. (2) The environment complexity ablation yields a non-obvious, actionable finding: linear hops drive transfer, comparisons target their matching real-world category, and constraints actively backfire via a diagnosed verbatim-query shortcut with verbatim trajectory evidence — a rare case of an ablation producing a mechanism, not just a number. (3) The emergent search-scaling observation (search calls linear in hop count for Qwen models only) is a genuinely interesting behavioral finding that connects environment design to model-capability-dependent skill acquisition. (4) The bidirectional anchor sampling fix for answer-position bias shows attention to subtle generator-bias artifacts most synthetic-data work ignores. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state that (1) the complexity analysis does not yet yield a recipe mapping known capability gaps to synthetic environment compositions; (2) synthetic environments are used standalone, and blending with real data (e.g., as mid-training) is unexplored; (3) compute limits prevent training larger LLMs and evaluating on long-context or open-web benchmarks like BrowseComp-Plus. They also frankly document the constraint-question backfire and RL training instability (entropy spikes) as limitations of the approach and training recipe. This is direct, non-minimizing limitation reporting — a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: (1) The motivating three-way comparison (human-curated vs LLM-synthesized vs rule-generated) is executed only two-thirds of the way: no LLM-generated environment is actually trained against, so "zero-marginal-cost beats or matches LLM synthesis" remains a claim, not a measurement. (2) Transfer is measured only on multi-hop QA over static curated corpora; the retrieved-document distribution of template articles differs from real Wikipedia prose in ways that may interact with the dense retriever, and the paper does not test BM25 or hybrid retrieval to show the skill is retriever-agnostic. (3) The constraint-shortcut finding is partly a property of the authors' own environment design (rare attributes make verbatim queries win); a reviewer would want to know whether constraint design can be fixed to reward decomposition rather than simply avoiding constraints. (4) The search-scaling claim rests on Qwen-family models (two models) with Llama partial and Phi absent — three families is thin support for an "emergent" capability claim. (5) FRAMES uses a June 2023 Wikipedia snapshot while training-time LLMs postdate it, leaving residual contamination ambiguity on one of the two benchmarks driving the "newer and harder" advantage narrative — though SynthWorlds-SM independently controls for this. (6) Search-budget linear-in-difficulty is reported as desirable but its downstream effect on accuracy-per-token cost is not quantified. Bottom Line: A practitioner training RL search agents gains concrete, well-evidenced tools and findings here — free verifiable environments that beat real training data out-of-domain, a shortcut failure mode to design around, and a hop-count-dominance result — making this worth reading despite the missing LLM-synthesized-environment baseline and the curated-corpus-only evaluation.

When Specifications Drift: Measuring Semantic Preservation Across LLM Representations

MA Patel, LC Corpaci · openreview.net · specification to code with formal verifications - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper presents a controlled 153,000-call empirical study measuring whether nine LLMs preserve the logical meaning of 500 small magma identities when the same identity is presented in 18 deterministic encodings, using a formal directional implication oracle (equivalent/weaker/stronger/incomparable) rather than a binary accuracy score. - Why it's important: If a model silently rewrites a specification into a strictly weaker one, downstream verifiers can certify implementations that the original requirement excludes, so specification validation is a distinct obligation from proof checking — a gap with direct consequences for AI-for-verifiable-coding pipelines. - How it does it: It exploits the Equational Theories Project's (ETP) precomputed implication matrix over 4,694 magma identities as a directional semantic oracle on model reconstructions, and separately reports oracle-coverage failures so that uncertified outputs are not mistaken for proven errors. - The good: The strict-weakening signal under confusable identifiers is formally certified and sharply concentrated: 30.3% of confusable-name responses are proven strictly weaker, and 93.7% of those use fewer distinct variables — a directional, oracle-backed failure mode, not a proxy-level claim. - The missing: The domain is short, pretraining-plausible single equations with no control flow or program state; contamination is not quantified, the homoglyph condition lacks the end-to-end inverse validation other encodings receive, and no end-to-end effect on verified code generation is tested. - Read it or not: Read it if you build or evaluate specification autoformalization or verification pipelines — the directional-oracle methodology and the demonstrated identifier/instruction sensitivity are directly actionable; skip it if you need evidence about realistic software specifications rather than toy equational laws.

Problem & Motivation: Verification certifies that an implementation satisfies the specification as submitted; it says nothing about whether an LLM-mediated translation of that specification preserved the intended meaning. A model that weakens a spec enables false assurance: a correct proof against the weakened statement proves the wrong requirement. Who has this problem: anyone using LLMs to autoformalize mathematics, translate specs into Lean/SMT/Python checks, or route natural-language requirements into solver input. Prior work (miniF2F, LeanEuclid, Verus-SpecGym, FormatSpread) either evaluates fixed formal statements, checks bidirectional equivalence in one representation, or studies prompt-format sensitivity in accuracy terms — none systematically vary the encoding of a fixed source specification and classify the direction of semantic change. The paper closes this gap in a domain where directional semantic relations are computable for every item. Key Idea: The core insight is to repurpose a finite, fully-certified implication catalogue (ETP's dense matrix over 4,694 magma identities) as a directional semantic oracle: present the same identity in many deterministic encodings, ask the model to recover it as a canonical explicitly-parenthesized infix equation, and classify the reconstruction as equivalent, strictly weaker, strictly stronger, or incomparable — while bucketing coverage failures (off-catalogue, unparseable, unknown) separately so that "uncertified" is never conflated with "refuted." A secondary analytical device is the logical observation that variable identification (σ with S ⊨ σ(S)) can only weaken a universal law, giving a principled explanation for the concentrated fewer-variable errors observed under confusable identifiers, with an explicit two-element right-projection magma as a strictness witness. Methodology: The pipeline is: (1) build 18 alternate renderings of the ETP catalogue (symbolic, Lean/TPTP/SMT-LIB, Python lambda/Cayley, mechanical prose, SSA/JSON/tree/DOT, slot/confusable variables), each validated by exhaustive inverse checks recovering all 4,694 source ASTs; (2) sample 500 laws (census of order 1–2, seeded samples of order 3–4, with post-stratification weights); (3) run a 9-model × 18-encoding × 500-law main sweep (81,000 calls via OpenRouter, temperature 0, 900-token cap), plus 48,600 repeat calls, 9,600 notation-note, 8,400 framing, and 5,400 naming calls; (4) grade via a fixed extraction ladder and the certified implication matrix, reporting nine outcome types with a denominator that excludes only content-filter and transport losses so unparseable answers cannot inflate scores. Statistics include Cochran's Q across encodings per model, exact McNemar versus canonical with within-model Holm correction on a 434-law common subset, Wilson intervals, and an exploratory clustered logistic regression. Critical design decisions: (a) the oracle is a historical snapshot with 190 uncertified directions, explicitly not an unrestricted decision procedure — well-justified and honestly bounded; (b) the anti-copy output contract ("Do not restate the input") turned out to conflict with the recovery task, motivating the framing probe — an initially under-justified choice the authors later expose themselves; (c) reported representation effects use a fixed 9-model roster with heterogeneous seed/reasoning support — the authors repeatedly label tier comparisons descriptive, which is appropriate but limits generalization. Key Results: Main sweep (81,000 calls, 80,931 analyzable): pooled certified recovery spans 65.2 points, from 73.7% (bracket words) and 72.2% (SSA) and 71.4% (LaTeX) down to 16.9% (Polish prefix) and 8.5% (RPN); the canonical infix control itself scores only 49.6%. All 153 noncontrol comparisons reject equality via Cochran's Q (p < 10⁻¹² for every model); 123 of 153 survive Holm correction versus control. Oracle outcomes across the main sweep: 42,151 equivalent, 7,705 weaker, 1,087 stronger, 7,576 incomparable, versus 19,472 off-catalogue and 2,925 parse/mapping failures — i.e., strict semantic disagreement is certified for 16,368 outputs and coverage loss is reported separately (e.g., 2,340 of RPN's off-fragment outputs are actually valid above-order-four identities). Confusable identifiers produce 1,365/4,500 (30.3%) proven strictly weaker (vs. 8.2% under LaTeX), with 93.7% of those using fewer distinct variables. The identifier study drops recovery from 64.4% (canonical letters) to 3.1% (Latin/Cyrillic homoglyphs), with the fewer-variable proxy rising from 33.4% to 98.0% and unparseable rates ≤3.0%. Generous notation notes with examples recover large losses (GPT-5.2 Polish 34.0%→93.3%; Opus 5 RPN 49.3%→94.0%), length-matched padding adds nothing (mean −2.2 points), and generous notes hurt LaTeX for Qwen (−15.3) and Gemini (−14.7). An anti-transformation sentence lifts canonical recovery by up to +72.7 points (Grok, with preamble removal) and LaTeX recovery by 14–22 points (all p < 0.001). Repeat sampling (3 draws on 150 laws) shows median cell recovery range of 2.0 points but a 20.0-point maximum and only 77.0% outcome agreement, cautioning against fine-grained format rankings. Strong model×format interactions appear (Qwen: 98.0% Lean vs. 44.4% canonical; Mistral: 0% Lean; Opus 5: 53% RPN vs. <10% for all others). Novelty Classification: NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING and NEW FORMULATION, with elements of NEW DATASET/BENCHMARK. Genuinely novel: the paired 18-representation design with directional formal verdicts and explicit oracle-coverage accounting, and the certified, concentrated strict-weakening effect under confusable identifiers. Not novel, as the authors themselves concede: bidirectional semantic checking (LeanEuclid's SMT-based equivalence engine), specification-faithfulness benchmarking (Verus-SpecGym), and prompt-format sensitivity (FormatSpread). The magma domain and oracle matrix are borrowed infrastructure (ETP); the contribution is the experimental design and the findings, not a new algorithm or tool. Rigor & Reproducibility: Rigor is above average for an empirical LLM study: paired designs, Holm-corrected tests, post-stratification and common-subset sensitivity analyses, repeat-sampling variability explicitly reported and used to police over-interpretation, and a denominator rule that prevents unparseable answers from inflating recovery. Ablations are extensive: note removal/padding/generous conditions isolate reading content from prompt length; framing probes isolate the anti-transformation instruction; naming schemes isolate identifier choice. Reproducibility is partial: an anonymous code-only supplement (oracle, converters, runners, prompt configuration) is prepared, but saved responses and analysis scripts are excluded, no public repository is claimed, and the NeurIPS checklist self-reports [No] for open data/code access. Concerns: (a) evaluation on a domain that may be heavily represented in pretraining, with contamination unquantified; (b) a mid-experiment model substitution (Kimi→DeepSeek) and changed denominator/ token caps documented in Appendix H.1, i.e., the design record is not an immutable preregistration; (c) condition-block dispatch of follow-ups admits temporal/provider confounds the authors acknowledge; (d) the same benchmark used to design and evaluate the protocol (though the representation contrasts, not the oracle, are the object of study). Cost transparency is unusually good: ~$103.92 in reported API spend for 153,000 calls. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (a measurement study with a reusable oracle methodology, not a deployed system). - Practical: Fully — the study runs entirely through commodity OpenRouter API endpoints, and the grading pipeline needs only Python standard library plus NumPy/SciPy/Matplotlib. - Efficient: Very — $103.92 for 153,000 calls; the oracle consumes a precomputed matrix rather than invoking ATPs at query time, so preservation checking at this domain's scale is essentially free per query. - Effective: The evidence shows the oracle detects real directional semantic drift and that instructions/identifiers causally move it; it does not yet show that any of this improves end-to-end verified code generation, which the authors explicitly do not claim. - Scalable: Untested beyond the 4,694-identity catalogue; scaling to arbitrary specifications requires an implication backend the paper does not provide, and the paper is careful to say the coverage boundary would need a stronger backend or human review. The work delivers a reusable code artifact (oracle, converters, experiment runners) and a measurement methodology, not a finished tool, CLI for practitioners, or trained model; it stops at paper-plus-supplement form. Strengths: - The directional oracle design converts a vague "models mistranslate specs" worry into certified, falsifiable per-item verdicts, and the explicit separation of proven inequivalence from oracle coverage loss is a methodological contribution that other specification-evaluation papers should copy. - The confusable-identifier finding is the strongest result: a formally certified 30.3% strict-weakening rate with 93.7% fewer-variable concentration and a concrete counterexample witness (Equation 2), connecting an attack-surface observation to a logical mechanism rather than a proxy heuristic. - The intervention studies (generous notes, padding control, anti-transformation probe) are properly controlled — length-matched padding rules out a mere token-count explanation, and the probe prevents misreading the 49.6% canonical score as intrinsic notation difficulty. - Unusual candor: model substitution, denominator changes, exploratory status of follow-ups, snapshot uncertified directions, and even a self-reported [No] on open data access are all disclosed in detail. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors confront limitations directly and at length (Section 6, Appendices D and H.1): short single equations possibly in pretraining with unquantified contamination; strata overrepresenting lower orders; a fixed historical API roster with heterogeneous seed/reasoning/routing support; follow-ups reusing a 150-law subset with condition-block dispatch; confounded Unicode naming schemes (script, similarity, length, tokenization varied together); shared helper code undermining independence of inverse checks; a homoglyph condition lacking full end-to-end validation; 69 content-filter losses and 499 token-cap finishes concentrated in particular encodings; and no evaluated linter or repair pipeline. This level of disclosure is a credibility positive; the authors do not minimize. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - No contamination probe of any kind (e.g., memorization checks on ETP identities or their renderings), despite the authors flagging the risk — the representation effects could partly reflect uneven pretraining exposure to encodings rather than uniform semantic sensitivity. - The variable-identification explanation for weakening is supported by a count proxy and one witness; no edit-level analysis (e.g., tree-diff of generated versus source ASTs) verifies that counted outputs are pure variable merges. - All nine models are evaluated at one snapshot in time through one aggregator (OpenRouter); no replication on an independent roster or later model generation, so stability of the format effects over model iterations is unknown. - The framing probe varies instruction and preamble jointly for some models (e.g., Grok's largest gain requires both), but the two factors are never tested at full factorial depth across all encodings, and the paper concedes the psychological mechanism (over-transformation) is not established. - Coverage of the oracle is limited to order ≤4 identities; the 52.0% of RPN responses that are valid but above-order go uncertified, meaning the headline 8.5% RPN recovery figure is a lower bound the paper cannot tighten — a reader skimming the abstract will not appreciate how much of the postfix deficit is measurement artifact. - No comparison against a non-ETP formal domain (e.g., group theory or library specifications) to test whether the representation effects are catalogue-specific. Bottom Line: A careful, unusually honest measurement paper whose directional-oracle methodology and certified strict-weakening findings are directly useful to anyone building specification-translation or verification pipelines, and which I would accept over most toy-benchmark submissions in this space — but its findings are bounded by a tiny, possibly contaminated equational domain and an unpublished artifact, so treat the headline numbers as domain-specific lower bounds rather than general laws of specification drift.

TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces a formal framework and toolchain that certify by proof the behavioral effect of a mechanistic edit — that a target skill is removed and a second skill preserved for every input in a continuous region — on piecewise-linear networks up to a small softmax + LayerNorm transformer, and proves no finite deterministic black-box test can ever deliver such a certificate. - Why it's important: Safety-critical edits (ablations, unlearning, steering) are currently validated only by finite test suites, and jailbreaks and unlearning reversals succeed precisely on inputs outside test coverage, so edits can ship while the harmful skill survives in undetected pockets. - How it does it: It encodes the edited network and the negation of the behavioral claim into Z3 as quantifier-free linear real arithmetic over exact rationals (with a hull relaxation over token choices), and extends past the exact solver's frontier with sound CROWN bound propagation, bracketed from above by projected-gradient attacks. - The good: The central impossibility result (P3) comes with a concrete, machine-checked witness — an edit that passes a 40,401-point grid plus 1,000 random probes yet provably retains the skill on a survivor pocket below 1.5×10⁻⁶ of the domain — and three of 160 naturally trained models exhibited such illusions unprompted. - The missing: All subjects are toy or known-formula models (up to a 64-wide, 2-layer transformer with contrived skills); no pretrained language model, no real safety-relevant capability, and the paper itself concedes the framework presupposes a decidable skill specification that real harms lack. - Read it or not: Read it if you work at the formal-verification × interpretability × unlearning boundary — it defines a genuinely new certification target and maps exactly where current provers stop — but skip it if you want deployable certificates for real LLM safety edits today.

Problem & Motivation: Mechanistic interpretability practitioners (unlearning, ablation, activation-steering communities) validate edits by running the edited model on held-out prompts. Testing answers the claim only at tested inputs; jailbreak and unlearning-reversal literature shows failures concentrate off-distribution. Prior formal work certifies descriptions of a model (accuracy floors, circuit faithfulness, circuit stability under resampling) or statistical unlearning guarantees — none certifies what an edit does behaviorally, worst-case, over a continuous input region. The paper frames the target property as feature non-interference in the information-flow-security sense: the edited component's output is provably independent of a forbidden input feature everywhere in a region. Key Idea: The core move is re-targeting formal verification from model descriptions to edit effects: state removal/preservation as a universally-quantified sign claim g_h(x) ≤ 0 / > 0 over a box region plus its inflations, prove it by showing the negation unsatisfiable in QF-LRA with an SMT solver, and measure robustness as a bisection-computed "certified radius" (the largest region inflation for which the claim still holds). The negative counterpart — a three-ReLU "tent" gadget hidden between test points with slopes that cancel exactly at every probe — is the constructive proof that no finite deterministic black-box test can certify removal. That duality (constructive positive certificates + constructive impossibility for testing) is the paper's intellectual center. Methodology: Pipeline: (1) define a model class (ReLU networks, rational weights, domain [0,1]^d), claims (head, region, sign), and edit types (ablation, weight edit, bias-add steering); (2) exact SMT encoding in Z3 — every weight as an exact fraction, each ReLU as an ite split; a claim is certified by unsat of its negation, refuted by a concrete counterexample; radii found by bisection with a query-count bound (P2d); token sequences handled either by Boolean selectors (intractable) or a "hull relaxation" over the embedding simplex that soundly over-approximates discrete inputs; (3) a CROWN/auto_LiRPA bound-propagation extension for softmax + LayerNorm, which the exact encoding cannot represent, with soundness validated by reproducing exact radii where both provers apply (M0: 0.5=0.5 removal, 0.0996=0.0996 preservation on the toy model) and bracketed from above by PGD attack (M1); (4) a siamese two-copy encoding certifying influence of a forbidden feature (non-interference). Propositions P1 (region monotonicity/union closure), P2 (radius well-defined and cheaply decidable), P3 (test impossibility), P4 (exact surgery-vs-steering separation with linear-in-dose collateral) each have machine-checked witnesses except P1. Critical design decisions: hull relaxation to avoid Boolean branching (justified by soundness via P1a, but the relaxation is reported "too loose" beyond 96 noise variables); explicit float-gap slack (γ=10⁻⁹ toy, 10⁻⁶ transformer) bridging exact-rational proofs to float64 execution (forward-error ceiling ≈10⁻¹³); replacing a component circuit with a position-scoped attention knockout on the softmax model because greedy search found no separable circuit — a concession that changes what is certified. Key Results: On a softmax + LayerNorm transformer (64-wide, 4 heads, 2 layers), CROWN certifies removal at radius 0.0091 (attack: 0.03) and preservation at 0.0079 (attack: 0.05) and 0.0098 (attack: 0.1) over 448 embedding-noise dimensions — roughly 9× the exact solver's frontier of 48 noise variables (threshold-gate transformer: removal 0.016, preservation 0.013, with collateral quantified as skill-B radius dropping 0.034 → 0.013). Constructed and naturally occurring intervention illusions: 3/160 trained models (all with ≥4 inputs) passed a 40,401-point grid plus 1,000 random inputs plus preservation checks while the solver exhibited a survivor input; survivor pockets below 1.5×10⁻⁶ of the domain (95% Clopper–Pearson, 2×10⁶ samples). P4 confirmed experimentally: diff-of-means steering erodes skill-B radius linearly in dose (0.0996 → 0.0908 at dose 4 → 0.0656 at dose 16; R² ≥ 0.999), ablation/weight-edit/targeted suppression certify zero collateral; on the transformer no steering dose both removes A and preserves B. Certified influence driven from 22 to <0.001 by surgical edit on the toy model; exactly 0 on the transformer. Certified edges stop within 0.0012–0.0039 of the model's own decision boundary, showing tightness. Exact frontier mapped: hull queries time out or go too loose at 128 noise variables / 16-wide 2-head depth-8. Subjects are toy-to-small scale throughout; all baselines are the authors' own provers plus conceptual comparison to BlockCert and certified unlearning, which certify different objects. Novelty Classification: NEW PROBLEM (certifying the behavioral effect of a mechanistic edit over continuous regions), NEW FORMULATION (edits as sign-claim certificates with certified radii; removal as feature non-interference), NEW METHOD (hull-relaxed SMT encoding + CROWN extension with attack bracketing for edit certification), and NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING (naturally occurring intervention illusions). The building blocks — Z3, CROWN, PGD, bisection — are standard; the novelty lies in the claim being certified and the impossibility/separation theorems, not in new solver technology. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations and validation are unusually careful: M0 cross-validation of CROWN against the complete exact solver, per-claim attack bracketing, machine-checked witnesses for P2–P4, explicit float-gap slack analysis, and a Clopper–Pearson bound on illusion pocket size. Every reported number maps to a committed script with fixed seeds (Table IV); code "will be released publicly with the final version" — not yet available at review time, so reproducibility is promised, not demonstrated externally. Concerns: the certified-to-attack gap on the transformer is large (removal 0.0091 vs 0.03), so true radii may be ~3× larger and the prover's looseness is the binding constraint; the softmax-model "edit" is a position path-patch, not a circuit ablation, so the headline transformer result certifies a coarser intervention than the circuit story in the title; no external baselines exist because the certification target is new — this is legitimate but means claims cannot be benchmarked against alternatives. This is an arXiv preprint; peer review status not stated. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (built systems and ran certifications; theorems are in service of the empirical pipeline). Practical: Runs on commodity hardware (numpy + Z3, ~32–230 s per exact query at the frontier; CROWN on a 64-wide 2-layer model) — yes, but only on models of comparable scale. Efficient: Exact certification cost is exponential in internal branching and already at its limit at 48 noise variables; CROWN is cheaper but loose. Effective: Within the evaluated scope (decidable toy skills, continuous embedding balls), the certificates provably do what they claim; but this is a proxy — no evidence yet on real capabilities or discrete prompt robustness (a single token swap is ~324× the certified ball). Scalable: Not tested beyond tiny models; the authors state the frontier is exponential and claim (not demonstrate) that pretrained-SLM certification is the next step. Deliverable: a runnable pipeline of scripts plus reusable proof techniques (P1–P4 with machine-checked witnesses); no library, trained model, or released artifact as of this preprint. Strengths: (1) The impossibility result (P3) is the strongest part: a constructive, machine-checked proof that finite deterministic black-box testing — adaptive included — cannot certify removal, with a witness that is not adversarially contrived (3/160 naturally trained models exhibit it), converting a methodological worry into a theorem. (2) P4 gives the first exact, dose-linear account of the surgery-vs-steering collateral trade-off for a model class, turning previously empirical observations into proven structure. (3) Verification hygiene exceeds field norms: float-gap slack transfer, M0 prover cross-validation, per-claim attack bracketing that separates prover looseness from edit fragility, and explicit mapping of where exact certification stops (Table III). (4) The related-work taxonomy (description axis vs. edit axis vs. statistical axis) is precise and positions the contribution against Verifiable Transformers, BlockCert, and certified unlearning accurately rather than dismissively. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors confront limitations unusually directly (§VI): guarantees hold only on small standard-architecture networks; the exact frontier is exponential; CROWN radii are sound-but-not-exact with reported prover-looseness gaps; the softmax edit is a position path-patch, not a component circuit; the continuous radius is not discrete-prompt robustness (token-swap ≈ 324× the ball); and — stated prominently — the framework presupposes a decidable skill specification, which real harmful capabilities lack, making the whole work a proof of concept. This candor is a strong credibility positive; the limitations are not minimized. Analyst-Identified Gaps: Beyond the authors' own scope statements: (1) the transformer skills are contrived (quote-content detection, modular addition on disjoint positions), so even the "known-formula" stepping stone is far from any capability a practitioner would want to remove; (2) the certified radii in embedding space are tiny relative to semantically meaningful input changes — the paper quantifies this (324× gap) but does not explore whether the continuous-ball framing can be made meaningful for discrete NLP inputs; (3) the 9× scale gain over the exact frontier is obtained partly by switching to a weaker intervention (position knockout) on a different subject, so the frontier comparison spans both prover and edit changes; (4) no experiment on any pretrained model, even a small GPT-2-scale network, leaves the practical-relevance claim entirely untested; (5) the hull relaxation's "too loose" failures are characterized only by the size ladder — no analysis of why looseness explodes, which would guide scaling; (6) P4 is proven only for one hidden layer, and the deeper-network generalization is acknowledged open but no partial result or experiment probes it. Bottom Line: For researchers at the verification–interpretability boundary this is a genuinely new and honestly scoped opening — a new certification target, a solid impossibility theorem, and a mapped prover frontier — but practitioners seeking certificates for real unlearning or de-fanning edits should treat it as a direction-setting proof of concept, not an applicable tool, and no existing alternative covers the same ground.

PLCWorld: Benchmarking LLM-Generated PLC Programs in Closed-Loop Plant Simulation

Y Kim, Y Lee, H Seo, J Choi, W Lee · arxiv.org · specification to code with formal verifications - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper builds PLCWorld, a closed-loop benchmark that executes LLM-generated Structured Text (ST) PLC programs against a simulated plant, and evaluates six LLMs and four generation-and-verification frameworks on it. - Why it's important: Prior LLM-for-PLC evaluations check syntax, compilation, or formal properties of the code but never observe whether commands actually produce correct and safe plant behavior — yet a command issued is not a physical result in industrial control, so upstream acceptance is a misleading proxy. - How it does it: Each generated ST program runs cyclically in PLC scans inside a task-specific plant simulator that updates device/workpiece states and returns derived sensor feedback, with evaluation split into separate Task Success and Safety Violation judgments plus an Execution Gap metric measuring failure after upstream acceptance. - The good: Validation is unusually thorough for a benchmark paper — 4 practitioners reviewed all 100 task specs, 100 reference programs succeeded on all 473 task-condition pairs, all 542 targeted counterexample programs triggered their designated evaluator rules, and cross-runtime comparison against MATIEC/GCC agreed on Safety Violation in 1,199/1,199 cases. - The missing: The plant simulator is never validated against measurements from physical equipment, and the difficulty-by-dependency-scope design is observational — the Hard-task collapse is not isolated as a causal effect of dependency scope (the authors concede this). - Read it or not: Worth reading for researchers building code-generation evaluation environments or working on LLM-based industrial automation; skippable for general LLM-for-code readers who only need the headline that frontier models collapse from ~83% to ~25% Task Success on multi-job coordination tasks.
Why this rank
Scored using Empirical profile. Rigor (80) is exceptional for a benchmark paper — 542 targeted counterexample programs, alternative-solution acceptance tests, cross-runtime trace agreement (1,199/1,199 on Safety Violation), and bootstrap CIs — held back from 85+ only by the unvalidated plant simulator and benchmark/evaluation on the same frozen condition set. Novelty (78) reflects a genuinely new closed-loop evaluation formulation for LLM-generated control code, not just another code benchmark. Non-Obviousness (75) rests on the Execution Gap construct (32–93% of accepted programs fail at plant level), a sharp quantified reframing of the upstream-acceptance proxy problem. Completeness (78) and Resilience (78) benefit from unusually direct, non-defensive limitation disclosure. Practical Impact (80) is supported by a fully released environment, evaluator, and baselines that plausibly become the default yardstick for this domain. Show full analysis
Problem & Motivation: Engineers increasingly use LLMs to generate PLC control code (IEC 61131-3 Structured Text) for industrial equipment, but existing validation pipelines — syntax checks, compiler feedback, formal verification of code or plan models (LLM4PLC, Agents4PLC, AutoPLC, Spec2Control, SemaPLC) — never observe whether the generated program's commands actually coordinate a plant to task completion without safety breaches. The core gap is that issuing a command does not establish a physical state: a gripper may grasp slower than a fixed wait timer, so a program with correct command ordering still lifts an unsecured workpiece. Prior studies partially or entirely lack plant-outcome evaluation (the paper's Table 1 shows only partial coverage of workpiece handling and safety violations among five prior systems). Evaluation on physical equipment is possible but lacks common tasks, conditions, and criteria, making cross-method comparison impossible. Key Idea: Evaluate LLM-generated PLC programs in closed loop with a simulated plant — control outputs change device and workpiece states each scan, and sensor inputs are derived from the resulting plant state (not replayed traces) — so that task completion and safety are judged from physical behavior, with difficulty defined by control-dependency scope (within one basic function → between functions of one job → between jobs sharing resources). The accompanying analytical insight is the Execution Gap: the fraction of accepted (profile-passing) submissions that nonetheless fail the task or violate safety, quantifying how poorly upstream checks predict plant outcomes. Methodology: Three components. (1) Plant execution environment: each case couples an ST program, device configuration with I/O bindings, initial plant state, and execution conditions; the program runs cyclic scan-by-scan per the recurrence (C_{t+1}, Y_t) = Exec(C_t, X_t; Δt), P_{t+1} = F(P_t, Y_t, θ_t, Δt), X_{t+1} = H(P_{t+1}, θ_{t+1}), with timers advanced by the scan interval. The plant models device response times, acquisition/holding/handover transitions, and occupancy/clearance geometry — explicitly not contact forces, friction, or multi-body dynamics. (2) Benchmark: 100 synthetic tasks (50 Motion Control, 50 Material Handling) grounded in control relations abstracted from 2,201 PLC/automation project files plus I/O lists, drawings, and equipment manuals from real manufacturing equipment; 473 registered task-condition pairs vary initial state, device timing, and external inputs within published operating ranges. (3) Evaluation protocol: Task Success requires the goal plant state, all required events and precedence relations, and retention by the deadline; Safety Violation is monitored through the endpoint including post-completion claims; both are computed from plant records with explicit error-accounting rules (submission failures count as SR failures, non-executed cases excluded from SVR, infrastructure errors excluded). Four validation tracks: practitioner review, reference/alternative/counterexample programs, spec–evaluator alignment audits, and cross-runtime comparison. Critical design decisions: difficulty by dependency scope rather than device count (defensible and practitioner-endorsed, but acknowledged as non-causal); safety monitored past completion claims (well-justified by the premature-completion failure mode); evaluation on a frozen spec (v6)/evaluator (v5.2.6) with replay of earlier-version artifacts. Key Results: On pooled direct generation, GPT-5.5 achieves 82.70% Task Success on Easy cases, 84.09% on Medium, but 25.10% on Hard; the Hard collapse recurs across all models and all four frameworks. Pooled SR: Gemini 3.1 Pro 65.61%, GPT-5.5 62.58%, Gemini 3.8 Flash 60.82%, Claude Sonnet 5 51.16%, Qwen3.5-Plus 37.63%, GPT-4o 6.77%. Completion and safety diverge: on Hard Material Handling, Gemini 3.1 Pro beats GPT-5.5 on SR (35.25% vs. 27.87%) but has higher SVR (51.95% vs. 32.24%). All four adapted verification frameworks (LLM4PLC, Agents4PLC, AutoPLC, SemaPLC, GPT-5.5 backbone) show no consistent plant-level gain over matched direct generation — paired framework-minus-direct differences include zero for all four against the matched run — while costing more (SemaPLC: median 18 calls and 523.9k tokens per task vs. 1 call and 11.5k for direct GPT-5.5). Execution Gap ranges from 32.10% (Gemini 3.8 Flash) to 92.75% (GPT-4o) among direct models; across frameworks, 16.7–19.3% of plant-entering cases show observed violations even after internal verification. Failure analysis over 4,339 adverse cases: completion timing failures dominate (73.0%), followed by completion retention (36.7%) and actuation-constraint violations (24.7%). Frameworks were tested on all 100 tasks; efficiency on an 18-task subset. Baselines are current (2024–2026 models) and the framework comparisons use each method's configured budget under authors' adaptations. Novelty Classification: NEW DATASET/BENCHMARK and NEW SYSTEM/TOOL, with a NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING (the Execution Gap and the Hard-task dependency-scope collapse). The genuinely novel element is the closed-loop plant-execution coupling of ST scan-cycle semantics with state-derived sensor feedback under registered operating conditions, plus the separation of completion, safety, and upstream acceptance as first-class metrics. The individual ingredients — scan-cycle simulation, IEC 61131-3 runtimes (MATIEC, S7-PLCSIM), task-cluster bootstrap evaluation, LLM code-generation pipelines — are standard; the abstraction of industrial control relations into synthetic task families and the validation methodology are competent applications of known simulation-V&V practice (citing Sargent 2013) to a new setting. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablation-style validation is strong: reference programs (100), alternative implementations (72 programs over 67 tasks, 378 executions), 542 targeted counterexamples with per-rule detection checks, a bidirectional spec–evaluator semantic audit, and cross-runtime comparison against MATIEC/GCC (trace agreement 1,162/1,199; Task Success 1,195/1,199; Safety Violation 1,199/1,199, with all four Task Success discrepancies traced to one program double-calling a TON instance per scan) and S7-PLCSIM Advanced (one corrected TON scan-boundary discrepancy). Statistics: 10,000-replicate task-cluster bootstrap CIs on pooled and paired SR, three generation repetitions per direct model, seeds documented; the authors explicitly note intervals are pointwise and unadjusted for multiple comparisons, and that SR comparisons across difficulty groups are between-task-groups, not causal isolations. Code, environment, tasks, evaluator, and baselines are publicly released at https://yunji0516.github.io/PLCWorld/; confidential industrial source materials are excluded. Methodological caveats: the benchmark and its frozen conditions are used for both construction validation and evaluation; framework adaptations are the authors' reconstructions (Agents4PLC was rebuilt from the paper because the release lacked orchestration); inference compute is not matched across models; one model (Qwen3.5-Plus) ran via OpenRouter at concurrency 8 while others used Batch APIs. Evaluator and reference programs are withheld from models, and PLCWorld content was excluded from AutoPLC's retrieval pool — good hygiene against contamination. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (a built environment plus controlled experiments). - Practical: Runs as software on commodity hardware (scan-cycle simulation of task-specific abstractions; only the optional Siemens cross-check needs S7-PLCSIM Advanced), so yes for any lab with API access to the evaluated models. - Efficient: Plant evaluation itself is cheap; the cost driver is generation — frameworks consume 3–45× the tokens of direct generation (SemaPLC 523.9k vs. 11.5k median tokens/task) for no consistent gain. - Effective: Within its scope, the evidence directly supports the thesis that upstream checks poorly predict plant outcomes (Execution Gaps of 32–93%), but effectiveness as a stand-in for real commissioning is unproven since plant models were never validated against physical measurements. - Scalable: Only claimed implicitly — the 100-task/473-condition scale is fixed by construction; scaling to broader industrial settings is limited by source-material coverage and manual task construction, which the paper does not test. Delivers a real software artifact: environment, benchmark, evaluator, submission interface, and baseline implementations on a public project site. Strengths: (1) The Execution Gap construct — measuring failure and violation rates conditional on passing a common upstream check, on the same submitted programs — is a sharp, reusable analytical instrument that turns the paper's motivation into a quantified result (32–93% gaps). (2) Validation depth is well beyond benchmark norms: adversarial counterexample coverage of evaluator rules (542 programs, all activating their designated rules), alternative-solution acceptance testing, and two-runtime ST semantics comparison with a diagnosed, mechanistically explained discrepancy. (3) The dependency-scope difficulty axis captures a control-engineering dimension (inter-function and inter-job coordination) that code length or device count miss, and practitioners largely endorsed it (3 of 4 fully; 1 of 4 after clarification). (4) Honest error accounting and statistics: infrastructure errors excluded and reported, SR/SVR denominators made explicit, bootstrap CIs with documented seeds, and explicit disclaimers that pooled signature percentages are descriptive. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state: cross-runtime comparisons cover only selected constructs and programs with residual differences; plant responses are not validated against measurements from physical equipment; limited source coverage constrains generalization and confidentiality prevents independent inspection of the industrial grounding; evaluation covers only specified requirements under registered conditions, leaving unmodeled hazards out of scope; Execution Gap is conditional on the authors' own submission-profile check; framework comparisons reflect their adaptations under method-specific budgets; and difficulty-group comparisons do not isolate the effect of dependency scope. They also frankly report that MATIEC rejects 31/100 reference programs due to conversion/type-typing incompatibilities, handling this by restricting cross-runtime comparison to the mutually accepted subset. This is direct, non-defensive confrontation of limitations — a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: (1) No physical-hardware validation anywhere — the entire safety story rests on an unvalidated plant abstraction, so "Safety Violation" should be read as "simulator-rule breach," a caveat the ethics statement makes but the headline metrics can blur. (2) Task construction is manual and grounded in one confidential archive; nothing shows the requirement-family distribution (Figure 4) generalizes, and independent researchers cannot audit the grounding. (3) The benchmark is developed and evaluated on the same frozen condition set — there is no held-out condition robustness test (the authors note this in Appendix G.5 but it is easy to miss). (4) Framework comparisons fix a single backbone (GPT-5.5) and one run per task per framework, while the direct baseline pools three repetitions; the authors acknowledge framework rerun variability is not captured in CIs. (5) Only single-turn, no-feedback direct generation is compared — an agent loop with plant-execution feedback would presumably change the Hard-task numbers, and its omission leaves the benchmark's most interesting regime (interactive repair) untested. (6) GPT-4o's 6.77% pooled SR is so extreme it may partly reflect spec-prompt incompatibility rather than plant capability; no diagnosis of GPT-4o's failure mode is offered. Bottom Line: For anyone building or evaluating LLM-based PLC/industrial code generation, PLCWorld is now the credible default yardstick — its closed-loop execution, safety separation, and validation rigor expose weaknesses that code-level verification papers obscure — but its conclusions are simulator-relative until the plant models are validated against physical equipment, so treat the absolute numbers as benchmark-internal.

#11 — Highly Innovative (77)

Learning Transferable Representations from Operating System Entities via Provenance Graph Distillation

T Bilot, X Han, T Pasquier · tfjmp.org · 10 new citations to your articles
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces SPIDER, a 5.2M-parameter text-only transformer encoder for OS entities (files, processes, sockets) that is trained by distilling behavioral knowledge from a graph-aware teacher operating on provenance graphs, so that a single pretrained checkpoint produces behavior-aware entity embeddings at inference from raw labels alone with no graph access. - Why it's important: Provenance-based endpoint intrusion detectors currently learn entity embeddings from scratch per dataset and require expensive graph traversal at inference, which is infeasible at enterprise scale; a reusable, deployable encoder removes this bottleneck and, per the paper's results, improves detection across detectors and operating systems for free. - How it does it: A teacher combines edge-type-conditioned graph attention over sampled neighborhoods ("who an entity interacts with") with multi-hot behavioral signatures of direction/event-type/semantic-class triplets ("how it interacts"), trained with supervised contrastive loss; an EMA-distilled transformer student matches the teacher's projections from tokenized text alone using a scaled-cosine-error distillation loss. - The good: The controlled ablation isolating graph distillation is convincing: a teacher-free student with the same tokenizer, semantic classes, and contrastive loss reaches only 0.62 avg AP versus SPIDER's 0.82 across five benchmarks, showing graph-contextualized targets cannot be recovered from text and semantic supervision alone. - The missing: Evaluation rests on the DARPA TC (E3/E5) and OpTC corpora, which have known weaknesses (small attack counts — e.g., 1–3 attacks per dataset, 34–749 attack nodes — synthetic/curated background traffic, and community-acknowledged tuning hazards); no independent non-DARPA deployment evaluation is provided, and the pretraining corpus is author-collected and not publicly characterized in detail. - Read it or not: Read it if you work on provenance-based detection, endpoint security ML, or graph-to-text distillation — it is a well-executed, well-ablated piece with a released artifact; skip it if you need evidence beyond DARPA benchmarks to believe the enterprise-scale story.
