Problem & Motivation: Endpoint intrusion detection systems built on provenance graphs (nodes = OS entities, edges = system-call events) must embed entities to flag anomalous interactions. Prior detectors (KAIROS, FLASH, ORTHRUS, VELOX) train node embeddings from scratch per dataset using generic text encoders (Word2Vec, feature hashing), which has two costs: (1) embeddings capture only lexical identity, missing behavioral regularities of OS entities (system binaries, config files, common services) that recur across executions and environments; and (2) structure-aware inference requires graph traversal at detection time, which industrial practitioners (Dong et al., CCS'23) report is incompatible with the ≤160 MB memory budget and real-time constraints of endpoint deployment. The paper targets security teams deploying provenance-based EDR who need behavior-informed entity representations computable in a single forward pass on commodity endpoints. Key Idea: The core insight is that OS entity behavior is a stable function of identity that can be learned offline from provenance graph neighborhoods and then approximated at inference from entity text alone — i.e., cross-modal distillation (graph → text) converts a structure-dependent representation problem into a text-only inference problem. The teacher's targets are deliberately structured by semantic classes (e.g., {PROC, nginx} → webserver, {SOCK, 22} → ssh_socket) so that the student can generalize across hosts, operating systems, and organizations rather than memorize deployment-specific neighborhoods. Methodology: SPIDER is a teacher-student knowledge distillation pipeline. (1) Tokenization: a two-phase, domain-specific tokenizer maps entity labels to tokens (path components like [/USR][/LIB], well-known ports like [PORT_SSH], collapsed [HASH]/[GUID]/[USER] tokens, type prefixes [PROC]/[FILE]/[SOCK]), followed by a domain-trained BPE; this is a deliberate anti-overfitting design (IPs anonymized during pretraining, reintroduced only during continued pretraining on target data). (2) Teacher: for each entity, a sampled, edge-type-stratified one-hop neighborhood (noisy hub edges like /proc filtered) is encoded by one graph-attention layer with learnable edge-type embeddings, over node features from an EMA copy of the student (λ=0.999); this graph embedding is L2-normalized, concatenated with an L2-normalized multi-hot behavioral signature over (direction, event type, semantic class) triplets (532 unique triplets in the corpus), and projected via an MLP. (3) Training objective: L = L_con + L_dis — a SupCon loss (temperature-structured, P×K batch sampling, e.g., 512 classes × 4 entities) pulling same-semantic-class entities together, plus a scaled-cosine-error distillation loss aligning the student's projection to the stop-gradient teacher projection. (4) Deployment: only the student remains; embeddings can be cached, and scoring reduces to hash lookups plus a detector head. Critical design decisions: edge-type-conditioned attention (justified — R-GCN matches at 0.82 avg AP while GraphSAGE/GIN drop to 0.74/0.72); supervised contrastive over curated semantic classes (justified — replacing SupCon with cross-entropy costs 0.20 avg AP); SCE over MSE distillation (justified — MSE degrades several datasets). The framework is unsupervised with respect to anomalies (no attack labels at pretraining). Key Results: Pretraining used a 42.3M-entity corpus (287.3M edges) spanning Linux, FreeBSD, Windows, and Android, disjoint from all evaluation data. (1) Drop-in detection: replacing the native text encoders of four detectors (VELOX, ORTHRUS, FLASH, KAIROS) on five benchmarks (CADETS-E3, THEIA-E3/E5, CLEARSCOPE-E5 (Android), OpTC (Windows)) matches or exceeds native featurization on 19/20 detector–dataset pairs frozen, with fine-tuning improving further on 17/20; e.g., VELOX on OpTC goes from 0.08 to 0.36 (frozen) / 0.56 (fine-tuned) AP, and FLASH on OpTC from 0.00 to 1.00 (frozen). (2) Encoder comparison: against 12 baselines pretrained on the same corpus and evaluated via VELOX frozen embeddings, SPIDER achieves the best average AP (0.82 vs. 0.80 for GPT-2 1.5B — a ~290× parameter reduction — 0.76 for GraphMAE, 0.53 for Word2Vec/FastText) and is the only encoder strong across all four OSes. (3) Efficiency: 35 ms per 10k-entity batch on GPU, ~2 ms/entity on CPU, 28–160 MB memory (vs. ~1.1–3.0 GB for transductive Word2Vec/FastText and ~2.9–8.6 GB fp16 for LLMs). (4) Robustness: leave-one-OS-out pretraining costs only 0.01 avg AP; unseen entities degrade gracefully (0.89 → 0.80 avg AP common → unseen); renaming and mimicry attacks (Goyal et al. protocol, 0–5,000 injected edges) fail to suppress detection; Wilcoxon tests over 10 seeds show p ≤ 0.004 with large effect sizes vs. Word2Vec. Baselines are current and represent the strongest recent detectors (S&P'24/USENIX Sec'24–'25 systems) and the community-standard evaluation framework (PIDSMaker). Headline numbers carry high variance on some cells (e.g., SPIDER 0.36±0.32 on OpTC via VELOX), which the authors attribute to extreme class imbalance — 7–75 attack nodes per dataset except OpTC. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD and NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING: the genuinely novel contribution is the setting and demonstration — pretrained, transferable, graph-distilled behavioral priors for OS entities that transfer across graphs, operating systems, and organizations — rather than the building blocks themselves (EMA teacher, SupCon, SCE distillation, graph attention are all standard). The paper is candid about this in its related-work section, positioning the contribution against GLNN/NOSMOG/GRAD as a difference of setting (open-vocabulary inductive student, behavior-prior targets, no task labels) rather than algorithmic novelty; an adapted GLNN baseline trails by 0.14–0.17 avg AP, supporting that the setting-specific design matters. Rigor & Reproducibility: Strong. Ablations cover every major component (tokenizer, both losses, both teacher channels, teacher GNN architecture) plus teacher-free controls; hyperparameter sensitivity is reported; 10-seed runs with standard deviations and paired Wilcoxon tests with effect sizes are provided; hyperparameter tuning uses a pretraining-internal self-consistency criterion (k-NN class accuracy) explicitly designed to avoid peeking at downstream detection performance. The pretraining corpus is disjoint from evaluation data (no shared hosts, organizations, or time periods), and leave-one-OS-out and frequency-stratified evaluations directly probe the transfer claim. Code is released at https://github.com/ubc-provenance/PIDSMaker/tree/spider, integrated into the PIDSMaker framework; a pretrained checkpoint is released. Concerns: (a) all detection evaluation is on DARPA TC/OpTC benchmarks, which are the community standard but have been criticized (including by these authors' own prior VELOX work) for fragility to tuning and protocol choices — the paper mitigates this by following the established PIDSMaker protocol; (b) the pretraining corpus is author-collected and its construction ("thousands of commands" in monitored environments) is not externally verifiable; (c) several Table 2 cells have very large standard deviations (±0.32, ±0.30), so per-cell claims in the high-variance regime should be read cautiously; (d) FLASH at 0.00–0.10 AP with native encoders on TH-E5/OpTC suggests some baseline configurations are weak, though frozen SPIDER rescuing them to 0.06–1.00 still supports the contribution. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL (with a SYSTEMS artifact — a released pretrained model and framework integration). Practical: Yes — 5.2M parameters, single forward pass, CPU-only operation demonstrated (~2 ms/entity), explicitly designed for endpoint deployment. Efficient: 28–160 MB memory within the industrial ≤160 MB endpoint budget, roughly 290× smaller than the competitive GPT-2 baseline and two orders of magnitude lighter than LLMs; training takes ~2 GPU-hours on A100. Effective: The evidence shows improved AP on the attacked-node benchmark suites versus strong baselines, which is the field's standard proxy; real-world false-positive burden on production fleets is not measured. Scalable: Inference cost is per-entity and cacheable, so 10×–100× host scaling is architecturally plausible, but the paper tests single-dataset benchmarks up to 3.8M nodes and does not evaluate fleet-scale (multi-host) deployment; the enterprise-scale claim rests on the cost analysis, not a deployment experiment. Delivers a software artifact: pretrained checkpoint (5.2M params) and code within the open-source PIDSMaker framework. Strengths: - The controlled graph-distillation experiment (teacher-free SupCon student at 0.62 vs. 0.82 avg AP) cleanly establishes that the claimed value comes from graph context and not from the domain tokenizer or semantic-class supervision alone — this is the paper's most credible piece of evidence and directly addresses the obvious confound. - The problem formulation is a genuine paradigm shift for the subfield: decoupling representation learning from the detection objective and making the encoder reusable across detectors, datasets, and OSes, with evaluation designed to test exactly that claim (frozen drop-in, leave-one-OS-out, unseen-entity strata). - Deployment realism is taken seriously throughout: the 160 MB industrial budget cited from practitioner literature, per-entity caching, adversarial evaluation under both renaming and mimicry threat models, and a defense-oriented analysis of why renaming fails against structure-aware downstream detectors. - The two-channel teacher (who + how) is a sensible, well-justified decomposition, and the ablation shows the channels are complementary (removing signatures hurts CD-E3 most: 0.84→0.38; removing graph embeddings hurts CS-E5/OpTC most). Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state that SPIDER is evaluated only as an entity encoder for intrusion detection, leaving transfer to forensics, alert triage, and malware classification open; they acknowledge that renaming attacks may succeed against applications consuming SPIDER embeddings directly (rather than through a graph-aware detector), that fine-tuning only mitigates rather than solves label-level mimicry, and that perfect behavioral mimicry remains open for all provenance-based detectors (citing Goyal et al., NDSS'23). They confront limitations directly and honestly, including an explicit adversarial threat-model analysis — a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - Evaluation relies entirely on DARPA TC/OpTC data, where attack node counts are tiny (e.g., 1 attack with 70 nodes in THEIA-E5; 3 attacks in CADETS-E3); the high-variance cells (±0.32) mean some per-dataset conclusions are fragile, and no non-DARPA or production telemetry validation exists. - The pretraining corpus is self-collected; its composition, diversity, and how well it represents enterprise traffic are unverifiable, and although the authors argue design choices limit spurious-correlation inheritance, the argument is indirect (transfer results) rather than a direct measurement of correlation leakage. - The semantic-class taxonomy (a few hundred curated prefix entries) is human-curated; its sensitivity to curation quality, coverage gaps on unfamiliar software ecosystems (e.g., industrial control systems, macOS), and maintenance cost are not analyzed — unseen or exotic entity classes fall back on generic tokens, and only frequency-stratified AP, not class-coverage stress tests, are reported. - The claim of being detector-agnostic is tested on four detectors that, per Table 10, share a similar encode/decode architecture family and come from an overlapping author community (VELOX and ORTHRUS share authors with this paper); a genuinely independent third-party detector would strengthen the drop-in claim. - Fine-tuning reintroduces raw IP octets and dataset-specific entities, which partially re-couples the encoder to the deployment environment; the paper does not quantify how much of the fine-tuned gain comes from such re-coupling versus genuine prior adaptation. Bottom Line: For anyone building or evaluating provenance-based detection, this is the strongest available demonstration that pretrained, transferable entity representations are practical on endpoints — the ablations, adversarial analysis, and released artifact clear the bar even though the evidence base is confined to DARPA benchmarks, and there is no comparable alternative covering the same ground.

AgentPersonaBench: Benchmarking Persona-Driven User Simulation

J Huang, Y Wang, H Shen, YD Lu, S Huang, M Oh… · arxiv.org · automated generated environments for agent testing - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces AgentPersonaBench (APB), a 2,460-task benchmark spanning 867 persona traits and four interaction surfaces (survey, chat, web, desktop app) that measures whether latent persona traits — never named in the task prompt — observably govern an agent's downstream actions, verified 78.5% by deterministic code predicates rather than self-reports. - Why it's important: Deployed agents (recommenders, synthetic survey respondents, user proxies in software testing) act on user profiles where a persona-flavored reply is worthless if the underlying trait (e.g., veganism, risk aversion) does not actually steer the concrete choice — and existing role-play and instruction-following benchmarks cannot detect this failure. - How it does it: Each task pins a single trait inside a complete synthetic persona drawn from a 1M-profile corpus, stages an identical everyday errand across four media of increasing realism, never names the trait or announces the test, and scores adherence from observable artifacts (option IDs, DOM state, app-written files, or rubric-judged dialogue), with every task passing automated leak/discrimination audits plus human review. - The good: The two-stage verification pipeline is unusually thorough — 3,882 candidate tasks, 504 independent reviews, 1,957 tasks returned for revision, content-blind pass-rate enumeration to kill guessing shortcuts — and repeat-run studies (σ ≤ 2.0 points, Cohen's κ 0.46–0.75) show leaderboard gaps are not sampling noise. - The missing: Cross-surface fragility — the headline finding — is quantified only on a matched cohort of 140 scenarios across six OpenAI arms (all-four pass 37.9–64.3%), so the generality of the paper's central claim rests on a single vendor's models. - Read it or not: Worth reading for anyone building or auditing persona-conditioned agents or synthetic-user evaluation pipelines; skippable for researchers working on unrelated agent-capability questions, since the benchmark itself and its verification protocol are the contribution.

Problem & Motivation: Teams deploying language models as persona-driven user simulators — recommender agents acting on consumer tastes, synthetic cohorts replacing human survey respondents, agents standing in for users in software testing — currently have no way to measure whether a persona's latent traits actually determine what the agent does. Existing evaluation falls into two camps, both inadequate: conversational role-play benchmarks (PersonaChat, CharacterEval, Sotopia) score whether text "sounds like" a character, which a model can pass while putting meat in a vegan's shopping cart; and demographic-simulation studies score aggregate distributional alignment, where individual infidelities cancel out across cohorts. Instruction-following benchmarks are equally inapplicable because they explicitly declare the target behavior, inviting sycophantic compliance, whereas a real user profile is a description, not a command. The gap is a behavioral, individual-level, leak-free measurement of whether an unmentioned trait governs an observable decision. Key Idea: Test persona adherence latently: embed the pinned trait as one attribute among hundreds in a complete synthetic persona, stage an everyday errand whose outcome differs depending on whether the trait or its contrast value holds, never mention the trait or the evaluation, and derive a binary verdict from the agent's observable action artifacts rather than its words. The secondary trick is cross-surface pairing — the byte-identical persona and errand realized in four media (multiple-choice survey, pressure-scripted chat, live browser, desktop GUI) — which turns "does the trait survive a change of interface" into a measurable quantity. Methodology: The construction pipeline has three dependency-ordered stages. (1) Sample the persona: draw a target trait and contrast value from a schema of 6,347 traits across 14 families, then sample a complete persona conditioned on holding the target value from a 1M-profile corpus; the full profile (hundreds of background attributes) is rendered into the system prompt, identical across all four surfaces. (2) Build the environment: stage an everyday errand whose adherent and contrast choices diverge, with all trait cues stripped from the task presentation — survey uses randomized unlabelled options against a host-side answer key; chat applies scripted progressive off-persona pressure over multiple turns; web records UI selections and submitted decisions from live DOM state; app records application-written state files from a desktop GUI operated by visual interaction. (3) Design the checker: 3,033 of 3,865 checks (78.5%) are deterministic predicates over structured artifacts; the remaining 832 free-text-only checks use a single frozen LLM judge (gpt-5.6-luna) with fixed rubrics. Tasks are single-trait (binary held/violated) or multi-trait (score out of N, e.g., three coding-style habits checked as comment density, indentation unit, and try-block count). Every candidate task passes a two-stage admission gate: five automated audits (contract integrity, exhaustive leak detection, content-blind discrimination/position-bias enumeration, cross-surface parity, verifier stress-testing with positive/negative/malformed submissions) followed by independent human review of threshold semantics, trait independence, duplicate coverage, and distractor plausibility. Scoring uses full-pass (all checks) as the headline metric with normalized credit (s/K) as a secondary. No training objective is involved; this is pure evaluation infrastructure. Key Results: Across 20 model arms from eight providers on 2,460 tasks (502 survey, 565 chat, 707 web, 686 app), the top arms are gemini-3-8-flash at 84.7% overall full-pass, opus-5-5 at 82.9%, and gpt-6-astra at 82.1%; the weakest (deepseek-v4-flash) reaches 50.5%. Chat is the lowest-scoring surface for 15 of 20 arms because of scripted off-persona persuasion. Multi-attribute co-exposure degrades sharply for lighter models: gpt-6-luna falls from 74.4% (single) to 45.7% (multi), gpt-5-6-luna from 72.1% to 40.8%, deepseek-v4-flash from 64.8% to 36.4%, while gpt-6-astra holds at 80.6% versus 83.6%. On a matched cohort of 140 single-attribute scenarios (44 personas, six OpenAI arms) executed on all four surfaces, all-four pass rates span 37.9% (GPT-5.6 Luna) to 64.3% (GPT-6 Astra) despite 80.0–89.3% per-surface rates; app is the largest conditional-failure surface for every arm (e.g., 14.3% of Astra's survey passes fail on app, 30.8% for GPT-5.6 Luna). Median trait-category adherence drops steeply from survey to chat for everyday preferences (food 81.2%→49.3%, media 85.1%→49.0%, sports 66.7%→34.4%) while health, values, and risk stay above 71.4% everywhere. Cross-vendor overlap analysis on 1,086 shared chat/web tasks shows only 229 tasks passed and 12 failed unanimously, with 77.8% mixed — models have complementary failure sets. Cost per task ranges from $0.008 (gpt-6-luna) to $0.869 (gpt-6-astra). Repeat runs (three passes, two GPT-6 arms) show surface-level rate SD ≤ 2.0 points and task-level κ of 0.46 (chat) to 0.75 (web/app); the sol–luna gap of 8.9–20.8 points is stable with 95% intervals excluding zero on every surface. Novelty Classification: NEW DATASET/BENCHMARK with elements of NEW PROBLEM and NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING. The genuinely novel move is the latent-measurement protocol — scoring unmentioned traits from verified actions across a realism gradient of interaction surfaces — which is a real inversion of both role-play judging and explicit instruction-following evaluation; the component substrates (survey harnesses, scripted interlocutors, browser sandboxes, desktop GUI agents, LLM-judge rubrics, deterministic verifiers) are all standard techniques competently recombined, and the findings (cross-surface inconsistency, multi-trait degradation, complementary failure sets) are new measurements rather than new mechanisms. Rigor & Reproducibility: This is one of the more rigorously verified benchmarks the reviewer has seen at the task-admission level: content-blind discrimination audits enumerate the decision space to bound guessing floors (e.g., 12.5% for the vegan survey), verifiers are stress-tested against malformed submissions, cross-surface parity is asserted programmatically, and human review is non-author (14 reviewers, 504 reviews over 3,882 candidates, 1,957 returned for revision). Uncertainty is handled properly where it matters: 95% persona-cluster bootstrap intervals on paired surface differences, three-repeat stability runs with Cohen's κ, and an error-inclusive audit confirming rankings survive scoring incomplete attempts as zero. The judge-reliance concern is partially addressed — model separations persist on the 1,905–1,905-task rule-only subsets (e.g., GPT-6 pair gap of 17.7 points on rules-only vs 11.4 on judge-only). Code, environments, and task definitions are publicly released (https://github.com/MatrAIx-ai/AgentPersonaBench; CC-BY 4.0 for tasks, Apache 2.0 for harness). Methodological concerns that remain: the leaderboard is a single run per task per model; the frozen judge is itself an OpenAI model (gpt-5.6-luna), though rule-only analyses mitigate this; and the benchmark is developed and evaluated by the same group with no external replication yet. Note this is an arXiv preprint (arXiv:2610.04379), not peer-reviewed, and the work is funded by OpenAI, Anthropic, Microsoft, AWS, and Meta while evaluating those same vendors' models — a disclosed but real conflict-of-interest vector. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (a built benchmark evaluated by running 20 model arms through 45,000+ interactive episodes). - Practical: Runs via standard commercial APIs plus sandboxed local web/desktop environments; nothing requires exotic hardware, though the app surface needs a GUI-agent stack that text-only models simply cannot run (hence N/A cells). - Efficient: Per-task cost is reported and cheap ($0.008–$0.869 depending on model), making a full 2,460-task sweep roughly $20–$2,100 per arm — inexpensive relative to typical agentic benchmarks. - Effective: The evidence shows it measures a real construct that existing benchmarks miss (models complete interfaces successfully while violating personas), but it measures trait adherence under synthetic conditions, not fidelity to real human behavioral distributions — the authors concede this explicitly. - Scalable: Already tested at meaningful scale (20 arms, 45,000+ episodes); the constraint on 100× scaling is the human-review stage of task admission, whose cost the paper does not quantify. The work delivers a concrete software artifact: benchmark tasks, execution harnesses, verifiers, and evaluation code, publicly released under permissive licenses. Strengths: - The latent-conditioning discipline is the real contribution: trait never named, evaluation never announced, ground truth isolated from the agent's view, and guessing floors computed by enumerating the content-blind policy space — this closes the sycophancy loophole that afflicts instruction-following benchmarks applied to personas. - Verification depth exceeds community norms: 1,957 of 3,882 candidate tasks were rejected or returned for revision at least once, and the discrimination audit (content-blind pass-rate enumeration, position-bias checks) is a concrete, reusable defense against benchmark inflation of the kind Kapoor et al. and the AGREE-style critiques describe. - The matched-cohort design (same persona hash, same pinned trait, four surfaces) cleanly isolates interaction modality from persona-sampling variance, and the paired bootstrap analysis honestly reframes the "chat deficit" as growing with model weakness rather than uniform — a more interesting and more defensible finding than a blanket claim. - Judge-reliance is actively audited rather than waved away: separations are shown to survive on rule-only task subsets, and repeat-run κ quantifies exactly how much of the cross-vendor "complementarity" is dialogue stochasticity. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors are candid across Appendices E–H: (1) APB tests internal construct validity (does the agent obey the declared trait) and explicitly does not predict real human population distributions, which they frame as a prerequisite rather than a substitute; (2) single-trait isolation sacrifices the trait-intersection structure of real human behavior, partially patched by 1,172 multi-attribute tasks; (3) the leaderboard is single-run, mitigated by three-repeat audits on representative arms (σ ≤ 2.0); (4) 21.5% of checks depend on an LLM judge, mitigated by rule-only sensitivity analyses; (5) coverage across trait families is highly uneven (1,404 Interests tasks vs 6 Professional tasks), which the authors state plainly in §3.1.2. They also address impersonation, stereotype, PII, and sandbox-containment risks proactively. This directness is a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - The abstract's headline cross-surface numbers ("only 37.9–64.3% pass all four surfaces") derive entirely from six OpenAI arms on 140 scenarios; no non-OpenAI arm is included in the four-surface matched cohort, so the paper's most-quoted fragility claim generalizes from one vendor's architecture family. The authors do not flag this restriction in the abstract or discussion. - The judge (gpt-5.6-luna) is a model from a vendor whose arms are also being ranked first-tier; the rule-only subset analysis is reassuring but covers only 78.5% of checks, and no alternative-judge ablation (e.g., a Claude- or Gemini-based judge) is reported. - Tasks are LLM-generated synthetic personas and scenarios from the authors' own 1M-persona corpus (from their companion MatrAIx work); there is no validation that adherence scores on synthetic personas correlate with adherence when real users' profiles are used, nor any contamination analysis for the web/app environments. - The category-imbalance problem is acknowledged but not corrected: any "domain-level" aggregate is dominated by Interests (57.5% of tasks), so statements like "health and values are most stable" ride on very small n per category (22–135 scored trials per cell at minimum). - Funding by OpenAI, Anthropic, Microsoft, AWS, and Meta while publishing comparative rankings of those vendors' models is disclosed, but no firewall or third-party audit of the evaluation runs is described. Bottom Line: A practitioner building or auditing persona-conditioned agents should read this — the latent-measurement protocol and two-stage task verification are genuinely better than the field's current practice, and the cross-surface fragility finding is actionable — but treat the leaderboard as a well-engineered vendor-adjacent preprint snapshot rather than an independently replicated standard.

Every Batch Is Its Own Validation Set: Leave-One-Out Gradient Matching for Online Data Selection in LLM Fine-Tuning

H Chen, X Luo, M Zhao, L Tang, Z Xu, J Li, Y Wang… · arxiv.org · karypis - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces LOOM, an online batch-selection method for LLM supervised fine-tuning that replaces the batch gradient targeted by validation-free gradient matching with a leave-one-out target, and shows theoretically and empirically that this correction lets a selected subset out-train the full batch. - Why it's important: Online selection promises better fine-tuning at lower cost without held-out data, but every existing validation-free gradient matcher underperforms plain full-batch training; this paper explains why (a covariance-penalty bias) and removes the barrier, which also yields strong robustness to label noise (3.6% of selected examples corrupted at a 20% base rate). - How it does it: The core trick is dropping the diagonal of the per-example gradient Gram matrix: since the other B−1 candidates form an independent sample of the data distribution, leave-one-out targets give an unbiased estimate of the update's error against the population gradient, whose optimum weights examples by gradient signal-to-noise ratio. - The good: The diagnosis-to-fix chain is validated end to end — on real Llama-3.1-8B batches the leave-one-out update error is 0.61× full-batch at b=B/2, the ablation that restores the diagonal loses 2.79 points, and LOOM's gain over full-batch training tracks the theoretically predicted SNR-heterogeneity index across 7 backbones × 4 tasks (Spearman ρ = 0.86). - The missing: All headline experiments are LoRA fine-tuning on single-task SFT with training and evaluation drawn from the same distribution, at most 8B parameters; pretraining, RL post-training, and shifted-target regimes (where the authors concede validation-guided methods can win) are untested, and no public code repository URL is given. - Read it or not: Read it if you work on data selection, coresets, or training-time data curation — the diagnosis that in-sample objectives select their own noise applies to CRAIG, GradMatch, and offline coresets broadly, and the fix is essentially free; skip it if you only need a production recipe for large-scale pretraining, which is out of scope.

Problem & Motivation: Practitioners fine-tuning LLMs on supervised data face a data-quality problem at training time: each optimizer step draws a candidate batch and should update on only the useful part of it. Validation-free gradient-matching selectors (CRAIG, GradMatch, DivBS, CoLM) are attractive because they need no held-out data, yet they have a puzzling property the paper exposes: if a selected subset reproduced the batch gradient exactly, the update would equal the full-batch update that is already available, so the best such a selector can do is match training on everything. Empirically, the authors show every in-sample matcher lands between random selection and full-batch training. The unserved audience is anyone doing SFT without a clean validation set — noisy web-scale or crowdsourced instruction data included — who currently must choose between biased heuristic scores (loss, gradient norm) and validation-guided methods that require held-out data. Key Idea: The single core insight is that in-sample gradient matching is a biased risk estimator: because each example appears in the batch-mean target it is matched to, the diagonal of the gradient Gram matrix injects exactly the covariance penalty that makes training error optimistic (Efron 2004), which (i) credits each example with its own gradient noise and thus prefers the noisiest examples, and (ii) makes the uniform full batch the minimizer of the objective. Replacing the in-sample target c_j = (1/B)Σ_i K_ij with the leave-one-out mean c_j = (1/(B−1))Σ_{i≠j} K_ij yields an unbiased estimate of the update's error against the population gradient — the candidate batch becomes its own validation set — and the resulting optimum weights examples proportionally to per-example gradient SNR with shrinkage, beating the full batch exactly when SNR heterogeneity H_ρ = AM_b/H_MB > 1/ρ (Theorem 1). Methodology: The framework is quadratic optimization over selection weights in the metric of the Adam preconditioner, analyzed through (a) a heteroscedastic signal-plus-noise gradient model g_j = a_jμ + ξ_j, (b) Efron-style covariance-penalty theory, (c) restricted strong concavity for greedy guarantees, and (d) a descent argument for preconditioned SGD showing the matched risk R_t is the only selector-dependent term in the convergence bound (Theorem 2). LOOM's per-step pipeline: (1) one ordinary backward pass with hooks materializes per-example LoRA gradients (21M entries for Llama-3.1-8B, rank-8, ~0.7 GB per GPU); (2) gradients are scaled by (√v̂_{t−1}+ε)^{−1/2} using the previous step's AdamW second moment — fixed before the batch is drawn, as the unbiasedness analysis requires — and the Gram matrix K = GG̃^T is accumulated module by module; (3) leave-one-out targets c_j are computed and a greedy forward selection maximizes G(S) = c_S^T(K_SS + λI)^{−1}c_S with ridge λ = λ̄·tr(K)/B, choosing the candidate maximizing r_j²/(K_jj + λ − ||U_:,j||²) with an incremental Cholesky and NNLS re-fit (Proposition 3 gives a (1−e^{−γ}) bound via submodularity ratio, very loose in practice: greedy attains 99.99% of exhaustive optimum on B=14 batches); (4) weights are normalized to sum 1 and an unchanged AdamW step is taken on the weighted mean. Critical design decisions: the leave-one-out target (the paper's contribution, well justified by Prop. 1 and ablated at −2.79 points if reverted); the Adam metric rather than Euclidean (justified: −0.82 points without it, because Euclidean geometry concentrates in the top 8 layers); and nonnegative weights (justified: signed weights lower gradient error to 0.58 but lose 1.51 points by taking ascent steps on single examples that first-order risk does not penalize). Key Results: Main benchmark: 4 SFT tasks (MMLU aux-train→test, ScienceQA, GSM8K, CodeAlpaca-20k→HumanEval pass@1), 7 backbones from 1.5B to 8B, b=64 of B=128 candidates per step, 4 seeds with standard deviations reported. LOOM averages 56.5 on Llama-3.1-8B (+2.3 over full-batch Regular at 54.2) and 70.9 on Qwen2.5-7B (+2.4); it exceeds all in-sample matchers (CRAIG 53.4, GradMatch 53.7, DivBS 53.9, CoLM 54.2 on Llama) by 2.4+ points and the validation-guided GREATS (54.6) and OPUS (54.9) by 1.6–2.0 points without held-out data. Mechanism evidence: against a 4,096-example held-out reference gradient, LOOM's update error is 0.61× Regular at b=B/2 while in-sample matchers never beat 1.0; real batches show H_{1/2} of 2–6 (break-even is 2). Noise robustness: with 20% corrupted responses, LOOM selects 3.6% corrupted (vs. 43.6% for MaxLoss, 27.5% for GradMatch) and drops only 1.1 points at 20% corruption vs. 3.1 for Regular. Efficiency: 0.95× throughput of Regular (5.4% overhead), reaching Regular's final accuracy in 57% of steps and 60% of wall-clock; a forward-only LOOM-fast variant reaches 1.17× throughput with −0.65 points. Baselines include current methods (UDS 2025, GREATS NeurIPS 2024, CoLM ICLR 2025) and all gradient-based baselines share LOOM's per-example gradients and metric, isolating the target as the only difference — a well-controlled comparison. Gains are smallest on ScienceQA (most homogeneous batches), consistent with theory. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD (LOOM) plus NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING (the diagnosis that in-sample gradient matching is optimistic by a Gram-diagonal covariance penalty and is therefore capped at full-batch performance — this reframes why a whole family of published selectors underperforms). The genuinely novel element is applying classical cross-fitting/U-statistic machinery (Efron's covariance penalty, Hoeffding U-statistics, Stein shrinkage) to the target of gradient-matching selection; the surrounding apparatus — per-example LoRA gradients, Adam-metric Gram matrices, ghost inner products, greedy submodular selection — is a competent recombination of existing techniques (explicitly credited to GREATS, DP-training, and Elenberg et al.). Rigor & Reproducibility: Rigor is above average for this area. Ablations isolate each component (target, metric, weights, ridge, budget) with both task scores and a direct gradient-error measurement; the theory is numerically verified by exact computation on synthetic gradients (Table 3: in-sample bias slope 0.998 vs. theory 1.0, Monte Carlo risk ratios matching Theorem 1 within ~8%, estimated-vs-true SNR Spearman 0.944); four seeds with standard deviations are reported, and margins over the strongest baseline exceed the larger standard deviation on most tasks. The correlation between predicted heterogeneity and realized gain (ρ = 0.86 over 28 backbone-task pairs) is a strong theory-consistency check. Weaknesses: no code or model release URL is stated (only internal paths like code/theory_checks.py), no formal significance tests, and the single hyperparameter λ̄ was tuned on an MMLU held-out split with Qwen2.5-1.5B before being frozen — reasonable, but a residual tuning pathway. The greedy (1−e^{−γ}) guarantee is admitted to be vacuous (bound 0.07 vs. achieved 99.99%). Evaluations are zero-shot on standard public benchmarks; no benchmark-gaming concern, though training and evaluation distributions coincide in the main setting, which flatters a training-distribution-matching selector (the authors acknowledge this in the shifted-target experiment). Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (with a SYSTEMS artifact component — a working selection pipeline evaluated in training runs). Practical: Yes — runs on 8×A100 80GB with rank-8 LoRA, the same hardware class as ordinary SFT. Efficient: 5.4% step-time overhead (499 ms of a 9.2 s step, dominated by per-example gradient I/O), 41.4 GB peak per GPU; it is slower than UDS (1.21×) but ends 0.5 points higher, and LOOM-fast offers a 1.17×-throughput alternative. Effective: The evidence supports the stated claim on in-distribution SFT — it beats full-batch training, all in-sample matchers, and validation-guided methods on the tested tasks — but effectiveness under distribution shift is conceded to validation-guided methods in one appendix setting. Scalability: Tested across 7 backbones (1.5B–8B), candidate batches to B=256, full fine-tuning of a 1.5B model, and one OOD transfer setting; pretraining-scale and RL post-training are claimed as future work, not tested — the 10× question is open. Deliverable: the paper describes a complete algorithm (Algorithms 1–2) with implementation details sufficient for reimplementation, but no released library, weights, or dataset artifact. Strengths: (1) A clean, falsifiable diagnosis: identifying the Gram diagonal as the exact covariance-penalty term (proved in Prop. 1, verified at slope 0.998) explains — rather than merely observes — why a published family of methods cannot beat full-batch training, and the diagnosis generalizes to offline coresets and data attribution. (2) The fix costs nothing: dropping the diagonal is a one-line change to an existing objective, yet it flips the sign of the achievable gain and comes with an exact condition (Theorem 1) for when selection helps, plus a convergence bound in which the estimated quantity is precisely the optimizer's error term. (3) The evaluation isolates the mechanism: all gradient-based baselines share LOOM's gradients and metric, so the −2.79-point ablation from restoring the diagonal is direct causal evidence for the diagnosis, and the heterogeneity-gain correlation across 28 settings tests the theory's scope condition, not just its average prediction. (4) Honest extended settings: the appendix includes a protocol (GREATS-style mixed pool with small validation sets) where a competitor wins, and the authors quantify it. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors confront limitations directly and specifically, which is a credibility positive. They state: (i) under training-pool/target-task shift, a validation gradient carries information the batch cannot, and GREATS beats LOOM on TydiQA in that regime (with a LOOM+val combination offered as a remedy); (ii) leave-one-out targets favor majority sources in pooled data, fixed by per-source stratification; (iii) the i.i.d.-candidate, fixed-metric, finite-variance assumptions, with near-duplicates reintroducing optimism; (iv) per-example gradients are LoRA-cheap but need ghosts/sketches for full fine-tuning of large models; (v) SNR weights correlate mildly with response length, and online selection may shift behaviors task accuracy does not measure; (vi) only SFT up to 8B was tested — pretraining and RL post-training are untested. The ethics statement additionally flags the risk of down-weighting rare but legitimate content (minority dialects, uncommon viewpoints). Analyst-Identified Gaps: Beyond the acknowledged limitations, a critical reviewer would flag: (1) no public code or artifact release is mentioned anywhere, which is notable for a paper with a reproducibility checklist and ~11,000 A100-hours of experiments; (2) the main results train and evaluate on the same distribution (MMLU aux-train→MMLU test, etc.), which is precisely the regime where matching the training-population gradient is optimal — the favorable-to-LOOM framing is structural, and the one shifted-target test appears only in an appendix; (3) the improvement over UDS (a simpler, faster, forward-only method) is 0.7–0.8 points on average, is negative on two task-backbone cells in Table 1 (UDS leads on Qwen2.5-7B ScienceQA and Llama GSM8K), and UDS beats LOOM in-distribution on the GSM8K transfer table — so the practical margin over the best cheap alternative is real but thin; (4) comparisons omit some recent external-resource selectors (BLADE, Filter-then-Weight are cited but not run); (5) the gain-over-heterogeneity correlation (ρ = 0.86) is across backbone-task pairs that share evaluation settings and is observational, not an intervention; (6) no wall-clock-matched comparison at equal total compute budget including the throughput deficit (the 57%-of-steps result partially addresses this, but LOOM-fast's retained gain suggests the speed/quality frontier deserves a fuller treatment); (7) all stated gains are 1–2.4 points on 4-seed means of largely saturated benchmarks, where small prompt or parsing choices can matter — the seed-wise standard deviations mitigate but do not eliminate this concern. Bottom Line: This is the rare data-selection paper whose main value is a correct and portable diagnosis rather than a leaderboard entry — anyone building gradient-matching selectors, coresets, or influence-based selection should internalize the leave-one-out correction immediately, and the thin margins over UDS in deployment do not diminish that contribution.

Recursive World-Model Self-Repair in PDDL Domains: Verifier Coverage Is the Binding Constraint, and Under-Verified Loops Stall Rather Than Diverge

E Zueco, DS Lewis, H Yi · openreview.net · recursive self-improvement - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper builds and measures a recursive self-repair loop over a corrupted PDDL world model, and shows experimentally that verifier coverage — the fraction of domain conditions a repair can be scored against — is the binding constraint on how far the loop gets, with the under-verified failure mode being stagnation rather than divergence. - Why it's important: Embodied agents carry world models that are wrong on arrival, and the self-correction literature treats verification as binary (oracle present or absent), so practitioners building self-repairing agents have no guidance on what partial verification does to multi-round repair. - How it does it: The core move is making verifier coverage an engineerable knob c ∈ {0.2,...,1.0} crossed with repair depth k, evaluated with a pre-registered factorial design, an exact k=0 negative control, and a pre-declared falsifier for the divergence mechanism. - The good: The coverage × k interaction is +0.530 (95% CI [+0.447, +0.615]), replicates per domain (+0.56/+0.60/+0.43), and the k=0 control is exactly 0.0000, so the effect cannot be a leak — and the authors report that their own pre-registered mechanism was refuted by their own falsifier, which is unusual evidential honesty. - The missing: The proposer proposes exactly the edit family used to seed the corruption (condition toggles), so the loop's high-coverage success (0.900 at c=1.0) may overstate repairability; there is no comparison to existing action-model acquisition methods, and the LLM-proposer arm is 8 seeds and non-reproducible. - Read it or not: Read it if you design self-correcting or self-improving agent loops and need an empirical answer to how partial verification shapes multi-round repair; skip it if you need results about LLM-based repair, continuous dynamics, or realistic sensor partiality — the authors explicitly exclude all three.

Problem & Motivation: Agents that carry an explicit symbolic world model (operators induced from skills, LLM-written PDDL domains) hold models that are wrong on arrival, so they need a plan–execute–diagnose–edit–replan loop: recursive self-improvement in miniature. Whether such a loop is stable is a question about the verifier, and real verifiers are neither absent nor complete — a robot's checker scores only the conditions it can sense. Prior self-correction work (Huang et al., Self-Refine, Reflexion, repeated-sampling-with-checker) grades verification as a binary or as a property of a trained reward model; nobody, to the authors' knowledge, has parameterised verifier quality as a continuous coverage fraction crossed with repair depth in a symbolic repair loop. Key Idea: Treat verifier coverage c as a controlled experimental variable rather than a fixed property of the system: the verifier scores a candidate edit-set only against a fixed, stratified subset V of the true domain's conditions, and acceptance requires strict domination of (verifier score, evidence fit) over the current model. This one design — partial-but-present oracle plus monotone acceptance — is what makes the divergence-versus-stagnation question decidable, because strict domination makes visible-model error non-increasing by construction, forcing any failure into the invisible components of the model. Methodology: A ground-truth STRIPS domain M defines real dynamics; the agent holds a corrupted copy M (4 seeded condition toggles: 2 true conditions dropped, 2 false conditions added, identical across coverage levels within a seed). Each round: plan with pyperplan (greedy best-first over h_FF, 1200 expansions / 5 s cap), execute against M, collect failure evidence, generate candidate edit-sets from a deterministic search-based proposer (never reads M*), score candidates against the visible set V only, accept the best candidate iff its (verifier score, evidence fit) pair strictly dominates the incumbent's. Evidence fit is recomputed on recorded (state, action, successor) tuples without ground truth. The grid is 3 IPC domains (blocks, gripper, logistics) × 5 coverages × 20 seeds = 300 runs, 10 instances per domain (5 repair, 5 held out), with k nested so within-seed contrasts are exact. Analysis: seed-clustered bootstrap (10,000 resamples, seed as unit of independence); exactly two confirmatory tests pre-declared — the coverage × k interaction (Δ = success(k=4) − success(k=1), high band minus low band) and the divergence falsifier. Critical design decisions: (i) strict-domination acceptance — well-justified for bounding divergence, but it also largely manufactures the stagnation result; (ii) a deterministic proposer instead of an LLM — forced by a pre-declared throughput fallback that fired, and justified as isolating the verifier constraint from proposer noise, though it means findings say nothing about LLM repair; (iii) corruption fixed at n=4 via a hypothesis-blind rule (A8) after a single-error rule was found to force the interaction to zero by construction — a near-miss handled correctly. Key Results: The interaction is +0.530 [0.447, 0.615]; held-out success at k=4 rises monotonically in coverage from 0.1733 (c=0.2) through 0.4200 (c=0.6) to 0.900 (c=1.0), against a flat k=0 baseline of 0.0133 everywhere. Per-domain interactions: blocks +0.56, gripper +0.60, logistics +0.43, all excluding zero. The pre-declared divergence falsifier fired: 2 of 360 divergence events at c≤0.4 vs 3 of 360 at c≥0.8 (gap +0.0028 [−0.0056, +0.0111], covering zero), refuting the self-poisoning mechanism. Edit distance to M* falls from 4.00 to 1.1833 at high coverage but only to 3.0167 at low coverage. Invisible-residual error increases in 22 of 360 low-coverage transitions vs 3 of 360 high (gap +0.0528 [+0.0278, +0.0750]) but never accumulates (mean 2.6333 → 2.4083). Stall counter: 0.6062 of repair rounds propose-and-accept-nothing at c≤0.4 vs 0.1437 at c≥0.8 (gap +0.4625). An 8-seed LLM-proposer arm (blocks only) shows a directional interaction of +0.0625 [0.0000, 0.1875] and near-zero success throughout. A pre-committed wallclock-removed replication (A12) reproduces every headline quantity (interaction +0.5383). Scale is standard: 3 small classical IPC domains, 10 instances each — toy-to-standard, not stress-scale. Novelty Classification: NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING (verifier coverage as a continuous knob governing repair depth, with stagnation not divergence as the under-verified failure mode) plus a NEW METHOD/BENCHMARK apparatus (the coverage-stratified verifier inside a self-repair loop). The genuinely novel element is the factorial manipulation of partial observability at repair time crossed with repair depth, with an exact negative control; the loop itself is a competent combination of known pieces — pyperplan planning, VAL-style STRIPS adjudication, seeded corruption, greedy repair — and the proposer is deliberately trivial. Rigor & Reproducibility: This is among the more rigorous experimental protocols I have seen at this scale: design fixed before data (citable pre-declaration, commit 5121253), amendments A1–A12 logged with rationale, exactly two confirmatory tests declared, a pre-declared falsifier that fired against the authors' own mechanism, an exact k=0 leak control, three pre-declared rival mechanisms measured and eliminated, seed-clustered bootstrap with the correct independence unit, per-domain replication, an anonymised artifact bundle (https://anonymous.4open.science/r/rsi-art-nemo-59CF/) with a machine-checkable ledger row per printed number, an independent re-implementation agreeing on 24/24 headline checks, and a pre-committed budget replication. Concerns: (i) the proposer's candidate space (evidence-localised condition toggles) is exactly matched to the corruption family, so repairability at high coverage is partly built in; (ii) held-out means unseen instances only — corruption and repair are domain-level, so the 5 held-out instances share the domain's learned repair; (iii) divergence events are too rare (2 vs 3 in 360) to resolve small effects, which the authors concede; (iv) the wallclock component of the planner budget made held-out success host-dependent — disclosed and empirically bounded by the A12 replication, but still a defect in the primary numbers; (v) no comparison against FAMA-style action-model acquisition baselines. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (the paper runs a system and reports measurements; no theory claims). - Practical: Yes — the full 300-run grid completes in roughly 50 minutes on ordinary hardware with an open-source planner (pyperplan); nothing requires special compute. - Efficient: The loop itself is cheap (deterministic proposer, bounded planner calls); the LLM alternative was 31–99 s per call in the pilot, which is the expensive variant and was demoted. - Effective: The evidence shows the loop solves the stated problem only at high coverage (0.900 at c=1.0); at low coverage success stays at 0.1733, so the deployed claim is conditional on verifier breadth — which is the paper's point, but also its limit. - Scalable: Not tested beyond 3 small domains and 10 instances per domain; the authors claim no scalability, and correlated (sensor-like) blind spots — the realistic scaling direction — are explicitly flagged as untested and potentially outcome-changing. The work delivers a reproducible artifact bundle (apparatus, run records, ledgers, pre-declaration, analysis tree) but no packaged library or trained model; it stops at paper-plus-artifact form. Strengths: - The falsifier-driven design: pre-declaring a mechanism and reporting that it was refuted by the pre-committed test, while the interaction survived, is a model of how to separate effect from mechanism claims — most self-correction papers conflate the two. - The exact k=0 negative control (coverage main effect identically 0.0000 before any repair) is a cheap, decisive leak detector that factorial agent evaluations rarely include. - The visible/invisible residual decomposition cleanly separates what the acceptance rule guarantees from what verification leaves unprotected, converting a vague "is self-repair safe" question into measurable quantities (0 vs 22 invisible-error increases per 360 transitions). - The actionable design rules are quantified and falsifiable: rounds pay +0.7383 at high coverage vs +0.2083 at low; the stall counter (no-accept rate) is a deployable, drift-detector-compatible monitoring signal that would be invisible to standard divergence monitoring. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state: results hold only on 3 classical IPC domains with discrete STRIPS semantics, one planner configuration, one corruption magnitude; no continuous dynamics, state uncertainty, or adversarial error; held-out means unseen instances with domain-level corruption/repair; coverage is uniform random, not the spatially correlated partiality of real sensors, under which local corruption could accumulate into the divergence not observed; the proposer is matched to the corruption family, so the finding isolates verification, not proposal; every primary number comes from a non-LLM proposer and the 8-seed LLM arm is underpowered and irreproducible at temperature 0; divergence events are too rare to resolve small effects; low-coverage success remains poor. They confront limitations directly and at length — a strong credibility positive; the one place they minimize is the strict-domination acceptance rule, whose role in producing stagnation is noted as "a property of the acceptance rule, not a result" but not pursued as a limitation of the design-rule generality. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - The strict-domination acceptance rule guarantees the visible component cannot degrade, so "stagnation, not divergence" is partly an artifact of the chosen acceptance policy; a threshold-based or LLM-judged acceptance rule could diverge, and the paper never runs an alternative acceptance rule to test whether R2 generalises beyond its own safety-by-construction harness. - No baseline from the action-model acquisition literature (FAMA, ARMS, LOCM) even on the full-observability cell, so there is no reference point for whether 0.900 at c=1.0, k=4 is good, bad, or trivial for this repair problem. - Domain-level repair with only 5 held-out instances per domain, 20 seeds, and 3 domains means the effective sample for the "does it generalise" question is tiny; CIs treat seeds as the unit but domains (n=3) are the coarser unit and are not resampled. - The corruption family (pure condition toggles, no corrupted preconditions of the planner's heuristic-relevant form, no structural damage) is the easiest possible error class; real LLM-written domains fail in ways (wrong typing, missing predicates, malformed effects) this loop's proposer cannot express. - The high no-plan rates (~27% of planner calls return no plan) are attributed to the corrupted model, but they interact with the strict-domination rule in an unexplored way: rounds where the model is unplannable may accept repairs on evidence-fit alone, and the paper does not decompose acceptance behaviour in those rounds. - The excluded full-parity LLM grid (dropped by a pre-committed contamination rule that was confounded with domain order, as the authors themselves note) represents a discarded ~300-run dataset whose within-domain analysis they say was flat or falling; publishing it descriptively would have cost nothing and materially informed the transfer question. Bottom Line: A practitioner building self-repairing agent loops gains a genuinely useful, unusually well-verified empirical result — buy verifier coverage before buying iterations, and instrument for stalls rather than corruption — but should treat the stagnation finding as a property of strict-domination acceptance in toggle-corrupted STRIPS domains, not yet as a law of under-verified self-repair; the obvious next paper (realistic sensor-correlated coverage, an expressive proposer, an unconstrained acceptance rule) is the one that will settle it.

Safety Must Survive Self - Improvement : Why Failures Persist and How Agents Recover

Y Zhang, J Wang, S Lyu, Y Ge, K Liang, Z Jin… · arxiv.org · recursive self-improvement - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper builds a controlled testbed of stateful authorization tasks with seeded event streams and independent effect traces, and uses matched interventions over recursive-self-improvement (RSI) loops to decompose why unsafe programs persist across agent generations and which controller decisions restore safety. - Why it's important: RSI systems (STOP, Darwin Gödel Machine, AlphaEvolve) inherit selected code across generations, so a program that passed yesterday's test suite can silently execute unauthorized actions after the environment changes — and detection alone does not end unsafe execution. - How it does it: The core move is separating three confounded decisions — what is evaluated, what is edited next, and what executes — via paired branches over the same archives, failed roots, and rejected candidate pools. - The good: The headline persistence mechanism is cleanly isolated: in 48 framework histories, historical archive scores retain the same 22 unsafe programs through iteration 100 even though every affected archive contains a correct alternative; score refresh fixes all 48 endpoints on the original suite (fully correct 7→48). - The missing: All evidence comes from author-constructed authorization tasks with assumed-correct validators and initially correct founders; the two persistence mechanisms are synthetic constructs fixed before the pilot, and no release of testbed code or data beyond a project page is stated. - Read it or not: Worth reading for researchers building self-improving agent loops or agent-safety benchmarks, because it converts a vague worry about "safety drift" into two named, causally isolated mechanisms (historical eligibility and keep-after-rejection) plus concrete controller rules; skip it if you only care about benchmark-style safety scoring.

Problem & Motivation: Recursive self-improvement loops let an LLM editor repeatedly revise executable agent components, and each selected revision becomes both the running program and the parent of the next revision. Prior agent-safety work (Agent-SafetyBench, ToolEmu, AgentDojo, SafeArena) scores whether risky actions occur, and misevolution studies document unsafe tool reuse and behavioral drift, but neither asks the operational question this paper targets: once a failure is observable, does the failed implementation stop running, and what determines whether the system recovers? Detecting a failure, having a correct repair in the archive, and deploying that repair are distinct outcomes — a correct final program says nothing about unauthorized effects during intervening generations. Key Idea: The key idea is a decision-theoretic decomposition of the RSI loop: safety depends on (1) eligibility for execution — revalidation against the current contract, since archived test passes are certificates about old conditions, not proofs; (2) the retention rule — what runs when all candidates are rejected (keep vs. fallback vs. pause); and (3) the editing source — whether the editor revises the failed incumbent or the initially correct founder. The paper's formalization of the keep rule (Equation 1: an empty eligible set returns the failed incumbent) is the crisp capture of why rejection alone does not end unsafe execution. Methodology: The testbed covers four stateful authorization families (session authorization, filesystem containment, tool approval, structured user consent), each with seeded event-stream generators spanning eight probe categories, split into public (eligibility/feedback), audit (rollback), and hidden (measurement) suites — 288 blocks, 20,736 stream assignments. The improvement loop fixes the LLM editor (Qwen3 Coder, Sonnet 4.5, GPT-5.6 Sol, plus Devstral 2 and GLM 4.7 Flash in recovery studies) while the selected program and archive evolve over 12 generations; the editor produces two children per generation under efficiency or maintenance objectives. Four matched-comparison studies follow: (a) 72 histories under a new authorization dependency (upstream delegation grants, resource classification) revealed at generation 4; (b) 48 OpenEvolve/DGM-derived histories where historical vs. current archive readouts rank the same stored programs, plus a score-refresh intervention; (c) 42 shared failed roots where only the editing source varies (42 × 6 generations × 12 conditions); (d) 288-block core trajectories measuring safety (no unauthorized effect via independent traces), full correctness (including completing permitted work), and founder-relative service-cost savings. Frameworks: evolutionary program search over executable code with a validation gate, archive selection, and retention rules; paired bootstrap CIs (10,000 resamples within model strata), exact paired tests, and Holm correction over 16 pre-declared contrasts. The independent-trace oracle (permission computed from environment state, effects recorded separately from program output) is a well-justified design decision that prevents blanket refusal from counting as repair; the pinning of upstream OpenEvolve (commit 411fb59) and DGM (commit a565fd2) components with AST-equality checks is another. Key Results: (1) Failure entry: the new dependency exposes unauthorized effects in 22 of 24 GPT checkpoints despite full initial validation, while all frozen founders remain fully correct; Sonnet checkpoints miss permitted work; Qwen stays correct. (2) Persistence via historical scores: historical readout retains the same 22 unsafe programs through iteration 100 (all GPT histories) though a correct repair exists in every affected archive; score refresh (matched 60-edit continuation) reduces unsafe selections from 22 to 0 on the original suite and raises full correctness from 7 to 48; on independently composed held-out streams, unsafe endpoints drop 25→3 and full correctness rises 6→43 (paired exact p = 2.98×10⁻⁶). A real Casbin policy-engine task replicates persistence with Sonnet (12 vs. 0 unsafe endpoints). (3) Persistence after rejection: under keep, 14 of 432 full-coverage candidate pools retain unsafe incumbents (from three Qwen lineages); founder fallback is 100% safe in the same pools. (4) Editing source: from 42 shared failed roots, current-code editing leaves 14 unsafe endpoints after six generations vs. 1 under founder editing (−31.0 pp, 95% CI 23.8–38.1, p = 0.000488); the effect is editor-dependent (GPT repairs nearly everything; the gap is largest for Qwen). (5) Utility: validated rollback and full validation achieve fully correct endpoints in all 288 blocks while retaining mean founder-relative deployment savings of 43.5%, 43.4%, and 42.8% (rollback, full validation, validation+rollback). (6) A native τ/τ²-bench dialogue transfer shows no systematic authorization failure increase — an honest negative. The counter-intuitive finding is that the same repair is available but unselected: repair availability alone does not ensure deployment (123 of 132 unsafe historical selections had a passing proposal available). Novelty Classification: NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING + NEW DATASET/BENCHMARK. The genuinely novel contribution is the causal decomposition — showing via matched interventions that stale archive eligibility and keep-after-rejection (not editor incapacity) sustain unsafe execution, and that editing source causally affects recovery from identical failures. The interventions themselves (revalidate before deploy, fallback to a known-good version, pause) are standard fault-tolerance/regression-testing practice applied to RSI archives; the four-family authorization testbed with independent effect traces is a new instrument, not a new algorithm. Rigor & Reproducibility: Rigor is unusually high for this area. Ablations and controls are pervasive: frozen-found controls, paired same-archive readouts, fixed 432-pool subset analysis with exact inclusion–exclusion probabilities, prompt-vs-ranking and tie-rule factors, price ablations, old-certificate replay, and an all-history-invalid control. Multiple editors (5 LLMs), multiple seeds (12 per cell in the core study), 10,000-resample stratified bootstrap CIs, exact paired tests, and Holm correction over a pre-declared 16-contrast family are reported, with exploratory contrasts separated. The pilots were run on 4 seeds and expanded to 12 after inspection — the paper flags this itself. No error bars are missing where claims are statistical. A code or dataset release URL is not stated (only a project page, RSI-Safety.github.io); this is the main reproducibility gap. Methodological concerns: the tasks, dependencies, and reveal schedule are author-designed and fixed before the pilot (Goodhart risk is mitigated but the ecology is narrow); the 14 unsafe keep-pools come from three Qwen lineages, so repeated mechanistic observations inflate apparent prevalence; savings exclude validation expenditure, which the paper handles honestly via a volume-sensitivity analysis (Eq. 2) showing validation outweighs savings at one workload batch per revision. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (a built testbed and controller study, not a shipped system). Practical: Yes — tasks run as restricted Python with commercial API access via Amazon Bedrock; no special hardware. Efficient: Interventions cost real validation compute (e.g., deployment validation raises probes from 439.0 to 540.5 per history, +23.1%), but repeated deployment amortizes it (total-cost ratio 0.628–0.648 at 100 batches per revision). Effective: The evidence shows the interventions solve the stated problem in these synthetic authorization tasks — fully correct endpoints with >43% savings — but only within test-coverage limits, which independent compositions expose (3/48 unsafe refresh endpoints persist). Scalable: Not tested; 12-generation histories, small task families, fixed editors; the authors state that larger deployments, longer histories, and jointly evolving editors are unexplored. Deliverable form: paper plus a project page; no code, dataset, or trained-model release is stated. Strengths: - The matched-comparison methodology is the paper's real contribution: holding the archive, proposals, and test outcomes fixed while varying one controller decision converts a correlational safety observation into a causal claim about selection and retention rules. - The independent effect-trace oracle (permission computed from environment state, effects recorded separately from program return values) cleanly prevents the standard failure mode where refusal or output suppression masks unauthorized actions. - The editing-source finding (founder vs. incumbent editing from identical failed roots, −31.0 pp) is non-obvious and useful: recovery depends on which implementation supplies context, not only on failure information. - Honest reporting: a negative native-dialogue transfer is included, residual post-refresh failures are reported rather than hidden, and the seed-expansion-after-pilot decision is disclosed. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state the setting is controlled authorization tasks with fixed editors, initially correct founders, and externally specified contracts; conclusions assume correct validators (validator implementation is not varied); larger deployments, longer histories, and jointly evolving editors remain open; service costs measure weighted operations, not model inference or latency; the native τ transfer "does not establish a systematic increase in authorization failures." This is direct, non-minimizing confrontation of scope — a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: (1) External validity beyond authorization caching: all four task families instantiate the same failure pattern (stale permission/consent reuse); whether editor-induced drift, memory tampering, or reward-hacking failures follow the same persistence mechanisms is untested. (2) The keep-after-rejection mechanism is heavily concentrated in Qwen3 Coder (345 of 346 post-gate unsafe states); the generality of persistence-after-rejection across frontier editors rests on few observations. (3) Correct validators are assumed, but in practice the validator is itself often an LLM or generated test suite — the paper's own score-refresh fix presupposes the expanded tests correctly capture the new contract. (4) No code or data release is stated, which limits independent verification of the pinned-component claims. (5) The two "mechanisms" have known analogues (stale regression-test oracles, failed-build deployment policies in CI/CD), so the finding's novelty is its instantiation in RSI loops, not the phenomenon; the paper does not engage with the software-engineering deployment-policy literature beyond one regression-testing citation. (6) The >43% savings headline is on the founder-relative redundant baseline; against single-check references, savings on correct endpoints are much smaller (median 16.6–25.8% in the framework cohorts), which the appendix reports but the abstract-level framing does not emphasize. Bottom Line: A rigorous, unusually well-controlled empirical study that gives anyone building self-improving agent systems two concrete, causally isolated failure-persistence mechanisms and cheap controller fixes (current-contract revalidation, validated fallback, founder-editing) — read it for the experimental design and the selection-rule insight, while treating the synthetic task ecology and missing artifact release as the price of admission.

Federated Targeted Maximum Likelihood Estimation

D Li, F Wang, K Gan · arxiv.org · Fei Wang, FAMIA, FIAHSI, FACMI - new articles
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces the first general federated algorithms for iterative targeted maximum likelihood estimation (TMLE) — FedTMLE-G, which aggregates local gradients to reproduce centralized targeting step-for-step, and FedTMLE-L, which averages locally fitted fluctuation parameters in a single exchange — together with communication, statistical-accuracy, disclosure, and personalized-retirement theory. - Why it's important: Hospitals, banks, and registries that cannot pool individual records currently cannot run TMLE, the standard machinery for efficient, doubly robust plug-in inference of causal and policy targets, on their combined evidence; this closes that gap for cross-silo collaborations. - How it does it: The core move is to federate the targeting step itself — the pooled fluctuation loss decomposes exactly across silos by sample-size weights — combined with a finite-precision protocol that transmits gradient changes (differentially Elias-gamma coded) and a description-length analysis of the accepted targeting history that controls data-dependent stopping without charging for every gradient query. - The good: The theory is unusually complete: Theorem 4.1 certifies a prescribed EIF residual within explicit round (R ≤ 1 + 64βΔ/(3δ²)) and bit (O(MdβΔ/δ²) leading-order) budgets, Corollary 4.1 shows finite communication suffices for √n-consistency and asymptotic normality, and Theorem 4.8 gives a nonconvex convergence bound for personalized retirement that cleanly separates averaging penalty from sampling variability. - The missing: All experiments are synthetic (n = 10,000, a 3-dimensional optimal-transport target, M up to 40 clients); there is no real multi-institution data, no empirical comparison against alternative federated causal estimators (e.g., Han, Shen and Zubizarreta 2023), no error bars or seed replication, and the statistical conditions in (18) are left unverified on any example. - Read it or not: Read it if you work on federated causal inference or targeted learning and need the definitive first formulation and its trade-offs; skip it if you want a deployable system or empirical evidence on real clinical data, which this deliberately does not provide.
