Problem & Motivation: Scientific and operational decisions increasingly require evidence pooled across institutions — hospitals assessing treatment effects, banks estimating credit risk — where privacy regulation, governance, and institutional boundaries forbid centralizing individual records. Cross-silo federated learning addresses computation over distributed data but delivers predictors, not statistically defensible estimates of a target parameter. TMLE delivers efficient, model-respecting, often doubly robust plug-in estimates, but in its general iterative form has remained a fully centralized procedure. Prior federated causal methods address nuisance estimation, transportability, or estimand-specific constructions (e.g., survival mediation) and do not federate the repeated, evolving fluctuation-fitting loop that defines standard TMLE. The gap: no general federated formulation of iterative TMLE existed for arbitrary targets, losses, and fluctuation families. Key Idea: The pooled empirical fluctuation loss and pooled EIF mean decompose exactly, in finite samples, as sample-size-weighted sums of local quantities (∇ℓ_k(0) = Σ_m (N_m/n)∇ℓ_{m,k}(0)), so targeting can be federated either by aggregating gradients (exactly reproducing the centralized trajectory) or by averaging locally solved fluctuation parameters (trading pooled fidelity for one-exchange autonomy). The second, subtler move is decoupling the cost of computing an estimator from the complexity of selecting it: the accepted targeting history (a short code of accepted fluctuation vectors) reconstructs the final density, so a prefix-free description-length bound on that history — not the full gradient transcript — controls the adaptivity penalty in the statistical guarantee. Methodology: The framework is semiparametric efficiency theory plus empirical nonconvex optimization. Stage 1: all silos share an initial density estimate p̂⁰ and, at each outer iteration, the loss L, efficient influence function D, and a targeted fluctuation submodel defined by ∇_εL(p_k(ε))|₀ = D(p_k)(o) (Definition 2.1); the target Ψ, loss, and fluctuation family stay abstract. Stage 2a (FedTMLE-G, Algorithm 2): the server broadcasts the submodel, silos return local gradient sums, and the server runs GD/SGD on the pooled submodel loss; in exact arithmetic this reproduces centralized targeting step-for-step under matched initialization, sampling, and stopping rules. Stage 2b (FedTMLE-L, Algorithm 3): each silo exactly minimizes its own fluctuation loss, the server averages the fitted ε̂ᵏₘ with weights α_m (uniform 1/M or sample-size N_m/n), and the average — which need not solve the pooled problem, and can cancel to zero — updates the shared density. Stage 2c (FedTMLE-LR, Algorithm 5): a client whose exact local fit is zero freezes its density and estimate (locally TMLE-stable, Δ_m(p) = 0) and retires. Stage 3: a finite-precision variant (Algorithm 4) rounds local gradients to a dyadic grid of spacing h tied to the EIF tolerance δ (δ/(8√d) < h ≤ δ/(4√d)), transmits only coordinatewise changes via signed Elias-gamma codes, and uses a 3-bit action protocol to distinguish inner stationarity from a certified origin EIF check. The communication analysis (Theorem 4.1) charges squared rounded gradients to the loss decrease Δ and gradient variation to the two Lipschitz constants (β for submodel smoothness, κ for EIF re-centering), yielding logarithmic dependence on κ/β. The statistical analysis (Theorem 4.2) applies Kraft/occupy-histories concentration to all valid decoded histories, giving an empirical-process penalty of order √(x_K/n)·‖D(p_K) − D(p⁰)‖_{L²} + 4G√d·x_K/(3n) with x_K = H_K log 2 + log(2d/ξ). The disclosure analysis (Theorems 4.3–4.4) models a corrupted server issuing adaptive queries under bounded transcript uncertainty η, proving a record-reconstruction minimax lower bound of order η^{1/s}T^{−1/(2s)} (via Chebyshev-polynomial moment cancellation and divided differences) and an attribute-recovery characterization through an optimal-recovery design modulus ω_T(η), showing reconstruction instability coexists with exact attribute recovery. The personalized analysis (Theorems 4.6–4.8) bounds the improvement forfeited by averaging through pairwise disagreement moments V²_k, V⁴_k and a sampling coefficient χ_k. Critical design decisions: (i) pooled batches must be drawn jointly, not silo-by-silo, to keep SGD pooled-uniform (justified explicitly); (ii) the stopping test uses the pooled EIF mean at a freshly reconstructed submodel origin (correct, since the derivative identity holds only at base points); (iii) averaging local minimizers is not claimed to minimize any pooled objective — the honest consequence, path divergence, is analyzed rather than hidden. Key Results: This is primarily a theory paper with illustrative synthetic experiments. Headline theoretical results: certified targeting accuracy r_K ≤ δ with R ≤ 1 + 64βΔ/(3δ²) rounds and B ≤ CMd[(1 + βΔ/δ²)log₂(4 + κ/β) + log₂(2 + G√d/δ)] bits; with δ_n = (a_n√n)⁻¹, R = O_P(na_n²) and B = O_P(Md·na_n²), and under conditions (18), √n(Ψ(p_K) − Ψ(p⁰)) ⇒ N(0, P⁰[D(p⁰)D(p⁰)ᵀ]). The averaging penalty bound (Theorem 4.8) scales as (2G₁ζ_n/3)√(χ_k V²_k) + (βζ_n/6)√(χ_k V⁴_k) + (β₄/18)V⁴_k, with χ_k differing by up to the arithmetic-to-harmonic mean ratio of active sample sizes between uniform and size weighting. Record reconstruction lower bound R^rec_T(η) ≥ (1/6s)min{ρ, (2sN_m(s−1)!η/(C_s√T))^{1/s}}. Experiments: n = 10,000 observations from anisotropic Gaussian or curved mixtures, an entropy-regularized optimal-transport target (d = 3, four fixed destinations), M ∈ {5, 10, 20, 40}, client size ratio ~5:1, random vs. spatially heterogeneous partitions. Findings: FedTMLE-L makes faster initial loss progress on the Gaussian mixture while FedTMLE-G leads early on the curved mixture; under a fixed 200-round budget FedTMLE-G has higher loss (multiple pooled queries per update) while its full-batch trajectory is invariant to repartitioning; uniform weighting degrades as M grows, especially with spatial heterogeneity; ordering by elapsed time differs from ordering by communication budget. Baselines are the two federated variants against each other — no external method is compared. Scale is small (toy), and all DPand distributions are synthetic. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD (first general federated formulation of iterative TMLE, for arbitrary target/loss/fluctuation family) with substantial NEW FORMULATION elements (the description-length separation of computation cost from selection complexity; the retirement-based personalization driven by local TMLE stability) and NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING (the reconstruction-vs-attribute-recovery asymmetry under bounded transcript uncertainty). The underlying primitives — gradient aggregation, differential quantization, Elias-gamma coding, federated averaging, Kraft/Chernoff concentration, Donoho-style optimal recovery — are standard; the genuine novelty lies in assembling them around the re-centering structure of TMLE, where Assumption 4.2 must control gradient changes across changing submodels, and in proving that the accepted-history code (not the full transcript) suffices for adaptive inference. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations: the paper decomposes its bit bound into inner-step, re-centering, and certificate contributions (Eqs. 13–14) and separates the two Lipschitz constants analytically, which serves the role of component-level ablation; empirical ablations vary partition type, client count, and budget type. Error bars, multiple seeds, and significance tests are not reported for the experiments; all plots are single trajectories. Probability statements in the theory carry explicit confidence (1 − ξ) and the constants (C = 256 in Theorem 4.1) are explicit. No code, data, or model release is mentioned. Methodological concerns: (i) experiments are entirely synthetic and defined by the authors; (ii) the statistical conditions (18) required for Corollary 4.1 — √n‖R₂(p_K, p⁰)‖ = o_P(1) and EIF convergence — are not verified on any concrete estimator or dataset, so the end-to-end efficiency claim remains conditional; (iii) exact local minimization is treated as an oracle, and the authors note a finite solver need not implement it; (iv) the communication analysis assumes public knowledge of β, a shared initial estimator, and reliable synchronous links with cryptographic/transport costs excluded; (v) the disclosure lower bound is worst-case over datasets and vacuous at η = 0, and no empirical attack or defense is evaluated. The theory is nonetheless internally rigorous: proofs are complete, self-contained, and careful about the gap between stationarity within a submodel and the targeting equation at the rebuilt submodel. Deployability: Profile: THEORETICAL with a small empirical illustration (the paper proves bounds and characterizations; the experiments illustrate trajectory behavior rather than validate deployment). - Sound: Assumptions are explicit (feasible smooth targeting, re-centering regularity, EIF envelope, covering-number complexity), proofs are complete, but Assumption 4.5's pre-sampled state family and the oracle exact-minimizer convention are restrictive. - General: The core communication bound holds for arbitrary silo heterogeneity and requires no gradient agreement; the statistical corollary additionally needs bounded β, G, κ/β, the conditions in (18), and fixed d; the personalized analysis requires a common law across silos, which the authors flag as a scope limit. - Tight: The bit bound is explicitly an upper bound on this protocol, not a lower bound for federated estimation; the record-reconstruction lower bound is sharp within its model (matching fixed-block affine upper bound for attributes) but vacuous at η = 0. - Implementable: Algorithms 2–5 are fully specified pseudocode with explicit rounding and coding rules, but no software artifact, library, or dataset is released; the work stops at paper form. Strengths: - Genuinely first contribution: federating the iterative targeting loop rather than a one-shot estimator, with an abstract interface (target, loss, fluctuation family) that covers the standard TMLE template. - The description-length argument (Theorem 4.2) is a genuinely new technical device in this literature: it controls data-dependent stopping and same-sample initialization through a prefix-free history code, replacing Donsker/sample-splitting conditions, and cleanly separates inner optimization cost from statistical selection cost. - The honest treatment of FedTMLE-L's failure modes — averaging does not solve the pooled problem, cancellation can stall targeting, stationarity and feasibility do not survive averaging — is analyzed rather than papered over, and the retirement mechanism converts cancellation into a certified per-client stopping rule. - The selective-disclosure analysis (Theorems 4.3–4.4) makes a non-obvious point with practical consequence: keeping data local is not privacy, and reconstruction instability does not imply attribute protection; the spectral modulus ω_T(η) explains exactly why. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state: the disclosure lower bound is an obstruction result, worst-case over datasets, silent about typical-case protection and about exact (η = 0) responses; equivalence to centralized computation offers no privacy protection; the personalized analysis assumes a common law across silos and does not establish that every client retires in finitely many rounds or that retained estimates are doubly robust; the efficiency corollary does not address regularity under local alternatives; conditions (18) refer to the estimator actually computed, and properties of an idealized exact trajectory do not establish them; the retirement analysis assumes exact local solves. These are confronted directly and precisely, which strengthens credibility. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - The statistical conditions (18) are never instantiated: no initial estimator (Super Learner, parametric nuisance fits) is shown to satisfy them, so the reader cannot judge whether the finite-communication asymptotic normality is achievable in practice. - No empirical comparison against existing federated causal estimators (Han et al. 2023; Tong et al. 2025) even as a reference point, and no real-world data despite the motivating hospitals/banks framing. - The finite-precision protocol requires a publicly known Lipschitz constant β for step sizing (ε_{t+1} = ε_t − ĝ_r/β), which is generally unknown and unestimated; sensitivity to a misspecified β is not studied. - Experiments measure loss and EIF residual but never the target estimate Ψ(p_k) itself — the actual estimand of interest — nor coverage of the Theorem 4.2 confidence bound, which is the paper's own inferential deliverable. - The disclosure model restricts queries to full-silo means with a bounded, distribution-free error budget; whether realistic adaptive attackers (state manipulation, participation games, which the authors mention) fall inside this model is untested, and no empirical leakage evaluation is run. - The communication bound's leading term O(MdβΔ/δ²) grows quadratically as δ tightens with n (δ_n = (a_n√n)⁻¹ gives R = O_P(na_n²)), which for any a_n growing with n may be prohibitive; the practical round counts at realistic n are not extrapolated. Bottom Line: This is the definitive first word on federated iterative TMLE — theoretically deep, unusually honest about its own failure modes, and essential reading for anyone building federated causal inference — but its practical case rests entirely on theory and synthetic plots, so practitioners awaiting real-hospital validation, released code, or verified efficiency conditions should treat it as a foundation to build on, not a tool to use.

Turbo Harness: Instance-Adaptive Harness Optimization

T Zhang, H Wang, K Xu, DN Metaxas · arxiv.org · long-horizon RL for agents - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces Turbo Harness, a framework that reuses the search archive from a completed global harness-optimization run — distilled into a playbook — to train a small RL-fine-tuned editor (Qwen3.5-9B with GRPO) that patches the globally optimized agent harness into an instance-specific harness for each test task. - Why it's important: Harness optimization is expensive, and existing methods (Meta-Harness, Harness-R1) discard instance-specific signal by deploying one global harness uniformly, leaving accuracy and compute headroom on tasks whose requirements differ (e.g., different repositories in SWE-bench-style evaluation). - How it does it: The core trick is recycling the outer-loop search "exhaust": successes and failures of discarded harness candidates are summarized into a conditional strategy playbook, and a GRPO-trained 9B editor learns to select and apply the right strategy as a single code patch to the global harness, conditioned on the test instance. - The good: A clean ablation shows neither RL nor the playbook alone beats the global harness (49.3–51.3% vs 50.7% on SWE-smith-MR), but their combination reaches 64.0% — and the RL-trained 9B editor matches a much larger Opus-4.6 editor (61.3%) that uses the playbook zero-shot. - The missing: Evaluation uses non-standard, self-constructed splits (a 150-issue SWE-bench Verified subset under a 40-step/$3 budget, a 50-issue SWE-smith-MR subset not held out by repository), the headline Harness-R1 comparison uses different runtimes and rollout budgets, and editor-training variability across seeds is not measured. - Read it or not: Read it if you work on agent scaffold/harness optimization or test-time adaptation of agentic systems — the instance-adaptation formulation and the reuse-of-search-artifacts idea are directly reusable; skip it if you only need leaderboard-grade SWE-bench numbers, since the evaluation setup is deliberately non-standard.

Problem & Motivation: Teams deploying LLM agents face a runtime-design problem: the harness (context construction, control flow, tool workflow, verification) around a frozen model heavily shapes task performance, and hand-designing it is a hard optimization problem. Automated harness optimization (Meta-Harness, Self-Harness, Harness-R1) addresses this but produces a single global harness applied uniformly to all instances, even though instances differ — e.g., SWE-bench issues from different repositories have different testing conventions, and a harness that wins on average can be suboptimal per instance. A second pain point: outer-loop optimization generates a rich archive of candidate harnesses, traces, and outcomes, and existing methods use this only to improve the global harness, discarding the instance-level signal once search ends. The paper targets practitioners running agentic evaluation/deployment on interactive, software-engineering, and terminal tasks. Key Idea: Recycle the exhaust of a completed global harness search: (1) distill the search archive into a structured playbook of conditional editing strategies and anti-patterns (via ACE-style extraction, reflection, curation), and (2) RL-train a small editor so that, given a new instance, the global harness source, and the playbook, it emits one code patch producing an instance-specific harness. The editor learns which prior strategy applies to which instance rather than discovering strategies from scratch — the key insight is that per-instance adaptation can be made cheap (one 9B-model call) by making the expensive strategy discovery happen once, offline, during the global search. Methodology: The pipeline is a two-loop construction around a frozen execution model M. Offline: an outer loop (Meta-Harness with Claude Sonnet 4.5/Opus 4.6 as the optimizer) produces a global harness H plus a search archive; the archive is summarized into a playbook P with three stages — extraction (contrastive/uniform record construction, source-level diffs between solving and failing variants), reflection (frontier model emits candidate strategies with confidence, anti-patterns filtered), and curation (deduplicated conditional strategies; e.g., the TB2.1 playbook has 6 strategies and 9 anti-patterns). Editor training: for each training instance, sample G candidate patches from the editor πθ (Qwen3.5-9B, full-parameter fine-tuning, FSDP), apply each to H, execute the frozen agent once, and update with GRPO using task-specific rewards (e.g., SWE reward = 1 − s/(2·40) for a successful fix using s steps; abstention penalized by 0.05 on non-coding benchmarks). Inference: one editor call produces a patch; if it fails to apply, the system falls back to H. Critical design decisions: (a) patch-not-generate — the editor only edits H, enabling a 9B editor (justified by the ablation showing small editors cannot exploit the playbook zero-shot but can after RL); (b) playbook-as-context rather than retrieval (the whole playbook sits in the editor's context — plausible at 6 entries, but never stress-tested for size); (c) reward integrity safeguards — scoring computed by a trusted runner outside the editor-generated harness code, reducing reward hacking. Decision (a) is well-justified empirically; (b) and (c) are reasonable but (b) is untested at playbook scale. Key Results: Seven benchmarks. Agentic (frozen Qwen3.5-9B executor, single run each): ALFWorld success 70.7% vs Meta-Harness 60.7%; ScienceWorld 42.4/100 vs 35.1; DBBench 69.2% vs 65.0%; WebShop Success@1 42.0% vs 40.0% (comparable to Harness-R1's author-reported 42.2%). Coding benchmarks (3 runs, mean±SEM, 40-step/$3 budget): SWE-smith-MR pass rate 64.0±1.2% (Haiku 4.5) vs Meta-Harness 50.7±2.9%, and 88.0±1.2% (Gemini 3.7 Flash) vs 70.7±2.4%; SWE-bench Verified 150-issue subset 59.3±1.4% vs 56.7±2.0% (Haiku) and 54.4±2.3% vs 38.4±0.4% (Gemini). Efficiency: on SWE-smith-MR with Gemini, 8.7 vs 23.1 steps and $0.046 vs $0.310 per issue (~6.7× cost reduction); on TB2.1 (Sonnet 4.5, 5 runs, 44 tasks) Turbo reaches 55.5±1.4% vs Meta-Harness 50.5±1.7%, Terminus-Kira 52.3±1.1%, Terminus-2 50.9±0.8%, OpenHands 47.3±1.5%, while also cheapest among competitive harnesses ($1.38/task, 2.65M input tokens vs Meta-Harness $1.56, 3.15M). Baselines are current and mostly strong (Meta-Harness, GEPA, ACE, Harness-R1, human-designed TB2.1 harnesses), though Harness-R1 numbers are partly author-reported or ported into a different runtime. Notable counter-intuitive finding: on TB2.1 the automated global harness loses to human-crafted ones, yet instance adaptation alone restores the lead — and the same control knob (forced tool use) is optimal ON for one task and a global anti-pattern costing −6.7% on the suite, directly illustrating the global-vs-instance tension. Novelty Classification: NEW FORMULATION (instance-adaptive harness optimization as distinct from global search) plus NEW METHOD (playbook-conditioned RL-trained patch editor reusing search exhaust). The components are standard — GRPO, ACE-style playbook curation, an existing outer-loop optimizer (Meta-Harness) as the substrate, LLM-as-editor — but the combination and the recycling framing are genuinely new relative to prior global or from-scratch-per-instance methods (JIT-Agent, Harness-R1); the reliability analysis (resolved-in-all-3-runs rising from 20→28 Haiku, 26→42 Gemini) and the same-knob-opposite-optimum case study are valuable new empirical findings. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are present and informative (RL × playbook factorial; editor-capability sweep Base-9B/Sonnet-4.5/Opus-4.6). Coding-benchmark results report mean±SEM over 3 execution runs and TB2.1 over 5 runs, with a reliability analysis over repeats. Code is released at github.com/Tyrion58/turbo-harness. Concerns: (1) no seed variation for editor training or playbook construction — the appendix explicitly states editor-training/split variability is not evaluated; (2) the four agentic benchmarks use a single evaluation run each; (3) the SWE-bench Verified numbers come from a self-constructed 150-issue subset under a 40-step/$3 budget, and the paper itself warns these should not be read as leaderboard results; (4) SWE-smith-MR holds out issues but not repositories, so cross-repo generalization of adaptation is untested; (5) the Harness-R1 comparison mixes author-reported numbers and a ported/RL-retrained engineer in a different runtime, and the paper honestly flags that it does not isolate the editor effect; (6) WebShop required a divergent, hand-tuned GRPO recipe (Dr. GRPO-style advantages, improvement bonus, filtered 65-goal training subset), a fragility signal; (7) checkpoint selection on SWE-bench Verified uses validation pass rate with an entropy-based exclusion rule — sensible, but a per-benchmark recipe inhomogeneity that complicates interpretation. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL (with a SYSTEMS artifact). Practical: Yes — the editor is a 9B open-weight model runnable locally, and code is released, though the playbook build requires frontier-model calls. Efficient: At inference it adds one 9B call per instance and frequently reduces executor cost (up to ~6.7× on SWE-smith-MR/Gemini), but reported costs exclude the offline Meta-Harness search and all editor GRPO training, which consumed up to 8 GPUs per benchmark for multiple epochs — the total-cost picture is not given. Effective: The evidence shows it improves pass rates over the global harness on all seven benchmarks under the authors' own splits and budgets, which is the stated claim; generalization to unseen repositories or domains is untested. Scalable: Not tested — playbook-grows-past-context behavior, transfer across benchmarks/domains, and cross-search reuse are acknowledged as open questions. The work delivers a released software artifact (code repo) plus trained editors/playbooks; weights of the editors are not explicitly stated as released. Strengths: - Genuine reframing: treating outer-loop search artifacts as reusable training experience ("exhaust") rather than disposable byproducts is a real conceptual contribution to the harness-optimization literature, and the turbocharger analogy is apt. - The central ablation is unusually clean: it shows a non-obvious interaction (RL-trained 9B + playbook = 64.0% vs 49.3–51.3% for either alone) and that the trained 9B matches an untrained Opus-4.6 editor (61.3%), isolating what RL buys. - Honest efficiency accounting: step and dollar costs are reported alongside accuracy, the Pareto position on TB2.1 is shown against human-designed harnesses, and the failure case (Haiku on SWE-bench Verified, +20.4 steps vs 18.8) is disclosed rather than hidden. - Reward-integrity engineering (trusted runner, source checks against scoring internals) and the qualitative patch case studies (per-instance step-budget reallocation, opposite optima for the same knob) substantively support the claim that adaptation reaches executable control flow, not just prompt text. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state two: (1) dependence on the quality/diversity of the prior search archive — weak search yields weak adaptation; (2) editor training requires environment rollouts, which is costly on agentic tasks. They also transparently disclose the non-standard SWE-bench Verified budget, that TB2.1 per-instance test patches were not persisted (case study uses training-task edits), the confounds in the Harness-R1 comparison, and that error bars do not cover editor-training variability. This is direct, non-minimizing treatment of limitations — a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: Beyond the authors' notes: (1) playbook construction depends on frontier models (Sonnet 4.5/Opus 4.6), so the "lightweight" pipeline has a hidden frontier-model dependency not counted in cost; (2) the playbook-conditioning mechanism is untested for context-length scalability — real archives could yield playbooks far larger than 6 strategies, and no retrieval fallback is evaluated; (3) the headline SWE-smith-MR gain (+17.3 points with Gemini, 88.0% on a 50-issue set) rests on 50 issues from 25 repositories with equal weighting — a few repository-level quirks can move the number substantially, and the training/test split shares repositories; (4) the WebShop recipe divergence (different advantage computation, bonuses, filtered training set) suggests the method may not be uniformly plug-and-play across tasks, but no analysis of when it fails is given; (5) gains correlate with the executor's remaining headroom (large for Gemini, +2.7 points for Haiku on Verified), implying the method's value shrinks as harness optimization improves — an unstated ceiling on the contribution; (6) no statistical testing beyond SEM, and no comparison to the concurrent JIT-Agent, the closest competing instance-specific method, which is discussed in related work but not benchmarked. Bottom Line: A practitioner building automated agent-harness pipelines should read this: the recycle-the-search-archive formulation is a practical, ablation-supported lever for accuracy and cost that no competing global-only method currently offers, but the evidence comes from self-built splits and budgets, so treat the absolute numbers as directional rather than leaderboard-comparable.

From Solo to Social Learning: Characterizing Recursive Social Improvement in LLMs

K Jha, M Kleiman-Weiner, N Jaques · arxiv.org · recursive self-improvement - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces a reinforcement-learning formulation of "recursive social improvement" — populations of self-interested LLM agents that each decide, under one shared token budget, whether to privately revise their skills, copy a peer's, or act — and reports a systematic empirical study of whether such populations beat independent learners at equal cost. - Why it's important: Deployed LLM agents increasingly share skills and scaffolding (e.g., via public repositories and multi-agent swarms), and whether peer learning helps or hurts self-interested agent populations determines if decentralized agent ecosystems can exceed the sum of their parts without central coordination. - How it does it: The core move is a matched-cost comparison (ΔJ(C)) that counts every token spent by every agent — including the private search behind a copied skill — and asks whether a social population outperforms N independent learners that spent the same total tokens, cleanly separating efficiency (reward per token) from effectiveness (performance at equal cost). - The good: The experimental design is unusually careful: an algorithmic hierarchical UCB baseline confirms the environment contains exploitable social information (+25.68 ± 2.87 cumulative reward over solo UCB, p < 0.001), so the LLMs' failure to benefit is attributable to their policies, not the task, and randomized causal interventions (protected execution, forced independent search, assigned observation timing) test specific mechanisms. - The missing: All social decisions come from fixed-weight LLMs making in-context choices — no agent is trained, fine-tuned, or incentivized to learn when and whom to copy — so the headline negative result may reflect the decision policy rather than a limit of social learning itself; the authors flag this only as future work. - Read it or not: Worth reading for anyone building multi-agent LLM systems or studying cultural evolution in machine populations, because it delivers a crisp negative result with a reusable evaluation methodology; skippable for practitioners seeking a method that improves multi-agent performance today — it does not provide one.

Problem & Motivation: Self-improvement methods for LLM agents (prompt optimization, reflection, evolutionary search over skill files) optimize one system at a time, while multi-agent frameworks typically make all agents pursue a shared goal under designed collaboration. The paper addresses the unstudied middle ground: what happens when many self-interested agents, each rewarded only on its own tasks, can see what their peers produce and must choose whether to pay for copying? This is the classic producer–scrounger tension from behavioral ecology and economics (Rogers 1988; Grossman & Stiglitz 1980): social learning is valuable only if someone pays to explore, yet each individual prefers that someone else pay, and copying from the wrong source can be worse than learning alone. The practitioners with the problem are builders of persistent agent ecosystems (skill libraries, agent marketplaces) where sharing is emergent rather than designed. The gap closed is that prior work either assumed a single improver or engineered collaboration; no prior framework measures whether uncoordinated, self-interested LLM improvers outperform equally funded independent learners. Key Idea: The key idea is methodological rather than algorithmic: evaluate social learning only at matched total token cost, counting every token — including the search that produced a copied skill — so that a positive ΔJ(C) cannot arise from merely redistributing discoveries across parallel searchers. This distinguishes "efficient social learning" (more reward per token, achievable by stopping search early) from "effective social learning" (beating independent learners at equal cost), and defines recursive social improvement as recursive transmission (a skill copied and revised again) plus ΔJ(C) > 0. The observation cost is made endogenous: reasoning about whether and whom to observe consumes the same budget as acting, mirroring deployed agent economics. Methodology: The framework is a two-stage, non-stationary RL problem for N agents over T rounds. Each round a policy πᵢ (either a fixed-weight LLM learning in-context or an algorithmic baseline) first selects a learning action — REVISE a skill using its own task feedback, OBSERVE a chosen peer (acquiring that peer's last-executed skill and reward), or SKIP — then selects a skill from its growing library and executes it, all within a per-round token budget B (Equation 1); invalid or exhausted actions earn zero. Performance J(π; C) is measured at the last round before cumulative population cost exceeds C, and ΔJ(C) = J(π_soc; C) − J(π_solo; C) is the headline metric. Two experimental phases: (1) a controlled 25-armed bandit adapting the Rendell et al. (2010) social-learning tournament (10 agents, 100 rounds, B = 4,096 completion tokens, 8 environment seeds, models Qwen3-14B, Ministral-3-14B, GPT-OSS-20B), with hierarchical UCB and DEOE algorithmic baselines and two randomized interventions — protected execution (PE: reserve 2,048 tokens for the pull) and independent search (IS: force an unpulled arm on 15% of agent-rounds); (2) skill-file evolution on IFBench using OpenEvolve for revisions (GPT-OSS-120B and GLM-5.3-Flash, six populations of five agents, 49 learning rounds on 100 training examples, 200 held-out examples, whole-answer constraint satisfaction as the metric), plus UCB and uniform source-selection controllers compared against full solo OpenEvolve. Critical design decisions: (a) counting discovery costs in the matched-cost baseline — well justified, explicitly argued in Appendix E.2 with a student-study analogy; (b) LLM policies with fixed weights and fixed prompts, never trained on the meta-decision — justified only as scope, not tested; (c) restricting each agent's view to only its latest full observation — a practical prompt-control choice whose effect on results is not ablated. Key Results: In the bandit, hierarchical UCB gains +25.68 ± 2.87 cumulative reward over solo UCB (p < 0.001), establishing exploitable social information. All three LLMs fail to convert it: at matched completion tokens, ΔJ(C) is +0.14 ± 0.33 (Qwen), +0.37 ± 0.34 (Ministral), and −1.24 ± 0.45 (GPT-OSS), none significant after correction; reward per token drops 29.6 ± 13.4%, 41.8 ± 11.6%, and 51.9 ± 7.8% respectively (significant for GPT-OSS, p < 0.01). Diagnostics show copying quality is not the problem — 93.2% of GPT-OSS copied arms beat the recipient's personal best — but social populations explore fewer distinct arms and Qwen's social agents complete pulls in only 81.0% of rounds vs. 98.1% solo. PE and IS each fix their targeted defect (PE: +19.53 ± 2.24 pp completion; IS: +1.27 ± 0.23 distinct arms) yet neither closes the social–solo gap. On IFBench, at matched learning tokens ΔJ(C) is +0.14 ± 0.35 pp (GPT-OSS-120B) and +0.98 ± 0.85 pp (GLM-5.3-Flash) — neither significant, so neither model meets the criterion for recursive social improvement. GLM's social populations improve sooner (+1.31 ± 0.61 pp trajectory average) while GPT-OSS's spend 17.34 ± 2.08M fewer learning tokens (p < 0.001) — efficiency without effectiveness. Randomized timing experiments show distributed observation beats early observation for GLM (+2.42 ± 0.46 pp, p < 0.01), and distributed-observation copying reaches skills where 95.83% differ from the initial file vs. 79.17% under early copying. Recursive transmission occurs (83.3% of GPT-OSS and 56.7% of GLM final deployed skills descend from copy-then-revise chains), but social runs concentrate on 1.0 (GPT-OSS) and 2.33 (GLM) founding lineages vs. ~5 under solo learning. Algorithmic UCB and uniform controllers reach accuracy within 1.03 pp of full solo OpenEvolve using 76–78% fewer learning tokens, with no advantage of adaptive over random source choice. Scale is modest: 10-agent/100-round bandits and 5-agent/49-round instruction-following runs; no larger-scale tests. The counter-intuitive headline — LLMs copy good things yet social populations do no better at equal cost, while dumb algorithmic rules capture most of the available savings — is well supported within the tested envelope. Novelty Classification: NEW PROBLEM (recursive social improvement among self-interested, self-improving LLM agents) and NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING (LLM-controlled social learning fails at matched cost where algorithmic social learners succeed). The formulation adapts the existing social-learning-tournament design of Rendell et al. (2010) with endogenous token costs — a competent re-engineering of known machinery — and the skill-evolution harness is a straightforward assembly of OpenEvolve plus a decision layer; the genuinely new contributions are the matched-cost ΔJ(C) evaluation criterion and the negative-result evidence base. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are unusually thorough: randomized causal interventions (PE, IS, assigned observation timing, early-access windows) rather than only correlational diagnostics; Bonferroni-corrected primary comparisons; bootstrap over held-out items; sensitivity checks over token-accounting choices (completion vs. prompt+completion, interpolated vs. last-round endpoints) that preserve direction; a retrospective minimum-detectable-effect calculation; and an explicit statement that non-significance is not equivalence. An implementation correction ("corrected loop") is disclosed and kept separate from earlier runs rather than pooled — a credibility positive. Code, configurations, and seed-level summaries are planned for release but not yet available ("We plan on releasing"); no URL is given. Concerns: the bandit LLM experiments use only 8 seeds, and several key contrasts (e.g., Qwen/Ministral efficiency drops, all IFBench ΔJ(C) values) are non-significant, so some conclusions rest on point estimates with substantial uncertainty; all agents train and evaluate on the same IFBench distribution; peer identity is confounded with fixed list position (acknowledged, unshuffled). No Goodhart-style benchmark gaming is apparent since held-out evaluation never feeds back into learning. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL (experiments run on API-accessible open-weight models; no primary theoretical claim). - Practical: Yes — every experiment uses publicly available models (Qwen3-14B, GPT-OSS-20B/120B, Ministral-3-14B, GLM-5.3-Flash) via standard API or open weights on commodity inference. - Efficient: The per-population API cost is modest (learning costs on the order of single-digit to tens of dollars per five-agent population per condition, per reported ledgers); the paper's own finding is that copying-based policies reduce cost by up to 76–78% versus private search. - Effective: The evidence shows social access does not yet solve the stated problem — no tested configuration beats independent learners at equal cost — though it does buy earlier improvement (GLM) or lower spend (GPT-OSS). - Scalable: Not tested: populations are 5–10 agents over 49–100 rounds; nothing measures whether concentration-on-few-lineages worsens or whether LLM decision-making improves at 10× population size — scalability is unclaimed, which is appropriate. The work delivers a methodology and negative result in paper form; the artifact release (code, configs, seed-level summaries) is promised but not yet published. Strengths: - The efficiency/effectiveness distinction operationalized through ΔJ(C) is a genuine conceptual contribution — most multi-agent LLM papers report raw gains or token savings without controlling for the discovery cost copied skills embed, and this metric makes "more than the sum of its parts" a falsifiable claim. - The two-tier evidence structure is well executed: the algorithmic UCB baseline proves the environment contains social value (+25.68 ± 2.87, p < 0.001), cleanly localizing the failure to LLM decision policies rather than the task. - Randomized interventions (protected execution, forced independent search, assigned observation timing) convert descriptive failure modes into causal tests, and the timing experiment genuinely reverses the tempting interpretation that GLM's early copying explains its speed advantage. - The lineage/concentration analysis (1.0 vs. 4.83 founding lineages for GPT-OSS) documents a real collective risk of copying — reduced diversity of discoveries — that individual-level reward metrics would miss. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state that findings rest on three bandit models and two models on a single benchmark (IFBench) and may not generalize; that fixed peer-list order confounds peer preference with position; that matched-cost comparison uses realized spend rather than a prospectively fixed budget; that agents keep only the latest observation in full, draw tasks from one distribution, use a single model per population, and cannot revise their decision prompts. They also carefully note in the appendix that non-significant differences are not evidence of equivalence and report minimum detectable effects. This is direct, non-minimizing acknowledgment — a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - The most important unacknowledged gap: the LLM social policy is never trained. The paper concludes that "using peers' discoveries well becomes a capability in its own right," but tests only fixed-weight in-context policies with fixed prompts; a fine-tuned or search-optimized meta-policy is the obvious next baseline, and its absence leaves open that the negative result is an artifact of prompting, not a capability limit. - The IFBench setting gives all agents identical training data, so copying confers no information advantage beyond saved search — a structurally harsh test whose restriction to this one task type is not ablated. - Populations of 5 agents with full observability are far from any ecosystem scale; network structure, heterogeneity, and larger N — the variables the cited human social-learning literature shows matter most — are unvaried. - The finding that UCB and uniform controllers match full solo OpenEvolve at 76–78% fewer tokens partially reflects a design choice (observation avoids the mandatory 100-example evaluation), which the authors note but which blurs how much of the "savings" is learning from peers versus skipping expensive search entirely. - Several headline-adjacent contrasts (Qwen and Ministral efficiency drops, both IFBench ΔJ(C) values) are not statistically significant even before correcting for multiple comparisons, so the sweeping claim that "three LLMs do not" benefit leans on GPT-OSS's significant result plus directional consistency. Bottom Line: A practitioner building self-improving or multi-agent LLM systems should read this for its matched-cost evaluation discipline and its sobering, well-controlled negative result — LLM agents currently copy well but coordinate exploration poorly — though anyone seeking a method that makes agent populations outperform independent learners will need to look elsewhere, since this paper diagnoses the problem rather than solving it.

TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces SafeActBench, a 656-case benchmark with a deterministic, provenance-bound trajectory evaluator that checks whether a tool-using agent established evidence for the correct entity and state before executing consequential actions, across static judgment, investigated non-action, single-action, and dependency-constrained multi-action protocols. - Why it's important: Agents increasingly issue refunds, disable devices, and update production records; Problem & Motivation: Tool-using LLM agents are moving from answering to acting: they issue refunds, dispatch couriers, disable home devices, and close compliance filings, all state-changing operations the authors call consequential actions. For such actions, correctness of the final environment state does not imply the action was justified — an agent can refund the right charge for the right amount without ever having verified the charge is a duplicate, as the paper's Figure 1 shows. Existing interactive benchmarks (AgentBench, AppWorld, τ-bench, ToolSandbox, OSWorld, WorkArena) score task completion, milestones, or policy violations, and concurrent work examines overtrust in observations (EnvTrustBench), latent policy failures (Near-Miss), or abstention (AgentAbstain), but none explicitly score whether each consequential action was supported by entity-bound evidence established in the observable trajectory before execution, nor whether downstream actions consume actual predecessor results. The gap: failures between observing the environment and changing it are hard to localize when the only signal is task success or failure. Key Idea: The core insight is that action support is a provenance-bound, observable property of the trajectory: a prerequisite is satisfied only if evidence for the required fact about the specific entity and state was established before execution — a matching value read from the wrong record does not count — and in multi-action settings, support extends to results of predecessor actions (a dependent call must use the actual returned identifier, not a look-alike). This decomposes the evidence-to-action chain into four checkable failure sites: incomplete investigation, evidence bound to the wrong entity, premature execution, and violated dependency/result-propagation, all verifiable deterministically without inspecting hidden reasoning or using an LLM judge. Methodology: SafeActBench contains 656 cases across six operational domains (customer/policy, engineering/infrastructure, legal/financial, research, smart-home, healthcare) in five protocols: Legacy (static ALLOW/BLOCK/DEFER on a fixed candidate, 86 cases), V0 investigated non-action (175), V1 single action (131), V2 linear multi-action (132), and V3 DAG-constrained multi-action (132). Each case specifies task context, information tools, consequential tools, hidden per-action evidence requirements R(a), expected actions, and dependencies (V3 aggregates 501 action nodes, 439 dependency edges, 103 forks, 96 joins). The formal success criterion is Supported(a) ⟺ ∀r ∈ R(a), r established before a; interactive success is conjunctive over investigation, evidence, exact arguments, receipts, dependencies, and terminal conditions. Evaluation is a deterministic replay of recorded trajectories — no LLM judge, no hidden-reasoning access. Validation includes author reference solutions passing 656/656, human audits (120 cases, two blinded annotators, κ = 0.87/0.81/0.74 for action support/requirement necessity/establishment), a 300-trajectory evaluator audit (2.0% false acceptance, 1.3% false rejection, with Wilson CIs), and replay tests of alternative evidence paths (395 additional reads, 132 action swaps, etc., all accepted; 20 wrong-entity and 30 stale-evidence controls all rejected) after a date-handling bug fix. Experiments run ten model–harness configurations (five models × family harness and shared Inspect ReAct harness), three rollouts per case, temperature 0.6/top-p 0.95 for open models, 600s per-case budget. Beyond the main benchmark, the paper runs matched-case static-vs-interactive comparisons (100 V1 cases; a 99-scenario class-balanced control), paired harness analyses with 5,000-resample case-paired bootstrap CIs, evidence-withholding and contradiction interventions on 43 V1 cases with three configurations, and mechanism probes (evidence-package vs requester-claim presentations, urgency cues, system warnings, distractor records). Key Results: Across ten configurations, overall exact case success (ECS) ranges from 37.7% (GLM–ZCode) to 67.2% (Claude–Claude Code). Two headline patterns: (1) static judgment does not predict interactive execution — GLM–ZCode scores 97.7% on Legacy but 12.1% on V1, while DeepSeek–DSH with similar Legacy (96.5%) reaches 61–65% on V1–V3; on the same 100 V1 cases, static accuracy is 95.0–99.0% against interactive ECS of 28.0–52.0% (gaps of 43–69 points, CIs excluding zero). (2) Failures arise before execution: premature-action rate (PAR) on V1 is 37.0–66.9%, stopped-before-investigation (BSR) on V0 is 21.7–62.9%, yet conditional action success given completed evidence (CAS) is 93.2–100% for nine of ten configurations — single-action execution is reliable once evidence is established. Multi-action protocols add unresolved-prerequisite (Gap) and incomplete-workflow (Part.) failures with model-specific signatures (e.g., GLM–ZCode: 80.3% Gap vs 33.3% Part. on V2). Harness effects are large and model-dependent: paired CIs show DeepSeek +4.4 points with DSH and GLM −6.8 points with ZCode, while Claude/GPT/Qwen intervals include or reach zero; Qwen's two harnesses disagree on 23.5% of cases. Interventions show withholding a decisive record reduces action probability by 37.2–45.2 points, but agents still act in 46.5–53.5% of Withheld episodes; contradiction reduces action more (54.5–70.0 points); and agents respond more to a requester's verbal claim that missing evidence was checked (action rates 14.0–23.3%) than to the actual evidence package being presented (30.2–41.9%). A supplementary structured runtime (SCGR-EG) yields ECS gains of +0.3 to +16.2 points across all ten configurations, while the selective variant (SCGR-Select) helps Qwen (+11.6) but hurts Claude (−9.1). Novelty Classification: NEW PROBLEM (operationalizing the evidence-to-action boundary as an evaluation target), NEW DATASET/BENCHMARK, and NEW SYSTEM/TOOL (the provenance-bound Evidence Ledger and deterministic evaluator). The genuinely novel element is the conjunction of entity/state-bound pre-action evidence requirements, result propagation, and investigated non-action scored from observable trajectories with a non-LLM evaluator — Table 5 shows each ingredient has partial coverage in prior or concurrent work (ToolSandbox's milestone DAGs, Near-Miss's read-before-mutate checks, EnvTrustBench, AgentAbstain), so the benchmark is best described as the first to check all four properties together rather than a wholly new evaluation primitive. The experimental apparatus (harness pairing, bootstrap CIs, intervention design) is competent application of standard methodology; the SCGR supplementary runtime is an engineering combination with mixed results. Rigor & Reproducibility: Rigor is above average for a benchmark paper. Ablation-style localization is present (BSR, PAR, CAS, Gap, Part. diagnostics; failure-mode decomposition by protocol), three rollouts per case with reported run-to-run SDs of 0.2–0.7 points, paired bootstrap CIs throughout, negative controls for the evaluator (wrong-entity/stale-evidence rejections), and a clearly disclosed evaluator bug (dynamic date handling) that was fixed before final evaluation. Human validation is stratified, blinded, and adjudicated, with honest reporting of low-coverage configurations (Qwen's balanced control omitted due to n=3 paired tasks). Concerns: (a) evidence requirements are author-defined; the audits check consistency and inter-annotator agreement but the authors themselves note the checks "do not by themselves establish that the specified evidence requirements are necessary or complete" — a specification-completeness risk the determinism of the evaluator does not remove; (b) the intervention analyses cover only 43 V1 cases and three configurations, so the most interesting behavioral findings rest on a small frozen cohort; (c) strict conjunctive ECS means a single wrong terminal label (e.g., BLOCK vs DEFER after complete investigation, trajectory D.1) fails the case, which conflates calibration failures with evidence failures; (d) human audits were performed by research-team members, not independent annotators. A project page (https://safeact.github.io) is cited; no direct code/data repository URL or model release is stated in the text. Deployability: (4-property check):** Profile: EMPIRICAL (a benchmark and evaluation study with a built evaluator; the SCGR runtime is a small secondary system). - Practical: Yes — all evaluation runs through commercial APIs and the Inspect AI framework with a 600s per-case budget, reproducible by any lab with API access. - Efficient: Moderate cost — correct trajectories require 5.6–7.1 specified reads per case (up to 17), and the full evaluation was 3 rollouts × 656 cases × 10 configurations, plus ~2,073 intervention episodes; cheaper than interactive benchmarks with simulated users but not trivial. - Effective: The benchmark demonstrably localizes failures that endpoint-based scoring misses (matched-case static-vs-interactive gap of 43–69 points), though it measures observable support, not internal reliance — a scope limit the authors state explicitly. - Scalable: Only claimed, not tested — case authoring is the bottleneck (656 researcher-authored cases with per-case hidden requirement specifications and multi-stage human review), and scaling to hundreds of DAG-heavy workflows would multiply the authoring and audit cost; no automated case-generation pipeline is offered. The work delivers a benchmark suite and deterministic evaluator (artifact promised at the project page); the SCGR runtime is a training-free analysis instrument, not a deployable mitigation. Strengths: - The matched-case static-vs-interactive design (same 100 V1 cases reformulated as static judgment vs interactive execution, plus a class-balanced 99-scenario control) is the strongest evidence in the paper: it rules out case-composition confounds and shows a 43–69 point gap that cannot be explained by task difficulty. - The deterministic, provenance-bound evaluator with audited alternative-evidence-path acceptance (778 valid variants accepted; 50 negative controls rejected) is a real methodological contribution — it shows the evaluator is strict about entity binding without being brittle about path choice, and the disclosure and repair of the date-handling bug is a credibility positive. - The evidence-withholding and requester-claim probes yield a non-obvious finding: agents weight a human's verbal assurance more than the absence or presence of actual evidence (requester claims reduce action to 14.0–23.3% vs 30.2–41.9% for evidence packages), which has direct implications for agent-safety design around social-engineering resistance. - The harness-effect analysis is honest about its own limits — the balanced control shows GLM–Inspect's gap reverses sign (−10.1 points) with format-failure imbalance, and the paper says so rather than overclaiming a universal static-interactive gap. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors confront limitations directly: they state the analysis captures observable support rather than internal reliance; that Gap and Part. are overlapping diagnostics, not an additive decomposition; that reduced action probability under interventions "does not necessarily indicate correct refusals"; that the balanced static control confounds evidence availability with action-construction responsibility and output-contract reliability; that SCGR-Select effects are model-, harness-, and protocol-dependent with mixed sign; that Qwen configurations lack sufficient paired coverage; and that benchmark results "should not be interpreted as certifications of safety" for real-world domains. The ethics statement notes all validation was done by research-team members without external human subjects. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - No strong-baseline or mitigation comparison: the paper never tests whether a simple scaffold (e.g., a mandatory pre-action checklist, a read-before-write tool wrapper, or an enforced plan-then-act harness) closes the PAR/BSR gaps — SCGR is presented as an "analysis instrument," but the natural next experiment (does structured evidence presentation fix the problem?) produced mixed results and is relegated to a supplementary study. - Requirement specification is a single point of failure: each case's R(a) set is authored and reviewed, but there is no automatic completeness check against tool semantics; an unlisted prerequisite makes a supported action unsupported, and the human audit covers only 120 of 656 cases for requirement construction (the 300-trajectory audit measures evaluator consistency, not requirement completeness). - The intervention cohort (43 V1 cases, three configurations, one model per finding class) is small relative to the claims in §5.3.3–5.3.4; the paper is careful with CIs but the qualitative conclusions ("agents respond more to requester claims than to absent evidence") rest on one frozen cohort not selected for representativeness. - Strict conjunctive ECS penalizes label calibration errors (BLOCK vs DEFER, trajectory D.1) and single-argument mismatches (D.2) in the same binary score as unsafe action, which the diagnostics partially but not fully separate; a graded safety-relevant score (e.g., unsupported-action rate alone) is never reported as a headline. - Model set is capped at five families under two harnesses each, all frontier-tier; the static-interactive gap for smaller or open-weight models, and the interaction of evidence-grounding with model scale, is unexplored. - The benchmark is fully synthetic with fictional records; whether the requester-claim susceptibility finding transfers to real multi-turn deployments with adversarial users is untested. Bottom Line: This is one of the more rigorous agent-evaluation papers of its cycle — the provenance-bound evaluator and matched-case static-vs-interactive design give practitioners a genuinely new diagnostic lens on why endpoint-correct agents still act unsafely, and it should be read by anyone building tool-use harnesses or safety evaluations, with the caveat that the behavioral findings need replication at larger scale and the paper offers no validated fix, only a diagnosis.

P Prakash, P Höllmer, A Fuhr, P Hirschfeld, P Ganesh… · arxiv.org · karypis - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces a GRPO-based reinforcement learning scheme that directly treats atom-type commit events in a masked discrete flow-matching crystal generator (OMatG) as discrete policy actions with exact per-event likelihood ratios, raising the metastable-unique-novel (mSUN) yield on LeMat-GenBench from 13.4% to 45.5%. - Why it's important: Generative crystal models are trained to match databases and are blind to design goals; composition determines a material's chemistry, yet prior RL approaches for 3D crystal generators froze the composition, relaxed it to continuous variables, or decoded it from a latent, leaving the most consequential decisions unsteered by the reward. - How it does it: The closed-form likelihood ratio for each discrete element-commit event plugs into a clipped GRPO surrogate with a reward that relaxes each structure under the UMA potential and scores clipped energy-above-hull, creativity (novelty/uniqueness), and diversity (composition-occurrence discount plus an MMD coverage bonus), with explicit guards: abstention on hulls with fewer than 12 near-hull reference phases and a penalty floor for single-element or implausibly below-hull structures. - The good: DFT spot-checks confirm 63 of 67 trusted-tier metastability claims with 0.016 eV/atom mean absolute deviation, and controls (best-of-N at 7.7%, frozen-composition at 9.8%) show the gain genuinely requires RL on the discrete composition channel rather than oversampling or geometry-only RL. - The missing: The reward shares novelty, uniqueness, and stability machinery with the benchmark it is scored on (circularity the authors quantify — 39.3% mSUN without the creativity term — but cannot eliminate), and headline results are effectively single-seed; the valid-structure rate also drops from 94.1% to 69.8% after RL, an unexamined cost. - Read it or not: Anyone doing RL-based generative materials design, or any generative-models researcher who wants a field-specific, forensically documented reward-hacking taxonomy and a demonstration that the S.U.N. metric is gameable, should read this; readers outside materials generation can skip the derivations but should read Sections 4.3 and 4.5.
Why this rank
Scored using Empirical profile. The composite is driven by Novelty (75) — the exact discrete-commit likelihood ratio making composition a first-class policy action, plus the first documented reward-hacking taxonomy for crystal generation — and Impact (78), with code, checkpoints, and generated structures publicly released and runs feasible on one B200. Rigor (72) is strong (DFT validation, controls, extensive exploit-closure ablations, current baselines) but capped by single-seed headline results and reward/benchmark co-adaptation the authors flag but cannot eliminate. Non-Obviousness (76) is high: the induction-from-zero single-element exploit and the benchmark-validity critique are surprising, field-relevant findings. Completeness (74) is a credibility positive — limitations are treated as findings — while Resilience (72) is solid given the out-of-reward DFT check and quantified circularity, and the unexamined valid-rate drop (94.1%→69.8%) is the main residual vulnerability. Problem & Motivation: Inverse materials design needs generative crystal models steered toward properties such as thermodynamic stability, but generators like OMatG, MatterGen, and DiffCSP are pre-trained only to match the distribution of structure databases (e.g., MP-20), so their training objective rewards neither stability nor novelty. Conditional generation requires property labels that most structures lack; RL requires only a reward evaluable on a generated structure. Prior crystal-generation RL either acted only on positions/lattice (OMatG-IRL, composition frozen), on latent spaces (Chemeleon2, composition decoded after the fact by a frozen decoder), or on continuous relaxations of composition — so the elemental constituents, which decide chemistry and hence stability, were never directly reinforced. The practitioners with this problem are computational materials scientists and ML researchers building RL-aligned generative models for 3D periodic structures. Key Idea: In masked discrete flow matching, each atom's element identity is chosen in a single categorical "commit" event whose likelihood ratio between current and old policies is exact — the schedule factors cancel, leaving a product of ratios of the model's predicted final-species distributions over committing atoms. This lets the policy gradient reach the composition channel natively as discrete actions rather than through frozen species, continuous relaxations, or latents. The second key move is defensive: because a reward rewarding low E_hull invites exploitation of sparse hulls and MLIP pathologies, the reward abstains (zeroes the advantage) on hulls with <12 near-hull references and penalizes single-element repackings — a guard set built by iteratively closing observed exploits. Methodology: The pipeline builds on OMatG, which models positions and lattice via stochastic interpolants (an SDE with drift combining a learned velocity field and denoiser, integrated by Euler–Maruyama steps) and atom types via masked discrete flow matching (a continuous-time Markov chain whose rate matrix unmasking term is the model's predicted species distribution). GRPO draws K=16 rollouts per group from a shared initial noise/mask state, computes the group-relative advantage Â = (r − mean)/std, and maximizes a per-channel clipped PPO-style surrogate summed over the position, lattice, and species channels, with per-channel KL penalties to the frozen pretrained model (β_species=0.05, β_pos=0.01, β_cell=0). The species-channel ratio (Eq. 4) is derived exactly in Appendix A for any remasking noise η. The reward (Eq. 5) is r = r_pen + c_occ·(r_stab + r_creat − r_pen) + 0.4·r_mmd, computed on UMA-relaxed structures (≤100 FIRE steps): r_stab = −clip(E_hull, 0, 1) against the UMA-consistent LeMat-Bulk hull, r_creat follows Chemeleon2's novelty/uniqueness term with clamped AMD partial credit, c_occ is a within-group composition-occurrence discount, and r_mmd is a leave-one-out MMD bonus matching the MP-20 composition distribution. Training: 750 rollout iterations × 4 groups × 16 structures, 3 inner epochs, ~8 hours on one NVIDIA B200. Critical design decisions: (1) routing sparse-hull structures to abstention rather than reward or penalty — justified by the observed exploit sequence, though the 12-reference threshold is a tuned knob; (2) relaxing inside the reward — justified because raw geometries move ~1 Å under relaxation, making unrelaxed terms nearly constant and gradient-free; (3) channel weights α set from logged gradient magnitudes — a reasonable but heuristic choice. Key Results: On the unmodified LeMat-GenBench protocol (2,500 generations per method, stability by a three-MLIP ensemble of Orb/MACE/UMA with two-of-three agreement, 0.1 eV/atom threshold, uniqueness/novelty against ~5.3M LeMat-Bulk structures): pretrained OMatG 13.4% mSUN (336/2,500); OMatGRPO 45.5% (1,138/2,500), a 3.4× gain; best-of-N over 47,795 prior samples 7.7%; frozen-composition control 9.8% (below the prior); released Chemeleon2 36.6% (915/2,500). The reward transfers: inside Chemeleon2's latent-VAE pipeline it reaches 43.7% versus that pipeline's native 36.6%, while Chemeleon2's reward in the OMatG pipeline reaches only 18.6%. Strict on-hull SUN counts are small (7 for OMatGRPO vs. 8 for the prior), so most structures are metastable, not on-hull. Without the single-element guard, 53.5% of the mSUN set is single-element repackings (e.g., fcc Mg counted as "novel"); the guard reduces this to 0.4% (4 structures). DFT (VASP, PBE, MP settings, no MP2020 corrections on either side) confirms 63/67 trusted-tier metastability claims (MAE 0.016 eV/atom); 20/22 for OMatGRPO alone. Sparse-hull share of mSUN: prior 21.7%, discovery (unguarded) run 63.4%, OMatGRPO 23.5%. Baselines are current — Chemeleon2 is a 2026 Nature Machine Intelligence method and the benchmark is the field's newest standard. The most striking finding is the exploit induced from zero: an Alexandria-pretrained prior emits no single-element mSUN structures, but RL produces 104 per 1,000 under the pre-creativity reward; the exploit also grows with group size (K=16: 253 → K=32: 307 per 1,000) at matched rollout budget. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD (GRPO applied to the discrete flow-matching composition channel of a crystal generator using exact per-event categorical likelihood ratios — prior crystal RL froze, relaxed, or latently decoded composition) plus NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING (a documented five-mode reward-hacking taxonomy in crystal generation, and a demonstration that single-element repackings on sparse hulls pass MatterGen's, Chemeleon2's, and LeMat-GenBench's mSUN filters, i.e., a benchmark-validity flaw). The GRPO/PPR machinery, stability/creativity/diversity reward components, and the benchmark are standard; the genuinely new parts are the exact discrete-commit likelihood ratio applied to crystal chemistry and the exploit-driven reward-guard methodology and benchmark critique. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are extensive and central to the argument: Appendix C catalogs five reward variants with per-run numbers, Table 4 gives LeMat-GenBench results for every named run, the creativity-term ablation (39.3% without it) quantifies the benchmark/reward circularity, a second pretrain (Alexandria) and a group-size sweep test whether the single-element exploit is training-induced, and a second MLIP (MatterSim, 0.015 eV/atom median agreement) checks potential dependence. Controls (best-of-N, frozen composition) isolate the contribution of species RL. Error bars (95% CIs) appear in Figure 2a, but headline mSUN numbers are single-seed; only the guard-stability claim is verified across three seeds, and the reward-swap runs are explicitly single-seed with an unseeded Chemeleon2 sampler. DFT spot-checks (88 structures, pre-registered sampling frames, per-structure table, two documented exclusions) are unusually careful. Code (github.com/paprakash/OMatGRPO), trained models, and generated structure sets (HuggingFace) are released, with hyperparameters fully tabulated. Methodological concerns: reward and evaluation share components (novelty, uniqueness, UMA, LeMat-Bulk hulls) — Goodhart risk the authors acknowledge and partially mitigate (novelty rewarded against MP-20 but tested against 5.3M LeMat-Bulk; DFT as an out-of-reward check); the 12-reference threshold was selected through exploit-closure runs on the same benchmark used for final evaluation. No significance tests are reported for the mSUN comparisons, though 1,138 vs. 336 counts make the headline gap statistically implausible to reverse. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL (with a SYSTEMS component via released models and code). - Practical: Runs on a single NVIDIA B200 (~8 hours per RL run) with public potentials (UMA) and public data; accessible to most academic labs. - Efficient: The reward requires a UMA relaxation per generated structure (≤100 FIRE steps), adding nontrivial but affordable per-rollout cost; sampling for evaluation is 2,500 structures per method. - Effective: The evidence supports the claim on the stated target — benchmark mSUN with DFT-validated metastability claims — though "metastable" (≤0.1 eV/atom above hull) is a weaker bar than on-hull stability, where the model yields only 7 strict SUN. - Scalable: Not tested beyond 750 rollout iterations and one pretraining dataset (MP-20; Alexandria only for exploit analysis); no evidence on larger models, other property rewards, or non-de-novo generation tasks — scalability is unclaimed rather than overclaimed. Deliverable: software artifact — training code, trained OMatGRPO checkpoints, and generated structure sets are publicly released. Strengths: - The exact likelihood ratio for discrete element-commit events (Eq. 4, Appendix A) is a clean, correct technical derivation that makes composition a first-class policy action — a genuine methodological advance over latent- or continuous-relaxation approaches for 3D crystal generators. - The reward-hacking analysis is exemplary: five distinct exploit modes with per-run numbers, cross-protocol confirmation (16/20 offending packings pass MatterGen's own evaluation), induction-from-zero on a second pretraining corpus, and a group-size sensitivity test — this is the paper's most transferable contribution. - The reward-transfer experiment (Table 2) cleanly separates reward quality from pipeline quality, and the off-diagonal analysis (Appendix D) including an audit of whether their pipeline exploited the transplanted reward is more honest than typical comparisons. - Tiering every result by reference-phase count and showing that DFT cannot adjudicate sparse-tier claims regardless of potential agreement converts a benchmark critique into an actionable reporting standard. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors explicitly confront: (1) reward/benchmark circularity — novelty, uniqueness, and stability machinery are shared, and they quantify that ~80% of the gain survives removal of the overlapping creativity term; (2) the single-element exploit and its origin in RL training pressure, plus the benchmark flaw that admits such structures; (3) that a stability claim is only as good as its reference hull, hence the per-result tiering; (4) single-seed status of the reward-swap runs and the unseeded Chemeleon2 sampler (Appendix D); (5) unverified MP2020 correction status of LeMat-Bulk energies, resolved by leaving both DFT sides uncorrected. The authors treat limitations as findings rather than minimizing them — a notable credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - The valid-structure rate drops from 94.1% (prior) to 69.8% (OMatGRPO) — nearly a third of generations now fail structural checks — and the paper never analyzes what these failures are or their cost to effective sample efficiency; the mSUN-over-nominal convention makes the method look better than per-valid rates suggest (0.652 vs. 0.143 mSUN on valid, per Table 7). - Headline mSUN is single-seed; the 3.4× gain is large, but no seed variance for the main result is given, and the reward-swap cells (Table 2) with differences as small as 6.9 points are single-seed with an unseeded sampler. - The 12-reference abstention threshold and reward weights were tuned through exploit-closure runs evaluated against the same benchmark used for the headline number, so the final recipe has been co-adapted to the metric — the authors flag the component overlap but not this co-adaptation. - Only one generator family (OMatG) is natively trained; the Chemeleon2 result, while valuable, is a single transfer experiment, and no experiment tests the reward on a property other than stability (e.g., band gap, superconducting Tc), so generality of the reward design beyond mSUN-type objectives is untested. - Strict on-hull SUN is essentially unchanged (8 → 7), and the metastable structures are near-threshold (mean E_hull 0.070 eV/atom); whether the method finds materials meaningfully closer to synthesizability than the prior is not established beyond the DFT spot-check count. Bottom Line: A practitioner doing RL-aligned generative materials design should read this for both the first working scheme that reinforces crystal composition natively through discrete flow matching and the best-documented reward-hacking case study in the field; the mSUN gain is real but metastable-tier, the guard thresholds are benchmark-co-adapted, and no published alternative currently covers the same ground.

#21 — Innovative (74)

Context Language Models

Rulin Shao, Shannon Zejiang Shen, Junjie Oscar Yin, Yuetai Li, Minheng Wang, Hamish Ivison, Radha Poovendran, Nathan Lambert, Teng Xiao, Mike Lewis, Wen-tau Yih, Luke Zettlemoyer, Pang Wei Koh · arxiv.org · 🥇Top AI Papers of the Week
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces Context Language Models (CLMs), which give a language model unrestricted read–write control over its own live context by mirroring the context as a file the model can edit via Bash, and shows that this beats human-designed context-management harnesses while enabling in-context and reinforcement learning of context-management strategies. - Why it's important: Long-horizon agents (deep research, terminal coding, 24-hour optimization swarms) are bottlenecked by fixed, harness-defined context compaction policies that lose information or waste compute, and this work removes that ceiling by making context management a learnable model capability. - How it does it: The core trick is context-as-a-file: the live context is a synced file the model can arbitrarily rewrite (including defining reusable editing functions and new internal roles), paired with a prefix-reuse FLOPs metric that charges for re-prefilling after mid-context edits, a success-gated efficiency advantage in stepwise GRPO that re-ranks successful trajectories by FLOPs, and a Suffix Cache Reuse patch to SGLang that reuses KV cache beyond the matching prefix. - The good: Zero-shot, with no method-specific training, CLM reaches 59.4% on BrowseComp-Plus (Qwen3.6-27B, 32K context) — 11.4% above the strongest baseline with 21.5% fewer prefix-reuse FLOPs — and the pattern holds across TerminalBench 2.1, TBLite, OpenEvolve math problems, 12-hour EdgeBench, and a 24-hour six-repository agent swarm. - The missing: The RL gain over a trained summary harness is only 0.4 points (42.5% vs 42.1%) with no significance testing, several headline comparisons (math optimization, Software World) are single runs without error bars, and CLM's advantage is model-dependent — the 9B model without RL underperforms summarization by 6 points. - Read it or not: Read it if you build or train agentic systems or study context/memory management — the formulation, benchmark, efficiency metric, and serving technique are all immediately reusable; skip it only if you need results on models you cannot give Bash access to.
Why this rank
Scored using the Empirical profile. Novelty (80) is the strongest in the cluster: the context-as-a-file formulation — model-controlled unrestricted context transition replacing harness-defined compaction — is a real conceptual move, backed by a new benchmark, a FLOPs cost metric that charges the method for its own edits, and an SGLang serving patch. Non-Obviousness (80): showing that the constraint itself, not the strategy, was the bottleneck is a surprising result with emergent-behavior evidence. Rigor (68) is mixed — K-sensitivity and EdgeBench results have seeds and error bars, and code/benchmark are released, but the 0.4-point RL headline has no significance test, the RL comparison is not perfectly controlled (asymmetric auxiliary penalties), and math/swarm results are single runs. Completeness (72) benefits from direct safety discussion but is reduced by missing head-to-heads with published competitors and the unanalyzed 9B capability dependency. Impact (82) is high: released code, benchmark, and a serving patch valuable beyond this method. Weighted composite: 0.20*80 + 0.25*68 + 0.15*80 + 0.15*72 + 0.15*65 + 0.10*82 = 74.
