Problem & Motivation: Agents operating over hundreds to thousands of turns (deep research, terminal coding, multi-repo optimization) must decide what stays in a limited context window. Prior solutions fix this in the harness: Codex/Cursor-style summarization compacts at a length threshold; action-based methods (Self-Compact, AutoCompact, ACM, Context-as-a-Tool, Sculptor) let the model trigger compaction/offloading only within a human-defined action space; RLMs externalize the input but leave the live context append-only. Across this whole progression, the update policy is prescribed by humans, and the paper's ContextBench pilot shows these strategies fail even on simple synthetic tasks under context pressure (e.g., summaries hallucinate needles; coding tools can offload but cannot evict from live context). The gap closed is autonomy: no prior method lets the model define its own context-management operations on its live context. Key Idea: Make the context transition itself a learned, model-controlled function — c_{t+1} = f_CLM(c_t) instead of the append-only c_{t+1} = c_t ⊕ f_LM(c_t) — implemented as a mirrored, synced context file editable with general Bash commands. This one move subsumes prior constrained tool interfaces, extends naturally to multi-agent settings (multiple context files, subagent create/delete), and, because the strategy now lives in the model rather than the harness, makes context management steerable by natural language, improvable by textual skill evolution, and trainable by RL. Methodology: Three stacked contributions. (1) Implementation: the live context is mirrored to a file whose path is given in the system prompt; Bash edits to the file are synchronized into the context sent to the LLM server for the next turn; unedited turns append by default. Multi-agent extension: multiple coexisting context files. Costs are measured with a derived prefix-reuse FLOPs formula (re-prefill of tokens from the first prefix mismatch onward plus decode FLOPs), with per-token and attention constants worked out for the hybrid-attention Qwen3.6-27B. (2) Learning: in-context steering (one-sentence instructions change compaction timing/placement/backup behavior); a GEPA-style skill-evolution loop optimizing an instruction document s = argmax E[R(τ(x;s))] with train/dev/test separation; and RL via stepwise GRPO where trajectory-level outcome advantages are broadcast to all segments of the trajectory (necessary because edits break append-only structure), plus a success-gated efficiency advantage A_eff that clips the normalized FLOPs deficit among successful trajectories only (zero if fewer than two successes in a group), combined as A = A_out + w_eff·A_eff with w_eff = 0.25. (3) Serving: Suffix Cache Reuse (SCR), a SGLang patch that diffs the new prompt against the previous one, relocates up to K=6 surviving post-edit spans (re-rotating RoPE positions), falls back to standard prefill if slots are unavailable, and extends to hybrid linear-attention layers via recurrent-state snapshots. Key design decisions — unrestricted Bash edits rather than a constrained action space, FLOPs-based rather than length-based efficiency reward (explicitly to prevent reward hacking via wasteful edits), and K-capped relocation — are each justified, the latter with a sensitivity study over K ∈ {1..64}. Key Results: All out-of-the-box (untrained) comparisons use Qwen3.6-27B with a 32K context limit against Mini-SWE-Agent base, Codex-style Summary, MEM1, Self-Compact, ACM, and RLM. BrowseComp-Plus (830 questions): CLM 59.4%, +11.4% over the best baseline with 21.5% fewer FLOPs. TerminalBench 2.1: matches the best baseline with 29.5% fewer FLOPs; TBLite: 73.7% vs 67.0% with 91% of FLOPs. Math optimization (Claude 4.6 Sonnet, one run per method): CLM beats OpenEvolve on all four AlphaEvolve problems, e.g., Heilbronn 0.03653 vs 0.03127 (+16.8%) and circle packing 2.618 vs 2.541. EdgeBench-10 (12h, 3 seeds): CLM 44.6 at 179 PFLOPs vs summarization 42.3 at 437 PFLOPs; with Claude Sonnet, 51.0 vs 42.3. Software World (24h, 6-repo swarm, GPT-5.6-Sol, 272K budget): 65% greater held-out downstream speedup (1.044 vs 1.026 geometric mean) at matched spend. Learning: evolved skills improve held-out ContextBench KV Store accuracy 38.3%→74.2% (+35.9 points); RL on Qwen3.5-9B lifts BrowseComp-Plus 28.8%→42.5%, edging a trained summary harness (42.1%) at 1.34 vs 2.19 PFLOPs/question. SCR serves at matched accuracy (60.2%) with 65.0% of standard SGLang FLOPs (10.98→7.14 PFLOPs/question); notably, 5.3 of the 7.8 reused-token percentage points come from reasoning-token stripping in standard chat serving, not from CLM edits. ContextBench pilot: no baseline solves the simple tasks perfectly at up to 24× context pressure while CLM does. Baselines are current (2025–2026 methods), and the test scale is serious — real 12–24-hour runs, contexts to 272K tokens. Novelty Classification: NEW FORMULATION (model-controlled, unrestricted context transition replacing harness-defined compaction), NEW METHOD (context-as-a-file implementation; success-gated FLOPs-based efficiency advantage in stepwise GRPO), NEW DATASET/BENCHMARK (ContextBench diagnostic), NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING (emergent behaviors like custom chat roles and reusable compact_turns functions), and an ENGINEERING OPTIMIZATION (Suffix Cache Reuse in SGLang, building on known non-prefix cache-reuse ideas from PIE/CacheBlend/EPIC applied to agent live context). The genuinely new element is the degree of autonomy — the formulation is a one-line generalization of Eq. 1, but prior work stopped at constrained action spaces, and the paper demonstrates the gap is real. SCR and the evolution loop are competent applications of existing techniques (cache relocation; GEPA-style prompt evolution) to this new setting. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are present and informative: reward ablations (with/without FLOPs reward), K sensitivity for SCR with repeat runs and error bars, model-size comparison (9B vs 27B), 128K-budget EdgeBench replication, and a context-length-awareness probe. ContextBench uses 4–8 seeds; EdgeBench 3 seeds; SCR figures report ±1 standard error. However, math optimization is one run per method, the Software World comparison appears to be a single swarm per condition, and the 0.4-point RL win over the trained summary harness carries no significance test despite being a headline claim. Code is released at github.com/facebookresearch/context-language-models. Methodological concerns: BrowseComp-Plus grading depends on LLM judges (Qwen3.5-27B for evaluation, GPT-5.4-nano for RL reward), a known noise source; prefix-reuse FLOPs are a theoretical model of server compute, not measured wall-clock, energy, or dollars (except Software World's USD); EdgeBench-10 is a 10-task subset of a larger benchmark, with selection criteria not fully justified; several baselines (MEM1) are re-implementations. The stated 47.6% RL improvement is measured on held-out BrowseComp-Plus after training on OpenResearcher, which is properly out-of-distribution, but the checkpoint is selected on 500 validation questions from the training distribution. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (with a SYSTEMS component in SCR). Practical: Yes — the method needs only a code-execution harness and any served or API model, with no architecture changes; SCR is an SGLang patch with a safe fallback. Efficient: The method's whole thesis is efficiency: 21.5–59% fewer FLOPs than baselines in most settings, though mid-context edits can spike re-prefilling cost up to ~7.7× an append-only turn if the model edits badly (illustrative calculation), and RL training cost 16 H200s for the policy plus 48 rollout GPUs for 70 steps. Effective: Evidence covers real benchmarks and held-out packages rather than proxies, though accuracy gains on coding are parity-not-better and the RL gain over a trained harness is marginal. Scalable: Tested to 24-hour wall-clock runs and 272K context budgets; claims about scaling RL and distilling harnesses into CLMs are explicitly future work, not experiments. The work delivers a software artifact (code, ContextBench, SCR patch), not trained weights. Strengths: (1) The formulation is a real conceptual move: collapsing the entire harness-vs-action-space spectrum into a single unrestricted context transition, and showing the constraint itself — not the specific strategy — was the bottleneck, with the Bitter Lesson framing backed by qualitative evidence of emergent strategies (custom roles, reusable editing functions, orchestrator scoreboards). (2) Honest cost accounting: the prefix-reuse FLOPs metric charges CLMs for the re-prefilling their own edits cause, so the efficiency wins are not artifacts of a favorable metric. (3) The learning stack is well-conceived — because context management is now intrinsic, the same artifact is steerable by a sentence, improvable by textual evolution, and trainable by GRPO with a reward design (success-gated, FLOPs-based) that explicitly anticipates reward hacking. (4) SCR's finding that 5.3 of 7.8 points of reuse come from reasoning-token stripping gives it value beyond CLMs, for standard reasoning-model serving. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors directly confront the safety surface — an editable context is a persistent channel for prompt injections and self-generated instructions, citing OpenAI's observed self-injection in compaction summaries — and flag it as an open problem rather than minimizing it. They also document (Appendix G) that existing LMs have poor context-length awareness (bucketed estimates, e.g., recurring 6.2K/9.8K guesses), necessitating temporary environmental hints; note that CLM gains grow with model capability (the 9B model edits rarely and underperforms without RL); and identify an SGLang hybrid-model caching limitation (coarse recurrent-state checkpoints leave redundant unchanged-prefix prefill) as distinct from SCR itself. This directness is a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: (1) Statistical support is thin where claims are smallest: the 0.4-point RL win and the single-run math-optimization and Software World comparisons carry no error bars, yet anchor the learning and swarm sections. (2) The RL comparison trains the summary harness with task reward alone while CLM gets auxiliary penalties for failed tool calls and malformed outputs, so the 0.4-point comparison is not perfectly controlled. (3) Several related methods with published results — Memento, AgeMem, CompactionRL, Context Folding (used only in the pilot) — are absent from the main head-to-heads. (4) The capability dependency is under-analyzed: with Qwen3.5-9B, zero-shot CLM trails summarization by six points, meaning the headline claim "existing models can be turned into strong CLMs" holds mainly for frontier-scale or RL-trained models, and the paper does not chart where the crossover lies. (5) Failure recovery is under-specified: the BCP harness silently rolls back and retries on budget overflow (up to six times), so the reported behavior may mask lost-information failure modes; there is no measurement of how often destructive edits corrupt state. (6) Safety is discussed but not measured — no injection-resilience experiment accompanies the acknowledged risk. (7) The main benchmarks (coding, BCP) are also used to motivate design choices like the editing reminder, a mild develop-on/evaluate-on overlap. Bottom Line: For anyone building or post-training long-horizon agents, this is worth reading as the clearest demonstration yet that unrestricted model-controlled context beats hand-engineered management and is learnable — the honest cost metric, released code and benchmark, and reusable SCR technique outweigh the thin statistics on the learning results, though follow-up work should confirm the RL and swarm findings with proper replication.

Graph Anomaly Detection as Finite-Horizon Control: Training-Free Scoring via Empirical Bayes

F Xu, T Markovich, F Regol, Y Sun · arxiv.org · karypis - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces EB-GAD, a training-free node-level graph anomaly detection framework that models normality as a graph-aware generalized Ornstein–Uhlenbeck relaxation toward a graph-filtered template, fits the prior by empirical Bayes on the residual-field likelihood, and scores nodes with a closed-form finite-horizon control-energy bank selected without labels. - Why it's important: Unsupervised fraud and abuse detection on graphs currently requires training GNN detectors whose scores are opaque, GPU-hungry, and unstable across graph regimes (several baselines score below chance on Elliptic and Facebook); a deterministic, CPU-runnable, label-free scorer with calibrated nulls directly targets deployment cost and interpretability. - How it does it: A graph-Matérn precision (parameters ρ for graph trust, κ for length-scale, γ for template bandwidth) is fitted by maximizing a closed-form residual-space likelihood; the GOU's Gaussian transition then converts anomaly scoring into minimum control effort to reach each node from a feature-neutral start, with a label-free selector routing each graph to one of four score families (equilibrium, control energy, control ratio, profile aggregation). - The good: On 11 benchmarks with no labels used at any step, EB-GAD achieves best or tied-best AUROC on 9, including 84.8 on T-Finance (best baseline 63.1), 74.5 on Elliptic, 66.8 on DGraph (3.7M nodes), and 71.7 on YelpChi, with an explicit relabeling gate and every number regenerated under one disclosed pipeline. - The missing: The finite-horizon machinery contributes little per se — a single finite-horizon score is at parity with or below its equilibrium limit on 9–10 of 10 datasets (Appendix C.4) — so the headline gains rest on aggregation/normalization tricks and a selector whose 21 cutoffs were developed on the same 11 benchmarks it is evaluated on. - Read it or not: Worth reading for practitioners in unsupervised graph anomaly detection and for anyone interested in training-free, calibrated scoring at scale; skippable for readers seeking new diffusion/control theory, since the components are standard and the contribution is their calibrated composition.
Why this rank
Scored using Empirical profile. Rigor (78) is the strongest dimension — exhaustive ablations, a relabeling gate that caught the authors' own artifact, and released code — but is reduced by the post-hoc bandwidth rule chosen after seeing labels and a selector developed on the same 11 benchmarks it evaluates. Novelty (70) and Non-Obviousness (70) reflect a well-executed calibrated composition of standard ingredients rather than new theory; the finite-horizon control framing is largely decorative per the paper's own Appendix C.4. Completeness (80) is high due to unusually direct limitation acknowledgment, but Resilience (70) is pulled down by the disclosed Goodhart exposure and the hand-crafted selector with no out-of-benchmark transfer test. Impact (72) reflects a CPU-only, artifact-backed pipeline that scales where GNN baselines OOM, though with mixed AUPRC evidence. Problem & Motivation: Node-level graph anomaly detection (GAD) must rank nodes whose attributes and interactions deviate from graph regularities, in fraud detection, cybersecurity, and scientific networks, without labels. The authors identify three coupled decisions that existing methods make implicitly through architectures, message passing, and loss design: how much the graph structure should define normality ("graph trust"), which graph-spectral scales matter, and how deviations become a score. Because these are entangled with hyperparameter sweeps, resulting scores are opaque, expensive to produce, and unstable across graph regimes — the paper shows several baselines falling below chance AUROC on Elliptic and Facebook under native-score evaluation. The gap closed is a detector where these three decisions are explicit parameters of a single linear-Gaussian model, selected from unlabeled data. Key Idea: The core insight is that a graph-aware GOU process with graph-Matérn precision, whose stationary law is the EB-fitted normal-data prior N(m, Q̄ρ⁻¹), yields closed-form Gaussian transitions; the negative log-density of the endpoint given a feature-neutral start — identically the minimum control energy to steer the process to the observed node — is a per-node anomaly score, and varying the relaxation horizon Γ and endpoint tolerance λc produces a bank of scores sharing one fitted prior and one plug-in chi-squared null. Equilibrium Mahalanobis scoring is the Γ, λc → ∞ limit, so the framework strictly generalizes it. This is a calibrated composition of known ingredients (graph Matérn GPs, OU bridges, empirical Bayes, quadratic scores); the authors say so explicitly. Methodology: (1) Modeling: features are z-scored (optionally PCA-projected), a low-pass Matérn template m = (γ²I + L)⁻ν X is formed, and residuals Δ = X − m are modeled as N(0, Q̄ρ⁻¹) with Qρ = ρ(κ²I + L)^ν + (1−ρ)I (ν = 1 fixed). (2) EB fit (Algorithm 1): for each γ on a bounded grid, (ρ, κ) maximize the closed-form residual-space log-likelihood −½Σⱼ qⱼSⱼ + (D/2)Σⱼ log qⱼ (Theorem 1); the likelihood is concave in ρ (clamped Newton) and κ is grid-searched. (3) Scoring: per-node control energies Cᵢ(Γ, λc) and scale-normalized ratios CRᵢ = Cᵢ/(‖δΓ,i‖₂ + ε), with equilibrium limits J⋆ and R, form the bank. (4) Selection: an ordered rule set over label-free statistics (cosine feature homophily h, edge density dₑ, feature dimension Dₓ, truncation ratio k/n, plus NullKS and Berk–Jones goodness-of-fit diagnostics) routes each graph to one of four families and picks a member by percentile-normalized fitted-null deviation plus neighboring-rank stability. Critical design decisions: (a) the dynamical reading is representational, not a claim that data evolved via the SDE — well-justified via reversibility of the linear diffusion with the fitted stationary law; (b) the anchor bandwidth rule γₐ (grid value nearest a graph-statistic center) was adopted after the likelihood-selected bandwidth was evaluated on labels — a post-hoc choice the authors disclose candidly; (c) the selector's 21 cutoffs are implementation defaults developed on these benchmarks — acknowledged as engineering, not derived from a principle. Key Results: On 11 benchmarks (Weibo, Reddit, Amazon, YelpChi, BlogCatalog, Facebook, ACM, Elliptic, Elliptic++, DGraph, T-Finance; up to 3.7M nodes), against LOF, DIF, ANOMALOUS, DOMINANT, AnomalyDAE, CONAD, CoLA, DiffGAD, and TAM, EB-GAD is best or tied-best on 9 with no labels used at any step: T-Finance 84.8 (margin 21.7 over TAM's 63.1), Elliptic 74.5 (vs CoLA 65.3), Elliptic++ 72.5, DGraph 66.8, YelpChi 71.7, Amazon 78.0, Weibo 95.1, Facebook 91.4 (tie with TAM), Reddit 60.6 (level with CoLA 60.3); second on BlogCatalog (78.6 vs TAM 82.5) and ACM (86.0 vs 88.8). AUPRC is less favorable: best on the five fraud graphs (T-Finance 53.0 vs 6.6 best baseline) but fourth on Facebook (17.2 vs TAM 22.3) and at base rate on Reddit. Isolation studies show the EB-fitted GOU bank leads generic spectral precisions by 10.2–12.6 AUROC on the three large financial graphs, driven by label-free selectability rather than a better best-member score; elsewhere (e.g., Facebook, where a heat-kernel bank leads by 11.6) no family is consistently better. The finite horizon adds +3.6 to +4.7 AUROC on three datasets via aggregation/normalization and is at parity elsewhere; a single finite-horizon score matches its equilibrium limit within 0.3 points on 9 of 10 datasets. The method runs on 16 CPU threads in 8 seconds (Facebook) to 33 minutes (DGraph, 30 of which is eigendecomposition), versus 65–69 GPU-minutes for the in-memory trained baselines. A supervised upper bound (logistic stacking of the same scores) shows 8–17 points of untapped headroom on four datasets. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD (with an ENGINEERING OPTIMIZATION component). The genuinely novel element is the calibrated composition: attaching a single EB-fitted graph-Matérn prior to a horizon-indexed family of closed-form control-energy scores with a shared plug-in null, plus a predeclared label-free selector — the paper itself and correctly frames each ingredient (graph Gaussian priors, OU processes, Mahalanobis scoring, EB) as established. The GOU-as-scoring-dynamics framing for GAD and the relabeling-gated evaluation protocol are the most non-obvious pieces; the finite-horizon generalization of equilibrium scoring is conceptually clean but empirically contributes little on its own. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are unusually thorough: precision-family isolation, selector cutoff perturbation (21 cutoffs × ±25/±50%, selection unchanged in 99.4%/97.4% of evaluations), contamination stress (24% contamination costs 1.1 points on Weibo), misspecification stress on SBM graphs, neighboring-anomaly tests, and supervised stacking bounds. Determinism is verified via a relabeling gate; truncated-spectrum entries report mean ± std over five node orders. Code, protocol file, and table-regeneration scripts are released at github.com/heraclixus/EBGAD. This is a preprint (arXiv:2609.38424, NeurIPS 2026 submission), not yet peer-reviewed. Methodological concerns, most of which the authors volunteer: the anchor bandwidth rule for Weibo and Reddit was adopted after both bandwidth choices were evaluated on labels (Weibo 95.1/Reddit 60.6 with the rule vs 92.5/48.5 without — a Goodhart's-Law exposure, disclosed in detail); the selector's cutoffs were developed on the same 11 benchmarks used for evaluation; the YelpChi result of the submitted version (95.3) was a node-order artifact exposed by the relabeling gate and corrected to 71.7; and 8 of 11 baseline cells are the authors' own runs with published hyperparameters, with some cells imported from the TAM benchmark. Error bars: baseline seed-std reported; EB-GAD is deterministic given the eigenbasis. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (with a built, released artifact). - Practical: Yes — the full pipeline runs on 16 CPU threads with no GPU, and it scales to 3.7M nodes where most deep baselines OOM, via LOBPCG truncated eigendecomposition and eigen-caching. - Efficient: 8 s (Facebook) to 33 min (DGraph) wall-clock on CPU, generally faster than GPU-trained baselines (e.g., 33 min vs 65–69 min for CoLA/DiffGAD on DGraph), though the table is a cross-hardware, order-of-magnitude comparison, and the implementation redundantly recomputes the eigendecomposition per bandwidth. - Effective: AUROC evidence is strong on fraud graphs (up to +21.7 over the best baseline); AUPRC evidence is mixed (fourth on Facebook, base-rate on Reddit, where the authors themselves read the column as unsolved), so top-of-ranking precision — often what matters in fraud triage — is only partially demonstrated. - Scalable: Tested at 3.7M nodes (standard-to-stress scale for GAD); further 10–100× scaling would require sublinear eigensolvers not tested here, and no experiment beyond DGraph is reported. The work delivers a software artifact (released code, protocol, and regeneration scripts) plus a reusable recipe (EB-fitted graph-Gaussian null + score-bank selection); it stops at paper-plus-code form — no trained model or library packaging is claimed. Strengths: - Genuinely useful reframing: decomposing GAD into graph trust, spectral length-scale, and score choice as parameters of one linear-Gaussian model, then fitting them label-free in closed form — the interpretability and the shared plug-in null across the whole score bank are the real contributions. - Exceptional evaluation hygiene: the relabeling gate that caught the authors' own YelpChi artifact, full disclosure of every change from the submitted version (including dropping 95.3 to 71.7 and admitting the Weibo/Reddit bandwidth rule was chosen post-hoc), and a supervised-stacking diagnostic that quantifies the selector's untapped headroom rather than hiding it. - Honest scoping of where the mechanism does and does not help: the isolation study (Appendix C.3) shows the EB-fitted GOU's advantage is selectability on three financial graphs and explicitly disclaims superiority elsewhere — rare restraint. - Practical scalability design: truncated LOBPCG spectra, O(nk) spectral operations, and CPU-only execution make the method deployable where GNN detectors OOM. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors confront limitations directly and in detail (a strong credibility signal): (i) the selector's cutoffs are implementation defaults developed on these benchmarks with no transfer claim; (ii) the model does not identify the template bandwidth — the anchor uses a graph-statistic rule adopted after label evaluation, and Weibo/Reddit entries depend on it; (iii) the Gaussian residual model fails on binarized features (AUROC below 61) and costs 9–19 points under multimodal normal populations; (iv) BlogCatalog and ACM trail TAM and richer (high-pass/band-pass) filters do not close the gap; (v) truncated eigenbases are non-unique, giving up to ~2 AUROC variation on YelpChi; (vi) fairness: scores can encode degree/activity bias and need subgroup audits. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - The headline abstraction — "anomaly detection as finite-horizon control" — is under-delivered by the evidence: Appendix C.4 shows single finite-horizon scores are at parity with or below equilibrium scores on 9–10 of 10 datasets, so the control-energy framing is mostly a device for generating aggregatable family members rather than a source of new detection signal. A reviewer could argue the paper's title overstates its own mechanism. - The label-free selector is effectively a hand-crafted expert system (7 ordered rules, 21 cutoffs, family-specific pool windows and Gini thresholds) validated only on the 11 datasets it was designed on; the ±25% perturbation study tests local sensitivity, not out-of-benchmark transfer. No held-out graph family is ever shown. - The post-hoc anchor-bandwidth rule (decided after seeing labels on both options) is disclosed but still inflates the 9-of-11 count: an a-priori pipeline would report 7 of 11. - The supervised-stacking result (8–17 points of headroom on T-Finance, ACM, Elliptic, Elliptic++) is presented as a diagnostic, but it also suggests the label-free selector extracts substantially less than the score bank contains — the practical ceiling of the training-free claim is untested in any semi-supervised regime. - AUPRC weakness on Facebook and Reddit receives less prominence than the AUROC headline, and Reddit (3.3% anomalies, no method above base rate +1.2) is admitted unsolved but still counted in the benchmark suite. Bottom Line: A practitioner in unsupervised graph anomaly detection — especially fraud on large graphs without labels or GPU budget — gains something concrete and unusually well-audited from this paper, but should read it as a strong calibrated Mahalanobis detector with a cleverly assembled score bank and a hand-tuned selector, not as a validated control-theoretic breakthrough; the finite-horizon story is thinner than the framing suggests.

From Traces to Agentic Worlds: Agentic Language World Models for Interactive Environment Simulation (97 ▲ )

Quanyu Long, Xiao Chen, Jianda Chen, Haozhen Zhang, Qisheng Hu, Jianzhu Bao, Wenya Wang · arxiv.org · Daily papers of 9 Oct 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces Trace2Env, a learning-free framework that converts historical agent interaction traces into a structured "environment worldbook" operated by an agentic language world model, so a dedicated LLM agent can simulate an environment (predicting observations and persistent state effects) when the original executable system is unavailable. - Why it's important: Training and evaluating LLM agents requires environment replicas, but reproducing original systems (terminals, enterprise software, internal tools) is often infeasible while historical traces remain accessible — this closes the gap between trace availability and usable simulators. - How it does it: An offline constructor distills traces into schemas, grounded evidence, induced behavioral rules, and provenance; at runtime, a world model agent inspects this fixed worldbook plus per-episode state and memory, proposes a typed transition (state effects + observation), and a shared harness validates and commits it. - The good: The multi-turn consistency result is the strongest evidence: on ALFWorld, action sequences generated inside the simulator succeed in the real environment at a 0.914 consistency ratio versus 0.032 for direct prompting, showing the simulator preserves real dynamics rather than just internally coherent fiction. - The missing: No head-to-head comparison against Terminal-Universe, the closest prior system (executable reconstruction from traces), and the single-step evaluation relies entirely on LLM-judge scores that could favor the system's structured output style. - Read it or not: Worth reading for researchers building agent evaluation environments or language world models — it defines a credible new trace-only simulation setting and delivers unusually careful ablations — but practitioners needing a ready simulator for a specific system may find the engineering details thin without the code.

Rigor (73) is the standout strength — trajectory-clustered bootstrap CIs, cross-fitting leakage control, paired ablation standard errors, two backbone portability tests, and released code — but it is held back by total reliance on LLM-judge scoring for all single-step results and the missing head-to-head against Terminal-Universe. Non-Obviousness (80) is high: the finding that in-simulation success anti-correlates with real-environment transfer (97% vs 3% W2R) is a genuinely surprising insight with value beyond the paper. Novelty (78) reflects a real new formulation (trace-only simulation) though the components are competent combinations of known techniques. Completeness (70) and Resilience (68) are dented by the unresolved harness-vs-knowledge conflation and the unevaluated closest baseline, while Impact (72) benefits from the open-source release. Problem & Motivation: LLM agent developers and evaluators need interactive environment replicas for training, testing, and benchmarking without touching original systems. Original environments (a terminal image, an enterprise portal, a software workspace) may have unavailable code, data, or infrastructure, but recorded interaction traces — actions, observations, failures — usually survive. Existing trace-distillation methods produce artifacts that help the task agent act (skills, workflows, memories), and Terminal-Universe attempts full executable reconstruction, which fails when implementation details are absent from traces. The gap: no method turns traces alone into a stateful behavioral simulator that maintains long-horizon state continuity (e.g., a deleted file producing a missing-file error many turns later), since flat prompting conflates reusable environment knowledge with episode-specific state in one context window. Key Idea: Separate environment knowledge by scope and lifetime — an immutable, cross-episode "worldbook" reconstructed from traces (how the environment behaves), a mutable per-episode state (what is currently true), and episodic memory (what happened) — and make simulation agentic: a world model agent actively inspects these resources via tools, separates retrieval relevance from applicability (a retrieved trace's facts must not leak into the current episode), and proposes typed transitions that a deterministic harness validates against schemas and constraints before committing. Crucially, cross-episode evidence is labeled supporting / uncertain / format-only so that foreign file names and values are masked, preventing trace contamination of a new episode. Methodology: Two-phase pipeline. Offline reconstruction: a constructor LLM (gpt-5.6-sol in all experiments) aligns actions with results, extracts facts/candidate effects with uncertainty, induces action and state schemas (world/session/surface/epistemic paths), proposes transition rules reviewed by a falsification pass against supporting and contrasting cases (only "supported" rules become executable), induces observation contracts and notes, and links every artifact to its source turns as provenance; effects with ambiguous attribution are withheld. Online rollout: for each action, the world model agent receives a structured brief, inspects the workspace through ~10 read-only tools (read_state, search_knowledge, read_evidence, apply_rule, dry_run, etc.) within an 8-request/20-call budget, and submits a transition proposal (typed state effects, outcome, exact observation text, citations). A harness canonicalizes the action, gates retrieved evidence applicability, applies candidate effects to a state copy, validates against schemas/mutability/constraints, rejects-then-falls-back to observation-only if invalid, resolves the observation under rendering contracts, and commits state and memory. The framework is learning-free (frozen LLM weights, no fine-tuning); there is no explicit loss — objectives are implicit in construction prompts. Critical design decisions: (1) the three-way scope split (worldbook/state/memory), well-motivated by the episode-transfer problem and confirmed by ablation; (2) the applicability gate for cross-episode evidence, justified qualitatively and via the leakage analysis; (3) harness-side validation of model-proposed effects, which is a safety mechanism whose benefit is less directly ablated (the harness-only baseline conflates harness structure with state tracking). Key Results: Single-step next-observation prediction on 7 environments (Terminal/SWE/Android/Web splits of AgentWorldBench; Food/Shopping/Benefits from EnvScaler) with two backbones: Trace2Env averages 75.94 (gpt-5.6-sol) and 75.75 (deepseek-v4.1-flash) on the official gpt-5.2-judged 0–100 scale, versus 69.51/68.71 for the official Direct Prompting protocol (+6.43/+7.04 points), best in 11 of 14 environment–backbone pairs and never below Direct Prompting. Trajectory-clustered bootstrap CIs (10,000 resamples) exclude zero for the gain over Direct Prompting in every AgentWorldBench environment. Ablations: raw-trace RAG +2.66, static worldbook-in-prompt +3.31, harness-only +4.38 over Direct Prompting on Terminal; evidence contributes +2.45±0.89 alone while abstraction alone is −1.12, but they are complementary (evidence given abstraction +4.26±1.02). Removing the adaptive loop costs −1.79±0.91; removing state tracking −0.97±0.78. Gains persist on unseen-task subsets (e.g., Terminal no-overlap +3.69 [+1.71, +5.63] with GPT, though only +0.61 with DeepSeek). Multi-turn on ALFWorld/SciWorld: Direct Prompting achieves higher in-simulation success (97% ALFWorld WM vs 88% for Trace2Env) but collapses on real-environment replay (W2R 3% vs 85%; CR 0.032 vs 0.914); SciWorld CR 0.706 vs 0.529. Cost: Trace2Env uses 5.0 model calls and $0.187/record on Terminal vs 1.0 call and $0.04 for Direct Prompting (~4.7× cost, ~1.5× latency). Construction scales from 64.89 (20 traces) to 66.42 (36 traces), still rising, with build cost around $40 at the largest setting. Baselines are the current official benchmark protocol plus reasonable retrieval/static-context variants; no comparison to Terminal-Universe or other trace-reconstruction systems. Novelty Classification: NEW FORMULATION + NEW METHOD + NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING. Genuinely novel: the trace-only simulation setting (original environment unavailable at simulation time), the agentic world model that actively inspects a trace-reconstructed worldbook with explicit separation of cross-episode knowledge from episode state, and the finding that in-simulation success is anti-correlated with real-environment transfer for prompted LWMs (Direct Prompting hits 97% simulated success but 3% real replay). Standard components — agentic tool use, retrieval-augmented prompting, induction-and-review rule extraction, state tracking — are competently combined, and the worldbook idea is a domain-shifted relative of Agent Workflow Memory / Trace2Skill applied to the environment side rather than the task agent side. Rigor & Reproducibility: Strong. Component ablations isolate worldbook contents, adaptive inspection, and state tracking with paired standard errors; trajectory-clustered bootstrap CIs (10k resamples) treat trajectories as the independent unit; leakage is controlled via five-fold cross-fitting on SWE/Android, disjoint task splits for EnvScaler/ALFWorld, and explicit overlap stratification (Appendix B.3). Two backbones test backbone-portability of frozen worldbooks. Code is released (github.com/ruyue0001/trace2env). Concerns: (1) evaluation is LLM-judged (gpt-5.2) for all single-step results — a known noise and bias source, partially mitigated by the official protocol but not validated against human judgment; (2) the construction and headline evaluation model are the same (gpt-5.6-sol), so self-improvement/leakage at the model level cannot be fully excluded; (3) all baselines are prompting variants of the same systems — no executable-reconstruction or fine-tuned world model baseline (e.g., Terminal-Universe) is run despite being the closest motivation; (4) multi-turn evaluation covers only 100 ALFWorld and 40 SciWorld tasks, small samples where the 85% vs 3% W2R contrast is dramatic but the SciWorld difference (60% vs 45%) has no reported interval. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL (a runnable system evaluated on benchmarks). Practical: Yes — API-only, no training, works with two commercial backbone models on standard benchmark hardware; requires only trace collection plus one-time construction. Efficient: 3–5× the per-prediction cost of direct prompting ($0.19 vs $0.04/row on Terminal, 5 vs 1 calls) plus one-time build cost (~$10–40 per environment), with a documented lighter mode (no adaptive loop) retaining ~80% of the gain at 29% of the cost. Effective: The W2R/CR replay evidence shows it solves the stated problem (behavior-preserving simulation), not just the judged-observation proxy; single-step Factuality remains the weakest judged dimension (e.g., 50.5 on Terminal), so raw content fidelity is imperfect. Scalable: Not stress-tested — the trace-scaling curve is still rising at 36 traces (the maximum available), construction cost grows roughly linearly, and environments with richer state (319 Android state fields) already strain the schema approach; behavior at 10× trace volume or in production-grade systems is claimed only implicitly. Delivers a software artifact (open-source code) plus a reusable methodology; worldbooks themselves are environment-specific. Strengths: (1) The real-environment replay protocol (W2R/CR) is a genuinely meaningful faithfulness metric — it exposes that internally coherent simulation can be catastrophically unfaithful (3% transfer), an insight valuable beyond this paper. (2) The worldbook's provenance-linked, three-tier design (evidence, abstraction, schemas) with a falsification review pass is a concrete, auditable answer to the reliability/applicability problem that raw RAG-style trace reuse has. (3) Statistical discipline uncommon in this literature: clustered CIs, paired differences, cross-fitting, and explicit unseen-task stratification rather than pooled memorization-friendly averages. (4) The DeepSeek-on-GPT-worldbook results show the constructed knowledge transfers across backbones, supporting the claim that the worldbook is a reusable artifact rather than an idiosyncratic prompt. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state that fidelity "remains bounded by what the traces reveal" (simulation cannot exceed observed behavior coverage) and that "some backbones rely on reconstructed evidence less consistently than others" (visible in the DeepSeek Terminal unseen-task result of +0.61, CI crossing zero). They also note the trace-scaling curve is un-converged at 36 traces and that construction cost grows with data. They confront limitations directly and do not overstate — a credibility positive — though the discussion is brief and confined to the conclusion. Analyst-Identified Gaps: (1) The missing comparison: Terminal-Universe shares the trace-to-environment motivation and is cited, but no head-to-head or even shared-task comparison is run, so the claim that non-executable behavioral simulation beats or complements executable reconstruction is asserted, not measured. (2) All single-step evidence flows through one LLM judge whose criteria (Format, Realism) could structurally favor harness-rendered templated outputs; no human evaluation or exact-match metric on a subset is reported. (3) The harness conflates two effects — agent-loop structure and state management — such that "Harness only" beating full prompting baselines (+4.38) suggests much of the gain may come from scaffolding rather than reconstructed knowledge, a distinction only partially resolved. (4) The multi-turn result rests on 140 tasks in two text-game environments; the single-step benchmark environments (terminal, web, Android, SWE) are never evaluated multi-turn against a real replay, which is where the method's practical value claims live. (5) Worldbooks are built from successful trajectories only (EnvScaler, ALFWorld, SciWorld), yet the motivating story emphasizes traces containing failures — the sensitivity of construction to failure-sparse traces is untested. (6) The Shopping worldbook is built from just 3 trajectories, making the reported generality across "nine environments" uneven in support. Bottom Line: This is a substantive and unusually well-controlled step toward building simulators from traces alone — the replay-consistency finding alone justifies a read by anyone working on agent evaluation or language world models — but the absence of a head-to-head with executable reconstruction (Terminal-Universe) and the total reliance on LLM-judge scoring for single-step fidelity leave the central paradigm claim partially unproven.

On the Divergence of Accuracy and Mechanism Consistency in Time Series World Models

H Zhang, J Guo, Z Xu, Z Plotkin, N Konz, Z Tan, T Chen · arxiv.org · 10 new citations to your articles
TL;DR - What it does: This paper formalizes the time series world model (TSWM) problem, builds a benchmark of eight public action-conditional datasets spanning 12,205 engineered and clinical systems, sweeps three design choices (prediction space, plan fusion, plan encoding) across seven forecasting backbones and five seeds, and shows that prediction accuracy and mechanism consistency — whether shifting an action moves the forecast in a declared direction — diverge, then fixes the divergence with a directional-supervision loss that raises consistency above 0.99 at no MAE cost. - Why it's important: A world model is used to compare plans that were never executed (e.g., raising a vasopressor dose in an ICU), but current practice trains and evaluates forecasters only on the executed plan, so models deployed for decision support can respond to intervention in exactly the wrong direction — a documented failure in clinical and building-control applications. - How it does it: The core moves are (1) a mechanism-consistency metric that quantile-shifts one action channel and checks the sign of the forecast response against a declared mechanism, and (2) directional supervision, a loss term penalizing the wrong-signed fraction of the response to a perturbed plan, using a second forward pass through the frozen encoder and fusion/decoder only. - The good: The negative result is demonstrated at unusual breadth — every design choice across 5,040 distinct runs scores 0.46–0.59 mean consistency (chance is 0.5) on four of five mechanism datasets while PREDIST hits ~0.97, isolating the failure in the training objective rather than the architecture; the fix is validated with a null control, paired bootstrap intervals, and a held-out-direction check. - The missing: Reported MAE is measured on the same held-out set used for checkpoint selection and early stopping (no separate test set), and all 21 declared mechanisms were authored by the paper itself, so both the accuracy and consistency numbers lack an independent test surface. - Read it or not: Worth a full read for anyone building action-conditional forecasters or clinical/control decision-support models — the accuracy–consistency divergence is a field-level caution and the recipe (frozen AE latent space + output-side gating + sign penalty) is immediately actionable; skip it if you only need generic long-horizon forecasting benchmarks, since the design-space findings do not transfer there.

Scored using the Empirical profile. Novelty (78) is strong — a new problem formulation (action-conditional TSWM on real data), a reusable mechanism-consistency metric, and a benchmark consolidation. Rigor (74) is high — 5,040 runs, five seeds, dataset-level bootstrap, pre-registered analysis rules, null control, released code — but reduced for the untouched-test-set conflation, self-declared mechanisms, and preprint status. Non-Obviousness (80) is the paper's engine: the accuracy–consistency divergence with observational confounding inverting clinical drug signs is a counter-intuitive, field-level negative result that no architecture choice escapes. Completeness (68) is buoyed by unusually honest failure reporting (three held-out mechanisms moving the wrong way) but dragged by the unacknowledged selection-set issue and sign-only metric coverage. Resilience (70) and Impact (70) are solid: claims are mostly well-bounded, the recipe is cheap and released, though magnitude/timing behavior and closed-loop use are untested. Problem & Motivation: Practitioners in control, building operation, and clinical care need models that predict how a regulated state (blood pressure, indoor temperature, glucose) responds to a plan of future actions and exogenous inputs — a world model in the RL sense, here instantiated on multivariate time series. Current practice builds these as covariate-aware forecasters (TimeXer, TiDE, NBEATSx-style models) trained on prediction error under the executed plan; each paper compares its own design against two or three alternatives within its own architecture, so the design space has never been swept with the backbone held fixed. Worse, the evaluation practice never tests the model's response to a changed plan, which is the only use case that matters for plan comparison — and prior domain studies report that models accurate under the executed plan respond incorrectly to interventions. The gap is twofold: no systematic comparison of TSWM design choices on real (non-simulated) action data, and no metric that scores the direction of the response to an intervention alongside forecast error. Key Idea: The central technical insight is that mechanism consistency — agreement between the sign of the model's response to a quantile-shifted action and a domain-declared sign (e.g., more vasopressor → higher blood pressure) — is a property of the training objective, not the architecture: observational confounding (drugs are given when the state is already bad) plants the reverse sign in the data, and no swap of prediction space, fusion, or encoding escapes it, so the sign must be supplied as a soft penalty on the response to a perturbed plan (directional supervision, Eq. 5.2), which costs one extra fusion/decoder pass per batch since the backbone is plan-blind. The metric itself (quantile shift τ_δ via the empirical CDF of the action channel, with response-magnitude and mode-conditioning exclusions) is the second reusable idea. Methodology: The paper first formalizes the TSWM: channels are assigned roles (state, action, exogenous input); actions are decomposed into continuous, mode, and event components; the model maps (history, plan) → horizon outcome and is trained on MSE. The architecture is a state encoder → plan-blind backbone → fusion adapter → decoder, with three swappable design choices: (1) prediction space — observation, frozen AE, frozen VAE, or jointly trained JEPA (latent width 32); (2) plan fusion — None, Concat, Res, Res-0, FiLM-0, Gate, or cross-attention, all with explicit formulas in Appendix B; (3) plan encoding — identity, learned decay, dilated convolution, or causal self-attention, all zero-initialized. Three one-factor-at-a-time experiments run each option with 7 backbones × 5 seeds on 8 datasets (5,040 distinct runs plus 1,120 shared entries). Mechanism consistency is computed on held-out windows via |δ| = 0.1 quantile shifts over 21 declared mechanisms, with windows excluded when the shift does not change the plan or the forecast does not move (|∆| > 10⁻³·MAD). Directional supervision adds L_dir — the fraction of response mass with the wrong sign, with a stop-gradient denominator — scaled by ρ = 0.1 (selected by a pre-registered rule on a Greenhouse pilot), with δ ~ U(0.05, 0.30), upward shifts only in training; 12 mechanisms penalized, 9 held out, Wastewater as null control. Well-justified decisions: one-factor sweeps with paired seed-matched comparisons; pre-registration of the penalized mechanism split and ρ rule. Weakly justified: reporting validation MAE on the checkpoint-selection set, and the frozen-AE-vs-JEPA explanation ("the frozen latent space helps") is a hypothesis, not an isolated cause. Key Results: (1) Frozen AE latent space lowers MAE by 9.87% versus observation space (95% bootstrap CI [−17.71, −3.93]%, better on 8/8 datasets); VAE is within 2.59% of AE; jointly trained JEPA is 20.21% worse than observation space (0/8 datasets) — a counter-intuitive result against the JEPA trend from video world models. (2) Gate (−12.73%) and FiLM-0 (−12.58%) fusion at the output beat Concat on 8/8 datasets; cross-attention (−7.27%, 113k params) underperforms adapters under 50k params. (3) Plan encoding matters little: best option (Conv) changes average MAE by −2.2% and helps on only 4/8 datasets. (4) Mechanism consistency: mean MC across five datasets is 0.46–0.59 for all design choices (chance 0.5); PREDIST reaches 0.92–0.99 (direct actuator effects with no confounding) while VitalDB and MIMIC-Cardio are at or below chance, with clinical drug mechanisms learning the opposite sign (e.g., norepinephrine → mean pressure: 0.13–0.15). (5) Directional supervision lifts MC on the 12 penalized mechanisms to >0.99 (lowest single run 0.991) in both the trained upward and untrained downward directions, with pooled median MAE change of −0.05% (per-dataset medians −1.54% to +0.35%); the null control (Wastewater) reproduces Gate MAE to 0.0002. (6) Honest negative result for generalization: held-out mechanisms mostly stay below chance, and three move away from their declared sign (PleiaData cooling setpoint 0.373 → 0.000; vasopressin 0.531 → 0.182; remifentanil-MAP 0.284 → 0.156). The benchmark spans sampling intervals of 2 s to 30 min and state dimension ≤ 6 — a standard, not stress, scale. Novelty Classification: NEW PROBLEM (systematic design-space study of action-conditional forecasting as "world modeling" on real data), NEW FORMULATION (the TSWM formalization with three action types and the mechanism-consistency metric), NEW METHOD (directional supervision — though it is a straightforward sign-penalty relative to prior monotonicity-constraint and treatment-effect-ranking work such as Runje & Shankaranarayana 2023 and Zou et al. 2024, its application to forecasters under confounded controller actions is new), and NEW DATASET/BENCHMARK (the eight-dataset consolidation with 21 declared mechanisms). The genuinely novel parts are the mechanism-consistency metric on real interventional data and the accuracy–consistency divergence finding; the individual model components (AE latents, FiLM/Gate adapters) are standard techniques arranged in a sensible, well-instrumented pipeline. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are the paper itself — the entire design space is a controlled factorial sweep with the backbone fixed. Uncertainty is handled carefully: five seeds per cell, paired geometric-mean effects, percentile bootstrap over whole datasets (so an effect must survive dataset resampling), and a null-control run for the proposed loss. Pre-registration discipline is visible (mechanisms fixed before training, ρ selected by a pre-stated rule, one post-hoc exclusion — the Wastewater mechanism, whose timescale exceeds the 32-minute horizon — is explicitly flagged as made after seeing the numbers). Code, preprocessing, the MIMIC-Cardio extraction script, and all run configurations are released at https://github.com/HaochenZhang717/TSWM-Official-Repo; MIMIC-IV data itself is not redistributable so only extraction code ships. Methodological concerns: (a) the reported "held-out" MAE comes from the same split used for checkpoint selection and early stopping — there is no untouched test set, so absolute MAE values may be mildly optimistic, though all comparisons share this bias; (b) mechanism signs are declared by the authors, and the evaluation metric is designed by the same authors who then propose the method that optimizes it — a self-referential loop, partially mitigated by held-out mechanisms and directions; (c) the MC metric conditions on the forecast moving, and 85 of 3,150 cells fail this condition, which is reported rather than counted as chance but still reduces coverage. This is a preprint (arXiv 2610.01842, October 2026) and has not been peer-reviewed. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL (benchmark + method with experiments the authors ran). Practical: Yes — adapters of 26–114k parameters, 32-d latent spaces, and TFB-default backbones run on commodity hardware; the MIMIC extraction requires credentialed access but that is a data-governance, not hardware, issue. Efficient: Directional supervision costs one extra pass through the fusion and decoder per batch (the backbone runs once), and frozen codecs are shared across seeds; overhead relative to plain Gate training is small. Effective: It demonstrably solves the stated problem — sign-correct response to a changed plan at unchanged accuracy — but only for supplied mechanisms; it solves a proxy for the deeper goal of correct interventional prediction, since magnitude, timing, and undeclared mechanisms are unconstrained. Scalable: Not tested — state dimension is ≤ 6 and horizons are 16 steps everywhere; behavior at longer horizons (where the Wastewater mechanism already fails), higher-dimensional states, or closed-loop use is untested, and the authors name closed-loop evaluation as future work. The work delivers a software artifact: a released repository with benchmark, metrics, training/evaluation code, and run configurations — not pretrained model weights as a standalone deliverable. Strengths: - The divergence finding is a real, broadly relevant empirical result: accuracy-selected configurations score at or below chance consistency on 4/5 mechanism datasets (e.g., Gate at 0.36 on VitalDB), across 7 backbones and 15 design configurations — this is evidence against a whole evaluation paradigm, not one architecture. - Exceptional experimental hygiene for a benchmark paper: paired seed-matched contrasts, dataset-level bootstrap, a true null control (Wastewater, MAE agreement to 0.0002), bitwise verification of counterfactual forecasts, and the DUET router-determinism wrinkle documented to 1.1×10⁻³. - The confounding explanation (dose responds to the state, so the observational sign inverts the mechanism) is stated, mechanistically plausible, and consistent with the PREDIST-vs-clinical contrast — the sharpest diagnostic in the paper. - The paper reports its own method's failures in full: three held-out mechanisms move away from their declared sign under directional supervision, and the PleiaData mode-anticorrelation analysis (ρ = −0.86 across 506 cells) is exactly the kind of self-audit most benchmark papers omit. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state that directional supervision enforces only the signs it is given and does not recover undeclared mechanisms or constrain effect sizes; that a wrongly declared sign would be enforced as faithfully as a correct one (ethics statement); that the metric checks sign only, saying nothing about magnitude or safety; that extension to event actions, clinical validation of declared pharmacological signs, and closed-loop control evaluation remain future work; and they transparently disclose the one post-hoc mechanism exclusion (Wastewater) and the two pre-evaluation exclusions. This is direct confrontation with limitations rather than minimization — a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - No untouched test set: the held-out split serves for checkpoint selection, early stopping, and reported MAE. All reported errors are selection-set errors; the paper never acknowledges this conflation. - The 21 mechanisms are authored by the paper's own authors and never validated by independent domain experts (the ethics statement recommends expert review), so both the metric and the method optimize against a self-declared ground truth. - Only sign, never magnitude or timing, is scored: a model could pass MC with a 10⁻³-scale response that is clinically useless; no calibration or effect-size evaluation exists. - Mechanism-consistency results rest on small per-dataset mechanism counts (1–4 after penalized/held-out splits), and the MIMIC-Cardio drug mechanisms inherit all the confounding of observational ICU charting — the paper shows the model fails there but cannot verify what the true sign structure is beyond pharmacology textbook priors. - The frozen-AE-beats-JEPA finding gets a one-sentence hypothesis ("the frozen latent space helps") without an ablation isolating whether the problem is joint training instability (JEPA's seed variance is noted as highest) or something else; the recipe's recommendation is therefore empirical, not explanatory. - Rolling-out evaluation exists only as an appendix diagnostic for the auxiliary loss, not for the directional-supervision model or for the main design-choice winners, so the recommended recipe is never tested beyond teacher-forced 16-step horizons. Bottom Line: Read it — this is the rare benchmark paper whose negative result (accurate forecasters respond wrongly to intervention, and no architecture fixes it) plus a cheap, validated fix (sign-supervised response at zero accuracy cost) will change how anyone building action-conditional forecasters for control or clinical use should train and evaluate them, provided they accept that the method certifies only the signs they explicitly supply.

How Much of a Harness Does a Strong Agent Need for Autonomous ML Engineering?

K Brilliantov, A Hernández-Cano, E Abbé · arxiv.org · 10 new citations to your articles
TL;DR - What it does: This paper builds Malena, a minimal baseline consisting of a single long-running, well-prompted coding agent session on OpenCode with three small tools (submission registry, system status, background jobs), and shows through controlled ablations that it matches or beats four open-source state-of-the-art MLE harnesses under matched backbones, hardware, and 24h time budgets on MLE-bench and NatureBench. - Why it's important: The autonomous ML engineering field is investing heavily in elaborate scaffolding (tree search, multi-agent orchestrators, memory hierarchies), and this work argues — with budget- and backbone-matched evidence — that most of that machinery yields no measurable return on frontier models, redirecting effort toward backbone and runtime instead. - How it does it: The core move is a ladder of harness interventions re-implemented in a single codebase — chat vs. coding-agent interface, four search strategies (Chain, Greedy, UCB1, Best-of-N), full agent autonomy, and three multi-agent coordination mechanisms — evaluated with paired-by-task bootstrap confidence intervals at fixed model and compute, then cross-checked against released external harnesses. - The good: The matched comparison is unusually rigorous for this literature: on the 30-task fixed MLE-bench split with GLM 5.2, Malena achieves a 62.5% any-medal rate vs. 47.1% for the best external harness, with paired-by-task 95% CIs favoring Malena significantly in most backbone pairs, and the authors document their tuning effort on baselines in detail. - The missing: Statistical power is the binding constraint — several key conclusions rest on overlapping confidence intervals (e.g., multi-agent arms, context-window ablations), and MLE-bench's known preparation bugs and Kaggle contamination risk mean the headline benchmark may flatter agentic capability in ways the NatureBench follow-up (only 3 harnesses, 2 backbones, 8h budget) cannot fully rule out. - Read it or not: Anyone building or reviewing MLE/agent harness papers should read it — it is now the reference null result and methodological template (paired-by-task CIs, seed-effort accounting) for the field, while readers outside agentic ML can skip it.

Completeness (80) is the highest in the cluster: limitations are quantified where claims weaken, and the authors correctly restrict themselves to no-worse-than statements. Non-Obviousness (75) reflects the genuinely counter-intuitive attribution result that search topology, autonomy shaping, and multi-agent orchestration are statistically redundant given strong coding-agent backbones, with a trace-analysis mechanism explaining why. Novelty (70) is a NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING rather than a new method, and Resilience (72) is bounded by acknowledged statistical power limits and MLE-bench contamination risk. Practical Impact (65) is discounted because no code release URL is stated despite the detailed reproducibility apparatus. Problem & Motivation: Autonomous machine learning engineering (MLE) agents — systems that produce Kaggle-style ML pipelines end to end — are evaluated on leaderboards like MLE-bench, but their published gains are confounded: harness performance has risen alongside backbone capability, evaluations rarely share backbones or seed counts, and a single 24h × 3-seed × 75-task rerun costs thousands of GPU hours, so faithful re-comparisons are rare. Meanwhile, harnesses have grown elaborate (search trees, populations, memory, agent teams) on the premise that a single LLM completion cannot execute code or manage context — a premise weakened by coding-agent-post-trained models with million-token windows. The open question the paper attacks: which parts of the harness still earn their keep when the backbone can already run code, inspect data, and debug in one session? Key Idea: Treat every harness component as a separable intervention and ablate them at fixed backbone, hardware, and time budget; the hypothesis is that coding-agent post-training substitutes for hand-crafted scaffolding, so the only high-leverage intervention is giving the model a shell, filesystem, and execution primitives (the coding agent environment), after which search topology, autonomy shaping, and multi-agent orchestration are redundant — an instance of Sutton's bitter lesson for MLE. Methodology: The pipeline is built on OpenCode v1.15.6, served locally with vLLM, with fixed resources (1×A100 80GB, 12 CPU cores, 144GB RAM) and a shared prompt template across iterations. The ablation ladder runs: (1) Chat (single completion, error-loop debugging) vs. Oneshot (one coding-agent session producing one submission in 6h); (2) search primitives chaining Oneshot iterations at a matched 24h budget — Chain (iterative refinement), Greedy (exploit best validation), UCB1 (rank-normalized upper-confidence bound with max-backup), Best-of-N (independent runs); (3) Malena — a single session spanning the full budget, re-prompted to continue, with submission/system/jobs tools; (4) orchestration interventions — delegation via subagents, 3-way parallelism, and a broadcast messaging tool. Primary benchmark is MLE-bench (a fixed30 task split: 5 Lite, 21 Medium, 4 High; four broken tasks repaired with documented diffs) plus NatureBench (40 Nature-family SOTA-matching tasks, 8h budget). Metrics are any-medal rate and mean percentile under self-select vs. oracle selection, macro-averaged with 95% bootstrap CIs and paired-by-task difference CIs; a trace analysis annotates checkpoints with ML-technique labels (Qwen3-Embedding-8B clustering, GLM 5.2 as judge) to compare search behavior. Critical design decisions: reimplementing interventions in one codebase for clean attribution (well-justified), fixing MLE-bench preparation bugs before comparison (well-justified, diffs published), and a fixed 0.1× cache-read cost model for USD estimates (acknowledged as approximate since harnesses don't report real cache hits). Key Results: With GLM 5.2 on MLE-bench fixed30 at 24h, Malena achieves 69.74 self-select / 71.56 oracle percentile and 62.5% self-select any-medal rate, versus the best external harness (AiScientist) at 61.39 / 62.35 and 47.1%; paired-by-task differences favor Malena significantly over all four harnesses at GLM 5.2 (e.g., +22.16pp percentile, +38.1pp medal rate over ScienceFlow) and over MLEvolve and AiScientist at Kimi K3. The coding agent environment is the dominant effect: frontier backbones (GLM 5.2, Kimi K3) improve dramatically from Chat to Oneshot, and even Gemma 4 31B benefits. Search strategy is indistinguishable (largest gap: UCB1 over Best-of-N by 2.71pp, CI [−1.44, +6.60]); Malena shows the lowest validation-selection gap (1.876pp vs. Best-of-N's 6.832pp). Multi-agent additions do not help: delegation lowers medal rate (45.2% vs. 55.7% base), broadcast+parallelism hurts significantly (+22.4pp medal-rate difference in favor of base), and parallelism raises oracle but not self-select performance. One exception: on the weak Gemma 4 31B backbone, MLEvolve beats Malena by 10.53pp percentile (CI [−14.72, −6.36]), suggesting harness priors still matter for weak models. Cost analysis shows Malena's modeled inference cost ($12.12/run at GLM 5.2) is ~6.2× AiScientist's due to cache-read resending of its ever-growing session, though hardware ($24–85/24h A100) dominates total cost. Trace analysis shows Malena shifts from balanced pipeline techniques toward ensembling/pseudo-labeling late in runs while using comparatively rare techniques, i.e., it performs the adaptive search harnesses hard-code. Novelty Classification: NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING — the genuinely novel contribution is the controlled, budget- and backbone-matched demonstration that harness machinery is statistically redundant given a strong coding-agent backbone, plus the paired-by-task statistical protocol applied to this domain. Malena itself is deliberately a minimal baseline (an engineering assembly of OpenCode plus three tools and a prompt), and the search/UCB1 components are standard techniques; the paper's value is the attribution result, not a new algorithm. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are the core of the paper and are systematic: four intervention families, paired-by-task 95% CIs, multiple backbones (7+ models), and separate self-select vs. oracle reporting that surfaces the selection gap honestly. Seed counts and per-task imputation of failed runs are documented; two data caveats (uneven seeds, tie creation from imputation) are acknowledged by the authors themselves. A dedicated appendix (D.3) documents tuning effort on each external harness, including adopted fixes (e.g., MLEvolve reasoning effort on DeepSeek V4 Flash, which alone moved its medal rate from 0% to 25% on the ablation subset) — a strong mitigation of tuning asymmetry. Notably, some published baselines were evaluated at what the authors found to be misconfigured settings, and their corrections are disclosed. The paper develops its interventions on MLE-bench and evaluates partially on the same benchmark, mitigated by NatureBench. No public code or model release URL for Malena is stated in the provided text; the reproducibility statement enumerates appendices (task lists, prompts, tool specs, diffs, statistical protocol) but does not name a repository. Confidence intervals are wide enough in several arms that the authors correctly limit themselves to no-worse-than claims in places. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (with a SYSTEMS artifact — the Malena harness). Practical: Yes — runs on one A100 80GB with locally served open-weight backbones via vLLM. Efficient: Inference token cost is 6.2× the cheapest harness at GLM 5.2 (dominated by cache-read tokens from single-session context resending), though total cost is hardware-dominated. Effective: Evidence shows it matches or beats harnesses on MLE-bench and NatureBench under matched conditions; the selection-gap result (1.876pp) supports that the reported submission quality is genuine, not just a proxy. Scalable: Not tested beyond 24h and 3-way parallelism; single-session context overflow is only probed via an artificial 64k cap (performance drops, CIs overlap), and the authors flag long-horizon coordination as open. The work delivers a concrete harness implementation described in detail, but no public artifact URL is stated; it stops at paper form plus detailed appendices. Strengths: - The controlled attribution design — all interventions re-implemented in one codebase with matched model, hardware, and time budget — finally separates harness effects from backbone effects, which prior leaderboard comparisons could not. - Unusually careful statistics for this area: paired-by-task CIs that cancel task difficulty, explicit self-select vs. oracle decomposition, and a transparent accounting of the validation-selection gap as a first-class metric. - The tuning-effort appendix (D.3) and the published MLE-bench repair diffs (data leakage in hubmap, smartphone, multi-modal; missing test geometry in champs) are concrete, verifiable contributions beyond the headline claim. - The trace analysis provides a mechanism, not just a null result: Malena trades rare techniques against late-run performance focus and reuses its own artifacts, explaining why hard-coded search structure adds nothing. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state four: (1) reliance on MLE-bench with its known task-preparation issues and plausible Kaggle contamination (mitigated by task fixes, contamination checks, and NatureBench); (2) limited statistical power, with CIs wide enough that only no-worse-than claims are strongly supported; (3) scope — interventions tested operate within a single worker, with deeper coordination protocols left to future work; (4) possible tuning asymmetry favoring Malena, mitigated and documented in Appendix D.3. They confront limitations directly and quantify where claims weaken — a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: Beyond the acknowledged limits: (1) the NatureBench generalization test covers only 3 of the 4 harnesses (ScienceFlow and Arbor absent), 2 backbones, and an 8h budget — half the MLE-bench budget — so the strongest cross-benchmark evidence is thinner than the headline; (2) the cache-read cost model (0.1× input price) is uniform and unvalidated against real provider telemetry, so the 6.2× cost figure for Malena is directional; (3) NatureBench's oracle-best-of-run metric mechanically rewards harnesses that make more /evaluate calls (the authors note Malena and AiScientist call ~2× more than MLEvolve), an asymmetry that could deflate MLEvolve's number; (4) imputing failed runs at worst-percentile creates ties between distinct failure modes with outsized leverage on point estimates — the authors note this in D.2 but headline tables still use it; (5) all backbones are open-weight models served locally; no closed frontier API model is tested, so the claim that scaffolding is redundant for "frontier" models rests on one vendor-agnostic class of backbones; (6) no code release URL appears in the text, limiting independent verification despite the reproducibility statement. Bottom Line: For anyone building or evaluating MLE agents, this is essential reading — it sets the statistical standard the field lacks and delivers a credible, well-controlled null result that hand-crafted scaffolding buys little on strong coding-agent backbones — though its conclusions should be quoted with the authors' own caveat that they are no-worse-than claims on a contaminated-prone benchmark rather than proven universal redundancy.

Leto: Fast In-Place Recovery for LLM Training on Surviving Hardware

GW Kim, JH Kim, D Kim · arxiv.org · 10 new citations to your articles
TL;DR - What it does: This paper builds Leto, a fault-tolerant LLM training system that recovers from hardware-operable failures (HOFs) in place by retaining the live model state and preinitializing a shadow trainer on the same node, avoiding checkpoint reload and recomputation entirely. - Why it's important: Large training jobs stall entire GPU fleets when a single trainer fails, and at projected failure rates for 131,072-GPU jobs, recovery overhead can consume over 10% of wall-clock time even with state-of-the-art in-memory checkpointing. - How it does it: Leto decouples state lifetime from process lifetime via a state manager owning GPU allocations across process failures, protects model state with two-tier Reed–Solomon erasure coding whose parity lives in host memory (not scarce HBM), makes in-place optimizer updates crash-consistent with chunk-level transactions, and reclaims a shadow trainer's prebuilt GPU state on demand to avoid OOMs. - The good: Measured recovery drops to 6–19 s versus 60–180 s for the strongest checkpointing baselines (Gemini, Gemini+, MoEvement, JIT-Ckpt) across five dense/MoE models, with a careful correctness experiment showing bit-exact loss reproduction after mid-update failures plus injected HBM page loss. - The missing: Real hardware evaluation stops at 72 GPUs; the 131,072-GPU claims come from the authors' own simulator, and all failures are injected via SIGKILL plus emulated page retirement rather than observed in production. - Read it or not: Read it if you build or operate distributed LLM training infrastructure — it demonstrates a concrete, quantified alternative to checkpoint-based recovery — but skip it if you need validated results beyond 72 GPUs or non-synthetic failure data.
