Problem & Motivation: Hybrid LLMs (Qwen3.8-27B with Gated DeltaNet, Kimi-Linear-48B-A3B-Instruct with Kimi Delta Attention) replace the growing KV cache with a fixed-size recurrent state, but each concurrent request still needs a persistent FP32 state matrix (plus reserved scheduling slots), so the state pool grows linearly with concurrency even for short contexts — in official SGLang deployment, Qwen's FP32 state pool exceeds its BF16 weight footprint at 70 concurrent requests. Uniform low-bit quantization of these states fails badly because quantization error is fed back into every subsequent Delta update (mean long-task accuracy drops to 45.04% for Qwen at INT6 and 12.73% at INT4), and prior state-quantization work (Quamba2, Q-Mamba) targets Mamba-style SSMs rather than GDN/KDA recurrences, while the concurrent DAMP method only reaches INT8-level precision (9.9 bits). Key Idea: Quantization error in a recurrent Delta-rule state matters along two coupled axes — temporally, error persistence is governed by the gate retention factor (Proposition 1: E_t = A_t E_{t-1} + ε_t with ‖A_t‖ ≤ 1, so errors in directions misaligned with future keys decay only via gate decay), and spatially, key rows with higher readout sensitivity ω_i = E[g²_{t,i}] amplify equal-magnitude errors into larger output error. These two diagnostic observations translate directly into a per-unit lifetime-weighted distortion objective for bit allocation and a row-impact-weighted dual-axis (row × column) scaling scheme. Methodology: The framework operates as an offline calibration phase plus an online decode path. Offline: on 32 WikiText-2 segments (2,048 tokens), it estimates (i) mean log retention ℓ_u per allocation unit (per-head for Qwen/GDN, per-key-row for KDA), yielding lifetime weights L_u = Σ_j exp(2jℓ_u); (ii) per-bit candidate distortions d_u(b); and (iii) key-row impact scores ω_i from the transported readout g_t = A_t^T q_t. Bit allocation solves min Σ_u L_u d_u(b_u) subject to a total bit budget (multiple-choice DP for Qwen, Lagrangian allocation for KDA), with ~1.39% of Qwen heads (32) and 512 KDA key rows kept as FP16 sparse pivots. Online: each updated state X is reconstructed as X̂_ij = r_i c_j z_ij where row factors r_i = m_i^{1/2} w_i^{-1/2} blend row magnitude and impact (w_i from fractional-power-normalized ω_i, γ = 0.25), and column scales c_j minimize a w²_i-weighted least-squares fit — a closed-form update on stored codes. A fused SGLang kernel (v0.5.12 pin) reconstructs, applies the Delta update, and computes the readout in one pass, with scale refitting and packed writeback overlapped on a separate CUDA stream. Critical design decisions: (1) gate-only lifetime as the persistence proxy — a simplification the authors acknowledge does not model the key-dependent transition; (2) FP16 pivot units chosen by residual allocation risk, justified by a +6.70-point ablation swing at 4 bits; (3) square-root magnitude scaling with γ = 0.25 impact tempering — heuristically justified by analogy to SmoothQuant-style smoothing rather than derived from first principles. Key Results: On Qwen3.8-27B BF16, STEPQuant@6bit achieves 80.59% mean over seven long-generation tasks (FP32: 80.60%) and 87.54% over six short tasks (FP32: 87.78%), versus 45.04%/82.49% for uniform INT6; at 4 bits it scores 80.51% (long) and 87.63% (short), beating uniform INT8 (71.86%/86.25%). On Kimi-Linear-48B, STEPQuant@6bit reaches 61.47% (long) vs. FP32's 61.52%, and 4-bit reaches 58.52% vs. INT8's 56.02%. With W4-AWQ weights, 6-bit STEPQuant is within 0.05 (Qwen) and 0.33 (Kimi) points of the FP32-state baseline. Ablations (Qwen, 3 tasks): at 4 bits, full method 84.72% vs. spatial-only 73.95%, temporal-only 12.87%, Q-Mamba DSQ 7.64%, uniform INT4 3.97%. Serving: 5.03×/5.08× recurrent-state compression (Qwen/Kimi), 68.7%/53.7% total serving memory reduction at batch 512, state-update speedup of 2.91× (Qwen) and 1.78× (Kimi), and full decode throughput gains up to +20.53% (Qwen) and +11.80% (Kimi) at batch 512. Against the concurrent DAMP (cross-study, uncontrolled), STEPQuant@6bit retains 100.51% of FP32 accuracy at 6.30 effective bits vs. DAMP's 100.99% at 9.9 bits. Uniform quantization also induces severe overthinking (Kimi INT4 averages 41.07K generated tokens vs. 11.87K for FP32); STEPQuant keeps lengths near FP32. Baselines (uniform INT4/6/8, Q-Mamba DSQ, AWQ weights) are reasonable but limited — no other mixed-precision or rotation-based state-quantization competitors are run directly. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD with a NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING component: the genuinely novel elements are (i) the lifetime-aware bit-allocation objective that couples per-unit gate retention with mixed-precision distortion, and (ii) the demonstration that recurrent-state outliers appear along both key-row and value-column axes (max-to-median RMS contrasts of 10.3×/19.4×), requiring dual-axis rather than single-axis scaling. The dual-axis scaling itself adapts known techniques (SmoothQuant-style smoothing, pivot/int4 mixed precision à la SpQR/IntactKV) to the recurrent-state setting, and the readout-impact score derives from a straightforward first-order sensitivity identity. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations isolate each component (temporal, spatial, pivots, and the Q-Mamba DSQ baseline) on both models under matched bit budgets, and the paper supports its analysis claims with controlled mechanism experiments (feedback-removal oracle showing 26.82× error reduction from Delta feedback, Spearman ρ ≈ 0.80 between gate half-life and accumulated error across all 2,304 Qwen heads and 81,920 KDA channels, held-out row-impact validation with direct-propagation checks to 7.1×10⁻⁷ relative error). However: no error bars, multiple seeds, or significance tests are reported for benchmark accuracies; calibration uses a single small source (32 WikiText-2 segments); the DAMP comparison is explicitly cross-study and uncontrolled; and the serving evaluation uses one hardware configuration (4× A800, TP4, fixed 128-token prompts, greedy 1,024-token decode). Code is stated as released at https://github.com/Dreamer-Toby/STEPQuant. The paper is an arXiv preprint (2609.38169), not peer-reviewed. The storage claims are candidly separated into analytical compact counts versus measured packed allocations, which is a credibility positive. Deployability (4-property check): EMPIRICAL/SYSTEMS profile — the paper both runs extensive accuracy experiments and ships a serving-integrated tool. - Practical: Runs on four commodity A800 GPUs within SGLang, a mainstream open-source serving stack; no exotic hardware. - Efficient: Reduces recurrent-state memory by ~80% (5.03×) and state-update time by 65.6% (Qwen, 2.91×), and even improves end-to-end decode throughput (+4.3% to +20.5%), because state I/O dominates at high batch. - Effective: Evidence covers both accuracy (near-FP32 at 6 bits, near-INT8-beating at 4 bits, on 13 benchmarks) and the real deployment target (total serving memory −68.7%), though with W4 weights at 4-bit state Qwen generates ~31.6% longer outputs, a partially unresolved side effect. - Scalable: Tested at batch sizes up to 512 on TP4; behavior under dynamic workloads, other hardware, and larger deployments is acknowledged as unverified. The work delivers a concrete software artifact: quantization code, checkpoint-specific precision maps, and fused packed-state kernels in SGLang 0.5.12, with a public GitHub repository. Strengths: - The error-propagation analysis (Proposition 1 and the oracle experiment isolating Delta feedback, +26.82× accumulated error) is a genuine mechanistic insight that explains why uniform quantization fails here, not just that it does — most PTQ papers lack this diagnostic layer. - The temporal and spatial components are complementary by design and the ablation proves it: neither alone recovers FP32 accuracy at 4 bits (12.87% and 73.95% vs. 84.72% combined on Qwen), which is unusually clean evidence for a two-component method. - Calibration statistics are validated at population scale across independent text sources (lifetime rankings stable across WikiText/C4/LiveCodeBench with Spearman ρ ≈ 0.98–0.99), supporting robustness of the offline phase beyond a single calibration corpus. - Honest accounting: analytical vs. measured bit costs are separated, the W4-weights configuration is evaluated (a setting most quantization papers skip), and generation-length/overthinking side effects are measured rather than hidden. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state (Appendix H) that the lifetime weight approximates persistence through gate decay only and ignores the time-varying, key-dependent transition; that KDA loses accuracy at 4-bit state on long-generation tasks with BF16 weights (92.91% retention) and Qwen produces longer outputs; and that evaluation covers only two GDN/KDA models under fixed hardware and workload settings, with dynamic serving workloads unverified. This is a direct and reasonably non-minimizing limitation statement. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - Only two models are evaluated, both from the same GDN/KDA family with 128×128 states; generalization to other hybrid ratios, state sizes, or other recurrent architectures is extrapolated from nothing. - The mixed-precision baseline landscape for states is thin: only uniform rowwise-absmax and an adapted Q-Mamba DSQ are run directly; no comparison against rotation/Hadamard-based state quantization, and the strongest competitor (DAMP) is compared via transcribed cross-paper numbers with different generation settings — an acknowledged but material weakness. - No error bars or seed variance on any benchmark accuracy; several margins (e.g., STEPQuant@6bit 79.27% vs. FP32 79.32% with W4) are within plausible run-to-run noise given sampling temperatures of 1.0 and up to 64 samples per question. - The claimed throughput/memory results come from a single serving configuration (fixed 128-token prompts, greedy decode, one TP topology); no results with real request-length distributions or prefix caching, where packed-state layouts might behave differently. - The ΔNLL drift probe (Appendix B.2) shows a negative excess NLL (−0.0120) on KDA, which suggests possible measurement subtleties in the drift methodology that the paper does not discuss. - It is not stated whether the 6-bit accuracy retention holds when state quantization interacts with speculative decoding, chunked prefill re-quantization, or multi-LoRA serving — features of real SGLang deployments. Bottom Line: For anyone serving GDN/KDA hybrid linear-attention models, this is the current reference work on sub-8-bit recurrent-state quantization — the mechanism analysis is credible, the ablations are convincing, and the SGLang integration makes it immediately actionable — while readers outside that narrow architecture family can safely wait for follow-up work confirming generalization beyond two models.

How Much Can Language Models Gain from Test-Time Computation?

B Yang, J Li, J Fan, YE Zhang, R Guo, H Ma, N He… · arxiv.org · Recommended articles
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces SELF-POT, a benchmark and evaluation framework that measures how much test-time computation (parallel sampling, selection, self-revision) actually converts into task success and dollar cost across 350 sealed tasks spanning competition mathematics, competitive programming, app workflows, and terminal-agent environments. - Why it's important: Practitioners are told that extra inference on a cheap model can replace a stronger model, but prior comparisons evaluate one domain at a time, count budgets in FLOPs or samples rather than dollars, and rarely charge selection/verification calls to the budget — so the deployment decision has been made on misleading accounting. - How it does it: It runs one frozen model through Direct, Parallel@2, Parallel@4 (same-model judge), and Revise@4 protocols under a hard output-token cap that is a fixed multiple of a single Direct attempt, charges every call including judges and critiques in USD, and decomposes accuracy into candidate coverage × conversion via the identity E[S] = P(O)·P(S|O), then replays alternative selection and fallback rules on the saved candidate pools. - The good: The controlled replays cleanly isolate where gains are lost: on programming, public-example selection converts 453/500 scheduled cells versus 376 for the model judge at 12–49% lower API cost, and a trivial output-preserving fallback recovers 61 submissions at unchanged cost, reversing a measured −8.6 pp loss into +3.6 pp. - The missing: Every cell is sampled exactly once (no repeated seeds), so within-task stochastic variability is unestimated; several headline effects (mathematics judging vs. voting: 186 vs. 182) have bootstrap intervals spanning zero; and the replays are accounting counterfactuals on saved pools, not fresh equal-budget trials. - Read it or not: Worth reading for anyone building or purchasing inference-compute pipelines — it supplies the first dollar-denominated, multi-domain accounting of where test-time-scaling gains actually go — but method developers seeking a new scaling algorithm will find none here by design.
Why this rank
Scored using Empirical profile. Rigor (75) is above the cluster norm — exact sign tests with Holm correction across all 44 comparisons, task-stratified bootstrap intervals, a second-grader sensitivity check, and sealed tasks with leakage exclusions — but held back by single-sample cells and headline replay effects within noise. Show full analysis
Problem & Motivation: A practitioner with a fixed model and a fixed budget must choose among a single attempt, parallel sampling with selection, and self-revision — and the right choice plausibly differs by domain, by selection rule, and by whether the environment allows discarded attempts. Prior controlled comparisons (Snell et al., Wu et al., Stroebl et al., etc.) leave three gaps: they mostly evaluate a single domain (usually mathematics), few charge selection or verification calls to the same budget as generation or count cost in money, and the headline comparison — a cheap model with extra compute versus a stronger model answering once — has been made only within model families and on narrow domains. The paper targets the resulting decision problem: where does the next unit of inference budget go — another candidate, a better selector, or a different base model? Key Idea: The core move is treating test-time potential as a conversion profile: separate candidate coverage (does any sampled candidate grade correct?) from conversion (does the pipeline actually submit a correct answer?), measure both under an all-calls-charged dollar budget, and then replay task-appropriate selection and fallback rules on the frozen candidate pools so that generation is held constant while the choice rule varies. This converts aggregate accuracy deltas into a diagnosis of which stage loses the opportunity — generation, selection (no choice vs. wrong choice), submission, or revision — and prices the marginal value of a model judge against free rules like voting and public-test selection. Methodology: The framework defines a measured quantity A(M, π; D, I, E, H, B) — expected success of model M under protocol π with budget cap B — where all calls in a cell satisfy Σ τ(c_t) ≤ m_π·B_d (Eq. 1), with B_d = 131,072 output tokens for math/code and 393,216 for agent episodes; caps on model calls, tool calls, and wall-clock scale with the multiplier m_π. Four protocols run on the same frozen model: Direct (one answer); Parallel@2 (two samples, token-free rule — majority vote in math, most public examples passed in code); Parallel@4 (three samples plus a same-model judge that reads all three and names one, i.e., joint selection); Revise@4 (one Self-Refine iteration: critique-only, PASS returns the initial answer, otherwise revise with up to 2B). On agent tasks, parallel protocols draft k plans, select one with a same-model call, and execute only that plan; Revise@4 inserts a review call every two executor turns. Grading uses a rule-based math grader (with CompassVerifier-3B as a sensitivity check), hidden tests in a pinned container for code, and native final-state evaluators for AppWorld/Terminal-Bench. Statistics: exact two-sided sign tests per model–domain with Holm correction across all 44 protocol-vs-Direct comparisons; panel means with task-stratified bootstrap (20,000 replicates, 95% pointwise intervals). Critical design decisions: (1) charging selection/critique to the same cap as generation — well-motivated by their own development evidence that critiques consumed ~58K tokens; (2) capping budget rather than matching realized cost — acknowledged as a limitation since protocols realize different actual spends; (3) replaying selectors post-hoc on saved pools rather than running fresh equal-cost trials — explicitly flagged as not new trials. Key Results: Across 6,165 recorded cells (68 configurations, 5 low-cost models, Opus 5.5 Direct as anchor, 350 sealed tasks): (RQ1) Protocol gains are domain-dependent — on code, Parallel@2 yields a panel mean of +6.2 pp [4.2, 8.2] with 31 wins/0 losses, while Parallel@4 yields −8.6 pp [−11.8, −5.4] (18W/61L) because joint selection fails to return usable choices; on math, Parallel@4 gives +4.0 pp [0.3, 7.7]; on workflows, no protocol raises the panel mean (Parallel@2 −4.2 pp; Revise@4 −7.2 pp, e.g., Flash drops 78→55/160, Holm p = 0.033); terminal tasks show no parallel gain. (RQ2) Coverage ≠ submission: Qwen3-Next covers 38/60 math tasks but submits 30 correctly; GLM-5 covers 88/100 code pools but submits 55, with 27 of 33 lost pools being no-choice failures. Replays: coding public-example selection 453/500 vs. 376 for the judge (+6.8 pp vs. Direct), saving 12–49% of logical API cost; fallback recovers 61 submissions (−8.6 → +3.6 pp); on math, judging with fallback reaches 186/292 pools vs. 182 for vote@3 — an interval spanning zero — while voting saves 12–21% of cost. (RQ3) Opus 5.5 Direct remains the most accurate configuration outside coding (math 57/60 vs. Flash's best 52/60; workflows 148/160 vs. 82/160; terminal 13/30 vs. 3/30), and at peak Flash rates both Flash judging ($0.176/task) and vote@3 ($0.144) are dominated by Opus Direct ($0.103); at half price they join the frontier. In coding, Flash Direct (99/100, $0.013/task) dominates — GPT-OSS Parallel@2's 97/100 exceeds the anchor's frozen 93/100, but the anchor scores 99/100 once numpy is installed. Baselines are current commercial reasoning models; test scale is modest (350 tasks, 60–160 per domain), each cell run once. Novelty Classification: NEW DATASET/BENCHMARK (a sealed four-domain, dollar-accounted test-time-scaling evaluation harness) plus NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING (failure handling and selector choice can reverse the sign of a measured TTS gain; the cheap-model-vs-strong-model comparison flips with price basis and runtime dependencies). The constituent techniques — Self-Refine, majority voting, model judging, plan-level parallelism — are all standard; the genuine novelty is the measurement design: all-calls-charged dollar accounting, coverage/conversion decomposition with same-pool selector replays, and the cross-domain frozen protocol matrix. The paper correctly disclaims that it proposes no new TTS method. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are present in an unusual form — the same-pool selector replays (judge vs. judge+fallback vs. public selection vs. vote@3, with a public-first gate variant) isolate the choice rule with generation fixed, and revision-transition tables (Table 10) separate content rewrites from lost submissions. Significance testing is careful: exact sign tests with Holm correction over all 44 comparisons, task-stratified bootstrap intervals with fixed seeds, and grading sensitivity via a second grader (Compass: 194 vs. 189, preserving direction). Concerns: each cell is sampled once, so within-task variance is unestimated (acknowledged); primary small effects (math judging vs. voting) are not significant; the DeepSeek half-price sensitivity flips frontier membership, showing conclusions are tariff-dependent (acknowledged); several post-hoc rules were specified after inspecting results (flagged as post-hoc); a dozen infrastructure/interface amendments after sealing are documented in Appendix H. Analysis scripts are named (analysis/audit_results.py, run_selector_replay.py, etc.) with source hashes, but no public repository URL is stated in the provided text — release status: Not stated. The sealed test set and hashed manifests strengthen contamination control. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL (a measurement campaign with an evaluation harness artifact). Practical: Yes — everything runs via commercial APIs (DeepSeek API, Amazon Bedrock) on the benchmark's pinned containers; no exotic hardware. Efficient: Costs are explicitly measured and small in absolute terms ($82–$282 total ledger per model family; per-task means from $0.013 for Flash code Direct to $1.93 for Opus terminal Direct), which is the paper's point. Effective: Evidence supports the diagnostic claim — selection/failure handling changes realized gains on static tasks — but the agent-side conclusion is only that interface failures mask any planning value, and the math judging-vs-voting difference is within noise. Scalable: Untested beyond 3–4 candidates and 350 tasks; the paper explicitly does not trace an accuracy–budget response curve and warns intervals describe the fixed five-model panel, not unseen families. Delivers a benchmark/evaluation framework with analysis scripts; no trained model weights or standalone library release is stated. Strengths: - The coverage/conversion decomposition with same-pool replays is a genuinely informative diagnostic: it converts the counterintuitive result that a more compute-intensive protocol loses 8.6 pp into the actionable finding that 56 of 61 lost coding outcomes are no-choice failures, fixable for free. - Charging every call in dollars, including judges and critiques, and anchoring against a paid strong model (Opus 5.5 Direct) makes the central deployment question (cheap model + TTS vs. strong model once) answerable, with honest price-basis sensitivity analysis showing frontier membership flips at half price. - Unusually careful failure accounting: 15 unfinished cells scored as failures, model outcomes never retried, the Opus-numpy runtime dependency investigated and reported (93%→99% without new inference), post-sealing amendments documented, and claims consistently scoped to the tested selectors rather than all possible judges. - The sealed test set with model-independent eligibility checks, fixed-seed stratified sampling, and leakage-group exclusions is a methodological step above typical TTS comparisons. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state: no accuracy–budget response curve (budget caps ≠ matched realized costs); cross-domain contrasts confound feedback, difficulty, and protocol instantiation; each cell sampled once so within-task stochasticity is unestimated; intervals describe this fixed model panel, not unseen families; replays are accounting counterfactuals, not fresh equal-cost trials; agent protocol results measure the model–protocol–interface combination, not plan quality (GPT-OSS 117/160 and MiniMax 159/160 workflow stage failures); two-way voting with earliest-tie cannot measure self-consistency value; the parallel-vs-judge code contrast is not a clean selector ablation (different candidate counts); development-informed design choices (judges, full budgets) were adopted before sealing but rested on small pilots; the long-reasoning protocol and domain-specific methods were not run. They confront limitations directly and repeatedly — a credibility strength. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - The headline replay numbers (453 vs. 376; 61 recovered submissions) are post-hoc counterfactuals computed after observing that the frozen judge failed; no fresh end-to-end run of the amended pipeline was performed, so the deployment-relevant number remains a projection. - Three candidates per pool is a narrow operating point; the finding that a judge underperforms public-example selection may not transfer to larger candidate pools where judging's discrimination could matter more (the authors' own citation of coverage-vs-selection saturation suggests this). - The five-model panel is convenience-sampled and the anchor is a single model at a single effort setting; 'low-cost' is defined by token rate, and price data are a snapshot — the RQ3 conclusion is already shown to be tariff-sensitive, so panel and price sensitivity compound. - Very low agent Direct scores for three models (GPT-OSS 9.4%, Qwen3-Next 0%, MiniMax 11.9% on workflows) suggest harness/interface mismatch for some models; protocol comparisons against such floors are of limited external validity, and adaptive omissions (GPT-OSS/MiniMax terminal protocols skipped after zero Direct) introduce non-random missingness, albeit disclosed. - No code or benchmark release URL appears in the provided text, which limits reproducibility of an explicitly artifact-oriented contribution. Bottom Line: For anyone deciding how to spend an inference budget across model choice, sampling, and selection — or designing a TTS evaluation — this paper is directly useful and arguably sets the accounting standard the subfield should adopt; readers seeking a better scaling algorithm or large-scale response curves will need to wait for follow-up work.

Wei Huang, Bohan Zhang, Chenzhi Liu, Isabella Liu, Shuai Yang, Weian Mao, Luozhou Wang, Yicheng Xiao, Weifeng Lin, Qixin Hu, Bryan Chu, Sifei Liu, Linxi Fan, Xiaojuan Qi, Song Han, Yukang Chen · arxiv.org · Daily papers of 8 Oct 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces Long-WAM, a world-action model and deployment system that shows robot-control success scales with visual-history length — but only when the video backbone is pretrained autoregressively — and delivers real-time inference at 107.4 ms per action chunk on an RTX 5090, including future-video latent prediction. - Why it's important: Real-time robot control is usually forced to choose between reactive single-frame policies (no motion context) and history-aware models (too slow); this work argues both constraints can be met simultaneously, which matters for dynamic manipulation like intercepting moving objects. - How it does it: Pretrain a causal video model on ~10,000 window-equivalent hours of robot and egocentric video, adapt it to actions while preserving the history-to-future causal structure (predict future latents, reuse their KV cache for action denoising), then recover latency through streaming VAE, asynchronous chunk execution, NVFP4 quantization, and device-specific kernel tuning. - The good: The controlled initialization comparison is the strongest evidence: on RoboCasa GR-1, AR-pretrained foundations gain +15.4 points (63.3%→78.7%) when context grows 0→19.2 s, while a bidirectionally pretrained (Wan2.2) foundation shows no net gain, isolating pretraining objective — not context access — as the driver. - The missing: Each context length is a separately trained model evaluated in simulation; no single policy adapts its window at test time, no real-robot context-scaling study is run, no error bars or seeds are reported, and the 38.4 s performance decline is explained by training-data padding coverage rather than tested. - Read it or not: Worth reading for robotics researchers and systems engineers working on world models, memory, or edge deployment of generative policies; skippable for practitioners seeking a ready-to-use general policy, since real-world gains are confined to two bespoke robot setups.

Problem & Motivation: Real-time robot manipulation needs enough visual history to infer object motion and task progress — a single frame cannot distinguish a stationary cup from one about to be lifted — but processing history delays the very actions it should improve. World-action models (WAMs) that couple video prediction to action generation have mostly adapted bidirectionally pretrained video generators (DreamZero, LingBot-VA) or trained memory modules post hoc; the authors identify a gap: prior systems give the model access to history without ever training it to predict from history. The work targets robotics labs and edge-deployment engineers who need both long-horizon context and sub-150 ms inference on consumer/embedded hardware. Key Idea: Access to history is not the same as using it: the value of longer context depends on whether the video foundation was pretrained autoregressively, because AR pretraining already learns the history-to-future causal factorization that action adaptation later reuses. The enabling trick is "causal-to-causal" adaptation — keep the pretrained causal video dependencies intact, let the video expert roll out K future latents to noise level σ*=0.9 (never decoded to pixels), then condition a separate action expert's flow-matching denoising on the joint visual KV cache of observed history plus predicted future (an "inverse dynamics modeling" / predict-then-act decomposition). Methodology: Three phases. (1) AR video pretraining (LongLive2.0-Robot): continue LongLive-2.0's 16 s checkpoint on ~2.29 M text-and-image-to-video samples from RoVid-X (82.7%), EgoDex, AgiBot World, EgoVerse, and VITRA, using teacher-forced block-causal flow matching (velocity prediction, Eq. 2) with error recycling, sequence-parallel over sequences up to 30 s; action-free supervision means embodiments need not share action spaces. (2) Causal-to-causal adaptation: asymmetric attention (video queries never read action tokens; action queries read history, noised futures, and the noisy action chunk); two-pass training — video flow matching on clean history, then action flow matching on a detached, forward-noised ground-truth-future cache — with weighted objective L = λ_v·L_video + λ_a·L_action. (3) Deployment: asynchronous chunk execution (stride S, overlap O=R−S, deadline T_ready ≤ O·Δt), streaming causal VAE that encodes observations during robot execution, within-call KV reuse, NVFP4 W4A4 for the video expert (BF16 for actions), CUDA Graph/compile fusion, shared-input quantization, online-softmax attention over split video/action KV buffers, and per-device GEMM/VAE tuning. Three design decisions stand out: (a) stopping video denoising at σ*=0.9 instead of a clean frame — justified as sufficient for conditioning and confirmed by IDM beating CoD on LIBERO-Long (99.5% vs 97.8%); (b) training one model per context window — clean for the scaling study but acknowledged as not test-time adaptive; (c) no blending or prefix guidance for asynchronous handoffs — well-justified empirically (IDM loses only 0.2 points sync→async while Fast-WAM loses 15.4 and LingBot-VA 45.5). Key Results: Simulation: LIBERO average 99.5% (IDM), beating LingBot-VA (98.5%) and Fast-WAM (97.6%), with the largest margin on LIBERO-Long (99.5% vs 95.2%/98.5%); RoboTwin 2.0 average 94.4% (vs ABot-M0.5 94.1%, LingBot-VA 2.0 93.6%); DOMINO 34.9% SR after dynamic fine-tuning, +15.0 SR over Fast-WAM and +10.1 MS over PUMA; RoboCasa GR-1 78.7% at 19.2 s context vs best baseline GR00T-N1.5 at 64.1%. Context scaling: GR-1 63.3%→78.7% (0→19.2 s), LIBERO-Long 94.5%→99.5% at 2.4 s, both declining at 38.4 s (75.2%/74.2%); the AR-vs-bidirectional gap grows from 3.3 points (0 s) to 17.1 points (19.2 s). Real world (20 trials/condition, no error bars stated): G1 conveyor grasping 100/100/95/90% at 3.0/4.5/6.0/7.5 cm/s while π0.5 and Fast-WAM drop to 0% at high speeds; dynamic cup stacking 19/20 vs 0/20 for both baselines; YAM long-horizon tasks (>40 s) at 80–85% (81.7% avg). Hierarchical: Long-WAM + GPT-6 Astra planner on RoboCasa365 lifts Overall from 31.4% to 54.4% (planner alone 25.2%), a +23.0-point gain vs +13.6 for π0.5 + planner. Efficiency: 107.4 ms/chunk on RTX 5090 (3.3× over BF16 eager; 4.1× on DGX Spark), 81.8 ms at V2/A2 (−1.0 SR point), 2.3× faster than Fast-WAM while also predicting future video. Baselines are current and strong (2025–2026 VLA and WAM models), though latency comparisons use each baseline's "native deployment configuration," and this is an NVIDIA-authored preprint with NVIDIA-hardware numbers. Novelty Classification: NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING (the AR-pretraining-conditionality of context scaling is the paper's genuinely novel and falsifiable claim) plus NEW SYSTEM/TOOL (the streaming-VAE + asynchronous + NVFP4 edge stack with reported per-stage ablation) and NEW METHOD at the component level (IDM predict-then-act with σ*-truncated latent rollout and KV reuse). The adaptation machinery (asymmetric video-action attention, flow matching, action-chunk denoising) is a competent assembly of existing ideas from DreamZero/LingBot-VA; the contribution is the staged AR-first recipe, the controlled initialization comparison, and the co-designed deployment — not any single new algorithm. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are unusually thorough for this genre: three video initializations (Wan2.2 bidirectional, LongLive-2.0 AR, LongLive2.0-Robot) under identical causal adaptation; three denoising strategies (w/o V, CoD, IDM); overlap-length sweep (S=12/16/20 with SR, RMSE, jerk); cumulative per-optimization latency table across three devices; latency-vs-context table (74.6→341.0 ms for 0→19.2 s). Missing: no seeds, error bars, or significance tests anywhere; 20 trials per real-world condition; the authors honestly flag that ~10,000 hours is a window-equivalent estimate, not unique footage, and that the 38.4 s decline may reflect 80.4% padding in training histories rather than an intrinsic limit. Code and project page links appear on page 1 but no specific repository URL or released weights are verifiable from the text. Methodological concerns: (1) each context length is a separately trained model, so "scaling" here is a training-compute sweep, not test-time memory extension; (2) the context-scaling study is simulation-only while real-robot experiments use a fixed 2.4 s window; (3) baseline latency numbers are self-collected under heterogeneous native configs; (4) vendor affiliation with the GPUs quantitatively benchmarked warrants independent replication. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: SYSTEMS (a built, deployed pipeline evaluated on physical robots) with a strong EMPIRICAL component. - Practical: Runs on a consumer RTX 5090, DGX Spark desktop, and Jetson AGX Thor robot computer — deliberately non-datacenter hardware. - Efficient: 107.4 ms (9.3 Hz) per chunk at 2.4 s context versus 356.0 ms BF16 eager and 244.1 ms for Fast-WAM, but latency grows ~3.2× at 19.2 s context (341.0 ms), so long context costs real response time. - Effective: Strong evidence it solves the stated problem on hardware (90–95% success at conveyor speeds where baselines score 0%), though simulation context-scaling gains are not directly replicated on real robots. - Scalable: Not tested beyond 38.4 s context, where success degrades; 10× longer histories would multiply KV/attention cost and require data that does not yet exist at density — the paper acknowledges this rather than claiming it. The work delivers a concrete software artifact (deployment stack, quantized models) plus presumably code/weights via the linked project page; the reusable techniques are the streaming-VAE scheduling discipline and the shared-input-quant/online-softmax kernel patterns. Strengths: - The central empirical claim is clean and falsifiable: three initializations, identical adaptation, monotone context sweep — showing the AR advantage grows with context (3.3→17.1 points) is exactly the right experimental design for the "access vs. use" thesis. - The efficiency work is ablated per optimization (Table 8: NVFP4+Graph+compile 2.1×, reuse to 2.5×, shared-input quant to 2.7×, online softmax to 2.8×, tuning to 3.3×) rather than reported as a single magic number, and honest details like NVFP4 yielding no RTX 5090 gain at V2/A2 without reuse (81.8 vs 81.3 ms) build credibility. - The asynchrony result — near-lossless chunk handoff without blending or prefix guidance (94.4→94.2% sync→async, vs −15.4/−45.5 for baselines) with measured overlap RMSE and jerk — addresses a known failure mode of chunked policies with quantified evidence. - The hierarchical experiment is a useful systems finding: planner gains scale with executor quality (+23.0 vs +13.6 points for π0.5), with the controls (policy queried every 15 steps without planner: only 11.2%/5.0% on composite splits) to rule out mere control-frequency effects. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state directly that: each context window is a separately trained model, so test-time adaptive windows remain future work; the 38.4 s decline coincides with sparse real history (80.4% padding) rather than demonstrating a memory limit; real-robot context-length studies were not run; the 10,000-hour figure is window-equivalent, not unique footage; the training surrogate for future latents is an approximation (noisy ground-truth at training vs pure rollout at inference); the appropriate context window is task- and compute-dependent, with no universal duration; and cross-embodiment transfer of the action-free pretraining was not evaluated. This is direct, well-instrumented limitation disclosure — a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: Beyond the acknowledged items: (1) no variance reporting anywhere — 20-trial real-robot comparisons and single-point simulation numbers leave statistical significance unknown, especially for the 0.3–1.0-point margins over ABot-M0.5 and LingBot-VA 2.0 on RoboTwin; (2) the headline context-scaling result (GR-1 78.7%) has no baseline at matched context — baselines were not given the history budget, so the +11.6-point margin conflates context with architecture; (3) the AR-vs-bidirectional claim rests on one bidirectional checkpoint (Wan2.2) at one scale; (4) DOMINO's 34.9% is after "dynamic-data fine-tuning" whose exact relationship to the benchmark's fine-tuning protocol is under-specified in the main text; (5) the streaming-VAE/asynchronous pipeline is evaluated only via its latency benefits and RoboTwin asynchrony ablation — the interaction between long context, streaming encoding, and real-robot timing is untested; (6) baseline latencies mix deployment quality with model size, so the 2.3×-over-Fast-WAM figure is not an apples-to-apples compute comparison. Bottom Line: For anyone building history-aware or dynamically deployed robot policies, this is one of the more convincing demonstrations that how a video foundation is pretrained determines whether memory helps — and the edge-deployment recipe alone is worth borrowing — but the headline context-scaling claim needs baseline-matched controls, seed-level variance, and real-robot replication before being treated as settled.

Problem & Motivation Formal verification establishes that code satisfies its contract, but the contract may omit obligations the author intended — verification then succeeds on a wrong program. The paper targets this specification-completeness problem in the LLM-assisted formal-verification workflow (Verus/Rust, drawing tasks from VeriContest). A useful audit searches for a specification-completeness witness: a program the weakened contract S− admits that violates intended behavior (fails official tests, and fails verification once the omitted postcondition is restored). The tension the paper identifies is that the habitual repair loop — feeding compilation, verifier, and test feedback back into the model — pushes the model toward the correct program before the admitted failure is captured, an effect the authors call objective reversal. The audience is developers of verified-code-generation and self-repair agent systems who currently treat correctness feedback as uniformly beneficial. Key Idea The key idea is that corrective feedback is objective-dependent: during adversarial discovery of specification gaps, verifier/test feedback reverses the search objective (it repairs instead of exposing), so the fix is procedural — separate the workflow into a no-feedback discovery phase whose selected candidate is frozen and certified, followed only then by feedback-driven specification repair and implementation synthesis. The phase boundary itself, not a new search algorithm, is the contribution. Methodology The pipeline has two stages. (1) Discovery: given a natural-language task and a contract S− with one postcondition removed, each of three calls per episode asks for a side-effect-free pure Rust expression that verifies under S− but violates intent; policies differ only in feedback — DIRECT carries nothing between calls, INTENTSHIELD feeds back rustc status, weakened-contract verification, and visible-test tables, Model-Judgment asks the model to self-assess, and PHASE re-executes the DIRECT protocol in separate API calls then freezes the selected candidate. Candidates are ranked lexicographically by parse success, S− acceptance, Rust compilation, visible-test divergence count, and call index; only the selected candidate is certified against the restored contract and full oracle bank. (2) Downstream (Campaign A2, 16 tasks, 2 models): synthesize implementations under Original (weakened), IS-Revised, or Phase-Revised specifications, three attempts each. The design is a 12-task × 4-model-family (Claude Sonnet 5, DeepSeek V3.2, Devstral 2, Qwen3-Coder-480B) × 3-episode matrix = 144 outcomes per policy, 1,728 calls, analyzed with task as the independent unit via task-cluster bootstrap and exact sign tests. Critical design decisions: (a) candidate selection uses visible oracles while certification replays the full bank — the authors correctly note this demonstrates incompleteness, not held-out generalization; (b) PHASE uses prompts byte-identical to DIRECT, so the comparison isolates the phase boundary, though this also makes PHASE a repeat-run rather than an independent method; (c) provider-default sampling settings with matched three-call budgets — reasonable but uncontrolled decoding parameters. Key Results On the primary matrix, DIRECT certifies 85/144 (59.0%) versus 39/144 (27.1%) for INTENTSHIELD: mean task-level difference +31.9 pp, 95% task-bootstrap CI [21.5, 38.9], sign test p = 0.00635, favoring DIRECT on 11 of 12 tasks (both strata: +38.3 pp on residual-contract tasks, +27.4 pp on total-omission controls; the sole reversal is cf50A at −16.7 pp). PHASE, an independent execution of the same protocol, reproduces 85/144 and matches DIRECT on every task exactly. Model-Judgment scores 34/144. Parse failures are 3.3× more common under INTENTSHIELD (49/144 vs 15/144), but a parse-clean sensitivity analysis retains a +23.6 pp Direct advantage. Downstream, Original specifications verify under the weakened contract 42/48 but only 14/48 after restoring the omitted postcondition (a 58.3 pp specification gap); Phase-Revised yields 39/48 (81.3%), IS-Revised 30/48 (62.5%), Original 14/48 (29.2%), with Phase−IS = +18.8 pp [10.4, 27.1], p = 0.00391. Critically, the effect does not transfer: in Dafny, the Qwen stratum slightly favors INTENTSHIELD (23/24 vs 21/24) with frontier models at ceiling; on 24 Lean tasks from Verina, PHASE is the worst arm (8/48 vs 12–14 for the others). Scale is modest — 12 primary competitive-programming functions, restricted expression language, three calls per episode. Novelty Classification NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING plus a NEW METHOD framing (phase-separated witness preservation). The genuinely novel element is the quantified demonstration that correctness feedback suppresses adversarial witness discovery — an inverse of the usual self-refinement story. The machinery (prompted LLM calls, verifier checks, test replay, sign tests) is standard; the phase-separated workflow is a procedural discipline rather than an algorithmic advance, and the 'objective reversal' concept reworks known specification-gaming and counterexample-guided-synthesis ideas with the sign flipped (preserve the admitted failure rather than eliminate it). Rigor & Reproducibility Statistical practice is above average for this kind of study: task-cluster bootstrap intervals, exact two-sided sign tests, an explicitly defined independent unit, within-task episodes honestly labeled as repeated stochastic samples rather than independent observations, and a parse-clean sensitivity analysis. Ablations exist but are admitted to be underpowered (verifier-feedback-only −25.0 pp p=0.0625; visible-test-only −20.8 pp p=0.125) and the feedback channels are changed together, so no causal attribution to a single message is possible. The anonymous supplement ships task-level CSVs, analysis scripts, and a reproduce.sh that regenerates all statistics and figures without model calls; full model-facing replay is admittedly incomplete (NeurIPS checklist answers [No] for reproducibility, data/code, and compute details). Methodological concerns: (a) the primary benchmark is only 12 tasks from one source (VeriContest) with a restricted candidate language; (b) DIRECT and PHASE sharing harness, prompts, and selection logic makes the identical per-task counts consistent with harness artifacts as well as genuine stability — the authors flag this themselves; (c) the downstream comparison is missing the Direct-Revised baseline, which the authors acknowledge; (d) provider-default decoding settings are uncontrolled across model families. No evidence of benchmark gaming, and the negative transfer results are reported prominently rather than buried. Deployability Profile: EMPIRICAL (an executed measurement campaign plus a workflow prescription; no new tool or library is released). - Practical: Yes — all experiments run through hosted APIs (Amazon Bedrock) with local Verus/Rust checking; nothing requires exotic hardware. - Efficient: Matching three-call budgets per policy; the phase-separated workflow adds no calls over Direct plus a standard repair loop, though the paper reports no cost/latency accounting (checklist item 8 answered [No]). - Effective: Within the studied Verus setting, yes — the 31.9 pp yield gap and the downstream 39/48 vs 14/48 contrast support the workflow on the tested proxy (pure Rust expressions), but effectiveness on realistic specifications with mutable state or repositories is untested. - Scalable: Not tested — 12 primary tasks and a 16-task downstream set; whether the feedback-suppression effect persists with richer candidate languages, longer search horizons, or larger task sets is claimed nowhere and measured nowhere, and the Dafny/Lean results suggest it may not hold elsewhere. The work delivers paper-form results plus an analysis-reproduction supplement (task-level data and scripts); it does not release a tool, trained model, or the raw model-facing replay material. Strengths - The finding is contrarian and quantified: a 31.9 pp suppression of certified-witness yield from feedback, consistent across 11 of 12 tasks and both task strata, with the honest inclusion of the one reversal (cf50A). - The paper's epistemic hygiene is unusually strong: failed transfer to Dafny and Lean is reported in the main results section, the missing Direct-Revised baseline is stated in the abstract itself, and selection-versus-certification is cleanly separated (visible oracles select, the full oracle bank certifies). - The phase boundary is a genuinely actionable engineering prescription — 'freeze and certify the witness before repair' — that costs nothing and is directly adoptable in agent workflows for verified code. - PHASE's independent execution reaching identical 85/144 provides at least some repeat-run stability evidence for the no-feedback protocol, even if shared-harness caveats apply. Author-Acknowledged Limitations The authors confront limitations directly, which is a credibility positive: they state the effect was measured only on 12 competitive-programming functions in a restricted expression language; that it did not reproduce in Dafny or Lean; that the feedback channels were changed together so no single message is identified as causal; that parse-failure differences complicate interpretation (with a sensitivity analysis); that the Direct-Revised baseline is missing so the downstream result compares witness sources rather than proving witness-guided repair is best; and that full replay material is pending. They explicitly disclaim application to repositories, mutable state, concurrency, and other proof workflows. The scope-limiting in the abstract and Section 5 is candid rather than minimizing. Analyst-Identified Gaps - The exactly-identical per-task counts between DIRECT and PHASE (e.g., 9/12 and 9/12 on cf124A across every task) are striking for independent API runs under provider-default sampling; the authors note shared-harness artifacts as possible, but a per-episode (not just per-aggregate) comparison, or released raw transcripts, would be needed to distinguish genuine determinism (e.g., temperature-0-like provider defaults) from an execution or logging artifact. - INTENTSHIELD's degradation may partly reflect prompt-format pathology rather than 'objective reversal' per se — the 3.3× parse-failure increase suggests the feedback-formatted prompts confuse models — and the mechanism ablations that could isolate this are underpowered (p = 0.0625, 0.125), so the headline interpretation is stronger than the mechanistic evidence. - The Dafny evaluation's frontier-at-ceiling result and the Lean result where PHASE is worst suggest the paper's framing ('correctness feedback erases evidence') may be substrate-specific in ways the title does not convey; the Dafny and Lean matrices also differ from the Verus matrix, confounding substrate with task difficulty. - Certification uses the same official test bank the prompts expose as visible cases for selection guidance, so certification of 'wrongness' is partly circular relative to search guidance (the authors acknowledge this demonstrates incompleteness, not generalization, but the downstream repaired specifications are also evaluated against the same tasks). - No human- or developer-facing evaluation of whether witnesses actually help practitioners repair real specifications — the 'potential use' claim rests entirely on the model-in-the-loop downstream synthesis numbers. Bottom Line A narrowly scoped but well-executed and unusually honest negative result that every builder of self-repairing verification agents should read for the phase-separation lesson alone, though the finding is confined to a 12-task Verus expression setting, transfers poorly to Dafny and Lean, and lacks the ablation power and the Direct-Revised baseline needed to elevate it beyond a well-documented case study.

H Liu, Y Sun, Q Tan · arxiv.org · long-horizon RL for agents - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces DAGent, a DAG-based multi-agent deep research framework that replaces upfront full-plan commitment ("Plan-then-Patch") with "Evaluate-then-Grow" incremental planning, plus DAGRPO, a GRPO reinforcement-learning variant that injects DAG-topology-conditioned credit assignment and structural compliance penalties. - Why it's important: Deep research agents waste large amounts of compute and lose accuracy when they commit a full task decomposition before any evidence exists; a planning paradigm that conditions each expansion on completed-node evidence could cut cost and raise accuracy simultaneously for long-horizon search systems. - How it does it: An Orchestrator grows the task DAG one batch at a time using structured per-node feedback (QueryDocs with answer, confidence, and uncertainty fields), propagates only compact summaries downstream with on-demand transcript recall, and exploits the resulting append-only graph to define on-chain/off-chain credit and plan-validity rewards for RL. - The good: The controlled same-architecture ablation isolates the paradigm effect directly — swapping only the planning behavior from Evaluate-then-Grow to Plan-then-Patch costs 5.3/4.8/4.0 Pass@1 points on BrowseComp-Plus/GAIA/xbench-DeepSearch while adding 40/29/18% more tokens, so gains come from better planning, not more compute. - The missing: RL is trained and evaluated on the BrowseComp-Plus train/eval split of the same benchmark with only 21 LoRA update steps on Qwen3-8B, so the DAGRPO gains are established at the smallest, most favorable setting and their persistence at scale is untested; training-free rows are single greedy passes with no variance estimates. - Read it or not: Read it if you build or train deep research or multi-agent DAG systems — the paradigm comparison and topology-conditioned credit are directly actionable; skip it if you only need another leaderboard entry, since the headline numbers sit on small (100–150 task) evaluation sets.

Problem & Motivation: Deep research tasks — navigating large knowledge spaces, synthesizing evidence across dozens of sources, and adapting to intermediate findings — strain LLM agents. DAG-based multi-agent systems suit this setting because independent branches run in parallel and each agent sees only its dependency context. However, existing DAG agents (Flash-Searcher, FlowSearch) use what the authors call Plan-then-Patch: the full task graph is committed before any node executes (in one decomposition call or several planner iterations), then edited during execution. The system makes its largest planning commitment when its evidence is weakest, and later revisions waste computation on branches that should never have been planned. Builders of deep research agents, both open-source and proprietary, face this planning brittleness and its compute cost. Key Idea: Grow the DAG incrementally — plan one batch of nodes, execute it, evaluate each completed node against a structured evidence record (QueryDoc: answer, explanation, key steps, confidence in [0,1], listed uncertainties), and only then decide the next expansion — keeping the graph strictly append-only. The append-only property is the linchpin: it guarantees that a node's ancestry in the final graph equals the context it actually saw, which (a) makes the answer-inclusive closure a well-defined credit-assignment signal for RL (something Plan-then-Patch trajectories, where nodes get deleted/rewired, cannot support), and (b) lets a cheap structural proxy replace counterfactual re-execution for per-node contribution. Methodology: The system has two layers. (1) Evaluate-then-Grow planning: an Orchestrator assigns each node in the latest executed batch a status (Success / Uncertain / Not Found); Uncertain or Not Found nodes spawn refine nodes (capped at one initial execution plus two refinements); targeted expansions instantiate new nodes with descriptions, prompts, and dependency edges; termination occurs when a singleton answer-type node is scheduled. Executors are standard ReAct loops with a 32K-token per-sub-task budget. Hierarchical context propagation ("Selective Propagation") passes only direct dependencies' QueryDocs by default, bounding context by fan-in rather than trajectory length; a RecallTool retrieves goal-conditioned snippets from a dependency's full InteractionTranscript as a fallback (invoked in 22.0/13.6/11.0% of tasks on the three benchmarks at Qwen3-32B). (2) DAGRPO: a GRPO objective with DAPO-style asymmetric clipping and role-separated group normalization, where Executor rewards are attenuated by α=0.5 for rollouts outside the answer-inclusive closure S(τ) (the answer node plus all ancestors), and Orchestrator rewards receive a structural compliance penalty rproc = −λproc·min(N(τ), Kproc) for planning turns violating format/status/refinement/answer-node constraints (λproc=0.3, Kproc=5). RL training uses LoRA (rank 64) on 2×H200, 32 tasks per batch, 8 rollouts per task, 21 update steps, three seeds. Critical design decisions: append-only growth (justified by the credit-signal well-definedness argument and anti-gaming analysis in Appendix B.2), multiplicative rather than subtractive off-chain attenuation (justified by the α=0 ablation collapsing below the GRPO baseline), and trajectory-level rather than token-level penalty aggregation. All three are supported by ablations, though the off-chain-attenuation justification is partly post-hoc. Key Results: On BrowseComp-Plus (150 tasks), GAIA (103-task text-only subset; full 165 for GPT-5), and xbench-DeepSearch (100 Chinese tasks), all with shared retrieval backends and judge: at Qwen3-32B DAGent reaches 47.3/55.3/65.0 Pass@1 versus FlowSearch (authors' released implementation, Coordinator enabled) at 43.3/51.5/63.0 and Flash-Searcher at 38.7/44.7/58.0. The lead over the strongest baseline holds at Qwen3-8B (+5.3/+7.8/+5.0) and Qwen3-235B-A22B (+5.3/+5.8/+2.0), replicates across Seed-OSS-36B, GLM-4-32B, and Nemotron-3-Nano-30B, and at GPT-5/327K context reaches 85.0/85.5/85.0 against the strongest reported baselines (e.g., Flash-Searcher GPT-5: 83.0/83.0/83.0). RL: DAGRPO improves Qwen3-8B DAGent from 40.0/46.6/60.0 (training-free) to 49.6/53.4/65.7 (mean±std over three seeds, std ≤1.5), exceeding same-budget outcome-only GRPO by 3.6/2.6/2.7 points. Ablations: removing Evaluate-then-Grow costs 14.0/12.6/10.0 points total (Plan-then-Patch swap −5.3/−4.8/−4.0; collapsing to single upfront plan a further −8.7/−7.8/−6.0); Selective Propagation −12.6/−10.6/−8.0; QueryDoc −8.0/−7.7/−5.0; InteractionTranscript/recall −4.0/−2.9/−2.0; DAGRPO's topology credit −2.0 overall and compliance regularization −1.1 overall; α peaks at 0.5 on every benchmark. Efficiency: the Plan-then-Patch variant uses 40/29/18% more tokens and 28/21/21% more steps than DAGent at lower accuracy; DAGent is cheaper than FlowSearch on every cost column, though single-agent Flash-Searcher is cheaper still (0.91M vs 1.20M tokens on BrowseComp-Plus) at 8.6 points lower accuracy. A judge-calibration study reports aggregate Cohen's κ=0.95 and 97.3% raw agreement between the GPT-4o-mini judge (GPT-4.1 tie-breaker) and a three-human majority. Baselines are current and reasonably configured (FlowSearch run with its refiner enabled, documented deviations recorded), and the strongest comparisons at frontier scale rely partly on numbers imported from prior papers. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD (Evaluate-then-Grow incremental DAG planning as a named paradigm contrasted with Plan-then-Patch) plus NEW FORMULATION for the RL component (topology-conditioned credit and structural compliance regularization enabled specifically by append-only growth). The ingredients are individually standard — DAG decomposition, ReAct executors, summary propagation, GRPO with reward shaping, LoRA RL — but the combination is genuinely new in two respects: conditioning every graph expansion on structured per-node evidence before that evidence exists nowhere else in the cited deep-research agents, and deriving credit assignment from the recorded append-only topology rather than role, turn, or entropy heuristics. The closest concurrent work (Graph-GRPO, M-GRPO, CCPO, DeepPlanner) is differentiated in Appendix B.3, and the differentiation is substantive rather than cosmetic. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are unusually thorough and well-targeted: the same-architecture Plan-then-Patch variant isolates the planning paradigm from confounds, and the RL ablations (α sweep, regularization removal) attribute DAGRPO's gain to the structural signals rather than the training budget. Training-based rows report mean±std over three seeds with per-seed breakdowns; the authors explicitly flag that smaller single-seed ablation deltas fall within seed noise and rely on sign consistency instead. Judge quality is validated against humans (κ=0.95), addressing the usual LLM-judge concern. Code is released at https://github.com/hanwenliu6825/DAGent. Methodological concerns: (1) RL is trained on BrowseComp-Plus and evaluated on its held-out split of the same benchmark, a development/evaluation coupling that Goodhart's Law applies to, partially mitigated by zero-shot transfer to the other two benchmarks (where the DAGRPO-over-GRPO deltas are smallest relative to seed noise); (2) training-free rows are single greedy passes — no error bars, and with 100–150 tasks, differences of 2–5 points are fragile; (3) the GAIA evaluation set changes between the main results (103 text-only) and the GPT-5 comparison (165 with multimodal inspector tools added), so the frontier-scale GAIA number is not directly comparable to the main table; (4) some GPT-5-scale baseline numbers are quoted from prior work rather than reproduced. The paper is a formatted NeurIPS 2026 submission (arXiv:2609.39154), i.e., a preprint, though the internal standard of the evaluation apparatus is above typical preprint practice. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (with a built framework — effectively EMPIRICAL/SYSTEMS hybrid; using the EMPIRICAL check). Practical: Yes — open Qwen3/Seed-OSS/GLM/Nemotron backbones on commodity GPUs; RL training needs only 2×H200 with LoRA; GPT-5 results use standard API access. Efficient: Mean per-task cost of 0.44–1.20M tokens and 381–542 s wall-clock at Qwen3-32B; cheaper than FlowSearch and its own Plan-then-Patch variant on every cost column, but more expensive than single-agent Flash-Searcher — the multi-context-per-node architecture carries real overhead. Effective: The evidence supports the claim on closed-form-answer deep research benchmarks with verified judges; open-ended report generation is explicitly outside the evidence. Scalable: Inference is stress-tested up to GPT-5 at 327K context, but RL is tested only at Qwen3-8B with LoRA for 21 update steps — the paper honestly states that DAGRPO gains at larger scale, longer schedules, or full fine-tuning are not established. Delivers a software artifact (released code and prompts) plus a reusable design pattern (append-only incremental planning as an enabler of topology-conditioned credit). Strengths: - The same-architecture Plan-then-Patch variant is the strongest single piece of experimental design in the paper: it converts a paradigm argument into a controlled measurement (−5.3/−4.8/−4.0 Pass@1, +40/29/18% tokens) and rules out the counter-explanation that the ablated system was merely weakened — its overall score (51.2) sits between the two released Plan-then-Patch systems (47.1, 52.6). - The append-only insight connecting planning paradigm to RL credit assignment is a real, non-obvious formulation: the answer-inclusive closure is only readable off the trajectory without re-execution because no node is ever deleted or rewired, and the authors provide an explicit anti-gaming argument (inflating dependencies costs accuracy under Selective Propagation and is contradicted by observed off-chain-ratio dynamics). - Judge validation against three human annotators (Cohen's κ = 0.95 aggregate, per-benchmark κ = 0.92–0.96) with stratified sampling across benchmarks and agent baselines — a step most agent papers skip. - Honest handling of statistical fragility: seed variance is reported, single-seed ablation deltas are explicitly flagged as within noise, and the structural-violation/accuracy association (14.7 points) is labeled correlational rather than causal. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state in Appendix F that DAGent is text-native (multimodal attachments are converted to text pre-planning rather than handled in-loop); that accuracy is bounded by retriever/embedding/page-extraction quality; that the answer-inclusive closure is a structural proxy, not causal attribution, and the compliance/accuracy association is correlational; that all three benchmarks have closed-form answers, excluding open-ended report generation; and that RL results cover one backbone (Qwen3-8B), LoRA, and 21 update steps, so persistence of DAGRPO gains at larger scale is unestablished. They confront limitations directly and with appropriate calibration — a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - RL development and evaluation share the BrowseComp-Plus benchmark (train/eval split of the same query distribution); the zero-shot transfer argument is the right mitigation but the DAGRPO-over-GRPO margins on the transferred benchmarks (2.6, 2.7) are comparable to the seed standard deviations (1.0, 1.5), so the transfer evidence for the structural signals specifically is thin. - Training-free results are single greedy passes on 100–150-task sets; a 2.0-point lead at 235B on xbench-DeepSearch is within plausible run-to-run or judge-noise range, and no significance test or bootstrap interval is offered for the training-free comparisons. - The α=0.5 optimum is selected on the same three benchmarks used for reporting, and only for the regularization-on configuration — the α sweep does not appear to include a held-out selection protocol. - The Plan-then-Patch variant is implemented by the authors rather than being an external system; although the variant scores between the two released Plan-then-Patch systems (a fair-faithfulness check the authors themselves run), the paradigm comparison is still self-implemented, and FlowSearch is evaluated at Qwen3-32B only. - First-batch planning still proceeds with zero evidence (61.9% first-batch success rate reported), so the paradigm does not eliminate upfront commitment — only reduces its scope; the sensitivity of overall performance to first-batch quality is not ablated. - The GPT-5 frontier comparison mixes reproduced numbers with numbers imported from Flash-Searcher and FlowSearch papers under differing tool stacks (multimodal inspectors added for DAGent on full GAIA), a configuration asymmetry the authors document but do not equalize. Bottom Line: For anyone building or training deep research agents, this is worth reading for the Evaluate-then-Grow paradigm and the append-only-topology credit-assignment trick — both immediately reusable and supported by the cleanest controlled comparison in the recent deep-research literature — while the RL contribution specifically should be treated as promising-but-small-scale until replicated beyond Qwen3-8B and outside its training benchmark.

UNREAL: Unifying Retrieval and Long-Context with a Single Model (15 ▲ )

Edan Kinderman, Elad Hoffer, Yochai Blau, Brian Chmiel, Ron Banner, Daniel Soudry, Boris Ginsburg · arxiv.org · Daily papers of 7 Oct 2026
TL;DR: - What it does: This paper introduces UNREAL, a framework that turns a frozen decoder-only LLM into both a corpus-scale retriever and a long-context evidence selector by training fewer than 500K parameters (retrieval tokens, layer-mixing weights, one soft prompt) on top of the model's own residual-stream representations. - Why it's important: Production RAG pipelines must train, serve, and keep aligned a separate retriever and reader; UNREAL collapses this into one model, and the same selection mechanism also removes distractors in long-context inference where full-context accuracy collapses. - How it does it: It encodes each chunk once from a chosen intermediate layer of the frozen LLM, appends learned retrieval tokens to the query, reads layer-wise residual states at those token positions, and scores chunks with a layer-weighted late-interaction MaxSim trained via a multi-positive InfoNCE loss with BM25-mined hard negatives. - The good: All four tested backbones (dense, linear-attention hybrid, Mamba-attention hybrid) beat strong dedicated retriever-reranker systems on a 21M-chunk Wikipedia index — e.g., complete-evidence recall@10 on HotpotQA rises from 49.1% to 73.2% — with 95% BCa confidence intervals and single-knob ablations. - The missing: Everything is trained and evaluated on Wikipedia-derived QA data only; no code or index release is stated, there is no end-to-end wall-clock comparison against an external-retriever pipeline (only against full-context inference), and the NoLiMa full-context baseline of 1.0% at 128K suggests a weak generator that inflates the headline gain. - Read it or not: Read it if you work on RAG systems, retrieval architectures, or long-context efficiency — the <0.005%-of-parameters trick and the retrieval-vs-long-context unification are directly actionable; skip it if you need non-Wikipedia or multilingual evidence, which is untested.
Why this rank
Scored using Empirical profile. Rigor (72) is solid — one-knob ablations, four diverse backbones, 95% BCa CIs — but is held back by no code/index release, a self-constructed 8K–100M benchmark that favors retrieval by construction, and a suspiciously weak NoLiMa full-context baseline (1.0%) that inflates the headline 24.83% gain. Novelty (78) is high: the unification of corpus retrieval and long-context selection via a <500K-parameter residual-stream readout is a NEW METHOD with a surprising existence-proof result. Completeness (72) and Resilience (70) are tempered by Wikipedia-only training/evaluation, the missing wall-clock comparison against an external-retriever pipeline (the relevant deployment baseline), and exhaustive 21M-chunk scoring with no ANN strategy. Impact (65) is limited by no released artifact. Weighted composite: 0.20*78 + 0.25*72 + 0.15*80 + 0.15*72 + 0.15*70 + 0.10*65 = 73.
