Problem & Motivation: Teams building generative multimedia applications need video with synchronized speech, sound effects, and lip-sync, but the strongest systems (Veo 3.1, Sora 2, Wan 2.6) are closed-source, blocking reproducibility and further research. Existing open audio-video models lag closed ones in clip duration, resolution, and synchronization accuracy. The paper targets this gap: an open, permissively licensed foundation model family that is competitive specifically on speech quality and audio-visual synchronization, and that runs on consumer GPUs (16–32 GB). The work is a technical report from Kandinsky Lab (Sber-affiliated lineage), positioned as the successor to Kandinsky 5.0 Video. Key Idea: The central trick is asymmetric continuous pretraining with independent per-modality noising: rather than training a joint audio-video model from scratch, the authors freeze-inherit a strong video DiT, train a smaller audio DiT from scratch on 40M audio-only clips, then wire the two together with newly initialized bidirectional cross-attention and jointly train on 7M paired audio-video clips where the video and audio diffusion timesteps t are sampled independently (independent_time mode). Independent timesteps force each stream to denoise conditioned on the other modality's partially noised state, which is what enables bidirectional use (e.g., video-to-audio) and, empirically, synchronization. Secondary tricks: a latent-face-region loss weighted 1.0 for lip-sync in SFT Stage 2, data-driven per-block gradient-surgery schedules for RL, and a deterministic Latent Upscaler that avoids per-tile pixel-space re-encoding in super-resolution. Methodology: The pipeline is flow matching (MSE velocity loss) with Hunyuan VAE for video, MMAudio autoencoder at 44 kHz, and Qwen2.5-VL-7B + CLIP ViT-L/14 text encoders. Stages: (1) separate pretraining — T2A (30–40k steps) and continued T2V from Kandinsky 5.0 checkpoints; (2) joint T2AV pretraining (46–57.5k steps, up to 121 frames at 23–25 fps) with independent_time noising and mixed modality dropout, followed by 4–5k steps with 25% I2AV samples using a channel mask, temporal RoPE positioning of the reference frame, and Token Role Embeddings (inference-time ablations show RoPE and mask are the load-bearing mechanisms; TRE is largely redundant, which the authors state honestly); (3) two-stage SFT — 11 per-domain models trained with frozen audio in Stage 1 (visual quality) and full unfreeze in Stage 2 (sync/lip-sync, loss = 0.85·video + 0.15·audio + 1.0·face loss), merged by uniform weight averaging into a model soup; (4) RL adapted from OmniNFT — GRPO groups of K=10 rollouts, LoRA r=16, eight reward terms (HPSv3, VideoAlign, AudioBox Aesthetics, CLAP, Whisper-ASR, AV-desync, AV-align, LatentSync-gated) routed into modality-wise advantages, DPO-like policy loss with region-wise reweighting from A2V cross-attention maps and a KL anchor; (5) two-stage distillation — π-Flow on-policy imitation to 10 NFE, then Sim-LADD adversarial refinement where adversarial states come from the student's own backward rollout (rather than forward noising as in LADD) with DRaFT-k truncated backprop (k=5); (6) super-resolution — a 1.41B text-free SR-DiT (flow matching with HQ first-frame anchor conditioning, pixel L1 + LPIPS + high-frequency Haar loss + masked Fourier loss) plus separately trained deterministic Latent Upscalers (1.44B at ×4, 0.76B at ×2), distilled to NFE=2 with a π-Flow DX policy. Key design decisions — independent timesteps, the face loss, and the gradient-surgery zones calibrated by the authors' own blockwise KV ablations (LTX-2's zones did not transfer) — are each justified with ablation evidence, a credibility positive. Key Results: VABench (Pro vs LTX 2.5 Full-HD config vs own Lite): Pro leads on speech_qn (1.496 vs 1.427), lipsync (2.072 vs 1.567), desync (0.396 vs 0.521), visual_realism (4.485 vs 4.366), tv_align (0.229 vs 0.185), av_align (0.268 vs 0.258); LTX 2.5 leads on VLM-judged alignment (4.527 vs 4.329), expressiveness, and WER (0.099 vs 0.117). Human side-by-side evaluations (~200+ pairwise comparisons per criterion, majority vote): clear win over Kandinsky 5.0 Video Pro on all criteria in T2V and I2V; significant win over LTX 2.5 on overall visual quality and speech quality; mixed vs Kling 2.6 (Kling leads visual aesthetics and audio quality, Kandinsky leads sound-prompt following); split vs Veo 3.1 Fast (Veo leads prompt following, sync, and audio; Kandinsky leads artifacts, camera motion, and I2AV image fidelity); loses to MiniMax H3 on the majority of criteria; loses visual criteria to Seedance 2.0 while leading speech quality. RL ablation: WER 0.235→0.124 (Pro, −47%, p<10⁻³) and 0.179→0.127 (Lite, −29%, p<10⁻³), with human-eval gains across speech-focused, general T2AV, and I2AV settings. Distillation ablation: 51%/49% preference vs the full model, no statistically significant difference. Deployment: Pro SD peaks at 72.8 GiB resident but 7.9–21.7 GiB with block offloading; 5-second Full HD generation in 402 s on H100, 854 s on RTX 5090, ~21 min on RTX 4090; SR adds ~40–131 s depending on route. Baselines are current (2025–2026 commercial systems), and the paper reports its losses as frankly as its wins. Novelty Classification: NEW SYSTEM/TOOL (the released model family) with components of NEW METHOD and ENGINEERING OPTIMIZATION. The genuinely new elements are Sim-LADD (on-policy adversarial states from the student's backward rollout combined with DRaFT-k truncated backprop), the data-driven per-block gradient-surgery calibration for cross-modal RL, the latent-face-region loss, and the deterministic latent-space upscaler replacing per-tile pixel re-encoding. The dual-stream CrossDiT with bidirectional cross-attention is a standard pattern (explicitly credited to Ovi and LTX-2), and the overall pipeline is a competent integration of known techniques (flow matching, GRPO-style RL, model soups, π-Flow distillation, Real-ESRGAN degradations) applied to a new model generation. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are present and unusually candid: RL vs SFT across three settings, distilled vs full model, I2AV conditioning-component ablations (mask/RoPE/TRE), SR stage-wise metrics, and gradient-surgery zone calibration. Significance testing appears for WER (paired Wilcoxon), and checkpoint selection uses sliding-window reward averaging. Human evaluation methodology is described in detail (anonymization, randomized ordering, tie options, majority vote), though annotator count and expertise are not stated. Code, weights, and diffusers integration are released under MIT (github.com/kandinskylab/kandinsky-6; Hugging Face collection). Concerns: (1) Whisper-large-v3 is both an RL reward model and the WER evaluator for the headline −47% result — the authors acknowledge this and add the Harvard-sentences confirmation, but the confirmation still uses the same Whisper-family transcriber; the VABench WER uses a different ASR (Qwen3-ASR-1.7B) where Kandinsky Pro actually loses to LTX 2.5 (0.117 vs 0.099), a discrepancy the authors flag but which tempers the RL claim; (2) evaluation is confined to the authors' own 5-second, SD-native operating point; (3) no total pretraining compute is disclosed, so the 29B result cannot be situated against compute-matched baselines; (4) reward models (HPSv3, VideoAlign, CLAP) overlap with benchmark-style metrics, inviting Goodhart-style optimization. This is an arXiv preprint (2610.05608), not peer-reviewed. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: SYSTEMS (built and released models evaluated by benchmark, human study, and deployment timings; substantial empirical content). Practical: Yes — explicitly engineered for consumer GPUs, with VRAM presets for 16/24/32 GB cards (16 GB preset: 7.9 GiB peak at SD) and tested on RTX 4090/5060 Ti/5080/5090, RTX PRO 6000, A100, and H100. Efficient: Mixed — the Lite model and distilled SR are fast (Lite SD: 239 s on H100), but Pro Full HD costs 402 s on H100 and 1,247 s on RTX 4090 for 5 seconds of output, with offloading requiring ~58 GiB host RSS for Pro. Effective: Evidence shows it solves the speech/sync slice of the problem (best-in-comparison speech quality, lipsync, desync on VABench) but only partially the visual-quality slice, losing to MiniMax H3 and Seedance 2.0 on visual criteria. Scalable: Not tested beyond 5-second clips and SD-native resolution; longer duration and higher native resolution are named as future work, not demonstrated. The work delivers a concrete software artifact: model weights (Lite and Pro), source code, diffusers integration, and a distilled SR model, all MIT-licensed. Strengths: - Honest, criterion-level human evaluation against five current commercial systems, including reporting statistically significant losses to MiniMax H3 and Veo 3.1 Fast rather than only favorable comparisons. - The RL result is the strongest evidence in the paper: a 47% relative WER reduction with significance testing, an out-of-distribution confirmation set, and a matching human-eval ablation isolating RL from SFT. - Deployment engineering is genuinely informative: measured per-GPU timings, block-offloading behavior, and explicit accounting of which optimizations are lossless (offloading to numerical epsilon) versus lossy (NF4 text-encoder quantization changes outputs). - Independent-timestep joint noising (independent_time) is a clean, well-motivated mechanism for making cross-attention bidirectional, and the accompanying conditioning ablations (RoPE position as the primary anchor-binding mechanism) transfer as insight to anyone building I2AV systems. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The conclusion states the models generate only 5-second clips, run at SD base resolution with Full HD obtained via super-resolution, and that a gap remains to the strongest proprietary systems in visual quality and overall audio quality. The authors also explicitly acknowledge the Whisper-as-reward/evaluator circularity, the non-comparability of the two WER numbers, that TRE's training utility cannot be established without an ablation training run, that SR no-reference metrics imperfectly capture SR-specific artifacts, and that warp error confounds detail with temporal quality. This direct confrontation with unfavorable results is a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - No total training compute (GPU-hours/cost) is reported for pretraining or the joint stages, making it impossible to judge efficiency of the 29B result against compute-matched alternatives; only SR training times (e.g., 4.5 days on 8 H100s) are given. - Human evaluation omits annotator count, expertise, screening, and inter-annotator agreement; ~200 comparisons per criterion with majority vote is a thin base for per-criterion significance claims, and the significance criteria for human-eval figures are not formalized. - VABench is run only against LTX 2.5; the stronger systems (MiniMax H3, Seedance 2.0) are compared only in human SBS, so no third-party benchmark covers the models where Kandinsky is weakest. - RL is trained at 512×768 while inference targets Full HD via SR; whether RL gains persist through the SR pipeline is not verified. - The Harvard-sentences WER confirmation still uses Whisper-family transcription, so the reward-circularity concern is reduced, not eliminated; a non-Whisper ASR (e.g., the Qwen3-ASR used in VABench, where the model loses WER to LTX 2.5) is not applied to the RL-vs-SFT comparison. - Audio-stream pretraining data (40M tracks) is extracted from the same video collection as the T2AV data, so train/eval contamination at the source-collection level is not discussed. Bottom Line: For practitioners building or deploying open audio-video generation, this is worth reading as one of the most transparent and honestly evaluated releases in the space — the training recipe, ablations, and consumer-GPU engineering are directly actionable — but as a research contribution it is primarily systems integration, and anyone seeking frontier visual quality should look at MiniMax H3 or Seedance 2.0, whose strengths the authors themselves concede.

#42 — Innovative (72)

Learning Functional Subspaces for Neural Network Compression

M Bini, A Christensen, S Alaniz, J Goldfeder, O Winther… · arxiv.org · 10 new citations to your articles
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces Learnable Subspace Projections (LSP), a low-rank compression method that learns, end-to-end and with the pretrained weights frozen, which subspace of each linear layer (or tied Q/K/V and gate/up group) to remove, by optimizing orthogonal projectors against the dense model's output KL or the task loss. - Why it's important: Existing low-rank LLM compression picks removed directions from local per-layer criteria (activation energy, reconstruction error, quadratic loss surrogates) that ignore how errors propagate through depth, so quality collapses at high compression; deployment-grade memory and speed savings at −70% compression are the practical stake. - How it does it: Each unit gets an orthogonal projector P = I − UU⊤ (U = QR factor of an unconstrained V) applied in activation space, initialized from a whitened SVD truncation with ranks allocated by measured output-KL per saved parameter, then all projectors are trained jointly against distillation to the frozen dense model and merged into plain low-rank factors with one shared input factor per tied group. - The good: At −70% compression on Llama-2-7B, LSP reaches 10.9 WikiText-2 perplexity and 42.2% mean zero-shot accuracy versus 13.3 and 36.0% for the strongest baseline (LoRA-recovered SVD-LLM), with the margin growing monotonically with compression ratio across 12 model–ratio settings, backed by three-seed standard deviations and component ablations. - The missing: The measured-KL allocation is an additive surrogate whose joint KL exceeds the sum of isolated costs by 1.5–14×, no code release is stated, the latent-cache numbers are partly analytical rather than measured, and nothing above 7B parameters is tested. - Read it or not: Read it if you work on LLM/ViT compression or efficient inference — it sets a new, well-ablated reference point for learned low-rank compression and latent-cache design; skip it if you only need training-free one-shot methods, since LSP requires a calibration-plus-training pipeline that activation-based methods avoid.
Why this rank

Problem & Motivation: Operators serving large transformers need to cut weight memory and KV-cache footprint, but the dominant low-rank compression recipes choose the discarded subspace with local closed-form criteria: activation energy (ASVD, SliceGPT, MoDeGPT), layer-wise output reconstruction (SVD-LLM, Swift-SVD), or local loss surrogates (FW-SVD's Fisher weighting, LLM-Surgeon's quadratic curvature model). These criteria are blind to the network output — a low-energy direction is discarded even if the output depends on it, and layer-wise optima say nothing about error compounding through depth, which is why training-free SVD methods collapse past −50% compression (e.g., ASVD exceeds 10⁴ perplexity on Llama-2-7B at −70%). The gap the authors identify is that in no prior low-rank method does the network loss itself select which directions are removed; Dobi-SVD optimizes loss but only the truncation rank within a fixed closed-form basis. Key Idea: Choosing a subspace to remove is equivalent to choosing an orthogonal projector, and that projector can be treated as a differentiable, learned parameter: apply P = I − UU⊤ to each weight (in activation space, avoiding materializing the dense projected matrix), initialize U from a whitened SVD so removal starts from a sensible basis, allocate how many directions each unit loses by directly measuring the output KL each candidate truncation induces per saved parameter, then jointly optimize all projectors against the dense model's output distribution while every pretrained weight stays frozen. The removed subspace, not the remaining weights, is the learnable variable — the same "learn what to delete against a global objective" shift that recently transformed structured pruning (MaskLLM, DISP-LLM), applied to a continuous subspace rather than discrete coordinates. Methodology: Pipeline: (1) replace each target linear layer with a projector-composed unit; layers reading the same activation (Q/K/V, gate/up) form tied groups sharing one input-side projector; other layers are projected on their smaller side. (2) Collect calibration activations, build whitened bases via Cholesky-whitened SVD of the (row- or column-stacked) weight, with a proved orthogonal recast of the input-side whitened truncation (Proposition 1 quantifies the excess error of the oblique-to-orthogonal replacement). (3) Allocate ranks greedily by marginal measured-KL per saved parameter — each unit truncated in isolation, dense outputs cached once, no gradients or new SVDs per candidate; units whose cost is too high stay dense. (4) Train only the unconstrained V's with Adam against L_KL (distillation to the frozen dense model's next-token distribution, teacher run without gradients so no second weight copy) or the task loss (LSPᵀ), plus an orthogonality penalty on V's columns; α ramps 0→1 over the first epoch, per-direction Bernoulli dropout (no 1/(1−p) rescaling, which would flip removed directions), fused-QR backward for O(dk + k²) state. (5) Merge: P = U⊥U⊥ᵀ factors exactly as W P = (W U⊥)U⊥ᵀ; tied-group members share the input factor A, enabling a latent KV cache storing z = Ax (MLA/Palu-style, keys rebuilt under rotary embeddings). A proposition establishes the orthogonal projector as the unique Frobenius-least-disruptive annihilator of a given subspace. Critical design decisions: activation-space application (justified by memory/gradient accounting), tied groups (ablated: tying raises mean zero-shot accuracy 0.3–3.1 points on Llama-2-7B), and measured-KL allocation (ablated against uniform-parameter, uniform-rank, and diagonal-Fisher budgets, leading by 0.2–0.9 perplexity on OPT-1.3B). Key Results: Tested at up to −70% compression on OPT-125M, OPT-1.3B, Qwen3-4B, Llama-2-7B, and ViT-B/16 (CIFAR-100). WikiText-2: one LSP variant has the lowest perplexity in all 12 model–ratio settings; at −70%, Llama-2-7B reaches 10.9 (LSP) vs 13.3 for LoRA-recovered SVD-LLM, 105.0 for LLM-Surgeon, and 222.8 for NoLSP (same initialization and ranks without training) — training the directions is what keeps the model usable. Zero-shot (six benchmarks): LSP leads the strongest training-free baseline by 6.7–10.5 points on Llama-2-7B (Alpaca calibration) and 6.2–10.8 on Qwen3-4B (C4 calibration) at every ratio, with both objectives within two points of each other. ViT: at −70% with in-domain calibration, LSP scores 85.9% CIFAR-100 accuracy vs dense 89.9% (best training-free baseline: 77.1%); on a size-matched diverse calibration pool it gains the most transfer (linear-probe on Pets/Aircraft/Places365, +6.6 to +7.1 points over the size-matched control), and is most robust to calibration shift. Efficiency: on Llama-2-7B at batch 1 on a GH200, LSP decodes 1.21×/1.36×/1.56× faster than dense at −30/50/70% (all untied factorizations are slower than dense at −30%); at −70% with a latent cache, weights + KV cache at 128k tokens take 13.5× less memory than dense (556 vs 8192 KV floats/token/layer; max context 322k vs 146k tokens). Analysis: allocation compresses Q/K/V far harder than MLP projections (the shared K/V latent is ~1/7 of full rank at −70%), later blocks keep more rank (53 of 128 units stay dense at −30%), and learning removes more of leading singular directions than NoLSP — the weight spectrum ranks functional importance poorly. Compression cost: 0.5–10 wall-clock hours including KL measurement (1.11 h on Llama-2-7B), Pareto-optimal against baselines on the cost–quality frontier. Baselines are current (SVD-LLM, Swift-SVD, Dobi-SVD from ICLR 2025–2026; LLM-Surgeon ICLR 2024) and run from official code with matched calibration, precision, and swept hyperparameters. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD (learned orthogonal subspace projectors optimized end-to-end against the network output for low-rank compression) plus NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING (the weight/activation spectrum is a poor proxy for functional importance — learning moves removal toward leading singular directions — and label-free KL distillation on diverse unlabeled calibration data improves compressed-model transfer beyond what feature distillation achieves). The individual ingredients — whitened SVD initialization, KL-based rank allocation, tied Q/K/V factors, latent KV caches (MLA/Palu), distillation — are each established; the genuinely new combination is making the removed subspace itself the learned variable with weights frozen, plus measured-KL rank allocation on the full network rather than a curvature surrogate. Rigor & Reproducibility: Strong. Component ablations isolate initialization (whitened vs plain Gram, before and after training), tying, and allocation (vs uniform-parameter, uniform-rank, diagonal-Fisher), each at matched realized savings; three full-pipeline seeds with standard deviations are reported (e.g., Llama-2-7B −70% LSP: 10.94 ± 0.12), epoch selection and hyperparameter sweeps use held-out validation splits only, realized compression lands within 0.25 points of nominal, and the additive-surrogate gap (joint KL 1.5–14× the sum of isolated costs) is disclosed rather than hidden. All baselines run from official code with matched budgets; unavailable official implementations (SVD-LLM-v2, MoDeGPT) are excluded and flagged. Methodological concerns: WikiText-2 calibration for WikiText-2 perplexity evaluation is acknowledged as domain specialization (mitigated by the zero-shot protocol with Alpaca/C4 calibration); latent-cache memory and context numbers are analytical estimates, with only throughput measured; no public code or model release URL is stated in the provided text. The paper is a preprint (arXiv, with an AI-use disclosure and a proof-checking protocol described). Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL (with a SYSTEMS component in the efficiency analysis). - Practical: Yes — runs on a single GH200 in bf16, with compression arithmetic in fp32/fp64 on commodity clusters; the deployed model is plain dense low-rank factors with no LSP-specific operations. - Efficient: Compression costs 0.5–10 wall-clock hours (one-off, measurements reusable across ratios and objectives); at inference, same FLOPs as untied factorizations at equal ratio but fastest measured decode (221 vs 191–193 tok/s at −70%, batch 1), and the latent cache halves per-token KV floats. - Effective: The evidence shows retained quality on perplexity, six zero-shot benchmarks, and cross-domain ViT transfer at −70%, not merely layer-wise proxy metrics — though the latent cache needs a dedicated attention implementation and serves capacity, not decode speed. - Scalable: Only claimed implicitly — largest model tested is 7B; the O(Σ dk) training state and per-unit KL measurements should extend, but nothing above 7B or beyond 128k-token cache accounting is measured. Deliverable: paper plus described pipeline; no released library, code, or compressed checkpoints is mentioned in the provided text. Strengths: - The reframing of low-rank compression as a search over orthogonal projectors trained against the global output is a clean, transferable idea, and the paper proves the two supporting pieces properly (orthogonal-projector optimality; exact error accounting for the whitened-input recast, including the tied-group Eckart–Young extension). - NoLSP — the untrained initialization at identical ranks and ties — is an unusually honest control: it isolates the contribution of learning (222.8 → 10.9 perplexity at −70% on Llama-2-7B), which most compression papers cannot do. - The efficiency section separates what is measured (CUDA-graph decode throughput) from what is analytical (cache size, context capacity), and the tied-factor latent cache yields a concrete, doubled memory advantage (13.5× vs ≤6.5× combined weights+KV at 128k tokens) over otherwise FLOPs-matched factorizations. - The ViT calibration-pool experiment cleanly isolates calibration composition from size (47k single vs 47k diverse pool, with a size-matched CIFAR-100-only control), showing LSP's distillation objective exploits unlabeled diversity in a way PELA's feature distillation does not. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: In Appendix A.7 the authors state: (i) measured-KL allocation is a local, additive surrogate with no global-optimality guarantee and uniform ranks can occasionally be preferred; (ii) compression is not free (KL measurements plus training), though measurements are reusable and the cost is one-off; (iii) the tied-group cache benefit requires input-side K/V tying, forcing a performance–efficiency trade-off on grouped-query models like Qwen3-4B (their best-accuracy configuration caches nearly as much as dense). The ethics statement also flags that compression losses may fall unevenly across subpopulations under-represented in the calibration distribution. These are confronted directly rather than minimized, which strengthens credibility. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - The additive KL surrogate is disclosed, but its 1.5–14× miscalibration is never corrected (e.g., no joint refinement of the allocation), so the allocation could be materially suboptimal in ways the greedy procedure cannot see; the authors report the gap but do not test a fix. - No code, weights, or configs are stated as released, which limits verification of a method whose results depend on many unstated-in-main-text implementation choices (fused QR backward, ridge handling, merge tolerance). - The model pool tops out at 7B and one ViT-B/16; the headline zero-shot gains come from two models and two calibration protocols, with no instruction-tuned or chat-model evaluation where distillation to a dense teacher's distribution might behave differently. - Baselines exclude hybrid pipelines that combine low-rank factorization with quantization (Dobi-SVD is deliberately run without its quantization step), so the comparison establishes dominance within low-rank-only methods but not against the practical compression stacks deployers actually assemble. - The task-loss variant's ability to drop below dense perplexity on OPT at −30% (24.5 vs 27.9) signals calibration-domain specialization; the paper names this for perplexity but does not quantify how much the zero-shot protocol itself is tuned toward LSP's strengths (the C4/Alpaca protocols are inherited from baselines, which mitigates this). Bottom Line: For anyone deploying or researching LLM compression, this is currently the strongest published low-rank-only recipe at aggressive ratios and worth reading in full — its measured gains over LoRA-recovered SVD-LLM at −70% (2.4 perplexity, 6.2 zero-shot points on Llama-2-7B) and the tied-latent cache are real, reproducible-looking advances — but the absence of a code release, the 7B ceiling, and the uncorrected additive allocation surrogate mean practitioners should wait for independent replication before replacing tuned quantization-plus-pruning stacks.

Towards Looped Models Done Right, Part II: Rethinking at Fixed Points (17 ▲ )

Benhao Huang, Chufan Shi, Junlin Chen, Shicheng Wen, Zhengzhong Liu, Eric Xing, Xuezhe Ma · arxiv.org · Daily papers of 6 Oct 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces a fixed-point account of looped language models under which the recurrent endpoint can replace the full trajectory, and delivers two training changes — a learned, entropy-regularized depth prior and orthogonal input injection (OrthoInj) — plus two new shortcuts built on fixed points: RL policy updates from saved rollout states (2× faster scoring/backward) and distilled prefill (up to 1.79× faster). - Why it's important: Every recurrence in a looped LM multiplies training memory, decode KV cache, prefill compute, and RL replay cost; if training shapes states toward fixed points, these depth-dependent costs can be decoupled from depth, making deep looped/test-time-compute models practical to train and serve. - How it does it: The core move is treating the loop recurrence z = F_θ(z; x) as approximately at a fixed point, so the endpoint stands in for the trajectory — exploited via truncated BPTT, terminal KV sharing, endpoint-predicting distillation, and truncated Neumann gradients from saved rollout states — with the depth prior learned from prediction feedback (a REINFORCE-style controller with PopArt-style advantages and an entropy term) and the carryover state projected off the injected input (OrthoInj). - The good: The empirical validation is unusually careful: the learned prior and OrthoInj are compared against current baselines (Huginn's PLN prior, Parcae-Decay, DEQ-QKV, fixed-depth) at three scales (100M/400M/1.6B) under matched token budgets, and the mechanism behind OrthoInj is directly measured (Parcae's carryover amplifies the injected input by 2.2×–3.4×; the projection fixes the gain at 1). - The missing: All headline results use one training seed per configuration (acknowledged), the RL reuse speedup is tested at a single depth (R=6) so the depth-scaling of the saving is unmeasured, and rollout generation dominates end-to-end RL time so the 2× update speedup does not translate to end-to-end speedup on the MBPP+ run. - Read it or not: Worth reading for anyone building or training looped/recurrent-depth/DEQ-style language models, since it is the most complete practical treatment of fixed-point shaping to date; general LLM practitioners can skip it, as the perplexity and downstream gains are modest (0.7–1.8% PPL improvements) and the guarantees rest on approximate fixed points.

Problem & Motivation: Looped language models apply a shared transformer block R times, so every recurrence adds cost in four places: stored activations during pretraining, KV cache during decoding, compute during prefill, and trajectory replay when scoring rollouts in RL. Prior work splits into camps that either avoid fixed points (fixed small loop counts, e.g., Ouro) or shape fixed points (Huginn, DEQ lineage), but no prior work systematically connects fixed-point behavior to per-stage cost reductions. The specific gaps closed here: fixed-depth training breaks terminal KV sharing (GSM8K collapses from 50.6 to 21.2 at 1.6B when sharing is applied); Huginn's fixed Poisson–log-normal depth prior spreads supervision uniformly and dilutes it at the target depth; and existing input injection schemes (Huginn-Linear, Parcae-Decay, DEQ-QKV) leave the state's component along the injected input unconstrained, so the input a fixed point retains depends on the state. The audience is researchers training looped models for latent reasoning and test-time compute scaling. Key Idea: Near a fixed point of the shared recurrence, the endpoint can stand in for the entire trajectory — and two controllable training choices (the depth prior and the input injection) determine whether such fixed points form. Exploiting this: (1) learn the depth-sampling distribution from detached cross-entropy feedback with an entropy bonus that keeps it broad enough to support terminal KV sharing, and (2) project the carried-over state orthogonally to the injected input (ζ = Q_q Λh + q with Q_q = I − qq^T/‖q‖²) so every recurrence receives the input at exactly unit strength and the projected carryover stays contractive since ‖Q_qΛ‖₂ ≤ ‖Λ‖₂ < 1. Methodology: The paper uses a Huginn-style architecture (1 prelude + 2×R shared recurrent blocks + 1 coda, Llama-style blocks) trained on TxT360-based multilingual mixtures with the Jais64k tokenizer. Four pipelines are presented. (1) Truncated BPTT (TBPTT): backpropagating only through the last b recurrences is shown (Appendix A.2, Lemma 2) to converge to the implicit equilibrium gradient D = (I − J)⁻¹B as states converge, without the warm-up that implicit-gradient methods require; truncation itself is shown to shape fixed points (Table 18: at fixed R=5, full BPTT raises R=64 perplexity 25%+ and KV-sharing perplexity 21%, while TBPTT b=2 costs only 2–3%). (2) RL rollout-state reuse: the policy gradient is computed as a truncated Neumann series v ← g + J_R^T v evaluated at the saved endpoint z_R via a single recorded recurrence (Algorithm 1), giving update cost independent of R. (3) Learned depth prior: a categorical prior over R ∈ {1,…,64} is optimized with J(ϕ) = −E[stopgrad(A) log p_ϕ(r)] − λ_H H(p_ϕ) + λ_m(E[R] − R̄)², where A is an inverse-perplexity reward centered by EMA and rescaled PopArt-style; gradients flow through only min(r, 10) recurrences. (4) OrthoInj:* the input-projection operator of equation (8), with a stabilizer ε = 10⁻⁶. Critical design decisions: TBPTT over implicit gradients (well-justified — endpoint Neumann estimates collapse from initialization at every LR); the entropy term in the prior (justified at L scale, where removing it drops GSM8K from 47.92 to 36.47, though it slightly raises PPL at the training depth); and dropping Parcae's prelude RMSNorm (ablated separately, gains add with the projection). Lemma 1 proves via the contraction mapping theorem that frozen-prefix (terminal-KV) decoding converges to the same limit as joint iteration when prefix context converges, with a finite-depth error bound (equation 12). Key Results: All trained from scratch at 100M (21.5B tokens), 400M (85.9B), and 1.6B (343.6B). Learned prior (λ_H=0.01): with terminal KV sharing (4 banks vs. 12), lowers MixVal PPL 0.7–1.8% vs. fixed PLN-5 at ≤1.6% extra FLOPs; at 1.6B it reaches 60.0% downstream average and 47.92 GSM8K, matching the full-cache downstream average of fixed-depth training; the lead over Untied-4 (matched parameters/cache) grows from 2.2 points (S) to 8.9 points (L) downstream. It still trails Untied-12 (3× parameters and cache) by 1.5 points downstream and 6.3% validation PPL at L, with the gap narrowing with scale. OrthoInj: lowest validation PPL at every scale (0.3–1.4% below Parcae-Decay), highest downstream average at every scale, and lowest final training loss at every scale. RL reuse: fine-tuning the 1.6B model with Dr. GRPO at R=6 raises GSM8K pass@1 from 40.63% to 60–63% across methods; reuse+Neumann-4 reaches 61.65% (within 1.6 points of full BPTT, consistent with measured run-to-run variation; gradient cosines 0.997–0.999 vs. the recomputation control) at 1.99× faster scoring/backward (244.1 s vs. 463.5 s median per update); MBPP+ pass@1 rises 30.88% → 37–41% with 2.02× update speedup. Distilled prefill: a two-block student trained on ¼ of the teacher's tokens prefills 8K prompts 1.54–1.79× faster than the R=5 teacher, trailing downstream average by 1.0 (S), 2.3 (M), and 4.5 (L) points — the gap grows with scale; at matched latency it beats early-stopped teacher prefill by 0.5–0.9 points. Baselines are current and appropriate (Huginn, Parcae, Ouro cited; DEQ-QKV, Huginn-Linear, Parcae-Decay, fixed-depth, Untied-4/12 all run). Tested at standard academic scale, not stress-scale. Surprising finding: truncation alone (without depth sampling or curriculum) shapes fixed points, and freezing the learned prior's final distribution from the first update matches or beats adapting it at S — the learned prior's main value is finding a good shape, not adaptation. Novelty Classification: NEW FORMULATION (the unified fixed-point account explaining four training/inference/post-training shortcuts, two of which — distilled prefill and RL rollout-state reuse — are new shortcuts) plus NEW METHOD (the entropy-regularized learned depth prior and OrthoInj). The individual ingredients are standard: TBPTT and Neumann series are classic (Williams & Peng 1990; Liao et al. 2018), REINFORCE-with-entropy depth controllers resemble Ouro and RL-Halting, distillation is FitNets-style, and KV projection is a one-line orthogonalization — but the observation that Parcae's carryover amplifies the injected input 2.2–3.4× at the fixed point, and that projecting it out helps at all three scales, is a genuinely new empirical finding, and the RL-from-saved-states algorithm is new to looped LMs. Much of the paper is competent engineering optimization of known ideas (Huginn + Parcae components) in a new regime. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are unusually thorough: entropy-coefficient sweeps (λ_H ∈ {0, 0.01, 0.05, 0.1}) with final prior distributions tabulated; reward-form ablations (raw CE, log CE, exp CE, inverse perplexity); two-switch factorial ablation of OrthoInj (Table 14); backward-window sweeps b ∈ {1,…,10, full}; distillation loss/initialization ablations; an R=25 teacher distillation showing the method's limits; and a recomputation control that isolates state reuse from the Neumann approximation in RL. Statistical treatment is mixed: paired bootstrap intervals and gradient-cosine diagnostics are reported for RL, but pretraining uses one seed per configuration (explicitly acknowledged; a few single-seed comparisons like Table 14 differ by ~0.04 PPL, plausibly within seed noise). Code is released at https://github.com/ifm-ai/xllm-loop. Concerns: several headline deltas are small relative to single-seed noise (e.g., OrthoInj vs. Parcae-Decay downstream averages differ by 0.02–0.13 points at S/M); evaluation includes the authors' own MixVal held-out set alongside standard benchmarks (mitigated by WikiText-103 and public downstream tasks); the RL comparison is at a single depth so the central claim that savings grow with depth is claimed but not measured; and the learned-prior comparison inherits a shared LR choice that favors one arm at some scales. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (with a SYSTEMS artifact — code release). Practical: Yes — models up to 1.6B parameters trained on standard hardware (peak allocation 48–124 GB for the ablated windows; BF16 training with FP32 projection inner products); no exotic hardware required. Efficient: The shortcuts reduce specific costs (3× smaller KV cache at R=5, 2× RL update time, up to 1.79× prefill), but the paper is honest that savings are partial: rollout generation consumes 72–82% of RL training time so end-to-end RL speedup is minimal on MBPP+, and distilled prefill requires training a student on 25% of the teacher's token budget. Effective: Yes for the stated problems — KV sharing is nearly lossless (≤0.85% PPL) under the learned prior, RL reuse matches full BPTT within measured variation — but distilled prefill only approximately solves prefill cost, trading 1.0–4.5 downstream points with a gap that grows with scale, and the R=25 distillation largely fails (loses the deeper teacher's generation gains). Scalable: Not tested beyond 1.6B; the paper claims savings grow with depth and scale but measures the depth-dependence of the RL saving at one point only; the narrowing gap to Untied-12 suggests potential at larger scale but this is extrapolation. The work delivers a software artifact (code) plus reusable training recipes and a distillation recipe; no model weights release is stated. Strengths: - The unifying fixed-point analysis converts four ad-hoc efficiency tricks into instances of one principle, and then derives two new tricks from it (distilled prefill only becomes possible because terminal KV sharing means the student must predict one endpoint bank, not per-recurrence banks) — this is real conceptual novelty, not just a survey. - The OrthoInj motivation is backed by direct mechanism measurement (Table 16: carryover-input cosine 0.81–0.91 and 2.2–3.4× input amplification in Parcae-Decay), not just end-to-end loss curves, and the projection preserves contractiveness by construction. - The demonstration that truncation alone shapes fixed points (Table 18) is a clean, well-controlled finding with the right controls (fixed depth, with/without injection, full-BPTT comparison, collapsed Neumann baseline). - Honest negative results are reported in detail: the R=25 distillation failure with a mechanistic explanation, the MBPP+ end-to-end timing showing reuse arms are not faster overall, and the entropy term's PPL cost at the training depth. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state: models trained up to 1.6B parameters with one seed per configuration; ablations do not exhaust the design space; larger scales and other model configurations untested; feasibility in real-world applications needs further study. They also note throughout that the distilled-prefill quality gap grows with scale and that a stronger (deeper) teacher need not give a better handoff. This is direct confrontation of limitations rather than minimization — a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - The central quantitative premise — that fixed-point shortcut savings grow with depth — is never directly measured: RL reuse is tested only at R=6 (where Neumann-4's four VJPs nearly match six recurrences, so the estimator saving is small by construction), and prefill saturation is shown only at S scale. - Several headline comparisons (OrthoInj vs. Parcae-Decay downstream averages at S/M differing by 0.02–0.13 points; learned vs. frozen prior at S differing by <0.1) are within plausible single-seed noise, and no seed-variance estimates for pretraining are provided despite the authors acknowledging one seed. - No comparison against the strongest alternative looped models at equal training compute beyond their own Untied baselines — e.g., no head-to-head with Ouro or Mixture-of-Recursions trained under the same recipe, though Ouro's KV-sharing failure is cited via third-party work. - The learned prior's reward uses detached per-microbatch cross-entropy as a proxy for final model quality; the connection between this bandit objective and long-run pretraining quality is empirical only, and the frozen-prior result (Table 12) suggests the learning machinery may be largely reducible to a one-time distribution search. - The theoretical guarantees (Lemma 1, Lemma 2) require contraction (κ < 1) and converged prefix context, but the empirically measured qualified prefixes need ~100–150 recurrences to converge — far beyond the R=5 sharing regime — so practical KV sharing rests on the finite-depth bound and measured PPL, which the authors do concede. Bottom Line: For anyone actually training looped or recurrent-depth language models this is now the reference paper — the fixed-point framing, the measured injection pathology, and the RL-state-reuse algorithm are immediately usable, and the code is public — despite modest headline gains and single-seed evidence; practitioners outside this niche will find stronger alternatives (or no need) elsewhere.

#44 — Innovative (72)

Adapting prior-data fitted networks for tabular anomaly detection

M Bershtman, N Cohen · arxiv.org · karypis - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces ZEN and FOCUS, two anomaly detectors for tabular data built by adapting a general-purpose prior-data fitted network (TabPFN): ZEN scores samples by k-nearest-neighbor distance in the frozen model's embeddings with contamination-robust 'soft cleaning', and FOCUS adds a trust-weighted compactness fine-tune of the same model. - Why it's important: Tabular anomaly detection (fraud, network intrusion, medical triage) has lacked strong reusable deep representations, so every deployment trains a detector from scratch, and ADBench found no unsupervised detector reliably best; a transferable representation-based detector would close that gap the way pretrained features did for images. - How it does it: It reads embeddings from the last four transformer blocks of TabPFN, runs the model on random feature subsets plus the full feature set to diversify the in-context representations, down-weights reference samples that sit far from their own neighbors (trust weights exp(-λ·â_i)) so contaminating anomalies cannot 'hide' test anomalies, and then fine-tunes the last blocks with a fixed-center, trust-weighted compactness loss, averaging epoch checkpoints. - The good: On all 47 ADBench datasets with five fixed seeds, ZEN (79.7 mean AUROC, training-free) and FOCUS (80.0) beat the strongest baseline (Isolation Forest, 76.4) under contamination with Wilcoxon significance in every pairwise comparison, and the frozen-embedding recipe transfers unchanged to four other tabular foundation models with +4.9 to +8.2 AUROC gains. - The missing: All evaluation is on a single benchmark (ADBench classical datasets, subsampled to ≤10,000 samples and capped at 200 features), no dedicated pretrained anomaly detectors (TACTIC, FoMo-0D, OutFormer, OFA-TAD) are run as baselines, and the per-regime constants (e.g., λ=0 clean vs λ=0.5 contaminated) presuppose the practitioner knows which regime holds, which the paper itself says is usually unknown. - Read it or not: Read it if you work on tabular anomaly detection or tabular foundation models — it is the first convincing demonstration that PFN representations carry anomaly-detection signal beyond their supervised pretraining objective; skip it if you need a production-ready detector for tables above 10,000 rows or wide feature spaces, where it is untested and expensive.
Why this rank
Scored using Empirical profile. Novelty (75) and Rigor (75) both contribute strongly: a new demonstration that general-purpose PFN embeddings carry anomaly-detection signal, with an ablation ladder, five pre-registered seeds, Holm-corrected significance tests, a five-backbone transfer result, and the discovery/fix of an ADBench pipeline leak. Completeness (72) is helped by direct limitation disclosure (cleaning misfires, FOCUS's thin margin) but hurt by single-benchmark evaluation and regime-conditional constants that presuppose knowledge the paper says is unavailable. Impact (60) is limited by a code-only artifact, GPU dependence, and untested scale above 10,000 samples. Weighted composite: 0.20*75 + 0.25*75 + 0.15*72 + 0.15*72 + 0.15*68 + 0.10*60 = 72.

Show full analysis
Problem & Motivation: Tabular anomaly detection is unsupervised: a reference set defines normal behavior and the detector must score new samples, facing two unknowns — the anomalies are rare and structurally unknown, and the reference set may itself be contaminated (e.g., unverified transactions recorded as normal in fraud data). Classical detectors (Isolation Forest, kNN, LOF) remain strong but start from zero on every dataset; deep detectors train one model per dataset with gains that do not generalize (ADBench's conclusion: no detector is reliably better, so 'algorithm selection' dominates). Image anomaly detection escaped this via transfer from pretrained features, but tabular data lacked comparably strong generic representations — the gap this paper closes now that PFNs like TabPFN provide them. Existing PFN-for-anomaly-detection work either pretrains dedicated anomaly detectors or uses TabPFN's predictions as a plug-in scorer; adapting the pretrained model itself was unexplored. Key Idea: Treat a supervised tabular foundation model as a feature extractor whose in-context embeddings encode 'normality' well enough that plain kNN distance in that space is a competitive anomaly score — then make the score contamination-robust by down-weighting reference samples that are themselves isolated (soft cleaning), and improve the space by fine-tuning the model so reference embeddings contract toward a fixed, trust-weighted center (DeepSVDD/PANDA-style compactness applied to a PFN). The soft cleaning is the crucial trick: a test anomaly near a reference anomaly no longer looks normal because the reference anomaly's distances are inflated by its low trust weight, without ever removing it from the set. Methodology: Pipeline: (1) embed the reference set with frozen TabPFN leave-one-fold-out (10 folds, arbitrary random context labels), reading the last 4 of 24 transformer blocks; (2) repeat over 5 random half-feature subsets plus the full feature set, with m=min(n,500) synthetic uniform [−1,1] samples added to each context to regularize the conditioning; (3) compute one pooled isolation estimate per reference sample (standardized mean leave-one-out kNN distance over all subset×block representations) and convert to trust weights w_i = exp(−λ·â_i); (4) score each test sample by mean distance to its k=50 nearest reference samples, with distances divided by trust weights, standardized per block and averaged (Eq. 4). FOCUS then minimizes a trust-weighted squared distance of final-block embeddings to a fixed center c (the trust-weighted frozen mean), updating only the last K blocks (K=6 contaminated, K=12 clean) for two epochs and averaging the epoch-1/epoch-2 weights (SWA-style). Framework: in-context/transformer representations plus density-based scoring; the fine-tune is a one-class compactness objective, not RLHF or variational. Critical design decisions: fixed (never-updated) weights and center to prevent collapse (justified by analogy to DeepSVDD, ablated); averaging random feature subsets so cleaning mistakes decorrelate (justified by ablation, +1.9 AUROC); checkpoint averaging instead of validation-based early stopping since no labeled validation exists (reasonable but only weakly justified — gains over alternatives are ≤0.2 points, and the two-epoch choice appears convenience-driven). Key Results: On 47 ADBench datasets, five seeds, both regimes. Contaminated: FOCUS 80.0 mean AUROC, ZEN 79.7, vs Isolation Forest 76.4 (strongest baseline), TabPFN-PL 74.6, raw-feature kNN 73.9, deep detectors TCCM 72.2/DTE 74.3/DeepSVDD 70.9, official unsupervised TabPFN extension (uTabPFN) 68.3; FOCUS is significantly ahead of all 16 ranked baselines (Holm-corrected Wilcoxon). Clean: FOCUS 85.9, ZEN 85.2, raw kNN 85.1 (best mean rank at 4.4). Notably, raw kNN loses 11 AUROC points from clean to contaminated while FOCUS loses only 5.9. The ablation ladder shows the plain frozen readout is only 74.1 — augmented context +0.9, feature subsets +1.9, soft cleaning +2.8 — so most of ZEN's advantage over the frozen readout comes from the authors' extraction/cleaning, not the backbone alone. ZEN transfers to TabPFN v2 (+8.2), TabICL (+7.2), Mitra (+5.4), TabDPT (+4.9); FOCUS on TabPFN v2 lifts the plain readout +3.0. AUPRC: FOCUS best mean in both regimes but its lead over Isolation Forest under contamination is not significant (p=0.08). Scale: standard benchmark scale (reference sets ≤10,000 samples, ≤200 features), not stress-scale. Baselines are current and include recent deep detectors with public code; none tuned per dataset, same as the proposed methods. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD and NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING. Genuinely novel: adapting a general-purpose PFN (never pretrained for anomaly detection) into a competitive detector via embedding readout plus trust-weighted contamination handling, and the evidence that this recipe transfers across five tabular foundation models. Standard components recombined: kNN scoring, fixed-center compactness fine-tuning (DeepSVDD/PANDA), feature-bagging ensembles, SWA — applied to a new backbone and modality; the contamination-driven motivation and transfer results are the substantive contribution. Rigor & Reproducibility: Strong. Ablations cover every component and constant: the ablation ladder (Table 10), block-window sweep (last 1–24 blocks, Table 11), readout constants k/λ/α/B (Table 12), fine-tune constants including learning rate and trainable depth (Table 13), context construction (Table 14), injected-contamination dose-response (Fig. 11), backbone transfer (Table 15), and an unusual negative-results appendix listing eight rejected design alternatives. Five pre-registered seeds; per-dataset seed-spread reported; Wilcoxon tests with Holm correction throughout; regret profiles included. Code released (github.com/Maximilianb1/zen-focus-tabular-anomaly-detection). The authors found and fixed a genuine leak in the official ADBench pipeline (resampling with replacement duplicates samples across the split for 12 small datasets — on average 88.5% of test samples have a training twin under the official protocol), a contribution to benchmark hygiene, though it makes their numbers non-comparable to published ADBench results. Concerns: fine-tune ablations run at one seed on mixed GPU types (mitigated by paired reruns); evaluation on a single benchmark family whose datasets the method's design was developed against, with regime-specific constants chosen per regime. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (with a SYSTEMS artifact — released code). - Practical: Needs a GPU (one A100); processes ~3,500 samples/minute; no consumer-hardware story given. - Efficient: Much slower than classical detectors — ZEN totals ~3,754 s and FOCUS ~10,219 s per seed over 47 datasets vs 7.8 s for Isolation Forest — dominated by TabPFN forward passes, reducible by cutting folds (5 folds cost nothing measurable) or subsets. - Effective: Evidence supports the stated problem under AUROC; the AUPRC advantage over Isolation Forest under contamination is not significant (p=0.08), and per-dataset wins over IForest are 28/47 — real but not dominant per dataset. - Scalable: Untested beyond 10,000 reference samples and 200 features (three datasets capped at 200 features for implementation reasons); scaling is claimed via TabPFN-3's 1M-sample capacity, not demonstrated. Delivers a software artifact (public code) plus a reusable recipe (PFN-embedding readout + soft cleaning) rather than a trained model. Strengths: - The soft-cleaning mechanism is a genuinely clever, well-motivated solution to reference-set contamination: trust weights pooled across 24 (subset, block) representations average 0.70 on reference anomalies vs 1.16 on normals, and the cleaning contributes the largest single ablation gain (+2.8 AUROC), with a controlled injection study showing the gain grows with contamination rate. - The five-backbone transfer experiment (identical constants, all gains significant, +4.9 to +8.2 AUROC) is the strongest evidence that the finding is about PFN representations generally, not one backbone — and it supports the appealing thesis that anomaly-detection capability is latent in models never trained for it. - Discovery and quantified correction of the ADBench resampling leak (byte-identical train/test twins in 12 datasets) is a service to the community that strengthens the credibility of the paper's own comparisons. - The negative-results appendix and plateau-level constant sensitivity (no constant at a sharp optimum) indicate honest engineering rather than benchmark-tuned magic constants. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state: GPU requirement and 3,500 samples/min throughput with concrete speedup paths; untested scale above 10,000 reference samples and the O(reference-set) cost growth; the 200-feature cap on three datasets; and that no method (including theirs) exceeds 55 AUROC on Speech. They also candidly report that the isolation-estimate cleaning misfires on Wilt (−6 AUROC) and costs >1 point on 10 of 47 datasets, and that the fine-tune's gain largely overlaps with soft cleaning (only +0.3 over ZEN under contamination). They confront limitations directly — a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - The regime-conditional configuration undercuts the deployment story: λ=0 vs λ=0.5, K=12 vs K=6, and different learning rates are fixed per regime, yet the paper emphasizes that which regime holds 'is often unknown at deployment time'. The claim that FOCUS 'matches the best classical detector if the reference set turns out clean' uses contaminated-regime constants, but the paper does not report a single constant set that works across both regimes (the contaminated configuration loses 1.7 AUROC on clean data via λ=0.5). - No comparison against the dedicated pretrained anomaly detectors the related-work section itself surveys (TACTIC, FoMo-0D, OutFormer, OFA-TAD), justified on scope grounds ('every compared method starts without anomaly-specific pretraining') but leaving the headline 'beats every baseline' relative to a deliberately restricted pool. - Single-benchmark evaluation: all 47 datasets come from ADBench, and the methods were developed on these same datasets; no held-out benchmark (e.g., ReTabAD) corroborates generalization, and the strongest-performing datasets (musk, satimage-2, shuttle at ~100 AUROC) suggest ceiling effects inflating aggregate means. - FOCUS's marginal value over ZEN under contamination (+0.3, and only +0.3 in the ablation ladder) is thin for a fine-tuning method whose per-dataset training cost is 7,340 s; the clean-regime gain (+0.6–1.2) is the better case for it, and the paper's own hypothesis that fine-tuning and cleaning 'repair the same defect' is untested. - Ablation arms run at one seed (Tables 13–14) leave fine-tune sensitivity estimates on a weaker footing than the main results, though the paired-rerun design partially compensates. Bottom Line: For anyone building tabular anomaly detectors or probing what tabular foundation models know beyond their pretraining objective, this is the strongest current evidence that PFN embeddings plus contamination-aware readout beat both classical and deep detectors under realistic contamination — read it, but treat FOCUS as an optional increment over the training-free ZEN and expect GPU cost and unproven behavior above 10,000 rows.

#45 — Innovative (72)

A Unified Scaling Law for Time Series Foundation Models

X Dai, Y Liu, Z Dong, JM Yang, Q Xu · arxiv.org · karypis - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper fits a five-parameter scaling law linking model capacity, input (lookback) length, and forecast horizon across 21 heterogeneous time series foundation model (TSFM) checkpoints, and pairs it with a Gaussian-regression-based theory of how full-shot models (in-weight) versus frozen TSFMs (in-context, via activations) convert historical data into predictive rules. - Why it's important: Whether pretrained scale actually pays off in time series forecasting is actively contested — several recent studies show supervised baselines beating TSFMs under some history budgets — and practitioners currently lack a quantitative guide for choosing model size, context length, and adaptation strategy. - How it does it: The law is derived by integrating local resource elasticities (capacity, context, horizon) estimated from robust regression on log-MASE contrasts, yielding log R = c + α·log H − γ·log L − β·log N·log L + q·(log L)²; the learning hypotheses are tested with matched-history comparisons, parameter exchanges between opposite-rule models, and activation patching in frozen TimesFM 2.5 and Chronos 2. - The good: Fitted without any Toto 2.0 data, the law predicts Toto 2.0's horizon-averaged capacity-scaling curves (4M–2.5B parameters) with mean absolute percentage errors of 1.09% (L=2048) and 1.50% (L=4096), a strong held-out-architecture validation. - The missing: Pointwise, the five-parameter Unified law (10.13% MAPE on Controlled points) does not statistically outperform a simpler capacity-independent baseline (9.96%), and the capacity coefficient β is identified almost entirely from four same-architecture checkpoint families, so capacity effects are confounded with architectural differences. - Read it or not: Read it if you build, evaluate, or deploy time series foundation models and need evidence on when capacity and context scaling pay off; skip it if you want a prescriptive recipe for a single model family, since the law is aggregate and the pointwise precision is modest.

Problem & Motivation: Teams building time series foundation models (Salesforce, Google, Amazon, Ant, and others) face an unresolved debate: critiques of domain universality and empirical results showing supervised baselines (DLinear, PatchTST, context-parroting) competing with TSFMs raise the question of when and why pretrained scale and long history translate into better forecasts. Prior scaling studies cover either training resources (Yao et al., Edwards et al.), capacity–lookback interaction with a fixed horizon (Shi et al.), or long-context behavior (Timer-XL), but none jointly characterizes capacity, input length, and forecast horizon across heterogeneous released checkpoints. Model users face the complementary problem: given a horizon and a history budget, how large a model and how much context should they allocate? Key Idea: Estimate local partial-derivative relations of log-error with respect to log-capacity, log-context, and log-horizon from controlled contrasts across heterogeneous checkpoints, integrate them into a single closed-form response surface whose key term is a capacity–history interaction (−β·log N·log L): capacity gains grow with available history, and context returns diminish at a capacity-dependent saturation scale L*(N) = exp((γ + β·log N)/2q). The learning half pairs this with a Gaussian regression decomposition separating rule identification (estimating dynamics from history) from rule retention (in weights) versus rule extraction (in activations). Methodology: (1) Evidence design: a fixed panel of 23 dataset-frequency tasks from GIFT-Eval across six domains; controlled experiments over input lengths L ∈ {128,…,8192} and horizons H ∈ {8,…,720} at shared origins, yielding 18,768 cells aggregated to 1,070 fitting points over 21 public checkpoints (4M–2.5B parameters). The response R is raw MASE normalized by matched Seasonal Naive MASE, making cross-dataset averages dimensionless. (2) Law construction: capacity slopes are pooled OLS fits within four registered multi-capacity checkpoint families (Toto 2.0, Moirai 1, Chronos 2, Chronos-Bolt); context contrasts come from adjacent input lengths within checkpoint–horizon slices; (γ, β, q) are fit with a robust soft-ℓ1 objective over these targets, α as the median horizon elasticity, and c as the median residual. Parsimony-driven model selection compares the Unified law against six- and seven-parameter alternatives (independent-capacity, conditional quadratic, rational saturation, capacity-gated saturation, and horizon-interaction extensions) under a three-fold dataset-held-out protocol. (3) Theory: a linear-Gaussian model where history supplies noisy observations of rule coefficients with precision L·ν_j; prediction error V_r(L) separates history-reducible variance from irreducible variance, and proofs show the marginal value of additional history increases for newly available coefficients and diminishes for already-estimated ones. (4) Hypothesis tests: matched-history comparisons (DLinear/PatchTST trained on L ∈ {1024–8192} records vs. frozen TSFMs given the same history), a crossed training-history × immediate-input experiment with TimesFM 2.5 adaptation, parameter exchange between opposite-rule-trained models (108 fits), and activation patching (add/erase donor history-state differences at a fixed Transformer block) with random, carrier-only, and shuffled-history controls. Critical design decisions — the common-horizon-shift assumption, active-parameter counting, and zero-intercept capacity elasticity — are mostly justified by ablation or comparison, though the zero-intercept choice is justified mainly by parsimony. Key Results: The fitted law is log R̂ = 0.9658 + 0.0429·log H − 0.3621·log L − 0.00185·log N·log L + 0.0222·(log L)². Predictive validation: 10.13% MAPE on 1,070 Controlled points, 12.82% on 111 non-overlapping GIFT Public points, 11.53% on 150 leave-Toto-out Controlled points; the headline held-out result is 1.09%/1.50% MAPE on Toto 2.0's horizon-averaged capacity curves at L=2048/4096. Dataset-bootstrap 95% intervals for β ([0.00090, 0.00322]) and q ([0.0131, 0.0310]) exclude zero, supporting history-dependent capacity gains and diminishing context returns; fitted saturation scales sit around 3.6k–4.6k input steps for 10M–1B models. Matched-history: extending training history from 1,024 to 8,192 improves DLinear's task-averaged MASE from 1.042 to 0.931 at H=96, while frozen TSFM means remain lower at every matched condition. Adaptation: task-tuned TimesFM 2.5 improves MASE from 0.9233 to 0.7877 (−14.68%), and the 96- vs 512-input gap shrinks 68% (0.2396 → 0.0768), evidencing partial substitution between in-weight and in-context information. Interventions: cross-query activation transfer reduces error 7.51%; recovery restores 41.67% of the erasure-induced loss in TimesFM 2.5, with positive paired 95% bootstrap intervals in all 18 confirmation conditions; matched-rule donors beat opposite-rule donors in all 324 TimesFM comparisons. Tested scale is standard-to-large (up to 2.5B parameters, 8,192-step contexts, one benchmark panel of 23 tasks) — not stress-scale. Novelty Classification: NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING and NEW FORMULATION — the genuinely novel elements are (a) a joint capacity–context–horizon scaling law fit across heterogeneous released TSFM checkpoints with held-out-architecture validation, and (b) causal-style activation/parameter interventions showing historical rule information is retained, transferred across queries, and recoverable in frozen models. The Gaussian regression framework is a standard adaptation of in-context linear regression analyses (Sander et al. 2024) to time series, the activation patching methodology is borrowed from mechanistic interpretability (Zhang & Nanda 2024), and the law's functional form is a low-degree polynomial in log-resources — competent combination rather than new machinery. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are unusually thorough: reduced-law restrictions (no-capacity, no-quadratic, additive) are shown without refitting; flexible alternatives are compared under a shared three-fold dataset-held-out protocol (Unified 11.77% vs. 11.78–13.10% validation MAPE); 1,000-fold dataset bootstrap gives coefficient intervals; dataset-held-out and leave-Toto-out procedures repeat every estimation step. Statistical care is high — paired bootstrap intervals for essentially every intervention claim, antithetic query pairs, three seeds for full-shot fits with reported relative seed SDs (±0.2–0.5%). Code and main results are released at https://github.com/Fifthky/UniScale. Concerns: (a) Table 5 shows the capacity-independent baseline slightly beats the Unified law pointwise (9.96% vs. 10.13% Controlled; 13.01% vs. 12.82% Public) and the paper reports paired MAPE-difference intervals that include zero — the law's advantage over the simpler baseline rests on the capacity-curve predictions, not pointwise accuracy; (b) capacity slopes come from only four checkpoint families in which architecture and capacity co-vary; (c) everything is on one benchmark panel (GIFT-Eval) with one evaluator, so Goodhart-style overfitting of the law's form to this panel cannot be excluded; (d) this is a preprint, not peer-reviewed. These are largely disclosed in the appendices, which is a credibility positive. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (with a theoretical component that is subordinate). Practical: Yes — all experiments use publicly released checkpoints and standard hardware-accessible forecasting models (DLinear, PatchTST, TimesFM, Chronos), and the law is a five-parameter formula any team can evaluate. Efficient: The law itself is free to apply; its actionable content (context saturation near L≈4k for mid-size models, adaptation shortening useful context) directly saves inference compute versus indiscriminate long contexts. Effective: Evidence supports the law as an aggregate allocator (capacity curves predicted to ~1–1.5% MAPE), but pointwise forecasts carry ~10–13% error and the paper itself frames outputs as starting regions for task-level validation, not guarantees. Scalable: Untested above 2.5B parameters and 8,192-step contexts; the increasing-capacity recommendation (d·L/d·log N > 0) is an extrapolation from four families, not a demonstrated 10–100× result. Deliverable: released code and result artifacts plus a reusable empirical methodology; no new model weights or library. Strengths: (1) The held-out Toto 2.0 experiment is a genuinely falsifiable test — the law was fit on 16 heterogeneous checkpoints and then quantitatively predicted a withheld 4M–2.5B architecture family's capacity response to ~1% error, which is rare in scaling-law studies. (2) The intervention program (parameter exchange showing trained rule retention; cross-query activation transfer and recovery showing activation-extracted rule reuse, with matched-vs-opposite-donor and shuffled-history controls) moves the in-weight vs. in-context debate from correlational to causal evidence in frozen TSFMs. (3) The normalized MASE response (relative to matched Seasonal Naive at identical origins) makes heterogeneous datasets commensurable in a way raw-error scaling studies are not. (4) Honest reporting of negative-comparison results, e.g., the capacity-independent baseline matching the full law pointwise and the Chronos 2 direct-transfer null result (0.28774 → 0.28776). Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state that the law describes average resource returns; that the horizon term measures performance relative to a baseline whose own error varies with H, so horizon-specific references must be retained in validation; that context gains may turn slightly negative beyond the saturation region (observed through 8,192); that the zero-intercept capacity form was selected for parsimony over an intercept extension; and that bootstrap intervals for prediction-MAPE differences versus alternatives include zero. They confront these directly in appendices C.1, C.3, and C.5 rather than burying them, which strengthens confidence in the headline results. They do not, however, explicitly flag the architecture–capacity confound in the multi-capacity families or the single-benchmark dependence. Analyst-Identified Gaps: (1) The capacity coefficient β — the paper's central claim that bigger models benefit more from longer history — is estimated from four checkpoint families where capacity and architecture change together; no within-architecture-at-scale experiment (e.g., training one architecture across a wider size grid) isolates the effect, and the Toto validation, while impressive, is itself a same-family extrapolation. (2) The matched-history comparison covers only two full-shot architectures (DLinear, PatchTST) on 23 tasks from one benchmark; conclusions about history value may not transfer to other model classes or domains. (3) The Gaussian theory assumes linear rules, Gaussian innovations, and fixed per-coefficient evidence precision — far from real multi-seasonal, heteroskedastic series — and the paper never tests the theory's quantitative predictions (e.g., the specific 1/L error decay), only its qualitative directions. (4) The connection between the two halves (scaling law and learning theory) is rhetorical: the Gaussian model does not derive the fitted functional form or the β·log N·log L interaction. (5) Activation-patching sites/strengths were selected on development data with only one confirmation setting per model; the recovery of 41.67% of erasure loss at a single chosen site may not reflect the model's overall reliance on historical activations. (6) All controlled data use a single evaluator and benchmark snapshot; information-leakage concerns raised about GIFT-Eval-style benchmarks (cited by the authors themselves, Meyer et al. 2026b) are not addressed. Bottom Line: This is the most careful joint capacity–context–horizon scaling analysis published for time series foundation models, and its held-out Toto validation plus causal intervention evidence make it required reading for TSFM builders and serious users — but the core capacity–history claim rests on architecture-confounded comparisons and a single benchmark, so treat its quantitative guidance as a well-supported prior to be re-validated per task, not a settled law.

Learn2Play Bench: How Well Do LLM Agents Learn from Experience in Unfamiliar Environments? (86 ▲ )

Yibo Li, Jinhang Qiu, Zhi Zheng, Qianyun Guo, Jiaying Wu, Shuo Ji, Bryan Hooi · arxiv.org · Daily papers of 9 Oct 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces Learn2Play Bench, a benchmark of 20 manually designed text-based games with novel or counterintuitive hidden rules, deterministic feedback, and automatic scoring, used to measure how well LLM agents learn from interaction without weight updates. - Why it's important: Existing self-evolving-agent benchmarks use tasks whose rules may already be in pretraining data, so reported 'improvement' conflates genuine learning with retrieval of prior knowledge; this benchmark isolates the learning signal. - How it does it: Agents play repeated episodes of newly designed games where hidden rules (e.g., stealing a colleague's lunch earns promotion) conflict with pretrained priors, across fixed and re-shuffled instance variants, scored by four metrics (Max, Mean, Learning Gain, Learning Slope) over 3 independent trials. - The good: A controlled comparison of 11 backbones, 5 self-evolving methods, 3 harnesses, and 21-30 human players per game shows raw history retention (MEMORY) beats Reflexion, EvoTest, ReasoningBank, and AWM on Learning Gain with Kimi K3 (+16.9 vs +1.8 to +14.8), with per-game rule-discovery evidence matrices backing the aggregate claims. - The missing: Single pinned seed per game template, only 3 trials per configuration (large trial SDs relative to metric differences), and the 'experience retention beats compression' finding rests on 3 backbones and qualitative log cases rather than a causal ablation. - Read it or not: Worth reading for anyone building self-evolving agents or agent-memory systems — it delivers a falsifiable negative result about distilled-memory methods that is directly actionable; skip it if you only care about RL/fine-tuning-based adaptation, which is out of scope.

Rigor (68) is pulled down by single pinned seeds per game, no significance testing, and headline method differences (MEMORY +16.9 vs Reflexion +14.8 LG) falling within one SD, despite commendable SD reporting and self-policing appendices.
