Problem & Motivation: Practitioners building LLM agents for unfamiliar environments (e.g., an agent controlling a robot through an undocumented command interface) need agents that acquire rules from interaction feedback. The evaluation community lacks a way to verify this: existing benchmarks (StreamBench, MemoryBench, LifelongAgentBench, J-TTL on Jericho games, SWE-Bench-CL) use tasks grounded in real-world settings or public game corpora whose rules may already be represented in pretraining, so an agent's score improvement cannot be attributed to new learning versus recovered prior knowledge. The paper targets researchers developing self-evolving agents who currently compare methods across incomparable models, tasks, and protocols. Key Idea: The core trick is rule novelty by construction — designing games whose hidden rules are deliberately counterintuitive relative to pretrained priors (hard work does not cause promotion; theft does), so that any improvement across episodes must come from in-context learning of interaction feedback, not retrieval. A second key move is the fixed-vs-re-shuffled split: ten games repeat the identical instance while ten change visible characters, objects, or layouts each episode while preserving the underlying rule, isolating knowledge transfer from instance memorization. Weight updates are disallowed everywhere; all adaptation is context-level. Methodology: The benchmark comprises 20 game templates (10 fixed, 10 re-shuffled; 5 flagged as challenge games after pilot difficulty estimation), each generating instances from seeds; agents interact via a black-box command interface (actions in, textual observations and a terminal score out) with no access to game source or oracles. Protocol: Tg = 5 episodes per trial for normal games, 10 for challenge games, 3 independent trials per game-configuration cell, with trials isolated (no cross-trial memory). Scores are normalized per game as z = 100x/C against reference scores labeled exact (oracle/proof), partial, or estimated. Four metrics are defined: Max (mean of per-trial peaks), Mean (episode-average), Learning Gain (late minus early k=min(3, floor(T/2)) episodes), and Learning Slope (linear regression coefficient of the episode-mean trajectory); aggregation weights challenge games 3x so challenge and normal sets each carry 50%. Five experimental arms: (1) backbone comparison — 11 models (GPT-6 Astra, Claude Opus 5.5/5, Sonnet 5, Gemini 3.5/3.7 Flash, GPT-5.6-SOL, GPT-5 Mini, DeepSeek V4 Pro, Kimi K3, Qwen 3.8 Max) under the OpenCode harness; (2) self-evolving method comparison — NAIVE, MEMORY (raw cumulative histories), Reflexion, EvoTest, ReasoningBank, AWM, each with backbone held fixed on three models; (3) harness comparison — OpenCode vs Claude Code (Opus 5) and vs Codex (GPT-5.6-SOL); (4) human study — 21-30 college students per game under the identical interface, with Top-1/3/5 selection by Max; (5) transfer — learning slopes in re-shuffled vs same-instance control conditions. Cost analysis uses logged token counts with a 30-August-2026 OpenRouter price snapshot, separating fresh/cached input and output, plus one confirmed vendor bill (GPT-6 Astra, $150/600 episodes = $0.25/episode). Critical design decisions: pinned single seed per game (justified for reproducibility but limits rule diversity), 3x challenge weighting (justified so neither game class dominates), and qualitative rule-discovery annotation (S/P/– labels per target) rather than an aggregated discovery rate — a defensible but weak choice the authors themselves flag. Key Results: Tested at standard benchmark scale (20 games, 3 trials, ~31 agent configurations, 620 complete configuration-game cells). Backbone results (all-20-game aggregates): Claude Opus 5.5 leads Max (80.1 ± 2.7) and Mean (61.0 ± 2.4); Qwen 3.8 Max leads LG (+25.2 ± 4.5) and LS (+6.30 ± 1.18); GPT-5 Mini trails sharply (Max 34.0). Method comparison with Kimi K3: MEMORY leads all four metrics (Max 63.3, LG +16.9, LS +4.69), beating Reflexion (LG +14.8), ReasoningBank (+8.3), EvoTest (+1.8), and AWM (+4.8); three-backbone averages show Reflexion best on Max (60.0) but MEMORY best on LG (+11.4) and LS (+3.04). Harness effect: Claude Code lifts Opus 5 from Max 74.5/LG +21.3 to 81.8/+27.1; Codex lifts GPT-5.6-SOL from 57.0/+14.5 to 74.3/+22.2, attributed to models being trained on their own harnesses. Transfer: re-shuffling hurts learning slope most for weaker backbones (Sonnet 5 LS drop 2.67; Gemini 3.7 Flash 2.15) while Qwen 3.8 Max and Codex show no drop (−0.41, −0.19). Humans: Human Top-1 achieves Max 84.3, exceeding every agent configuration, with lower consecutive-episode action-sequence similarity (0.54 vs 0.66) and higher post-setback recovery (33% vs 22% of decreases followed by a new personal best); agents beat humans on execution-heavy games (REDEYE, MODEL AUDITOR). Cost: OpenCode-Kimi K3 uses 56% fewer input tokens than MEMORY and 71%/41% fewer generated tokens than EvoTest/ReasoningBank at higher Max; Codex-GPT-5.6-SOL delivers Max 74.3 at $0.144/episode. Baselines (Reflexion, AWM, EvoTest, ReasoningBank) are current and representative of the self-evolving literature. Novelty Classification: NEW DATASET/BENCHMARK plus NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING. The genuinely novel elements are (a) the counterintuitive-hidden-rule design principle that decouples learning from pretraining recall, (b) the fixed-vs-re-shuffled transfer protocol, and (c) the finding that raw-history retention outperforms distilled memory methods — a non-obvious, actionable result. The metrics (linear-trend learning slope, early/late gain contrast) and the compared methods are standard; the harness comparison is a competent evaluation of known artifacts rather than a technical contribution. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are present in the form of the backbone/method/harness factorial structure and the transfer control condition, though not component-level ablations of the benchmark games themselves. Trial standard deviations are reported for all 31 configurations and all four metrics (Appendix C), with an honest derivation of the propagated aggregate SD; the paper explicitly notes that 3 trials make SD estimates imprecise and that human Top-k groups are not repeat trials. No significance tests are reported, and several headline differences (e.g., MEMORY LG +16.9 ± 4.0 vs Reflexion +14.8 ± 4.7 with Kimi K3) fall within roughly one SD of each other. The paper is commendably careful about mechanism claims — the appendix repeatedly states that qualitative log cases 'illustrate possible mechanisms rather than their frequency' and explicitly disclaims that compression causally causes the MEMORY advantage (B.1.3). A project website exists (https://liushiliushi.github.io/learn2play-bench-website/); no separate code repository URL is given in the provided text. Methodological concerns: one pinned seed per template risks seed-specific difficulty; the human study has no pre-registration and Top-k selection introduces selection effects (acknowledged); cost figures mix standard-price estimates with one confirmed bill; and the Opus 5.5 / GPT-6 Astra rows lack rule-discovery annotations entirely, with score validation alone not establishing rule discovery. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (benchmark + measurement study). Practical: Yes — all games run through text command interfaces and commercial APIs; human study used the same interface on student hardware. Efficient: Cost per episode ranges from $0.0063 (OpenCode-GPT-5 Mini) to $3.09 (MEMORY-Opus 5), so evaluation cost is modest but non-trivial at 620 cells; the paper quantifies this frontier explicitly. Effective: The evidence shows the benchmark measures what it claims (deterministic scoring, controlled novelty), though whether agents 'learn' versus 'accumulate context' is only partially disentangled — NAIVE shows near-zero LG while MEMORY shows large LG, which is the paper's strongest internal validation. Scalable: Not tested beyond 20 games and 5-10 episodes; the paper does not claim scale and gives no evidence about generalization beyond its own templates. Deliverable: a benchmark artifact (game suite, scoring harness, archived interaction logs, per-game evidence matrices) via the project website; no trained model or library is released. Strengths: - The counterintuitive-rule design principle is a real methodological contribution: it converts 'did the agent improve?' into a question that pretraining recall provably cannot answer, addressing a confound that plagues J-TTL, StreamBench, and similar benchmarks. - The MEMORY-beats-distillation finding is genuinely useful and well-evidenced relative to the field's prior: it comes with a concrete mechanism (EvoTest turning one failed jade-opal fusion into a blanket ban on untested tier-2/3 combinations in GEMFORGE, freezing Max at 83) and per-game discovery matrices that show where distilled rules outrun the evidence. - The evaluation machinery is unusually transparent: reference scores are labeled by evidence level (exact/partial/estimated), normalization and weighting formulas are fully specified, and the appendix separates scored-window evidence from supplementary log evidence. - The human comparison produces specific, quantified behavioral contrasts (action-sequence similarity 0.54 vs 0.66; recovery-after-setback 33% vs 22%) rather than vague claims about exploration. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors explicitly acknowledge: (a) rule-discovery labels mix complete-rule discovery with successful execution and cannot be aggregated into percentages; (b) qualitative cases illustrate mechanisms but do not establish their frequency; (c) the MEMORY-vs-compression claim is correlational ('does not establish that compression causes the aggregate difference'); (d) behavioral statistics are descriptive, not causal, due to non-independence of repeated observations; (e) 3 trials make SD estimates imprecise; (f) terse logs (especially GPT-5.6-SOL) can leave targets unverified despite successful policies; (g) no rule-discovery annotation exists for Opus 5.5 or GPT-6 Astra. This is a credibility positive — the paper consistently polices its own claims in the appendix. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - Single-seed evaluation: each template is scored on one pinned seed, so game-level and aggregate results may be idiosyncratic to that instance's difficulty; no cross-seed variance for the benchmark itself is reported. - Key methodological conclusions rest on differences within one standard deviation: MEMORY's LG advantage over Reflexion with Kimi K3 (+16.9 ± 4.0 vs +14.8 ± 4.7) and over three-backbone averages (+11.4 vs +10.0) is suggestive, not established; no paired significance testing is attempted despite the fully crossed design making pairing feasible. - The harness finding ('models are trained on their harnesses') is asserted from two matched pairs and vendor-blog citations rather than tested (e.g., by evaluating one harness family against a model not trained for it in both directions beyond the two pairs given). - The human study lacks controls for effort asymmetry — the paper notes humans stopped probing in MODEL AUDITOR but does not control time budgets between humans and agents, so the Human Top-1 > best-agent comparison may partly reflect human motivation incentives rather than learning ability. - Transfer analysis compares archived re-shuffled trajectories against newly run control trajectories; any protocol drift between archived and fresh runs is not discussed. - No evaluation of whether benchmark rankings predict downstream agentic performance (e.g., on web or coding tasks), so external validity is unestablished — a standard but real gap for a benchmark paper. Bottom Line: For researchers building or evaluating memory-based self-evolving agents, this benchmark and its raw-history-beats-distillation finding are directly consequential and the paper's self-critical appendix raises it above typical benchmark releases; its single-seed design and sub-SD headline differences mean the ranking tables should be read as directional, but the benchmark itself is a contribution the field should adopt and extend.

Optimizing the Optimizer: Language Models Discover Faster Molecular Relaxation (17 ▲ )

Artem Tsypin, Vladimir Deshchenya, Kuzma Khrabrov, Denis Potapov, Maxim Radchenko, Artur Kadurin, Michael G. Medvedev · arxiv.org · Daily papers of 6 Oct 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper builds a gated LLM-driven autoresearch loop that rewrites the Sella molecular geometry optimizer, producing AutoSella-F and AutoSella-A — evolved optimizers that cut force-call counts to 40.2–77.2% of Sella's at the r2SCAN-3c DFT level while matching or exceeding Sella's energy recovery. - Why it's important: Each optimizer step requires one force evaluation, and at DFT level that evaluation dominates wall time and cost of the geometry optimizations that pervade computational chemistry and drug design, so a 1.3–2.5× reduction in force calls translates directly into proportional compute savings. - How it does it: A single-trajectory LLM agent (Karpathy-style autoresearch) repeatedly edits a pinned single-file version of Sella 2.5.0, with every candidate admitted only through a validity gate (no errors, mean energy recovery ≥ Sella's on training) and a generalization gate (same conditions on a held-out validation split), so 'faster' cannot mean 'stops too early' or 'overfit.' - The good: The savings transfer to two potentials never seen during the search — GFN-FF and r2SCAN-3c DFT — despite the search running entirely on cheap GFN2-xTB, and the paper reports an honest negative control: the same loop run with Grok 4.6 produced only 97.8–98.1% cost and regressed badly on fragment systems, showing the gates do not hand out wins for free. - The missing: One run per LLM (no seeds), no significance testing or error bars on the headline cost ratios, web access allowed during agent runs (raising contamination questions about whether the agent could read published Sella improvements), and the 'same minimum' structural check fails on most solvated systems (1.0% agreement for AutoSella-F), leaving final-state equivalence on multi-fragment systems asserted mainly through energy, not structure. - Read it or not: Read it if you work on automated algorithm discovery, LLM-driven program search, or computational chemistry software — it is a concrete, well-gated instance of the autoresearch paradigm on a real cost-bearing scientific task; skip it if you only want a better hand-designed geometry optimizer, since the mechanisms are described qualitatively rather than formalized.

Problem & Motivation Molecular geometry optimization is among the most frequently executed operations in computational chemistry, and its cost is measured in force evaluations: on an empirical force field the optimizer overhead matters, but at DFT level each force evaluation dominates wall time, so the number of optimizer steps sets the price of a relaxation. This hits anyone running DFT-level conformational searches, ligand preparation, or biomolecular relaxation at scale. Decades of manual design (quasi-Newton updates, rational-function steps, redundant internal coordinates, model Hessians, preconditioners) have converged on a handful of packages — ASE, geomeTRIC, pysisyphus, Sella — and the gap the authors target is whether an automated search can beat the best of these hand-designed optimizers on force-call count without degrading relaxation depth. Prior LLM program-search work (FunSearch, AlphaEvolve, Lion, EoH, ReEvo) targets kernels, heuristics, and neural optimizers, not molecular geometry optimization, and prior chemistry relaxation benchmarks (GOLF, ∇²DFT, PubChemQCR) evaluate potentials, not optimizers. Key Idea The core trick is to run the LLM autoresearch loop on a cheap surrogate potential (GFN2-xTB) rather than the target DFT level, and to replace a single imperfect objective with two admission gates — a validity gate that rejects candidates with any evaluation error or mean relative energy recovery below the champion's (blocking reward hacking via premature stopping or convergence-criteria gaming), and a generalization gate that demands the same cost reduction on a held-out validation split of molecules — so that accepted edits must genuinely reduce force calls at equal relaxation depth on unseen structures. Methodology The pipeline has four stages. (1) Baseline selection: 27 configurations from six open-source optimizer packages are benchmarked under an identical protocol (GFN2-xTB, a five-criterion Gaussian-style convergence test of ΔE, max/RMS gradient and max/RMS displacement, 200-call cap); Sella 2.5.0 in internal coordinates uses the fewest force calls on all four datasets, so its code is consolidated into a single pinned file (trace, concatenate, prune, collapse-device-layer, verified numerically identical). (2) Data: 469 training and 465 validation structures drawn from SPICE 2.0.1 (PubChem drug-like molecules via greedy Tanimoto-fingerprint diversity selection, DES370K dimers, 25 RowanSci drugs); four held-out test sets: 500 out-of-distribution PubChem molecules, 673 dipeptides, 475 amino acid–ligand pairs, 100 solvated PubChem systems. (3) The loop (Algorithm 1): the agent reads per-molecule evaluation records, a narrative log, and a backlog of rejected ideas, proposes one coherent edit to algo.py, and the candidate is scored remotely (192 distributed workers, evaluator inaccessible to the agent, SSH-relay JSON protocol, diagnostic bundles for failures). Acceptance requires C_per-mol below champion minus δ=10⁻⁴ on training with energy recovery ≥1 and no errors, then the same on validation. (4) Evaluation on held-out molecules and on two potentials the search never saw (GFN-FF, r2SCAN-3c via ORCA). Metrics are pooled and per-molecule force-call ratios (Eq. 1) and mean relative energy recovery (Eq. 2). Two agents ran 66 active research hours each — Claude Fable 5.1 (max) via Claude Code producing AutoSella-F (108 candidates, 37 accepted) and GPT-6 Astra (high) via Codex producing AutoSella-A (672 candidates, 29 accepted); Grok 4.6 ran as a third arm (Appendix H). Critical design decisions: the δ noise floor (justified as excluding numerical noise), the recovery-ratio validity condition (directly blocks the under-relaxation failure mode), and per-molecule diagnostic tables given to the agent (enables chemically grounded hypotheses); the recovery condition is well justified, while the choice of a 200-call cap is argued as loose (Sella uses ≤155 on train/val) but is set using the same splits the search runs on. Key Results On GFN2-xTB held-out sets, AutoSella-F costs 73.25% (Test, N=500), 65.28% (Dipeptides, N=673), 69.79% (AA–ligand, N=475), and 39.86% (Solvated PubChem, N=100) of Sella's per-molecule force calls, with mean energy recovery above 1 on all four; AutoSella-A costs 78.14–92.57% on the first three but regresses to 118.77% with ¯r=0.999125 on Solvated PubChem. On r2SCAN-3c DFT, AutoSella-F requires 77.20% (Test), 73.14% (Dipeptides), 68.61% (AA–ligand), and 40.24% (Solvated) of Sella's calls with greater mean recovery everywhere — achieved without the search ever evaluating a DFT gradient. Transfer to GFN-FF is similar (34.08–74.14% for AutoSella-F). Structural checks: AutoSella-F reaches the 'same minimum' as Sella (RMSD <0.1 Å, |ΔE| <0.1 kcal/mol, no mode below −50 cm⁻¹) on 97.2% of Test and 93.2% of Dipeptides, but only 39.8% of AA–ligand pairs and 1.0% of Solvated systems — where endpoints often lie lower in energy instead (median ΔE = −1.30 kcal/mol on Solvated). The baseline panel is current and strong: Sella beats all 26 other configurations (e.g., pysisyphus/DLC at 105.4% on Test; geomeTRIC/TRIC at 129.6%; Cartesian BFGS at ~600%). Ablations attribute the largest single-block effects to model Hessian/coordinates (+18.7 points for AutoSella-F on validation), fragment handling (+11.3), and Hessian updates (+10.2). A Grok 4.6 run reached only 97.79%/98.14% cost and 239.85% cost with 64/100 non-convergences on Solvated. Scale: ~1,650 evaluation structures per potential, xTB candidate evaluation 60–90 s on 192 CPU workers. Novelty Classification NEW METHOD and NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING, with a NEW SYSTEM/TOOL component: the genuinely new elements are the gated autoresearch loop applied to molecular geometry optimization and the demonstration that surrogate-potential search transfers to DFT without ever evaluating DFT gradients; the individual evolved mechanisms (model Hessians with non-covalent stiffness terms, fragment coordinates, Hessian-pair reuse with geometry correction, trust-radius control, a Gaussian-process step model) are competent recombinations of known computational-chemistry concepts assembled automatically rather than invented from scratch. Rigor & Reproducibility Ablations are present and informative: every functional block of both optimizers is removed individually and in four pairs, on both training and validation splits, with validity criteria for ablation runs — this is above the norm for autoresearch papers. Structural verification (heavy-atom RMSD after superposition, energy differences, numerical-Hessian vibrational analysis) goes beyond energy-only claims. Error bars, multiple seeds, and significance tests are not reported; each optimizer is deterministic per molecule but each LLM run is a single trajectory, so Fable-vs-Astra-vs-Grok comparisons are one sample per model. Code is released at https://github.com/vdeshchenya/autosella. Methodological concerns: (i) evaluation on GFN2-xTB is the same potential the search optimized on for training/validation results, though held-out molecules and the two unseen potentials mitigate this; (ii) web search is allowed in the agent container, so the agent may have accessed published Sella documentation or literature — the paper does not audit for this; (iii) the 200-call cap and the data-preparation structure-selection procedure were tuned on train/validation splits that also drive the search; (iv) the 5-criterion convergence test is geomeTRIC's, applied uniformly, which is fair, but the training-time inclusion of non-converged runs in averages is a protocol choice the reader must track. Deployability Profile: EMPIRICAL (with a SYSTEMS component — the autoresearch harness and released optimizers). Practical: Yes — both AutoSella variants are pure-Python descendants of Sella running on CPU with any ASE-compatible force evaluator, including standard DFT codes through ORCA. Efficient: The optimizer itself adds negligible overhead relative to force evaluations, and it reduces DFT force calls by 23–60% per molecule, a direct proportional cost cut; the search cost (66 active research hours × 3 frontier-agent runs plus 192-worker xTB evaluation) is a one-time investment that is not itemized in tokens or dollars. Effective: The evidence supports force-call reduction at equal-or-greater mean energy recovery across three potentials and four held-out molecular domains, but endpoint equivalence on multi-fragment systems is not established structurally (1–18% same-minimum agreement on Solvated), only energetically. Scalable: Not tested beyond 3–110-atom drug-like systems and solute+20-water clusters; behavior on larger systems, periodic materials, or transition-state (order=1) optimization is unexamined, and fragment-handling mechanisms that drive the savings may behave differently at larger scale. Deliverable: software artifact (two evolved optimizer implementations plus the autoresearch harness) at the GitHub URL above; the discovered mechanisms are documented qualitatively in Appendix G rather than as a reusable formal technique. Strengths - The two-gate admission scheme (validity + generalization) is a clean, well-motivated answer to the two most obvious failure modes of LLM program search on this task — premature stopping and training-set overfitting — and the gates are enforced by an evaluator the agent cannot touch, with per-molecule diagnostics that turn failures into next hypotheses. - The transfer result is the paper's strongest evidence: improvements found entirely on a ~cheap tight-binding surrogate carry to r2SCAN-3c DFT (40.24% of Sella's calls on Solvated PubChem, with 1.27% greater mean energy recovery), validating the surrogate-search methodology itself, not just the specific optimizers. - The honest negative control — reporting that Grok 4.6 under the identical harness, data, and gates produced essentially no improvement (97.79% training) and 239.85% cost on Solvated — makes the Fable/Astra results far more credible than a single-success story would be, and the Fable-vs-Astra analysis (108 considered candidates at 36.3-min mean intervals vs. 672 at 5.9-min intervals) gives a genuine, if anecdotal, look at agent research styles. - The classical panel benchmark (27 configurations under one protocol) independently yields useful findings — coordinate system and initial Hessian each change cost by ~4× — giving the field a reference beyond the specific evolved artifacts. Author-Acknowledged Limitations The authors acknowledge that AutoSella-A regresses on Solvated PubChem (118.77% cost at xTB, 109.06% at DFT, with lower energy recovery); that 'same minimum' agreement collapses on fragment systems (39.8% AA–ligand, 1.0% Solvated for AutoSella-F), hypothesizing alternative fragment poses and water arrangements; that the ablation blocks are non-additive (joint removals cost less than the sum of single removals); and that AutoSella-G performed poorly and was excluded from main-text comparisons. They confront limitations directly rather than minimize them — the appendix structure (per-molecule energy distributions, structural-agreement tables, full Grok run) is a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps - No seed replication or variance estimate: each LLM's result is a single 66-hour trajectory; nothing distinguishes a robust methodology outcome from a lucky run, and the model-ranking claims (Fable > Astra > Grok) rest on one sample each. - Web access during agent runs is allowed but unaudited; the agent could plausibly have retrieved Sella papers, documentation, or issue threads describing exactly the mechanisms it 'discovered' (fragment handling, model Hessian terms). A contamination audit or a no-web ablation is absent. - The initial Sella configuration for evolution uses allow_fragments=False (the costlier variant) while the evaluation reference uses allow_fragments=True — defensible and disclosed, but it means part of the evolved gain over the starting program reflects simply recovering a setting the reference already had; the Appendix G ablations compare against the False variant, which inflates the fragment-handling block's apparent contribution relative to the deployed reference. - Transfer is tested on the same four molecular benchmark sets under new potentials; no test of transfer to a new molecular domain selected after the search (e.g., inorganic clusters, periodic systems), so the scope of 'general optimizer' claims is narrower than the framing suggests. - Token/compute cost of the autoresearch runs is never quantified, so the reader cannot judge whether the savings outweigh the search investment for a typical lab's workload — a nontrivial omission for a paper whose selling point is cost reduction. - The energy-recovery metric is referenced to Sella's own final energy; on systems where AutoSella-F lands in different (often deeper) wells, ¯r > 1 partly reflects reaching different minima rather than matching quality — the authors show this, but the headline 'same energy reduction' phrasing in the abstract glosses over it for solvated systems. Bottom Line A practitioner running DFT-level molecular relaxations should absolutely try AutoSella-F — it is a free 1.3–2.5× cost reduction with released code and unusually honest evaluation — and anyone building LLM autoresearch systems should read the gates-and-negative-control design, even though the single-run-per-model evidence and unaudited web access leave the methodology's generality less proven than the artifact's value.

Problem & Motivation: LLM serving systems execute one logical request many different ways: continuous batching changes co-batched companions, chunked prefill changes chunk budgets, speculative decoding changes prefill/decode structure, and paged KV-caches share, evict, or recompute prefixes. Because floating-point addition is not associative and kernels pick tilings and reduction orders from tensor shapes, these execution variations change logit bit patterns. This matters to operators running RL post-training (rollout/training log-probability mismatch), speculative decoding (draft acceptance depends on exact logits), and anyone needing reproducible responses independent of server load. Prior work (Thinking Machines' batch-invariant kernels, vLLM's batch-invariant mode, SGLang's deterministic mode, DeepSeek-V4's in-stack kernels) addresses only batch-dependent kernel selection, empirically, with no system-level definition of what deterministic inference requires. Key Idea: Make determinism a formally specified, machine-checked property of the whole system by decomposing the proof at the engine/GPU-kernel boundary: the engine is verified in Verus against an invariant that every live or retained KV entry bitwise-equals the value a cold forward would produce for its causal token prefix (so runtime scheduling cannot change a position's logical inputs), while a separate relational analyzer proves each Triton kernel's selected output is bitwise-equal across invocations that differ in batch layout, query length, and physical page tables — the two proofs meet at uninterpreted kernel functions f_K. The enabling trick for the kernel side is value-aware relational analysis: abstract interpretation tracks cells known to be zero/−∞/masked, letting extra causally-masked attention tiles be proved identity steps so prefill and decode paths align despite different loop ranges. Methodology: Three layers. (1) Specification: Definition 2.1 formalizes determinism as prefix-comparability of per-request output views (logit bit patterns plus tokens) across any two finite executions sharing a fixed deployment configuration W — a safety property, explicitly not liveness or functional correctness. (2) Engine (Rust + Verus, ~14K LoC implementation, ~65K LoC proof): implements vLLM-style continuous batching, paged KV storage, and prefix caching; key design decisions are (a) fixed, runtime-independent kernel/tiling choices bound at initialization — justified as trading dispatch flexibility for verifiability, (b) exact prefix matching where hash candidates are confirmed by full token comparison to make cache hits deterministic — well-motivated, (c) separation of cache reuse from generation, with shared pages immutable and writes confined to private suffix slots. Theorem 4.1 (engine-step preservation of the invariant Inv(E,W) plus logits = Forward(W, history)) is proved by induction, with sampling handled as a deterministic function of logits and sampler state. (3) Kernel verifier (~17K LoC): translates an annotated Triton subset to a tile IR, performs relational control-flow alignment (isomorphism of value-relevant operations, Z3-checked scalar obligations), backward regional dependency rules (e.g., D[I,J] ← A[I,H], B[H,J] for tl.dot), and conservative abstract interpretation for attention causality; unsupported constructs are rejected and missing configurations abort rather than autotune. Explicitly trusted: the Triton compiler, contract translation, tensor-representation correspondence, tile-operation numerical rules, and finiteness of loaded values. Key Results: (1) Measurement of production systems (vLLM 0.28.0, SGLang 0.5.19, BF16, single NVIDIA H200, Llama3.1-8B and Gemma3-4B): default modes fail broadly (e.g., vLLM default FA3: 177/296 batch pairs, 53/384 prefill-decode pairs matched on Llama3.1-8B); vLLM batch-invariant and SGLang Det. FA3 pass all 784 comparisons per model on Llama3.1-8B but all four production deterministic configurations fail on Gemma3-4B (e.g., vLLM Inv. FA3: 193/296 batch, 0/90 chunk, 5/384 prefill-decode); SGLang Det. Triton matches only 3/384 prefill-decode pairs. (2) Vosti passes all 784 comparisons per model across seven models (Llama3.1-8B, Llama3.2-3B, Gemma3-4B/12B/27B, Gemma4-12B/31B), totaling 5,488/5,488 bitwise-matched pairs. (3) Performance on H200: decode throughput 1.36–3.19× vLLM's invariant modes, but prefill throughput lower than both default engines; in a synthetic 4-session, 6-turn agentic workload with 16K-token prompts and 768 output tokens/turn, Vosti completes sessions 1.14–2.20× faster than vLLM's invariant modes while remaining slower than default modes and SGLang deterministic modes (e.g., Gemma3-27B: 143 s vs 90 s vLLM default vs 106 s SGLang Det. FA3). Root-cause analyses attribute production mismatches to FA3's batch-wide K-length masking specialization and to fully-masked softmax tiles flipping a −∞ running maximum to zero. Baselines are current production systems; throughput results are single-GPU with no error bars or repeated-run variance reported. Novelty Classification: NEW PROBLEM (first system-level formal specification of deterministic LLM inference, as opposed to kernel-level batch invariance), NEW METHOD (composition of a mechanized engine-state proof with relational Triton kernel verification meeting at uninterpreted kernel functions, including value-aware identity-step alignment for causal attention), and NEW SYSTEM/TOOL (Vosti). The engine architecture (continuous batching, paged KV, prefix caching) is a competent reimplementation of vLLM's known design; Verus, Z3, abstract interpretation, translation-validation-style relational checking, and FlashAttention-style tiled online softmax are all existing techniques — the novelty lies in the specification, the invariant that ties KV-cache provenance to causal prefixes, and the cross-layer proof composition. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are partially present: the paper isolates which execution variation (batch, chunk, prefill-decode, prefix reuse) breaks each engine/backend combination and gives controlled root-cause experiments for selected mismatches, but there is no ablation showing which engine invariants or verifier components could be relaxed. No error bars, seeds, or significance tests for the throughput numbers. The specification, implementation, and proofs are quantified (Table 2: 14,043 impl / 876 spec / 64,952 proof LoC for the engine; total verification 52.9 s + ~34 s kernels) and source code is public at https://github.com/QDelta/Vosti. Methodological concerns: the motivating test suite and the determinism evaluation share the same construction (the tests are the authors' own, not a community benchmark, though no standard benchmark exists for this property); the verified determinism claim is conditional on a trusted computing base (compiler, translator, numerical rules) validated only by testing on the evaluated configurations; the finiteness premise for attention is unchecked at runtime; all evaluation is single-GPU, two model families (dense attention only), single node. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: SYSTEMS (a built, verified inference engine evaluated by measurement), with an EMPIRICAL component (the production-system measurement study). - Practical: Runs on a single commodity NVIDIA H200 with Triton kernels and standard Llama/Gemma checkpoints in BF16 — no exotic hardware required. - Efficient: Verification is cheap (52.9 s engine, ≤17.3 s per kernel configuration); runtime cost is real — prefill throughput trails both production engines, and the paper attributes Vosti's decode advantage (1.36–3.19× over vLLM invariant) to smaller tiles that conversely hurt prefill. - Effective: The evidence shows bitwise determinism (5,488/5,488) at tested variations, which is the stated goal, but the guarantee is conditional on trusted components and does not extend to functional correctness, cross-platform, or cross-dtype agreement. - Scalable: Not tested beyond one GPU and 0–16K cached context with batch 4; the paper only discusses (does not evaluate) multi-GPU, MoE, and linear-attention extensions, and rejects missing kernel configurations at runtime rather than scaling the verified set. The work delivers a software artifact (engine, kernels, verifier, proofs) released as open source, not just a paper. Strengths: - The proof decomposition is the real contribution: separating 'the engine supplies the right logical inputs' (Verus, cache-provenance invariant) from 'the kernel computes bitwise-identical selected outputs' (relational tile analysis) makes an otherwise intractable end-to-end verification tractable, and the interface (uninterpreted f_K with contracts imported as trusted assumptions) is precisely scoped. - The measurement study is genuinely useful independent of the system: it demonstrates with 784 comparisons per configuration that production 'deterministic' modes fail on Gemma3-4B in every category and identifies concrete mechanisms (batch-wide K-length masking specialization; −∞-to-zero running-maximum flips in masked tiles), converting an anecdotal concern into characterized behavior. - The value-aware identity-step argument for causal attention — proving extra fully-masked key tiles bitwise-preserve state so prefill and decode loop ranges need not match — is a non-obvious technical move that makes the prefill/decode equivalence proof work. - Intellectual honesty: the paper repeatedly distinguishes determinism from correctness, mismatches from bugs, and proof from tested evidence, and states its trusted computing base explicitly. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state that determinism does not imply functional correctness (an all-zero engine is deterministic); the guarantee is fixed to one model, dtype, kernel configuration, compiler version, and hardware; cross-kernel dispatch is future work; linear-attention and MoE architectures are unsupported; multi-GPU determinism is future work; the translator, solver encoding, numerical rules, engine/kernel interface, and compiler/GPU execution are trusted; attention finiteness is an unchecked runtime premise; the motivating tests are not exhaustive verification; and Vosti is slower than default modes. This is an unusually direct and complete acknowledgment section — a strong credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - The trusted computing base is larger than the headline 'verified' framing suggests: the compiled Triton binary is never checked against the verified source, so compiler miscompilations or hardware-level non-determinism silently void the guarantee; testing on evaluated configurations is the only support for these assumptions. - Model coverage is narrow for the claim's generality: two families (Llama, Gemma), all dense causal attention, BF16, single-GPU; no evidence the invariant framework extends to the MLA-style or GQA-variant architectures common in current serving, and no stress-testing of the kernel verifier's rejection rate on real-world kernel code (unsupported constructs abort at load time — how often? Not stated). - Performance comparison lacks variance reporting and multi-run medians; the agentic workload is synthetic and authored by the evaluators, so the 1.14–2.20× session speedup claim has no independent workload validation. - The end-to-end verification covers the tested kernel configurations for the tested models, but there is no story for configuration drift (a Triton version bump silently invalidates the guarantee) beyond the runtime rejection mechanism — operational implications for real deployments are unexamined. - No comparison against LLM-42 or MarginGate (cited related systems for deterministic/verified inference) on either determinism or performance, so the claimed advantage of ahead-of-time verification over per-request replay is argued, not measured. Bottom Line: This is the first serious end-to-end formal treatment of deterministic LLM inference and a clear advance over empirically-validated batch-invariant kernels, but its verified guarantee is narrower than it sounds (trusted compiler and numerical rules, single GPU, dense attention only) and it costs throughput against default engines — so serving practitioners should read it for the specification and proof architecture, while adopting it in production only if bitwise reproducibility is a hard requirement their current deterministic mode fails.

Long-Horizon Textual World Modeling through Structured Reasoning

F Wang, X Gao, Y Yao, K Dong, N Walia, K Das · arxiv.org · generating environments for agent testing in enterprises - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces latent-SR, a non-recursive textual world-model transition that emits sparse, replayable state edits for an entire future action sequence in a single autoregressive decode, and trains it with a trajectory-level reward that supervises intermediate as well as endpoint predictions. - Why it's important: Recursive one-step world-model rollouts compound intermediate errors with horizon, while direct endpoint prediction provides no intermediate targets — so long-horizon prediction, the core capability agents need for planning and counterfactual reasoning, has lacked a good factorization for partially observable text environments. - How it does it: The model predicts only typed sparse deltas per action; Problem & Motivation Language-based agents operating in partially observable environments must predict how the world evolves under a sequence of future actions to compare possible futures before acting. The dominant approach — learning a one-step transition and recursively rolling it forward — lets intermediate prediction errors become inputs to later calls and compound with horizon (e.g., obs-recursive drops from 94.45 to 73.66 Fact-F1 from h1 to h10 on ScienceWorld). The alternative, direct endpoint prediction from the full action sequence, avoids error feedback but fragments learning: either one model must cover all horizons with weak endpoint-only supervision, or separate models per horizon discard shared structure. The paper targets the gap between these two factorizations, in settings where the model must retain history information while tracking action-dependent sparse changes over 10–20 steps. The intended beneficiaries are builders of LLM-based agents in interactive text environments. Key Idea Treat a multi-step transition as structured reasoning over a textual world state: the model emits only sparse per-action edits in one decode, and every intermediate state (including the endpoint) is mechanically replayed by code rather than generated — which simultaneously eases state tracking, keeps the computation non-recursive, and exposes semantically grounded intermediate targets that can be individually scored and rewarded during training. Methodology The framework is a POMDP-style encode–transition–decode factorization, all instantiated with a shared Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 backbone via stage-specific prompts. Encoding maps the interaction history to a textual JSON state Ẑt (flat free-text key-value pairs on ScienceWorld/CEO-Bench, nested JSON with dot-path set/remove operations on Jericho); the SR transition conditions on Ẑt plus the full action sequence a_{t:t+k−1} and outputs a list of sparse deltas Δ̂_{1:k}; decoding renders a state into observation text (on CEO-Bench the replayed state is scored directly, no decode call). The APPLY operator deterministically merges edits, so unchanged facts are copied forward by code rather than regenerated — a deliberate design decision that removes a generation-error source and is well justified by the delta-vs-full-state ablation (Fact-F1 0.556 vs 0.499 with Qwen3-4B on a 500-example ScienceWorld subset). Because no ground-truth state trajectories exist, training is two-stage: (1) rejection-sampled distillation, where a GPT-5.2 teacher generates full traces filtered by terminal-prediction quality and format validity, used as SFT targets; (2) trajectory-level GRPO over a rollout tree with branching factors (b_enc, b_trans, b_dec), where each node receives the mean reward of its descendants and siblings form GRPO groups. The reward is fmt · (α1·obs_quality + α2·obs_quality_gain + α3·obs_quality_mid_avg), where the predictive-gain term max(0, policy − baseline)/τ compares the state-conditioned prediction against the same policy predicting directly from raw history (a frozen, pre-computed baseline — a sensible stability choice), and the mid term averages the same metric over all replayed intermediate states. A third key decision — never re-entering reconstructed states as transition inputs — is what distinguishes SR from the recursive baseline while still exposing a supervised trajectory. Key Results On fixed-target evaluation (all horizons scored against the same target step), latent-SR achieves the best average on every metric across three environments. ScienceWorld: 92.44 Fact-F1 / 92.37 BLEU average vs 88.94/85.92 for obs-direct (the strongest baseline), with the h10 gap of roughly +10 Fact-F1 and +13 BLEU points. CEO-Bench: 87.35 SE-score average vs 81.85 (obs-direct) and 80.17 for test-set-selected GPT-5.2; at h10 the margin is ~7 SE-score points (81.73 vs 74.81). Jericho: 24.5 average BLEU and 1.728 average Score MAE vs 1.956 for obs-direct, with latent-SR overtaking obs-recursive from h10 onward. Baselines are reasonably current and include matched learned variants (obs/latent × recursive/direct/SR), test-set-selected GPT-5.2 prompts, Copy-last, and oracle-selected Chronos-2/TimesFM forecasters — the test-set selection is conservative toward baselines. Three further results stand out: (1) the perturbation study shows an injected relevant fabricated fact costs latent-recursive 11.1 average SE-score points but the full latent-SR only 1.7, while an irrelevant distractor harms nothing (selective intervention); (2) the recursion gap widens with training (+0.8 at SFT → +3.1 at Distill+GRPO on matched CEO-Bench comparisons), suggesting RL does not close it; (3) counterfactual sensitivity is null for every latent-SR training stage until the intermediate (mid) reward is added, pinning the action-tracking capability to that specific reward component. Surprising and honest: RL without distillation warm-start collapses to 61.12 average SE-score, and obs-recursive/obs-direct show significantly negative action sensitivity after geometry correction. Scale: horizons up to 10 (ScienceWorld, CEO-Bench) and 20 (Jericho), test sets of 298/415/128 fixed targets; this is standard benchmark scale, not stress-scale. Novelty Classification NEW METHOD (the replayable sparse-edit transition with deterministic intermediate-state reconstruction inside a non-recursive call) plus NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING (the recursion gap persists and widens under matched training, and action sensitivity emerges only with intermediate supervision). The ingredients are individually standard — chain-of-thought-style structured reasoning, GRPO, rejection-sampling distillation, predictive-state objectives — and the closest prior work (direct multi-step models of Asadi et al./Lambert et al., latent overshooting in Dreamer) already combines non-recursion with multi-step supervision in continuous latents; the genuine novelty is instantiating the trajectory explicitly as a textual edit sequence whose intermediate states can be scored without reintroducing recursive feedback. Rigor & Reproducibility Ablations are unusually thorough: reward-component ablations (Table 4/Table 10), a distillation-necessity ablation, a matched-stage recursion comparison (Table 11), delta-vs-full-state-vs-free-form-CoT reasoning comparisons across two backbones, a controlled state-perturbation study with an irrelevant-fact control, and a two-test counterfactual analysis with company-level clustering, a permutation test, and a model-independent within-model action-swap test — plus transparent discussion of when the median-based permutation statistic degenerates. Error bars or multi-seed runs for the main prediction tables are not reported (single runs per cell; the counterfactual and sign tests are the only inferential statistics). No code, data, or model weights release URL is stated — the reproducibility statement describes environments, prompts, hyperparameters, and metrics (including exact GRPO settings and 8×A100/H100 compute) but promises no artifact. Methodological concerns: baseline model/prompt configurations for GPT-5.2 and time-series models were selected directly on the test set (disclosed and conservative, since it favors baselines); the mid-reward ablation and the counterfactual sensitivity share the benchmark used for development, so some Goodhart risk applies to the CEO-Bench numbers; the distillation teacher (GPT-5.2) is also an evaluated baseline, which is handled cleanly by matching prompts. Main results are vendor-free and the preprint is not yet peer-reviewed. Deployability Profile: EMPIRICAL (a trained system with experiments actually run; no closed-form theory). - Practical: Yes — a 4B model trained on 8×A100-80GB (Jericho RL on 8×H100), well within commercial reach, though it depends on a GPT-5.2 teacher for the distillation stage. - Efficient: Favorable relative to recursive baselines — one decode per multi-step prediction regardless of horizon, versus k model calls for recursive rollout; replay is programmatic. - Effective: The evidence shows it solves the open-loop observation-prediction proxy on three benchmarks, with the counterfactual study strengthening the claim that predictions track actions; whether it improves closed-loop agent performance is untested. - Scalable: Untested beyond horizon 20 and 4B parameters; the sparse-edit representation could degrade under very dense state change (every fact edited) or horizons where the action sequence exceeds the context window — the paper claims neither, which is appropriate. The work delivers a method and evaluation protocol in paper form; no reusable library, dataset release, or checkpoint artifact is stated. Strengths - The replayable-edit design is a genuine architectural insight: it decouples "exposing intermediate structure" from "recursive feedback," resolving the apparent trade-off between recursive and direct factorizations rather than just picking a side. - The evaluation methodology is a model for the subfield: fixed-target protocol isolating horizon from target difficulty, geometry-corrected counterfactual margins, company-clustered significance testing, and a perturbation study with a negative control — most textual world-model papers report only per-horizon accuracy. - The ablation that localizes action sensitivity to the intermediate-state reward (Table 12: every pre-mid stage is null under both tests) is a specific, falsifiable finding about why the method works, not just that it does. - Honest negative results are reported prominently: RL without distillation collapses (61.12), and both raw-history baselines are significantly anti-correlated with branch actions — informative for anyone training these models. Author-Acknowledged Limitations The conclusion states directly that experiments cover only textual, partially observable simulated environments, and that whether the factorization helps visual/continuous world models or improves downstream closed-loop planning remains open. The case-study section explicitly hedges its own interpretations (paired examples are "selected illustrations, not independent significance tests," and improved terminal stocks do not imply accurate intermediate flows). This is direct, non-minimizing limitation disclosure — a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps - No closed-loop or planning evaluation anywhere: the abstract motivates agents that "reason about counterfactual actions before acting," but the model is never placed inside an agent loop, so the practical payoff claim rests entirely on the open-loop proxy. - Main tables lack seeds/error bars; given GRPO's known variance and small test sets (128 CEO-Bench anchors, 60 test trajectories on ScienceWorld), some per-cell differences (e.g., latent-direct 89.16 vs latent-recursive 88.43 on ScienceWorld) may not be robust — the paper's own statistical care in Section 5.5 is not extended to the headline tables. - The predictive-gain baseline is frozen and computed once (Appendix C.3); a stale baseline could make the gain reward trivially easy or trivially hard over training, and no analysis of gain-term dynamics is provided. - CEO-Bench is a synthetic simulator with a single scripted CEO policy generating both train and test trajectories — distribution shift under different policies (the counterfactual set aside) is unmeasured. - The distillation filter keeps only traces whose terminal predictions exceed a quality threshold, which biases the state representation toward the teacher's own predictive blind spots; no analysis of distillation-data diversity is given. - Latent-space Faithfulness of the textual state is assumed rather than tested: the perturbation study shows the model is robust to injected errors, but no probe verifies that the learned states actually encode the claimed latent variables (trends, drivers) rather than exploiting decoder shortcuts. - No artifact release despite a detailed reproducibility statement; independent verification currently requires rebuilding data collection and prompts from scratch. Bottom Line This is the strongest paper I have seen on the recursive-vs-direct factorization question for textual world models — the sparse-edit/replay design and the counterfactual evaluation protocol alone justify a read by anyone working on LLM world models or agent memory, even though the absence of any closed-loop experiment and of released artifacts means its practical impact for actual agents remains a well-supported hypothesis rather than a demonstrated result.

Representation-Space MMD for Diffusion Language Models (16 ▲ )

Ilya Drobyshevskiy, Ilia Sudakov, Maksim Semenov, Denis Kuznedelev, Maksim Ignatov, Pavel Temirchev, Nikita Balagansky, Viacheslav Meshchaninov, Nikita Gushchin, Dmitry Baranchuk · arxiv.org · Daily papers of 6 Oct 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces a post-training method for diffusion language models (both discrete and continuous) that minimizes Maximum Mean Discrepancy (MMD) between generated and reference token-level features from a frozen pretrained DLM, enabling faster/fewer-step generation without teacher trajectories or jointly trained auxiliary models. - Why it's important: Few-step diffusion language models currently need expensive distillation pipelines (teacher rollouts, learned discriminators or auxiliary denoisers); a distribution-matching signal computable directly from samples makes cheap post-training of DLMs practical, including a demonstrated 16B-scale deployment. - How it does it: The core trick is to use contextual features at individual token positions from a single frozen extractor pass, yielding B×|S| kernel observations per batch, estimated with an unbiased sequence-kernel MMD (excluding same-sequence pairs), optimized via grouped REINFORCE with a leave-one-out baseline for discrete models and direct differentiation for continuous ones. - The good: The evaluation is unusually thorough for this space: 5-seed error bars on generative perplexity and GSM8K accuracy, extensive loss/representation/group-size ablations, and a real 16B-scale result (DMax-Math/Coder-MMD: 10.3–16.5% more tokens-per-forward at equal-or-better accuracy on GSM8K/MATH500/Minerva/ASDIV; +2.4 and +3.8 points on HumanEval-Instruct and MBPP-Instruct). - The missing: There is no direct comparison of the training-compute cost of MMD post-training against the distillation baselines it beats (e.g., total GPU-hours vs. IDLM/DiDi-Instruct), and the kernel bandwidth, feature layer, and batch size appear tuned per setup without a held-out selection protocol. - Read it or not: Read it if you work on diffusion LLM sampling efficiency or distribution-matching post-training — it is the strongest released-code demonstration of frozen-feature MMD for text generation — skip it if you only care about autoregressive LLM post-training, where the related EBFT line (Jelassi et al., 2026) covers the same ground.

Rigor (72) is hurt by Goodhart risk (GSM8K hyperparameters tuned and evaluated on the same benchmark, no held-out selection protocol) and baselines compared via copied numbers; 5-seed error bars and extensive ablations partially offset this. Problem & Motivation Diffusion language models (DLMs) need many denoising steps at inference, and existing accelerations — distillation from teacher trajectories (SDTT, ELF-PD, FMLM⋆), or distribution-matching with jointly trained auxiliary models (IDLM, D-MMD, DiDi-Instruct) — require either expensive teacher rollouts or additional learned networks. The authors ask whether a useful distributional training signal can be computed directly from generated and reference samples, with no auxiliary model and no full sampling trajectories. This matters for anyone deploying DLMs (e.g., LLaDA-2.0-scale masked models) where decoding parallelism (tokens per forward pass) is the key efficiency metric and post-training cost must stay low. Key Idea The central trick is to treat token-position features from a frozen pretrained DLM as i.i.d.-style observations of the conditional distribution: one extractor forward pass yields |S| feature samples per sequence, and MMD is computed with a positive-semidefinite sequence kernel formed by averaging pairwise RBF similarities between token features — with same-sequence pairs excluded to preserve unbiasedness. The repulsive generated–generated term plus the attractive reference–generated term jointly prevent mode collapse, and the resulting reward needs only one reference per condition, making conditional post-training feasible. Methodology The method (Section 3) defines a conditional MMD objective L_MMD over contextual features φ(x) extracted from a frozen DLM at scored positions (masked positions for masked DLMs; response positions for prompted generation; all positions for unconditional latents), using a Gaussian RBF kernel. The training loss (Eq. 6) averages the generated–generated kernel term over B≥2 independently sampled sequences minus twice the reference–generated term; the real–real term is dropped since it is θ-independent. Two realizations: (1) Discrete — MDLM-MMD and DMax-MMD sample B token sequences from a single denoiser pass, compute MMD reward, and optimize with REINFORCE using G groups and a leave-one-out baseline (Eq. 8–9); (2) Continuous — ELF-MMD initializes a one-step latent generator from pretrained ELF and backpropagates MMD gradients through the frozen extractor, with bootstrapped self-conditioning steps (sampled uniformly in {0,…,n−1}) to match multi-step inference, plus optional Iterative Refinement Distillation (IRD) to compress K refinement steps into one. Critical design decisions: token-level RBF rather than mean-pooled sequence-level RBF or linear-kernel feature matching (justified by ablations in Sec. 4.4, where attraction-only and feature-regression variants collapse for continuous models); the exclusion of same-sequence kernel pairs for unbiasedness (well argued); and the presence of the repulsive term (ablation shows collapse without it). A theoretical justification that token-feature MMD identifies the true sequence distribution is only sketched via injectivity results for causal transformers — the authors explicitly note this does not establish identifiability for their estimator. Key Results On OpenWebText unconditional generation (L=1024, 1000 samples, GPT-2-Large generative PPL), MDLM-MMD achieves 43.50±0.86 gPPL at 8 steps, 26.84±0.48 at 16, and 21.46±0.18 at 32 (matched to data entropy ≈5.43), versus IDLM's 56.20/33.77/29.30 — a 17–21% reduction at matched entropy. For continuous models on GSM8K (trained on TinyGSM), ELF-MMD+IRD reaches 20.8% accuracy at 4 steps (vs. 15.9% for ELF-PD), 32.5% at 8 (vs. 23.5%), and 36.3% at 64 steps (vs. 31.6% for ELF), averaged over 5 seeds; it beats ELF-GAN at most budgets. At 16B scale, DMax-Math-MMD increases tokens-per-forward by 10.3–16.5% over DMax-Math operating points with equal or higher accuracy (e.g., GSM8K 92.1→92.1 with TPF 5.48→6.15; Minerva-Algebra 91.5→92.1 with TPF 7.03→8.19), and DMax-Coder-MMD improves pass@1 by 2.4 and 3.8 points on HumanEval-Instruct and MBPP-Instruct with higher TPF. Post-training cost is modest: 400 steps, ~1.7–2.5 GPU-hours on 8×H100. Baselines are current and reasonably strong (IDLM, DiDi-Instruct, D-MMD, TokenDrift, ELF/ELF-PD/ELF⋆/FMLM+), though two baselines without released code (D-MMD, TokenDrift) are compared only via numbers copied from their original papers. A counter-intuitive practical finding: MMD post-training works with only 400 steps at 16B, and a single bootstrap step captures most of the bootstrapping benefit. Novelty Classification NEW METHOD (representation-space MMD post-training for both discrete and continuous DLMs) plus NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING (frozen-feature MMD scales to 16B hybrid masked–uniform models with only 400 steps). The individual ingredients — MMD objectives, frozen pretrained feature spaces (from MMD-GAN/GFMN/SwD in vision), REINFORCE with group baselines, self-conditioning, and flow-map distillation — are all established; the genuine novelty is the token-level sequence-kernel construction that multiplies observations per extractor pass, and the unified application across discrete and continuous DLM state spaces. It is a competent, well-executed transfer of visual-generation distillation ideas (SwD-style patch-level MMD) to text, not a fundamentally new learning principle. Rigor & Reproducibility Ablations are a clear strength: kernel choice (linear vs. sequence-level vs. token-level RBF), attraction-only variant, feature regression, representation space (input embeddings, external AR encoder, diffusion encoder), policy-gradient group size G∈{1,2,4,8}, model-size scaling (ELF-B→ELF-M), and bootstrap-step count — each isolates a component. OWT and GSM8K tables report 5-seed means with standard deviations; the 16B results average 5 training runs with error bars. Code is released at github.com/yandex-research/dlm-mmd. Concerns: the DMax comparison uses baseline numbers from the original DMax paper (partially self-reproduced); D-MMD and TokenDrift comparisons rely on copied published numbers without re-running; RBF bandwidth (σ from 10 to 3330), feature layer, and batch size vary per setup and appear tuned on the evaluation tasks (GSM8K results are tuned-on and evaluated-on the same benchmark's training set, so test-set selection is not flagged either way); no significance tests beyond reported standard deviations; generative perplexity under GPT-2-Large is a known imperfect proxy for sample quality. Deployability: (4-property check) Profile: EMPIRICAL (with a strong SYSTEMS component at 16B). — Practical: Yes — uses standard hardware (8×H100 for 16B models; small models for OWT/GSM8K experiments), and all components are standard training loops. — Efficient: The method's selling point is cost: 400 post-training steps (~1.7–2.5 GPU-hours at 16B) with no teacher trajectories or auxiliary models, though the paper never reports the compute of the small-scale MMD runs relative to IDLM/DiDi-Instruct training. — Effective: Evidence covers both proxy metrics (generative perplexity at matched entropy) and end tasks (GSM8K accuracy, HumanEval/MBPP pass@1), so it demonstrates more than a proxy; however, no human or likelihood-free quality assessment of unconditional text is reported. — Scalable: Tested up to 16B and from ELF-B to ELF-M, but 10–100× beyond 16B is untested and only implied; the REINFORCE estimator's variance at larger scale is not analyzed. The work delivers a software artifact (released code and hyperparameter tables) plus the recipe; no trained checkpoints are mentioned for the small-scale models. Strengths - The token-level sequence-kernel MMD construction (averaging pairwise token-feature RBF similarities, excluding same-sequence pairs for unbiasedness) is a genuine, non-obvious technical move that turns one extractor pass into many MMD observations — this is what makes the method cheap for conditional generation with a single reference. - Unified treatment across discrete (masked, hybrid masked–uniform) and continuous (latent flow) DLM state spaces with one objective, which is rare and strengthens the claim that the mechanism is general rather than architecture-specific. - The 16B DMax result is the most credible evidence in the paper: real released checkpoints, official dInfer evaluation stack, five-seed error bars, and accuracy–TPF curves across eleven decoding thresholds — a deployment-relevant metric (tokens per forward), not just perplexity. - Honest theoretical framing: the authors explicitly state that injectivity results motivate but do not prove identifiability of their estimator, rather than overclaiming. Author-Acknowledged Limitations The authors acknowledge that performance depends on RBF bandwidth and representation choice (calling representation design an open direction), that they use features from a single layer on clean inputs only, and that combining MMD with other objectives (e.g., the demonstrated IRD gains) may be needed in practice. They also note that retaining same-sequence kernel pairs introduces bias even if useful in practice, and that the identifiability argument is incomplete. These limitations are confronted directly rather than minimized, which is a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps - No comparison of training compute against the distillation baselines the method beats — 'no teacher trajectories needed' is claimed but the total GPU-hour parity is never shown, so the efficiency argument rests on architecture of the method, not measurement. - Hyperparameters (bandwidth, layer, batch size, learning rate) vary widely across setups (e.g., σ from 10 to 3330) and there is no stated protocol for selecting them without tuning on the test benchmark; this raises Goodhart risk for the GSM8K headline numbers. - Two discrete baselines (D-MMD, TokenDrift) are compared via numbers copied from their papers under possibly different extractors/evaluation protocols, which weakens the strongest OWT table (Table 2). - The 16B experiments train on LLaDA-2.0-mini-generated data rather than curated ground truth, so the DMax gains measure improvement over a self-distillation-style data distribution, not over the true data distribution — an unstated distributional caveat. - No evaluation of instruction-following, factuality, or long-form coherence at 16B beyond math/code; the general-purpose text quality impact of MMD post-training at scale remains unmeasured. - The 2-step ELF-MMD results with the T5 encoder are notably worse than ELF (gPPL 192.28 vs. 34.02), indicating the method can degrade very-low-step regimes, which the narrative does not discuss. Bottom Line Practitioners working on fast diffusion LLM decoding should read this paper — it delivers a cheap, code-released post-training recipe with credible 16B evidence that meaningfully shifts the accuracy–parallelism trade-off — while readers seeking a general theory of distribution matching for text will find the identifiability story only sketched and the alternative distillation literature still essential.

Pivot-SD: Efficient Self-Distillation for Masked Diffusion Language Models (50 ▲ )

Seo Hyun Kim, Sunwoo Hong, Younwoo Choi, Chen-Hao Chao, Se-Young Yun, Rahul G. Krishnan · arxiv.org · Daily papers of 5 Oct 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces Pivot-SD, an offline self-distillation framework for masked diffusion language models (dLMs) that supervises only the handful of denoising commitments ("pivots") that most reduce uncertainty over remaining masked positions, using cross-entropy for successful trajectories and unlikelihood for failed ones. - Why it's important: Post-training dLMs currently requires either full-sequence SFT that weights trivial fills the same as decision-shaping tokens, or online RL that is compute-hungry and stalls under zero-reward batches; a cheap offline alternative makes dLM post-training feasible on academic hardware. - How it does it: The core move is scoring each denoising step by its normalized entropy drop over still-masked positions (information gain, computed from forward passes the sampler already runs), selecting the top-K steps, then applying CE/UL loss only at those committed tokens in the exact masked state where they were originally generated. - The good: With 200 questions × 4 rollouts, Pivot-SD beats budget-matched and 5,000-step RL baselines (diffu-GRPO, wd1++) on 3 of 4 benchmarks at 256 tokens with non-overlapping one-standard-deviation intervals (e.g., MATH 37.47±1.21 vs. best baseline 35.47±0.23), using 2.8 vs. 5.4–22.9 wall-clock hours on two L40 GPUs. - The missing: The method is only tested at 200–2,000 questions on an 8B model with verifiable math/code tasks, the sampler setting (one token per step) is load-bearing for the pivot definition, and the MBPP+ margin (0.8 points) is within noise — no evidence yet at larger data, longer context, or open-ended generation. - Read it or not: Read it if you are post-training or studying masked diffusion LMs and care about credit assignment or compute efficiency; skip it if you work on autoregressive LLM post-training, where the token-selection ideas (entropy-based filtering, unlikelihood on critical tokens) are already familiar.

Novelty (70) is moderate — entropy-based token filtering and unlikelihood are standard; the new element is where the loss is applied.
