Problem & Motivation: Masked diffusion language models generate by iteratively unmasking positions, and under confidence-based samplers a small number of early commitments sharply reduce uncertainty over the remaining masked positions and largely determine the response. Existing post-training recipes for dLMs either (a) train on the final text with uniform per-position loss, giving a pivotal early commitment the same weight as a trivial late fill and penalizing correct intermediate steps in failed trajectories, or (b) use online RL with rewards at trajectory or step granularity, which is expensive and unstable at small budgets (the authors observed zero-reward batch stalls for wd1++ on code). Practitioners post-training 7–8B dLMs on verifiable reasoning tasks lack a cheap, stable way to decide which tokens to learn from. The gap closed is credit assignment at the granularity of the individual denoising commitment, using a signal (entropy over masked positions over time) that autoregressive generation does not expose. Key Idea: Score each denoising step by its information gain — the average entropy reduction per remaining masked position caused by that step's commitment — and train only on the K highest-gain committed tokens, replaying the exact partially-masked state in which each was committed, with the loss sign set by the trajectory-level verifier outcome (CE for correct, unlikelihood for incorrect). Because the same token at the same position matters more early in denoising than late, the supervised object is the event (t, p, y_p) rather than the final-sequence position — a distinction only available in dLMs. Methodology: Pivot-SD is a three-stage offline pipeline. (1) Trajectory generation: sample T-step denoising trajectories (800 total: 200 prompts × 4 rollouts) from the frozen base model θ₀ with the confidence-based sampler (block length 64, one token per step), giving candidate commitments (t, p, y_p) per step. (2) Pivot selection: compute pre/post entropy sums over positions still masked after step t, normalize by their count to make scores comparable across steps (Eq. 9), exclude block-boundary steps and EOS tokens, and keep the top-K steps (K=10, fixed a priori; results stable for K∈[5,20]). Selection reuses sampler forward passes, adding zero model calls. (3) Outcome-conditioned training: each pivot tuple (M_t, y, p, y_p, s(τ)) trains with cross-entropy −log P_θ(y_p|M_t) if the verifier marked the trajectory correct, or unlikelihood −log(1−P_θ(y_p|M_t)) scaled by λ_neg if incorrect; no loss lands on any other token, and the objective (Eq. 14) is minimized by standard gradient descent on the fixed cached dataset. Critical design decisions: (i) normalizing information gain by remaining-masked-count (justified — unnormalized differences would mechanically favor early steps); (ii) applying unlikelihood only at pivots, sparing valid content in failed trajectories (supported by the Pos+Neg All-token ablation losing 2.5–5.1 points); (iii) λ_neg set from the positive:negative trajectory ratio for math (1 and 5) but log-scale searched on ~100 held-out examples for code (0.02) — the only tuned hyperparameter, a mild inconsistency in the "no tuning" narrative. Key Results: On LLaDA-8B-Instruct at the 256-token training-matched budget, Pivot-SD scores 37.47±1.21 (MATH500), 79.51±1.30 (GSM8K), 40.43±2.75 (HumanEval+), 47.12±1.20 (MBPP+), best mean on all four among SFT-GT, SFT-SD, and budget-matched diffu-GRPO/wd1++ (all run 3 seeds with full re-randomization of question set, trajectory pool, and seed). It also beats the 5,000-step extended RL runs (e.g., MATH 37.47 vs. 35.20 for diffu-GRPO) while using 1,875 vs. 3,093 PFLOPs (~1.65×) and 2.8 vs. 5.4–22.9 wall-clock hours. Ablations show selectivity matters once unlikelihood is applied: Random-Step Pivot drops MATH to 29.93±3.13 (below the untrained base model's 31.40) and Random-Token to 34.87, vs. 37.47 for information-gain selection. On Dream-v0-Instruct-7B, Pivot-SD beats both SFT baselines on all four benchmarks (e.g., MATH 42.20 vs. 40.80 SFT-SD). At 512 tokens it leads on MATH/GSM8K/MBPP+ but scores 41.46 on HumanEval+, below the base model (42.07). OOD transfer: best overall micro-average (48.61) but third among MATH-trained models. MBPP+'s 0.8-point margin over SFT-GT is within one standard deviation and honestly counted as a tie. Baselines are current (2025–2026 dLM RL methods) and reasonably strong; the RL baselines were even given a bootstrap reward-shaping fix to un-stall them on code, and still lost. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD (Pivot-SD's combination of information-gain pivot selection with outcome-conditioned pivot-local CE/UL) plus a NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING (supervising ~4% of tokens from 200 prompts suffices to beat 10×-data RL on dLMs). The genuinely novel element is using trajectory-recorded information gain to localize offline supervision inside the denoising process, distinct from inference-time info-gain sampling (KLASS, Yang et al.), final-sequence entropy weighting (GIFT), and step-level online RL (AGRPO, DiSPO). The ingredients — entropy-based token selection, unlikelihood training, rejection-style self-distillation — are all standard; the novelty is the unit of supervision and where the loss is applied. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are well-designed: they separately isolate state selection (IG vs. random step), token selection within the state (pivot vs. all vs. random token), and selection criterion (IG vs. local entropy), each with and without the negative branch — a genuine attempt to show which components matter. Three fully re-randomized seeds with standard deviations are reported for all budget-matched methods; no significance tests are claimed, and the authors explicitly decline to claim statistical significance and count MBPP+ as a tie — commendably honest. Notably, the appendix reports a failed/negative result (wd1++ zero-advantage stall, Appendix I) transparently. However: extended RL baselines and the 512-token evaluations are single runs; the K-sweep and budget-sweep tables are single runs; and random controls show large variance (HumanEval+ std up to 5.51). Code: the paper states trajectories and evaluation scripts "will be open-sourced" under MIT (project page sunwoohong.github.io/pivot-sd), but no released repository is confirmed in the text. Methodological concern: λ_neg for code was tuned on a held-out split, a (small) deviation from the hyperparameter-free story; also, all evaluation benchmarks are standard and the method is not evaluated on the same data it selects pivots from, so no Goodhart-style contamination is apparent. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (with a strong SYSTEMS-adjacent flavor given the compute accounting). Practical: Runs on two consumer-adjacent NVIDIA L40 GPUs — genuinely modest hardware for an 8B model. Efficient: 1.65× fewer FLOPs and 2–8× less wall-clock than matched/extended RL, with training taking only 0.3 h after 2.5 h of one-time offline sampling. Effective: The evidence shows it improves verifiable math/code accuracy on two backbones under matched budgets; it does not address open-ended tasks without reliable verifiers, and the 512-token HumanEval+ regression shows the gains do not uniformly transfer across lengths. Scalable: Not tested beyond 2,000 questions / 8B parameters; the authors themselves flag that block-local credit assignment and per-configuration hyperparameters may not extend to long contexts or larger models. Deliverable: a described method with promised open-sourced trajectories/eval scripts; no trained checkpoint or library release is confirmed in the text. Strengths: - The unit-of-supervision insight is real and dLM-specific: using the entropy trajectory over masked positions to identify which commitments shaped the response is a signal no final-text method can access, and the paper positions it carefully against inference-time info-gain sampling, GIFT, and step-level RL (Table 6 is a useful map). - The ablation design is unusually clean — crossing positive/negative branches with state/token/random selections demonstrates that pivot selection matters specifically because of unlikelihood (Random-Step falling below the base model is a striking, informative negative result). - Compute accounting is unusually thorough and honest: FLOPs, NFE, wall-clock, and supervised-token counts are all broken out (Tables 3, 11), and the appendix documents the wd1++ stall and the reward-shaping rescue given to the baseline rather than hiding it. - Genuine data-efficiency result: 200 prompts and 10 supervised tokens per trajectory beating 5,000-step RL on 3 of 4 benchmarks is a practically meaningful claim, and it replicates across two backbones. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state that λ_neg and other hyperparameters are set per configuration rather than learned and require adjustment across domains/backbones; that credit assignment is local to a denoising block and would need extension across block boundaries for long-context reasoning; and that experiments cover only two masked diffusion backbones at comparable (7–8B) scale. They also acknowledge in the risks section dependence on automated verifiers (reward-hacking risk on open-ended tasks) and possible amplification of base-model biases via self-distillation. This is direct, non-minimizing disclosure — a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - The pivot definition silently depends on the one-token-per-step sampler configuration; how information gain and pivot selection behave under multi-token or block-parallel unmasking (common in faster dLM samplers) is unexamined, so the method's applicability to the inference configurations practitioners actually deploy is unclear. - Only one round of self-distillation is evaluated. There is no comparison against iterative rejection-sampling/self-distillation (e.g., STaR-style loops), which is the natural alternative use of the same compute and the strongest missing baseline for the offline setting. - Several headline-adjacent results rest on single runs (extended RL, the 512-token columns, the K-sweep, the budget sweep), while random-selection controls exhibit standard deviations up to 5.5 points — the selectivity story is convincing at K=10 with 3 seeds, but boundary claims (e.g., the 512-token HumanEval+ regression, K=40 collapse) are under-powered. - The extended RL baselines (5,000 steps) are compared in wall-clock/FLOPs against a method that caches its data offline; a fair extended comparison would let RL also see 2,000 questions at matched total FLOPs with multiple seeds, which the paper partially does (budget sweep, single-seed) but cannot fully resolve. - No investigation of why unlikelihood at pivots generalizes rather than merely suppressing tokens that correlate with failure — the risk that pivot unlikelihood encodes verifier noise or spurious solution-path features is not probed. Bottom Line: For anyone post-training masked diffusion LMs on verifiable tasks, this is worth reading and likely adopting as a cheap first-line baseline — it demonstrably beats current online RL at 8B scale for a fraction of the cost — but it is a narrowly-scoped (200–2,000 prompts, 8B, block-local, verifier-dependent) result whose scaling behavior and robustness beyond that regime remain open.

Rethinking Multi-Image Re-Representation in Multi-Image Understanding

G Zhang, X Han, X Xie, T Liu, V Tresp · arxiv.org · karypis - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces Mosaic, a visual tool harness with ten composable image operations (crop, rotate, homography, collage, overlay, pixel differencing, coordinate grids, etc.) that lets a multimodal LLM construct and reuse visual intermediates during multi-image reasoning, plus MosaicBench, a 560-example grounding-focused benchmark, and MosaicAgent-8B, an RL-trained agent that uses the harness. - Why it's important: Current MLLMs encode multi-image evidence into compressed visual tokens, and it is unclear when actively manipulating images (visual re-representation) beats reasoning in text — a question that determines how agentic vision systems should be built and where tool investment pays off. - How it does it: The core move is a controlled five-setting comparison (no re-representation, free-form CoT, guided re-description, online visual tools, prefabricated visual intermediates) plus GRPO training with only binary accuracy and format rewards, with no demonstration trajectories or tool-specific reward shaping. - The good: The cleanest evidence is the harness ablation on identical training data: CoT-only RL lifts the Qwen3-VL-8B backbone from 45.2% to 53.0% on MosaicBench, while RL with Mosaic reaches 63.3% — a 10.3-point gain attributable to the harness, corroborated by a crossed trajectory-probing analysis (+11.0 pp final-prefix answerability from post-RL trajectories with the solver fixed). - The missing: The headline benchmark (MosaicBench) is constructed by the authors from the same generation pipeline and task taxonomy as the training suite (overlap removed only at sample/source/image level), so the agent's largest gains are measured on data distributions its training task types were designed around; results on genuinely external benchmarks are mixed (MMIU drops from 61.0% to 57.2% with training). - Read it or not: Read it if you work on agentic vision, tool-use RL for MLLMs, or multi-image benchmarks — the five-setting taxonomy and the construction-vs-utilization probing analysis are reusable; skip it if you only want evidence that visual tools help on externally established benchmarks, since that case is thinner here.

Scored using Empirical profile. Rigor (70) is the strongest driver — harness-on/off ablations with seed error bars and the crossed prefix-probing protocol — but it is held back by the circular MosaicBench construction (Goodhart flag), an unaddressed missing-agent-baseline gap, and the unexplained MMIU regression. Novelty (80) is high (new formulation + benchmark + probing method), while Completeness (65) and Resilience (62) are dragged down by the fact that the headline gains live on a self-authored benchmark with only +2–4 pp external evidence. Problem & Motivation: Multi-image understanding (video frames, multi-view scenes, image collections) requires MLLMs to organize visual evidence distributed across images, not just recognize each image. Prior approaches either reason over the encoded context textually (CoT, caption chains like QG-CoC) or use agentic visual tools (DeepEyes, Visual Sketchpad, PyVision, VipAct), but no controlled study identifies when visual manipulation beats textual re-organization. Existing multi-image benchmarks (BLINK, M4Bench, MMIU) mix tasks with different evidence demands, so gains from visual tooling cannot be attributed cleanly. The authors target two audiences: practitioners deciding between textual and visual reasoning strategies, and researchers training tool-using vision agents. Key Idea: Formulate both textual CoT and agentic image manipulation as instances of one abstraction — multi-image re-representation, a re-representer p(z|x) feeding a solver p(y|x,z) — and then decompose visual tool benefit into two separable factors: whether prefabricated visual intermediates help the solver (PV-Re2 vs. textual settings) and whether online construction by the agent itself helps (V-Re2). The single most transferable insight is the crossed prefix-probing protocol: deterministically replay trajectories from pre- and post-RL policies, force-answer at every prefix with pre- and post-RL solvers, and separate gains in trajectory construction from gains in answer readout. Methodology: The pipeline has three stages. (1) Harness: Mosaic exposes ten deterministic operations (crop, rotate, resize, flip, affine, homography, coordinate grid, per-pixel difference, collage, overlay) over a persistent asset workspace with RGBA editing views and RGB observation views; outputs become reusable assets with stable [imgN] references. (2) Benchmark suite: 32 task types across six challenge categories (resolution, orientation, precision comparison, hypothesis testing, context interference, spatial reference) are built by annotation augmentation from 12 public datasets (VisDrone2019-MOT, TT100K, CAMELYON16, MVTec AD, CARPK, PubLayNet, LEVIR-CD, SmartDoc15, MSD, Rico, COCO, BDD100K) plus two synthetic generators; ground truth derives from source annotations or known construction parameters, with shortcut probes and reprojection/seam-error validation. Training selection uses rollout filtering (incorrect without tools, correct in 2–7 of 8 tool-enabled rollouts), yielding 3,509 of 12,800 examples; MosaicBench holds out 560 examples across 28 task types with three-level overlap exclusion. (3) RL: GRPO on Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct (8 rollouts/prompt, group-normalized advantages, no critic, no KL, lr 1e-6, 4×H100, max 10 assistant turns), reward r = acc(y, y*) + fmt(τ, y), both binary. Critical design decisions: rollout-based curriculum filtering (reasonable but optimizes for the initial policy's difficulty band); prefabricated intermediates generated by the RL-trained agent and shared across all solvers (introduces a solver-generator coupling they partially acknowledge); and the closed-evidence conditional-independence framing, which the authors correctly label a property, not an empirical finding. Key Results: Five-setting comparison across Qwen3-VL-8B, Qwen3-VL-32B, and GPT-5.4 on BLINK, M4Bench, and MosaicBench shows task-dependent benefits: on M4Bench Detailed Difference, Qwen3-VL-8B improves 7.3% → 46.1% (T-Re2) → 59.9% (V-Re2); on State Comparison, all three models do worse with visual tools than with CoT. PV-Re2 (78.2–82.3% on BLINK Relative Depth) can beat V-Re2 (74.2%), separating intermediate usefulness from construction skill. On MosaicBench, MosaicAgent-8B reaches 63.3% (best open-weight baseline: Qwen3.5-27B at 60.9%), 61.8% on M4Bench (+4.3 pp over the strongest open baseline), and the standout is hypothesis testing: 62.9% vs. 31.7% for the best open-weight baseline. GPT-5.4 + Mosaic reaches 61.3% on MosaicBench vs. 58.0% without. Training raises mean accuracy reward from 0.48 to 0.63 and tool calls 1.66× (1,830 → 3,037), shifting usage toward crop (36.7% → 54.8%) and collage (0.5% → 6.2%). Post-RL trajectories improve final-prefix answerability by +11.0/+10.5 pp with pre-/post-RL solvers fixed, and gains emerge only after ~2 tool steps. Failure analysis shows training reshapes failure modes (fewer answer-destroying trajectories) but total failures barely change (231 → 221). Baselines are current (Qwen3-VL, InternVL3.5, GLM-4.6V, GPT-5.4, Claude Sonnet 5); evaluation scale is standard, not stress-scale. Novelty Classification: NEW FORMULATION + NEW METHOD + NEW DATASET/BENCHMARK + NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING. The re-representation framework unifying textual CoT and visual tooling under one factorized model, and the construction-vs-utilization decomposition (PV-Re2 vs. V-Re2 plus crossed prefix probing) are genuinely new analytical contributions. Mosaic itself is a competent recombination of known operations (crop/zoom tools, sketching, differencing) in a persistent-workspace design; RL with accuracy+format rewards follows the DeepEyes/VTool-R1 recipe. The empirical finding — that visual re-representation benefits concentrate in precision/geometry-grounding tasks and can hurt semantic tasks — is the most valuable non-obvious result. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are strong: RL with vs. without the harness on identical data, full toolset vs. crop-only (+9.4 pp on MosaicBench), and a crossed re-representer×solver probing design with ±1 SE bands. Key numbers report standard deviations over seeds (e.g., 63.3±1.1 on MosaicBench). Code and data are promised at github.com/gengyuanmax/Mosaic (release, not confirmed available in the text). Methodological concerns: (a) MosaicBench is authored by the same group, from the same construction pipeline and taxonomy as the training suite, with only 20 examples per task type — small per-task cells despite reported error bars; (b) Appendix A.2 concedes the tool-mode vs. vanilla-mode prompts differ in image metadata, planning instructions, and conventions, so the V-Re2 vs. T-Re2 comparison conflates tool access with prompt differences — a confound the authors flag honestly in the appendix but not in the main results narrative; (c) MMIU results decline with training (61.0% → 57.2%), an off-benchmark regression the text mentions but does not analyze. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (with a SYSTEMS component in the harness and released data). Practical: Runs on 4×H100 for training; inference requires any tool-calling MLLM plus a CPU-side image workspace, so commercially feasible. Efficient: Multi-turn tool use multiplies forward passes (5.41 vs. 3.16 mean tool steps post-RL, up to 10 turns, 20K-token responses), so cost is substantially higher than direct CoT answering; no latency/token-cost comparison is reported. Effective: Evidence supports solving fine-grained grounding tasks (hypothesis testing, precision comparison) well beyond CoT RL, but semantic-task gains are absent or negative, so it solves the stated grounding problem specifically, not multi-image understanding broadly. Scalable: Not tested — no experiments at larger backbones, more operations, or longer horizons; the claim that construction of visual representations is generally learnable is extrapolated from one 8B model and 3,509 curated examples. The work delivers concrete artifacts (harness, benchmark, training suite, checkpoints promised) beyond paper form. Strengths: - The five-setting taxonomy (No-Re2 / T-Re2 / PG-Re2 / PV-Re2 / V-Re2) is a genuinely useful decomposition; the PV-Re2 vs. V-Re2 contrast (prefabricated intermediates beating online construction on BLINK Relative Depth, 82.3% vs. 74.2%) is an insight prior agentic-vision work does not isolate. - The crossed prefix-probing protocol is a methodological contribution in its own right — a faithful-CoT-style intervention adapted to multimodal tool trajectories that separates trajectory quality from answer readout. - Benchmark construction hygiene is above the norm: three-level train/test overlap checks, perceptual-hash filtering, blind shortcut probes (centroid/outlier heuristics), source-provenance fingerprints, and seeded reproducibility (seeds 20260807/08) documented per sample. - The failure-mode analysis (Fig. 7) is candid: training leaves total failures nearly unchanged while reshaping their timing — an honest characterization most tool-RL papers omit. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors explicitly note in Appendix A.2 that the tool-mode and vanilla prompts differ in metadata and instructions, so their comparison measures tool access plus prompt differences, and that isolating tool availability requires a matched control. They also state the closed-evidence property is a stated assumption, not an empirical finding, and acknowledge that gains are task-dependent, with semantic tasks showing "smaller or less consistent" benefits. The MMIU decline and the small per-task MosaicBench cells are visible in their tables but not discussed as limitations. Overall they confront the prompt confound directly — a credibility positive — though it belongs in the main text, not only the appendix. Analyst-Identified Gaps: (1) Circular construction: MosaicBench tasks are designed around exactly the operations Mosaic exposes (homography, rotation, collage, coordinate grids), so the agent's headline hypothesis-testing gain (62.9% vs. 31.7%) may partly reflect alignment between the toolset and the benchmark's task grammar rather than generalizable grounding skill; external-benchmark gains are much smaller (+2.4 pp on M4Bench, near-parity on Mantis, negative on MMIU). (2) No comparison to the closest agentic-vision systems (DeepEyes, OpenThinkIMG, PyVision-RL, VipAct) under the same evaluation — the tool-RL baselines in Table 1 are plain MLLMs, so the community cannot tell if Mosaic's training recipe beats existing visual-tool agents, not just untuned backbones. (3) The rollout-based training filter biases toward tasks solvable by the initial policy in 2–7 of 8 tries, and the hard subset (4,032 examples where the policy fails almost always) is held out but never used for evaluation, leaving the difficulty frontier unmeasured. (4) Proprietary baseline numbers (GPT-5.4, Claude Sonnet 5) are single-run API results without error bars, unlike the open-weight entries. (5) The prefabricated intermediates for PV-Re2 come from the RL-trained agent itself, entangling the PV-Re2/V-Re2 comparison with the generator's policy. Bottom Line: A practitioner building tool-using vision agents gains real, reusable assets here — the five-setting taxonomy, the construction-vs-utilization probing method, and a carefully documented benchmark — but the strongest quantitative wins are on a benchmark built by the same authors from the same task grammar as the training data, so treat the external-benchmark evidence (roughly +2–4 pp over strong open baselines, mixed on MMIU) as the honest headline rather than the MosaicBench number.

Sibyl: An Efficient Small-large Model Collaboration Framework for Long-horizon Tasks

Z Fang, Y Zhang, Z Shao, M Li, Z Lin, L Chen, Z Yu… · arxiv.org · karypis - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces Sibyl, a three-stage reinforcement-learning training pipeline that teaches a 0.6B-parameter on-device agent to (a) treat "call cloud" as a native action, (b) learn which states justify a one-step cloud consultation, and (c) internalize cloud guidance so similar states are later handled locally. - Why it's important: Edge-deployable sub-1B agents fail at long-horizon tasks while cloud-only execution is expensive and latency-bound, so the practical barrier to on-device agents is exactly the success–cost trade-off this work targets. - How it does it: The core trick is counterfactual state mining — replaying failed SLM trajectories with a one-step cloud action to identify "decisive-disagreement" states where a single cloud intervention flips failure to success — combined with consultation-specific credit from matched-state returns and skill-conditioned on-policy distillation for guidance internalization. - The good: With Qwen3-0.6B, Sibyl reaches 95.2% success on ALFWorld at 0.8 cloud calls/episode ($0.4 total test cost) versus 37.4% for the strongest device-only baseline, and it beats the cloud-only Qwen3.7-Max (82.4%) it consults, showing learned collaboration outperforms pure cloud execution. - The missing: Main results are on the ALFWorld Seen split only (OOD numbers relegated to an appendix), WebShop success is statistically indistinguishable from the training-time GiGPO w/SFT baseline (80.4% vs 80.6%), and there are no latency or on-device deployment measurements. - Read it or not: Worth reading for anyone building edge–cloud LLM agent systems or agentic RL credit assignment; skip if you only care about methods validated beyond ALFWorld/WebShop, since generalization is untested.

Non-Obviousness (79) is the top dimension — decisive-disagreement mining and matched-state consultation credit are genuinely clever answers to a real credit-assignment problem — and Novelty (75) benefits from a new formulation (consultation as in-policy action). Problem & Motivation: Operators of latency- and resource-constrained applications (mobile/edge agents) want small language models to execute long-horizon tasks — embodied household instructions (ALFWorld) and web shopping (WebShop) — but SLMs at ≤3B have weak planning and reasoning, so trajectory quality degrades over many interdependent steps. Existing SLM–LLM collaboration methods route independent one-shot requests and do not fit agentic settings: the decision of when to call the cloud is a sequence of decisions over an evolving trajectory, the utility of any single cloud call is entangled with subsequent actions and observable only in the final sparse outcome, and a separately trained external router (as in Hera and RouteLLM) becomes misaligned as the agent policy is updated. The paper targets closing this gap: step-level collaboration that maximizes task success while minimizing cloud invocations, without a separate router. Key Idea: Treat cloud consultation as a native action in the SLM's policy and optimize it jointly with local actions from trajectory-level outcomes; the enabling insight is counterfactual supervision — mine the exact states in failed self-rollouts where swapping in a single cloud action flips the final return from 0 to 1, and use those "decisive-disagreement" states to cold-start and then credit-assign consultation decisions. Methodology: The formulation augments the SLM action space with {call cloud}; when invoked, a fixed cloud policy πθL receives the full state and returns one executable action, after which the SLM resumes control. The objective is a cost-regularized return max E[R(τ) − λC(τ)], pursued indirectly through three stages. (1) Consultation-free self-evolving RL: a cloud trajectory teacher distills hindsight skills (episode summary + reusable behavioral rule) from SLM self-rollouts; the SLM is fine-tuned on trajectory–skill pairs, bootstrapped into its own trajectory analyzer TθS, cold-started on cloud-generated state–action pairs, then trained with GRPO-style clipped group-relative RL (Eq. 10) plus skill-conditioned on-policy distillation — a detached confidence weight w = σ(βopd·sg[ℓz − ℓ∅]) re-weights token-level distillation from skill-augmented re-scoring onto the ordinary branch (Eq. 9). (2) Consultation cold start: roll out the frozen Stage-1 policy, collect failures, and for each visited state form a disagreement branch by substituting one cloud action and completing with the SLM; states where this flips R from 0 to 1 define decisive-disagreement states, converted to supervised prefixes ending in "call cloud" and mixed with successful consultation-free trajectories for SFT. (3) Consultation-aware RL: the combined advantage A_Sibyl = A_i,n + αstep·A_step + αcf·A_cf adds (i) a matched-state advantage computed by grouping states across the N rollouts per task via an exact-state key (observation + admissible actions), and (ii) a consultation-specific term A_cf = R̄_call − R̄_local comparing mean returns of cloud vs. local continuations from matched states; the OPD loss is reused to internalize cloud guidance, and the trajectory analyzer is removed at inference. Design decisions: exact-state matching is a strong simplifying assumption that works because ALFWorld/WebShop states are discrete and repeatable across rollouts — plausibility is argued implicitly, not defended; counterfactual completion with the SLM after the swapped action is reasonable but adds rollout cost; αcf acts as an implicit knob over the λ in Eq. 4 rather than optimizing it directly, which the authors acknowledge is indirect. Key Results: All numbers are averaged over three runs. With Qwen3-0.6B assisted by Qwen3.7-Max: ALFWorld Seen success 95.2% (vs 37.4% device-only GiGPO, 91.7% GRPO w/SFT, 91.7% GiGPO w/SFT, 65.0% Hera, 65.7% RouteLLM, 82.4% cloud-only Qwen3.7-Max, 98.6% cloud-only Gemini 3.1 Pro); WebShop score 90.7 and success 80.4% (vs 86.7/80.6% for GiGPO w/SFT). Cloud cost: 0.8 calls/episode and $0.4 total test cost on ALFWorld (21.5× cheaper than cloud-only Qwen3.7-Max), 3.9 calls and $16.1 on WebShop (3.0× cheaper). With Qwen3-1.7B: 97.4%/84.6% success at 43–44× lower cost, exceeding the strongest training-time baselines by 5.4 and 7.3 points. Ablations: Stage 1 alone lifts success from 0.7%/0.8% to 90.0%/60.8%; random cloud calls add little; Stage 3 reaches 94.3%/80.2% while cutting call ratios to 7.7%/64.8%, and neither αcf=0 nor αcf=1 reaches the frontier. The Pareto frontier (Figure 3, from a first-run checkpoint, not the averaged model) shows 94.3% success at ~8% call ratio on ALFWorld. Substituting Gemini 3.1 Pro as the cloud at inference without retraining improves both benchmarks, suggesting transfer across cloud models. Baselines are current and reasonably strong (GRPO, GiGPO, SEED, RouteLLM, Hera), including training-time cloud-assisted variants. Tested scale is standard benchmarks, not stress-scale. Novelty Classification: NEW FORMULATION (step-level SLM–LLM consultation as an in-policy action rather than an external router) plus NEW METHOD (the decisive-disagreement mining procedure and consultation-specific matched-state credit). The underlying machinery is a competent recombination of established components — GRPO, on-policy distillation, counterfactual replay — applied to a setting (long-horizon edge–cloud collaboration) where the combination is genuinely non-obvious, particularly the credit-disentanglement of a single cloud call from downstream actions. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are present and informative: the three-stage trace (Figure 4) isolates each stage's contribution, and the αcf sweep (0, 0.25, 1) shows the credit term matters at intermediate weight. Results are averaged over three runs with ± reported; however, the Pareto-frontier analysis in §5.3 explicitly uses a single first-run checkpoint, and no significance tests are given — several headline margins (WebShop 80.4% vs 80.6% against GiGPO w/SFT) are within noise. Code and trained weights are released at https://github.com/real-fzw/Sibyl. Methodological concerns: (i) primary results are on the ALFWorld Seen split, with the 134-task Unseen split (96.3%) reported only in the appendix — a favorable choice, though the OOD result actually exceeds Seen; (ii) the exact-state key for matched-state credit could be gamed or trivially satisfied in these two deterministic, low-variety environments — nothing tests it in stochastic or open-ended settings; (iii) the same cloud model (Qwen3.7-Max) supplies SFT data, hindsight skills, and consultation, so distillation and consultation effects are not fully disentangled; (iv) hyperparameters (αcf=0.25, λopd=0.01) are stated but the tuning procedure and its benchmark-split hygiene are not described. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (a trained method with benchmark evaluation; no production deployment). Practical: Yes — the 0.6B/1.7B SLM runs on-device and the cloud side is a commercial API; training needs 8 AMD MI308X GPUs (149.7–205.7 GPU-hours per benchmark). Efficient: Inference is cheap relative to cloud-only ($0.4 vs $8.6 on ALFWorld), but training costs $105.1–$145.5 in API charges per benchmark, breaking even only after ~1,794 (ALFWorld) or ~2,245 (WebShop) tasks, excluding GPU time — a real fixed cost the paper honestly reports. Effective: Evidence on the two text benchmarks shows it solves the stated problem (success + low call rate, beating the very cloud model it consults on ALFWorld), but effectiveness in stochastic, visually grounded, or open-web environments is a proxy gap. Scalable: Not tested — no experiments beyond 0.6B/1.7B SLMs, one cloud model family per run, and two environments; the paper claims but does not demonstrate scaling behavior. Delivers a software artifact: released code and model weights, though the paper is a preprint (arXiv 2610.05383) and not peer-reviewed. Strengths: (1) The decisive-disagreement mining procedure is a genuinely clever, cheap way to extract counterfactual consultation supervision from sparse-reward failures — it directly attacks the credit-assignment problem the paper identifies. (2) The matched-state consultation credit A_cf is a concrete, well-motivated answer to disentangling one cloud call's contribution from subsequent local actions, with an ablation showing intermediate weighting is necessary. (3) Beating cloud-only Qwen3.7-Max while calling it for <8% of steps is the strongest single result — it demonstrates the learned policy composes local and cloud actions into trajectories better than cloud-only execution. (4) Honest cost accounting: the paper reports training API expenditure and break-even task counts rather than hiding the substantial Stage-3 cost ($92.7 on ALFWorld, $126.0 on WebShop). Author-Acknowledged Limitations: Appendix F states the formulation assumes cloud availability and sufficient context sharing; that privacy-sensitive applications and intermittent connectivity require context limitation and safe fallback when consultation fails; and that the cloud is treated as a single fixed source rather than a menu of models with differing capability, price, and latency (future work: choose which model to consult). The authors confront these directly and concretely — a credibility positive. They do not, however, acknowledge the training-cost break-even horizon, the Seen-split presentation of main results, or the single-checkpoint basis of the frontier analysis in the main text. Analyst-Identified Gaps: (1) Environment breadth: both benchmarks are text-based, deterministic-ish, with discrete admissible action sets — precisely the conditions that make the exact-state matching for A_step/A_cf tractable; no evidence the credit mechanism survives in stochastic or continuous-state environments. (2) The WebShop headline masks a parity result: on exact success the training-time baseline GiGPO w/SFT (80.6%) statistically matches Sibyl (80.4%), and only the softer score metric separates them. (3) Latency is never measured — the motivating constraint is on-device latency, yet the paper reports only API cost and call counts, not wall-clock time for SLM steps vs. cloud round-trips. (4) Stage 2 mining requires cloud action queries at every state of every failed trajectory and Stage 3 requires dense rollouts with a fixed cloud; the marginal value of Stage 2 vs. simply relying on Stage 3 RL exploration is not isolated (the ablation reports stages cumulatively, not Stage 3-without-Stage-2). (5) The claim that consultation "transfers across cloud models" rests on swapping in one stronger model at inference; no weaker or differently-shaped cloud model is tested. (6) Reported training hyperparameters give no seed or search protocol, and the frontier figures come from a single checkpoint despite three-run averaging elsewhere. Bottom Line: A practitioner building cost-sensitive edge–cloud agent systems should read this — the counterfactual consultation-supervision recipe and the honest cost analysis are immediately reusable — but the evidence is confined to two discrete text benchmarks and a preprint without peer review, so treat the generality of the matched-state credit mechanism as unproven until tested outside ALFWorld/WebShop.

Prompt2Skill: Unsupervised Skill Optimization From Natural Language Instructions

B Ni, L Li, RA Rossi, F Dernoncourt, T Derr · arxiv.org · karypis - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces Prompt2Skill, a multi-agent framework that converts a bare natural-language task description into a model-optimized skill document for a frozen LLM, via agentic data retrieval/synthesis followed by closed-loop reflective editing with statistical acceptance. - Why it's important: Existing automated skill optimizers (Trace2Skill, SkillOpt) require a curated, in-distribution labeled training set, which deployed users typically lack; expert-authored skills are expensive and not tuned to the consuming model's failure modes. - How it does it: A Data Agent derives a task specification and builds a validated proxy dataset from Hugging Face/Wikipedia retrieval, format adaptation, and grounded synthesis; a Skill Agent then iterates rollouts → reflective edits, accepting an edit only when it wins a paired win/loss statistical screen on a fresh held-out batch, with a frozen validation set consulted exactly once for final selection. - The good: Under a matched budget of 7,400 solver evaluations, Prompt2Skill beats SkillOpt head-to-head (SearchQA EM 48.71 vs 45.79; SQuAD EM 82.50 vs 81.30), and it improves over direct prompting on 19 of ~20 model–benchmark pairs across five target models. - The missing: Ablation conditions are single-run (some matched zero-example runs failed during data acquisition), the acceptance statistic uses κ=1 without multiple-comparison correction across candidates and rounds, and the proxy-to-test distribution gap is only bounded theoretically, not measured. - Read it or not: Worth reading for researchers in prompt/skill optimization and agent self-improvement who want the data-free problem formalization and the acceptance/selection machinery; practitioners can skip to the released code and Appendix D/E for the concrete recipe.

Problem & Motivation: LLM "skills" — markdown artifacts placed in context at inference time — are currently authored by human experts, which is expensive per task and not adapted to the specific target model whose failure modes vary with version, scale, and training. Recent automated skill optimizers presuppose a curated, labeled, in-distribution training set; SkillOpt's own results show gains collapse to a data-blind draft when the training set shrinks to one example. The paper targets the realistic regime where a user has only a task in mind ("I want a model that reads a passage and answers questions about it"), possibly a couple of examples, and no labeled data from the task distribution. Key Idea: Since the target distribution D is never observed, synthesize the missing training signal from the task description itself: an LLM Data Agent turns the description into an executable task specification plus a proxy dataset assembled from retrieved public data (adapted to the task's input–output contract) and grounded synthetic items, then run standard reflective prompt optimization against that proxy — treating proxy-data construction, not the optimizer, as the bottleneck. A secondary key move is statistical hygiene in editing: paired win/loss evaluation against the incumbent on fresh batches, plus retention of all accepted skills and a one-shot frozen selection set, so the final export does not inherit overfitting from the adaptive refinement trajectory. Methodology: The pipeline has three phases. (1) Task setup: a single LLM call jointly produces a task specification τ (input structure, task type, answer style, an executable proxy metric µ̂τ such as normalized exact match, numeric equivalence, or containment) and a seed skill s0, before any data is inspected. (2) Data Agent: generates retrieval requests over tools (Hugging Face catalog, Wikipedia), including hypothetical-dataset-card queries; inspects candidate sources and proposes conversion plans executed by deterministic row mappers; generates new items when conversion is insufficient, targeting diagnosed model weaknesses; validates items via structural checks, LLM compatibility reports against τ, an answerability screen (rejecting sources where the seed-equipped model scores zero), and a consistency check for synthetic items; deduplicates into a pool P split into per-round reflection sets Tt, fresh acceptance batches Bt, and a frozen selection set V (e.g., 400 initial text items: 150 selection, 250 reflection; 150 more reflection items and 120 acceptance items per round). (3) Skill Agent: runs the skill-equipped target model on Tt, proposes candidate skill edits from failure feedback (GPT-5.5 as reflector in all reported runs), and accepts a candidate only if it has strictly more wins than losses on Bt and a screening statistic z = (|w−ℓ|−1)/√(w+ℓ) ≥ 1, choosing the largest net gain. All accepted skills and initial skills are then scored on V and the argmax is exported as SKILL.md. Appendix A proves a selection guarantee (Hoeffding + union bound): the exported skill is within 2(ε_dist + ε_eval) + √(2log(2K/δ)/n) of the best retained skill under bounded distribution and evaluator mismatch. Critical design decisions: constructing the proxy distribution rather than assuming one (well-motivated, but its quality is the framework's main unmeasured risk); retaining accepted skills and selecting on a frozen set once (well-justified by the theorem); and κ=1 as a heuristic screen rather than a corrected significance test (acknowledged as non-standard, less well justified). Key Results: Across four benchmarks (SearchQA 1,400-item test split; SQuAD 1,000 validation examples; AIME 120 problems; SpreadsheetBench 280 held-out tasks) and five target models (Qwen3-8B, Qwen3-32B, Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct, Claude Haiku 4.5, GPT-5.5), Prompt2Skill achieves the highest average relative gain for every target model: +29.1% (Qwen3-8B), +26.1% (Qwen3-32B), +93.5% (Llama-3.2-1B, three text tasks), +22.0% (Haiku 4.5), +24.3% (GPT-5.5), versus direct prompting. Concrete examples: SearchQA/Qwen3-32B 0.613→0.778; SQuAD/Llama-3.2-1B 0.207→0.492 (an off-the-shelf skill regressed this to 0.048); SQuAD/Haiku 4.5 0.416→0.793. Gains are not universal: SpreadsheetBench is essentially flat for frontier models (Haiku 0.297→0.269; GPT-5.5 0.266→0.263), AIME for GPT-5.5 is best with the off-the-shelf skill (0.914 vs 0.861 for P2S), and SearchQA for Haiku slightly regresses (0.857→0.839). Aggregated over 19 model–benchmark pairs, the conclusion reports 36.1% average relative gain over direct prompting and 83.0% over off-the-shelf skills. Baselines are current and reasonable for the skill-setting (direct prompting, off-the-shelf public skills, one-shot LLM-authored skills, and a matched-budget SkillOpt comparison), though no comparison to fine-tuning on the proxy data is reported in the main table. The relative-gain aggregates are inflated by low baselines (the authors say so themselves in Appendix E.4). The 36.1%/83.0% relative figures in the conclusion and the "10.8% points" figure in the abstract/intro are different aggregations and are not reconciled explicitly. Novelty Classification: NEW PROBLEM (skill optimization with no user-supplied task data — the prompt-to-skill setting is a genuine and well-motivated generalization of SkillOpt/Trace2Skill) plus NEW SYSTEM/TOOL. The components are standard: reflective editing follows GEPA/ProTeGi, paired acceptance and held-out validation are standard optimization hygiene, and retrieval-then-synthesize data construction follows Prompt2Model/AutoML-Agent. The genuinely novel combination is using an LLM data agent to manufacture the optimization signal (including failure-targeted synthesis and solver-agreement screens) so that text-space skill optimization can run distribution-free, with a formal selection guarantee attached. Rigor & Reproducibility: Strengths: error bars (± std) reported for main-table results; a matched-budget head-to-head with SkillOpt isolating the optimization procedure from data acquisition; two ablations (seed-skill initialization; 0/1/4 user examples); a thorough retrospective train–test overlap audit (exact/containment/near-text shingle checks on text; dual SHA-256 workbook-hash checks over 1,884 proxy vs 560 target workbooks — zero flags); a theorem with complete proof bounding selection error. Code is released at github.com/Arstanley/Prompt2Skill, and all prompts, skill texts, and data sources are reproduced in the appendix. Concerns: ablation conditions use a single run each, and the matched zero-example runs "failed during data acquisition" (replaced by main-table three-run means), so ablation conclusions rest on thin evidence; the acceptance rule does not correct for multiple comparisons across candidates and rounds (the authors flag κ=1 as a screening threshold, not a 5% test); the overlap audit covers "recorded proxy sources" with the authors conceding that HotpotQA "had no bulk-fetch progress in most runs" and that source cursors don't identify retained items — so the audit is honest but partially retrospective; and the proxy-distribution gap (ε_dist in the theorem) is never estimated empirically. The framework is developed and evaluated on the same four benchmarks whose task descriptions drive retrieval, which is exactly the leakage surface the audit tries to rule out. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (a built system, evaluated by benchmark experiments). Practical: Yes — needs only API access (GPT-5.5 reflector, commercial targets) or a consumer GPU for the 1B–32B open-weight targets, plus Hugging Face/Wikipedia tools. Efficient: Not free — the SkillOpt comparison caps at 7,400 solver evaluations per task, and the text loop requests hundreds of proxy items per round, so optimization costs thousands of target-model calls; inference-time cost is only the skill text in context. Effective: Evidence supports the stated problem on text QA and for weak/small models, but the near-zero spreadsheet gains for frontier models and the AIME result for GPT-5.5 show the method does not help where the model is already strong or the domain is tool-driven. Scalable: Claimed, not tested — only four task families are evaluated, all with public, well-indexed proxy data; behavior on tasks where no suitable retrieval source exists (the pure-synthesis fallback) is essentially untested at evaluation strength. Deliverable: a software artifact (code plus exported SKILL.md skills), not just a paper. Strengths: (1) Clean problem formalization — casting supervised skill optimization's labeled-set assumption as the special case of a description-plus-few-examples regime makes the contribution legible and positions it against SkillOpt/Trace2Skill precisely. (2) The data-agent-as-problem-understudy insight: rather than inventing a new optimizer, the paper shows that manufacturing a validated proxy distribution is the missing piece, and the matched-budget SkillOpt comparison credibly supports this. (3) Statistical discipline unusual for prompt-optimization papers — paired fresh-batch acceptance, retention of all accepted skills, one-shot frozen selection, and a formal (if simple) selection bound. (4) Unusually transparent appendices: full prompts, full baseline and exported skill texts, recorded data sources, and a concrete overlap audit with stated thresholds. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors acknowledge that κ=1 is a per-candidate screen without cross-candidate/round correction (Appendix D); that the audit's zero-match result applies only to audited artifacts and recorded sources, with incomplete fetch attribution for some sources (Appendix C); that the theorem's ε_dist and ε_eval mismatch terms "remain separate sources of error" not controlled by the framework; that the paired-batch and ablation figure mixes single-run and multi-run conditions (Figure 3 caption); that Llama-3.2-1B could not complete SpreadsheetBench; and that solver agreement in validation "does not establish reference correctness or representativeness." They confront limitations directly — a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: (1) No fine-tuning baseline: the AutoML appendix compares against Prompt2Model-style fine-tuning only on two small auxiliary tasks with "comparable scores" and no numbers in the main text, leaving the headline claim of skill-based adaptation as a weight-update alternative under-evidenced. (2) The proxy/test distribution gap is never measured — no experiment estimates how often retrieval returns distribution-mismatched data or how performance degrades when it does; the four chosen tasks are all ones where abundant public data exists, which is close to assuming the conclusion. (3) The conclusion's 36.1%/83.0% relative aggregates and the abstract's "10.8% points" are not reconciled, and equal-weighting pairs with tiny baselines (e.g., Llama AIME at 0.017) inflate relative claims. (4) Ablations are single-run with failed conditions, so the claims that initialization and user examples don't matter are fragile. (5) The evaluator µ̂τ is chosen by the setup LLM and shared between optimization and testing; if µ̂τ is mis-specified for a task, both the acceptance signal and the reported metric are wrong in the same direction. (6) Self-reflection asymmetry: GPT-5.5 is the reflector for all targets including itself, and the paper does not test whether a weaker reflector — the realistic deployment case — preserves gains. Bottom Line: A practitioner or researcher working on automated prompt/skill optimization should read this: the data-free problem formalization, the matched-budget SkillOpt comparison, and the selection machinery are genuinely useful, but the evidence is concentrated on four retrieval-friendly tasks with thin ablations, so treat the headline relative gains and the AutoML claim as promising rather than settled.

Beyond Heuristics? Rethinking Targeted Unit Test Generation in the Era of LLM Agents

J Liu, Y Wu · drops.dagstuhl.de · automated generated environments for agent testing - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper presents the first systematic empirical evaluation of general-purpose LLM coding agents on targeted unit test generation — reproducing a bug at a specified line — using a refined benchmark of 210 real-world Java runtime exception bugs across 66 projects. - Why it's important: Targeted tests underpin static-analysis alarm validation, crash reproduction, and patch testing, but existing tools (EvoSuite, Randoop, UnitCon) rely on heuristics that fail on semantics-heavy bugs, leaving this task largely unsolved. - How it does it: The study runs a 3×3 factorial over agent scaffolds (Claude Code, OpenHands, OpenCode) and frontier models (GPT-5, Claude-4.5-Sonnet, DeepSeek-V3.2) under a fixed minimal prompt, 15-minute budget, and $2 cost cap, comparing against UnitCon, EvoSuite, and Randoop on an execution-based oracle. - The good: The best combination (Claude Code + GPT-5) achieves an 89.5% success rate versus 49.6% for the strongest baseline UnitCon, with 41.8% of agent successes unreachable by any baseline tool, and stability confirmed over five runs. - The missing: Evaluation is confined to Java runtime exceptions (60% NullPointerException), so generalization to assertion failures, logical faults, concurrency bugs, or other languages is argued, not measured; test quality beyond reproduction (maintainability, readability) is only spot-checked on 90 samples. - Read it or not: Read it if you work on automated test generation, bug reproduction, or agentic software engineering — it is the first controlled evidence on where agents beat heuristic tools and where they still fail; skip it if you need a new technique, since the paper delivers measurement, not a method.
Why this rank

The composite is capped by Novelty (62) — this is measurement, not a method, and extends Mündler et al.'s agent-tester line to a subtask — and Non-Obviousness (60), since 'agents beat heuristics' is broadly anticipated. Completeness (78) is strong thanks to direct, quantified limitation acknowledgment; Resilience (72) and Impact (68) are dented by the missing LLM-prompt baseline, NPE-dominated instance distribution, and the fact that the deliverable is a benchmark rather than a tool. Weighted composite: 0.20*62 + 0.25*82 + 0.15*60 + 0.15*78 + 0.15*72 + 0.10*68 = 71.

Problem & Motivation: Targeted unit tests must drive a program to a specific buggy location and trigger the fault there — a fundamentally harder objective than the coverage-maximizing heuristics of mainstream generators like EvoSuite and Randoop, which waste budget on unrelated code. UnitCon (FSE 2025) added heuristics for this task but remains brittle on loops, cross-class state, and project-specific conditions. Prior LLM work on unit testing used prompt engineering with hand-crafted context selection and repair loops, which the authors argue is costly and constrained by context limits and the lost-in-the-middle effect. The open question the paper targets: do general-purpose LLM agents, given only a codebase path and a raw bug location, already solve targeted test generation — and what can they not yet do? The audience is software engineering researchers and practitioners building testing infrastructure. Key Idea: The core move is methodological rather than algorithmic: treat off-the-shelf general-purpose coding agents as the test generator, and isolate the scaffold and model contributions via a factorial design with a deliberately minimal, fixed prompt. The hypothesis under test is that agentic capabilities — repository exploration, tool use, and iterative execution-feedback refinement — substitute for task-specific heuristics without any task-specific engineering. There is no new algorithm; the intellectual contribution is the controlled comparison, the refined benchmark, and the qualitative attribution of the performance gap to three named agent capabilities. Methodology: The study formalizes each instance as a tuple ⟨P, e, l⟩ (buggy program, exception type, target line); the system must output a JUnit suite T that, when run on P in a Docker container, throws exception e with location l at the top of the stack trace — an objective, execution-based oracle. Benchmark construction has two phases: (1) Incorporating — deduplicated Java runtime-exception bugs from Defects4J, BEARS, Genesis, NPEX, VFix, and UnitCon, containerized and filtered by a 15-minute build threshold, yielding 169 bugs across 66 projects; (2) Refining — 41 additional bugs disclosed October 2025–May 2026 (post-cutoff for all studied models) to probe contamination, totaling 210 bugs. Nine scaffold-model combinations are evaluated alongside UnitCon (static-analysis-based, targeted), EvoSuite (search-based), and Randoop (feedback-directed random), all under a 15-minute budget; agents additionally face a $2.00 monetary cap and temperature 0. Metrics: reproduction success rate, completion time, monetary cost. Each experiment is repeated five times. Critical design decisions: (a) minimal zero-shot prompting to measure intrinsic capability — justified by the study's framing but acknowledged as leaving headroom; (b) execution-oracle strictness (exception type + stack-trace position) — well justified, with manual verification that degenerate trigger paths occur in only 5.6% of sampled successes; (c) post-cutoff data collection — a strong, well-executed contamination control backed by stratified statistical testing (Fisher's exact and Z-tests, all p > 0.05). Key Results: Tested at standard scale (210 instances, 66 real-world projects including Apache Commons IO and Log4j2). Headline: Claude Code + GPT-5 achieves 89.5% success at $1.09/instance and ~326s average, versus UnitCon 49.6%, EvoSuite 39.4%, Randoop 21.3% — absolute margins of 39.9, 50.1, and 68.2 percentage points. All proprietary-model configurations exceed 81%; even the weakest open-source configuration (OpenHands + DeepSeek-V3.2, 63.8%) beats every baseline. DeepSeek-V3.2 trails by 16.0–24.4 points but costs $0.04–0.05/instance. Scaffold choice matters little (81.4–89.5% spread driven mostly by model); model choice dominates. Five-run repetition shows no significant variation (max Fisher p = 0.43). Qualitative analysis of 210 successful trajectories attributes the gap to three capabilities: direct code comprehension for synthesizing complex structural inputs (e.g., order-sensitive JSON payloads), adaptive execution-guided refinement (≥1 refinement round in 74.8% of successes), and adaptive choice between public call paths and Java reflection. Failure analysis of 200 trajectories (Cohen's κ = 0.76 between two annotators) identifies four modes: Insufficient Exploration 41.5%, Inadequate Reasoning 25.5%, Tool Misuse 14.0%, Incorrect Focus 11.5% — the last including agents drifting into fixing the bug instead of testing it, even at temperature 0. A time-budget sensitivity check (30 instances, OpenCode) shows closed-source models plateau by 25 minutes while DeepSeek-V3.2 gains ~12 points from 15→20 minutes. Baselines are current (UnitCon is FSE 2025, the targeted-generation state of the art), not strawmen. Counter-intuitive finding: heuristic tools remain complementary on shallow, easily-reachable bugs where agents over-analyze and burn their budget. Novelty Classification: NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING and NEW DATASET/BENCHMARK. Genuinely novel: the first controlled factorial measurement of general-purpose LLM agents on the targeted unit test generation task, plus a refined benchmark with post-cutoff instances addressing contamination and subjective-oracle flaws in prior suites. What is a standard combination: the agents, scaffolds, models, and evaluation harness are all existing, off-the-shelf components applied to a new setting; no new generation technique is proposed. The paper's self-description as the "first empirical evaluation of LLM agents for targeted unit test generation" is consistent with the related-work coverage, with the caveat that Mündler et al. (2024) showed agents are competitive SOTA software testers generally — this paper extends that line to the targeted subtask. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations and sensitivity analyses are present and substantive: budget sensitivity (10/15/20/25 minutes), scaffold-vs-model attribution, pre-/post-cutoff contamination stratification with formal hypothesis tests, and five-run repetition with reported p-values. Qualitative analyses use defined protocols (dual annotation, κ = 0.76; fixed sample sizes of 30/70/90/200). Artifacts — the 210-bug benchmark, containerized environments, and evaluation scripts — are released on Zenodo (https://zenodo.org/records/20283766). Methodological concerns: (1) the contamination check relies on only 30 post-cutoff instances, so it has limited statistical power even though p-values exceed 0.05; (2) baseline tools and agents are tuned under somewhat different resource regimes (agents get execution servers and tool use within the same time budget, while EvoSuite/Randoop receive only the target class), which the authors defend via construct validity of each tool's original interface but which is not a perfectly symmetric comparison; (3) qualitative capability attribution is by the authors' own manual inspection, inherently subjective despite the kappa reported only for failure modes. Commercial model APIs introduce potential drift/non-reproducibility over time, which is not discussed. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL (with a SYSTEMS artifact in the form of the released benchmark and harness). - Practical: Yes — everything runs in Dockerized environments on commodity hardware; the only external dependency is API access to a frontier model, and a fully open-source path (OpenCode + DeepSeek-V3.2) is demonstrated. - Efficient: $1.09/instance at ~326s for the top configuration, versus effectively free-per-instance heuristic tools; DeepSeek-V3.2 offers 65–67% success at ~$0.05, a ~20× cost reduction for a 16–24 point accuracy trade. - Effective: Strong evidence for the stated proxy (reproducing a known runtime exception at a given line), but the paper's own quality audit shows generated tests are less maintainable and readable than developer tests, so effectiveness as drop-in developer tests is weaker. - Scalable: Not tested at 10× scale — 210 instances is the entire evaluation; the authors' own failure analysis suggests scaling to very large repositories worsens the dominant failure mode (budget-consuming exploration), so scaling beyond the tested size is claimed only implicitly. The work delivers a reusable dataset and evaluation harness; it does not deliver a deployable test-generation tool of its own (agents are third-party). Strengths: - The factorial scaffold×model design cleanly separates which layer of the agent stack drives performance — a question usually conflated in agent evaluations — and yields a concrete, actionable finding that scaffolding matters far less than the underlying model. - The contamination control is unusually careful for this literature: post-cutoff bug collection aligned to explicit model knowledge cutoffs, plus stratified statistical testing, rather than the usual hand-waving. - The failure-mode taxonomy (with inter-annotator agreement) converts an otherwise cheerleading "agents win" result into an actionable research agenda — notably the observation that agents spontaneously drift into bug fixing due to pre-training priors, and that shallow heuristics still beat agents on simple bugs. - The oracle design (exception type plus stack-trace position) plus manual audit of degenerate paths (5.6%) addresses the most obvious way this kind of evaluation could be gamed. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors explicitly restrict quantitative conclusions to Java runtime exceptions in open-source projects and flag that extrapolation to dynamic languages, concurrency bugs, and industrial codebases is untested (asserting only theoretical plausibility for the latter). They acknowledge the minimal zero-shot prompt may understate achievable performance, that extended reasoning modes are disabled for cost, that resource budgets bind open-source models disproportionately (quantified), and that generated tests are structurally fragile (16.7% bypass public APIs) and poorly readable (72.2% with generic naming). They confront limitations directly, with sensitivity analyses for the most consequential choices — a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - The NPE-heavy distribution (126/210 = 60% NullPointerException) means the headline number is dominated by one bug class; per-category success rates are not reported, so the 89.5% could mask large variance across exception types. - The post-cutoff contamination subset (41 instances, 30 sampled) is small; with ~83–87% rates on 30 instances, the confidence intervals are wide enough that moderate contamination effects cannot be excluded — the paper states p > 0.05 as absence of evidence. - No LLM-based targeted-generation baseline (e.g., prompt-engineered LLM pipelines like ChatUniTest or CodaMosa-style hybrids) is compared; the comparison jumps from non-LLM heuristics straight to general-purpose agents, leaving open how much of the gain comes from agentic autonomy versus simply using a frontier LLM. - No cost-matched comparison: baselines cannot spend on API calls, so "agents beat tools" partially reflects an injected $1–2/bug budget; a cheaper LLM-prompt baseline at equal cost would sharpen the attribution. - Time-budget fairness is defended via prior work, but the sensitivity analysis itself shows DeepSeek-V3.2's result is highly budget-dependent (relative >50% drop at 10 minutes), so the 15-minute choice materially shapes the open-source story. - API drift and model versioning over the October 2025–May 2026 evaluation window are not discussed, which weakens exact reproducibility despite the released artifacts. Bottom Line: This is the reference empirical evidence that off-the-shelf LLM agents decisively beat heuristic targeted test generation (89.5% vs 49.6%) on Java runtime exceptions, and any researcher or practitioner in automated testing or agentic software engineering should read it for its failure-mode taxonomy and benchmark — with the caveat that it measures rather than builds, and its conclusions are bounded to one bug class in one language.

Selection-Based Structured Reasoning: Toward Efficient Multimodal Search Agents (14 ▲ )

Feiyu Gavin Zhu, Xiaoyu Zhu, Jiqi Yang, Rui Yang, Arnab Kumar Mondal, Yancheng Wang, Xinke Deng, Jean Oh, Reid Simmons, Joerg Liebelt, Xiang Kong, Zhongyu Jiang · arxiv.org · Daily papers of 7 Oct 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces Selection-based Structured Reasoning (SSR), a framework that replaces freeform chain-of-thought generation in multimodal search agents with selection among six pre-written reusable reasoning candidates, scored by length-normalized likelihood and computed in a single batched prefill pass. - Why it's important: Small (2B–4B) on-device agents pay a large sequential decoding cost for reasoning text before every tool call, and for capacity-limited models this verbose reasoning often adds latency without improving action quality. - How it does it: Because all candidate reasoning texts are fixed in advance, the language model itself acts as a zero-shot classifier — teacher-forced prefill scores every candidate token in parallel, within and across candidates, against a shared history KV cache, and the selected candidate is injected as context for action generation. - The good: The gains are demonstrated across four training objectives (GRPO, GSPO, SAPO, SFT) and two model sizes on seven benchmarks, with a 4B GRPO-SSR agent reaching 61.37% average success (matching the best trained 4B baseline at 61.25%) while cutting mean per-turn reasoning latency from 0.896s to 0.061s (−93.2%). - The missing: The reasoning library is six manually written, task-specific candidates for multimodal search only; nothing evaluates whether the approach transfers to domains where the useful reasoning space is not so easily enumerable, and no error bars, seeds, or significance tests are reported. - Read it or not: Worth reading for anyone building latency-constrained small agents or working on structured/efficient reasoning, because it demonstrates a genuinely different mechanism (selection-as-scoring instead of generation) with solid controlled comparisons; skippable if you only work with large frontier models where reasoning latency is less binding.

Rigor (68) is solid on paired controlled comparisons and ablations but capped by zero seeds/error bars with a 0.12-point margin against the strongest baseline and author-reproduced baselines.
