Problem & Motivation: Organisations running large asset fleets depend on EAM platforms like IBM Maximo to record maintenance, but once a system goes live, what users actually type into it is rarely inspected. Two structural problems motivate the work: (1) an accredited consultancy under a fixed-hour service contract has no standing mandate to inspect the client system — nothing happens until a ticket arrives, so defects accumulate silently; and (2) acceptance testing checks functionality, not longitudinal user behaviour, so documentation and timestamp defects build up invisibly. The domain gap the authors identify is that prior EAM quality work either stops at diagnosis (Lu et al.), is preventive-only (Oyoo), or requires dense narrative text this dataset lacks (Santos et al.); nobody converts a measured behavioural pattern into a configurable platform rule. Key Idea: The core move is to promote data-quality defects into mineable features: missing work logs, missing attachments, backdated timestamps, instant closures, and overlapping labour bookings become binary indicator items, so that "the gap is the observation" and association rule mining can run over an 11-item matrix where documentation failure is a co-occurring behaviour rather than a nuisance to impute away. Supporting this is a "sponge effect" ablation — near-constant items (no-attachment at ~98% prevalence, no-worklog at 99.5% in PM) must be removed from the item space, not merely filtered from the output, because they otherwise absorb all rule structure. Methodology: The study follows CRISP-DM across six phases. Phase 1 fixes acceptance thresholds (confidence ≥ 0.70, lift > 1.0) before any query is written, plus a four-part practical-significance criterion (support ≥ 0.10, lift ≥ 1.25, OR ≥ 3, blockable consequent). Phase 2 profiles completeness and integrity across seven DB2 tables (Lee et al. metrics), excluding only user-visible attributes. Phase 3 collapses child tables (WORKLOG, DOCLINKS, LABTRANS, MULTIASSETLOCCI, WOSTATUS) to order level via DB2 CTEs and recodes 12,368 orders (5,790 CM, 6,578 PM) into binary transactions of eleven items C–M, with three explicit item-inclusion rules (portability across Maximo deployments, user-editable fields, nameable procedural obligation). Phase 4 runs Apriori and FP-Growth (mlxtend 0.23.4, Python 3.11) at support 0.10 / confidence 0.70 / lift > 1.0 over four scenarios (work type × ablation step), with timings averaged over 30 runs after 3 warm-ups. Phase 5 adds one-sided Fisher exact tests on each rule's 2×2 table, Benjamini-Hochberg correction across all m = 155 tested rules, multivariable logistic regression (IRLS) re-estimating each syndrome with all other items as simultaneous predictors, and a pre-fixed 4×4 support-confidence grid with rule-identity (not just count) comparison across cells. Phase 6 designs three artefacts: a per-client validation package via custom system properties, a blueprint checklist, and a Node.js rule engine rendering rules as natural-language sentences. Well-justified design decisions: pre-registered thresholds (removes post-hoc tuning), removing saturated items from the search space rather than filtering output (shown empirically necessary via four ablation variants in Table 8), and the CRISP-DM loop back to data preparation after a definitionally trivial failure-report item produced confidence-1.000 rules. Key Results: The data quality profile splits cleanly: administrative fields reach 100% integrity while execution fields collapse (actual start 71.10%, actual finish 66.29%, failure code 46.34%, WOACTIVITY long descriptions 1.97%). PM work logs run at a ratio of 0.01 logs per completed order versus 0.56 for CM; 97.97% of CM orders close with no attachment; over 95% of CM status changes are backdated; 63.4% of completed CM closures occur within two minutes; ~70% of PM and 27% of CM orders contain overlapping technician intervals. Apriori and FP-Growth returned numerically identical rule sets in all four scenarios (strong robustness evidence), with Apriori 23–98× faster (all runtimes under 0.19 s) on the 11-item space — a finding the authors correctly bound as a property of low-dimensional binary matrices, not a general ranking. After redundancy pruning (211 rules to 35/30/18/7 per scenario), the two syndromes emerge: {F} ⇒ {E} at support 0.470, confidence 0.980, lift 1.350, OR 49.50 (CM); {E, G} ⇒ {L} at support 0.305, confidence 0.968, lift 1.759, OR 54.46 (PM); all syndrome rules survive BH correction at q < 0.001 (log10 q as low as −1048.8) and Bonferroni (129 of 155 rules at 0.05). Logistic models retain adjusted ORs of 49.3 (CM) and 69.7/7.1 (PM) and correct a marginal-rule misreading: high priority's association with backdating reverses sign (adjusted OR 0.67) once instant closure is controlled — priority acts through instant closure. Exactly two rules per work type appear in all sixteen threshold cells, and only rules leave the grid as thresholds tighten, never enter. Three statistically significant but practically empty Step-1 rules (lift 1.003–1.020) are correctly excluded by the pre-registered practical criterion. Baselines are the authors' own ablation variants and threshold grids — there are no external benchmarks, which is appropriate for a single-site audit but limits external comparison. Novelty Classification: NEW FORMULATION and NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING with an engineering component; this is not a NEW METHOD in the algorithmic sense. Genuinely novel: the encoding of documentation absence as mineable items for compliance auditing in EAM, the prevalence-driven ablation, and the three-layer validation-to-deployment pipeline (statistical significance, mutual adjustment, practical significance) carried through to configurable platform controls. The authors are explicit and credible that Apriori, FP-Growth, CRISP-DM, and Fisher's test are established and unmodified — the contribution is their disciplined integration in a domain where this combination had not been applied end-to-end. Rigor & Reproducibility: This is unusually rigorous for an applied association-rules paper. Ablations are present and load-bearing (Table 8 tests four ablation choices per work type); the threshold sensitivity grid compares rule identity across cells, not just counts; multiple testing is corrected with both BH and Bonferroni; effect sizes are reported with 95% Wald intervals; runtime means carry standard deviations over 30 runs on a controlled machine. Limitations are confronted directly rather than minimized (six explicit limitations, §4.2). Weaknesses: no code or data repository is cited — the SQL and analysis code are "available on request" and the data cannot be released at all (single-site proprietary records); there are no error bars on the mining results themselves (though the exact tests and CIs partly cover this); no stratification by site, crew, asset class, or shift (acknowledged as the principal confound); no temporal train/test validation of the rules. The first author is a paid consultant on the audited account — a declared conflict of interest that provides access but introduces incentive risk; the behavioural interpretations were validated only by the authors' own consulting team. Not a preprint: this appears in Statistics, Optimization and Information Computing (peer-reviewed venue), though with placeholder volume/date metadata in the PDF. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL (with a SYSTEMS-flavoured deployment design that was not actually deployed). - Practical: Yes — the entire analysis ran on a single Apple M3 laptop with 8 GB RAM, and the controls deploy through Maximo's configuration layer (custom system properties) without source-code modification. - Efficient: Extremely — every mining run completes in under 0.19 seconds; compute cost is negligible relative to any alternative. - Effective: Partially — the evidence establishes that the two syndromes exist and are statistically robust, but effectiveness of the proposed controls is an argument, not a measurement; the before-and-after protocol (including a per-site controlled rollout and three displacement indicators) is specified but never executed. - Scalable: Only claimed by inference — the framework is argued to transfer across Maximo installations via its stable table schema, but nothing beyond 12,368 orders at one site was tested, and the three portability preconditions (retained status history, interval-based labour booking, post-go-live stability) are themselves restrictive. The work delivers a deployment design and one working rule-engine prototype, not an installed artifact; the reusable output is the framework (encoding, ablation, validation layer), with code available only on request. Strengths: 1. The missingness-as-feature encoding is a genuinely useful reframing: in a dataset where work logs cover ~20% and attachments ~4% of orders, imputation would have erased the phenomenon, and treating documentation gaps as indicators is the correct instrument for auditing rather than estimation. 2. The validation layer is layered correctly and pre-registered: statistical significance (Fisher + BH over 155 rules), mutual adjustment (multivariable logistic), and practical significance (four pre-fixed conditions) are kept distinct, and the paper demonstrates the payoff concretely by exhibiting three significant-but-useless rules the criterion correctly excludes. 3. The algorithm comparison is honest to an unusual degree: identical rule sets establish robustness, and the 23–98× speed-up is explicitly bounded as a property of 11-item matrices with the mechanism (candidate-space size vs. tree overhead) explained, refusing the tempting over-generalization. 4. Causal discipline: the paper repeatedly distinguishes co-occurrence from mechanism, enumerates at least three competing explanations per syndrome, and uses the logistic models to catch and correct a misleading marginal association (priority → backdating). Author-Acknowledged Limitations: Six, stated in §4.2 and confronted directly: (1) single installation, single industry — the framework transfers, the numbers do not, with three data preconditions named for replication; (2) deployment artefacts are designs and one prototype, with no post-intervention measurement (a credibility positive that the section title states plainly); (3) presence indicators measure completeness, not accuracy or informativeness of documentation — findings are a lower bound; (4) rules capture association, behavioural readings are expert-validated interpretations, not established causes; (5) contextual confounders (site, asset class, crew, shift, technician) were not extracted into the matrix, called "the single most consequential open question"; (6) the sensitivity grid covers a defensible but bounded parameter range with lift held fixed. This is candid limitation reporting. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - The authors' interpretation of the syndromes is validated only by their own consulting team — the same team whose service model the paper argues should be restructured — with no independent domain validation; this is acknowledged obliquely but not as an incentive problem. - The three remaining confounder candidates (unavailable mobile access, batch coordinator entry, platform defaulting of execution stamps) are all checkable with data the authors describe but did not obtain (interface logs, shift rosters); the paper flags this as open rather than pursuing it within the study window. - No temporal holdout: deriving the rules on an earlier window and testing on a later one is listed as future work, but the two-to-three-year extract makes an inner split feasible now, and its absence leaves rule stability over time untested. - The single-CRISP-DM-loop correction of the failure-report item is reported transparently, but it means the item selection was itself data-driven after seeing first-pass results — the pre-registration discipline applied to thresholds was not applied to item definitions. - The practical-significance thresholds (lift ≥ 1.25, OR ≥ 3, support ≥ 0.10), while fixed before mining, were fixed by the same first author whose client relationship motivates the conclusions; no sensitivity to those particular cut-offs is reported. - Data, SQL, and analysis code are not publicly released (proprietary data, code on request), so no independent reproduction is currently possible. Bottom Line: A practitioner in EAM consulting, Maximo administration, or transactional data-quality auditing gains a concrete, unusually well-validated playbook worth reading in full, while readers seeking algorithmic or cross-site evidence will find the same ground better covered by the process-mining and maintenance-analytics literature the paper itself positions against.

Problem & Motivation: Teams formalizing mathematics in Lean — from single theorems toward textbooks and research papers — face a gap the proof assistant cannot close: Lean checks formal correctness, not whether a formal statement preserves the source's meaning. A statement can compile, admit a proof, and still omit a hypothesis, shift a quantified domain, or substitute a different formal construction; at document scale, downstream units import such statements automatically. Existing faithfulness signals (bidirectional provability/BEq+, prompted judges, structural distances like GTED/TransTED, expert references) are theorem-level signals that do not by themselves make document-level acceptance decisions: whether a generated statement may advance, whether a deviation is justified, and what evidence downstream reuse requires. The paper distinguishes proof capability, semantic faithfulness, and formal correctness, and targets the second at document scale. Key Idea: Make semantic faithfulness an auditable, graded relation with a single pre-fixed standard of equivalence: an LLM may only propose structured evidence over slot-level correspondences (binder domains, hypothesis conjuncts, goal conjuncts, used definitions), while deterministic code — not the model — checks coverage, logical polarity, scope, and admissibility, and computes the statement grade as a non-compensatory minimum (grade 3 aligned, 2 trivially equivalent, 1 modified, 0 failed). The genuinely non-obvious move is the treatment of grade-1 deviations: a directionally admissible change (candidate conclusions stronger, candidate assumptions weaker, per a polarity calculus where negation and implication antecedents reverse direction) is not reclassified as faithful, but must carry a Lean-checked bridge obligation S1 → S0 witnessed by explicit transfer maps (object coverage e, hypothesis transfer a, claim transfer g), with a compositional theorem (Appendix E.2) showing scope-aware local certificates compose into a global proof transformer on the supported logical fragment. Methodology: FYAN maps PDF/TeX/Markdown sources into a dependency-aware Lean project through a staged pipeline: (1) Intake/SPECIFIER extract self-contained theorem units (problem.tex) and a document-level dependency DAG, with deterministic validation of unit coverage, cycle-freedom, and recomputed topological layering; (2) an ORCHESTRATOR schedules ready units in topological order; (3) REASONER (built on the open-source QED system) produces a natural-language proof (proof.md) that may reuse proved upstream units as black boxes; (4) PLANNER converts this into a lemma-level DAG, a blueprint, and a compiling Statement.lean scaffold with := by sorry bodies, frozen read-only during proving; (5) FORMALIZER (a Pi-runtime agent, forked from Archon v0.2.0) runs a plan–prove–review loop; (6) the semantic audit sits between statement generation and proof search; (7) a deterministic completion gate requires zero sorry, full project build, discharged bridges, intact frozen signatures, and a transitive axiom audit (no sorryAx). The audit's grade function is grade(R) = min({3} ∪ {s_i}), i.e., a single unresolved comparison fails the statement. Three critical design decisions: (a) models/experts/human guidance are advice-only while a gateway is the sole writer of stage state — well-justified by the trust-boundary table (Appendix F.5); (b) unpaired source slots score as omissions via replacement with ⊤/⊥ under the polarity rule, which handles deleted conjuncts/disjuncts without a separate heuristic — well-justified with worked examples; (c) the closed list of admissible 'trivial equivalent' conversions (bundling, currying, standard unfolding, etc.) defines evident agreement — this is the policy locus and is discussed candidly but is ultimately a judgment call (e.g., whether Mathlib's subgroup infimum equals textual intersection is graded 1, not 2). Key Results: On FormalTCS (143 theorems, one output per item, DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash in both arms, Lean 4.32.2/Mathlib 905b958, released graders): strict Lean pass (FT2FP) 86/143 (60.1%) vs 69/143 (48.3%) for a general agent harness (+17); T2NP rubric mean 0.851 vs 0.501; NT2FT BEq+ 8 vs 5 (both near-floor — the strongest published result with Claude Opus 5 at 8 samples/item is 11.2%). On ConsistencyCheck (300 of 835 eligible items, balanced 150/150), recall on inconsistent statements: original labels 0.873 (FYAN) vs 0.820 (direct judge); author-verified labels 0.777 vs 0.636, with accuracy 0.813 vs 0.750, precision 0.941 vs 1.000, and exact McNemar p = 0.027; 95% bootstrap intervals are reported. The audit's 39 false alarms under original labels include 18 grade-1 reports, of which 13 re-verification found were genuinely not the text's statement (e.g., exercise 1 13a omits domain connectedness and the Lean statement is false). Case studies show failures of competing yardsticks: BEq+ cannot identify independently declared types (all 5 control NT2FT passes lie among the 52/143 references without a declared structure; one-sided Fisher p = 0.0056), and a direct judge accepts a miniF2F arithmetic-series statement with a free variable that makes it false. ODENumLib: 20 of 23 units formalized (no sorry, no new axioms), 9,355 lines of Lean, 34 theorems, 118 lemmas, 17 replaying under the pinned environment; notably, Appendix D discloses that ODENumLib was built before the semantic audit was added, and that 9 of 19 units with retained scaffolds underwent substantive statement changes, including scaffold-weakening (runge_kutta_4 assumes the local truncation estimate; dahlquist proves one direction only). Baselines are contemporaneous (2025–2026 references) but the control harness is a generic agent using benchmark prompts verbatim, not a competing formalization-specific system. Scale is standard-benchmark (143–371 items) plus one small case-study project. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD (evidence-grounded semantic audit with deterministic validation, polarity-aware admissibility, and non-compensatory grading) plus NEW FORMULATION (proof-transfer obligations with a compositional transfer theorem linking local slot certificates to a global Lean-checkable bridge), and a modest NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING (structured auditing beats direct judgment on recall, and the audit's rejections under original benchmark labels are largely correct upon re-verification). The document-level DAG workflow itself is a competent combination of existing ideas — Archon for proving loops, QED for natural-language reasoning, blueprint-style dependency management — and the paper says so explicitly; the genuinely novel element is the acceptance discipline, not the orchestration. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations of CURATOR and ORCHESTRATOR supervision are absent (the authors state they do not attribute independent empirical effects to either, and list their ablation as future work — honest, but it means the harness is evaluated only as a bundle). The semantic audit versus direct judge comparison is clean: same model, same per-call reasoning settings, same inputs; confusion counts, bootstrap intervals, and exact McNemar testing are reported. The FormalTCS comparison controls model, Lean environment, graders, and one-candidate-per-item sampling, with a bwrap sandbox hiding benchmark references. Single trajectory per item and a single model are acknowledged limitations; there are no multi-seed variance estimates for the proving results. Code, prompts, configurations, and artifacts are released at an anonymous repository (https://anonymous.4open.science/r/fyan-release-78C6). Methodological concern: the 'verified labels' were produced by screening with Claude Opus 5.5 plus author confirmation under a criterion (differing only by conversions a reader sees at a glance) that closely matches the audit's design intent; the authors argue the criterion is the same one the direct judge was instructed to apply, and that the direct judge accepts 48 of the 56 relabelled statements, but the relabeling still moves 56 of 300 labels in the direction that favors a recall-oriented audit. A second concern is self-grading asymmetry: the audit's cost and failure analysis is self-reported. The ODENumLib project predates the audit, so the document-level case study does not exercise the paper's central contribution end-to-end. This is a preprint (arXiv, dated Sep 2026 in the text), not peer-reviewed. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (with a SYSTEMS component). Practical: Yes — it runs on a commercial API model (DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash), standard Lean/Mathlib toolchain, and commodity per-theorem workspaces. Efficient: Proving costs are modest, but the audit costs ~0.15 CNY per statement versus 0.007 CNY for a direct judgment (~21×), and the multi-stage pipeline adds up to 50 proving iterations, 4 concurrent provers, and up to 3 concurrent theorem units per configured run. Effective: Evidence supports improved proof throughput (+17/143) and better inconsistency recall, but faithfulness of the final accepted project is shown only through audit behavior on a benchmark, not by demonstrating that ODENumLib's statements are faithful (the authors themselves document substantive, unaudited statement changes in it). Scalable: Only claimed, not tested — ODENumLib is 20 units, 3 units remain open, 3 need porting; behavior at 10–100× units (DAG scheduling, bridge accumulation, audit cost) is extrapolation. The work delivers a software artifact: an anonymous repository with implementation, prompts, and configurations, plus the ODENumLib Lean library; the compositional transfer theorem is a reusable proof technique but its checker constructs symbolic recipes, not kernel-checked Lean terms. Strengths: - The separation of proposal from acceptance — LLMs propose evidence, deterministic code decides grades, stage transitions, and completion — is implemented as concrete, inspectable machinery (trust-boundary table, gateway-as-sole-writer, fail-closed defaults), not just a principle. - The polarity calculus for admissible one-way changes and the omission-as-⊤/⊥ treatment yield a principled, checkable answer to 'what counts as a dropped hypothesis,' with worked examples (e.g., (A ∧ H) → G recoverable vs A → (G ∧ H) → A → G not). - The evaluation is unusually self-critical: the authors relabel their own benchmark against a stricter criterion, report that 13 of the audit's grade-1 'false alarms' were actually correct rejections (one Lean statement is outright false), disclose that their case-study library predates the audit and contains weakened scaffolds, and expose BEq+'s structural blind spot with a statistical argument (Fisher p = 0.0056). - The bridge-obligation mechanism converts a semantic judgment into a Lean-checkable obligation, so accepted deviations are backed by machine-checked implications rather than the judge's word. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state: evaluation uses one model (DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash) and one trajectory per item; ODENumLib covers a single domain (numerical analysis of ODEs); the audit costs more per statement than a single judgment; CURATOR and ORCHESTRATOR supervision are not ablated; and future work will replace more of the Judge's conversions with mechanically checked rules. Appendix D further concedes the library was built before the audit existed and that 9/19 units changed statements substantively. The authors confront limitations directly and in detail — a credibility positive; they do not minimize. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - Circularity risk in the verified labels: the re-verification criterion ('same statement up to conversions a reader sees at a glance') is effectively the audit's grade-2 definition, the screening was done by a different frontier model with author confirmation, and 56/300 labels moved in the direction that improves the audit's headline recall. The paper argues the direct judge was given the same criterion, which mitigates but does not eliminate the concern. - The control baseline is a generic agent harness with benchmark prompts verbatim, not a competing formalization system (e.g., Archon unmodified, or ProofFlow-style dependency-graph pipelines), so the +17/143 gain conflates the semantic audit with the whole document-level harness (REASONER, PLANNER, DAG scheduling). - No end-to-end demonstration that the audit improves the faithfulness of an actually built library: the flagship artifact (ODENumLib) was constructed without it. - Single grading-model dependence: all audit evidence comes from one LLM judge; sensitivity of grades to the judge model is unmeasured. - The closed conversion list for 'trivial equivalence' is a fixed policy whose boundary cases (e.g., Mathlib infimum of subgroups vs textual intersection; implicitly assumed finite dimensionality) are shown to decide outcomes, but there is no study of how often the list misroutes in either direction beyond the 300-item sample. - Precision degradation on original labels (0.771 vs 0.939) is substantial; the recall-first framing is well-argued for library gates but the paper does not measure the downstream cost of the resulting extra repair rounds in wall-clock or token terms. Bottom Line: For anyone building autoformalization or agentic proving systems, this paper offers the most concrete and honestly evaluated acceptance discipline for semantic faithfulness I have seen in this line of work — read it for the audit-and-bridge design, while discounting the headline numbers as single-model, single-trajectory results against a generic control.

TL;DR - What it does: This paper presents an empirical study of cross-tokenizer On-Policy Distillation (OPD) showing that strict 1:1 token alignment plus a student-selected top-16 subset of the shared vocabulary captures nearly all distillation gains, while adding span-level MSE supervision on mismatched token groups to broaden coverage systematically hurts accuracy. - Why it's important: Cross-tokenizer distillation lets teams transfer capability from a strong teacher (e.g., Qwen) to students with different tokenizers (e.g., Llama, Phi) without retraining on teacher tokenizations, and recent work assumes recovering excluded supervision (multi-token spans, byte interfaces) is where the gains are; this paper challenges that assumption. - How it does it: The core move is decomposing cross-tokenizer supervision into strict 1:1 aligned positions (reverse KL over a renormalized shared vocabulary) versus mismatch groups (span log-probability MSE), then measuring token coverage, probability-mass concentration, and mismatch-vs-strict gradient cosine/norm ratios to explain why more coverage yields worse students. - The good: The probability-mass and coverage measurements are convincing and quantitatively strong — static vocabulary Jaccard overlap is only 39.49–64.87%, yet strict 1:1 groups cover 85.57–96.98% of student tokens, and the shared vocabulary retains 99.69–99.90% of teacher probability mass at strict positions. - The missing: No error bars, seeds, or significance tests are reported for the downstream comparisons, and the margin over the strongest baseline (SimCT) is small (0.51–1.05 full-average points), so method ordering could plausibly flip under run-to-run variance. - Read it or not: Worth reading for anyone building cross-tokenizer distillation pipelines (it directly rebuts the premise of SimCT-style coverage-recovery methods) or studying why auxiliary distillation losses fail; skippable if you work only within a single tokenizer family, where standard GKD/MiniLLM results already apply.

Problem & Motivation: Practitioners who want to distill a teacher LLM into a student from a different model family face two obstacles: token boundaries and vocabularies differ, so teacher and student predictions cannot be compared token-by-token or distribution-to-distribution directly. Recent cross-tokenizer OPD methods (SimCT, Byte-Prefix Marginalization, GOLD, ULD) invest in recovering supervision beyond strict 1:1 alignment via multi-token units, learned mappings, or byte interfaces, implicitly assuming more alignment coverage means better learning. This paper asks whether that assumption holds: how much useful supervision does strict matching already retain, and does recovering the excluded targets actually improve student accuracy? Key Idea: The central insight is that static vocabulary overlap is a misleading proxy for the actual supervision gap. Because token frequency and probability mass are heavily concentrated, (a) most tokens on student trajectories fall in strict 1:1 groups even when only ~40–65% of vocabulary entries overlap, and (b) the shared vocabulary plus a 16-entry student-selected subset carries almost all predictive probability at strict positions. Consequently, compact, reliable supervision at strict positions beats structurally complete supervision that injects weakly aligned or conflicting signals from mismatch groups. The supporting evidence for why span supervision hurts is a gradient diagnostic: span-loss gradients have weak-to-negative cosine with strict-loss gradients (consistently below a split-half control) while their norm ratio grows up to 28× over 100 training steps. Methodology: The setup is on-policy distillation: the student samples rollouts, both models re-tokenize the decoded response, and token-group alignment partitions the response into R span-aligned token-group pairs split into strict 1:1 groups and mismatch groups. The strict objective (Eq. 5) sums reverse KL between teacher and student distributions restricted and renormalized on the shared vocabulary V∩ at strict positions. The span objective (Eq. 8) is an MSE on log-probabilities of the observed token paths within each mismatch group; the total loss is L1:1 + λ·Lspan, swept over λ ∈ {0, 0.25, ..., 1.5}. The compact variant restricts the strict reverse KL to a student-selected top-k subset of V∩ (k ∈ {4,...,128}, emphasis on 16 and 128), renormalizing both models on the same subset. Diagnostics include strict token coverage (Eq. 6), retained probability mass for teacher and student on shared/top-k subsets (Eqs. 10–11), and gradient cosine/norm-ratio comparisons against a split-half control (Eq. 13). Three critical design decisions: (1) measuring coverage and mass on student-generated rollouts rather than static vocabularies — well justified, this is the paper's central corrective; (2) using student-selected top-k as the loss support — justified by the measurement that student selection also captures most teacher mass, and empirically it retains ≥96% of the full objective's gains; (3) using span log-probability MSE as the coverage-recovery mechanism — reasonable but specific; whether other mismatch losses (e.g., byte-prefix marginalization) behave differently is not tested, so the anti-coverage conclusion generalizes beyond this one span formulation only via the gradient argument. Key Results: Across three pairs (Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct→Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct, Granite-4.1-8B→Phi-4-mini-instruct, Granite-4.1-8B→Qwen2.5-7B-Base) trained on 20k prompts (10k DAPO-Math-17K, 10k CodeForces) for 100 on-policy iterations: (1) Strict token coverage is 85.57–96.98% (student) despite Jaccard overlap of 39.49–64.87%. (2) Shared vocabulary retains 99.69–99.90% of teacher and 98.99–99.81% of student mass at strict positions; top-16 retains ≥93.54%/≥94.55% respectively. (3) Adding span MSE lowers accuracy at all 18 positive-λ settings by 0.27–1.20 full-average points relative to λ=0. (4) Strict full achieves full averages of 32.86/42.49/47.35 across the three pairs, beating ULD, Extended ULD, GOLD, and SimCT on all pairs; top-16 leads the strongest baseline by 0.51–1.05 full-average points and retains ≥96% of the strict-full improvement over the undistilled student. (5) With a Qwen3-235B-A22B teacher, Strict top-16 reaches 62.46 full average vs 56.25 for the best baseline; on ALFWorld it reaches 30.34% overall success rate vs 28.52% for SimCT. (6) Gradient diagnostics: mismatch–strict cosine near 0 or negative (e.g., −0.360 at step 0 for Granite→Qwen) versus split-half control of 0.208–0.977; norm ratio grows 6.6×–28.0× from step 0 to 100. Evaluation uses MATH500, GSM8K, AIME-2024/25/26, AMC23, Minerva-Math (mean@32) and HumanEval, MBPP, LiveCodeBench (mean@8). Baselines are recent (2024–2026) and implemented in the KDFlow framework, so the comparison is credible. The finding that λ=0 strictly dominates is consistent across all three pairs and both domains, which is the paper's most robust and somewhat counter-intuitive result given SimCT's published gains from coverage recovery. Novelty Classification: NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING with supporting ENGINEERING OPTIMIZATION (the top-16 compact objective). The genuinely novel contribution is the negative result plus mechanism: complete structural coverage via span MSE hurts, with gradient-direction/magnitude evidence explaining why, and the demonstration that a 16-entry student-selected support suffices under heterogeneous tokenizers. The individual techniques — reverse KL at aligned positions, top-k support restriction (closely following Li et al. 2026 in the shared-vocabulary setting), span log-probability MSE, and gradient-surgery-style cosine diagnostics (Yu et al. 2020) — are all existing ideas; the novelty lies in the cross-tokenizer instantiation and the coverage-versus-reliability analysis, not in any new algorithmic primitive. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are present and substantive: the λ-sweep (7 weights × 3 pairs), the top-k sweep (6 subset sizes × 3 pairs), and benchmark-level tables for every configuration are all reported. The split-half gradient control is a thoughtful methodological touch that strengthens the diagnostic. However, no error bars, multiple seeds, or significance tests appear anywhere; mean@32/mean@8 sampling reduces eval noise but training-run variance is unaddressed, and several headline margins (0.51–1.05 points) are within plausible run-to-run variation. Code is released via an anonymous.4open.science link; prompts, training configs, baseline implementations, and scoring pipelines (Math-Verify, EvalPlus, LiveCodeBench v6) are documented in detail in Appendix A. Methodological concerns: the probability-mass and coverage probes are run before distillation only, so the concentration claims describe the pre-training student distribution; the gradient analysis covers only 4 checkpoints per run with medians over replay units; and the paper's strict objective outperforming SimCT directly contradicts SimCT's own reported results — the authors attribute this to their framework, but the discrepancy is not independently investigated. One student is a base model (Granite→Qwen), a useful robustness check. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (training and evaluation experiments actually run; the top-16 objective is a lightweight tool-level contribution). - Practical: Runs on a single node of 8 NVIDIA H20 GPUs with FSDP2 and SGLang rollouts — commercially standard hardware for 3B–8B students. - Efficient: Restricting to top-16 strictly reduces the per-position support versus full shared-vocabulary KL, so the compact variant is cheaper than the full objective and cheaper in principle than baselines requiring mapping structures or byte interfaces; exact cost comparisons are not reported. - Effective: The evidence shows the strict objective solves the stated problem (cross-tokenizer distillation gains) on standard math/code benchmarks, a 235B-teacher setting, and ALFWorld, though the accuracy transfer is modest relative to the teacher (e.g., Llama student reaches 32.86 vs teacher 49.03 full average). - Scalable: Tested only on 3B–8B students, 100 iterations, 20k prompts; the 235B-teacher experiment is the largest scale probe, but 10× more prompts/students or much longer training is untested and the gradient-ratio growth trend raises unresolved questions about long-run behavior. The work delivers code (anonymous repository) and a recipe; no trained model weights are reported as released. Strengths: - The coverage-versus-reliability reframing is supported by three independent measurement types (token coverage, probability mass, gradient geometry) that all point the same way, giving the negative result unusually strong triangulation for an empirical paper. - The static-overlap-is-misleading finding (39.49% Jaccard but 96.98% strict token coverage for Granite→Phi) is a crisp, quantified corrective to how the field estimates the cross-tokenizer supervision gap. - The split-half gradient control distinguishes "span gradients disagree with strict gradients" from generic gradient noise across positions, which most ablation-only papers would omit. - Breadth of validation: 3 main pairs, a 235B→8B transfer, and an interactive agent benchmark (ALFWorld) beyond static math/code — competent execution beyond the minimum for this claim type. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors are appropriately measured rather than overclaiming: they scope the span-supervision conclusion to "the evaluated cross-tokenizer baselines" and the specific MSE formulation, hedge the gradient explanation with "may help explain," and restrict the top-k claim to "retains most of the observed distillation gains." They do not include a dedicated limitations section; boundaries are conveyed through careful wording and the experimental scoping rather than explicit confrontation. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - No seeds/variance reporting for training runs; given SimCT published the opposite ordering, a 0.5–1 point margin without variance evidence is a real fragility, and the SimCT contradiction is left unexplained beyond framework differences. - Only one mismatch-supervision formulation (span log-probability MSE) is tested; the anti-coverage conclusion would be stronger if a second coverage-recovery mechanism (e.g., byte-prefix marginalization, which its own authors found needs masking to avoid collapse) were also shown to hurt. - The probability-mass and coverage probes use the pre-distillation student; mass concentration could degrade as the student trains, and the paper measures coverage during training (stable) but not mass during training. - The gradient diagnostic is correlational: weak/negative cosine plus growing norm ratio does not establish that span-gradient conflict causes the accuracy drop; no intervention (e.g., gradient projection or normalization of span gradients) is attempted, which would have been the direct causal test. - Training uses only 20k prompts and 100 iterations — well below modern post-training budgets — so conclusions about whether coverage matters at longer training horizons are extrapolated. - The human-annotation "methodological research at the beginning of the work" mentioned in the ethics statement is never described in the paper. Bottom Line: A practitioner doing cross-model distillation should read this paper — its measurements dismantle the coverage-maximization premise underlying recent cross-tokenizer OPD methods and hand you a simple, cheap recipe (strict reverse KL on a student-selected top-16 shared-vocabulary support) that beat every evaluated alternative — but the absence of variance reporting and the unresolved conflict with SimCT's published results mean the method ordering should be re-verified in your own stack before adoption.

ALoDLM: Adaptively Looped Diffusion Language Models (55 ▲ )

Liancheng Fang, Zhuowei Li, Youngeun Kim, Tianchen Zhao, Rajat Koner, Jiaye Wu, Linghan Xu, Xuanbai Chen, Xiang Xu, Zheng Zhang, Jakub Zablocki, Nishant Sankaran, Yifan Xing · arxiv.org · Daily papers of 6 Oct 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces ALoDLM, a diffusion language model that replaces the fixed-depth denoiser with token-adaptive latent recurrence — confident tokens commit early within a denoising step while difficult tokens keep refining persistent hidden states — and trains it at 1.7B and 8B scales to beat both diffusion and autoregressive baselines on average across 11 benchmarks. - Why it's important: Diffusion LMs promise parallel-decoding speedups over autoregressive decoding but consistently lose on quality to same-size AR models, and closing that gap without surrendering the speed advantage is the central obstacle to their practical adoption. - How it does it: Within each outer denoising step, an inner loop lets a learned exit gate and an entropy-based commitment rule decide per-token when to halt latent refinement; committed tokens feed their embeddings back as context, and the token-wise exit schedule is treated as a latent variable optimized via a conditional NELBO with a single-trajectory REINFORCE-style gradient estimator plus variance reduction. - The good: The headline result is concrete and at scale: ALoDLM-8B reaches an 80.3 average across 11 benchmarks versus 78.5 for its Qwen3-8B AR teacher and 75.1 for the strongest DLM baseline (WeDLM-8B), while delivering ~2.7× the GSM8K throughput of vLLM-served Qwen3-8B at comparable accuracy, with ablations (depth K, loop placement, variance reduction) that individually justify the design. - The missing: No multi-seed runs, significance tests, or error bars on the headline benchmark comparison — the 1.8-point margin over Qwen3-8B rests on a single training run, and the quality table is measured in a one-token-per-step mode distinct from the parallel-decoding mode used for the throughput claims. - Read it or not: Read it if you work on diffusion LMs, adaptive computation, or looped/recurrent-depth architectures; skip it if you only care about pushing AR model efficiency, since the speedup is benchmark-specific (GSM8K) and the authors themselves admit it can vanish on out-of-domain prompts.

Problem & Motivation: Diffusion language models decode many tokens in parallel but trail comparably sized autoregressive models in quality. The authors diagnose the root cause as a computation–difficulty mismatch: within one denoising step, some masked positions are easy to predict while others need more computation, yet standard DLMs apply the same fixed denoiser depth to every position. Confidence-based decoding (e.g., in LLaDA) only defers hard tokens to later steps, where the computation spent on their latent representations is discarded and the token is recomputed from its mask embedding. Anyone serving LLMs at scale — where AR token-by-token decoding is the latency bottleneck — is affected by either the DLM quality gap or the AR latency gap. The paper targets closing this gap inside the DLM framework itself, rather than via semi-autoregressive block diffusion or diffusion-as-drafter schemes. Key Idea: Treat the per-token exit depth from an inner latent recurrence loop as a latent variable and jointly learn the denoiser and the halting policy through a conditional ELBO, so that easy tokens commit early (their embeddings become discrete context for later passes) and hard tokens carry their evolving hidden states forward through additional recurrent passes — computation scales with token difficulty rather than being uniform. The counterintuitive move that makes this work where prior looped DLMs (which apply uniform recurrent depth) stop: backpropagating through the recurrent passes trains earlier latent states to support future predictions, instead of discarding them like self-conditioning schemes do. Methodology: The architecture partitions a Qwen3 backbone into Prelude (embedding + prefix blocks), Recurrent Core (the shared blocks applied up to K=4 times), and Coda (suffix blocks plus an LM head and an ExitGate head). Inference alternates an outer denoising loop with an inner recurrence loop: each pass produces a readout, high-confidence (low-entropy) tokens are committed and their embeddings substituted into the recurrent state, and a learned halting gate accumulates halt probabilities; the inner loop stops when the masked set empties, the mean cumulative halt probability exceeds q, or depth K is reached, with a forced lowest-entropy commitment guaranteeing progress. Training uses a conditional NELBO (Eq. 5) with a truncated geometric prior over exit depths; because a single token's exit depth changes the context for all remaining tokens (making exact summation over joint schedules intractable), gradients for the gate are estimated with an unbiased score-function (REINFORCE) estimator (Proposition 1), regularized by a relaxed depth-KL that weakly penalizes per-token deviation while matching the minibatch-average depth to the prior, and variance-reduced via intermediate supervision (weighted averaging of pre-commitment readout losses) and a first-pass control variate. Models are converted from Qwen3-1.7B/8B by direct SFT on a 5B-token corpus using WeDLM's streaming block-diffusion framework, skipping the expensive continued-pretraining phase used by SDAR and WeDLM. Critical design decisions: (1) middle-layer recurrence [10,26) at 8B — justified by an ablation showing it beats last-layer recurrence; (2) K=4 — justified by an ablation where K=2 plateaus lower and K=8 matches but costs more; (3) score-function over Gumbel-Softmax relaxation — argued qualitatively (discrete commitments complicate partial-commitment extensions) but not empirically compared against the alternative. Key Results: Across 11 benchmarks (ARC-E/C, MMLU, MMLU-Pro, GPQA-Diamond, GSM8K, MATH-500, HumanEval(+), MBPP(+)), under the OpenCompass protocol: ALoDLM-1.7B averages 65.5 (vs. 63.8 for Qwen3-1.7B, 61.0 for SDAR-1.7B); ALoDLM-8B averages 80.3, leading on 10 of 11 tasks, vs. 78.5 for Qwen3-8B, 75.1 for WeDLM-8B, 74.2 for SDAR-8B, 61.0 for Fast-dLLM-v2, 53.3 for LLaDA-8B, 60.5 for Dream-7B. Notably, these averages come from direct SFT on 5B tokens, no continued pretraining. Efficiency: on GSM8K single-stream on one B200, ALoDLM-8B reaches ~2.7× vLLM-served Qwen3-8B throughput at comparable or higher accuracy; at matched 93.25% accuracy it delivers 612.4 tok/s vs. WeDLM's 564.2 (+8.5%) and needs 133.5 vs. 154.6 GFLOPs/token (−13.6%). The frontier crosses near 650 tok/s, with WeDLM leading at the fastest operating points. Test-time scaling: raising exit threshold q from 0.1 to 0.4 raises loops/token from 1.60 to 2.34 and the 11-benchmark average from 77.9% to 79.1%. Learned allocation: numerical tokens get the lowest mean first-pass halt probability (0.369 vs. 0.417 cross-dataset mean, −11.5%) without difficulty labels. Variance reduction: removing intermediate supervision raises gradient variance to 1.76×/1.49×/1.42× at steps 1k/6.5k/17k (measured on a 4,096-parameter subset). Baselines are current and served with their own optimized engines (dInfer, JetEngine, vLLM, Fast-dLLM). One caveat on the headline figure: the 2.7× speedup over Qwen3-8B is reported at 'comparable or higher accuracy' on GSM8K only, and the paper's own frontier shows the advantage over WeDLM narrows to 8.5% at matched accuracy. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD (primary) + NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING. Genuinely novel: token-wise adaptive latent depth inside a diffusion denoising step — prior looped DLMs apply uniform recurrent depth per step, and FReDA's token-level commitment revises explicit drafts rather than propagating latent states — plus the conditional-ELBO formulation of joint exit schedules as latent variables with a single-trajectory unbiased estimator, which is a non-trivial extension of PonderNet/Ouro-style objectives to the case where exits interact through context feedback. The components (looped transformers, ACT/PonderNet halting, masked diffusion, Qwen3 conversion via WeDLM) are established; the combination and the joint variational treatment are the new contribution. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are present and target the right questions: recurrent depth K ∈ {2,4,8}, loop placement (middle vs. last vs. full stack), intermediate-supervision variance reduction (with paired 95% bootstrap CIs on eight fixed input packs), and decoding hyperparameter (τ, q) sweeps covering 94 configurations. However, the main 11-benchmark comparison is a single training run per model with no error bars, seeds, or significance tests — the 1.8-point average margin over Qwen3-8B is within plausible run-to-run variance for some of these benchmarks. Code (github.com/amazon-science/ALoDLM), model weights (huggingface.co/amazon/ALoDLM-8B), and a project page are released, which is a strong reproducibility positive. Concerns: (1) the quality table (Table 1) is measured in a one-token-per-step mode where ALoDLM uses preset q without entropy gating, while the efficiency claims use a different parallel mode — the reader cannot directly verify that the deployed fast mode reproduces the table's quality numbers across all 11 benchmarks (only GSM8K is shown for the frontier); (2) gradient-variance analysis covers only a 4,096-parameter subset of the 8B denoiser; (3) the score-function estimator is not compared against the Gumbel-Softmax alternative the authors themselves name; (4) the GFLOPs/token comparison is an estimate from execution records, not a hardware counter measurement, though the wall-clock throughput numbers are direct. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL (trained models run and measured, plus a serving implementation). - Practical: Yes — runs on a single NVIDIA B200 via vLLM with depth-aware KV caching, and weights are publicly released. - Efficient: Mixed — 13.6% fewer GFLOPs/token than WeDLM at matched accuracy, but the depth-aware KV cache needs L+(K−1)m = 84 logical buffer pairs vs. 36 physical layers at 8B (~2.3× KV memory), and recurrent computation is input-dependent. - Effective: Evidence supports quality gains on the 11 benchmarks and GSM8K speedups, but effectiveness under the fast parallel mode is verified in depth only on GSM8K; the 11-benchmark table uses the slow single-token mode. - Scalable: Tested at 1.7B and 8B (the largest looped DLM reported to date); behavior at 10–100× data, longer generation horizons, or larger models is claimed via the test-time-scaling axis but not measured; the authors explicitly warn throughput can degrade on underrepresented domains. The work delivers concrete artifacts: released code, an 8B model checkpoint, and a vLLM-compatible serving path. Strengths: - A genuine architectural-variational contribution: formulating interacting per-token exit schedules as latent variables and deriving a tractable single-trajectory unbiased estimator with proofs in the appendix is substantive, not a mechanical combination — the intractability of exact summation when commitments alter context is handled cleanly. - The efficient recipe is a practical result in itself: reaching AR-beating average quality (80.3 vs. 78.5) via direct SFT on 5B tokens without continued pretraining, undercutting the conversion cost of SDAR and WeDLM. - Honest efficiency methodology: the paper separates arithmetic cost (GFLOPs/token) from execution efficiency, sweeps 94 operating points to draw a real frontier against WeDLM, and measures baselines under their own tuned engines rather than strawman settings. - The emergent token-adaptive finding (numeric tokens receive ~11.5% lower halt probability than the mean, learned without difficulty labels) directly corroborates the motivating computation–difficulty hypothesis with interpretable evidence. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state two: (1) longer time-to-first-token than a comparable AR model because the KV cache is built for full recurrent depth at prefill, hurting short responses and latency-sensitive use; (2) inherently input-dependent throughput — on domains underrepresented in training data the model may need more recurrent refinement and fewer parallel commitments, potentially reducing or reversing the speed advantage over optimized AR serving. They confront both directly and quantitatively frame the second; this candor is a credibility positive, though they do not quantify the out-of-domain degradation. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - No statistical rigor on the headline comparison: single runs, no seeds, no significance testing, and no per-benchmark variance — the 1.8-point average margin over Qwen3-8B (and 5.2 over WeDLM) is asserted without uncertainty. - The 2.7× speedup claim is anchored to GSM8K, a math benchmark where the model's strength is greatest; no throughput figures for the other ten benchmarks or for open-ended generation are given, so the generality of the speed advantage is unverified — precisely where the authors' own input-dependence caveat bites. - The AR baselines are the Qwen3 models ALoDLM was SFT'd from; no comparison against stronger 8B-class instruct models (e.g., Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, DeepSeek-R1-distill-8B) to establish whether the quality claim extends beyond the teacher pair. - The quality-vs-efficiency discrepancy between evaluation modes (single-token for Table 1, parallel for Figure 1/3) means the community cannot confirm the deployed configuration achieves the table's quality; a full 11-benchmark evaluation of the parallel mode is the obvious missing experiment. - Evaluation is confined to 4,096-token generations and short math/code problems; long-context behavior with the 84-buffer KV scheme (memory ~2.3× baseline) is unexamined. - The Gumbel-Softmax alternative to the score-function estimator is dismissed in a footnote without an experiment, leaving the gradient-estimation choice under-validated. Bottom Line: For anyone building or studying diffusion LMs and adaptive-computation architectures, this is the strongest publicly-released demonstration to date that token-adaptive latent recurrence closes the DLM-vs-AR quality gap while keeping parallel-decoding speed — read it — but a practitioner primarily optimizing AR inference will find the speedup confined to math-style tasks and the statistical support for the quality margin thin.

Problem & Motivation: Cross-variate attention in time series foundation models must serve two distinct regimes: multivariate (MV) forecasting, where variates are time-aligned sensors measuring the same instants, and in-context learning (ICL), where example windows from other times are not time- or phase-aligned. Univariate models remain strong baselines, and prior work suggests learned covariate handling often adds little over uniform alternatives, but no one had decomposed which part of a cross-variate attention head earns or costs performance. Chronos-2's group attention is an ideal probe because it treats univariate forecasting as a first-class mode — suppressing cross-variate flow leaves the model in a trained configuration — and because it advertises both MV and ICL service from one mechanism. The paper targets researchers and practitioners deciding whether to trust cross-variate attention for ICL-style forecasting. Key Idea: Treat one attention head's α matrix as the sum of two functions — routing (Q/K decides the weights) and pooling (V/O determines what a weighted average is worth) — and separate them by progressively restoring α from identity (α = I, pure univariate), to uniform (α = 1/V, pooling only), to row-shuffled (preserves entropy and self-weight but randomizes which variate gets which weight), to learned. The shuffled condition is the clever move: learned-minus-shuffled measures whether variate identity in the weighting matters, independent of weight sharpness. Methodology: The authors use the public Chronos-2 checkpoint and edit α where it leaves the softmax in each of twelve encoder blocks, leaving W_OV, layer norm, and the univariate time-domain attention untouched. The pipeline has three phases: (1) the four-setting α ladder, scored as contributions in percentage points of univariate-baseline MAE; (2) restriction — activating group attention in subsets of blocks (α = I elsewhere) against univariate inference — to localize where the ICL harm arises; (3) repair — forcing one block to uniform pooling in the otherwise-shipped model against the released model. Statistical treatment is unusually careful: 95% paired bootstrap over windows (10,000 resamples), with a materiality threshold of ±0.1 points calibrated using block 5, where the shipped model's attention is already near-uniform, so forcing it uniform is a real but negligible edit (moves forecasts ≤0.081 points yet 14 of 20 intervals exclude zero). Critical design decisions: choosing Chronos-2 specifically for its univariate-first training (well justified — Moirai-style flattened variate/time offers no such separation); the shuffled-weighting control to isolate identity-dependence (well justified, with an entropy/self-weight preservation argument); and inference-time-only edits (acknowledged as a limitation — findings may not transfer to retraining). Appendix B rules out the trivial explanation that uniform α just reduces to averaging: replacing the learned V/O projection with a raw cross-variate mean costs −216.8 points on one configuration, dwarfing every reported effect. Key Results: On five sensor networks (Atlantic/Gulf and Pacific tide gauges, USCRN climate stations, PJM and Central-European load zones) at two context/horizon protocols (204/52 and 320/96), giving 20 configurations plus 6 standard LSTF corpora (ETTh1/h2/m1, electricity, exchange_rate, solar_AL, traffic) and relatedness controls (39 configurations total): uniform pooling is positive on 18 of 20 sensor-network configurations; shuffled weighting is near-zero (median −0.04); learned weighting is positive on 8 of 10 MV conditions but negative on 9 of 10 ICL conditions. The same eight Atlantic tide gauges score +8.15 points as an MV group but −1.85 as an ICL group (+8.37 vs −3.81 at the longer protocol). On 4 of 10 ICL configurations the shipped model is worse than univariate inference; the worst case is EU load ICL at −18.59 learned / −15.39 total. Restriction shows harm is a depth property: no single block other than block 0 moves the forecast more than 0.52 points, but cumulative leading-block subsets reach −16.09 on Pacific tides ICL. Repair: forcing block 0 uniform improves all ten ICL configurations (materially on eight, +0.4 to +20.5 points), and removing every group-attention Q/K weight (11.8% of parameters) yields +5.92 mean improvement over shipped Chronos-2 on ICL, while removing block 0's Q/K alone yields +7.2. Baselines are the model's own ablated configurations rather than external competitors, which is appropriate for a mechanism decomposition; the standard LSTF corpora reproduce the ICL pattern (e.g., electricity −14.08 learned). No result is surprising in direction so much as in the sharp MV/ICL split within one mechanism. Novelty Classification: NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING, with elements of a NEW FORMULATION (the pooling/routing decomposition of a cross-variate head via α-editing). The genuinely novel contribution is the demonstration that a single shipped attention mechanism helps and hurts by mode, and that the harm is depth-composed with block 0 as the break point; the techniques (activation patching in the style of Zhang & Nanda, uniform-attention nulls from Wiegreffe & Pinter and You et al.) are standard interpretability tools applied to a new setting. The paper itself frames Chronos-2's Q/K and V/O as instances of the established Transformer Circuits head decomposition. Rigor & Reproducibility: This is a rigorously ablated paper: the four-setting ladder, row-shuffled control, block-level restriction sweep (Tables A3–A4), repair sweep (Tables A5–A6), a raw-mean control establishing that V/O is not trivial averaging (Table A2), and an empirically calibrated materiality floor are all present, and the appendix reports every configuration behind every aggregate count. Error quantification is via 95% paired bootstrap over windows; however, the paper does not report multiple independent runs beyond the eight shuffle permutations, and per-window n (39–400) is modest. No code or data release is mentioned — reproducibility depends on the public Chronos-2 checkpoint plus the authors' evaluation pipeline, which is not stated as released. Methodological concerns: everything rests on one model checkpoint, and the authors candidly flag that Chronos-2 acquires its multivariate ability from synthetic structure on univariate series, so results may partly reflect its training distribution (a Goodhart-adjacent risk for generalization); the intervention is inference-time only, so claims about depth and position are claims about the shipped stack, not about training-time architecture choices. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL (inference-time measurement study with an actionable architectural edit). - Practical: Yes — the interventions require only the public Chronos-2 checkpoint and weight edits at inference; no specialized hardware is introduced or needed. - Efficient: Removing Q/K from group attention drops 11.8% of parameters and strictly reduces computation; the block-0 repair is free at inference. - Effective: The evidence shows the fix recovers ICL performance on the authors' five sensor networks and six LSTF corpora, but effectiveness on genuinely new deployments is untested beyond these. - Scalable: Not tested beyond 5 networks and standard LSTF corpora; the paper claims nothing about larger scale, and the depth-chain account is unverified at other model sizes. Deliverable: the paper stops at paper form — no library, patch, or modified checkpoint release is stated. Strengths: - The row-shuffled α control is a genuine methodological contribution: it separates weight sharpness from variate identity, letting the paper show the harm is specifically identity-dependent routing rather than attention entropy. - The materiality threshold is calibrated against an empirical near-null (block 5), a discipline almost no interpretability paper applies; 14 of 20 intervals excluding zero on a negligible edit motivates the ±0.1 floor convincingly. - The restriction/repair design attacks the depth question from both ends of the stack, and the conclusion — block 0 is not the guilty block but the cheapest place to break a chain — is a more honest and more useful claim than a naive single-block localization. - Table A2 (raw-mean vs. learned V/O, −216.8 points vs. +7.7) preempts the obvious misreading that uniform-α results imply cross-variate attention is just averaging. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state they cannot explain why tidal networks are the exception where learned weighting pays, nor why depth is what makes the cost material; their edits localize effects to a pathway and block without showing what the block computes, and rank-collapse-style accounts cannot be adjudicated. They acknowledge the phase-alignment hypothesis for the MV/ICL difference is untested, that inference-time findings may not hold under retraining, that only one alternative covariate attention design (Cohen et al.) is suggested for comparison, and that Chronos-2's synthetic multivariate training structure means the result may partly be a statement about the training distribution. This is a direct, non-minimizing limitations section — a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - Single-model evidence: every claim rests on one Chronos-2 checkpoint. The retraining experiment the authors defer to future work (or a comparison against Cohen et al.'s single-block covariate attention, which they name but do not run) is the experiment that would turn this from a case study into a general finding about cross-variate attention. - The phase-alignment explanation for the MV/ICL split is the paper's central interpretive claim, yet no ablation controls for phase alignment; a synthetic dataset with phase-aligned ICL examples would test it directly and cheaply. - No significance treatment beyond the bootstrap interval: with n as low as 39 windows (EU load MV), and a materiality floor chosen post hoc relative to a calibrated null, borderline results (e.g., USCRN ICL +0.40, marked not material) sit close to the threshold. - No code release is stated, which limits reproduction of the patching pipeline and evaluation splits despite the public checkpoint. Bottom Line: A practitioner deploying or building on Chronos-2 should read this for the immediately actionable block-0 finding and the rare statistical discipline, while anyone seeking a general theory of when cross-variate attention helps must wait for the retraining and phase-alignment experiments the authors themselves flag as missing.

#66 — Innovative (69)

SkillGym

Zhilong Ge, Yuting Shao, Yutao Yang, Yuxuan Cai, Jie Zhou, Kai Chen, Bo Zhang, Qin Chen, Liang He · arxiv.org · 🥇Top AI Papers of the Week
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces SkillGym, a pipeline that converts human-written agent skills into 2,756 Docker-packaged, code-verified task environments, and uses 8,364 verified trajectories collected there to fine-tune Qwen3.5-35B-A3B into SkillGym-Agent. - Why it's important: Human-authored skill documents (workflow instructions, scripts, constraints) are currently used only as external inference-time prompts; this work tests whether practicing on them builds internalized procedural competence rather than dependence on retrieval and prompt-following. - How it does it: Category-specific human-designed templates instantiate skills into concrete tasks with executable outcome verifiers, a contrastive with-skill/without-skill run labels tasks as empirically skill-dependent, and multiple harness-model combinations sample long-horizon trajectories for supervised fine-tuning. - The good: Under Claude Code, the fine-tuned 35B model gains +199 Elo on GDPval-AA v2, +19.10 points on Terminal-Bench 2.1, and 51.47% on skill-assisted SkillsBench v1.1 — above reported scores for Claude Sonnet 4.6 (47.2%) and DeepSeek V4 Pro Preview (50.1%) — and it beats its own skill-assisted base even when given no skills at inference. - The missing: Reinforcement learning in these environments is promised as future work but never run, only one base model is fine-tuned, evaluation has no error bars or significance tests, and the headline comparison against frontier models mixes the authors' controlled runs with harness-mismatched public leaderboard numbers. - Read it or not: Worth reading for agent-training and data-construction researchers who want a reproducible recipe (code, environments, and data are released on GitHub/HuggingFace) for turning skill corpora into verifiable training tasks; practitioners seeking RL-trained agents or multi-backbone evidence can wait.
Why this rank

Impact (80) is the strongest dimension — environments, trajectories, and a trained 35B checkpoint are all released, with the skill-free-beats-skill-assisted-base result directly supporting the internalization claim. Novelty (70) rests on the contrastive skill-dependency labeling protocol rather than any new training method; Rigor (65) is materially reduced by zero error bars or significance tests anywhere, a single backbone, uncontrolled frontier-model comparisons, and no adversarial testing of the verifiers that generate every label and reward. Completeness (72) is a credibility positive (honest harness-confound and non-controlled-comparison caveats), while Resilience (65) suffers from the unexamined contamination risk against SkillsBench and the SFT-only gap between the 'gym' framing and what was actually run.
