Problem & Motivation: Teams building LLM-based browsing agents lack an evaluation that reflects real-world search: open web, non-English information ecosystems, and evidence embedded in videos, scans, audio, maps, and tables. The original BrowseComp (Wei et al., 2025) is English-centric and predominantly textual; BrowseComp-ZH and K-BrowseComp cover single languages; BrowseComp-Plus/XBCP uses translated documents in a static corpus; MM-BrowseComp and BrowseComp-V3 add multimodality but only in English. Additionally, trivia-style questions saturate as models absorb more parametric knowledge. The gap HyperBrowseComp closes is a benchmark whose questions are natively authored per language (not translated), grounded in language-specific web ecosystems, and whose decisive evidence frequently requires discovering which medium to consult at all — 'interpretive search' rather than keyword lookup. Key Idea: The core move is combining natively-authored multilingual questions with a parametric-knowledge filter: questions start from an obscure publicly verifiable answer, validators add non-leading disambiguating 'fingerprints' (constraints unhelpful for searching but definitive for uniqueness), and any question a no-internet model answers — twice, or once with a highly specific answer — is excluded. The surviving 423 questions require locating evidence that is poorly indexed, timestamped inside videos, or hidden in scans, so difficulty comes from evidence discovery rather than answer interpretation. Methodology: Benchmark construction runs in three stages. (1) Question writing: annotators (native or near-native speakers, co-authorship for significant contributors) submit question, canonical answer with aliases, URLs, exact evidence locations (timestamps, page numbers, quotes), access dates, and a solution trace, following a source policy that bans paywalled, authenticated, fragile individual social-media, and private-person content. (2) Validation: a second annotator checks interpretability, uniqueness, evidence accessibility, and time-bounded wording; a core team member performs a final check; validators can demand harder questions, and group discussions iteratively raised difficulty as model weaknesses surfaced. (3) Difficulty auditing: seven no-internet models (Gemini 3.1 Pro Preview, Gemini 3.7 Flash, GLM-4.7, GPT-OSS-120B, Kimi K2 Thinking, MiniMax-M2, DeepSeek-V3.2) screened 500 submitted questions; 54 questions solved by ≥2 models and 23 solved by one model with LLM-judged (human-confirmed) 'highly specific' answers were excluded, leaving 423. Evaluation uses Inspect AI with a ReAct loop (≤25 steps) under three harnesses — provider built-in search, Exa search+fetch, and OWL (a CAMEL multi-agent workforce with DuckDuckGo/Wikipedia search, screenshot-based visual browsing, and multimodal inspection, limited to 2,400s and 50 external/250 model calls per sample) — scored by binary LLM-judge matching, with the generator as its own judge validated by a cross-judge sensitivity study (≥98.7% agreement, ≤0.80pp accuracy shift across three fixed judges). Notable design decisions: the no-internet exclusion threshold of 2 (justified against single lucky guesses), self-judging (justified empirically via the sensitivity analysis), and encoded release with a decoding key for contamination control (explicitly acknowledged as defeatable by bad-faith actors). Key Results: Best configuration: Gemini 3.7 Flash with built-in search at 31.68% (134/423), Gemini 3.1 Pro 25.53%, GPT-5.6 Sol 19.15%, Terra 15.84%, Luna 11.58% — all built-in. Harness sensitivity is the headline empirical finding: swapping built-in search for Exa raises GPT-5.6 Sol from 19.15% to 26.71% but drops Gemini 3.1 Pro from 25.53% to 18.20% and Gemini 3.7 Flash from 31.68% to 22.22%, while consuming 10–60× more tokens (Exa runs use 1.32–2.20M tokens/question vs ~0.1–0.4M built-in). OWL with Gemini 3.7 Flash scores 17.73% overall (22.73% on its 330 completed attempts, with 93 terminal failures counted incorrect). On 30 human-evaluated questions (Indonesian, Thai, Vietnamese), humans solved 15/30 (mean 89.5 min, median 54.6 min) versus 13/30 for Gemini 3.7 Flash, with overlap on only 8 questions. 244/423 questions (57.68%) were solved by no model under native search; 49 were solved by exactly one model. Shared failures concentrate on visual modalities (plots/graphs 75.0%, images 74.4%) and low-resource-language ecosystems (German 73.7%, Indonesian 69.2% shared failure). Scale is standard-benchmark, not stress-scale: 423 questions, 1 epoch, five API models, three harnesses. Novelty Classification: NEW DATASET/BENCHMARK plus NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING. The genuinely novel contribution is the conjunction: natively authored (non-translated) multilingual questions grounded in language-specific web ecosystems, combined with multimodal evidence and a parametric-knowledge exclusion audit — no prior BrowseComp variant does all three. The evaluation harnesses, ReAct loop, LLM judging, and no-internet screening are competent applications of existing techniques (Inspect AI, OWL, BrowseComp's own screening methodology). Rigor & Reproducibility: Strengths: a full validation pipeline with second-annotator checks and fingerprints; a seven-model no-internet audit with threshold-sensitivity analysis (Table 7 reports exclusions at k=1..7); a judge-sensitivity study quantifying self-judge bias at ≤0.80pp over 3,384 paired judgments; detailed token/time/cost accounting per language, modality, and harness; failure-mode taxonomy for OWL (51 worker-step timeouts, 28 budget exhaustions, etc.); prompts, tool schemas, model identifiers, and preserved traces promised for release, with the encoded dataset and site at HyperBrowseComp.github.io. Concerns: no error bars, seeds, or significance tests anywhere — accuracy differences of a few points across models or languages are not statistically supported; each configuration ran once on a live, non-stationary web; modality and domain labels come from LLM post-hoc annotation (human-verified but on unverified per-item bases); the difficulty analysis is explicitly descriptive (TF-IDF word associations, per-category failure rates) with known confounds — per-language question sets differ, so language rankings do not isolate language ability, which the authors concede. No Goodhart-style training-on-test is evident, but live-web drift means exact reruns will differ, as the authors state. Deployability: Profile: SYSTEMS/EMPIRICAL (a released benchmark plus evaluation harness, exercised via API calls). Practical: Yes — everything runs on commercially available API access plus open-source tooling (Inspect AI, Exa API, OWL); no special hardware. Efficient: Mixed — built-in search is cheap (~0.1–0.4M tokens/question, up to ~130 cumulative hours per full run), but Exa harnesses cost 1.3–2.2M tokens/question and OWL ~462K tokens plus 133 model calls per attempt, so a full harness comparison is expensive (the authors report single runs taking days). Effective: The evidence shows the benchmark discriminates current agents well (best at 31.68%, 57.68% shared failures) and correlates imperfectly with human difficulty — effective as a stress test, but it deliberately does not represent natural query distributions. Scalable: Not tested — the 423-question set, 13 languages, and single-epoch runs are fixed; scaling question counts or harness iterations is claimed as future work only. Deliverable: a dataset (encoded release with decoding key), annotation guidelines, evaluation code, prompts, and traces promised public upon paper release; site: https://HyperBrowseComp.github.io/. Strengths: (1) Natively authored, non-translated multilingual questions — a design decision that captures language-specific terminology, search behavior, and local web ecosystems that translation-based benchmarks (XBCP) structurally cannot. (2) The dual quality gate of human 'fingerprint' validation plus a multi-model no-internet audit with threshold sensitivity analysis is a rigorous, transparent operationalization of 'not answerable from parametric knowledge.' (3) The harness-sensitivity result (Exa helping GPT-5.6 Sol but hurting both Gemini models by 7–9 points) is a genuinely useful empirical finding showing that model and retrieval ecosystem are co-adapted and cannot be evaluated in isolation. (4) Unusually honest cost accounting: token totals, wall-clock time, per-question amortization, and a full OWL failure taxonomy, including counting terminal failures as incorrect rather than silently dropping them. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state: the benchmark is an intentional stress test, not representative of everyday queries; live-web variability makes exact reruns impossible (mitigated by preserved traces); language selection is non-representative and searchable information density differs across languages; privacy risks of obscure-information search are mitigated by excluding private individuals and authenticated sources; the model evaluation is limited to five frontier systems because single runs cost days and hundreds of millions of tokens; and Exa was tested on only a subset of models, with broader harness studies left to future work. They confront limitations directly and at appropriate length — a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: (1) No statistical treatment: single-epoch accuracy differences across models, harnesses, and languages carry no confidence intervals, yet the paper draws comparative conclusions (e.g., 'Larger variants of ChatGPT yielded better performance') from gaps of a few percentage points on n≈34–39 per language. (2) Cross-language difficulty is admittedly unstandardized, which undermines the benchmark's headline multilingual claim — per-language leaderboard comparisons are confounded by annotator-dependent difficulty. (3) The no-internet audit uses the same model family (Gemini 3.1/3.7) for both screening and evaluation, so memorization by evaluated models is not directly probed, only parametric answerability by other models. (4) Modality/domain annotations are LLM-generated from question text and proof cells without opening sources (acknowledged in the prompts themselves), so the '64.3% multimodal' figure is a documented-route estimate, not a verified property. (5) The human evaluation covers only 3 of 13 languages and 30 questions with single highly-selected annotators (top-of-class undergraduates), limiting the human-vs-model comparison's generality. (6) The 'fingerprints' mechanism, while solving uniqueness, is not analyzed for whether it inadvertently makes questions easier to verify-by-guess, and the encoded-release contamination control is acknowledged as symbolic. Bottom Line: For anyone building or benchmarking browsing/deep-research agents, this is currently the most demanding multilingual, multimodal open-web testbed available and the harness-sensitivity analysis alone justifies reading it, despite the small question counts, missing statistical rigor, and single-epoch evaluation that mean its language-level numbers should be treated as provisional.

Taming VLAs under Robot Execution Errors: Self-Compensation and Stress Testing (25 ▲ )

Sohyun Lee, Yoonjae Baek, Jaesang Won, Jinnyeong Kim, Kang Hyunwoo, Seung-Hwan Baek, Ivan Laptev, Suha Kwak · arxiv.org · Daily papers of 7 Oct 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces self-compensating VLA, a deployment-time adaptation method that fine-tunes a VLA policy online using the residual between commanded and executed robot motion, plus RoboStress, a simulation benchmark of seven joint-level execution-error scenarios for stress-testing VLA robustness. - Why it's important: Real robots develop execution errors from wear, payloads, and thermal conditions that existing VLA robustness work ignores (it tests only synthetic command noise), and building a fleet of degraded robots to evaluate against is impractical. - How it does it: The residual between a commanded delta pose and the proprioceptively measured executed motion is turned into a pseudo-target, and only rank-4 LoRA adapters on the action expert are updated with a flow-matching loss plus an anchor regularizer, leaving the base weights and the low-level controller frozen. - The good: On two physical AgileX Piper arms with different usage histories, the method raises average task success from 43% to 76% (π0.5) and 40% to 72% (π0) on Robot A, and from 43% to 74% and 38% to 71% on Robot B — gains that also transfer to unseen object variants (64% vs. 16% base). - The missing: There is no comparison against the test-time adaptation baselines the paper itself cites (EVOLVE-VLA, TT-VLA), no variance or significance testing despite three seeds, and the real-robot evaluation covers only four tasks on one 6-DoF arm model. - Read it or not: Read it if you deploy or fine-tune VLA policies on physical manipulators and care about deployment-time adaptation or realistic robustness evaluation; skip it if you only work with synthetic perturbation robustness, where the delta is the execution-error modeling rather than the adversarial-robustness toolkit.
Why this rank
Scored using Empirical profile. Novelty (75) is the strongest dimension — a genuinely new problem formulation (physical execution-error robustness for VLAs, distinct from synthetic command noise), a new benchmark (RoboStress) with physically-motivated joint-level error injection, and a new method — though each rests on competent recombination of known ideas (feedback-error learning, LoRA, flow-matching). Rigor (65) is solid but capped: targeted ablations cleanly isolate the residual signal (23.6% vs 44.2%), a rare DTW reality-check validates the simulation, but three seeds come with no variance reporting, the closest test-time-adaptation baselines are absent, and evaluation episodes populate the adaptation buffer. Non-Obviousness (72) is high — the command-execution residual as a free reward-free adaptation signal, and the finding that even a new arm carries 32.9% residual, is a physically grounded insight that changes practitioner defaults. Completeness (62) and Resilience (62) are dragged by the missing EVOLVE-VLA/TT-VLA comparisons and narrow real-robot scope (4 tasks, one arm model); Impact (70) reflects an immediately usable, cheap deployment-time recipe with promised code. Weighted composite: 0.20*75 + 0.25*65 + 0.15*72 + 0.15*62 + 0.15*62 + 0.10*70 = 68.

Problem & Motivation: Operators deploying VLA policies on physical manipulators face execution errors — the executed motion deviating from the commanded action — caused by mechanical wear, heavy payloads, and temperature changes. These errors vary across robots and operating conditions, so a policy trained once cannot anticipate them. Prior VLA robustness work evaluates visual corruptions, distractors, or synthetic noise injected directly on end-effector commands; none of these capture execution errors that (a) depend on the robot's state and motion history and (b) originate per-joint with different end-effector effects. Evaluating against real degraded hardware requires an impractical fleet of robots in varied operating conditions, some of which risk hardware damage. Key Idea: The command-execution residual — the difference between what the VLA commanded and what proprioception says the robot actually did — is a free, self-supervised adaptation signal available at deployment without task rewards, labels, or knowledge of the error source. Constructing a compensated pseudo-target by subtracting the observed residual from the executed command, and regressing the policy onto it via LoRA updates, teaches the policy to pre-compensate future commands. This is a clean, physically-grounded formulation of the residual-learning idea (feedback-error learning) recast for flow-matching VLA backbones. Methodology: The method has two stages. (1) Compensation signal: for each executed action step, compute η_obs = Δx − a_policy, where Δx is the achieved end-effector displacement measured via proprioception, converted to the normalized action space using the SO(3) logarithm map for rotations and the command scale factors for translation. (2) Deployment-time adaptation: build a pseudo-target chunk a_target = a_policy − η_obs, store executed chunks in a 32-chunk FIFO buffer, and every 8 chunks take one Adam step on a batch of 4 chunks minimizing a flow-matching objective L_comp that regresses the velocity field toward the pseudo-target, plus an L2 anchor term (λ_anc = 10^-4) keeping LoRA weights near initialization. Only rank-4 LoRA adapters on the 300M-parameter action expert train (2.76M parameters, 0.085% of π0's 3.24B); the base weights are frozen. RoboStress injects four established joint-level models — Coulomb-Stribeck friction (torque-level), gravity-compensation residual fraction (torque-level), Tao-Kokotović backlash deadband (position-level, history-dependent), and Spong elastic-joint compliance (position-level, second-order dynamics) — at their physically correct stages of the operational-space control pipeline in MuJoCo, combined into seven deployment scenarios (Heavy Payload, two Thermal Drift ramps, three Aged Joint variants, Aged Transmission) over LIBERO's four task suites. Critical design decisions: injecting noise at joint level rather than end-effector level (well-justified by dynamics coupling arguments and validated against a real payload replay), the anchor term (justified by ablation: removing it costs 2.4 points), and freezing the base policy with LoRA-only updates (reasonable for stability, though the choice of rank 4 is not ablated). Key Results: On RoboStress, self-compensating VLA beats base policies and both training-time robustness baselines (action-space domain randomization, RobustVLA adversarial training) in all seven scenarios with both backbones: average success 49.1% → 56.6% with π0.5 and 41.7% → 44.2% with π0, while DR and RobustVLA sometimes fall below the base policy (e.g., 38.8% vs. 41.7% average with π0). Real-world results on two AgileX Piper arms (new vs. one-year-old): average success across four tasks rises from 43% to 76% (π0.5, Robot A), 40% to 72% (π0, Robot A), 43% to 74% (π0.5, Robot B), 38% to 71% (π0, Robot B), at 25 episodes per task. OOD generalization to five unseen bowl variants: 64% vs. 16% base and 36% RobustVLA with π0.5. A disturbance-observer comparison shows complementarity: DOB alone 56% vs. 84% for the method alone vs. 80% combined (Task 1, Robot A, π0.5). A validity check shows the calibrated Heavy Payload simulation matches a real 1 kg payload replay better (DTW 0.027) than Gaussian action noise (DTW 0.388). Scale is standard (LIBERO 40 tasks, 20 episodes × 3 seeds in simulation; 4 real tasks × 25 episodes), not stress-scale. Somewhat counter-intuitively, even a brand-new arm shows a 32.9% normalized command-execution residual. Novelty Classification: NEW PROBLEM (VLA robustness to physical execution errors, as distinct from synthetic command perturbations), NEW DATASET/BENCHMARK (RoboStress — repurposing classical robot dynamics models as evaluation noise rather than for control), and NEW METHOD (self-compensating VLA). The genuinely novel pieces are the joint-level, state/history-dependent error modeling in RoboStress and the use of proprioceptive residuals as a reward-free deployment-time adaptation signal for VLAs. The method itself is a competent combination of known ideas — feedback-error learning, LoRA, flow-matching regression, anchoring — applied to a new setting; the benchmark's models are all pre-existing dynamics formulations. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are present and targeted: per-noise-component analysis (Table 3), residual-vs-adaptation decomposition (direct chunk-mean correction gets only 23.6% vs. 44.2%; zero-residual updating gets 40.8%), anchor-loss effect (−2.4 points without), and a five-level severity sweep across all scenarios and suites (Figure D1). DOB compatibility is tested rather than assumed. The protocol is transparent: same pretrained checkpoints, action horizons, and initial states across methods; hyperparameters, hardware (single A6000), and scenario parameters are documented in appendices. Code release is promised but no URL is given in the text. Concerns: results are reported as means over three seeds with no error bars, variance, or significance tests, and several real-robot comparisons (e.g., 38% vs. 40% base on Robot A π0.5 Task 1) involve small per-cell counts (25 episodes) where differences may not be reliable. The simulation validation against reality rests on a single replayed pick-and-place trajectory with one payload; the benchmark's realism for other scenarios (thermal drift, backlash aging) is argued from the dynamics literature, not measured. RobustVLA is a recent (2025/2026) adversarial baseline, so the comparison set is current, though the two test-time adaptation methods discussed in related work are absent from experiments. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL (a runnable adaptation method plus a simulation benchmark, evaluated in simulation and on hardware). - Practical: Yes — runs on a single NVIDIA A6000 (48 GB) with an asynchronous server/client loop at 20–30 Hz on consumer-relevant robot arms. - Efficient: Cheap — LoRA updates are 2.76M trainable parameters (~50 ms per Adam step) plus ~80 ms flow-matching inference per chunk, on top of standard VLA inference cost. - Effective: The evidence supports effectiveness on the tested tasks (30+ point gains on two arms), but these are four tabletop tasks on one arm model; effectiveness on longer-horizon or contact-rich tasks is only proxied by LIBERO-Long in simulation, which degrades most under severity. - Scalable: Untested beyond two arms and four tasks; the method carries adaptation state across episodes within a task, and behavior under many tasks, drift accumulation, or catastrophic forgetting over long deployments is unexamined. The work delivers a method plus a benchmark with promised code and scenario configurations; no trained model weights or dataset release is stated. Strengths: - The core insight — using command-execution residuals as a label-free, reward-free adaptation signal available on any proprioceptive robot — is simple, general, and well-executed, and the ablation cleanly isolates that the residual carries the signal (23.6% for direct correction vs. 44.2% with adaptation). - RoboStress's decision to inject noise at the joint level at the physically correct pipeline stage (torque vs. position) distinguishes it from prior end-effector command-perturbation benchmarks, and the DTW comparison against a real 1 kg payload replay (0.027 vs. 0.388 for Gaussian noise) is a rare and commendable reality-check for a simulated robustness benchmark. - Real-robot evaluation spans two arms with genuinely different usage histories, and the finding that even a new arm has a 32.9% normalized residual substantiates the problem's practical relevance. - The DOB experiment (56% DOB alone, 80% combined, 84% method alone) tests complementarity with classical control rather than framing the method as a replacement — an unusually honest systems comparison. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state that reported success improvements are not safety guarantees and that deployment in human environments requires additional safety evaluation. The conclusion names one limitation: the method relies on proprioception, and future work should incorporate external sensing to reduce that reliance. They do not otherwise dwell on limitations, but the limitations they do name are direct rather than minimized. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - No comparison against the test-time adaptation baselines the paper itself situates against (EVOLVE-VLA, TT-VLA), even though they are the closest methodological relatives; the comparison set is limited to two training-time robustness methods. - Real-robot evaluation is narrow: four tabletop tasks, one 6-DoF arm model (AgileX Piper), 25 episodes per task, with evaluation episodes themselves populating the adaptation buffer — so the reported numbers conflate adaptation and evaluation, and behavior when adaptation state is not carried across episodes is unreported. - No variance or significance testing despite three seeds; several simulated margins (e.g., 44.2% vs. 40.8% for the zero-residual ablation) and real-robot per-task gaps may be within noise. - Simulation-to-reality validation of RoboStress covers only Heavy Payload via one replayed trajectory; friction, backlash, and compliance scenarios are never checked against physical degradation, so RoboStress's realism for wear/thermal scenarios remains a modeling assumption. - Robustness of the adaptation itself is unexplored: no experiments on failure cases, policy collapse under adversarial or noisy residual signals (e.g., a slipping gripper or slipping object would corrupt the pseudo-target), or performance when execution errors are non-stationary in ways the anchor does not handle. - LoRA rank 4 and update schedule (every 8 chunks, batch 4) are fixed without ablation; sensitivity to these hyperparameters across robots is unknown. Bottom Line: Practitioners deploying VLAs on real manipulators gain something concrete and immediately usable here — a cheap, reward-free online adaptation recipe with strong physical-robot evidence and a genuinely more realistic robustness benchmark — and this is the strongest available treatment of execution-error robustness for VLAs despite the narrow task coverage and missing test-time-adaptation baselines.

Recursive Organization Improvement: A Modeling Specification for Human-- Agent Organizations

Z Wang · arxiv.org · automated generated environments for agent testing - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces a formal modeling specification — plus an executable checker, a small public-record mapping, and a controlled simulation study — for 'recursive organization improvement' (ROI), i.e., how human–agent teams evaluate, retain, and revise changes to their own workflows and to the procedures used to evaluate those changes. - Why it's important: Teams adopting AI agents conflate capability gains with organizational gains, and a workflow change can look beneficial because of how evidence was sampled and reused rather than because the change helped; the paper targets exactly this attribution problem, which currently has no explicit modeling standard. - How it does it: The core move is a declared change boundary that jointly makes explicit (a) the object being revised, (b) the evidence the revision may access, and (c) the procedure that authorizes and retains it — operationalized as versioned 'change contracts' (p = target, version, transformation, evidence, comparator, costs, horizon, retention rule) that a finite checker can validate. - The good: The mechanism study's acquisition-matched controls are unusually honest: they show that the apparent gain from periodically replacing the evaluation program shrinks from 0.00607 to 0.00191 (interval spanning zero at two of three tested reversal timings), demonstrating that evidence acquisition and reuse — not evaluator replacement — drive the observed improvement. - The missing: All empirical content is simulation with synthetic error probabilities and a three-template catalog; no human participants, no deployed LLM agents, and no evidence that the specification reduces modeling effort or improves predictions relative to alternative notations. - Read it or not: Worth reading for researchers designing multi-agent workflow-optimization or organizational-learning experiments who need a vocabulary for evidence provenance, decision rights, and retention; practitioners looking for validated tooling or empirically grounded design guidance will not find it here yet.

Problem & Motivation: Teams using AI agents face a measurement problem when they revise work arrangements: a new review or routing policy changes both which cases receive attention and which failures become visible, so if the same selected cases determine whether the policy is retained, organizational learning can favor a locally successful but globally harmful arrangement. The paper further notes that comparing agent capabilities while holding the organization fixed answers a different question than comparing organizations that can revise their workflows, and that an improvement procedure can itself become a target of revision. Prior formalisms (MOISE+, OperA, process mining, organizational-learning theory, agentic workflow search) supply representational pieces but none makes the object of revision, its evidence base, and its evaluation procedure jointly explicit and checkable. The intended users are designers and researchers of human–AI teams and multi-agent organizations. Key Idea: Make every organizational change carry a versioned, evidence-carrying contract with a declared boundary separating execution events, operational adaptations, and procedure revisions — so that any retained change can be reconstructed from its available evidence, checked against admission conditions, and compared under a fixed external criterion. The single most transferable insight from the study: distinguish evidence acquisition, evidence retention (memory horizon), and evaluator replacement as separable interventions, because conflating them mis-attributes organizational improvement. Methodology: Three evaluation legs. (1) A reference implementation provides a finite checker for unique event/artifact identifiers, actor-visible inputs, version matching, target-specific permissions, and patch budgets, validated on constructed fixtures (a valid trace, a hidden-input rejection, five invalid patch variants, and an authority test distinguishing a release owner from a review board). (2) A feasibility mapping of three merged Flask pull requests (4 commit artifacts, 56 events: 8 reviews, 42 head-commit check runs, 6 opening/merge records) demonstrates recoverability of required fields and exposes instrumentation gaps. (3) A mechanism study crosses 3 environments (stationary harm, workflow reversal before round 25, uniform gain), 3 memory conditions (reset, cumulative, window-8), and 6 decision arms (Biased/Balanced/Neyman fixed programs, successive rejection, discover-once, repeated discovery) with 128 replicates per cell (6,912 core trajectories; 2736-label budget per 8-round block; 48 rounds × 4096 production tasks; error probabilities e.g. (.08, .46) for the specialized template shifting to (.08, .08) at reversal). Workflow choice is a fixed-budget best-arm identification problem using a population-weighted Beta posterior (Eq. 5); net value per task subtracts error penalties (3 units), label (0.20), generation (0.02), and program-change (0.50) costs. Critical design decisions: identical resource ceilings and shared potential-label streams across arms (well justified, enables causal attribution); the core protocol frozen before runs, with the trial-matched control and reversal-timing checks honestly labeled exploratory and run on fresh streams (well justified); program-score history treated separately from workflow-label memory (justified by the pooling/score-reset ablations, which show pooling matters and score reset does not). Key Results: Under stationary harm, cumulative evidence raises Balanced's normalized net value per task from 0.45224 to 0.48007 (paired gain 0.02783, 95% MC interval 0.02659–0.02907), exactly matching the reduction in selection regret (0.02939 → 0.00156). Repeated discovery's disadvantage versus Balanced falls from −0.01702 (reset) to −0.00007 (cumulative). Under workflow reversal, indefinite accumulation costs 0.1025 versus reset on the full horizon (0.48026 vs 0.58280), while the 8-round window recovers late performance (0.72163 vs 0.48280 cumulative in final eight rounds) at a transition-delay cost. In exploratory acquisition-matched controls, the repeated-discovery advantage over Balanced drops from 0.00607 to 0.00191 (reversal before round 25) and to −0.00063/−0.00057 (reversals before rounds 21/29, intervals spanning zero) — no stable gain from program replacement across tested timings. A 9-cell budget grid (shares 0.2/0.4/0.6 × trials 1/3/6) and a supplementary value-of-information audit model (Appendix D, e.g., EVSI underperforming a heuristic under strong priors: 0.5673 vs 0.8795 with prior 1:19, stationary) are reported in full. Baselines are appropriate for the contrived setting (Neyman allocation, successive rejection per Audibert et al., an ex-ante fixed-program mixture); scale is small and entirely synthetic. Novelty Classification: NEW FORMULATION and NEW SYSTEM/TOOL (the checkable change-contract specification plus checker), with a NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING (acquisition-matched controls eliminate the apparent benefit of evaluator replacement). The representational machinery — roles, norms, event logs, bandit-style allocation, Beta posteriors — is standard; the novelty is the explicit, checkable joint organization of revision target, evidence provenance, authority, and retention into one comparison contract, and the demonstration that this decomposition changes attribution. The mechanism study itself is a well-executed combination of known bandit/sampling ideas in a new organizational framing. Rigor & Reproducibility: Strong for a specification paper: 128 replicates per cell with paired 95% Monte Carlo intervals on shared random streams, a 6,912-trajectory core plus 4,608 ablation and 6,144 exploratory trajectories, a frozen core protocol recorded before the first run, scalar reconstruction checks to 10⁻¹² tolerance, negative fixtures for the checker, and full factorial grids reported (no cherry-picking visible). No multiple-testing correction and no equivalence claims where intervals span zero — the authors flag this themselves. Code, data, frozen protocols, per-trajectory results, and checksums are released under MIT/CC BY 4.0 at https://github.com/wizardlancet/recursive-organization-improvement (tagged release research-2026-09-30). Concerns: the error probabilities and cost schedule are hand-set synthetic parameters ('not fitted organizational parameters'); the public-record mapping covers only 3 PRs from one repository chosen by convenience; the trial-matched control was designed after inspecting core results (disclosed as exploratory); and the entire efficacy evidence lives in the authors' own simulation, not on any external benchmark. This is a preprint, not peer-reviewed. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (a checker plus simulation study; no deployed system or human users). Practical: The checker and simulator run on commodity hardware — the simulation is a lightweight label-budget process, though no runtime figures are given. Efficient: The intervention itself costs nothing to compute; the modeled economics (label 0.20, program change 0.50 per unit) are synthetic, so real-world cost ratios are unverified. Effective: Evidence supports the attribution claim within the simulation; it does not show the specification solves any real organization's improvement problem — the Flask mapping is explicitly a feasibility check, not efficacy. Scalable: Untested beyond 3 templates, 2 strata, 48 rounds, and 3 PRs; behavior with richer catalogs, continuous action spaces, or heterogeneous human actors is unexamined. Delivered artifacts: an executable reference checker, simulation/analysis code, frozen protocols, and a pseudonymized data snapshot — a genuine software artifact, not just paper form. Strengths: - The acquisition-matched control is a genuine methodological contribution to a literature prone to attributing gains to the most conspicuous changed component; showing the reassessment gain collapse from 0.00607 to 0.00191 (and to zero at other reversal timings) is a result most workflow-optimization papers never run. - The change-contract formalism with executable admission predicates converts a vague organizational-learning notion into inspectable obligations (Table 3's failure conditions: hidden inputs, stale patches, unauthorized changes, uncovered strata, changed criteria, omitted costs) — this is real, checkable modeling, not just notation. - Unusually candid reporting: exploratory analyses labeled as such on fresh streams, complete negative results (no stable program-replacement benefit) given headline placement, and conditional-on-retained-program means explicitly marked non-causal. - The paper cleanly delineates itself from MOISE+/OperA/process mining via Table 1, framing its contribution as required records for change comparison rather than an expressiveness claim — an honest and correct positioning. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state that the evaluation does not establish lower modeling effort, better inter-rater agreement, or better predictions than alternative notations (this requires user studies); that all distributions, catalogs, and costs are synthetic; that program-score memory is a heuristic over trials conducted at different knowledge states; that reset/cumulative/window retention rules are crude stand-ins for principled change-point or switching-bandit methods; that exploratory controls were specified after core results; that no equivalence claims attach to intervals spanning zero; and that the public mapping lacks historical authority, actual message exposure, effort, and AI-involvement records. These limitations are confronted directly and precisely rather than minimized — a substantial credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - The 'human–agent organization' framing outruns the evidence: no humans and no language-model agents appear anywhere in the experiments; every actor is a script over synthetic Bernoulli labels, so behavioral phenomena (reliance, anchoring, correlated human–AI errors) discussed in Section 5 are untested. - The candidate space is three fixed templates and a three-program catalog with a fixed outer selector; the paper's own admission that positive results for 'open-ended procedure discovery' would require a broader candidate space underscores that the recursive part of ROI is essentially unexercised — no run revises the revision procedure itself. - Effect sizes are tiny in absolute terms (headline gains of ~0.006–0.028 normalized units per task, on a scale where one task is worth 1 unit); the paper does not discuss whether such differences would matter under realistic cost measurement noise. - No adaptive/change-point baseline (e.g., Bayesian online changepoint detection, which the paper cites) is actually run against the window-8 heuristic in the reversal condition, leaving the retention-rule comparison among deliberately naive rules. - Single author with a commercial affiliation (CataX AI), self-built simulation, self-defined criteria, and no external review (preprint) — the closed loop between specification author, checker author, and experiment author weakens independent validation of the checker's completeness. - The three-PR Flask mapping is too small to support any generalization about real-world trace availability; it functions as an illustration, though the surrounding text occasionally reads as a validation leg. Bottom Line: A carefully executed, unusually honest position-plus-simulation paper that gives the human–agent-organization field a genuinely useful formal vocabulary and a cautionary attribution result, but whose empirical content is confined to small synthetic simulations — researchers building workflow-optimization or org-learning systems should read it for the contract formalism and the acquisition-matched-control lesson, while anyone seeking validated methods or tooling should wait for follow-up work with real agents, humans, and principled retention baselines.

Zhiming Liu, Yikun Miao, Ying Chen, Hongrui Yin, Fangqi Zhu, Xiaoyi Pang, Quanxin Shou, Zhengyang Yan, Haodong Wang, Song Guo · arxiv.org · Daily papers of 7 Oct 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces WING, a framework that distills interaction-centric latent actions from ~200 hours of egocentric human video and injects their low-frequency temporal structure as guidance tokens into a world-action model, raising robot manipulation success rates across three simulation benchmarks and four real-world bimanual tasks. - Why it's important: Teleoperated robot demonstrations are expensive and hard to scale, while egocentric human video is abundant — but camera motion and human-robot temporal dynamics mismatches have prevented latent-action methods from transferring that experience to robot control. - How it does it: A point-tracking-based teacher decomposes each frame transition into a global camera warp and residual hand-object interaction motion, distills an RGB-only student latent-action encoder, and a lightweight predictor estimates DCT low-frequency (K=4) latent components that condition action generation via gated cross-attention. - The good: The mechanism is validated at each level — WING-LAM shows the lowest camera-motion decodability (R²≈0.00 on EgoDex MLP probe) while retaining interaction decodability (R²=0.48), and low-frequency latents separate matched from mismatched human-robot pairs by 0.51 cosine-similarity gap versus 0.26 (full) and 0.05 (high-frequency). - The missing: No public code or model weights are available yet (only a project page; deployment code "will be released"), and the camera-interaction decomposition relies on a single global affine warp whose failure modes under parallax and 3D camera motion are acknowledged but not quantified. - Read it or not: Read it if you work on ego-to-robot transfer or latent-action pretraining — it is one of the most carefully ablated entries in a crowded 2025-2026 WAM field — skip it if you need a deployable low-latency policy (500.6 ms median inference vs 90.6 ms for π0.5) or reproducible artifacts today.

Problem & Motivation: Robot learning labs building generalist manipulation policies need large-scale interaction data, but teleoperation costs limit scale. Egocentric human videos (Ego4D, EgoDex, EgoVerse) offer interaction experience from a first-person visual viewpoint resembling robot observations, but two specific gaps block their use: (1) reconstruction-based latent action models entangle task-irrelevant observer/camera motion — which dominates ego footage — with hand-object interaction dynamics; and (2) human and robot executions of the same task differ in speed and control granularity, so even correct interaction latents transfer poorly as direct action targets. The paper closes the gap between latent-action pretraining (LAPA, UniVLA, CD-LAM, DreamDojo), which models full visual transitions, and the selective, cross-embodiment-consistent interaction structure robot policies actually need. Key Idea: The core trick is a two-part factorization of the visual transition signal: (1) geometric motion routing — background point tracks fit an invertible global affine warp (camera motion) while camera-compensated residual displacements of hand-region tracks define interaction motion, giving privileged two-channel supervision for a teacher whose interaction latent is distilled into an RGB-only student with camera-intervention consistency; and (2) spectral truncation — applying an orthonormal DCT-II along the temporal axis of latent-action trajectories and keeping only the K=4 lowest frequency components, which the paper empirically shows carry the cross-embodiment-consistent interaction semantics, used as auxiliary guidance tokens rather than action targets. Methodology: The pipeline has three stages. (1) WING-LAM training: an offline motion-supervision builder uses AllTracker point tracks, EgoHOS hand seeds, and deterministic RANSAC to construct camera/interaction targets; a two-branch DreamDojo-style teacher (Dc=16 camera latent, Di=32 interaction latent) is trained with Smooth-L1 motion losses plus camera-intervention consistency and variance/covariance regularization (Eq. 29); the frozen teacher distills into an RGB-only student via L2 distillation plus a view-consistency term (Eq. 2). (2) Egocentric pretraining: a Wan2.2-TI2V-5B video backbone is trained for future-frame generation while a 4-query Transformer predictor (hidden dim 1024) is trained to predict the 4×32 normalized DCT guidance from current observation and instruction (MSE loss, Eq. 3), on 200h of ego video at 0.2s sampling, H=8 transitions, 40 epochs on 32 H100s. (3) Robot policy learning: the pretrained backbone and predictor are jointly fine-tuned with an action expert on robot demonstrations (Ltotal = λvideo·Lvideo + λaction·Laction + 0.1·Lpred); predicted guidance is projected to K×Dhid tokens with learned frequency embeddings and injected via gated residual cross-attention (Eq. 4). Design decisions: K=4 is justified by ablation (K=2 too restrictive, K=8 full spectrum worse); guidance-as-auxiliary-conditioning rather than direct action target is justified by the Q4 pretraining-strategy comparison; the affine warp approximation is acknowledged as the weakest link. Key Results: On LIBERO (one checkpoint, 4 suites, 50 rollouts/task): 99.20% average (Spatial 99.0, Object 100.0, Goal 98.8, Long 99.0), beating LaWAM (98.6), LingBot-VA (98.5), and π0.5 (96.9). On RoboTwin 2.0 (50 bimanual tasks, 100 rollouts/task/condition): 93.80% average (Clean 94.56, Randomized 93.04) vs LingBot-VA 92.20 and LaWAM 91.22. On RoboCasa-GR1 (24 humanoid tabletop tasks): 57.7% vs LDA-1B 55.4, FastWAM reproduction 51.9, GR00T-N1.6 47.6. Real world (Agilex Cobot Magic, 4 bimanual tasks, 20 trials/setting): 75.0% standard-setting success, comparable to π0.5 under generalization settings with slightly higher progress scores, and clearly above FastWAM and GR00T-N1.7. Pretraining ablations (200h budget): spectral guidance pretraining beats video-only, hand-pose, and LAPA-style latent-action pretraining; gains grow as downstream robot data shrinks (e.g., real-world 25% data: 67.5% with pretraining vs 60.0% without). Latency: 500.6 ms median / 517.1 ms P95 on one RTX 4090 — 5.5× slower than π0.5 but faster than Motus (1532.8 ms). Baselines are current (2025-2026) and strong; two RoboCasa/RoboTwin baseline numbers are the authors' own reproductions. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD with a NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING component. The genuinely novel elements are (a) using explicit camera-vs-interaction point-track decomposition as separate supervision channels for latent-action learning, and (b) the demonstration that low-frequency DCT components of latent-action trajectories are where human-robot correspondence concentrates — an empirical finding with a supporting linear-PCA analysis (Proposition 1) and reproduced with a second LAM. The surrounding machinery — teacher-student distillation, Wan2.2 video backbone, gated cross-attention conditioning, flow/diffusion action expert — is a competent combination of standard techniques applied to a new supervision signal. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are unusually thorough: both components (WING-LAM, DCT guidance) are individually ablated with controlled replacements (DreamDojo LAM; full time-domain trajectory), K is swept over {2,4,8}, denoising steps are swept, four pretraining strategies are compared at matched 200h budget, and data-efficiency curves at 25/50/100% downstream data are reported. Representation evaluations report 95% grouped-bootstrap confidence intervals across three probe families, and the matched/mismatched pair protocol was pre-registered (pairs finalized before computing latents) with inter-annotator agreement checks. Concerns: (1) main simulation tables report single numbers without seeds or error bars — 50-100 rollouts per task mitigates but does not eliminate variance concerns; (2) two baseline entries are the authors' own reproductions, and a reproduced FastWAM (51.9) underperforms its class; (3) the spectral-similarity analysis is run primarily with the authors' own WING-LAM (a DreamDojo replication confirms the ordering, which helps); (4) code and weights are not yet released — only a project page and a promise to release deployment code. The preprint is not peer-reviewed. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (with a built system artifact). Practical: Runs on commodity hardware at inference (single RTX 4090), but pretraining required 32 H100s for 40 epochs; Efficient: 500.6 ms median inference is a real cost — 5.5× π0.5, 2.2× FastWAM — acknowledged as a limitation; Effective: Evidence supports the claim on the tested manipulation tasks, but the benefit is a guidance prior, so a policy still needs robot demonstrations — the method augments rather than replaces robot data; Scalable: Not stress-tested — 200h of ego video is modest (Ego4D alone is 3,000h), and whether the affine-warp decomposition survives at petabyte-scale wild video is untested, only claimed. Deliverable: a trained policy and pipeline; deployment code promised but not released at publication time. Strengths: - The frequency-domain finding is a real, falsifiable empirical claim with pre-registered pair construction, bootstrap CIs, a control excluding the dominant q0 component (matched similarity 0.42 vs 0.08 mismatched for q1:q3), and replication with a second LAM — this is the paper's most durable contribution. - The linear-PCA analysis (Proposition 1) gives a clean theoretical account of why reconstruction-based LAMs retain observer variation (retained observer variance = tr(PΣobs) in the top-dz subspace), connecting mechanism to diagnosis rather than just patching symptoms. - The pretraining-strategy ablation (video-only vs hand-pose vs latent-action-target vs spectral-guidance, all at matched 200h) directly answers the question practitioners actually have: ego latents work best as auxiliary conditioning, not as action targets. - Motion-routed teacher distillation is a concrete, reusable recipe for removing a known nuisance factor from latent-action representations, validated by controlled camera-intervention probes rather than only downstream success rates. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state that (1) the teacher relies on a single global affine warp that degrades under strong parallax, large depth variation, or pronounced 3D camera motion, potentially injecting noise into interaction supervision; and (2) latent-action pretraining plus spectral guidance adds training cost and pipeline complexity. They confront both directly and propose depth-aware motion modeling and cheaper guidance mechanisms as future work. They also candidly report their own latency disadvantage in a dedicated table. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - No statistical treatment (seeds, CIs) on the headline simulation results, where several baselines sit within ~1 point (RoboTwin: 93.80 vs 92.20); differences this small need error bars to be actionable. - The interaction/camera decomposition is supervised by the same affine-warp proxy it is evaluated against on two of three datasets (only EgoDex uses ground-truth 6D head pose), so the camera-suppression claim is partially circular — the cleanest evidence is the single EgoDex head-pose readout. - The cross-embodiment spectral analysis uses WING-LAM trained on ego video to encode robot clips (out-of-domain), and the 100/100 matched/mismatched pairs come from one source (EgoDex/EgoDex-Eval, 25 tasks) — the finding's breadth across embodiments and datasets is under-sampled. - Real-world evaluation is 20 trials per setting across 4 tasks on one platform; the generalization study changes one factor at a time only, and no multi-factor compounding is tested. - The 200h pretraining corpus (85h EgoDex + 95h EgoVerse) likely overlaps in task style with the robot tasks (tabletop pick-and-place, stacking); no cross-domain evaluation (e.g., kitchen/EPIC-style footage) shows whether the benefit survives when ego and robot domains diverge — the dogs-not-barking question of whether this is ego-video transfer or near-domain transfer. - No cost comparison of the full two-stage pipeline against simply collecting the equivalent hours of teleoperated demonstrations it is meant to substitute. Bottom Line: A practitioner in ego-to-robot transfer or latent-action pretraining should read this for the frequency-domain cross-embodiment finding and the matched-budget pretraining-strategy comparison, which are the strongest evidence yet that ego latents help as guidance rather than targets — but wait for the promised code release and multi-seed replication before treating the sub-point benchmark margins as decisive over LaWAM or LingBot-VA.

#75 — Innovative (68)

RACE: Residual-Aware Test-Time Adaptation for Neighbor-Rich Time-Series Foundation Model Forecasting

HN Shi, T Wu, CC Sun, Y Jiang, HJ Ye, DC Zhan · arxiv.org · karypis - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces RACE, a two-stage test-time framework that retrieves residuals from a frozen time-series foundation model's own completed same-domain windows and selectively applies an aggregated residual correction to improve future forecasts without touching backbone weights. - Why it's important: Deployments of TSFMs (continuous glucose monitoring, Web/cloud capacity planning) accumulate related historical series whose realized errors are currently discarded; exploiting them could improve forecasts cheaply, without per-domain fine-tuning or backbone modification. - How it does it: A training-free stage retrieves neighbors using a joint context-plus-frozen-forecast descriptor, aligns their residuals to the query scale, filters conflicting residuals via a MAD-based consensus rule, and averages the survivors into a correction proposal; a lightweight XGBoost "Utility-Aware Gate" (30 inference-visible features) then decides per query whether applying the correction reduces MSE. - The good: Gains are consistent and cross-backbone: domain-aggregate MSE improves ~+19.7% to +22.8% on CGM and ~+1.0% to +2.0% on Web across all four backbones, and a Gate trained on one TSFM transfers to the other three with all 72 cross-backbone metric comparisons beating the frozen target. - The missing: There is no publicly downloadable code or data release (the reproducibility package is prepared but not bundled with no public link), CGM results rest on a single 109-patient public target dataset with private retrieval libraries, and the Web gains (~1–2%) are small enough that per-subset win/loss counts (e.g., 26/14 MSE) show substantial heterogeneity. - Read it or not: Read it if you deploy frozen TSFMs in settings with reusable domain histories and want a backbone-agnostic, output-side correction recipe; skip it if you need general-purpose forecasting gains — the broader GIFT-Eval diagnostic shows the method mostly neutral outside explicitly neighbor-rich domains.
Why this rank
Scored using Empirical profile. Novelty (72) is anchored by the NEW FORMULATION of using a frozen model's own realized residuals under a strict information boundary as the correction object, and Non-Obviousness (75) by the genuinely surprising cross-backbone gate-transfer result (all 72 off-diagonal comparisons beat frozen targets). Rigor (72) reflects strong protocol discipline — leakage audits, chronological splits, bootstrap intervals, error-stratified reporting — but is reduced by the missing comparison against per-domain fine-tuning, private CGM retrieval collections that make the headline ~20% gains unverifiable, and a single 109-record public target. Completeness (65) is helped by unusually honest failure-case reporting, while Resilience (65) is capped by thin general-domain value (~1-2% Web gains, near-zero on most of GIFT-Eval) and the overstated 'test-time adaptation' naming. Practical Impact (45) is low: the reproducibility package ships with no public link and no released tool or weights. Weighted composite: 0.20*72 + 0.25*72 + 0.15*75 + 0.15*65 + 0.15*65 + 0.10*45 = 68.

Problem & Motivation: Operators deploying time-series foundation models (Chronos-2, Chronos-Bolt, TimesFM 2.5, Toto-2.0) typically forecast each query series in isolation, even when the deployment environment has already accumulated many related but non-identical historical series with observed outcomes — e.g., CGM trajectories from other patients/devices, or workload traces from related cloud services. Prior remedies either fine-tune the TSFM per domain (costly, backbone-specific) or append retrieved series as input augmentation without verifying whether the retrieved material actually supports the current forecast. The paper identifies the core difficulty: retrieved neighbors' residuals may conflict in scale and direction, and useful-looking evidence can still harm an individual query. Key Idea: The core trick is to treat the frozen TSFM's own past errors on completed, temporally legal same-domain windows as reusable test-time evidence: retrieve windows similar in both context and the frozen model's forecast, align their residuals to the query scale, discard conflicting residuals via robust consensus filtering, average the rest into a dimensionless correction, and use a cheap learned gate to decide per query whether to apply it. The correction object is the model-specific residual, not the sequence content — this is what makes the gate transferable across backbones. Methodology: The pipeline has two stages. (1) Residual Evidence Construction (training-free): each completed window's residual r_i = y_i − f_θ(c_i) is stored with a raw-z descriptor (z-normalized context concatenated with z-normalized frozen forecast); for a query, FAISS retrieves K=60 neighbors by squared Euclidean distance; each residual is normalized by its own history scale and rescaled to the query by a ratio clipped to [1/4, 4]; a mean-centred, MAD-based consensus filter removes neighbors whose residuals deviate from or vary more than the retrieved set (threshold γ=2.5, with a 50% retention floor); survivors are coordinate-wise averaged into the consensus-mean proposal Δ_q. The final forecast is ŷ_q + a_q·s_q·Δ_q with a_q ∈ {0,1}. (2) Utility-Aware Correction Gate: an XGBoost classifier maps a fixed 30-dimensional inference-visible feature vector (evidence availability, aligned-residual statistics, retrieval similarity, forecast/context shape, proposal magnitude, weight concentration, direction consistency) to a probability; the label is whether applying the always-on correction would have reduced MSE on development windows; the threshold τ is frozen on calibration data via accepted-MSE-utility maximization, with fit/model-select/calibration/test roles split chronologically 70/10/10/10. Critical design decisions: (a) joint context–forecast retrieval descriptor (justified by ablation — history-only retrieval roughly halves CGM gains), (b) residual consensus filtering (justified — unfiltered averaging degrades Web MAE/CRPS by −5.8/−8.0 points), (c) restricting the gate to a 30-dim output-side schema with no backbone identity or hidden states (this enables the cross-backbone transfer result, though it caps expressiveness). Key Results: Tested with four frozen backbones (Chronos-2, Chronos-Bolt Base, TimesFM-2.5 200M, Toto-2.0-313m) at 512-step context / 64-step horizon. On CGM (ShanghaiT2DM target, 109 records, 821–847 test windows), RACE improves domain-aggregate MSE by +20.8% (Chronos-2), +22.8% (Chronos-Bolt), +19.7% (TimesFM-2.5), +22.0% (Toto-2.0). On Web/cloud (six GIFT-Eval + four LOTSA subsets, 15,541 series), improvements are smaller: +0.98% to +1.99% MSE, with the largest gains concentrated in the highest frozen-base-error quintile (e.g., +55.1% to +60.9% MSE in bin 5, versus roughly 0 in bins 1–3). RACE/RACE-TF take best results in 19 of 24 backbone–task–metric comparisons against RAF (input augmentation) and TS-RAG (evaluated only on its Chronos-Bolt interface, where fine-tuned TS-RAG wins CGM MAE/CRPS with +20.8%/+14.7%); the direct learned residual regressor (CERR) achieves higher CGM MSE (+26.6%) but collapses on Web MAE/CRPS (−6.5/−9.0 four-backbone mean). A GIFT-Eval-wide diagnostic over 34 subsets shows much smaller gains (four-backbone mean +2.1% MSE) with one slightly negative metric (Chronos-2 CRPS −0.089%). Cross-backbone gate transfer: all 72 off-diagonal comparisons beat frozen targets, with transferred gates within ~0.06 percentage points of target-trained ones on domain averages. Acceptance-rate audits (Tables 11–13) show the gate enriches precision among accepted corrections, and case studies honestly display a Web failure mode where all corrections hurt. Novelty Classification: NEW FORMULATION + NEW METHOD. The genuinely new element is the formulation of "test-time neighborhood scaling" — using a frozen model's own realized residuals on temporally legal same-domain windows as the correction object — and the consensus-filter-plus-utility-gate decomposition. The constituent techniques (kNN retrieval via FAISS, MAD outlier filtering, XGBoost gating, residual/bias correction) are standard; their combination and the cross-backbone transfer claim are the new contribution. Retrieval-augmented forecasting baselines (RAF, TimeRAG, TimeRAF, TS-RAG, RAFT) operate on sequence content or learned predictors, not on self-residuals. Rigor & Reproducibility: Rigor is above average for this area: extensive factorized ablations (retrieval descriptor, K, consensus, gate target, representation, retrieval scope), 95% target-parent bootstrap intervals with 2,000 draws and fixed seeds, a documented leakage audit (zero test-window matches with the residual pool, causal same-parent filtering, test loader created only after all choices frozen), figure-provenance documentation, and pre-specified case-selection rules. The gate-label construction (oracle MSE-utility on development windows) is sound and clearly separated from test. Reproducibility is a weak point: a "prepared reproducibility package" with result ledgers and fixtures is described, but the paper states it "is not bundled with this preprint, and this version provides no public download link"; CGM retrieval collections are private (de-identified fixtures only, with acknowledged numerical deviations from reported numbers). Methodological concerns: the CGM evaluation uses one public dataset of 109 patients, so the ~20% gains carry clinical-sample uncertainty the bootstrap only partially addresses; the Web effect size is ~1–2% at the aggregate level with 14–23 subset-level losses per metric; RAF and TS-RAG are the only external baselines and both are weaker method families, so there is no comparison against strong per-domain fine-tuning of the backbone itself — the alternative the paper says it avoids but never prices against in accuracy terms. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (with a built pipeline artifact). Practical: Yes — the pipeline runs on a single consumer GPU (RTX 5070 Ti for measured runs) plus small backbones (200–313M parameters); retrieval uses a flat FAISS index with sub-3ms query latency. Efficient: Post-hoc replay costs 8.7–93.7s per backbone-task (RACE-TF) and 19.5–170.8s (RACE with gate fitting), excluding forecast-cache construction — cheaper than RAF on three of four backbones because it avoids a second backbone forecast, and far cheaper than fine-tuned TS-RAG (814s on Web). Effective: Evidence supports the stated problem in neighbor-rich domains (consistent CGM gains, targeted high-error-bin Web gains), but the broader GIFT-Eval diagnostic shows near-zero effect outside that regime, so effectiveness is conditional on the deployment having coherent neighbor structure. Scalability: Not tested — the retrieval libraries are capped (4,000 windows per Web subset; ~500 CGM retrieval series), and the authors explicitly defer larger libraries and scaling characterization to future work. The work stops at paper form: no publicly downloadable tool, library, or model weights. Strengths: (1) The reframing of retrieval-augmented forecasting around model-specific residuals under a strict information boundary is a clean, well-motivated idea that yields the genuinely surprising cross-backbone result — a gate trained on one TSFM's residual statistics transfers to another with essentially no loss. (2) The two-stage separation of training-free evidence construction from selective application is well executed and independently ablatable; RACE-TF alone is a useful zero-fit method (+20–23% CGM MSE). (3) The error-stratified audit is unusually honest and informative: it shows gains come almost entirely from the top error quintile and that the method is roughly neutral-to-harmful on easy queries, and the included Web failure case names the mechanism (smooth residual adjustment cannot help a bursty future). (4) The chronological-protocol discipline, leakage audit, and per-window ledger with a verifier that recomputes reported tables exceed typical preprint standards. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state (Appendix J) that the method is designed for neighbor-rich settings and that broader GIFT-Eval results "do not establish uniformly large gains"; that the architecture is intentionally low-capacity and they do not study high-capacity retrievers or large-scale libraries; that clinical experiments are retrospective and not validated for diagnosis or dosing; and Appendix E.4 that domain-level gains do not imply per-subset wins. They confront limitations directly rather than minimize them, which strengthens credibility, and Appendix I explicitly discloses that the reproducibility package has no public download link in this version. Analyst-Identified Gaps: (1) No accuracy comparison against the head-to-head alternative the paper positions against — per-domain fine-tuning of the backbone — so the cost/benefit claim versus fine-tuning rests on argument, not measurement. (2) CGM evidence comes from a single 109-record public target; the four large external retrieval collections are private, and the released CGM fixture is transformed and stride-subsampled with acknowledged metric deviations, so independent verification of the headline ~20% gains is not currently possible. (3) The Web gains (~1–2% aggregate) are small relative to the harness's complexity, and the MSE metric on Web raw units (base errors ~10^5) makes percentage improvements sensitive to heavy tails; MAE/CRPS gains are similarly ~1–2 points. (4) The gate's 30 features are inference-visible by construction, but the consensus filter threshold (γ=2.5) and K=60 are fixed without hyperparameter sensitivity reported for γ. (5) The "test-time adaptation" framing may overstate what happens: nothing adapts at test time except a binary accept/reject from a frozen gate — a naming choice that could mislead readers expecting parameter or prompt updates. (6) Only 34 of 55 GIFT-Eval subsets are evaluable under the fixed 512+64 window; behavior on short-series or multi-horizon regimes is unexamined. Bottom Line: A rigorously disciplined and unusually honest preprint whose residual-evidence-plus-gate recipe is genuinely worth adopting for frozen-TSFM deployments with reusable same-domain histories (especially CGM-like settings), but whose general-domain value is thin, whose headline clinical gains are unreplicable without the private data, and which ships no public code — so treat the transfer result as the real contribution and the rest as strong supporting evidence.

#76 — Innovative (68)

VERA: Scaling Verifiable Environments for Agentic co-Evolution

J Liu, Y Pan, Z Jiang, D Li, B Zhang, X Ling, S Wang… · arxiv.org · long-horizon RL for agents - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces VERA, a pipeline that converts benchmark trajectories into 9,000+ stage-wise restartable, rubric-scored sandbox environments and runs an alternating model (GRPO) + harness (skill-edit) co-evolution loop on them, releasing the environment corpus openly. - Why it's important: Long-horizon agent training (e.g., medical research workflows with dozens of dependent steps) lacks environments that score intermediate stages from observable evidence, so self-improvement loops currently train only on outcome signals and cannot localize failures. - How it does it: A coding agent writes binary rubric items from trajectories, executable checks plus an interacting Agent Judge gate every sandbox before admission, and an LLM Attribution step converts stage-wise rubric evidence into two reports that route updates to either GRPO training on stage rubric rewards or skill additions/merges/removals, each gated by a development-set verifier. - The good: The axis-level ablation at 9B is the strongest evidence — full co-evolution reaches 31.0 Overall on AutoCoWorkBench and 69.1 on AutoMedBench versus 18.9/43.3 for LLM-only and 18.2/56.1 for harness-only, showing neither axis alone captures most of the gain. - The missing: Full baseline comparisons are run only at 9B, no error bars or significance tests are reported on a 40-task CoWork evaluation core, and the ADAS baseline adaptation degenerated (all 27 eligible candidates scored zero on its own selection metric, so a tie-break picked the harness), leaving the headline 10.3-point margin over that baseline questionable. - Read it or not: Worth reading for researchers building agent RL environments or self-improvement loops — the environment-construction recipe and open corpus are reusable — but frontier-comparison readers should treat the 27B headline numbers as configuration-specific rather than general rankings.
Why this rank
Scored using Empirical profile. Practical Impact (78) is the standout — the open 9,000+ verifiable stage-wise environment corpus and released harness fill a real resource gap no competing release covers. Novelty (75) is anchored by the dual-use rubric design (admission gate, attribution evidence, and RL reward from one rubric set) and the verifier-gated co-evolution loop. Resilience (58) drags the composite: no error bars or significance tests on a 40-task evaluation core, headline margins within plausible noise, and a silently degenerate ADAS baseline undermine the frontier-comparison claims. Rigor (60) is middling — informative axis ablations at 9B, but judge/attribution/verifier circularity through GPT-5.6-Sol and a scale claim confounded by backbone change are unaddressed.
