Problem & Motivation: Long-horizon agentic workflows (software work, office automation, and especially medical research, where an agent must ground findings in images, classify them, and compose reports under expert scrutiny) cannot be learned by current systems because practical training environments do not exist: trajectory data is rare outside coding, and hand-curated benchmarks score only final outcomes without stage-level, restartable scoring. Existing environment pipelines either define success by repository test suites (restricting to coding, rewarding only episode end) or are static evaluation sets. The authors argue the bottleneck for agent self-improvement is the environment, not the learning algorithm, and that environments must be resumable at any stage and score intermediate behavior from observable evidence. Key Idea: The core insight is that benchmark trajectories already contain everything a verifiable environment needs (initial states, tool interactions, observable effects), so an automated pipeline (Auto-Rubric) can convert them into stage-wise sandboxes where binary rubric items — verifiable only from execution records and workspace artifacts, never from agent claims — serve simultaneously as the sandbox admission gate, the failure-attribution evidence, and the RL reward. Combined with alternating frozen-axis updates and verifier-gated acceptance, this turns single-axis self-improvement into evidence-attributed co-evolution of the LLM and its harness. Methodology: Two pipelines. (1) Auto-Rubric: benchmark trajectories (Terminal-Bench, SWE-Bench, MLE-Bench for CoWork; AutoMedBench, MedXpertQA for Med) are segmented into five stages (plan, setup, verify, execute, submit); a coding agent writes binary rubric items over action arguments, execution effects, artifacts, and outputs; stage-wise sandboxes restore each stage's start state for independent practice, and end-to-end sandboxes use an LLM surrogate to simulate slow tool calls; every candidate passes executable checks plus Agent Judge inspection (failed executable checks override judge scores) before entering the training bank. (2) Co-evolution loop: each round, LLM Attribution reads stage-wise scores and traces to produce an LLM Report (target stage) and Harness Report (skill gaps). Model rounds run full-parameter GRPO with rubric rewards following the Agent Lightning execution/training separation: stage reward r_k = h_k·Σw_kj·z_kj / Σw_kj (h_k a mandatory-check gate), end-to-end reward R = g[λp + (1−λ)c] with λ=0.2 (CoWork) or 0.5 (Med), g a hard gate zeroing verified reward hacking. Harness rounds propose skill additions/merges/removals (max three per round), accepted only if paired frozen-model runs on the development set improve the target stage by ≥5 Overall points with no end-to-end regression; model checkpoints are accepted if dev score drops ≤20% relative to the prior checkpoint. Critical design decisions: freezing one axis per round for attribution (justified by the ablation), executable-check-overrides-judge for hack resistance (partially justified via case studies), and the permissive ≤20% model acceptance rule (weakly justified, no sensitivity analysis). Key Results: At 9B (Qwen3.5-9B), VERA Agent reaches 31.0 Overall on AutoCoWorkBench versus 20.7 for ADAS (+10.3) and 69.1 on AutoMedBench versus 56.1 for its harness-only variant (+13.0), also leading SWE-Bench Verified (54.2 Pass@1) and MedXpertQA Text (50.8). Ablations show LLM-only and harness-only each recover roughly half the gain. At 27B (Qwen3.8-27B), VERA scores 71.6 Overall on AutoCoWorkBench (1.0 below GPT-5.6-Sol at 72.6, above Claude-Opus-4.8's 66.6 under benchmark-default runners) and 80.7 on AutoMedBench (1.2 below Claude-Opus-4.8's 81.9), with the highest AutoMedBench Agentic score (94.1). Transfer: 43.8% pass on Automation-Bench (rank 2) and 76.4% on AgentClinic (rank 3). Capability retention is scale-dependent: at 4B/9B, AIME 2026 drops 15.8–59.7 points, while the 27B CoWork agent improves on all four general benchmarks (e.g., AIME +10.0 to 96.7). Cost analysis estimates ~$240k for the Medical Research pipeline, with environment preparation at 54.7% of cost and each 27B run consuming ~5,000–8,000 H100-hours. Baselines (SFT, GRPO, RaR, OPD, ReflectRL, ADAS, COS-PLAY) are recent and matched on update budgets, though several required adaptation. The general-capability collapse at 4B/9B is a notable, honestly reported negative finding. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD (verified model–harness co-evolution with attribution-driven axis selection) and NEW DATASET/BENCHMARK (the 9,000+ open verifiable stage-wise sandbox corpus). The genuinely novel elements are the dual use of one rubric set as admission gate, attribution evidence, and training reward, and the verifier-gated alternation between weight and harness updates. The constituent techniques — GRPO, rubrics-as-rewards, agent-as-judge, skill libraries, ADAS-style harness search, paired A/B acceptance — are existing; the contribution is their coordination under verified evidence, plus the first large-scale environment bank for joint LLM/harness evolution. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations isolate each axis (LLM-only vs. harness-only vs. joint) at 9B with matched RL budgets, which is the paper's methodological strength. However: no error bars, seed variance, or significance tests are reported for Table 2 (AutoCoWorkBench Lite has only 40 evaluation tasks, and the paper states a tie-breaking rule rather than statistical separation); the ADAS baseline adaptation is effectively degenerate (all 27 eligible selection candidates scored zero, so the first registered candidate was chosen), weakening the headline 10.3-point claim; the 4B→9B→27B scaling trend confounds parameter count with backbone generation (Qwen3.5 vs. Qwen3.8); and GPT-5.6-Sol serves as judge, attribution model, and verifier throughout, with judge-choice sensitivity untested. The authors acknowledge they do not ablate environment counts, reward formulations, or reasoning-effort settings. Code, a blog, and the 9,000+ environment corpus are open-sourced (links in the header); no model weights release is stated. Verifier and harness case studies are partly synthetic and explicitly labeled as such, which is honest but limits evidential weight. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (a trained system with benchmark evaluations, plus a released environment corpus). Practical: Runs on standard infrastructure (H100s, SGLang serving, MCP tooling, off-the-shelf Qwen backbones), though full reproduction needs thousands of GPU-hours. Efficient: The 27B co-evolution run costs ~5,000–8,000 H100-hours per domain, and environment construction is over half the total ~$240k pipeline cost — environment preparation, not training, is the dominant expense. Effective: Evidence supports domain gains and partial transfer to unseen workflows, but evaluation on a 40-task CoWork core and judged process scores for Med means some metrics are proxies rather than ground truth; the paper itself distinguishes training rubrics from official scoring. Scalable: Only claimed via the 4B/9B/27B trend, which is confounded by backbone change; environment-count scaling is explicitly untested. The work delivers a software/data artifact (open environment corpus, harness, blog) in addition to the paper; trained weights are not stated as released. Strengths: - The dual-use rubric design (one binary rubric set as admission gate, attribution evidence, and GRPO reward) is a real conceptual contribution that closes the gap between judged evaluation and trainable rewards for long-horizon tasks. - The axis-level ablation is genuinely informative: at 9B it shows co-evolution (31.0/69.1) substantially exceeds either axis alone (18.9/18.2 CoWork; 43.3/56.1 Med), establishing that the interaction, not either component, drives the gain. - Honest negative results — capability collapse at 4B/9B (AIME −56.4 to −59.7 at 4B), the degenerate ADAS selection outcome, harness-friction observations in Table 3 — are reported rather than hidden. - The admission-loop verification (executable checks overriding judge scores, container replay, paired A/B harness acceptance) is a concrete, reusable mechanism against reward hacking in agent RL, backed by case studies. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state five: (1) environment-count scaling and alternative construction methods are not varied; (2) harness runtime settings including reasoning effort are fixed and not ablated; (3) judging, verification, and attribution all depend on GPT-5.6-Sol with judge-choice sensitivity untested; (4) full baseline comparisons are limited to 9B because a 27B co-evolution run costs ~5,000–8,000 GPU-hours; (5) they compare learning algorithms rather than ablating alternative reward operators within VERA. They confront these directly and also candidly flag that frontier rankings are configuration-specific (Claude scores 80.5 with its productivity harness vs. 81.9 with the benchmark-default runner). This is a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - Statistical fragility: AutoCoWorkBench Lite contains only 40 evaluation tasks, and no confidence intervals or significance tests appear anywhere; several headline margins (e.g., 10.3 points, or the 1.0-point gap to GPT-5.6-Sol) are within plausible seed noise, especially given the acknowledged harness-configuration sensitivity of rankings. - The ADAS baseline adaptation failed silently (all eligible candidates scored zero on the selection metric), so the strongest single-axis harness baseline may be under-tuned; the 10.3-point margin over it is not firm evidence of co-evolution superiority over competent harness search. - The ≤20% relative dev-score drop acceptance rule for model checkpoints is permissive and unexamined; over rounds this could accumulate degraded checkpoints, and no analysis of fallback frequency or checkpoint quality drift is provided. - Judge circularity: GPT-5.6-Sol writes rubric judgments, performs attribution, verifies rewards, and gates harness edits; a systematic judge bias could be reinforced across rounds rather than corrected, and the anti-hacking case studies are largely synthetic. - The scaling claim ("stronger backbones better support self-evolution") changes both size and model generation simultaneously, so the capability-retention conclusion cannot be attributed to scale alone. - Process scores for MedResearch are judged rather than programmatic, partially undercutting the "verifiable from observable evidence" framing for that domain's end-to-end reward. Bottom Line: A practitioner building agent training environments or self-improvement loops gains real, reusable machinery here — the trajectory-to-verifiable-sandbox recipe, the open 9,000+ environment corpus, and the verified co-evolution loop — but should discount the frontier-comparison and baseline-margin claims given the tiny evaluation core, missing statistics, and the degenerate ADAS baseline, and no competing released resource currently covers the same ground.

OmniReasoning: Pushing the Limits of Audio-Visual Joint Reasoning (17 ▲ )

Junming Lin, Yuxuan Wang, Zhenxin Lei, Yuxin Liu, Ruixun Liu, Yinsong Yan, Ling Wang, Minghao Han, Yunfei Chu, Shun Lei, Xueyao Zhang, Qize Yang, Jin Xu, Yiwu Zhong · arxiv.org · Daily papers of 6 Oct 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces (1) OmniReasoningBench, a 1,150-question benchmark where questions are constructible only by chaining audio and visual evidence, (2) OmniQA, a data engine that yields 112K SFT and 19K human-checked RL samples with timestamped modality-specific clue annotations, and (3) MFSD, an RL method that converts the non-additive log-likelihood gain from joint versus individual modality clues into token-level credit assignment. - Why it's important: Existing audio-visual benchmarks are largely solvable without audio (a visual-only model scores 57.9–68.8% on WorldSense/Daily-Omni), so neither evaluation nor training reliably elicits genuine cross-modal reasoning, a core gap in omni-modal LLMs. - How it does it: MFSD scores each sampled response under four clue contexts (none, audio, visual, joint) and uses the contrast S_t = ΔAV − ΔA − ΔV — proven to be a token-wise increment in conditional pointwise mutual information — combined with the joint-clue gain to shape bounded, sign-preserving token-level advantage weights on top of RLSD. - The good: The benchmark-validity evidence is unusually careful: joint inputs beat a single-modality oracle (credit when either audio-only or visual-only succeeds) by 9.9–26.7 points across three frontier models, and their visual-only accuracy collapses to 17.2%/8.7% (MCQ/open-ended) versus 44.9–74.1% visual-only on four prior benchmarks. - The missing: There are no error bars, seeds, or significance tests anywhere, the data pipeline (Qwen3.8 question generation, DeepSeek-V4-Flash judge) overlaps the model family being evaluated, and MFSD's component ablations are presented algebraically rather than empirically. - Read it or not: Worth reading for anyone building or benchmarking omni-modal LLMs or designing credit-assignment schemes for multimodal RL; skip if you only care about the model results, which are a competent but single-model post-training run still 15 points behind Gemini-3.7-Flash.
Why this rank
Scored using Empirical profile. Rigor (55) is the binding weakness: no error bars, seeds, or significance tests anywhere — the headline MFSD-vs-RLSD delta of 3.3 points rests on a single seed and single RL budget — plus an unvalidated LLM judge used for both RL rewards and open-ended evaluation, and a Qwen-family data-generation/evaluation loop that partially measures fit to the generator's question style. Novelty (80) is genuinely strong: the four-condition shortcut-screening methodology and the conditional-PMI interaction contrast S_t = ΔAV − ΔA − ΔV are real, reusable contributions, and the oracle-validated benchmark-validity analysis is rarely done. Non-Obviousness (78) is high; Completeness (68) suffers because MFSD's component ablations are algebraic only and the 112K SFT set is never human-checked despite supplying the largest gain; Resilience (65) drops given single-run evidence for the method claim. Impact (70) reflects released benchmark, datasets, and a trained model. Weighted composite: 0.20*80 + 0.25*55 + 0.15*78 + 0.15*68 + 0.15*65 + 0.10*70 = 68.

Problem & Motivation: Omni-modal LLMs (Qwen-Omni, Gemini, Nemotron) claim unified audio-vision-language understanding, but the community cannot measure audio-visual joint reasoning because current benchmarks mostly admit single-modality shortcuts. The authors show Qwen3.5-Plus answers 57.85% (WorldSense), 68.76% (Daily-Omni), 44.90% (OmniVideoBench), and 60.43% (JointAVBench) with visual-only input — i.e., audio is dispensable for most questions. The same gap afflicts training data: existing audio-visual instruction corpora pair modalities without enforcing that both are necessary. The intended audience is omni-modal model developers and benchmark designers. Key Idea: The single core insight is to make cross-modal dependency an explicit, first-class object at every stage: questions are constructed from timestamped audio/visual clue chains such that no single modality suffices (enforced by a shortcut screen that rejects any question solvable under question-only, audio-only, or visual-only conditions), and those same clue annotations become privileged contexts for RL — where the non-additive likelihood gain (joint clues minus each modality alone) isolates genuine cross-modal interaction for token-level credit assignment. Once you see "clue-conditioned likelihood contrasts as credit," both the data engine and MFSD are reconstructable. Methodology: Three coupled components. (1) OmniReasoningBench: 750 reasoning-over-video questions (375 MCQ, 375 open-ended, 10 task types) and 400 reasoning-beyond-video questions (250 MCQ, 150 open, 9 task types), each with a reference answer and an annotated evidence chain; beyond-video questions carry a new figure/table not in the video. (2) OmniQA data engine: event segmentation → Gemini-3.1-Pro timestamped audio/visual captioning → Qwen3.8 question/answer/dependency-chain generation → structural checks, caption-conditioned answer verification, per-clue media verification, and four-condition shortcut screening → thinking-process synthesis from verified chains (without the source video). Outputs: OmniReasoning-SFT-112K (112,463 samples, 42,200 videos, avg. 8.1 min) and OmniReasoning-RL-19K (18,991 human-validated questions). (3) MFSD: GRPO-style group rollouts with group-normalized outcome advantages; each response is re-scored by the same actor under four clue contexts; detached gains ΔM = ℓM − ℓ∅ for M ∈ {A, V, AV}; the interaction score S_t = ΔAV − ΔA − ΔV is centered within each response, scaled by an EMA-calibrated κ, and mixed with the joint gain via a gated β into token weights w = exp(sign(A)g), clipped to [1−εw, 1+εw] and interpolated with the outcome advantage (λ = β = 0.5 after warm-up). Appendix B proves S_t is a conditional PMI increment under a joint-consistency assumption, that centering is zero-sum and offset-invariant, and that reweighting is bounded and sign-preserving. Critical design decisions: (a) rejecting questions solvable by any restricted condition — well justified by the paired oracle analysis; (b) centering the interaction so it redistributes rather than rescales credit — clean, with honest acknowledgment that exponentiation breaks exact zero-sum; (c) reusing RLSD's weighting rather than a new objective — prudent, isolating the contribution to the interaction term, though it means MFSD's merit is inseparable from RLSD's machinery. Key Results: OmniReasoning-30B-A3B (from Qwen3-Omni-30B-A3B-Thinking) reaches 42.5% on OmniReasoningBench (+9.3 over base; MCQ 48.0, open-ended 30.1 on over-video), 50.0% on OmniVideoBench (+12.8), 44.7% LVOmniBench (+7.0), 74.4% Video-MMMU (+6.1), 44.0% Video-MME-v2 (+7.5) — but remains 15.1 points below Gemini-3.7-Flash (57.6%) on their benchmark. Under an identical RL budget (150 steps, 8 rollouts, batch 256, 64 GPUs), MFSD beats GRPO and RLSD: 42.5 vs 38.3 and 39.2 on OmniReasoningBench; notably GRPO (44.8) and RLSD (45.4) fall below SFT-only (47.0) on OmniVideoBench while MFSD reaches 50.0. Modality ablations across three frontier omni models show joint-input accuracy of 42.3–50.1% versus 10.9–14.9% video-only and 16.3–20.4% audio-only, with joint beating the single-modality oracle by 9.9–26.7 points. Tested at standard, not stress, scale: 30B-A3B MoE, videos up to 30 min, single model size. Novelty Classification: NEW DATASET/BENCHMARK (a benchmark with enforced modality-necessity via four-condition shortcut screening and oracle-validated joint gains is a genuine advance over prior audio-visual benchmarks) and NEW METHOD (the modality-factored PMI interaction contrast for token credit assignment is genuinely new, with a correct information-theoretic derivation); the data engine is a competent engineering pipeline of known LLM-generation-and-verify patterns, and the weighting machinery is inherited from RLSD. Rigor & Reproducibility: The modality-necessity validation is rigorous and unusually honest — the paired single-modality-oracle analysis (Table 6) is the right test and is rarely done. The RL method comparison controls budget and initialization, and per-group OmniVideoBench breakdowns rule out cherry-picked gains. However: no error bars, seeds, or significance tests are reported for any comparison, including the MFSD-vs-RLSD deltas of 3.3 points that drive the headline method claim; MFSD's β and λ are analyzed only as algebraic limits, with no empirical ablation table isolating the interaction term's contribution; the RL reward and all open-ended evaluation use the same DeepSeek-V4-Flash judge, and open-ended RL questions are scored by a model judge whose calibration is not validated; question generation uses Qwen3.8, an Alibaba model, while evaluation uses Alibaba's Qwen3-Omni base — a partial vendor-loop concern, though shortcut screening and human validation of the RL set mitigate it. No explicit code/data URL appears in the text beyond the project homepage (pku-value-lab.github.io/OmniReasoning-Homepage); datasets are described as "released." This is a preprint. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (with a SYSTEMS artifact in the datasets/benchmark). Practical: The 30B-A3B MoE with frozen encoders is trainable on 64 GPUs, within reach of well-resourced labs but not typical academic budgets. Efficient: MFSD adds three extra actor scoring passes per update but reuses media features and rollouts — no extra rollouts or teacher parameters — a favorable cost profile versus teacher-based distillation. Effective: Evidence supports the stated problem on their benchmark and transfers to four public benchmarks, but the transfer claim rests on single-run numbers, and the remaining 15-point gap to Gemini shows the problem is far from solved. Scalable: Not tested beyond 30B-A3B and 150 RL steps; scaling behavior of the interaction signal (whose variance the κ cap suggests can be small) is unexamined. Delivers concrete artifacts: a benchmark (1,150 QA with evidence chains), two training datasets, a post-trained model, and a documented method; whether model weights or only data are public is not explicitly stated. Strengths: - The benchmark-validity methodology — four-condition shortcut screening at construction time plus a paired single-modality-oracle comparison showing +9.9 to +26.7 points for joint inputs — converts a widely hand-waved claim ("our benchmark needs both modalities") into measured evidence, and exposes that 44.9–68.8% of questions on four prior audio-visual benchmarks are answerable without audio. - MFSD's interaction score is a substantive, well-motivated idea: the S_t = ΔAV − ΔA − ΔV contrast with a correct conditional-PMI derivation gives the field a principled, cheap-to-compute signal for cross-modal credit, and the honest decomposition of "joint support" vs "interaction" (they can differ in sign) is conceptually clarifying. - The finding that GRPO and RLSD underperform SFT-only on general benchmarks while MFSD does not (e.g., 44.8/45.4 vs 47.0/50.0 on OmniVideoBench) is a practically important negative result about outcome-reward and coarse-clue RL on top of targeted SFT. - The data engine's dependency-chain annotations are reused as RL privileged context, so benchmark, data, and method are one coherent design rather than three bolted-together artifacts. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state a clear accuracy gap to the strongest proprietary model (57.6% Gemini-3.7-Flash vs 42.5%), indicating joint reasoning "is far from solved." They carefully qualify the PMI interpretation: positive S_t does not imply positive joint support or reasoning correctness, centering does not conserve advantage mass after exponentiation, and κ calibration is approximate. In the qualitative appendix they explicitly note that model-claimed timestamps and inscriptions were not independently verified. Limitations are confronted directly rather than minimized — a credibility positive — though there is no dedicated limitations section and no discussion of single-run variance, judge-model risk, or the Qwen-family data/eval overlap. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - The headline method claim (MFSD > RLSD by 3.3 points on OmniReasoningBench) is supported by one seed, one base model, one RL budget; with 8 rollouts per question and group-normalized advantages, run-to-run variance in RL post-training is commonly large enough to make such deltas ambiguous. No variance reporting anywhere in the paper. - The data pipeline (Qwen3.8 generation, Gemini-3.1-Pro captioning) and the shortcut screen are tuned on the same distribution the trained model is evaluated on (their own benchmark); the +9.3 gain on OmniReasoningBench partially measures how well the model fits the generator's question style, not just joint-reasoning capability — the public-benchmark transfer partially addresses this, but those are also largely speech/lecture-style videos like the training domains (8 content domains, YouTube-style source material). - No empirical component ablation of MFSD (β = 0, λ = 0 variants are described only algebraically); the reader cannot tell how much of MFSD's edge comes from the interaction term versus simply having better-calibrated token weighting or hyperparameters. - Open-ended RL rewards and all open-ended evaluation use a single LLM judge (DeepSeek-V4-Flash) with no judge-accuracy validation against human labels reported. - "Reasoning beyond video" questions sometimes require only audio (e.g., a single spoken rule plus a figure); the paper does not report a modality ablation for the beyond-video subset, so its necessity claim is empirically established only for over-video questions. - Human validation covers only the 19K RL set; the 112K SFT set is model-verified, yet SFT contributes the largest single jump (33.2 → 36.1 base, and 47.0 on OmniVideoBench), so most of the training signal rests on unhuman-checked synthetic reasoning chains. Bottom Line: Yes — anyone designing audio-visual benchmarks or multimodal RL credit assignment should read this for the shortcut-screening methodology and the PMI-factored interaction signal, which are real, reusable contributions despite single-seed evidence and an in-family data/evaluation loop that temper confidence in the exact margins.

Self- Spec Verifiable Code Generation

J Qian, Y Dong, Y Li, H Zhu, B Gu, G Li · arxiv.org · specification to code with formal verifications - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces VeriCodeBench, a 400-problem benchmark for "self-spec" verifiable code generation — where an LLM must generate both a formal specification and an implementation, with the code verified only against its own specification — plus CodeNova, a constraint-guided specification and verifier-guided repair pipeline that raises end-to-end success on it. - Why it's important: Existing verifiable-code benchmarks evaluate specification and code generation stage-wise against oracle specifications, which inflates end-to-end estimates and hides error propagation from a bad specification into downstream verification; specification quality is shown here to be the actual bottleneck for autonomous verified code generation. - How it does it: The benchmark freezes the model-generated specification into code generation and repair (preventing spec weakening for easier proofs) and scores joint success as verifier acceptance AND full coverage of curated requirement obligations via a deterministic SMT-based Constraint Entailment Framework; CodeNova extracts atomic constraints, self-checks the specification, and repairs code from verifier diagnostics under a frozen contract. - The good: The oracle-vs-self diagnostic is the strongest evidence: mean code validity across 16 model–language settings is 71.0% under Direct self-spec but joint success is only 44.1%, and supplying oracle specifications lifts validity by up to 36 points (e.g., Qwen3.6-plus on C: 50→86), cleanly demonstrating that specification adequacy, not implementation ability, caps end-to-end performance. - The missing: There is no comparison against any existing agentic repair or specification-refinement baseline (e.g., prior verifier-feedback loops like AutoSafeCoder or AlphaVerus-style bootstrapping), so CodeNova's gains cannot be attributed to its specific design rather than to generic multi-attempt repair with verifier feedback. - Read it or not: Worth reading for researchers building verifiable-code-generation systems or benchmarks who need the self-spec protocol and the multilingual (C/Java/Rust/Python) task distribution; practitioners seeking a drop-off-the-shelf verification tool will find only a prompt pipeline and should look elsewhere.

Problem & Motivation: Formal verification offers machine-checkable correctness guarantees that test-case-based evaluation of LLM-generated code cannot (tests cover a limited input slice). Prior benchmarks (CLEVER, VERINA, AlgoVeri, FormalBench) evaluate the requirement→specification→code→verification pipeline stage-wise, typically conditioning code generation on a human-written oracle specification and combining stage scores into an "end-to-end" estimate. This masks two failure modes: code that verifies against a vacuous or over-restrictive self-generated specification, and error propagation where a poor specification changes the difficulty or objective of downstream code generation. Existing benchmarks also concentrate on single proof-oriented ecosystems (mostly Lean or Dafny) with mathematically structured tasks, under-covering software-engineering concerns like pointer validity, aliasing, frame conditions, object mutation, and exceptions. The gap is an end-to-end-by-construction evaluation that preserves the dependency between a model's own specification and its code, across developer-facing language/toolchain pairs. Key Idea: Make the model's own generated specification a frozen mandatory artifact for code generation and repair, and score success jointly on two independent conditions — (a) specification adequacy measured by deterministic SMT entailment against curated requirement-level obligations, and (b) native-verifier acceptance of the code against that exact specification. The core insight is that a specification is simultaneously a prediction to be graded and an intermediate artifact constraining downstream work, so only propagating it end-to-end exposes both failure classes; the reversed entailment direction for preconditions (guarantees must imply the target precondition) specifically prevents credit for unnecessarily restrictive input domains. Methodology: VeriCodeBench defines instances (requirement, signature/context, curated target obligations, reference spec/implementation, native verifier) across four tracks of 100 problems each: C/ACSL with Frama-C/WP (pointers, aliasing, frames), Java/JML with OpenJML ESC (nullability, mutation, exceptions), Rust/Verus (ownership, borrowing, panic freedom), and Python/Nagini (permissions, Optional, exception freedom). Specification adequacy is scored by the Constraint Entailment Framework (CEF): language-specific canonicalization, then SMT-based entailment (L ∧ ¬R unsatisfiability) over conjunctions of up to N=5 generated clauses, capped at 2,000 search attempts, returning the fraction of curated targets entailed. Code validity is binary native-verifier acceptance (syntax errors, timeouts, unproved obligations count as failures). Joint success requires both on the same problem; the protocol is fully automated and deterministic. CodeNova has two stages: Constraint-Guided Specification (extract atomic constraints Q, translate to specification, model-driven self-check/refine loop with a budget) and Verifier-Guided Candidate Repair (plan subgoals from verifier diagnostics, generate up to K focused repair candidates per round from a shared plan, check each as a complete program, accept the first valid one; the specification and its coverage denominator stay frozen — only bodies, helpers, and loop invariants may change). Critical design decisions: (1) freezing the specification during repair — well-justified, it prevents the trivial cheat of deleting postconditions; (2) the reversed entailment direction for preconditions — well-justified against over-restrictive domains; (3) LLM self-assessment as the CGS stopping criterion — acknowledged by the authors as only a heuristic, since CEF independently grades the output; (4) verifier timeouts (e.g., 10s in one cited case) treated as failure — reasonable but timeout sensitivity is not systematically characterized. Key Results: Across 16 model–language settings (DeepSeek V3.2, Kimi-K2.7-Code, Qwen3.6-plus, Claude-Sonnet-5; 100 problems per language), Direct generation averages 71.0% code validity but only 44.1% joint success; Claude-Sonnet-5 leads with 60.3% average joint success under Direct. CGS raises mean requirement coverage from 0.7162 to 0.7761 in all 16 settings but lowers validity in several (Kimi on Rust: valid implementations 91→60), and aggregate joint success rises only 44.1%→45.6%. VGCR added to Direct and CGS combined lifts validity from 65.6% to 75.7% and joint success from 45.6% to 49.1%; full CodeNova is best, with Claude-Sonnet-5 reaching 65.5% average joint success. The oracle diagnostic (Table 4) shows oracle specifications improve validity in nearly every comparison — e.g., DeepSeek V3.2 on C: 34→69 valid (Direct), Qwen3.6-plus on C: 50→86 — yet CodeNova with self-specs remains 12.4 points below oracle-conditioned aggregate validity, and the paper correctly cautions this gap conflates information content with changed proof obligations. A striking case study: Kimi on Rust has identical 91/100 validity under self and oracle specs, but joint success is 57 vs 91, because the self-generated contracts omit requirement coverage — equal validity can conceal a large adequacy gap. Pass@k analysis (DeepSeek V4.1 Flash) shows CGS is conditionally helpful (harmful at small budgets on some tracks) while VGCR curves dominate more consistently, and sampling cannot remove the specification bottleneck. Baselines are the paper's own ablation configurations (Direct/CGS/VGCR/CodeNova) — no external methods are compared. Tested at benchmark scale (400 problems), not stress scale. Novelty Classification: NEW DATASET/BENCHMARK and NEW FORMULATION (the self-spec protocol with frozen-specification propagation and the dual adequacy/validity metric is a genuinely new evaluation formulation), plus a modest NEW METHOD (CodeNova) and NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING (specification adequacy, not implementation ability, is the end-to-end bottleneck). The genuinely novel part is the evaluation protocol and the four-language-native task distribution; CodeNova itself is a competent combination of known ideas — constraint extraction, self-refinement, and verifier-guided repair loops all exist in prior work (AutoSpec, SpecGen, AutoSafeCoder, AlphaVerus) — applied here in a unified pipeline with a frozen-contract constraint that is the main structural twist. Rigor & Reproducibility: The component ablation is well-controlled by design: VGCR reuses the exact specification and initial code from the corresponding no-repair run, isolating repair gains from specification effects, and Table 3 cleanly separates coverage, validity, and joint counts. The CEF scorer is deterministic and LLM-free, avoiding judge-model circularity, and the pipeline stores layered evidence (specs, code, raw verifier diagnostics, coverage reports) for traceability. Concerns: (1) no error bars, seeds, or significance tests are reported anywhere — with joint-success differences as small as 44.1%→45.6% on 400 problems, several headline conclusions rest on differences of 6–10 problems; (2) no external baselines (other agentic repair frameworks or even a naive multi-sample-and-verify loop) are compared against CodeNova; (3) the benchmark's target obligations and reference specifications were curated by the authors, and CEF's conservative matching for "exceptional constructs outside the shared Boolean fragment" introduces unverifiable scoring discretion; (4) verifier timeout thresholds are mentioned but their effect on results is not systematically reported. Code is released at https://github.com/JiaruQian/VeriCodeBench, including manifests, reference implementations, and prompt templates — a strong reproducibility artifact. This is a preprint, not peer-reviewed. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (a benchmark plus a prompting/repair pipeline evaluated empirically; the "system" is prompt templates plus open-source verifiers, not new infrastructure). Practical: Yes — it runs on commercially available LLM APIs (Claude, DeepSeek, Qwen, Kimi) and open-source verifiers (Frama-C, OpenJML, Verus, Nagini) in containerized toolchains. Efficient: CodeNova is expensive relative to Direct — multiple LLM calls per problem (extraction, translation, self-check loops, then K repair candidates per round each requiring a full native verification) — and the paper reports no token or wall-clock cost figures. Effective: Partially — even the best configuration reaches 65.5% joint success, so roughly a third of problems still fail end-to-end, and the paper itself shows repair cannot fix inadequate specifications; this is real progress on a genuinely hard task, not a solved problem. Scalable: Not tested — 400 problems is a moderate benchmark; scaling behavior of CEF entailment search (worst case 2^N−1 checks per target) and of repair candidate scheduling beyond the tested budgets is unexamined. The work delivers a concrete artifact: the benchmark dataset, scorer, pipeline scripts, and prompts at the GitHub URL. Strengths: - The self-spec formulation is a real conceptual contribution: freezing the model-generated specification into downstream generation and repair is a simple but principled protocol change that converts a vague "end-to-end" claim into a measurable error-propagation property, and the Kimi/Rust case (equal validity 91, joint success 57 vs 91) is a memorable demonstration that verifier acceptance and specification adequacy are non-interchangeable. - The dual-metric design with a deterministic, LLM-free adequacy scorer (CEF) avoids the circularity that plagues LLM-judged specification quality, and the reversed entailment direction for preconditions is a thoughtful guard against specification-gaming. - The multilingual, language-native task distribution (C memory/frame obligations, Java mutation/exceptions, Rust ownership, Python permissions) is a substantive expansion over Lean/Dafny-centric predecessors, with 400 author-curated problems, reference implementations validated by the same verifiers, and released manifests. - The controlled ablation (specification held fixed across repair conditions) is an unusually careful experimental design for this subfield, and the paper honestly reports where its own method hurts (CGS lowering Kimi/Rust validity from 91 to 60). Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors explicitly confront several limitations directly, which is a credibility positive: CGS improves coverage but can make verification harder or introduce unprovable obligations (with dedicated case studies in Appendix D.2); a more sophisticated specification does not necessarily raise joint success; the oracle-vs-self gap "should not be interpreted as a direct measurement of specification errors" because it changes both information and proof obligations; downstream repair is bounded by the frozen specification (DeepSeek on C: validity 34→60 but joint only 8→11); CGS self-checking is a heuristic based on model-generated constraints, not ground truth; and pass@k curves flatten, indicating sampling cannot remove the specification bottleneck. They also note cross-language comparisons reflect task–toolchain combinations, not controlled measurements. Notably absent is any dedicated limitations section addressing benchmark-construction bias or comparison baselines. TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces ArgGYM, a procedural benchmark and RLVR-compatible training environment that decomposes structured defeasible reasoning into twelve separately verifiable tasks over a common ASPIC+ argumentation substrate. - Why it's important: Current LLM reasoning benchmarks concentrate on mathematics, code, and monotonic logic where answers are fixed; real-world reasoning under incomplete, conflicting, and revisable information remains poorly measured, and a verified environment for it enables both reliable evaluation and contamination-free RL training. - How it does it: Each instance is generated by task-specific procedural generators, validated by structural gates, and scored against formal states computed by a pinned PyArg argumentation engine, so constructive answers are evaluated by executing the submitted intervention and recomputing the resulting argumentative state. - The good: The matched counter_argument/counter_argument_strict ablation (120 theory-matched pairs differing only in intervention language) plus the native-vs-complete success gap produce the paper's most credible finding: models can recover most of a structured answer locally while failing to compose the globally correct state (e.g., Qwen3.5-27B scores 88.7 native on status_query but only 35.8% complete success). - The missing: No RLVR training experiment is actually run — the RLVR interface is provided but untested, so the central claim that the environment supports effective verifiable-reward training remains unevaluated; additionally, only symbolic theories with template-generated language are tested, leaving natural-language transfer unmeasured. - Read it or not: Read it if you build reasoning benchmarks, train with verifiable rewards, or study argumentation-based reasoning; skip it if you only need another headline LLM capability number, since the paper's value is in its infrastructure and diagnostic decomposition rather than a single result.

Problem & Motivation: Researchers training and evaluating LLMs for reasoning have access to mature verifiable-reward environments in mathematics, code, and formal logic, but not in defeasible (non-monotonic) reasoning, where adding information can invalidate previously supported conclusions. Prior defeasible benchmarks (LogicNMR, BoardgameQA, Belief-R, DEFREASING) each test a narrow inference problem under a single formalism; procedural environments like Reasoning Gym cover many task types but not structured argumentation. The gap is a unified, executable environment where multiple structured defeasible-reasoning operations share one formal substrate, can be separately verified, and can generate fresh instances to reduce contamination risk and serve as RL training rewards. Key Idea: The core move is grounding evaluation in the formal consequences computed by a symbolic argumentation engine (pinned PyArg 2.0.2 for ASPIC+), so that (a) constructive tasks are scored by executing the model's submitted intervention and recomputing the resulting argumentative state rather than by string-matching a reference answer, and (b) the same generators and verification contracts produce both a frozen benchmark and unlimited fresh instances. This enables a controlled decomposition of defeasible reasoning into twelve operations (formalization, support-chain recovery, defeat diagnosis, status/semantics query, perturbation prediction, and six intervention types) whose failures can be localized without changing the underlying formalism. Methodology: An ASPIC+ argumentation theory (knowledge base, strict/defeasible rules, conflicts, preferences) is generated from a deterministic seed (τ, ℓ, p, c, s) where τ indexes one of twelve tasks, ℓ one of fifteen curriculum configurations, p ∈ {last-link, weakest-link} argument preference ordering, and c ∈ {elitist, democratic} set ordering. Generation follows a generate-verify loop: structural gates check that the candidate exhibits the target reasoning phenomenon, then the engine computes the relevant argumentative state; rejected candidates are discarded. Verification separates complete-task success (exact satisfaction of the task's output contract; for constructive tasks, all requested postconditions hold after executing the submitted intervention and the resulting theory remains consistent) from a task-native partial-credit score in [0,1] with task-specific semantics (e.g., key-status F1 for status_query, content F1 times ordering-fraction for claim_chain, 0.5+0.5·min(1,m/n) for intervention economy). Three critical design decisions: (1) grounded semantics for all tasks except semantics_query, justified because it has a unique extension and is polynomial-time decidable — well-justified for verification tractability; (2) behavioral-equivalence scoring for the formalization task rather than exact directive matching — well-justified because it tolerates legitimate paraphrase; (3) independent generation of last-link and weakest-link instances rather than matched pairs — acknowledged by the authors as making ordering comparisons descriptive rather than causal, and honestly flagged. Key Results: Across 42 model-reasoning configurations (18 model variants from Gemma, GPT-OSS, Qwen, DeepSeek, and Gemini families), complete-task success ranges from 0.0% (Qwen3.5-0.8B/2B) to 82.4% (Gemini 3.8 Flash at high reasoning effort). Models with similar aggregate scores diverge sharply at task level: Qwen3.5-27B with thinking reaches 88.7 native on status_query but only 35.8% complete success; Gemini 3.8 Flash reaches 93.6 native on defeat_diagnosis but 57.5% complete success. Performance degrades in later curriculum bands: GPT-OSS-120B falls from 45.2% (L1-L5) to 16.0% (L11-L15); Gemini 3.8 Flash from 88.1% to 76.5%. Last-link generally outperforms weakest-link (e.g., 92.9% vs. 71.8% for Gemini 3.8 Flash), but task-level reversals occur (DeepSeek-v4.1-Flash scores 66.7% vs. 53.3% on claim_chain under weakest-link). The matched counter-argument ablation shows non-uniform response to expanded intervention language: Gemini 3.8 Flash drops from 86.7% to 60.0% when strict rules are added; Qwen3.8-27B drops from 50.8% to 11.7% at xhigh effort, while Qwen3.5-9B rises from 20.8% to 44.2%. Baselines are current frontier and open-weight models; the benchmark is tested at standard scale (1,440 frozen instances). Novelty Classification: NEW DATASET/BENCHMARK and NEW SYSTEM/TOOL. The genuinely novel element is the combination of a shared ASPIC+ substrate, twelve separately verified tasks spanning analysis and constructive intervention, and a matched intervention-language ablation within one executable environment — this combination does not exist in prior work. The individual components (procedural generation, symbolic verification, RLVR interfaces, ASPIC+ itself) are standard; the paper's positioning against DeFAb, DeReLab, DPG, and Reasoning Gym is candid about this complementarity. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are present: the matched counter-argument pair (120 frozen matched pairs holding theory and semantic objective fixed while varying only the intervention language) is a clean controlled experiment, and a frozen-gold re-execution audit re-runs all 1,440 instances checking for zero decoding, rescoring, ordering-propagation, and engine-invariant failures. No error bars, multiple seeds, or significance tests are reported for model performance comparisons; the 1,440-instance benchmark provides 120 instances per task (or 60 per ordering condition), which limits statistical power for within-cell comparisons. Code, benchmark, generators, verifiers, and evaluation harness are publicly released at https://github.com/ieddeveci/ArgGYM. No Goodhart concern arises from evaluating on the same benchmark used for development since the benchmark is new and frozen; however, the evaluation relies entirely on a single pinned implementation (PyArg 2.0.2) of ASPIC+ semantics, and the authors explicitly note the audit is not an independent second implementation of those semantics. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL (a benchmark and evaluation environment with model experiments actually run). - Practical: Yes — all open-weight models run on NVIDIA H200 GPUs via TRUBA; only Gemini and DeepSeek require API access. - Efficient: Verification is polynomial-time (grounded semantics), and instance generation is deterministic from a seed; the cost is dominated by model inference, not the evaluation harness. - Effective: The evidence shows the environment successfully discriminates between models and localizes failure modes, but it measures symbolic defeasible reasoning — a proxy for natural-language argumentative competence that the authors do not claim transfers. - Scalable: Not tested beyond 1,440 frozen instances and 12 tasks; scaling curriculum depth, task count, or training-loop use is claimed but unverified. The work delivers a software artifact: a frozen benchmark, procedural generators, verifiers, and an evaluation harness released publicly. Strengths: - The matched counter-argument ablation is a genuinely controlled experiment (same theory, same semantic objective, only the intervention language differs across 120 pairs), which is rare in LLM benchmarking and produces the most interesting finding about intervention affordances. - The separation of task-native partial credit from complete-task success exposes a composition failure mode (high native, low complete) that single-metric benchmarks systematically hide, and the paper quantifies it precisely (e.g., 88.7 native vs. 35.8% complete on status_query). - Execution-based scoring of constructive tasks (recompute argumentative state after applying submitted directives) avoids string-matching brittleness and allows any semantically valid intervention to succeed. - Honest handling of confounds: the authors explicitly label curriculum and ordering analyses as diagnostic rather than causal, report the frozen-gold re-execution audit, and identify where democratic/elitist contrast is formally inactive in the generated theories. Author-Acknowledged Limitations:\- Proprietary frontier models (Claude, GPT-series) are excluded from the evaluation panel, so findings may not generalize to all top systems. - Almost all tasks use symbolic theories with opaque literal names (ko9, ls2, etc.); the single natural-language task (formalization) uses template-generated descriptions, so transfer to realistic language is untested. - Only grounded semantics is used for most tasks; findings may not extend to preferred, stable, or other acceptance notions. - Curriculum and ordering analyses are diagnostic, not causal, because configurations vary multiple structural properties simultaneously and ordering conditions are generated independently. The authors confront these limitations directly and thoroughly rather than minimizing them — a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - No RLVR training experiment is run despite RLVR compatibility being a headline contribution; the training loop, reward signal quality, and whether improvements on one task transfer to others (the stated motivation for the decomposition) are entirely untested. - The symbolic substrate uses opaque atom names (e.g., ko9, mp0), which conflates "cannot reason defeasibly" with "cannot track opaque referents" — a within-symbolism baseline using meaningful atoms is absent. - Only 2 accepted instances per (task × level × ordering × set-ordering) cell limits statistical reliability of within-cell claims; no variance estimates are possible from the frozen benchmark. - The re-execution audit checks internal consistency against the same PyArg implementation, so a bug in the pinned engine would propagate undetected to all gold labels; no cross-implementation validation is performed. - Scaling claims about fresh instance generation are untested — no evidence that generators produce well-distributed instances indefinitely rather than exhausting their candidate space for harder configurations. Bottom Line: A practitioner building RLVR training pipelines or studying argumentation-based reasoning gains real infrastructure and a well-designed decomposition that no prior benchmark provides, but those seeking evidence that this environment improves models — or that findings transfer beyond opaque symbolic theories — will need the follow-up work this paper only enables, not delivers.

TabJoinBench: A Benchmark for Joinable Table Discovery

TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces TabJoinBench, a benchmark with three subsets (semantic WikiTables, relational MMQA, hybrid NYC Open Data) for evaluating joinable table discovery methods under equi-join, fuzzy, and semantic join semantics, released with a composable perturbation framework and a public generation pipeline. - Why it's important: Join discovery methods have been evaluated on method-specific, unreleased preprocessed datasets, so results are neither reproducible nor comparable, and existing shared benchmarks (e.g., LakeBench) only test equi-joins between closely related table partitions, not the semantic heterogeneity of real data lakes. - How it does it: The benchmark builds validated seed query–candidate pairs from three sources (Wikidata entity overlap, ground-truth SQL join predicates, LLM-assisted vertical partitioning scored against a 1,000-sample random-partition null), then applies composable structural, representation, and semantic perturbations to candidates while provably preserving the join relationship. - The good: The evaluation of 6 specialized methods plus 2 LM-embedding baselines yields genuinely non-obvious findings — a set-containment sketch (LSH Ensemble, P@1 0.969 on WikiTables) beats learned methods, generic Qwen3/Gemma embeddings match specialized ones (P@R 0.688–0.749 vs. DeepJoin's 0.762 on WikiTables), and no method dominates across subsets. - The missing: Ground truth contains verified positives only with no exhaustive negative annotation, so methods may be penalized for retrieving valid joins the single-author annotator never labeled; there is no inter-annotator agreement, no error bars, and the released-artifact URL is not stated. - Read it or not: Read it if you build or benchmark data-lake join/discovery systems and need a defensible evaluation protocol spanning semantic joins; skip it if you want new algorithms or large-scale results — the largest lake here is 13,106 tables with ~1,270 rows on average.

Show full analysis
Problem & Motivation: Organizations storing data in heterogeneous lakes (enterprise, partner, open-government sources) need to find tables that can complement a query table via joins, but unlike relational databases, lakes lack declared keys, consistent naming, or standardized value formats. Researchers have proposed set-similarity, learned-representation, and feature-based join discovery methods, yet each evaluates on its own preprocessing of public corpora (WDC, WikiTables, Open Government data) without releasing processed queries or ground truth, making fair comparison impossible. Prior shared benchmarks (LakeBench and successors) construct pairs by vertically/horizontally partitioning tables around a shared column, which tests only equi-joins between near-duplicate tables, assumes the shared column is a valid key without verification, and misses the semantic diversity and quality issues of practice. The gap TabJoinBench closes is a reproducible benchmark covering semantic, relational, and hybrid join settings with validated ground truth. Key Idea: The core trick is seed-and-perturb construction: establish a small number of validated join pairs from sources with independent ground-truth evidence (Wikidata entity co-occurrence, SQL JOIN clauses, partitioned single tables), then mechanically transform candidate tables with composable operators that provably preserve the join relation — so a perturbed candidate remains a true positive by construction, yielding a heterogeneous lake with reliable labels and no need to annotate negatives exhaustively. The perturbations come in three tiers (structural reorganization, representation changes like JSON serialization and case changes, and semantic changes like synonym column names and entity rollups) that let the authors measure which signal each method depends on. Methodology: The pipeline has three stages. (1) Seed generation per source: for WikiTables, tables (≥10 rows, 5–75 columns, single-row headers) are entity-linked to Wikidata QIDs; candidate column pairs sharing ≥5 entities pass length/entropy filters, are ranked by a heuristic (weighted sum: 0.2 entity overlap, 0.2 context similarity, 0.2 value similarity, 0.4 schema complementarity), and 983 pairs were manually classified, retaining 543 joinable seeds. For MMQA, 574 unique pairs are parsed directly from ground-truth SQL JOIN predicates over Spider databases. For NYC Open Data, 620 datasets (10–50 columns, 15–5,000 rows) are split by GPT-4o into two column groups sharing exactly one column; partition quality is scored with an attribute-affinity formula (mean in-group embedding similarity minus out-group similarity) and accepted only if its z-score against a 1,000-random-partition null exceeds 1.96; 70 of 82 inspected partitions survived manual review. (2) Perturbation: candidate tables only receive composable structural (reorder, partition, duplicate rows, drop non-join columns), representation (JSON serialization, prefixes, case, missing values, ID re-sequencing), and semantic (anonymized/synonym column names, entity-aware value rewrites, schema merge/split) operators. (3) Assembly: original plus perturbed candidates form the lake (WikiTables: 11,932 lake tables / 295 queries; MMQA: 13,106 / 408; NYC: 2,638 / 70), with 32–40 relevant candidates per query. Evaluation computes Precision@k and Recall@k for k ∈ {1, 5, 15, 30} plus P@R for 6 specialized methods (LSH Ensemble, PEXESO, D3L, Freyja, WarpGate, DeepJoin) and 2 serialized-column LM embeddings (Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B, embeddinggemma-300m) with HNSW indexing. Critical design decisions: source-specific validation strategies (well-justified — each source needs different ground-truth evidence); perturbing candidates only (justified as increasing heterogeneity, though it asymmetrically disadvantages value-overlap methods); LLM partitioning of NYC datasets from metadata only (partially justified — the z-score null test is clever, but only 82 partitions were checked and data never exposed to the LLM, so affinity is a proxy for true joinability). Key Results: On the WikiTables subset, LSH Ensemble leads precision (P@1 0.969, P@30 0.937) while DeepJoin leads P@R (0.762), with Gemma embeddings close behind (P@R 0.749); D3L (P@R 0.101) and WarpGate (0.133) collapse. On MMQA — the hardest subset — DeepJoin dominates every metric (P@1 0.585, P@R 0.478), and all methods degrade sharply; the authors attribute this to numeric identifier keys with no semantic content. On NYC Open Data no method dominates: LSH Ensemble tops P@5/15/30 (~0.94/0.94/0.76), DeepJoin tops P@1 (0.952), Freyja tops R@30 and P@R (0.655). The headline empirical finding is that task-agnostic LM embeddings are competitive with specialized join-discovery systems across all subsets without join-specific training. Perturbation analysis (P@R by category) shows value-overlap/profile/sketch methods degrade most under representation perturbations on MMQA (e.g., LSH Ensemble falls to 0.078), while name-using methods (DeepJoin, LM embeddings) degrade most under semantic perturbations on NYC (DeepJoin 0.464 vs. 0.583 structural). Tested scale is modest: lakes of 2,638–13,106 tables, average 56–1,270 rows, on a single H200 GPU per run. The surprise is that a 2016-era sketch method beats nearly everything on two of three subsets. Novelty Classification: NEW DATASET/BENCHMARK, with a secondary NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING (generic LM embeddings have closed the gap with specialized join-discovery methods, and no method family is robust across join semantics). The genuinely novel elements are the Wikidata-entity-based semantic-join ground truth and the perturbation framework that extends verified seeds into heterogeneous lakes while preserving labels. The individual components — WikiTables entity linking, SQL parsing from MMQA, LLM-driven vertical partitioning, embedding retrieval with HNSW, standard perturbation operators — are established techniques combined competently for a new evaluation purpose; the closest prior (LakeBench) differs mainly in join semantics coverage rather than methodology. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablation-style analysis is present and is the paper's strength: per-perturbation-category results (Tables 4, 6–8) and per-method hyperparameters (Appendix E) are reported, with full P@k/R@k grids. However, no error bars, seeds, or significance tests appear, and Precision/Recall are averaged over as few as 70 queries (NYC subset), where single-query swings matter. Manual verification was performed by the primary author alone with no inter-annotator agreement measurement — the authors admit this. Ground truth is positives-only and non-exhaustive, so precision figures are upper bounds affected by unlabeled true joins; the paper does not quantify this risk. DeepJoin's training configuration is given (MultipleNegativesRankingLoss, batch 32, 4 epochs) but the training corpus is not identified in the main text, raising an unresolved question of whether it was trained on data overlapping the benchmark. Code, datasets, ground truth, and the generation pipeline are stated as publicly released, but no URL or repository identifier appears in the provided text. All baselines use default or paper-derived hyperparameters; some (Freyja, 2026) are current, and the inclusion of 2025-era embedding models is a credibility positive. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (a benchmark artifact plus evaluation study; no new method is deployed). - Practical: Yes — construction and evaluation run in Python 3.10 on one GPU per execution; the benchmark's tables are small enough for a laptop-scale evaluation, though one H200 and 96 cores were used. - Efficient: The benchmark itself adds no runtime overhead beyond standard retrieval indexing (HNSW, LSH); constructing the NYC subset required LLM calls (GPT-4o) but only over dataset metadata, not values. - Effective: The benchmark demonstrably discriminates between methods and perturbation sensitivities, which is the stated goal, but because ground truth is positives-only, it measures retrieval against a partially known answer set rather than true precision. - Scalable: Not tested — tables are capped at 15–5,000 rows and lakes at ~13K tables, orders of magnitude below industrial lakes; the authors argue sampling is standard practice, but 10×–100× behavior is claimed nowhere and unmeasured. Deliverable: a released dataset/benchmark with generation pipeline and annotations (repository URL not stated in the provided text); no trained model or library. Strengths: (1) The seed-and-perturb construction methodology is a real methodological contribution: it converts three heterogeneous, independently validated ground-truth sources into a controlled benchmark where label correctness survives transformation by design, sidestepping the annotation-cost wall that has kept prior benchmarks limited to partitioned equi-joins. (2) The statistical validation of LLM-generated partitions (z-score against a 1,000-sample random-partition null, borrowed from attribute-affinity partitioning theory) is a thoughtful, reusable quality gate for LLM-assisted benchmark construction. (3) The perturbation-tier analysis produces actionable, non-obvious diagnostics — e.g., that representation perturbations destroy sketch/value methods on identifier-heavy data while semantic perturbations specifically degrade name-dependent learned methods — which is more useful to method designers than a single leaderboard. (4) Honest evaluation of generic embeddings against specialized systems, showing the specialization gap has largely closed, is a finding the join-discovery community needs stated with numbers. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state that (a) manual verification was done by the primary author alone so inter-annotator agreement could not be measured; (b) source-specific heuristic ranking prioritized which pairs got inspected, with final inclusion at annotator discretion; (c) only verified positive joins are provided — the benchmark does not exhaustively enumerate all valid joins in the lake, so additional true joins may exist outside the ground truth; and (d) the perturbation framework cannot capture the full diversity of real transformations, and entity-aware rewrites are applied non-exhaustively, so some pairs retain lexical overlap. This is a direct, non-minimizing limitations section — naming the positives-only ground truth and single-annotator risk explicitly is a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: Beyond the acknowledged issues, a reviewer would flag: (1) the incomplete-negative problem is more serious than stated — since semantic perturbations are applied non-exhaustively, perturbed candidates that retain valid joins are guaranteed true positives, but unperturbed candidate tables from the same sources that happen to be joinable but were never annotated will be counted as false positives, systematically deflating precision for high-recall methods (this plausibly contributes to LSH Ensemble's odd dominance, since containment search surfaces exactly the unannotated true joins); (2) no runtime, indexing-cost, or memory comparison across methods, despite efficiency being a stated selling point of several baselines (PEXESO, Freyja); (3) DeepJoin's training data is unspecified, leaving open train-test contamination of the benchmark; (4) the NYC subset has only 70 queries and its seeds derive from splitting single tables, so intra-source join difficulty may not generalize to cross-dataset discovery, the actual data-lake use case; (5) no baseline tuned per-subset — default hyperparameters may favor some methods on some subsets (e.g., PEXESO's GloVe-50d embeddings are known-weak for domain entities, which the authors themselves note); (6) the WikiTables seed-pair heuristic weights (0.2/0.2/0.2/0.4) are unjustified and un-sensitivity-tested. Bottom Line: For anyone building or evaluating join-discovery systems, this is currently the only benchmark that pairs validated semantic-join ground truth with controlled perturbation analysis, so it is worth adopting despite the positives-only labels and modest scale — but its leaderboard should be read as an upper-bound diagnostic, not a deployment-grade ranking, and the incompleteness of its negative set deserves a follow-up paper more than the next method does.

Problem & Motivation: Agents that improve their own workflows via RSI (outer loop optimizing the procedure, inner loop solving tasks like Lean 4 proofs or Verus-verified code) typically behave as first-order optimizers: they patch surface parameters in response to failure symptoms. The authors' motivating audit of five real RSI trajectories (134 optimization attempts) shows 64.2% of attempts are direct repairs and only 11.2% include any observable diagnostic check — and that 8 of 9 zero-progress editing loops consist purely of direct repairs. The immediate consequence is oscillation: the same symptom (unsolved proof goals) prompts raising retrieval count k to 20 for recall, then lowering it to 15 for context overflow, then back to 18, never investigating that the real mechanism is poor retrieval ranking. Practitioners running costly self-improvement sessions (24-hour budgets here) need a principled way to decide when to stop patching and start diagnosing; the gap prior work (SICA, HarnessFix) leaves open is not whether diagnosis is possible, but when repeated failures should trigger it and how evidence should persist across improvement rounds. Key Idea: Borrowing the second-order problem-solving distinction from organizational research (Tucker & Edmondson, 2003), the core insight is that RSI should escalate to mechanism investigation only when structural anomalies — recurrence, reversals, expectation mismatches — appear in its own edit history, and that the investigation must produce executed evidence (diagnostic probes that discriminate between causal hypotheses), not just LLM-generated explanations. Untested plausible hypotheses are explicitly not enough; the paper's audit shows agents articulate mechanisms in 44 attempts but test only 15 of them (34.1%), so the contribution is turning explanation into verification with persistent memory linking evidence across RSI rounds. Methodology: The system is a Python controller orchestrating a single fixed LLM (GPT-5.6-sol) with distinct prompts for detection, investigation, and editing — no additional training. Stage 1 (Detection): after each RSI attempt, a structured record X_t (version, component, edit, rationale, outcome) is compared against related prior records by a short LLM call that flags one of three anomalies: recurrence (targeted failure persists after a remedy), reversal (opposing parameter changes for similar symptoms, formally (k_t − k_{t−1})(k_{t−1} − k_{t−2}) < 0), or expectation mismatch (observed outcome contradicts the recorded rationale). Stage 2 (Mechanism Investigation, I): hypothesis formation contrasts historical attempts (successes included), proposes non-mutually-exclusive causal hypotheses each with mechanism, supporting/conflicting observations, prediction, and proposed check, optionally consulting external docs; hypothesis testing generates a diagnostic script or tool call executed in an isolated workspace, preferring artifact inspection and stage replay over new model calls, with results classified as supported/contradicted/inconclusive. Stage 3 (Evidence-Guided Intervention, G): the ordinary editing agent receives the verified explanation plus probe results and proposes a workflow patch, which merges only via the normal dev-benchmark acceptance rule. Persistent JSON investigation memory tracks hypotheses, probes, and open questions across rounds with statuses (open/deferred/ready_for_G/monitoring). The objective (Eq. 1) maximizes held-out task success subject to a budget B on total research cost; all detection and investigation calls count against the budget. Critical design decisions: (a) anomaly detection from logs rather than extra benchmark evaluations — well-motivated for cost but unvalidated for recall/precision of triggers; (b) requiring an executed check before handoff to G — the paper's central claim, directly supported by the probe ablation; (c) one investigation step per RSI round with oldest-pending scheduling — plausible but not ablated. Key Results: On Lean 4 proving (92 train / 48 test problems from RSI-Exam + VeriSoftBench) under a 24-hour outer budget with per-task limits of 3 model calls, 12,000 tokens, 4 verifier checks, 180s: SO-RSI achieves 71.2% ± 1.9 held-out pass rate vs. 49.4% ± 2.8 for Naive RSI and 29.4% for the seed workflow — a 21.8-point advantage over Naive RSI. On Verus VCG (113/46 hard problems from VeriContest): 59.2% ± 3.7 vs. 33.4% ± 5.2 and a 14.8% seed — a 25.8-point advantage. All figures are means over three independent outer runs. Ablations: removing executable probes drops pass rate to 63.4% (Lean) / 33.0% (VCG); removing investigation memory drops it to 60.9% / 36.7%. Behavioral analysis: mechanism-testing rate rises from 14.8% to 46.0% (Lean) and 8.9% to 41.6% (VCG) vs. Naive RSI; diagnosed-mechanism recurrence drops by 31.4/35.7 points (vs. 7.3/10.9 for Naive RSI); zero-progress loops fall from 18.7 to 7.2 per 100 evaluated edits (Lean) and 21.4 to 8.6 (VCG). The baseline (Naive RSI on the same seed workflow) is a fair but weak comparison — no external RSI system is run. Testing is at a moderate scale (48/46 test problems, 5 audit trajectories); the audit's group comparisons (e.g., mean gain +14.3 pp for I/G edits on 11 evaluated edits) rest on very small samples and are explicitly descriptive. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD (a selective-escalation controller for RSI: anomaly-triggered, probe-verified, memory-persistent mechanism investigation) plus NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING (quantified evidence that first-order patching dominates RSI behavior and that diagnostic inquiry correlates with larger per-edit gains and fewer zero-progress loops). The genuinely novel part is the operationalization of second-order inquiry — detection triggers, executable probes, and persistent investigation memory — atop an existing RSI loop; the underlying components (LLM reflection, tool execution, log analysis, agent memory à la AutoManual) are standard, and the framing adapts known organizational-behavior theory rather than deriving new theory. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations isolate exactly the two components the paper claims matter (probes, memory), and each ablation is run at full budget across both domains with 3-run means and standard deviations for headline numbers. The methodological hygiene is unusually good: held-out tasks never guide optimization, checkpoint workflows are frozen before testing, behavioral annotation is reconstructed from full traces without method-specific IDs, and reviewers auditing interventions were blind to method identity. Concerns: (1) the behavioral metrics in Table 5 are point estimates with no run-level variance; (2) no inter-annotator agreement statistics are reported for the F/H/I/G coding scheme despite the appendix prescribing that reviewers should compute one; (3) the audit corpus is five trajectories of (presumably) Naive-RSI-style runs — 15 I/G attempts underpin the RQ2 gain comparison; (4) the only baseline is Naive RSI; SICA and HarnessFix are discussed but not compared; (5) aggregate token cost is explicitly not reported, so matched wall-clock budget does not guarantee matched cost. No public code, data, or model release is stated — the reproducibility statement points to appendices only, and cited evidence files (e.g., evidence/reversal_cases.json) are not linked to a repository. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (a method run end-to-end on real verifier-in-the-loop tasks, not just a system claimed to deploy). Practical: Runs on standard API access to a single frontier LLM plus Lean/Verus verifiers in Docker-style isolated workspaces — no special hardware. Efficient: Detection is a short LLM call per attempt and probes prefer artifact replay over new generations, but investigation consumes budget within the same 24-hour envelope; token totals are unreported, so true cost parity with Naive RSI is asserted, not measured. Effective: The evidence shows it improves held-out pass rate and reduces failure recurrence on two formal-verification domains — a real outcome, not only a proxy, though the mechanism-recurrence metric is the authors' own construction audited by their protocol. Scalable: Untested beyond 24-hour runs and ~100-problem benchmarks; whether anomaly detection remains precise as workflows and histories grow by 10× is claimed implicitly but not measured. Deliverable form: the paper describes a full implementation (controller, JSON investigation records, probe executor interfaces) but no software artifact or repository is publicly released, so it currently stops at paper form. Strengths: (1) The motivating audit is a genuine empirical contribution: 134 classified attempts with explicit, defensible coding rules (a parameter change is labeled by the inquiry behind it, not its scope), yielding a quantified diagnosis (64.2% direct repair, 11.2% diagnostic checks) rather than an anecdote. (2) The design enforces epistemic discipline unusual in agent papers — probes must discriminate hypotheses, LLM confidence alone cannot flip a hypothesis to supported, diagnostic support alone never merges an edit — which makes the system's central claim testable. (3) The ablation table cleanly attributes the gains: probes and memory each contribute double-digit points on VCG, and the w/o-probes ablation falling to near-Naive-RSI on VCG (33.0 vs 33.4) shows the mechanism, not the extra scaffolding, drives results. (4) The behavioral analysis applies the same annotation standard to all methods including their own, and reports that Naive RSI spontaneously investigates 14.8% of the time — an honest baseline characterization. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state that evaluation covers only two formal-verification domains and one outer improvement model, and that generalization to other models and workflows remains open. They also candidly note that second-order investigation does not eliminate all regressions, that the RQ2 group comparisons are descriptive and cannot isolate causal effects, and that reversal edits are not always harmful. This is direct, non-minimizing acknowledgment — a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: (1) No comparison against any existing RSI or harness-repair system; SICA and HarnessFix are cited as establishing the capabilities SO-RSI builds on, yet neither is run, so the 21.8/25.8-point margins cannot be situated against the actual frontier of agent self-improvement. (2) The anomaly detector's precision/recall is never measured — every downstream result assumes the three signatures fire when they should; false triggers would waste budget and true misses would silently reduce SO-RSI to Naive RSI. (3) The F/H/I/G annotation rubric's reliability is unvalidated: Appendix A prescribes reviewer agreement statistics, but none are reported, and the behavioral metrics central to the paper's explanation of why it works depend on this rubric. (4) The audit trajectories underpinning the motivation are only five runs in one domain; the claim that first-order thrashing is a general RSI pathology is extrapolated from that corpus. (5) Budget matching is wall-clock only with token costs unreported — SO-RSI's extra LLM calls (2,017–3,223 investigation episodes vs 1,249–1,840 for Naive RSI) could represent a substantially higher spend that the 24-hour cap happens not to penalize. (6) Test sets are small (48 and 46 problems), so the 3-run standard deviations of 1.9–6.2 points sit on narrow denominators. (7) A potential confound the paper does not address: the investigation modules themselves add structured prompts and tool access that might improve the editing agent's context quality independent of any diagnostic evidence, a factor the w/o-probes ablation only partially separates. Bottom Line: For anyone building self-improving LLM agents, this is the most concrete and honestly evaluated treatment I have seen of the patching-versus-diagnosis problem, and the ablations make the core claim stick within its scope — but with only Naive RSI as a baseline, no code release, and a single outer model on two small formal-verification benchmarks, it is a strong proof-of-concept rather than an established method, and the reader should weigh it against HarnessFix-style diagnosis pipelines before adopting it wholesale.
