Problem & Motivation: Current I2V models excel at visual realism and physical dynamics, but existing benchmarks (VBench, EvalCrafter, FETV, and physics-focused benchmarks) evaluate explicit action alignment ('a man opens a box') or physical continuation, which incentivizes statistical shortcut learning — mapping action verbs to visual priors without causal reasoning. The authors argue real-world behavior is driven by unobservable mental states (belief, desire, perception), formalized in cognitive science as Theory of Mind (ToM). No existing benchmark tests whether a generative video model can synthesize behavior conditioned on latent mental states — ToM work in vision (e.g., MuMa-ToM, R³-VQA) is restricted to understanding tasks. The gap is the inverse task: given a world state (image) and a mental state (text), generate the behavior the mental state implies, even when it contradicts objective reality (e.g., a man opening an empty box he falsely believes contains an object). Key Idea: Zero-Action Prompting combined with counterfactual minimal pairs: the image anchors the objective World State while the text injects only subjective mental variables (formalized via a BDI-P causal graph: Perception → Belief, then Belief × Desire → Intention → Action), and prompt pairs that flip exactly one mental variable under a fixed image make single-prompt luck distinguishable from genuine counterfactual mental-state tracking (joint success on both members of a pair). The 'trick' is the physical-mental decoupling: withholding any action verb from the prompt forces the model to internally infer the latent chain Mental State → Intention → Action. Methodology: The paper formalizes the task with a causal graph p(W_{t+1}|W_t, M) = p(W_{t+1}|W_t, A)p(A|I)p(I|M), operationalized as an end-to-end generation mapping (W_t, M) → V where M ⊆ {P, B, D}. Dataset construction: five experts design cognitive graphs over world state, perception, belief, desire, intention, action; each graph is independently reviewed by two experts with consensus required; images are sourced from public repositories or AIGC platforms (frontal faces excluded); prompts are synthesized without revealing the ground-truth intention; a final audit condenses 2,000+ candidates into 744 prompts over 372 images. The taxonomy spans 3 primary dimensions (Perception, Belief, Desire), 12 secondary categories, 34 sub-dimensions. Evaluation uses five metrics — Visual Quality (1–5), Commonsense Plausibility (1–5), Action Occurrence (intended/no/other action), Intention Accuracy (binary), World-State Maintenance (binary) — scored by Gemini 3.1 Pro with a structured multi-step judging pipeline (identify world state → manipulated mental condition → candidate behaviors → rubric-based scoring). Diagnostic analyses add action completion vs. conditional correctness, counterfactual pair outcomes (Both/One/Neither Correct), and an action–state 2×2 decomposition. Critical design decisions: (1) withholding action verbs — well-motivated as the core causal isolation mechanism; (2) counterfactual pairs — well-justified against chance success and directly credited from contrastive-evaluation literature; (3) LVM-as-judge — pragmatically necessary at this scale but the weakest link, validated on only 100 videos. Key Results: Across 11 I2V systems (Veo 3.1, Kling V3, Seedance 1.5 Pro, Hailuo 2.3, Runway Gen-4, Wan 2.6/2.2, CogVideoX, HunyuanVideo 1.5, LongCat-Video, LTX 2.3), Visual Quality clusters in 3.8–4.4 and Commonsense Plausibility in 3.8–4.6, while Intention Accuracy spans only 11.9% (LTX 2.3) to 59.5% (Veo 3.1) and World-State Maintenance 32.5% (Hailuo 2.3) to 68.3% (HunyuanVideo 1.5) — a clear dissociation between perceptual fidelity and mental-state reasoning. Veo 3.1 leads in all three dimensions (Belief 58.3%, Perception 58.6%, Desire 61.6%). Counterfactual pair analysis shows Veo 3.1 achieves only 54.2% Both-Correct (Wan 2.6: 51.1%, Kling V3: 50.0%; LTX 2.3: 8.3% Both-Correct, 47.9% Neither-Correct). The action–state decomposition reveals the key asymmetry: State-Correct-Only far exceeds Action-Correct-Only for most models (Veo 3.1: 45.6% vs. 8.9%; HunyuanVideo 1.5: 42.4% vs. 18.5%), showing preserving the world state is easier than selecting the mental-state-appropriate action. The named finding, Omniscient Bias, is that models default to the objective world state rather than the character's limited subjective belief (e.g., generating the action consistent with where the object actually is, not where the character believes it is). Baselines are current commercial and open-source frontier models; testing scale is a standard benchmark (744 prompts, 720p, 5–8 s videos), not a stress test. Novelty Classification: NEW DATASET/BENCHMARK and NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING. The genuinely novel elements are the inverse-ToM generation task formulation (synthesizing behavior from latent mental states, versus prior ToM work on visual understanding) and the Zero-Action Prompting + counterfactual-pair methodology. The constituent techniques — BDI agent theory, minimal-pair contrastive evaluation (cited from SyntaxGym/Vamvas & Sennrich), and LVM-as-judge pipelines — are standard; the contribution is a well-executed adaptation of them to a new evaluation target, plus the Omniscient Bias empirical finding. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations/diagnostics are present and informative: the action-type distribution, conditional correctness, counterfactual pair outcomes, and action–state decomposition each isolate a distinct failure component. Validation of the automated judge against 10 human experts (92%/89% exact agreement on binary metrics; PLCC/SRCC 0.78/0.76 and 0.81/0.79 on continuous metrics) is reported and above typical LLM-judge validation standards. However: no error bars, multiple generation seeds, or significance tests are reported despite binary metrics on ~372 cases where adjacent models may not be separable; the dataset's public release is implied by a project website but not explicitly stated with a repository link in the provided text; all images were partially AIGC-sourced, which could interact with generation-model priors. Methodological concern: a closed-source judge (Gemini 3.1 Pro) scoring outputs from closed-source generators (including Google's own Veo 3.1, which ranks first) creates an unquantifiable same-family-judge risk — Veo 3.1's top ranking should be interpreted cautiously. Also, the evaluator is never tested for its own ToM competence on the benchmark's reasoning questions. Deployability: Profile: SYSTEMS (a built benchmark and evaluation pipeline, evaluated by deployment across 11 models). - Practical: Yes — evaluation requires only API/model access for generation plus a Gemini 3.1 Pro judge; the 744 prompts and 372 images are lightweight, though closed-source model APIs (Veo, Kling) and a paid judge are dependencies. - Efficient: Automated judging removes the need for large-scale human annotation (only 100 videos needed expert validation); cost per video is one structured LVM call. - Effective: The evidence shows it diagnoses a real capability gap (IA far below visual-quality scores, counterfactual pair failures), though the measured construct depends on judge reliability that was validated on only 100 of thousands of generated videos. - Scalable: The pipeline scales linearly in prompts; whether the taxonomy's 34 sub-dimensions remain populated with sufficient cases at 10× scale is untested, and benchmark contamination (models trained on or prompted to exploit mental-state templates) is unaddressed. The work delivers a benchmark artifact (744 prompts, 372 images, evaluation protocol, project website: https://richard2049-lee.github.io/MindWorldBench/) rather than a trained model or library. Strengths: - The physical-mental decoupling design — image for world state, action-verb-free text for mental state — is a clean causal isolation that no prior video-generation benchmark implements, and it directly blocks the verb-to-visual shortcut that plagues instruction-following evaluations. - The counterfactual pair requirement (joint success on minimally-paired prompts) is imported from contrastive evaluation methodology in NLP and applied rigorously, exposing that single-prompt accuracy overstates capability (e.g., Veo 3.1 drops from ~59.5% IA to 54.2% Both-Correct). - The action–state decomposition is a genuinely insightful diagnostic: it separates two orthogonal capabilities (choosing the right action vs. preserving world state) and produces the paper's clearest quantitative asymmetry (45.6% vs. 8.9% for Veo 3.1). - The Omniscient Bias finding is a concrete, memorable, and actionable characterization of why models fail — defaulting to objective truth over subjective belief — rather than a generic 'models are bad at reasoning' conclusion. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors acknowledge that outputs lacking either candidate action 'cannot reveal whether the model has correctly translated the mental state into behavior' (an action-realization bottleneck affecting up to 16% of outputs for some models), that the automated evaluation 'remains complementary to human assessment', and that action reasoning and world-state maintenance are 'related but non-equivalent capabilities'. They state the benchmark highlights 'a need for explicit mental-state modeling' without proposing a fix. They confront limitations moderately directly, though they do not discuss judge bias, dataset release, or statistical uncertainty. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - Single-judge dependency: all headline numbers come from one Gemini 3.1 Pro run with no ensemble, second judge, or ablation on judge sensitivity to prompt phrasing; the judge's own false-belief competence is never tested, yet the benchmark's hardest cases are exactly false-belief scenarios. - No statistical treatment: 372 images mean Belief/Perception/Desire sub-scores and 34 sub-dimensions rest on small strata; differences of a few points between adjacent models are likely within noise, yet rankings are presented without confidence intervals. - Possible judge–generator confound: Veo 3.1 (Google) is evaluated by Gemini (Google) and ranks first on the subjective reasoning metric; the authors do not address this. - Training/contamination risk: closed-source commercial models could have encountered ToM-style prompting patterns in their text-image training data; no decontamination or perturbation robustness check (e.g., paraphrased prompts) is reported. - The two candidate actions per case constrain the evaluation to a forced-choice structure; models generating a plausible but non-listed rational action are penalized as 'Other Action' (up to 28.8% for LTX 2.3), which may conflate creativity with failure. - Images partly AIGC-generated may distribute visual priors in ways that interact with the tested models' own synthetic-data training distributions; this is unexamined. Bottom Line: This is the strongest current instrument for measuring a capability (mental-state-driven behavior generation) that every existing video benchmark ignores, and its counterfactual methodology and Omniscient Bias finding will genuinely inform world-simulator research — read it if you build or evaluate video generation models, but treat the model rankings, especially the top one, with caution given the single-judge and judge-vendor confounds.

#98 — Innovative (66)

Prospective Hindsight: Self-Calibrating Reinforcement Learning via Prediction-Reality Gaps

J Zhang, X Peng, Q Chen, Y Li, H Hayashi, CS Wu · arxiv.org · long-horizon RL for agents - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces Prospective Hindsight (PH), a one-line modification to retrospective agent-RL methods (GRPO, on-policy distillation, and their combination) that upweights rollouts where the agent's action-time prediction of its own success disagrees with the eventual verifier outcome, via the loss ℓ_PH = (1 + α·ξ)·ℓ_base with a stop-gradient surprise indicator ξ. - Why it's important: Long-horizon LLM agents trained with hindsight-only RL become confidently wrong — a failure mode retrospective signals structurally cannot see — and existing fixes add explicit calibration losses that trade off against task accuracy. - How it does it: Before the verifier scores each rollout, the same policy is re-prompted to predict its outcome (ternary −1/0/+1); the binary disagreement with the realized outcome is the surprise, and because the predictor shares parameters with the policy, calibration improves implicitly without an added loss term. - The good: The ablations are convincing at the mechanism level: random reweighting with identical total gradient mass leaves calibration nearly unchanged (OFR 33.3% vs. PH's 20.9% on Science Q&A), so the gain comes from surprise-based selection, not added weight, and the PH weight self-anneals as the prediction–reality gap closes. - The missing: No empirical head-to-head against the calibration-augmented RL baselines the paper positions against (CaOPD, Leng et al., Damani et al.) despite reusing CaOPD's exact datasets and preprocessing — the claimed removal of the capability–calibration trade-off is asserted, not measured. - Read it or not: Worth reading for anyone doing RL post-training of LLM agents or working on calibration-in-training, because the core idea is a cheap, plug-in-compatible reweighting with a clean theoretical framing; skimmable if you only care about benchmark SOTA, since absolute gains are modest and the evaluation footprint is small.
Why this rank
Scored using Empirical profile. Rigor (65) is anchored by unusually clean reweighting controls (random/failure-only, matched gradient mass), cross-scale replication, and an honest α=2.0 negative result, but is capped by the missing head-to-head against the calibration-augmented baselines (CaOPD et al.) the paper positions against, no error bars, and GPT-4.1 serving as both simulator and judge. Novelty (70) and Non-Obviousness (72) benefit from the LUPI-framed surprise-gated reweighting and the non-obvious finding that the dominant miscalibration cell flips between single-turn and multi-turn regimes. Completeness (72) is a credibility positive given direct, non-minimizing limitation reporting; Resilience (60) and Impact (50) are limited by the untested central trade-off claim and no confirmed code release. Weighted composite: 0.20*70 + 0.25*65 + 0.15*72 + 0.15*72 + 0.15*60 + 0.10*50 = 66.

Problem & Motivation: Agentic RL for LLMs (GRPO-style binary RL, on-policy distillation, PRM-scored multi-turn training) constructs every learning signal from post-action quantities — rewards, next states, hindsight-teacher distributions. The agent's prospective belief at action time ("did I expect this to work?") never enters the gradient, so a lucky success and a calibrated success receive identical reinforcement, as do an anticipated failure and a surprising one. The authors call this the "hindsight trap" and argue it explains why retrospective training raises accuracy without fixing overconfidence. Practitioners deploying agents in tool-use, tutoring, and coding contexts have this problem: confidently wrong actions propagate down trajectories and suppress recovery, while failures the agent itself flags invite fallbacks. Prior calibration work is either inference-time (temperature scaling, verbalized confidence) or adds a separate calibration loss to RL that trades against task performance. Key Idea: Convert the gap between the agent's prospective belief and the retrospective outcome into a per-rollout training weight: a binary surprise indicator ξ = 𝟙[(z, y) ∈ {overconfident failure, underconfident success}] multiplies the base loss by (1 + αξ), with ξ treated as a stop-gradient constant. The conceptual move is reframing this gap as a per-rollout realization of the privileged-information gap I⋆ from Vapnik's LUPI framework — rollouts with ξ = 1 are exactly where action-time information falls short of post-action information, so upweighting them concentrates gradient budget where the agent's self-model is most wrong. Methodology: Three components. (1) A prospective self-evaluator: the same policy is prompted (with a task-specific template) to predict whether its just-emitted action will succeed, parsed to a ternary z ∈ {−1, 0, +1}; M samples are majority-voted (M=1 single-turn, M=3 multi-turn where the PRM is stochastic). (2) A four-cell calibration taxonomy (CS/OF/US/AF) crossing prospective belief with verifier outcome; z = 0 is a neutral class with weight 1. (3) The update: ℓ_PH = (1 + α·ξ)·ℓ_base with default α = 1; multi-turn uses a continuous gate ξ = ½|z̄ − r| ∈ [0,1]. The theory frames the expected PH loss as base loss plus a surprise residual R(θ) = c(θ)·M(θ) (exact identity), where M(θ) is the miscalibration rate (equivalently the binary Brier score of the deterministic predictor), and proves a gradient-flow decomposition (Theorem 4) showing the PH update contains a −α·c̄·∇M component plus a remainder bounded via Cauchy–Schwarz. Critical design decisions: parameter-sharing between policy and evaluator (justified by the co-evolution argument and the implicit-calibration mechanism); the discrete/continuous gate split by verifier determinism (reasonable); and honest uncertainty (z = 0) treated as neutral weight (conservative but not ablated). The authors are appropriately careful to frame Theorem 4 as motivation, not a monotone-descent guarantee. Key Results: Single-turn (SciKnowEval Chemistry, ToolAlpaca Tool Use; OLMo-3-7B-Instruct, SDPO base, 3 seeds): late-training OFR on Science Q&A drops from 34.2% (baseline) to 20.9% at α=0.5 with validation accuracy slightly up (65.7 vs. 63.0 avg mean@16); on Tool Use α=1.0 gives the joint best (58.2/61.7 mean@16, OFR 33.6%). The gpt-oss-20B replication shows comparable or larger gains (e.g., OFR 10.3 vs. 9.1, capability +1.4). Multi-turn (OpenClaw-RL personal agent, GSM8K tutoring, GPT-4.1 simulator, OLMo-3-7B PRM/teacher): PH lifts trajectory-averaged evaluator score over baseline at α=1.0 by +7.2 (RL), +15.3 (OPD), +3.9 (Combined); OFR drops in every block; prospective accuracy peaks at 87.8%. A genuinely interesting structural finding: the dominant miscalibration cell flips between regimes — single-turn is OF-dominated (OF 34.1% vs. US 2.7%) while multi-turn is US-dominated (US grows 13.8% → 27.9% → 34.5% across RL → OPD → Combined), yet the same scalar α works in both. α = 2.0 in multi-turn collapses the predictor toward constant z = −1 (calibration improves via self-model degradation, not genuine alignment) — an honest negative result. Overhead is ~6% wall-clock single-turn and ~0% (asynchronous) multi-turn on a single 8×H200 node. Baselines are current for the reweighting controls (random, failure-only, both matched on total weight), but absent for the calibration-in-RL competitors the paper positions against. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD (surprise-gated reweighting of any retrospective RL loss) plus NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING (the regime-dependent flip of the dominant miscalibration cell, and calibration emerging as a byproduct of stop-gradient reweighting). The genuinely novel element is using the per-rollout prediction–reality disagreement as a sample-level training weight — the authors' claim that this is the first use of the LUPI gap I⋆ as a sample-level signal in agent RL is plausible. The ingredients are standard: importance-style loss reweighting, self-ask confidence elicitation, and the law of total variance; the combination and its placement inside GRPO/OPD training loops is the contribution, and the theory (Prop. 1, Prop. 2–3) is a direct application of known identities. Rigor & Reproducibility: The ablations are the strongest part: the random/failure-only reweighting controls isolate selection from gradient mass, the α-sweep spans {0.1–2.0} with per-step dynamics, cross-scale replication (7B → 20B) and a second user simulator (GPT-5.4) are included, and the α=2.0 predictor collapse is reported rather than hidden. Headline numbers aggregate over 3 seeds, but the main tables report point values without error bars or significance tests; no statistical testing appears. A D.4 section header promises a code release, but no URL or repository is given in the provided text — artifact availability is not stated. Methodological concerns: (i) the multi-turn capability metric is a GPT-4.1-judge score where GPT-4.1 is also the user simulator, a partially circular LLM-judge setup; (ii) calibration metrics (OFR, surprise) are computed from the agent's own ternary self-evaluation, so improvements could partly reflect changes in the verbalized self-report rather than true belief–outcome alignment; (iii) single-turn evaluation reuses exactly CaOPD's two datasets but CaOPD itself is never run as a baseline; (iv) training and evaluation of calibration happen against the same PRM judge, creating a mild Goodhart risk the paper acknowledges only implicitly (via the "deceptive calibration" broader-impact note). Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL (trained systems with measured outcomes, plus supporting theory that is motivation rather than the contribution). - Practical: Yes — runs on one 8×H200 node with standard stacks (verl/vLLM, slime/Megatron-LM/sglang) on 7B–20B models. - Efficient: Very — ~6% single-turn overhead, ~0% multi-turn (asynchronous predictor), zero added parameters, one hyperparameter α. - Effective: Calibration improvements are well-evidenced against matched reweighting controls; task-capability gains are smaller (single-turn +1–3 points, multi-turn +4 to +15 on an LLM-judged score) and the OFR metric is self-report-derived, so effectiveness on true downstream miscalibration (e.g., failure-triggered recovery behavior) is a proxy, not directly measured. - Scalable: Not tested beyond 20B and 48-turn sessions; the authors claim applicability to longer-horizon agents (SWE, terminal, GUI) as future work, and the α=2.0 gradient-norm instability at long horizons suggests scaling is not friction-free. Deliverable: a method with detailed prompts, hyperparameters, and an implementation flag (SURPRISE_MODE), but no publicly confirmed code, dataset, or model artifact in the provided text. Strengths: - The reweighting-control design (random and failure-only, matched on per-step total weight) is the right experiment and cleanly demonstrates that surprise-based selection, not added gradient mass, drives the calibration gains. - The LUPI framing gives the heuristic a principled substrate: the privileged-information-gap decomposition (Prop. 1) and the exact residual identity R(θ) = c(θ)·M(θ) are simple but genuinely clarifying, and the authors resist overclaiming (Theorem 4 is explicitly "motivation, not guarantee"). - The structural finding that the dominant miscalibration mode flips from overconfident failures (single-turn) to underconfident successes (multi-turn, scaling with OPD's privileged teacher) is a non-obvious empirical observation that survived three base methods. - The self-extinguishing weight dynamic (mean weight annealing from ~1.35 to ~1.09 as the pass rate rises) means no schedule tuning is needed — a practical property verified across two orders of magnitude of α. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: Explicitly listed in App. G: variance amplification and gradient-norm spikes at α ≥ 2.0 in long horizons; the uniform-base-loss assumption behind the calibration-alignment claim (alignment is "quantitative rather than absolute"); training-time compute overhead; dependence of the surprise signal on initial self-model quality; and evaluation scope limited to verifiable tasks and a math-tutoring agent. The paper also honestly reports the α=2.0 predictor collapse and the Combined block being a "partial exception" to its OPD-vs-RL ordering. It additionally flags in Broader Impact the risk of "deceptive calibration" (agent avoids hard tasks to minimize surprise). This is direct, non-minimizing limitation reporting — a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - The central comparative claim — that PH avoids the capability–calibration trade-off exhibited by explicit calibration-augmented RL — is never tested against those baselines; CaOPD, Leng et al., and Damani et al. appear only in related work while their datasets are reused. This is the largest evidentiary hole. - Multi-turn capability is scored by a GPT-4.1 evaluator against preferences that GPT-4.1 (as simulator) also enforces during training; a human or independent-judge evaluation is absent. - No ablation removes parameter sharing (e.g., a frozen or separately-parameterized evaluator) to verify the co-evolution mechanism the theory leans on; PAcc rising from ~30% to ~80% is attributed to the shared-parameter channel without an alternative-architecture control. - The "hindsight trap" gradient-invariance claim (Eq. 2) is stated but not demonstrated experimentally (e.g., by showing base-method gradients really are invariant to z), and the hindsight-trap → overconfidence causal story is asserted from citation, not isolation. - Single-turn datasets are ~4–5k prompts with 3-epoch runs; no error bars in main tables despite 3 seeds; no significance testing. - The z = 0 neutral class handling (folding parse failures into "honest uncertainty") could mask evaluator-pathology rates; its empirical frequency is described only qualitatively. Bottom Line: A practitioner training RL-post-trained LLM agents should read this: the surprise-gated reweighting is a cheap, framework-agnostic addition with unusually clean ablations and one genuinely new empirical finding, but the headline claim of eliminating the capability–calibration trade-off remains unverified against the very baselines it targets, so treat it as a strong promising mechanism, not a settled improvement over calibration-loss methods.

AgentGarten: Code Worlds for Evolving Agents (131 ▲ )

Jiawei Chi, Shangchen Miao, Zhiyuan Shi, Kailu Wu, Hanyang Wang, Weiliang Chen, Qiyu Dai, Jinshan Ren, Jun Gao, Mingsheng Long, Yueqi Duan, Jiangran Lyu, Jialong Wu, Fangfu Liu · arxiv.org · Daily papers of 9 Oct 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces AgentGarten, a framework that couples simulators/game engines maintaining persistent, code-defined world state with a shared real-time neural renderer, plus Adversarial Forcing, a distillation method that turns a pretrained bidirectional video model into a geometry-conditioned renderer running at 36.5 frames/s on one H100. - Why it's important: Building interactive environments with both faithful dynamics and realistic visuals is a stated bottleneck for agent training; this removes the need to author per-scene visual assets while keeping state inspectable and editable as code. - How it does it: The engine exports structured conditions (colorized depth or surface normals) through a common interface; the renderer is distilled from a Cosmos 3-Nano video model via DMD-style distribution matching on its own rollouts, with bitwise-exact replay making history prefilling differentiable, and an adversarial loss on real video with an exact R1/R2 penalty computed without double-backward through fused attention. - The good: The exact replay result is the strongest evidence — block-by-block SDPA replay achieves bitwise-identical recomputation (0% relative L2 error) versus 3.99% for the SGF-style FlexAttention alternative, at 5.4% lower forward time and essentially unchanged memory, directly enabling history-gradient learning. - The missing: Agent evaluation is extremely thin — one episode per round per world, no seeds or variance, no baseline (e.g., the same agents on engine-rendered frames or with state access), and the headline Self Forcing vs. Adversarial Forcing comparison (Figure 8) is qualitative only, with no FVD or human metrics. - Read it or not: Worth reading for researchers building neural-rendering-based simulation or distilling causal video models (Sections 3–4 are technically dense and reproducible); the agent-learning sections (Section 5) can be skimmed, as they are anecdotal demonstrations rather than controlled experiments.
Why this rank
Scored using Systems profile. Practical Impact (72) and Novelty (75) drive the composite — the bitwise-exact replay mechanism and the JVP-based exact R1/R2 construction are genuinely reusable technical advances, and the framework ships as a real-time artifact on a single H100. Rigor (55) and Resilience (55) are the weak links: this is an unreviewed vendor preprint with no error bars or seeds anywhere, the central Adversarial-vs-Self Forcing comparison is qualitative only (no FVD or human metrics), the agent study is one episode per round, and there is no control isolating the renderer's contribution. Non-Obviousness (78) is strong — matching execution structure to achieve bitwise-identical differentiable recomputation is a non-obvious systems insight. Problem & Motivation: Teams training embodied or interactive agents need environments whose state, rules, and dynamics are faithful (persistent, inspectable, editable) and whose observations are realistic (matching real-world visual distributions). Simulators/game engines provide the former but require costly 3D asset authoring for visual diversity; video world models provide the latter but bury task-relevant state in generated history, making it non-inspectable, non-editable, and error-accumulating. The paper targets the gap between these two: programmable dynamics with learned, diverse appearance shared across many environments. Key Idea: Separate world evolution from appearance: the engine owns state and exports a three-channel geometry condition (depth or normals) through a unified interface, and a single shared neural renderer turns conditions plus an appearance reference and text into the agent's visual stream — so rendering errors cannot corrupt state, and new worlds need only coarse geometry, not visual assets. The enabling training trick, Adversarial Forcing, makes history prefilling differentiable via "exact replay" (re-running the rollout block-by-block with identical kernels/shapes so recomputation is bitwise identical, allowing later losses to update the KV-cache-writing computation without a fully differentiable rollout), and computes exact R1/R2 gradient penalties through a frozen discriminator backbone using VJP/JVP products instead of double backward. Methodology: Three training stages on 32 H100s. (1) Geometry conditioning: adapt Cosmos 3-Nano (36 layers, 4096 hidden) to depth/normal tokens — encoded by the frozen Wan video encoder, spatially pooled, injected via joint sequence-level attention with zero-initialized modality embeddings — with robustness augmentations (modality dropout, warps, latent noise). (2) Teacher-forcing adaptation: block-causal training with parallel clean (P_j) and noisy (Q_j) copies of each block under a mask where noisy copies never see their own clean target; flow-matching loss (Eq. 6). (3) Adversarial Forcing: DMD distillation against the frozen stage-1 teacher plus a fake-score model, a two-pass scheme (no-gradient rollout recording inputs/outputs, then differentiable replay under the Eq. 5 mask), and a relativistic GAN objective (R3GAN-style) with a trainable head over frozen teacher features; exact R1/R2 via the frozen-backbone identity ∇_φ R = ∇_φ[2 J_z h_φ(z) sg(v)] (Eqs. 11–13). Inference uses a bounded KV cache (5 sink + 44 recent latent frames), top-aligned RoPE remapping beyond the training horizon, custom Triton kernels, CUDA graphs, and a distilled tiny VAE decoder (<10 ms). Agent experiments use pretrained foundation-model agents (cited as GPT-6 Astra) acting through short Python programs on rendered first-person frames only, writing Markdown "playbook" skill files that later rounds inherit. Key design decisions: joint-attention conditioning instead of ControlNet-style branches (justified by avoiding pixel-aligned bias, though un-validated against that alternative); frozen text tower and VAE (reasonable efficiency choice); depth/normals as the condition interface (well-justified by estimator availability from real video, but acknowledged as lossy for rotation-symmetric state and material). Key Results: Replay: SGF-style FlexAttention replay diverges from the rollout by 3.99% relative L2; block-by-block SDPA replay is bitwise identical (0% error), with forward time 2.79 s vs 2.95 s (−5.4%) and peak memory within 0.2% on one H100, BF16, 480×832, 61 latent frames. Throughput: 438.8 ms per 16-frame block steady-state (condition encoding 10.6 ms, transformer 414.4 ms, decode 8.8 ms), i.e., 36.5 frames/s on one H100 including all stages. Adversarial vs Self Forcing: 30-second rollouts show Self Forcing developing repetitive patterns and losing detail while Adversarial Forcing retains texture — reported qualitatively only, with no perceptual metrics. Agents: in hide-and-seek, hiders built shelters by round 4 and seekers used ramps by round 10, versus ≈25M and ≈100M training episodes respectively in Baker et al.'s self-play RL — a comparison the authors explicitly flag as paradigm-dependent, not a sample-efficiency ratio. Four additional worlds (one episode per round, four rounds): companion-dog engagement 13→19; bridge swap 71→41 s; herding 3/4→4/4 sheep (score 60→88.3 with a round-3 dip); quarry loader 30→0→30→90.9 (round-2 regression). Scale: renderer training on DL3DV-10K, OpenDV, and gameplay/robotics video; agent study is small-n demonstration scale. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD (Adversarial Forcing's exact bitwise replay and exact R1/R2 for a frozen-backbone discriminator are specific, well-executed technical advances over Self Gradient Forcing and APT's approximation) + NEW SYSTEM/TOOL (the code-world framework with a shared geometry-conditioned real-time renderer and playable environment library) + NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING (playbook-based multi-round improvement by pretrained agents observing only neural-rendered frames). The core architecture — explicit state outside the video model, rendered through it — is an anticipated combination the authors themselves situate against Magpie, OmniDreams, Code2Worlds, and state-aware game world models; the genuinely novel parts are the bitwise-exact replay schedule, the JVP-based exact regularizer, and the empirical demonstration of text-playbook evolution in this setting. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are present but partial: Self Forcing vs. Adversarial Forcing is compared only qualitatively (no FVD, LPIPS, or human study), while replay error and throughput are measured carefully with stated hardware, precision, and protocol. No error bars, seeds, or significance tests anywhere; the agent study reports single episodes per round. Code is claimed at https://github.com/MirroS-Lab/AgentGarten with a project page, and appendices give training hyperparameters, cache policies, and verbatim task files — unusually strong reproduction detail for a corporate technical report. Concerns: this is a vendor technical report (MirroS) and a preprint, not peer-reviewed; one cited component (WildDet3D) has "Citation to be completed" and the agent model (GPT-6 Astra) is a proprietary 2026 system, making the agent experiments hard to replicate end-to-end; there is no baseline isolating the renderer's contribution (e.g., the same agents on ground-truth engine renders, or on a competing world-model renderer such as Matrix-Game or Genie 3); and the four extra worlds show non-monotonic scores (herding 90.1→87.6, loader 90→0) that are narrated but not analyzed statistically. Deployability: Profile: SYSTEMS (a built, served framework evaluated in deployment) with a substantial EMPIRICAL component. Practical: Inference runs on a single H100 with a browser/WebRTC client; training requires 32 H100s, so only well-resourced labs can retrain the renderer. Efficient: 36.5 frames/s at 480×832 on one H100 is competitive for a diffusion-based renderer, aided by the tiny decoder and fused kernels; the paper does not compare GPU cost against conventional engine rendering, which would be far cheaper per frame. Effective: The system demonstrably supports real-time closed-loop agent interaction across six environments, but evidence that the renderer is necessary or sufficient for the agent gains is weak (no rendering-free controls). Scalable: Only claimed — the authors state worlds "were built one at a time" and that scaling world generation to coding agents is future work; no experiment tests 10×–100× more worlds or longer-horizon playbooks. The work ships a software artifact (code, environment library, trained renderer weights implied by links) plus a reusable proof technique (the exact R1/R2 construction, Appendix B). Strengths: (1) The exact replay mechanism is a real contribution: achieving bitwise-identical differentiable recomputation of a cached rollout by matching execution structure (block-by-block SDPA, identical call shapes and KV ordering) is a non-obvious systems insight with a measured payoff over SGF-style full-sequence replay. (2) The exact R1/R2 derivation for a frozen-backbone discriminator (VJP for g, JVP for v, explicit head JVP for the φ-gradient, Eqs. 11–13) removes the double-backward barrier that has forced approximations in adversarial post-training of large models, and is independently reusable. (3) The authors confront their headline comparison honestly, explicitly stating the round-4/round-10 vs. 25M/100M episode numbers reflect different paradigms rather than a sample-efficiency ratio — a credibility positive. (4) Unusually thorough reproduction material: training stages, LR schedules, sampling endpoints, cache policies, augmentation probabilities, and full verbatim task files. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The Future Work section is candid: depth/normal conditions are redundant yet lossy (cannot represent spin of rotationally symmetric objects, material, color, object identity beyond the visual-history window); thin structures are destroyed by pooling; texture leakage and misalignment in estimated conditions motivate augmentations but are not solved; all worlds were hand-built one at a time, and automated verification of whether a generated world "deserves an agent's time" is open; playbook management across many worlds (selection, merging, retrieval) is unsolved. The authors also explicitly demote their RL comparison to a paradigm contrast, not a benchmark. These limitations are confronted directly rather than minimized. Analyst-Identified Gaps: Beyond the acknowledged limits: (1) No quantitative visual-fidelity evaluation of the renderer against any baseline — the central claim that Adversarial Forcing fixes long-rollout degradation rests on four screenshot pairs; FVD or human ratings against CausVid/Self Forcing/APT-style baselines are needed. (2) The agent study lacks any control isolating the renderer: no run with the same agents and playbooks on conventional engine renders, so the claimed benefit of neural rendering over cheap graphics rendering is unevaluated. (3) One episode per round with non-monotonic scores (loader 90→0, herding dips) cannot support claims of "improvement across rounds" — the observed trends are within plausible run-to-run variance for a stochastic agent. (4) Round-based playbook gains may largely reflect the pretrained model's existing competence; a no-playbook or shuffled-playbook ablation is absent. (5) The renderer was trained on a data mixture including gameplay/robotics internet video, so agents may benefit from distributional familiarity with exactly the evaluation-style worlds — a potential Goodhart-like overlap between training data and the hide-and-seek evaluation domain that is not discussed. (6) Comparison to the closest competing systems (Matrix-Game 2.0/3.0, WorldPlay, Magpie) is limited to related-work prose; no head-to-head control, latency, or consistency measurement. Bottom Line: A technically substantive systems paper whose distillation machinery (bitwise exact replay, exact R1/R2 without double backward) is genuinely worth adopting by anyone building real-time causal video renderers, but whose agent-learning study is a demonstration rather than evidence — practitioners should read Sections 3–4 and appendices and treat Section 5 as an inspiring anecdote pending controlled evaluation.

#100 — Innovative (66)

Foundations of Proactive Agents: Principles, Technical Layers, and Proactivity-Gym (21 ▲ )

Jio Oh, Seunghyun Do, Young-Jun Lee, Steven Euijong Whang, Dongyeop Kang · arxiv.org · Daily papers of 6 Oct 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper proposes a conceptual foundation for proactive LLM agents built on three joint objectives (Task Capability, Temporal Allocation, Trust — the "3T"), a five-dimension design space for realizing them, and PROACTIVITY-GYM, a multi-day simulation testbed with 10 hand-crafted scenarios, 3 personas each, and a 30-participant human study evaluating 23 model–harness configurations. - Why it's important: Proactive assistance converts idle compute into useful work, but poorly timed or over-intervening agents impose review costs and destroy user trust — and current evaluations conflate task success with trustworthiness, so failures cannot be diagnosed separately. - How it does it: The core move is decomposing "proactivity" into three separately-measured objectives and instrumenting a stateful, simulated-clock environment where agent actions change task state, resources, and user trust over days, so downstream consequences of proactive decisions are scored. - The good: The human study provides the most credible evidence: correct-but-misaligned interventions drop trust by 1.86 points on a 5-point scale versus +1.27 for the reverse transition, and acceptance of sleep-time assistance reaches 97.8% versus 26.7% for competing immediate assistance — directly validating that the 3T objectives are dissociable. - The missing: TA is evaluated on exactly one two-task decision window per scenario and TR-D is a binary depth match against predefined personas, so headline claims about temporal allocation and trust rest on narrow, hand-authored proxies with LLM judges whose calibration differs materially between judge models. - Read it or not: Read it if you build or evaluate personal-agent systems and need a vocabulary and testbed for proactive behavior beyond static request-response benchmarks; skip it if you want a method that improves proactive agents, since this paper delivers principles and measurement, not a training or optimization technique.
Why this rank
Scored using Empirical profile. The paper is pulled down primarily on Impact (55) and Resilience (63): no method or intervention is delivered — only a specification, a testbed, and diagnostics — the code and data are merely 'planned for release,' and TA scores rest on a single engineered two-task decision window with a strict AND rule that partly measures whether agents verbalize 'later.' Rigor (68) shows thorough diagnostics and bootstrap CIs for the human study, but no significance tests for model comparisons, Goodhart-prone author-authored rubrics, and a demonstrably miscalibrated LLM-judge pair. Novelty (70) and Non-Obviousness (68) are supported by the 3T dissociation finding and the trust-loss asymmetry result (−1.86 vs +1.27), which is real and load-bearing, while Completeness (70) benefits from honest limitation reporting. Weighted composite: 0.20*70 + 0.25*68 + 0.15*68 + 0.15*70 + 0.15*63 + 0.10*55 = 66.

Show full analysis
Problem & Motivation: Personal AI agents running on consumer hardware (e.g., via OpenClaw, OpenJarvis) sit idle between user requests, and the authors argue this idle compute could deliver proactive assistance — work prepared before the user asks. The pain point: current agents and benchmarks are almost entirely reactive, and the few proactive benchmarks (ProactiveBench, ContextAgentBench, ProAgentBench, PROBE, PARE-Bench, ProPerSim, π-Bench, VibeLifeBench, ProactiveMobile) measure only need prediction, timing, or intervention success. Crucially, correct work can still be harmful: an off-time intervention imposes review cost, competes for the user's compute, and erodes trust. Existing evaluations collapse these failure modes together, so a system designer cannot tell whether an agent failed at doing useful work, at scheduling it, or at preserving trust. The intended audience is agent researchers and harness builders designing always-on personal assistants. Key Idea: The single core insight is that proactivity requires three distinct, jointly-weighted objectives — Task Capability (anticipate needs and execute well), Temporal Allocation (allocate compute across "interaction time" vs. "sleep time" per resource availability and deadlines), and Trust (estimated behaviorally via intervention depth: prepare/suggest/execute) — and that because these are empirically dissociable (TC correlates only r=0.31 with TA and r=0.34 with TR-D), they must be measured separately in dynamic multi-day simulations rather than at single static responses. The 3T idea is a synthesis of Horvitz's mixed-initiative principles, sleep-time compute (Lin et al., 2025), and Madsen & Gregor's five trust constructs, rather than a new algorithmic mechanism. Methodology: The paper has three layers. (1) A formal framework: a weighted objective max over agent designs of λ_TC·S_TC + λ_TA·S_TA + λ_TR·S_TR (Eq. 1), plus a POMDP-like update where a situation representation z_t = R(c_t) feeds a policy a_t ~ π_A(·|z_t, c_t) and context updates c_{t+1} = U(c_t, a_t, o_{t+1}) (Eq. 2); no method for optimizing this objective is given — it is a specification, not an algorithm. (2) A five-dimension design space (task scope, anticipation horizon, activation trigger, processing timing, intervention depth) mapped onto the 3T objectives, with situation modeling (user/environment state) and system modeling (backbone LLM + harness orchestrating scheduling, permissions) as realization requirements. (3) PROACTIVITY-GYM: 10 manually-authored 7–10 day scenarios (124 total tasks) across domains like research, travel, and finance; three personas per scenario (Reviewer/Planner/Operator) with different approval policies; a Qwen 3.8-27B user simulator gated by a deterministic state machine that decides approve/decline/defer; and 23 model–harness configurations (GPT 5.6 Luna/Sol, Claude Sonnet 5/Opus 5, Qwen 3.5 2B/9B/27B, Gemma 4 12B/31B × Codex/Claude Code/OpenClaw), 90 runs per configuration (3 runs × 3 personas × 10 scenarios), reasoning disabled in main runs. Metrics: TC (0–100) mixing rule-based checks (evidence retrieval, required outputs, content constraints) with two LLM-judge components (semantics, completion) averaged over two judges; TA (%) as a strict AND of selecting the urgent task now and explicitly deferring the competing one in one decision window per scenario; TR-D (%) as fraction of tasks matching the persona's expected intervention depth; TR-J (1–5) as judges' ratings of the five trust constructs. Critical design decisions: separating depth agreement (TR-D) from judged trust (TR-J) — well justified by the human study's divergent results; the strict AND scoring of TA — acknowledged by the authors to conflate prioritization failure with failure to verbalize deferral; and persona-gated user simulators — reasonable, though the simulator is a single model whose fidelity is not validated against humans beyond a plausibility rating. Key Results: On the gym (preprint, not peer-reviewed), Claude Opus 5 on OpenClaw leads with TC 67.4 (Table 7 reports 67.38), TA 62.2%, TR-D 50.5%, TR-J 4.15; every other configuration scores below 20% on TA, with most small models near 0%. Within TA components, models select the urgent task (now) 44.3% on average but explicitly defer the competing task only 10.8% of the time — deferral is the bottleneck. TC correlates weakly with TA (r=0.31) and TR-D (r=0.34) but strongly with LLM-judge trust (r=0.70), and raising GPT 5.6-Sol reasoning effort from none to xhigh raises TC 50.0→58.9 while TR-D and TR-J plateau (~51–54%, ~4.0). Harness effects are model-dependent: switching Claude Opus 5 from Claude Code to OpenClaw raises TC by 4.6 and TA by 21.1 points but lowers TR-D by 3.8. LLM judges are insensitive to intervention-depth misalignment (Claude Opus 5 scores 4.72 understandability despite 52.4% TR-D). The 30-participant human study: participants prefer correct outcomes 92.2% of the time and aligned intervention depth 88.3% when content is equal; acceptance of proactive help rises from 26.7% (correct but competing with ongoing work) to 97.8% (sleep-time, even when output needs correction), and 64.4% still prefer sleep-time when immediate help costs only 10 minutes with no resource conflict; trust drops 1.86 points after an aligned→misaligned transition versus +1.27 for the reverse, and in A→M→A sequences trust recovers only to 3.43 from an initial 4.43 despite the final action being rated 4.71 in appropriateness. Judge-model agreement is high in rank (configuration-level r = .993–.980) but differs substantially in absolute calibration (e.g., TA NOW-correct rates .313 vs .574 between judges). Novelty Classification: NEW FORMULATION and NEW DATASET/BENCHMARK. The genuinely novel elements are (a) the joint 3T decomposition with separately operationalized TA and trust metrics in a longitudinal, stateful evaluation, and (b) PROACTIVITY-GYM as the first testbed to score intervention-depth alignment against persona trust state across multi-day simulated interactions. The design space dimensions, the trust constructs, the sleep-time/interaction-time distinction, and the mixed-initiative framing are all standard or directly borrowed (Horvitz 1999, Lin et al. 2025, Kraus et al. 2023, Isbell & Pierce 2005, Madsen & Gregor 2000); the human study is a competent application of established trust-in-automation methodology rather than a new measurement technique. No new method for achieving proactivity is proposed. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations and diagnostics are unusually thorough for a benchmark paper: per-component TC breakdowns (rule-based evidence/output/constraints vs. LLM-judged semantics/completion), now/later/continuation-quality splits for TA, per-construct trust scores, scenario and persona variation, reasoning-effort sweeps, and judge-agreement statistics (Pearson/Spearman, Cohen's κ, MAE across 2,070 trajectories). Three repetitions per scenario-persona pair address run-to-run stochasticity, and bootstrap 95% CIs appear for the human-study figures. However: no significance tests or error bars are reported for the headline model comparisons; all rubrics are authored by the same team that designed the scenarios (Goodhart risk — agents are scored against the authors' own gold criteria, and the TA gold decision pairs are predefined); evaluation depends on LLM-as-judge with demonstrated calibration gaps between the two judges; and the user simulator is a single LLM whose behavioral fidelity to real users is validated only by a 73.3% scenario-plausibility rating from study participants. Code and data are stated to be "planned for release upon publication" — not released at the time of writing; project page: https://harryoh99.github.io/foundations_of_proactive_agents/. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL (a built simulation testbed and evaluation study; no trained model or optimization method is delivered). - Practical: Yes — the gym orchestrates commercially available models and open-source harnesses (Codex, Claude Code, OpenClaw) in isolated environments, so any lab can replicate the setup. - Efficient: Not stated in compute terms; each configuration requires 90 multi-day runs plus dual LLM-judge scoring, which is nontrivial but unquantified, and the premise is that proactive work uses otherwise-idle compute. - Effective: The evidence shows current agents fail at TA and TR-D (all but Claude Opus 5 below 20% TA), which supports the diagnostic claim, but no intervention is shown to improve 3T performance — the testbed detects the problem without demonstrating a solution. - Scalable: Untested and acknowledged as limited: TA evaluation covers one two-task decision window per scenario, scenarios are 7–10 days with simplified resource models, and the authors state that wall-clock, longer-horizon, and real-workflow evaluation is future work. Deliverable: a benchmark/testbed artifact plus measurement protocol (code and data promised at publication); no trained model, library, or method ships with the paper. Strengths: - The 3T decomposition is genuinely useful framing: the empirical dissociation (TC↔TA r=0.31, TC↔TR-D r=0.34, but TC↔TR-J r=0.70) is a real finding showing that existing task-centric evaluations cannot diagnose scheduling and trust failures. - The human study is the paper's strongest evidence and is well designed for its purpose: paired comparisons isolating TA and TR effects, longitudinal week-long trust trajectories with 20,000-sample bootstrap CIs, and the asymmetric trust-loss result (−1.86 vs +1.27; incomplete A→M→A recovery to 3.43 from 4.43) quantifies a phenomenon LLM judges demonstrably miss. - The methodological honesty of the metrics: the authors separate behavioral depth agreement (TR-D) from judged trust (TR-J) and then show LLM judges are poor proxies for human trust penalties — an important negative result for the LLM-as-judge literature. - Coverage analysis (Table 2) mapping 16 prior systems/benchmarks against 3T is a substantive synthesis that positions the field usefully for the thematic grouper. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state the gym has "simplified resource constraints and user models," that TA evaluation is a starting point limited to single decision windows (variable task durations, changing compute budgets, and preemption are future work), that TR-J ratings "estimate perceived interaction quality" rather than measuring human psychological trust directly, and that longer-term real-world evaluation is needed (Limitation & Future Work; App. H). The AI-use statement discloses LLM-generated synthetic data for the user simulator. This is direct confrontation of limitations rather than minimization — a credibility positive — though the framing of PROACTIVITY-GYM as "initial" implicitly concedes that the headline quantitative gaps may not transfer to messier settings. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - Construct validity of TR-D: intervention depth is treated as a behavioral proxy for trust, but the paper never validates that depth agreement actually predicts trust for real users — the human study shows trust responds to alignment, not that alignment is the right causal lever in deployment. - TA is scored on a single engineered decision window per scenario with a strict AND rule; the authors admit low TA "does not necessarily mean that the agent selected the wrong priority," yet headline figures ("all models below 20% TA") are reported without this caveat — the metric partially measures whether agents verbalize "later," which harness prompts could trivially fix. - Benchmark authoring and evaluation rubrics come from the same small team with LLM-assisted refinement; no inter-annotator agreement for the human-authored rubrics or gold TA pairs is reported. - The 30 participants are Korean-speaking students and professionals in adjacent fields (compensated KRW 10,000) — a narrow, WEIRD-adjacent sample for claims about trust dynamics; the trust-trajectory scenarios are vignettes read in 40–60 minutes, not lived experience with a real agent. - No baseline method or harness modification is attempted despite the paper's own design space (Sec. 4.2) suggesting concrete mechanisms (pending-task tracking, scheduling, permission control) — the natural experiment of whether any 3T-aware intervention helps is left entirely to future work. - Judge-calibration deltas (e.g., TA NOW-correct rates differing by 26 points between judges) mean absolute scores like "51.7% TA" carry judge-dependent uncertainty the paper does not propagate into its conclusions. Bottom Line: This is a worthwhile read for agent-benchmark builders and HCI-leaning agent researchers because the 3T decomposition, the trust-loss asymmetry findings, and the demonstration that LLM judges misjudge trust are genuinely load-bearing; practitioners looking for a method to make agents proactive will find principles and a testbed here but no solution, and the benchmark's narrow TA windows and unreleased code mean its numbers should be treated as directional rather than definitive.

My FAULT: Self-Diagnosis as Credit Assignment in Self-Evolving Agentic Reinforcement Learning

Y Zhu, Q Liu, W Qiao, X Ren, W Xu, W Li, W Wang… · arxiv.org · long-horizon RL for agents - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces FAULT, a credit-assignment method for agentic RL that converts verified self-diagnosed errors into explicit step-level penalties, with each error type's cost learned from terminal outcomes rather than hand-specified. - Why it's important: Group-relative agentic RL (GRPO-style) loses all learning signal when rollouts of the same task share an outcome — 59–64% of groups in their ALFWorld runs — and broadcasts trajectory-level advantage to every step, so long-horizon agents cannot learn which specific decision caused a failure. - How it does it: It separates error localization from error valuation: a shared actor/diagnoser produces structured error records (class, step, verbatim quote) that are mechanically verified by quote-matching, while relative error prices are fit by conditional logit (with Firth small-sample correction) regressing within-task terminal outcomes on verified error rates, then a bounded penalty budget is redistributed across diagnosed steps inside a GiGPO-style dual-channel advantage. - The good: The mechanism analysis is unusually thorough: on ALFWorld, signal coverage rises from 41% (GRPO) and 72% (GiGPO) to 95% of groups, decisive-step localization MRR reaches 0.494 versus 0.303 (GiGPO) and 0.266 (random), and diag-SFT-controlled baselines isolate the RL-stage gains (e.g., +10.4 points over GiGPO (diag-SFT) on ALFWorld at 4B). - The missing: Every result comes from a single training run per configuration with no seeds, error bars, or significance tests; several ablations are admittedly confounded ('not matched controls'); and the headline coverage comparison measures budgets for FAULT but advantages for baselines, which the authors concede is a 'contrast proxy, not a common-scale' quantity. - Read it or not: Read it if you work on agentic RL credit assignment or process rewards — the localization-from-valuation separation and the econometric pricing estimator are genuinely reusable ideas — skip it if you only need another benchmark-topping agent recipe, since absolute gains over the strongest baseline (SEED) are 0.7–6.7 points on single seeds.
Why this rank
Scored using the Empirical profile. Novelty (74) and Non-Obviousness (72) are the drivers — the localization/valuation separation and the conditional-logit/Firth pricing estimator imported from econometrics are genuinely reusable, non-obvious ideas — and Completeness (74) is a credibility positive thanks to exceptionally precise self-auditing (failed quality gates, confounded ablations, proxy metrics all disclosed). But Rigor (58) is materially reduced by single-run results with no seeds anywhere, ablations the authors admit are 'not matched controls', and an asymmetric coverage comparison; Resilience (55) falls because the 0.7–6.7 point margins over the strongest baseline are within plausible single-run RL variance and the title's 'self-evolving' mechanism is never cleanly isolated. Impact (62) reflects the released code, prompts, and raw fits. Weighted composite: 0.20*74 + 0.25*58 + 0.15*72 + 0.15*74 + 0.15*55 + 0.10*62 ≈ 66.

Problem & Motivation: Practitioners training LLM agents with reinforcement learning on multi-step interactive tasks (embodied households, web shopping, tool-augmented QA) rely on terminal outcome rewards because final outcomes are easy to verify while intermediate decisions are not. Two credit-assignment failures follow: (1) in group-relative methods like GRPO, when all G rollouts of a task succeed or all fail, normalized advantages vanish and the group contributes no gradient — and such same-outcome groups constituted 59–64% of ALFWorld training groups in the authors' preliminary runs, rising toward 75% as training progresses; (2) even in mixed groups, the trajectory-level advantage is identical across all steps, so a single decisive mistake is not distinguished from otherwise reasonable actions. Natural-language reflection/diagnosis approaches supply richer process information but remain descriptive — their error claims are unverifiable and carry no quantitative weight. The paper targets the gap between these two lines: process signals that are both trustworthy (verifiable localization) and calibrated (outcome-grounded relative importance). Key Idea: Separate error localization from error valuation. Self-diagnosis answers only 'what went wrong and where' as structured, mechanically checkable records (error class from a frozen taxonomy, step number, verbatim quote matched against the cited step's text); terminal outcomes answer 'how much does each error type cost' by fitting outcome-association coefficients βk over verified error rates via a conditional (within-task) likelihood that removes task difficulty intercepts — a conditional logit with Firth correction from econometrics. Negative coefficients become relative prices; a per-trajectory penalty budget (capped below the success–failure reward gap so successes always outrank failures) is split across diagnosed steps proportional to priced localization weights and folded into a GiGPO-style dual-channel advantage. Because priced error rates differ even among same-outcome rollouts, all-fail and most all-success groups regain a learning signal. Methodology: Two-stage pipeline. Stage I (cold start): a teacher model (GPT-5.6 Sol) diagnoses initial-policy trajectories; entries pass verification (valid taxonomy class, valid step, verbatim case-sensitive quote match); an LLM induction pass freezes a two-level taxonomy (8 L1 families, 25 L2 mechanisms for ALFWorld, K=20 priced classes); a diagnosis-SFT loss (Eq. 2) trains a shared actor/diagnoser on verified diagnoses; initial prices come from a conditional logit fit with a length covariate, Firth log-determinant correction, and shrinkage (Eq. 14), or group-centered ridge for graded rewards (Eq. 16). Stage II (self-evolving RL): per batch, the frozen policy samples G=8 rollouts and M=3 self-diagnoses per trajectory; entries are verified and aggregated into error-rate vectors (Eq. 9); a warm-up-plus-cosine penalty strength λu scales a clipped error score into a budget P=min(λuS, ηΔR) with η=0.9 (Eq. 23); the budget is conserved-split across steps proportional to price-weighted localization counts with a 1.5× boost to the earliest penalized step (Eq. 25); dual-channel advantages (episode and anchor-state step channels, Eqs. 6–7) drive a clipped PPO objective with dual clipping and low-variance KL (Eq. 8). Diagnosis tokens receive no policy gradient, preventing the diagnoser from learning to suppress error reports. Prices are refit every 10 updates from a 50-update sliding window via the same conditional likelihood, with a sign-gated EMA update (Eq. 20). Two propositions with proofs (order preservation under the cap; advantage structure in same-outcome groups) are provided. Critical design decisions: (a) quote-based verification is cheap but verifies existence, not semantic correctness of the error claim — partially justified, and the authors concede the initial diagnoser's step localization (0.48 accuracy at ±2 tolerance) misses their own 0.60 quality bar; (b) the η=0.9 cap provably preserves success–failure ordering (Proposition 1) — well-justified and clean; (c) diagnosis rate x=n/T rather than count avoids rewarding short trajectories — reasonable but the first-error boost term reintroduces a 1/T dependence. Key Results: On ALFWorld (134 unseen tasks) with Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507, FAULT reaches 91.0% success versus SEED 84.3%, GiGPO 73.9%, GRPO 49.3%, vanilla 19.4%; at Qwen3-1.7B, 68.7% versus SEED 65.7%. On WebShop, FAULT scores 88.5 (4B) and 87.5 (1.7B) task score versus SEED 86.2/86.8, though SEED leads strict purchase success by 2.7 and 3.9 points — a comparison the authors admit is confounded because FAULT trains on the graded score. On Search-based QA, FAULT is slightly behind SEED (43.8 vs 44.4 at 4B; tied 38.9 at 1.7B). Mechanism results: signal coverage 95.1% (FAULT) vs 72.5% (GiGPO) and 41.4% (GRPO); decisive-step MRR 0.494 vs 0.303 (GiGPO) and 0.266 (random), with 82/300 exact top-1 matches; credit entropy 0.29 vs 0.72 (GiGPO) and 0.91 (GRPO); pooled signal-retention index 0.821 vs ~0.42 for both baselines. Ablations on ALFWorld 4B: removing online pricing costs only 1.4 points (91.0→89.6), constant λ costs 11.9, fixed judge 8.2, GRPO+trajectory-level diagnostic penalty 13.4 — but the authors state these variants 'differ in more than their named components' and the runs are 'not matched controls.' Diagnostic quality: teacher verification retains 95.4% of mentions; the SFT diagnoser reaches L1 precision 0.81/recall 0.56 (above thresholds) but dominant-error step accuracy 0.48 and off-table rate 0.31 both fail their own quality gates. Tested scale is standard: 1.7B/4B models, 160 RL updates, 16 tasks × 8 rollouts per batch; baselines GRPO, GiGPO (NeurIPS 2025) and SEED are current and, with the diag-SFT controls, reasonably strong. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD with an EMPIRICAL FINDING component. The genuinely novel move is converting verified natural-language self-diagnoses into quantitative step-level credit via outcome-fitted error prices (a conditional-logit/Firth estimator imported from econometrics), decoupling localization from valuation so same-outcome groups regain signal. The surrounding machinery — GiGPO-style anchor-state step channels, PPO clipping, diagnosis SFT — is a competent assembly of existing techniques, and the problem (same-outcome group collapse in GRPO) is already documented; the pricing mechanism, not the setting, is the contribution. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations exist but are explicitly confounded: the fixed-judge variant also changes λ and other settings, and the authors flag that the ablations 'assess recorded design variants rather than isolating localization, pricing or the judge one factor at a time.' No multi-seed runs, error bars, or significance tests anywhere — Appendix C.2 states each result is one training run and differences are point estimates. The code repository is released (github.com/SKYLENAGE-AI/FAULT_Agentic_RL) with prompts and hyperparameters (Table 4) documented in unusual detail. Two methodological concerns deserve flags: (1) Goodhart-adjacent measurement asymmetry — the headline 95%/72%/41% coverage numbers use trajectory diagnostic scores for FAULT but optimizer advantages for baselines, which the authors themselves call 'a contrast proxy, not a common-scale advantage estimate'; (2) the localization gold standard is a blind LLM judge (Qwen3.8-Max) with only a 48-trajectory relabel-agreement check (75% within one step), not human or counterfactual verification. To the authors' credit, they repeatedly and precisely qualify their own claims (propositions 'concern advantage contrast, not semantic correctness'; coefficients are 'predictive associations, not causal effects'), and the diag-SFT-controlled baselines are a real attempt to separate cold-start from RL gains. This is a preprint (arXiv, dated October 2026 in the text). Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL (trains and evaluates LLM agents; also ships a reusable method). Practical: Runs on Qwen3-1.7B/4B backbones with standard PPO-style RL infrastructure, but the cold start requires a frontier commercial API (GPT-5.6 Sol) for teacher diagnosis, adding per-benchmark setup cost. Efficient: Adds 3 self-diagnoses per trajectory per batch plus periodic L-BFGS-B refits on ≤50-update windows — a modest overhead relative to rollout generation, though total teacher/cold-start cost is not quantified. Effective: The evidence shows it improves step-level signal availability and localization and transfers to higher task success on two long-horizon benchmarks, but the link from diagnostic-penalty mechanism to final success rests on single-seed point estimates and partly confounded ablations; effectiveness on the shortest-horizon benchmark is nil-to-negative, consistent with (and honestly reported as) the length-dependence of the mechanism. Scalable: Only claimed implicitly — the pricing fit scales with class count K and window size, but nothing beyond 4B/30-step tasks is tested, and diagnosis quality gates (off-table rate 0.31, step accuracy 0.48 below the authors' own thresholds) could worsen on longer, messier trajectories. Delivers a software artifact (code, prompts, hyperparameters, raw fits released); no trained model weights mentioned. Strengths: - The localization/valuation separation is a real conceptual contribution: it converts unverifiable free-text reflection into mechanically checkable records while keeping terminal outcomes as the only trusted supervision, directly addressing the reward-hacking risk of learned process rewards. - The conditional-logit-with-Firth-correction pricing estimator is a genuinely non-obvious import: conditioning on within-group success counts removes task-difficulty intercepts without estimating them, and the Firth correction + shrinkage + sign-gated EMA shows unusual statistical care for this literature. - The evaluation goes beyond end-task scores to measure the mechanism itself (signal coverage, MRR against a blind judge, credit entropy, no-op targeting at 3.67× uniform vs 0.48×/0.57× for baselines), and includes diag-SFT-controlled GRPO/GiGPO runs that credibly isolate the RL-stage contribution (+10.4 points over GiGPO (diag-SFT) on ALFWorld 4B). - Unusually candid self-auditing: the paper reports that its own diagnoser fails two of its four pre-registered quality gates, that ablations are unmatched, that its coverage metric is an asymmetric proxy, and that WebShop strict-success comparisons are reward-confounded. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors explicitly state: (1) initial self-diagnoser step localization (0.48 at ±2-step tolerance) and off-table rate (0.31) fall below their own acceptance thresholds; (2) verification checks quotes and steps but 'is not an independent judgment of semantic correctness'; (3) ablation variants 'differ in more than their named components' and are 'not matched controls'; (4) all results are single-run point estimates without significance claims; (5) LLM-judge labels are model judgments, not human or counterfactual ground truth; (6) the WebShop strict-success comparison is confounded by FAULT's graded training reward; (7) fitted prices are associations, not causal error costs; (8) gains concentrate on long-horizon tasks and shrink or reverse on 4-step QA. This is a credibility positive — the limitations are confronted directly and precisely rather than minimized. Analyst-Identified Gaps: (1) No multi-seed replication anywhere: the headline margins over SEED (6.7 points ALFWorld, 0.7 WebShop score at 4B; 1.7B margins of 1.7–3.0) are within plausible single-run variance for RL, so the practical claim over the strongest baseline is not established. (2) The 95%-vs-41%-vs-72% coverage headline compares incomparable quantities (budget range vs advantage range), and the applied-budget version of FAULT's own coverage drops to 84.6% and to 20% in the final annealed window — the strongest-sounding number is the least commensurable one. (3) Teacher dependence is unexamined: cost, latency, and diagnosis-quality sensitivity to the GPT-5.6 Sol teacher are unreported, and the frozen taxonomy covers only 90.6% of accepted mentions, so ~9% of errors fall outside the priced system with no analysis of what those errors cost. (4) The fixed-judge ablation (8.2-point drop) is the only evidence that the co-evolving diagnoser matters, yet it is confounded with the constant-λ schedule, so the central 'self-evolving' claim — the paper's title mechanism — is never cleanly isolated. (5) All three benchmarks are text-based with ≤30-step horizons; the motivation invokes long-horizon credit assignment, but nothing tests genuinely long horizons (50+ steps) or visual/multimodal environments where diagnosis is harder. (6) No comparison against process-reward-model baselines (e.g., learned PRMs or Monte Carlo step scorers), so the claim that diagnosis-anchored credit beats numerical process rewards is asserted via related-work argument, not measured. Bottom Line: A methodologically careful and unusually honest paper whose localization-from-valuation trick is a real and reusable advance in agentic credit assignment, but whose practical superiority over SEED rests on single-seed margins of 0.7–6.7 points with confounded ablations — read it for the mechanism and the measurement practices, not for a proven new default recipe.

Certificate-Carrying Patch Promotion: Verifier-First Gates for AI-Generated Repository Changes

D Erman · openreview.net · specification to code with formal verifications - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces a typed 'certificate-carrying patch promotion' contract in which trusted repository policy derives the mandatory obligation set for an AI-generated patch from an authenticated cumulative diff against a fixed anchor, and a fail-closed gate admits the patch only when every obligation carries evidence of sufficient scope from a sound, independent verifier. - Why it's important: Passing a build and test suite is the de facto acceptance bar for AI-generated patches (e.g., on SWE-bench-style workflows), but it silently misses forbidden dependencies, provenance breaks, scope-limited evidence, and non-decomposable cross-file invariants — gaps that become attack surface as agents write repository-scale changes. - How it does it: The core move is computing the required obligation set D_B(x) = Φ(F_B(x)) from a fixed trusted anchor rather than from generator metadata or per-step diffs, which makes the requirement set path-independent and closes split-edit and under-declaration evasions. - The good: The paper is unusually honest about its own epistemics: it proves its properties relative to explicitly stated trust assumptions, gives an exact two-file counterexample where step-local discovery fails, labels its 16/16 gate result as a deterministic regression test rather than a benchmark win, and ships an independent replay implementation that recomputes the same confusion matrices. - The missing: There is no evaluation on real repositories or real agent-generated patches — the 16 cases were authored by the same authors to exercise each gate branch (so the perfect score is circular by construction), and the paper never demonstrates the contract on SWE-bench or any non-synthetic workload despite citing SWE-bench as the motivating setting. - Read it or not: Worth reading if you design CI admission, supply-chain attestation, or agent-safety gates and want a crisp vocabulary for scope/trust boundaries; skip it if you want empirical evidence that any of this improves real-world code-agent safety — that study does not exist here.
Why this rank
Scored using Systems profile. Practical Impact (55) is capped by the evaluation's circularity — the 16-case suite is self-authored and no real agent patches or OPA/Sigstore baseline are tested — though the dependency-free checker and independent replay script do ship. Rigor (55) is similarly limited by zero out-of-sample evidence despite strong reproducibility discipline. Completeness (72) and Resilience (75) benefit from exceptional limitation disclosure, and Novelty (75) anchors the contribution in a genuine new formulation (anchored path-independence, four-way gate separation). Weighted composite: 0.15*75 + 0.15*55 + 0.10*70 + 0.15*72 + 0.15*75 + 0.30*55 = 65.
