Problem & Motivation: Robotic control policies built on video-generation backbones (world action models) can inherit visual-dynamics priors from large action-free video corpora, addressing the data hunger of VLAs that rely on expensive robot demonstrations. The core dilemma: full-imagination WAMs (e.g., DreamZero) condition actions on dense generated rollouts, which costs many denoising passes through a multi-billion-parameter video backbone per action chunk; zero-imagination and single-frame WAMs (FastWAM, ImageWAM) are fast but provide no explicit intermediate-progress guidance, hurting long-horizon and OOD execution. Practitioners building closed-loop robot policies need visual foresight that is both informative and cheap enough for real-time replanning. Key Idea: Parameterize the visual future as k sparse sub-goal frames indexed by normalized progress r ∈ [0,1] relative to the current observation (r=0 now, r=1 trajectory end), and train the video expert to predict these slots via flow matching with the progress value injected as an additive modulation on the diffusion timestep embedding — so one model, trained with random k ∈ {1,...,K_max}, can generate any number of sub-goals at any requested progress positions at inference, all in a single cached forward pass. Final-goal prediction is the special case k=1, r=1. Methodology: The system is a mixture-of-transformers on Wan2.2-TI2V-5B with a video expert and a lightweight diffusion action expert, trained with a combined flow-matching objective L = λ_video·L_video + λ_sub·L_sub + λ_act·L_act (all weights 1.0), where video and action branches use independent timesteps. The latent sequence is [current frame X0 | clip transitions X | sub-goals G]; sub-goal frames are VAE-encoded ground-truth future frames selected at τ(r_i) along the demonstration. Attention is structured: sub-goals attend bidirectionally among themselves and to X0; transitions condition on X0 and G; action tokens attend to {X0, G} but the video expert never attends to actions (preserving the pretrained generative prior). Training is two-stage: (1) video-only pretraining on action-free robot/egocentric video (DROID/AgiBot/OpenX mix, 60/30/10; 128 H100s, ~79k steps, ~2×10⁷ clips) learning clip and sub-goal prediction; (2) joint fine-tuning on task demonstrations. Critical design decisions: (i) relative (re-anchored) progress rather than absolute time — justified by the horizon ablation showing near schedules (r ∈ [0.1, 0.5]) beat far ones (75.7% vs 68.4% OOD); (ii) KV-cache single-pass sub-goal inference instead of joint denoising — justified by Table 12 showing identical OOD SR at 86.7% less compute; (iii) asymmetric attention to protect the video prior — motivated by prior MoT WAMs, ablated only indirectly via ProWAM-Light (85.8% → 80.3% OOD without explicit sub-goals). Key Results: On LIBERO-Plus (zero-shot perturbations), ProWAM reaches 85.8% vs 83.1% for the best prior WAM (Being-H0.7) and 80.5% for the best VLA (ABot-M0); in-domain LIBERO is saturated (~98.8%). On randomized RoboTwin (trained only on 2,500 clean demos), 75.7% vs 55.7% for MV-WAM and 6.3% for FastWAM — a +20.0 absolute gain over the strongest WAM. On RoboCasa365, 48.1% overall / 18.2% Composite-Unseen, placing 4th on the leaderboard behind Paimon-0 (58.1%), Xiaomi-Robotics-1 (57.4%), and Phasor-m7 (56.8%) — methods of unstated provenance. Zero-shot real-world on a Franka FR3 using DROID training: 70.0% average over 4 tasks vs 55.0% for DreamZero (14B) and 50.0% for π0.5 (3B), with 100% on spatial placement. Efficiency: 18.7 TFLOPs / 313 ms per 16-action chunk vs 115.5 TFLOPs / 581 ms for naive joint denoising, benchmarked on one H100. Baselines are current (2024–2026 VLA/WAM literature), and the k=1 configuration (73.8% OOD at 15.2 TFLOPs) crushes FastWAM (6.3% at 13.2 TFLOPs) at comparable cost. Surprising finding: sub-goals from a single denoising step suffice — photorealism is unnecessary for control, consistent with prior single-frame WAM observations. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD (with an EMPIRICAL FINDING component). The genuinely novel element is the progress-indexed sparse sub-goal parameterization embedded natively in the WAM's video pathway with progress-conditioned adaLN modulation and variable-k training — it occupies a previously empty point on the imagination spectrum (between ImageWAM's single endpoint and full dense rollouts) without an external planner. The remaining machinery (flow matching, mixture-of-transformers, asymmetric attention, KV caching, two-stage pretraining-then-finetuning, hierarchical sub-goals) is a competent assembly of established techniques. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are present and informative: sub-goal count k (stable for k∈[1,3], peak at k=4 with only +3.5 TFLOPs), sub-goal horizon (Near > Mid > Far, monotonic 68.4→70.2→75.7%), KV-cache depth (KV-1/KV-3/KV-10 vs Joint-10), and the ProWAM-Light no-sub-goal control (isolating the sub-goal's contribution: −5.5 OOD). A pilot study (Appendix A) separately validates final-goal prediction across two WAM paradigms and three data fractions. However: no seeds, error bars, or significance tests are reported anywhere; simulation run counts are stated (50–100 trials/task) but real-world evaluation is 5 trials/task across only 4 tasks; the ProWAM-Base vs ProWAM comparison (80.3% vs 85.8% LIBERO-Plus OOD) involves a single training difference with no variance estimate. No code or weights release is mentioned — only a project page. Methodological concern: on RoboTwin, the video expert was trained with action-free videos from both clean AND randomized scenes, so the headline OOD number (75.7%) partially reflects visual-domain exposure the action-supervised baselines may not have had; the authors state this framing explicitly, which mitigates but does not eliminate it. The RoboCasa365 comparisons are leaderboard submissions of unknown training data/compute. Internal inconsistency: the abstract says "ranking 4th overall" on RoboCasa365 while Section 4.2 claims "ranks second overall" — the table supports 4th. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (with a SYSTEMS artifact — a trained policy deployed on real hardware). - Practical: Runs on a single H100 for inference and required 128 H100s for pretraining — within reach of well-funded labs but not small academic groups for the full pipeline; the ProWAM-Base variant (skip pretraining) is far cheaper. - Efficient: 15.1–18.7 TFLOPs and 313 ms per replanning step is comparable to FastWAM/ImageWAM and ~6× cheaper than naive joint denoising, a genuine advance over full-imagination WAMs. - Effective: Strong evidence on OOD simulation benchmarks and a real zero-shot result, but the real-world evidence base (20 trials) is thin and the Composite-Unseen RoboCasa365 number (18.2%) shows the method still trails proprietary leaders on long-horizon compositional generalization. - Scalable: Not tested beyond a 5B backbone; the authors concede that scaling behavior of backbone and pretraining corpus is unexplored, and sub-goal schedule selection is manual. The work stops at paper-plus-project-page form; no library, CLI, dataset, or model weights are stated as released. Strengths: - The progress-indexed sub-goal parameterization is a clean, general formulation: FGP, ImageWAM-style endpoint prediction, and multi-milestone planning are all special cases of one trained model, and k becomes an inference-time knob rather than a retraining decision. - The efficiency result is decisive and well-isolated: identical OOD success (85.8%) with 86.7% less compute by caching KV features after one video-expert pass, with an explicit control (ProWAM-Light) showing explicit sub-goal conditioning — not just backbone knowledge — drives the OOD gain. - The paper is unusually candid about its own evidence structure: the RoboTwin OOD protocol's video-pretraining caveat is stated openly, the pilot study motivated FGP with data-fraction sweeps, and the failure analysis (blurred sub-goal geometry preceding premature release) connects predicted plans to execution failures. - The near-vs-far horizon ablation yields a non-obvious actionable insight: nearer sub-goals give tighter grounding (+7.3 OOD), which contradicts the intuition that long-horizon planning needs distant targets. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors explicitly list (Appendix F): (1) the inference sub-goal schedule (k and progress values) is manually specified per benchmark rather than learned or adaptive; (2) model and pretraining scale are unexplored due to compute constraints; (3) tested task horizons and dexterity are limited relative to extended real-world deployment. They also openly flag that LIBERO in-domain saturation (~99%) makes it non-discriminative, and they disclose the RoboTwin video-data asymmetry. This is a direct, non-minimizing limitations section — a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - Statistical rigor: zero seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests across all tables; several headline margins (85.8% vs 83.1% LIBERO-Plus) are within plausible run-to-run noise given no variance is reported, while the authors themselves note LIBERO differences fall "within run-to-run noise." - Real-world evidence is thin: 4 tasks × 5 trials, with success criteria scored by the authors' own protocol; per-task numbers for the real-world table are not broken out in the main text shown. - The RoboCasa365 ranking claim is internally inconsistent (abstract: 4th; Section 4.2 text: 2nd; table: 4th), and the top-three leaderboard methods are not characterized in terms of architecture, data, or compute, so the comparison's meaning is unclear. - No ablation isolates the asymmetric attention mask or the progress-modulation mechanism itself (vs. simply conditioning on r as an input token); the design is justified by analogy, not by component-wise evidence. - No code or weight release is stated, which materially limits reproducibility of a system with many unstated-but-critical details (composite view layouts, per-benchmark schedules). - The dream of "scales naturally via action-free video pretraining" is tested with a single corpus mix and a single backbone; no data-scaling curve for the pretraining stage is provided. Bottom Line: A practitioner in robot learning or world modeling should read this: the progress-indexed sub-goal formulation and the demonstrated single-pass KV-cached inference are practical, reusable ideas that meaningfully advance the efficiency–foresight trade-off for WAMs, even though the missing statistical rigor, thin real-world evaluation, and unreleased code mean the headline numbers deserve moderate confidence.

Show full analysis
Problem & Motivation: Time-series practitioners face heterogeneous requests from a single system: point/probabilistic forecasting from history, forecasting conditioned on textual context describing interventions or constraints absent from the data, and language-based temporal reasoning (anomaly identification, series comparison, causal questions). These have been served by disjoint model families — numerical time-series foundation models (TSFMs like Chronos-2, TimesFM, Toto) give strong forecasts but accept no text; time-series language models (TSLMs like OpenTSLM, ChatTS) handle context and reasoning but lag numerically. Existing generalist temporal models (UniTS, TsLLM, TimeOmni) broaden task coverage but the paper argues (and its ablations partially confirm) that breadth usually comes at the cost of specialist performance. The gap addressed is unification without dilution. Key Idea: Train each temporal capability as a separate frozen LoRA expert over a shared frozen backbone with its own data and objective, then learn only a lightweight request-level controller that mixes the frozen parameter updates (π-weighted LoRA composition, one mixture shared across all adapted layers) and routes to either a numerical forecast-decoder head or the language-model head. The aggregation expert adds a second layer to the trick: instead of forecasting natively, it exposes an XGBoost-weighted ensemble of 8 foundation models blended with the public Toto-FnF 10-model ensemble (13 unique candidates) as a continuous "reference forecast" token encoding, and the backbone learns only a bounded residual correction d_t with |d_t| ≤ ½ and a disagreement gate — a zero-initialized editor that can never degrade far below the strong reference ensemble. Methodology: Four training phases: (1) fit the numerical ensemble — XGBoost (1,200 rounds, depth 10) predicts per-candidate CRPS ranks over 576,920 windows from GIFT-train, BOOM, RMISC, LOTSA, and UTSD-1G; pooled CDFs are blended with Toto-FnF at a learned scalar α ≈ 0.386; (2) train the aggregation expert (LoRA rank 4) on 4,096 GIFT-train windows with a weighted SmoothL1 loss on normalized corrections plus a squared-edit penalty, using ten-fold cross-fitting to construct out-of-fold reference forecasts; (3) train native forecasting (rank 32, 20,000 examples, forward-KL-regularized cross-entropy) and temporal analysis (rank 16, 12,000 examples, forward+reverse KL) adapters; (4) freeze everything and fit a linear controller (h = (1−α)h_text + αh_full → softmax over three experts) on 1,000 examples with per-capability prediction losses plus a numerical-vs-textual format loss. The backbone stays frozen throughout; total trainable parameters are LoRA adapters, encoder/decoder, and a linear map. Critical design decisions: (a) request-level (not per-layer) mixture weights, borrowed from X-LoRA — justified by simplicity but limits expressiveness; (b) the bounded-correction editor that preserves quantile ordering and only shifts location — well-motivated for calibration safety; (c) the rank-32 (not rank-52) joint-training baseline — explicitly and carefully justified against a capacity-expansion confound. Key Results: On GIFT-Eval (97 cells, 371,330 windows, 134-entry recomputed roster), TeeMoE achieves a mean MASE rank of 19.990, third behind STRIDE + Synapse (15.412) and EXAONE Forecast Agent (19.928), and ahead of TimesFM-3 (29.216), Chronos-2 (49.665), and Toto-2.0-2.5B (46.062). On Context is Key (355 instances, 71 task types), it reaches RCRPS 0.115, behind only Gemini-2.5-Pro direct prompting (0.108) and Claude-Sonnet-4.5 + Chronos-Large CorDP (0.110), and well ahead of locally evaluated TSLMs (ChatTS-14B 0.322, TS-Reasoner-7B 0.374) and history-only numerical ensembles (0.283–0.292). On TimeSeriesExam v1.1 (746 questions) it leads with 78.552% vs GPT-oss-120B hybrid at 78.000%. At ~40B total parameters it outperforms Llama-3.1-405B on CiK and GPT-oss-120B on TSE. The most informative results are the ablations: top-1 routing nearly matches soft composition (CiK RCRPS 0.123 vs 0.115), equal-weight adapters slightly beat learned routing on GIFT, composition improves TSE accuracy over the analysis expert alone by only 0.134pp, and modular training costs 30.756 vs 58.657 H100-hours for the joint recipe. The benchmark scale is standard (GIFT-Eval is the de facto forecasting leaderboard); no stress-scale testing beyond these panels. Novelty Classification: NEW SYSTEM/TOOL with a secondary NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING. The genuinely novel elements are (a) the first MoE-composed generalist TSLM spanning forecasting, contextual prediction, and reasoning, and (b) the demonstration that independently trained specialists with different objectives and schedules can be composed without a shared recipe. However, the ingredients are standard: LoRA-library composition and routing near-oracle selection comes from Ostapenko et al. (2024), the two-pass request-level gating from X-LoRA, forecast combination from FFORMA/Synapse/CastStar, and the expert-refines-ensemble interface extends OpenTSLM's Chronos-2 encoder idea. The empirical finding that modular training is cheaper and better-balanced than joint training is valuable but confirms expectations from the adapter-fusion literature. Rigor & Reproducibility: Rigor is high on protocol transparency but has notable gaps. Ablations directly target which components matter (individual experts, top-1/equal/full-strength mixtures, joint training, ensemble pooling vs refinement) and are honestly reported — several ablations beat the full system on individual metrics. No error bars, multiple seeds, or significance tests are reported anywhere; given that composition improves TSE by 0.134pp over the analysis expert alone, some margins are likely within noise. Code is on GitHub (github.com/OpenTSLM/OpenTSLM-TeeMoE) and checkpoints on Hugging Face, with detailed training recipes, source manifests, and pinned leaderboard rosters. The authors audit train–test leakage, cross-fit the editor's references, and meticulously document excluded comparisons (Tables 8–9). Methodological concerns: (1) the aggregation expert and reference blend are fitted on the GIFT training split and evaluated on GIFT-Eval test cells — permissible, but it gives TeeMoE supervised exposure to the benchmark distribution that zero-shot TSFM baselines lack, and the GIFT gain over the unedited reference blend (rank 20.660 → 19.990) is small; (2) GIFT comparisons with TSLM competitors are skipped via a predeclared 1,000-H100-hour OOT budget, so the "top-three" placement partially rests on which competitors could afford to run; (3) several published CiK/TSE numbers come from proprietary vendor models under their own reported settings. No evidence of Goodhart-style benchmark fitting in the native or analysis experts, though CiK training sources and evaluation were audited. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL/SYSTEMS (a built, released system evaluated on public benchmarks). - Practical: Runs on 8×H100 80GB for training (~130 GPU-hours total for the composed model including caches), but inference depends on 13 external foundation-model forecasts plus a 27B backbone, so the numerical path is a heavy multi-model pipeline. - Efficient: Modular training is ~1.9× cheaper than the joint baseline (30.756 vs 58.657 H100-hours), and expert-plus-controller revision avoids full retraining; per-request cost includes two backbone passes plus ensemble inference, which is substantially costlier than any single TSFM. - Effective: Evidence supports all three capabilities at near-specialist level on the three benchmarks, but these are proxy panels; the authors concede that alternating forecast-then-revise workflows are untested. - Scalable: Not tested at 10× scale; the OOT budget analysis actually shows that scaling this token-generation approach to GIFT-sized workloads costs other TSLMs 35,000–500,000 projected H100-hours, and TeeMoE's own native path was among the profiled-expensive configurations — deployment economics at scale are unproven. The work delivers a concrete software artifact: code, checkpoints, training/evaluation workflows, and cached forecast infrastructure. Strengths: - The composition-vs-joint-training comparison is the paper's real intellectual contribution: a carefully matched joint baseline (rank-32 width-matching argument, inherited optimization scale, matched training exposure) showing modular training wins on all three benchmarks while costing roughly half as much — this is a transferable finding for multi-capability LLM systems generally, not just time series. - The bounded-residual aggregation design (zero-initialized editor, disagreement gate, quantile-order-preserving shifts) is a disciplined way to attach a language model to a strong numerical ensemble such that it can only help — Table 5 confirms refinement improves the already-strong blend (rank 20.660 → 19.990). - Evaluation hygiene is well above field norms: pinned 134-entry leaderboard roster recomputation, ten-fold cross-fitting of reference forecasts, leakage audits, explicit documentation of every excluded comparison and why, and reporting of both capped/uncapped RCRPS. - Honest ablation reporting: the paper states plainly that expert interaction contributes "only small additional predictive gains" and that top-1 routing captures most of the benefit, rather than overselling the MoE machinery. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors acknowledge: (a) composition gains over the best single expert are small and routing gains "unsurprising"; (b) evaluation is confined to three capability-separated benchmarks, with interleaved forecast-and-revise workflows left to future work; (c) only one backbone family (Qwen3.6) is studied, so generality of the findings is unverified; (d) the joint-training baseline admits "a broader study of joint-training configurations is left to future work"; (e) benchmark accuracy does not establish fitness for autonomous high-stakes decisions. They confront limitations directly rather than minimize them — a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - The central claim — that MoE composition preserves capability — is only weakly stress-tested: with three experts, top-1 routing nearly suffices, so the paper does not establish that learned soft composition is necessary; a harder expert set with genuinely conflicting behaviors would be needed to show the controller matters. - No variance reporting: TSE differences of 0.134pp and CiK differences of 0.004–0.007 RCRPS between configurations are presented without seeds or confidence intervals, yet placement claims (e.g., 3rd vs 4th on GIFT by 0.05 rank) hang on margins of this size. - The aggregation expert's supervised exposure to GIFT training data (XGBoost fitted on 300,000 GIFT-train windows) is not compared against TSFM baselines given equivalent in-domain supervision, so the GIFT "top-three" placement conflates ensemble strength, benchmark-specific fitting, and LM refinement. - TSLM competitors on GIFT are excluded by compute budget while TeeMoE's own GIFT score was obtained via the cheap numerical path — the comparison is asymmetric in TeeMoE's favor, and the TimeOmni-VL TSE score (14.745%) is presented as a capability ranking despite the authors' own note that it likely reflects failed transfer. - The two-pass architecture doubles backbone compute per request relative to single-pass routing; no latency or inference-cost analysis per request is provided. - Only three fixed output paths exist; mixed requests (e.g., forecast then explain the forecast) are outside the interface, so "generalist" is bounded to one-shot, single-capability requests. Bottom Line: A practitioner building multi-capability time-series LLM systems should read this for the best-documented modular-vs-joint training comparison available and a safely-deployable ensemble-refinement design, but should treat the "top-three generalist" framing as a leaderboard artifact shaped by favorable comparison selection rather than evidence that the MoE machinery itself drives the performance.

SimTrace: Grounded Multimodal User Trajectories Generation for Online User Modeling

Y Lu, S Xie, M Allamudi, M Zhao, H Li, L Wang, Z Yu · arxiv.org · generating environments for agent testing in enterprises - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces SIMTRACE, an open-source framework that converts private, coarse activity logs into faithful, fine-grained multimodal clickstream trajectories (HTML + screenshot per step) by anonymizing logs, building a simulated twin website, and having an LLM teacher agent replay behavior inside it. - Why it's important: Fine-grained, environment-grounded user interaction data are locked behind privacy rules and unavailable to low-traffic organizations, blocking work on virtual clients for A/B testing, recommendation, and interface evaluation. - How it does it: The core trick is conditioning a computer-use agent on an anonymized reference trajectory as guidance (not a script) while a nested outer reflection loop expands coarse logged events into interface-level steps and an inner verifier rejects infeasible or off-trajectory actions before execution. - The good: The framework wins 7 of 8 fidelity metrics against prompting and agentic baselines (e.g., Outcome JSD of 7.98e-5 vs 1.86e-3 for UXAgent on gemini-3-flash), and synthetic-only training matches real-only training on purchase prediction and session-based recommendation within statistical bounds. - The missing: The headline 'synthetic ≈ real' downstream result is computed on very small training sets (739 purchase sessions, 357 recommendation sessions) with all confidence intervals spanning zero — evidence of parity is as consistent with low statistical power as with true equivalence, and the 1,513-session dataset is three orders of magnitude smaller than the item-ID datasets it positions against. - Read it or not: Read it if you build user simulators, synthetic data pipelines, or e-commerce agent environments; skip it if you need large-scale behavioral data or general-domain (non-e-commerce) evidence, which the paper does not provide.

Problem & Motivation: Practitioners building LLM-based virtual clients for A/B testing, recommender development, usability studies, and interface evaluation need trajectories that pair every user action with its web observation and user context. Two data regimes fail this need: large public clickstream datasets (Coveo 203k, YOOCHOOSE 9M, Tmall 8M sessions) reduce behavior to item IDs or coarse event types, discarding interface context, while context-rich datasets (OPeRA at 692 sessions) are small, costly, and platform-locked. Organizations' own logs are private, traffic-limited, and privacy-constrained (GDPR). Prior LLM user simulators prioritize plausible task completion over step-level fidelity and, per Zhang et al. (2026), diverge substantially from real sessions at the action level. The gap is a scalable way to produce semantically faithful, environment-grounded, shareable multimodal trajectories. Key Idea: Treat a real logged trajectory as flexible behavioral guidance rather than a replayable script: anonymize it to a semantic-action sequence with inferred intent/persona, then have a teacher agent regenerate the fine-grained interaction inside a sandbox twin of the website, using a two-loop control structure — an outer plan/act/reflect loop to expand coarse logged events into the interface-level actions the log omitted (the authors' 'granularity mismatch'), and an inner pre-execution verifier scoring each proposed action on executability, trajectory consistency, and realism to prevent 'interface drift' from irreversibly corrupting the session. This observation-grounded regeneration, not persona prompting, is what the fidelity gains hinge on. Methodology: Three-stage pipeline. (1) Log transformation: greedy session selection that cycles through three conversion-funnel outcomes (Browse-only, Cart Abandonment, Checkout) maximizing marginal product coverage; standardization of heterogeneous logs onto a MECE 9-action taxonomy (search, detail, add, remove, checkout, goto, back, stay, terminate) extended from Requena et al. (2020); keyed HMAC-SHA-256 identifier hashing; SimGym-style 5-dimension persona and intent inference. (2) Twin environment construction (adapted from ShopGym): a coding agent (Pi harness with GPT-5.5) explores nine configured interface areas via Playwright, produces a design manual plus structured element specs plus prefetched static data; sensitive content is replaced via a two-stage image pipeline (caption original image, regenerate from caption + synthetic vendor identity — no pixel access); two verifiers gate release: an LLM screenshot scorer (layout, color theme, component correspondence, content density, language consistency) and a Playwright action-replay checker that replays sampled real trajectories. Cost: 28–30M tokens, 2.9–4.2 hours, $60–64 per site. (3) Generation: teacher agent (gemini-3-flash or gpt-5.6-sol) runs the nested reflection–verification loop; the inner verifier returns per-criterion rationale/score/confidence and failed actions are revised before execution. Downstream evaluation covers SFT of Qwen3.5-4B (QLoRA) for purchase prediction, RAIN and DIMO for session recommendation, and SFT + GDPO reinforcement learning of Qwen3.5-9B for next-action prediction, with a hierarchical partial-credit target reward (LCS similarity 0.6, validity 0.1, exact-match 0.3) plus action and format rewards. Critical design decisions: guidance-not-script conditioning (well-justified via the granularity-mismatch analysis); pre-execution verification (justified by the interface-drift failure mode of UXAgent-style loops); LLM-judged visual fidelity for the sandbox (weakest justification — self-referential quality control with a threshold, no human validation reported). Key Results: Fidelity (200 synthetic sessions per method, two backbone models): SIMTRACE best on 7/8 metrics on gemini-3-flash — Outcome JSD 7.98e-5 (significant at p<0.05 over all baselines), Action Frequency JSD 4.96e-3 (significant), Trajectory Levenshtein 0.180 vs 0.218–0.674 for baselines; Product Diversity Ratio (0.085) and Transition Matrix distance (0.227) were not won. Rankings hold on gpt-5.6-sol, where Outcome JSD reaches 0.00 (significant). Downstream utility: TSTR vs TRTR on a held-out real test set shows no significant differences — purchase prediction F1 65.52 vs 64.36 (Δ +1.16, 95% CI [−3.00, +5.00]); RAIN MRR@10 13.64 vs 13.20; DIMO results mixed (HR@10 40.46 vs 39.86, MRR@5 16.49 vs 17.84). Low-resource next-action prediction (50 OPeRA real sessions, Qwen3.5-9B): SFT on synthetic data gains 11.9–20.6 points over the base model; real+synthetic SFT adds 1.5–8.5 points over real-only; GDPO RL adds a further 1.7/1.8/5.0 points on exact match, action-type F1, and accuracy, eliminating malformed JSON (1.99% → 0%). The abstract's '11.0% relative' augmentation improvement is a claimed aggregate; per-metric point gains in Figure 2 are the measured quantities. Tested at toy-to-small scale throughout: 200-session fidelity comparisons, ≤739-session downstream training, a 1,513-session released dataset vs 9M-session item-ID datasets. Novelty Classification: NEW DATASET/BENCHMARK (first public multimodal, sandbox-paired, multi-platform fine-grained trajectory dataset, 1,513 sessions across 5 stores and 4 languages) and NEW SYSTEM/TOOL (the open-source generation framework). The method itself is a competent combination of existing pieces — ShopGym's twin construction, SimGym's personas, UXAgent-style reflection loops, DeepSeek-style SFT→RL training, GDPO — applied to a new setting; the genuinely novel element is the observation-grounded regeneration of anonymized logs inside a sandbox with pre-execution action verification, which no prior public pipeline offers end-to-end. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are implicit but effective: the UXAgent baseline isolates the value of the inner verifier (it has the outer loop but not the inner one), and the prompting baselines isolate the value of agentic grounding; the RQ3 analysis decomposes augmentation gains into target-coverage expansion (search-suggestion cases: 0/40 → 22/40 correct) and RL effects (parent-path accuracy 40.71% → 44.26%). Statistical care is real but the key downstream claim rests on null results: three seeds with bootstrap 95% CIs, where parity is inferred from CIs including zero on n=434–500 test sessions — a low-power design where 'not significantly different' is weak evidence of equivalence. Fidelity metrics are largely authors' own constructions (product coherence/diversity/alignment metrics), defined in the appendix but not validated against human judgment. Code (github.com/agentic-foundation-modeling-research/SimTrace) and data (huggingface.co/datasets/luyunan/SimTrace, CC BY-NC 4.0) are released. Concerns: the LLM-judge visual verifier creates a self-grading loop for sandbox quality; generation and fidelity evaluation share the same environments (Goodhart exposure on the metric suite); baselines are the authors' own prompting variants plus UXAgent but not the strongest RL-based simulators (Shop-R1, Customer-R1) on fidelity; this is a preprint (arXiv 2609.38397), apparently Shopify-affiliated, and the small training sets for the TSTR experiments deserve skepticism before treating parity as established. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL (and SYSTEMS — an open-source package with modules for collection, generation, and training). Practical: Yes — runs on commodity APIs plus a single multi-GPU node for downstream training (H200s, 8 GPUs for RL); the released models are 4B/9B. Efficient: Twin construction is cheap ($60–64, ~3–4 hours per site), but trajectory generation depends on frontier-model teachers (gemini-3-flash / gpt-5.6-sol), and RL takes ~24 hours per run; the paper's stated motivation is that generated data offsets repeated frontier-model inference at use time via small trained user models. Effective: Evidence supports fidelity and augmentation utility, but the core 'replace real data' claim is a null result at low power, and cross-platform transfer is explicitly shown to be lossy (synthetic-only trails real-only on next-action prediction). Scalable: Untested beyond 1,513 sessions and 5 stores; whether generation cost and quality hold at 100× scale, or across non-e-commerce domains, is claimed (domain-adaptive design) but not measured. Delivers a concrete software artifact: open-source package, generation framework, and a public multimodal dataset. Strengths: - The granularity-mismatch / interface-drift failure analysis is the paper's best intellectual contribution: it explains precisely why one-shot trajectory prompting produces broken sessions and maps each failure to a mechanism (outer reflection, inner verification), supported by the UXAgent ablation rather than assertion. - End-to-end system completeness: log standardization, anonymization, twin construction with dual automated verifiers, generation, and downstream training are all released, and the twin-construction cost ($60–64/site) is honestly reported — rare transparency for this kind of pipeline. - Honest statistical reporting in RQ2: the authors report TSTR−TRTR differences with 95% CIs and explicitly state all intervals include zero, rather than spinning null results as wins. - The RQ3 error analysis is unusually actionable — quantified failure decomposition (77.4% of targets occur once; 24.03% of real training mass on two overpredicted targets; the search-suggestion 0/40 → 22/40 recovery) gives practitioners a real account of where synthetic data helps and where it cannot. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state (Section 7): (1) evaluation is confined to e-commerce while the method's taxonomies and privacy handling are domain-specific, so finance/education/healthcare remain unvalidated; (2) the cold-start problem is not solved — trajectory-conditioned generation still requires initial activity logs; (3) synthetic data from a related environment remains less effective than real target-domain data for next-action prediction, with cross-platform mismatches in interaction granularity, target vocabulary, and operation semantics analyzed in Appendix F.2. This is direct, non-minimizing treatment of limitations — a credibility positive; the Appendix F.2 diagnosis of why transfer fails (click-then-type vs type-then-click, missing review/recommendation modules) goes beyond boilerplate. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - The headline parity claim (RQ2) is underpowered: 739/357 training sessions and 434–500 test sessions with CIs that all include zero cannot distinguish 'synthetic ≈ real' from 'experiment too small to detect a real gap'; an equivalence-test framework (e.g., TOST) is needed, and no sample-size justification is given. - No human evaluation anywhere: fidelity is judged entirely by distributional statistics and LLM-judged semantic metrics, and sandbox quality by an LLM screenshot scorer — a circular judge with no inter-rater or human-validation anchor. - Missing fidelity baselines: Shop-R1 and Customer-R1, the strongest trained simulators in the paper's own related work, are cited but not compared against; UXAgent is the only agentic baseline. - The fidelity suite is developed and evaluated on the same generated environments and metrics designed by the authors, with no held-out environment or external benchmark to guard against metric gaming (Product Diversity and Transition Matrix — the two metrics SIMTRACE loses — suggest the suite is not vacuous, but also that no method dominates). - The released dataset's 1,513 sessions are small relative to the data-scarcity problem the paper targets; the multi-platform advantage is real structurally but thin empirically (5 stores, all one domain). - Privacy claims rest on HMAC hashing and content regeneration without any formal privacy analysis (no membership-inference or leakage testing of the released synthetic sessions derived from real logs). Bottom Line: A practitioner building e-commerce user simulators or synthetic interaction data should read this — the failure-mode analysis and the released pipeline/dataset are immediately usable — but researchers seeking large-scale behavioral data, cross-domain evidence, or a statistically solid 'synthetic replaces real' result will find the evaluation too small to settle that question, and there is currently no stronger alternative covering the same grounded-generation ground.

CHAIN: Calibrated LLM Forecasting via Causal-Temporal Hypergraph Inference

W Liu, C Wang, Y Lu, Z Cui, H Luo · arxiv.org · Recommended articles
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces CHAIN, an inference-time calibration framework that structures retrieved evidence as a causal-temporal hypergraph and calibrates LLM event-forecast probabilities by targeting three stages of bias — evidence weighting, chain aggregation, and source fusion — rather than correcting outputs post hoc. - Why it's important: LLM forecasters are systematically overconfident with bias that varies across domains and question types, and untrustworthy probabilities break threshold-based decisions in prediction markets, risk management, and clinical planning. - How it does it: CHAIN modulates an exponential temporal-decay function by causal BFS topological distance to the question's target entities, deduplicates redundant same-polarity causal chains (Jaccard-θ) before Noisy-OR aggregation over ~independent paths, and adaptively blends the causal estimate with the LLM's own estimate using a sigmoid fusion weight driven by causal coverage and directional balance. - The good: Gains are consistent and statistically supported: CHAIN wins all 24 (dataset, backbone) configurations for ECE, Brier, and Accuracy against the per-metric strongest baseline, wins all 120 question-level paired comparisons directionally, and remains significant after Holm correction in 44/120 ECE comparisons vs. RAG baselines. - The missing: The LLM-extracted causal edges that the entire pipeline depends on are never validated against ground truth, test sets are only 128 instances per dataset (making bin-based ECE high-variance), and the method carries ~14 fixed hyperparameters (e.g., Ω0=0.3, α0=0.6, dmax=4) with sensitivity swept for only a subset. - Read it or not: Read it if you work on LLM forecasting, calibration, or graph-based RAG — it is the most thorough evaluation of structural (in-process) vs. post-hoc calibration I have seen — skip it if you need validated causal-extraction accuracy or deployment-scale evidence.

Show full analysis
Problem & Motivation: LLM-based event forecasting has progressed from direct prompting and CoT to retrieval-augmented and graph-structured prediction, but probability outputs remain systematically overconfident with heterogeneous bias across domains and question types. Existing calibration is almost entirely post hoc (temperature/Platt/isotonic scaling, conformal adjustment, verbalized confidence): it corrects the final number after prediction completes and never touches the structural sources of bias inside the prediction process. The authors identify three such sources: (i) evidence at different causal distances from the question target is treated equally, so stale background influences estimates as much as proximate causes; (ii) multiple retrieval paths referencing the same fact act as independent evidence, inflating confidence via redundant Noisy-OR-style accumulation; (iii) the trade-off between external evidence and the LLM's internal estimate is fused with a fixed weight regardless of evidence quality. The affected users are anyone making decisions under uncertainty from LLM forecasts — market participants, risk analysts, policy and trial planners. Key Idea: Recast calibrated forecasting as probabilistic inference over a causal-temporal hypergraph and place a bias-correction mechanism at each of three pipeline stages, so calibration happens inside prediction rather than after it. The single most load-bearing trick is the Causal-Temporal Validity Function: use reverse-BFS causal distance from question-resolved target anchors to modulate the temporal decay rate (ρ=0 ⇒ no decay for causally direct evidence; ρ=1 ⇒ 1/√Δt decay for distal evidence), which down-weights distal and stale evidence in one coupled operation. Methodology: The pipeline has three phases. (1) Hypergraph construction: an LLM extractor (GPT-4o-mini) converts each retrieved news chunk into factual propositions and typed directed causal edges (causes/enables/prevents) with strength scores; hyperedges carry source timestamps, forming G = (V, E_H, C), built once per corpus. (2) Per-query causal estimation: a cutoff-safe active graph view G_q is built; a reasoning-direction LLM call resolves target anchors T(q) with polarity axis; causal distances d(n,q) are computed by reverse BFS capped at d_max; the CTVF validity V_CTVF = min(V_rec + V_sal, 1) combines distance-modulated exponential recency with a sub-linear recurrence-salience term (µ(N)·√N·M_r); chains are enumerated by forward BFS with fan-out cap F_max and score pruning τ_Φ, gated to terminate at oriented targets; chain confidence Φ(π,q) = ι_q(π)·∏ w_ℓ·ω(c_ℓ); chains are split by polarity δ_q(π) = a_q(v_L)(−1)^{P(π)}, deduplicated greedily by Jaccard-θ within each polarity, aggregated by per-polarity Noisy-OR, and combined via a neutral-anchored log-odds difference into P_causal. (3) Adaptive fusion: a coverage score Ω(q) = min(k·Φ̄·κ(k)·β̃(q)/Z, 1) (chain count, mean confidence, saturated reliability, floored directional balance) maps through a sigmoid to α(q) ∈ [0, α0], and the final forecast is the convex combination p̂ = α·P_causal + (1−α)·P_llm. Three "Propositions" are given conditional proofs in Appendix A (Prop. 1 requires that proximal evidence has lower error and that within-subset reweighting does not increase error; Prop. 3 requires stratum-invariant LLM error moments and conditions on variance terms — they are structured inequalities, not unconditional theorems). Critical design decisions: distance-modulated decay (justified by ablation: removing CTVF raises ECE on every dataset); polarity-aware Jaccard dedup before Noisy-OR (justified by ablation and Prop. 2); the α0 = 0.6 cap on causal contribution (a sensible hedge, but its value is a fixed default with limited sensitivity analysis). Key Results: On four in-distribution datasets (AI-Futures, Metaculus, Polymarket, Future-as-Label) with GPT-4o-mini, CHAIN averages ECE 10.23% / Brier 18.79% / Accuracy 72.27% versus the best baselines (ConformalAdj: 15.00/24.36/58.98; LLM CoT: 16.79/24.62/62.70); per-backbone gains over the strongest baseline are −4.77 to −3.07 ECE points, −5.57 to −3.30 Brier points, +9.57 to +7.42 Accuracy points across GPT-4o-mini, Gemini-2.0-Flash, and DeepSeek-V3. On four OOD datasets (Clinical Trial Outcomes, FOReCAst, Golf-Forecasting, KalshiBench) with DeepSeek-V3, CHAIN averages ECE 5.75% / Brier 21.87% / Acc 64.45% vs. TempScaling 6.63/22.82/62.70. Against modern post-hoc calibrators under leakage-safe five-fold cross-fitting (including Beta calibration, Venn–Abers, Dirichlet), CHAIN lowers ECE 12.81→8.53 and Accuracy 61.49→69.47 vs. Temperature Scaling. A compute-matched control (five-sample averaged Direct-MO at 5 LLM calls/case, same as CHAIN) improves ECE only 15.21→14.91 vs. CHAIN's 8.14, ruling out mere ensembling. Ablations show each component removal degrades ECE on every dataset. A perturbation study shows reversing causal-edge directions degrades Accuracy by 5.37 points while shuffling strengths is nearly harmless, supporting direction-sensitivity. Statistical support: Wilcoxon/paired-t/binomial all p < 10⁻³ at config level; question-level tests with Holm correction reported. Test scale: 128 instances per dataset (small); baselines are current and reasonably strong (five graph-RAG variants, five post-hoc calibrators, conformal adjustment), though no fine-tuned forecasting specialist baseline appears. Novelty Classification: NEW FORMULATION + NEW METHOD (with an ENGINEERING OPTIMIZATION component in pruning/search). The genuinely novel move is diagnosing and correcting calibration bias stage-by-stage inside a causal-temporal hypergraph inference pipeline — proximity-modulated temporal decay, polarity-aware dedup, and coverage-driven fusion are each individually standard ingredients (exponential decay, Jaccard dedup, Noisy-OR, sigmoid gating), but their composition as structural calibration targeting three named bias sources is new relative to the post-hoc-calibration literature. The theoretical propositions are conditional decompositions rather than new analytic tools. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations isolate each of the three components (Table 3); extensive sensitivity analyses cover chain budget, depth, fan-out, pruning threshold (Table 9), graph scale (Table 11), extractor choice (GPT-4.1-nano vs. GPT-4o-mini, Table 12), alternative calibration-error estimators (Adaptive ECE, debiased RMSCE, Jackknife, Table 16), and domain-specific retrieval corpora with a documented boundary audit (Table 21). Results are averaged over three runs; question-level significance tests with bootstrap CIs and Holm correction are in Appendix U — well above typical calibration-paper standards. Concerns: (a) no error bars on the headline tables themselves; (b) ECE with 128 test instances per dataset has substantial finite-sample bias despite the appendix's estimator-robustness checks; (c) the ConformalAdj baseline is a custom scalar adjustment, not a native conformal method with coverage guarantees; (d) FOReCAst has acknowledged knowledge-cutoff leakage risk (applied uniformly, but not quantified); (e) numerous hyperparameters are given as defaults without stating how they were selected, which weakens the "calibration-set-free" positioning — the fixed constants (Ω0, α0, ζ, Z, β0, k_sat, η) act as implicit calibration choices. Code and materials are stated as released at github.com/QwenQKing/Chain. Preprint (arXiv 2609.36689), not peer reviewed. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL (with a SYSTEMS artifact in the released code/graph pipeline). Practical: Yes — built entirely from commercial API models (GPT-4o-mini extraction, GPT-4o-mini/Gemini-2.0-Flash/DeepSeek-V3 backbones) plus standard embeddings; no exotic hardware. Efficient: This is the weak point — 13,371 tokens/case vs. 550 for single Direct-MO (~24×), i.e., ~5 LLM calls but far heavier prompts; offline path search drops from 10.48s to 2.47s with pruning at τ_Φ=0.005, and hypergraph construction amortizes across queries. Effective: Evidence supports the stated problem on real resolved-outcome benchmarks (calibration and accuracy both improve), not just a proxy; the single-question case study (IBM "Sovereign Core", 39 chains, Brier 2.56% vs. 28.89–98.01% for baselines) is illustrative only. Scalable: Not stress-tested — 128 test instances/dataset, corpora of 2,048 construction instances per ID dataset, OOD corpora as small as 9–12 documents; graph-scale experiments (25–100% source fractions) show monotone Brier/Accuracy improvement, but behavior at 10–100× corpus or question volume is claimed, not measured. Delivers a software artifact (code, prompts, pipeline) beyond paper form. Strengths: - The three-stage bias diagnosis (weighting / aggregation / fusion) is a crisp, actionable decomposition of why LLM forecasts miscalibrate, and each stage maps to a mechanism with a dedicated ablation — this is a real conceptual contribution over "rescale the output" calibration. - Evaluation rigor is unusually high: 8 datasets × 3 backbones × 13 baselines, a leakage-safe cross-fitted comparison against modern post-hoc calibrators (Venn–Abers, Beta/Dirichlet), a call-matched multi-sample control, an extractor-swap robustness check, an alternative-estimator robustness check, and a corpus-boundary audit for OOD comparisons — most of the obvious fairness objections are pre-empted. - The perturbation study (direction reversal degrades Accuracy by 5.37 points; strength shuffling does not) is a clever, targeted test of whether the causal structure itself carries information, not just extra context. - Honest reporting of the adaptive-α behavior (Table 18: 49.22% of records have Ω=0 and fall back fully to the LLM) shows the mechanism degrades gracefully to the base forecaster when evidence is absent. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors acknowledge that FOReCAst contains some questions whose resolution dates precede model knowledge cutoffs (leakage risk, applied uniformly); that OOD evaluation uses a unified in-distribution retrieval corpus, so it tests cross-source rather than domain-disjoint transfer with varying topical overlap (Appendix D); and that post-hoc significance tests at the configuration level are "descriptive rather than confirmatory" because the strongest baseline is selected from the same results. The limitations are confronted directly where stated — a credibility positive — though the paper does not include a consolidated limitations section. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - No validation of causal extraction quality. The entire pipeline rests on LLM-extracted typed causal edges and strengths, yet edge precision/recall or strength calibration is never measured against human-annotated ground truth; edge strengths are shown to matter little under shuffling (which is reassuring), but wrong-direction edges would silently corrupt the polarity logic, and the direction-reversal result only shows directions matter, not that the extractor gets them right. - Hyperparameter provenance. Fourteen CHAIN-specific constants are reported with defaults; sensitivity is swept only for search-related parameters (B_π, d_max, F_max, τ_Φ) and θ. The fusion parameters (Ω0, α0, ζ, Z, β0, k_sat, η, v_fb) are never swept in the main text, leaving open whether defaults were tuned on the evaluation data — directly relevant to the "calibration-set-free" claim. - Small evaluation samples. 128 test instances per dataset makes per-dataset ECE/MCE estimates noisy; the multi-estimator robustness check mitigates but does not eliminate this, and no per-dataset confidence intervals on headline tables are given. - Missing specialist baselines. No comparison against fine-tuned forecasting systems or ensemble/aggregation methods from the forecasting literature (e.g., trained forecaster pipelines), so CHAIN is only compared against prompting/RAG/post-hoc families. - Runtime/token cost is reported but not positioned against what accuracy a 24× token budget spent on better prompting or more retrieval would buy for a strong non-CHAIN method at matched cost — the multi-sample control tests averaging, not richer prompting or retrieval. Bottom Line: A practitioner in LLM forecasting or calibration should read this — the staged structural-calibration formulation and the unusually fair, multi-control evaluation make it a meaningful advance over post-hoc correction, but its practical value hinges on causal-extraction quality that the paper never validates, so treat the large accuracy gains (up to +9.6 points over the strongest baseline) with the caveat that the evidence graph itself is unverified.

AdaStep: Adaptive Step Credit Weighting for Agentic Reinforcement Learning

X Wang, W Wu, M Zhang, Z Wang, K Shao, J Luan · arxiv.org · long-horizon RL for agents - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces AdaStep, a modification of GiGPO-style agentic RL that replaces the fixed step-level advantage coefficient with a per-anchor-state shrinkage weight derived as the optimal solution to a mean-squared-error objective, computable as a signal-to-total-variance ratio from existing rollout statistics. - Why it's important: Training long-horizon LLM agents with sparse outcome rewards suffers from either coarse trajectory-level credit (GRPO) or noisy step-level credit whose reliability varies across states; mis-weighted local signals can reinforce irrelevant actions or penalize correct ones, wasting compute and destabilizing training. - How it does it: Under an explicit noise model for the step-level advantage estimate, the MSE-optimal rescaling of the local correction is the fraction of return variance at a state attributable to differences in expected return across actions (1 − within-action variance / total variance), estimable from group mean/variance statistics with no critic, extra rollouts, or extra forward passes (~1% added credit-computation time). - The good: Consistent gains over GiGPO and HGPO across 3 backbones and 3 benchmarks with 3 seeds and standard deviations — e.g., +9.36 points on ScienceWorld with Qwen3-1.7B (29.93 vs 20.57) and +4.99 on ALFWorld with Qwen3-4B — plus a fixed-weight sensitivity sweep showing AdaStep beats every tested global coefficient. - The missing: The method depends on exact anchor-state matching across rollouts, which only works in deterministic text worlds; generalization to continuous, partially observable, or non-repeating environments is explicitly left open, and the i.i.d.-within-group assumption underlying the estimator is violated in correlated multi-rollout data. - Read it or not: Read it if you are building group-based RL for LLM agents and use GiGPO/HGPO-style step-level credit — the derivation is short and the drop-in change is cheap — but skip it if your setting lacks repeatable states or if you need results beyond three discrete text benchmarks.
Why this rank
Scored using the Empirical profile. Rigor (72) is the top contributor — 3 seeds with std everywhere, a normalization/fallback/fixed-weight ablation matrix, and fully proved supporting theory — while Completeness (72) benefits from honest treatment of the fallback result and proxy-diagnostic caveats. The composite is pulled down by Novelty (62) and Non-Obviousness (66): this is a principled but incremental replacement of one scalar in GiGPO, with scope confined to deterministic, exactly-repeatable text worlds where the estimator's requirements are trivially met. Resilience (62) is dented by the i.i.d. assumption being untested and the fallback analysis partially undercutting the adaptive-weighting story, and Impact (48) is low with no code, data, or checkpoint release. Weighted composite: 0.20*62 + 0.25*72 + 0.15*66 + 0.15*72 + 0.15*62 + 0.10*48 ≈ 65.

Problem & Motivation: Group-based post-training methods (RLOO, GRPO) broadcast a single trajectory-level advantage to every token of a rollout, which is accurate about eventual success but blind to which individual decisions caused it. GiGPO adds a step-level correction by grouping state–action pairs that share an anchor state across rollouts, but this local estimate is noisy: for the same correct action, discounted-return differences driven by stochastic downstream behavior or longer trajectories can flip the advantage sign (the paper's Example 1 shows GiGPO assigning −1.51 to a correct `click[three meat]` action in one trajectory and +3.33 to the same action in another). A fixed global coefficient ω cannot distinguish groups where return variation reflects action quality from groups where it reflects downstream randomness. The open question the paper targets is: how strongly should each step-level group's local correction be trusted? Key Idea: Formulate per-group weighting of the step-level advantage as a one-dimensional least-squares projection of the latent true step advantage onto the noisy estimate. The resulting optimal shrinkage coefficient, w(s) = E[A_S·A_S|s] / E[A²_S|s], reduces via the law of total variance to the ratio Var_a[Q(s,a)] / Var(R|s) — the fraction of return variance at state s explained by action-dependent value differences. High ratio means local credit is credible (weight near 1); low ratio means variation is dominated by downstream randomness (weight near 0). The key lemma is that the estimate's 1/N_s conditional bias cancels after marginalizing over actions, so reweighting — not sign-flipping or discarding — is the correct intervention. Methodology: The method sits inside the GiGPO pipeline: sample N rollouts per task, compute episode-level relative advantages A_E (Eq. 1), hash states to build step-level groups G(s) of state–action–return triples, and form the combined advantage A(s,a) = A_E + w(s)·A_S inside a clipped PPO objective with KL penalty (Eq. 20). The theoretical framework is a per-group MSE minimization: Theorem 1 gives the projection weight; a three-term noise decomposition (Eq. 8) establishes that the GiGPO estimator is conditionally biased by −A*_S/N_s but marginally unbiased; Lemma 1 computes numerator and denominator in closed form under i.i.d.-conditional-on-s sampling with finite variance; Theorem 2 gives the computable ratio. The finite-sample estimate (Eq. 17) is ŵ(s) = 1 − Σ_a p̂(a|s)·v̂_{s,a} / v̂_s, using counts, sums, and sums of squares already collected by GiGPO. Three critical design decisions: (1) computing the coefficient from unnormalized return statistics before any advantage normalization — justified by an explicit robustness experiment (Table 2) showing gains both with and without std normalization; (2) a fallback weight of w=1 for non-estimable groups (single action, one return per action, zero variance) — empirically supported in Table 3(b) where w=1 beats w=0 and w=mean, though this reveals the estimated coefficient frequently wants to down-weight a signal that is still better retained; (3) eligibility requirements of ≥2 distinct actions and ≥2 returns per action — reasonable but understates how many groups in sparse data will fall back to the default. The clipped objective with KL regularization is standard GiGPO machinery, unchanged. Key Results: On ALFWorld, WebShop, and ScienceWorld (8 simple tasks) with Qwen3-1.7B, Qwen3-4B, and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, AdaStep beats all trained baselines in every model–benchmark cell, averaged over 3 seeds. Headline deltas vs GiGPO: ScienceWorld +9.36 (Qwen3-1.7B: 29.93±1.9 vs 20.57±1.8), ALFWorld +4.99 (Qwen3-4B: 93.01±0.9 vs 88.02±0.9), WebShop +4.82 (Qwen2.5-7B: 82.42±1.2 vs 77.60±1.7). Baselines are current and strong: GRPO, RLOO, PPO, GiGPO (NeurIPS 2025), and HGPO (ICLR 2026), plus ReAct/Reflexion prompting and two frontier-model reference points. The fixed-weight sensitivity sweep (Fig. 3a,b) shows AdaStep exceeding every fixed ω on both ALFWorld and WebShop, and offline diagnostics on 3,666 WebShop groups show AdaStep reducing within-action credit variation to 35.8% of GiGPO's while achieving the lowest held-out reference MSE (65.8 vs GiGPO's 100). Efficiency: 0.5018s vs 0.4968s per-iteration credit computation (~1% overhead), faster than HGPO's 0.6340s. Tested scale is modest: 160 training steps, ≤16 hours on 8×H100, small open-weight backbones; no scaling study. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD with a supporting NEW FORMULATION. The genuinely novel element is deriving the step-level correction strength from an explicit MSE-estimation objective rather than a tuned hyperparameter, yielding the variance-fraction interpretation of w*(s). The surrounding machinery — GiGPO's anchor-state grouping, GRPO's group-relative advantages, PPO clipping — is a standard combination of existing ideas; the contribution is a principled replacement of one scalar, and the shrinkage-to-noise-ratio idea connects to well-known variance-control work (GBMP-style shrinkage baselines, GAE's λ trade-off). It is an increment on GiGPO, not a new paradigm. Rigor & Reproducibility: Strong for the empirical claims: ablations cover normalization on/off, fallback weight choice, fixed-coefficient sensitivity, and offline estimation diagnostics; all main results report means ± std over 3 seeds; baselines share identical training pipelines and hyperparameters, with GiGPO's ω=1 taken untuned from the original paper (the sensitivity sweep in Fig. 3 partially compensates by sweeping fixed weights). The theory is self-contained with full proofs in Appendix A, and the paper is honest that the held-out MSE diagnostic is a proxy estimated from finite rows, not ground truth. Methodological concerns: (1) all three benchmarks are discrete, deterministic text worlds where exact anchor-state matching is trivially available — the setting is chosen to fit the estimator's requirements; (2) the i.i.d.-conditional-on-s assumption used in Lemma 1 is violated in practice, since rollouts come from the same policy and trajectories share states within a task group; (3) some Qwen2.5-7B prompting baselines in Table 1 lack error bars (single values with "-" for ALFWorld Out-Success); (4) no code, data, or model release is mentioned anywhere in the paper; (5) the offline diagnostics use historical samples where rows may share trajectories and groups recur across updates, which the authors correctly flag as non-independent. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (with a small THEORETICAL component that is fully proved and constructive). Practical: Yes — runs on 8×H100, standard small open-weight backbones, no critic or extra model inference. Efficient: ~1% overhead over GiGPO credit computation (0.5018 vs 0.4968 s/iteration) and cheaper than HGPO. Effective: The evidence shows consistent success-rate gains on the tested text worlds over strong recent baselines; whether it improves the underlying credit signal is supported only by the proxy MSE diagnostic, not ground-truth step advantages. Scalable: Untested beyond 160 steps, 7B parameters, and 30–50-step episodes; no evidence at 10× scale, and the anchor-state matching bottleneck likely worsens as environments become larger or stochastic. Deliverable status: paper only — no released library, code, or trained checkpoints are mentioned. Strengths: - The core derivation is clean and genuinely useful: identifying the optimal local-correction weight as a variance-decomposition ratio gives practitioners an interpretable, hyperparameter-free quantity computable from statistics GiGPO already collects — the kind of result that can be re-implemented from the paper in an afternoon. - The noise decomposition (Eq. 8 / Lemma A.1) is a real analytical contribution: it precisely characterizes the 1/N_s conditional bias of GiGPO's group-mean baseline and proves marginal unbiasedness, which justifies reweighting over other interventions and will be quotable beyond this method. - Honest diagnostics: the authors distinguish within-action variation (a stability metric that trivially shrinks as c→0) from held-out reference MSE, and explicitly disclaim that the proxy is not ground truth — a rigor level many adjacent papers lack. - The ablation matrix (normalization × fallback × fixed-weight sweep) directly tests the design decisions rather than only the end-to-end system. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The paper states plainly (Appendix F) that AdaStep relies on constructing step-level groups via exact anchor-state matching, which is only feasible because the three benchmarks have discrete, exactly reproducible states; extending to continuous, partially observable, or open-ended environments where states are not revisited verbatim is left open, including the design of state abstractions or learned grouping criteria that preserve the reliability interpretation. Appendix E also acknowledges that the offline diagnostics use non-independent historical samples and are proxies. The authors confront these limits directly rather than minimizing them — a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - The fallback analysis (Table 3b) shows w=1 outperforming the estimated-coefficient regime on the very benchmarks where estimation is possible, which suggests the estimated weights are frequently too conservative; the paper reports this without probing why, and it partially undercuts the story that adaptive down-weighting is the active ingredient on real groups. - The i.i.d.-conditional-on-s sampling assumption is stated but never tested; in practice rollouts within a task group come from one shared policy and one environment instance, so group statistics are correlated, and the variance-ratio estimate's bias under dependence is unquantified. - Evaluation is confined to three discrete, deterministic, sparse-reward text worlds — the ideal conditions for the method; no experiment introduces even mild stochasticity in transitions, which would stress the noise model the method is built to handle. - GiGPO's ω=1 is inherited untuned; while the fixed-weight sweep exists, it is only run on one backbone (Qwen2.5-7B) and two benchmarks, so per-benchmark tuned fixed-ω baselines cannot be ruled out for the other cells. - ScienceWorld evaluation is restricted to "eight simple tasks" — a narrow slice of a broader benchmark — and this restriction is stated only in the appendix. - No code or artifact release is mentioned, which limits independent verification of the advantage-computation details (e.g., hash-key construction for anchor states, which is notoriously fiddly). Bottom Line: For anyone training LLM agents with GiGPO-family methods, this is a worthwhile read — the derivation is short, the change is a one-line drop-in with ~1% overhead, and the +0.5 to +9.4 point gains over a strong 2025/2026 baseline are credible — but its scope is firmly bounded to repeatable-state text environments, and practitioners in stochastic or continuous settings will need the follow-up work on state abstractions that this paper explicitly does not provide.

LMBuild: Evaluating LLM Agents for Generating Buildable and Functional Structures (24 ▲ )

Jiateng Liu, Rushi Wang, Cheng Qian, Xuejun Zhang, Sun Li, Jiayu Liu, Yifan Shen, Xu Cao, Jiarui Yao, Bingxuan Li, Ruhi Sarikaya, Heng Ji · arxiv.org · Daily papers of 6 Oct 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces LMBuild, a benchmark and interactive tool-based environment for evaluating whether LLM agents can generate 3D structures that are not just visually plausible but buildable, articulated, materially specified, and physically operable, evaluated across 30 systems (6 closed APIs, 13 open LLMs, 11 domain-specific generators). - Why it's important: Existing 3D-generation evaluation rewards geometry and visual alignment while ignoring whether an artifact can actually be fabricated, assembled, and used — a gap that matters for anyone targeting language-driven design-to-manufacturing pipelines. - How it does it: Agents construct objects through 19 environment tools (retrieve or create parts via CSG programs, place, joint, assign materials, declare assembly sequences), and outputs are scored on a 12-sub-metric hierarchy spanning structural soundness, functional affordance, design quality, and physical realization, with annotations grounded in a traceable Wikidata/Wikipedia evidence pipeline. - The good: The headline finding is quantitatively crisp: frontier closed models score 83–97 on collision-freeness but only 38–43 on kinematic correctness (A.3) and 17.7–22.1 on simulation-based operability (R.3), cleanly demonstrating that physical function, not geometry, is the bottleneck. - The missing: There is an internal inconsistency about benchmark size (the appendix repeatedly describes a "50-task LMBuild-Core" while the main text and Table 1 report 200 core objects), and the text provided is truncated before the full definitions of the affordance and realization metrics — the dimensions driving the paper's conclusions. - Read it or not: Worth reading for anyone building 3D-generation or agentic-assembly systems who needs a shared evaluation target beyond visual fidelity; skip if you only need text-to-3D appearance metrics, which existing benchmarks already cover.

Problem & Motivation: LLM agents can now produce impressive 3D geometry, but a visually convincing object may be disconnected, unassemblable, missing its functional parts, or inoperable — and existing evaluations (text-to-3D alignment, VLM-judged appearance, geometric consistency) do not measure physical realizability. The authors target researchers building LLM-based structure-generation agents, motivated by "speaking structures into existence" fabrication systems. No prior benchmark jointly scores soundness, affordance, design, and physical realization across heterogeneous object types (LEGO assemblies, CAD, articulated everyday objects, complete open-source hardware products). Key Idea: Reframe 3D-generation evaluation from "does the geometry look right" to "can this object be built and work," by (a) representing outputs as assemblies — parts with roles, joints, materials, and an assembly sequence — and (b) grounding the required parts/kinematics in externally verifiable Wikipedia/Wikidata evidence rather than the authors' intuition. The knowledge-grounding pipeline (evidence-constrained claim extraction by Qwen3.5-27B with every claim required to quote retrieved text verbatim, then independent verification by Gemma-4-31B, with provenance to pinned Wikipedia revisions) is the most distinctive technical move; the environment and metric hierarchy are competent assemblies of known techniques. Methodology: Three components. (1) Environment: a stateful pure-Python tool environment with 19 tools; part creation accepts declarative CSG programs (DAG of ≤96 nodes over box/cylinder/sphere/torus/extrude/revolve with Boolean ops) compiled by manifold3d to guarantee watertight solids; budgets of 160 tool calls, 6 check calls, 4 render calls per episode; headless Blender renders six fixed viewpoints. Three access tiers (retrieval-only, retrieval+creation, creation-only) isolate the effect of part creation, plus multi-round revision (K=1–3) with rule-based diagnostic reports and renders. (2) Data: stratified, coverage-oriented selection from ~368K assets (BrickNet 320,808; PartNeXt; Fusion 360 Gallery; Artiverse; 27 open-source hardware projects) down to 2,549 (LMBuild-Full) and 200 (LMBuild-Core) objects, each ≥4 parts, grounded via Wikidata/Wikipedia/WordNet claim extraction with verbatim-quote constraints. (3) Evaluation: 4 dimensions / 12 sub-metrics on a 0–100 scale, mixing rule-based geometric checks (voxelized at 4 mm; connectivity via assembly graph with volume-weighted largest component, fragmentation, and fastener-count terms; collision via absolute 1 cm³ + relative 10–25% overlap thresholds; tipping stability via critical tilt angle and lateral-force proxies normalized to the reference object), Wikipedia-grounded part/kinematic checks, and human-calibrated VLM judgments. Domain-specific systems lacking articulation outputs are augmented with Particulate, or scored N/A on metrics outside their native output space. Design decisions are mostly well-justified (reference-relative stability normalization, evidence-constrained annotation), though many metric hyperparameters are admittedly heuristic. Key Results: On LMBuild-Core under the baseline protocol: frontier closed models dominate — GPT-6 Astra scores 83.0/95.9/86.7 on connectivity/collision/stability but only 45.3 (A.2 parts), 41.7 (A.3 kinematics), and 19.2 (R.3 operability); Claude Opus 5 reaches the best operability at 22.1. Open models trail broadly (Qwen3.5-27B is the strongest open model; ERNIE-4.5-VL-28B scores 1.3–4.9 on affordance metrics). Domain-specific systems score near-perfect soundness (BrickGPT: 99.6/100.0 on S.1/S.2) but are N/A on realization metrics or, when Particulate-augmented, collapse on kinematics (≤3.8). Under access tiers (25 sampled objects), Qwen3-VL-32B drops from 61.7 (retrieval-only) to 34.1 (creation-only) average Soundness+Design, while frontier models hold or improve; closed models succeed on 95.7% of part-creation calls vs 51.7% for open models, and open models reference never-placed parts at 7.2 errors per 100 calls vs 0.3 for closed. Explicit functional prompts raise functional-part completeness by 10.3 points and operability by 12.0 points (Wilcoxon p < 0.001), whereas three revision rounds yield only ~+2% overall. Baselines are current frontier systems as of the paper's date, and the tested scale is moderate (200 objects, single seed 0, temperature 0.6 for open models). The capability split — geometry solved, function unsolved — is the key finding. Novelty Classification: NEW DATASET/BENCHMARK and NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING. The genuinely novel elements are the four-dimension affordance/realization evaluation hierarchy grounded in traceable external knowledge, and the quantified capability dissociation (creation-vs-retrieval stratified by model strength; prompt specificity outweighing iterative revision). The environment, CSG part creation, and VLM+rule evaluation are standard combinations of existing tools (manifold3d, Blender, trimesh, VLM judges) applied to a new setting. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are present and informative: the three access tiers isolate retrieval vs creation; the revision and prompt-enrichment experiments are reported with 95% bootstrap CIs and Wilcoxon signed-rank significance over episodes. Code, dataset (HuggingFace: Lumos-Jiateng/LMBuild), environment, and model trajectories are promised for release, with GitHub and project-page URLs given; the full pipeline was not yet public at writing ("will open-source"). Methodological concerns: (a) VLM-judged metrics (aesthetics, alignment, parts) are human-"calibrated" but the calibration protocol and judge identity are not visible in the provided text; (b) single seed/temperature for open models; (c) the appendix internally contradicts the main text on core-set size ("50 core objects"/"50-task LMBuild-Core" in A.3 vs 200 in Table 1 and §2.2), suggesting the appendix predates an expansion — a reproducibility red flag; (d) the provided text is truncated mid-A.4, so the full definitions for the affordance and realization metrics — the paper's central claims — could not be verified here; (e) the Wikipedia-grounded annotations are extracted by the same model family (Qwen3.5-27B) that is evaluated, though only as an annotator, not a judge of its own outputs. Deployability: Profile: SYSTEMS (a benchmark plus executable environment, evaluated by running 30 systems through it). Practical: Yes — pure-Python environment, NumPy/SciPy geometry kernel, headless Blender; runs on commodity hardware. Efficient: Expensive per episode (50+ tool calls per round for a <20-part object; the authors state millions of LLM turns would be needed for exhaustive evaluation, motivating the 200-object core). Effective: The benchmark measures buildability/operability proxies, not physical fabrication — operability is simulation- and Wikipedia-grounded rather than demonstrated on real hardware. Scalable: Not tested at 10× scale; all headline experiments use the 200-object core, with the 2,549-object full set deferred. The work delivers a reusable artifact set (environment, dataset, evaluation scripts, promised trajectories), not just a paper. Strengths: - The benchmark attacks a real evaluation blind spot: functional affordance and physical operability are measured, not assumed, and the finding that frontier models score 95+ on collision-freeness but ~20 on operability is a clean, decision-relevant dissociation no prior 3D benchmark provides. - The evidence-constrained annotation pipeline (verbatim-quote requirement, two-model extraction/verification, pinned Wikipedia revisions, conservative taxonomic inheritance) is a unusually careful approach to benchmark grounding that resists hallucinated requirements. - The tiered retrieval/creation design produces a genuinely non-obvious empirical insight: part creation is a capability that flips from harmful (weak models, 61.7→34.1) to beneficial (frontier models) as model strength increases. - Honest accounting of comparability: domain-specific systems are scored N/A rather than penalized for unsupported outputs, and the failure-mode analysis (CAD-convention violations, scene-state tracking at 7.2 vs 0.3 errors/100 calls) is diagnostic, not just leaderboard reporting. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state that benchmark performance is not evidence of readiness for safety-critical engineering without domain validation; that operability, aesthetics, and assembly feasibility "remain difficult to quantify in a fully unbiased and model-independent manner"; that all metric hyperparameters are heuristic, empirically chosen proxies fixed before evaluation; that budget constraints limited experiments to the 200-object core; and that bridging to real fabrication requires further validation with manufacturing constraints, physical assembly, and functional testing. This is direct, non-minimizing limitation disclosure — a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - Internal inconsistency on core-set size (50 vs 200 objects in A.3 vs main text) undermines confidence in which results correspond to which data and suggests version drift between appendix and main text. - The VLM-judge calibration for A.2, D.2, D.3 is asserted but not demonstrated in the visible text; VLM judges are known to favor outputs from models in their own training distribution, and no inter-judge agreement or human-correlation statistic is reported in the provided material. - Particulate-augmented domain systems score 0.7–4.2 on A.3, meaning the comparison between domain generators and LLM agents on kinematics mostly measures Particulate's failure, not the generators' — the paper flags comparability caveats but the kinematic rows of Table 2 are close to uninterpretable as model comparisons. - Operability (R.3) is the headline bottleneck at scores ≤22, yet "simulation-based" is only sketched as a "Wikipedia-grounded simulation check"; without the truncated metric definition, the reader cannot assess whether low R.3 reflects model failure or an unforgiving proxy (e.g., rigid tolerance to declared-joint graph errors). - No test of whether benchmark performance predicts downstream robotic assembly or fabrication success — the stated end goal — even on a handful of objects. - Part annotations are extracted with Qwen3.5-27B, which is also the strongest evaluated open model; systematic annotation biases aligned with that model's priors cannot be ruled out. Bottom Line: For researchers building agents that must produce manufacturable, functional 3D assemblies, LMBuild is the most credible and diagnostic evaluation target currently available and worth adopting despite its heuristic metrics and the core-set inconsistency, which should be resolved before relying on exact numbers.
