TokenRouter: Efficient Serving System for Token-Level LLM Routing (103 ▲ )

Tianyu Fu, Tengxuan Liu, Ruoxi Wang, Yixin Dong, Yi Ge, Yichen You, Yu Wang · arxiv.org · Daily papers of 9 Oct 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper builds TokenRouter, a serving system on top of SGLang that efficiently executes token-level routed LLM inference, where the model generating each token can change at every decoding step. - Why it's important: Token-level routing algorithms promise large efficiency gains (e.g., matching 32B-model quality while invoking the 32B for only ~5% of tokens), but no existing serving stack supports them efficiently, so the algorithmic gains have been unattainable in practice. - How it does it: The core move is a "request-centric programming, model-centric execution" split: developers write a route-send-receive lifecycle per request, while each LLM runs as an autonomous asynchronous subserver with a decoupled inter-model loop, a KV-state-preserving handoff-resume mechanism, and a delayed-batching scheduler whose threshold is chosen by a DTMC throughput model. - The good: The gain breakdown is credible and mechanistic: extended CUDA graphs give 1.71×, asynchronous execution +1.12×, and delayed batching +1.31× over the official R2R implementation (2.76× total at concurrency 8), and the DTMC model predicts the empirically optimal batching threshold at every tested concurrency. - The missing: The strongest headline number (64.15×) is measured against official implementations that lack continuous batching, and the fairest baseline — one SGLang server per LLM with an external dispatcher — is self-built rather than a published third-party system, so the margin over a genuinely well-engineered competitor is thinner than the headline suggests. - Read it or not: Read it if you build LLM serving infrastructure or want to deploy token-level routing (R2R, CITER, R-Stitch, Co-LLM, mixture ensembles); skip it if you only care about routing algorithms or quality, since routing accuracy is evaluated only in a single Pareto figure.

Problem & Motivation: Token-level routing decides, at each generated token, whether to continue with a small model or delegate to a larger/expert model. Algorithmic work (R2R, CITER, R-Stitch, Co-LLM) shows this beats query-level routing on the cost-quality frontier, but production and academic serving stacks (SGLang, vLLM) assume a single LLM: all active requests synchronize per decoding step. This creates three concrete failures: (1) step desynchronization — mixed batches wait for the slowest model's per-step latency; (2) batch admission delay — frequently re-routed requests arrive mid-batch and stall until the next admission window; (3) implementation complexity — no API exists for per-step routing inside these codebases. The constituency is routing-algorithm researchers and anyone deploying small-large model collaboration. Key Idea: Treat token-level routing as an asynchronous message-passing lifecycle — receive → decode → route → send — so routing logic is expressed as three per-request hooks (route, send, receive), while each model runs as an independent subserver with its own continuous batching and KV cache. Cross-model handoff is made cheap by a "pending" request state that preserves serving state, reducing a model switch to little more than a token append instead of re-doing prefix matching and KV allocation (the profiled baseline spends ~53% of per-step latency in prefix matching and radix-cache maintenance). A delayed-batching scheduler absorbs irregular routed arrivals by buffering until a threshold B, with B* chosen to maximize throughput in a discrete-time Markov chain model of the system. Methodology: Three pipeline stages. (1) Programming interface: developers implement route(result) → destination model index per request, send(req) → a PeerReq carrying the peer-unseen token suffix and a position anchor, and receive(peer_req) → local request conversion; five diverse algorithms (CITER, R2R, R-Stitch, Co-LLM, ME) are shown to fit this pattern, including multi-model ensembles. (2) Asynchronous execution: each subserver runs three decoupled event loops (client-server, decoding, inter-model) in a subprocess, communicating over ZeroMQ; handoff marks the request pending, and resume appends peer tokens without prefix re-matching. Routing-specific engineering includes joint KV-cache budget allocation across co-located models, CUDA-graph capture over extend-mode batch shapes (the dominant handoff path), and in-process routers. (3) Delayed batching: the system is modeled as a finite-state DTMC over (queue length, batch size, residual time) per model, with stationary routing probabilities and geometrically distributed inter-send token counts; steady-state throughput T(B) = E[g(s,M)]/E[τ(s)] is solved via the stationary distribution, and B* = argmax over a feasible threshold set. The model is validated on R2R: predicted optimal B₁ coincides with measured optimum at N = 2, 3, 4. Critical design decisions: asynchrony over synchronization (justified by Figure 4's latency accounting and ablations), pending-state handoff (justified by the baseline latency profile), and the geometric/stationary routing assumption (acknowledged as a limitation). Key Results: On an 8×A100-80G server, across 15 algorithm–workload combinations (three workloads: AIME short/long-output reasoning, SWE-Smith agentic trajectories) at concurrency 4, TokenRouter achieves 2.01–64.15× higher throughput than the stronger baseline (official implementations or a self-built SGLang standard-serving baseline) and 2.03–63.64× latency reduction. Under each algorithm's original settings (original model pairs like DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B/32B, LLaMA2-7B/70B), throughput improves 2.73–21.97× at concurrency 4 and 1.93–10.20× at concurrency 1. Ablations at concurrency 8 attribute the 2.76× gain over official R2R (134.9 → 372.48 token/s) to CUDA graphs (×1.71 base), async execution (×1.12), and delayed batching (×1.31); interestingly, at concurrency 1 only CUDA graphs matter (async/delayed add nothing). Across SLM–LLM pairs (0.6B/8B up to 4B/32B), gains are 1.99–3.21× over official R2R. At concurrency 16, TokenRouter delivers 18.58× higher throughput than official R2R at concurrency 1 while retaining 1.13× higher per-user speed. A throughput–accuracy Pareto plot on AMC23 shows token-level routing via TokenRouter dominating query-level RouteLLM baselines. Baselines are mixed in strength: official CITER and R2R code lack continuous batching (weak), the Co-LLM baseline uses per-model vLLM servers (moderate), and the strongest comparison is the authors' own SGLang-based dispatcher. Scale is modest: concurrency 1–16, single server. Novelty Classification: NEW SYSTEM/TOOL with an ENGINEERING OPTIMIZATION core and a secondary NEW FORMULATION (the route-send-receive programming abstraction). The genuinely novel pieces are the pending-state handoff-resume mechanism, extend-mode CUDA graph capture for the handoff path, and the DTMC-based delayed-batching threshold derivation. The subservers-plus-dispatcher structure is a natural application of known continuous batching and CUDA graph techniques to a new setting; the throughput model is standard Markovian queueing analysis competently applied. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are present and informative (per-component gain breakdown at three concurrencies, tensor-parallelism sweep, overlapping vs. non-overlapping GPU deployment, single- vs. multi-node at 3.7 GB/s RoCE, baseline latency profile). The throughput model is empirically validated against measurements rather than left theoretical. However: no error bars, seeds, or variance reporting anywhere; the strongest headline figures (up to 64×) come largely from baselines without continuous batching, which flatters the comparison; the fair SGLang baseline is author-built rather than an external strong competitor; concurrency is capped at 16 (latency–throughput trade-off at higher load is untested); accuracy is measured only in one Pareto figure on one benchmark (AMC23), with no verification that the handoff-resume token-append semantics preserve generation quality across all five algorithms and workloads. Code is released at https://github.com/thu-nics/TokenRouter. No Goodhart-style train-on-test issue arises since nothing is learned on the serving benchmarks, but the system is tuned and evaluated on the same hardware/configuration class throughout. Deployability: Profile: SYSTEMS (a built tool evaluated by deployment; the DTMC model is auxiliary). - Practical: Runs on a single 8×A100 node with tensor parallelism and CUDA MPS; co-locating a 0.6B and a 32B model is within ordinary commercial hardware budgets. - Efficient: The system is itself the efficiency contribution — 2.01–64.15× throughput over existing token-routing implementations — though serving a 32B model (TP=2) alongside the SLM doubles-plus the GPU footprint relative to SLM-only serving. - Effective: Evidence shows it solves the throughput/admission-latency problem for five routing algorithms on three workloads; whether routed outputs remain quality-neutral under fast handoff is only checked on AMC23, a proxy. - Scalable: Only claimed beyond concurrency 16 and 3 models; the DTMC model scales with state-space size, but multi-model, high-concurrency, and high-QPS production behavior is untested. Cross-node deployment is tested and shows only ~5–15% throughput loss. The work delivers a software artifact: a released SGLang-based serving framework implementing five routing algorithms. Strengths: - The route-send-receive abstraction genuinely generalizes: five heterogeneous algorithms (confidence-based, entropy-based, learned-deferral, multi-model ensembles) are shown expressible in a few lines each (Figure 3), which is real evidence the abstraction, not just the optimizations, is the contribution. - The pending-state handoff-resume is a well-motivated mechanism, and the baseline latency profile (Table 10: prefix matching + radix-cache work ≈ 53% of per-step latency) directly implicates the single-model assumption the mechanism removes. - The DTMC throughput model is closed-form, validated against measurement, and its predicted optimal batching threshold matches the empirical optimum at every tested concurrency — a level of analytic grounding rare in systems papers. - Honest ablation accounting separates commodity engineering (CUDA graphs, 1.71×) from the research contributions (async + delayed batching, ~1.46× combined), so readers can weigh the novelty themselves. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state that the mathematical model assumes the token count between consecutive sends follows a geometric distribution (stationary routing probabilities), which holds for most but not all token-level routing algorithms; corner cases violating this are deferred to future work. This is a narrow acknowledgment — the authors confront the modeling assumption directly but do not discuss baseline strength, quality-preservation under handoff, or concurrency scaling limits. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - The 64.15× headline is dominated by the weakest baselines; against the strongest comparison (their own SGLang standard-serving baseline, itself not CUDA-graph-extended to parity in all configurations), the gap is far smaller. A published, competitively tuned token-routing server would strengthen the claim. - No statistical rigor: single runs, no confidence intervals, and several reported gains (e.g., SLM TP 1→2 adding 0.4–0.8%) are within plausible noise. - Correctness of the handoff semantics is under-evaluated: send excludes or includes the just-sampled token depending on the algorithm, and resume commits all peer tokens; only one figure on AMC23 checks accuracy, so silent quality degradation on agentic or long-reasoning workloads cannot be ruled out from the evidence given. - Concurrency capped at 16 on a single node; the interaction of delayed batching with admission control, preemption, and heterogeneous SLOs at production load is unexplored. - The DTMC model assumes stationary routing probabilities and independent requests; realistic reasoning traces have strongly non-stationary difficulty (difficulty spikes mid-chain), and the paper does not measure model violation on real workloads beyond R2R. Bottom Line: For anyone deploying or researching token-level LLM routing, this is currently the only credible open-source serving substrate for it and the ablations are honest about where the speedup comes from — but the headline multipliers are inflated by weak baselines, so read it as a solid, well-analyzed systems contribution rather than the last word on serving routed inference.

EVISKILL: Grounding Skill Evolution in Replayable Evidence (36 ▲ )

Yan Zhou, Yili Wang, Yiwei Dai, Qinggang Zhang, Xin Wang · arxiv.org · Daily papers of 7 Oct 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces EviSkill, a framework for LLM-agent skill evolution that attaches every proposed skill edit to a Replayable Evidence Card (persistent ID + trigger ranges + correction), verifies each edit by re-executing its cited trajectory ranges, and carries locally-supported-but-globally-rejected edits across epochs in a Provisional Edit Ledger until global validation admits them. - Why it's important: Existing experience-driven skill-evolution methods commit edits based on trajectory plausibility alone, and their preliminary study shows 25–45% of such edits fail or degrade behavior when re-executed — meaning errors compound silently across evolution rounds in parameter-free agent improvement. - How it does it: The core trick is provenance-preserving edits: each edit keeps links to the exact trajectory intervals that justify it, enabling localized prefix-replay of only those ranges under the edited skill, with an LLM evaluator returning accept/reflect/reject, plus post-rejection replay that rescues useful edits from globally rejected revisions. - The good: Mechanism analysis over 18 runs and 3,361 evidence cards shows the machinery actually works as claimed — 20.7–42.5% of candidate edits fail initial replay, 72.9% of the 96 provisionally retained edits are later promoted into validated skills, and trigger-range replay cuts replay steps by 66–69% versus full-trajectory replay. - The missing: No error bars, multiple seeds, or significance tests are reported despite temperature-0.7 rollouts and shuffled task order, all meta-roles (extractor, editor, evaluator) use GPT-5.5 with no validation of judge reliability, and evolution runs only 4 epochs on ≤96 training tasks, so cost-scaling and long-run stability of the provisional ledger are untested. - Read it or not: Read it if you build self-improving agent memory/skill systems and need a concrete pattern for verifiable, revisable non-parametric knowledge updates; skip it if you only want frontier benchmark numbers, since the strongest gains concentrate on ScienceWorld and the margins over SkillOpt are modest on ALFWorld/AppWorld.

Problem & Motivation: LLM agents accumulate reusable procedural guidance as external skill documents (markdown procedures, tool-use rules) edited across interaction epochs without parameter updates. The paper identifies two failure modes in the prevailing experience-driven paradigm: (1) edits distilled from trajectories do not consistently produce the behavioral change they target — re-executing Trace2Skill edits shows only 55–75% actually improve the motivating tasks on the three benchmarks (Sec. 2.1), and once a bad edit is committed it contaminates subsequent evolution rounds; (2) global validation is all-or-nothing — a revision rejected on validation accuracy may contain constituent edits that are individually beneficial, which the paper demonstrates by selectively retaining rejected-revision edits for +4.16/+3.34/+12.50 pp on ALFWorld/AppWorld/ScienceWorld (Sec. 2.2). Anyone running continual agent improvement over long horizons inherits both problems: overfit edits that persist, and useful signal discarded with failed revisions. Key Idea: Treat skill evolution as evidence management rather than lesson extraction: never convert a trajectory observation directly into a committed edit — instead preserve a replayable pointer to the exact execution intervals that justify the edit, verify the edit by re-running those intervals under the edited skill, and keep the edit provisional across epochs until global validation (not local replay) decides it becomes permanent. The separation of Validated Skill from Working Skill (validated plus provisional ledger) is what lets a rejected revision's good parts survive. Methodology: The pipeline runs for E=4 epochs, each with three phases. (1) Evidence-Grounded Edit Synthesis: an LLM extractor f_ext consumes the Working Skill and current trajectories to emit Trajectory Evidence Cards, and compares adjacent-epoch trajectory pairs for tasks referenced by Tracked Edits to emit Contrastive Evidence Cards; cards pass a grounding verifier, are embedded with Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B, clustered with HDBSCAN into Evidence Windows, and an LLM editor f_edit consolidates each window into candidate edits that retain their supporting card IDs (Eq. 5). (2) Replay-Guided Edit Verification: for each edit, the recorded trajectory prefix before the trigger range is copied to reconstruct state, the Action Agent re-executes the range under Working Skill ⊕ edit, and an evaluator f_eval returns accept/reflect/reject; reflected edits get one revision-and-re-replay cycle (Eq. 7–8). Accepted edits are consolidated into a candidate revision. (3) Cross-Epoch Evidence Propagation: global validation on D_val gates the candidate into the Validated Skill (Eq. 9); if rejected, each consolidated edit is re-replayed in isolation under Validated Skill ⊕ v (post-rejection replay), accepted edits enter the Provisional Edit Ledger (capped at 16 live edits), and card lifecycle states (active/protected/archived/stale) govern what evidence carries forward. The objective is simply strict validation-accuracy improvement — a hill-climbing selection rule; there is no learned component. Critical design decisions: (a) trigger-range replay rather than full-trajectory replay (well-justified: 66–69% step reduction, Appendix F.2); (b) provisional ledger with post-rejection replay (well-justified by the Sec. 2.2 preliminary study and the 72.9% eventual-promotion figure); (c) replay decisions made by a GPT-5.5 judge (weakly justified — no agreement study against human or ground-truth judgments). Key Results: Evaluated on ALFWorld (134 test tasks), AppWorld (168), and ScienceWorld (211) with six Action-Agent backbones (GPT-5.5, GPT-5.4, GPT-5.4-mini, Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, Qwen3.5-9B, Qwen3.5-4B) against NoSkill, a fixed LLM Skill, and four skill-evolution baselines (Trace2Skill, EvoSkill, SkillGrad, SkillOpt — all concurrent 2026 arXiv preprints, so current but not peer-reviewed). EviSkill is best in 14 of 18 model–dataset settings and top-two in 16, averaging +17.93 pp over NoSkill. Largest margins: ScienceWorld with Qwen3.5-9B, 37.91% vs SkillOpt's 22.27% (+15.64 pp); with GPT-5.4, 76.78% vs SkillOpt's 63.03% (+13.75 pp). Ablations (averaged over three GPT backbones): removing replay costs 2.49/4.56/2.85 pp on ALFWorld/AppWorld/ScienceWorld; removing cross-epoch propagation costs 1.49/4.16/1.11 pp; a decomposition on ALFWorld (Qwen family) shows both sub-pathways (cards-only +1.74, edits-only +2.24) contribute. Efficiency: 3.77 validation-accuracy points per 100 training rollouts vs 1.55 (EvoSkill) and 0.84 (SkillGrad), though EviSkill consumes 376 mean rollouts vs SkillGrad's 120. Notably, several baselines degrade below the fixed initial skill (e.g., EvoSkill at 54.50% on ScienceWorld/GPT-5.5 vs LLM Skill's 76.78%), which the paper presents as evidence that unchecked evolution is actively harmful. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD with a supporting NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING. Genuinely novel: the Replayable Evidence Card abstraction — persistent, replayable provenance links between skill edits and trajectory ranges, combined with the provisional-ledger mechanism that decouples local edit support from global revision acceptance. The empirical findings (40%+ of trajectory-derived edits fail behavioral verification; rejected revisions contain promotable edits) are themselves contributions. Standard components applied in a new combination: LLM-as-judge accept/reflect/reject loops, validation-gated hill climbing (from SkillOpt), clustering for grouping (HDBSCAN), and reflection-with-revision — each individually known; the contribution is the provenance architecture binding them together, not any single mechanism. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are present and target the two headline components, including a finer decomposition of cross-epoch propagation into cards-only and edits-only variants, and full six-backbone ablation tables in the appendix. Mechanism analysis is unusually thorough: 18 runs spanning 72 epochs, edit-level and card-level counts (155 consolidated edits, 96 post-rejection acceptances, 3,361 cards with lifecycle statistics). However: no error bars, seeds, or significance tests are reported despite stochastic rollouts (temperature 0.7, shuffled task order), and success-rate differences of 1–2 pp (common on ALFWorld) could fall within run-to-run variance. Code is released at https://github.com/Zhouyaner/eviskill, with dataset splits, prompts (Appendix H), and hyperparameters documented. Methodological concerns: (1) the extractor, editor, and evaluator are all GPT-5.5 — self-verification circularity is not addressed and judge accuracy is never validated against human labels; (2) skill selection repeatedly optimizes the same 48–57-task validation sets over 4 epochs, a mild Goodhart risk shared by all baselines but not quantified; (3) the preliminary studies (Sec. 2) that motivate the design use Trace2Skill, the authors' own framework's target — appropriate, but the retained-edits analysis uses a GPT-5.5 selector whose choices could leak the conclusion. Baselines are current and reasonably strong (SkillOpt in particular), which strengthens the comparison. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (framework run in simulated environments; no deployment). - Practical: Runs on any hardware that can call GPT-5.5-class APIs and host the three open-source simulators; no training infrastructure required, but the meta-pipeline needs a frontier model for extraction, editing, and judging — a real cost barrier for smaller teams. - Efficient: Higher upfront cost than cheaper baselines (376 vs 120 mean training rollouts), partially offset by localized replay (66–69% fewer replayed steps than full-trajectory replay) and a 2.4–4.5× better validation-gain-per-rollout ratio; the paper provides this accounting explicitly, which is commendable. - Effective: Strong evidence on ScienceWorld and ALFWorld that verified, provenance-linked edits beat both no-skill and unverified evolution; evidence on AppWorld is weaker (second place in two settings, e.g., 83.93 vs EvoSkill's 85.12 with GPT-5.4-mini), so the claim holds fully on two of three benchmarks. - Scalable: Untested beyond 4 epochs and ≤96 training tasks; the 16-edit ledger cap, 15-edit post-rejection replay budget, and 128-edit epoch budget are hand-tuned ceilings whose behavior under 10× more tasks or epochs is claimed by design intent only. The work delivers a released code artifact (GitHub repo) plus documented prompts; the reusable contribution is the evidence-card/lifecycle design pattern rather than a library with a stable API. Strengths: - The two preliminary studies are the paper's best move: before proposing the method, it empirically quantifies both motivating failure modes (per-edit re-execution outcomes in Fig. 2; recoverable value inside rejected revisions in Fig. 3), so the design is driven by measured failure, not intuition. - Provenance-preserving edits with trigger-range replay is a genuinely reusable design pattern — it converts the vague notion of "grounding edits in evidence" into a mechanical, checkable procedure (reconstruct prefix, re-execute range, compare), and the localized-replay audit (Appendix F.2) quantifies exactly what this saves. - Mechanism analysis goes beyond accuracy: promotion trajectories of retained edits (72.9% eventually incorporated), card reuse depth (23% used in ≥2 epochs), and cross-task-vs-single-task card utilization (Table 6) let a reader verify that the claimed mechanisms, not side effects, produce the gains. - Honest handling of a subtle confound: the cross-task-evidence analysis shows broader support does not substitute for replay (cross-task cards have lower replay-retention rates), which cuts against an intuitive hypothesis the authors could have exploited. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: There is no dedicated limitations section, but the authors flag several things inline: the AppWorld advantage "is less consistent" across backbones; cross-task evidence breadth "does not ensure... generalization to unseen tasks"; 27.1% of provisionally retained edits remain un-promoted when the 4-epoch budget ends, so their eventual value "remains unobserved"; and "identifying a deficiency does not ensure an effective repair" (9 of 29 tracked-edit lineages yielded no accepted correction). These are stated accurately rather than minimized, which is a credibility positive, but the omission of variance/significance reporting and judge-reliability validation is not acknowledged. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - Statistical rigor: with temperature-0.7 rollouts and shuffled task orders, single-run accuracy differences of 1–2 pp on ALFWorld (e.g., 96.27 vs 95.52 vs 94.78) are not distinguishable from noise without seeds or confidence intervals; the "best in 14/18 settings" claim inherits this. - Judge validity: all accept/reflect/reject decisions — the load-bearing mechanism — come from one GPT-5.5 evaluator with no human agreement study, no ablation substituting a weaker/cheaper judge, and no analysis of judge errors on the acceptance cases in the case studies. - Replay assumes the environment can be faithfully reconstructed by copying a recorded prefix; this holds in the three deterministic simulators used but the paper does not discuss applicability to stochastic, networked, or non-restartable environments, which limits the practical scope of the core mechanism. - Frontier-model asymmetry: the meta-pipeline always uses GPT-5.5 even when the Action Agent is a 4B model, so the framework's value for resource-constrained deployments (its most natural audience) is untested — does the overhead still pay off when meta-model ≈ action model? - Only 4 evolution epochs: the provisional-ledger mechanism is justified by cross-epoch dynamics, but 4 epochs is too short to observe ledger saturation, stale-card accumulation at scale, or degradation loops the framework is designed to prevent. - No comparison to a trivial alternative for the second failure mode: a simple "apply each edit individually and keep those that improve validation" strategy would address rejected-revision recovery without evidence cards; its absence makes it hard to attribute gains to the provenance machinery specifically versus per-edit selection alone. Bottom Line: For researchers building self-evolving agent memory or skill libraries, this is worth reading for its evidence-provenance design pattern and unusually honest mechanism analysis; for everyone else, SkillOpt-style validation-gated revision plus per-edit selection likely covers most of the practical benefit at a fraction of the machinery.

Problem & Motivation: Clinical diagnosis is a long-horizon, multi-turn process in which physicians iteratively gather history, order tests, and integrate imaging, but medical LLMs are trained and benchmarked mostly on static single-turn VQA. Groups building interactive medical agents face a gap: EHR-driven benchmarks (AI Hospital, AgentClinic, MedAgentBoard, DiagGym) match clinical distributions but are small (506–2.4k cases per the paper's Table 1), noisy, and hard to verify, while synthetic benchmarks scale but produce idealized, inconsistent evidence. There is no large-scale, multimodal, verifiable environment for training agents via RL on realistic clinical workflows. Key Idea: The core trick is hybrid grounding for simulation plus confidence-based process reward. On the environment side, an "EHR-first → knowledge-base → no-evidence fallback" routing policy lets a patient simulator answer factually from real records while using a disease-level knowledge base to patch missing EHR signals, keeping long multi-turn dialogues answerable without inventing evidence. On the training side, the process reward g_t = log π_θ(y|H≤t) − log π_θ(y|H<t) — the increase in the policy's own probability of the correct diagnosis after each turn — converts sparse terminal correctness into dense per-turn credit for informative questioning, retrieval, and test ordering, with a penalty for turns that trigger the no-evidence fallback. Methodology: (1) Data pipeline: MIMIC-IV, MIMIC-IV-Note, and MIMIC-CXR admissions are packaged into structured episodes (demographics, labs, microbiology, medications, notes, radiology reports, CXR images, diagnosis labels), restricted to a pre-medication observation window with de-leakage of discharge summaries to avoid outcome leakage. (2) Environment: a patient simulator with the three-tier evidence routing; three MCP-callable tools for the doctor agent — guideline retrieval, imaging exam ordering, and visual grounding via Grounding DINO. (3) Agent training: SFT cold start on ~3k trajectories synthesized by Gemini-3-Pro, then difficulty-aware filtering (8 stochastic rollouts per case; keep only non-uniformly-correct/incorrect cases), then GRPO with combined reward R = λ_res·r_res + Σ r_proc_t (weights 1.0/0.5), λ_auto penalty on fallback turns, trained on 8×H200 GPUs with group size 8, lr 1e-6, horizon 15. Critical design decisions: (a) knowledge-base augmentation to handle EHR missingness — motivated but not ablated against an EHR-only simulator, so its isolated contribution is unverified; (b) difficulty filtering to keep reward variance — reasonable but heuristic; (c) evaluation by LLM-as-judge (Qwen3-8B) with binary consistency over synonyms plus ICD matching — pragmatic but under-validated (no human agreement study reported). Key Results: On the MedEnv benchmark, Diagnosis-R1 (Qwen3-VL-8B base) scores 41.95% accuracy without images (80.99% efficient turns, 10.58 avg turns) vs. 35.99% for Qwen3.5-397B-A17B, 34.84% for GPT 5, and 34.15% for Gemini-3-Flash among general models, and vs. 28.59% for the best medical model (Hulu-Med-32B); the best baseline with images is 37.56% (Qwen3.5-397B). With images enabled, Diagnosis-R1 slightly degrades (41.15% accuracy, 77.87% efficient turns), while several baselines improve. Tool ablations show retrieval helps most, especially for small models; grounding adds little, attributed to coarse-grained CXR cues. Scaling RL data improves accuracy monotonically but plateaus around 50K trajectories. Baselines are current frontier models (GPT 5, Gemini-3-Flash, Qwen3.5-397B) and recent medical models, so the comparison set is strong; testing is at standard single-GPU-inference scale on a single benchmark. Novelty Classification: NEW DATASET/BENCHMARK (496K+ trajectories, an order of magnitude larger than the 506–48k cited prior environments, with EHR-grounded fallback verification) plus NEW METHOD for the confidence-based dense process reward applied to clinical interaction. The individual ingredients — MIMIC-derived simulation, MCP tool interfaces, SFT→GRPO training, LLM-as-judge evaluation — are standard; the genuinely new combination is the EHR-first/KB/fallback routing and the per-turn log-probability-gain reward tied to ground-truth diagnosis confidence. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are present and well-controlled: training-stage ablation (base/SFT/RL-outcome/full) holds model, data, steps, and hyperparameters fixed, and tool ablations span model scales. Missing: no error bars, seeds, or significance tests; no inter-rater or human validation of the Qwen3-8B judge; no ablation of the knowledge-base routing component itself. Code and data are released at https://github.com/FanZT6/MedEnv, which is a strong reproducibility positive. Methodological concerns: (a) the method is developed and evaluated on the same environment (inherent to environment papers, but generalization is untested); (b) the judge shares a model family (Qwen) with the base policy, a potential self-preference bias; (c) the KB is matched to cases via ICD codes and disease cues extracted from the EHR, which may leak diagnosis-adjacent information the baselines without equivalent grounding cannot access. This is a peer-review-stage paper (MICCAI 2026 submission); results should be treated as pre-publication. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (a built environment plus trained agent, evaluated by experiments). - Practical: Yes — the environment runs on public MIMIC data (credentialed access required) and the 8B agent runs on commodity GPU hardware; training required 8×H200, which is substantial but routine for RL fine-tuning. - Efficient: Diagnosis-R1 reaches the best accuracy with an 8B model and the fewest average turns among top performers (10.58), so inference cost is low relative to the 397B-parameter baseline it outperforms. - Effective: The evidence shows it improves accuracy and efficiency on its own benchmark, which is a proxy — the paper itself states MedEnv is a research environment, not a deployable diagnostic system, and no clinician or external validation exists. - Scalable: Not demonstrated beyond ~50K RL trajectories, where the paper reports a plateau; 10×–100× scaling is explicitly said to require better data quality and reward design rather than volume. The work delivers a concrete software artifact (environment, data pipeline, code, and a trained agent checkpoint) rather than stopping at paper form. Strengths: - The confidence-based process reward is a real methodological contribution: it gives dense, interpretable credit for evidence acquisition in long-horizon diagnosis, and the ablation attributes ~10 accuracy points to it over outcome-reward-only RL (31.51% → 41.95%). - Scale and grounding of the environment: 496K+ trajectories from real ICU records with paired CXR, roughly 200× the size of AI Hospital and ~200× MedAgentBoard per the paper's own table, with a verifiable fallback mechanism that blocks unsupported information. - Honest negative results: the paper reports that image evidence hurts its own trained agent, that grounding contributes little, and that RL scaling saturates at ~50K — an unusually candid reporting posture that raises credibility. - Full release of code and data enables independent reproduction of both the benchmark and the training pipeline. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors explicitly state that MedEnv is a research environment rather than a deployable diagnostic system, that EHR-first grounding does not establish clinical safety without clinician and external validation, that the current environment covers only CXR (limiting grounding-tool value), that image integration currently degrades their agent's performance, and that further gains require better data quality, hard-case coverage, and reward/sampling design rather than volume. They confront limitations directly rather than minimizing them — a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - No validation of the LLM-as-judge against clinician or human labels; judge reliability for binary free-text diagnosis consistency is asserted, not measured, and the judge's Qwen lineage overlaps the base policy family. - The knowledge-base routing is never ablated; the possibility that ICD-based KB retrieval effectively reveals the diagnosis (label leakage through the environment) — which would inflate both trained-agent accuracy and the process-reward signal — is not ruled out. - Baselines are prompted frontier models interacting with the environment, but only the authors' model receives the ~3K SFT trajectories and RL; no baseline (e.g., GPT 5 or Qwen3.5-397B) is fine-tuned on MedEnv data, so the comparison conflates architecture/scale with access to environment-specific training. - Generalization is untested: everything is measured on MedEnv itself; there is no transfer evaluation to an external multi-turn medical benchmark (e.g., AgentClinic or AI Hospital) to show the agent or reward design generalizes beyond the authors' own environment. - Missing-data robustness — the central motivation for KB augmentation — is not evaluated with any controlled experiment on EHR missingness rates. Bottom Line: For researchers building interactive medical agents, this is worth reading and using as the current largest EHR-grounded training environment with released code, but the headline accuracy claims rest on self-benchmarked, LLM-judged evaluation and should be treated as provisional until the judge reliability and potential KB leakage are independently checked.

Questioning the Questions: Sustaining Self-Evolution in Reasoning Models (64 ▲ )

Jinyuan Li, Chengsong Huang, Langlin Huang, Donghong Cai, Shiping Gao, Yuyi Yang, Jiaxin Huang · arxiv.org · Daily papers of 8 Oct 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces R-Quest, a self-evolution framework for reasoning LLMs that injects two feedback signals — question validity judgments from a validity-trained solver and task-level novelty judgments from a frozen base model — into the questioner's GRPO reward to prevent performance collapse during prolonged self-play. - Why it's important: Self-evolving models that train on their own generated questions collapse after a few rounds (R-Zero drops 11.57 points below its base model after ten rounds), which currently caps the practicality of label-free, self-play RL training. - How it does it: The core move is diagnosing collapse as two data-quality failures (rising invalid-question rates and task-type repetition that BLEU clustering misses) and gating the questioner's uncertainty reward on a solver majority-vote validity check plus O(BK) sampled pairwise same-type judgments by the frozen base model. - The good: The longitudinal evidence is convincing: on Qwen3-4B-Base over ten rounds, R-Quest peaks at 51.92 average math score in the final round while R-Zero falls to 34.60, and GPT-judged question validity rises to 94.5–97.5% under R-Quest versus falling to 49.0% under R-Zero. - The missing: All novelty judgments, validity annotations, and concentration analyses rely on GPT-5.6-Sol or the model's own judgments without human-verified ground truth at scale, and the evaluation reports best-checkpoint-per-domain averages over only 3B/4B models without multiple seeds or significance testing. - Read it or not: Read it if you are building questioner–solver self-play or label-free RL pipelines, because the diagnosis (consistency filtering inflates invalid-question share; lexical clustering fragments repeated task types) is directly actionable; skip it if you only work with large frontier models or verified-data training.

Scored using Empirical profile. This is a solid, actionable diagnosis of self-evolution collapse — the finding that consistency filtering enriches for invalid questions is genuinely counter-intuitive and the matched repair experiment converts it into a causal argument, which supports Non-Obviousness (72) and Novelty (70). Problem & Motivation: Self-evolving reasoning models (e.g., R-Zero) train a questioner and solver in alternation using only model-generated data, removing dependence on human-curated corpora. Practitioners adopting these frameworks observe that early gains reverse: R-Zero's average math score peaks at 49.10 in round three and falls to 34.60 by round ten on Qwen3-4B-Base, below the 46.17 base model. The paper asks why performance collapses and what mechanism sustains improvement. It identifies two failure modes in self-generated question pools: (1) invalid questions (contradictory, unsolvable, ambiguous, missing conditions) become more prevalent each round — the valid-question rate drops from 76.5% to 39.5% over five R-Zero rounds — and R-Zero's answer-consistency filter makes this worse, cutting valid share to 27.64% in round five because solvers give inconsistent answers to ill-posed questions, which the filter misreads as desirable difficulty; (2) the questioner recycles the same underlying mathematical task with reworded surface forms, and BLEU-based repetition clustering fragments one task type into up to 22 clusters, so the cluster-size repetition penalty never fires — the top three task types cover 59.5% of round-five training data. Key Idea: The core insight is that self-evolution needs the training loop itself to evaluate the questions, not just the answers: teach the solver to say INVALID for ill-posed questions during an initial GRPO mid-training phase, then use that capability both as a reward gate for the questioner and a data filter, and replace lexical diversity control with an atomic semantic judgment — "are these two questions the same exercise pattern?" — issued by a frozen copy of the base model on randomly sampled within-batch pairs. Methodology: The pipeline has three phases. (1) Validity-aware solver initialization: 2,240 questions sampled from five R-Zero rounds are annotated as valid/invalid by GPT-5.6-Sol (two-stage: attempt-solve-then-classify, then independent answer derivation with an automated review pass); the base model is GRPO-trained (15 steps, 512-question rollout batches, 8 responses/question) with reward R_init = 1[a = a(q)] − λ·1[a = INVALID ∧ a(q) ≠ INVALID], λ = 0.5, teaching it to reject invalid questions without over-refusing. (2) Novelty assessment: for each of B candidate questions in a questioner rollout batch, the frozen base model judges K = 8 uniformly sampled within-batch references as SAME_TYPE or DIFFERENT; a single same-type match rejects the candidate, giving pass probability ≈ (1−p)^K where p is the same-type fraction — reducing O(B²) exhaustive comparison to O(BK). (3) Co-evolution: the questioner's GRPO reward is g_valid(q) = ½ − u(q) for invalid-classified questions (u(q) = fraction of 9 solver responses returning INVALID) and g_novel(q)·min{s(q), 1−s(q)} otherwise, restricting the uncertainty reward to questions that are both valid and novel; the solver is trained on consistency-filtered questions (s(q) ∈ [0.3, 0.8]) with majority-vote pseudo-labels, mixed with 10% replay of the validity-initialization data. Critical design decisions: using the solver itself (continuously trained) rather than a frozen judge for validity — ablated and supported (+1.71 math points over frozen judge); using the frozen base model rather than an external stronger model for novelty — justified by self-containment but validated only against GPT-based concentration metrics; and setting K = 8 rather than 16 — the paper shows K = 16 over-suppresses challenging variants within recurring patterns and hurts performance (a thoughtful negative result). Key Results: On Qwen3-4B-Base across seven math benchmarks (AMC, Minerva, MATH-500, GSM8K, OlympiadBench, AIME24/25), R-Quest averages 51.64 versus 49.82 (R-Diverse), 49.57 (OCNR), 49.10 (R-Zero), and 46.17 (base) — +5.47 over base, 1.87× R-Zero's gain. On OctoThinker-3B it averages 30.69 versus 28.61 for the best baseline. Over ten rounds, R-Quest reaches 51.92 in the final round while R-Zero falls to 34.60 (Δ = 17.32 at round ten; R-Zero ends 11.57 points below base, R-Quest 5.75 above). Code generation: 62.69 average pass@1 (HumanEval+/MBPP+) on Qwen3-4B versus 58.79 base and ≤60.50 for baselines; general reasoning (SuperGPQA/MMLU-Pro/BBEH): 32.75 versus 28.79 base. Ablations show both components matter (w/o validity: 50.27 math; w/o novelty: 51.02; w/o both: 49.10) and validity feedback is the critical one for ten-round stability — its removal causes late-stage collapse. Mechanistic evidence: solver invalid-recall rises from ~15% (R-Zero throughout) to 86.36% by round ten; majority-answer accuracy on valid questions retains 54.69% at round ten versus R-Zero's 2.06%; top-five task-type concentration is held at 24.0% versus R-Zero's 69.0% at round five. Baselines (R-Zero, OCNR, R-Diverse) are recent and relevant; scale is modest (3B/4B models, 10,000 candidate questions per round). Novelty Classification: NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING (systematic characterization that answer-consistency filtering increases invalid-question share and that BLEU clustering fragments repeated task types, weakening repetition penalties) plus NEW METHOD (validity-gated and semantic-novelty-gated questioner rewards within the questioner–solver GRPO loop). The novelty judgment mechanism itself — sampled pairwise LLM comparisons with a (1−p)^K acceptance model — is a straightforward, well-motivated design rather than a new algorithmic primitive; the contribution is the diagnosis plus the integration of these two gates into self-play training, not any single component. Rigor & Reproducibility: Component ablations are present and informative (Table 3, Table 9 per-benchmark), including a frozen-judge control and a K-sensitivity study that surfaces a genuinely non-obvious trade-off (stricter diversity control lowers concentration but hurts scores). The preliminary repair experiment (repaired vs. original 1,273-question matched datasets: 49.91 vs. 46.54) causally links invalid questions to solver degradation. Wilson 95% confidence intervals are reported for validity-rate plots. Concerns: no multiple seeds or significance tests on headline results; each method's score is the best checkpoint across rounds, a favorable selection rule; all validity, novelty-ground-truth, and concentration measurements use GPT-5.6-Sol, which is also used to build the training data — the judge is never validated against human labels beyond a stated manual review of flagged answers; the paper is a preprint and self-references co-authors across much of the related self-play literature (Huang et al.). No code, data, or model weights are stated as released (the first page shows Project Page and Code markers, but no URLs appear in the provided text). Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (with a SYSTEMS-adjacent flavor, as it is a training recipe rather than a deployed tool). - Practical: Yes — everything runs on 3B/4B open-weight models with GRPO and self-generated judgments; the only external model (GPT-5.6-Sol) is needed once, offline, for the 2,240-question initialization set. - Efficient: The novelty check costs O(BK) = O(2,048×8) pairwise judgments per rollout batch, plus 9 validity responses per question; OCNR requires 2× question oversampling by comparison, but a full FLOP accounting against baselines is not reported. - Effective: The evidence supports the stated problem at 3B/4B scale on math, code, and general reasoning benchmarks, though evaluation-on-own-curriculum selection (best checkpoint per round range) slightly inflates all methods including baselines. - Scalable: Untested above 4B parameters and 10 rounds; whether validity self-assessment remains reliable for larger or more capable models (where solvers may confidently answer subtly invalid questions) is claimed implicitly, not shown. Deliverable: a training recipe and (apparently) a code artifact, but no released weights or dataset URLs are visible in the paper text. Strengths: - The diagnostic section is genuinely valuable and could stand alone: quantifying that consistency filtering enriches for invalid questions (27.64% valid in round five post-filter vs. 39.5% pre-filter) is a counter-intuitive, actionable finding for anyone using majority-vote pseudo-labels. - The causal repair experiment (matched 1,273-question datasets, +3.37 points from repairing 507 invalid questions) converts a correlation into a reasonably clean causal argument. - The K = 8 vs. K = 16 analysis resists a naive "more diversity control is better" conclusion and identifies the exploration-within-pattern trade-off, backed by the (1−p)^K acceptance model. - The 10-round longitudinal tracking of mechanism variables (invalid recall, question validity, majority-answer accuracy, top-five concentration) ties performance curves to the hypothesized causes, not just end metrics. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors acknowledge that overly strict diversity control (K = 16) suppresses challenging variants within recurring exercise patterns and reduces performance; that either feedback alone yields a higher peak than R-Zero but validity is essential for sustained gains (novelty's removal causes only milder decline); that minor fluctuations occur between rounds; and that R-Zero's BLEU clustering and OCNR/R-Diverse's embedding-based novelty are inadequate in specific ways they demonstrate. They do not include a dedicated limitations section in the main text; the limitations they do state are confronted with data rather than minimized. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - GPT-5.6-Sol is simultaneously the annotator of the initialization data, the judge of validity rates, the source of reference answers for accuracy evaluation, and the grouper for diversity analysis — a single-model evaluation stack with no reported human inter-annotator agreement; a systematic bias in this judge would propagate through every diagnostic figure. - The validity-initialization data is drawn from R-Zero's own question distributions, so the solver's notion of "invalid" is calibrated to R-Zero's failure modes; transfer to questioners with different generation styles is untested. - Only 3B/4B models are evaluated; the claim of sustained self-evolution is untested at 7B–70B scale, where the self-assessment dynamics may differ qualitatively. - Best-checkpoint reporting per method (standard in this line of work, but still favorable) combined with no multi-seed runs leaves the 2.5-point margins over R-Diverse/OCNR statistically unevaluated; AIME scores (13.44 vs. 12.29 on ~30-problem sets) are within noise. - The code-generation and general-reasoning gains arise from a math-only self-evolution curriculum; the paper speculates about grounded reasoning but offers no analysis of why transfer to code is larger for R-Quest than baselines. - The frozen base model's novelty-judgment accuracy is never directly measured (only its downstream effect via concentration metrics), so the sampler-based gate could be silently admitting or rejecting at unknown error rates. Bottom Line: For anyone running or designing questioner–solver self-play pipelines, this is worth reading for the failure diagnosis and the demonstrated 17.32-point ten-round advantage over R-Zero, but the modest margins over recent baselines, single-judge evaluation stack, and 4B-scale-only evidence mean it is a strong engineering contribution to an active subfield rather than a definitive solution to self-evolution collapse.

Problem & Motivation: Real shopping conversations involve users who start with underspecified intents, reveal constraints gradually, revise preferences, reject candidates, and coordinate multiple subgoals (bundles, split orders, urgent vs. deferrable items). Agents must therefore elicit hidden needs, track evolving state, ground recommendations in real catalog evidence, and converge to an actionable purchase. The authors argue existing benchmarks miss this: outcome-oriented ones (LLM-ReDial, CONCEPT, PEPPER, RecUserSim) score final-item relevance in simplified product spaces, while execution-oriented ones (ShoppingBench, DeepShop, EComStage, RecoWorld) score tool-call completion but ignore the conversational decision process. Practitioners deploying shopping assistants consequently lack a way to measure state tracking, constraint updating, and grounded convergence. Key Idea: The core insight is that conversational shopping should be evaluated — and implemented — as a session-level decision-control problem rather than single-turn recommendation or isolated tool execution. For the benchmark, this means decomposing each episode into ⟨P, S, Π⟩ (profile, scenario, session plan) with an explicit latent/visible profile split so agents must infer hidden constraints through dialogue, plus a metric hierarchy that scores turn quality, session process quality, and final convergence separately. For the agent, it means externalizing state, action timing, evidence grounding, and consistency checking into four executable modules rather than leaving them to free-form LLM generation. The idea is sound but incremental: it re-packages dialogue state tracking, action policies, and grounded retrieval guards into one coherent harness. Methodology: Benchmark. (1) Product inventory: category-driven crawls of a real e-commerce platform, rule-filtered to shippable physical goods, deduplicated to 3.28M SKUs with price/attribute/category/fulfillment fields; treated as a fixed snapshot. (2) Episodes: a category-anchored two-stage pipeline maps category seeds to scenario archetypes (bundle construction, upgrades, repairs, restocking, mixed errands, urgency purchases) with constraint modifiers, then a session plan Π specifies intent ambiguity, subgoal count, and disclosure timing of hidden constraints; each episode carries diagnostic metadata (scenario type, interaction phenomenon, user style) assigned at construction, not from agent outcomes. (3) Profiles: structured schemas separating hard/soft/negotiable constraints, with visible prior P̃ split from latent state; catalog grounding during synthesis downgrades unverifiable constraints. (4) Evaluation: Kimi-K2.6 simulates the customer under an action-first policy (validated at 0.93 profile faithfulness, 0.95 action controllability on 200 sampled profiles); a three-stage GPT-5.5 judge scores {0,1,2} turn dimensions (need understanding, rec. accuracy, rationale), five session dimensions (clarification, state tracking, constraint updating, decision pacing, personalization), and holistic overall_success plus convergence_quality; sessions terminate as SUCCESS, EARLY-EXIT-WITHOUT-CONVERGENCE, or MAX-TURN (30). Held-out diagnostic set: 100 episodes per slice across 6 scenario types, 6 phenomena, 6 user styles; each system evaluated 5 times, mean reported. Agent. RealShop_Agent maintains explicit state M_t (intents, subgoals, constraint stack, rejected options, stale dependencies), selects among six actions, retrieves structured evidence records with stale-evidence invalidation, and applies three runtime guards (ToolBudget, FabricationGuard, StateConsistencyGuard). Backbone: Qwen3.5-27B, SFT on 10K examples then GRPO (8 rollouts/prompt, 1.5K training prompts, lr 1e-6, slime framework) with reward r = r_task + r_ground + r_constraint + r_tool − p_invalid. Critical design decisions: the action-first simulator (well justified — decouples behavior from surface realization and is validated); the latent/visible profile split (well justified — enables partial observability); and grading the agent's RL with rubric-aligned reward signals (thinly justified — see gaps). Key Results: On RealWorldShop's held-out diagnostic set: (1) Turn-to-session gap is universal — general LLMs average Turn Avg. 1.08 vs. Sess. Avg. 0.80; GPT-5 drops 1.45→1.20 yet still leads baselines with 0.71 success, 2.49 convergence, 0.10 early exit; Gemini-2.5-Flash and GPT-4o succeed on only 0.38. (2) Early exits correlate with state-tracking collapse (state tracking 0.98 in non-exit vs. 0.23 in early-exit sessions) rather than poor clarification (1.43→1.25); bundle re-planning success falls to 48%. (3) Ambiguity and complexity amplify the gap: explicit single-item success 72% (gap 0.11) vs. ambiguous single-item 57%; ambiguous + long-horizon sessions show the largest gap (0.33); low-patience/high-skepticism/efficiency-first users raise early exits to 27–32% vs. 12–19% for tolerant styles. (4) RealShop_Agent (full) reaches Sess. Avg. 1.39, success 0.82, gap 0.07, early exit 0.09, versus the Qwen3.5-27B base at 0.55 success and the SFT/RL-adapted backbone at 0.65 — explicit control on the unadapted base already gives 0.71. Ablations: removing the State Manager widens gap 0.07→0.24; removing the Flow Controller drops success 0.82→0.66; Retriever and Guards removals cost 0.65 and 0.68. Diagnostic gains: constraint-update success 0.55→0.83, rejection recovery 0.50→0.78, multi-intent 0.49→0.76. Baselines include current frontier models (GPT-5, DeepSeek-V3.2, Kimi-K2.6) tested at standard diagnostic scale (~100 episodes/slice), not stress scale. No error bars or significance tests are reported — only means over five runs. Novelty Classification: NEW DATASET/BENCHMARK + NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING + NEW METHOD (moderate). Genuinely novel: the session-process evaluation protocol with explicit process metrics (state tracking, constraint updating, decision pacing) under catalog grounding, partial observability, and convergence pressure, at 3.28M-SKU scale; and the quantified turn-to-session gap finding. The agent framework is a competent combination of known techniques — dialogue state tracking, action policies, retrieval-augmented verification, output guards, GRPO post-training — packaged as an integrated control loop; each module is individually standard, and the contribution is the diagnosis-driven integration rather than any new algorithm. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are present and interpretable — each of the four modules is removed on the same SFT/RL backbone, with distinct signatures (State Manager → state/constraint scores; Retriever → rec. accuracy/personalization), which supports the complementarity claim. Judge reliability is assessed against 150 stratified human-annotated sessions with three annotators (QWK/κ 0.76–0.89; MAE 0.03–0.19) and three repeated judging passes (ICC(2,1) 0.86–0.92, flip rate ≤0.04); simulator faithfulness and action controllability are validated on 200 profiles. Five evaluation runs per system are reported as means, but no variances, confidence intervals, or significance tests are given. No code, data, or model weights release URL is mentioned. Methodological concerns: (a) the evaluation rubric and the RL reward both encode the authors' session-control philosophy, so RealShop_Agent is trained against signals that mirror the benchmark's judging criteria — a Goodhart risk partially mitigated (disjoint training prompts) but not eliminated; (b) the judge (GPT-5.5) and simulator (Kimi-K2.6) are also evaluated as baseline agents, creating self-reference; (c) specialized baselines are re-instantiated on a DeepSeek-V3.2 backbone, which may disadvantage methods designed around their own backbones; (d) all results are on the authors' own benchmark with no external validation. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL (benchmark plus a system actually run end-to-end). - Practical: Requires API access to large judge/simulator models (GPT-5.5, Kimi-K2.6) and training a 27B backbone — feasible for well-resourced labs and e-commerce platforms, not for small teams; the product inventory depends on proprietary platform access. - Efficient: Cost relative to prompt-only baselines is not reported — no latency, token, or tool-call budget numbers beyond a qualitative ToolBudget mechanism; five full role-play runs per system plus multi-stage judging imply substantial evaluation cost. - Effective: Evidence that the harness solves the stated problem is strong on the authors' own benchmark (success 0.55→0.82, gap 0.31→0.07); effectiveness on third-party benchmarks or live users is untested. - Scalable: The 3.28M catalog and 30-turn sessions are realistic, but RL training used only 1.5K prompts and evaluation covered ~3,600 diagnostic episodes; behavior at 10–100× session volume or with dynamic price/stock drift (explicitly excluded by the snapshot design) is claimed only implicitly, not tested. Deliverable status: paper form only — no released library, dataset, or trained weights is stated. Strengths: - The turn-to-session Gap metric is a genuinely useful evaluation construct: it is simple, defined precisely (Turn Avg. minus Sess. Avg.), and yields a quantified, generalizable finding across seven LLMs and five specialized methods. - The termination taxonomy (SUCCESS / EARLY-EXIT-WITHOUT-CONVERGENCE / MAX-TURN) separates voluntary abandonment from capacity-limited timeouts, which most role-play benchmarks conflate; linking early exits to state-tracking collapse (0.98→0.23) rather than under-clarification is a non-obvious, actionable finding. - The latent/visible profile split with planned disclosure schedules and pre-assigned diagnostic metadata makes the partial-observability evaluation controlled rather than emergent, and the simulator is validated on both profile faithfulness (0.93) and action controllability (0.95) — most simulator-based benchmarks skip the latter. - The module ablations have distinct, interpretable failure signatures, so the complementarity claim rests on evidence rather than assertion. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors directly confront three limitations: (1) LLM-judge sensitivity to surface fluency, style, and prompt wording, which may bias absolute scores and cross-family comparisons; (2) simulator-based users may miss real shopper behaviors (emotion, impulsivity, brand attachment), so results are a controlled approximation rather than a substitute for live studies; (3) coverage gaps — no after-sales, returns/refunds, promotions, cross-platform price comparison, lifecycle modeling, or live commerce. They also document IRB-approved data collection, PII removal, and misuse considerations. This is a candid limitations section; the authors do not minimize. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - Benchmark-method circularity: the judge rubric's session dimensions (state tracking, constraint updating, decision pacing) are exactly the agent's modules, and the RL reward graders score the same behaviors; the 0.82-vs-0.71 headline should be read as "the system optimized for this rubric wins on this rubric." No third-party benchmark or human live-session study corroborates the agent's advantage. - Judge/simulator/baseline self-reference: GPT-5.5 judges and Kimi-K2.6 simulates, while both are also baselines; judge familiarity or bias toward certain response styles could differentially affect them, and the authors' acknowledged judge-bias caveat does not address this role overlap. - No variance reporting: five runs are averaged but no standard deviations or significance tests are given, so margins like 0.71 vs. 0.68 (Guards ablation) cannot be judged. - Specialized baselines under a foreign backbone: all five shopping-agent methods run on DeepSeek-V3.2; several (AgentCF, AFL) were designed with their own memory/feedback loops, and prompting them into a fixed harness may understate them. - No release: with 3.28M SKUs from a proprietary platform, reproducibility outside the authors' organization is unlikely unless the inventory and episode generator are published, which is not stated. - Static catalog: price/stock/promotion dynamics are excluded by design, so "real-world" grounding is real schema but frozen evidence — recommendation timing and availability reasoning, central to real shopping, are untested. Bottom Line: A practitioner building or benchmarking conversational shopping agents should read this for the session-process evaluation protocol and the quantified turn-to-session gap, but should treat RealShop_Agent's 0.82 headline as rubric-internal evidence and wait for independent replication or a public release before adopting the framework over simpler state-tracking + guard stacks.

AutoGym

Aarati Andrea Noronha, Kavya Ravikumar, Carly Xiaoyu Lin · arxiv.org · 🥇Top AI Papers of the Week
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces AutoGym, a pipeline that automatically generates complete agent RL gyms — task, executable environment, and verifier — by first authoring a solution blueprint that fixes the valid solution space and verification criteria before the environment is materialized. - Why it's important: Manually built agent environments are expensive ($500–$1,000/task by the authors' estimate), static, saturate as models improve, and are exposed to contamination, so anyone training or evaluating agents is bottlenecked on gym construction. - How it does it: The core move is inverting generation order: specify solvability and verification constraints in a blueprint (with explicit generation parameters for topology, obfuscation gradient, and distractor budget), reconcile the blueprint, then materialize the environment and derive ground truth by executing the blueprint's solution path against it, rather than generating tasks and discovering solvability problems post-hoc. - The good: The difficulty-steering result is concrete and controlled — flipping only topology weights, obfuscation, and distractor budgets (C1→C2) moves hard-task share for Claude Opus 4.6 from 10.0% to 39.0% while holding domain and tool interface fixed, with cross-model separation (70% hard for gpt-oss-120b on the same C2 gym) arguing the hardness reflects genuine capability demands rather than broken tasks. - The missing: No code, data, or generated-gym release is mentioned; open-ended verification still routes through a three-stage LLM judge whose reliability is never validated against human agreement; and downstream RL evidence is a single 8B model run for 500 GRPO steps in an appendix with only a training-reward curve and no held-out evaluation. - Read it or not: Worth reading for anyone building synthetic agent-training environments or RL curricula — the blueprint-first formulation and the difficulty-parameter ablation are directly transferable ideas — but skippable for readers seeking validated training recipes or a released tool.
Why this rank
Scored using Empirical profile. The composite is pulled down by Practical Impact (48) — no released code, gyms, or blueprints despite the paper's core value being a reusable pipeline — and by Resilience (60): the verification claim leans on an unvalidated LLM judge for exactly the task classes where judges are least trustworthy, the generator and primary frontier reference model share a family, and the RL evidence is a single 500-step reward curve with no held-out evaluation. Novelty (72) is real — the blueprint-first inversion making solvability a construction-time invariant is a clean NEW FORMULATION — and the C1/C2 difficulty-steering ablation with cross-model separation is the right causal test, supporting Rigor (58) and Non-Obviousness (68) at moderate levels; but missing error bars, asymmetric baseline filtering, and no release cap the execution score. Completeness (72) benefits from candid limitations. Weighted composite: 0.20*72 + 0.25*58 + 0.15*68 + 0.15*72 + 0.15*60 + 0.10*48 = 64.

Problem & Motivation: Teams doing RL post-training of LLM agents need gyms: a task, an executable environment, and a verifier that reliably separates success from failure. Manually authored suites (WebArena, OSWorld, WorkArena, τ-bench, AppWorld) are realistic and programmatically verified but fixed at authoring time, expensive to extend, and saturate as models improve. Single-pass LLM synthesis offers scale but produces tasks whose difficulty is largely cosmetic (same-capability models solve them despite convoluted phrasing) and whose correctness must be adjudicated post-hoc by LLM judges with known position and verbosity biases. Existing environment-generation systems (AgentGen, AgentGym, AgentSynth, EnvScaler, Agent World Model) improve executability but typically generate the task before establishing whether the environment contains a valid, verifiable solution path. The specific gap AutoGym closes is the absence of a generation framework where solvability, verifiability, and difficulty are construction-time constraints rather than downstream checks. Key Idea: Blueprint-first generation: invert the conventional task→environment order so that a blueprint specifying the solution space (entities, attributes, dependencies), environment requirements, obfuscation (which solution-relevant values are withheld from the question and must be recovered from the environment), and distractor composition is reconciled for solvability before the environment is materialized; ground truth is then computed by walking the blueprint's solution derivation against the built environment, and verifiers are derived from blueprint criteria. An answerability invariant (all withheld information is discoverable in the environment) plus a reconciliation check make broken tasks a repair trigger rather than an evaluation artifact. Methodology: Six-stage pipeline: (1) blueprint initialization from a domain seed, tool specification, and optionally prior model trajectories — a scenario and persona plus sampled generation parameters (task topology tiers 1–3 with 8 named patterns, capability axes, a 0–1 obfuscation gradient, distractor budget across persona/content/tool channels); (2) blueprint construction — solution space, obfuscated values, distractors, and a reconciliation check that at least one valid solution route survives the distractors; (3) maze materialization — the blueprint induces an executable environment (relational store in the main experiments; a declarative cloud-API emulator substrate in Appendix E) exposed through the supplied tool interface; (4) ground truth and verifier assembly — ground truth is computed by executing the blueprint's solution derivation, then a 4-signal verifier is built (programmatic outcome checks, distractor-resilience checks, LLM-scored process quality via a process/outcome/meta-judge pipeline, persona constraints); (5) evaluation — 8 rollouts per task scored to a mean verifier reward, banded hard (<0.30)/medium/easy (≥0.80); (6) failure analysis feeding active curriculum synthesis — dimensions with success <0.30 are relaxed, >0.80 strengthened, with bounded updates to reduce oscillation. Critical design decisions: (a) ground truth computed from the materialized environment rather than trusting generator-proposed values — well justified, it directly blocks a common synthesis failure; (b) difficulty via explicit parameters decoupled from domain — justified by the C1/C2 ablation; (c) the repair loop discards rather than publishes defective tasks — pragmatic but introduces survivorship selection (yields 80–92%). Key Results: Two main settings plus appendix studies. (1) Seed-driven productivity gym (7-tool interface): compared against a human expert-authored suite (21.5% hard for Claude Opus 4.6) and Agent World Model (4.0% hard, 90.0% easy for Opus after manual filtering to 217/300 tasks), AutoGym C1 gives 10.0/34.7/55.3% hard/medium/easy and C2 gives 39.0/10.0/51.0% for Opus 4.6, while gpt-oss-120b on the same C2 gym shows 70.0/17.0/13.0% — a cross-model separation the authors argue certifies genuine capability demand. Repair retained 84.9% (C1, 297/350) and 80.0% (C2, 280/350). LLM certification of C2 scored 78–92.7 across 7 rubric dimensions, weakest on interface realism (78.0). (2) Failure-driven temporal-reasoning gym (92/100 retained): 89.1% easy for Opus 4.6 but 41.3% hard+medium for gpt-oss-120b, with a strictly one-sided task ordering (no task harder for the stronger model), consistent with targeting the identified gpt-oss-120b capability gap. Appendix F: 600 tasks across six domains in under ten hours at $100–200 per 50-task batch (~$2–5/task, claimed 100× wall-clock and two-orders-of-magnitude cost reduction vs. expert authoring). Appendix G: GRPO on an 8B model over an instruction-following gym shows a rising training-reward curve over 500 steps. Baselines are recent (Agent World Model, 2026 arXiv) but the AWM comparison benefits AutoGym asymmetrically: AWM tasks were hand-filtered for correctness, while AutoGym tasks pass its own repair loop. All difficulty numbers are point estimates from 8 rollouts with no error bars or significance tests. Novelty Classification: NEW FORMULATION + NEW SYSTEM/TOOL, with an ENGINEERING OPTIMIZATION component (cost/speed of gym production). The genuinely novel element is the blueprint-first ordering — making solvability and verification construction-time invariants rather than post-hoc properties — plus the validated difficulty-steering ablation showing the parameter set actually moves the difficulty distribution. The individual ingredients (LLM task generation, programmatic verifiers, distractors, curriculum from failure analysis) exist in τ²-bench's compositional generators, APIGen's multi-stage verification, WebRL's curriculum RL, and Agent World Model (which the authors credit as inspiring their prototype); the contribution is the disciplined assembly and the demonstrated causal link between generation parameters and difficulty, not any single new algorithm. Rigor & Reproducibility: The strongest rigor element is the C1/C2 parameter ablation, which isolates topology weights, obfuscation, and distractor budgets while holding everything else fixed — a real causal test of the steering claim. The gpt-oss-120b cross-model check on C2 addresses the obvious confound (broken tasks also score low). Human inspection of ground-truth reachability is described for retained tasks, plus manual checks of the 10 non-easy temporal tasks. Weaknesses: no error bars, seeds, or significance tests on any difficulty percentage despite an 8-rollout protocol that supports them; no code, generated gyms, blueprints, or tooling are stated as released; the certification audit is an LLM judge scoring LLM-generated tasks with no validation of the judge itself; the AWM baseline filtering protocol differs from AutoGym's own retention protocol; and the frontier claim rests on one model (Claude Opus 4.6) evaluated against tasks generated by a same-family model (Claude Sonnet 4.6), a possible self-family bias never discussed. The RL experiment lacks any held-out-task evaluation or baseline data mixture. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (with a SYSTEMS component — a built generation pipeline). Practical: Yes — environments are relational stores behind mocked tool wrappers or a cloud-API emulator, runnable with commercial API access and no exotic hardware. Efficient: Strong on paper — $2–5 per task and 15.6 minutes wall-clock at mid-tier pricing, versus $500–$1,000 and 1–1.5 hours for expert authoring; the per-task human-validation cost is excluded from these figures and noted as a one-time study. Effective: The evidence supports difficulty steering and cross-model discrimination for deterministic-style tasks, but the headline claim of reliable verification is only a proxy for open-ended tasks, which still pass through an unvalidated three-stage LLM judge. Scalable: 600 tasks in under ten hours with 20-way parallelism demonstrates throughput at the tested scale, but 10–100× diversity (distinct domains, personas, capabilities) is claimed, not tested, and curriculum stability over many adaptation rounds is unmeasured. The work stops at paper form: no released library, dataset, or trained model is mentioned. Strengths: (1) The blueprint-first inversion is a clean, articulable formulation that plausibly generalizes (the cloud-emulator substrate sketch shows the same declarative-state/truth-from-spec trick applies beyond relational stores); (2) the C1/C2 ablation is exactly the experiment needed to make the difficulty-control claim falsifiable, and the cross-model separation on identical tasks is the right triangulation against the broken-task confound; (3) the answerability invariant with tracked obfuscated values (each removed value recorded with the entity where it can be discovered) is a concrete, checkable mechanism rather than a slogan; (4) the reconciliation-before-materialization step, with repair instead of post-hoc filtering, converts the most common synthesis failure into a pipeline event with a measurable yield (80–92%). Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state four directly: interface realism is the weakest certification dimension (78.0) due to the tool-mocking layer; open-ended verification still depends on LLM semantic judgment; the RL experiment is limited to one 8B model over 500 GRPO steps; and the cloud-API substrate is demonstrated but not empirically evaluated for difficulty or discrimination. This is a candid limitations section that confronts the real weak points rather than minimizing them — a credibility positive, particularly the explicit admission that LLM adjudication for free-form tasks is not solved. Analyst-Identified Gaps: (1) The abstract positions AutoGym against unreliable LLM judges, but process quality, open-ended outcome correctness, and the meta-judge reward are all LLM-scored; the deterministic fraction of the verifier is never quantified per gym, so the reader cannot tell how much of the measured difficulty rests on unvalidated LLM judgment — and no human-agreement study of the judge pipeline is reported. (2) The certification rubric is itself an LLM judge with no grounding (e.g., no check that its scores correlate with human judgment), making the gym-quality numbers weakly interpretable. (3) The generator (Claude Sonnet 4.6) and the primary frontier reference model (Claude Opus 4.6) share a family; a third-party frontier model (e.g., Gemini or GPT frontier tier) is absent from the headline experiments. (4) The AWM baseline underwent manual filtering to 217/300 while AutoGym's tasks survive its own repair loop, so the difficulty-distribution comparison conflates generator quality with retention-protocol differences. (5) No error bars despite an 8-rollout protocol — several comparisons (e.g., 21.5% vs 39.0% hard) are presumably robust, but others (e.g., the 6.5% vs 4.3% hard/medium split in Table 4) are on 92 tasks and fragile. (6) The RL result is a reward curve only: no held-out benchmark, no comparison against training on AWM-style or human tasks, so the central practical claim — that these gyms produce better training signal than alternatives — is untested. (7) The repair loop's 15–20% discard rate is reported but not analyzed: which generation parameters produce unrecoverable defects is unknown, limiting a practitioner's ability to tune yield. Bottom Line: A practitioner building synthetic agent RL environments should read this for the blueprint-first formulation and the rare parameter-ablation evidence that difficulty can be steered by construction — but should treat the verification and downstream-training claims as partially unproven, since the released-artifact-free paper still leans on unvalidated LLM judges for exactly the task classes where judges are least trustworthy.
