Safe Hypergraph Contraction via Capacity-Aware Repair Certificates

Y Deng, X Yang, K Zhu · arxiv.org · karypis - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces Certified Safe Coarsening (CSC), a preprocessing module that certifies which vertex contractions in capacitated hypergraph bipartitioning provably preserve the globally optimal cut value, without ever computing that optimum. - Why it's important: Multilevel partitioners used in VLSI flows (KaHyPar, TritonPart) can destroy the optimal partition during coarsening even when each merge looks locally safe and capacity-feasible, leaving quality on the table in physical-design pipelines that are extremely sensitive to cut quality. - How it does it: The core trick is a repair-certificate argument: for each candidate contraction, exhibit a capacity-feasible repair of any optimal partition that does not increase the cut, with repair-cost bounds tightened by excluding nets that capacity constraints force to be cut anyway; component-level safety is decided by a directed minimum-cut computation. - The good: The safety claim is validated where it can be checked exactly: on all 323 exactly solvable instances, every certified configuration preserved the optimum, while capacity-filtered HeiCut variants preserved it on only 131/323 and classical heuristics on 70–137/323 — direct evidence the certificates do real work beyond capacity filtering. - The missing: The end-to-end evaluation covers only k = 2 with a single imbalance (ϵ = 0.04) on 40 instances against KaHyPar alone; no other k, no Mt-KaHyPar or TritonPart baseline, no comparison against spectral coarsening (HyperEF/SHyPar) end-to-end, and no code release is stated. - Read it or not: Worth reading for researchers in hypergraph partitioning, persistency/reduction theory, or EDA tool builders who want provable preprocessing; practitioners using k > 2 or multi-objective flows will find it not directly applicable yet.

Problem & Motivation: Hypergraph partitioning under hard block-capacity constraints is central to VLSI netlist partitioning, and multilevel tools shrink the hypergraph via vertex contraction before solving the coarsest instance. The problem: contraction restricts the representable partition set, and a merge that satisfies block capacity and has the highest local affinity score can still eliminate every optimal balanced bipartition (the paper's Fig. 1 gives a unit-weight example where the uniquely best-rated merge raises the optimum from 3 to 4). Existing coarsening criteria (heavy-edge, community structure, spectral methods like HyperEF, SHyPar) provide no guarantee; uncapacitated exact reduction rules (HeiCut, following Padberg–Rinaldi style contractions) lack capacity handling, and the paper shows experimentally that capacity filtering of HeiCut preserves the optimum on only 40.6% of instances. Who has this problem: anyone running balanced bipartitioning on circuit netlists where solution quality directly affects wiring, timing, or FPGAbitstream decomposition cost. Key Idea: The single core insight is a sufficient condition for OPT-safety via directional repair: a contraction is safe if, for any optimal feasible partition, one can repair it — moving one side of a split contraction group into the other's block — such that (i) the move respects the fixed capacity B (guaranteed by c(u)+c(v) ≤ 2B − C + 1, using integrality of weights), and (ii) the cut does not increase, with the repair-cost bound tightened by excluding capacity-forced-cut nets (nets with total vertex weight c(e) > B are cut in every feasible partition, so they contribute zero marginal change). This couples feasibility and nonincrease in the same direction, which is what prior uncapacitated reductions miss. Methodology: The paper develops three certificates over a hypergraph H = (V, E, c, w) with positive integer weights, fixed capacity B < C, and the cut-net objective (minimize total weight of nets intersecting both blocks). (1) FPDC (Filtered Pair Dominance Certificate) for pairs (u, v): certify when c(u)+c(v) ≤ 2B − C + 1 and the shared two-pin-net weight p(u, v) ≥ max{F_u(v), F_v(u)}, where F_u(v) sums weights of u-exclusive nets with c(e) ≤ B; the first condition ensures a feasible repair direction, the second makes that direction non-increasing. (2) BMCC (Bidirectional Min-Cut Component Certificate) for a component S: define µ(S) = min over nonempty proper A ⊊ S of (internal saving ι_S(A) minus boundary exposure ρ_B(A)); µ(S) ≥ 0 certifies that every split of S has a non-increasing repair. This is computed without split enumeration via a directed network construction (Lawler-style hypergraph cut representation extended with boundary-contact nodes), solved with 2(|S| − 1) max-flow computations. (3) PCDC checks one feasible non-increasing direction per reachable outside-weight state, using pseudo-polynomial subset-sum dynamic programming over block weights; it is strictly weaker than BMCC in one direction but can succeed where the aggregate bound fails. The CSC loop (Algorithm 2) repeatedly contracts a greedy vertex-disjoint batch of FPDC-certified pairs, falling back to component certification (BMCC, then PCDC) when no pair certifies, with recertification on each updated quotient; batch and sequential composition are proved safe by induction (OPT(H_t, B) = OPT(H, B) for all rounds t). A lifted quotient partition is then refined on the original hypergraph; if an incumbent is supplied, the same repairs transfer it without cut increase. Critical design decisions: restricting pair candidates to explicit two-pin nets (a search restriction, justified as such), excluding capacity-forced-cut nets from bounds (justified by the c(e) > B invariant), and individual component contraction with recertification (justified by the composition proof). Failure to certify is explicitly one-sided: it does not imply unsafety. Key Results: Two experimental tracks. (1) Optimum preservation: on 323 exactly solvable small hypergraphs (subhypergraphs sampled from circuit netlists plus random hypergraphs), FPDC, FPDC+BMCC, and FPDC+BMCC+PCDC each preserved the exact optimum on 323/323 instances with zero infeasible quotients, versus 131/323 for capacity-filtered HeiCut (HEICUT-ALLCUT-CAP), 137/323 for capacity-filtered heavy-edge (HE-CAP), and 58/323 with 265 infeasible quotients for unmodified HEICUT-VALUE. The full certificate stack achieved 92.90% of the mean vertex reduction of HEICUT-ALLCUT-CAP and 79.43% of HE-CAP (mean K of 7.734 vs. 8.325 and 9.737), so safety costs reduction power but retains most of it; component certificates roughly tripled mean reduction relative to FPDC alone (6.975–7.734 vs. 3.269). (2) End-to-end: integrating CSC into KaHyPar (CSC-KaHyPar, k = 2, ϵ = 0.04, seven paired seeds) on 40 instances (22 Titan23, 18 unit-weight ISPD98) matched or improved KaHyPar's best cut on 39/40, raised best-result coverage from 42.5% to 97.5%, cut the sum of per-instance best cuts by 3.36%, with mean runtime rising from 6.12 s to 6.81 s (11.3% total overhead; median paired overhead 8.0%). Largest per-instance best-cut improvements: gsm_switch +35.69%, minres +23.62%; worst: stereo_vision −4.71%. The KaHyPar baseline is current and strong for k = 2; the exact-optimality track uses correctly constructed baselines under identical constraints. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD (certified optimum-preserving coarsening under hard capacity constraints for balanced bipartitioning) plus an EMPIRICAL FINDING (uncapacitated safe reductions and capacity-filtered heuristics destroy the optimum on the majority of instances, quantifying a real gap). The building blocks — persistency arguments from quadratic/multicut optimization, Lawler's directed hypergraph-cut networks, max-flow, HeiCut-style exact reductions — are all established; the genuinely new element is the capacity-coupled repair-certificate framework (forcing the exclusion of capacity-forced-cut nets and the 2B − C + 1 feasibility slack) and its composition proofs for batches and rounds. This is not a benchmark or system paper; the KaHyPar integration is a competent application of the new certificates. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are present and informative: three certificate configurations are compared, showing each component (BMCC, PCDC) adds reduction while preserving the guarantee, and the one-sidedness of certification ("failure does not imply unsafety") is stated. Seven paired seeds with per-instance seed-matched runtime medians give reasonable variance control for the end-to-end track; exact optimum verification on the small-instance track is a strong methodology. However: no formal significance tests or error bars on the 3.36% aggregate; no code or data release is mentioned anywhere in the paper; the small instances are sampled from the same domain (circuit netlists) as the end-to-end benchmarks, so the two tracks are not independent domains; the end-to-end evaluation tests only k = 2 and a single ϵ = 0.04, which limits external validity of the quality claims; the budget parameter B in Algorithm 2 is not ablated; and PCDC's pseudo-polynomial DP (O((n − s)B + 2^s(m + B))) is acknowledged but its practical cost profile is not characterized empirically. Some cited works carry 2026 dates (HeiCut at ALENEX 2026, Lassiter et al. MOR 2026, SHyPar TCAD 2026), and the arXiv stamp reads 1 Oct 2026 — consistent with a contemporaneous preprint; peer-review status is not stated. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL (with a strong theoretical core: proofs of OPT-safety under batch and sequential composition, though the guarantees are sufficient conditions, not characterizations). Practical: Yes — the pipeline is KaHyPar plus min-cut/DP subroutines on commodity CPUs (tested on dual Intel Xeon Platinum 8358); no exotic hardware. Efficient: Modest cost — 11.3% total runtime overhead for 3.36% aggregate quality gain, with FPDC computable via one filtered pass per round and BMCC requiring 2(|S| − 1) max-flow calls per candidate component. Effective: The evidence shows the guarantee holds exactly where testable (323/323) and improves end-to-end quality on real benchmarks, but only for k = 2 bipartitioning with the cut-net objective — the exact setting the theory targets, so effectiveness and claim scope align. Scalable: Not stress-tested: 40 instances and seconds-scale runtimes; behavior on very large netlists (where max-flow per component and per-round recertification could dominate, or where certified contractions become too sparse to matter) is untested and unclaimed. Deliverable form: paper only — no library, CLI, dataset, or trained artifact is reported as released. Strengths: - A clean, correct-looking theoretical contribution: the repair-certificate framework yields provable OPT-safety under capacity constraints, with explicit composition theorems (vertex-disjoint batches, successive rounds with recertification) — a guarantee class absent from the coarsening literature for this problem. - The directed min-cut component certificate (BMCC) is a substantive construction: it converts a condition over exponentially many component splits into 2(|S| − 1) flow computations via an exact contact-set aggregation, and Fig. 2 demonstrates a component FPDC provably cannot certify. - The experimental design attacks the right question first: validating the guarantee on exactly solvable instances, where capacity-filtered HeiCut (131/323) and heuristics (70–137/323) demonstrably fail, establishing that the certificates — not capacity filtering alone — carry the guarantee. - Honest one-sidedness framing: the paper repeatedly states that failure to certify does not imply unsafety and that candidate restriction to two-pin nets is a search limitation, not a theoretical one. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The paper explicitly scopes the method to bipartitioning with positive integer vertex/net weights, fixed hard capacities B < C, and the cut-net objective; it notes PCDC is pseudo-polynomial in B and that bounding component size does not remove this dependence; it states FPDC's candidate search restriction; it reports the runtime cost of end-to-end integration (11.3%); and it acknowledges that component certificate computation is budgeted and that "budget exhaustion never authorizes contraction." The authors confront these boundaries directly rather than minimizing them — a credibility positive. They do not, however, explicitly discuss the k = 2 restriction as a deployment limitation or the absence of a code release. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - Single operating point end-to-end: only k = 2 and ϵ = 0.04 on the 40-instance track. Real VLSI flows use varying imbalance and sometimes k > 2; the certificates' capacity conditions (e.g., 2B − C + 1 slack) depend on tightness of B, so behavior at loose or very tight capacities is unexplored. - No comparison against spectral coarsening (HyperEF, HyperEF 2.0, SHyPar) or SpecPart end-to-end, even though these are the current quality-oriented coarsening competitors cited in the introduction; KaHyPar's default coarsening is the only baseline. - No ablation of the contraction budget parameter in Algorithm 2, and no sensitivity analysis of how often component certification (the expensive path) fires on large instances. - The 323 exact-solvable instances are small by construction; the distribution of certificate yield (fraction of vertices certifiable) on full-size industrial netlists is never measured, so the practical throughput of CSC at scale is extrapolated from 40 aggregate runs. - No significance testing or confidence intervals on the 3.36% aggregate improvement; with 40 instances and seven seeds, per-instance variance (e.g., −28.48% mean regression on stereo_vision) deserves statistical treatment. - No code or artifact release, which for a paper whose value proposition is a drop-in preprocessing module substantially limits immediate adoption and verifiability. Bottom Line: For researchers and tool builders in hypergraph partitioning, this is a genuinely useful and theoretically careful contribution — the first capacity-aware optimum-preserving coarsening certificates with a working KaHyPar integration — but its restriction to bipartitioning, single-imbalance evaluation, and missing artifact release mean practitioners with k > 2 or large-scale flows should treat it as a promising direction rather than an immediately adoptable component.

Bingxuan Li, Siqi Song, Yizhuo Wu, Jiarui Yao, Tong Zhang, Huan Zhang · arxiv.org · Daily papers of 5 Oct 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces MotorMind, an execution harness that lets a frozen, general-purpose VLM control a robot arm zero-shot by proposing mid-level actions (parameterized translations, rotations, gripper commands in the base frame) coordinated through five VLM roles — Planner, Executor, Monitor, Verifier, Memory — with asynchronous monitoring and background memory updates. - Why it's important: Fine-tuned VLA policies fail to transfer zero-shot to new tasks and environments, and their specialized training disconnects them from rapidly improving general-purpose VLMs; a training-free harness could make robot competence ride directly on foundation-model progress. - How it does it: It exposes a compact, revisable mid-level action interface between semantic reasoning and deterministic controllers, and runs a sequential execution loop with concurrent background monitoring that can cancel pending actions at action boundaries when observations contradict the active subgoal. - The good: The headline result is strong and well-instrumented: 66.7% zero-shot success on LIBERO-PRO base suites and 53.8% under perturbations — versus 13.3%/19.2% for the best zero-shot baseline (CaP-X) and comparable to fine-tuned OpenVLA-OFT's 51.2% on perturbations — plus 95% pooled success on a real xArm6. - The missing: There are no error bars, seeds, or significance tests on the main results (the backbone comparison is explicitly single-seed), and the core simulation evaluation rests on one benchmark (LIBERO-PRO) with a comparatively weak zero-shot baseline field. - Read it or not: Read it if you work on robot manipulation, agentic VLM systems, or VLA alternatives — the diagnostic study, failure taxonomy, and asynchronous-scheduling design are genuinely useful; skip it if you only need evidence about scaling trained policies.

Problem & Motivation: VLA policies (π0.5, OpenVLA-OFT, GR00T N1.5, MolmoAct2) achieve strong in-distribution manipulation but require task-specific demonstrations or fine-tuning to handle changed objects, layouts, instructions, or tasks, and their robotics specialization prevents them from inheriting improvements in general-purpose VLMs. Agentic robotics systems that do use VLMs typically stack external components — learned action experts, coding agents, segmentation tools like SAM3, motion planners — adding complexity, latency, and cost. The paper targets practitioners who need zero-shot manipulation across embodiments and environments without collecting robot data. The gap it claims to close: no prior system lets a single general-purpose VLM perform the entire perception–decision–control loop, teleoperator-style, without external models or policy training. Key Idea: Treat zero-shot robot control as a harness-design problem rather than a policy-learning problem: give the VLM a compact mid-level action vocabulary (move/rotate/gripper with VLM-chosen magnitudes, validated and resolved by a deterministic controller), then protect the VLM's known weaknesses — unreliable action selection and progress/completion judgment — with a scheduling architecture in which monitoring and memory run asynchronously around a sequential propose–execute–verify loop, so invalid continuations can be interrupted at the next action boundary instead of blocking execution. Methodology: The pipeline is a frozen VLM instantiating five roles plus a deterministic Controller. (1) The Planner converts a natural-language instruction into an ordered subgoal list, each with a success criterion; it replans when evidence invalidates remaining subgoals. (2) The Executor receives the active subgoal, camera images, measured robot state (tool pose, gripper state, measured motion), recent cycle history, and a memory note; it emits a structured proposal — assessment, optional action batch A_t = (a_{t,1},...,a_{t,K_t}) with types (τ, η) over move (direction + mm distance), rotate (axis + degrees), gripper (open/close, optional width), plus wait/home, completion signal, and expected outcome. (3) The Controller validates commands, resolves them to Cartesian motion, and records measured outcomes. (4) The Monitor runs on a background thread during execution, emitting alerts; a STOP alert cancels pending queued actions at the next action boundary. (5) The Verifier judges subgoal completion from observations and measured state (direct measurements like a lost grasp can settle the attempt without a model verdict), routing to advance, retry, or replan. (6) Memory summarizes execution evidence on a background writer; readers take the latest completed note, with pending requests consolidated. The design is grounded in a 240-question diagnostic (80 each for action selection, progress assessment, subgoal completion) built from LIBERO expert demonstrations with Codex-assisted labeling and human review, which found action selection weakest (18.75–60% across models, e.g., 36.25% for Qwen3.8-Flash-Next vs. 55.0% progress and 65.0% completion) and an accuracy–latency trade-off (GPT-6 Astra at 72.92% overall but 8,724 ms/query vs. 276 ms for Qwen3.8-Flash-Next). Critical design decisions: mid-level parameterized actions rather than joint commands or code (justified by the diagnostic's action-selection weakness and ablation of alternatives like CaP-X's code generation); asynchronous interruption at action boundaries (justified qualitatively and by the adaptive-task results, though not by a targeted scheduling ablation); backbone choice Qwen3.8-Flash-Next on latency grounds (justified by the latency table, with GPT-6 Sol as the quality alternative). Key Results: On LIBERO-PRO (Goal/Spatial/Object suites, 10 tasks each; 40 base and 160 perturbed task configurations), MotorMind (Qwen3.8-Flash-Next) achieves 66.7% average zero-shot base success (45.0/75.0/80.0 per suite) and 53.8% under Semantic/Object/Position/Task perturbations, at 223.4 s mean base wall time (TimeScore 17.91 pp/min). The strongest zero-shot baselines are far behind: CaP-X at 10 loops reaches 13.3% base / 19.2% perturbed; all four zero-shot VLA policies score 0.0% base (OpenVLA-OFT 0.8% perturbed). Against fine-tuned policies, MotorMind's 53.8% perturbed exceeds fine-tuned OpenVLA-OFT (51.2%) and π0.5 (63.3% perturbed but at 997 s vs. 248.5 s wall time), though fine-tuned π0.5 (98.3%) and MolmoAct2 (100%) dominate on base suites. Adaptive tasks (30 tasks in four suites): 70% Dynamic Reasoning, 90% Scene Shift, 80% Dynamic Manipulation, 60% Prompt Shift — best in every group, with the best baseline at 30/70/40/60%. Real xArm6 (RealSense D455, no fine-tuning): 95% pooled success — 97% Direct Perception, 93% Human Perturbation, 80/100/100/60% on four Semantic Understanding tasks. Backbone swap to GPT-6 Sol raises LIBERO-PRO base success from 66.7% to 83.3% (with wall time rising, e.g., Spatial 370.4 s vs. 199.0 s). Ablations: removing replanning drops success 30.0 points (66.7%→36.7%), removing the verifier 6.7 points (→60.0%), removing the planner to 0.0%. Failure analysis attributes most errors to visual grounding (e.g., 49 grounding errors per 60 episodes under Task perturbations) and premature completion claims (false-done in 9% of perturbed episodes). Tested at standard academic-benchmark scale, not stress scale. Novelty Classification: NEW SYSTEM/TOOL and NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING. The genuinely novel elements are the empirical demonstration that a single frozen general-purpose VLM across all five reasoning roles reaches competitive-with-fine-tuned zero-shot manipulation, and the asynchronous scheduling design (concurrent monitoring with action-boundary cancellation, non-blocking background memory) layered on a mid-level action interface. The mid-level action vocabulary itself, planner–executor–verifier decomposition, and memory notes are competent combinations of ideas already present in Code-as-Policies, VoLo, Harness VLA, and the concurrent Show-Harness; the paper itself carefully differentiates from Show-Harness rather than claiming priority on the core intuition. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are present and informative (replanning, verifier, planner, execution budget), and the execution-budget ablation honestly reports a non-monotonic result (900 s budget yields 50% success vs. 66.7% at 450 s). However, no error bars, multiple seeds, or significance tests appear anywhere; the backbone comparison is explicitly single-seed. Baselines are current and correctly configured (published checkpoints, model-specific transforms retained, a shared π0.5 checkpoint across agent baselines), and baseline configurations are documented in detail. The diagnostic benchmark was built by the authors (Codex-generated labels with human review) on the same LIBERO ecosystem used for the main evaluation, creating mild Goodhart risk, though the diagnostic informs design rather than serving as the success metric. No code release is stated; the project page (motor-mind.github.io) is cited and complete prompt files are promised in supplementary material. Preprint (arXiv:2609.38078), not peer-reviewed. A strength is the paper's repeated, explicit caution about what its own evidence does and does not establish (e.g., the diagnostic "does not establish that a particular control abstraction causes those errors"). Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (with a SYSTEMS component — a built harness deployed on real hardware). - Practical: Yes — runs on a local Qwen3.8-Flash-Next (FP8, ~0.28 s/query) with a commodity xArm6 and RealSense D455; no SAM3, IK solver, or coding agent required. - Efficient: Mean episode wall times of 223–249 s in simulation; the GPT-6 Sol variant trades roughly 1.5–2× wall time for +16.6 points of success; the paper explicitly notes TimeScore is not a compute or monetary cost measure, so actual API/compute cost is not quantified. - Effective: The evidence supports zero-shot placement and adaptive tasks in simulation and constrained real table-top tasks, but real-robot evaluation is limited to simple cube/food-item placements (10 trials per setting) — effectiveness on dexterous or contact-rich tasks is not shown. - Scalable: Not tested — long-horizon tasks, cluttered scenes, higher-DOF embodiments, and multi-robot settings are unexplored; the failure analysis suggests grounding errors (up to 49 per 60 episodes) could compound with horizon length. The work delivers a system artifact (the MotorMind harness with role prompts) demonstrated on a real robot; no public code or weights release is confirmed. Strengths: - The diagnostic-first methodology is a real intellectual contribution: decomposing manipulation into action selection / progress assessment / subgoal completion and measuring each per model with latency grounds the harness design in evidence rather than intuition. - The asynchronous scheduling design — background monitoring that cancels queued actions at action boundaries, non-blocking memory writers that read the latest completed note — is a concrete, transferable systems contribution distinguishing it from sequential agentic baselines. - Honest, unusually careful epistemic framing: the authors repeatedly flag what their results do not show, report the non-monotonic budget ablation, and publish a granular failure taxonomy (false-done 9%, grounding errors by perturbation type) rather than only headline numbers. - The backbone-swap result (66.7%→83.3% by changing only the VLM) is the most consequential empirical finding: it directly evidences the paper's thesis that manipulation competence can track general VLM progress without retraining. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state that the diagnostic does not establish that a control abstraction causes the observed errors; that answer spaces differ across diagnostic tasks so accuracies are not comparable as intrinsic difficulty; that remaining failures concentrate in visual grounding, embodied reasoning (premature completion), and action knowledge; that TimeScore is descriptive and not a cost measure; that the adaptive-task evaluation is a stress test rather than precise quantitative evidence; and that Show-Harness is concurrent work not directly compared experimentally. They confront limitations directly and repeatedly — a credibility positive — though they minimize the absence of statistical uncertainty reporting, never mentioning seeds or variance. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - No multi-seed evaluation or confidence intervals anywhere; with 10 tasks per suite and 10 trials per real-robot setting, several headline gaps (e.g., 53.8% vs. 51.2% perturbed, a 2.6-point difference) are well within plausible single-run noise. - The zero-shot baseline field is thin: the strongest zero-shot competitor is CaP-X (13.3% base), while much stronger zero-shot agent systems cited in related work (e.g., Show-Harness, Guava, VIA) are dismissed as concurrent or absent from the table — the comparison that would most stress-test the "VLM-only, no tools" claim is missing. - The diagnostic and all main evaluations derive from the LIBERO ecosystem; LIBERO-PRO perturbations probe instruction/layout changes, but all environments share LIBERO's table-top, pick-place structure — generalization to fundamentally different tasks (articulated objects beyond drawers, tool use, deformables) is untested. - The five-role architecture is justified by the diagnostic, but there is no ablation of the asynchronous scheduling itself against a sequential version of the same roles (the closest, VoLoAgent, differs in more than scheduling alone), so the paper's second headline design principle rests partly on confounded comparisons. - Real-robot success is pooled over 3 objects and 4 semantic tasks with randomized-but-limited arrangements; trial counts (10 and 5) are too small to support the reported precision (e.g., 95% pooled implies a 95% CI roughly spanning 85–99%). - Compute and monetary cost of the many role-specific VLM calls per episode (planner, replans, executor cycles, monitor polls, verifier, memory writers) is never reported despite being the obvious deployment concern for a harness that multiplies inference volume. Bottom Line: A practitioner in zero-shot robot control or VLM-based agents should read this: even granting the missing error bars and the thin zero-shot baseline field, the diagnostic methodology, asynchronous monitoring design, and backbone-swap evidence make it the most concrete current demonstration that harness engineering — not policy training — can deliver competitive zero-shot manipulation, and it sets the comparison standard that concurrent systems like Show-Harness must now meet.

Problem & Motivation: Disordered crystal structure prediction (CSP) asks: given only a chemical formula, generate a crystallographic structure where sites can be fractionally shared by multiple species, partially vacant, or interstitially occupied. Practitioners in materials discovery (batteries, solid electrolytes, magnets, superconductors) face this constantly because disorder controls functional properties. Prior ordered generators (CDVAE, DiffCSP, FlowMM, MatterGen, OMatG) fix one species per site; recent disordered generators (Dis-Gen, DMFlow) still require site-level annotations stating which sites are doped and with what occupancies—supervision that is unavailable when the formula is the primary input. The gap: a generator that infers the full site-by-species occupancy allocation from stoichiometry alone. Key Idea: Represent a disordered crystal's occupancy as an Occupancy Distribution Matrix (ODM) constrained to a formula-dependent transportation polytope (row sums = 1 per site, column sums = stoichiometric counts c, non-negativity), then canonicalize all these heterogeneous polytopes into one shared linear space by double-centering log(A). In that zero-marginal space M0(N,M), ordinary linear flow matching works, and the map Ψ = D∘log is a bijection onto the polytope interior (proved via Sinkhorn uniqueness), so a Sinkhorn projection on exp(A′) exactly recovers feasible occupancies. Vacancies are handled as a pseudo-species that pads the formula so Σcj = N, unifying ordered, substitutional, vacancy, and interstitial disorder in one representation. Methodology: The pipeline has three stages. (1) Canonicalization: each training ODM A is ε-smoothed, log-transformed, and double-centered (masked algorithm given) to A′ = D(log Aε) ∈ M0(N,M); the inverse is A = S(exp(A′), 1, c) via Sinkhorn iterations with a truncation threshold τ = 0.005 for trace occupancies followed by a second projection. (2) Joint flow matching: linear interpolation paths on A′ (velocity projected by D to stay in M0), geodesic velocities for fractional coordinates on the 3N-torus, and FlowMM-style unconstrained parameterization (log lengths, Niggli-reduced angles) for lattice parameters; the loss is a weighted sum of MSEs over four velocity heads (occupancy, coordinates, lattice lengths, lattice angles), conditioned on the stoichiometry vector c. (3) Inference: 200 ODE steps, then Sinkhorn recovery to the target polytope. The backbone is a 6-layer, 512-hidden-dim message-passing network over a fully connected per-crystal graph with sinusoidal periodic-displacement embeddings and an energy-difference edge feature ΔA′ij; it is SO(3)- and translation-invariant by construction (proofs in Appendices A.3–A.4). Critical design decisions: (a) working in log-domain double-centered space rather than the raw polytope—justified both by the bijectivity proposition and by the ablation showing raw-polytope learning fails; (b) the vacancy pseudo-species to make site count consistent—well-motivated with worked examples (Appendix D.2); (c) the Boltzmann/thermodynamic analogy (Appendix B)—explicitly labeled heuristic, not a derivation, which is honest but adds no algorithmic content. Key Results: Benchmarks are self-constructed from COD (17,239 structures) and MPDS (110,966 structures), split into Sub-20/Sub-50 (substitutional) and Disorder-20/Disorder-50 (with vacancies) subsets, ≤50 sites, ≤6 species, 8:1:1 splits with structural deduplication. Against author-adapted FlowMM, OMatG, and DMFlow, EP-Flow attains the best Match Rate on all 8 dataset×subset combinations: 17.10%–60.82%, versus 0.13%–0.67% for Ada-FlowMM, 3.28%–11.78% for Ada-OMatG, and 9.74%–45.17% for Ada-DMFlow (e.g., MPDS Sub-20: 60.82% vs. 45.17% for DMFlow). Occupancy error (OccMAE) is lowest for EP-Flow on most subsets (e.g., 0.0069–0.0075 on MPDS Sub-50/Sub-20); RMSD is mid-pack on some subsets, which the authors correctly attribute to higher Match Rates including harder matches. Validity ranges 77.70%–97.80%. An occupancy-tolerance sweep (occtol 0.30 → 0.01) shows Match Rate degrades gracefully from 60.82% to 50.09% with OccMAE dropping to 0.0004, arguing the metric is not gaming-friendly. Ablations on MPDS Sub-20: w/o Formula conditioning drops Match Rate to 20.01%; w/o Energy-diff to 35.23%; w/o Double Centering to 46.06%; w/o Projection leaves Match Rate at 15.78% with OccMAE 0.1277; w/o both DC & Sinkhorn collapses to 0.00%. Case studies cover oxygen-vacancy disorder in a cuprate, interstitial N in a ThMn12 magnet, and multi-sublattice O/F + cation mixing in a perovskite, with maximum site occupancy errors of 0.0013–0.0371 on mixed sites. No error bars, seeds, or significance tests are reported. Novelty Classification: NEW FORMULATION + NEW METHOD + NEW DATASET/BENCHMARK. The genuinely novel pieces are (1) the transportation-polytope formulation of formula-conditioned disordered CSP via the vacancy-extended ODM, and (2) the double-centered canonicalization + Sinkhorn inverse map as a way to run flow matching on a formula-dependent family of polytopes—this is a real methodological contribution to constrained generative modeling, not just materials science. The backbone (message passing over a fully connected crystal graph, torus-aware coordinate flows, FlowMM-style lattice parameterization) is a competent assembly of existing components. The benchmark is new but exists only because no public disordered-CSP benchmark existed; DMFlow (same overlapping author group, cited as arXiv 2602.04734) already covers disordered generation under annotations, so the delta is the no-site-annotation setting. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are present and well-designed—they target exactly the components the method claims matter (centering, projection, formula conditioning, edge features), and the w/o-DC-&-Sinkhorn collapse is convincing. However: no multiple seeds, error bars, or significance tests anywhere; Match Rate differences of 7–15 points are reported as point estimates. Code, data, or trained weights are not stated to be released. Methodological concerns: (1) the evaluation benchmark, matching metric, and occupancy tolerance (occtol = 0.3) are all authored by the paper—while the tolerance sweep mitigates gaming, no independent benchmark validates the metric's semantics; (2) all baselines are author-adapted, and adaptation quality directly determines the size of the reported gap (Ada-FlowMM at <1% Match Rate may reflect a poor adaptation as much as a weak base method, though the appendix describes the adaptations fairly and applies identical Sinkhorn post-processing to all baselines); (3) evaluation is reconstruction-flavored (matching generated structures to test-set ground truth), so a model could score well by memorizing common disorder motifs—partially checked via the transfer analysis in Fig. 4 but not via any novelty/diversity metric. The bijectivity proof and trajectory-feasibility proofs are correct and complete for the stated setting (strictly positive matrices; ε-smoothing moves data off the polytope boundary, which is handled). Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (with a SYSTEMS artifact in the form of a benchmark). Practical: Yes—training ran on 1–2 NVIDIA RTX 4090 GPUs (24 GB) with 16-bit precision, i.e., consumer hardware. Efficient: 1,000 training epochs, 6 message-passing layers, 100 Sinkhorn iterations, and 200 ODE steps at inference; Sinkhorn over an N×M matrix is cheap, so cost is comparable to other flow-based crystal generators, though no wall-clock or parameter-count comparison to baselines is given. Effective: Evidence shows accurate reconstruction of test-set disordered structures under the authors' own matcher; no downstream validation (DFT relaxation, stability, property prediction, or experimental refinement) demonstrates the generated structures solve a real materials problem. Scalable: Tested up to N=50 sites and ~111K training structures; behavior beyond that (larger cells, more species, higher site counts) is untested, and the ODE/sinkhorn cost grows with N×M. Deliverable form: paper plus benchmark; no software artifact is stated to be publicly available. Strengths: (1) The polytope-canonicalization idea—log-domain double centering into a shared zero-marginal space with provable bijectivity via Sinkhorn uniqueness—is a clean, transferable technique for any generative task whose support is a transportation polytope, well beyond crystals. (2) The ablation design is unusually decisive: each removed component maps to a distinct, interpretable failure (0% match without normalization, 10× occupancy error without projection), so the mechanism is validated, not just the end-to-end number. (3) The vacancy-pseudo-species device that makes site count well-defined for vacancy/interstitial disorder is a simple but genuinely enabling representation choice, worked through carefully with examples. (4) The occupancy-tolerance sweep (Table 5) preempts the most obvious metric-gaming objection with data rather than argument. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state three: (1) the number of crystallographic sites must be specified or sampled externally and cannot yet be determined from the formula alone—an open problem for disordered structures; (2) no property-conditioned generation (no ionic conductivity, magnetism, stability targets); (3) no conditioning on experimental measurements (PXRD, PDF, spectroscopy). This is a direct, non-minimizing limitations section, which is a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: (1) No seed variance or significance testing despite headline gaps of 7–15 Match Rate points on test sets of ~900–11,500 structures—some margins are large enough to survive, but the smaller ones (e.g., COD Disorder-50: 17.10% vs 9.74%) are not obviously robust. (2) All baselines are adapted by the authors; there is no sanity check that the adaptation pipeline recovers near-original performance on the ordered special case, which would calibrate trust in Ada-FlowMM's <1% numbers. (3) The disorder-type distribution, sparsity statistics, and degree of site-preference learnability in COD vs MPDS are not characterized, so the consistent COD-vs-MPDS performance gap is explained only speculatively ("richer supervision"). (4) No comparison against a trivial baseline (e.g., sampling occupancies uniformly on the polytope or from a compositional prior plus an ordered generator), which would establish how much of the task's difficulty the flow actually solves versus how much the Sinkhorn post-processing shared by all methods already handles. (5) No diversity/novelty metric on generated structures—only reconstruction matching—so the model's usefulness for discovery (generating new structures, not recovering known ones) is unmeasured. (6) No code or data release is stated, which limits reproducibility of a benchmark paper. Bottom Line: This is the strongest and most principled treatment to date of formula-conditioned disordered crystal generation, and the polytope-canonicalization technique alone justifies a read by anyone working on constrained generative models—provided one treats the headline numbers as self-benchmarked and adapted-baseline results pending independent reproduction.

Research on multi-objective scheduling optimization of emergency resources based on simulated annealing algorithm

Z Song · nature.com · simulation environments for business processes - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper builds a multi-objective ED resource scheduling model (physicians, consultation rooms, beds, 15-min time slots, triage-weighted waiting time plus threshold-violation penalty plus labor cost) and solves it with a customized simulated annealing algorithm featuring three clinically feasible neighborhood operators and a constraint-repair procedure. - Why it's important: Emergency departments face long patient waits, unbalanced resource utilization, and high staff overtime under fixed resource budgets; the paper quantifies exactly what timeliness gains can be bought and at what additional labor cost (an 11.4% cost increase, not a saving). - How it does it: A weighted-sum scalarization of three normalized objectives is minimized by SA using discrete neighborhood moves (patient swap, cross-doctor reassignment, shift fine-tuning) that, after a deterministic repair pass, keep every candidate solution feasible by construction. - The good: On a full year (2023) of real tertiary-hospital ED data across three calibrated scenarios, the SA schedules cut mean waiting time 20–35%, dropped threshold-violation rate from 26.7% to 14.2%, and matched NSGA-II solution quality in 12.4 s versus 34.7 s of CPU time. - The missing: All evidence is in-silico from a single center with deterministic resource availability and NHPP arrivals that under-represent bursty demand; there is no prospective or multi-center validation, so reported gains are explicitly upper bounds. - Read it or not: Worth reading for healthcare operations researchers and hospital analytics teams deploying metaheuristic scheduling under clinical constraints; algorithm designers seeking novelty can skip it, as the authors themselves state the method is a well-established metaheuristic applied with domain adaptations.

Problem & Motivation: Emergency department managers at hospitals with ~100k+ annual visits face prolonged patient waits, uneven physician/space utilization, and persistent overtime, with limited ability to expand costly resources. Prior approaches fall into three categories the paper critiques: exact MILP (intractable at multi-resource ED scale), heuristic priority rules (long-tail waits at peak demand), and intelligent metaheuristics (GA, PSO, TS, MOEA) that struggle to embed strict clinical constraints like triage priority and doctor-room-bed coupling. The authors identify three gaps: single-objective focus in most ED scheduling work, lack of benchmarking against multi-objective baselines (NSGA-II, MOEA/D, TS) on identical instances, and limited attention to joint three-resource scheduling with explicit time-slot coupling. Key Idea: The core move is not algorithmic novelty but a domain-fitted constraint architecture around standard SA: triage-level-weighted waiting time and per-level maximum-wait thresholds in the objective (weights 0.5/0.3/0.2 derived from a Delphi-style clinician consultation plus a 9×9 Pareto grid search), each objective component normalized by its value under current practice so the acceptance probability exp(−ΔF/T) is dimensionless, and three clinical neighborhood operators paired with a deterministic repair procedure (up to ten passes) that guarantees feasibility by construction, eliminating penalty terms from the objective. Methodology: Closed-loop pipeline: (1) preprocess 2023 HIS/triage/scheduling data from one tertiary ED (~105,000 visits/year, 38 physicians, 15 rooms, 42 observation + 8 resuscitation beds; 3.2% incomplete records removed, ~6.4% missing service durations imputed with triage/complaint medians, timestamps discretized to 15-min slots, NHPP fitted hourly to arrivals); (2) construct a heuristic initial solution preserving the existing rota, sorting patients by triage then arrival, and load-balancing physician assignment; (3) run SA with operators drawn at probabilities 0.4/0.4/0.2, geometric cooling (T←γT), 1,000-iteration budget, single candidate per iteration; (4) evaluate via event-driven Monte Carlo simulation (≥100 replications per scenario) on Typical Day (285 arrivals), Peak Demand (353 arrivals, 1.5× intensity), and Night Shift (35 arrivals) scenarios. The objective F(S) = α·F_wait/F_wait⁰ + β·F_penalty/F_penalty⁰ + (1−α−β)·F_cost/F_cost⁰, subject to constraints on waiting-time definition, service duration, physician capacity, room/bed capacity, overtime, and unique patient assignment. Critical design decisions: constraint repair instead of penalties (well justified — guarantees feasible outputs), baseline-anchored normalization (well justified — makes temperatures transferable across scenarios), and equal-iteration benchmarking against population methods (the authors themselves flag this as unequal effort, correctly redirecting comparisons to wall-clock CPU time). Key Results: Versus current practice, SA reduced mean waiting time from 59.1 to 38.5 min (−34.9%, d=1.42), threshold-violation rate from 26.7% to 14.2% (−46.8%, d=1.31), and overtime hours from 18.2 to 12.8/day (−29.7%), while physician utilization rose from 58.3% to 71.2% and workload CV fell from 0.42 to 0.28. The gains cost money: daily labor cost rose from CNY 31,680 to 35,280 (+11.4%) and cost per visit from CNY 102.3 to 113.1 (+10.6%), driven by +CNY 4,380/day regular staffing offset partly by −CNY 780/day overtime. Versus the priority heuristic, SA still improved waiting time by 7.9 min (d=0.81). Against NSGA-II, MOEA/D, and adaptive-tenure Tabu Search on identical instances, SA matched NSGA-II waiting time (41.2 vs 40.8 min typical day) at ~35% of its CPU time (12.4 vs 34.7 s), achieved the lowest threshold-violation rate under peak demand (22.6% vs 24.5/28.7/26.3%), and the lowest cost on night shift; SA also attained the highest hypervolume under peak demand. Scaling tests on bootstrap-resampled instances up to 4,800 patients/day showed ~O(N·log N) runtime growth, with the largest instance solved in under 4 minutes on a single-thread i7-12,700. Baselines (NSGA-II, MOEA/D with standard parameterizations) are current and reasonably configured; the primary comparison target — the hospital's actual practice — is a weak baseline by construction. All results are simulation-based on one center; effect sizes, BCa bootstrap CIs (5,000 resamples), and 30 fixed-seed runs are reported. Novelty Classification: NEW FORMULATION (applied) + NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING + ENGINEERING OPTIMIZATION. Genuinely novel: the triage-weighted, threshold-penalized, three-resource-coupled formulation with baseline-normalized objectives and clinically feasible repair-based neighborhoods, evaluated on a real year of tertiary-ED data. Standard components: simulated annealing, weighted-sum scalarization, geometric cooling, and the metaheuristic benchmarks are all textbook; the authors explicitly disclaim a new algorithm, positioning the contribution as applied, data-driven optimization with domain adaptations. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are unusually thorough for this venue tier: a 9×9 weight grid (Sup Table 1), five imputation/resampling robustness schemes (KPIs move <4%, Sup Table 2), one-dimensional sensitivity on weights, thresholds, arrival rate, and service time (Table 10), convergence curves, and effect sizes with BCa bootstrap CIs (Sup Table 3). All results are means over 30 fixed-seed runs; multi-benchmark comparison against NSGA-II, MOEA/D, and TS was added on identical instances with shared encoding and repair. The authors are unusually candid that Monte Carlo p-values quantify within-simulation reproducibility, not clinical generalizability. Code, seeds, scenario files, and figure-regeneration scripts are released (github.com/SYYY3789/Simulated-Annealing-Algorithm.git, archived on Zenodo); record-level EHR data is restricted by ethics approval. Methodological concerns: the model is developed and evaluated on the same single-center data (no held-out hospital); resource availability is deterministic, which likely inflates attainable gains; and the equal-iteration benchmark budget, while self-flagged, still shapes the headline speedup narrative. Deployability: (EMPIRICAL profile):** - Practical: Runs on a commodity single-thread desktop CPU (i7-12,700, 32 GB RAM) in ~12 s for a real ED day — no specialized hardware needed. - Efficient: 2.5–2.8× faster than population-based baselines at equivalent solution quality; per-iteration cost 0.0124 s, comparable to Tabu Search and one-third of NSGA-II's. - Effective: Solves the stated problem convincingly in simulation, but only against simulated counterfactuals — no real ED ever operated the optimized schedule, so real-world effect is unproven and, per the authors' own structural-uncertainty analysis, likely smaller than reported. - Scalable: Tested up to 4,800 patients/day via empirical bootstrap resampling with ~O(N·log N) growth and a stated warm-start path to 30-min rolling-horizon re-optimization; the warm-start variant itself is only described (Sup Fig. 1c), not independently validated in this text. The paper delivers a software artifact (executable Python solver, benchmark implementations, scenario inputs, analysis scripts) rather than an integrated hospital system; no prospective deployment. Strengths: - Rare honesty in cost accounting: the paper repeatedly and explicitly reports that clinical gains were purchased with an 11.4% labor-cost increase rather than framing the schedule as a pure win, and reframes Fig. 7 as a cost-effectiveness frontier rather than a saving. - The constraint-repair design that guarantees feasibility by construction is a clean, transferable engineering pattern for strongly constrained scheduling and removes penalty-tuning from the objective. - The multi-benchmark study against NSGA-II, MOEA/D, and Tabu Search with shared encoding and wall-clock-based comparison addresses the most common weakness of applied metaheuristic papers (missing strong baselines), and includes hypervolume analysis. - Thorough uncertainty treatment relative to venue norms: effect sizes, BCa bootstrap intervals, imputation robustness checks, weight/threshold/demand sensitivity, and explicit separation of parameter vs. structural uncertainty. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors directly confront: single-center data limiting generalization; static (not real-time/dynamic) scheduling only; exclusion of staff preferences, skill mix, and cross-department resource coupling; NHPP under-representing bursty ambulance-batch arrivals; median imputation producing optimistic utilization; exclusion of no-shows, interruptions, and equipment failures making results an upper bound; p-values on Monte Carlo replications not indicating clinical significance; no alternative arrival-process family fitted; and purely in-silico validation with prospective multi-center work required. This is a credibility positive — limitations are stated repeatedly, quantified where possible, and never minimized. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - The comparison baselines within the headline Table 5 (current practice, priority heuristic) are weak; the strong metaheuristic benchmarks appear only in a late section, and the abstract/intro lead with the weaker comparison's 20–35% improvement numbers. - Patient outcomes like "patient satisfaction score" (72.3 → 84.2) appear in Table 5 without any stated measurement instrument or derivation — a simulated construct presented alongside measured KPIs. - Scaling experiments hold nominal load constant by scaling physicians proportionally, so the 4,800-patient result tests runtime growth, not whether solution quality holds under genuinely strained capacity. - No ablation isolating the contribution of each neighborhood operator or the repair procedure to end-to-end performance; the scenario-specific mechanism story in the Discussion is plausible but not experimentally verified via operator-level ablation. - The warm-start/rolling-horizon re-optimization claim central to the deployability narrative is not evaluated in the main text. - Single-author paper with no external validation of the Delphi weight-elicitation process; clinician weight rankings (5:3:2) are documented but unverifiable. Bottom Line: A rigorously executed, unusually honest applied OR study that hospital analytics teams can practically reuse — the code, formulation, and benchmark protocol are worth adopting — but its contribution is a well-engineered application of standard simulated annealing, and readers seeking algorithmic novelty or evidence of real-world clinical impact should look to prospective multi-center validation studies before citing its improvement percentages as achievable in practice.

Memadapter: Counterfactual Adaptation Against Memory-induced Sycophancy (27 ▲ )

Ruqing Ning, Haibo Meng, Zhishang Xiang, Zerui Chen, Jinsong Su, Xin Wang, Qinggang Zhang · arxiv.org · Daily papers of 6 Oct 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces MemAdapter, a three-stage post-retrieval prompting framework (Counterfactual Induction, Context-Aware Reflection, Evidence-Based Reasoning) that adaptively regulates how retrieved memories influence an LLM agent's reasoning to suppress memory-induced sycophancy without modifying the upstream memory system. - Why it's important: Long-term memory agents inherit users' past beliefs and preferences across sessions, and even factually correct memories can silently override objective evidence — a persistent behavioral bias affecting any deployed personalized assistant. - How it does it: The core trick is to hold each retrieved memory fixed, probe it under counterfactually constructed task settings to induce conditional-use boundaries (what the memory can and cannot justify), then resolve those boundaries against the current query and evidence into per-memory usage instructions that constrain final generation. - The good: A controlled preliminary study cleanly isolates the phenomenon: with only verified-accurate, task-relevant memories, accuracy drops from 96.0% to 77.3% across three benchmarks, and 19.4% of otherwise-correct predictions flip to memory-aligned errors — directly motivating the post-retrieval framing. - The missing: No error bars, seeds, or significance tests are reported for the headline gains, evaluation relies entirely on LLM-as-judge rubrics, and one of the three evaluation benchmarks (MemSyco-Bench) has substantial author overlap with the paper itself. - Read it or not: Worth reading for researchers building memory-augmented agents or studying sycophancy — the reframing of memory risk as context-dependent rather than content-dependent is a genuinely useful conceptual contribution — but practitioners seeking training-free mitigation should note it is pure prompting and the margin over simpler interventions on strong backbones is modest (e.g., +0.44 to +2.33 points over the best baseline with A-MEM).

Problem & Motivation: Long-term memory systems for LLM agents (A-MEM, Mem0, MemoryBank, etc.) extract, store, and retrieve user information across sessions. A growing set of benchmarks (Recalling Too Well, PersistBench, OP-Bench, MemTrapBench, MemSyco-Bench) shows that retrieved memories can induce sycophancy — the agent over-aligns with remembered user beliefs even against evidence. Existing mitigations intervene before reasoning: filtering at extraction (lossy extraction fixes, forgetting policies), at retrieval (MemGate's learned gating, Self-ReCheck's relevance filtering), or via restructuring (Dynamic Partition). The paper argues these share a flawed assumption: that memory risk is an intrinsic property of memory content. It demonstrates the opposite — accurate, relevant memories still cause sycophancy, and the same memory warrants different influence in different contexts (a 'user is a cardiologist' memory legitimately shapes explanation style but should not override patient-specific evidence in a treatment decision). The problem is real for anyone deploying personalized assistants in domains where user preference must not become decision authority. Key Idea: Treat memory-induced sycophancy as a conditional failure and reformulate memory-risk identification as counterfactual boundary discovery: instead of asking 'is this memory safe?', ask 'under what downstream conditions does its influence become inappropriate?' — derived by varying hypothetical task contexts while holding the memory fixed, then inducing condition-to-influence rules that are resolved per-task at inference time. Methodology: MemAdapter is a training-free, three-stage LLM pipeline operating strictly after retrieval (no modification of memory construction, content, or retrieval). Stage 1, Counterfactual Induction, consumes each retrieved memory m_i (without the current query), derives memory-specific task types, constructs a counterfactual task space H_i of hypothetical request/evidence settings, assesses the memory's support/scope/limitation in each, and consolidates substantive differences into conditional-use boundaries B_i (Algorithm 1). Stage 2, Context-Aware Reflection, consumes the current query q, context/evidence c, memories M, and B, and produces natural-language per-memory use instructions U (what the memory may support, on which response components, to what degree, and what it cannot justify), accounting for cross-memory updates and conflicts. Stage 3, Evidence-Based Reasoning, generates (y, L) = R_EBR(q, c, M, U), where L is an internal answer-support trace verifying that each major response span's source exists, supports the span, and that memory uses stay within their instructions; only y is returned. Critical design decisions: (i) deriving task types from memory content rather than a fixed global checklist (plausible but unvalidated — coverage of the counterfactual space is untested); (ii) expressing boundaries as natural-language 'boundary cards' rather than structured constraints (interpretable, but the final generator is asked to self-enforce them, so compliance is not guaranteed); (iii) keeping memory content intact in Stage 3 while the instructions regulate use (preserves legitimate personalization, which the ablation supports). The output is a JSON-structured boundary card and instruction schema, with full prompts in Appendix H. Key Results: Evaluated on MemSyco-Bench (1,550 instances), MemTrapBench (1,050), and PersistBench (500), across five memory systems (A-MEM, Mem0, NaiveRAG, MemoryBank, LightMem) with DeepSeek-V4-Flash as primary backbone, plus GPT-5.6-sol and Qwen3-8B. Baselines are direct generation and four contemporary post-retrieval interventions (Anti-Sycophancy, Self-ReCheck, Dynamic Partition, MemGate), all given identical frozen retrieved-memory sets — a fair-comparison protocol. Headline numbers: on MemSyco-Bench with LightMem, When-to-Use accuracy jumps from 32.11% to 88.78% (+56.67); with Mem0, avg accuracy rises from 49.30% to 85.48% (+36.19). On PersistBench, sycophancy failure rate at three inferences drops consistently, e.g., 80.00%→53.50% (NaiveRAG), 82.00%→51.00% (MemoryBank); cross-domain failure rates also drop for four of five systems. On MemTrapBench, the Task Boundary scenario gains 0.74–1.50 points. Cross-backbone: with Qwen3-8B, avg accuracy improves 42–61 points over very weak direct-generation baselines (e.g., 24.57→85.74 with LightMem); with GPT-5.6-sol, gains are smaller (+3.10 to +39.84 depending on system) and personalized-memory use degrades in two of five settings (e.g., −9.00 with A-MEM). Ablations show Counterfactual Induction alone accounts for most of the gain (NaiveRAG avg 70.25→84.26), Reflection adds ~1 point, Evidence-Based Reasoning adds ~4.8 more (→89.94). Runtime: mean 6.63–6.95 s/sample, within the range of competing interventions. A notable counter-intuitive preliminary finding: adding verified-correct, relevant memories flips 19.4% of correct answers to memory-aligned errors. The beneficial-memory failure rate degrades for some systems (up to +6 points with LightMem), an acknowledged trade-off. Novelty Classification: NEW FORMULATION and NEW METHOD. Genuinely novel is the reframing of memory risk as a relational, context-dependent property requiring post-retrieval calibration rather than pre-retrieval filtering — prior work assumed risk was detectable from memory content. The three-stage mechanism is a competent combination of known techniques: counterfactual probing, self-reflection (Reflexion-style), and grounded generation with support verification (Self-RAG-style), applied to a new setting (memory-use regulation). The preliminary study is a solid NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING supporting the formulation, though the phenomenon's existence is arguably implied by prior benchmarks. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are present and well-designed: the B / B+R / full variants isolate each stage's contribution, and complete results across all five memory systems are in Appendix C.4, with the full configuration winning in every block. However, no error bars, multiple seeds, or significance tests are reported anywhere; PersistBench failure rates over 200-sample splits have nontrivial sampling error that the deltas (sometimes ~0.1 point margins over Self-ReCheck on MemTrapBench averages) do not statistically support. Code is released at https://github.com/DEEP-JLU/MemAdapter, with full prompts, hyperparameters, and preserved per-instance artifacts. Methodological concerns: (i) the paper's own prior work (Xiang et al., 2026a) is MemSyco-Bench, so the framework was developed with knowledge of at least one headline benchmark; (ii) all primary metrics are LLM-as-judge rubrics (the paper states judges follow official benchmark protocols, but judges are LLMs and MemAdapter's outputs — explicit boundary-respecting language — may align more readily with judge rubric phrasing than baselines' outputs, a potential evaluation-bias channel); (iii) the LightMem and Mem0 direct-generation baselines are extremely weak (37.03 and 49.30 avg accuracy), so some gains reflect recovering baseline failures rather than beating strong competitors — against the strongest intervention margins narrow to 0.44–2.33 points. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL. Practical: Yes — runs on API-accessible backbones (DeepSeek-V4-Flash, GPT-5.6-sol) or a locally hosted 4-bit Qwen3-8B, with no training. Efficient: Mean 6.63–6.95 s/sample (P99 up to 16.23 s), comparable to single-pass baselines despite multiple LLM calls, though the paper does not report token-cost overhead, which for per-memory counterfactual construction should scale linearly with memory count and could be substantial. Effective: Evidence is strong on the tested proxies — it improves sycophancy, scope-control, and conflict metrics across five memory systems and three backbones — but all evidence is on sycophancy-focused benchmarks with LLM judges; no open-ended deployment or human evaluation. Scalable: Only claimed implicitly; the counterfactual stage cost grows with per-query memory count (PersistBench uses 4–16 memories), and behavior with hundreds of memories or streaming agent sessions is untested. The work delivers a code artifact (GitHub repo with prompts and pipeline) but no trained model or library; it stops at paper-plus-repo form. Strengths: (1) The preliminary controlled study (75 manually verified paired instances where the memory is the only systematic input difference) is a clean causal isolation of the phenomenon — accuracy drops 96.0%→77.3% with verified-correct memories, and all reversals are memory-aligned — which genuinely establishes that content-level filtering is insufficient. (2) The fair-comparison protocol (one frozen retrieved-memory set reused across all interventions per instance) removes retrieval as a confound, making the intervention comparison meaningful. (3) The ablation is honest and informative: Counterfactual Induction alone delivers most of the gain, and the paper reports where it does not win (Beneficial FR trade-offs, GPT-5.6-sol personalized-use degradation, per-dimension losses to Self-ReCheck/Dynamic Partition). (4) Reducing cross-memory-system performance spread from 34.68 to 4.97 percentage points on MemSyco-Bench is a practically interesting result — the method largely equalizes weak and strong memory backends. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors explicitly state that the beneficial-memory failure rate is a memory-system-dependent trade-off that increases for some systems (e.g., +6 with LightMem), that gains vary across memory systems and task dimensions (Obs. 5), that improvements on high-scoring MemTrapBench scenarios (Trauma, Safety) have limited headroom and should not be compared to gains on low-scoring scenarios, that cross-domain improvement on LightMem is mixed, and that personalized-memory accuracy degrades under GPT-5.6-sol for some systems. They confront these directly in observation paragraphs rather than burying them — a credibility positive. They do not, however, acknowledge evaluation-methodology limitations (LLM judges, benchmark overlap, absence of statistical testing). Analyst-Identified Gaps: (1) Evaluation integrity: MemSyco-Bench is authored by a heavily overlapping author set (Xiang, Chen, Ning, Zhang, Su), so performance on the paper's largest benchmark (1,550 of 3,100 total instances) is on home turf; independent-benchmark-only results (PersistBench, MemTrapBench) show smaller margins. (2) LLM-judge circularity: MemAdapter's outputs articulate boundaries and evidence-grounding in exactly the vocabulary the judge rubrics reward (e.g., 'preference is context, not evidence'), creating a plausible judge-affinity bias the paper does not control for (no judge-robustness or human-agreement check is reported). (3) No significance testing or seeds — several claimed advantages (e.g., MemTrapBench average over Self-ReCheck by 0.07–0.26 points) are within plausible judge noise. (4) The counterfactual task-space construction (Stage 1) is never evaluated for coverage or quality — no analysis of whether induced boundaries miss the failure conditions that actually occur, or how often Reflection overrides them. (5) The extremely weak LightMem/Mem0 direct-generation baselines inflate aggregate gains; against the strongest competing intervention, the effective margin on strong backbones is under 2.5 points on the primary benchmark. (6) Token/cost accounting beyond wall-clock latency is absent, despite the method making several LLM calls per memory. Bottom Line: A practitioner building memory-augmented agents should read this for the context-dependent-risk framing and the fair post-retrieval comparison protocol — the framework itself is a reasonable training-free mitigation, but with modest margins over simpler interventions on strong backbones, judge-based evaluation on partially home-turf benchmarks, and no statistical rigor, it is a promising direction paper rather than a settled solution.

Data Unlearning via Inverse Distillation (16 ▲ )

Aleksei Leonov, Nikita Kornilov, Zhenhe Zhang, Evgeny Burnaev, Iaroslav Koshelev, Alexander Korotin · arxiv.org · Daily papers of 6 Oct 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces Inverse Distillation Unlearning (IDU), a min-max objective that simultaneously distills a multi-step matching model (flow or score-based diffusion) into a one-step generator while suppressing generation of a designated forget subset, without access to retained training data. - Why it's important: Generative models trained on web-scale data can memorize and reproduce private, copyrighted, or unsafe content, and unlearning methods for efficient one-step generators were essentially missing; IDU removes forget-set influence at one-step inference cost with a single tunable hyperparameter (ρ). - How it does it: It reparametrizes the optimized data distribution in the inverse-distillation min-max scheme as a mixture ρ·p_F + (1−ρ)·p_θ of forget and generated data, so that matching the full teacher distribution forces the generator to produce only the retained data. - The good: Across four dataset–backbone combinations (MNIST/CIFAR-10 × flow matching/SiD), forgotten-class generation rates drop to at most 0.56% (FM) and 1.25% (SiD) with Retain FID close to retrain-distillation oracles (e.g., 3.15 vs 2.82 SiD-CIFAR-10), with mean±std over five runs and a single-class robustness sweep over all 10 classes per setting. - The missing: There is no privacy-attack evaluation (e.g., membership inference or sample extraction) to verify the forget data's influence is genuinely removed rather than merely not sampled, and all experiments are on 28×28/32×32 toy benchmarks; the authors also report FM instability (forgotten-class frequency rebounds after ~20k updates, divergence at ρ=0.9). - Read it or not: Worth reading for researchers working on unlearning in generative models or distillation of matching models, since it is the first unified data-unlearning-plus-distillation framework and exposes real stability trade-offs; practitioners needing deployed, audited unlearning at scale will find the evidence still too early-stage.
Why this rank
Scored using Empirical profile (with a theoretical anchor). Novelty (78) is the highest in the cluster — the mixture reparametrization casting unlearning as inverse distillation is a new formulation with a correct theorem and the weakest requirement profile among competitors — and the paper's honesty about failure modes (divergence at ρ=0.9, FGR rebound, collateral suppression) makes Completeness (75) exemplary. However, Rigor (55) and Resilience (50) drop sharply: all evaluation is on 28×28/32×32 toy benchmarks, baselines rely on self-reported numbers rather than re-runs, the empirically best ρ deviates unexplained from the theoretical π, and — most damaging — no privacy-attack evaluation (membership inference, extraction) verifies that forget data influence is actually removed rather than merely unsampled, which strikes at the core unlearning claim the paper must survive. Impact (48) is limited to promised code at toy scale. Weighted composite: 0.20*78 + 0.25*55 + 0.15*74 + 0.15*75 + 0.15*50 + 0.10*48 = 64.
