Problem & Motivation: Autoregressive (AR) video diffusion models generate long videos chunk-by-chunk, conditioning each chunk on a KV cache of prior chunks. Beyond the fixed training horizon (N chunks), a rolling KV window attends to configurations never seen in training, causing 'drifting': colors and textures shift and motion dynamics decay toward frame freezing. Prior test-time fixes (Deep Forcing, ∞-RoPE, MemRoPE) only modify KV conditioning — which cached entries are read and where they are positioned — implicitly assuming the cached entries themselves are in-distribution. The authors argue this assumption fails because nothing constrains how entries are cached at test time, and no amount of training-horizon extension removes the boundary for arbitrarily long generation. The problem affects anyone building world models, streaming video, or long-form narrative generation on top of open AR video backbones. Key Idea: The single core insight is the KV-provenance problem: a KV entry's distributional status depends not only on the chunk it encodes but on which prior entries it attended to when it was cached (its provenance). Beyond the training horizon, every chunk is cached under an unseen provenance, so cached entries become OOD before any conditioning policy reads them — and no conditioning policy can recover from that. The fix is to control both levels: cache early window entries with self-caching (attending to nothing, as chunk 0 does in training) and cache the rest autoregressively on top of the last self-cached entry, so every cache-write pattern matches one seen in training. Methodology: The framework is a test-time, training-free procedure on a chunked AR diffusion model with a few-step denoiser G_θ (here a Wan2.1-T2V-1.3B DiT, 4-step schedule at timesteps {1000, 750, 500, 250}, 3 latent frames per chunk). Two levels of KV management: (1) KV caching (self-caching): for a window of L entries, the first ℓ entries are cached as E(x_j; ∅) — attending to nothing — and the remaining L−ℓ are cached autoregressively on top of the last self-cached entry, exactly mirroring training's incremental caching of κ_1…κ_{N−1} on top of κ_0. (2) KV conditioning: keep the first chunk κ_0 permanently in slot 0 (justified by the causal 3D-VAE making κ_0 distributionally unique — it is encoded from a single pixel frame, unlike all later chunks), hold the L−1 most recent entries in the remaining slots (L < N, so the window fits the training budget), evict the oldest non-sink entry each step, and re-rotate stored keys by R^{−f} so all temporal RoPE distances match trained configurations. The output is Algorithm 1, a short rolling-window loop. Critical design decisions: (a) self-caching is justified by Observations 1–2 (drift can only enter through the conditioning window; entries are in-distribution only if their provenance was trained) — argued, not empirically proven with distributional measurements; (b) retaining exactly one sink (κ_0) rather than several is justified distributionally, distinguishing it from attention-sink heuristics; (c) the ℓ parameter (2 for Self-Forcing, 3 for LongLive) is set empirically without sensitivity analysis. Key Results: On 120- and 240-second videos (480×832, first 128 MovieGen prompts refined by Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct), built on two base models (Self-Forcing, LongLive) and compared against Deep Forcing, ∞-RoPE, and MemRoPE — contemporaneous 2026 methods, so baselines are current. On Self-Forcing at 120 s, ID-Forcing reaches Color Drift 72.37 (vs. 25.54 base, 59.65 Deep Forcing, 54.15 ∞-RoPE, 59.25 MemRoPE) and Motion Drift 89.06, with the highest Dynamic Degree (65.65 vs. 30.04 base). On LongLive at 240 s: Color Drift 71.76, Dynamic Degree 56.13 vs. base 39.79. Gains persist across 30/60/120/240 s (Appendix Table 3), while baselines' Dynamic Degree degrades with length (e.g., base Self-Forcing 44.58 → 29.61). A 20-participant 2AFC user study with a balanced Latin-square design shows 86–100% preference for ID-Forcing across all baselines and dimensions. The one weakness: Motion Smoothness is lower than base models, which the authors attribute to that metric rewarding near-frozen frames — plausible but self-serving, since it is the only metric where they lose. Tested scale is minute-level generation on a 1.3B model; drift metrics are first-vs-last-frame proxies, and the paper does not evaluate semantic/prompt-adherence quality over long horizons. Novelty Classification: NEW FORMULATION + NEW METHOD + NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING. The genuinely novel element is the KV-provenance framing — recasting drift as an OOD failure at the cache-write level rather than the cache-read level — and self-caching as the corresponding fix; the accompanying mechanisms (persistent sink, RoPE re-rotation) are adaptations of known attention-sink and positional-realignment ideas, and the overall system is a small modification to a standard rolling-window AR pipeline. The distinction from attention sinks (one distributionally-unique chunk vs. several stabilizing chunks) is a real conceptual contribution. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are present and well-designed: sink, re-rotation, and self-caching are added cumulatively (Fig. 5, Table 4), showing self-caching is the component that most reduces drift and that sink/re-rotation alone leave Color Drift at 60.66. No error bars, seeds, or significance tests are reported for any metric; the user study has only 20 participants across 20 prompts. Code release is not stated — only a project page (https://in-distribution-forcing.github.io/) with videos; the method is simple enough to reimplement from Algorithm 1. Methodological concerns: the two drift metrics are custom (Color Drift from a prior arXiv work, Motion Drift self-constructed from VBench's Dynamic Degree), evaluated only on 128 MovieGen prompts from a single base architecture (Wan2.1-1.3B); the core in-distribution claim is argued from mechanism, never verified by measuring KV-entry distributions; and the claim that Motion Smoothness penalizes them is asserted, not substantiated with a frozen-frame control. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (a test-time inference procedure run on open models). Practical: Yes — it runs on an open-weight 1.3B DiT with only KV-management changes, no retraining. Efficient: Window is strictly bounded at L < N entries, so memory and attention cost stay constant per chunk; no added compute beyond a re-caching pass over L entries, though exact overhead numbers are not reported. Effective: Strong evidence it suppresses drift (the stated problem) at 120–240 s on both drift metrics and human preference, but long-horizon prompt adherence and content coherence are not measured, so effectiveness on full generation quality is partially proxy-based. Scalable: Behavior past 240 s is untested — the in-distribution argument predicts stability at any length, but this is a claim, not an experiment; 10–100× scale (hours-long, larger backbones) is unexamined. Deliverable: a method + project page with videos; no released library, checkpoint, or dataset. Strengths: - The KV-provenance problem is a genuinely new and useful abstraction: it explains why conditioning-only fixes fail and converts an empirical mystery (drift) into a distribution-matching condition that suggests an algorithm directly. - The diagnostic Figure 2 experiment (same conditioning, three different caching provenances for one chunk, with visibly different downstream drift) is a clean, targeted piece of evidence for the central claim. - Self-caching is a one-rule intervention with large measured effect (Color Drift 60.66 → 72.37 in the ablation), and it composes with, rather than replaces, base models trained at different horizons (both Self-Forcing and LongLive improve). - Evaluation is disciplined relative to field norms: two base models, four durations, contemporaneous training-free baselines, and a balanced-design user study rather than metrics alone. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors acknowledge the Motion Smoothness deficit, attributing it to that metric rewarding collapsed, near-frozen output (supported qualitatively by the base model's low Dynamic Degree). They note that extending the training horizon cannot solve the problem in principle and that their method is orthogonal to better-trained backbones. They do not include a dedicated limitations section; failure modes such as content incoherence over minutes, dependence on the causal-VAE structure of the first chunk, or sensitivity to ℓ and L are not discussed, so limitation coverage is partial rather than direct. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - The central in-distribution claim is never tested: no experiment measures KV-entry distances to the training distribution, compares self-cached vs. AR-cached entries in feature space, or tests what happens when provenance is only partially matched. The claim rests on Observations 1–2 plus downstream metrics. - Both drift metrics reduce each video to first-vs-last-5-second statistics (HSV hue histogram; Dynamic Degree difference), which is blind to mid-sequence color oscillation, periodic resets (visible in their own ablation frames), or subject-identity drift that returns by the end — a measurement gap for a paper about progressive degradation. - Only one base architecture (Wan2.1-1.3B) and one denoising schedule are tested; whether the KV-provenance fix transfers to other causal-VAE AR models (e.g., CogVideoX-style, SkyReels-V2) is unknown, and the first-chunk argument depends on Wan's VAE specifics. - No combination experiments: ID-Forcing is framed as orthogonal to conditioning-level methods (∞-RoPE, MemRoPE, Deep Forcing), but the obvious test — stack them — is absent, which would either strengthen the orthogonality claim or reveal overlap. - No variance reporting: 128 prompts, single run per setting, no seeds or confidence intervals, and the Motion Drift metric (a difference of two noisy Dynamic Degree estimates) is reported to two decimal places without uncertainty. - The per-chunk re-caching of the L−ℓ tail entries each step adds compute that is never quantified (latency, memory, or wall-clock vs. baselines). Bottom Line: For anyone building or deploying autoregressive video diffusion beyond a few seconds, this paper is worth reading — the KV-provenance insight and the near-free self-caching fix are likely to matter more than any single conditioning-level trick in the current literature, even though the in-distribution story is argued rather than measured and the evaluation is confined to one 1.3B backbone and coarse drift proxies.

When code does not run: reproducibility challenges in materials machine learning benchmarks

B Lyu, J Bonini, M Zhang, A Sadeghi, A Jaberi… · oaepublish.com · automated generated environments for agent testing - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper presents a systematic re-execution audit of 28 algorithm submissions to the MatBench materials-property benchmark, measuring how often a runnable software environment can be reconstructed from the released dependency metadata and how often the original reported results can be regenerated. - Why it's important: Benchmark leaderboards in AI-for-materials are only useful if submissions actually execute months or years later; this paper quantifies that dependency rot silently invalidates most of them, wasting community effort and undermining trust in published comparisons. - How it does it: It runs a three-stage escalating remediation pipeline — strict installation from author-supplied metadata in clean GitHub Actions runners, error-guided automated constraint relaxation, then human/LLM-assisted repair — classifying each submission by the minimum intervention needed, followed by code re-execution and RMSE comparison on representative tasks. - The good: The headline finding is stark and quantified: only 2 of 28 submissions install and pass import checks from the original metadata, and even after full remediation only 13 of 28 (46.4%) complete a benchmark task, while the 13 that do re-execute reproduce their five-fold mean RMSE within 7.2% maximum deviation. - The missing: Numerical reproducibility is tested on only the single smallest representative task per input class (steels for composition, jdft2d for structure), not across MatBench's 13 tasks, so the finding that "results are highly reproducible once environments run" rests on a thin slice of the benchmark. - Read it or not: Read it if you maintain a scientific ML benchmark platform, submit to one, or package scientific software for reproducibility; skip it if you want new ML methods — there are none here.
Why this rank
Scored using Empirical profile. Novelty (55) is the ceiling here: the staged install→execute→match funnel is a sound measurement protocol and the first systematic executability audit for a materials ML benchmark, but the constituent techniques (CI validation, Nix, lockfiles) are standard engineering applied to a new setting. Non-Obviousness (55) is modest — dependency rot failing submissions is the expected finding; the mild surprise is that numerically reproduced results match within 7.2% once environments run. Rigor (65) is reduced by numerical reproducibility being tested on only the two smallest MatBench tasks while the claim is stated broadly, unquantified LLM-assisted repair, and no error quantification on the ΔRMSE comparisons. Completeness (72) is a credibility positive — the authors candidly flag constraint relaxation risks and GPU-Nix gaps — and Impact (70) reflects genuinely released GitHub Actions workflows and usnistgov Nix packages that benchmark maintainers can adopt immediately. Weighted composite: 0.20*55 + 0.25*65 + 0.15*55 + 0.15*72 + 0.15*70 + 0.10*70 = 63.

Problem & Motivation: Reproducibility in machine learning benchmarks is commonly assumed to follow from releasing source code plus a requirements file, but this assumption fails when the dependency specification cannot actually reconstruct an executable environment. The affected parties are the materials-informatics community — benchmark maintainers (MatBench, JARVIS-Leaderboard), method authors whose leaderboards entries decay, and practitioners who cannot re-run or compare published models. The specific gap the paper closes: prior reproducibility discussions treat environment reconstruction as a solved formality, and no systematic, sandboxed, staged measurement of executability failure rates exists for materials ML benchmarks. The motivating analogy is a chemistry synthesis protocol that only works with "one beaker the chemist never washes" — a computational workflow that only runs on the author's machine should be judged equally incomplete. Key Idea: The core insight is to treat environment reconstruction difficulty as a measurable, staged quantity: submit each benchmark entry to progressively more aggressive remediation (exact metadata → error-guided automated constraint relaxation → human-supervised repair, with an LLM as a supervised troubleshooting aid) and classify each entry by the minimum intervention tier that yields an import-valid environment. This separates "environment installable" from "code executable" from "numbers match" — three failure levels prior work conflates. The key idea is sound but is a measurement protocol, not an algorithmic contribution. Methodology: The pipeline has three sequential levels. (1) Environment reconstruction: each of 28 MatBench submissions (info.json metadata, source code, results.json.gz) is installed in clean isolated Linux GitHub Actions runners across Python 3.6–3.12 via pip and conda; the workflow scans all import statements and requires them to load. Stage 1 uses metadata unmodified; Stage 2 applies predefined error-classification rules that only relax dependency constraints; Stage 3 adds manual review and LLM-assisted troubleshooting (GPT-5.4 via ChatGPT, human-supervised, explicitly declared). Categories: Cat. 1 (direct install, 2/28), Cat. 2 (auto-fix, 15/28), Cat. 3 (human effort, 9/28), Cat. 4 (failed, 2/28: DeeperGATGNN, rf). (2) Code re-execution: Cat. 1–3 environments are installed on an HPC node (Rocky Linux 9.4, NVIDIA A100-80GB, CUDA 12.8); each submission runs one selected representative task — the smallest per input class (steels, composition-based; jdft2d, structure-based) to bound compute cost. (3) Numerical comparison: signed relative difference ΔRMSE (%) between regenerated and reported five-fold mean RMSE, with no arbitrary binary threshold. A parallel effort packages 14 JARVIS-Leaderboard exfoliation-energy models with the Nix functional package manager (nixpkgs + PDM/pyproject.toml via dream2nix), patching scripts for CLI flags and path purity. Critical design decisions: three-level separation (well justified — they demonstrate installable-but-unrunnable cases like the empty run.py in cgcnnv2019); testing only the smallest task per class (justified by cost, but limits the strength of the reproducibility conclusion); refusing to modify submitted model/evaluation code (well justified, preserves fidelity to the original artifact). Key Results: From original metadata, 2/28 submissions install and pass import checks (Auto-sklearn via environment.yml; Ax_10_90_CrabNet_v1.2.7 on Python 3.7). Rule-based automated remediation recovers 15 more; human/LLM-assisted repair recovers 9 more; 2 remain unrecoverable (26/28 total). Of the 26 reconstructed environments, 13 (46.4% of all 28) complete a benchmark task and generate outputs. Dominant failure modes: unavailability of pinned versions (matbench==0.1.0 missing from repositories, breaking 11 environments), dependency conflicts among matbench/scikit-learn/pymatgen/matminer, missing packages in metadata (e.g., torch_scatter for Matformer), and API drift at runtime (renamed entry points in alignn, relocated pymatgen Structure import in modnet, gptchem hitting a dead OpenAI endpoint returning HTTP 404). For the 13 re-executed submissions, the maximum absolute ΔRMSE was 7.2%, with most near zero. On JARVIS-Leaderboard, 11 of 14 exfoliation-energy models were packaged with Nix after patching; 3 (alignn, cgcnn, matformer) needed substantially more work. Baselines here are the submissions' own reported metrics — appropriate for this audit design. Tested scale is small in absolute terms (28 + 14 models, 2 tasks) but exhaustive within its scope; the finding that reconstruction difficulty, not model correctness, is the bottleneck is the paper's most useful and mildly counter-intuitive result (Figure 6). Novelty Classification: NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING + NEW SYSTEM/TOOL. The genuinely novel element is the first quantified, staged executability audit of a materials ML benchmark (2/28 → 26/28 → 13/28 funnel) plus a working Nix-based functional-packaging demonstration for JARVIS-Leaderboard models with released workflows. The individual techniques (CI environment validation, lockfiles, conda-pack, Docker, Nix) are all standard software-engineering tools; the contribution is their systematic application to, and measurement on, a scientific benchmark platform — a competent combination of known ideas in a setting where they had not been systematically tested. Rigor & Reproducibility: The paper's own artifact is well-reproduced: GitHub Actions workflows are released (github.com/BohuiLyu/matbench_reproduce.git) and the Nix packaging is at github.com/usnistgov/reproducible-models. The staged category taxonomy is a genuine ablation of intervention level. However: no multiple seeds or error bars are needed for the executability counts, but the ΔRMSE comparison on 13 submissions has no uncertainty quantification; the LLM-assisted Stage 3 introduces irreproducible human/LLM judgment the authors acknowledge but do not bound (they do note Cat. 4 "should not be interpreted as proof that reconstruction is impossible"). A methodological concern: the numerical reproducibility claim is evaluated on the two smallest MatBench tasks only, chosen by the authors for cost — a narrow slice that could overstate stability. The two-year age of submissions is correctly identified as a confound driving failure rates, but it is also part of the phenomenon being measured. The paper does not game its own benchmark; it evaluates the benchmark ecosystem itself. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL (with a SYSTEMS component — the released CI workflows and Nix packages). Practical: Yes — the workflow runs on commodity GitHub Actions runners plus one A100 node, and most reconstruction stages need only CPU. Efficient: The audit itself is cheap by design (smallest tasks selected explicitly to bound cost); the remediation effort, however, consumed substantial human time for 9 of 26 environments, which the paper does not quantify in hours. Effective: The evidence shows the workflow diagnoses and partially repairs executability — 13/28 fully re-executed — but half the reconstructed environments still failed at runtime, so it solves the diagnosis problem more completely than the repair problem. Scalable: Not tested at 10× — the authors extrapolate that CI-based validation is low-maintenance for future submissions but provide no measurement of throughput across a larger submission corpus; GPU/Nix reproducibility is explicitly deferred to future work. Deliverables: working CI workflows, Nix packaging scripts, and a strategy comparison table (Table 5) — a real software artifact, not just a paper. Strengths: - The staged-funnel measurement design (install → execute → match numbers) cleanly decouples failure modes that prior reproducibility discussions conflate, and the taxonomy (Cat. 1–4) is immediately reusable by other benchmark platforms. - The headline numbers (2/28 installable as-is; 46.4% fully re-executable) are concrete, exhaustive within scope, and directly actionable for MatBench and JARVIS-Leaderboard maintainers. - The Table 5 comparison of six environment-preservation strategies (requirements.yml, conda-lock, conda-pack, Docker/Apptainer, Nix, hosted services) with honest maintenance-burden and limitation columns is a genuinely useful engineering synthesis absent from most reproducibility papers. - Transparent disclosure of LLM use (GPT-5.4, human-supervised, non-autonomous) in both remediation and manuscript preparation. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors explicitly state: (i) relaxing version constraints may change environments from those that produced original results, creating risk of altered outcomes; (ii) they did not patch execution scripts or package sources to fix runtime incompatibilities, so 13 executable-environment failures may be repairable with more intervention; (iii) Cat. 4 does not prove reconstruction is impossible under all configurations; (iv) OS, drivers, hardware, and numerical nondeterminism are outside their scope; (v) GPU reproducibility under Nix was "not fully addressed at this stage"; (vi) preservation strategies impose real packaging, storage, and maintenance burdens with trade-offs that "should be carefully considered." This is a candid limitation treatment — the authors confront rather than minimize their boundaries, which strengthens credibility. Analyst-Identified Gaps: (1) Numerical reproducibility is claimed broadly ("results are generally highly reproducible") but measured on exactly two small tasks (steels, jdft2d) — the larger, harder 11 MatBench tasks are untested, and larger tasks could exhibit larger ΔRMSE or more runtime failures. (2) The remediation effort is unquantified in human hours, making the "low maintenance burden" claim for the proposed CI solution an argument rather than a measurement. (3) The 28 submissions are 2–3 years old; the paper does not report whether failure rates differ for recent submissions, so the urgency of its recommendations for new submissions is extrapolated. (4) Stage 3's LLM-assisted repair is not repeatable by an independent team following the paper — the boundary between legitimate environment repair and outcome-altering substitution is asserted but not audited (e.g., no check that remediated dependency versions match known-original versions). (5) The JARVIS-Leaderboard Nix study deliberately did "no attempt to constrain dependency versions to those used by the original authors," so it demonstrates packaging feasibility, not numerical reproducibility, yet the two platforms' results are presented as parallel evidence of the same phenomenon. (6) One reproducible "submission" is the `dummy` baseline, slightly inflating the apparent method-reproducibility count. Bottom Line: Any maintainer or contributor to a scientific ML benchmark should read this — it converts a vague anxiety about dependency rot into precise failure counts, a reusable audit workflow, and a pragmatic preservation menu — even though the numerical-reproducibility evidence is thinner than the executability evidence and more rigorous multi-task audits will be needed to confirm that "runnable equals reproducible" across the full benchmark.

TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces COMMON-TSQA, a 2,600-sample unified benchmark across six time-series QA tasks, plus an intervention-based protocol (six numerical-evidence perturbations) and a staged rationale audit, to test whether four time-series QA systems (TimeOmni-1, ChatTS, TimeOmni-VL, Time-MQA) actually use the supplied numerical series. - Why it's important: Specialized time-series LLMs report large accuracy gains over their backbones, but final-answer accuracy cannot distinguish genuine temporal-structure use from shortcut or fallback behavior, so the field's headline numbers may overstate what these models can do. - How it does it: Each system sees identical canonical samples through its native interface under the original input plus six series interventions (Shuffle, Flat, Noise, Swap, Answer-only, Zero) with the question and target held fixed; Problem & Motivation: Time-series QA systems built on LLMs (TimeOmni-1, ChatTS, TimeOmni-VL, Time-MQA) report large accuracy gains over their backbones on forecasting, anomaly detection, pattern recognition, cross-series comparison, causal diagnosis, and decision tasks. Practitioners cannot tell from final-answer accuracy whether these gains depend on the supplied numerical series: the same answer is compatible with temporal structure, coarse level cues, or non-series cues in the question and options. The problem also afflicts evaluation infrastructure itself — systems are evaluated on different, often unreleased test sets, making reported scores non-comparable. Prior work (Tan et al. 2024 on LMs for forecasting; Merrill et al. 2024 on time-series reasoning; TSQueryBench) questioned LLM usefulness and explanation quality in fragments, but no work had combined cross-system common evaluation, systematic evidence intervention, and staged rationale auditing for time-series QA. Key Idea: Treat evidence use as a causal question: hold the question and target fixed, transform only the numerical series, and read system behavior off the response pattern — prediction turnover (sensitivity), fallback (a fixed-class or reference-forecast response), and target-aware updating (does the system answer correctly when the intervention changes the correct answer?). For rationales, decompose the evidence-to-answer path into three separable failure points — factual grounding of stated numerical claims, validity of intermediate inference, and consistency of the conclusion with the final answer — so that a fluent, answer-consistent rationale can be shown to fail upstream. The target-aware recomputation of ground truth under transformation (e.g., Flat makes two series' amplitudes equal, changing the correct comparison) is the sharpest single move, because it prevents the protocol from penalizing appropriate responses as errors. Methodology: Three stages. (1) Native reproduction: three systems with released evaluation data are re-run through their native interfaces; reproduced results track reported values within 3.3% on most metrics, with a larger gap on TimeOmni-1 OOD forecasting MAE (186.12 vs. 145.53 reported). (2) Intervention study on COMMON-TSQA (2,600 samples from ten public sources — GIFT-Eval, SciTS, TIME, TSB-AD-U, TSAQA, CaTS-Bench, FactoryBench, SenTSR-Bench, TSRBench, TSR-Suite-OOD — deduplicated against training data): each sample is scored under Original plus six transformations of the numerical series (Shuffle, Flat, Noise, Swap, Answer-only, Zero), using MASE for forecasting and accuracy/relation-accuracy for discrete tasks; diagnostics include Original→Answer-only transition matrices, a distance-to-history-mean-forecast reference for Flat, and recomputed targets for cross-series pairs whose correct answer changes. (3) Rationale audit of TimeOmni-1 and TimeOmni-VL under Original using GPT-5.6 as judge: atomic numerical claims are extracted and labeled supported/unsupported/not-verifiable, and outputs are scored on factual grounding, inference validity, and conclusion consistency; the judge is validated on a blinded 240-claim / 100-output human subset (κ 0.837–0.969). Critical design decisions: evaluating through each system's native interface rather than a forced common format (justified — avoids penalizing systems for rendering); recomputing targets under intervention (justified — avoids mislabeling correct updates); no intervention is scored against a changed target in the main table, with the target-aware analysis segregated (well-justified and clearly documented in Appendix D.3). Key Results: RQ1: specialization consistently beats matched backbones — e.g., TimeOmni-1 reaches 88.50% scenario ACC vs. 41.00% for Qwen2.5-7B (ID) and 47.87% vs. 23.94% decision ACC; ChatTS improves over Qwen2.5-14B on all six metrics; TimeOmni-VL improves over BAGEL-7B on all four OOD metrics. RQ2: Original is not uniformly best — Flat yields the lowest forecasting MASE (1.321 for TimeOmni-1 vs. 1.739 Original; 2.106 vs. 2.258 for Time-MQA), and paired diagnostics show Flat moves nearly all forecasts toward a history-mean reference rather than improving modeling. Aggregate scores hide turnover: on pattern recognition under Answer-only, 47.95% of TimeOmni-VL predictions change while accuracy barely moves (58.35%→58.91%). Under Answer-only, all four systems collapse to single-class anomaly-detection fallback (three always "normal", ChatTS always "anomalous"), so residual accuracy (~45–54%) reflects class frequency, not discrimination. On target-changed cross-series pairs, correct updates dominate stale answers (e.g., 78.90% vs. 14.98% for TimeOmni-1), and scoring against recomputed targets raises accuracy substantially (41.55%→72.80%). RQ3: only 49.4% (TimeOmni-1) and 50.1% (TimeOmni-VL) of extracted numerical claims are grounded; output-level factual grounding pass rates are 2.1% and 11.2%, inference validity 27.3% and 34.3%, but conclusion consistency 64.0% and 92.2%. A Time-MQA base-vs-LoRA contrast shows adaptation raises correct updates (17.13%→44.04%) and validity on some tasks while lowering paired-valid accuracy on pattern recognition (73.91%→53.42%). Baselines (matched Qwen2.5-7B/14B, BAGEL-7B) are current and appropriate for the questions asked. Testing scale is standard benchmark scale (2,600 samples), not stress-scale. Novelty Classification: NEW DATASET/BENCHMARK (COMMON-TSQA as a unified cross-system evaluation surface) and NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING (first combined evidence-intervention + staged rationale audit for time-series QA systems, including the target-aware recomputation distinction between stale answers and correct updates). The genuinely novel elements are the benchmark harmonization across ten sources and the finding that answer-consistent rationales are largely numerically ungrounded; the intervention menu (shuffle, noise, ablation, swap) and LLM-as-judge rationale auditing are standard behavioral-evaluation techniques from Merrill et al. 2024, Lanham et al. 2023, and ERASER, competently adapted to a new domain rather than newly invented. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are present in a meaningful form: per-task and per-intervention decompositions (Table 11), a base-vs-LoRA checkpoint contrast as a proxy for training-stage ablation, and an alternative last-value forecasting reference in Appendix D.2. The LLM judge is validated against blinded human annotation with strong agreement (κ 0.837–0.969 over 240 claims and 100 outputs), a credibility positive most faithfulness papers omit. However, no error bars, seeds, or significance tests are reported for any headline number, and some intervention subsets are small (e.g., 9 target-changed pairs under Shuffle for Time-MQA). Reproduction of prior results is honest, including a disclosed +40.59 MAE discrepancy on TimeOmni-1 OOD forecasting. Data sources are public with links (Table 8); the paper does not explicitly state a repository release for COMMON-TSQA itself ("Not stated"). Methodological flags: the rationale audit covers only 2 of 4 systems; GPT-5.6 as judge introduces potential shared-model bias even though the audited systems are differently trained; the benchmark is assembled from existing sources rather than newly annotated, so source annotation noise propagates; and all evaluation data are drawn from public benchmarks that overlap in provenance with the systems' own evaluation sets (mitigated by deduplication against training data, but not verifiable in full). Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL (an evaluation study with a benchmark artifact, no new model). Practical: Yes — evaluation runs four 7B–14B-class open checkpoints through public APIs/weights on commodity hardware, with no training required. Efficient: Seven evaluation conditions per sample means ~7× inference cost of a standard benchmark run, but at 2,600 samples this is modest. Effective: The evidence shows the diagnosis (accuracy masks fallback, turnover, and ungrounded rationales) on the tested systems and tasks; it does not yet show the benchmark predicts behavior on proprietary or larger systems. Scalable: Not tested beyond 2,600 samples and four systems; the intervention protocol and target-recomputation machinery should extend, but cross-series target recomputation is only feasible on the exact-oracle subset (669 pairs), which may not scale to tasks lacking deterministic targets. The work delivers a benchmark artifact (with public source links and documented construction rules) and a reusable evaluation protocol; no trained model or library is released ("Not stated" for a dedicated code release). Strengths: - The three-way rationale decomposition (factual grounding / inference validity / conclusion consistency) yields a genuinely non-obvious result: conclusion consistency of 92.2% (TimeOmni-VL) coexists with 11.2% strict grounding, and the Case 1 walkthrough (correct amplitudes 14 vs. 7.29, reversed comparison) makes the failure mode concrete and mechanical rather than anecdotal. - The target-aware recomputation distinguishes stale answers from correct updates, fixing a real flaw in naive intervention scoring that would otherwise penalize appropriate behavior — a methodological contribution other faithfulness evaluations lack. - Transparent reproduction with disclosed discrepancies (e.g., +40.59 MAE on TimeOmni-1 OOD forecasting) and explicit treatment of what the Time-MQA base–LoRA contrast can and cannot support (a checkpoint contrast, not a training ablation) reflects unusually careful epistemic hygiene. - The human validation of the LLM judge with per-criterion κ (0.837–0.969) substantiates the audit pipeline instead of asserting judge reliability. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state that the analysis identifies limitations "after specialization" rather than attributing errors to specific training choices; that no public release provides intermediate training checkpoints, so training-design discussion is diagnostic rather than causal; that the Time-MQA comparison is a checkpoint contrast with an unpinned base revision, not an exact ablation; that ChatTS corpus tags are rule-based and not gold annotations, and the audited 50 candidate groups cannot establish absence of evidence-change supervision in private training; that the Swap donor procedure and intervention semantics are documented as approximate (rounded means, unrecentered Gaussian noise); and that reproduction discrepancies concentrate in OOD forecasting. They confront limitations directly and at appropriate granularity — a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - No statistical uncertainty anywhere: many task × system × intervention cells are small (e.g., 9 changed targets under Shuffle for Time-MQA; 175 decision-intervention samples total), and several headline contrasts (e.g., Flat beating Original on MASE) are single-point estimates with no variance. - The rationale audit excludes ChatTS and Time-MQA entirely, yet the discussion draws conclusions about "systems" broadly; the two audited systems are also both from the same research group (Guan et al.), limiting generalization. - GPT-5.6 judging of numerical claims about time series is itself a time-series reasoning task the paper shows models fail; the blinded human validation on 340 items mitigates but does not eliminate systematic judge error, and no second judge or judge-ablation is reported. - Four systems is a thin sample for field-level conclusions; the strongest systems in the space (PATRA, ARTIST are cited but not evaluated) are absent, so it is unknown whether the failures are universal or specific to these checkpoints. - The Answer-only single-class fallback finding is arguably confounded by class imbalance in the 285-sample anomaly subset (45.61% appears repeatedly as the majority-class rate), and the paper does not report chance-corrected scores (e.g., Cohen's kappa against class priors) for any task. - No explicit statement of a code/benchmark release repository for COMMON-TSQA beyond source-dataset links. Bottom Line: A practitioner building or evaluating time-series LLM systems should read this: the benchmark harmonization, target-aware intervention scoring, and the demonstration that answer-consistent rationales are largely ungrounded (~2–11% strict grounding pass rates) expose evaluation blind spots that leaderboard accuracy hides, and no comparable unified audit currently covers this domain.

Explore-on-Graph: Hybrid Embedding-LLM Reasoning for Knowledge Graph Question Answering under Incompleteness

OE Khatib, D Difallah · arxiv.org · 10 new citations to your articles
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces XoG, a multi-hop knowledge graph question answering (KGQA) framework that recovers broken reasoning paths using graph-grounded signals — type-level entity–relation co-occurrence statistics and ComplEx embedding-based link prediction — instead of LLM parametric knowledge or LLM-generated triples. - Why it's important: Real-world knowledge graphs are incomplete, and existing LLM+KG methods either fail when required triples are missing (traversal-based) or hallucinate missing facts (generation-based); XoG targets this reliability gap directly. - How it does it: An iterative planning–exploration–reasoning loop in which the LLM prunes curated candidate sets (relations from a type-conditioned co-occurrence matrix via hierarchical bucketing prompts, entities from top-K KGE link-prediction scores filtered by DistilBERT), keeping the LLM as a selector rather than a knowledge generator. - The good: On the GoG incompleteness protocol, XoG reaches 77.6% Hits@1 on WebQSP and 55.7% on CWQ at IKG-40% with GPT-3.5-Turbo (vs. GoG's 66.6%/44.3% and PoG's 69.7%/53.7%), holds up to 85.4%/75.9% with stronger backbones, and cuts token consumption by up to 33% versus PoG. - The missing: Incompleteness is entirely synthetic — triples are removed at random along gold reasoning paths (IKG-20%–80%) or via rule-mined removal (BRINK), so the method's behavior under natural, non-uniform real-world KG incompleteness is untested. - Read it or not: Worth reading for researchers building LLM–KG hybrid systems or working on KGQA robustness, since the graph-grounded-recovery-versus-LLM-generation comparison and the retrieval-gap error analysis are directly actionable; skippable for readers only interested in complete-KG settings, where XoG's gains are marginal.
Why this rank
Scored using Empirical profile. Novelty (65) is solid but not high — a competent assembly of known components (PoG planning, ComplEx, DistilBERT) around one genuinely new design move (graph-grounded recovery with the LLM demoted to selector). Rigor (62) is dragged down by absent error bars/significance tests, baseline numbers transcribed from GoG, and a synthetic incompleteness protocol that leaks gold-path supervision; code release and six-backbone evaluation partially compensate. Completeness (65) benefits from direct limitation acknowledgment, while Resilience (58) suffers because the robustness claim collapses to a proxy under natural incompleteness, and Impact (62) reflects a released pipeline with measurable token savings. empirical Novelty 65 Rigor 62 Non-Obv 62 Completeness 65 Resilience 58 Impact 62
Show full analysis
Problem & Motivation: Multi-hop KGQA degrades sharply when the knowledge graph lacks triples on the path from topic entity to answer. Who has this problem: anyone deploying KG-grounded LLM agents over real KGs (Freebase, Wikidata), where incompleteness is endemic due to scale, dynamics, and long-tail relations. Prior options form a trade-off: traversal-based planners (ToG, PoG) terminate prematurely on broken paths or take long detours; generation-based methods (GoG) fill gaps from LLM parametric memory and risk hallucinated evidence; embedding-only and fine-tuned methods (RoG, GNN-RAG, EmbedKGQA) require task-specific KGQA training data. The paper closes the gap of recovering missing triples without hallucination and without task-specific KGQA supervision. Key Idea: Recover missing reasoning-path evidence from learned graph structure, not LLM knowledge: (1) prune the relation search space using a type-level entity–relation co-occurrence matrix F (frequency that entities of type t co-occur with relation r), which surfaces relations likely relevant even when absent from the entity's neighborhood; and (2) retrieve plausible tail entities via ComplEx link-prediction scores φ(e_c, r, e), with the LLM restricted to semantically pruning the resulting curated candidate sets. The LLM is demoted from knowledge source to noise-filtering selector over KG-grounded candidates. Methodology: XoG runs an iterative planning–exploration–reasoning loop (planning and status tracking inherited from PoG). Planning: an LLM decomposes question Q into sub-questions {SQ_i} with explicit answered/unanswered status. Exploration has two components. Relation exploration: candidate relations R_cand = R_KG ∪ R_cur (neighbors plus type-level co-occurrence, scored ψ(r_j|e_c) = F[t_c, j]/Σ_k F[t_c, k]); when |R_cand| exceeds a bucket size (~30 works best over ~98 candidates/query), a hierarchical bucketing strategy has the LLM prune random buckets independently with multi-retention, then merges and refines across rounds. Entity exploration: for each (e_c, r), ComplEx ranks entities via φ in the appropriate direction, top-K candidates are filtered by DistilBERT semantic similarity to Q when K is large, then an LLM prunes to E(e_c, r), extending reasoning paths. Reasoning: the LLM updates sub-question status and either extracts the answer from explored paths or iterates back to exploration up to a maximum depth. Critical design decisions: (i) hierarchical bucketing — justified by an ablation showing bucket size 30 beats no-hierarchy (80.4 vs 77.4 hit rate on WebQSP CKG); (ii) KGE recovery at inference rather than one-shot graph completion — motivated qualitatively but the non-monotonic IKG-40%/80% ablation results are only informally hypothesized; (iii) ComplEx as the scorer — acknowledged as a deliberately simple, replaceable choice. Offline costs: one ComplEx training pass (~5 hours on one A100 for Freebase) and one linear pass to build F. Key Results: Evaluated on WebQSP, CWQ (Freebase; GoG's synthetic incompleteness protocol removing 20–80% of crucial gold-path triples) and BRINK (Wikidata5m with rule-mined incomplete split), reporting Hits@1 for the first two and F1 for BRINK. With GPT-3.5-Turbo under IKG-40%: XoG 77.6 (WebQSP) and 55.7 (CWQ), beating all no-task-training baselines (PoG 69.7/53.7, GoG 66.6/44.3, ToG 63.4/37.9); supervised RoG is higher at 78.2/54.2 but requires task-specific fine-tuning. On complete graphs XoG is competitive but only slightly ahead (83.7 WebQSP vs PoG 82.0; 64.4 CWQ vs PoG 63.2). Gains persist across six backbones (GPT-3.5, Qwen3-32B, LLaMA-3.3-70B, GPT-4, GPT-5.5, Claude Opus 4.8); best IKG-40% results are 85.4 (WebQSP, Opus 4.8) and 75.9 (CWQ, GPT-5.5). Notably, GPT-5.5 CoT without KG reaches 74.0 on CWQ — approaching traversal baselines — yet XoG with GPT-5.5 still exceeds it (80.5/75.9), supporting the claim that stronger LLMs do not substitute for missing graph evidence. On BRINK incomplete, XoG scores 0.52 F1 vs PoG 0.34 and ToG 0.32, but supervised GNN-RAG (0.68) and RoG (0.62) remain ahead. Efficiency: up to 33% fewer total tokens and 33% fewer LLM calls than PoG at IKG-40% on WebQSP; ~12 s/question end-to-end with KGE scoring only ~0.3 s. Error analysis: retrieval gaps account for 84–93% of errors and grow with sparsity, while LLM selection errors stay at 7–16%. Baselines are recent and appropriate (GoG, PoG, ToG are the current no-training frontier); several baseline numbers are copied from the GoG paper rather than re-run. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD with a NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING. Genuinely novel: the combination of type-level co-occurrence relation curation plus embedding-based link prediction as in-loop recovery mechanisms within an LLM planning–exploration–reasoning agent, and the demonstration that graph-grounded recovery dominates LLM-generated recovery under incompleteness. The scaffolding (PoG-style planning, ComplEx, DistilBERT, LLM pruning prompts) is a competent assembly of existing techniques; hierarchical bucketing is an engineering refinement of prompt-context management rather than a conceptual advance. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are present and informative: removing link prediction costs 7.5–15.6 points on WebQSP (76.2 CKG, 62.0 IKG-40%), removing relation selection costs little on CKG but ~3.8–5.7 points under incompleteness, and replacing LLM pruning with embedding top-1/top-3 or DistilBERT selection consistently degrades results. Sensitivity analyses cover bucket size and retrieval quality (LLM selection accuracy tracks KGE Hits@100 almost linearly). Missing: no error bars, seeds, or significance tests anywhere; single runs per configuration. Code, prompts, and setup are released at https://github.com/colab-nyuad/XoG. Methodological concerns: (i) the incompleteness protocol removes "crucial" triples identified from gold reasoning paths, which leaks supervision signal about which triples matter and may not reflect natural incompleteness — the authors acknowledge this; (ii) several baseline rows are transcribed from GoG rather than re-executed; (iii) the paper references future-dated models (GPT-5.5, Claude Opus 4.8) and a 2026 BRINK citation, consistent with a late-2026 arXiv preprint; peer-review status is not stated. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (a running pipeline evaluated experimentally, with a released code artifact). - Practical: Yes — built on GPT-3.5/4-class APIs, ComplEx (LibKGE, one A100 for ~5 hours offline), DistilBERT, and SPARQL; no exotic hardware. - Efficient: KGE scoring adds only ~0.3 s/question; LLM inference dominates (~85% of ~12 s), and XoG uses 2–33% fewer tokens than PoG depending on sparsity. - Effective: The evidence shows it answers multi-hop questions over synthetically incomplete Freebase/Wikidata graphs better than comparable no-training baselines, but effectiveness under natural incompleteness is only a proxy claim. - Scalable: Not directly tested at 10–100× scale — relation candidate pools are ~98/query and per-question runtime is characterized, but behavior on much larger KGs, higher query throughput, or heavily multi-topic questions is extrapolated, not measured. Delivers a software artifact: released code, prompts, and evaluation setup (no trained model weights beyond per-GKG ComplEx embeddings, which are retrained per sparsity setting). Strengths: - The central design move — constrain the LLM to select from KG-grounded candidate sets rather than generate missing facts — cleanly isolates and resolves the hallucination-vs-traversal trade-off, and the PoG/GoG/ToG comparison across five sparsity levels substantiates it. - The error decomposition (retrieval gap vs selection error) is the paper's most useful analytical contribution: it shows 93%+ of failures at IKG-80% are retrieval-side, redirecting future work toward KGE quality rather than better LLM reasoning — and the retrieval-quality sensitivity curve supports this causally. - Multi-backbone evaluation across six LLMs (including open-weight Qwen3-32B and LLaMA-3.3-70B) shows the robustness claim is not an artifact of one model family, and the backbone-matched CoT control addresses parametric-memorization confounds honestly (while admitting CoT cannot fully rule memorization in or out). - Cross-KG generalization to Wikidata (BRINK) strengthens external validity beyond Freebase, and the token-efficiency gains (−33% vs PoG at IKG-40%) are measured, not claimed. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors explicitly state: (i) ComplEx is a deliberately simple KGE and results depend on its quality, though the framework is model-agnostic; (ii) the incompleteness protocol is synthetic (random crucial-triple removal; BRINK's rule-mined removal) and may not capture real-world patterns like uneven class coverage or long-tail gaps; (iii) generalization beyond Freebase/Wikidata5m is unestablished; (iv) XoG requires accessible entity-type information to build co-occurrence statistics, limiting applicability to KGs without type structure. They confront limitations directly, including the synthetic-benchmark concern and a call for naturally incomplete benchmarks — a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - The IKG protocol removes triples along gold reasoning paths, so the recovery task is partially supervised by ground truth about where paths break; a natural-incompleteness test (or perturbation of non-crucial triples as a control) is absent. - No significance testing, seeds, or variance estimates despite LLM-based pipelines with stochastic pruning; several margins (e.g., XoG 83.7 vs PoG 82.0 on WebQSP CKG) are small enough that variance could matter. - No fine-tuning-free comparison against GNN-RAG/RoG under matched supervision constraints on Freebase incompleteness — the supervised baselines that actually beat XoG on BRINK (GNN-RAG 0.68 vs 0.52) are not evaluated on WebQSP/CWQ incompleteness curves. - The claimed benefit of link prediction on complete graphs (disambiguating many-to-many relations) is a hypothesis offered without direct evidence. - Type-level co-occurrence statistics inherit long-tail bias: relations rare within an entity type's observed triples get near-zero ψ scores, and the paper does not test behavior on type-poor or novel-type entities beyond noting the type-information requirement. - The LLM-as-selector pruning step injects a single LLM judgment per hop; no analysis of pruning failure propagation across multi-hop chains (compounding error) is reported. Bottom Line: A practitioner building LLM–KG QA systems should read this: the graph-grounded-recovery design, the retrieval-gap error analysis, and the sparsity-robustness curves provide concrete, reusable evidence that KGE-assisted candidate curation beats both pure traversal and LLM hallucination under missing edges — with the caveat that its robustness is proven only under synthetic incompleteness, and supervised retrieval methods remain stronger if task-specific training is an option.

Scaling Trajectories for Complex Tasks through Recursive Self-Rewrite

Z Li, Y Shi, Z Li, J Yang, R Wang, C Huang, F Liu, H Mi… · arxiv.org · recursive self-improvement - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces Recursive Self-Rewrite (RSR), a pipeline in which a single 27B model (Qwen-3.8-27B) discovers successful terminal-task solutions under three different agent harnesses, then a planner-critic-executor loop rewrites those harness-assisted successes into verified trajectories under one general harness for self-supervised fine-tuning. - Why it's important: Agent success depends heavily on the harness, but training on harness-specific trajectories teaches the model controller conventions it won't have at inference time — so harness-assisted wins are usually lost as reusable capability; this targets converting them into durable model skill. - How it does it: The model itself plays three roles: a planner distills each successful trajectory into a runbook (milestones, checks, recovery strategies), a critic screens runbooks for verifier/solution leakage, and an executor re-solves the task in a fresh sandbox under the general Terminus 2 harness, keeping only verified passing rewrites. - The good: The multi-harness discovery claim is well-supported by coverage data — the three-harness union solves 759 of 2,929 tasks vs. 565 for the best single harness (+194 tasks, 34.3% relative), with an equal-rollout-count control showing the union still adds 23.5% — and RSR beats both the base model and direct SFT on all five evaluation benchmarks. - The missing: There are no error bars, no external method baselines (e.g., Harness-Zero or DCAS, which the related work cites as closest), and three of the five evaluation benchmarks (TBH, SWR100, LHTB) are self-curated by overlapping author groups, so headline gains are partly measured on non-independent benchmarks. - Read it or not: Worth reading for practitioners building terminal-agent training loops or self-improvement pipelines at modest scale (27B), since the multi-harness-as-discovery-tool framing and the leakage-audit mechanics are concretely reusable; skippable if you only care about frontier-scale agent results.
Why this rank
Scored using Empirical profile. Novelty (72) is genuine — treating harnesses as complementary discovery engines and the leakage-audited runbook rewrite loop are new framings with a reusable mechanism. But Rigor (55) is the key drag: no error bars or significance tests anywhere, no external baselines despite citing the closest prior work, a single-run harness ablation, and three of five evaluation benchmarks self-curated with train/eval provenance overlap. Completeness (60) is undercut by the unacknowledged benchmark-independence issue and the unidentifiable attribution among rewriting, leakage filtering, and 5.5× more data. Resilience (55) suffers from the evaluation-harness-equals-rewrite-target confound and the 'recursive' label covering only one round; Non-Obviousness (70) is buoyed by the honest negative result that direct SFT on raw trajectories hurts. Impact (62) reflects released model weights but no pipeline code. Weighted composite: 0.20*72 + 0.25*55 + 0.15*70 + 0.15*60 + 0.15*55 + 0.10*62 = 62.

Problem & Motivation: Teams building terminal agents face a supervision bottleneck: hard tasks are rarely solved, so successful trajectories are scarce and valuable. Harness engineering (Terminus, StateM, etc.) raises solve rates without weight updates, and different harnesses solve complementary task subsets — but trajectories collected under a specialized harness contain controller interventions, workflow conventions, and stopping rules that a general harness will not provide at inference. Naively pooling these trajectories for SFT risks teaching the model to depend on external control it will not have. The gap: how to convert harness-assisted successes into training signal that transfers to a general-purpose harness the deployed model runs under. Key Idea: Treat harnesses as discovery tools rather than deployment systems: solve once under diverse harnesses, then have the same model rewrite each success — via a runbook intermediate that carries procedure (checks, recovery, pitfalls) but not the finished deliverable — into fresh, independently verified executions under the general harness, so the final demonstration contains only public interaction history. The runbook-plus-critic loop is the trick: it abstracts away harness-specific mechanics while a leakage audit blocks answer transfer. Methodology: The pipeline has three stages. (1) Multi-harness discovery: Qwen-3.8-27B runs under Terminus 2 (general act-observe loop), StateM (persistent workflow states with checked transitions), and RSRT (verifier-outcome-triggered reflection/debug up to 180 min per task), producing 14,598 rollouts and 2,001 passing trajectories over 759 unique tasks from a ~3K-task pool (2,509 self-curated SWR tasks across 50 domains + 420 modified RST tasks). (2) Trajectory rewriting: source trajectories are compacted (harness-specific control messages stripped), the planner samples K=4 runbooks, deterministic and model-based critics screen for schema violations and leakage (verifier details, harness references, finished deliverables), and each retained runbook guides M=4 fresh executions at temperature 0.7 in fresh sandboxes under Terminus 2; a final audit flags underived values indicating hidden answer transfer. (3) Filtering and SFT: only passing, leak-free public histories are kept, yielding 11,094 training trajectories (12,893 rewriting rollouts, ~86% pass), supplemented with the 766 Terminus-2-native passing trajectories. The framework is rejection-sampling-style self-distillation with verifier-verified rollouts; no explicit loss is stated beyond standard SFT on these trajectories. Critical design decisions: the runbook must not contain the deliverable (justified by the critic audit and final leak filter), private runbooks are excluded from training data (justified — otherwise the model learns behaviors it cannot execute at inference), and rewriting targets the general harness Terminus 2 (reasonable but conflates the general harness with the evaluation harness). Key Results: Discovery: pooled harness union solves 759/2,929 tasks (25.9%) vs. 565 (19.3%) for the best single harness; 288 tasks are exclusive to one harness. Evaluation (pass@3, base → direct SFT → RSR): Terminal-Bench 2 (89 tasks) 57.0% → 53.4% → 74.2%; Terminal-Bench 3 (74) 0.0% → 5.4% → 9.5%; Terminal-Bench 4 (66) 1.5% → 4.5% → 9.1%; Terminal-Bench Hard (100, self-curated) 39.0% → 56.0% → 63.0%; SWR100 (100, self-curated) 3.0% → 3.0% → 6.0%. Mean per-run pass rates follow the same ordering (e.g., TB2: 51.7% → 43.8% → 70.1%). LHTB process reward rises 0.21 → 0.25 → 0.29, but all three checkpoints solve 0/46 tasks. Notable counter-intuitive findings: direct SFT on raw multi-harness trajectories hurts TB2 (-3.6 pass@3, -7.9 mean), with inspected checkpoints showing dead-end looping behavior; and runbook guidance does not guarantee success — the same runbook yields both passing and failing rewrites (58.3% pass on the Markdown case). Tested scale: one 27B model, ~15K rollouts — standard, not stress-scale. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD plus NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING. The genuinely novel elements are (a) the framing of multiple harnesses as complementary discovery engines for training-data generation rather than inference-time controllers, and (b) the planner-critic-executor runbook rewrite loop with leakage auditing for cross-harness trajectory transfer. The components are standard in isolation — rejection sampling, self-critique, verifier-filtered distillation — combined in a new setting; the closest prior work (Harness-Zero, DCAS, cross-scaffold transfer studies) is cited and differentiated only at the framing level. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations exist and are informative: an equal-rollout-count control (1,247 tasks) confirming harness complementarity is not a sampling artifact, per-domain coverage analysis (87 labels), execution-style statistics, and a command-similarity analysis showing same-runbook rewrites are measurably more similar (e.g., 19.1 vs. 12.1 exact command overlap for Markdown). However: no error bars or significance tests anywhere; main results average three runs but the harness ablation (Table 6) is single-run; no variance across training seeds or runs of the full pipeline. Model weights are released (huggingface.co/IntelligenceLab/RSR-27B); code and the SWR task pool release is not stated. Methodological concerns: three of five evaluation benchmarks (TBH, SWR100, LHTB) trace to overlapping author groups or their prior work, and the training pool includes 420 modified RST tasks from the same lineage as TBH — a train/eval provenance overlap; comparisons against external self-improvement baselines are absent, so RSR is only compared to its own ablation (direct SFT). Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL (the paper runs the full discovery-rewrite-train loop and evaluates the resulting model). - Practical: Yes — the entire loop uses one 27B open-weights model and containerized terminal sandboxes, feasible on a multi-GPU node plus CPU-heavy sandbox orchestration. - Efficient: Expensive relative to plain SFT — 14,598 discovery rollouts plus 12,893 rewriting rollouts (K=4 runbooks × M=4 executions per source, up to 180 min per RSRT discovery rollout) to produce 11,094 training trajectories. - Effective: The evidence shows gains on terminal benchmarks, including an independent one (TB2 +17.2 pass@3 over base), but the process-reward gain on LHTB (0.29) comes with zero fully solved tasks, so long-horizon transfer is only partial progress, not solved capability. - Scalable: Not tested beyond ~3K tasks and one 27B model; the authors claim rewriting 'scales experience' (2,001 → 11,094 trajectories) but provide no experiment at 10× scale or with a second base model. Delivers a software/training artifact: released fine-tuned model weights; the RSR pipeline code and SWR task set are not stated as public. Strengths: - The multi-harness complementarity finding is quantified carefully, including the equal-rollout-count control and the per-domain breakdown showing each harness is uniquely strongest in different domains — this is the paper's most defensible contribution. - The leakage-audit design (critic on public instruction only, deterministic checks, post-hoc underived-value filter, runbooks excluded from training data) directly addresses the obvious failure mode of answer transfer, which most trajectory-distillation work ignores. - Honest negative result: the paper reports and diagnoses why direct SFT on raw multi-harness trajectories degrades TB2 performance (dead-end loops, >100-step trajectories from RSRT), which motivates the whole method rather than hiding the baseline failure. - Case studies with command-similarity metrics give mechanistic texture on what runbooks do and do not control, rather than only end-to-end scores. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors note that sandbox/task errors caused unequal rollout counts across harnesses (footnote 2), that shorter or cleaner rewrites do not guarantee success (the Markdown case), that direct SFT introduces circular/dead-end behaviors, that all checkpoints solve 0/46 LHTB tasks (process reward reflects partial progress only), and that verifier success does not imply quality-audit acceptance. They confront the LHTB and direct-SFT limitations directly. They do not, however, acknowledge that their strongest relative gains appear partly on benchmarks of their own construction, nor the single-run nature of the harness ablation. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - No external baseline: the paper cites Harness-Zero and DCAS as closest prior work but compares against neither, nor against any off-the-shelf SFT or RL self-improvement recipe — the only comparison is RSR vs. its own ablated variant. - Benchmark provenance: TBH, SWR100, and LHTB are self-curated (and TBH derives from the authors' RST dataset, 420 tasks of which are in the training pool), so the largest reported gain (+7.0 pass@3 over direct SFT) is on the least independent evaluation; gains on public TB2 are real but smaller in task count (89 tasks, so 66/89 vs. 48/89 — differences of 15–18 tasks with no significance testing). - Single model, single iteration: one 27B base model, one round of self-improvement; no evidence the loop composes over multiple iterations despite the 'recursive' name, and no evidence the method works for larger or smaller models. - The rewriting target (Terminus 2) is also the evaluation harness, so part of the gain may be distribution matching to the eval interface rather than general capability; a second general-harness transfer target would disentangle this. - Runbook/leak-filter effectiveness is validated only by construction and two case studies; no ablation of the critic's contribution (e.g., RSR without the leakage screen) is reported, so which component drives the gain over direct SFT — rewriting, leakage filtering, or sheer trajectory count (5.5× data) — is unidentifiable. Bottom Line: A practitioner building agent self-improvement loops should read this for its careful multi-harness coverage analysis and its leakage-audited rewrite recipe, but should treat the magnitude of the training gains as provisional given self-curated benchmarks, missing external baselines, and no component-wise ablation — there is no stronger published alternative covering this exact ground yet, though the claims outrun the controlled evidence.

#139 — Innovative (62)

Learning Latent Specifications from Structural Peers

L Cui, S Chakraborty, M Musuvathi, S Fakhoury · openreview.net · specification to code with formal verifications - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces INTENTMINER, a neuro-symbolic pipeline that uses symbolic program analysis to group structurally related functions ("peers") and LLM agents to infer undocumented "latent specifications" from those groups, then flags deviations from them as candidate bugs. - Why it's important: Automated testing and verification of real codebases are blocked by missing functional specifications, and inferring them from a single implementation enshrines existing bugs; recovering intended behavior could expose security-critical defects (e.g., authentication bypasses) that conventional tools cannot express. - How it does it: Joern-derived call-graph, data-flow, and rule-based "bases" construct candidate peer groups; one LLM agent per group synthesizes a natural-language specification plus properties and assumptions, and validator agents judge whether apparent deviations are bugs or legitimate exemptions. - The good: On a pinned wolfSSH checkout (~35k LOC C), it recalls 5/5 CVEs and 414/567 (73.0%) of later-fixed defects versus 4/5 and 299/567 (52.7%) for an unstructured LLM baseline at the same model and code scope, and uniquely localizes CVE-2024-2873, a dispatcher-spanning authentication bypass with no individually-wrong function. - The missing: The baseline is not budget-matched (INTENTMINER costs ~8× more AI credits, 704,178 vs. 88,272), results come from a single run with no variance, and all bug-specimen matching relies on an LLM judge with maintainer confirmation still pending. - Read it or not: Worth reading for researchers in LLM-based program analysis, specification mining, and security auditing — the peer-grouping-as-context idea and the honest limitations section are instructive — but practitioners wanting a deployable bug-finder should wait for confirmed precision numbers and a second codebase.
Why this rank
Scored using Empirical profile. Rigor (55) is the main drag: a single run on a single author-constructed codebase, no per-basis ablation despite RQ2 promising one, ground-truth matching and precision both resting on an LLM judge, and an 8× budget-unmatched baseline that makes the 20-point recall gain partly a compute effect. Novelty (70) and Non-Obviousness (72) are real — the structure-selects-evidence/LLM-argues-correctness reframing and the CVE-2024-2873 dispatcher-spanning localization demonstrate a bug class unstructured agents miss. Resilience (60) suffers from untriaged candidate bugs and possible CVE contamination asymmetry, and Impact (40) is low: no released artifact, 6,000 unreviewed reports, and a closed commercial-model dependency. Weighted composite: 0.20*70 + 0.25*55 + 0.15*72 + 0.15*70 + 0.15*60 + 0.10*40 = 62.
