Problem & Motivation: Testing and formal verification require specifications of intended behavior, but real codebases leave most functional contracts unstated: documentation covers interfaces, not implementation-specific constraints on state transitions, ownership, and protocol ordering. Inferring constraints from the code alone risks enshrining bugs as intended behavior. Classic deviance miners (Engler et al., PR-Miner, Juxta, APISan) need many comparable implementations or frequency statistics to declare a minority deviation a bug; LLM-based specification generators (SpecGen, KBSpec, AutoVerus-style) target formal contracts for verification-aware languages or memory-safety classes, not cross-module, application-specific obligations in a single legacy C codebase. The gap: recover latent, undocumented specifications from within one codebase using structural relations rather than frequency, and distinguish genuine violations from legitimate variation. Key Idea: Structural relatedness is evidence of shared intent: instead of using frequency across many implementations to decide correctness (prior work), use symbolic analysis only to select peer evidence, and let an LLM argue correctness from that evidence plus docs, tests, and domain knowledge. Critically, the pipeline separates the shared specification φ from "assumptions" — explicit hypotheses about why a deviating peer might still be correct — which are then validated codebase-wide by a dedicated agent, avoiding circularity (a spec inferred from a group is checked against code beyond that group). Methodology: Three stages. (1) Structural peer grouping: Joern extracts the call graph, intraprocedural data flow, and control dependence; nine deterministic "bases" (callers_of, callees_of, path_to/path_from, dispatch_slot, field_family, object_family, unguarded_flow, unchecked_return) each produce a group G = (basis, R, Π, M) with root R, peer set Π (|Π| ≥ 2), and member functions M. Call-graph groups get a value-flow refinement keeping only peers carrying a value to/from R, while the coarse group is retained (a peer whose bug is the omitted flow is only comparable there). (2) Latent specification synthesis: one LLM agent per group either rejects the group or emits (a) a natural-language specification φ with its inference source (latent vs. documented) and type (memory-safety vs. not), (b) properties Pφ breaking φ into checkable cases, and (c) assumptions Aφ — candidate exemptions with anchor sites and conditions. (3) Bug finding: a property-validation agent judges each peer against Pφ (upholds/deviates/not applicable/unclear), and an assumption-validation agent searches the whole program for paths violating an assumption's condition; violated assumptions are candidate bugs. No defect is confirmed dynamically; the framework is LLM-agent reconciliation over natural-language obligations, not a formal objective. Design decisions worth noting: the coarse/refined group duality and the property/assumption split are argued explicitly and appear well-motivated; the reliance on a fixed set of hand-designed bases is asserted as sufficient for wolfSSH but not systematically justified. Key Results: On wolfSSH 1.4.16 (commit 13598c7, ~35k LOC src/), with 5 CVEs and 567 later-fixed bugs as ground truth: dataset recall 419/572 (73.3%) vs. 303/572 (53.0%) for the baseline (5/5 vs. 4/5 CVEs; 414/567 vs. 299/567 later-fixed defects). INTENTMINER recovers 201 defects the baseline misses; the baseline finds 85 INTENTMINER misses. Precision by LLM judge: 64.4% (3,862/6,000 findings) vs. 78.8% (993/1,260) for the baseline — higher recall, lower precision. The headline qualitative result: CVE-2024-2873 (CVSS 9.1 authentication bypass) is localized to the unguarded DoPacket dispatch in 56 reports by INTENTMINER and missed entirely by the baseline, because the fault is a missing guard spanning the whole dispatch table rather than any individually-wrong handler. Specification characterization (RQ1): 4,663 specifications — 55.1% temporal protocols, 32.2% function contracts, 12.7% state invariants; 58.4% compound; 4,313/4,663 inferred latently rather than from documentation. Manual validation on a 93-specification sample (2%): 72% human–LLM-judge agreement, with disagreement concentrated on compound specs. Scale: one checkout, one model (gpt-5.5 via Copilot CLI, xhigh effort), single run, up to 32 concurrent agents on a 128-core AMD EPYC node. Baseline is an unstructured LLM agent at the same model, effort, code scope, and sandbox — current in spirit but budget-unmatched; no off-the-shelf static analyzer, fuzzer, or deviance miner is compared (the authors argue none is apples-to-apples). Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD with a NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING component. The genuinely novel move is reframing deviance detection: symbolic structure selects evidence while an LLM decides correctness, replacing the frequency-based minority-report heuristic of Engler-style cross-checking with evidence reconciliation, and constructing small peer groups within a single codebase (including peers without a shared declared interface) where prior work required multiple implementations or large peer populations. The LLM-agent components themselves are standard (per-group synthesis agents, validator agents, LLM judge); the engineering contribution is the basis taxonomy and the property/assumption decomposition, which are competent combinations of known ideas in a new setting. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are absent in the strongest sense — no per-basis breakdown shows which of the nine grouping bases accounts for the recovered defects (the paper promises "which peer bases account for the defects" in RQ2 but the results section does not deliver this analysis). No seeds, no error bars, no significance tests: explicitly a single run, which the authors attribute to compute cost. Human validation is 2% of specifications by one author, blind to LLM labels — thin but honestly reported. Code and data are not released (anonymity plus pending responsible disclosure; an anonymized artifact is promised upon acceptance); the pinned commit, model, sandbox policy, and judging protocol are described in enough detail to make reproduction plausible in principle. Methodological concerns: (1) the ground-truth dataset is the authors' own construction from upstream fixes, and evaluation is only on that dataset for one codebase; (2) the LLM judge both matches findings to ground truth and estimates precision — no maintainer-confirmed numbers exist yet, so all precision figures are self-referential model judgments; (3) CVEs are likely in the training data (acknowledged); (4) the baseline is budget-unmatched, so the recall gain may partly be a compute effect (acknowledged). The reported recall difference (73.0% vs. 52.7% on 567 defects) is large enough that it plausibly survives these caveats, but the paper cannot show this statistically. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (a pipeline the authors actually run on a real codebase). - Practical: Yes in hardware terms — LLM agents over a 35k-LOC C project on a single 128-core/503 GB server with a commercial Copilot CLI backend — though the closed model dependency means it runs only via a paid vendor API. - Efficient: Poorly: 704,178 Copilot credits vs. 88,272 for the baseline (~8×) at equal model and effort, producing 6,000 candidate reports whose review burden the authors call out as bounding practical utility. - Effective: Partially — bug recovery is a proxy for specification correctness, deviations are never executed or mechanically verified, and precision is only an LLM-judge estimate (64.4%), so the evidence shows recall on known defects rather than confirmed deployable detection. - Scalable: Untested beyond one 35k-LOC codebase; the pipeline's whole-repository, thousands-of-groups analysis (4,663 specs from ~4,000+ groups) suggests it scales to mid-sized C projects, but the authors themselves note whole-program taint analysis does not scale and they deliberately avoid it; no 10×–100× claim is tested. Deliverable: paper form plus a promised (unreleased) anonymized artifact and a mined wolfSSH defect dataset; no library, CLI, or trained model is available now. Strengths: - The core reframing — structure selects evidence, the LLM argues correctness — cleanly separates INTENTMINER from frequency-based deviance mining and enables small-peer-group inference within one codebase, including peers with no shared declared interface. - The CVE-2024-2873 case study is the strongest evidence in the paper: a CVSS 9.1 authentication bypass whose fault is a missing guard across an entire dispatch table is localized by the method and missed by 51 baseline reports on surrounding code, precisely demonstrating what structured context buys over unstructured agent search. - The property/assumption decomposition is a thoughtful mechanism: it keeps synthesis focused on shared intent while deferring exemption analysis to a dedicated codebase-wide validator, mitigating the circularity of checking a group's spec against only that group. - Unusually candid limitations section: single run, budget-unmatched baseline, training-data contamination, LLM-judge dependence, and 8× cost are all stated by the authors rather than left for reviewers to find. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state that specification correctness is evaluated only indirectly via bug-finding as a proxy; that human annotation covers 2% by a single annotator; that matching relies on an LLM judge; that high-severity CVEs are probably in the model's training data regardless of network restrictions; that the baseline matches model/effort/scope/sandbox but not budget, so results speak to capability, not efficiency; that all numbers come from one run on one checkout with one model without variance; that outputs are natural-language obligations, never executed or mechanically verified; and that cost, runtime, and the 6,000-report review burden limit practical utility. This is direct confrontation with limitations, not minimization — a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - No ablation over the nine grouping bases: RQ2 asks which bases account for unrecovered defects, but no per-basis results are reported, so the reader cannot tell which of the taxonomy's families carry the 20-point recall gain or whether several bases are dead weight. - The recall gain may be substantially a budget effect: 8× the AI credits with an explicit 'investigate everything via peer groups' structure versus a 'find bugs' instruction; a compute-matched baseline (or a sampled down-costed INTENTMINER) is absent. - Single-codebase evaluation on a dataset the authors built themselves for this paper, with the matching step performed by an LLM judge using the authors' own protocol; the 419/572 headline depends on judge-validated matches against author-defined ground truth, and no inter-rater or independent adjudication of the matched set is reported. - The 43 candidate new security bugs and 609 non-security candidates are untriaged at submission time, so the method's true precision — the number a practitioner actually needs — is unknown; only judge-estimated precision (64.4%) exists. - Generalization is untested: wolfSSH is chosen partly because its defects "concentrate in a single checkout," a favorable setup; whether peer-grouping works on codebases with thinner structural regularities, or in languages beyond C, is not examined. - Possible contamination asymmetry: both methods may have seen the CVEs in training, but the structured pipeline could more effectively reactivate memorized fixes around peer groups; no probe of memorization (e.g., mutated variable names or synthetic bugs) is attempted. Bottom Line: A practitioner in LLM-driven program analysis or security auditing should read this for the evidence-selects/LLM-argues design and the dispatcher-bypass case study, which genuinely demonstrate a class of cross-function bug unstructured agents miss — but the 8× cost, single-run single-codebase evidence, LLM-judged matching, and missing per-basis ablation mean this is a promising direction paper, not yet a validated alternative to existing tooling.

Multi-Agent Egocentric World Model with Fine-Grained Embodied Interaction (43 ▲ )

Dahyun Chung, Siyoon Jin, Hyunwook Choi, Honggyu An, Junyoung Seo, Hyunsung Kim, Seung Wook Kim, Seungryong Kim · arxiv.org · Daily papers of 9 Oct 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces ME-World, a video diffusion-based world model that jointly generates synchronized first-person video streams for multiple embodied agents whose fine-grained body/head actions and interaction outcomes stay consistent across all viewpoints in one shared world. - Why it's important: Real embodied settings (multi-user VR, embodied AI simulation, multi-robot collaboration) involve several agents acting in one environment, but existing multi-agent world models only handle coarse controls (discrete commands, camera trajectories), leaving fine-grained embodied interactions unmodelled. - How it does it: The core move is joint denoising of all ego-stream latents in a single shared token sequence, supported by shared action conditioning (every stream sees all agents' rendered poses plus Plücker-ray head trajectories) and shared environment memory (depth-warped history evidence per view plus unwarped anchor reference tokens shared across streams). - The good: The ablation table isolates each component on the same backbone and data, showing clear metric gains at every stage — e.g., Full-Body-PCK jumps from 0.385 (variant 3) to 0.881 (full model) and rotation error drops from 4.998 to 2.256 on the real benchmark — giving credible evidence that all three mechanisms matter. - The missing: The headline shared-world consistency metrics are self-proposed DINOv3 feature-similarity scores validated only on 100 clips per benchmark, with no error bars, no human study, and no third-party validation that these metrics track human perception of cross-view consistency. - Read it or not: Read it if you work on multi-agent or embodied world models and need the current formulation, data recipes, and evaluation protocol for coupled ego-stream generation; skip it if you only care about single-agent egocentric generation or non-video world models.
Why this rank
Scored using Empirical profile. Novelty (78) is the strongest dimension: a new problem formulation (fine-grained multi-agent ego-stream consistency) plus a new benchmark and unusually fair controlled baseline retraining. The composite is pulled down by Rigor (61) — self-proposed DINOv3 consistency metrics with no human validation, no error bars, 100-clip benchmarks, author-built evaluation on the paper's own proposal — and by Resilience (55) and Practical Impact (48): N=2 quantitative validation with scalability asserted, minimization-by-omission limitations, and no released code or weights. Weighted composite: 0.20*78 + 0.25*61 + 0.15*68 + 0.15*55 + 0.15*55 + 0.10*48 = 62.

Problem & Motivation: Egocentric world models predict an embodied agent's future first-person observations conditioned on its actions, but virtually all existing systems assume a single agent. Real settings — collaborative kitchen work, multi-user VR, multi-robot teams — have multiple agents whose actions are simultaneously (i) first-person controls, (ii) events visible in other agents' views, and (iii) causes of persistent state changes to shared objects and the environment. Existing multi-agent world models abstract actions into discrete game commands or camera trajectories and cannot represent fine-grained articulated interaction (hands, arms, gaze-driven viewpoint change) consistently across viewpoints. The gap is threefold: cross-view action consistency, shared-environment consistency, and consistent propagation of interaction-induced state updates across all generated streams. Training also requires synchronized multi-ego data, which mainstream egocentric datasets (Ego4D, Ego-Exo4D, EPIC-Kitchens) do not provide. Key Idea: Treat the N agents' ego streams not as independent videos but as coupled observations of one evolving world, realized by concatenating all agents' noisy latents (plus shared anchor-reference tokens) into a single token sequence that a pretrained video DiT jointly denoises with full self-attention — so cross-stream agreement is enforced by the denoising process itself rather than by post-hoc consistency losses. Shared action conditioning (projecting every agent's pose into every target view) and stream-aligned warped geometric memory then make each stream explicitly aware of the other agents' actions and the common scene. Methodology: ME-World fine-tunes Cosmos-Predict2.5 2B (multi-view DiT) with a rectified-flow objective, freezing the video VAE and text encoder. Pipeline per training sample: (1) encode each agent's 77-frame 480×480 ego stream into latents Z(n) via frozen VAE; (2) build conditions — per-stream skeleton maps for self body/hand motion, other agents' 3D poses projected into the target camera (identity-colored), Plücker ray maps for head/camera motion in a shared canonical frame, a depth-warped RGB observation with visibility mask (history frame with max reprojection coverage, humans removed via SAM3), and K=4 greedily selected unwarped anchor references shared across streams; (3) concatenate all agents' noisy latents along the token dimension, add learnable agent embeddings (identical RoPE across streams to align space-time positions), channel-concatenate the pose/ray/warp conditions, and append anchor tokens Z_ref; (4) train with flow-matching MSE against the joint clean latents. Per-stream cross-attention handles agent-specific text prompts while self-attention shares visual information. Design decisions: joint self-attention over the concatenated sequence (justified by ablation variant 4 vs 8), identical RoPE with agent embeddings rather than stream-specific RoPE (asserted, not ablated), and greedy coverage-maximizing anchor selection (heuristic, not ablated against alternatives). Key Results: On a 100-clip real benchmark (CoMind validation, unseen kitchens/participants) and a 100-clip synthetic benchmark, ME-World beats all baselines on every reported metric. Real benchmark: Senv 0.468 vs 0.417 (GEN3C) and 0.421 (MetaWorld adaptation); Supdate 0.466 vs 0.412; rotation error 2.256 vs 4.086 (best baseline); Full-Body-PCK 0.881 vs 0.837; FVD 637.9 vs 689.9 (best baseline). Synthetic benchmark: Senv 0.441, Sid 0.561, FVD 465.5 vs 841.5 for the best baseline. Baselines span three categories (multi-view generation: GEN3C, AnyView-DVS; single-ego world models: EgoSim, JointControlVideo; general world models: DreamX-World, LingBot-World) plus four multi-agent world models (MultiWorld, Solaris, γ-World, MetaWorld) re-trained on the same backbone, data, and shared action conditioning for a controlled comparison — a fairly strong and fair baseline set, though the multi-agent adaptations are reimplementations (MetaWorld from the paper, no official code). Off-the-shelf Cosmos-Predict2.5 fails entirely (Senv 0.289–0.290), showing the conditioning is necessary. Qualitative extensions show 3-agent generation and 221-frame autoregressive rollout, but these are visual demos without quantitative evaluation. Novelty Classification: NEW PROBLEM (fine-grained embodied multi-agent egocentric world modeling as synchronized ego-stream generation), NEW FORMULATION (joint conditional p(X(1..N)|C) with cross-view action, environment, and state-update consistency as explicit requirements), NEW METHOD (shared action conditioning + dual-path shared environment memory), and NEW DATASET/BENCHMARK (synthetic Inter-X/InterHuman-based multi-ego corpus of 4,736 clip pairs plus real/synthetic evaluation sets with Senv/Supdate/Sid metrics). The individual techniques — token-concatenation joint denoising, Plücker-ray camera conditioning, depth-warping of history frames, DINOv3-based similarity evaluation — are standard components; the novelty lies in assembling them for this setting and in the problem formulation and evaluation protocol, not in any single mechanism. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are the strongest rigor element: an 8-variant ladder (Table 4) adds each component cumulatively and in a crossed configuration (variant 7: shared action + shared env. without joint generation), cleanly attributing gains (e.g., Full-Body-PCK 0.385 → 0.881 across the ladder). The controlled metric validation (Table 5) injects temporal misalignment, environment conflicts, and state conflicts into 100 clips and shows Senv/Supdate respond differentiably (−0.090 for env. conflict on Senv vs −0.019 on Supdate). Missing: no error bars, multiple seeds, or significance tests anywhere; benchmark sizes are small (100 clips each); the metrics and benchmarks are introduced by the same paper that proposes the method (self-defined evaluation); PSNR/SSIM against ground truth is a weak proxy for stochastic video generation; and the multi-agent baseline adaptations are author reimplementations. A project page exists (https://cvlab-kaist.github.io/ME-World); no code or data release URL is stated in the provided text. Real-data training uses estimated depth/pseudo-labels (DA3, Sapiens2) and LLM-generated captions, introducing label noise not quantified. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (a trained generative model with quantitative evaluation; no system deployment). - Practical: Runs on 4×A100 80GB for training a 2B model; inference requires only a consumer-adjacent GPU in principle, though the Cosmos/DA3/SAM3 toolchain is nontrivial. - Efficient: 35 denoising steps for 77 frames at 480×480 is far from real-time interactive simulation — the very use case the motivation invokes; no inference-latency numbers are reported. - Effective: Evidence covers two-agent, fixed-length generation on author-built benchmarks; it solves the stated consistency problem on that proxy, but real-time, long-horizon, many-agent interactive simulation is only claimed/demonstrated qualitatively. - Scalable: Only claimed — the 3-agent and 221-frame results are single qualitative examples; token-sequence joint attention over all streams will grow quadratically with agent count, and no quantitative scaling study is provided. Deliverable: currently paper form plus a project page; no released library, weights, or dataset is confirmed in the text. Strengths: - Genuinely new problem formulation: decouples the three distinct consistency requirements (cross-view actions, shared environment, state-update propagation) and designs targeted mechanisms for each, rather than treating multi-agent generation as generic multi-view synthesis. - Disciplined controlled comparison: retraining four prior multi-agent world models on the identical backbone, data, and action conditioning isolates architectural differences and preempts the "weak baseline" objection common in this area. - The dual-path environment memory (view-aligned warped evidence + shared unwarped anchors) is a sensible and ablation-supported solution to the partial-observability problem each ego stream faces. - The evaluation protocol is thoughtfully constructed — restricting Senv to regions unsupported by warped memory specifically measures model-established consistency rather than consistency inherited from shared input, an unusually careful distinction. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The paper has no dedicated limitations section. The conclusion frames extensions rather than failures: jointly modeling actions and observations for planning, efficient cross-agent communication and memory for larger groups, and efficient video generation for real-time interactive simulation — implicitly conceding that the current model is not real-time and is untested beyond small agent counts and short horizons. This is minimization by omission rather than direct confrontation. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - The headline metrics are self-proposed DINOv3 cosine similarities. No human study correlates them with perceived cross-view consistency, and feature-space similarity of foundation-model patches is a gameable proxy that future methods could optimize directly (Goodhart risk on the authors' own benchmark). - Two-agent only in all quantitative results; the N-agent formulation is asserted general but validated quantitatively at N=2 — the scalability claim to larger groups is extrapolation. - The synthetic benchmark's identity metric (Sid) depends on SAM3 detection of the partner agent, coupling metric validity to a specific segmenter's behavior on generated (possibly degraded) characters. - Evaluation data is constructed by the authors from the same sources as training data (CoMind val split is disjoint, but the same recording distribution and processing pipeline); no cross-dataset generalization test is reported. - No comparison to simply running a strong single-ego model with the other agent's rendered pose injected as conditioning (a cheaper alternative that variant 5/7 partially probes but not as a standalone cheap baseline). - Autoregressive rollout quality (221 frames) is shown only qualitatively; error accumulation over long horizons — the standard failure mode — is unmeasured. Bottom Line: A practitioner building multi-agent or embodied world models should read this for its problem formulation, data pipeline, and unusually fair baseline methodology, but should treat the consistency metrics as a proposal needing external validation rather than settled ground truth.

What to Preserve in Recursive Computation: A Local Predictive Sufficiency Principle

P Wang, F Shiyang, H Gao, C Zhao, D Yuan, H Chen… · arxiv.org · recursive self-improvement - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces a task-agnostic training principle — local predictive sufficiency at recursive compression interfaces — and an optimization procedure (predictive feasibility projection) that constrains host-optimizer updates so compressed intermediate states retain predictive information for downstream computation. - Why it's important: Recursive systems (temporal graphs, recurrent memory, embodied memory, self-improving agents) lose long-range information through repeated compression before it reaches the final prediction, and existing reconstruction or future-prediction objectives do not guarantee the retained information suffices for subsequent recursive use. - How it does it: It proves that controlling local conditional mutual information I(Sv; Uv | ZΓv, C) for adjacent predictive pairs (Yv, Ypa(v)) composes to root-target sufficiency, then enforces this via an empirical predictive deficiency (finite tests + ridge profiling + covariance balancing) whose first-order sensitivities define margin-relaxed half-space constraints on the optimizer's task proposal, solved by a dual QP projection. - The good: The method improves four different recursive hosts under matched compression budgets with gains that grow with recursion depth (e.g., DailyDialog PPL −4.53% at depth 13 vs −1.98% at depth 4; LIBERO-Mem T3 success 1.67±2.89% → 11.67±2.89%), and ablations show the constrained-update realization beats additive predictive gradients by ~2 AP points (94.52 vs 92.64 on UCI). - The missing: The VLA headline gain rests on 2/60 vs 7/60 successful rollouts across three runs (20 rollouts each), the SRI comparison uses one paired recursive-search run per backbone with mixed task-level deltas, and all ablations are single-seed — the cross-domain evidence is directionally consistent but statistically thin in three of four domains. - Read it or not: Worth reading for researchers designing memory/compression mechanisms in recurrent, graph, or agentic systems who want a principled alternative to reconstruction or fixed future-prediction objectives; practitioners seeking plug-and-play accuracy gains on standard benchmarks can skip it, since gains over strong hosts are modest and the method trails DyGFormer at shallow graph depths.

Problem & Motivation: Recursive computation — temporal graph propagation (TGN, TGAT), recurrent context compression (CCM), embodied memory (MemoryVLA), and iterative self-improvement (Metan/Reflexion-style loops) — repeatedly summarizes intermediate states and reuses them. Information that must survive longer recursive paths passes through more compression interfaces, so it is exposed to more attenuation (the oversquashing/information-contraction phenomenon). Existing supervision for what a compressed state should retain is inadequate: reconstruction objectives preserve input-recovery information, predictive-state or future-prediction objectives require pre-specified targets, and full information-bottleneck criteria are intractable for high-dimensional states. None of these ensures the retained information remains sufficient for the next recursive transformation, which is the actual requirement. The affected practitioners are anyone training models with deep recursive state compression, where long-range signal degrades before reaching the loss. Key Idea: Local predictive sufficiency: instead of asking each intermediate state to preserve information about the distant root target (increasingly indirect as depth grows), require that at each recursive interface the compressed state retain the predictive information for the adjacent predictive pair Sv = (Yv, Ypa(v)) — the event at that interface and its parent. Because consecutive pairs share intermediate events along rootward paths (under tree conditional-separation conditions M1–M3), these local conditions compose: Proposition 1 shows zero local deficiencies at all interfaces imply I(Yρ; U | ZΓ, C) = 0 at the root, and Proposition 3 gives the quantitative bound E[TV(L(Yρ|U,C), L(Yρ|ZΓ,C))] ≤ sqrt(½ Σ_v I(Sv; Uv | ZΓv, C)). The second half of the trick is operational: estimate a tractable surrogate (empirical predictive deficiency via finite tests, ridge-profiled readouts, and full-covariance balancing) and use its parameter-space gradients not as an additive penalty but as half-space constraints that project the host optimizer's task proposal — active only when preservation would otherwise be violated. Methodology: The pipeline has three stages. (1) Predictive deficiency estimation: the exact variational criterion inf_q Vv(Γ, qv) is approximated in three steps — restrict prediction to a fixed finite test family Pv = TS(χ(Cv) ⊗ φ(Yv, Ypa(v))), profile the readout to ridge regression with full-covariance balancing to get a predictive value Jbal, and estimate the population quantity from a shared optimization window B, yielding D̂B(Γ) = Ĵbal,B(U) − Ĵbal,B(ZΓ), with the pre-compression term held as a stop-gradient reference. (2) Constraint construction: predictive sensitivities ai = ∇zΓi D̂B are pulled back through the compressor Jacobian to qi in parameter space, grouped per constraint (e.g., per computation tree and interface type in temporal graphs), and stacked into Ht with margin-relaxed bounds bt = κ‖tt‖₂·1m defining the feasible set Ft = {d : Ht d ≤ bt}. (3) Predictive feasibility projection: the host optimizer produces a task proposal tt (without advancing its state); Proposition 2 characterizes the unique constrained update dt = tt − Ht⊤αt via an m-dimensional dual QP, which is written back to the compressor parameters. The method modifies only the compression/retention mechanism of each host (TGN, CCM-merge, MemoryVLA, Metan), leaving backbone, task, and evaluation protocol fixed; the SRI instantiation is non-differentiable and instead trains a query-conditioned slotted-fusion reducer offline on frozen lineage archives to decide which execution traces survive the context budget. Critical design decisions: using the adjacent pair rather than a single event or the root target (justified by Proposition 1 and ablated — single-event costs 2.1 AP), constrained projection rather than additive gradients (ablated: 94.52 vs 92.64 AP), and full-covariance over diagonal balancing (ablated: 94.52 vs 91.51 AP). The κ tolerance requires a validation sweep; the paper shows an interior optimum. Key Results: Across four domains under matched compression budgets. (a) Temporal graphs (TGN host, 5 seeds, Wikipedia 9,227 nodes/157,474 interactions; UCI 1,899 nodes/59,835 interactions): Ours reaches 88.81±0.77 and 89.17±0.67 AUC on Wikipedia at depths 2–3, beating CTAN (87.31, 87.38); on UCI at depth 4, 94.89 AP / 94.47 AUC, comparable to DyGFormer (94.92/94.14), though trailing DyGFormer at depth 3 (94.14 vs 95.47 AP). (b) Language memory (CCM-merge, 3 seeds, LLaMA-7B and Gemma-4-E4B-It): DailyDialog dialogue-equal PPL improves from 5.98→5.86 at depth 4 up to 5.63→5.38 (−4.53%±2.03) at depth 13 on LLaMA-7B; MSC gains are smaller (−0.84% to −1.39% on LLaMA-7B; near-zero on Gemma). (c) VLA (MemoryVLA on LIBERO-Mem T3, 3 training runs × 20 held-out rollouts): strict success 1.67±2.89% → 11.67±2.89%, SGC 20.00±1.67% → 27.22±1.92%; π0 and SlotVLA report 0.00% SR in prior work. (d) SRI (Metan on a 6-task CO-Bench cohort, one paired run per backbone, 3 evaluations of frozen strategies): held-out cohort means +0.51 (gpt-5.5), +1.41 (gemini-3.1-pro), +2.98 pp (DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash), with task-level deltas ranging from −0.60 to +17.08 pp. Mechanism analyses show slower attenuation of the finite-test predictive value J across interfaces, constraint-violation density decreasing from 0.020 to 0.012 during training (confirming the projection is non-vacuous), and a first-order bridge audit where measured statistic change tracks the linearized prediction within ~10% across a 16× perturbation sweep. Baselines are current (DyGFormer, CTAN, CCM, MemoryVLA, Metan), though prior-work VLA/SRI numbers are contextual rather than protocol-matched. Novelty Classification: NEW FORMULATION (local predictive sufficiency and recursive predictive closure as a local-to-global principle for what recursive states must preserve) plus NEW METHOD (predictive-feasibility projection, where the constrained region is generated dynamically from predictive sensitivities of an information-theoretic deficiency at recursive interfaces). The ingredients are standard — finite-test/spectral predictive-state approximation, covariance balancing, GEM/A-GEM/PCGrad-style gradient projection (the authors explicitly disclaim the projection operator itself as a contribution) — and the genuine novelty lies in the compositional locality argument and in applying the constraint to the post-optimizer task proposal rather than the raw gradient. The four-domain instantiation is competent recombination of these known pieces under a new organizing principle. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are present and well-designed (target choice, pair structure, statistical realization, constrained vs. additive update, global vs. interface-wise constraint) but all are single-seed on UCI depth 3, explicitly labeled as mechanism diagnosis rather than variability estimates. Multi-seed results exist for the main comparisons (5 seeds temporal graphs, 3 seeds/runs language memory and VLA) with mean±std reported; no significance tests. No code URL is given in the main text, but the paper states executable commands and frozen configuration files ship with a supplementary code release, and Appendices C–E provide an unusually detailed reproduction map (splits, checkpoint selection, frozen hyperparameters, per-run artifacts, resource accounting for SRI). Methodological concerns: the VLA comparison is 20 rollouts per run against the authors' own MemoryVLA host (prior-work numbers are not re-evaluated); the SRI main table reports only development-defined "modified tasks" (the full six-task record is in the appendix, which mitigates cherry-picking concerns); the ablation benchmark is the same setting used for headline claims; and the theory-to-practice bridge involves several acknowledged approximation layers (test coverage, readout restriction, context localization, first-order linearization) between the population guarantee of Proposition 3 and what training actually controls. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (with a built tool-like training wrapper per host). Practical: Yes — runs on a single RTX 5090D for temporal graphs and A100 80GB for 7B-scale language memory and OpenVLA-7B-based VLA; SRI is API-backed. Efficient: Training costs 1.9–2.2× vanilla epoch time on TGN with +10.1% parameters (0.38M on a 3.77M host); inference is unchanged (within ±3% of vanilla, no projection at test time). Effective: The evidence shows consistent directional improvement over matched hosts under matched budgets, with mechanism-level diagnostics tying gains to preserved predictive information — but effect sizes are under 3% PPL in most language-memory cells and the VLA gain sits inside a high-variance small-sample regime, so it solves a proxy-backed version of the stated problem rather than demonstrating large end-task wins. Scalable: Not stress-tested — largest graph is 157K interactions, deepest language-memory history is 13 utterances, VLA is one benchmark task with 20 initializations; claims of depth-dependent benefit are supported only up to these scales. The work delivers methods, protocols, and a promised supplementary code release rather than a standalone library or trained model artifact. Strengths: - A genuinely clarifying theoretical move: decoupling "what to preserve" from the distant root target and proving local-to-global composition (Propositions 1 and 3), including a converse-style argument (Appendix F.6) that root-target supervision alone permits merging states with distinct recursive posteriors — this is the paper's real intellectual contribution. - Honest separation of claims from evidence: the paper repeatedly distinguishes the population quantity δv from the trained surrogate D̂B, audits the first-order bridge empirically (Table 9), and shows the constraint is actually active during training (violation density 0.020→0.012). - Controlled comparison discipline: the method modifies only the retention/compression mechanism while holding backbone, budget, and evaluation protocol fixed across all four domains, with dev-only checkpoint selection and frozen held-out evaluation; the SRI protocol's paired realized initialization and pre-registered modified-task rule are unusually careful for that setting. - Ablations that isolate the right questions — in particular showing constrained projection (94.52 AP) beats the same supervision as an additive gradient (92.64 AP) and a single global constraint (90.32 AP), which is the non-obvious part of the method. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state that the formulation relies on statistical support for estimating local predictive constraints and may be unstable in data-sparse regimes; that the feasibility tolerance κ requires validation-based calibration and may not transfer across tasks; and that the VLA evidence is restricted to the 20 held-out LIBERO-Mem T3 initializations and should not be read as out-of-distribution generalization. They confront these directly rather than minimizing them, which strengthens credibility; they do not, however, flag the small-sample character of the VLA/SRI comparisons as a limitation of statistical strength, only of scope. Analyst-Identified Gaps: (1) The VLA headline (1.67% → 11.67%) corresponds to a difference of 7 vs 2 successful rollouts out of 60 each; with 20 initializations per run and ±2.89% standard deviation, this is not statistically decisive, and the initialization-level table shows most rollouts (33/60 for Ours) complete zero repetitions. (2) SRI uses one paired recursive-search realization per backbone — downstream divergence after the shared Layer-1 state is part of the evaluated mechanism, but a single realization cannot separate the retention rule's effect from search-path stochasticity; task-level held-out deltas include negatives (−0.60, −0.30, −0.28 pp). (3) Ablations are single-seed while headline ablation gaps (~2 AP) are comparable to seed-level standard deviations reported elsewhere (±0.33 to ±1.73 AP). (4) The depth-dependent-gain narrative is supported strongly only in DailyDialog/LLaMA-7B; MSC on Gemma shows ~0% gains and UCI shows Ours trailing DyGFormer at shallow depth, so the pattern is domain- and backbone-conditional. (5) The theoretical guarantee concerns population deficiencies, while training controls a grouped first-order surrogate of a finite-test, ridge-profiled statistic — the chain of approximations (test coverage, readout class, context localization, independence conditions in Corollary F.1) is disclosed but never quantified end-to-end beyond the single UCI bridge audit. (6) No evaluation on larger temporal graphs (e.g., TGB-scale) where the pooled window statistics and m×p constraint machinery would face real scale pressure. Bottom Line: A researcher building memory or compression into recurrent, graph, or agentic systems should read this for the local predictive sufficiency formulation and the unusually disciplined matched-host evaluation, but should not expect the reported gains (often 1–3%, occasionally larger under deep recursion) to transfer without per-domain calibration — the theory is the durable contribution; the empirical evidence is promising but thin.

#142 — Innovative (62)

Time-series Foundation Models for Predictive Control: The Role of Excitation

M Amria, J Hoffmann, P Bordne, A Rothenhäusler… · arxiv.org · karypis - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper shows that time-series foundation models (TSFMs) like Chronos-2 can recover the control-relevant input–output relationship needed for model predictive control (MPC) only when the inference context contains sufficient independent excitation of the control input, and quantifies how fine-tuning and multiscale features reduce (but do not remove) that requirement. - Why it's important: Zero-shot forecasting accuracy is what TSFMs are sold on, but a forecaster that predicts the factual trajectory well can be blind to what the controller actually varies — so deploying TSFMs as MPC models could silently produce controllers acting on models that do not respond to the controls at all. - How it does it: Matched intervention probes — same building, context, initial state, and weather, with only the future control trajectory offset or replaced by APRBS signals — scored by a pooled least-squares "response gain" coefficient that isolates the control-response component from shared forecast error. - The good: The excitation finding is clean and dose-dependent: gain approaches 1 under high-amplitude excitation (24 K APRBS) and long context (21 d), while gain stays near 0 under unexcited MPC context regardless of context length, and the result replicates qualitatively on a real single-family house. - The missing: The evaluation is almost entirely synthetic (the i4b 4R3C simulator, whose linear thermal dynamics match the linear baseline's inductive bias), the real-building test has no ground-truth interventional response to score against, and no code or data release is stated. - Read it or not: Read it if you are considering TSFMs as dynamics models for control or doing building MPC — the observation-vs-intervention distinction and the response-gain probe are directly reusable; skip it if you need closed-loop evidence at scale or non-building domains, since both are only sketched here.
Why this rank
Scored using Empirical profile. Non-Obviousness (72) is the standout: transplanting the control-theoretic excitation question to in-context learners, with a crisp dose-responsive finding that context length buys forecast accuracy but not control relevance, is a genuinely surprising and actionable insight. Novelty (68) is supported by the new matched-probe response-gain metric, though the ingredients (APRBS, LoRA, EWMA, iCEM) are standard. Rigor (60) is the main drag: the primary test bed is a near-linear simulator that flatters the linear baseline, the real-building test cannot score interventional correctness, open-loop sweeps lack error bars, no competing action-conditioned TSFM baselines are run, and no code or data is released. Completeness (65) is a positive — limitations are confronted directly, including the unverified closed-loop mechanism — while Resilience (60) is capped because the most decision-relevant number (closed-loop gains under unexcited context) has no causal account. Practical Impact (42) reflects a paper-only deliverable with promising but preliminary deployment economics. Weighted composite: 0.20*68 + 0.25*60 + 0.15*72 + 0.15*65 + 0.15*60 + 0.10*42 = 62.

Problem & Motivation: Practitioners deploying MPC on buildings (or any system lacking a first-principles model) must identify a predictive model per site, which is expensive because thermal dynamics vary across buildings, operating conditions, and hardware, and are confounded by weather and occupancy. TSFMs offer zero-shot transfer, and recent models (Chronos-2) natively accept candidate control trajectories as known-future covariates, making them drop-in candidates for the MPC prediction map. The gap: standard forecast metrics are observational — they score predictions under the data-generating (closed-loop) policy — while MPC queries the model interventional-ly under candidate controls that may be far out of distribution. A TSFM can therefore achieve low MAE while capturing only passive dynamics or regularities of the historical controller, giving a controller a model with no usable input–response relationship. Prior HVAC work had reported exactly this failure but without a systematic way to measure it. Key Idea: Separate forecasting from control-relevant identification using matched intervention probes and a response-gain metric: hold the context, initial state, and disturbances fixed, vary only the future control across K=7 probes (constant offsets of ±2 K and ±6 K plus two 6 K APRBS signals), re-simulate the plant for each probe, then compute the pooled least-squares coefficient of predicted on realized deviations-about-per-step-probe-means. Gain ≈ 1 means the model scales the control response correctly; gain ≈ 0 means it is insensitive to the control. This isolates a necessary condition for model-based control that nominal MAE cannot detect. The paper's second key move is treating the inference context as a system-identification dataset — asking the classical excitation question (how much, how long, how amplitude) of an in-context learner rather than of a fitted model. Methodology: The MPC setup is a finite-horizon formulation where a multi-step predictor maps context (past targets, past/future controls, exogenous weather) plus a candidate control trajectory to future outputs; the linear baseline is a direct multi-step linear map with learned operators on target, control, and exogenous blocks (subspace-predictive-control style). The pipeline: (1) simulate 191 single-family buildings in i4b (4R3C thermal models + air-source heat pump, TABULA parameters, 7 countries, real ERA5 weather with ECMWF IFS forecast covariates at 15-min sampling; 131/30/30 building splits with disjoint weather years); (2) construct evaluation tasks from nominal MPC rollouts with 24 h horizons and contexts of 1, 2, 5, or 21 days; (3) generate contexts under no excitation (MPC) or APRBS excitation at 1.5, 6, and 24 K amplitude with 1–6 h dwell times; (4) evaluate zero-shot Chronos-2, TimesFM-2.5, the linear estimator, LoRA fine-tuned Chronos-2 (2,000 steps, batch 256, lr 10⁻⁵, ~36 min on one A6000, supervised on T_room and T_hp,ret on 4,061 windows from 131 training buildings), and an EWMA variant augmenting the control channel with causal moving averages at 30 min, 2 h, and 8 h scales; (5) a preliminary closed-loop study on 17 held-out test buildings using iCEM trajectory optimization (replanning every 15 min, ~95 candidate plans per step, 2-day episodes). Critical design decisions: centering predictions and outcomes on per-step probe means before computing gain (well-justified — it removes probe-invariant error and prevents scoring well on accuracy alone); using interventions on the plant rather than model-implied counterfactuals (well-justified); and the per-window linear estimator as baseline (well-chosen but, as the authors admit, its inductive bias nearly matches the simulator's true dynamics, making the comparison favorable to it). Key Results: On nominal forecasting, zero-shot Chronos-2 beats the multi-step linear predictor on real building data (MAE 0.2–0.6 K for room temperature across context lengths 2–21 d; 0.25–1.0 kW for heat-pump power). Under MPC (unexcited) context, Chronos-2 fits the observational trajectory but shows essentially zero response to 6 K control-offset interventions (gain ≈ 0), while the linear estimator on the same context recovers a substantial part of the response — a striking result where the simpler model separates what the TSFM cannot. Under excited context, Chronos-2's gain rises toward 1 with increasing excitation amplitude and context length; longer context without excitation improves MAE but not gain. EWMA features cut the context length needed for a given gain level but do not raise the maximum attainable gain. Fine-tuning on excited data helps most at short contexts; fine-tuned Chronos-2 + EWMA recovers substantial response from just 1 day of context even under no/low excitation, without a nominal-MAE penalty, but under fully unexcited operation gain stays well below 1 and does not improve with more context. Across most of the sweep the per-window linear estimator achieves the best gain and long-context MAE; TSFMs match or exceed it only under the strongest excitation with the longest context. In the preliminary closed-loop study (17 buildings, paired differences vs. the multi-step linear baseline, mean ± SE), Chronos-2 + EWMA with 2-day excited context improves the objective (energy + 10× comfort violation) by −362.2 ± 121.0 relative to a baseline absolute value of 500.2, and even unexcited-context variants improve the objective at 2-day contexts — which the authors attribute, without direct verification, to implicit excitation from executed iCEM actions entering the rolling context. Baselines are current (Chronos-2 is recent, TimesFM-2.5, a strong domain-tailored linear identifier) and honestly reported, including where the baseline wins. Scale is standard for the domain: 191 simulated buildings, one real house, 17 closed-loop test buildings. Novelty Classification: NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING plus a NEW METHOD in the evaluation instrument (the matched-probe response-gain metric). The genuinely novel content is the demonstration that in-context identification by TSFMs is gated by control excitation — a control-theoretic requirement transplanted into the foundation-model setting — and the quantification of how fine-tuning and multiscale features shift the excitation/context requirement. The individual ingredients (APRBS excitation, LoRA fine-tuning, EWMA features, iCEM, multi-step linear MPC) are all standard; the contribution is the systematic measurement and the observation-vs-intervention framing, not a new architecture or algorithm. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are present and load-bearing: excitation amplitude (three levels), context length (four values), EWMA features, and fine-tuning data type (excited vs. MPC-only) are each varied, and the paper correctly identifies which components matter. Closed-loop results report standard errors over n=17 paired building comparisons; open-loop results do not report error bars or seeds across probe construction, though the probe design is deterministic given the corpus. No code, data, or model weights release is mentioned. Methodological concerns: (1) the primary test bed is a simulator whose 4R3C linear thermal dynamics align closely with the linear baseline's inductive bias — the authors acknowledge this and interpret the linear estimator's advantage accordingly, but it means the simulator flatters the baseline and possibly understates how hard identification is for real nonlinear systems; (2) the real-building experiment (one house, 131 days, April–August, i.e., heating-light season) has no ground truth for the ±6 K offset plans, so it only tests whether forecasts move, not whether they move correctly; (3) the surprising positive closed-loop result under unexcited initial context rests on an unverified hypothesis (implicit excitation from executed actions). The gain metric's interpretation is handled carefully, including explicit discussion of what gain 0 and gain > 1 do and do not imply. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (with a small SYSTEMS component via the closed-loop study). Practical: Yes — fine-tuning takes ~36 minutes on a single 48 GB GPU and inference is a pretrained TSFM call, all on commodity hardware. Efficient: Mixed — model-side cost is low, but the closed-loop planner scores ~95 candidate plans per 15-minute step (150–600 s per 2-day building episode), which dominates the budget and would be the bottleneck for real-time deployment. Effective: Partially — open-loop evidence shows the TSFM solves the input–response identification problem only under sufficient excitation (and is then often matched by a linear identifier), and the closed-loop gains are promising but explicitly not linked to the open-loop gain metric. Scalable: Untested beyond 17 closed-loop buildings and 2-day episodes; the cross-building fine-tuning transfer claim is supported at 30 test buildings open-loop but nothing at 10–100× deployment scale on real stock. The work delivers no software artifact, dataset, or trained weights — it stops at paper form. Strengths: - The matched-probe response-gain metric is a real methodological contribution: it cleanly decouples observational forecast accuracy from interventional control fidelity, is cheap to apply, and the paper is unusually precise about what the metric can and cannot certify (a necessary, not sufficient, condition for control). - The headline finding — that context length alone does not buy control relevance, but excitation amplitude does, with gain approaching 1 only under high excitation and long context — is a crisp, dose-responsive, and practically actionable result that reframes TSFM context curation as an experiment-design problem. - Honest baseline treatment: the linear multi-step estimator wins most of the open-loop sweep, and the paper says so plainly and draws the correct conclusion (explicit identification remains strong given sufficient excited data), rather than burying it. - The fine-tuning result is well-targeted at the practical deployment question: excited fine-tuning plus EWMA features recovers substantial response from 1 day of context, transferring a system-identification prior across buildings — exactly the trade practitioners care about. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state directly that the evaluation is primarily synthetic and that transfer to real-world systems is open; that the closed-loop results are preliminary and do not establish a relationship between open-loop response gain and closed-loop performance; that the good closed-loop performance under unexcited initial context is explained only by an unverified hypothesis (implicit excitation from executed iCEM actions); that in-context identification requires disruptive excitation and rarely beats explicit identification; and that the linear baseline's inductive bias closely matches the simulator, making it a very competitive reference. They also flag the open questions of retaining control-informative observations in context and of exploiting naturally occurring variation (e.g., price-responsive operation). This is a credibility positive — the limitations section confronts the weak points rather than minimizing them. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - The real-building validation cannot score interventional correctness (no ground truth under offset plans) and uses a single house observed over a heating-light April–August window; it shows the forecasts move under longer context, not that they move correctly — the paper is careful about this, but the practical transfer claim rests entirely on simulation. - The simulator's near-linear plant dynamics mean the central question (can a flexible function approximator extract input–response behavior from context?) is tested in the regime where a linear model is near-optimal; a nonlinear plant would likely widen the gap in both directions and is not tested. - No comparison against the action-conditioned TSFM hybrids and distillation approaches the paper itself cites ([9], [10], [12]), which are the closest competing strategies for making TSFMs control-ready — the paper positions against them narratively but not empirically. - No error bars, seeds, or probe-set sensitivity for the open-loop gain/MAE sweeps, and no significance testing for the closed-loop paired differences beyond standard errors. - The closed-loop result that most favors TSFMs (strong improvement even from unexcited initial context) is the least understood mechanism in the paper, and the honest hypothesis is unverified — the most decision-relevant number in Table 1 currently has no causal account. - No code or data release is stated, and the evaluation corpus (custom i4b population, ERA5/ECMWF weather) would be nontrivial to reconstruct. Bottom Line: Practitioners considering TSFMs as MPC dynamics models should read this for the response-gain probing methodology and the concrete warning that forecast accuracy is nearly uninformative about control fidelity, but they should not read it as evidence that TSFMs beat a well-executed linear identifier for building control — on this paper's own numbers, they mostly do not.

#143 — Innovative (62)

The Price of Proof: A Pilot Study of API Cost and Verifier Acceptance in LLM Generation of Formally Verified Code

A Patodiya · openreview.net · specification to code with formal verifications - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces a token-metered economic measurement of LLM-based formally verified code generation, proposing "cost per verifier-accepted function" (reasoning tokens included) as a metric benchmarks should report alongside acceptance rates, and delivers a priced pilot on 30 stratified vericoding tasks across Dafny, Verus, and Lean 4. - Why it's important: Verifier-in-the-loop benchmarks report who wins on acceptance rate but not what winning costs, so budget holders cannot decide which model to buy, how many repair rounds to pay for, or whether the price list predicts delivered cost — and this paper shows all three decisions currently lack the right denominator. - How it does it: It reruns matched prompting/repair arms (description-only, formal-spec one-shot, spec-plus-up-to-8-verifier-feedback-repair rounds) on seven hosted models, records every billed token (including hidden reasoning tokens) at provider list prices, and audits accepted units for spec-dropping before dividing attributed dollars by verified units. - The good: The accounting is unusually honest and self-auditing — a statement-level spec-preservation audit catches 16 vacuous compiles (all 12 apparent Lean description-only "successes" had silently dropped the required theorem), and every headline contrast comes with task-clustered bootstrap intervals plus a fully reconciled dollar ledger. - The missing: The headline price-list inversion (F3) rests on 6 paired Lean tasks with a 2.8× cost-ratio CI of [0.63, 8.72] spanning parity and a McNemar p of 0.125 — the pilot sizes the effect but the abstract's strongest claim is underpowered at n=10 tasks per language. - Read it or not: Read it if you build or fund verified-code-generation systems or run verifier benchmarks — the metric, the audit methodology, and the repair-ladder economics are immediately reusable; skip it if you want settled effect sizes, since this is explicitly a pilot feeding a preregistered 870-task confirmatory study.
Why this rank
Scored using Empirical profile. The spec-preservation audit and cost-per-verified-function metric (Novelty 62, Non-Obviousness 65) are real contributions with unusual accounting candor, but Rigor (62) is capped by 10 tasks per language, and Resilience (56) is materially weakened by the abstract leading with the 2.8× price-list inversion that the paper's own statistics (CI [0.63, 8.72], McNemar p = 0.125) do not support — a claim/evidence register mismatch under adversarial questioning. Practical Impact (58) is helped by the Zenodo-deposited harness and preregistration but the pilot defers all settled effect sizes to a future study. Weighted composite: 0.20*62 + 0.25*62 + 0.15*65 + 0.15*70 + 0.15*56 + 0.10*58 = 62.
empirical Novelty 62 Rigor 62 Non-Obv 65 Completeness 70 Resilience 56 Impact 58
Show full analysis
Problem & Motivation: A family of benchmarks (DafnyBench, Verina, vericoding, AlgoVeri, VeriContest) now measures whether LLMs produce code a formal verifier accepts, but none reports the provider-billed cost of earning that acceptance. The gap is economic, not academic: verifier-feedback repair multiplies token spend, reasoning models bill for tokens that never appear in the transcript, and an acceptance rate cannot tell a deploying team which of seven models to run, for how many repair iterations, before the next attempt stops paying for itself. The author — a single unfunded researcher paying API costs personally — argues the deployment question ("given a task, language, and budget, which model and how many rounds?") is unanswerable from published acceptance numbers alone. Key Idea: The core insight is that a formal verifier supplies free ground truth against a fixed specification, so the marginal value of any intervention (showing the spec, feeding back errors, choosing a model) can be denominated in dollars per machine-checked acceptance — and that between 85.6% and 99.8% of billed output for reasoning models is hidden reasoning text, making posted per-token prices a poor predictor of delivered cost. The enabling methodological trick is a statement-level spec-preservation audit: because Lean spec theorems are model-editable text, a unit can "verify" while deleting the theorem, so accepted units are reassembled and their fixed declarations compared against canonical statements, reclassifying theorem-droppers as failures. Methodology: The pipeline samples a seeded, stratified 30-task subset (10 per language, 3 per 2025 difficulty-prior tercile plus one uncovered task) from vericoding's QA-clean split (10,481 deduplicated tasks), then runs 7 hosted models (claude-opus-5, gpt-5.5, claude-sonnet-5, gemini-3.1-pro-preview, gpt-5.4, deepseek-v4-flash, deepseek-v4-pro) under three ordered regimes: P0_vibe (natural-language description only), P1_formal (full formal task, one shot), P4_repair (P1 plus up to 8 verifier-feedback rounds). Verification is version-pinned (Dafny 4.11.0, Verus 2025 build, Lean 4.23.0-rc2 with Mathlib). Every generated unit passes an anti-cheat gate (sorry/admit/axiom/{:verify false}) and the post-hoc spec audit; accounting records billed input, output, and reasoning tokens at list prices. Statistics use a stratified task-clustered bootstrap (B=10,000, seed fixed) for 95% CIs — units sharing a task are correlated — with Wilson intervals for two degenerate near-zero cells and exact McNemar tests for paired regime contrasts. Three critical design decisions: (1) treating the continuous difficulty prior, not the degenerate stratum label, as covariate of record (well-justified — 73%/59% of Lean/Verus covered tasks have prior exactly 0); (2) excluding 18 lost units (all Claude arms, concentrated in Lean) with an impute-as-failure sensitivity (reasonable, though it thins exactly the cells carrying F3); (3) quoting the "campaign price" (whole attributed bill over all acceptances, $0.43) alongside the retrospective winning-run price ($0.093) and all-in recorded view ($0.63) — a three-tier framing that is transparent but demands reader attention. Of $133.23 recorded spend, $113.96 (85.5%) sits in P4_repair; a logging gap left 331 truncation-retry first calls unpriced, with a minimum-charge sensitivity bounding all-in spend at $144.42. Key Results: On the 612 completed units (213 accepted after audit), pooled acceptance orders 11.1% (P0) → 34.8% (P1) → 59.5% (P4) across 7 models. P0 almost never works in the proof languages: 0/26 on Lean (all 12 apparent successes were spec-dropping vacuous compiles) and 1/42 on Verus, vs. 34.9% (22/63) on Dafny. Repair's exact McNemar tests reject at p < 10⁻³ in all three languages. The repair ladder is steeply front-loaded: the first repair round's 25 acceptances cost $10.79 total ($0.43 each) versus $48.45 for 26 acceptances across rounds 2–8 ($1.86 each, a 4.3× ratio), while 77.1% of repair dollars ($56.07 of $72.72) went to the 81 units that never verified. The F3 price-list inversion: on six paired Lean tasks, claude-opus-5 (listed at 1.7× claude-sonnet-5's rate) delivered accepted functions at $0.97 versus sonnet's $2.73 — a 2.8× ratio, but with CI [0.63, 8.72] and McNemar p = 0.125, so the pilot sizes rather than settles it. On Dafny the ranking flips: deepseek-v4-flash hit 70% (7/10) at $0.036 per accepted function, 12.3× cheaper than opus's $0.44 at 90% (9/10). Reasoning tokens were 85.6% (gpt-5.5) to 99.8% (deepseek-v4-flash) of billed output where reported, so visible-text-only metering understates billed output by up to 411×; 47 of 612 units (7.7%) ended TRUNCATED. Syntax failures were the largest final-failure class (41.9% of 322 model-attributable failures), and on Verus, 142 syntax-repair rounds were never followed by an accepting call. Baselines are current in the sense that the 2025 benchmark-author campaign (9 models, 55,397 runs) provides a difficulty prior and a 7.4% mean Lean solve rate on the 9 covered sampled tasks — against which this study's 50.8% Lean P4 rate marks model-generation progress, though the comparison bundles newer models, longer repair budgets, and harness differences. Tested scale is small: 10 tasks per language, a deliberately labeled pilot. Novelty Classification: NEW METRIC (cost per verifier-accepted function) + NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING (repair-ladder marginal pricing, price-list inversion, reasoning-token share of bills, spec-dropping under description-only prompting) + NEW DATASET/ARTIFACT (the ProofSpend harness, records, and preregistered confirmatory corpus). Genuinely novel is the joining of token-metered list-price accounting to verifier acceptance across three verifier ecosystems under matched regimes; the constituent mechanisms (verifier-feedback repair, spec-in-prompt prompting) are established, and the metric is Cost-of-Pass applied to a verifier setting — the author says as much, and the repair-depth accounting extends Olausson et al.'s self-repair cost critique to verifiers. This is a measurement study, not a method paper. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablation-grade transparency is high: the dollar ledger reconciles planned→attempted→completed→accepted units line by line; the spec audit's 16 reclassifications are itemized; sensitivities cover lost-unit imputation, minimum-charge retry pricing, and the sonnet promotional window (invoiced rates move the F3 ratio to ~1.9×). Intervals are task-clustered bootstrap with the clustering rationale explicit, degenerate cells flagged and switched to Wilson intervals, and exact paired tests reported with p-values. Raw attempt-level records, audited tables, and an offline pipeline regenerating every number ship as supplementary material; the harness and frozen splits are deposited at Zenodo (DOI 10.5281/zenodo.22074866) with a frozen preregistration (DOI 10.5281/zenodo.21897887) for the confirmatory stage. Concerns: n=10 tasks per language yields wide intervals (Verus P4 spans 55 points); the headline F3 claim is not statistically settled; results come from one benchmark (vericoding) with possible contamination of 2025-era tasks into training data; list prices reflect one point in time; prompt caching was disabled, inflating repair costs relative to a caching-enabled deployment. This is a workshop paper (NeurIPS 2026 Workshop on AI for Verifiable Coding), not peer-reviewed conference proceedings, though the internal audit discipline partially compensates. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL (a measurement study with a built harness). Practical: Yes — everything runs on hosted APIs plus an M2 laptop with 0.5 h of aggregate verifier time; no GPUs or training. Efficient: The measured campaign price is $0.43 per accepted function overall, spanning over fifteenfold across models while acceptance spans under twofold — the cost spread itself is the paper's efficiency finding. Effective: The evidence shows the metric is computable and that it reorders purchasing decisions on this pilot; whether the specific orderings generalize is explicitly deferred to the preregistered 870-task study. Scalable: Not tested beyond 30 tasks; the author claims the confirmatory run (870 tasks, caching enabled) uses the same instrument but no scaling result exists yet. The work delivers a concrete artifact set: collection harness, task splits, raw records, and an offline reproduction pipeline (ProofSpend on Zenodo), not just a paper. Strengths: (1) The spec-preservation audit is the paper's best contribution — it exposes a failure mode (deleting model-editable spec theorems) that syntactic anti-cheat filters and verifier exit codes cannot see, and shows that an entire benchmark regime's apparent Lean success rate was measuring theorem deletion. (2) The three-tier cost decomposition (retrospective / campaign / all-in) is the right taxonomy; most cost papers blur exactly this distinction between what a success costs in hindsight and what finding it costs in advance. (3) The marginal pricing of repair depth ($0.43 at k=1 vs. $1.86 pooled across k=2–8, with the at-risk hazard decaying 34.0% → 18.9% → 7.5% → ≤4.3%) turns a vague "self-repair helps" claim into a purchasable policy statement. (4) Unusual accounting candor: an unfunded author itemizing $12 of un-invoiced promotional spend, 331 unpriced retry calls, and $36.60 of aborted-run overhead, with all of it in the ledger. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The paper confronts limitations directly and in detail: pilot scale (10 tasks/language, Verus P4 interval spanning 55 points, clustering moving endpoints by up to 16 pp); the 18 lost units concentrated in the Claude arms on Lean, with imputation showing opus's $0.97 is a lower bound because its lost tasks are the hardest; acceptance certifying only conformance to the fixed spec, not intent; one benchmark, one harness, one price epoch; possible contamination making the 2025 prior confound capability with training exposure; the degenerate Lean/Verus difficulty prior leaving hard strata unordered; Lean spec preservation enforced only post hoc in the pilot. F3's cost-ratio CI spanning parity is stated in the text, though the abstract's framing ("delivered each accepted function 2.8× cheaper") is firmer than the paired statistics warrant. Analyst-Identified Gaps: (1) The abstract leads with the 2.8× price-list inversion, but the paper's own primary statistics (CI [0.63, 8.72], McNemar p = 0.125 on 4 discordant pairs) do not establish it — this is a claim/evidence register mismatch at headline level, even though §3 is honest about it. (2) The F3 comparison is structurally fragile: 18 lost units sit disproportionately in exactly the two models being contrasted, on exactly the hardest language, and no model other than the Claude pair completed enough Lean units for a third competitor. (3) The spec-audit asymmetry — the Lean P0 zero is partly by construction (the prompt withholds the theorem, so acceptance requires reconstructing it verbatim from prose), which the paper concedes but the abstract's "every apparent Lean success had silently dropped the required theorem" framing flattens. (4) List-price accounting without caching inflates repair-depth costs precisely where the paper's steepest economics claim (F4) lives; caching-enabled repair could flatten the 4.3× ladder ratio, and the confirmatory study will test this but the pilot cannot. (5) No open-weight or self-hosted models — "delivered cost" for a deployer who can run DeepSeek locally may differ qualitatively from list-price API economics. (6) The 77 description-free units (11 tasks shipping empty natural-language descriptions) are a benchmark metadata defect that contaminates denominators and regime contrasts, patched statistically rather than excluded at sampling time. Bottom Line: A practitioner buying or benchmarking verified code generation should read this now for the spec-integrity audit and the cost-metric playbook, while treating every specific effect size — especially the 2.8× price-list inversion — as a hypothesis awaiting the author's own 870-task confirmatory study rather than a settled finding.

#144 — Innovative (62)

Joint Decomposition and Learned Deformation for Part-to-Whole MRI to Histology Registration

C Athalye, W Trotman, LM Levorse… · papers.miccai.org · karypis - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces an end-to-end implicit neural representation (INR) framework that jointly performs histology image decomposition and 3D-to-2D deformable registration of a single LFB-CV histology section to a postmortem 7T MRI volume, replacing error-prone sequential pipelines. - Why it's important: Validating neuroimaging biomarkers against cellular-level histopathology requires accurate MRI-histology alignment, and existing multi-stage pipelines fail or require manual intervention, blocking high-throughput clinico-pathological studies. - How it does it: Three SIREN networks jointly decompose the histology into a shared-anatomy "support" image and a stain-specific "residual" image while learning a bounded 3D deformation field, trained in two phases (affine+decomposition, then deformation with frozen affine) via eight scheduled loss terms. - The good: With automated initialization, the method completed 17/18 registrations (94%) versus 16/18 (89%) for Greedy and 12/18 (67%) for TIRL, while matching baseline accuracy on successful cases (Wilcoxon p=0.39 vs TIRL, p=0.89 vs Greedy) — robustness without an accuracy penalty. - The missing: The evaluation covers only 18 pairs from 16 subjects, a single stain (LFB-CV), a single metric (S-RMSD on manually traced GM-WM boundaries), and relies on a resource-intensive MRI-guided 3D-printed mold protocol for initialization, so scalability and generalization claims are untested. - Read it or not: Worth reading for anyone building postmortem MRI-histology pipelines or working on INR-based registration, since it is the first method to jointly handle slice localization, part-to-whole, and cross-modal deformable alignment; skip if you need only volumetric histology registration or large-scale learned registration.
Why this rank
Scored using Empirical profile. Novelty (68) is moderate — the joint support-residual decomposition with 3D-to-2D part-to-whole registration is a real new formulation for this problem, but it is competent integration of standard components rather than a new framework. Rigor (58) is limited by n=18 pairs from a single site, one stain, one custom metric on manually traced boundaries with no inter-rater reliability reported, and no ablation isolating the decomposition's contribution — the paper's central mechanistic claim is asserted, not tested. Completeness (60) is boosted by direct, non-minimizing limitation discussion, but the mold-protocol dependency undercuts the high-throughput claim, and Resilience (62) is only moderate because success-rate ranges at this sample size carry wide uncertainty. Practical Impact (60) reflects an open-source pipeline that runs in ~2 minutes on commodity hardware, valuable for a niche but not demonstrated at scale. Weighted composite: 0.20*68 + 0.25*58 + 0.15*65 + 0.15*60 + 0.15*62 + 0.10*60 = 62.
