#150 — Innovative (61)

DuoMatching: Joint-Marginal Distribution Matching for Few-Step Video Generation (69 ▲ )

Jiahao Zhan, Yan Wang, Yongrui Ma, Qunliang Xing, Ruchang Yao, Runtao Liu, Shijie Zhao, Tianfan Xue · arxiv.org · Daily papers of 7 Oct 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces DuoMatching, a distribution matching distillation framework for few-step video generation that augments standard joint (whole-video) DMD with an explicit frame-level marginal DMD objective supervised by a frozen image generation model (Qwen-Image by default). - Why it's important: Few-step video generators built on DMD drift in quality and miss prompt-specified details (textures, object attributes, composition) during autoregressive rollouts, and existing fixes (adversarial or reward supervision) do not close this frame-level quality gap without extra inference cost. - How it does it: The core move is a weighted joint-plus-marginal KL objective, where a lightweight pretrained module (LatentBridge, 10.75M params) maps temporally compressed video VAE latents into the image teacher's latent space so frame-level score differences can backpropagate to the video student, with Latent Variation Sampling distributing the K=4 per-step marginal supervision across high-motion temporal segments. - The good: Ablations cleanly isolate the mechanism — swapping in stronger image teachers (Qwen-Image HPSv3 9.05 vs Wan2.1-14B 5.87) monotonically improves student VBench Total (83.53 vs 81.43), and LatentBridge preserves Dynamic Degree (93.61) where direct marginal DMD on video latents collapses it to 76.94. - The missing: No seed variance, significance tests, or confidence intervals on any VBench or human evaluation number (e.g., the 0.72-point Total gain over Causal Forcing++ at 4 steps, 83.51 vs 82.79, could be within noise), and no code or model release is mentioned. - Read it or not: Worth reading for researchers working on video distillation or DMD-style training who want to combine heterogeneous teacher latent spaces; practitioners just seeking a better real-time video generator can wait for released weights.
Why this rank
Scored using Empirical profile. Novelty (70) and Non-Obviousness (70) are the strengths — the joint-marginal DMD formulation with an image teacher is genuinely new in this setting, and the LatentBridge ablation cleanly separates latent-space mismatch from dynamics suppression via a rare negative control. Rigor (58) and Resilience (55) are dragged down by the absence of any variance reporting (the 0.72-point margin over Causal Forcing++ at 4 NFE may be noise), a 23-participant human study with no rater statistics, and an advertised challenge set that is never scored quantitatively; Completeness (58) lacks an explicit limitations section, and Impact (48) is capped by no code or weight release. Weighted composite: 0.20*70 + 0.25*58 + 0.15*70 + 0.15*58 + 0.15*55 + 0.10*48 = 61.
empirical Novelty 70 Rigor 58 Non-Obv 70 Completeness 58 Resilience 55 Impact 48
Show full analysis
Problem & Motivation: The paper targets the residual quality gap in few-step (1–4 NFE) video generators produced by distribution matching distillation. Streaming/autoregressive video generation systems (CausVid, Causal Forcing++, Self Forcing) reach near-real-time inference, but DMD training against a video teacher's joint frame distribution leaves students with degraded fine-grained texture, weaker prompt adherence, and worse composition — visible as drift in Q-Align quality scores over rollout frames and missing prompt-specified attributes (e.g., a feather on a hat). Prior fixes add adversarial loss (One-Forcing), reward signals (Reward Forcing, DMDR), or real data (Data-Forcing), but none add a dedicated per-frame distributional reference; the paper argues joint matching alone under-constrains individual-frame marginals. Key Idea: Treat the real video distribution through a joint-marginal decomposition: keep the video teacher for joint (cross-frame) KL matching, and add a second DMD term matching the student's single-frame marginal to an image generator's distribution, which is a closer proxy for the true frame marginal than the video teacher's marginal (supported by an idealized forward-KL argument in Appendices C–D proving that a small positive marginal weight strictly improves the ideal optimum). The practical enabler is mapping between incompatible latent spaces: LatentBridge converts a temporally compressed video latent slice (conditioned on the preceding slice and a local frame index) into the image teacher's per-frame latent, letting gradients flow without decoding/re-encoding through both VAEs. Methodology: The pipeline has four stages. (1) Joint DMD: the student generator (initialized from the Causal Forcing++ causal CD checkpoint, or Wan2.1-T2V-1.3B for bidirectional mode) produces a video latent; a frozen video teacher and a trainable fake score estimator supply the standard DMD gradient over all temporal slices, following Causal Forcing's procedure. (2) Marginal DMD: Latent Variation Sampling computes MSE between adjacent latent slices, splits the sequence into K contiguous segments at the K−1 largest-difference positions, and samples one slice per segment plus one local frame index; LatentBridge (8 FiLM residual blocks, 256 channels, frozen) maps the slice to an image latent, which is noised under the image teacher's schedule and scored by the frozen image teacher (Qwen-Image) and a second trainable fake estimator. (3) The generator minimizes L_joint + ω·L_marginal with ω=0.4, warmed up over training; fake estimators update on fresh student samples with flow-matching targets (Algorithm 1). (4) LatentBridge itself is pretrained with an ℓ1 reconstruction loss against image-VAE encodings of ground-truth frames on 29,400 curated OpenVid videos (~15 minutes on 8×80GB GPUs). Critical design decisions: conditioning LatentBridge on the preceding latent slice to respect causal temporal VAE encoding (justified qualitatively and by reconstruction results); the ω warm-up (justified by the ω ablation showing ω=0.8 degrades Dynamic from 93.61 to 87.78); and LVS versus uniform sampling (justified by Table 5, LVS beats uniform at every K and uniform K=8 drops Total to 81.04). The theoretical justification for improvement is idealized: it assumes exact minima over infinite-capacity distribution families, finite KLs, and differentiability of the optimum path. Key Results: On VBench (official prompt suite), DuoMatching reaches Total 83.51 vs Causal Forcing++'s 82.79 at chunk-wise 4 NFE, 83.53 vs Causal Forcing++'s 80.67 at frame-wise 2 NFE (a 2.9-point gain, the largest margin reported), 82.65 vs One-Forcing's 82.09 at 1 NFE, and 81.45 vs CausVid's 80.63 for bidirectional full-video generation. Semantic scores improve most for the 2-step setting (72.84 vs 68.42). A 2AFC human study (23 participants, 40 prompt pairs per comparison) reports overall preference above 80% against all four baselines: 94.35% vs One-Forcing, 91.30% vs CausVid, 83.91% vs Reward Forcing, 80.87% vs Causal Forcing++, with Temporal & Motion preference near parity (49.57–60.87%), indicating motion is preserved rather than improved. Ablations: image teacher quality tracks student quality (Qwen-Image HPSv3 9.05 → Total 83.53; Wan2.1-14B HPSv3 5.87 → 81.43); LatentBridge beats direct marginal DMD (Total 83.53 vs 81.78) while direct DMD collapses Dynamic to 76.94; decode-encode alternative runs out of memory (OOM) at the training configuration. Baselines are current (2025–2026 works) and matched on NFE and the same Wan2.1 video teacher. Tests are at standard scale: 81-frame 480×832 videos, Wan2.1-1.3B student, 1,000–1,200 distillation steps on 8×80GB GPUs. The gains at 4 NFE (0.72 Total) are much smaller than at 2 NFE (2.86), and the 400-prompt curated challenge set is shown only qualitatively (Figure 4/5), not quantitatively. Novelty Classification: NEW FORMULATION and NEW METHOD with an ENGINEERING OPTIMIZATION component. The joint-marginal reformulation of DMD with a cross-modality (image) teacher for the marginal term, plus the proof that a small marginal weight strictly improves the ideal objective, is genuinely new in this setting; using image priors to aid video distillation has precedents (MCM's image-trained discriminator, AVDM2's image score matching on AnimateDiff-style models), so the marginal-DMD-with-image-teacher concept is an evolution of known ideas, while LatentBridge and LVS are competent, well-motivated engineering for temporally compressed video latents. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are thorough and well-targeted: image teacher choice (Table 3), marginal-loss weight ω (Table 6), number of sampled slices K and sampling strategy (Table 5), and latent-mapping strategy including the informative negative result that direct marginal DMD suppresses dynamics (Table 4). Hyperparameters (ω=0.4, K=4, training steps, dataset sizes, LatentBridge architecture) are fully specified, and the training algorithm is given in pseudocode. However: no error bars, seeds, or significance testing appear anywhere; the human study has only 23 participants and 40 prompt pairs per comparison with no inter-rater statistics; the headline VBench margin over the strongest baseline (Causal Forcing++) is 0.72 Total at the 4-step setting, unverifiable without variance estimates; no code, weights, or data release is mentioned (only a project page); and the theory holds only under idealized assumptions (infinite-capacity feasible families, exact minimizers) that the authors flag but that do not quantify real behavior. No Goodhart-style train/eval contamination is apparent — training uses VidProM (causal) or Mixkit (bidirectional), evaluation uses VBench prompts. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (a trained distillation method with automatic and human evaluations; includes a small theoretical component but the primary claim is empirical). Practical: Training needs 8×80GB GPUs, but inference adds zero extra NFE and reuses the Causal Forcing++/CausVid serving stack. Efficient: LatentBridge adds only 10.75M parameters and ~2.9GB peak training memory over the direct baseline (59.41 vs 56.49 GB), and trains in ~15 minutes. Effective: Evidence covers the stated problem (visual quality, semantic alignment, composition on VBench plus human preference), though the human eval is small and the curated 400-prompt stress set lacks quantitative results. *Scalability beyond Wan2.1-1.3B at 480p is untested and only implicitly claimed — behavior at 10× model or resolution scale, or with video VAEs lacking the shared-encoder coincidence that enabled the Direct baseline, is unknown. Deliverable: paper plus a project page; no library, CLI, or model weights are stated as released. Strengths: - The core insight — that a dedicated marginal objective with an image teacher supplies frame-level supervision that joint DMD structurally cannot, because joint score gradients for one slice are conditioned on the others — is crisp, well-motivated by the Figure 1 drift analysis, and validated by the direct ablation showing quality gains even without external image priors (Wan2.1-14B as image teacher already improves Total from 80.67 to 81.43). - The LatentBridge ablation is the paper's most convincing experiment: it separates the two confounded effects (latent-space mismatch vs dynamics suppression) and shows the failure mode (Dynamic 76.94) is a property of naive marginal matching, not of the method, while the decode-encode OOM result justifies the module practically. - The Appendix D proof, though idealized, is a correct and non-trivial local-improvement result (strictly negative right-derivative of forward KL at ω=0) that gives the loss weighting a principled footing rather than pure heuristic tuning. - Honest NFE- and mode-matched comparisons against contemporaneous strong baselines (One-Forcing, Reward Forcing, Causal Forcing++) on the same video teacher, with the potentially damaging temporal-quality numbers reported at parity rather than hidden. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state that excessive marginal supervision (ω=0.8) degrades dynamics, that K=8 is counterproductive, and that the theoretical improvement result requires idealized assumptions (matched marginal capacity, exact minima, differentiability) detailed in Appendices C–D. They acknowledge that Direct marginal DMD suppresses motion and that the Decode-Encode alternative is memory-infeasible. They do not include an explicit limitations section; limitations emerge from ablation discussion rather than a direct confrontation, which is a mild credibility deduction. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - No statistical uncertainty anywhere: single-run VBench numbers with sub-point margins over the strongest baseline (83.51 vs 82.79 at 4 NFE) and a 23-participant human study with no rater agreement analysis cannot support the stated effect sizes. - The Direct-latent baseline in Table 4 is only possible because Qwen-Image and Wan2.1 share a VAE encoder; generality of the approach for arbitrary video/image VAE pairs rests on LatentBridge's ℓ1 reconstruction quality alone, and no end-to-end ablation tests an image teacher with a truly incompatible VAE beyond the FLUX/SDXL bridge reconstructions (Figure 6), which are not linked to final video metrics. - The marginal term's benefit is entangled with the image teacher's text-to-image prompt-following ability: since the marginal loss conditions on the text prompt, the semantic-alignment gains may partly reflect distilling a stronger prompt-adherence model rather than the joint-marginal formulation per se; a control using the image teacher without text conditioning is absent. - The 400-prompt curated challenge set is advertised as a key evaluation asset but is never scored quantitatively — only cherry-picked side-by-side figures are shown. - The 1,000–1,200-step training budget is short; whether gains persist or degrade with longer training, and whether LVS's segment heuristic (MSE on clean latents) transfers to other VAEs or resolutions, is unexamined. Bottom Line: For anyone actively building DMD-style few-step video generators, this is worth reading — the joint-marginal formulation is a credible, well-ablated idea with a rare negative-control ablation — but the absence of variance reporting, code, and quantitative results on the authors' own challenge set means practitioners should treat the headline margins over Causal Forcing++ as promising rather than established.

Action Conditioned Bisimulation For GUI Agent Memory

H Zhang, L Song, Q Li, D Yang, Y Wen, Z Yao · arxiv.org · karypis - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces an action-conditioned bisimulation criterion that decides when two GUI pages may be merged in an agent's memory, replacing observation-similarity merging with a rule based on whether shared actions lead to agreeing outcomes and successor blocks. - Why it's important: GUI memory systems that merge look-alike pages (two tabs, two menu rows) pool evidence across different action semantics and recall confident but wrong actions, so the merge rule is the load-bearing decision in every episodic memory for frozen agents. - How it does it: States are compared only through their empirical predictive profiles — immediate outcome and distribution over successor blocks per shared action, under an affordance label — computed by fixed-point iteration on the transition counts a frozen agent already recorded, with nothing trained. - The good: The closed-loop ablation ladder on MiniWoB++ isolates the merge rule cleanly: the shortlist control and SR merge are flat against ReAct (+0.000, +0.005), the observation merge is negative (−0.015), and only the proposed criterion moves (+0.060, 95% CI [+0.033, +0.090], McNemar p < 10⁻³). - The missing: Everything rests on a single seed, 10 hand-picked MiniWoB++ navigation tasks, and a Qwen3-8B policy; no evidence exists beyond this narrow setting, one container task moves against the method and its cause is unresolved, and no code release is stated. - Read it or not: Read it if you build memory or state-abstraction for LLM agents and want a rigorous, minimal, training-free counterexample to similarity-based recall; skip it if you need evidence beyond toy-scale MiniWoB++ before committing to bisimulation-style partitioning.
Why this rank
Scored using Empirical profile. The ablation ladder, paired McNemar tests, pre-declared subset prediction, and passed negative control make this the cleanest isolation design in the cluster (Rigor 60), and Non-Obviousness (72) is high — refusing to merge on missing shared actions directly blocks the aliasing failure mode that observation-similarity merging provably exhibits. The composite is dragged down by Impact (35) — no code, dataset, or artifact release — and by Resilience (55): everything rests on a single seed, 10 hand-picked MiniWoB++ tasks, one 8B policy, and the authors' own memory consumer, with no end-to-end comparison against the modern memory systems the paper surveys. Weighted composite: 0.20*70 + 0.25*60 + 0.15*72 + 0.15*65 + 0.15*55 + 0.10*35 = 61.
empirical Novelty 70 Rigor 60 Non-Obv 72 Completeness 65 Resilience 55 Impact 35
Show full analysis
Problem & Motivation: A GUI agent that is frozen between episodes can only improve if its memory decides correctly whether two observations are the same state. Existing memories — Synapse (embedding retrieval), ExpeL, Agent Workflow Memory, AutoGuide, A-MEM, and successor-representation memories — all recall by observation similarity, which answers "which memory is relevant here" rather than "is this the same state." GUIs break this adversarially: two tabs of one widget or two rows of one menu are near-identical as observations but answer the same click differently, so merging them pools evidence across distinct action semantics and produces confident wrong recalls. The gap is a merge criterion that never consults appearance. Key Idea: Recast the bisimulation criterion — normally used to learn reward-conditioned embeddings offline in continuous RL — as a hard partition computed by counting the transitions a deployed agent has already made: two states merge only when, for every action both have actually tried, the immediate outcomes and successor block-distributions agree within a threshold, and never when they share no action (refusing to merge on missing data is the substantive move that blocks the similarity-rule failure mode). Action templates abstract element IDs into (role, label, slot) descriptors so cross-episode actions share a vocabulary; without this the shared-action restriction would collapse the partition to the identity. Methodology: Three stages. (1) Graph construction: a frozen agent's episodes accumulate into a transition multiset over observation signatures and action templates; per-state descriptions are empirical outcome frequencies ρ⁺/ρ⁻/ρ△, with progress graded by reachability (−1 self-loop, 0 can-reach-back, 1 otherwise) so repainting oscillation is not credited as progress. (2) Partition: bisimulation distance (Eq. 3) = mean outcome gap + γ·TV between pushforward successor block distributions, worst-cased over shared actions, gated on an invariant affordance label (goal slot pattern, element role set, fillable slots); the partition is computed as a monotone fixed point via union–find on thresholded distances, starting from the γ=0 partition. Empty-action states (terminals, the state being decided) are placed by incoming signature. (3) Inherited consumer: the partition is dropped into an existing outcome-value memory — normalized discounted terminal occupancy V, advantage scoring, block-pooled q with κ-prior and λ rank penalty — as a subclass overriding only B, so the comparison is closed-loop. Design decisions well-justified: shared-action restriction (the observation merge ablation fails exactly as predicted); the affordance label (needed to avoid a degenerate coarse fixed point, argued via the open/closed menu example); ϵ-greedy detours over the first third of each run, seeded by environment and step but never by system, so a memoryless control takes identical detours. Degenerate-scale caveat: under greedy execution |A(s)|=1 and no pooling is possible, which the detour mechanism addresses but which also means the method's premise depends on this exploration protocol. Key Results: MiniWoB++ via BrowserGym, 10 navigation tasks, frozen Qwen3-8B with thinking disabled, greedy decoding, 8-step cap, 60 episodes/task (20 with detours, 40 greedy), 400 paired evaluation cells, single seed. SR: ReAct 0.723; shortlist control 0.723 (Δ +0.000, p=1.000); SR merge 0.728 (+0.005, CI [−0.007, +0.018]); observation merge 0.708 (−0.015); APSG 0.782 (+0.060, CI [+0.033, +0.090], p < 0.001). A hand-written shortcut fired ~equally across systems (171 vs 170 times), ruling it out as confound. On the pre-declared container-task subset the gain is +0.075; on non-container tasks no discordant pairs exist (a passed negative control). Mechanism diagnostics: both merge rules have similar evidence coverage and override rate, but APSG moves most overridden outcomes failure→success while the observation merge moves them success→failure. The memory starts behind from exploration, crosses ReAct by ~episode 35, and ends ahead over all episodes; on the 272 cells all systems solve, APSG is more direct (1.70 vs 1.81 steps). Baselines (ReAct, SR-based memory, observation-similarity merge) are reasonable for the isolation being claimed but exclude modern agentic-memory systems like AWM or A-MEM as end-to-end comparators. Tested at toy scale; one task (click-menu-2) moves against the method with cause unresolved. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD plus NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING. The genuinely novel move is repurposing bisimulation as a training-free, empirical-count-based partition for a deployed LLM agent's memory rather than an offline-learned embedding, plus the shared-action merge restriction; the downstream value memory, the bisimulation-metric fixed-point machinery (Ferns et al., Castro), and the ϵ-greedy exploration protocol are standard components reassembled competently in a new setting. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are unusually clean: four rungs changing exactly one thing each, with three flat rungs that eliminate the second model call, the exploration detours, and non-action-conditioned merging as alternative explanations. Paired per-cell statistics with exact McNemar tests and bootstrap CIs; a pre-registered-style split (container vs non-container) with a directional prediction stated before the run; a negative control the mechanism passes; and a failed task reported with cause unknown. Concerns: single seed; 10 of MiniWoB++'s ~100 tasks chosen for a stated property; all merge rules evaluated only inside the authors' own outcome-value memory, so the criterion is never tested against a modern external memory system (A-MEM, AWM); no code or data release is mentioned; hyperparameters (ϵ=0.35, τ_b=0.30, γ=0.8, K=6) fixed by hand with no sensitivity analysis. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (a system component run closed-loop in a browser environment). Practical: Yes — runs on a locally served 8B model plus BrowserGym, all commercially available hardware. Efficient: One extra greedy model call per decision for the action shortlist plus an exploration tax over the first third of episodes; the partition computation over counted transitions is negligible. Effective: Evidence shows it solves the aliasing problem on the tested container tasks, but only under a specific exploration protocol and at toy benchmark scale. Scalable: Not tested beyond 10 tasks and a 8B model; the fixed-point iteration is monotone and reportedly settles in a few rounds, but behavior on open-ended websites with non-recurring layouts — where cross-episode state identity is harder — is untested and only claimed by analogy. Deliverable form: paper only; no software artifact, dataset, or weights release is stated. Strengths: (1) The isolating experimental design — a control that pays the identical exploration and model-call costs while keeping nothing — is a model of how to attribute gains to a single component. (2) The refusal to merge on missing shared actions is a sharp, well-argued design choice that directly addresses the failure mode it targets, and the observation-merge ablation empirically confirms the aliasing mechanism at the decision point (override precision moving in opposite directions). (3) Applying bisimulation as a count-based partition over a deployed agent's logged transitions, rather than a learned embedding, is a genuinely fresh use of a classical tool with a clear argument for why the cap is self-consistent at the fixed point. (4) Honest negative results: a flat SR-merge rung, a harmful observation merge, and one task that moves the wrong way are all reported. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state that the gain is bought with exploration (and quantify its repayment), that one container task (click-menu-2) moves against them with the cause unreolved, and that the criterion depends on affordance labels inherited from the base memory — dropping the label provably lands in a bad coarse fixed point. They also acknowledge the greedy-execution degeneracy that forces the detour protocol. They confront limitations directly; this is a credibility positive. Notably, they do not explicitly flag the single-seed design or the narrow task selection as limitations. Analyst-Identified Gaps: (1) Single seed across all ten tasks — the ±0.03 CI width on a paired design partly mitigates this, but seed-level variance in agent benchmarks is known to be large and unmeasured here. (2) The 10 tasks were fixed beforehand for the property that pages recur across episodes; performance on the other ~90 MiniWoB++ tasks, or on WebArena-style non-stationary sites, is extrapolated without evidence, despite the paper itself citing WebArena alignment work. (3) No end-to-end comparison against the modern memory systems the introduction surveys (Synapse, A-MEM, AWM), so the reader cannot tell how the full pipeline stacks up, only that the merge rule beats its own ablations. (4) The affordance label and action templates are substantial engineering layers whose individual contributions are not ablated — the paper's "nothing is trained" claim covers the partition but the signature extraction is doing unstated representational work. (5) The paper is a preprint and has not, as far as the text indicates, undergone peer review. Bottom Line: A practitioner building memory for frozen LLM agents should read this for its unusually clean causal isolation and a genuinely new angle on state abstraction, but should not treat the +6-point MiniWoB++ result as evidence the approach survives contact with realistic web workloads or modern memory baselines.

Problem & Motivation: The paper addresses the symbolic-search substrate of formal theorem proving. Practitioners building learned Lean provers (DeepSeek-Prover, Goedel-Prover, HunyuanProver) currently treat the proof assistant as a terminal accept/reject oracle, discarding verified intermediate structure. The gap: while semantic guidance from language models has advanced rapidly, the algorithmic design space of the symbolic environment itself — how verified consequences are retained, how equivalent goals are merged, how operator families are scheduled, how far speculative expansion runs under a finite budget — has remained comparatively underexplored since miniF2F's 2022 tidy baseline (18.0%). The paper argues these two capability sources (semantic priors vs. proof-space organization) are complementary and that the second is a substantial, underexploited lever. Key Idea: Treat a proof attempt as a bounded, persistent AND/OR graph of semantically-identified proof states, where the unit of accounting is the proof state rather than the path prefix — so convergent tactic routes share verified downstream work, and a kernel-checked graph (not a raw transcript) becomes the reusable memory and interface for both symbolic scheduling and future neural agents. Each of the four mechanisms (perspective-balanced frontier, transposition persistence, bounded futures, local synthesis) is a recognizable search technique; the persistent semantically-keyed Atlas as the central substrate is the unifying move. Methodology: The pipeline is: (1) canonicalize each Lean goal into a strict semantic key (alpha-normalized local names, ordered context, declaration kinds, types, let-values; 64-bit hash with structural equality confirmation, so hash collisions never merge states); (2) expand via nine symbolic perspectives (normalization, contradiction, rewriting, elimination, construction, backward application, typed forward closure, equality reasoning, bounded futures), merged as round-robin interleave of per-perspective capped lists truncated to a global budget B — with a first-round coverage guarantee when B ≥ number of active perspectives; (3) merge states hitting existing Atlas identities, reusing outgoing transitions, failures, and verified descendants (transposition table); (4) preview depth-3/width-6/24-node BFS future graphs under saved metavariable state with transactional rollback; (5) synthesize exact and partial inhabitants of local hypotheses plus reflexive-equality/True closures at every visited state; (6) close leaves with bounded mathlib automation (normalization, rewriting, arithmetic, Aesop-style search). Every accepted branch is elaborated to a Lean term and kernel-checked. Boundedness is enforced via a 10-dimensional budget vector (time, nodes, transitions, work units, meta-ops, rendered chars, regions, future depth/width, provider capacity) under one global cancellation deadline. Critical design decisions: separating the per-perspective cap q from global budget B (justified by a coverage lemma, Appendix C); BFS rather than DFS for futures (argued, not measured); preview/execution separation so speculative state never touches the trusted proof path (well-argued, transactional pattern in Appendix F). The objective is implicit — solve the target within budget — with a hand-tuned structural transition potential (Eq. 6, clip[c,1](c_p/max(0.1, c_p + c̄ + 0.20(m−1)))) used only as a ranking signal. Key Results: Headline: 122/244 = 50.0% pass@1 on the complete miniF2F-test split, model-free, with theorem-answer declarations excluded and target-theorem retrieval disabled. Reference points (from different proof environments, honestly caveated in Appendix O): Lean tidy 18.0% pass@1 deterministic; Isabelle Sledgehammer 10.4%; Lean grind 32.4% (79/244); Dafny SMT-backed verification 38.9% (95/244). Learned rows for context: DeepSeek-Prover-V1.5-RL 50.0% at whole-proof pass@32; Goedel-Prover-SFT 57.6% pass@32. Baselines are current for symbolic automation, though the comparison is cross-system and cross-toolchain. The evaluation is a single standard benchmark at standard scale; no per-problem timing distributions, compute budget, or failure breakdown on miniF2F are reported in the main text. The striking (and unexplained) finding is a 17.6-point absolute jump over grind from pure search organization with no learned component. The agentic interface (Section 5, planner/interactive/policy modes, Atlas-delta process supervision) is presented as design only — no neural experiment is run. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD plus NEW SYSTEM/TOOL, with a secondary NEW FORMULATION (finite-budget Lean search as persistent proof-space exploration with explicit mode coverage). Genuinely novel: the persistent semantically-keyed Proof Atlas serving simultaneously as transposition table, agentic workspace, and process-supervision substrate. Standard ingredients applied in combination: perspective balancing is round-robin fair scheduling, bounded futures are shallow lookahead with transactional rollback, local synthesis is type-directed inhabitant search, and leaf closure is off-the-shelf mathlib automation — competent integration rather than new algorithms per component. Rigor & Reproducibility: Weak on ablations. The paper builds matched-compute benchmark modes (Appendix L, eight configurations isolating frontier, Atlas persistence, futures, synthesis) but explicitly reports "No additional empirical numbers are inserted here" — the ablation infrastructure exists while the ablation results do not. No error bars, seeds, or significance tests (deterministic search makes this partly moot, but timeout sensitivity is unaddressed). Code is public at https://github.com/RuoranXu/ViaLean, with a module-by-module implementation map (Appendix P) and a suggested reproduction record — a credibility positive. Methodological concerns: (1) evaluation on a single benchmark that is also the field's most-mined target; (2) cross-environment baselines (Isabelle, Dafny) retained but not directly comparable; (3) the evaluation timeout/configuration used for the 122/244 run is not stated in the main text (Table 2's 10 s default is labeled an implementation default the harness "may override"); (4) no comparison against Aesop or a hammer-style baseline within the same Lean toolchain, which would isolate VIALEAN's contribution from mathlib's leaf portfolio; (5) the headline comparison (grind 32.4%) is cited from a 2026 arXiv preprint. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL (a built system with one benchmark measurement; the neural interface is untested design). - Practical: Yes — runs as ordinary Lean 4 metaprogramming on consumer hardware with a 10 s-class wall-clock budget; no GPUs or providers needed in the evaluated configuration. - Efficient: Bounded by an explicit 10-dimensional budget vector (≤96 Atlas nodes, ≤160 transitions, ≤256 work units in defaults), so cost is strictly capped, but absolute compute is not compared against grind or tidy under matched budgets. - Effective: The 50.0% kernel-checked result shows the system solves the stated problem on miniF2F, though the mechanism attribution (which component earns the gain) is unverified. - Scalable: Not tested — the Atlas is deliberately finite (hard caps on nodes/transitions/meta-ops), and behavior at 10× budget or on harder corpora (Putnam, Lean Formalgym, mathlib) is unmeasured; the paper claims, rather than demonstrates, that the substrate scales. The work delivers a software artifact (public Lean 4 repository with benchmark and trace schemas); the neural-epoch interface stops at paper form. Strengths: - The persistent semantic state identity (Appendix A) is a careful, correct piece of engineering: alpha-stable keys, hash buckets with structural confirmation, order-preserving context — this is the load-bearing detail that makes transposition reuse sound, and the paper exposes it fully. - The proof/observation trust separation is unusually clean for this literature: preview transactions never mutate the trusted path, validation never confers truth (a typed cut stays an obligation), and search memory is explicitly distinguished from Lean's acceptance criterion. - Honest baseline accounting: Appendix O explicitly preserves the incomparability of cross-system reference points instead of laundering them into a leaderboard. - The matched-compute benchmark modes and structured failure taxonomy (14 classes distinguishing timeout from type mismatch from budget denial) are reusable infrastructure beyond the headline number. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors acknowledge that Table 1 rows come from different proof environments, libraries, and inference budgets and must be read as context rather than controlled comparison (Appendix O); that the reported score is a "system-level measurement" of the full configuration with component attribution deferred to a matched-compute protocol (Appendix L) that they do not execute; and that their boundedness claim concerns search control, not complexity of Lean elaboration (Appendix G). They are candid about the evaluation boundary (target retrieval disabled, theorem-answer exclusions). This is direct confrontation of the main comparability weakness — a credibility positive — though stating an ablation design without running it is a notable self-acknowledged shortfall. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - The central empirical question is unanswered: no ablation numbers exist, so the 17.6-point gain over grind cannot be attributed to perspective balancing, persistence, futures, or synthesis individually. The infrastructure exists; the experiment was not run or not reported. - The evaluation timeout and full configuration for the headline run are not stated in the paper (defaults are flagged as overridable), so the result is not exactly reproducible from the text alone. - No within-toolchain baseline: Aesop, plain mathlib tactics, or a simple best-first search over the same leaf portfolio would isolate what the Atlas adds versus what mathlib automation already solves. - miniF2F is small, olympiad-style, and heavily saturated by years of optimization; no second benchmark or out-of-distribution corpus tests whether the perspective taxonomy generalizes beyond competition arithmetic/algebra. - The agentic Section 5 (neural epochs, Atlas-delta supervision) is a design sketch with zero experiments, yet it occupies substantial paper real estate — claims about "sparse neural intervention" and process-level supervision are entirely unevaluated. - The 0.20 branch-penalty constant and all scheduler weights appear untuned/unvalidated; no sensitivity analysis. Bottom Line: A practitioner in automated theorem proving should read this: the model-free 50.0% on miniF2F-test is a real, kernel-checked advance over the symbolic frontier, the released implementation contains genuinely reusable machinery, but the paper's inability to attribute the gain to its four mechanisms means the reader must treat it as a strong empirical artifact with an unvalidated internal theory, not a validated methodology.

Problem & Motivation: Robot foundation models face a fork: VLAs (π0, OpenVLA, RT-2) inherit semantic understanding from vision-language pretraining but get little grounding in world dynamics from action-only supervision, while world-action models (DreamZero, Motus, 4D-WAM) inherit spatiotemporal dynamics priors from video generators but degrade in reasoning under distribution shift. The motivating question is how to get both capabilities in one generalist policy. The intended users are robotics labs building generalist manipulation systems; the specific gap closed is the absence of a single architecture and training recipe that jointly optimizes understanding, generation, and action with heterogeneous data sources without one objective destroying the others' pretrained capabilities. Key Idea: Route supervision, not just data, to the right expert: represent continuous end-effector actions as deterministic natural-language templates ('physical language,' following LAP) so the frozen-distribution VLM can absorb embodied control without catastrophic forgetting, and assign VQA data to supervise only the reasoner, human egocentric data to reasoner+generator (avoiding low-precision human action labels for the action expert), and robot data to all three experts. Secondary ideas: future-frame latent noise augmentation (forces the action expert to use coarse visual predictions rather than near-clean future latents) and initializing the action flow from perturbed action history instead of Gaussian noise (action-to-action generation), which jointly enable 2–4 step inference. Methodology: The model is a Mixture-of-Transformers with three 30-layer experts exchanging information via joint token-concatenated attention with modality-specific projections and an attention mask; the objective is p(y, o_{t+1:t+h}, a_{t+1:t+h} | o_t, s_t, I). Pipeline: (1) data cleaning — median/Savitzky-Golay filtering with jerk/acceleration thresholds, cross-correlation state-action lag checks, percentile-based outlier removal, forward-kinematics joint-EEF consistency, frame-quality filtering; (2) human-data annotation — the EgoANT VLM pipeline (coarse-to-fine contact-sheet temporal segmentation with Qwen3.6-27B, multi-candidate description generation with Qwen3.5-397B, text-only candidate selection) to segment EgoDex into atomic subtasks; (3) pretraining for 7 days on 32 H800s with two flow-matching losses (video and action velocity fields, weights 1:1) plus an autoregressive language loss weighted 0.1, on ~4,958h robot + ~5,072h human + 8.293M VQA pairs; (4) post-training with future-frame noise augmentation (latent retention scale ~ U(0.5,1), prob. 0.5) and history-conditioned flow matching (source = previous 16-action chunk + N(0, 0.02²I)). Critical design decisions: language-verbalized actions (justified by preserving VLM capabilities and enabling cross-embodiment human-robot supervision, supported by a t-SNE representation-overlap analysis), per-expert data routing (justified via source-level ablation), and history-based flow initialization (justified by the step-count ablation showing A2A at 2–4 steps beats N2A at 10). Key Results: LIBERO average 99.2% (vs. 98.7% Xiaomi-Robotics-0, 98.5% for several 2025-26 baselines); LIBERO-Plus total 92.6% (vs. 89.0% Kairos, 86.2% π0.5), leading on robot-state (89.5%), language (92.2%), light (97.9%), and background (97.6%) perturbations. RoboTwin 2.0: 75.14% C2C and 68.32% C2R, average 71.73% — highest average in the table, but OpenWAM-α scores 89.4% C2C and GigaBrain-0.7 scores 67.9% C2R. Real-world (dual-arm AgileX Piper, 200 demos/task, 40 trials/task): average success 67.5% and instruction-following 82.5% across four grounding tasks versus π0.5 (54.4%/60.6%) and Motus (36.9%/43.1%); long-horizon 'Tidy up the desk' Task Progress 5.0/6 vs. 4.8 (π0.5) and 3.2 (Motus). Scaling: OOD task completion rises monotonically 0.35→0.67 from 250h to 5k robot hours; validation loss follows L(D) ≈ 0.03205 − 0.00302 ln(D) with R² ≈ 0.983; human data degrades performance below 1k total hours and helps beyond. Ablations attribute gains to robot data (46.23%→67.53%), human data (+3.81 avg points), VQA (+0.39), physical language supervision (46.49%→51.74%), and full pretraining (→71.34%). Baselines are current (2025–2026) and mostly strong; testing spans standard sim suites plus a modest 4-task real setup. Novelty Classification: NEW SYSTEM/TOOL and NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING, with elements of NEW FORMULATION (explicit formulation of history-conditioned action flow and perturbed-future-latent post-training). The genuinely novel pieces are the systematic complementary-supervision routing across a tri-expert MoT, the quantified human-robot co-training scaling law with the small-data-regime crossover, and the history-initialized flow matching for action generation. The architecture itself is a standard combination of known components (Mixture-of-Transformers, flow matching from π0, language-action verbalization from LAP, video backbones from WAMs) applied to a new unified setting. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations cover data composition, VLM training strategy, and action-generation strategy, with a step-count study and task-level RoboTwin results in appendices — component attribution is genuinely present. However, no error bars, multiple seeds, or significance tests are reported; differences of 0.5 points on LIBERO (99.2 vs 98.7) are within plausible run-to-run noise. Code is on GitHub and checkpoints on ModelScope, with a project page and released VQA data — good artifact availability. Methodological concerns: the scaling-law fit is on pretraining loss with downstream tracking shown only at a few points; the t-SNE human-robot representation-overlap evidence is qualitative; real-world evaluation uses the authors' own four tasks rather than a community benchmark; and the two simulation benchmarks (LIBERO/RoboTwin variants) are the same ones used to tune training designs, creating mild Goodhart risk. The paper is a preprint (arXiv v3, Oct 2026), not stated as peer-reviewed. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (a trained system with simulation and real-robot experiments). - Practical: Runs on commodity accelerators (H100/H800) and a ~$30k-class dual-arm Piper platform, but requires a 2B VLM + 5B video generator backbone with future-frame latent prediction at 384×320, which is heavy for embedded robot deployment. - Efficient: The A2A initialization cuts action denoising to 2–4 steps (vs. 10 for N2A), a concrete inference speedup, though total inference still carries the full video-generation expert per step. - Effective: Simulation and real results support OOD robustness and instruction grounding, but real-world evidence covers only four custom tasks plus one long-horizon task on a single embodiment. - Scalable: The log-linear fit covers only 250h–10k hours with no saturation point identified, and 10–100× scaling is extrapolated, not tested. Delivers a real software artifact: code, checkpoints, and a released VQA dataset, plus the reusable EgoANT annotation pipeline (described in a companion report). Strengths: - The supervision-routing recipe is a clear, transferable insight: showing that human egocentric data should supervise dynamics but not the action expert, and that verbalized actions protect VLM capability, is more actionable than generic co-training. - The human-data crossover finding (harmful below ~1k hours, beneficial above, with a 0.983-R² log-linear fit) is a genuinely useful empirical contribution for anyone budgeting mixed-data pretraining. - EgoANT is a concrete, well-specified contribution: coarse-to-fine contact-sheet segmentation plus multi-candidate description selection that turns EgoDex into subtask-level language-annotated data. - The history-conditioned flow matching yields a measurable, practically valuable result — A2A at 2–4 steps (75.14/68.32% C2C/C2R at 4 steps) matches or exceeds N2A at 10 steps. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors acknowledge that human egocentric data degrades performance at small data scales (below ~1k hours), attributing this to visual/physical distribution mismatch, and that near-clean future visual latents are 'sometimes unreliable at inference' (motivating noise augmentation). There is no dedicated limitations section in the main text; limitations are confronted implicitly through ablations rather than stated directly, which is a moderate credibility deduction. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - No statistical treatment anywhere: single-run results, no seeds, no confidence intervals, yet headline claims rest on 0.4–0.5 point margins on LIBERO. - The in-distribution RoboTwin result (75.14% C2C) is 14 points below OpenWAM-α (89.4%); the paper claims SOTA via the average but does not explain or dwell on the C2C deficit. - History-conditioned flow initialization risks compounding action-history errors and autocorrelated failure modes during rollout; the paper reports no analysis of error accumulation or recovery behavior, only static success rates. - The claim that physical language supervision 'enables strong generalization' (Q4) is supported mainly by a t-SNE plot and LIBERO-Plus language-dimension numbers; no direct causal ablation isolates physical language's contribution to OOD generalization specifically (the cumulative ablation conflates it with unfreezing and pretraining). - Real-world evaluation uses the authors' own tasks, 200 demos/task, and their own platform; no transfer to an external real-robot benchmark or third-party reproduction is reported. - The world generator's actual contribution is never isolated by an ablation that removes the video expert entirely — the data-composition ablations vary data sources, not architecture components. Bottom Line: A practitioner building generalist manipulation policies gains concrete, reusable guidance here — the supervision-routing recipe, the human-data scaling threshold, and the data/annotation pipeline justify reading despite the single-run statistics and the mixed SOTA picture, though anyone prioritizing pure in-distribution performance should also consult OpenWAM-α.

Problem & Motivation: The essay addresses the orientation problem that precedes platform strategy. Prior work covers multihoming, platform constellations, multi-platform integration (Schreieck et al.), inter-platform ecosystems (Carballa-Smichowski et al.), and situational platform awareness (Burström et al.) — the author explicitly acknowledges this gap is not an absence of work on multiple platforms. The less-developed problem is upstream: how can an organization identify the several platforms it is simultaneously situated in, distinguish the different positions it occupies across them, and interpret dependencies arising from their interconnection — before any focal platform has been chosen? The analytical anchor shifts from the platform (as in Burström et al.) to the organization trying to determine which systems should be focal. The motivating tension is sharpened by the Shopify case: a successful Platform Owner ($378B GMV in 2025, $248.1B Payments volume) can find itself a participant in an agent-mediated commerce layer whose customer interface it does not own. Key Idea: The core insight is that platform roles are relational, not identities: "is this firm an Owner or a Provider?" is ill-posed until the reference platform is specified, so strategic analysis must begin with explicit multi-platform position-finding rather than with a single focal system. The enabling move for practice is the Platform Landscape — connected PBMC Core Frames, one per platform the organization participates in — so that simultaneous, potentially contradictory positions (e.g., Shopify as Owner of its commerce ecosystem and Provider within AI-agent-mediated commerce) can be externalized, compared, and contested. Methodology: This is a conceptual essay, not an empirical study; the author states this explicitly in a "Note on Method." The method is constructive-analytical: (1) a prehistoric boundary case (Ohalo II, Göbekli Tepe) stress-tests how far a technology-neutral language of platform-like coordination extends without anachronism, establishing that structured interdependence precedes both digital technology and ownership; (2) five historical cases each isolate one positional movement — Lloyd (recognizing the platform around you), Western Union (a second transaction on owned infrastructure), Sears (scaling on non-owned infrastructure), AWS (the platform already inside), Shopify (a platform becoming a participant above); (3) Chapter 8 names the pattern; (4) Chapter 9 formalizes the Platform Landscape from PBMC Core Frames, with Landscape and full PBMC claimed to "correct one another." Design decisions worth noting: cases are selected for variation in positional type (well-justified for concept exposition, but this also guarantees the pattern appears); the author refuses to attribute platform reasoning to historical actors without documentary support (a credibility positive); and no loss function, formal model, or falsifiable propositions are stated — the essay deliberately stops at concept formation. Key Results: Not applicable — no hypotheses are tested and no quantitative outcomes are reported as findings. The closest things to results are: (1) a measured descriptive indicator showing classified platform firms' share of the global Top-10 market capitalization rising from 8.5% (~$0.163tn) in 2009 to 57.0% (~$13.6tn) in 2026, offered as evidence of economic salience, not causation; (2) case-level documented facts (e.g., Western Union's 1868 admission of telegraphic money orders predating its formal 1871 service; Sears's order volume rising five-fold in 1913 after Parcel Post; Ewens et al.'s finding that AWS-exposed startups raised ~20% less first-round capital), used as raw material rather than tests. The essay's own claims are conceptual and the author explicitly disclaims causal inference: the cases "do not establish a causal relationship between awareness and performance." Novelty Classification: NEW FORMULATION and NEW CONCEPT (construct proposal), not a new method or empirical finding. Genuinely novel: the organization-centric reframing of platform positioning as a prior orientation problem, and the Platform Landscape as connected PBMC Core Frames — an extension of the existing PBMC tool rather than a replacement. What is a standard combination: the synthesis draws directly on established platform economics (Rochet & Tirole, Katz & Shapiro), ecosystem-as-structure (Adner, Jacobides et al.), boundary resources (Ghazawneh & Henfridsson), and situation-awareness research; the prehistoric chapter borrows niche construction and archaeology for rhetorical framing rather than analytic work. Rigor & Reproducibility: There are no ablations, seeds, or significance tests by design — this is conceptual work, and internal rigor takes the form of source discipline: extensive archival citation (Wright & Fayle 1928, Smithsonian Western Union records, Asher Papers, SEC/DOJ filings, AWS blog posts), explicit separation of documented fact from inference, and open acknowledgment of contested or uncertain provenance (e.g., conflicting Sears origin stories, Barr's uncertain recollection of the Bezos brainstorm). No code, dataset, or instrument is released; the Platform Landscape is described but not operationalized as a usable artifact with coding instructions in the visible text. Methodological concerns: the cases are illustrative, selected because each exhibits a positional shift, which makes the pattern-confirming structure unavoidable; there is no negative case (an organization that failed due to low platform awareness), which the author implicitly concedes by listing negative cases as open agenda items. The prehistoric chapter, while intellectually charming, does minimal argumentative work and would not survive a strict reviewer's cost-benefit test. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: this is a conceptual essay that fits none of the three profiles cleanly — it is closest to THEORETICAL, but contains no proofs, bounds, or formalisms, only a proposed construct and framework. Applying the theoretical check in spirit: Sound: the construct is defined with care and explicitly scoped, but it is unfalsified and unfalsified-able as stated. General: the positioning is deliberately technology-neutral (prehistoric to AI-era), which is broad but risks vagueness. Tight: not applicable — there are no formal statements; the boundary against Burström et al.'s situational platform awareness and Spurava's media-literacy sense is drawn, which is the relevant precision here. Implementable: the Platform Landscape is intended as a practical artifact, but no procedure, worksheet, or worked application to a live firm is provided beyond the cases themselves. Deliverable: paper form only — a conceptual glossary and a research agenda; no tool, dataset, or trained artifact ships with it. Strengths: - The five-case architecture is genuinely well-designed: each case is selected to isolate a distinct positional movement, and the sequence (Lloyd → Western Union → Sears → AWS → Shopify) builds the concept cumulatively rather than redundantly. - Exceptional source discipline for a conceptual essay — the author repeatedly corrects founder myths against the archival record (Lloyd was probably not an underwriter; Western Union's money orders predate the 1871 launch as a constrained internal practice; the AWS "eureka" session is flagged as uncertain by its own participant), modeling exactly the fact/inference separation the framework preaches. - The relational-role claim — that Owner/Provider/Consumer/Partner are meaningless without specifying the reference platform — is a crisp, teachable insight that genuinely reorganizes how multi-platform questions should be asked. - Honest self-limitation: the essay states up front that the cases are illustrative, non-causal, and non-representative, and converts every weakness into an explicit research agenda item (construct validity, role coding, negative cases, longitudinal change, capability formation). Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors confront limitations unusually directly. The abstract alone concedes: cases are illustrative rather than representative; no causal link between awareness and performance is established; the capacity to develop and revise awareness is treated as a separate untested empirical question; construct validity, role coding, negative cases, and longitudinal change are open, not settled. Chapter 10.3 is devoted to limits and the research agenda. The Shopify chapter refuses to declare agentic commerce the inevitable next layer while it is still unfolding. This level of self-scrutiny is a strong credibility signal. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - No negative cases and no counterfactual: without even one documented organization that suffered from low platform awareness, the construct's practical value rests entirely on suggestive historical reading, and selection bias toward awareness-driven successes is possible even within illustrative framing. - The Platform Landscape is proposed but never applied end-to-end to a single live organization in the visible text; the reader cannot assess whether connected Core Frames are tractable for a real multi-platform firm or produce insight beyond an ecosystem map plus role labels. - The relationship to existing multi-platform constructs (platform constellations, multi-platform integration typologies, inter-platform ecosystems) is positioned as "one step earlier," but no analytic criterion distinguishes when Platform Awareness adds explanatory power versus when these prior lenses suffice — a boundary the essay asserts rather than demonstrates. - The prehistoric chapter, while serving the technology-neutral claim, is rhetorically heavy and analytically thin; a reviewer could argue the same work could be done in a paragraph. - The pending chapters (8 onward are partially truncated in the provided text) mean the formal treatment of the concept and the research agenda cannot be fully assessed from the material supplied; judgments above rest on the abstract, contents, and Chapters 1–8 opening. Bottom Line: For a management or information-systems researcher working on platforms and ecosystems, this is a genuinely useful construct-development essay whose relational-role insight and historical case design merit engagement — but it stops deliberately at concept formation, so anyone seeking tested theory, a validated diagnostic, or formal propositions should read it as an agenda-setter, not a result.

TimeNet: An Extensible Unified Data Infrastructure for Next-Generation Temporal Foundation Models

M Maritsch, T Stoffregen, T Kaar, B Riemer, MA Xu… · arxiv.org · karypis - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces TimeNet, an open-source data standard (TimeF) and software infrastructure that decouples time-series recordings from task definitions, enabling heterogeneous temporal datasets to be combined for multi-task training of temporal foundation models through configuration changes alone. - Why it's important: Time-series foundation model development is bottlenecked by fragmented, task-specific dataset formats that force an N×M integration burden between datasets and consumers; a shared representation (N+M integrations) lowers the cost of scaling pooled training across domains, modalities, and tasks. - How it does it: The core move is a relational object model (Records → recursive Sources → Signals, with reusable Annotations and Tasks as many-to-many references) stored as a DuckDB control plane over sharded Parquet/Zarr values, paired with a compositional task taxonomy where tasks are typed by a signature φ(τ) = (output kind, target position, arity) instead of ad-hoc task names. - The good: The paper shows pooled training on four QA datasets via TimeNet raises OpenTSLM's average F1 from 29.16 to 33.28, improving F1 on all four datasets, with detailed I/O benchmarks (6 datasets, pandas and PyTorch consumers) showing practical parity with native formats on several datasets (e.g., ECG-QA full-read time 2,351 s native → 644 s TimeF). - The missing: The training evaluation covers only the question-answering family with two model families, one seed, no significance tests, and no ablation isolating whether gains come from data diversity versus simply more data — while the headline claims about forecasting, generation, editing, and localization remain unexercised in training. - Read it or not: Worth reading for anyone building or serving time-series ML datasets and training pipelines (the schema design and task taxonomy are directly reusable); model researchers seeking evidence that cross-dataset training improves TFM capabilities will find only a narrow, small-scale proof of concept.

Problem & Motivation: Builders of Temporal Foundation Models (TSFMs and Time-Series Language Models) must train on many heterogeneous datasets, but time-series data is published as self-contained, task-specific packages with bespoke formats, preprocessing, and loaders. The same underlying recordings (e.g., PTB-XL ECGs) are repeatedly repackaged for classification, QA, reasoning, and instruction tuning, each effort introducing its own representation. This fragmentation blocks pooled, multi-task training across domains, modalities, temporal scales, and supervision types — the scaling recipe that enabled general foundation models in other modalities. Prior resources either curate benchmarks (UCR/UEA, Monash, GIFT-Eval), harmonize numerical pretraining corpora (LOTSA, UTSD, Time-MMD), or provide domain-specific storage (AtriumDB for physiological waveforms), but none provide a general, task-aware storage and serving layer for TFM training. Key Idea: Two ideas combine here. First, an interface-compression argument: represent all datasets in one model-independent data model (TimeF) so integrating N datasets with M consumers requires N connectors + M adapters instead of N×M dataset-specific pipelines. Second, a compositional task algebra: instead of naming tasks, characterize each task by its signature φ(τ) = (κ, Δ, α) — output kind (Value/Span/Signal/Index), target position relative to observed support (Obs/Gap/Fut/Past/Chan/Null), and arity (1 vs ≥2 temporal objects) — which partitions all well-posed tasks into six constructions grouped into five semantic families (attribute inference, temporal localization, future-directed inference, relational inference, temporal synthesis), with task constructors (Shift, Mask, Pair, Ask, Explain, Stream, Reduce, Restrict) deriving new tasks without duplicating data. The signature taxonomy is the paper's most intellectually distinctive piece; the storage layer is competent engineering of known ideas (relational metadata + columnar values). Methodology: TimeNet's pipeline has three stages. (1) Ingestion: dataset-specific connectors run download→convert→derive_schema→store, producing immutable versioned TimeF entries in a registry (org/name@version) where non-redistributable data can be rebuilt locally. (2) Representation: TimeF's object model (Records, recursive Sources, Signals with regular/irregular/ordinal axes, Spans, normalized Annotations, Tasks) maps to a DuckDB control plane (hierarchy, annotations, task references) plus sharded Parquet/Zarr values, keeping relational filtering off large arrays. (3) Collation: a model-specific function C_m maps resolved task instances to (X_m, M_m, C_m, Y_m) tensors — windowing, padding, resampling — reusing one loader across all datasets. The formal appendix specifies the task tuple (views, conditioning, output type, support, interface, rationale, protocol, scoring) and proves the signature grid partitions well-posed tasks (Proposition 1) and that constructors are type-closed (Proposition 2). Critical design decisions: many-to-many Task↔Record references with targets stored as annotation references rather than copies (justified by avoiding repackaging, though it adds referential complexity); DuckDB+Parquet split (justified by the I/O benchmarks); and the signature-based taxonomy (well-argued, but its practical payoff is only demonstrated for QA training). Key Results: (1) Pooled training: OpenTSLM (Llama 3.2-1B Flamingo variant) trained jointly on Sleep-EDF Expanded CoT, ECG-QA CoT, HEARTS, and ARFBench improves F1 on all four versus per-dataset training — Sleep-EDF 37.49→41.80, ECG-QA 31.19→34.21, HEARTS 15.03→19.70, ARFBench 32.94→37.41; average F1 29.16→33.28 (a 14% relative gain; absolute gains are 4–5 points on a low baseline). SLIP (400M parameters) improves on Sleep-EDF (31.78→42.27 F1) and HEARTS (9.98→24.78 F1) but degrades on ECG-QA (33.93→30.00 F1), which the authors attribute to its smaller capacity — an unverified explanation. (2) I/O benchmarks across six datasets (canonical item counts 750 to 618,508; up to ~282 s full-read, 8.7 GB HTTP payload): TimeF is sometimes faster (ECG-QA: 2,351 s → 644 s PyTorch full-read; HEARTS: 95 s → 17 s) and sometimes slower (SLIP: 116 s → 283 s; Sleep-EDF: 171 s → 432 s PyTorch), with the honest concession that memory-mapped native formats can be faster. Baselines are the original dataset loaders, appropriately current by construction. Scale is standard (a 1.51M-instance registry: 899k QA, 484k classification, 131k generation, 441 temporal localization, 292 scalar prediction — note the last two are nearly empty). No counter-intuitive findings beyond the SLIP regression. Novelty Classification: NEW DATASET/BENCHMARK (the 1.51M-instance registry and connectors) and NEW SYSTEM/TOOL (the TimeNet infrastructure and TimeF format), with a NEW FORMULATION component in the compositional task signature taxonomy. The genuinely novel part is treating tasks as first-class, typed, derivable views over shared recordings with a formal signature space and constructors; the storage layer (relational metadata over Parquet/Zarr) and the pooled-training demonstration are competent applications of known ideas (HuggingFace-Datasets-style registry patterns, DuckDB analytics) to the time-series setting, where prior equivalents are either benchmark-only or single-modality (AtriumDB). Rigor & Reproducibility: No ablations isolate which TimeNet components matter for the training gain — the pooled-vs-single comparison conflates data diversity, data volume, and the format itself (there is no non-TimeNet pooled-training baseline using a naive concatenation loader). No error bars, seeds, or significance tests are reported for either the training or I/O experiments, and I/O numbers are single-run. Code is open source (github.com/OpenTSLM/TimeNet, timenet.ai, HuggingFace OpenTSLM), all external datasets are open, and the reproducibility statement is credible. Methodological concerns: the training evaluation uses only four QA datasets and two model families, one of which (SLIP) contradicts the headline claim, and the "14% improvement" is a relative number on F1 values below 42 — absolute accuracy ranges from 33% to 88% and the pooled accuracy gain on ARFBench is slightly negative for OpenTSLM. Some loaders for the I/O comparison were implemented by the authors with "verified parity" but no parity protocol is described. The registry's temporal-localization (441) and scalar-prediction (292) counts are too small to support the claimed breadth of task families. Deployability: Profile: SYSTEMS (a built tool and infrastructure, evaluated by I/O benchmarks and a training use case; also EMPIRICAL for the pooled-training experiments). Practical: Yes — it runs on commodity hardware using DuckDB, Parquet, and Zarr; the training experiments used a 1B-parameter model on standard infrastructure. Efficient: Mixed — memory footprint is comparable to native formats (roughly 0.8–2.0 GiB peak RSS), transfer volume is often lower, but full-read throughput can be 1.5–2.5× slower than tuned native loaders on some datasets. Effective: The evidence shows the infrastructure enables pooled training and modest QA gains; it does not yet show it solves the broader stated goal of task-general TFMs, since forecasting, editing, generation, and localization training are untested. Scalability: Not tested beyond ~1.5M instances and 6 datasets; no evidence at 10–100× scale, and no demonstration of concurrent multi-user registry operation — only claims. The work delivers a real software artifact (library, connectors, versioned registry, HF models), not just a paper. Strengths: (1) The compositional task signature φ(τ) = (κ, Δ, α) with its proved partition of the signature space is a genuinely clarifying formal contribution — it dissolves the anomaly-detection/forecasting/QA naming confusion into checkable properties, and the constructor algebra (Shift, Mask, Pair, etc.) with explicit preconditions is more principled than ad-hoc task taxonomies in prior time-series resources. (2) The N×M→N+M interface-compression framing is correct and consequential, and the design follows through: tasks reference shared annotations rather than copying data, so new task views over existing recordings require no signal duplication. (3) The I/O benchmark is unusually honest for an infrastructure paper — the authors report where TimeF loses to native formats rather than cherry-picking. (4) The SLIP result contradicting the pooled-training claim is reported rather than buried, which raises confidence in the rest of the evaluation. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state that training experiments cover only selected models and tasks rather than the full TFM space, that the evaluation spans only six datasets for I/O and four for training, that only QA and time-series reasoning were trained (leaving a model spanning all task families to future work), and Appendix B.11 explicitly lists settings the specification does not cover (interventional/counterfactual tasks, sequential decision-making, multi-turn agentic interaction, structured outputs beyond the registry). This is a direct, non-minimizing treatment of limitations — a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: (1) No control for data quantity: the pooled-training gain could come entirely from 4× more training instances rather than heterogeneity, so the central claim that the shared representation enables better models is not isolated from the trivial benefit of more data. (2) No comparison against the obvious alternative baselines — HuggingFace Datasets, PyHealth 2.0, or MEDS — for either I/O or integration effort, so the claimed superiority over existing standards is asserted, not measured. (3) Single-run experiments with no seeds or significance tests; given F1 deltas of 1–4 points, statistical support is weak. (4) The taxonomy's practical value is unexercised: the registry's 441 localization and 292 scalar-prediction instances mean five of eight built-in task types are essentially unrepresented, so the schema's breadth is theoretical. (5) The SLIP capacity explanation for its ECG-QA regression is speculation; a scaling ablation would settle it. (6) The I/O benchmarks measure sequential read patterns; training workloads involve random access, shuffling, and streaming, none of which are benchmarked. (7) The "1.5M task instances" headline counts overlap-derivable instances (e.g., SLIP overlaps Sleep-EDF and PTB-XL per Table 4), so effective dataset diversity is smaller than the count implies. Bottom Line: This is the most complete attempt yet at a shared, task-aware data layer for temporal foundation models and is worth adopting or contributing to for anyone publishing or consuming time-series datasets, but its empirical evidence is a narrow QA-only proof of concept — read it for the schema and taxonomy, not for proof that unified data infrastructure makes better TFMs.

Large language models discover complementary heuristics for combinatorial optimization

H Gong, S Wang, D Song, JB Sheu, R Yan · nature.com · 10 new citations to your articles
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces LACE, a framework in which LLM agents automatically construct a verified problem interface and evolve a portfolio of complementary heuristics for combinatorial optimization problems, evaluated on 36 CO-Bench problems plus four newly formulated container-terminal scheduling problems. - Why it's important: Writing competitive heuristics for new combinatorial problems requires scarce human algorithm-design expertise; automating this with reliability guarantees could let practitioners get working solvers from a natural-language problem description alone. - How it does it: The core trick is separating a machine-verified problem contract (Input–Output–Tools) from the heuristic search itself — no module is accepted on LLM say-so, only after execution-grounded validation (parsers must parse real instances, the feasibility checker must accept a deterministic feasible witness, heuristics must run end-to-end) — followed by evolutionary refinement of a heuristic portfolio selected by a rank-based MILP objective that maximizes complementarity rather than average performance. - The good: The ablation program is genuinely informative: rank-based complementary selection beats the best alternative by ~11 percentage points on Survival Rate (0.633 vs 0.525) despite only ~3 points on Avg Score, and removing the two reactive repair operators causes the largest drops (Avg Score 0.850 with ER disabled, Valid Rate 0.73), cleanly showing that reliability, not raw quality, is what the design buys. - The missing: The provided document is the supplementary material only, so headline main-text comparisons (exact margins over the six metaheuristics and Gurobi) cannot be verified here; additionally, all ablation figures come from single runs with no seeds or error bars, and the pipeline is anchored to a proprietary o3-mini backbone. - Read it or not: Worth reading for researchers in LLM-for-optimization and algorithm discovery — the verified-contract design and the complementarity-versus-averaging finding are transferable — but skip if you need the actual benchmark tables, which live in the main text not included here.
