Problem & Motivation: Practitioners who face novel combinatorial optimization problems (here, port and tugboat scheduling in maritime logistics, where berth, tugboat, and timing decisions are tightly coupled) have no off-the-shelf solver and no benchmark in the LLM pretraining corpus. The paper targets two gaps at once: (1) existing LLM-based algorithm-search systems lack a trustworthy way to define feasibility and scoring for a problem the LLM has never seen, and (2) a single LLM-generated heuristic typically excels on some instances and fails catastrophically on others, so the system needs a principled way to assemble a set of heuristics with balanced tail coverage. The four novel problems (PSP, TRS, MB-TRS, TRS-VS) are constructed specifically so their constraint structure "does not match any standard benchmark and is therefore unlikely to appear in LLM pretraining corpora," making them a zero-shot generalization test. Key Idea: The central insight is a verified-contract separation: factor a solver into a problem-defining contract (I: input parser/schema, O: output schema plus a trivially feasible placeholder solution, T: feasibility checker and objective evaluator authored by the LLM itself) and free-form heuristic solve-functions, then accept every contract module only through a generate–validate–repair loop whose acceptance test is execution on real instance data — the checker must accept the deterministic O-placeholder witness, and a temporary heuristic must traverse I→O→T end-to-end and score a feasible solution, proving the contract composes. The second insight, in Stage Two, is that portfolio selection should minimize mean best-achieved rank (a scale-invariant, complementary-coverage objective implemented as a MILP) rather than average objective value, because averages hide systematic failure on hard instances. Methodology: Stage One invokes four sequenced LLM designer agents — Input Designer, Output Designer, Tool Designer, Helper Designer — each wrapped in a bounded repair loop (default 3 attempts) with stage-specific acceptance gates: machine smoke tests plus a substantive-defects-only reviewer LLM for I and O; a heuristic-witness end-to-end run for T; and an instrumented invocation check for optional helpers (invalid helpers are silently discarded). Stage Two runs an evolutionary loop for Nmax = 6 iterations, each generating n new candidate heuristics via five operators (Local Refinement, Reflective Redesign, Complementary Crossover, Comparative Synthesis, Diversity Injection) plus two reactive repair operators (Error Repair, Efficiency Improvement), then reduces 2n candidates to a portfolio of n via the rank-based MILP selection. For the 36 CO-Bench problems, the input layer and scoring oracle are adopted from CO-Bench to keep scoring fair; for the four novel problems the entire contract is generated. The novel problems are formalized as MILPs: PSP integrates berth assignment with two asymmetric tugboat maneuvers per vessel (horsepower-pooling coalitions, sequencing tolerances, four weighted objective terms); TRS/MB-TRS/TRS-VS are routing formulations on a task graph with multi-depot home-base return (MB-TRS) and speed discretized into three levels with cubic speed–power fuel coupling linearized via McCormick constraints (TRS-VS). Baselines are six metaheuristics (GA, PSO, ACOR, GWO, KOA, EO) sharing a continuous-chromosome feasibility-preserving greedy decoder, run 60 s per instance with 5 seeds, and Gurobi 11.0 at 1-min and 30-min budgets. Backbone: o3-mini; per-instance budgets 10 s (CO-Bench) and 60 s (novel problems). Key Results: In the supplementary material, the reported headline is Avg Score 0.950 over the 40 problems (0.945 over the 36 CO-Bench problems alone), with Survival Rate 0.633 under the full system. Ablations: (1) selection rule — Rank-MILP 0.950 Avg / 0.633 Survival vs Avg-scalarization 0.920/0.525, greedy 0.899/0.477, top-n-by-mean 0.801/0.362, random 0.753/0.299; (2) leave-one-out operators — removing Complementary Crossover costs the most among generators (0.904), removing Error Repair or Efficiency Improvement is worst overall (0.850 with Valid Rate 0.73, and 0.878 with Valid Rate 0.85, respectively); (3) runtime budget — Avg Score rises monotonically and saturates (e.g., Location & Assignment 0.874→0.990 from 5 s to 10 s; novel problems 0.918 at 30 s, 0.980 at 60 s, 0.989 at 90 s); (4) iterations — family-mean Avg Score climbs from 0.852 (initial portfolio H0) to 0.949 at iteration 6 while marginal gain decays from +0.039 to +0.003 and cumulative token cost reaches ~154 M, justifying Nmax = 6. On the novel problems, Gurobi at the tested scales does not close the optimality gap and 30 min yields only modest gains over 1 min, so no certified optima exist. Exact head-to-head numbers against the six metaheuristic baselines are in the main text, which is not included in this document; the baselines themselves are current and tuned per problem on a development set, which is a strength. Testing scale: 100–500 vessels (PSP), 10–290 tasks (tugboat variants) — standard-to-moderate, not stress-scale. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD (LACE's verified-contract construction plus complementary portfolio evolution) and NEW DATASET/BENCHMARK (the four novel container-terminal MILP problems: PSP, TRS, MB-TRS, TRS-VS), with a NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING (survival rate, not average score, is what complementary selection protects, and repair operators rather than generation operators drive reliability). The individual ingredients — LLM code generation, generate-validate-repair loops, evolutionary heuristic search — are established; the genuinely novel elements are the execution-grounded contract acceptance tests (the placeholder-witness and end-to-end heuristic-witness gates) and the rank-based MILP portfolio selection objective, both of which are more than a standard recombination. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are the strongest rigor feature: selection-rule comparison across five alternatives, leave-one-out over all seven operators, budget sweeps, and iteration sweeps, each isolating one component with backbone and split held fixed. However, each ablation configuration is explicitly a single run — no seeds, error bars, or significance tests are reported for the pipeline-level results (the metaheuristic baselines do get 5 seeds). Code including all agent prompts is stated to be openly available in a repository (URL not given in this document), and all problem instances are in a supplementary repository. Methodological concerns: (a) on the four novel problems, both the feasibility checker and the scoring function are LLM-authored by the same system being evaluated — the risk of a self-consistent but subtly wrong contract is real, though mitigated on CO-Bench by adopting CO-Bench's own evaluator; (b) the novel-instance generator, feasibility screens, and per-instance weight calibration are all author-controlled; (c) no certified optima exist at tested scales, so all quality claims on novel problems are relative to incumbents. The adoption of CO-Bench's official scoring oracle for the 36 standard problems is a credibility positive that avoids self-grading there. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL (a system with experiments; also delivers reusable problem formulations). - Practical: Yes — the pipeline needs only API access to an LLM (o3-mini) and a standard CPU for solving/scoring; Gurobi is the only commercial dependency and only for the exact baseline. - Efficient: Per-instance solve cost is a fixed 10–60 s wall-clock budget, deliberately near the saturation point of the quality–time curve; discovery cost is nontrivial (~154 M tokens for a full 6-iteration Stage Two over 40 problems). - Effective: Evidence supports the claim on both adopted (CO-Bench, third-party scoring) and novel problems, but with a 0.633 Survival Rate the portfolio still fails on roughly a third of held-out instances — effectiveness on the tail is partial. - Scalable: Only claimed implicitly through the budget-saturation and instance-scale spread (up to 500 vessels); no experiment probes 10× instance sizes or portfolio scaling beyond 6 iterations, and rising per-iteration token cost suggests discovery cost grows superlinearly. The work delivers a software artifact (LACE pipeline with prompts, plus instance repositories for four new MILP problem families) rather than stopping at paper form. Strengths: - The execution-grounded contract validation is a real design contribution: requiring the feasibility checker to accept a deterministic feasible witness and a heuristic to run the full I→O→T loop converts "the LLM says the contract is right" into a mechanical, composable proof, directly addressing the most fragile failure mode of LLM-as-evaluator systems. - The finding that Avg Score and Survival Rate diverge sharply under alternative selection rules (0.801 Avg for top-n alongside 0.362 Survival) is a non-obvious, actionable insight: average objective is the wrong selection signal for heterogeneous instance sets. - The four novel MILP formulations are carefully constructed and documented (horsepower coalitions, asymmetric dual tugboat maneuvers, McCormick-linearized speed–fuel coupling), giving the community pretraining-free test problems with matching metaheuristic and exact baselines. - Fair-scoring discipline on CO-Bench — adopting the third-party parser and evaluator rather than self-authoring them — is exactly the control a skeptical reviewer would demand. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors acknowledge that PSP "is not intended to be solved to proven optimality" and serves only as a testbed for feasibility, robustness, and quality–time trade-offs; that Gurobi returns improving incumbents rather than certified optima at tested scales; that helpers which fail validation are silently discarded (a deliberate non-blocking choice); and that ablation values come from single runs (stated in figure captions). They confront the evaluation-fairness issue directly by adopting CO-Bench's oracle. The limitations are generally confronted rather than minimized, which is a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - The circularity risk on the four novel problems is understated: the same LLM authors the feasibility checker, the objective, and the heuristics, so a systematically wrong contract would be self-consistently satisfied; no human verification of the generated contracts for PSP/TRS/MB-TRS/TRS-VS is reported. - No seeds or variance for any Stage-Two pipeline result — given known LLM output stochasticity, a 0.950 vs 0.920 ablation gap (3 points) may not be robust, and the paper does not test this. - The single backbone (o3-mini) leaves open whether the verified-contract machinery or the specific model's coding ability drives the results; no cross-model ablation appears in this document. - Survival Rate 0.633 means 37% of held-out instances have no portfolio member finding any feasible-quality solution, but the paper does not characterize which instances fail or why. - Instance-generation for the novel problems is author-designed with calibrated weights and feasibility screens; no sensitivity analysis over instance-distribution assumptions is provided. - Head-to-head quantitative results against the six metaheuristics and Gurobi are referenced but not contained in this document, so the central comparative claim cannot be verified from the provided text. Bottom Line: A researcher in LLM-driven algorithm design should read this for the verified-contract pattern and the complementarity-selection finding, which are genuinely useful and well-ablated — but should treat the novel-problem results as self-graded until independently verified, and consult the main text for the actual benchmark numbers this supplementary volume omits.

Automatically Building Machine-Checked Assurance Cases from C Codebases to Requirements

H Li, Z Wang, G Li, X Yi, S Qin, J Yin, M Chen · arxiv.org · specification to code with formal verifications - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces CCV, an LLM-assisted framework that builds machine-checked assurance cases for C codebases in VST/Rocq, jointly synthesizing function specifications, body proofs, and a resource-aware interface protocol that models permitted cross-interface call sequences for open libraries. - Why it's important: Verifying real C code in an interactive theorem prover normally requires expensive expert labor to write contracts and proofs, and function-level proofs alone do not show that a library's interfaces compose to meet its stated requirements — the gap that historically makes verification of open libraries a manual burden. - How it does it: A two-phase workflow co-evolves specifications and proofs (top-down NL contract derivation from requirements, then bottom-up formalization and proof with feedback-driven revision), while a state-based interface protocol with per-edge subsumption obligations yields a machine-checked conditional safety theorem for protocol-following call sequences, with explicit human conformance review gates outside the kernel-checked evidence. - The good: It verifies memory safety and leak freedom for all 299 function definitions across six C benchmarks, including four industrial cryptographic components of openHiTLS (ML-DSA, SLH-DSA, SHA-256/224, FrodoKEM), with no admitted obligations and under one person-day of reported human effort per benchmark. - The missing: There is no controlled baseline comparison — no head-to-head run against AutoRocq, FM-Agent, or manual verification on the same inputs — and the six benchmarks are self-selected, so the reported cost figures cannot be interpreted as a success rate over arbitrary C codebases. - Read it or not: Read it if you work on LLM-assisted deductive verification or formal assurance of C libraries; the interface-protocol formalism and honest trust-boundary accounting are substantive, but practitioners seeking a ready-to-use tool or a measured comparison of automation strategies will find only an early framework and a case-study evaluation.

Show full analysis
Problem & Motivation: Safety-critical C codebases need formal verification, but Hoare-style verification in an ITP requires both expressive function contracts and machine-checked body proofs, and the two are coupled: a proof stalls exactly where a specification is too strong, too weak, or mis-shaped (illustrated with a signed-overflow obligation on `c = c + 1` in a linked-list length function). Existing LLM work splits into proof-generation methods that take specifications as given, and contract-synthesis methods validated by auto-active backends rather than an ITP kernel — neither co-evolves the pair. A second, harder problem arises for open libraries with no designated client: requirements are stated over sequences of interface calls, and per-module proofs do not establish that the exported interfaces support those sequences. This is the problem of the maintainers and assurance engineers of safety-critical C libraries (e.g., cryptographic libraries), who currently must absorb both costs as manual expert work. Key Idea: The core move is to insert a reviewable, resource-aware interface protocol — a state machine whose states carry separation-logic interpretations (global invariants, borrowed resources, library-owned objects), whose edges are source-state-specific Hoare triples, and whose per-edge subsumption obligations connect it to the verified function contracts — into the assurance chain. This converts the vague question "do the library's interfaces conform to its requirements?" into (i) machine-checkable subsumption proofs and a protocol soundness theorem (conditional safety for all client executions realizing a valid run, given verified contracts and caller obligations) plus (ii) an explicit, documented human conformance judgment over the protocol and specifications. The second key mechanism is specification–proof co-evolution: proof feedback drives revisions to contracts, protocol, and proofs rather than treating initial specifications as fixed. Methodology: CCV builds a five-component assurance case (C codebase → Clight AST via CompCert's front end → verified specifications → interface protocol → requirements) with three kernel-checked relations and one human review relation. Preprocessing establishes a frozen Clight program with a regeneration check and distinguishes trusted translation from semantics-changing adaptations. Phase I (V_Analyze, V_Specify) derives natural-language contracts top-down from requirements and caller demands (inspired by FM-Agent's caller-expectation view), then formalizes bottom-up callee-to-caller, producing resource predicates, funspecs, and a protocol configuration (states S = S_G × S_B × S_L, guards G_f, branch families Br_f, transition judgment, edge specifications). Phase II (V_Prove) constructs modular body proofs by VST forward symbolic execution and discharges per-edge subsumption entailments P^E ⊢ F ∗ P and F ∗ ∃o. Q ⊢ Q^E, plus a generic run-lifting proof for protocol soundness; failed proofs feed back into specification and protocol revision. Human gates (optional early V_Review, mandatory V_Confirm) assess scope and conformance to design intent. Model-quality checks include logical realizability via a covering witness run. Critical design decisions: (1) the LLM agent is deliberately outside the TCB (Rocq kernel re-checks everything); (2) conformance is an explicit, recorded human judgment rather than something the theorem pretends to establish — well justified by cited evidence that statement review cannot be eliminated; (3) branches are existentially quantified in postconditions, handling nondeterministic outcomes — the formalism (Definitions 1–9, Theorem 10) is worked out carefully, though the proof sketch is only sketched in the paper and the mechanization is in the artifact. Key Results: Six C benchmarks totaling 299 function definitions across 18 translation units: red–black tree (287 LOC, 12 functions), linked list (148 LOC, 10), ML-DSA (~2,439 LOC, 105), SLH-DSA (1,981 LOC, 97), SHA-256/224 (667 LOC, 25), FrodoKEM (1,747 LOC, 50). All 299 functions verified for memory safety and leak freedom under disclosed contracts, with zero admitted obligations, in Rocq 9.0.0 / VST 2.16 / CompCert 3.17. For four open-library cases, interface protocols with per-edge subsumption proofs and covering witnesses were delivered. Recorded costs: elapsed times of 1.55 d (tree) to 17.03 d (FrodoKEM, of which 193.1 h was confirmed model-service downtime, giving 8.99 d net), token usage up to ~25.9B (ML-DSA), and under one person-day human effort per benchmark — but token records are missing for SLH-DSA and the red–black tree, and runs used different models (GLM-5.3/GLM-5.3-Flash via OpenCode for SHA-256/224; Claude Opus 5 via Claude Code for FrodoKEM), so the authors themselves state no controlled efficiency comparison is possible. There is no success-rate measurement over unselected code. A notable qualitative finding: reviewing the SHA-256/224 case exposed a genuine library defect (a self-copy `CopyCtx(ctx, ctx)` excluded by the generated contract due to overlapping memcpy operands), demonstrating that conformance review catches things proof success does not. There is no baseline comparison — the evaluation is a case-study, not a controlled experiment. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD (in integration) and NEW FORMULATION (partially) plus NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING (weak). The authors are explicit and credible about what is not new: resource-transformer interfaces (VST, RefinedC), API-call automata (typestate, behavioral interface synthesis, specification mining), and caller-driven specification inference (maximal specification synthesis, angelic verification, FM-Agent) all predate this work. What is genuinely new is the organization: a reviewed, separation-logic-interpreted protocol layer whose enabled edges are justified by machine-checked subsumption to kernel-checked function contracts, embedded in an end-to-end assurance workflow with an explicit soundness theorem and human gates. The interface-protocol formalism itself is a competent composition of known separation-logic and typestate ideas rather than a new theory. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are absent: there is no experiment isolating whether the interface protocol, the co-evolution loop, or specific prompting/model choices drive the results, and no measurement of how much review effort the protocol adds. No error bars, seeds, or significance tests — understandable for a verification artifact, but cost figures are single uncontrolled runs with mixed models and missing records. The paper states results are "supported by archived source, specifications, proofs, certificates, and verification reports," but no public URL or repository is given in the text provided. Methodological concerns: (1) benchmarks were selected by the authors and developed with the tool, so the effort and cost numbers are not representative (the authors acknowledge this); (2) the human-effort figure (<1 person-day) is self-reported without a described measurement protocol; (3) model identity varies across benchmarks, confounding any cross-benchmark cost reading. On the positive side, the trust-boundary accounting is unusually rigorous: the TCB is enumerated (Rocq kernel, VST + CompCert Clight semantics, configured front-end path, correctness-critical gate code), admitted obligations are gated to zero, and axioms/premises are audited and disclosed. Deployability: Profile: SYSTEMS (a built workflow/tool evaluated on real codebases, though delivered as a research framework). - Practical: Runs on LLM API access plus a Rocq/VST/CompCert toolchain — commercially available, though VST expertise is needed for review. - Efficient: Token consumption is large (up to ~25.9B tokens for ~2.4K LOC of ML-DSA) and wall-clock runs span days (8.99–17 d for the largest cases); cost relative to a human expert is plausibly favorable but relative to other automation is unmeasured. - Effective: Machine-checked memory safety and leak freedom for all functions is solid evidence for the stated (narrow) scope; conformance to requirements rests on human review, and functional correctness, termination, and concurrency are explicitly out of scope — the delivered artifact solves a proxy, by design. - Scalable: Tested up to 105 functions / ~2.4K LOC per benchmark; behavior at 10–100× scale is untested and only implied, and review burden (currently the explicit human gate) may become the bottleneck. The work delivers a verification workflow and archived proof artifacts rather than a packaged library or CLI; no trained model or reusable tool release is described beyond the archived case materials. Strengths: - The interface protocol formalism with per-edge subsumption and a conditional protocol soundness theorem is a genuine technical contribution: it makes the previously manual "do the interfaces compose?" obligation partially machine-checkable while honestly bounding what the theorem does and does not claim (caller obligations, realizability limits, non-maximality of the accepted language). - The specification–proof co-evolution loop is well-motivated by a concrete, convincing failure example (the overflow goal forcing a strengthened precondition) that shows why proof-only or spec-only automation is insufficient. - Trust-boundary discipline is exemplary: the LLM is kept outside the TCB, admitted obligations are gated to zero, axioms and adaptations are disclosed per-case, and human conformance judgment is positioned on the critical path rather than papered over — directly informed by documented failures elsewhere (silent theorem weakening in machine-generated developments). - Evaluation on four industrial cryptographic components of openHiTLS (ML-DSA, SLH-DSA, SHA-256/224, FrodoKEM) is far above the usual benchmark-toy scale for VST verification, and the SHA-256/224 self-copy defect found during review is a real, satisfying demonstration that the review layer earns its keep. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state that guarantees are conditional on disclosed contracts, external-function specifications, allocator premises, and the CompCert Clight semantics (executable code requires a downstream verified-compilation step); that conformance of specifications and the protocol to intended requirements is a human judgment, not a theorem; that the accepted protocol language is not proven maximal or complete; that the covering witness does not prove state/branch satisfiability in general; that there is no client-side checker, no termination or liveness guarantees, and no callback or concurrency protocols; and that functional correctness of the cryptographic algorithms is out of scope. They also state plainly that the cases show completed verification on selected programs, not a success rate over arbitrary C. This is direct, non-minimizing confrontation of limitations — a strong credibility signal. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - No controlled comparison against any alternative (AutoRocq, FM-Agent, CLEVER-style pipelines, or manual verification on a slice), so neither the cost claims nor the framework's contribution over a simpler LLM-plus-VST pipeline is isolated. - No ablation of the interface protocol: for the two cases delivered without one, the function-level results are similar in kind; the protocol's cost–benefit (extra tokens, extra review time, extra proofs vs. assurance gained) is never quantified. - Heterogeneous models across benchmarks (GLM-5.3 vs. Claude Opus 5) and missing token records for two benchmarks undermine the cost table's comparability; the authors note this but the evaluation design could have avoided it. - The "less than one person-day" human effort is self-reported with no description of who reviewed, for how long, or how conformance review of e.g. ML-DSA's 105 functions was actually performed — the very gate the whole assurance case rests on is the least measured quantity in the paper. - Benchmark selection is circular: the tool, the benchmarks, and the reviewers share authors and institutional context (openHiTLS collaboration), and no external or adversarial codebase is attempted. - The paper reports two safety properties only; claims about the framework's generality to richer requirement classes (functional correctness of the crypto primitives, resource bounds) are left entirely untested. Bottom Line: For researchers in LLM-assisted formal verification and assurance of C systems, this paper is worth reading for its interface-protocol formalism and unusually honest trust-boundary treatment; for practitioners, it is an early, expensive, expert-supervised case study rather than a deployable alternative, and the missing baselines and self-selected benchmarks mean no conclusion about relative cost-effectiveness can yet be drawn.

nanoMuse: An Open-Source Personal Agent for Every Device You Own (83 ▲ )

Guangyi Liu, Yong Liu, Jiangning Zhang · arxiv.org · Daily papers of 8 Oct 2026

Problem & Motivation: Personal agents — programs that act for one person across their accounts, devices, and files over weeks — arrived commercially in September 2026 (Muse, Today, Manus Cue, OpenAI dots), but all share one architecture: a cloud VM per person, thin clients, a vendor-trained model, closed code, and (for Muse) US-only availability. Prior open projects each cover only a slice: Hermes Agent and OpenClaw have no screen access, OpenMinis is a phone-only agent without cross-device identity or memory, and OpenMuse (CopilotKit) is a server with windows onto it. The gap is that no open system lets one agent hold accounts, memory, and screen-level hands on the devices where a person's actual life lives (banking and government apps have no API or web page), while remaining inspectable and self-hostable. Key Idea: Two ideas carry the paper. First, invert the vendor architecture: instead of one agent in the cloud with thin clients, put a whole agent (its own Sentinel and file memory) on every device and let them meet over an optional relay, so a device works alone with just an API key and the shared surface is the only network component. Second, the "governable hands" trick: in the screenshot-action loop, the model must emit a one-sentence natural-language statement of what it is about to do, because a deterministic policy cannot judge a picture but can judge words — enabling label-based sensitivity rules ("confirm payment," "send," "delete" force per-step approval) that no mode or list can waive. Methodology: This is a systems paper, not an experimental one. The pipeline is: (1) a definitional section — five questions (what it knows, where it acts, whom it answers to, how it learns, how it is paid for/governed) and three horizons — that functions as the design spec; (2) a source-attributed reconstruction of Muse's architecture from four Meta public documents plus an unverifiable copy of its production system prompt, with every statement tagged documented/prompt/observed/inferred; (3) the nanoMuse construction: Android app built on modified OpenMinis (sandboxed Alpine Linux, shell, browser, MCP servers), desktop app as an Electron shell around the DeepSeek harness carrying a Python runtime, phone Hands in the MemGUI-Bench operator dialect (one action per screenshot, goal, per-step one-sentence history, accessibility elements), computer Hands ported from UI-TARS-desktop; (4) a Sentinel with a fixed decision order (denied tools → user rules → allow/ask lists → taint → risk-vs-mode → unwaivable warnings), scoped grants (once / this conversation / always-for-recipient) with a revocation UI, and full decision logging; (5) cross-device execution where any device's agent can invoke another's as a tool, with jobs running under the target device's own Sentinel so a requester cannot lend permissions it lacks. Critical design decisions: policy-boundary-in-process rather than privilege boundary (acknowledged as a real compromise), lowest-rung-first action ladder (skill/CLI/MCP → fetched page → browser → screen), and trajectory-as-chat-record instead of Muse's dimmed live stage. Justification is argumentative, not experimental. Key Results: There are no accuracy, success-rate, or benchmark results. The quantitative content is system footprint and cost self-reported by the authors: Android app 38 MB (arm64); desktop 256–498 MB download, 928 MB installed on Linux, ~0.5 GB idle memory; relay one Python process + SQLite at ~85 MB idle, sized for 1 vCPU/1 GB; self-hosting ¥30–60/month (China) or US$4–6/month plus model usage; model pricing from Bailian's October 2026 list (¥2/¥8 per million tokens chat, ¥3/¥12 for the hands model). The comparison table against Muse, Today, OpenMuse, Manus Cue, OpenAI dots, Hermes Agent, OpenClaw, and OpenMinis is a feature matrix, not a measurement. No baselines are run, and the authors state plainly: "We have no success rate and no count of human take-overs to report." Stress-scale is not tested; the relay is explicitly sized for the smallest server tier. Novelty Classification: NEW SYSTEM/TOOL with elements of NEW FORMULATION (the five-questions definition of a personal agent and the approvals-as-grammar-of-trust framing) and NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING in a weak sense (the source-tagged reconstruction of Muse's architecture). Genuinely novel: the first open-source system combining on-device agents, phone-screen control, per-device Sentinels, and a shared relay in one account — per the paper's own table, no prior system (including OpenMinis, its base) has all of these. The parts are standard combinations of existing ideas: OpenMinis, DeepSeek harness, UI-TARS-desktop operator, MemGUI-Bench operator dialect, MCP, Markdown memory files echoing OpenClaw's convention. The Sentinel-as-decision-order and the natural-language action sentence as a policy-judgable interface are the most original technical moves. Rigor & Reproducibility: There are no ablations, no seeds, no significance tests, and no benchmarks run — rigor is architectural rather than empirical. Code is released at github.com/nano-muse/nanoMuse with a live demo at nanomuse.cn, versioned to v0.1.40, and the release notes/changelog are cited as the record. Methodological concerns: (1) the Muse reconstruction rests partly on a production prompt copy whose provenance the authors admit they cannot verify beyond internal consistency; (2) all size and cost figures are self-described estimates from the project's own documentation and provider price lists, not measurements of third-party usage; (3) the system is evaluated on nothing except its own existence — no AndroidWorld, OSWorld, MemGUI-Bench, or OS-Harm numbers despite these being named as the right tools in the roadmap. To the authors' credit, the absence of evaluation is stated rather than hidden, which is unusual and increases trust in the reported numbers that do exist. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: SYSTEMS (a built, released, versioned tool evaluated by existence and footprint, not deployment metrics). - Practical: Yes — it runs on consumer phones and laptops, needs only an OpenAI-compatible API key or a ChatGPT plan, and a single device requires no server at all. - Efficient: Roughly one order of magnitude leaner than a per-person cloud VM (0.5 GB RAM idle per device, ~85 MB relay, ¥30–60/month hosting) plus token costs of a few fen per day of chat by the authors' estimate. - Effective: Only partially — the architecture exists and works end to end, but whether the Hands actually complete real phone/desktop tasks is unmeasured; the evidence is functional, not performance evidence. - Scalable: Untested — the relay is one Python process with SQLite, fine for a household, but behavior at 10×–100× concurrent users on a shared community relay is only claimed via sizing guidance, not measured. The work delivers a substantial software artifact (five apps, relay, console, self-hosting script) plus a reusable design framework, not just a paper. Strengths: - The Sentinel's fixed decision order with taint-in-conversation, unwaivable warnings, and scoped grants (a payment is never remembered "however often the person says always") is a concrete, inspectable trust grammar that goes beyond the usual "human in the loop" slogan. - The governable-hands trick — requiring a natural-language action sentence so a deterministic policy, not the model, classifies sensitivity — is a genuinely clever interface between probabilistic and rule-based safety. - The source-tagged (documented/prompt/observed/inferred) reconstruction of Muse is careful epistemic practice for reverse-engineering a closed system, and is independently useful as the most detailed public anatomy of a shipped personal agent. - Honest self-reporting: publishing that no success rates exist, flagging the least-sure design choice (default-on training data switch), and explicitly separating claims from estimates build real credibility. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors are unusually direct: (1) the Sentinel is a policy boundary, not a privilege boundary — a device compromise is an agent compromise, and the taint rule and sandbox mitigate but do not solve this; (2) Hands are unmeasured — no success rate, no take-over counts, icon-only buttons in unlabeled apps defeat the label-based policy, and Linux support is X11-only; (3) memory lacks provenance — no model, date, or confidence per line, and no re-checking rule, so a weak model's guess is read as fact by a stronger one; (4) the community relay keeps synced text on a machine the project runs, and the default-on model-training switch is flagged as the choice they are "least sure of"; (5) the Muse account rests on an unverifiable prompt copy that may be stale. These are confronted head-on, not minimized — a strong credibility signal. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - The single largest gap, only partially acknowledged: the paper names its own evaluation suite (AndroidWorld, OSWorld, MemGUI-Bench, OS-Harm) as future work while shipping none of it — even a small run on one benchmark would have transformed the paper's evidentiary standing. - No security evaluation of the Sentinel: the decision order is asserted, never tested against a prompt-injection corpus or an adversarial agent attempting to phrase a committing action in innocuous words — the exact attack the sentence-based policy invites (a model can write "tapping the button" for a payment button). - Heavy self-citation concentration (five of the key technical substrates — MemGUI-Bench, MAS-Bench, MobileForge, LearnAct, the survey — are the first author's own work), which is not disclosed as a potential conflict in positioning. - The iOS story is thin: the iPhone agent has no hands and no stated plan beyond citing Apple's restriction, leaving a major device class structurally limited. - The claim that one device can "ask" another's agent as a tool crosses a trust boundary between devices whose interaction with the taint rule (does taint propagate across device invocations?) is not specified in the text. - The report reads partly as project advocacy (roadmap, community recruitment); a reviewer must discount the unmeasured superiority claims against Muse accordingly. Bottom Line: For practitioners building personal agents or thinking about trust boundaries for screen-operating AI, this is worth reading as the most complete public anatomy of the personal-agent product category and a serious open reference architecture — but it is a v0.1 system with zero performance evidence, so anyone needing measured capability should wait for the promised evaluation suite rather than treat this as proof the approach works.

TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces EmbodiRSI, an agentic real-to-sim-to-real system in which a robot manipulation policy recursively improves itself by using its own rollout failures in a reconstructed task-specific simulation to steer corrective-trajectory generation and targeted data collection. - Why it's important: Adapting manipulation policies to new environments is bottlenecked by expensive physical data collection; this work attacks the cost of adaptation data, claiming 83.1% real-world success from 10 real trajectories per subtask versus 75.0% for a baseline using 200 real demonstrations per subtask (a 20× reduction in physical data). - How it does it: The core mechanism is a closed loop that converts policy execution feedback into experience: an agentic monitor diagnoses failures, generates corrective trajectories from policy-reached failure states without task reset, attributes failures to reset configurations on a normalized grid, and shifts the demonstration-collection distribution toward diagnosed weak configurations, with advantage-conditioned behavior cloning (RECAP-style) updating the policy. - The good: The matched-budget control is credible: with identical 50-trajectory initialization, architecture, and training recipe, adaptive collection beats static collection by 20.6 percentage points of scene-balanced simulation success at 400 trajectories per subtask, and the advantage persists after real-world refinement (+14.2 pp). - The missing: There is no component-wise ablation isolating Collaborative Error Correction from Adaptive Data Collection (acknowledged by the authors), no comparison against external self-improvement baselines such as SOAR, RECAP, or RoboClaw, and no evidence of generalization to held-out workspaces or more than two RSI rounds. - Read it or not: Read it if you work on robot self-improvement, real2sim pipelines, or agentic data collection and want a well-documented systems blueprint with honest statistics; skip it if you need theoretically grounded or ablation-decomposed evidence about which feedback mechanism matters.

Problem & Motivation: Practitioners deploying general-purpose manipulation policies (π0.5-class VLAs) face systematic, shifting failure modes when a policy moves to a new environment: states reached after a missed grasp are absent from nominal demonstrations, and the configurations where the policy fails change as it improves. Prior approaches address pieces of this — DAgger-style aggregation, intervention/recovery methods, agentic collection pipelines, and real2sim2real transfer systems (RialTo, ReBot, X-SIM, RoboTwin 2.0) — but none, per the authors, couple within-episode recovery to across-episode recollection driven by the evolving policy's own failure distribution. The gap is a system that turns observed failures into targeted, low-cost training experience without human involvement at every iteration. Key Idea: Treat the deployment-specific simulation not as a one-time data generator but as a persistent practice environment, and use the policy's failure statistics as a curriculum: attribute each final failure to the source-object reset, the target-anchor reset, or neither; compute attributed-failure rates on a normalized grid over each reset range; and sample new demonstration configurations from a mixture p_{k+1}(c) = (1−α)p0(c) + α·p_hard,k(c) concentrated on weak cells. This is paired with Collaborative Error Correction, where a nominal grasp is transported to the object's current pose via T_g^cur = T_o^cur (T_o^0)^{-1} T_g^0 so recovery solves the task from the state the policy actually reached. Methodology: The pipeline has three stages. (1) Real2Sim construction: SAM 3 masks and SAM 3D meshes reconstruct the tabletop; support-aware collision rectification (parallel horizontal rectification across groups, relation-specific intra-group fixes) and coarse-to-fine agent-guided layout refinement produce an initial scene S0 and organized target scene Sorg. (2) Trajectory generation: an agent proposes object-space routes, projects them through GraspGen grasps, validates programs with cuRobo under swept-mesh, multi-view VLM review, sequential-motion, and execution-time checks (Eq. B.7), and re-grounds stored waypoints to measured poses after each reset. (3) The RSI loop (Algorithm 1): roll out πk under an agentic monitor (decide continue/recover/complete from images, action history, and simulator state), retain rollout-derived episodes, attribute failures, form p_{k+1}, generate new validated demonstrations, and retrain with advantage-conditioned BC — L(θ) = E[ℓ_BC(π_θ(·|o_t,l,z_t), a_t)] where z_t is a binary advantage label from a value-model estimate (Â_t^(50) > δ) following RECAP. After two simulated rounds, ten real HIL trajectories per subtask refine the policy. Critical design decisions: simulator state is available to the training-time monitor but never to the learned policy (justified, avoids privileged-information leakage); evaluation disables all agent takeover (clearly separated in logging); unsuccessful rollouts inform collection but are excluded from policy training data — a decision disclosed in Appendix D.4 but not ablated, and arguably in tension with the stated advantage-conditioning objective that supposedly supports learning from failures. The number of rounds and data quotas are fixed in advance; feedback only shapes what is collected within that schedule, so this is bounded, budgeted recursion rather than open-ended RSI. Key Results: On a 14-DoF dual-arm ALOHA across three tabletop scenes and 14 subtasks (one policy per scene, initialized from π0.5, GPT-5.5-based agents, Isaac Sim): scene-balanced autonomous simulation success rises from 50.4% (R0) to 70.7% (R1) to 83.5% (R2), with all 14 subtasks improving (e.g., black-pen placement 14.0%→76.5%). In the matched-budget comparison (S1 and S3, 400 retained trajectories per subtask), adaptive collection reaches 79.9% versus 59.3% for static collection (+20.6 pp simulation; +12.9 pp real before HIL; +14.2 pp after ten HIL trajectories). Real-world: 83.1% scene-balanced success with 400 simulated + 10 HIL trajectories per subtask versus 75.0% for Real-only adaptation with 200 real demonstrations per subtask; Real-only 10/100 yield 26.1%/57.2%. Zero-shot R2 achieves 62.8% real success before refinement. Real tests are ten autonomous trials per task per setting (140 episodes per fully evaluated setting). Baselines (static collection, real-only demonstrations) are reasonable internal controls but no external self-improvement system is compared against. Scale is modest: tabletop scenes, two RSI rounds, single training run per scene policy. One counter-intuitive detail: S1 mouse placement decreases from 67.6% to 59.1% as static data grows, and one S3 task is slightly better under static collection — task-level exceptions are honestly reported. Novelty Classification: NEW SYSTEM/TOOL with an NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING component. The genuinely novel element is the configuration-level adaptive collection mechanism — grid-based failure attribution over reset ranges steering demonstration generation within a fixed budget — combined with the coupling of within-episode corrective recovery and across-episode recollection inside a retained deployment-specific simulation. The rest is a competent integration of existing components: RECAP's advantage conditioning, MimicGen-style demonstration amplification, GraspGen/cuRobo motion tooling, SAM 3/SAM 3D reconstruction, and the real2sim2real paradigm of Torne et al. and successors. No new learning algorithm is proposed; the recursion operates through data, not through the learning formulation. Rigor & Reproducibility: Statistical hygiene is better than typical robotics papers: Wilson 95% intervals per task (n=10 real trials), explicit distinction between subtask-dispersion SDs and independent runs, scene-balanced versus pooled weighting, and per-subtask differences with means and SDs. However, there are no multiple training seeds — each scene policy is trained once, so round-over-round gains carry no run-level error bars. Ablations are absent: the system is evaluated only as a whole, and the authors concede that component attribution (recovery vs. recollection vs. agent reasoning) is not done. The static-collection control is a fair internal ablation of feedback-driven acquisition but is not an external baseline. Code is promised ("will be released soon") but not released; the pipeline depends on proprietary GPT-5.5 and pre-release models (SAM 3, π0.5), which limits reproducibility regardless. Evaluation is on the authors' own three workspaces with the simulation built from observations of those same workspaces, so sim and real test distributions are coupled by construction. The arXiv preprint has not (per the text) undergone peer review. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL (a built system with real and simulated rollouts). Practical: Requires an ALOHA-class dual-arm robot, multi-camera setup, Isaac Sim, GPU training of π0.5-scale policies, and paid LLM API calls — beyond hobbyist hardware but standard for robotics labs. Efficient: The headline is data efficiency (20× fewer physical trajectories than the matched-performance baseline), but the paper counts only retained trajectories, not VLM calls, recovery interventions, validation-repair cycles, or total simulation attempts — the true compute and engineering cost is not stated. Effective: The evidence shows it solves the evaluated adaptation problem on the authors' own scenes and tasks; success on these 14 scripted tabletop rearrangement subtasks is a proxy for general adaptation. Scalable: Not tested — only two RSI rounds, tabletop only, scenes where the policy starts at 50.4%; behavior at harder initial performance, more rounds, or non-tabletop geometry is unexamined, and the fixed-budget schedule sidesteps the question of whether the loop sustains improvement. Deliverable: a system with a promised (not yet available) full-pipeline code release; currently stops at paper form. Strengths: - The matched-trajectory static-collection control directly tests the paper's central claim (feedback-driven acquisition beats static distribution) rather than only comparing against real-data baselines, and the +20.6 pp simulation / +14.2 pp real gap is large and consistent across 9 of 10 compared subtasks. - Clean separation of training-time agent assistance from autonomous evaluation, with logging that distinguishes recovery requests, executed corrections, and final outcomes — this pre-empts the most common way such systems overstate results (planner-assisted test rollouts). - The adaptive collection mechanism is concrete and inspectable: attributed-failure rates on a normalized grid, a documented mixture distribution, and reuse of stored VLM attributions without repeated calls. - Transparent data accounting (Appendix D separates D0, monitored rollouts, corrections, and new demonstrations) and honest reporting of task-level regressions and ties. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state (Section 5) that evaluation is limited to the selected workspaces with no held-out scenes and only short improvement runs, and that no component-wise ablation separates recovery, recollection, and agent reasoning. They confront these directly rather than minimizing them, and defer targeted ablations to future work. They also candidly note in the analysis that the pretrained policy's prior capabilities contribute to final performance and that the failure-concentration statistic is a heuristic, not an estimate of learning gain. Analyst-Identified Gaps: Beyond the acknowledged limitations: (1) no external baseline from the RSI literature the paper itself surveys (SOAR, RECAP, RoboClaw, RISE, VERITAS), so it is impossible to tell whether the gains come from the specific feedback mechanisms or from simply adding more curated simulation data over more training; (2) only ultimately-successful trajectories are retained for policy training despite the advantage-conditioning formulation nominally supporting failure learning — this undisclosed-in-advance choice needs an ablation; (3) failure attribution rests on VLM judgments whose accuracy is never measured, and mis-attribution would silently corrupt the collection distribution; (4) simulation test-episode counts vary by task–checkpoint pair and are not reported in the main text, complicating comparison of sim numbers; (5) Real2Sim fidelity is never quantified (no reconstruction-error or dynamics-gap measurement), so the sim-real transfer margin is unknown; (6) all gains are within the same scenes used to build the simulation, leaving Goodhart-style coupling between the training environment and test environment untested; (7) the computational budget of agent calls, replanning, and rejected candidate trajectories is unreported, so the claimed efficiency is measured only in retained trajectories. Bottom Line: For robotics researchers building self-improving or real2sim systems, this is a worthwhile and unusually well-accounted systems reference whose adaptive-collection mechanism is genuinely useful — but its evidence base (two rounds, three own-built scenes, no component ablation, no external baseline, code not yet released) means it should be read as a credible blueprint, not as proof that recursive self-improvement generalizes.

Recursive Self - Improvement of Visuomotor Policies through Local Recovery Supervision

Y Zhang, X Liu, Y Zhang · arxiv.org · recursive self-improvement - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces a recursive self-improvement (RSI) framework in which an offline auditor localizes unresolved failures of a frozen visuomotor student, a fixed tool-using multimodal teacher generates local recovery demonstrations from evidence-supported entry states, and the frozen student's own continuation behavior determines how far each demonstration must extend before the corrected data is distilled back into the student via quality-weighted post-training. - Why it's important: Visuomotor policies execute familiar tasks but cannot recover from their own mistakes, and human-in-the-loop correction (DAgger-style intervention) is expensive; an automatic teacher that targets a policy's actual failure states could close the recovery gap without a human in the loop or a deployed teacher. - How it does it: Three boundary decisions are decoupled and driven by different evidence — failure evidence selects the intervention state (entry), the student's executed continuation from the teacher endpoint decides whether the demonstration is long enough (endpoint, with restore-and-extend on failed handoffs), and an offline per-action quality grader selects continuous training windows (η=0.75 threshold) with validity masks so only teacher actions become imitation targets. - The good: The matched-budget comparison is well-controlled — from the same π0 checkpoint with identical 2,000 additional updates, recovery augmentation converts 18 previously failing validation episodes to successes versus 8 the other way, and the honest reporting of the non-significant McNemar p-value (0.0755) is a credibility positive. - The missing: The headline result rests on one training seed, validation scenes that were also used to select the source checkpoint, and no statistically significant paired difference — and the central 'recursive' claim (multi-round improvement) is never run; Section 5 is a protocol, not results. - Read it or not: Worth reading for robotics/IL researchers working on automated correction-data generation or self-improvement loops (a thoughtful decomposition of where interventions start, end, and get trusted), but practitioners seeking validated recipes should wait for the multi-round, multi-seed evaluation the authors themselves specify as unfinished.

Problem & Motivation Visuomotor policies (π0, Octo, generalist VLAs) learn tasks from demonstrations but fail to recover when execution deviates — e.g., continuing a transport motion with an empty gripper after a missed grasp. Recovery benchmarks (RoboRecover, LIBERO-RECOVER) show this gap explicitly. Existing remedies either require human intervention (HG-DAgger, human-in-the-loop teleoperation), complete the task from the failure state without deciding where the demonstration should start or end, or generate recovery data without conditioning on the recipient policy's competence. The open question the authors pose: when an automatic teacher turns a policy's failures into supervision, what determines the demonstration's entry, endpoint, and which of its actions deserve imitation? This becomes acute under recursion — updating the policy changes the states it visits, so a fixed recovery dataset stops targeting its weaknesses. Key Idea Decouple the three boundary decisions of a corrective demonstration and ground each in different evidence: (1) entry is chosen by offline coarse-to-dense temporal evidence of an unresolved failure (with Focus/Coverage selection modes), not at the first anomaly; (2) endpoint is determined by the frozen student's actual continuation from the teacher's saved state — if the student cannot sustain progress, the system restores the teacher endpoint and extends the demonstration, so demonstration length depends on the recipient's behavior rather than teacher confidence; (3) imitation targets are continuous intervals above a per-action quality grade, so detours and retreats within an accepted path can be excluded while a necessary retreat is retained. The student's failed branches supply diagnostic evidence only, never labels. Methodology The pipeline is: (a) Audit — a localization model reads a coarse rollout (~1 frame/sec plus motion-change centers), then dense inspection (~96 samples over a ±0.5s local window) to characterize an unresolved event and return 0–3 supported entry states with evidence citations; (b) Specification freeze — a model writes a structured local goal Γr = (gr, Er, br; Pr, fr, cr) with 1–3 AND-composed teacher completion checks grounded in observable RGB/proprioception, and OR-composed student progress alternatives; (c) Teacher execution — a fixed tool-using multimodal agent (reported as 'gpt-6.1-sol', medium reasoning) runs observe/compute/act/inspect loops through native actions (1–40 steps per request), must justify completion from observation records, and gets no privileged state; (d) Student handoff test — the frozen student branches from the saved endpoint, an observer checks preserved relations plus new progress (HS=60, Δ=10, C=10) with a formal acceptance rule (Eq. 7); on failure, the endpoint is restored by simulator replay and the teacher appends a further stage (≤5 stages, ≤300 teacher actions, ≤7200s per attempt); (e) Offline grading — a separate privileged evaluator assigns each executed teacher action an ordinal quality qi ∈ {0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1}; maximal continuous runs with qi ≥ 0.75 and length ≥ 5 become training windows with true pre-action observations; (f) Post-training — the student's native objective (flow matching for π0) is weighted as L = Σ mᵢqᵢℓᵢ / max(1, Σ mᵢ), with validity masks clearing action targets, noisy action inputs, flow targets, and attention for π0's action chunks. The outer loop (Eq. 11) re-audits the updated student each round. Critical design decisions: student-driven endpoint extension (justified by the failed-grasp example but not ablated), quality weighting without renormalization (denominator counts valid targets, not weight mass — plausible but not justified experimentally), and teacher/student sensor alignment with an information gap only via the specification document (reasonable, but the teacher still holds session memory and tool documentation the student lacks). Key Results π0 on a custom LIBERO-Goal split (seed 7, 30/10/10 scenes per task): the 3,000-update checkpoint M0 scores 77/100 on 100 validation scenes; after 2,000 matched additional updates, original-data continuation reaches 78/100 while recovery-augmented continuation reaches 88/100 (+10 points; paired McNemar two-sided p = 0.0755, not significant at 0.05). Recovery data was small: 27 accepted teacher paths / 3,974 native actions from 67 audited failures, yielding 1,639 windows covering 2,095 distinct actions — 4.14% of training anchors. Gains are non-uniform: 5 tasks improve, 4 unchanged, 1 declines (e.g., 'put cream cheese in bowl' 3→8, 'push plate' 10→9). The earlier BC-RNN study on robomimic Can: 26 recovery segments (+2,547 labels) raise success from 102/130 (78.46%) to 112/130 (86.15%) over matched continuation (source policy: 91/130); this study predates endpoint extension and quality windows, so it tests only the local-supervision principle. Both comparisons use one training seed and a teacher absent at evaluation. No multi-round recursion was run; Section 5 is a prospective protocol only. Scale is standard-benchmark (LIBERO-Goal, robomimic Can), not stress-scale. Novelty Classification NEW FORMULATION and NEW METHOD, with a candidate NEW SYSTEM/TOOL. Genuinely novel: the decomposition of recovery-demonstration boundaries into evidence-supported entry, student-execution-supported endpoint, and quality-supported imitation intervals — particularly the frozen-student handoff test with endpoint restore-and-extend, which makes demonstration length a function of the recipient policy; no cited prior work (IntervenGen, Kintsugi-VLA, WM-DAgger, MAGMA-GEN) uses the recipient's continuation to bound the demonstration. The components are largely known techniques — DAgger-style correction data, LLM/tool-agent teachers (Agent as Policy, Code as Policies), quality-weighted behavior cloning (SSDF), flow-matching fine-tuning of π0 — combined in a new, well-motivated configuration. The 'recursive' framing inherits from RoboCat/EmbodiRSI. Rigor & Reproducibility Method-level care is high: formal acceptance rules, explicit evidence constraints, matched optimization budgets, paired episode reporting, and separate accounting of diagnostic vs. target actions. But the empirical evidence is thin: (1) one training seed per comparison, with the authors' own McNemar test failing the 0.05 threshold (p = 0.0755); (2) the validation scenes used to report results were also used to select M0 (checkpoint 3,000 of 5,000), and the reserved test split was never evaluated — a Goodhart/selection-bias exposure the authors acknowledge; (3) the recovery dataset was assembled during system development with changing retry limits and prompts, so the teacher yield is not a fixed-protocol measurement; (4) no ablation of the method's own components (entry selection, endpoint extension, quality weighting, masking) — Section 5 specifies these as future work; (5) the BC-RNN result does not test the two most distinctive components (endpoint extension, quality windows). The teacher is identified only as 'gpt-6.1-sol' — a vendor-model dependency with no cross-teacher comparison and self-reported selection. No code, data, or weights release is mentioned. Preprint, not peer-reviewed. Deployability Profile: EMPIRICAL (simulation studies of a collection-and-training pipeline; no deployed system). Practical: Yes in simulation — three RTX A6000 GPUs, LoRA fine-tuning of π0 (~468M of 3.288B parameters trainable); on hardware it requires a control bridge to an LLM agent plus simulator-grade state restoration. Efficient: Training cost is matched to the baseline, but the true cost is collection-side (audit calls, teacher sessions, failed attempts, grading, replay) which the paper itself notes is uncharged and unquantified in wall-clock/dollar terms. Effective: Evidence shows improved nominal task success on one custom split with a non-significant paired difference; recovery-from-held-out-failure-states — the stated motivation — was specified but not measured. Scalable: Untested; the recursive loop ran zero complete rounds, so whether gains compound, plateau, or collapse across audits is open, and the teacher's per-attempt budgets (5 stages, 300 actions) cap per-failure cost but not per-round scaling. Deliverable status: paper with a described implementation; no released library, dataset, or trained model is stated. Strengths - The recipient-driven endpoint test is a genuinely new mechanism: using the frozen student's continuation (with restore-and-extend from saved teacher endpoints) to determine demonstration length, cleanly separating 'teacher can do it' from 'student can use it.' - The three-way boundary decomposition (entry/endpoint/targets) is a reusable conceptual contribution — it makes explicit design choices that prior recovery-data-generation work leaves implicit, and the formal acceptance rule (Eq. 7) is implementable as written. - The training-view engineering is careful and correct where most work is sloppy: true pre-action observations for each window anchor, validity masks that clear noisy action inputs and attention (not just the loss) for π0's chunked flow-matching, and no recovery oversampling — the gain comes from ~1.5% of target occurrences. - Unusually honest reporting: the authors volunteer the non-significant p-value, the validation/test-selection contamination, the development-time protocol drift, and specify the exact controls (Section 5) their claims still need. Author-Acknowledged Limitations The authors state: single seed; validation scenes used for checkpoint selection; non-significance (p = 0.0755); only one post-training update evaluated, not the recursive loop; teacher grading semantics are fallible LLM judgments with no ground-truth local-success oracle; exact state restoration requires simulation and multi-stage physical extension needs a validated reset procedure (untested on hardware); the BC-RNN study predates the endpoint-extension and quality-window components; collection cost is not equal across conditions. They confront limitations directly and extensively — Section 5 is essentially a self-review — which is a strong credibility signal, though it also concedes that most headline claims (recursion, generalization, physical deployment) are currently unverified. Analyst-Identified Gaps - No ablation isolates the contribution of the paper's signature mechanisms: whether student-driven endpoint extension beats simply demonstrating to local completion (the authors' own length-matched control, proposed but not run), and whether quality weighting beats whole-path imitation on the same archive. - The +10-point gain is within noise by the authors' own test; with one seed and no confidence intervals across training runs, the effect could plausibly be ±8 points of run-to-run variance under the 'edge of the statistical precipice' standards they cite. - Only 67 failures produced 27 accepted paths — the yield and the reason for ~60% of failures yielding nothing are unexamined, and Focus/Coverage selection is never compared to a trivial baseline (uniform sampling, coarse-only), so entry-selection value is unattributed. - The offline evaluator uses privileged simulation state to grade actions the student cannot observe — the paper notes this mismatch (scores are not 'inferable from the student's restricted input') but never tests whether graded quality correlates with student learning, and the teacher's own completion judgments are never validated against ground truth. - Single-teacher dependence ('gpt-6.1-sol') means the pipeline's sensitivity to the underlying model is unknown; no cross-family comparison or even a second checkpoint of the same model. - Nominal task success from standard starts is measured, but the motivating outcome — recovery success from a fixed bank of held-out failure states — was specified and omitted; the evaluated quantity is a proxy. Bottom Line A methodologically careful and conceptually fresh framework whose key mechanism — recipient-driven demonstration endpoints via frozen-student handoff tests — deserves attention from anyone building automated correction-data pipelines, but with one-seed, non-significant results on a contaminated validation split and zero completed recursion rounds, this is a well-specified research program in its first, unproven step rather than validated evidence, so read it for the formulation and Section 5 protocol, not for the numbers.

TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces EvoRiskBench, an executable benchmark of 450 adversarial tasks that evaluates runtime security of complete Model × Harness agent configurations under indirect prompt injection (IPI), organized around a 9-entry-point × 5-risk-effect taxonomy with independent outcome verification. - Why it's important: Workspace agents turn LLM outputs into real file, command, and network operations, and organizations currently have no systematic, executable way to measure which agent configurations are exploitable before deployment — existing benchmarks leave multi-agent and ecosystem entry points (peer-agent communication, subagent delegation, MCP services, skill invocation) largely uncovered. - How it does it: Each risk case is represented as EP→Path→EF (entry interface, agent-mediated execution path, one-hop technical effect);
