Problem & Motivation: Autoregressive video diffusion models generate frames sequentially, and each generated block must simultaneously be denoised (current content) and encoded into key-value representations (context for future blocks). Prior work (Self Forcing) blocked gradients to context writing for tractability, creating a supervision gap; the authors' predecessor SGF restored context-writing gradients via a two-pass differentiable replay, but both roles still updated the same parameters. Practitioners building streaming video generators and world models observe visual degradation and inconsistency on long rollouts; SGF additionally showed occasional worse initial-frame quality than SF. The paper asks whether shared parameters can at all serve both optimization demands, and answers no based on measured gradient conflict. Key Idea: The single core insight is that the context-writing gradient and the denoising gradient under the same generation objective are systematically anti-aligned (angles exceeding 90°, all measured pairs negative), so on shared weights they partially cancel; separating the two roles into distinct parameter sets θc and θd — while retaining forward coupling through causal attention — removes this cancellation at negligible inference cost, since each token still uses only one role's parameters per forward pass. Methodology: Training is a two-pass procedure built on SGF. Pass 1 runs a no-gradient autoregressive rollout of the denoiser D(θd) with the context writer C(θc) encoding each clean estimate into the KV cache, recording detached clean latents X and noisy exit latents Z*. Pass 2 reconstructs the computation in parallel under a causal mask with stop-gradient on X but differentiable KV construction, and applies the DMD distribution-matching loss L = L_DMD to target denoising predictions; gradients reach θc through the differentiable KV state and θd through target denoising. The only change from SGF is untying θ: C(θc) and D(θd) replace the shared D(θ)/C(θ). Critical design decisions: (1) full parameter separation rather than LoRA adapters or partial (Attention-only/FFN-only) separation — justified by the ablation in Table 2 showing partial separation underperforms full separation; (2) no auxiliary context loss — gradient supervision flows solely through the future-generation objective, argued as simpler than gradient-projection or loss-weighting alternatives; (3) Appendix G provides a local optimization analysis (Propositions G.1–G.2, Corollaries G.1–G.3) proving first-order descent advantages of split versus tied updates under both fixed-budget and common-learning-rate protocols. The theoretical analysis is a nice complement, though it is local/first-order and the authors themselves note the common-learning-rate protocol's comparison is regime-dependent (positive alignment would favor sharing). Key Results: Evaluated on VBench (5s in-horizon), VBench-Long prompts (60s = 12× training horizon), and MovieGen-128 prompts (240s = 48× horizon), in framewise and chunkwise modes, all three methods sharing initialization, prompts, and seeds. At 240s framewise, SGF+ reaches 98.74 Subject Consistency vs 97.07 (SGF) and 96.36 (SF), and 97.81 Background Consistency vs 96.81/96.42; similar ordering holds for flickering, motion smoothness, aesthetics, and imaging quality across horizons. SGF+ trained on 5s rollouts generates continuously for up to 24 hours (qualitative only, Appendix D). The Dynamic Degree metric drops sharply (e.g., 55.38 vs 71.19 for SGF at 60s framewise); the authors argue — plausibly but unverifiably — that baselines' higher scores reflect incoherent artifacts (scene jumps, deformed subjects) rather than better motion. Efficiency: doubling generator parameters from 1.4B to 2.8B raises training time per step by 8.2% (11.79→12.76 s), inference memory from 24.85 to 27.96 GB, with inference latency essentially unchanged (4.962→4.969 s for 81 frames). Baselines are not current strong external methods — they are SF and SGF from the same research group, at 1.3B student scale with a frozen 14B Wan2.1 teacher. Novelty Classification: NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING (the measured systematic negative alignment between context-writing and denoising gradients, shown also to exist at TF initialization) plus NEW METHOD (role-specific parameterization within self-forcing-style autoregressive video diffusion training). The training machinery — self-generated rollouts, two-pass differentiable replay, DMD distillation — is inherited wholesale from SGF; the genuinely novel element is the gradient-conflict diagnosis and the simplest possible architectural response (untied parameters), with supporting local optimization theory. This is an incremental but well-motivated step in a fast-moving lineage rather than a new formulation. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are present and informative: Attention-only vs FFN-only vs full parameter separation (Table 2) shows partial separation underperforms, supporting the claim that conflict exists in both module families. The gradient-conflict analysis is replicated at three points: during SGF training, at TF initialization, and layer-wise across 30 blocks (silhouette scores reported). However, no error bars, multiple seeds, or significance tests are reported for any generation metric, despite shared seeds across methods making variance estimation feasible. A project page exists (https://zihan-su.github.io/self-gradient-forcing-plus), but no code, data, or model weights release is stated in the provided text. Methodological concerns: (1) all baselines are the authors' own prior methods sharing the same initialization and training stack — no external long-video methods (LongLive, Self-Forcing++, Rolling Forcing, FreqForcing) are empirically compared despite being cited and discussed; (2) evaluation is exclusively VBench-derived metrics, whose correlation with perceived long-video quality is asserted rather than validated (no human study is mentioned in the provided text); (3) the Dynamic Degree dismissal, while plausible, conveniently converts a metric loss into a non-issue without a replacement motion-quality measurement. This is a preprint (arXiv v2), so claims carry pre-review confidence. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL (a trained system with quantitative and qualitative evaluation). Practical: Yes — built on Wan2.1-T2V-1.3B with ~28 GB inference memory, runnable on a single 32 GB+ GPU. Efficient: Favorable — inference latency is essentially unchanged versus SGF (+0.007 s per 81 frames) because each token uses only its role's parameters, at the cost of doubled stored weights and an 8.2% training-time increase. Effective: The evidence shows improvements on VBench-style consistency/quality proxies and qualitative long-rollout stability versus two same-family baselines, but not against the strongest external methods; the 24-hour claim is demonstrated only with sampled frames, not measured end-to-end. Scalable: Extrapolation to 48× the training horizon is actually tested at 240s, which is genuine evidence, but the 24-hour regime (≈17,000× the training window) is untested quantitatively; whether the sink-plus-FIFO context policy (12–21 latent window) suffices at that scale is asserted through examples only. The work delivers a trained model and method description; no released software artifact is confirmed in the paper text. Strengths: - The gradient-conflict analysis is a real, quantified empirical finding — 104.2°/106.3° mean angular separation, 512/512 negative cosine pairs, replicated at initialization and per-layer — rather than a post-hoc story; it gives the field a reusable diagnostic (role-stratified gradient cosine) for any shared-parameter autoregressive diffusion model. - The intervention is minimal and honest about it: no auxiliary losses, no extra data, no longer training horizon — the ablation attributing gains purely to parameter separation is clean because everything else is held fixed from SGF. - Appendix G supplies a genuine local optimization theory (quantifying the sharing restriction Γ = ½ − ⟨gC,gD⟩/E, and finite-step descent gaps), correctly distinguishing negative alignment from general gradient inequality and acknowledging where its own comparison protocols diverge — unusually careful for this literature. - The efficiency accounting is concrete and preempts the obvious objection that doubling parameters doubles cost, with per-step training time, memory, and latency measured for all three methods. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: - Dynamic Degree is lower for SGF+ across settings; the authors confront this directly and argue the metric rewards incoherent large motion (scene jumps, deformation, subject disappearance), backed by qualitative examples — credible, though they substitute argument for measurement. - Full parameter sets (2.8B) are used rather than LoRA or partial separation, doubling stored parameters; the cost is quantified but not optimized away. - The future-work section acknowledges that model merging or lightweight/asymmetric context writers might be better than naive duplication, and that world-action-model extensions are unexplored. The authors are generally forthright about scope; they do not, however, flag the absence of external baselines or human evaluation. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - The comparison set is a family reunion: SF and SGF share the authors' initialization, prompt pipeline, and context policy. Without at least one external long-video method (LongLive or Self-Forcing++ are the obvious candidates), the claim of "best visual quality and long-horizon consistency among the three methods" is technically accurate but scoped to the authors' own lineage — this is the single largest weakness. - No human evaluation or perceptual study is mentioned; the entire quality case rests on VBench-style proxy metrics plus selected qualitative frames, and the paper itself argues one of those metrics (Dynamic Degree) is unreliable, which weakens confidence in the others as sufficient evidence. - The 24-hour claim is a headline (abstract, Figure 1) supported only by eight sampled frames in Appendix D; no drift metrics, no self-similarity measurements, no failure-mode census at that horizon. - Because both roles are initialized identically and trained jointly, the paper does not test whether the context writer eventually diverges into a degenerate solution (e.g., collapsed KV diversity) over very long training, nor whether the separation gain persists when the base model is larger or trained longer than the reported schedule. - The theoretical analysis (Appendix G) is local and first-order; the authors correctly note the common-learning-rate comparison can favor sharing under positive alignment, but the paper does not measure the minibatch-aggregated alignment condition (Proposition G.2's own caveat) that its practical advantage depends on. Bottom Line: A practitioner building autoregressive video diffusion or world models should read the gradient-conflict analysis (Sections 3.2, 4.4, Appendices C/E) and seriously consider role-specific parameterization, since it is cheap, well-diagnosed, and likely transfers — but should treat the benchmark results as evidence within one research lineage rather than proof of state of the art, and the 24-hour claim as a qualitative demonstration, not a measured result.

From Ad Hoc to Systemic Circular Construction: Evidence of a Legislative Bottleneck in an Emerging Economy

A Al Mahruqi, MS Saleh, M Al Alawi, K S. Al-Jabri · link.springer.com · specification to code with formal verifications - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper presents a cross-sectional survey of 114 Omani construction professionals analyzed with PLS-SEM, hierarchical regression, and mediation analysis to show that perceived legislative barriers are most strongly associated with end-of-life circular-economy adoption (β = -0.47, p < 0.001) and weakest with design-phase adoption (β = -0.12, p = 0.180), supporting a phase-specific 'legislative bottleneck' framework. - Why it's important: Oman landfilled over 408,000 tons of construction and demolition waste in 2023 (a 22% year-on-year increase) despite Vision 2040 circularity mandates, and the paper argues the binding constraint is regulatory architecture, not awareness or finance — a diagnosis that generalizes to rapidly developing economies. - How it does it: It operationalizes circular strategies as twelve Likert items across design, construction, and end-of-life phases, then tests whether a legislative-barrier latent construct shows phase-gradient associations with adoption, using bootstrap contrasts to formally compare the three coefficients within one sample. - The good: The paired bootstrap contrast directly demonstrates the end-of-life association is significantly more negative than both design (Δβ = -0.541, p < 0.001) and construction (Δβ = -0.320, p = 0.008) phases, and hierarchical regression independently corroborates the headline effect (β = -0.47 to -0.51), with legislative barriers alone accounting for 87.1% of the explanatory power of all five barrier categories. - The missing: The design is cross-sectional and perceptual — the paper never measures actual legislation, actual waste flows, or actual adoption behavior, so the 'bottleneck' remains a correlation between stakeholders' opinions about regulation and their opinions about practice. - Read it or not: Read it if you work on circular-economy policy or socio-technical transitions in GCC/developing-market construction; skip it if you seek causal identification, behavioral (non-self-report) evidence, or methods beyond standard PLS-SEM practice.
Why this rank
Scored using Empirical profile. This is the strongest paper in the cluster: Rigor (65) benefits from measurement-model validation, triangulation across three estimators, robustness checks, and — unusually — a paired bootstrap contrast the authors used to weaken their own stepwise-gradient claim, mirroring the self-correcting, mechanism-level style the reader values. Novelty (55) and Non-Obviousness (60) rest on the phase-resolved 'legislative bottleneck' formulation with a role-differentiated mediation result. Completeness (70) is high given unusually candid limitation acknowledgment. The composite is pulled down by Resilience (55) — reverse causality and single-source perceptual data remain unaddressed beyond design caveats — and Impact (35), as nothing beyond the paper is released and the causal story is untested.

Show full analysis
Problem & Motivation: Oman's construction sector is caught between high-level policy ambition (Vision 2040's circular-economy mandate) and fragmented project-level practice: circular strategies that fit within a single project's boundaries (design adaptability, standardization) get adopted, while cross-project practices (pre-demolition audits, material certification, secondary-material markets) do not scale. Prior circular-construction research classifies barriers statically — technical, economic, informational, institutional, legislative — but offers little explanation of where in the project lifecycle adoption breaks down or which stakeholder is blocked. This matters for emerging economies whose regulatory systems were built for linear flows and landfill management; the authors also document Oman-specific context (only 8.8% of respondents' organizations had any formal CE strategy, versus 38% of U.S. firms per Guerra & Leite 2021). The gap addressed is the absence of phase-specific, stakeholder-resolved evidence on how legislative weakness shapes circular adoption in an emerging market. Key Idea: The 'legislative bottleneck': regulatory and institutional weakness is not a uniform dampener on circularity but a phase-specific constraint — it barely binds upstream design decisions that can be made within project boundaries, while it strongly binds downstream end-of-life practices (recycling, deconstruction, selective demolition) that require waste codes, reporting, liability rules, and secondary-material markets. The paper links this to Institutional Theory (a weak Scott regulative pillar stunting normative/cognitive acceptance) and Geels' Multi-Level Perspective (niche innovations that cannot escape into the regime without regulatory pressure). A secondary mechanism is stakeholder-specific: contractors report the highest legislative-barrier exposure, and this fully mediates their lower end-of-life adoption relative to government/clients. Methodology: Quantitative cross-sectional survey (Google Forms, October–November 2024, six weeks) of 114 Omani construction professionals (47.4% government/client, 26.3% contractors, 16.7% design consultants, plus small waste-management and project-management groups), 49.1% with ≤5 years' experience, using purposive convenience sampling. The instrument, adapted from validated CE barrier/driver frameworks and pilot-tested, measured 12 circular strategies, 16 barriers, and 16 enablers on 5-point Likert scales. Analysis pipeline: (1) CB-CFA with MLR estimation to validate a five-factor barrier measurement model (CFI = 0.91, RMSEA = 0.07, SRMR = 0.06; CR ≥ 0.82, AVE ≥ 0.55, α ≥ 0.79); (2) PLS-SEM (SmartPLS 4.0, 5,000 bootstrap resamples) regressing design-, construction-, and end-of-life adoption on legislative barriers, with technological and institutional barriers as secondary end-of-life predictors; (3) Hayes PROCESS multi-categorical mediation with stakeholder-type dummies (government/client reference), legislative barriers as mediator, end-of-life adoption as outcome; (4) hierarchical regression (three nested models predicting end-of-life adoption); (5) confirmatory checks: restricted-sample sensitivity analysis (n = 103, excluding the two smallest subgroups), non-response bias (Mann–Whitney U), multicollinearity (VIF ≤ 3.18), outlier diagnostics (max Cook's d = 0.18), and power/sensitivity analysis (80% power at f² ≈ 0.099 for the three-predictor model); (6) a paired bootstrap phase-contrast (5,000 resamples, BCa CIs) formally testing whether the three phase-specific coefficients differ. Key design decisions: PLS-SEM over CB-SEM for non-normality and modest n (reasonable), composite-score bootstrap contrasts as a fix for the paper's initial failure to formally compare coefficients (well-justified and honestly framed as supplementary), and mediation through perceived barriers using observational cross-sectional data (weakly justified for any causal reading, which the authors largely avoid). Key Results: Descriptively, adoption declines across the lifecycle: design-phase mean 3.29 (highest item: design for adaptability, M = 3.52), construction 3.24, end-of-life 3.06 (lowest items: design for disassembly M = 2.95, selective demolition M = 2.96). PLS-SEM shows legislative barriers weakly and non-significantly associated with design adoption (β = -0.12, p = 0.180, f² = 0.01), more negatively with construction adoption (β = -0.29, p = 0.002, f² = 0.09), and most negatively with end-of-life adoption (β = -0.47, p < 0.001, f² = 0.28). The bootstrap contrast confirms the end-of-life coefficient is significantly more negative than construction (Δβ = -0.320, 95% BCa CI [-0.550, -0.081], p = 0.008) and design (Δβ = -0.541, 95% BCa CI [-0.790, -0.261], p < 0.001), but construction and design are statistically indistinguishable (Δβ = -0.220, p = 0.139) — the paper correctly reinterprets its claim from a 'stepwise gradient' to a distinct end-of-life bottleneck. Mediation: contractors report higher legislative barriers than government/clients (path a β = 0.45, p = 0.002) and show a significant indirect effect on lower end-of-life adoption (β = -0.22, 95% CI [-0.42, -0.06]), robust in the restricted sample (β = -0.147, CI [-0.322, -0.035]); no other stakeholder's indirect effect is supported. Hierarchical regression: Model 2 explains R² = 0.40 of end-of-life adoption, with legislative barriers the dominant predictor (β = -0.47 to -0.51), institutional barriers secondary (β = -0.19, p = 0.034), and economic barriers non-significant — legislative items alone carry 87.1% of the barrier block's explanatory power. All baselines are descriptive or perception-based rather than behavioral; the U.S. 38% institutionalization figure is drawn from prior literature, not measured here. Tested scale is a single-country, single-sector perception survey of 114 — toy by quantitative social-science standards, adequate for medium-to-large effects as the authors' power analysis shows. Novelty Classification: NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING (phase-specific pattern of legislative-barrier associations, with a formal within-sample contrast, in an under-studied emerging-market context) plus a NEW FORMULATION of the 'legislative bottleneck' as a phase-resolved transition constraint bridging Institutional Theory and the Multi-Level Perspective. The underlying tools — PLS-SEM, Hayes PROCESS mediation, hierarchical regression, standard barrier taxonomies from Guerra & Leite, Hossain et al., Munaro & Tavares — are entirely standard; the novelty lies in the phase-resolved framing, the formal coefficient contrasts, and the Omani evidence base, not in method. The proposed three-pillar policy framework (codification, enforcement, market-enabling procurement) is a synthesis of well-known circular-procurement and waste-code instruments mapped to Omani institutions. Rigor & Reproducibility: Methodologically this is careful for a survey study: measurement-model validation (CB-CFA with fit indices, Fornell-Larcker discriminant validity, cross-loading checks), common-method-bias tests (Harman's single factor at 24.8% variance; CLF ΔCFI < 0.10), four post-hoc robustness checks, a restricted-sample sensitivity analysis, power/sensitivity analysis, and — unusually and commendably — a paired bootstrap contrast that the authors used to weaken their own initial stepwise-gradient interpretation. Ablation-like evidence exists via hierarchical models isolating the legislative block. No multiple-seed or significance-testing concerns apply as in ML research; error is quantified via bootstrap CIs throughout. No code, data repository, or instrument is publicly released — data are 'available from the corresponding author upon reasonable request.' Concerns: single-source perceptual data measuring both predictor and outcome (partially mitigated but not eliminated by CMB tests); purposive convenience sample with 47.4% government/client respondents and only 6 waste-management and 5 project-management respondents, making several subgroup estimates uninformative; 49.1% of respondents have ≤5 years' experience, yet experience is treated only as a control; the CB-CFA text has apparent typographical corruption in the fit-index equations (inline-eq placeholders), and TLI = 0.89 and NFI below 0.90 are marginal though acknowledged; the ad hoc/systemic dichotomy is admittedly not a validated construct. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL (a survey-based observational study; also delivers a policy framework). - Practical: Yes — SPSS 26 and SmartPLS 4.0 on ordinary hardware; the 'deployment' relevant here is policy design, and the framework names specific Omani institutions (Environment Authority, Be'ah, MoHUP, Tender Board). - Efficient: Not applicable in a compute sense; the analytical cost is trivial, but the data-collection cost of replication is high given the small, hard-to-reach expert population. - Effective: The evidence shows an association between perceived barriers and self-reported adoption, not that legislative reform would increase actual circularity — effectiveness of the proposed policy pillars is entirely untested and flagged as such. - Scalable: Not tested; generalization beyond Oman and the building sector is explicitly deferred to future cross-national and longitudinal work, so 10× scale (multi-country, longitudinal, behavioral measurement) is claimed as a research agenda, not demonstrated. The work stops at paper form: no dataset release, no tool, no trained artifact. Strengths: - The paired bootstrap phase-contrast analysis is the paper's genuine methodological contribution: instead of inferring a lifecycle gradient from three separately significant paths, it tests coefficient differences within one sample and then honestly downgrades its own 'stepwise' narrative to a single end-of-life bottleneck — a self-correcting move rarely seen in this literature. - Triangulation across three distinct estimators (latent-variable PLS-SEM, composite-score PROCESS mediation, hierarchical regression) with convergent effect sizes (β = -0.47 to -0.51 for the legislative→end-of-life path), plus a preregistered-in-spirit restricted-sample sensitivity analysis, gives the headline finding more resilience than typical construction-management surveys. - The stakeholder-specific mediation result (contractor-only indirect effect, β = -0.22) is a non-obvious empirical pattern that refines the bottleneck from a sector-wide claim to a role-differentiated mechanism with clear policy targeting. - The theoretical synthesis — connecting Scott's regulative pillar and Geels' MLP to explain why upstream strategies flourish while downstream loops fail — is a coherent framing that other emerging-market researchers can operationalize. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors are unusually forthcoming: they state (1) the cross-sectional design supports associations, not causation; (2) all data are self-reported perceptions, not site audits or behavioral measures; (3) n = 114 fell below the n = 385 target, subgroups are unbalanced (waste-management n = 6, project-management n = 5), and small-subgroup estimates are exploratory; (4) 'ad hoc' and 'systemic' circularity are analytical interpretations, not validated latent constructs; (5) materials are lumped into one category, and infrastructure projects are excluded; (6) generalizability beyond Oman requires cross-national replication; and (7) the policy framework is evidence-informed recommendation, not tested intervention. They repeatedly reframe causal-sounding language ('confirms the hypothesis') into associational language in Tables 10 and the discussion — this candor is a credibility positive. They minimize only mildly: the abstract's 'Evidence of a Legislative Bottleneck' title is stronger than the perceptual, correlational warrant acknowledged inside the paper. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - Reverse causality and confounding are unaddressed beyond design acknowledgment: respondents who practice little end-of-life circularity may rationally perceive legislation as the binding constraint (perception of barriers may be a consequence, not a cause, of low adoption), and the contractor mediation could equally reflect contractors' cost exposure or waste-handling responsibility driving both their barrier perceptions and low self-reported adoption. - The mediation model omits the four other barrier categories (economic, informational, institutional, technological) as candidate mediators, so 'full mediation by legislative barriers' is established only within a single-mediator specification; institutional barriers' near-significant path (p = 0.059) suggests a competing mechanism. - No comparison jurisdiction: the claim that the pattern is a legislative bottleneck would be far stronger with a parallel sample from a regulated market (e.g., EU, where the 70% C&DW recovery mandate applies) showing the phase gradient flattens — the paper cites the EU directive but does not test the contrast. - Sampling reach is opaque: response rate, denominator of invitations, and potential self-selection of circularity-interested professionals are not reported; a 47.4% government/client sample may inflate both barrier perception and adoption self-reports. - Common-method-bias tests (Harman, CLF) are weak detectors by construction; a marker-variable or time-separated design would be needed for the perceptual data to carry the interpretive weight placed on it. - An internal inconsistency: the conclusion section repeats the phase-point estimates 'as phase-specific point estimates rather than as proof of statistically different phase effects, because no formal within-sample contrast... was performed,' directly contradicting the paired bootstrap contrast analysis the paper itself conducted — likely a stale paragraph, but a reviewer would flag the sloppy synthesis. - The descriptive adoption means cluster tightly (3.06–3.29 phase averages on a 5-point scale); the 'declining gradient' is a 0.23-point difference whose practical significance is unquantified beyond statistical significance. Bottom Line: A methodologically self-aware and unusually honest perception survey that convincingly documents where Omani circular construction stalls (end-of-life) and who is blocked (contractors), but its bottleneck causal story rests entirely on cross-sectional self-reports — worth reading as a template for phase-resolved transition diagnostics in emerging markets and as policy input for Oman specifically, while anyone seeking tested regulatory remedies should look to quasi-experimental work (e.g., on the EU Waste Framework Directive) instead.

Recursive Harness Self - Improvement for Frontier Reasoning Data Synthesis

W Zhang, Z Jiao, C Zhang, L Jiang, SY Ma, Q Zhang… · arxiv.org · recursive self-improvement - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces task–harness co-evolution, a recursive reasoning-data synthesis framework in which a meta-agent co-evolves the problem-generation harness (skills, prompts, workflows, verifier/revision placement) alongside the tasks themselves, via online skill updates during generation and gated post-batch harness revisions. - Why it's important: Static and task-only-recursive synthetic data pipelines cannot keep producing progressively harder training problems as solver capability rises, starving post-training of frontier-level reasoning data; adapting the construction procedure addresses that ceiling. - How it does it: A Director/Meta-Agent loop converts intermediate solver failures into reusable construction skills mid-batch, then a post-task optimizer proposes harness revisions that are adopted only if they lower fixed-solver accuracy, do not decrease validity, and keep cost growth within 1.5× the relative difficulty gain (capped at +50%), with model weights and verifier logic frozen. - The good: The ablation cleanly isolates the mechanism: at round 14, full co-evolution reaches 50.0% solver accuracy versus 73.5% for fixed-harness task recursion, and a frozen evolved harness H14 still yields 52.0% versus 70.0% for H0 on 50 held-out math seeds — evidence the gains live in the harness, not the task chains. - The missing: No error bars, single-run trajectories, no comparison to the closest harness-evolution baselines (RST, BenchEvolver, Autodata, DataFoundry), difficulty measured only against the same DeepSeek-V4-Pro model that powers generation, and no code/data release. - Read it or not: Worth reading for researchers building self-improving synthesis or agentic-data pipelines who want a concrete, gated, rollback-protected recipe; skippable if you only need evidence that synthetic math data helps SFT, which OpenMathInstruct-2 and successors already cover.
Why this rank
Scored using Empirical profile. Rigor (52) pulls the composite down hardest: no seeds, no error bars on single-run trajectories, solver-generates-and-solves circularity with DeepSeek-V4-Pro, no code/data release, and the closest recursive baselines (RST, BenchEvolver, Autodata, DataFoundry) are discussed but never run. Practical Impact (42) is minimal — paper only, with the learned harness artifact unverifiable. Completeness (70) is a credibility positive given unusually candid scope-of-evidence caveats, and Non-Obviousness (68) is supported by the complementary-schedule ablation and the frozen-harness transfer experiment, but these cannot compensate for the unestablished core claim. Weighted composite: 0.20*65 + 0.25*52 + 0.15*68 + 0.15*70 + 0.15*55 + 0.10*42 = 59.

Problem & Motivation: Teams training reasoning models need a supply of problems hard enough to expose the gap between current solver capability and the frontier. Static datasets (OpenMathInstruct-2, MetaMath) cannot increase difficulty, and task-level recursion (RST) reuses generated problems as seeds while leaving the construction harness — the reusable skills, prompts, and workflows that turn a seed into a verified problem — frozen, so difficulty plateaus (the paper's Task-only ablation plateaus around 70–73.5% solver accuracy). The gap this paper targets: can the generation procedure itself improve as its own outputs become the inputs to later rounds? Key Idea: Co-evolve the task distribution and the synthesis harness, with adaptation split into two schedules: (1) online self-improvement converts attributed solver-failure traces into reusable construction transformations (skills with intent/method/difficulty_effect/tool_hint fields) that are admitted mid-batch and immediately readable by the next Director call, and (2) post-task self-improvement runs an outer search over harness edits (skills, prompts, workflow, verify/revise placement) whose candidates are accepted only under a three-part gate — strictly lower mean solver accuracy, no validity decrease, and cost growth ≤ min{1+1.5(r_D−1), 1.5} of the online baseline — with rollback to the online snapshot after three rejections. Freezing model weights and verifier logic prevents the system from editing its own acceptance criteria. Methodology: The pipeline has three stages. Stage 1 curates seeds/sources, screens for benchmark overlap, and distills an initial skill library into harness H0. Stage 2 (online) runs a Director selecting skills and controlling Extend/Revise/Verify operators until budget exhaustion; a solver miss on a valid QA yields a trace that the skill Meta-Agent converts into a candidate skill admitted into the working library (Eq. 3). Stage 3 (post-task) freezes the online harness H_online_n as the baseline, prepares execution logs/metrics/failure traces, applies skill updates to a copy, and proposes up to three harness candidates (Eq. 4); each candidate and the baseline independently synthesize one round from a frozen 150-task cohort (four solver attempts per task, 600 outcomes per side), and the Critic applies the acceptance gate of Eq. 5. Difficulty is mean solver accuracy p̂(q) over four attempts; relative difficulty r_D is a ratio of cohort means. Key design decisions: (a) verifier logic is immutable — well-justified, since otherwise the gate could be gamed; (b) candidates are evaluated by generating a new round from shared inputs rather than reusing recorded scores — sound, avoids selection on stale metrics; (c) the 1.5× cost coefficient is an explicitly uncalibrated engineering preference — honest, but arbitrary. No formal objective beyond the empirical gate is given; this is agentic search (ADAS/AFlow-style workflow optimization) applied to data generation, not a differentiable or RL method. Key Results: Difficulty: DeepSeek-V4-Pro accuracy on 150 seed chains (50 each math/coding/science) falls monotonically from 100.0% (round 0) to 54.8% (round 14); domain endpoints 50.0/58.5/56.0%. Ablation (50 shared seeds, round 14): Task-only 73.5%, Online-only 67.0% (regressing from 64.5% at round 10), Post-task-only 59.0%, Full 50.0%. Frozen-harness transfer: H14 vs H0 on 50 held-out math seeds gives 52.0% vs 70.0% after ten rounds. Operator cost (Extend/Revise/Verify only, excluding Director/search): $1.065 vs $1.332 per seed at round 14 for Full vs Task-only (−20.0%), though Full costs 2.0–2.9% more at rounds 2–4. Downstream: GRPO on Qwen3.5-4B Thinking (10K examples) gives 62.7% overall mean-16 across APEX Shortlist/HMMT Feb 2025/LCB v6/SciBench versus 59.5% for IQC and 58.4% for the untrained checkpoint, with the highest score on all four benchmarks; SFT on Qwen3.5-35B-A3B (12K examples) gives 55.7% overall versus 51.1% for MMIQC/IQC; Qwen3.8-27B + SFT on 10K math reaches 62.5% mean-16 on APEX 2025, second only to Kimi K3 (Think) at 65.6% among self-evaluated frontier references. Baselines are reasonable static-data competitors but the closest recursive/harness-evolution methods are not run. Scale is modest: 150 seed chains, 14 rounds, ≤2,400 solver attempts per gate evaluation. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD (task–harness co-evolution for data synthesis) plus NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING (the two update schedules are complementary, and the evolved harness transfers to new seeds). The genuinely new element is applying gated harness-level RSI to the data-synthesis loop with an explicit cost-bounded acceptance criterion; the components — recursion over verified tasks (RST, BenchEvolver), meta-agent workflow search (ADAS, AFlow), prompt evolution (Promptbreeder), and archiving with rollback (Darwin Gödel Machine) — are standard, and notably Lee et al. 2026a (cited, titled "Recursive harness self-improvement") already establishes harness RSI, so the contribution is the co-evolution coupling and its data-synthesis application rather than the mechanism itself. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are present and well-designed (four configurations sharing seeds and harness; a transfer experiment that correctly controls for the harder-starting-tasks confound). However: no multiple seeds, no error bars, no significance tests — the paper itself states the 600 gate outcomes are clustered within 150 tasks and that no run-level uncertainty is inferred. Difficulty is measured by DeepSeek-V4-Pro, which is also the Extend/Revise/Director model — a circularity risk the authors do not discuss. No code, data, or harness release URL is mentioned, limiting reproducibility of a paper whose artifact is a learned harness. Contamination control is described as a protocol, but the paper concedes the audit records that would establish non-contamination are not presented. The authors are unusually explicit about accounting scope (operator cost ≠ total cost; gate cohort is not a generalization test), which raises rigor of interpretation even as headline numbers stay unaccompanied by uncertainty. Total evolution cost, candidate validity rates, and fallback rates are unreported. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (a synthesis pipeline run at moderate scale with real downstream training). Practical: Yes — it uses commercially available API models (DeepSeek-V4-Pro, GPT-5.6, Qwen3.8-Max) and trains students on 16× NVIDIA H20 GPUs. Efficient: Per-seed operator cost drops to $1.065 at round 14 (vs $1.332 Task-only), but total search cost including candidate evaluation is unmeasured, so end-to-end efficiency is unproven. Effective: The evidence supports producing harder tasks that improve SFT/GRPO on the tested benchmarks, but "harder" is only demonstrated against one solver that shares provenance with the generation stack. Scalable: Untested beyond 150 seed chains and 14 rounds; nothing shows the mechanism survives 10–100× scale or whether the difficulty decline continues or the skill library saturates. Deliverable: paper only — no library, dataset, or trained model release is mentioned. Strengths: (1) The frozen-harness transfer experiment (H14 at 52.0% vs H0 at 70.0% on held-out seeds) is the paper's best piece of evidence — it correctly rules out the trivial explanation that H14 looks better merely because it starts from harder tasks, and ties the difficulty gain to a reusable procedure. (2) The complementary-schedule ablation is clean and reveals a non-obvious finding: Online-only regresses in late rounds while Post-task-only keeps improving, showing batch-level re-evaluation does work online skill admission cannot. (3) The immutable-verifier constraint plus candidate-vs-baseline generation-on-shared-inputs evaluation is a well-constructed defense against self-grading gate collapse. (4) The "Scope of the evidence" paragraph and Appendix cost-accounting caveats are more candid than is typical; the authors distinguish claims from measurements explicitly. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state that matched-token training on fixed-harness versus evolved-harness data was not run (so harness evolution's isolated downstream contribution is unmeasured); total evolution cost, candidate validity, fallback rates, and independent-run uncertainty are unreported; difficulty transfer was tested within mathematics only, under the same solver, not across solvers or domains; the cost-growth constants are engineering preferences, not calibrated thresholds; the gate guarantees no improvement on unseen tasks; and the curation protocol does not by itself establish absence of contamination. This is direct, non-minimizing confrontation of limitations — a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: (1) Solver circularity: the difficulty metric, Director, Extend, and Revise all use DeepSeek-V4-Pro; "harder for DeepSeek-V4-Pro" may not mean harder for the Qwen students actually trained, and no independent-solver difficulty check is reported despite the authors flagging cross-solver transfer as untested. (2) Missing strongest baselines: RST, BenchEvolver, Autodata, and DataFoundry are discussed as the closest related work but none is run; IQC is the only recursive baseline. (3) Downstream gains could partly reflect data composition/mixture effects (10K math + 2K coding) rather than difficulty; the static baselines are used at fixed example counts without token matching. (4) Single trajectory per configuration with no variance reporting makes the ablation gaps (e.g., 9.0 points between Post-task-only and Full) impossible to attach uncertainty to. (5) The APEX frontier comparison is self-evaluated and mixes models with wildly different inference budgets, which the authors note but which weakens the headline. (6) No skill-library analysis — what skills were admitted, whether they generalize, or whether late-round difficulty comes from a few high-leverage skills, is unexamined despite the framework's central claim being about skill accumulation. (7) No release artifact, so the learned harness itself cannot be verified. Bottom Line: A practitioner building self-improving data-generation pipelines gains a concrete, well-gated blueprint and the useful finding that online and batch-level harness updates are complementary, but the absence of independent-solver validation, variance reporting, released artifacts, and head-to-head comparison with the closest recursive baselines means the core claim — that harness co-evolution, not just co-evolved tasks, drives the difficulty frontier — remains plausible rather than established.

SpecAgent: Empowering Program Verification with Agentic Synthesis of Formal Program Specifications

L Ma, H Wang, S Liu, J Wang, L Bu · arxiv.org · specification to code with formal verifications - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces SpecAgent, a multi-agent LLM framework that synthesizes ACSL formal specifications (function contracts and loop invariants) for real-world C programs, achieving 96.82% precision and 88.95% recall on a 50-program benchmark from 14 repositories and discharging 604 of 811 real-world verification targets with Frama-C/WP. - Why it's important: Deductive verification of real C software is bottlenecked by the labor of hand-writing ACSL annotations (the authors cite five calendar months of manual effort for one X.509 parser), and prior LLM synthesizers get trapped repairing downstream failures whose root cause is a weak, already-finalized upstream specification. - How it does it: It replaces the forward-only generate-repair pipeline with a closed-loop agentic workflow — dependency-aware planning, RAG-style generation from a fingerprint-indexed ACSL knowledge base, verifier-gated repair that can trace failures back across specification dependencies, and a critique stage whose "Postcondition Completeness Probe" (a harness calling f(x) twice and asserting equal returns) detects under-constrained postconditions via verifier counterexamples. - The good: The ablation isolates component value (repair lifts precision from ~89.8% to ~94.8%; critique adds +6.9% recall over repair-only on DeepSeek-V4), and SpecAgent beats even Codex with GPT-5.6-sol (96.14%/82.39%) while costing $0.62/program, less than Preguss ($0.72) or Codex ($0.71). - The missing: No statistical variance reporting (no seeds, error bars, or significance tests despite acknowledged LLM stochasticity), no released artifact or code URL, and the benchmark/tooling originate from the authors' own prior work (SpecSyn/SpecGen), with the primary strength metric gated by ground-truth specifications from that same artifact. - Read it or not: Read it if you work on LLM-assisted formal verification or specification synthesis (ACSL/Frama-C or Verus/Dafny analogues); skip it if you want general agentic-architecture insights, since the machinery is ReAct plus tool calls and the core value is domain-specific verification-loop design.
Why this rank
Scored using Empirical profile. The dependency-aware repair loop and verifier-native completeness probe are genuinely clever (Non-Obviousness 70), but Rigor (52) is pulled down hard: single-run results with no seeds or error bars despite acknowledged LLM stochasticity, a self-referential benchmark inherited from the authors' own prior work, and no released artifact of any kind. Practical Impact (42) suffers from the absent code/knowledge-base release, and Resilience (58) is weakened because the headline margin over Codex rests on unmeasured run-to-run variance. Weighted composite: 0.20*65 + 0.25*52 + 0.15*70 + 0.15*65 + 0.15*58 + 0.10*42 = 59.

Problem & Motivation: Teams doing deductive verification of C programs with Frama-C/WP must write loop invariants and function contracts by hand; this is expertise-intensive and does not scale to real repositories with entangled function/loop dependencies. LLM-based synthesizers (AutoSpec, SpecGen, Preguss, SpecSyn) are forward-only: once a specification passes verification it is frozen, and repair is confined to the failure site. The paper motivates the problem with deficiency propagation — a weak but locally verifiable postcondition S1 (for a callee) starves the downstream S2 of semantic information, so localized repair of S2 loops futilely while the root cause in S1 is never revisited. Practitioners verifying real-world codebases with interprocedural dependencies are the target audience. Key Idea: Treat specification synthesis as an iterative, dependency-aware decision-making process rather than a one-pass pipeline: when verification fails downstream, an agent can trace specification dependencies, diagnose whether the root cause is upstream, and revisit (replan/refine) previously finalized specifications. The second key mechanism is the Postcondition Completeness Probe — exploiting the over-approximation view of postconditions, it proves (or fails to prove) m = n for m := f(x); n := f(x) using only the contract, turning 'is this postcondition strong enough to pin the return value?' into a decidable verifier query whose failed proof obligations serve as counterexample-guided refinement evidence. Methodology: SpecAgent runs four stages coordinated by a deterministic central orchestrator (agents follow ReAct; agents share state only via a workspace; per-invocation budgets N_step = 10 for planning/critique and 30 for generation/repair; total N_invoke = 10). (1) Planning Agent: consumes a deterministic program context (function signatures, caller-callee relations, loop positions from syntax analysis) plus source, and emits a natural-language synthesis plan naming targets, intended semantics, dependencies, and processing order. (2) Generation Agent: converts the plan into ACSL annotations (requires/ensures/assigns/loop invariants/predicates) via search-and-replace edits restricted to annotations only; prompts are augmented with up to 3 examples retrieved from a knowledge base of 184 function-level annotated units built from the official ACSL tutorial, indexed by a 32-bit structural fingerprint bitvector (parameter types, pointers/arrays, branches/loops, memory access, calls, ACSL constructs), filtered by loop-structure/return-type compatibility and ranked by Jaccard similarity over fingerprints. (3) Verification Gate + Repairing Agent: Frama-C/WP outcomes are parsed into structured JSON failure reports with provenance (caller, callee, source line); the Repairing Agent may invoke WP and Frama-C/Eva for extra evidence and iterates until the gate passes or budget expires. (4) Critique Agent: for verified specs, assesses semantic strength, using the Postcondition Completeness Probe, and outputs ACCEPT, IMPROVE (feedback to Generation), or REPLAN (reinitiate from Planning). Critical design decisions: annotation-only edits (preserves program semantics — well-justified); verifier-in-the-loop as ground truth for correctness (sound for correctness, but solver-incompleteness biases the pipeline — acknowledged); the probe checks only return-value determinacy, which is a sound proxy for but not a complete measure of postcondition strength (only justified informally; a contract could be return-determinate yet still weak on preconditions/generality — the Critique Agent's LLM judgment covers the remainder, which is itself an unverified component). Key Results: On the 50-program, 14-repository benchmark from Ma et al. (average 456.44 LoC/file, 7 files over 1,000 LoC), SpecAgent with DeepSeek-V4 achieves 96.82% precision / 88.95% recall versus SpecSyn 84.07%/61.61%, SpecGen 95.17%/74.47%, Preguss 93.71%/28.22%, AutoSpec 93.71%/20.26%, and Codex (general coding agent) at 91.69%/82.42% (DS-V4) and 96.14%/82.39% with GPT-5.6-sol; SpecAgent with GPT-5 reaches 96.10%/82.77%. On 811 verification targets (X509-parser 140, Contiki 163, Atomthreads 239 RTE-style targets; 269 SV-COMP reachability targets), SpecAgent discharges 604 vs. Codex 523, Preguss 512, SpecSyn 435, AutoSpec 363, SpecGen 312; on SV-COMP alone SpecAgent gets 218/269 with Codex close at 206. Ablations show the full pipeline beats generation-only (+8.02%/+10.63% recall for DS-V4/GPT-5) and that planning alone is inconsistent (GPT-5 recall drops 72.14%→71.51%). Quality evolution analysis shows most gains by 6–8 invocations (verification-gate pass rate 36%→62% from 2→6 invocations, then plateau). Cost: 1,684 s wall time, 25.58 Frama-C calls, 99.40 LLM calls, $0.6228 per program — cheaper than Preguss (7,750 s, 351 calls, $0.72) but 3× the wall time of AutoSpec (582 s, $0.03). Baselines are current (2024–2026 LLM-based synthesizers plus a frontier coding agent), though baseline numbers for GPT-5 are partly imported from Ma et al.'s earlier study. Scale is standard-to-moderate: hundreds-of-LoC files, not whole-codebase verification. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD with an NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING component. The genuinely novel elements are (a) the non-forward-only agentic repair loop that revisits upstream specifications upon downstream failure, and (b) the verifier-based completeness probe integrated as counterexample-guided refinement evidence rather than a binary assessment. The rest — RAG over annotated examples, ReAct agents, an orchestrator, verifier-gated iteration — is a competent assembly of existing techniques (aider-style edits, ReAct, Frama-C/WP) applied to ACSL; the fingerprint/Jaccard retrieval is a simple hand-crafted heuristic, not a learned retriever. Rigor & Reproducibility: A four-variant ablation (G, P+G, P+G+R, full) exists and is informative, but the authors themselves note that incrementally adding components conflates component effect with changed execution trajectories, so attribution is not strictly causal. No multiple seeds, error bars, or significance tests are reported despite explicitly acknowledging LLM output stochasticity as an internal threat — for margins like SpecAgent 604 vs. Codex 523 targets or recall gaps of a few points on some repositories, run-to-run variance could matter. No code, data, or artifact URL is mentioned anywhere in the paper. Methodological concerns: the benchmark and the specification-equivalence checking script are inherited from Ma et al. (SpecSyn), i.e., the authors evaluate on their own prior artifact with their own metric pipeline; baseline statistics for GPT-5 are adopted from that prior study rather than re-run; and specification 'recall' depends on the availability of verifiable ground-truth specifications, which only exists on this curated benchmark (the SV-COMP evaluation instead uses target-discharge count, a cleaner end-to-end metric where Codex is nearly competitive). Frama-C/WP incompleteness induces false negatives, which the authors acknowledge and mitigate by holding the verifier constant across all methods. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (a built framework evaluated through experiments, closest to SYSTEMS but with no released artifact stated). Practical: Yes — runs on a 24-core desktop CPU with 16 GB RAM; the LLM is accessed via API, so no accelerator hardware is needed locally. Efficient: Moderate — $0.62 and ~28 minutes wall time per program, cheaper than verification-heavy baselines (Preguss, SpecSyn) but 3× the cost of lightweight ones (AutoSpec), and it needs ~100 LLM calls per program. Effective: The evidence supports the stated problem on the tested distributions — 604/811 real verification targets discharged and ~89% ground-truth recall — but effectiveness is entangled with Frama-C/WP decidability limits and only demonstrated on C/ACSL. Scalable: Only partially claimed: the benchmark tops out at ~1,741 LoC files and 811 targets; behavior at whole-codebase scale (10⁴–10⁵ LoC per project, full dependency graphs) is untested, and the fixed N_invoke = 10 budget plus centralized orchestration may not transfer. The work stops at paper form: no library, CLI, dataset release, or trained model is stated as available. Strengths: - The core insight — that forward-only specification synthesis fails on interdependent specifications and that repair must be allowed to revisit upstream artifacts based on downstream evidence — is a real, articulable diagnosis of prior systems, backed by a concrete failure mode (Fig. 1) rather than anecdote. - The Postcondition Completeness Probe is a clever, cheap, and verifier-native strength check (double-call return-determinacy harness) that converts a semantic-judgment question into a proof obligation and feeds failed obligations back as refinement evidence — more principled than mutation- or test-based completeness heuristics that require test suites. - The evaluation goes beyond specification-quality proxies to end-to-end verification outcomes on 811 targets, and the cost analysis (time, verifier calls, API dollars) is a practice the subfield needs more of. - The RQ3 diminishing-returns analysis (most gains by 6–8 invocations) gives practitioners actionable budget guidance rather than an arbitrary hyperparameter. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors confront limitations unusually directly in Section 6.2: LLM stochasticity without seed-level variance reporting (mitigated only by fixed configurations and aggregate reporting); ablation non-causality (components interact with execution trajectories); sensitivity to invocation budgets; a small benchmark (50 programs) despite real-world provenance; scope restricted to C/ACSL/Frama-C with possible non-generalizability to other languages and verifiers (e.g., Verus/Dafny); and Frama-C/WP incompleteness causing potential false negatives in correctness assessment. This candor is a credibility positive, though the stochasticity mitigation does not actually resolve the missing variance reporting. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - No released artifact (code, knowledge base, prompts, or benchmark additions) is mentioned — for an agentic system whose behavior depends heavily on prompt and tool design, this severely limits independent reproduction. - Author overlap with the benchmark source (Ma et al. / SpecSyn / SpecGen) means the head-to-head comparison is self-referential: the metric script, ground truths, and dataset curation all originate from the authors' own line of work, and no fully independent benchmark is used for RQ1–RQ3. - The probe measures only return-value determinacy; specifications that are return-determinate but semantically vacuous on other behavioral dimensions (e.g., caller-visible memory via assigns, or weaker ensures on heap state) escape the probe, and the Critique Agent's coverage of those cases is itself an unvalidated LLM judgment — no measurement of critique-stage precision (how often ACCEPT is wrong) is given. - Single-run results: given that Codex trails by 4–7 recall points and 81 verification targets, and that the authors admit stochastic variance, the absence of repeated trials is the largest unaddressed validity threat for the headline margin over Codex. - On SV-COMP, Codex achieves 206 vs. SpecAgent's 218 on toy-sized programs (27.79 avg. LoC), suggesting the advantage concentrates on large programs; a per-size breakdown of the verification-target results is not provided. - The retrieval knowledge base is 184 units from a tutorial — small and pedagogically skewed; no ablation of the retrieval component (e.g., random examples vs. fingerprint ranking) is reported, so its contribution is unquantified. Bottom Line: For anyone building LLM-driven specification synthesis or verifier-in-the-loop agents, this is worth reading for its dependency-aware repair loop and completeness probe, which represent a genuine step beyond forward-only pipelines — but the self-referential benchmark, single-run results, and absent artifact mean its headline margins over Codex-style baselines should be treated as promising rather than settled.

VigilSAM3: Reinforcement-Optimized Memory Gating for Ultra-Long Surgical Video Segmentation

X Yao, Y Yang, Z Song, K Guo, H Tao, J Yang, L Zhu · papers.miccai.org · long-horizon RL for agents - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces VigilSAM3, a SAM3-based surgical video segmentation system in which a learned causal-Transformer agent decides per-frame whether to Trust the tracker, Correct via a heavier detector, or Reset contaminated memory, backed by a hierarchical pixel/class/frame-level memory firewall, plus a new 39-video, 21,734-frame hepatectomy segmentation dataset (Hepa-Vein). - Why it's important: In laparoscopic hepatectomy, missed or drifted segmentation of thin vessels and transient bleeding points (<0.1% of frame area) can lead to uncontrolled hemorrhage, and existing memory-based trackers irreversibly cascade a single corrupted memory entry across thousands of frames while frequent manual re-prompting is impractical during live surgery. - How it does it: The core move is framing memory-write decisions as an MDP solved with GRPO using softmax inverse-Dice class-aware rewards, so the policy learns when invoking the expensive detector prevents future drift, combined with a multiplicative gating hierarchy (residual memory writer × per-class MLP gate × agent frame gate) that filters what enters the memory bank. - The good: Ablations isolate real component synergy: the full system reaches 69.18 mean Dice vs. 66.32 for the ungated SAM3 baseline, and the paper honestly shows Memory Firewall alone under SFT hurts (-0.74 Dice vs. agent-only) and only helps once GRPO calibrates the correction policy. - The missing: No comparison against the long-horizon SAM2 robustness methods the paper itself cites as closest related work (SAM2Long, DAM4SAM), no error bars/seeds/significance tests, and the dataset/code are only promised, not released. - Read it or not: Worth reading for researchers in surgical video understanding or memory-based VOS who care about learned memory management; skippable if you only need a general SAM3 application, since the gains over a tuned SAM3 baseline are modest (~+1–2.9 Dice) outside the small-target class.

Problem & Motivation: Laparoscopic hepatectomy requires real-time identification of Glisson's pedicle, hepatic veins, and transient bleeding points to enable pre-emptive vessel clamping before hemorrhage occurs. Three properties of these targets break existing memory-based video segmentation: extreme scale imbalance (bleeding points occupy <0.1% of frame area), intermittent visibility across procedures spanning 1,000+ frames, and temporal drift, where one low-quality prediction written into the memory bank contaminates all future frames. Existing surgical benchmarks (CholecSeg8k, Endoscapes, DSAD) cover cholecystectomy and colorectal procedures but not hepatectomy. Prior SAM2-style surgical adaptations (ReSurgSAM2, SurgSAM2) require clinician re-prompting, which is impractical intraoperatively, and no prior work provides a principled mechanism for deciding when predictions are reliable enough to commit to memory. The intended users are surgeons and surgical-data-science researchers needing autonomous, minimal-interaction guidance. Key Idea: Treat the memory-write decision as a sequential decision problem with long-horizon credit assignment: a lightweight policy agent observes tracker quality signals (SAM quality token, pooled memory features, per-class quality statistics) and chooses Trust/Correct/Reset, where corrections promote frames to permanent, non-evictable "anchored" memory. Because an unnecessary correction wastes compute (System 2 detector shares an 815.6M ViT backbone with the 11.7M-param System 1 tracker) and can inject noise, while a skipped correction can cause catastrophic drift hundreds of frames later, fixed thresholds fail and RL (GRPO, critic-free, group-relative advantages) is used to learn the schedule with class-aware rewards that weight underperforming small classes via softmax inverse-Dice. Methodology: The pipeline is streaming: at frame 0 the System 2 detector initializes from a text prompt; thereafter the System 1 tracker produces a draft mask D_t, the agent observes state s_t = [z_iou; z_mem; b̄_t] and emits an action a_t ∈ {Trust, Correct, Reset} plus a continuous frame gate g_t. Trust writes the gated tracker prediction as FIFO-evictable temporal memory; Correct/Reset invoke the System 2 detector and promote the result to persistent anchored memory with a dedicated spatial embedding. A key design decision bypasses SAM's geometric-prompt pathway on correction frames, instead feeding the detector's dense semantic logits S_t directly as a mask prompt into the tracker decoder — justified because geometric prompts re-predict rather than adopt corrections, destroying small-target signals through downsampling. The hierarchical firewall composes multiplicatively: m_t,c = g_t · ĝ_t,c · f̃_t,c, where f̃_t,c is output of a lightweight residual CNN memory writer (learnable scalar α initialized to zero), ĝ_t,c is an MLP gate over an 8-D per-class quality descriptor, and g_t is the agent's frame gate. Training is two-stage: supervised imitation on oracle actions, then GRPO (loss = policy gradient + KL anchor to SFT reference + entropy bonus + behavioral-cloning warm start) with reward r_t = (q_final − q_draft) − C(a_t) − λ_rep·(redundancy penalty over a δ-frame window), augmented by unspecified "horizon-aware shaping." Design decisions are mostly well-justified in text, though the horizon-shaping term and how the reward's q_final is computed during training (does it require running the detector for every candidate action?) are under-specified. Key Results: On the authors' Hepa-Vein dataset (39 videos, 21,734 frames, 3 classes, 7:1:2 split), VigilSAM3 attains Dice 80.36 (Glisson), 66.73 (Blood Point), 82.33 (Vein), beating the strongest baselines ReSurgSAM2 (MICCAI'25: 75.49/64.53/78.23) and MedSAM3 (arXiv'25: 78.12/57.79/79.17); the headline gain is +27.41 Dice over MedSAM3 on the small Blood Point class. On DSAD (colorectal, vascular classes only), it reaches 74.65 Dice (Mesenteric Artery) and 64.71 (Intestinal Veins), the latter +5.69 over MedSAM. Baselines include 10 methods from 2015–2025, mixing image-level (U-Net, nnU-Net, MedSAM, SAMUS) and video methods (HRVVS, Vivim, GDKVM, ReSurgSAM2, MedSAM3) — reasonably current, though the cited long-horizon memory competitors SAM2Long and DAM4SAM are absent. Throughput is 22.53 FPS on one A800, slightly below MedSAM3's 26.76 and roughly 7× slower than U-Net; this is marginal for 25–30 FPS surgical video. Ablations (Table 3): baseline M0 66.32 Dice → +agent (SFT) 67.21 → +MF+GRPO 69.18; notably M2 (agent+MF, no GRPO, 67.95) underperforms M3 (agent+GRPO, no MF, 68.54), and the authors attribute this to the SFT-only policy triggering too few corrections — a counter-intuitive and honestly reported interaction. All results are single-run on the authors' own dataset plus one public dataset; no seeds, error bars, or significance tests are reported. Novelty Classification: NEW DATASET/BENCHMARK (Hepa-Vein, claimed largest hepatectomy segmentation dataset), NEW METHOD (RL-optimized memory-write scheduling with anchor promotion — the GRPO-gated Trust/Correct/Reset policy over a VOS memory bank appears genuinely new), and partially NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING (the MF–GRPO synergy ablation). The memory-firewall components (residual refinement, per-class gating, FIFO vs. persistent memory) are competent combinations of known ideas from XMem-style hierarchical memory and SAM2Long-style memory curation; the genuinely non-obvious step is optimizing the write/correct/anchor decision with critic-free RL rather than heuristics, and the mask-prompt adoption trick for authoritative corrections. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations exist and are informative, isolating each of the three components and exposing the negative M2 result. However: no multiple seeds, error bars, or significance tests; the ablation table reports only mean Dice/Jaccard/HD-95/ASSD/FPS without per-class breakdowns; the GRPO hyperparameters (K trajectories, δ window, λ values, reward-shaping form) and RL training compute are not given. Code and dataset are promised at a VigilSAM3 release but not available at submission time. Methodological concerns: (1) the method is developed and headline-evaluated on the authors' own dataset, with DSAD serving as a secondary check but only on two vascular classes and as still images rather than video; (2) the closest long-horizon robustness baselines (SAM2Long, DAM4SAM) are discussed in the introduction but excluded from all tables; (3) M0, the ablation baseline, is not precisely defined (what scheduling does SAM3 use without the agent?). No Goodhart-style training-on-test contamination is apparent, but the 7:1:2 split procedure and annotation inter-rater agreement are not reported. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (a built system with quantitative evaluation; the dataset is also a SYSTEMS-adjacent artifact). Practical: Runs on a single NVIDIA A800 with standard training (50 epochs, batch 8), so hardware requirements are unexceptional for a research lab, though the 815.6M shared backbone is heavy for bedside/edge deployment. Efficient: 22.53 FPS is below reliable real-time for 25–30 FPS endoscopic video and 7× slower than lightweight baselines; each System 2 correction adds cost, which the reward explicitly penalizes but the paper does not report correction frequency at inference. Effective: Evidence supports improved small/transient-structure segmentation on two datasets, but the target application (intraoperative hemorrhage prevention) is only proxied by offline Dice; no latency-under-drift or human-in-the-loop study. Scalability: Videos up to ~1,000+ frames are tested and the anchored-memory mechanism targets ultra-long video, but no experiment beyond the dataset's length distribution, and anchor accumulation over multi-hour unedited procedures is untested. Deliverables: promised code and dataset release (not yet available); the method itself stops at paper form plus a forthcoming artifact. Strengths: (1) The problem formulation is the real contribution: recasting memory-bank write/evict/anchor decisions in SAM3 as an MDP with delayed, compounding consequences — a framing that plausibly generalizes beyond surgery and that fixed thresholds demonstrably handle poorly. (2) The ablation honestly exposes a non-obvious interaction (MF without GRPO is harmful), which strengthens the credibility of the claimed synergy rather than a generic "everything helps" story. (3) The mask-prompt adoption trick (dense logits as mask prompts instead of geometric prompts) is a concrete, well-motivated fix for small-target destruction in SAM correction pathways. (4) Hepa-Vein fills a genuine benchmark gap with a three-tier clinical annotation pipeline on a clinically critical procedure, with useful dataset statistics (area ratios, temporal presence curves) motivating the method design. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The conclusion acknowledges three forward-looking limitations: the need for a lightweight variant of what appears to be the gating module ("lightweight GMC" — a term used nowhere else in the paper, an apparent writing error), backbone-agnostic validation (currently tied to SAM3), and "safeguards for rare false anchors" — implicitly admitting that promoting a wrong correction to permanent, never-evicted anchor memory is an unhandled failure mode. The authors confront the MF-requires-GRPO interaction directly in the ablation discussion, which is a credibility positive. They do not discuss the sub-real-time FPS, the absence of SAM2Long/DAM4SAM baselines, or single-run evaluation. Analyst-Identified Gaps: (1) The most dangerous unaddressed failure mode is internal to the design: a false anchor is permanent and always attended to, so a confidently wrong correction could be strictly worse than drift — no experiment quantifies false-anchor frequency or recovery, and the authors only gesture at future safeguards. (2) SAM2Long and DAM4SAM, the directly relevant training-free long-horizon memory methods, are omitted from all comparisons, leaving the claimed advantage over existing drift mitigation untested. (3) The RL training loop is underspecified: computing r_t = q_final − q_draft presumably requires executing both paths per frame during rollouts, so RL training cost is unknown and potentially large; the "horizon-aware shaping" term is described in one sentence with no formula. (4) The GRPO citation points to "DeepSeekMath-v2" (arXiv 2511.22570) rather than the original GRPO paper, and the method section contains internal inconsistencies (undefined "GMC" in the conclusion; "Blood Pts." drift figure described as a simulation). (5) Hepa-Vein inter-annotator agreement and annotation protocol details for <0.1%-area bleeding points are absent, yet label noise on such tiny targets directly caps achievable Dice. (6) FPS comparisons mix resolutions ("SAM-based methods use their default resolution, others 512×512"), so the throughput column is not apples-to-apples. Bottom Line: A practitioner in surgical video understanding should read this for the memory-scheduling-as-RL formulation and the new hepatectomy dataset, but should treat the headline numbers cautiously — the decisive comparison against existing long-horizon memory methods (SAM2Long, DAM4SAM) is missing, and a stronger verified baseline combination (MedSAM3 + SAM2Long-style memory curation) may already cover much of the same ground.

AutoSciBench: Autonomous Benchmark Generation for Evaluating Scientific Agents

D Kim, N Lee, S Nair, C Edwards, X Li, E De Brouwer… · arxiv.org · automated generated environments for agent testing - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces AutoSciBench, a framework that automatically generates, verifies, and iteratively refines benchmark tasks for scientific agents in computational biology, materials science, and clinical imaging, using solver behavior as feedback to close shortcut solution paths. - Why it's important: Scientific-agent benchmarks saturate quickly and are expensive to build or update by human experts, so agent capabilities in domains like drug discovery currently outrun the evaluations meant to measure them. - How it does it: It factors each benchmark task into a high-level "concept" (domain, data modality, required operations) and a low-level "recipe" (data, question, and ground-truth construction plan), then runs a generate–solve–judge–revise loop that patches tasks the solver can answer via shortcuts, and distills completed refinement histories into "experience cards" that steer subsequent concept generation. - The good: The difficulty gain is substantial and transfers: generated benchmarks drop average solver accuracy by 22.4pp (computational biology) and 25.5pp (materials science) relative to the human-curated seed benchmarks across 10 different solver models, not just the generator-solver pair. - The missing: Benchmark quality is judged exclusively by the same two LLMs that generated the tasks (Opus 4.8 and GPT-5.6 Sol); no human domain-expert evaluation of the generated tasks is reported, which leaves the core quality claim resting on self-referential LLM judges. - Read it or not: Worth reading for anyone building agent benchmarks or evaluating scientific LLM agents, since the concept/recipe/refinement decomposition and the difficulty-transfer evidence are directly reusable; skip it if you only care about general (non-scientific) agent evaluation, where prior auto-benchmark work covers similar ground.
Why this rank
Scored using Empirical profile. The composite is pulled down primarily by Rigor (55) and Resilience (55): benchmark quality is judged exclusively by the same two LLMs that generated the tasks, no human domain-expert validation is reported, difficulty rests on K=3 solver trials with no error bars or significance tests, no code repository URL is stated, and no contamination check on generator training data exists — and the authors do not engage the self-evaluation circularity at all. Practical Impact (48) is limited by the absence of a stated release and dependence on commercial CLI products. Novelty (68) is real — extending autonomous benchmark generation to scientific agent tasks with concept/recipe revision against solver-discovered shortcuts — and the difficulty-transfer result across 10 solvers plus the non-obvious finding that a weaker generator produces harder, cheaper tasks support Non-Obviousness (65) and a moderate Completeness (55), the latter capped by thin limitations treatment. Weighted composite: 0.20*68 + 0.25*55 + 0.15*65 + 0.15*55 + 0.15*55 + 0.10*48 = 58.
