Problem & Motivation: Single LLM agents are bounded by one context window, one action stream, and sequential execution, which imposes high latency on complex tasks. Current multi-agent harnesses (Codex sub-agents, Claude Code agent teams, Copilot fleet, Kimi Agent Swarm) use an orchestrator-worker structure in which a main agent plans, decomposes, assigns, and integrates work; the authors argue this central coordinator becomes the scalability bottleneck, and cite Anthropic engineering reports and AgentNet as evidence of coordinator-limited designs. The target users are practitioners running agentic software engineering on complex, long-horizon tasks under fixed time budgets. The gap addressed: no existing published harness demonstrates self-organized (orchestrator-free) coordination that scales to four orders of magnitude of agent count on a hard benchmark. Key Idea: Remove the orchestrator and let every worker run the same asynchronous five-step loop — gather context, claim a sub-task (announced as a CLAIM on a shared board), act, verify against acceptance criteria, merge into the shared workspace — with all coordination state externalized into three lightweight services (Git workspace, message channel, typed shared-context board). Sub-task discovery, conflict resolution, and integration are thereby emergent peer behaviors rather than centrally planned. This is a coordination-structure insight, not an algorithmic one: the trick is making the shared state cheap enough to access that planning can be distributed. Methodology: Each worker runs a single-agent harness (Copilot) locally, and Agensh layers organization-level behavior on top via prompts rather than hard-coded runtime logic — every worker receives an identical prompt except for its ID. The five-step loop consumes the shared goal, peer progress, messages, and board entries, and produces claimed sub-tasks, local work, verified patches, and merge updates. The shared context uses typed entries (OBSERVED, FACT, FAIL, CLAIM, PATCH_SUMMARY) with length caps, an append-only store, a `board_grep` tool for history beyond recent memory, and mid-turn delivery of new entries and direct messages via MCP tool-result wrapping. The runtime is event-driven: routers listen to Gitea server-sent events and Mattermost messages, enqueue deduplicated events per worker, and dispatch them with retry, liveness detection (10-minute idle prompts), and session recovery. Critical design decisions: (1) implementing the loop purely in the worker prompt (plug-and-play across harnesses) — justified by showing it works with Copilot, though only that harness is tested; (2) Git for merge conflict handling — reasonable, provenance-preserving, but textual conflicts at 1,024-writer scale are not stress-analyzed; (3) mid-turn injection of direct messages and board entries into tool results — plausible for coordination speed but the interrupt mechanism is not ablated. In experiments, agents are staggered (one every 30s for the first hour, then one every 3s), and centralized reminders are injected at T−45min and T−5min to freeze features and land merges. Key Results: On the five hardest ProgramBench tasks (FFmpeg 1.55M LOC, gromacs 816K, pandoc 104K, PHP-src 2.81M, ctags 246K; reference behavior must be reproduced from a pre-compiled binary in 6h with no internet), scaling 1→8→32→128 agents raises mean final test-pass rate from 19.31% to 20.68%, 26.52%, and 28.78% — a 9.47-point (≈49% relative) gain. On pandoc, 1→128→1,024 agents yields 33.89%→50.94%→55.06%. Larger organizations hit score thresholds earlier: on pandoc, 128 agents exceed 30% test-pass rate at the 30-minute checkpoint versus 60 minutes for 32 agents and 90 for 8, while single agents stay below it for the first two hours. Baselines are the paper's own single-agent runs; there is no comparison to orchestrator-based systems at matched agent count or budget. The 1,024-agent deployment spanned 16 nodes with 64 agents each. Qualitatively, trajectories show claimed emergent structure: interface-agreement and claim-conflict resolution at 8 agents, multi-worker code review and integration at 32, reviewer specialization and reusable merge protocols at 128, and redundant integrator roles at 1,024. The monotonic gains are the notable finding; absolute pass rates still top out near 55%, so most tests remain unsolved. Novelty Classification: NEW SYSTEM/TOOL plus NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING. The genuinely novel elements are the demonstrated scaling curve to 1,024 self-organized agents with a fixed model/harness, and the qualitative taxonomy of cooperation forms emerging at each scale tier. The core mechanism is a competent combination of known ideas: DeLM's shared context (explicitly adopted), Git-based decentralized coordination without an orchestrator (prefigured by Carlini's 16-agent compiler-building experiment), and standard chat/messaging tooling. The contribution is scale and systemization, not a new coordination primitive. Rigor & Reproducibility: Weak on statistical rigor: each configuration appears to be a single run; no seeds, error bars, or variance estimates are reported despite the benchmark being stochastic (LLM agents, 6h free-running). No ablations isolate the contribution of the message interface, shared context, or workspace — the three claimed components are never independently varied. The five tasks are selected post hoc as the hardest by existing model scores, which sharpens the demonstration but narrows generalization. Task selection, prompts (full worker prompt in Appendix A), model, harness, and evaluation protocol are documented in detail, and code is released at https://github.com/microsoft/Agensh, which supports reproducibility. Methodological concerns: (1) the harness injects centralized reminder prompts at T−45min and T−5min — a form of central intervention in a system pitched as fully self-organized; (2) the protocol prompt embeds ProgramBench-specific instructions (compile.sh contract, ulimit sandbox), so the loop's tuning may be benchmark-coupled; (3) all results come from one vendor's model (GPT-5.6-sol) and one underlying harness. This is a Microsoft technical report / arXiv preprint, not peer-reviewed. Deployability: (SYSTEMS profile):* This is a built system evaluated empirically by deployment. - Practical: Yes — it assembles off-the-shelf components (Gitea, Mattermost, Copilot harness, frontier LLM API); the 1,024-agent run needed 16 nodes, which is commodity infrastructure. - Efficient: Unclear — no token or dollar cost is reported, and 1,024 agents on a high-reasoning frontier model for 6 hours implies very large spend; whether the 49% relative gain justifies 128× the agent compute is not analyzed. - Effective: The evidence shows genuine test-pass-rate improvements on the actual benchmark (not a proxy), though a large fraction of hidden tests still fail at best (55.06%). - Scalable:* Tested to 1,024 agents (a real strength); behavior beyond that — Git/Mattermost contention, shared-context prompt growth, and merge-conflict load — is untested, and the paper only claims the frontier "expands." Strengths: (1) The 1→1,024 scaling demonstration with model and harness held fixed is the cleanest published evidence to date that agent count alone improves long-horizon agentic task performance, including the latency-reduction result (threshold crossing at 30 vs 90 minutes on pandoc). (2) The minimal-interface design — loop implemented entirely in prompts, pluggable onto existing single-agent harnesses — is a genuinely practical architectural choice and is fully documented (complete worker prompt in the appendix). (3) The emergent-cooperation analysis offers a concrete, tier-by-tier taxonomy (peer coordination → integration → workflow standardization → role specialization) that gives the field testable hypotheses about multi-agent scaling. (4) Engineering completeness: event-driven runtime with deduplication, retry, liveness detection, and mid-turn message injection is a substantive systems contribution. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The paper has no explicit limitations section ("Not stated."). Implicitly, the authors acknowledge that the shared-context mechanism is adopted from DeLM, that single-agent baselines rarely sustain the full 6-hour budget (mitigated with a stop-hook prompt), and that the qualitative emergence observations come from recorded trajectories rather than controlled measurements. They do not confront the absence of variance reporting, cost analysis, or orchestrator baselines. Analyst-Identified Gaps: (1) Single-run results on five hand-picked tasks with no variance — the 4.12-point gain from 128 to 1,024 agents on pandoc could plausibly be run-to-run noise, yet no repeats are shown. (2) No matched-budget comparison against an orchestrator-based baseline (e.g., Claude Code agent teams or Kimi Swarm) — the central claim that removing the orchestrator is what enables scaling is never tested against the alternative of scaling an orchestrator. (3) No cost/benefit analysis: without token spend, the "scaling dimension" claim is unactionable for practitioners deciding whether 1,024 agents beat 128 agents plus more time or a better model. (4) The T−45min and T−5min centralized reminders partially undercut the self-organization narrative and are never ablated. (5) Emergence claims are anecdotal trajectory excerpts, not quantified (e.g., no measure of how frequently specialized roles form or protocols propagate). (6) The closing claim that agent scaling "expands the frontier of general intelligence" extrapolates far beyond a 55% pass rate on one benchmark with one vendor model. Bottom Line: Practitioners building multi-agent harnesses gain real, reusable engineering detail and the first 1,024-agent scaling data point, but a careful reader should wait for multi-seed, cost-reported, orchestrator-baselined follow-up before accepting "agent count as a scaling dimension" as an established result.

Problem & Motivation: Repository-level software engineering agents (SWE-bench-style tasks) run long trajectories of code inspection, search, editing, and testing, during which exploratory hypotheses, failed attempts, and tool outputs become stale. The paper argues context management is a three-part decision problem—when to compact, what to preserve, and how to continue—and that prior work covers only slices: length-triggered methods (CompactionRL) compact on a fixed budget threshold regardless of task stage; proactive methods either use inference-time rubrics with no training signal (SelfCompact) or fine-tune on trajectories where compression calls were inserted offline, leaving post-compaction actions unsupervised (SWE-Compressor). The beneficiaries are practitioners training coding agents under context or cost constraints. Key Idea: Close the supervision loop: instead of annotating trajectories after the fact, a judge reviews each proposed action using only the history available at that step, replaces flawed compaction triggers, summaries, or continuations with corrected outputs, and lets the environment execute the corrections—so the policy generates subsequent actions from the repaired state and the SFT data demonstrates not just how to compact but how to behave after compaction. This is the central trick; everything downstream (SFT, then outcome-only RL) is standard machinery built on it. Methodology: The pipeline has three stages. (1) An augmented scaffold exposes a model-invocable compact() action that replaces prior history with a model-generated working-state summary (`# Auto Context Summary`) while retaining the original task. (2) Judge-guided data collection: the base policy (Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B-Instruct, terminal REPL scaffold) rolls out on 379 SWE-rebench tasks; the judge checks three decision types—trigger (is this a good compaction point), working-state (does the summary preserve needed findings, code/workspace state, and next actions), and continuation (do the first post-compaction actions follow the summary)—and writes replacements that are executed in place, yielding 1,052 corrected trajectories split 24%/53%/23% across the three decision types. SFT uses standard next-token prediction (2 epochs, LR 5×10⁻⁷). (3) RL: GRPO on SWE-Gym with binary task-success reward, 8 rollouts per task, no KL penalty or entropy bonus; trajectories are split into segments at each compact() call (since compaction rewrites the context prefix), with all segments of a trajectory sharing its group-relative advantage and the policy loss averaged at token level. Critical design decisions: online correction before execution (justified by the ablation against offline insertion via SWE-Compressor), segment splitting with shared advantages (a technical necessity for training through context rewrites, argued but not ablated), and no compaction-specific reward shaping (justified by Figure 4 showing RL reduces summary omissions from the task reward alone). Prompting alone fails to induce proactive compaction—stated from preliminary experiments, not shown. Key Results: On SWE-bench Verified with a 256K window and no cost cap, AutoCompact reaches 39.6% vs Base 30.4%, Fixed Compaction 28.8%, CompactionRL 32.7%, SelfCompact 31.7%, SWE-Compressor 31.0%, and AutoCompact-SFT 32.2%; on SWE-PolyBench Verified, 24.5% vs 19.5% (Base), with the same ordering. All figures are three-run averages. Under six per-task inference budgets ($0.10–$4.00, priced from Alibaba Cloud token rates with cached tokens at 20%), the trained policy wins at every budget; RL's largest gains over SFT come at low budgets (+38 additional tasks per 500 at $0.10). At a 16K forced-compaction threshold, AutoCompact beats Base 38.0% vs 28.8%. Behavior metrics: proactive compact() use goes 0% (Base) → 44.3% (SFT) → 58.5% (RL), while key-state omissions in summaries drop 3.1%→0.2% and next-action omissions 8.2%→2.2% (keyword-based screening plus manual spot checks on all 500 SWE-bench Verified tasks). The summary-ignored ablation shows 37.7% vs 39.6% for the same checkpoint, with a 19.9% relative advantage for executing compaction at $0.10 shrinking to 1.9% at $4.00. The baselines are recent (2026) and reasonably current, though several are self-implementations or numbers taken from papers using different scaffolds—comparability depends on the authors' reimplementation. A notable qualitative finding is summary self-consistency: SFT summaries can record a state while proposing an incompatible next action (Figure 5), which RL corrects because the summary is rewarded only through downstream task success. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD with an ENGINEERING OPTIMIZATION component. Genuinely novel: the online judge-correction loop in which corrected outputs are executed in the environment so that post-compaction behavior is directly supervised—prior proactive methods (SWE-Compressor, SWE-MeM) insert or synthesize memory actions without supervising the actions that follow. The compact() action, single-summary representation, SFT→GRPO training recipe, and binary-success RL are competent combinations of existing techniques (MemGPT-style summarization, GRPO, multi-turn RL); the contribution is the data-collection scheme and the evidence that it matters, not a new learning algorithm. Rigor & Reproducibility: The key ablations are present and well-chosen: summary-ignored inference isolates the effect of executing compaction; the SWE-Compressor comparison with matched base model, scaffold, and training-data volume isolates the effect of online versus offline correction; the 16K and 256K regimes separate overflow-driven from preference-driven compaction; and Figure 4 provides behavioral evidence for the mechanism. No error bars, confidence intervals, or significance tests are reported despite three-run averaging. Hyperparameters are stated, but no code, data, or model release is mentioned. Methodological concerns: (a) the judge (GPT-5.5-Codex) is a substantially stronger model than the base policy, so SFT distills judge behavior—the paper does not bound how much of the gain is judge capability rather than the correction scheme; (b) the summary-quality metrics in Figure 4 use keyword-based screening, which is acknowledged but is a noisy proxy; (c) SWE-rebench training tasks and SWE-bench Verified evaluation are related distributions and no decontamination check is reported in the paper; (d) RL trains on 32K-token sequences but is evaluated at 256K, so the training-evaluation regime mismatch means the RL gains at long context are extrapolated rather than trained for. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (a trained agent policy evaluated on standard benchmarks). Practical: Yes—Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B-Instruct is an open-weights MoE with ~3B active parameters, runnable on commodity multi-GPU hardware, and the judge is needed only during training. Efficient: Costs are measured directly—the paper reports pass rate versus per-task inference spend from $0.10 to $4.00 with explicit token pricing, and shows trained compaction dominates Base at every budget; the RL/SFT training compute is not reported. Effective: The evidence supports task-success gains on two standard benchmarks and under a hard 16K constraint, but the claim that compaction learns "what information matters" rests partly on keyword-screened summary metrics and a single qualitative case study. Scalable: Untested beyond 30B parameters, one scaffold, and 50-step/32K-token RL rollouts; whether the judge-correction scheme scales to stronger base policies (which need fewer corrections) or longer horizons is claimed via the 256K results but not demonstrated at training scale. Delivers: a trained model/checkpoint and method, with no released code, data, or weights stated. Strengths - The online judge-correction design is a real methodological advance over offline trajectory annotation: because corrections are executed, the SFT data teaches post-compaction behavior, and the matched comparison against SWE-Compressor (same base, scaffold, data volume; 32.2% vs 31.0% on SWE-bench Verified) isolates this effect credibly. - The summary-ignored ablation is the strongest piece of evidence in the paper: it holds model parameters fixed and shows that executing compaction contributes up to 19.9% relative at tight budgets, ruling out the alternative explanation that gains come purely from better general agent behavior learned in training. - Outcome-only RL reducing summary omissions (3.1%→0.2% key-state, 8.2%→2.2% next-action) without any compaction-specific reward is a genuinely interesting emergent-behavior finding, and the self-consistency case study (Figure 5) articulates a summary-quality dimension (state–action coherence) that existing coverage metrics miss. - Evaluation across two orthogonal regimes (256K preference-driven, 16K fallback-driven) and six cost budgets makes the cost-effectiveness claims concrete rather than aspirational. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state that RL training uses 32K-token sequences, shorter than the 256K evaluation window, and argue the budget-sweep gains justify this; they also note the study covers a single scaffold (terminal REPL with Qwen3-Coder-30B) and explicitly position integration with production harnesses (Codex, Claude Code) as future work. They confront these directly rather than minimizing them, and the 32K/256K mismatch is disclosed prominently in the Limitations section. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - The judge is GPT-5.5-Codex, likely far stronger than the 30B base policy; no experiment ablates judge strength or measures correction frequency/agreement, so the reader cannot tell how much of the gain is the correction loop versus access to a stronger teacher's behavior. - No variance reporting or significance testing across the three runs; several headline margins (e.g., AutoCompact-SFT 32.2% vs SWE-Compressor 31.0%, a 1.2-point gap) could fall within run-to-run noise. - No contamination check between the 379 SWE-rebench training tasks and the SWE-bench Verified / SWE-PolyBench Verified evaluation sets is reported, which matters because SWE-rebench is a web-scraped task pipeline covering similar repositories. - Baseline comparability is uncertain: CompactionRL, SelfCompact, and SWE-Compressor results appear to be reimplementations or transplanted numbers under this scaffold, and the paper does not state per-baseline which applies. - The behavioral metrics (Figure 4) rely on keyword-based screening validated only by "random manual spot checks" with no reported sample size or agreement rate. - The claim that prompting alone fails to induce proactive compaction is asserted from "preliminary experiments" with no data shown, yet it is the premise motivating the entire data-collection pipeline. - Only one base model is tested; the interaction between base-policy capability and the value of judge correction (weaker models need more corrections; stronger ones may compact competently already) is unexplored. Bottom Line: For anyone training long-horizon agents, this is worth reading for the online judge-correction data-collection scheme and the unusually clean compaction-execution ablation—both directly reusable ideas that a competent practitioner can port to their own stack—but the single-model, single-scaffold evidence and absent significance testing mean the headline numbers should be treated as promising rather than settled.

Recursive Game Creator: An Agentic Product-Level Experience-Oriented Game Harness (78 ▲ )

Jiajun Chen, Haoyu Wu, Mingda Jia, Xihui Liu · arxiv.org · Daily papers of 8 Oct 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper builds Recursive Game Creator, a four-role agentic harness (Designer, Builder, coding-native Player, Reviewer) that iteratively refines LLM-generated games toward player-experience quality rather than mere runnability. - Why it's important: Code-correct games are often unfun; converting functional prototypes into engaging, player-tuned products is the stated gap between current coding agents and real game development. - How it does it: The Player writes executable code policies that play the game programmatically to collect diverse trajectories cheaply (no LLM call per action), and the Reviewer turns trajectory metrics, screenshots, and user preferences into structured feedback that the Designer converts into the next revision plan. - The good: Consistent gains across three refinement rounds on two benchmarks — 71.26 → 77.89 overall on GameCraft-Bench and 9/47 → 25/47 (53.2%) task success on GameASG-Bench — with a 93.4% mean L2 runtime-check pass rate, the highest among compared configurations. - The missing: No component ablations (the contribution of the coding-native Player vs. the Reviewer vs. mere extra refinement rounds is never isolated), no variance/seeds, a tiny uncontrolled user study, and code is only "coming soon." - Read it or not: Worth reading for researchers building agentic game-generation or experience-driven evaluation loops; skippable if you only want rigorous evidence that programmatic playtesting beats GUI-agent playtesting, since that comparison is illustrative, not measured.

Problem & Motivation: Coding agents can produce runnable games, but successful execution does not imply engaging play — difficulty balance, feedback responsiveness, readable presentation, and coherent progression all shape player experience. Prior agentic game-development systems (GUI-agent testers like VibeGame-style pipelines, Harness-of-Harness, RSIGame) either test via slow screenshot-driven agents, which miss structured state and cannot run many rollouts, or stop at bug repair. The target users are game developers and end users who want product-level, customizable games rather than prototypes; the gap the paper closes is connecting repeated, cheap playtesting with experience-oriented, preference-informed revision inside a closed loop with fixed model parameters. Key Idea: Replace the GUI-agent playtester with a coding-native Player: the agent writes reusable executable policies against the game's programmatic interface, so gameplay-trajectory collection requires no per-step model inference or visual interpretation. Collected trajectories (state, action, events, progress, time, termination) plus screenshots then feed an experience-oriented Reviewer that produces game-specific rubric diagnoses and structured preference records, which the Designer converts into testable revision plans — a trajectory-to-feedback-to-plan recursive self-improvement loop. Methodology: The harness is a closed loop over four stages. (1) The Designer emits a structured plan P_t = (h_t, Δ_t, A_t, X_t): an experiential hypothesis, concrete changes, acceptance goals, and asset requests. (2) The Builder drafts the game (Z_t = Draft(G_t, Δ_t)), generates requested assets, integrates them, and runs targeted self-checks. (3) The Player reads the state schema and action space, writes K policies varied in skill/strategy/risk tolerance, and executes them as jobs to produce trajectories τ_t,k with visual records (τ_t,k = Rollout(C_t, π_t,k)); policies are repaired on failure. (4) The Reviewer, blind to source code and version order, estimates success rates and playtime from trajectories, applies shared rubrics (control responsiveness, content richness, pacing, visual coherence) instantiated per genre, examines screenshots for readability and action feedback, produces a structured preference record distinguishing observed behavior, inferred preference, and explicit user requests, and issues an anonymized A/B judgment to retain the better version. The framework is an agentic workflow (no parameter training) with no explicit objective function beyond rubric satisfaction and acceptance goals. Critical design decisions: (a) programmatic over GUI playtesting — justified qualitatively and by coverage analysis, but the GUI comparison in Fig. 4 is explicitly illustrative, not a controlled measurement; (b) blind Reviewer evaluation — well-motivated for bias control; (c) separating fast control from slow visual review — sensible but unquantified in cost terms. Key Results: On GameCraft-Bench (45 selected Godot tasks, following Yan et al.'s subset), using GPT-6 Astra (high) as the base model, the harness scores 77.89 overall at round 3 vs. 72.70 at round 1 (+5.19 across rounds, +6.63 over the same-model baseline of 71.26), exceeding the strongest prior baseline (HoH@3, 71.52) by 6.37 points; all five categories improve, with Action rising most (67.96 → 77.62, +9.66), though rounds 1–2 of Action fall below the one-shot baseline. On GameASG-Bench (47 tasks), the harness reaches 25/47 (53.2%) strict task success (+34.1 points over the same-model Codex CLI baseline at 9/47, and above GPT-6-Astra ultra's 26/47-adjacent 55.3% only in L2 mean, which is 93.4% vs. 93.2% — note ultra still wins task success), with L1 = 98.3%, L2 P0/P1/P2 = 99.0/92.2/93.9%. The Player-exploration analysis reports 97.1% grid coverage of an FPS scene from 48 policy rollouts. A user study (Table 3, no participant count given) reports round-level expert means rising from 2/1/3/2 (controls/playability/depth/art) at round 1 to 8/7/6/8 at round 3, and average playtime from 1.50 to 12.41 minutes. Baselines on GameASG-Bench are taken from Zhang et al.'s Table 3; the strongest same-budget baseline (GPT-6-Astra ultra, 26/47) actually outperforms the harness on task success, which the text does not foreground. Benchmarks are standard for this emerging area; scale is modest (45–47 tasks, single game engine per benchmark). Novelty Classification: NEW SYSTEM/TOOL and NEW METHOD, with an ENGINEERING OPTIMIZATION component. The genuinely novel element is the coding-native Player — code policies as the playtesting mechanism feeding an experience-oriented Reviewer inside a recursive retention loop. The surrounding machinery is a competent composition of established ideas: multi-role agent pipelines (MetaGPT/ChatDev/GameGPT), executable-skill libraries (Voyager), self-refinement loops (Self-Refine/Reflexion), and preference-informed revision without parameter updates (RLHF-adjacent, but text-level). The experience-oriented, trajectory-based Reviewer rubrics applied per genre is the second substantive novelty; the recursive loop itself overlaps with concurrent work (RSIGame, HoH). Rigor & Reproducibility: No component ablations are reported — the paper never isolates whether gains come from the Player, the Reviewer's rubrics, the Designer's structured plans, or simply three extra refinement rounds against a one-shot baseline. No seeds, error bars, or significance tests appear anywhere. Code is "coming soon" (not released), and no prompts or policy examples beyond Fig. 2 are provided, so reproducibility is currently low. Methodological concerns: (1) GameCraft-Bench evaluation involves "replayed gameplay and game-specific rubrics" — if the Reviewer/judge shares lineage with the generating model (GPT-6 Astra), self-evaluation bias is possible and unaddressed; (2) results are on a 45-task selected subset rather than the full benchmark, with selection criteria inherited from prior work but not justified here; (3) the user study reports only round-level means with no n, protocol, or controls; (4) the GUI-vs-coding-native comparison (Fig. 4) is explicitly not a controlled experiment, so the claimed efficiency advantage of the core contribution is asserted, not measured. The authors deserve credit for stating these caveats themselves (Sections 3.2, 4.1, 4.3), which is unusual and credible. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL/SYSTEMS (a built agentic harness, evaluated by benchmark and user study). Practical: Yes in principle — it orchestrates existing LLM coding agents and game engines (Godot, browser games), requiring no special hardware beyond LLM API access. Efficient: Claimed cheaper than GUI-agent testing because policy execution needs no per-step model calls, but total cost including policy generation, repair, and review is acknowledged and never quantified. Effective: The evidence (benchmark gains, runtime-check pass rates, rising expert scores and playtime) supports improvement on proxies for enjoyment (rubrics, playtime) more than demonstrated player enjoyment itself. Scalable: Untested beyond three rounds and ~47 tasks; behavior over many rounds (e.g., Reviewer drift, policy exhaustion, credit assignment across versions) is unexamined. The work delivers no released artifact yet — code and generated games are promised, and the paper itself is currently the only deliverable. Strengths: - The coding-native Player is a genuinely useful reframing: treating playtesting as policy-writing makes trajectory collection cheap, parallelizable, and reproducible, and it aligns playtesting with what coding agents are actually good at. - The Reviewer's epistemic discipline — separating observed behavior from inferred preference from explicit user requests, evaluating blind to version order and source code, and outputting A/B/tie/unavailable judgments — is a thoughtful evaluation design rare in this literature. - Consistent, multi-benchmark quantitative gains (77.89 GameCraft-Bench; 53.2% strict task success with 93.4% L2 pass on GameASG-Bench) against baselines that include strong recent systems (HoH@3, Codex CLI configurations). - Unusually honest self-limitation: the paper repeatedly flags that proxy playtime and success rate do not establish human enjoyment and that the GUI comparison is not a measured speedup. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state that proxy policies do not represent the human player population, that proxy playtime alone does not show enjoyment, that total testing cost includes policy generation/repair/execution/review, that the Fig. 4 GUI comparison shows coverage rather than a measured speedup, that Action-category gains emerged only late and the category scores alone do not identify the cause, and that success rate should target appropriate difficulty rather than maximization. This direct confrontation of limitations is a strong credibility positive; the paper does not minimize. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - No ablation of the four roles or of refinement-round count, so the marginal value of each component — the paper's actual contribution — is unknown; a plain "generate, then refine 3× with any feedback" baseline is absent. - The headline GameASG-Bench comparison is against the same model (GPT-6 Astra high at 9/47); the stronger GPT-6-Astra ultra configuration achieves 26/47 (55.3%) task success, beating the harness, so the "state-of-the-art" claim holds on GameCraft-Bench and on L2 pass rate, not on strict task success overall. - Potential judge-generator coupling: how GameCraft-Bench's rubric scoring is mechanized and whether it is independent of the generating model is unspecified. - The user study lacks participant count, task assignment, and statistical treatment; playtime as an engagement proxy can be inflated by confusion, not fun. - Generalization of the coding-native Player is untested on games lacking clean programmatic interfaces (the two benchmarks use Godot and browser games with exposed state); the approach may not transfer to engine-external or asset-heavy 3D games. - No released code, prompts, or trajectories at publication time. Bottom Line: A practitioner building agentic game-generation systems gains a concrete, well-argued design pattern — programmatic playtesting policies feeding a blind, trajectory-based experience Reviewer — that is likely the most reusable idea in this subfield right now, but the absent ablations, unreleased code, and a baseline configuration that beats the system on strict task success mean the reported numbers should be treated as promising rather than settled.

Self-Evolving Harness on Multiple Tasks with the Agent as Its Own Optimizer

TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces a self-evolving agent-harness framework in which a single frozen frontier model (GPT-5.6 Sol), running on the same harness it is improving, alternates between solving tasks as the solver and editing the harness code as the proposer, starting from a 49-line seed and evolving it to 430–524 lines across seven iterations. - Why it's important: Existing harness-evolution methods use a separate human-designed proposer harness, evolve one harness per benchmark, and often report gains on the tasks used for evolution — so their improvements do not compound in the improver and frequently fail to generalize to unseen tasks. - How it does it: The core move is a recursive setup (same model, same harness for both roles) combined with an explicit analogy to deep-learning training: mixed multi-benchmark batches as "pretraining," a decaying new-line edit budget as a learning-rate schedule, and free-text evolution notes as optimizer state, with success anchors replayed during a continual-training stage on a new domain. - The good: The evaluation is unusually careful for this line of work: strictly separated held-out tasks, five never-seen out-of-distribution benchmarks, and an explicit reward-hacking audit pipeline; Problem & Motivation: Agent performance depends heavily on the harness — the control code around the model that manages prompts, tools, context, and termination. Prior self-evolving-harness work (Meta-Harness, HarnessX, HarnessBank, AHE, etc.) shares four weaknesses the authors identify: the proposer runs on a fixed human-designed harness so gains never compound in the improver; the proposer model differs from the solver model (frontier models are used to improve weaker ones, which the paper argues is the less interesting question); editable scope is restricted to preset components or edit types; and evolution typically targets a single benchmark, so the resulting harness overfits that domain. Practitioners deploying agents face tasks from many domains and cannot maintain a bespoke harness per benchmark, so a single harness that improves itself from mixed-domain experience and generalizes to unseen tasks is the target gap. The paper also cites prior findings that evolution gains shrink or vanish when evaluation tasks are separated from evolution tasks, motivating its strict generalization protocol. Key Idea: The key insight is to make harness evolution genuinely recursive and treat it as model training: the same frozen agent, on the same version of the harness, plays both solver and proposer (the proposer literally runs on the harness it is editing, so improvements compound), and the training analogy supplies concrete design rules — new-lines-allowed-per-iteration as the learning rate (cosine-annealed 500→100 in stage 1, re-warmed to 200 then decayed to 100 in stage 2), free-text evolution notes as Adam-style optimizer state, mixed five-benchmark batches as multi-task pretraining data, and solved old tasks replayed as "success anchors" during continual training on a new domain. The analogy is inspired by SkillOpt but extended from skill documents to the entire harness source code, with unrestricted edit scope. Methodology: The framework is formalized as optimizing an external state Ht = (Ct, Nt) — full harness source code plus evolution notes — for a frozen model M on a fixed execution kernel K. Each iteration has three steps: (1) rollout — the solver runs the batch Bt once per task, producing records Et = {(x, τx, rx, vx)} of trajectories, scores, and grader outputs; (2) update — the same agent receives an update task It containing the raw, un-summarized run records, the current code and notes, and the previous update session's record, and edits the harness directly (Eq. 4); (3) check — engineering checks only (edits confined to the harness, non-empty, within the new-line budget at, passes a smoke run with a mock model), with rollback and a repair session on failure (Eq. 5). Notably, acceptance is purely runnability — there is no validation set and no score comparison between old and new versions. Stage 1 uses five iterations × 60 tasks (12 each from Terminal-Bench 2.1, GAIA2, OfficeQA Pro, τ³-Bench banking, SWE-Bench Pro train sets); stage 2 runs two iterations on Claw-Eval (40 new + 20 success-anchor tasks each). Three critical design decisions: (a) identical model configuration for solver and proposer — justified by the RSI motivation, though it pins the whole result to one frontier model; (b) the cosine edit-budget schedule — borrowed from learning-rate practice, plausible but un-ablated against alternatives like fixed budgets; (c) acceptance without score-based validation — explicitly acknowledged as the framework's weakest link, deliberately kept for minimal human priors. All experiments use GPT-5.6 Sol (high reasoning, 258,400-token input limit), with anti-reward-hacking constraints (pre-hoc task instructions, post-hoc scripted trajectory audits plus independent-agent review; no confirmed cheating). Key Results: On held-out tasks of the five in-distribution benchmarks, Iteration 5 averages 60.17 — 4.48 above the seed and 2.99 above Codex (Codex CLI 0.146.0, same model, same context-compaction tools) — with gains concentrated on Terminal-Bench 2.1 (66.67→83.91) and SWE-Bench Pro (51.00→61.00), both above Codex. On five OOD benchmarks never used in evolution, Iteration 5 averages 70.45, 12.64 above the seed and within 0.12 of Codex (70.57); BrowseComp-Plus jumps 34.00→90.00 (Codex: 93.00) because output truncation eliminated context-overflow aborts (the seed aborted on 65 such tasks; Iteration 5 answered 57 correctly). Excluding BrowseComp-Plus, the OOD margin narrows to 65.56 vs 63.76 (seed) and 64.97 (Codex). Stage 2 raises Claw-Eval from 66.17 to 68.06 (passed tasks 52→57), driven by multimodal tasks (39.3→47.8) via a visual-inspection quota and delivery deadlines; Iteration 7 exceeds Codex (66.2) there. The paper honestly reports regressions: Iteration 5 falls below Seed on τ³-Bench banking (−1.1; compaction deleted the customer's original request in all 11 triggered runs, only one passed; misuse of configure_run cut short 2 runs) and OfficeQA Pro (attributed to ambiguous questions affecting all harnesses equally). The analysis chapter traces mechanism emergence (output truncation and history compaction in Iteration 1, independent fresh-context review in Iterations 2–3, visual budget in Iteration 6) with trigger-rate statistics per benchmark (Appendix C). Baselines are current and strong (Codex on the same model). Tested scale is small: 300 stage-1 tasks, 80 stage-2 tasks, held-out sets of 29–100 tasks, 7 iterations. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD (with elements of NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING). The genuinely novel combination is the fully recursive configuration — same model, same (self-hosted) harness for proposer and solver, unrestricted edit scope, mixed multi-domain task batches — plus the systematic transfer of training-recipe mechanics (learning-rate annealing as edit budget, notes as optimizer state, replay anchors) to code-level harness evolution. Each ingredient individually exists: SkillOpt pioneered the bounded-edit/textual-learning-rate analogy, RRSI (concurrent) anneals edit counts, DGM/SICA keep multiple versions, and the training-analogy framing itself is derivative; what is new is their composition into a minimal-prior recursive loop validated on held-out and OOD multi-domain tasks, and the honest mechanistic analysis of what evolution actually built. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations in the loose sense are present: the paper attributes gains to specific mechanisms via trajectory analysis (truncation → BrowseComp-Plus; review → OfficeQA correction example uid0029; visual budget → Claw-Eval multimodal) and reports mechanism trigger rates per benchmark. However, there are no component ablations of the framework itself (e.g., no comparison against a non-recursive proposer, a per-benchmark-evolved harness baseline, or a simple-baseline-under-equal-budget comparison that the cited "Simple Baselines" and "Rethinking the Evaluation" papers explicitly demand), no multiple seeds, no error bars, and no significance tests — with only one evolution chain, the stochasticity of the process is unmeasured, and the authors admit rerunning could yield different mechanisms. The OOD average gain is heavily leveraged on a single benchmark (BrowseComp-Plus contributes ~11 of the 12.64 points), which the authors partially mitigate by reporting the four-benchmark average. Held-out sets are small and repeated runs (e.g., Terminal-Bench 29×3) substitute for statistical power. No code, data, or harness release is mentioned. The reward-hacking audit protocol is a methodological strength, and the anti-overfitting protocol (train/held-out separation, OOD evaluation) addresses the Goodhart concern that plagues this subfield — though the update prompt itself encodes the evaluation intent ("evaluated on unseen tasks"), a soft leakage channel the authors do not discuss. Deployability: (4-property check):** Profile: EMPIRICAL (a system/experiment actually run, on commercial API access). - Practical: Yes — it needs only API access to one frontier model plus a container execution kernel; the harness is plain Python. - Efficient: The evolution phase consumed 7 proposer sessions plus ~380 task rollouts, but each rollout uses a high-reasoning frontier model, and the evolved harness itself adds calls (independent review fires on ~100% of non-interactive tasks, capped at 150s/8 calls in stage 2) — the paper discusses but does not quantify per-task token cost versus seed or Codex. - Effective: Evidence shows real, mechanistically explained gains on held-out and OOD tasks, including a continual-training stage; but the headline OOD gain is one-mechanism-driven, and two in-distribution benchmarks regressed. - Scalable: Untested beyond 7 iterations and 5 benchmarks; the authors note edit diversity collapses over iterations and acceptance lacks validation, both of which likely worsen over longer horizons — no 10× evidence exists, only a vision. The work delivers no public artifact (no code repo or evolved harness is stated as released); it stops at paper form plus a described procedure. Strengths: - The recursive same-model/same-harness design is a real conceptual step over the proposer-on-fixed-harness paradigm: it removes the ceiling where the improver never improves, and the comparison table (Table 2) against 12 recent methods shows this configuration is rare and that Self-Harness's claimed equivalent has a material caveat. - The evaluation protocol is above the bar for this subfield: strict train/held-out separation, five genuinely OOD benchmarks, an explicit multi-stage reward-hacking audit (scripted flagging plus independent-agent review), and per-benchmark mechanism trigger rates that connect causes to effects. - The training-analogy is operationalized into concrete, transferable design rules (budget schedule, replay anchors, notes-as-momentum), not just rhetoric, and the two-stage pretraining/continual-training structure yields a testable prediction (Claw-Eval gain) that held. - The analysis of regressions (compaction destroying multi-turn dialogue state; tool exposure causing step-limit misuse) is unusually candid and mechanistically specific — genuinely useful negative knowledge for harness designers. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors confront limitations directly and at unusual length: (1) results use only one strong model, and whether weaker models need a prescribed outer pipeline is untested; (2) evolution is stochastic and a single chain cannot estimate variance; (3) some held-out sets are small, so small score differences should be interpreted cautiously; (4) continual training covers only one new domain; (5) Section 5.7 names three structural costs — local fixes with cross-task side effects, acceptance without any score-based validation (explicitly called "the framework's missing piece" and the sharpest divergence from gradient training, where a small step provably lowers batch loss), and narrowing edit diversity (skills, memory, sub-agents were prompted but never emerged), with proposed remedies (update validation, multi-version evolution à la DGM). This is a credibility positive: the limitations section matches the severity of what a reviewer would find. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - No equal-budget simple baseline: the cited "Simple Baselines are Competitive with Code Evolution" result makes the absence of a tuned static harness or prompt-only baseline under the same rollout budget a notable omission — the +4.48 in-distribution gain over Codex could partly be generic prompt/context engineering any competent engineer would add (truncation, timeouts, compaction are all standard). - The update prompt leaks evaluation intent ("will be evaluated on unseen tasks and entirely different benchmarks"), which functions as an implicit generalization regularizer that human harnesses being compared against do not receive — an asymmetry not acknowledged. - One evolution chain means the reported mechanisms (truncation, compaction, review) may be path-dependent; the authors note this but the framing of Section 5 as "how the harness evolved" overstates what a single run can establish. - Per-task token/cost accounting is absent, so "surpassing Codex" claims ignore that independent review on nearly every non-interactive task adds substantial inference cost — a practitioner comparing against Codex needs this number. - The 12.64-point OOD gain is largely a truncation artifact on one retrieval benchmark; the paper reports the corrected four-benchmark average but the headline framing still leans on the aggregate. - Claw-Eval training tasks (80) share a benchmark with a 100-task held-out set, so stage-2 "continual training" gains are on a benchmark the harness has been fed tasks from — weaker generalization evidence than the OOD-never-seen claims elsewhere. Bottom Line: Worth reading for anyone doing agent-harness research or RSI-style self-improvement — the recursive same-harness design and the candid failure analysis are genuinely instructive — but a practitioner should treat the headline numbers as one stochastic run from a single frontier model, likely dominated by a handful of well-known engineering mechanisms (truncation, timeouts, compaction, review) that could be transplanted directly without any evolution loop.

Continuous Verification of Evolving Architecture Models: A Testing Framework for MontiArc

T Bursch, A Marin, B Rumpe, D Schmalzing · se-rwth.de · specification to code with formal verifications - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces MaUnit, a testing framework that adapts xUnit-style test specification and automated execution to the architecture description language MontiArc, so tests are written as MontiArc components rather than in a general-purpose language. - Why it's important: Architecture models, like code, evolve continuously and need regression testing, but modelers of executable ADLs typically lack language-integrated test support and are forced down to JUnit-level GPL code, raising the barrier for domain experts. - How it does it: Tests are declared as complete MontiArc component topologies (system-under-test plus a test oracle) via a «test» stereotype, compiled to Java, and run on top of the JUnit Platform so results flow into standard Gradle/IDE tooling. - The good: The authors re-implemented 152 of 176 existing MontiArc simulator test files in MaUnit, cutting an average of 78.67 lines per test file (a 28.6% reduction), demonstrating the notation covers the language's real test workload. - The missing: The evaluation is a self-comparison against the authors' own Java tests with semantic equivalence judged by the authors themselves; there is no user study, no external codebase, and no measurement of whether the abstraction actually helps non-GPL modelers. - Read it or not: Read it if you build or adopt executable DSLs/ADLs and need to design language-integrated testing infrastructure; skip it if you want empirical evidence about test effectiveness beyond a single in-house case study.
Why this rank
Scored using Systems profile. Practical Impact (65) is solid — a real artifact integrated into an open-source toolchain and CI — but Rigor (45) is dragged down by a self-referential evaluation against the authors' own test suite, no ablation, and a single uncontrolled LOC metric. Novelty (35) is low: a competent port of established xUnit concepts to one ADL, classified as engineering. Completeness (65) benefits from honest enumeration of the 24 inexpressible tests. Problem & Motivation: Testing frameworks like JUnit, NUnit, and Pytest let developers write and run tests at the same abstraction level as the implementation, but comparable language-integrated testing support is largely absent for architecture description languages. Modelers of executable models must either write tests in a GPL (needing deep knowledge of the simulator and generated code, per the authors' 'semantic gap' argument), or lose traceability when failures reference compiled artifacts rather than model-level constructs. The target audience is MontiArc component developers and, by claimed generalization, anyone modeling cyber-physical systems in an ADL with executable semantics. Key Idea: Treat a test as a MontiArc component: a test is a fully connected, port-free component topology whose subcomponents are the SUT and a test oracle, marked with a «test» stereotype. This single move makes xUnit concepts (annotation-based discovery, assertions, parameterization, structured reporting) expressible entirely within the ADL, and compiling tests to Java annotated classes lets the framework piggyback on the JUnit Platform for discovery, execution, and toolchain compatibility. Methodology: The framework has three layers. (1) Notation: tests are MontiArc components composed with reusable library components — Emitters (Emit, EmitList, EmitSync, EmitTimed) that generate input streams and Asserters (AssertTrue/False, and an AssertEquals family with timed/untimed/synchronous variants) that check output streams — plus class-based assertion methods mirroring JUnit Jupiter and a fluent assertion API. A «test, ticks = N» annotation bounds simulation length, guaranteeing termination; a test passes if no assertion fails within N ticks. Parameterized tests take parameters with annotation-supplied argument sets. (2) Compilation: the MontiArc simulator generates Java; test components get a @MAUnitTest annotation and a generated MAUnitTestContext class carrying test metadata and parameter assignments. (3) Execution: a MaUnit test engine built on the JUnit Platform runs a discovery phase (find @MAUnitTest classes, create container descriptors) and an execution phase (per-case invocation descriptors, a custom scheduler that records scheduling traces, simulation for the specified ticks), and reports results in JUnit-compatible XML, HTML, and a binary format via a Gradle plugin. Critical design decisions: (a) tests as component topologies rather than a separate test DSL — justified by reusing existing language semantics and enabling gray-box integration testing; (b) building on the JUnit Platform rather than a bespoke runner — justified by free toolchain integration, though it ties the framework to the Java ecosystem; (c) tick-count as the termination mechanism — acknowledged by the authors as a leaky abstraction requiring low-level stream understanding. Key Results: The evaluation re-implemented MontiArc's own simulator test suite: 176 active test files exist in Java/JUnit; 152 were directly expressible in MaUnit and 24 were not (deployment tests asserting on internal subcomponent messages, scheduling tests using invalid input streams not producible by valid models, and simulator setup tests). Reported metrics: an average of 78.67 fewer lines of code per MaUnit test file versus the analogous Java test file, a 28.6% reduction; semantic equivalence was established by 'experienced MontiArc users' during construction (i.e., the authors). The resulting tests run in the MontiArc project's CI pipeline and reportedly need no updates when the simulator evolves. No runtime performance figures, error bars, or significance statistics are reported; the sole baseline is the authors' own pre-existing Java test suite, and the scale is a single language's test suite, not external projects. Novelty Classification: NEW SYSTEM/TOOL with an ENGINEERING OPTIMIZATION component (28.6% LOC reduction). The genuinely novel element is the realization of tests-as-component-topologies with a JUnit-Platform-backed engine for a concrete ADL; the individual ingredients — xUnit concepts, oracle/SUT composition, emitter/asserter libraries, parameterized tests, CI integration — are all established ideas from GPL testing, and the related work (Gamma's tracing language, HAMR contract testing, Simulink Test blocks) already covers model-level testing for adjacent formalisms. The contribution is a competent, well-integrated port of known testing concepts to one textual ADL, not a new testing technique. Rigor & Reproducibility: There is no ablation: the paper does not isolate which framework features (parameterization, library components, oracle composition) drive the LOC reduction, nor does it report per-test-category breakdowns. No error bars, seeds, or statistical tests — appropriate for a deterministic tool demonstration, but the 28.6% LOC figure is a single uncontrolled measurement. Code availability is implicit rather than stated: MontiArc lives at github.com/monticore/montiarc and the framework integrates into its Gradle plugin, but the paper never explicitly says MaUnit is released. Methodological concerns: (1) the evaluation tests the framework on the authors' own tool's tests — a self-referential benchmark with no external validity check; (2) semantic equivalence is judged by the developers, an unavoidable but unblinded standard; (3) the paper conflates 'applicability' (expressiveness) with the broader claim of 'continuous verification' benefit — no data on defect detection, maintenance cost, or adoption is presented. The title's 'Continuous Verification' overstates what is measured: the system runs tests in CI, but verification effectiveness is not evaluated. Deployability: Profile: SYSTEMS (a built tool evaluated by re-implementation and CI deployment). Practical: Runs on any machine with a JVM, Gradle, and the MontiArc toolchain — no specialized hardware needed. Efficient: No runtime cost data is reported versus direct JUnit tests; the LOC reduction (78.67 lines/file, 28.6%) is the only efficiency measure. Effective: Evidence shows it can express 86% of an existing in-house test suite at lower LOC, but does not show it finds defects faster or that domain experts without GPL skills can actually use it. Scalable: Untested — the evaluation covers one repository's test suite; behavior on large model bases, slow simulations, or thousands of parameterized cases is unexamined. The deliverable is a concrete software artifact (test notation, engine, Gradle plugin, component/assertion libraries) shipped inside the open-source MontiArc toolchain. Strengths: - The tests-as-complete-component-topologies design is a clean unification: one construct covers unit tests, mocked integration tests, and gray-box topology testing, avoiding a separate test DSL. - Building the engine on the JUnit Platform is a smart reuse decision — MontiArc tests appear natively in Gradle summaries and any JUnit-compatible tool at near-zero integration cost. - The evaluation against the project's own 176-file test suite is an honest applicability check, and the paper candidly enumerates the 24 inexpressible tests (deployment, scheduling, setup) with reasons, including the fundamental monitoring limitation (MaUnit only observes external ports). - The reported simulator-evolution benefit — MaUnit tests survive simulator changes without modification while Java tests must track generated-code APIs — is a real, concrete advantage of the abstraction. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state: (1) debugging is not improved — failing tests may still require inspecting generated simulator code, so requirement R4 (model-level traceability) is 'only partially fulfilled'; (2) tick-based test-length specification leaks low-level stream semantics and should be replaced by SI time units; (3) the simulator resolves model underspecifications (scheduling, incomplete automata) in one concrete way, so a test passing in simulation may fail on target hardware — tests must ultimately run on the final platform; (4) system-in-the-loop testing and reuse of test artifacts against the deployed product are deferred to future work. These limitations are stated directly and not minimized, which strengthens the paper's credibility. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - No user study or even anecdotal evidence that the target beneficiary — a domain expert without GPL knowledge — can write tests; the 'lowers barrier to entry' claim (R1) is argued, not measured. - The LOC-reduction metric confounds notation with suite history: the Java tests were written to test the simulator's Java-facing behavior, and no effort is reported to hand-optimize either side. - No comparison with the closest related systems (Gamma's tracing language, HAMR contract tests, Simulink test blocks) on any common workload, so claims of comparative usability advantage rest on qualitative argument in Section 8. - Failure-detection capability is never evaluated: no mutation analysis, fault injection, or regression-detection experiment shows MaUnit tests catch defects the Java tests do or do not. - Performance characteristics of the two-phase JUnit-Platform execution over the MontiArc simulator are unreported, leaving CI-time impact unknown. - The 24 inexpressible test categories reveal a structural ceiling (external-port-only observation) that the authors wave off as rare, but real integration testing often needs mid-topology observation points. Bottom Line: A solid, honestly-reported tool paper that usefully demonstrates how to give a textual ADL first-class xUnit testing infrastructure, but with a self-referential evaluation and no effectiveness evidence — read it as a design reference for DSL/ADL test frameworks, not as proof that model-level testing improves verification outcomes.

SuperNav: An Agentic Navigation System for Any Task in Any Scene (62 ▲ )

Jinkai Zhang, Jingyi Xu, Yuanhong Yu, Jiarui Guo, Ruizhen Hu, Hujun Bao, Xiaowei Zhou, Sida Peng · arxiv.org · Daily papers of 9 Oct 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces SuperNav, an agent harness that lets a pretrained (non-fine-tuned) MLLM drive embodied navigation across instance-level, multi-object, demand-driven, and category-level tasks by delegating motion to interchangeable tools, with Navigation Skills, task-progress tracking, and context management. - Why it's important: Fine-tuned navigation VLMs generalize poorly beyond their training environments (the paper's own cross-environment tests show e.g. UniNaVid dropping to 1.33% SR on multi-object tasks), and service robots need systems that handle new requests in unseen scenes without retraining. - How it does it: The MLLM stays untrained for navigation and only picks destinations as normalized image points in four-view RGB; a harness of Tools executes motion (geometric back-projection + navmesh planner, or a learned NoMaD-style flow policy), while Markdown-packaged Skills provide read-on-demand procedural guidance for search, recovery, and completion. - The good: The ablation is convincing — removing Navigation Skills collapses HM3D-OVON success at the 0.25 m threshold from 68.33% to 35.00%, and removing agent-oriented tool design drops it to 52.50%, showing both components materially matter rather than the raw MLLM alone. - The missing: All headline results depend on proprietary frontier models (GPT-5.6 Terra / GPT-6 Astra) via Codex CLI, with no error bars, multiple seeds, or significance tests, and the real-robot deployment on a Unitree Go2 is qualitative only. - Read it or not: Worth reading for embodied-AI and robot-learning researchers deciding between fine-tuned VLA policies and harness-style agentic systems, and for anyone building tool-based embodied agents; skippable if you only need the fine-tuning track, whose baselines here are notably weak.

Problem & Motivation: General-purpose service robots must navigate to fulfill heterogeneous requests — find a specific object instance, visit ordered multi-target sequences, or satisfy abstract needs like "prepare a workspace" — in environments unseen during development. Modular zero-shot pipelines (VLFM, SG-Nav, ApexNav) hard-code task-specific workflows that break when the request changes the goal semantics, progress tracking, or completion condition. End-to-end fine-tuned models (NaVid, UniNaVid, StreamVLN, OmniNav) encode observation-instruction-action associations that the paper argues (and measures, in Section 4.1) fail to transfer across environments. The gap addressed is a single zero-shot system that achieves both task generality and scene generality without navigation-specific training of the decision model. Key Idea: The core insight is a strict division of labor: keep the MLLM as an untouched general-purpose reasoner and move all navigation-specific machinery into an external harness. The enabling trick is a unified visual-point interface — PointNav(d, [u,v]) where the model clicks a destination in one of four direction-labeled RGB views — which decouples the model's decision (pick a pixel) from the motion backend (geometric planner or learned policy), and is supplemented by Skills (Markdown guidance loaded on demand) that steer when to search, recheck, recover, and stop, without programmatically enforcing any action sequence. Methodology: The system has three layers. (1) An agent loop (implemented on Codex CLI with MCP-exposed tools) maintains the request, textual history, goal-progress records, and current images; it prunes image media payloads once superseded while retaining textual history and image paths the model can re-fetch. (2) Agent-oriented Tools cover initialization, four-view observation, turning, visual-point navigation, progress query/update, and termination; the visual-point Tool internally grounds the pixel via depth and camera calibration to a navmesh location (Geo-based Executor: back-projection, Recast/Detour path query, GreedyGeodesicFollower) or drives a learned policy (Learned Executor: DINOv2 ViT-S/14 encoder, variable-length age-aware history of up to 12 frames, a 4-layer Transformer, and a 1-D U-Net conditional flow head trained by flow matching on 8 displacement increments plus a stop head, imitation-trained on Habitat greedy-follower trajectories with loss L_flow + 0.5·L_stop + 0.002·L_remaining). (3) Navigation Skills are Markdown bundles for search, recovery, and completion, discovered and loaded on demand. Termination is the model's own achieved/blocked judgment; benchmark scoring is independent of that declaration. Critical design decisions: (a) direct point selection instead of external language grounding — justified by an ablation where a LocateAnything-based grounding tool underperforms direct pointing (62.50 vs 68.33 SR at 0.25 m); (b) media-only context pruning — reasonable but un-ablated; (c) interchangeable backends sharing one interface — well executed, with the Learned Executor retaining most success but losing SPL (0.1443 vs 0.4105 at 1 m on OVON). Key Results: On the authors' InteriorGS benchmark (Habitat-GS), SuperNav + Geo-based Executor achieves 78.00% SR / 0.4127 SPL on 150 single-object tasks versus 34.00% for the strongest baseline (UniNaVid), and 59.50% / 0.1801 on 200 demand-driven AI2-THOR tasks versus 37.50% for OmniNav's Action Former. Multi-object SR is 34.00% for both backends versus ≤4.00% for all four baselines, with baseline SR5 at 0.00%. On HM3D-OVON val-unseen (120-episode subset), Geo-based Executor reaches 73.33% SR / 0.4105 SPL at 1 m and 68.33% / 0.3837 at 0.25 m, exceeding published MTU3D (40.80/0.1210 at 0.25 m), SoftNav (66.70/0.2570), AstraNav-Memory (62.50/0.3490 at 1 m), and OmniNav slow+CoT (59.20/0.3320). On 1,000 HM3Dv2 validation episodes it reports 80.30% / 0.3338 at 0.2 m and 86.50% / 0.3638 at 1 m, exceeding ApexNav (76.20/0.3800 at 0.2 m) and WMNav/MSGNav at 1 m. Ordered-progress tables (Table 4) show SuperNav leads every multi-object stage. A model-swap variant with GPT-6 Astra (medium) improves OVON to 71.67%/79.17% SR. Notably, the authors themselves flag that published HM3D comparison protocols and evaluation subsets differ from theirs, weakening direct numeric claims. Real-robot results on a Unitree Go2 are demonstration videos/figures only, with no quantitative success rates. Novelty Classification: NEW SYSTEM/TOOL and NEW FORMULATION (of navigation as harness-mediated agentic tool use with a visual-point action interface), plus a NEW DATASET/BENCHMARK (InteriorGS instance-navigation set). The genuinely novel element is the complete zero-training-harness design with the image-space point interface spanning two motion backends and four task types; individually, the components — MLLM prompting, VLM relevance scoring, NoMaD-style learned locomotion, context pruning, Markdown skills — are existing ideas, and concurrent work (AgenticNav, HarnessVLN, DemandAgent) applies very similar harness concepts to navigation, so the contribution is as much a well-engineered synthesis and empirical demonstration as a fundamentally new mechanism. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are present and substantive: Skills removal, tool-design removal, grounding-vs-pointing, backend swap, and decision-model swap, each on the shared 120-episode OVON manifest with interaction statistics (Table 6). However, no seeds, error bars, or significance tests are reported anywhere — a serious omission for stochastic LLM-agent evaluations where a 120-episode subset makes single-run differences of a few points noisy. Reproducibility is a major concern: the decision model is a proprietary frontier API (GPT-5.6 Terra / GPT-6 Astra) accessed through Codex CLI, so results cannot be exactly replicated once the model changes; the Learned Executor training is well specified (Appendix C), but no code, weights, or benchmark release is stated (a project page exists, contents not verified). Methodological flags: (1) the instance benchmark is the authors' own construction with AI-assisted annotations, evaluated only by them; (2) several HM3D comparisons use differing episode subsets, step budgets, and STOP rules, which the authors disclose but which means the table's cross-method ranking is not apples-to-apples; (3) baselines on the multi-object task are so weak (SR ≤ 4.00%) that the comparison there mostly shows the baselines fail, not that SuperNav's margin is calibrated; (4) the demand-driven protocol is a re-scoring of Demand-Bench that the authors explicitly note is incomparable to DemandAgent's numbers. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL (system built and run in simulation and on one robot; also arguably SYSTEMS). - Practical: Yes for the harness itself (Codex + MCP + a four-camera RGB robot), but the decision model requires access to a frontier proprietary LLM, and the Geo-based Executor needs depth/LiDAR or simulator geometry. - Efficient: Not efficient — the authors concede substantial MLLM inference cost and latency variability, with 3,600 s per-episode budgets and 300 s per tool call; the Learned Executor (ViT-S/14 + 4-layer Transformer) is lightweight but loses path efficiency. - Effective: The simulation evidence covers all four task types credibly, but effectiveness on a real robot is shown only qualitatively, and demand-driven "success" measures ordered navigation to regions, not completion of the underlying activity. - Scalable: Untested beyond 1,000-episode simulation benchmarks and a handful of real demos; long demand sequences collapse (SR6+ = 0 for all methods, only 3 tasks have ≥6 stages), and nothing addresses 10–100× task counts or fleet deployment. The work delivers a system artifact (harness, Skills, Learned Executor policy, benchmark) referenced at a project page, but public code/weights are not confirmed in the text. Strengths: (1) The ablation design is unusually decisive for a systems paper — Skills removal alone halves OVON success (68.33→35.00 SR at 0.25 m), isolating the harness's contribution from raw MLLM capability. (2) The unified visual-point interface is a genuinely useful abstraction: one decision loop demonstrably drives both a privileged geometric executor and an RGB-only learned policy, and transfers from Habitat to a real Unitree Go2. (3) Honest evaluation writing: the authors document protocol mismatches with published HM3D numbers, state that termination judgments are not independent semantic verification, and provide an unusually transparent AI-use statement. (4) The Learned Executor (point-marked NoMaD variant with age-aware history and flow head) is a competent, fully specified piece of policy engineering in its own right. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state that semantic judgments are bounded by the underlying MLLM's capability, that geometric execution depends on available maps/scene geometry, that MLLM latency makes task duration unpredictable, that demand-driven evaluation scores ordered navigation to relevant targets rather than actual activity completion, and that real-world coverage and long-sequence reliability are future work. This is a direct, non-minimizing limitations section — a credibility positive; the acknowledgment that demand-driven scoring is a proxy is particularly candid. Analyst-Identified Gaps: (1) No variance reporting: every headline number is a single run of a stochastic frontier-model agent on 120–200-episode sets, so the 3–6 point margins over SoftNav/ApexNav on HM3D could be noise. (2) Baseline asymmetry: baselines keep "native inputs and history mechanisms," which is fair in one sense but means SuperNav's four-view panorama and re-fetchable image history are capabilities the baselines structurally lack; a harness-equipped baseline ablation on the same observations would isolate this. (3) The cross-environment generalization argument (the paper's core motivation) is supported by simulation-to-simulation transfers (Habitat-GS, AI2-THOR, HM3D) plus an anecdotal real demo — there is no quantitative real-robot success rate across environments, the setting the motivation actually targets. (4) The decision model is identified only by a codename (GPT-5.6 Terra / GPT-6 Astra); without capability disclosure or a smaller open-model variant, the reader cannot judge how much of the result is harness versus raw model scale — the Astra/Terra swap shows model sensitivity of ±3–6 SR points but not the trend. (5) Skills content is described only at the level of topics; the actual Markdown guidance — the component the ablation shows is most critical — is not reproduced in the paper text, hindering reproduction of the headline effect. (6) The instance benchmark's annotations were AI-generated and manually checked, but no inter-annotator agreement or annotation-audit statistics are given. Bottom Line: A practitioner building zero-shot embodied agents should read this: it is the most complete demonstration to date that a harness + visual-point interface around a frozen frontier MLLM beats fine-tuned navigation VLMs across task types, but the proprietary-model dependence, single-run numbers, and qualitative-only real-robot evidence mean its exact results — though not its design pattern — should be treated as provisional.

TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces the Agent Reliability Profile (ARP), a standardized, per-deployment artifact through which financial institutions can state a bounded, falsifiable claim — this agent operates at a defined autonomy tier, within a defined operational design domain, for defined action classes, under a defined control envelope — backed by a three-level assurance ladder and a separate cross-institution benchmark flag. - Why it's important: No shared vocabulary currently exists for describing, validating, or benchmarking agentic-AI reliability in finance; each institution, vendor, and regulator uses its own schemas, and the April 2026 U.S. interagency guidance (SR 26-2) explicitly places agentic AI outside model risk management, leaving a supervisory vacuum that could trigger coarsely calibrated regulation after a harm event. - How it does it: The core move is converting the open-ended question "is this agent reliable?" into a scoped tuple S(D) = (T, O, A+, A−, C) over four standardized axes — autonomy tier (T0–T4 plus unprofiled status U), operational design domain (borrowed from automotive SAE J3016), a twelve-class action ontology graded by reversibility, and a six-layer, 55-control containment catalogue — with each axis value determining specific tests that can fail. - The good: The design is unusually self-aware for a standards proposal: it grounds the T2/T3 boundary in the human-factors literature on automation complacency (Bainbridge 1983; Bahner et al. 2008), proposes behavioral evidence (approval latency, edit rates, habituation testing) rather than configuration-only classification, and includes a five-phase implementation program with explicit off-ramps. - The missing: Nothing in the paper is built or measured — no pilot Profile exists, no inter-rater consistency study has been run, no cost figures for Profile production are given, and the benchmark environment is explicitly future work; every claim about usability is prospective. - Read it or not: Read it if you work on AI governance, agent assurance, or agentic-AI risk in regulated industries — it is the most concrete deployment-level assurance articulation in this space — but skip it if you need evaluated methods or empirical evidence, because it offers none.

Scored using Systems profile (nearest fit for a standards proposal; nothing is built). Novelty (70) and Non-Obviousness (70) are the strengths — the four-axis bounded-claim formulation attached to deployment identity, the behaviorally defined autonomy tier (reflexive approval = de facto T3), and the min-based separation of evidence independence from benchmark comparability are genuinely sharp, non-obvious design insights grounded in the automation-complacency literature. However, Rigor (25) reflects that there is zero empirical validation: the central standardization claim (inter-institution classification consistency) is the authors' own unexecuted Phase 1 criterion, no cost data exists, and the machine-readability machinery is aspirational. Completeness (75) is unusually strong given the eight directly confronted limitations, and Resilience (65) benefits from well-bounded claims with explicit off-ramps. Practical Impact (40) is capped because no tool, schema, or pilot exists — only a proposal soliciting its own adoption.
