Problem & Motivation: Deployers of AI agents — enterprises, security teams, public agencies, individual developers — now field systems that plan multistep tasks, call tools, spend money, and act on untrusted input, with authority delegated by principals who cannot observe every step. The book argues this raises questions no benchmark or product release settles: how to allocate tokens/compute/human attention, how to secure an agent that reads attacker-controlled content while holding real permissions, what interoperability protocols (MCP, Agent2Agent) must guarantee, how accountability flows through the developer–deployer–user–agent chain, what emergent risks (correlated errors, cascades, pricing collusion) appear at scale, and what collective behavior emerges in agent networks. Without foundations, the author contends, engineering proceeds by trial and error, which is dangerous precisely because in adversarial settings the attacker may be the first to find the failure. This is a legitimate, well-motivated gap: the agentic-AI literature is fragmented across RL, systems, and security communities with no unifying formal treatment. Key Idea: The single load-bearing idea is that agency is a property of the whole deployed system, not of the model weights (Definition 1.3): an agentic system is (i) goal-directed, (ii) engaged in sustained environment interaction, and (iii) exercising delegated authority, with agency a matter of degree along each clause. From this follow the book's two most reusable sub-ideas: autonomy should be assigned per action class rather than per system (level 4 in a sandbox, level 2 for the merge), and over long horizons recovery is worth as much as accuracy, because success probability is governed by the effective per-step failure probability ε(1−ρ), giving a half-success horizon T₁/₂ = ln 2 / −ln(1−p) ≈ 0.69/p. Both are framing contributions rather than new mathematics. Methodology: This is a textbook, so its "method" is pedagogical architecture rather than an algorithmic pipeline. Part I (Foundations, Ch. 1–6) treats agents as sequential decision-makers: expected utility and its departures (risk sensitivity via entropic/CVaR objectives, robust MDPs, bounded rationality), finite discounted MDPs with Bellman operators and value iteration (contraction-based dynamic programming, with a full proof that deterministic stationary policies suffice), POMDPs with Bayesian belief updates, approximate information states as a formalization of the context window, and a formal language-agent interface — action aₜ ~ π(·|cₜ), observation oₜ₊₁ ~ Env(·|aₜ), context update cₜ₊₁ = U(cₜ, aₜ, oₜ₊₁) — with tool calls, parse failures, and budget-terminated episodes. Part II (Systems, Ch. 7–12) covers architectures, tools/environments, memory/RAG/context engineering, multi-agent orchestration, evaluation, and domain case studies. Part III (Ch. 13–18) covers threat models (prompt injection, privilege misuse, poisoning), game-theoretic defense (Stackelberg formulations, moving targets), resilience and runtime assurance, alignment/oversight, and governance/mechanism design. Three critical design decisions: (1) three running examples (R1 research assistant, R2 software engineering agent, R3 security operations agent) chosen to stress different failure surfaces — well justified, as they span untrusted-content exposure, verifiable feedback, and adversarial inputs; (2) dating volatile facts in "In Practice" boxes to separate durable principles from September-2026 state of the field — well justified and unusual discipline for the genre; (3) six-level autonomy scale condensed from Sheridan–Verplank and Parasuraman et al. — justified by explicit appeal to the human-factors literature, though the condensation itself is asserted rather than validated. Key Results: No empirical results are reported — there are no benchmarks, no baselines, no model evaluations, and none are claimed. The quantitative content is illustrative formal work: (a) the error-compounding model, where ε = 0.02 per step yields ~36% success at 50 steps and ~13% at 100 steps, rising to ~67% at 100 steps with recovery probability ρ = 0.8, and the half-success horizon formula T₁/₂ ≈ 0.69/p (34 steps at p = 0.02, 173 steps with 80% recovery); (b) a worked value-iteration example on a three-state MDP where the greedy action flips from "patch" to "investigate" at k = 3, with the contraction error bound met exactly; (c) a numeric belief-update example for R3 where an alert raises P(compromised) from 0.10 to 0.433 but attacker-editable "clean" logs only lower it to 0.213 — twice the prior. External quantitative anchors are cited with appropriate hedging: METR's task-horizon doubling every ~7 months (2019–early 2025), revised to ~4 months in METR's January 2026 update with wide confidence intervals explicitly noted; Gartner's August 2025 forecast of 40% enterprise-agent integration by end-2026 alongside its prediction that >40% of agentic projects will be canceled by end-2027. These are claims from third parties, not measurements made by this work. Novelty Classification: This is best classified as a NEW FORMULATION (synthesis) with minor elements of NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING — and I use "empirical" loosely, since the finding is analytic. What is genuinely novel: the unified formal agent–environment interface (Eq. 1.1 / Theorem 2.15) binding contexts, tool calls, budgets, and memory into one object used across all three parts; the explicit definition of agency as system-level delegated authority (Definition 1.3); the per-action-class autonomy assignment; and the half-success-horizon framing connecting recovery engineering to measured capability trends. What is standard: nearly all the underlying mathematics (Bellman equations, POMDP belief updates, CVaR, Stackelberg games, mechanism design) is textbook material restated with proofs or proof sketches; the history, taxonomy, and threat-model organization synthesize known literature (ReAct, Toolformer, Voyager, SWE-agent, Greshake et al. on prompt injection) rather than contribute to it. A reader hoping for new methods or results will not find them here. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations, seeds, and significance tests are not applicable — no experiments are run. Internal mathematical rigor is adequate: Theorem 2.4 (optimality of deterministic stationary policies) carries a complete induction proof; the Appendix C machinery (contractions, stochastic approximation) is cited to support convergence claims; assumptions in the information-state material (bounded rewards, stationary policy-independent dynamics) are stated explicitly. The compounding-error model's independence and constant-rate assumptions are flagged by the author as unrealistic, with the general model deferred to Theorem 2.13. No code repository, dataset, or model weights are mentioned as released, though Appendix D describes six laboratory exercises (minimal agent loop, MCP integration, retrieval, debate, prompt-injection red-teaming in a sandbox, evaluation harness) whose artifact availability is not stated. One methodological caution: the bibliography shows heavy self-citation (Zhu, 2025a–f; Yang and Zhu; Ge and Zhu; Li and Zhu; Huang and Zhu; Zhang and Zhu; Chen and Zhu — roughly twenty references), so the "foundations" as presented lean substantially on the author's own research program, and claims from industry (METR, Gartner, vendor releases) are reported, not independently verified. There is no peer review in the journal sense; this is a self-published manuscript sample. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: THEORETICAL (a textbook/formal synthesis with no primary experimental claim). Sound: The formal material is standard and correctly presented with explicit assumptions; the original formulations (information states for contexts, action-class taxonomies, the injection-advantage and audit-compliance quantities in the notation tables) are stated as definitions and theorems whose proofs are not shown in the sample, so their completeness cannot be verified from this PDF. General: The framework is deliberately broad — it spans thermostats to computer-use agents — which is a strength for organization but means the formal results invoked (e.g., Theorem 2.15) must make strong idealizations (stationary dynamics, budgeted episodes, parseable actions) that real LLM deployments routinely violate. Tight: Not applicable in the bound-tightness sense; the one quantitative result, T₁/₂ ≈ 0.69/p, is exact under its assumptions and the author proves the 1% approximation quality for p ≤ 0.02, but the assumptions (independent, identically distributed per-step failure) are admittedly loose fits to real agent trajectories. Implementable: Yes in the pedagogical sense — Appendix D labs and the per-action-class approval-gate design (Theorem 8.7's action classes {R,V,I}×{C,X}, the audit-compliance condition q(d−f)F ≥ s in Theorem 17.6) are directly actionable for practitioners. The deliverable is a book manuscript (sample chapters); no software artifact, library, or trained model is released with it. Strengths: - The system-level (not model-level) definition of agency with three graded clauses is the sharpest and most consequential contribution — it correctly relocates security and governance questions away from model safety, and the one-model-four-deployments example (chatbot → read-only → approval-gated reset → overnight queue triage) makes the abstraction immediately operational. - Assigning autonomy per action class, grounded in the Sheridan–Verplank and Parasuraman human-factors tradition, is a practically important design principle that most agentic-AI writing ignores; the observation that the level-2→level-3 transition silently reverses the default (silence = stop vs. silence = go) is a genuinely non-obvious point. - The half-success-horizon analysis converts the abstract observation "agents fail over long horizons" into a quantitative design lever (halving ε or raising ρ each double the horizon), and Exercise 1.7 explicitly connects it to — and stress-tests — the METR time-horizon methodology rather than merely citing it. - Disciplined epistemic hygiene: volatile facts are dated, scoped to "In Practice" boxes, and caveated (METR's confidence intervals and estimated human baselines are reported), and the preface's pairing of Gartner's adoption and cancellation forecasts frames the stakes without hype. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The author explicitly flags that the compounding-error model's independence and constant-rate assumptions are unrealistic (steps differ in difficulty, errors are correlated, some errors are repairable much later), that the belief-MDP equivalence is "computationally sobering" and requires a model a language agent does not have, that survey literature on language agents "grows quickly, and any survey dates fast," that long contexts do not solve context engineering, and that METR's horizon estimates carry wide confidence intervals with estimated rather than measured human baselines. The preface also concedes that theory without systems misses real failure modes and vice versa. This is direct, non-defensive confrontation of limitations — a credibility positive. What is not acknowledged: the absence of any empirical validation of the framework itself, and the extent of self-citation in the foundations. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - No validation loop: the book's central claim — that system-scientific foundations produce better agent engineering than trial and error — is never tested, even in the small (e.g., no case study where the framework's per-action autonomy assignment or information-state formalism changed a deployed system's outcome). The evidence for usefulness is entirely rhetorical. - The formal interface (Eq. 1.1, Theorems 2.15, 8.1–8.2, 8.7, 9.7, 13.x) is asserted in the notation table and chapter summaries but its proofs and the conditions under which the approximations hold are not shown in the sample; the framework's actual mathematical content beyond classical restatements cannot be assessed from this PDF. - Heavy self-citation creates a monoculture risk: the "foundations" are anchored disproportionately to one research group's game-theoretic and control-theoretic program (Zhu and coauthors appear across foundations, security, economics, and governance chapters), with little engagement against alternative framings (e.g., interpretability-first, empirically-driven safety agendas, or the constitutional/legal literature) that might disagree. - Several load-bearing 2025–2026 facts (Gartner forecasts, the Anthropic espionage-campaign report, the Agentic AI Foundation, NIST initiative) are reported from press and vendor sources with no way to verify them from the text; a reader in 2027+ inherits a narrative built partly on unverifiable industry claims, dated or not. - The taxonomy of fourteen systems (Table 1.3) mixes types, prototypes, and products under one schema with "typical rather than definitive" entries, which weakens its use as a classification instrument. Bottom Line: For an instructor or a control/game-theory-trained researcher entering agentic AI, this is currently the most coherent structuring of the field available and worth reading closely; for anyone seeking new technical results, empirical evidence, or deployable artifacts, there is no stronger alternative here to skip it for — the value is organizational, not discovery.

Problem & Motivation: Repository-editing coding agents (e.g., SWE-agent-style systems) repeatedly reconstruct repository state, regenerate plans, and re-run validation. Shorter prompts and cached results reduce cost but can omit dependencies and silently upgrade evidence — a stale test pass or an out-of-scope proof gets treated as current, valid justification. The population with this problem is builders of autonomous software-engineering agents and automated testing/verification pipelines. The gap in prior work: agent–tool boundaries are typically unstructured conversation histories or ad-hoc caches with no typed notion of what a piece of evidence proves, in which environment, and until when. Key Idea: Treat evidence as a first-class typed record — (claim, subjects, assumptions, scope, dependencies, translation profile, checker result, environment, policy, provenance) — admitted only via integrity, applicability, required-check, and policy gates, never collapsed into a scalar confidence score. Three separations carry the design: (1) semantic state vs. operational state vs. durable artifacts, each with distinct authority; (2) candidate proposals vs. admitted knowledge (a model's plan or patch is never self-accepting); (3) incremental reuse with a visible unknown frontier (dynamic dispatch, reflection, plugins widen the invalidation frontier rather than vanish from it). Loss-aware translation is the second key discipline: a proof of a lossy projection of an obligation proves nothing about the original obligation, and unsupported translations must be rejected or bound to an independently justified preservation relation. Methodology: The pipeline is a supervision loop over a frozen repository forest F: (1) a semantic compiler extracts symbols, typed relationships, and limitations, sealing them into immutable content-addressed facts and dependency capsules; (2) a formalization layer maps intent (goal/legal/security IR families sharing a domain-neutral kernel) into bounded obligations, with translation validation checking each transformation; (3) a supervisor maintains an obligation frontier and routes each obligation down a cheapest-adequate ladder — exact dependency analysis, abstract interpretation (product lattice of constants, integer intervals, nullness, exceptions, effects), assume–guarantee implication checks (G ∧ ¬A via SAT/UNSAT), bounded QF_LIA CEGAR, CEGIS synthesis, then an explicitly authorized neural residual; (4) candidate edits apply in isolated fenced worktrees, trigger additive invalidation, and admitted test/proof evidence is sealed into source-addressed proof units under a requirement manifest, published via a WAL + pointer-CAS scheme governed by a stated acceptance invariant (Eq. 2). Fixture-aware test reuse (PCTDD) binds collection seed, fixture-definition closure, fixture-instance commitment, and per-phase setup/call/teardown evidence as separate cache-key stages. Critical design decisions: separate CEGAR (refines abstraction) from CEGIS (refines candidates); require positive-path authorization witnesses so a deny-all gate cannot masquerade as safety; treat queue exhaustion and budget exhaustion as distinct terminal outcomes, never success. These decisions are argued carefully but justified by design reasoning, not by executed comparisons. An inductive preservation argument for the accepted lineage (Appendix I.3.1) is offered explicitly as a proof sketch, not a machine-checked theorem. Key Results: Essentially none are measured. The results section is a preregistration-style plan: paired A/B arms (raw vs. semantic context, then +symbolic routing/reuse, then +governed lifecycle), frozen task populations, cold validation oracles, adversarial reuse attacks, and full cost/statistical reporting protocols — all tables marked [TBD]. The only quantitative data, self-described as "repository-reported preliminary evidence; not experiments rerun during this paper revision," are: a semantic context harness on 40 controlled tasks showing 58.90% median estimated context reduction with no model receipts; an incremental sealer on 40 transitions showing 43.6161% reuse and 43.0539% estimated compute reduction; and source inspection confirming typed state, routing, formalization, bounded synthesis, and storage mechanisms exist but that no single integrated deployment or passing runtime qualification has occurred. No baselines are compared; no benchmark is named as run. The Appendix A end-to-end example (denied-request-must-not-write repair cycle) is explicitly illustrative, not an observed run. Novelty Classification: NEW FORMULATION plus a partial NEW SYSTEM design. The genuinely new element is the composition at the agent's operational boundary: persistent typed evidence with explicit admission predicates, obligation-driven routing with residual model authorization, phase-aware fixture/test-certificate reuse, and accepted-transition publication as one governed loop. The constituent mechanisms — proof-carrying code (Necula 1997), abstract interpretation, CEGAR, CEGIS, translation validation, build-system à la carte scheduling, Groth16 attestation — are all established, and the paper says so plainly. Nothing here is a new algorithm; the value is the evidence-governance discipline and the honest separation of evidence classes, which is genuinely non-obvious relative to current agent scaffolding. Rigor & Reproducibility: As a measurement paper, rigor is absent by the authors' own accounting: no executed ablations, no error bars, no seeds, no significance tests, no code or artifact release stated, and the paper checklist is an explicitly marked placeholder. As a design paper, the rigor is unusually high: the paper distinguishes source-present vs. integrated vs. qualified vs. measured component statuses (Appendix H.2's independent status dimensions), specifies matched raw-context baselines, cold oracles, deny-all controls, positive-path witnesses, and adversarial reuse/crash cohorts before any experiment, and flags its own weak points — the SMT wrapper rebuilds Z3 per check so no retained-clause speedup is established; the Groth16 path is opt-in with a limited propositional-fragment derivation helper, not a validated temporal/deontic prover; the preliminary numbers are unrerun repository reports. No methodological gaming was found; the opposite — the paper is a sustained exercise in anti-overclaiming. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (intended), but currently only a design/specification artifact with source-present prototype components and two small unrerun repository observations. Practical: The design targets ordinary Python repositories and standard tooling (pytest, Z3, Git, optional Rust/Groth16 backend); nothing suggests exotic hardware is required. Efficient: Claimed savings (≈59% context reduction, ≈43% compute reduction) are small-sample estimates with an unquantified overhead from compilation, sealing, and proof checking that the paper itself says the paired evaluation must justify. Effective: Not demonstrated — no end-to-end task completion, false-admission rate, or cost result exists; only proxy observations on 40 items each. Scalable: Untested; the Merkle/CAS/incremental-invalidation machinery is designed for scale, but nothing beyond 40 tasks and 40 transitions has been observed, and multi-repo, distributed, and crash-recovery paths are specified only. Deliverable status: a paper plus unspecified prototype repository heads; no released library, dataset, or trained model. Strengths: - The typed evidence model (Table 6 evidence record; Table 3 evidence-class taxonomy) cleanly solves a real and under-addressed problem: agent pipelines conflating "a hash matched," "a signer asserted," "a solver proved an encoding," and "a program ran." The insistence that these are incomparable evidence classes is the paper's sharpest insight. - The loss-aware translation discipline (a proof of a projected formula cannot lift to the source obligation; Eq. 3; the concrete temporal-operator loss test in Appendix I.1) is a correct and rarely enforced rule for neurosymbolic agent stacks. - The evaluation plan is a model of experimental hygiene: frozen populations, paired arms, deny-all controls, positive-path witnesses, cold oracles, adversarial reuse mutations, non-additive cost accounting, and preregistered noninferiority margins — specified before results exist. - The paper's self-audit culture (source-presence vs. integration vs. qualification vs. measurement; refusal to credit a zero-provider-hook gate with saved model calls) is a credibility asset few submissions match. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: Extensive and direct. The authors state: Python reflection, native code, external state, concurrency, and unsound translations bound what can be proved; a sound checker cannot repair a mis-formalized requirement; default-deny can mask broken positive paths; the acceptance invariant is a design invariant, not an enforced theorem; the ZK helper proves only a propositional fragment; the reference enforcement layer does not connect to real tools; the receipt-consumption rollout defaults to off/shadow; no integrated deployment, unpushed worktree behavior, or runtime qualification exists; and the thesis that persistent obligations displace repeated neural reasoning "must be determined by the paired evaluation." These limitations are confronted head-on, not minimized — a strong credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - The central hypothesis — that obligation-governed state reduces total cost at preserved quality — is tested nowhere; the two preliminary observations (context reduction, reuse rate) are precisely the cheap proxies the paper's own methodology warns against crediting. - The mechanism set is enormous (formalization layers, four IR families, CEGAR/CEGIS adapters, ZK attestation, proof forests, world-model federation, learned continuation models, remodularization) relative to zero integrated evidence; the paper risks specifying a research program rather than delivering a validated method, and reviewer effort goes to auditing scope rather than findings. - Key overheads that could dominate the ledger — semantic recompilation cost per edit, obligation-manifest construction, proof-unit sealing latency — are named as reportable but never even estimated. - No external baseline system (SWE-agent, SWT-bench harnesses, LLMLingua-style compression) is actually run; they appear only as citations for future comparison. - The single-author anonymous submission with placeholders raises provenance questions the paper itself flags ("Important model use... must be disclosed") but cannot resolve in this draft. Bottom Line: This is a rigorously self-skeptical design and evaluation-protocol paper whose ideas about typed evidence and obligation-governed agent supervision are worth stealing, but with zero measured results a practitioner seeking validated techniques should look elsewhere, while anyone building verifiable coding-agent infrastructure should read it as a specification and preregistration template, not as evidence.

SQD- Agent : LLM-driven agentic framework for Quantum Chemistry workflows

K Tiwari, A Ray · arxiv.org · automated generated environments for agent testing - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper builds SQD-Agent, an LLM-based multi-agent orchestration framework that translates natural-language requests into executable sample-based quantum diagonalization (SQD) quantum-chemistry workflows spanning PySCF, Qiskit, ffsim, and IBM quantum hardware. - Why it's important: Assembling hybrid quantum-classical chemistry experiments currently requires expertise across electronic structure, quantum programming, transpilation, shot budgets, and error mitigation; an orchestration layer could lower that barrier for application researchers new to quantum computing. - How it does it: The LLM acts only as a planner that emits a validated structured run specification (SQDRunSpec) consumed by a deterministic, library-backed execution layer, with specialist agents for hardware submission, mitigation comparison, profiling, debugging, and reporting, plus a cache-first artifact policy. - The good: The strongest evidence is a real end-to-end hardware demonstration — N2 with a LUCJ ansatz on the 156-qubit ibm_kingston backend (100,000 shots, 298 two-qubit gates post-transpilation) — where the framework executed and compared four mitigation settings, with DD achieving |Δ| = 0.0018 mHa vs FCI at 48.6 s. - The missing: The evaluation is tiny and single-shot: six small molecules in the STO-3G minimal basis on simulators, one molecule/ansatz/backend on hardware, single unseeded runs with no error bars, no user study, and no code release yet (repository promised only after acceptance). - Read it or not: Worth reading for systems builders targeting LLM agents over quantum hardware stacks who want a concrete blueprint of planner/executor separation; skippable if you want evidence that agentic frameworks actually improve quantum-chemistry productivity — the authors themselves call this a proof-of-concept.
Why this rank
Scored using the Systems profile. The central weaknesses are Rigor (40) — single unseeded hardware runs with no error bars, no ablations of agent components, no comparison against manual execution or El Agente Q, and code unavailable at submission — and Practical Impact (45), since the framework exists but is unreleased and demonstrates no measured productivity gain over a skilled human. Novelty (60) is moderate: the first agentic framework covering quantum-native SQD workflows end-to-end is a genuine new-system contribution, but the planner/executor contract, typed tool specs, and multi-agent routing are known engineering patterns, keeping Non-Obviousness (45) low. The paper's honesty is its strongest asset: unusually direct acknowledgment of toy scale, single-run statistics, and proof-of-concept status lifts Completeness (65) and Resilience (60), as the claims are deliberately well-bounded and would survive adversarial review. Problem & Motivation: Application researchers in computational chemistry (catalysis, materials, drug development) face a steep learning curve when using hybrid quantum-classical workflows like SQD: they must choose geometries, basis sets, active spaces, ansätze, transpilation profiles, shot budgets, and error-mitigation strategies, then assemble libraries (PySCF, Qiskit, ffsim, qiskit-addon-sqd) manually into reproducible pipelines. Existing LLM chemistry agents (ChemCrow, Coscientist, El Agente Q) coordinate classical chemistry software but do not handle quantum-native concerns such as circuit transpilation, QPU submission, mitigation policies, and quantum–classical cost trade-offs. The paper targets the gap of an agentic control layer specifically for sampling-based subspace-iteration workflows on near-term quantum-centric supercomputing platforms. Key Idea: The core design move is strict separation of LLM planning from deterministic execution: the LLM never generates or runs free-form code; instead, specialist agents populate a validated, typed run contract (SQDRunSpec: geometry, basis, charge/spin, active-space policy, ansatz, backend, shots, batching, transpilation profile, mitigation policy, cache policy), and a fixed Python execution layer — wrapping existing libraries — executes the run and returns a structured SQDRunResult with energy, convergence trace, circuit metrics, timings, and artifact paths. This makes every agent-mediated run auditable and reproducible while keeping the agent layer independent of backend or solver changes. Methodology: The architecture has two tiers. (1) An agent-callable execution engine with modular interfaces for chemistry preparation (PySCF Hartree–Fock, integrals; active-space selection via HOMO–LUMO window, natural occupation, or CCSD-amplitude scoring, with a capacity-preserving refit), ansatz construction (Jordan–Wigner mapping; HF reference, UCJ from CCSD amplitudes via ffsim, localized UCJ, hardware-efficient), the SQD loop (sampling → bitstring filtering/configuration recovery → subspace batching in single/merged/independent modes → projected Hamiltonian diagonalization via qiskit-addon-sqd's solve_fermion), backend abstraction (Qiskit Aer simulators and IBM Quantum Runtime behind a common bitstring-count interface), error mitigation as a configurable policy object (DD, twirling, both, or none) with pre-execution compatibility suggestions and post-execution MitigationReport of accuracy–cost trade-offs, and cache-first artifact management keyed on a run signature. (2) An agentic orchestration tier: a lead orchestrator routes natural-language intents to specialist agents (SQD execution, hardware, mitigation advisor, performance, reporting, debugging), each restricted to a narrow scope, with human-in-the-loop confirmation required for fetched geometries and any QPU submission. The LLM is used for parameter resolution and routing, not computation. Key design decisions — the structured-contract constraint on agent actions, backend-agnostic sampling interface, and treating the diagonalizer as a replaceable solver component — are argued for extensibility and auditability but are design assertions, not ablated choices. Key Results: On simulators (STO-3G basis, 300,000 shots, 100,000 samples/batch, 8 iterations, seeded MPS), across six molecules, full-space UCJ/LUCJ SQD recovers FCI references closely: H2O/LUCJ +0.000 mHa, LiH/LUCJ +0.016–0.031 mHa, N2/UCJ +0.856 mHa, O2/UCJ +0.806 mHa, CH2O/UCJ +1.164 mHa, while active-space runs show expected truncation errors (e.g., N2 active-space +31.0 mHa, matching active-space CASCI). Hardware: N2/LUCJ (20 logical qubits, 298 post-transpilation two-qubit gates, depth 210) on ibm_kingston with 100,000 shots — unmitigated |Δ| vs FCI = 0.0195 mHa at 149.4 s; dynamical decoupling 0.0018 mHa at 48.6 s; twirling 0.130 mHa at 49.5 s; twirling+DD 0.122 mHa at 50.2 s. Notably, the mitigation ranking is molecule/context-specific and the authors explicitly decline to generalize it. Baselines (RHF, MP2, CCSD, CASCI, FCI) are standard and appropriate for the toy scale, but all tested molecules are small enough for exact diagonalization; the reported 12,635-atom protein-scale SQD results are cited from other work, not demonstrated here. Agent overhead example: a LiH workflow took 7 LLM calls and 5 tool calls (~67,978 tokens). Novelty Classification: NEW SYSTEM/TOOL with an ENGINEERING OPTIMIZATION component: the genuine novelty is the first agentic framework managing quantum-native SQD workflows end-to-end, including real-QPU submission and mitigation-strategy comparison under a planner/executor contract — a setting not covered by classical-chemistry agents like El Agente Q. The underlying algorithms (SQD, UCJ/LUCJ ansätze, DD, twirling) and libraries are entirely pre-existing; the contribution is their orchestration, which is a competent combination of known ideas (typed tool contracts, cache-first design, multi-agent routing) applied to a new domain. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are absent in the LLM sense — no experiments isolate which agent components (caching, specialist routing, mitigation advisor) matter, and no comparison against direct manual SQD execution or against El Agente Q on the same tasks. No error bars: hardware energies come from single unseeded runs, and the authors state this explicitly. The cache-first policy is described as evaluated by repeating saved tasks, but no quantitative hit-rate or time-savings numbers are given. Code availability is promised ("GitHub repository, whose link will be added after acceptance") — currently unavailable, so results are not independently verifiable. The hardware claim rests on one molecule/ansatz/backend combination, which the authors flag as path validation rather than a benchmark. A meta-concern: the framework itself was developed with LLM assistance (OpenCode + Gemini 2.5 Flash), with human review asserted but not audited. Deployability: Profile: SYSTEMS (a built tool evaluated by execution on simulators and real hardware). - Practical: Yes — it runs on standard Python with PySCF/Qiskit/Aer and accesses IBM Quantum via Qiskit Runtime; no exotic hardware beyond QPU access itself. - Efficient: Simulator overhead is modest (SQD runs of 0.4–1,129 s plus ~68K tokens of LLM calls per workflow); hardware costs are dominated by QPU queue time (142 s for the first job), which the caching policy mitigates. - Effective: The evidence shows the system executes correct SQD workflows and produces useful mitigation reports on toy problems; it does not yet show that it saves expert time or enables chemistry beyond what a skilled user could do directly — no user study or productivity measurement is included. - Scalable: Not tested — the architecture is argued to extend to transition-metal clusters and larger active spaces, but the largest demonstrated system is CH2O (24 qubits, STO-3G); scaling claims are explicitly disclaimed by the authors. The work delivers a software artifact (modular Python framework: runner.py, chemistry.py, active_space.py, plus agent specifications), but it is not yet publicly released. Strengths: - The planner/executor contract (SQDRunSpec/SQDRunResult) is a genuinely sound safety and auditability design: it prevents free-form LLM code execution in a domain where a hallucinated parameter costs real QPU budget, and it cleanly decouples agent logic from library churn. - The hardware demonstration is real and detailed: actual transpilation statistics (156 physical qubits, 2Q depth 42, 298 two-qubit gates), a VF2 calibration-aware layout, per-strategy mitigation costs including queue time caveats, and saved job IDs for retrieval — this is more operational transparency than most agentic-LLM papers provide. - The mitigation comparison honestly reports that the unmitigated baseline was cheapest and that DD won on accuracy for this instance, refusing to overgeneralize — a credibility positive. - The cache-first, signature-keyed artifact policy with environment-aware profiling signatures is a practical reproducibility mechanism tailored to the heterogeneous quantum-classical setting. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors are unusually direct: experiments are restricted to small molecules in STO-3G where FCI is computable; the hardware run is one molecule/ansatz/backend included only to validate the execution path; energies come from single unseeded runs with no error bars; reproducibility is via cached artifacts, not bitwise recomputation; the agent layer depends on the underlying LLM's reliability; reconfiguration is human-supervised, not closed-loop; the system is a proof-of-concept with preliminary, statistically insufficient informal user feedback; and the framework makes no claim of quantum advantage or new SQD algorithms. This candor is a strong credibility signal. Analyst-Identified Gaps: Beyond the acknowledged limits: (1) No baseline demonstrating that the agent actually reduces expertise or effort — the central motivating claim is unmeasured, and the planned user study is future work; (2) no head-to-head comparison with El Agente Q or direct scripting despite positioning the paper against it; (3) no evaluation of LLM reliability metrics (task success rate, hallucination incidents, intervention frequency) across many diverse prompts — the NL-to-workflow validation uses essentially one hand-crafted prompt, so robustness to ambiguous or erroneous user intent is unknown; (4) the mitigation advisor's pre-execution suggestion logic is never evaluated for accuracy — only post-hoc comparison is shown; (5) the choice of Gemini 2.5 Flash via OpenCode as the underlying LLM is not ablated against other models, leaving the framework's LLM-dependence unquantified; (6) code unavailability at submission time prevents verification of all reported artifacts. Bottom Line: A well-engineered, honestly reported proof-of-concept that shows LLM agents can orchestrate real SQD workflows on IBM hardware, but with a toy-scale evaluation and no evidence yet of the productivity gains that would justify adoption — read it for the planner/executor blueprint, not for demonstrated value over manual workflows.

Zero-Shot Transfer of Foundation Time-Series Forecasters to Datacenter Operational Telemetry: Mapping a Domain Nobody Gets to Study

D Pace jr · scholarworks.uno.edu · 10 new citations to your articles
TL;DR - What it does: This Master's thesis builds an audited forecasting benchmark on private, single-site datacenter telemetry (8 targets × 4 horizons = 32 slices) and shows that zero-shot foundation forecasters (Moirai-2.0, Chronos-Bolt, TimesFM-1.0) beat thirteen locally trained classical models under input-matched conditions (27 of 32 slices), while a naive persistence baseline (mean MAE 0.4028) still beats every learned method overall. - Why it's important: Published zero-shot transfer claims for time-series foundation models rest almost entirely on public corpora, so this is a rare out-of-distribution test on private operational data absent from pretraining — the setting where practitioners actually need these models to work. - How it does it: The core move is an input-semantics fairness ablation: because the foundation wrappers forecast channel-wise, the thesis retrains all classical baselines univariate (S-mode) on the target's own history, plus provenance fingerprinting of every run and a persistence-baseline skill gate. - The good: The foundation lead survives the fairness ablation, a 3-seed rerun of a competitive classical challenger (TimeKAN loses on all seeds for 29/32 slices), gap-exclusion sensitivity analysis, and per-slice Diebold–Mariano tests that never reverse — while the persistence result is honestly reported as bounding the whole learned field. - The missing: The evidence base is one site, ~900 training rows per category, three comparatively small channel-independent foundation checkpoints, and a post-hoc mechanism story (level-adaptivity plus pretraining) that the thesis itself flags as associative rather than experimentally isolated. - Read it or not: Worth reading for time-series benchmarking methodologists and anyone deploying forecasters on operational telemetry; skip if you need multi-site generalization, native-multivariate foundation models (e.g., Chronos-2), or causal mechanism evidence — none are here.

Completeness (66) is strong — the threats-to-validity candor, provenance fingerprinting, and S-mode fairness ablation are exemplary — which keeps the paper above the incremental band. Resilience (50) is limited by the n=8 post-hoc mechanism split and the synthetic-control reversal, and Practical Impact (30) reflects an unreleasable private dataset and no artifact. Problem & Motivation: Datacenter operators want advance warning of thermal, electrical, and workload risk from continuous telemetry, but real facility telemetry is noisy, operationally coupled, and full of measurement artifacts (SNMP fleet changes, sensor commissioning lags, infrastructure shifts) unlike curated public benchmarks (Monash, ETT, ECL, even GIFT-Eval). Prior evaluations of foundation forecasters (Moirai, Chronos, TimesFM) are concentrated on public data, and existing public datacenter resources (Google/Azure cluster traces, Building Data Genome 2) capture either workload scheduling or building energy, not multi-year daily subsystem telemetry from one operational facility. A second methodological gap: the two model families cannot be compared naively because TSLib classical models consume full multivariate input while foundation wrappers forecast channel-wise — so published head-to-heads conflate input semantics with model-family advantage. Key Idea: The key idea is not a new model but a decision procedure: treat the target-only (S-mode) classical retraining as a decisive fairness check that isolates the input-semantics confound, then gate any remaining ranking against the naive persistence baseline so that "genuine forecasting skill" is defined as beating persistence, not beating other models. The mechanistic insight that emerges — that persistence and foundation wrappers share per-window level re-anchoring while locally trained models learn patterns from a 2021–2024 regime that the 2025 test span no longer follows — is a genuinely useful framing for where foundation priors add value. Methodology: A five-phase pipeline: (1) dataset curation with an explicit variable-exclusion audit that classifies candidate series into defect classes (SNMP aggregation artifacts, sensor-commissioning lag, infrastructure shifts, externally driven signals, semantic defects, near-constant grid-regulated signals), retaining 8 of ~24 candidate targets; (2) a 13-model classical benchmark in TSLib (PatchTST, iTransformer, FiLM, TimeMixer, TimesNet, DLinear, TimeKAN, Autoformer, FEDformer, FreTS, MICN, plus committee-requested LSTM/GRU), trained with MAE loss and early stopping, in multivariate-to-univariate (MS) mode; (3) zero-shot evaluation of three foundation checkpoints under identical targets/horizons/splits; (4) fine-tuning of Chronos-Bolt and Moirai-2.0 with a fixed 500-step budget; (5) mechanism diagnostics relating per-slice foundation advantage (Δ = MAE_best-classical − MAE_best-foundation) to raw-data properties (roughness, volatility shift, dominant-state fraction, clean training windows). Tasks use L=96 input length, horizons H ∈ {7, 14, 30, 60} days, 70/10/20 chronological split, MAE as the sole ranking metric. Two critical design decisions: (a) the target-only ablation retrains all classical models with inputs restricted to the target's own history, matching the channel-wise wrappers — well-justified and well-executed; (b) every run passes a two-layer provenance check (row-count assertion at launch, exact numerical reconstruction of normalized test windows at collection, 10⁻⁴ tolerance) — unusually rigorous provenance hygiene for this literature. One design choice is weaker: foundation fine-tuning gets no validation-based early stopping, an asymmetry the authors acknowledge. Key Results: On the original MS comparison, the best foundation forecaster wins 26 of 32 slices; Moirai achieves mean MAE 0.4209 vs. 0.5030 for the strongest trained baseline (DLinear); per-slice Diebold–Mariano tests (Newey–West HAC, HLN correction) show Moirai significantly better on 16 slices, indistinguishable on 16, never significantly worse — 9 remain significant under Bonferroni. On the input-matched target-only ablation, foundation wins 27 of 32 (foundation mean 0.4143 vs. classical 0.4652, a 10.9% margin); GRU is the strongest trained model (0.4796). The persistence baseline posts the lowest mean MAE of any method (0.4028) and wins the four-way per-slice contest 17/32 vs. 11 for foundation; foundation beats persistence on 14 slices, concentrated on messy, regime-shifting targets (network/temperature, power/temperature at all horizons, server/power at 7–30 days, 60-day horizons of smoother targets). Foundation advantage is 0.0688 on audit-flagged messy targets vs. 0.0345 on cleaner ones; dominant-state fraction separates the groups (messier ≥0.196, cleaner ≤0.040). Synthetic controls reverse the ranking (classical wins 214 of 264 slices); linear regression (MAE 32,629) and XGBoost (1.31) win zero datacenter slices. Fine-tuning is heterogeneous: Moirai FT 0.4172 (≈1% gain), Chronos FT 0.4923 (16% degradation). Baselines are current (2023–2025 architectures including TimeKAN), and the benchmark is a small single-site case study, not a stress-scale evaluation. Novelty Classification: NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING and NEW DATASET/BENCHMARK. The genuinely novel element is the external-validation finding on private operational telemetry that zero-shot foundation forecasters dominate locally trained classical models under input-matched conditions while losing to persistence on average — plus the audited 8-target single-site benchmark, which the thesis argues (plausibly) has no public analogue. The individual techniques (TSLib benchmarking, DM tests, persistence baselines, instance-normalization explanations) are standard; the honest negative controls and provenance fingerprinting are competent execution of known benchmarking best practice rather than methodological invention. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are unusually thorough for a thesis: input-semantics ablation, 3-seed rerun of one classical challenger (median per-slice CV 5.5%), gap-exclusion sensitivity analysis (25/32 vs. 27/32), objective ablation (MSE-default moves counts further against classical, with the caveat that these runs predate the recurrent additions), and per-slice significance testing with multiplicity sensitivity. Provenance is verified numerically for every run. However: no code, data, or model checkpoints are stated as publicly released (the dataset is private and cannot be released by construction, limiting external replication); most classical results are single-seed; n=32 dependent slices limits formal inference (the authors note slices share test series); and the benchmark population was selected partly using test-period behavior, which the authors confront directly as a threat to validity. The foundation-vs-classical selection asymmetry (best of 13 vs. best of 3) is correctly identified as favoring the classical side. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL (a benchmark study with no deployed artifact). Practical: Yes — the recommended method on messy targets is zero-shot inference with public checkpoints on GPU, and the overall default (persistence) is one line of code. Efficient: The thesis argues a cost gradient (persistence free, foundation models moderate inference cost with zero training, locally trained models highest total cost for worst accuracy) but reports no timing or throughput measurements. Effective: The evidence supports the bounded claim — foundation models are the strongest learned method on this telemetry and add skill over persistence on messy targets — but only on one site at daily cadence; the operational value at finer cadences is asserted from an exploratory export, not demonstrated. Scalable: Untested and unclaimed beyond 8 targets and 32 slices; multi-site replication is explicitly future work. The work delivers a paper (thesis) form only — no released library, dataset, or tool is mentioned. Strengths: - The target-only S-mode ablation directly kills the strongest objection to the headline result before a reviewer can raise it, and the answer (input formulation changes classical means by ~1%) makes the conclusion robust in a way few forecasting comparisons are. - Reporting that naive persistence beats every learned method — including the paper's favored family — and then re-scoping the contribution to where learned methods beat persistence, is an unusually honest framing that raises the credibility of the foundation-model wins that remain. - The provenance fingerprinting protocol (reconstruction of every stored ground-truth array to 10⁻⁴) addresses a real failure mode in multi-run benchmark aggregation that most papers ignore entirely. - The variable-exclusion audit (Table 3.2, with per-variable evidence: SNMP scope jumps, 72-row commissioning prefixes, >30σ test shifts) is a transferable checklist for anyone building forecasting benchmarks on operational telemetry. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The thesis confronts limitations directly and extensively (a dedicated 8-item threats-to-validity section plus a limitations chapter): single-site generalization, associative-only mechanism evidence, test-window-visible target selection, unauditable pretraining corpora, synthetic controls failing to reproduce the effect, single-seed results for twelve of thirteen classical models, scope to small channel-independent foundation checkpoints (explicitly naming Chronos-2 as untested), and the best-of-13-vs-best-of-3 selection asymmetry. The fine-tuning checkpoint-selection asymmetry is also acknowledged. This candor is a credibility positive; the authors minimize nothing material. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - The fine-tuned Moirai result (0.4172) is the best learned method but is essentially tied with zero-shot Moirai; with no early stopping on the fine-tuned variants and a single fixed budget, the fine-tuning comparison is under-powered for the H5 conclusion — the authors partially note this but do not quantify how sensitive the Chronos degradation is to the checkpoint choice. - The dominant-state-fraction mechanism split is derived from the same 8 targets it explains (n=8 points, post-hoc threshold at 0.10), so the clean separation could be an artifact of eight data points; the authors flag the post-hoc nature but not the overfitting risk of the threshold itself. - The "private data absent from pretraining corpora" guarantee is asserted, not verified — no deduplication or membership-inference check against Chronos/Moirai/TimesFM training corpora is possible or attempted, and Moirai-2.0's August 2025 release overlapping the test span weakens the temporal argument more than "partial secondary reassurance" concedes. - The persistence baseline's dominance raises the question of whether seasonal-naive or simple exponential-smoothing baselines (which exploit more than the last value at daily cadence, e.g., weekly seasonality) would also beat the learned methods — only last-value persistence is tested, so the true naive frontier may be stronger or the learned skill set larger than reported. - Evaluation is exclusively MAE on train-normalized data; no raw-unit or operational-cost metrics are given, so a practitioner cannot judge whether a 0.05 MAE difference is operationally meaningful (e.g., degrees Celsius or watts). Bottom Line: A practitioner deploying forecasters on operational telemetry gains real, actionable guidance (always compute persistence; use zero-shot foundation models only where the data is regime-shifting; skip local training at this scale) from a methodologically honest case study, but the single-site, single-cadence, unreleased-data evidence means no broader claim about foundation-model transfer should be updated much — read it as an exemplary benchmarking template more than a generalizable result.

#204 — Moderately Innovative (52)

Symbolic Turbulence Modelling with Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning

ZS Tan · repository.tudelft.nl · neural symbolic - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces Multi-Agent Deep Symbolic Regression (MADSR), a framework that reformulates data-driven turbulence-closure discovery as a cooperative multi-agent RL problem in which each agent learns one scalar coefficient function of the Reynolds-stress anisotropy tensor expansion. - Why it's important: RANS turbulence closures carry large model-form uncertainty, and prior DSR-based closure methods learn the coupled coefficient functions independently with high-variance REINFORCE, yielding inconsistent multi-equation models. - How it does it: The trick is mapping each basis-tensor coefficient α^(n) to an agent sharing a common R² reward from frozen-RANS evaluation, then grafting PPO clipping and a centralized critic (CTDE/MAPPO-style) onto the DSR risk-seeking policy gradient. - The good: Four algorithm variants are compared over ten random seeds each with reported standard deviations, plus an ablation study and flow-field error analysis — unusually careful experimental hygiene for a method paper at this level. - The missing: Evaluation is confined to the periodic-hill benchmark in a frozen-RANS (a posteriori uncoupled) setting; no closed-loop RANS validation, no external flow cases, and the full 10-tensor Pope basis is reduced to 3–4 tensors. - Read it or not: Worth reading for researchers in data-driven turbulence closure or RL-based symbolic regression who want a concrete recipe for extending DSR to multi-output problems; skip it if you need validated, deployable closures or evidence beyond one canonical flow.
Why this rank

Rigor (52) and Resilience (45) drag the composite down: despite commendable 10-seed hygiene and a clean 2×2 factorial design, the method is developed and evaluated on the same periodic-hill benchmark, no external closure baselines (SpaRTA, TBRF, M-GEP) are compared, no closed-loop RANS validation is performed, and the work is an unreviewed MSc thesis with key results truncated in the available material. Novelty (62) is real but modest — mapping tensor-basis coefficients to cooperative agents is a natural, sensible reformulation rather than a surprising insight — and Completeness (50) is weakened by missing external baselines, a single flow family, and only 3–4 of 10 basis tensors. Problem & Motivation: RANS simulations require closure models for the Reynolds-stress tensor, and linear eddy-viscosity models (e.g., k-ω SST) fail in separated flows with strong pressure gradients. Data-driven model-form correction expresses the anisotropy error Δb_ij as a Pope tensor-basis expansion Δb_ij = Σ α^(n)(I₁,...,I₅) T^(n)_ij, and the task is to discover the scalar functions α^(n) from DNS/LES data. Symbolic regression is attractive for interpretability, but standard Deep Symbolic Regression (Petersen et al., 2019) is single-output, and prior DSR-for-EARSM attempts (Hemmes 2022's TBDSR; Tang et al. 2023) learn each coefficient function independently — ignoring the coupling between terms that jointly form one tensor — and use REINFORCE, whose high gradient variance is aggravated in the larger joint search space. The practitioners affected are CFD engineers and the data-driven turbulence modelling community. Key Idea: Treat EARSM discovery as a cooperative multi-agent POMDP — one agent per basis-tensor coefficient, all agents rewarded identically by the R² of the assembled tensor prediction — so that a centralized critic and parameter sharing coordinate learning across coupled equations, while PPO clipping enables multiple policy updates per sampled batch. This is a clean structural insight: the tensor-basis expansion already factorizes into N scalar sub-problems with a shared objective, which is exactly the cooperative-MARL shape. Methodology: The pipeline follows DSR: each agent's LSTM policy (3 layers, hidden size 48, with agent-ID one-hot input for parameter sharing) emits tokens in pre-order traversal to build an expression tree; priors (length, no-inputs, repeat limits on constants, relational constraints against nested unary operators, soft length prior) constrain generation. Constants are fitted per expression with BFGS; the N coefficient expressions are assembled via the tensor basis and scored by an R² reward on min-max-normalized tensor elements (invalid expressions get −10). Four variants are implemented, differing only in the training step: (1) vanilla MADSR (risk-seeking REINFORCE baseline R_ε, independent agents); (2) vPPODSR (adds PPO clipping to the risk-seeking gradient); (3) ACDSR (replaces the risk-seeking baseline with a centralized critic producing Monte-Carlo advantages — notably, the critic is trained on the full batch, not the top-ε subset, to avoid biased value estimates); (4) PPODSR (centralized critic + PPO clipping). A deliberate design decision retains the risk-seeking top-ε subset selection for the actor in all algorithms, justified by preliminary tests. Two targets are studied: EARSM anisotropy correction with 3 and 4 basis tensors, and the k-corrective RANS production term R of SpaRTA, on periodic-hill flow cases (α_PH = 1.0 and 1.5, varying domain aspect ratios) with features (invariants, D_k/C_k, D_k/P_k) computed from frozen-RANS fields. The justification for PPO and CTDE is argued from variance-reduction and non-stationarity reasoning rather than demonstrated ab initio; the empirical comparison in Chapter 4 serves as the justification. Key Results: The thesis reports best R² values per algorithm for the three-tensor EARSM, four-tensor EARSM, and R-correction tasks (Tables 4.1–4.3), with training curves across ten seeds per algorithm (standard deviations shaded). The abstract claims MADSR "outperforms single-agent DSR in frozen RANS evaluations of the periodic-hill benchmark" and that the multi-agent structure improves exploration efficiency and model interpretability/consistency. However, the provided text is truncated before the results chapter's numeric content, so the specific R² values and the exact margins over the single-agent baseline are not stated in the material available. Ablations (Section 4.4) examine input-feature combinations for the R-correction model via R² per combination, and flow-field analyses map predicted-vs-true error fields for Δb_ij and R at α_PH = 1.0 and 1.5. Testing scale is modest: one benchmark flow family, 3–4 of the 10 Pope basis tensors, small LSTMs. No results on full RANS re-integration of the discovered models are reported in the available text. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD. The genuinely novel element is the mapping of multi-equation symbolic regression onto cooperative MARL with centralized critics and PPO — prior DSR-for-EARSM work (TBDSR, Tang et al.) used independent per-coefficient training with REINFORCE. Everything else is competent recombination of existing components: DSR expression generation, MAPPO (Yu et al., 2022), hierarchical entropy regularization and soft length priors (Landajuela et al., 2021), and the frozen-RANS/k-corrective targets from SpaRTA. No new theorem, dataset, or system is contributed. Rigor & Reproducibility: Strengths: ten random seeds per algorithm with reported standard deviations; a controlled 2×2 factorial comparison (baseline/critic × no-clip/PPO-clip) isolating the contribution of each MARL ingredient; a dedicated ablation study (Section 4.4) and per-cell error-field visualizations. Concerns: (i) method development and evaluation occur on the same benchmark (periodic hills) — a Goodhart risk since the discovered models are selected on the data they are scored on, with only α_PH = 1.5 as a quasi-holdout within the same geometry family; (ii) no significance tests are mentioned, only visual standard-deviation bands; (iii) no comparison against non-DSR baselines from the closure literature (SpaRTA, TBRF, M-GEP) in the available text — the comparison set is only the four MADSR variants plus implied single-agent DSR; (iv) code release is not stated. The thesis is an unreviewed MSc dissertation (defended November 2025), which warrants tempered confidence relative to peer-reviewed results. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL (the paper trains and evaluates RL-based symbolic regression pipelines; no proofs). - Practical: Yes — the models are tiny (3-layer, 48-unit actor LSTM; 2-layer, 64-unit critic) and the frozen-RANS evaluation avoids running CFD during training, so standard workstation hardware suffices. - Efficient: Not stated — no wall-clock times, FLOP counts, or comparison of training compute against single-agent DSR are visible in the provided text; PPO's multiple epochs per batch should improve sample efficiency but this is asserted, not measured. - Effective: Partially — evidence covers R² fit to frozen-RANS correction fields on periodic hills, which is a proxy; whether discovered closures improve actual RANS flow predictions when coupled into a solver is not demonstrated in the available material. - Scalable: Untested beyond 4 agents/tensors and one flow family; the full Pope basis has 10 tensors and realistic applications involve multiple geometries and Reynolds numbers, so the 10×–100× scaling claim remains unexamined. Deliverable form: a paper (MSc thesis) describing a framework; no public code repository, library, or trained models are mentioned. Strengths: - The core reformulation — coefficient functions of a tensor-basis expansion as cooperative agents under a shared reward — is a natural, well-motivated idea that directly addresses a documented weakness (independent learning) in prior DSR-for-EARSM work, and it opens a previously unexplored intersection of MARL and symbolic regression. - The 2×2 algorithm decomposition (risk-seeking baseline vs. learned critic × no-clip vs. PPO clipping) is a clean experimental design that attributes performance to specific MARL ingredients rather than to a monolithic system. - Careful engineering details that materially affect correctness: training the critic on the full reward distribution while restricting actor updates to the top-ε subset; min-max normalization of tensor elements so small-magnitude components are not ignored by the shared R² reward; adaptation of DSR priors (allowing constant-only expressions, capping per-agent expression length at 10 tokens) to the multi-agent setting. - The evaluation goes beyond scalar metrics to per-cell error-field analysis and an input-feature ablation, which supports the interpretability claims. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The thesis contains a dedicated Limitations section (5.1) and future-work recommendations (5.2), but their content lies beyond the truncated excerpt provided, so the specific limitations the authors acknowledge cannot be quoted here — Not stated (in the available text). The abstract itself is modest, calling MADSR "a promising step toward" end-to-end RL-based symbolic turbulence modelling rather than claiming a solved problem, which is an appropriately hedged framing. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - No closed-loop validation: the reward and all reported metrics come from frozen-RANS field fitting; a closure that fits Δb_ij fields offline can still destabilize or degrade a coupled RANS solver, and this step — standard in the SpaRTA/RITA line the thesis builds on — is absent from the visible material. - Missing external baselines: the algorithm comparison is internal to MADSR variants; SpaRTA, TBRF, M-GEP, or plain GP on the same targets would establish whether MARL machinery beats far cheaper deterministic or evolutionary alternatives, not just whether it beats vanilla DSR. - Single-flow-family evaluation: periodic hills at two geometries is a narrow evidentiary base for claims of "more consistent and interpretable turbulence closures"; canonical cases used by prior work (converging–diverging channel, curved backward-facing step, NASA hump) are not evaluated in the provided text. - The claim that multi-agent structure "enhances exploration efficiency" is asserted from training curves on one problem; no exploration metrics or cross-task transfer evidence are shown. - Truncation to 3–4 of the 10 Pope basis tensors means the approach has not been shown to handle the full problem dimensionality for which the MARL coordination argument matters most. Bottom Line: A technically careful MSc thesis that offers a genuinely new and sensible formulation (cooperative MARL over tensor-basis coefficients) and a well-controlled algorithm comparison, but with single-benchmark, frozen-RANS-only evidence and no external baselines — useful as a methodological starting point for the DSR-for-closures community, while practitioners seeking validated turbulence models should stay with SpaRTA/RITA-style approaches until MADSR is shown to survive closed-loop RANS and multi-geometry testing.

Balancing relevance and redundancy: An optuna-tuned QUBO formulation for feature selection in recommender systems

B Prajapat, A Kuila · ceur-ws.org · karypis - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces a hybrid pipeline that wraps a QUBO feature-selection formulation for Item-KNN recommenders in an Optuna Bayesian loop that automatically tunes the QUBO penalty weights (relevance α, redundancy β, budget λ) against downstream NDCG@10, and evaluates the resulting matrices on both simulated and physical D-Wave quantum annealers as a submission to QuantumCLEF 2026 Task 1B. - Why it's important: QUBO-based feature selection requires hand-calibrating Lagrange multipliers, which prior qCLEF teams did manually or with static heuristics; automating this removes the main practical bottleneck to using quantum annealing for dimensionality reduction in recommender systems. - How it does it: The QUBO energy combines a Random-Forest-Gini relevance term, a cosine-similarity pairwise redundancy penalty, and a squared budget constraint; Optuna's TPE proposes (α, β, λ), a Simulated Annealing backend solves the QUBO, and validation NDCG@10 is fed back over 1,000 trials before the tuned matrix is run on the QPU. - The good: On the official qCLEF 2026 leaderboard, the pipeline achieved the best Simulated Annealing score of all teams (NDCG@10 = 0.0287, vs. 0.0256 for the runner-up) using the smallest feature budget (k = 59 vs. 75–97 for competitors), and all feature subsets beat the full 100-feature baseline (0.0226). - The missing: No classical wrapper baseline (greedy forward selection, genetic search, mRMR) is compared — so the reader cannot tell whether the QUBO machinery, quantum or otherwise, outperforms simple classical subset search at N = 100 features, a scale where exhaustive or greedy methods are trivially feasible. - Read it or not: Worth reading for researchers in quantum-assisted feature selection or qCLEF participants who want a concrete recipe for automated QUBO weight calibration; skippable for recommender-systems practitioners, since the scale (100 features) and the below-baseline QPU accuracy limit practical takeaway.

Problem & Motivation: Content-based recommender systems, particularly Item-Based KNN, degrade when high-dimensional item metadata introduces noise, multicollinearity, and computational overhead into similarity computations. The specific audience is participants of QuantumCLEF Task 1B, who must select a compact feature subset from a 100-dimensional Item Content Matrix of a private music recommendation dataset to maximize NDCG@10. Existing QUBO feature-selection formulations (MI-QUBO, QUBO-Correlation, PDQUBO from prior qCLEF teams) are sensitive to their penalty weights (Lagrange multipliers): prior teams tuned these manually or with static heuristics like the Auto-α estimator, and poor calibration makes it impossible to attribute performance changes to the feature subset rather than the energy landscape. The paper targets this hyperparameter bottleneck. Key Idea: Embed the QUBO solver inside a Bayesian optimization loop (Optuna's TPE) that treats the QUBO penalty weights (α, β, λ) as hyperparameters and the downstream validation NDCG@10 as the objective, so the energy landscape is calibrated automatically against end-task recommendation quality rather than by hand. This is a wrapper-over-QUBO composition; the underlying QUBO formulation (relevance linear term, redundancy quadratic term, squared budget penalty) and the quantum/simulated annealing solvers are existing techniques from Ferrari Dacrema et al. and standard D-Wave tooling. Methodology: The pipeline has four stages. (1) Coefficient construction: a Random Forest on the URM/ICM yields normalized Gini importance scores forming the linear relevance vector R; cosine similarity between ICM feature columns yields the pairwise redundancy matrix S. (2) QUBO formulation: minimize E(x) = −α Σᵢ Rᵢxᵢ + β Σᵢ Σ_{j>i} Sᵢⱼxᵢxⱼ + λ(Σᵢ xᵢ − k)² over binary x ∈ {0,1}ᴺ. (3) Hybrid tuning: Optuna (TPE) proposes (α, β, λ) for 1,000 trials; each trial builds the Q matrix, solves it with the dwave-neal Simulated Annealing backend (250 reads), and, if the returned subset exactly matches budget k, evaluates it with Item-KNN (top-K = 100, cosine similarity, shrinkage τ = 5), feeding validation NDCG@10 back to Optuna. (4) Quantum execution: tuned matrices are submitted to D-Wave Leap via EmbeddingComposite(DWaveSampler()) with 1,000 reads, budget-violating samples are filtered, and the five most stable lowest-energy subsets across repeated runs are submitted for official held-out evaluation. Data is split 80/20 into an optimization split (further subdivided into train_opt/val_opt for the tuner) and a final untouched 20% holdout. Critical design decisions: (a) using Random Forest Gini importance for R (reasonable but unvalidated against alternative relevance measures — no ablation); (b) tuning weights on SA but deploying on QPU (acknowledged by the authors as causing simulator overfitting); (c) the two-tier split to prevent leakage (well justified and cleanly executed). A 500-trial Bayesian search over the budget k identified two performance peaks at k = 48 and k = 59. Key Results: All experiments use the private qCLEF 2026 music dataset (3,209,730 implicit interactions, 20,428 users, 14,607 items, 100_ICM configuration with N = 100 features) — a toy-to-standard scale by recommender standards. Headline numbers: best SA submission achieves NDCG@10 = 0.0287 (k = 59) vs. the full-100-feature Item-KNN baseline of 0.0226 (+27.0% relative); internal holdout evaluation reports test NDCG of 0.0312 at k = 48 and 0.0309 at k = 59, both beating the baseline. On the official leaderboard, the team ranks first among SA submissions (0.0287 vs. R2AI's 0.0256 at k = 97, SYZYGY's 0.0243 at k = 85, FAST-NUCES's 0.0229 at k = 75). Pure-QPU executions peak at NDCG@10 = 0.0211 — below the classical baseline of 0.0226 and consistent with all other teams' pure-QPU results — but solve in ~2.5×10⁵ μs versus 9.4×10⁶–2.1×10⁷ μs for SA, a 35–80× time-to-solution advantage. Surprising finding: the k = 48 subset, found with only 0.4% of search density, generalized better on holdout (0.0312) than the optimizer's heavily-sampled k = 59 peak (0.0309). Baselines against other teams are current (same 2026 evaluation); the missing classical-wrapper baselines are the notable omission. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD (partially) + NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING. The genuinely novel element is the automated Optuna-driven calibration of QUBO penalty weights against downstream NDCG, which the related-work section substantiates as an open gap among qCLEF submissions; the QUBO formulation, relevance/redundancy coefficients, and annealing execution are standard combinations of existing ideas (Ferrari Dacrema et al.'s QUBO family, Random Forest importance, cosine similarity, D-Wave tooling) applied to the qCLEF 2026 setting. The budget-space analysis (peaks at k = 48/59) is a dataset-specific empirical finding, not a general result. Rigor & Reproducibility: The evaluation protocol is careful on the data side: a strict two-tier 80/20 split isolates the Optuna tuner from the final holdout, and all headline scores come from the official qCLEF assessment infrastructure — this is a credibility strength. Ablations are partial: a 500-trial search over k is reported in detail, but there is no ablation over the relevance estimator (RF Gini vs. alternatives), no sensitivity analysis of read counts, and no per-component decomposition of the QUBO terms. No error bars or significance tests are reported for SA runs (QPU stochasticity is mitigated by aggregating over repeated runs, but SA variance is not quantified). SA-compatible code is released at https://github.com/Novaa-a/qCLEF-2026-skywalkers; the dataset is private (qCLEF-provided), limiting full reproduction. Methodological concerns: (1) the tuning pipeline optimizes against SA feedback, then the paper reports QPU results — an acknowledged train/deploy mismatch (Goodhart-style overfitting to the simulator); (2) there is an unexplained inconsistency between the internal test NDCG of 0.0312 (k = 48, Section 6.1) and the best official submission score of 0.0287 (k = 48/59, Table 2) that the paper does not reconcile; (3) the annealing-time speedup compares QPU annealing time against SA wall-clock without accounting for QPU access overhead, embedding time, or retry rates; (4) no classical wrapper baseline is run. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (with a SYSTEMS flavor via the released pipeline), evaluated through the qCLEF competition harness. - Practical: Yes for the SA path — it runs on commodity hardware via dwave-neal; the QPU path requires paid D-Wave Leap cloud access. - Efficient: SA convergence takes 9–21 seconds per matrix (manageable), but the 1,000-trial Optuna loop over full KNN evaluations is the dominant cost and is not quantified; QPU sampling is ~250 ms, 35–80× faster. - Effective: The evidence shows the selected subsets beat the full-feature baseline and all competitor SA scores on the official holdout, so the core claim (better feature subsets) is supported; the claim of quantum utility is only supported on the speed axis, since QPU accuracy falls below baseline. - Scalable: Not tested — N = 100 features is trivially small; the paper only claims (does not demonstrate) that hybrid solvers will scale to enterprise-scale matrices, and dense pairwise redundancy matrices scale O(N²), which will become the binding constraint. The work delivers a released code artifact (SA pipeline) but no library, trained model, or dataset; the QUBO-weight-tuning recipe is the reusable technique. Strengths: (1) The Optuna-over-QUBO-weights loop is a clean, well-motivated solution to a real, documented bottleneck in the qCLEF literature, and it is validated where it matters — on the official leaderboard against all competing teams, where it wins the SA track with the smallest feature budget (k = 59 vs. 75–97). (2) The two-tier data-split protocol cleanly separates tuning from final evaluation, and all reported submission scores come from the organizers' infrastructure rather than self-measured numbers. (3) The paper is unusually candid about the QPU accuracy deficit: it reports all QPU results below the classical baseline, attributes the gap to both NISQ noise and its own SA-tuning-induced simulator overfitting, and cross-checks against competitors' Q-type submissions. (4) The budget-space analysis (Table 1), including the honest footnote that some zero-density rows came from an initial fixed grid, shows the search actually explored and rejected low/high-k regions. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors explicitly acknowledge: (a) physical QPU accuracy (max 0.0211) falls below both their SA results and the classical baseline, driven by analog noise, thermal decoherence, and minor-embedding limitations; (b) their own pipeline overfits the digital simulator because fine-tuning used SA feedback only; (c) hardware-native QPU hyperparameters (chain strength, annealing schedules) were not independently tuned; (d) the SA-to-QPU gap is listed as a current limitation of the approach. They confront these directly and propose QPU-specific hyperparameter optimization as future work — this candor is a credibility positive. They do not acknowledge the absence of classical baselines or the small problem scale. Analyst-Identified Gaps: (1) Missing classical wrapper baselines: at N = 100, greedy forward selection, exhaustive search over k-sized subsets sampled heuristically, genetic algorithms, or mRMR filtering are all computationally trivial; without them, the paper cannot establish that the QUBO/annealing machinery itself adds value over simple classical subset search — the entire quantum motivation rests on an untested counterfactual. (2) The speedup claim conflates QPU annealing time with SA wall-clock: QPU access via Leap includes queuing, embedding, and readout overheads that are not reported, so the 35–80× figure likely overstates end-to-end advantage. (3) Unreconciled numbers: Section 6.1 reports test NDCG 0.0312 at k = 48 while Table 2's best official submission is 0.0287 — the relationship between the internal holdout and the official test set is never explained, leaving ambiguity about which number to trust. (4) The relevance term depends entirely on Random Forest Gini importance, which is known to be biased toward high-cardinality features and unstable on sparse matrices; no alternative (mutual information, permutation importance) is compared. (5) No confidence intervals or seeds for SA runs despite the authors' own emphasis on annealer stochasticity. (6) Single dataset, single task, N = 100: all generalization claims about scalability to enterprise-scale matrices are extrapolation beyond the evidence. Bottom Line: A competently executed competition paper whose automated QUBO weight-tuning loop is a genuine, leaderboard-validated incremental contribution, but whose quantum component wins only on speed at a problem scale (100 features) where classical methods are untested and probably sufficient — read it for the tuning recipe, not for evidence of quantum advantage.
