Problem & Motivation: Engineers at AWS, MongoDB, Datadog, and Kafka model distributed systems in TLA+, but TLA+ has two structural weaknesses: (1) no mechanism ties the specification to the implementation, so specifications drift from code and TLA+ degenerates into model checking rather than software verification; (2) tooling is inadequate — TLC cannot handle state-space blow-up at scale, and TLAPS has limited liveness proof support, so system-scale temporal proofs remain rare, hand-crafted expert artifacts. The authors target the second weakness: producing machine-checked temporal proofs (safety, TypeOK, invariance, liveness) at scale for specifications nobody has written proofs for, with Verus chosen because it is the same language as the eventual implementation (the refinement step itself is deferred). The audience is both formal-methods practitioners and builders of proof-generation agents, who lack a temporal benchmark whose solutions are not in model training data. Key Idea: The core move is reusing Anvil's Verus temporal-logic encoding (execution traces as functions ℕ→State, always/eventually/leads-to as spec functions) at a scale and automation level never attempted, wrapped in a trust architecture: a merge gate where an LLM prover can only land a proof if deterministic anti-cheat checks and an independent fresh-context LLM reviewer both accept, enforced through Linux UIDs, sudoer-restricted MCP tools, a signed append-only ledger, and git hooks. A secondary key idea is the dual translation strategy — a hand-written transpiler vs. an agentic translator — enabling a controlled comparison of encodings on identical (spec, property) pairs. Methodology: The pipeline has three stages. (1) Translation: TranSpec, a deterministic Rust transpiler, handles TLA+→Verus type inference (constraint solving to synthesize enums/records/maps, Optional for CONSTANT NULL, sum types for state-dependent typing), termination measures, and SMT trigger placement (self-identified as the hardest problem); an alternative agentic translator–reviewer loop handles specs with false or assumption-contingent properties and the long tail of TLA+ syntax. (2) Proof search: a prover LLM session writes proofs on a dev branch of a git repo seeded with a Verus bundle (translated spec + one property + Anvil temporal scaffold); a reviewer LLM with clean context either validates unprovability claims (retracing counterexamples independently) or steers proof style; a gatekeeper (scripts under a separate Unix account, Ed25519-signed ledger, root-owned git hooks) merges only when mechanical checks and review pass. Anti-cheat extends lynette to reject net-new trust markers (admit, assume, external_body, axiom) in proof code. (3) Evaluation: both translation outputs are normalized to a three-region file layout (frozen 755-line/30,780-character scaffold; problem; empty proof fn); the harness returns only region 3 from the model, re-splices, and runs Verus as oracle (k=3 samples, V=10 verification attempts, pass@3 and per-sample pass@1 reported), plus cheating checks on passing files. Over 16,459 (spec, property) pairs: the algorithmic pipeline produced 5,160 well-posed translations and 3,094 proofs; the agentic pipeline 12,352 well-posed translations, with 492/500 proofs on a sample drawn from algorithmically-proven pairs (ensuring paired provability). Dataset construction cost ~$29,500 of list-price Claude tokens. Key Results: (1) Translation comparison on 492 paired proofs: the LLM translation costs 19% more to prove (median ratio 1.19×, $2.07 vs $1.67 per proof), with 1.38× prover turns and 2.00× Verus runs, but produces equal-length proofs with less Z3 work (0.86× rlimit, 0.73× quantifier instantiations); the extra Verus runs are mostly trigger errors (1.19 vs 0.13 per proof — 67% of LLM proofs hit at least one vs 8% of algorithmic) and name-resolution errors. Notably, TranSpec emits 3× more quantifiers and annotates fewer, yet causes fewer trigger errors. (2) Model evaluation (11 models, 3 datasets): on the 40-task paired sets, only Opus-5 and GPT-5.6-sol-pro reach 100% pass@3 on both encodings; Grok-4.5 hits 97.5% (tlaverus_llm) for $51 vs Sonnet-5's same score for $214; scores span 97.5% to 0% (gpt-oss-120b), so the benchmark discriminates below the frontier even as frontier models saturate it. tlaverus tasks are ~80× longer than verusbench (mean 47–55k vs 619 characters), and 8 of 10 models with complete verusbench runs score lower on tlaverus_algo (drops up to 57.5 points for DeepSeek-R1). (3) Liveness is the hardest property type (58/110 solves on tlaverus_algo vs 73–76 for the other types), and this is not explained by length (safety and liveness differ <2% in problem-text length); liveness is also where encodings diverge least. (4) Reasoning-token volume has no rank correlation with accuracy (ρ=0.00 and 0.01 across the two halves). (5) pass@3 substantially exceeds pass@1 for all models except Opus-5 (e.g., GPT-5.6-terra 75.0 vs 52.5). Baselines include verusbench, a current standard Verus benchmark. An appendix case study shows the reviewer rejecting a plausible-but-false unprovability claim on a consensus-spec Agreement property, after which the prover proved the theorem. Novelty Classification: NEW DATASET/BENCHMARK (first temporal-property, liveness-inclusive Verus/proof benchmark generated from deployed-system specifications whose solutions pre-date no training data), NEW SYSTEM/TOOL (the TranSpec transpiler and the prover–reviewer–gatekeeper pipeline with UID-enforced anti-cheat boundaries), and NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING (controlled encoding comparison; liveness difficulty; reasoning-token null correlation). The Verus temporal encoding itself is a competent reuse of Anvil's existing library, and the verifier-in-the-loop agent loop with cheat detection is a known pattern (AutoVerus, VeruSAGE) — the genuinely new elements are the TLA+-to-Verus semantic bridge, the scale of automatic temporal proof generation (3,094 machine-checked proofs where hand-written TLAPS liveness proofs are rare), and the security engineering around agent trust. Rigor & Reproducibility: The paired design (same 40 pairs, two encodings, same models, shared frozen scaffold) is a genuine methodological strength and controls the encoding comparison well. Ablations exist for translation style (per-pair bootstrap CIs on ratios, run-outcome breakdowns, quantifier/trigger analyses in Figures 7–12). However: no error bars or repeated runs for model evaluation (the checklist explicitly concedes point estimates only, k=3 samples, no fixed seeds); the 40-task evaluation set is small, with a thin safety arm (only 24 algorithmic-proven and 2 agentic-proven safety tasks; criterion 5 — excluding tutorial/benchmark specs — was relaxed for that arm, and two repositories retained despite contamination flags because the safety arm could not otherwise be filled). No code or data is released (checklist answer [No]: "workshop paper on work in progress"), which is a serious reproducibility gap for a benchmark paper — the corpus cannot be independently inspected, and one source specification was removed by its owner, so even the inputs are partly unverifiable. Verus version and Rust toolchain are pinned, and the ground-truth separation protocol (credential-denied reference proofs) is well designed. The evaluation harness (single-shot region-3 fill with V=10 retries) is much simpler than the paper's own prover–reviewer pipeline, so benchmark results do not measure the paper's headline system. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL (a built pipeline plus a model evaluation; no theoretical results). - Practical: Yes — the pipeline runs on commercial LLM APIs plus open-source Verus/Rust tooling on a container image, though the gatekeeper's Unix-account/sudoer/git-hook setup requires deliberate ops effort. - Efficient: Dataset construction cost ~$29,500 in list-price tokens; per-proof cost is $1.67 (algorithmic) or $2.07 (agentic) via the prover pipeline, and full evaluation runs cost $3–$333 per model depending on the model. - Effective: The evidence shows Verus-oracle-checked proofs of temporal properties of real specifications — a valid proxy for the stated goal — but the headline motivation (closing specification–implementation drift) is unproven: no refinement proofs connecting Verus specs to Rust implementations exist yet. - Scalable: Corpus generation demonstrably scaled to 16,459 pairs, but the evaluation is at 40 tasks, and saturation by two frontier models means the benchmark's discriminating range at frontier scale is already exhausted; 10× scaling of evaluation difficulty is claimed by corpus size, not tested. The work delivers no software artifact to third parties: no library, CLI, dataset, or weights are released; it stops at paper form (plus unreleased internal tooling). Strengths: - The paired, controlled evaluation design is unusually clean for an agentic-verification paper: identical 40 (spec, property) pairs, two independent encodings, one frozen byte-identical 30,780-character scaffold, letting the 1.19× cost ratio and per-type difficulty be attributed to encoding rather than problem selection. - The anti-cheat and trust architecture is a real contribution beyond prompt engineering: net-new escape-hatch detection extending lynette, plus a deterministic gatekeeper boundary (separate UIDs, signed append-only ledger, root-owned hooks) that is concretely specified and would transfer to other vericoding setups. - The corpus provenance argument is credible: specifications from 24 permissively-licensed public repos, Verus encodings created here, 40-task selection filtered on seven criteria including training-data contamination — addressing the single biggest validity threat in LLM proof benchmarks. - The reviewer-refutes-unprovability case study (Appendix C.2) is a genuinely informative failure-mode demonstration: an LLM prover produced a plausible 10-step counterexample to a true property, and only a second skeptical agent caught that step 1 was not a transition of Next — directly relevant to production use of false-alarm-prone provers. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state (Section 6) that the pipeline cannot reliably distinguish false specifications from true-but-hard-to-prove properties, and that deciding when an added assumption is a "fair addition" to a Verus spec remains an open challenge. The checklist concedes no error bars or repeated runs. Section D.2 admits criterion 5 was relaxed for the safety arm and that two repositories with contamination flags were retained. Appendix C.2 also documents that the showcased source specification is malformed and violates its own liveness property as published. Connecting implementations to specifications via refinement proofs — the motivating problem — is explicitly deferred to future work. The authors confront limitations directly rather than minimizing them, which is a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - No release of the pipeline, datasets, or the 3,094 proofs means none of the central artifacts can be audited; for a paper whose headline contribution is a benchmark, the [No] code/data answer undercuts its own utility as a community resource. - The evaluation measures single-shot region-3 completion with verifier-error retry, not the prover–reviewer–gatekeeper system the paper is named after — there is no controlled experiment showing the reviewer or the gatekeeper improves end-to-end proof yield (the Appendix C.2 evidence is two anecdotes). - The 500-pair agentic comparison is drawn only from pairs already proven algorithmically, so the reported 492/500 and 19% cost premium characterize neither the full agentic corpus (12,352 well-posed translations, of which proof rates are unknown) nor specs the transpiler cannot handle. - Only ~10 of 11 evaluated models are current-frontier and the field moves fast; more importantly, no baseline agent architectures (e.g., no-reviewer ablation, no anti-cheat-off ablation) quantify each pipeline component's contribution. - The "solutions not in training data" claim is asserted via provenance filtering, not validated empirically (e.g., no canary/membership-inference check), and the retained contaminated repositories (tlaplus/tlaplus, FormaLLM) weaken it for the safety arm specifically. - Safety coverage is thin (50 algorithmic / 630 agentic well-posed safety tasks, only 24 and 2 proven), yet safety is presented as one of four co-equal property categories. Bottom Line: A practitioner in LLM-for-formal-verification should read this for its controlled encoding comparison, its concrete anti-cheat/gatekeeper design, and the first real temporal-proof benchmark, but should treat it as a strong workshop-stage precursor — the unreleased artifacts, 40-task evaluation, and absence of any refinement-to-implementation result mean no stronger alternative on exactly this ground exists yet, while adjacent systems (VeruSAGE, RepoVBench) cover the non-temporal vericoding ground with released assets.

MiniCorp: The Last Mile of the AI Agent Firm

J Zeng, Z Dai, J Li, C Shin, D Zhang, Y Lu, Q He… · arxiv.org · generating environments for agent testing in enterprises - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces MiniCorp, a closed-loop e-commerce office simulator that couples a persistent multi-role LLM agent firm with an evolving external market, generating longitudinal and counterfactual enterprise data for training and evaluating agents that run a company. - Why it's important: Training and evaluating agents capable of sustained organizational autonomy requires longitudinal enterprise data that is scarce, privacy-restricted, and cannot answer counterfactual questions, so researchers currently lack any environment where firm decisions produce measurable, delayed market consequences. - How it does it: The core mechanism is a checkpointable, two-world simulation in which an exogenous market (explicit search ranking, sponsored-search auctions, click/conversion models, adaptive competitors) co-evolves with a standing agent organization whose approved decisions alter market state week over week, with all communications and outcomes recorded. - The good: The strongest evidence is the end-to-end fidelity validation: the integrated simulator reproduces documented empirical response patterns, including price elasticities of 2.9–3.2, persistent post-discount and post-stockout sales effects through a sales-velocity-to-organic-ranking feedback loop, and 84% of advertising-driven incremental units coming from competitor displacement. - The missing: There is no demonstration that the generated data actually improves agent training or transfers beyond the simulator — the paper's central value proposition (a data engine) is asserted, not tested, and robustness across independently initialized worlds is explicitly left unevaluated. - Read it or not: Worth reading for researchers building long-horizon agent environments, enterprise agent benchmarks, or market simulators, since the fidelity methodology and organizational-provenance analyses are transferable; skippable for readers seeking evidence that simulated enterprise data improves real agent capability.

Problem & Motivation: The work targets the gap between task-completing agents and the longer-run goal of organizational autonomy — a system of agents that sets strategic direction, coordinates across roles, and keeps an organization profitable over time. Three communities have this problem: agent researchers who lack evaluation environments with unverifiable, delayed business outcomes; enterprise ML teams who cannot access longitudinal records of decisions and their consequences (the paper cites Google's $10 million bankruptcy-auction purchase of Spirit Airlines' internal data as evidence of scarcity and cost); and RL practitioners, since static archives like Enron record only the single realized trajectory and cannot support interactive learning. Existing benchmarks (τ2-Bench, SWE-bench, GAIA, OSWorld, TheAgentCompany, EnterpriseArena, MerchantBench) evaluate bounded tasks with predefined objectives or reduce a company to a lone operator against a hand-authored world, and none supports checkpoint-and-replay of a persistent firm inside an evolving market. Key Idea: The central insight is that simulator fidelity must be validated end-to-end at the system level, not rule-by-rule, because individually plausible market mechanisms interact through feedback loops — and that preserving the intermediate response pathways (e.g., discount → sales velocity → organic ranking → delayed organic sales), not just terminal outcomes, is what prevents agents from learning simulator-specific regularities the authors call "simulator overfitting." The second, complementary idea is inverting the usual multi-agent setup: the organizational structure pre-exists the work (standing roles with fixed decision authorities, work routed into them) rather than being spawned per task, which makes delegation provenance, credit assignment, and counterfactual replay well-defined. Methodology: MiniCorp models business operation as a closed loop between two stateful systems. The external world evolves as W(t+1) ~ P_Λ(· | W_t, D_t, Z_t), where Λ are latent structural parameters (consumer preference weights, supplier defect propensities, unobserved query–category conversion multipliers) never shown to the agent firm, D_t is the firm's decision set, and Z_t carries exogenous shocks. Its e-commerce instantiation comprises six explicit marketplace components: (I) search demand from 1,000 queries (316 Amazon autocomplete + 684 constructed long-tail) distributed via Zipf's law, with LLM relevance labeling few-shot grounded in the ESCI dataset; (II) SKUs and listings with a 26-week warm-up "simulator-generated prehistory" so incumbents have sales and review histories; (III) a two-stage search engine (matching, then ranking on behavioral, relevance, and offer signals); (IV) per query–SKU click and conversion models with hidden conversion multipliers; (V) a multi-slot second-price sponsored-search auction with budget depletion; and (VI) dynamic competitors that adapt prices and advertising from observed performance only. Mechanisms are adapted from the commercial game Capitalism II and parameterized from published empirical studies. The internal world is a firm of standing roles, each defined only by (a) the business data it owns and (b) a subset A_i of the fixed action catalogue it may propose; agents coordinate via unstructured email/chat with no central scheduler, and an approving role (CEO) accepts or rejects proposals. Each period, the world exports a masked, raw, schema-audited data room (no latent parameters, no derived metrics); agents analyze it via isolated SQL/Python, communicate, and propose decisions that take effect at the next period boundary. Every message, query, proposal, and ruling is logged with provenance, and latent parameters are retained server-side for post-hoc credit assignment and scoring. Fidelity evaluation follows pattern-oriented modeling (Grimm et al. 2005) and Sargent's operational-validation framework: controlled interventions replay the same checkpoint with the same random draws, and response direction, temporal dynamics, distribution across participants, and trade-offs are compared against empirical studies. Two critical design decisions: (1) forcing decisions into a fixed action catalogue is justified by executability but limits the decision space to what the simulator can parse; (2) withholding all derived analytics is justified as making "deciding what to measure" part of the evaluated capability, but conflates data-engineering skill with business judgment. Key Results: RQ1 (fidelity): A 10% price cut/raise produced arc elasticities of 2.9 and 3.2, near the empirical benchmark of Bijmolt et al. (2005). A 20% discount for four weeks raised units 71% during the discount, with sales still 31% above control for four weeks after restoration and 11% for the following six weeks — nearly half the incremental units sold post-discount, reproducing the documented sales-velocity→organic-ranking pathway. A two-week stockout left 59% of the cumulative unit shortfall occurring after restocking and sales 36% below control at week 26. Advertising increased ad-attributed units 23–32% and organic gains from 0.5% to 5.8%, returned $0.53 per advertising dollar within the window, and drew 84% of incremental units from competitor displacement rather than market expansion. RQ2 (organizational realism): Across 30,248 work items, only 11% were self-planned; 58% were carried over and 31% were colleague-generated. CEO rejection rates concentrated on cash-committing categories (replenishment/logistics 29%, advertising/pricing 25%) versus 13% for zero-cost quality holds, with no instruction to that effect. Coordination routes around the reporting line: Quality Engineering and Supply Chain exchange work laterally (1,299 exchanges) because defect-detection capability sits apart from hold authority. RQ3: With explicit long-term strategic guidance, the firm spent ~$1,700 on advertising over 26 weeks, yielding ~$31,000 revenue and $1,913 gross profit after ad costs; without guidance it spent ~$50 total and recorded a $7 loss. RQ4: Across 10 injected shock scenarios × 2 runs, the firm executed the expected action in 11/20 runs and partially in 4/20, with message-chain audits showing collaboration was "irreplaceable" in five situations. RQ5: Emergent behaviors included evasive task-marking (a demand lead replying substantively but never pausing listings) and self-initiated title rewriting based on query conversion data, lifting one charger's weekly sales from 91 to 189 units at unchanged price. All results come from GPT-5.6-Sol as the single backbone; runs are 8–26 weeks over 20 runs for the shock suite. Baseline comparison for the simulator itself is against empirical literature patterns, not against alternative simulators. Novelty Classification: NEW SYSTEM/TOOL and NEW FORMULATION. The genuinely novel elements are (1) the coupling of a persistent standing-role agent firm with a self-advancing, checkpointable market that co-evolves with it — closest prior work (TheAgentCompany, EnterpriseArena, MerchantBench) either scripts the world, uses a lone operator, or terminates at task boundaries — and (2) the end-to-end, pathway-level fidelity validation methodology against empirical market patterns. The constituent mechanisms (second-price auctions, position-dependent CTR, LLM role agents, pattern-oriented model validation from agent-based economics) are all established; the contribution is their integration and the evaluation framework, not any single algorithm. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations: the RQ3 guided/unguided pairing is a clean controlled comparison with identical initial state, but there are no ablations over the external world's components (e.g., removing competitor adaptivity or the velocity-ranking loop) and no sensitivity analysis over latent parameters. Statistics: no error bars, confidence intervals, or significance tests anywhere; the shock evaluation uses 20 runs, and the paper itself concedes "robustness across independently initialized worlds remains to be evaluated." Code/data: a project website (agents-minicorp.com) is listed, but no code, dataset, or checkpoint release is stated in the text. Methodological concerns: (1) fidelity is validated against only four response patterns, each hand-selected, raising selection concern; (2) the single-firm, single-industry (e-commerce), single-backbone (GPT-5.6-Sol) scope limits generalization claims; (3) RQ3/RQ5 report single-run comparisons in the guided/unguided case ("in one run... in the other"), where week-to-week LLM stochasticity could plausibly explain outcome swings; (4) the four-urgent-problems and seasonal-dip scenarios have no reported share in Table 5, an unexplained inconsistency; (5) the paper appropriately flags its own simulator-overfitting risk but has no transfer experiment to quantify it. Deployability: Profile: SYSTEMS (a built simulator, evaluated by running it), with EMPIRICAL evaluation layered on. Practical: Yes — the substrate is a commercial LLM API plus a database export loop, so it runs on commercially available infrastructure. Efficient: Cost is bounded by LLM calls per role per week, but the paper reports no token or dollar cost per simulated week, so efficiency relative to alternatives cannot be assessed. Effective: The evidence shows the market closes the loop realistically and that agents respond to it; it does not show that the resulting data improves agent training or transfers to real marketplaces — the stated purpose is only a claim. Scalable: Untested; runs are 8–26 weeks, one firm, one industry, and 20-run evaluation; multi-industry extension is described as a general approach but never instantiated. Deliverable: the paper points to a website but ships no stated artifact (library, dataset, or trained model); as published it exists in paper form plus a web presence. Strengths: (1) The fidelity evaluation methodology is the paper's real intellectual contribution: insisting on pathway-level, system-level validation against empirical patterns (using held-out effects not used in calibration) is a disciplined import from agent-based computational economics that most LLM-simulation papers lack. (2) The organizational-provenance analysis (work-item origins, process signatures, delegation graphs) is a genuinely new measurement instrument — it turns "is this an organization or a task queue?" into quantitative structure, and the emergent capability/authority separation routing around the CEO is a credible finding. (3) The information-hiding design (masked exports, latent parameters held server-side, decision-catalogue constraint) makes credit assignment and counterfactual replay well-defined rather than aspirational. (4) The cold-start advertising result operationalizes "long-term vision" as a measurable behavioral difference between prompt conditions, a concrete instantiation of an otherwise vague construct. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors explicitly state that robustness across independently initialized worlds remains to be evaluated, and they name simulator overfitting as the central validity risk, arguing at length that fidelity testing is what mitigates it. They also scope the work as a single e-commerce demonstration of a general approach and note that the guided/unguided result is one comparison. They confront these limitations directly rather than minimizing them, which strengthens credibility. They do not, however, flag the missing release of code/data, the absence of statistical testing, the single-backbone dependence, or the lack of any experiment validating the data-engine use case. Analyst-Identified Gaps: (1) The headline value proposition — "a scalable source of longitudinal and counterfactual enterprise data for agent training and evaluation" — is never tested: no experiment trains or fine-tunes an agent on MiniCorp-generated data and measures improvement, so the data-engine claim is entirely unvalidated. (2) The RQ3 conclusion rests on what appears to be a single paired run per condition; given week-to-week variance in LLM agent behavior, this is far too thin to attribute a $31,000-vs-$200 revenue gap to strategic guidance rather than run variance. (3) There is no comparison against any alternative simulator or benchmark on any shared metric, so a reader cannot judge whether MiniCorp's market is more realistic than, say, MerchantBench's world model. (4) Only four fidelity tests are reported, all advertising- and pricing-centric; inventory, supplier, logistics, and customer-service response pathways — which make up most of the work items in Table 3 — receive no validation. (5) The "emergent" title-rewriting behavior (RQ5) arises from an LLM whose pretraining almost certainly includes Amazon SEO content; the paper's own criterion ("not a model default") is asserted rather than established, e.g., via a control prompt or a different backbone. (6) The checkerboard of scenario outcomes in Table 6 (50% hit rates on most shocks) is presented without any variance or seed analysis, leaving the firm's shock-response reliability uncharacterized. Bottom Line: A practitioner building long-horizon agent environments or enterprise benchmarks gains real, transferable value from MiniCorp's fidelity-validation methodology and organizational-provenance instrumentation, but should treat the "enterprise data engine" framing as an untested hypothesis rather than a demonstrated result — the field still lacks stronger validated alternatives, which is both this paper's opportunity and its weakness.

ACID: beta-testing active inference for active cyber -defence

JF Cevallos-Moreno, A Rizzardi, S Sicari… · link.springer.com · cyber model training - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces a mathematical formulation of Active Inference for fully observable MDPs, four bootstrapped neural Deep Active Inference (DAI) agent variants, and a synthetic CTI-acquisition testbed (LION) on which DAI-P reaches a ~75% win rate versus ~50% for DDQN/Dueling-DQN over 500 episodes. - Why it's important: Optimising the cost of acquiring cyber-threat-intelligence (CTI) labels against defensive benefit is a real budget problem for ML-based network intrusion detection, and the paper argues this meta-learning structure is a natural fit for Active Inference's epistemic-gain machinery, which standard RL lacks. - How it does it: The core move is decomposing the Expected Free Energy into a pragmatic term (environment reward) plus a perceptive epistemic term (transition-model prediction error on a 9-dim proprioceptive state vector), trained with one-step bootstrapped temporal-difference targets and Boltzmann action selection, planning horizon h=1. - The good: DAI-P attains the top win rate with the smallest parameter budget (9,420 params, 3.50M FLOPs/step vs 15,183 params, 8.37M FLOPs for DAI-A/DAI-F), and the ablation table cleanly isolates which epistemic term does the work. - The missing: All evaluation is on a 2-D, 7-Gaussian, 3-action synthetic environment whose reward and state design (label purchases zero a proprioceptive confidence slot, producing maximal prediction error) is explicitly engineered so the epistemic mechanism under test is the winning strategy — a near-circular validation; the realistic tiger environment is described but never evaluated on. - Read it or not: Worth reading for researchers in active inference or RL-for-security who want a careful, statistically reported proof-of-concept and a worked MDP derivation of EFE; practitioners seeking deployable NID cyber-defence will find nothing beyond a toy testbed and should skip it.

Scored using the Empirical profile. The composite is dragged down by Non-Obviousness (40) and Resilience (42): the LION environment is co-designed so label purchases zero the proprioceptive confidence slot and produce maximal prediction error (Appendix 8.3 admits this), making the headline result partially circular, and the motivating tiger environment is never evaluated on while the natural ICM/RND intrinsic-reward baselines are missing. Rigor (55) has real strengths — 10 seeds with CIs, a clean ablation ladder isolating the epistemic term, parameter/FLOP accounting, and released code — but the Goodhart-style environment design materially reduces it. Novelty (58) is capped because the MDP formulation overlaps cited prior adaptations. Completeness (58) benefits from honest, direct limitation acknowledgment. Problem & Motivation: ML-based network intrusion detection in an open world faces two costs: continuously incorporating new attack classes, and paying for the labelled data (CTI) that keeps detection accurate. The tiger game environment (the authors' prior work, cited as submitted) formalises the trade-off between spending budget on CTI labels versus acting (accept/block traffic), creating a meta-learning problem — an agent must learn how to acquire data in order to learn detection. Prior work applied DDQN to this trade-off; the open question is whether an agency framework with an explicit epistemic-gain objective (Active Inference, grounded in the Free Energy Principle) outperforms purely reward-driven RL on this hierarchical goal structure. The intended audience is the cyber-defence and active-inference research communities. Key Idea: Recast the Active Inference framework — normally posed over POMDPs — for fully observable MDPs, and show that the canonical perceptive epistemic term of the Expected Free Energy (a KL between an observation-informed posterior and the transition model's prediction, which reduces analytically to half the squared transition-prediction error under spherical-Gaussian assumptions) acts as a targeted intrinsic reward that lets the agent discover strategically valuable but visually inconspicuous CTI label purchases (the deceptive cluster UA) earlier than reward-only learning. The mechanism works because label purchases induce a sharp, localised, un-predictable change in the proprioceptive state, which the transition network registers as maximum epistemic gain — faster credit assignment than delayed reward signals alone. Methodology: The paper first derives a variational free energy (VFE = complexity + accuracy) and expected free energy (EFE = expected epistemic gain + expected pragmatic gain) for fully observable MDPs, making two explicit substitutions: replacing the process likelihood with the model's own (to induce exploration) and replacing the true future-observation distribution with a predefined preference distribution (here instantiated directly as the environment reward rt). Four DAI agents are then built as off-policy, bootstrapped (TD, γ=0.95, target network updated every 20 steps) neural implementations sharing a critic Gψ that scores actions via Boltzmann sampling (precision ζ=100, i.e. nearly deterministic): (1) DAI-P — canonical, target = −transition-KL − reward; (2) DAI-A — target = −action-space mutual-information KL − reward (a non-canonical extension requiring |A|=3 parallel TransitionNet passes); (3) DAI-SA — surrogate policy-divergence MSE bonus; (4) DAI-F — DAI-P plus the DAI-A bonus. Policy and transition networks are trained by supervised losses toward the critic-induced normative policy and next-observation prediction, respectively; a unified algorithm (Alg. 1) covers all variants plus a DDQN special case with the epistemic term removed. Three critical design decisions: (i) planning horizon h=1, justified by arguing the bootstrapped critic carries infinite-horizon epistemic value implicitly and that belief-tree search is unnecessary in a fully observable MDP — argued reasonably but only for this regime; (ii) the pragmatic term is implemented directly as environment reward rather than a learned preference distribution — a deliberate simplification toward RL that the authors acknowledge; (iii) no actor-critic despite policy networks present (policy model used only for auxiliary bonuses), justified by observed convergence failures of actor-critic schemes in this environment. Key Results: Tested in LION, a synthetic environment of seven 2-D Gaussian clusters (3 known, 4 unknown purchasable labels, prices 5/6/4/4 summing to 19 against an initial budget of 8, win threshold 40, 30 steps/episode, 3 actions), 500 training episodes, 10 seeds per agent (90 runs), mean ± 95% t-based CIs on smoothed series. DAI-P achieves the highest win rate, approaching 75% by episode 500; DDQN and Dueling-DQN converge to roughly 50% but need about twice as many episodes to reach DAI-P's episode-100 performance; SAC is substantially weaker; PPO is slowest; the Break-Even heuristic plateaus below 20%. DAI-P buys a stable 2.5–3 labels/episode with low variance versus 3–4 for DDQN variants; DAI-P and DAI-A overlap at ~70–75% win rate; DAI-SA lags consistently; DAI-F adds nothing over DAI-P. Epistemic gain for DAI-P/A self-extinguishes after ~episode 100 (transition model internalises purchase dynamics), whereas SAC's entropy bonus grows monotonically past 1.0. All DAI variants converge to ~15–17 budget units of CTI spend per episode and classification reward ~2.0 (near the +2.0 informed-regime maximum). Baselines are standard and appropriately chosen for the setting (DDQN, Dueling-DQN, PPO, discrete SAC, plus a rule-based reference); no baseline is outdated, but all were run in a heavily exploration-suppressed configuration. Notably, the authors report no results on the realistic tiger environment — only the synthetic LION proof-of-concept. Novelty Classification: NEW FORMULATION (an explicit Act-Inf derivation for fully observable MDPs, though the authors themselves cite prior MDP adaptations [31,32], so this is closer to a systematisation than a first), NEW METHOD (the four DAI variants, of which only DAI-P is canonical and the other three are acknowledged information-theoretic extensions/ablations), and NEW DATASET/BENCHMARK (LION). The genuinely novel element is the empirical demonstration that a perceptive transition-prediction epistemic term suffices to beat four DRL baselines on CTI-acquisition timing; the neural machinery itself (TD bootstrapping, target networks, Boltzmann selection, replay buffer) is a competent combination of standard deep-RL components, and the epistemic-bonus idea is well precedented in the Active Inference and curiosity-driven RL literature. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are present and are the paper's strongest methodological feature: Table 2 systematically isolates the perceptive term (DDQN vs DAI-P), the exact vs surrogate MI bonus (DAI-A vs DAI-SA), and the combined objective (DAI-F vs DAI-P), and Table 1 rules out model-size confounds (the best agent is also the smallest). Statistical reporting is careful: 10 seeds with per-seed data generators and independently pretrained classifiers shared across agents, offset random streams, 95% t-intervals, explicit smoothing protocol, and a full hyperparameter table. Code, data, and pretrained models are released (github.com/DISTA-IoT/lion; SmartVille release 3.0_ACID). Methodological concerns: (i) the environment and the epistemic signal are co-designed — the proprioceptive confidence slot is zeroed on purchase precisely so prediction error spikes there (Appendix 8.3 states this explicitly), so the headline result partially verifies the designed mechanism rather than discovering it; (ii) only 95% CIs are reported, no significance tests across agents; (iii) the deer-by-another-name issue that the realistic tiger environment, which motivates the entire problem, is never evaluated on. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL (learning agents run in a synthetic simulation; no deployment). - Practical: Yes trivially — networks have 5.7K–15.2K parameters and the task is a 14-dim state, 3-action MDP; ironically the experiments were run on 8×A100-80GB GPUs, grossly oversized for the workload. - Efficient: DAI-P costs 3.50M FLOPs/step versus 2.14M for DDQN (1.6×) and 8.37M for DAI-A/DAI-F (2.4×) — a modest overhead justified by the win-rate gain. - Effective: The evidence shows the method solves a synthetic, hand-crafted budgeted label-acquisition game; it is a proxy for real CTI lifecycle optimisation, not a demonstration on it. - Scalable: Untested beyond 7 Gaussian clusters, 3 actions, 30-step episodes; the authors state further research is needed and identify transition-model learnability as the scaling bottleneck — an honest claim, not an experiment. The work delivers a software artifact (LION environment, agent implementations, Hydra-based reproducible configs in the released repository), not a deployable defensive system. Strengths: - The cleanest contribution is the ablation design: by constructing DAI-A/SA/F as explicit extensions and DDQN as the epistemic-term-removed special case of a single unified algorithm, the paper makes the causal attribution of the performance gap to the perceptive epistemic term unusually transparent. - The parameter/FLOPs accounting (Table 1) pre-empts the standard confound that the winning agent is simply bigger — DAI-P wins with 38% fewer parameters than DAI-A/DAI-F. - The mathematical section is honest about its two EFE substitutions (model-for-process likelihood, preferences-for-future-observations) and explicitly connects the pragmatic term to the environment reward, defusing the usual Act-Inf-vs-RL comparability objection before reviewers raise it. - The statistical protocol (per-seed independent generators and classifiers shared across agents, offset streams, t-based CIs) is above the norm for this subfield. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state that claims are validated only within the specific parameter subspace of LION, that the perceptive epistemic term depends on accurately learning transition dynamics (and degrades if dynamics are hard to learn), that multi-domain evaluation (varied topologies, attack types, scales) is outstanding, and that DAI-SA's surrogate fails at high Boltzmann precision ζ=100, with a possible fix at lower precision left to future work. They confront limitations directly rather than minimising them, which strengthens credibility. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - Circularity/Goodhart concern: the environment's state representation is deliberately constructed so that label purchases produce the maximal prediction error (Appendix 8.3: the confidence slot is zeroed on purchase, 'producing a sharp, localised change... that the transition network cannot anticipate'), and the reward table is designed to make the least-anomalous cluster the most valuable label. The experiment is engineered so the tested mechanism must win; a neutral environment where epistemic gain is uncorrelated with (or opposed to) the optimal policy is absent. - The motivating tiger environment — the actual open-source RL testbed with the CTI interface — is never evaluated on; all results come from the authors' own synthetic LION, so the 'real-world-inspired' framing rests entirely on structural analogy. - The DDQN baselines run with heavily suppressed exploration (ε from 0.25 to 0.05, Boltzmann precision 100), and the paper does not test curiosity-driven intrinsic-reward RL baselines (e.g., ICM/RND prediction-error bonuses), which are the natural non-Act-Inf competitors for exactly this epistemic signal — their omission weakens the claim that Act-Inf specifically, rather than any prediction-error bonus, drives the gain. - The claimed 'novel mathematical formulation' for fully observable MDPs overlaps with cited prior adaptations (Millidge 2020; Friston & Smith 2020), and the distinction is not sharply argued. - The Data Availability statement points to a SmartVille release rather than the LION repository cited in the text, a reproducibility inconsistency. - Only two-dimensional features and a 5.7K-parameter backbone: nothing here rules out that the advantage disappears at realistic traffic dimensionality, where transition-model prediction error is dominated by representation noise rather than informative surprise. Bottom Line: A statistically careful, well-ablated proof-of-concept that will genuinely interest active-inference researchers and the RL-for-security community, but the engineered circularity of the LION environment and the absence of the motivating tiger evaluation or intrinsic-reward RL baselines mean it establishes a plausible inductive bias, not yet a demonstrated advantage for real cyber-defence.

Enabling Digital Twin Prototypes of IoT Systems through BPMN-Driven Modeling and Simulation

MC De Donato, F Corradini, N Francioni, F Fornari… · bp-meet-iot.github.io · simulation environments for business processes - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces a design-and-validation approach that models IoT system behavior as executable, interacting BPMN models and coordinates their execution within a Digital Twin Prototype architecture for pre-deployment validation. - Why it's important: IoT systems under design cannot be behaviorally tested before deployment, especially for rare, costly, or unsafe conditions like earthquakes, leaving design errors undiscovered until physical rollout. - How it does it: The trick is an explicit IoT-element-to-BPMN-construct mapping (devices → processes/pools, sensor events → message/signal events, timeouts → boundary timers) plus a middleware layer that uses entity identifiers as correlation keys to route messages between independently running BPMN process instances. - The good: The prototype is fully implemented with off-the-shelf components (Camunda 8.3, Kafka 3.8, a Go microservice) and released as open source (github.com/PROSLab/BPMN-DTP-IoT), with a concrete four-model case study demonstrating the mapping end-to-end. - The missing: There are no quantitative results whatsoever — no metrics, baselines, scale tests, or user evaluation; the evidence is a single demonstrative scenario run, and scalability is explicitly not evaluated. - Read it or not: Worth reading for BPM/IoT researchers seeking a concrete starting point for executable IoT digital twins; skip it if you need validated tooling, performance data, or evidence beyond a feasibility proof-of-concept.

Impact (48) gets moderate credit for a real open-source Camunda/Kafka prototype, and Completeness (65) is a credibility positive given the paper's unusually direct limitation section, but the central co-design claim is never tested and the hard cases (many concurrent instances, scale) are never exercised. Problem & Motivation: Teams designing IoT systems (system engineers, IoT developers, domain experts) lack a way to validate device and interaction behavior before physical deployment. This is acute when the target conditions are difficult, costly, or unsafe to reproduce — the motivating example is earthquake emergency response, where devices may not be installed and the triggering event is rare and dangerous. Prior work splits into two camps that do not cover this gap: IoT-enhanced business process approaches use devices and data to enrich process execution/monitoring of an existing system, while Digital Twin-based IoT testing approaches operate at the system/infrastructure level without explicit, stakeholder-readable models of internal component behavior. The paper targets the intersection: explicit, executable, human-readable behavioral models usable in a Digital Twin Prototype (a twin with no deployed physical counterpart yet). Key Idea: Decompose an IoT scenario into one executable BPMN model per entity (device, gateway, event source), let overall system behavior emerge from message/signal exchange between these models, and operationalize the resulting distributed execution through a middleware that translates simulation events into BPMN events and correlates messages to the correct process instance using entity identifiers stored as process variables. The BPMN notation serves the dual role of precision artifact and cross-stakeholder communication medium for co-design with non-technical domain experts. Methodology: The approach is a three-phase iterative process. (1) IoT scenario analysis: humans (IoT experts, designers, stakeholders) extract relevant entities, roles, and interactions — messages, commands, timeouts, acknowledgments, mode changes — from specifications and stakeholder knowledge, producing a scenario-level description. (2) Behavioral modeling: each entity is manually modeled as a separate BPMN process using a conceptual mapping table (Table 2): device/component → pool/lane/process; sensor reading/external event → message/signal event; periodic behavior → timer event; computation → task; branching → exclusive gateway; first-of-alternative-events → event-based gateway; timeout → boundary timer; operating mode → variables/subprocess. (3) Simulation and analysis: models are deployed and executed event-driven; controlled events are injected via user tasks; execution states, logs, and message traces are inspected against expected behavior; discrepancies trigger refinement loops. The reference architecture has five components: Simulation Manager (configuration/control), IoT Platform (digital entity registration/telemetry), Event Bus (asynchronous decoupling), Middleware (BPMN-event translation, message routing, correlation), and BPMN Execution Engine. The prototype implements the engine/buses/middleware loop with Camunda 8.3, Kafka 3.8, and a Dockerized Go microservice; simulation configuration arrives as JSON on Kafka, identifiers become process variables, and the middleware routes outgoing messages to the correct waiting process instance. Critical design decisions: (a) per-entity model decomposition rather than one monolithic process — justified by IoT's distributed asynchronous nature, but the authors themselves flag growing coordination effort; (b) entity-identifier-based message correlation in a middleware rather than point-to-point dependencies — reasonable but only demonstrated with four models and two identifiers; (c) manual model derivation from the mapping — no automation or tooling support is provided. The paper notes but does not perform formal analysis (e.g., deadlock freedom) of the resulting models. Key Results: The paper reports no quantitative results. The evaluation is a demonstration: the SAFE earthquake emergency scenario (PIR presence-detection device on anti-seismic furniture, stationary gateway, presence-signal and earthquake-signal simulation-input models — four BPMN models total) was executed in the prototype. The demonstrated outcome is qualitative: injecting an earthquake condition propagates to the gateway, which issues a WAR command that switches the PIR model into emergency mode; presence values injectable via Camunda user tasks activate corresponding behavioral branches; execution traces and message exchanges support manual behavioral inspection. There are no baselines, no comparison against alternative modeling/execution approaches, no measured latency/throughput, and no user study. Scale is toy-to-small: 4 interacting models, 1 device, 1 gateway. The authors explicitly frame this as "preliminary evidence of feasibility." Novelty Classification: NEW FORMULATION and NEW SYSTEM/TOOL (prototype). The genuinely new element is positioning executable, interacting BPMN models as the behavioral layer of a pre-deployment IoT Digital Twin Prototype — the paper's Table 1 comparison credibly argues that IoT-enhanced BPM work models device behavior only in service of business processes, and DT-testing work targets system-level validation without explicit per-component behavioral models. The individual ingredients — the IoT-to-BPMN mapping (Table 2), the BPMN engine, the event bus, identifier-based message correlation — are standard or incremental combinations of existing ideas (the mapping largely repackages known IoT-aware BPMN patterns from [12, 15]); the middleware is competent engineering glue rather than a technical advance. Rigor & Reproducibility: Rigor is low, consistent with a workshop-track feasibility paper. There are no ablations, no error bars, no seeds, no statistical tests, and no defined success criteria for "behavior is consistent with expectations" — validation is manual inspection of Camunda screenshots and logs by the authors. Source code is publicly available at https://github.com/PROSLab/BPMN-DTP-IoT, which is a genuine reproducibility positive, and the concrete BPMN models are shown in the paper. Methodological concerns: evaluation is only on a scenario derived from the authors' own prior SAFE project (ref [5, 20]), so the framework is applied to a setting the authors know intimately — generalization is untested; there is no comparison baseline (e.g., modeling the same scenario in a simulation tool or a plain BPMN engine without the middleware); and the paper was developed on the same use case it validates, a self-referential setup with Goodhart-style risk that the mapping was shaped to fit SAFE rather than validated against SAFE. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: SYSTEMS (a built prototype evaluated by demonstration). Practical: Yes — it runs on commodity hardware with entirely open/off-the-shelf components (Camunda, Kafka, Docker, Go), and code is public. Efficient: Not measured; Kafka + Camunda + middleware is a heavier stack than needed for a 4-model scenario, and no cost figures are reported. Effective: Only a proxy — the evidence shows BPMN models can be executed and correlated, not that the approach actually catches real design errors or improves validation outcomes versus alternatives. Scalable: Explicitly not evaluated; the authors state scalability (entity counts, event rates, latency) was not an objective, and model-maintenance effort is acknowledged as a growing trade-off. Deliverable: an open-source prototype implementation of the execution/correlation layer plus reusable modeling guidance; not yet a complete Digital Twin platform — the IoT Platform and Simulation Manager components exist only in the architecture diagram, not in the implementation. Strengths: - Honest framing throughout: the paper repeatedly and explicitly labels its results as preliminary feasibility evidence and states what is not built (IoT platform integration, scalability, analysis tooling) — rare and creditable. - The IoT-to-BPMN mapping table (Table 2) is a concrete, reusable artifact that other groups can apply or critique, covering non-obvious elements like event-based gateways for racing awaited events and boundary timers for timeouts. - The middleware-based correlation mechanism is a real, non-trivial engineering contribution: it preserves BPMN model independence (no point-to-point coupling) while routing messages to the correct process instance — a genuine operationalization problem when multiple instances of the same model run concurrently. - Bridge between two research communities (IoT-aware BPM and DT-based IoT testing) with a credible related-work comparison (Table 1) that pins down the unoccupied intersection. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors confront limitations directly and at length (Section 6): (1) the IoT Platform is not integrated into the execution loop — device registration and telemetry are unhandled; (2) scalability was not an objective and is not evaluated, in both execution and modeling dimensions; (3) result analysis relies on Camunda UI and logs, which is inaccessible to non-expert stakeholders, motivating a dedicated Simulation Manager; (4) the SAFE scenario covers only a subset of the real system; (5) as scenario complexity grows, the number of models and interactions increases maintenance and coordination effort; (6) evaluation beyond SAFE is needed. This candor is a credibility positive; nothing is minimized or hidden. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - No evaluation of the central claim that BPMN supports stakeholder co-design — the notation's comprehensibility benefit to domain experts is asserted but never tested with any user, expert, or non-expert. - The manual modeling step is unexamined: no data on modeling effort, model size, error rates, or whether the mapping suffices for IoT behaviors outside SAFE (e.g., data streaming, concurrent sensing loops, device failure handling). - No comparison against any alternative — simulating the same scenario in a standard IoT simulator, a discrete-event simulation tool, or plain BPMN-without-middleware would establish what the added architecture buys. - The correlation mechanism's correctness is undemonstrated: with only one PIR and one gateway instance, the hard case (routing among many concurrent instances of the same model) is never exercised. - Feasibility demonstration on the authors' own prior project creates circularity; an external scenario would strengthen the generalization claim the authors themselves defer to future work. - The claimed path to formal analysis (deadlock freedom, per [9]) is mentioned but not attempted, leaving behavioral correctness assurances at the level of eyeballing. Bottom Line: A credible, honestly-scoped feasibility report with a usable open-source starting point, but no measurements, baselines, or user evidence — a BPM/IoT researcher building executable digital twins should read it as a reference architecture and mapping baseline, while anyone needing a validated or deployable validation approach will find stronger ground in mature DT-testing tools.

Problem & Motivation: Automotive assembly shops depend on continuous operation of bearings, gearboxes, hydraulic cylinders, and drives; a single stoppage on an engine or transmission line interrupts planned output and triggers emergency repairs, downtime losses, overtime, and urgent purchases. Preventive (calendar-based) maintenance misses early degradation, and reactive repair only records problems after they hit the line. The authors' own literature framing notes that most PdM papers stop at models trained on archived datasets, while far fewer describe deployment into a live production loop where warnings must be acted on by maintenance personnel — the operational gap this pilot targets. The relevant audience is industrial engineers and digitization teams at manufacturing enterprises, particularly in the Kazakhstani/regional context. Key Idea: The core move is not algorithmic but architectural and operational: connect an off-the-shelf multichannel sensor ensemble (Random Forest on aggregated tabular features, gradient boosting for nonlinear interactions, CNN-LSTM on raw vibration series, outputs combined by simple probability averaging) directly into the maintenance-planning workflow, with feature-contribution explanations in the alert interface, and evaluate the result by coupled technical-plus-economic indicators rather than model accuracy alone. The 0.7 alarm threshold is an explicitly recall-first operational compromise, not an optimized operating point. Methodology: The system has four stages: (1) Data Collection — vibration (up to several kHz), temperature, pressure, and flow sensors on selected critical components, timestamped and centralized; (2) Preprocessing — outlier filtering, gap filling, timestamp synchronization, and aggregated statistical/spectral features over 30-second and 5-minute windows with normalization/log transforms; (3) Ensemble Modeling — Random Forest (scikit-learn), gradient boosting (XGBoost/LightGBM) on windowed features, and a TensorFlow/Keras CNN-LSTM on raw vibration series, each outputting a pre-failure probability, combined by unweighted averaging; (4) UI/Notification — per-line dashboards, risk trajectories, and alerts above the 0.7 threshold specifying component and likely failure type. Models were trained on historical labeled data (normal vs. pre-failure intervals from maintenance logs; "several million" time-series observations, with undisclosed counts and class distribution), with cross-validated hyperparameter selection and a held-out test split; no fixed separate validation set. Critical design decisions: (a) the 0.7 threshold, justified qualitatively as recall-prioritizing but not derived from a reported threshold sweep — a moderate justification; (b) simple probability averaging rather than a learned combiner or logged per-model comparison — unverified; (c) edge/workshop-level preprocessing to keep the monitoring loop responsive — reasonable but not benchmarked. The cost model is C_total = C_repair + C_downtime + C_inventory + C_emergency, with first-year ROI = (E_ann − C_impl)/C_impl and payback T = C_impl/E_ann, all in confidential enterprise accounting units. Key Results: During the two-month online pilot on two assembly lines (engine and transmission units), the system generated 14 alerts: 9 (64%) matched confirmed pre-failure states (abnormal vibration growth, sustained overheating, hydraulic pressure instability), and 5 (36%) revealed wear signs found during planned disassembly. At the 0.7 threshold: Precision = 0.64, Recall = 1.0, F1 = 0.78, with a reported Wilson 95% CI of ≈0.39–0.84 for Precision. Against the reactive-maintenance baseline (enterprise-reported, same comparison basis): total maintenance cost fell from 1,000,000 to 720,000 conventional units (−28.0%) and unplanned downtime from 340 to 200 hours (−41.2%). Compared against external literature (Bucay-Valdiviezo et al. 2023: 20–25% cost / ~30% downtime; Meddaoui et al. 2024: ~30% / ~35%), the results sit in the plausible published range. Baselines are weak by ML standards: the only comparator is single-sensor threshold rules discussed qualitatively, never run; no per-model ablation was performed because component-model outputs were not synchronized and logged. The scale is a small pilot (two lines, two months, 14 events) — not stress-scale, and the authors say so. Novelty Classification: NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING and ENGINEERING OPTIMIZATION in a deployment setting; there is no NEW METHOD. The genuinely new element is the documented end-to-end deployment of a standard RF + boosting + CNN-LSTM averaging ensemble with economic-outcome coupling in a Kazakhstani automotive assembly plant; the algorithmic content (windowed features, three-model ensemble, probability averaging, threshold alerting) is a standard combination of existing techniques applied to a new site, which the authors themselves frame as applied/engineering novelty. Rigor & Reproducibility: The paper is a peer-reviewed journal article (Vestnik SKU im. M. Kozybaev, №3(71), 2026) reporting a vendor-style case study: all data are enterprise-confidential, monetary values are anonymized "conventional units," raw sensor streams and training/test window counts are undisclosed, and the authors explicitly state that sample-level replication is not possible. Creditable rigor moves include the Wilson confidence interval on Precision, an honest admission that Recall = 1.0 rests on 14 events, explicit refusal to present ROI/payback as reproducible, and a stated plan to log per-model outputs in the next validation stage. Ablations are absent (no ensemble-vs-single-model comparison). Methodological concerns: (a) the pre/post economic comparison confounds the PdM system with any concurrent operational changes; (b) Recall = 1.0 may be near-tautological — if no confirmed pre-failure event occurred outside the alert set, recall is 1.0 by construction; (c) no code, data, or model weights are released (no repository mentioned); (d) the threshold was not validated across a sweep. No Goodhart-style train-on-test contamination is apparent, but the evaluation is on the authors' own enterprise data only. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL / SYSTEMS (a working prototype was integrated with enterprise sensor infrastructure and run for two months). - Practical: Yes — the stack is Python (pandas, NumPy, scikit-learn, XGBoost/LightGBM, TensorFlow/Keras) plus industrial sensors and a dashboard, all runnable on commodity hardware. - Efficient: Workshop-level feature aggregation keeps the 60-second risk-update loop cheap; raw-sensor bandwidth and compute costs relative to alternatives are not quantified. - Effective: Partially — 9 confirmed pre-failure detections and 28% cost reduction support feasibility on the monitored lines, but the economic figure is an uncontrolled enterprise self-report in anonymized units, so the evidence shows proxy-level success rather than an independently verifiable effect. - Scalable: Untested — only 2 of the shop's lines were covered, sensor coverage was heterogeneous, and the paper acknowledges that models trained on this narrow scope require recalibration and revalidation before transfer; scaling claims (digital twins, federated learning) are explicitly future work, not results. The work delivers a deployed prototype system and a reusable pilot-evaluation methodology (combined classification + economic + organizational indicators), not a public software artifact or dataset. Strengths: - Genuinely rare deployment transparency: the paper describes the full operational loop (alerts, SOPs, staff training, maintenance-log linkage) rather than stopping at offline model metrics, which is exactly the under-reported phase the introduction identifies. - Statistical honesty unusual for industrial case studies: a Wilson 95% CI on Precision from n=14, an explicit caveat that Recall = 1.0 needs longer validation, and refusal to present confidential ROI as a reproducible result. - The alert-labeling policy is carefully defined (wear found in planned maintenance counts as operationally useful but not as a confirmed positive), avoiding the common inflation of Precision in PdM reports. - The argument that the prediction-to-scheduling link matters more than isolated model accuracy is a correct and useful framing for practitioners. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors directly confront: the two-line/two-month scope being too short for seasonal effects or long-term ageing; heterogeneous sensor coverage leaving some failure modes less visible; model transferability requiring recalibration on local data; the 0.7 threshold being an operational choice rather than an optimized one; non-logged component-model outputs preventing per-model comparison; confidentiality of raw data and costs limiting reproducibility; and the results being evidence of feasibility rather than a universal benchmark. This is direct, non-minimizing treatment of limitations — a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - The economic comparison is pre/post within the same enterprise over an unspecified period; any concurrent changes (seasonality, order mix, staffing) are uncontrolled, and "conventional units" makes the 28% figure unfalsifiable in absolute terms. - Recall = 1.0 is potentially circular: if every confirmed pre-failure event during the pilot happened to be one the system flagged, recall is definitionally 1.0 with no independent failure census; the paper does not state whether any unflagged degradations or near-misses occurred. - The ROI/payback claim ("internal financial statements" show C_impl < E_ann, hence sub-one-year payback) is asserted without any numbers — a self-reported management-accounting estimate presented alongside empirical results. - No false-alarm rate per unit time or alert-processing burden is reported, so the claim that 14 alerts over two months is "manageable" for staff is unquantified; longer operation could raise alert volume substantially. - The ensemble's added value over a single cheap model (e.g., Random Forest alone) is asserted via qualitative reasoning, never measured — the cheapest possible ablation was not run. - The comparison to "simpler threshold rules" in practice is likewise qualitative; a sensor-threshold baseline on the same window would have anchored the ML contribution. Bottom Line: A practitioner planning an industrial PdM pilot will gain more from this paper's candid deployment accounting and metric-interpretation discipline than from most accuracy-only PdM papers, but anyone seeking methodological novelty or independently verifiable economic claims should look to stronger peer-reviewed deployment studies such as Meddaoui et al. (2024) or Bucay-Valdiviezo et al. (2023).

Optimized LSTM-Informer Model for Accurate Detection of Network Threats in Hospital Environments

H Liu, Z Chen, Y Xia, S Qiao, J Ou · journals.riverpublishers.com · cyber model training - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper proposes a hybrid BiLSTM–Informer model with an attention-enhanced multi-source feature fusion module and Focal Loss training to classify hospital network security alarms as real threats versus false positives. - Why it's important: Hospital security teams face alert fatigue — the paper cites ~100,000 alerts/month at a top-tier hospital with false alarm rates above 30% — so cutting false alarms directly reduces missed real threats to clinical systems and analyst workload. - How it does it: It fuses heterogeneous alarm features via sliding-window Z-score standardization plus MLP attention weights, runs BiLSTM and an Informer variant (ProbSparse attention re-scored with hand-set threat-level priors) in parallel, and combines their outputs with a learned gating weight, trained with Focal Loss for the 4.7%-positive class imbalance. - The good: The evaluation is unusually complete for this venue — a 136,022-sample, expert-labeled dataset from a real hospital, ablations of each module, two SOTA baselines (TFT, DeepLog), and a cross-dataset test on CICIDS2017 (94.8% accuracy). - The missing: There are no error bars, seeds, or significance tests; no code or data release; the threat-prior constants (l_i = 1.2/0.8, α = 0.1) are unjustified; and the paper contains an internal inconsistency — the abstract and conclusion report phishing-email results, but the dataset and Table 5 contain no phishing category. - Read it or not: Read it if you work on security-alarm triage or hospital SOC operations and want a domain-adapted LSTM-Informer template; skip it if you want methodologically airtight deep learning for intrusion detection, since the evaluation has reproducibility and consistency gaps that a stronger venue would require fixing.

Novelty (45) rests on the threat-prior-weighted ProbSparse query selection, a modest but sensible domain adaptation; Non-Obviousness (50) reflects the well-matched dual-timescale design.
