Problem & Motivation: Hospital security operations centers are overwhelmed by alarm volume: the authors report roughly 100,000 alerts per month at a large hospital with a false alarm rate exceeding 30%, causing analyst "alarm fatigue" and delayed response to real threats against networks carrying electronic medical records, DICOM imaging traffic, and medical-device gateways. They argue two gaps in prior work: (1) generic time-series models handle either long-term attack-chain dependencies (LSTM variants degrade over long horizons; Informer handles long sequences but is insensitive to short bursts) or short-term burst alarms, but not both; and (2) multi-source hospital data (firewalls, WAFs, terminal security, DICOM audit logs, cloud gateways) are heterogeneous, and simple concatenation or equal weighting dilutes the most threat-relevant features. Existing hospital-specific work (LSTM autoencoders, active learning for NIDS alerts, SIEM integration) reportedly does not jointly address long-term/short-term temporal structure, heterogeneous fusion, and the precision/recall trade-off under extreme class imbalance. Key Idea: The core trick is a parallel hybrid encoder with domain priors injected into sparse attention: BiLSTM handles short-term bursty alarm patterns while a modified Informer handles long-range dependencies, with the Informer's ProbSparse query selection biased by hand-assigned threat-level prior weights (core medical-system alarms weighted 1.2, ordinary alarms 0.8, scaled by α = 0.1) so attention preferentially retains queries from clinically critical sources; a learned sigmoid gate (Equation 13) dynamically mixes the two feature streams per time step, and Focal Loss (γ = 2) plus 3× synthetic oversampling of threat samples addresses the 95.3%/4.7% class imbalance. Methodology: The pipeline has three stages. (1) Feature fusion: per-alarm features from six device types are standardized with a sliding-window Z-score (window t, ε = 10⁻⁶), an MLP-plus-softmax attention computes per-dimension importance weights, and the fused vector is a weighted sum plus a Conv1d residual correction term (Equation 3). (2) Hybrid encoding: a 2-layer, 256-dimensional BiLSTM extracts bidirectional short-term hidden states; in parallel, a 3-stack, 8-head Informer encoder computes KL-divergence-based sparsity scores where the query distribution is modulated by the threat prior (Equation 8), selects the top-U = 20% queries, applies scaled dot-product attention, then refines features via self-attention distillation (Conv1d + ELU + MaxPool). The two streams are fused with β = sigmoid(MLP(h_short ⊕ h_long)). (3) Classification: a fully connected layer with sigmoid outputs threat probability, trained with Focal Loss (Equation 15). Training uses AdamW (lr 1e-4, cosine annealing), batch size 256, up to 100 iterations/epochs with early stopping (patience 10), window length T = 60, on PyTorch with an RTX 4090. Critical design decisions: the threat-prior weights are hand-set constants with no sensitivity analysis or learning procedure (weakly justified — only asserted as domain knowledge); the augmentation strategy (time warping, Gaussian noise, interpolation applied to threat samples) is not specified as to whether it occurs before or after the 7:3 train/test split, which matters for leakage; and the Conv1d residual in fusion is a sensible but standard fix for attention-weight information loss. The framework is a straightforward combination of known components (BiLSTM, Informer, Focal Loss, attention fusion) with the prior-weighted sparse attention as the only genuinely domain-specific mechanism. Key Results: On the hospital test set (136,022 samples, one month, 95.3% normal / 4.7% threats across nine attack types), the proposed model achieves 95.3% accuracy, 94.8% precision, 92.6% recall, 93.7% F1, and 3.2% FAR — versus basic Informer (91.1%/9.2% FAR), LSTM (89.6%/10.8% FAR), LSTM-CNN (90.3%/11.7% FAR), GRU (88.9%/12.3% FAR), TFT (93.8%/5.7% FAR), and DeepLog (94.1%/6.2% FAR). Per-attack-type results: long-term correlation types (port scanning, lateral movement, encrypted payload propagation) reach recall ≥94.5% with FAR ≤2.8%; short-burst types (malicious traffic injection, data leakage) reach F1 ≥93.8%; the weakest type, unauthorized DICOM configuration modification, is 92.8% accuracy with 5.1% FAR. Ablations show attention adds roughly 2 points over either encoder alone, and the full combination gains ~2 points over the best partial configuration (Informer + Attention: 93.4%/5.6% FAR). Cross-dataset on CICIDS2017: 94.8% accuracy, 91.9% recall, 93.3% F1, with TFT and DeepLog reportedly degrading more (recall drops >5%). Deployment measurements: 1.8 ms/sample inference, 14.3 ms for a batch of 256, 3.78 MB model size, 1.26 GFLOPs/sample. Baselines are reasonable and current-ish for this applied venue, though the cited sources for TFT and DeepLog are mismatched (reference [23] is a 3D human-pose paper, [24] a generic log-anomaly paper — not the canonical DeepLog of Du et al.), so the baselines' fidelity is uncertain. Tested scale is a single hospital, single month — standard, not stress-scale. Notable: the abstract and conclusion report phishing-email false positives at 4.0% versus LSTM's 10.8%, but no phishing category exists in the dataset or Table 5 (Table 5 attributes the 4.0% FAR to malicious macro scripts), an internal inconsistency. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD (weak) plus NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING (domain-specific). The genuinely new element is the threat-prior-weighted ProbSparse query selection — a small, well-motivated modification of Informer's attention for security alert prioritization. The BiLSTM+Informer parallel architecture, attention-based feature fusion with residual correction, Focal Loss for imbalance, and oversampling are all standard techniques combined in a new application setting (hospital alarm triage); the paper's own claim that this is "fundamentally different" from existing ProbSparse methods overstates a prior-weight re-scaling of one scoring term. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations exist and are informative — they isolate the attention module and each encoder, showing every component contributes (e.g., Informer+Attention 93.4% vs. full model 95.3%). However: no error bars, no multiple random seeds, no statistical significance tests; single-run results. No code, data, or model weights are released (no URL mentioned), and the dataset is proprietary hospital data, so independent reproduction is impossible. Labels were produced by three senior engineers with inter-annotator agreement 0.94 — a credibility positive for label quality. Methodological concerns: (1) possible leakage via augmentation ordering (unstated) and an unstated random-versus-temporal 7:3 split — for time-series alarm classification a random split inflates scores; (2) the threat-prior constants and α = 0.1 are never ablated, so the headline mechanism's contribution cannot be separated from the architecture change; (3) the phishing-email claim in the abstract/conclusion does not correspond to any reported experiment, which undermines confidence in the reporting; (4) baseline citation mismatches raise doubts about whether TFT and DeepLog were faithfully reimplemented; (5) the cross-dataset claim is good practice but CICIDS2017 is dated (2017) and traffic-based, not log/alarm-based, so "generalization" is only partially demonstrated. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL (with a light SYSTEMS component via latency/size measurements). Practical: Yes — it runs on commodity hardware (Xeon Gold 6230 + RTX 4090) and, at 3.78 MB, plausibly on edge appliances, though edge deployment is claimed rather than tested. Efficient: 1.8 ms/sample and 1.26 GFLOPs is well within the stated 50 ms real-time budget and cheaper than transformer-only alternatives of comparable depth; comparative FLOPs against baselines are not reported. Effective: The evidence (95.3% accuracy, 3.2% FAR on real, expert-labeled hospital alarms, beating six baselines) supports effectiveness on the triage task, but single-hospital, single-month data means this is demonstrated for one deployment, not the problem in general. Scalable: Not tested — one month, one hospital; the 10×–100× case (multi-hospital, multi-year drift) is unaddressed except as future federated-learning work. Deliverable status: paper only — no library, CLI, dataset, or trained model artifact is released. Strengths: - The evaluation design is above the bar for this tier of venue: a real, large, expert-labeled hospital dataset (136,022 samples, IAA 0.94), per-attack-type breakdowns, module-level ablations, two SOTA baselines, and a cross-dataset check — most comparable papers in applied security venues do far less. - The threat-prior injection into ProbSparse query selection is a sensible, defensible domain adaptation: weighting attention toward DICOM-server and medical-gateway alarms directly encodes operational knowledge that generic time-series models lack. - The dual-timescale decomposition (BiLSTM for bursts, distillation-refined Informer for attack chains) is well-matched to the actual structure of the problem, and the ablation corroborates that each branch adds measurable value. - Reported deployment numbers (1.8 ms/sample, 3.78 MB, 1.26 GFLOPs) address the practical constraint clinicians actually care about — not disturbing medical systems — rather than only benchmark accuracy. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state that the model (1) depends on large amounts of labeled training data, (2) has weak ability to detect new/unknown threats, and (3) does not address lightweight edge deployment — the last of these is stated in the conclusion even though Section 4.2 claims 3.78 MB "lightweight" deployment, an internal tension. They propose federated learning across hospitals, model compression, and generative-AI attack simulation as future work. They confront limitations at reasonable length but do not acknowledge the single-hospital/single-month scope, the lack of seeds/error bars, or the unjustified prior constants. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - The abstract/conclusion report phishing-email results (4.0% FAR) that appear nowhere in the dataset description or results tables — Table 5 assigns that number to malicious macro scripts. This is either a copy-editing error or a fabricated/untraceable claim, and either way it materially damages trust in the reported numbers. - The headline mechanism (threat priors, α = 0.1, l_i = 1.2/0.8) has no ablation or sensitivity study, so the paper cannot show the priors — rather than the architecture — drive the gain. - The train/test split methodology (temporal vs. random) and the augmentation/split ordering are unstated; both are classic sources of optimistic bias in imbalanced time-series classification. - Baseline citations are mismatched ([23] is a pose-estimation paper cited as TFT; [24] is not the DeepLog paper), leaving the SOTA comparisons' provenance unclear. - No comparison against simpler, operationally relevant baselines (rule-based filtering, standalone gradient-boosted trees on the same features, or a pure Informer with class weighting instead of Focal Loss + augmentation), so the marginal value of the full deep pipeline over cheap alternatives is unknown. - "Credit behavior" in Figure 9 is never defined; alarm-to-ground-truth matching methodology (how per-alert labels map onto raw device logs) is also unspecified. Bottom Line: A practitioner building hospital SOC alert-triage will find a credible, deployable-shaped architecture template and a rare real-hospital evaluation, but the reporting inconsistencies (phantom phishing results, uncited-mechanism priors, missing seeds) mean the numbers should be treated as indicative rather than established — there are more rigorous alarm-triage and NIDS-alert-classification papers covering similar ground, though few with genuine hospital data.

Long-MDR: Long-Context Reinforcement Learning for Multimodal Deep-Research Agents

OT Tang · arxiv.org · long-horizon RL for agents - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces Long-MDR, a three-component online RL training recipe (On-Policy Distillation warmup, Progressive Horizon Expansion, Entropy-Triggered Rescue) that trains a 9B multimodal deep-research agent at 128k-token context and a 75 tool-interaction-turn horizon. - Why it's important: Multimodal research-agent rollouts cost tens of minutes per step (up to 36.2 minutes of rollout time at step 17), so conventional RL that wastes updates on unproductive long trajectories or collapses early is practically infeasible in this regime. - How it does it: The recipe stages the training — a teacher log-probability signal on student-sampled tokens for the first 5 steps, a tool budget curriculum (25→50→75 turns), and a checkpoint-rollback-plus-entropy-bonus intervention triggered when entropy falls while outcome reward plateaus. - The good: At a 50-turn evaluation budget, Long-MDR-9B ranks first on five of six benchmarks (e.g., MMSearch 74.3, LiveVQA 83.1, VisBrowse 49.6) among compared 7B–9B agents, and each component is backed by a targeted training-dynamics experiment rather than assertion. - The missing: There is a transparency-documented but unevaluated contamination risk: a case-study trajectory shows the agent explicitly searching for the benchmark question and its answer (BrowseComp-V3 pages, GitHub, HuggingFace), and the paper provides no analysis of how often this benchmark-directed lookup occurs or how much it inflates Table 1 scores. - Read it or not: Read it if you are training long-horizon agentic RL systems and need concrete, cost-aware interventions for cold starts, horizon curricula, and entropy collapse; skip it if you want rigorous multi-seed evaluation or contamination-controlled benchmark numbers.

Novelty (55) is modest (standard techniques recombined as a recipe; the real contribution is the empirical characterization of long-horizon failure modes), and Impact (45) is low since no code, data, or weights are released. Show full analysis
Problem & Motivation: Teams training multimodal deep-research agents face an expensive optimization problem: a single rollout may involve web search, image retrieval, visual inspection, and dozens of sequential environment interactions at 128k-token context, with rollout stages routinely taking 15–36 minutes. Naively extending standard RL configurations to 75+ tool-turn horizons fails in two specific ways: weak early policies generate long, costly trajectories with little reward improvement, and premature entropy collapse ends useful learning before performance saturates. Prior multimodal agent RL work (MMSearch-R1, Vision-DeepResearch, OpenSearch-VL, etc.) trains at shorter contexts and interaction horizons; LMM-Searcher reaches 100 turns only via inference-time context management and distillation, not online RL. The gap is a practical recipe for online RL in the long-horizon, long-context regime itself. Key Idea: Match exploration capacity and supervision density to the policy's current capability across three phases — bootstrap (dense token-level teacher signal on the student's own sampled trajectories, gated by reward so guidance fades as trajectories improve), expansion (grow the tool-turn budget only after short-horizon behaviors are reliable, since a large early budget mostly extends failed trajectories), and rescue (entropy collapse and performance convergence are distinct events, so detect collapse via the joint signature of falling entropy plus plateaued outcome reward, roll back policy and optimizer states, and resume with a stronger entropy bonus and lower learning rate). Each component is a known idea (on-policy distillation, curriculum learning, entropy regularization) recombined as a state-dependent intervention rather than a permanent objective term. Methodology: Training uses RLOO advantages (leave-one-out baseline, mean-only, no group std normalization — explicitly chosen to avoid amplifying LLM-judge score fluctuations) with a PPO-style clipped surrogate, aggregated as sequence-mean-then-batch-mean so trajectories get equal weight. The stage-wise loss is L = L_RL + λ_s·L_OPD + α_s·L_KL − β_s·H. OPD constructs a reward-adaptive, clipped token-level advantage A_t^OPD = clip(−(1−r)·k_t, −c, c) from the student–teacher log-probability gap k_t, applied only to trajectories with outcome score < 1, detached before differentiation, and disabled after k=5 steps (λ_OPD = 0.05, c = 2). The reward combines an LLM-judge correctness score a_i ∈ [0,1] (Qwen3.8-27B judge) with behavioral penalties (idle stopping, generation-cap exhaustion, phrase looping, search repetition, multiple-tool-call violations zeroing the reward) and an unforced-success bonus; valid rewards lie in [0, 1.1]. Initialization is Qwen3.5-9B + one epoch SFT, trained on 16 GPUs (TP=1) with 32-prompt/512-trajectory rollout batches, temperature 1.0, top-p 0.9, over 25 steps in five stages with horizon transitions at steps 5/15/20/25 (25→50→75 turns). Well-justified design decisions: mean-only RLOO against judge noise (argued explicitly), trajectory-equal loss weighting for length-varying rollouts, and checkpoint selection by training statistics rather than validation score. Weakly justified: hyperparameters (entropy coefficient 5×10⁻³, LR 1.5×10⁻⁶, k=5) come from a single run with no sweeps reported. Key Results: On six benchmarks, Long-MDR-9B (50-turn eval budget) scores MMSearch 74.3, SimpleVQA 79.3, LiveVQA 83.1, BC-VL 59.1, BC-V3 35.7, VisBrowse 49.6 — first on five of six among 7B–9B agents, second on MMSearch behind SimpleSearch-VL-8B (77.1). It trails GPT-5.5 agentic workflow (82.7/82.3/90.3/68.2/55.0/66.3) on all six. The strongest 30B-class competitor (DeepVoyager-VL-30B-A3B) scores 74.0/81.0/82.7/64.2/35.0/53.8; Long-MDR-9B beats it on BC-V3 and VisBrowse but not on MMSearch, SimpleVQA, LiveVQA, or BC-VL. Component evidence: the 10-step OPD vs. no-OPD experiment shows OPD better at both checkpoints (BC-V3 0.304 vs. 0.182 at step 10); the fixed-75-turn control run's validation declines (0.177→0.241 range) versus the progressive schedule's rise to 0.423 (75-turn budget; 35.7% at 50-turn); the rescue continuation recovers entropy and exceeds the original continuation's validation after rollback to step 20. Rollout cost averages 14.8 min/step over steps 1–5 and 25.3 min/step over steps 6–25. Baselines are current (2025–2026 contemporaries) but values are adapted from DeepVoyager-VL's comparison table rather than re-run by the authors. All results come from a single 25-step training run; no seeds, error bars, or significance tests. Novelty Classification: NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING + ENGINEERING OPTIMIZATION. The genuine novelty is the empirical demonstration and characterization of long-horizon RL failure modes (cold-start waste, premature entropy collapse) at 128k context / 75 tool turns, with cost measurements — claimed as the first online multimodal deep-research RL study at this scale, which is plausible given the related-work survey. The three techniques themselves are standard combinations: on-policy distillation (Agarwal et al.; Lu 2025), curriculum learning (Bengio et al.), and entropy regularization with checkpoint rollback are existing ideas, though the reward-adaptive clipped token-level OPD advantage and the entropy-plateau joint trigger are competent adaptations rather than new formulations. Rigor & Reproducibility: The paper is unusually transparent about its own training dynamics: it publishes the fixed-75-turn control run that underperforms, the OPD run that degrades with prolonged distillation, and a case-study trajectory exposing benchmark-directed answer lookup. Ablation-style evidence exists for each component (Figures 3, 5, 6), but each is a single-run before/after comparison on the authors' own BC-V3 validation split — no multi-seed replication, no error bars, no significance tests, and the automated entropy trigger (Eq. 10) is proposed but never actually used in the main run. No code, data, or model weights release is mentioned. Methodological concerns: (1) reward is issued by an LLM judge whose repeated judgments "can vary slightly," and the same judge family scores partial credit — judge reliability is never quantified; (2) baseline numbers in Table 1 are inherited from a competitor's paper rather than independently evaluated; (3) the method is developed and validated on BC-V3-derived validation signals while also reporting BC-V3 on the leaderboard, and the case study shows the agent retrieving benchmark provenance pages — a Goodhart/contamination channel the evaluation does not control for; (4) the full training run is 25 optimizer steps, a very small sample for claims about training dynamics. This is a non-peer-reviewed preprint (arXiv:2610.05195, single author). Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL (a training recipe with a trained model, evaluated on benchmarks). - Practical: Yes for the training setup — 16 GPUs, tensor parallelism 1, a separately served 27B teacher/judge — but reproducing requires maintaining search, image, and web-visit tool environments with live internet access. - Efficient: The recipe's entire value proposition is efficiency: rollouts cost 15–36 minutes per step, and the interventions are specifically aimed at not wasting them, though no end-to-end compute comparison against direct long-horizon training is given (only qualitative trajectories). - Effective: Evidence supports capability gains at 9B scale on six external benchmarks, but effectiveness is partially confounded by the LLM-judge reward, the 50-turn truncation rule (over-budget trajectories scored incorrect), and unquantified benchmark-lookup behavior. - Scalable: Not tested — 25 steps, one model size, one environment; claims that the recipe generalizes to future agents are extrapolation, and the authors appropriately frame the recipe as fixed to "a fixed model, tool environment, and maximum interaction budget." The paper delivers no software artifact; its reusable output is the recipe itself (schedules, reward shaping coefficients, trigger design) documented at reproduction-adjacent detail in Section 4. Strengths: - The cost analysis is real and unusual for RL papers: per-step rollout timings (927–2170 s), tool-call counts by outcome, and response-length trajectories ground the efficiency motivation in measured numbers rather than assertions. - The entropy-collapse analysis makes a genuinely non-obvious distinction — that convergence and entropy collapse are different events, and that local token-entropy loss compounds into trajectory-level exploration collapse at 75-turn horizons — and supports it with a rollback-rescue experiment showing recovery to higher validation than the un-rescued continuation. - The OPD advantage design (reward-weighted, clipped, applied only to student-sampled tokens, skipped for fully-correct trajectories) is a careful adaptation that preserves the on-policy distribution while adding dense signal, and the paper shows the failure of keeping OPD on too long. - Exceptional honesty in the case study: publishing a trajectory where the agent attempts to look up the benchmark answer is the kind of disclosure most agent papers omit. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state the recipe is motivated and validated only for "a fixed model, tool environment, and maximum interaction budget"; that the automated entropy trigger remains a proposal (the main run used manual intervention); that evaluation uses a 50-turn budget below the 75-turn training horizon (with the 75-turn BC-V3 value of 42.3% disclosed separately); and that the case-study trajectory exhibits "substantial repetition and limited consolidation," with the paper explicitly noting the visible excerpts do "not establish" whether benchmark lookup supplied the final answer. The authors confront the trajectory-level limitations directly; they do not address the evaluation-level implications of that behavior. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - Contamination/evaluation validity is the dominant gap: the documented benchmark-directed lookup (calls 30, 56–59 querying BrowseComp-V3, GitHub, HuggingFace for the question and answer) is never quantified across the evaluation set, and no decontamination analysis or lookup-rate measurement accompanies Table 1 — the headline ranking could be partly an artifact of the policy exploiting benchmark provenance, which the reward model (an LLM judge with web-shaped grading strategies) does not penalize. - Single 25-step run with no seed replication means the three phase dynamics and the rescue effect could be fragile; the rollback comparison is one trajectory pair, not a distribution. - The horizon-expansion evidence is a two-arm comparison (fixed-75 vs. progressive) run once, without intermediate schedules (e.g., 50→75) or an ablation of stage transition points; the claimed curriculum benefit is not separated from simply training longer at small horizons. - Behavioral reward shaping coefficients (−0.10 penalties, +0.10 bonus) are un ablated; the paper cannot show which shaped terms matter or whether they distort the outcome signal. - Judge-based reward and judge-based evaluation share a failure surface: no human-verified subset or deterministic-verifier cross-check is reported for any benchmark. Bottom Line: A practitioner training long-horizon agentic RL will gain concrete, cost-quantified interventions (especially the entropy-plateau rollback trigger and the reward-gated OPD design) that are not assembled this way elsewhere, but should treat the benchmark rankings as unverified until the contamination channel the paper itself exposes is measured.

Skeleton-and-Strategy Prompting: Training-Free Negation Understanding for Vision-Language Models

Y Cai, M Rostami, J Thomason · arxiv.org · karypis - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces Skeleton-and-Strategy Prompting (SSP), a training-free inference-time method that improves VLM accuracy on negation-focused VQA by abstracting each question into a reusable structural skeleton, pairing it with a cached one-sentence reasoning strategy, and prepending both to the prompt. - Why it's important: VLMs systematically answer negated questions as if the negation were absent, which undermines reliability in deployed VQA systems, and prior fixes rely on computationally expensive fine-tuning of large models. - How it does it: The core trick is shifting guidance from instance level to question-type level: a rule-based POS/parsing pipeline extracts a skeleton (e.g., "Which X is not Y?"), and a VLM synthesizes one strategy sentence per skeleton from a small pool of GPT-4o-rewritten negation examples, cached and reused across all questions sharing that skeleton. - The good: Consistent accuracy gains across all six tested VLMs on two benchmarks (e.g., InternVL3-8B on NegVQA: 65.1→79.1), backed by ablations showing matched skeleton-strategy pairs beat random pairs and that caching costs at most 0.4% accuracy while cutting strategy-generation time ~43×. - The missing: No error bars, seeds, or significance tests; the DNVQA benchmark is LLM-generated by the authors themselves; and there is no check for overlap between the VQA-v2-derived example pool and NegVQA's 20 source datasets, nor any test of whether SSP degrades performance on non-negated questions. - Read it or not: Worth reading if you work on VLM robustness or training-free prompting and want a concrete example of type-level (rather than instance-level) in-context guidance; skimmable if you already know the multimodal ICL literature, since the machinery is straightforward.
Why this rank
Scored using Empirical profile. The composite is pulled down primarily by Rigor (42): no error bars, seeds, or significance tests anywhere, a self-built LLM-generated benchmark (DNVQA) verified only by its own generation pipeline, an unexamined contamination channel between the VQA-v2-derived pool and NegVQA, and comparisons only against three weak prompting baselines with no artifact released. Novelty (55) is modest — skeleton extraction, strategy prompting, and caching are standard primitives combined sensibly — and Completeness (45) suffers from the absence of any limitations section and no check of negative transfer to non-negated questions. The consistent cross-model gains keep it above 'incremental', but the evidence base places this at roughly minimum publishable expectations. Weighted composite: 0.20*55 + 0.25*42 + 0.15*55 + 0.15*45 + 0.15*45 + 0.10*50 = 48.25 ≈ 48.
empirical Novelty 55 Rigor 42 Non-Obv 55 Completeness 45 Resilience 45 Impact 50
Show full analysis
Problem & Motivation: Vision-language models consistently fail on visual questions involving negation ("Is there a dog but no cat?"), answering as though the negation were absent. Prior work on negation in VLMs targets CLIP-style image-text alignment and typically requires full-model fine-tuning with LLM-generated negation captions (e.g., Alhamoud et al. 2025, Singh et al. 2024, Cai et al. 2025), which is expensive for large pretrained models. Meanwhile, multimodal in-context learning methods transfer knowledge through instance-level demonstrations, forcing the VLM to infer the reasoning pattern from examples — inadequate for negation, where success hinges on interpreting linguistic structure (absence, exclusion, contradiction) rather than content. The gap SSP closes: a training-free method that gives the VLM explicit structural guidance about how to reason under negation, reusable across questions. The intended audience is anyone deploying VLMs in VQA settings where negated queries occur. Key Idea: Treat negation VQA as a structure-sensitive reasoning problem and lift prompting from instance level to question-type level. Questions sharing a negation format ("What [X] is not [Y]?", "Is it not [X]?") need the same reasoning procedure, so SSP extracts a skeleton via rule-based POS tagging and dependency parsing, retrieves or synthesizes a one-sentence answering strategy for that skeleton from a small pool of negation examples, caches the skeleton→strategy mapping, and prepends both to the test prompt. Once a skeleton is seen, its strategy is reused with no regeneration — converting recurring question formats into reusable prompting units. Methodology: SSP is a three-stage inference-time pipeline with no parameter updates. (1) Example pool construction (offline): K examples are sampled from VQA-v2; GPT-4o rewrites each positive question into negation form (absence, exclusion, incorrect attributes) while preserving the image and answer space, and the correct-answer label is swapped to the alternative binary option. (2) Skeleton extraction: the test question is POS-tagged and dependency-parsed; the interrogative word is located, the negation operator (not/no/without) is located, the noun phrase between them is replaced by placeholder X, and the noun following the negation operator is replaced by Y (Algorithm 1). The framework is prompt construction plus a key-value cache D: s → r, not a learned model. (3) Strategy generation and caching: if the skeleton is cached, the stored strategy is reused; otherwise N=3 same-structure negation examples from the pool are given to the VLM, which produces a one-sentence strategy (constrained to not mention specific objects); the pair is cached. The final prompt prepends "Question Type: s / Reasoning Strategy: r" before the image-question pair. Critical design decisions: (a) rule-based rather than LLM-based skeleton extraction — justified by determinism and reuse but limits coverage of syntactically complex negation; (b) label-swapping on binary VQA-v2 pairs to construct negation supervision — cheap but restricts the pool to binary-choice negation; (c) per-skeleton (rather than per-sample) strategy generation — justified by the ablation showing ≤0.4% accuracy loss for a ~43× speedup (51.45s vs 2,237.84s for GPT-4o over 1,000 samples). Key Results: On NegVQA (a benchmark spanning 20 VQA datasets), SSP beats Plain Prompt, a hand-written CoT negation rule, and 4-shot example attachment across all six VLMs: InternVL3-8B 65.1→79.1, Qwen3VL-8B 70.6→75.5, LLaVA-OneVision2-8B 73.2→76.3, InternVL3-2B 61.2→67.8, Qwen3VL-2B 51.0→54.4 (GPT-4o numbers on NegVQA appear only in Figure 3, not in text). On the authors' own DNVQA benchmark (1,000 LLM-generated implicit-negation pairs), gains range from +2.45 (InternVL3-2B, 57.60→60.05) to +17.17 points (Qwen3VL-8B, 50.45→67.62), with GPT-4o improving 56.58→64.24. Baselines are reasonable but basic — plain prompting, a single hand-written rule, and 4-shot demonstration attachment — with no comparison to stronger training-free methods (self-consistency, retrieval-augmented ICL with larger exemplar sets, or negation-specific prompt engineering). Notably, the CoT rule is unstable across model families (it drops Qwen3VL-2B from 51.0 to 29.8), while SSP is consistent. Ablations on 8B models show Strategy Only (77.6 on InternVL3-8B) comes within 1.5 points of full SSP (79.1), Skeleton Only is much weaker (72.3), and Random Skeleton+Strategy (76.1) underperforms matched pairs — the strategy sentence carries most of the gain. Sensitivity analyses: accuracy saturates at a 256-example pool (76.2% at 32 → 79.1% at 256, flat at 512) and at 3 strategy-generation samples (77.4% at 1 → 79.1% at 3, flat at 4–5). Testing scale is standard (benchmarks of ~1,000-sample subsets for efficiency analysis), not stress-scale. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD (training-free type-level prompting for negation VQA) and NEW DATASET/BENCHMARK (DNVQA for implicit negation). The genuinely novel element is the skeleton→cached-strategy abstraction, which replaces per-instance demonstration retrieval with reusable question-type guidance; the skeleton extraction itself is standard POS/parsing, strategy generation is standard LLM prompting, and caching is standard memoization — the contribution is a sensible combination of known techniques applied to a problem (negation VQA) where prior solutions were fine-tuning-based. The framing of negation VQA as structure-sensitive reasoning is the paper's clearest conceptual move. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are a strength: component-wise (skeleton/strategy/random-pair), caching vs per-sample, pool size (32–512), and sample count (1–5) are all isolated on 8B models. However, no error bars, multiple seeds, or significance tests are reported anywhere, and the arXiv-preprint status (2610.01180) means no peer review yet. No code, data, or strategy-cache release URL is mentioned. Two methodological concerns: (1) the DNVQA benchmark is generated by the authors via LLM rewriting and evaluated only on their own construction, with correctness of the rewritten target answers verified only by the generation pipeline itself; (2) the example pool is built from VQA-v2 while NegVQA spans 20 VQA datasets — the paper does not check whether VQA-v2-derived negation questions overlap with NegVQA test items, a potential contamination channel given GPT-4o performed both the pool rewriting and one of the evaluated models. The baselines, while appropriate, are weak-to-moderate; no stronger training-free negation baseline (e.g., self-consistency or negation-aware retrieval) is included. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (prompting method with benchmark experiments; no system deployment). - Practical: Yes — training-free, runs via commercial APIs (GPT-4o) or open-weight 2B–8B models on single-GPU hardware, with only POS tagging and prompt assembly as extra machinery. - Efficient: Caching cuts strategy-generation cost from 1,182–2,238 seconds to 27–51 seconds per 1,000 samples (~43×) and output tokens from ~19,000–20,300 to ~420–490 (~42–45×) at ≤0.4% accuracy cost; the example pool saturates at 256 pairs. - Effective: The evidence shows consistent gains on two negation benchmarks, but only under binary/multiple-choice evaluation with three simple baselines; effectiveness on open-ended VQA or on non-negated questions (possible negative transfer from the prepended strategy) is not measured. - Scalable: Not tested — the efficiency analysis covers 1,000 NegVQA samples, and behavior when unseen skeletons arrive at high rate or when the skeleton space is much larger is only claimed via the caching design, not measured. The work stops at paper form: no software artifact, dataset release, or cached strategy library is mentioned. Strengths: - The type-level abstraction is a real conceptual step beyond instance-level ICL: the Random Skeleton+Strategy ablation (76.1 vs 79.1 on InternVL3-8B) demonstrates the gain is not from adding arbitrary text, and the caching analysis shows the abstraction costs almost nothing in accuracy while yielding a ~43× generation speedup. - The cross-model consistency is convincing: SSP is the top method for all six VLMs across both benchmarks, at three model scales, including a commercial API model — this is stronger evidence than a single-model result. - The component ablation cleanly attributes the gain: Strategy Only reaches 77.6 vs full SSP's 79.1 on InternVL3-8B, showing the strategy sentence does most of the work while the skeleton adds complementary type identification. - DNVQA is a useful addition — testing implicit negation ("missing", "absent") rather than lexical markers probes a genuinely harder and less-studied failure mode. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The paper has no dedicated limitations section and does not explicitly confront scope boundaries. It does acknowledge indirectly that the fixed CoT negation rule does not generalize across model families (Qwen3VL-2B drops from 51.0 to 29.8 under that baseline), and it notes pool-size and sample-count saturation — but these are framed as properties of baselines and design spaces, not as limits of SSP itself. The absence of a candid limitations discussion is a mild credibility negative. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - No variance reporting: single-run accuracies with no seeds, error bars, or significance tests; several claimed margins (e.g., SSP 79.1 vs per-sample 78.7, Strategy Only 77.6) are within plausible noise. - Possible train/test contamination: the example pool is built from VQA-v2 with GPT-4o rewrites, while NegVQA spans 20 VQA datasets; no de-duplication or overlap check between pool questions and NegVQA test items is reported. - Self-built evaluation: DNVQA is LLM-generated by the authors with correctness of the rewritten answers enforced only by the generation pipeline, and is evaluated on no external system — a self-referential benchmark risk. - Missing robustness checks: no measurement of whether SSP hurts accuracy on non-negated questions (the prepended strategy could mislead), and the rule-based skeleton extractor's coverage of syntactically complex or multi-clause negation is untested. - Narrow answer format: the example pool is built from binary VQA-v2 answer pairs, leaving open-ended negation VQA unaddressed despite the method being pitched for VQA generally. - The "state-of-the-art" claim rests on comparisons against three basic prompting baselines; stronger training-free reasoning methods (self-consistency, multimodal CoT with rationale generation) are cited but not compared. Bottom Line: A practitioner deploying VLMs on negation-prone VQA gains a concrete, cheap, and consistently effective prompting recipe here, but the evidence base (weak baselines, no variance reporting, a self-built second benchmark, and unexamined contamination risk) means the headline numbers should be treated as promising rather than settled — read it for the skeleton-caching idea, not for the exact accuracy figures.

Automated, Standardized, and Adaptive Abstraction of IoT Data into Process -Level Events

E Brzychczy, HH Beyel, J Grüger, K Kluza, L Malburg… · bp-meet-iot.github.io · business process mining or process mining - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper presents a position/challenge paper that decomposes the problem of abstracting raw IoT sensor streams into process-mining-ready event logs into six sub-challenges, identifies seven research gaps, and proposes short-, medium-, and long-term community recommendations. - Why it's important: IoT-heavy industrial environments generate massive sensor data that process mining cannot consume because event-log construction (event recognition, case identification, semantic enrichment, standardized formats) remains manual, brittle, and domain-specific, so the data goes unused. - How it does it: The authors partition the IoT-to-event-log pipeline into six sub-challenges (automated event recognition, case identification, semantic models/ontologies, IoT-enriched log formats, domain-agnostic adaptive abstraction, and LLM-assisted abstraction), survey the state of the art per sub-challenge, and derive gaps and an action roadmap. - The good: The seven identified gaps — especially the mismatch between continuous sensor signals and discrete event semantics, and the lack of ground-truth-labeled industrial IoT benchmark datasets — are genuinely well-articulated and map tightly onto the surveyed literature, many of which the co-authors themselves produced. - The missing: The paper reports no experiments, no measurements, and no empirical validation of any kind; it is entirely a synthesis-and-agenda artifact, so every claim about what will help is a claim, not a result. - Read it or not: Worth reading if you are entering or funding research on IoT-driven process mining and want a curated map of sub-problems and literature; skip it if you want technical methods, algorithms, or empirical evidence.
Why this rank

The composite is dragged down by Rigor (40) — no validation of any kind is possible or attempted, and the selection methodology is expertise-driven with visible self-citation bias — and Novelty (50), since the six-sub-challenge decomposition largely reorganizes the authors' own prior manifesto and surveys, with only the gap list (evaluation under fuzzy targets, LLM non-determinism) as a modest increment. Completeness (55) is helped by candid limitation disclosure, and Non-Obviousness (50) gets credit for the sharp continuous-signal/discrete-event tension analysis, but the artifact is a map, not a vehicle. Show full analysis
Problem & Motivation: Process mining algorithms require structured event logs (case ID, activity, timestamp, attributes), but IoT environments — smart factories, heavy industry, smart homes, healthcare — produce high-frequency, heterogeneous, noisy, continuous sensor streams with no notion of discrete activities or process instances. The paper uses a running example of a CNC machine instrumented with vibration, temperature, and power sensors, where a process analyst needs events like "Tool change" or "Drilling" inferred from correlated multi-signal patterns and linked to a production order that the sensor stream itself does not identify. Prior work addresses pieces of this problem in isolation (CEP rules, ontologies, log-format extensions, LLM labeling), leaving the field without end-to-end, adaptive, reproducible solutions. The intended audience is the BPM/process-mining and IoT research communities, and this paper explicitly frames itself as an agenda-setting contribution for the BP-Meet-IoT workshop series. Key Idea: The paper has no single technical trick — the authors should be credited with not pretending otherwise. Its organizing move is a decomposition: the end-to-end abstraction pipeline is split into six sub-challenges chosen by (a) coverage of essential pipeline stages (abstraction, correlation, representation, automation) and (b) recurrence as open problems across prior surveys and manifestos (notably van Zelst et al.'s event-abstraction taxonomy and Brzychczy et al.'s sensor-data process-mining review). The most substantive intellectual position embedded in this structure is Section 2.6's treatment of LLMs: they are positioned as a complement — a semantic interpretation/labeling layer atop unsupervised pattern discovery — rather than a replacement for CEP, ontologies, or model-driven engineering, with the explicit warning that LLM non-determinism and hallucination directly threaten the standardization and reproducibility the field needs. Methodology: This is a position paper, not a method paper; the "methodology" is a structured literature synthesis. The authors state their selection criteria (pipeline-stage coverage plus recurrence across prior surveys/manifestos), use targeted searches and snowballing from two key surveys, and have each sub-challenge elaborated by co-authors with direct research experience in that area. They explicitly state this is not an exhaustive systematic literature review. For each of the six sub-challenges, Section 3 surveys representative approaches: CEP-based recognition pipelines, learning-based abstraction (IoT Miner, LLM-based log integration), four categories of case-identification methods, IoT ontologies (SOSA/SSN, IoTStream, MASON, MSDL, FTOnto, SAREF), IoT-enriched log formats (DataStream XES extension, NICE, CAIRO, and a unifying CORE metamodel built as an OCEL 2.0 extension), MDE/BPMN-extension frameworks, and LLM-as-semantic-layer work. Section 4 derives seven gaps from this synthesis; Section 5 maps them to 14 recommendations across short-, medium-, and long-term horizons with stakeholder assignments (Table 1). No objective function, algorithm, or formal framework is defined, and the gap-derivation step is expert judgment rather than a stated systematic procedure. Key Results: Not applicable — the paper reports no quantitative results, experiments, benchmarks, or measurements. Its outputs are analytic: six sub-challenges, seven research gaps (limited automation/adaptability; no generic case-ID methods for raw mixed-type industrial IoT data; unreliable evaluation under fuzzy abstraction targets, aggravated by LLM non-determinism; no explicit modeling of temporal dynamics and transition states; fragmented integration of abstraction/correlation/semantics; limited explainability and human-in-the-loop validation; no public real-world labeled industrial IoT benchmarks), and 14 recommendations. Notable qualitative observations from the survey include that neither XES nor OCEL meets ten distilled requirements for IoT-enhanced logs, that only a handful of case-identification approaches work without activity labels or process models, and that there is no accepted open benchmark for event abstraction. Novelty Classification: This is best classified as a NEW PROBLEM decomposition / research agenda rather than any of NEW METHOD, NEW DATASET, or NEW SYSTEM — the six sub-challenges largely reorganize problems already flagged in the 2020 IoT-BPM manifesto and subsequent surveys, and several co-authors authored that prior work. What is genuinely (if modestly) novel is the consolidated gap list — particularly elevating evaluation-under-fuzzy-abstraction-targets and LLM non-determinism as first-class gaps — and the staged, stakeholder-tagged roadmap. Everything else is a competent synthesis of existing taxonomies, surveys, and the authors' own prior tools (IoT Miner, DataStream XES, FTOnto) applied to frame the agenda. Rigor & Reproducibility: As a position paper there are no ablations, seeds, error bars, or significance tests to assess, and no code, data, or artifacts are released. The selection methodology is disclosed honestly (non-systematic, expertise-driven, snowballing from two surveys), which is a credibility positive, but it means coverage bias toward the authors' own research line is possible — and indeed a substantial fraction of cited works involve the co-authors. No evaluation of the gap analysis itself is possible or attempted. The paper's own Gap 3 and Gap 7 (reproducibility and benchmark scarcity) correctly diagnose the field's evaluation problems, including the authors' acknowledgment that existing "ground truth" labels are often too coarse to serve as evaluation targets. Deployability: Profile: THEORETICAL — more precisely, a position/survey paper with no proofs and no primary experimental claim, so the theoretical check applies loosely. Sound: The gap analysis is internally consistent and well-evidenced by the surveyed literature, but it is expert argument, not a validated result. General: The sub-challenge decomposition is claimed to cover the "minimal and essential pipeline" across domains, but this coverage claim is asserted, not demonstrated against workflows the authors did not consider. Tight: Not applicable — there are no bounds; the closest analogue, the completeness of the six-way decomposition, is untested (e.g., actuation/closed-loop control and privacy/edge deployment are absent from the challenge list). Implementable: Yes in a weak sense — the recommendations are actionable research directions (dataset curation, LLM-experiment checklists, sensor-data-quality schemas, benchmarking pipelines), several of which the community could start immediately. The paper delivers no software artifact; its product is the agenda itself. Strengths: - The six-sub-challenge decomposition is a genuinely useful community-coordinating artifact: it names the pipeline stages where progress is blocked and makes gaps discussable and assignable. - The treatment of LLMs is unusually sober for 2026: the paper neither hypes LLM-based abstraction nor dismisses it, but precisely identifies the tension between LLM usefulness (semantic labeling without manual knowledge engineering) and the reproducibility/standardization the field requires. - The diagnosis that discrete event semantics fundamentally conflict with continuous, fuzzy physical processes (Gap 4, citing the fuzzy-boundary problem from the event-abstraction taxonomy) is the sharpest intellectual point in the paper and is under-addressed in prior literature. - The recommendation table with time horizons and named stakeholder classes (academic vs. academic+industrial) converts diagnosis into a concrete, prioritizable program rather than generic calls for "more research." Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors explicitly state that their literature selection "does not constitute an exhaustive systematic literature review" and reflects deliberate, expertise-driven selection — a candid disclosure. They also directly acknowledge that LLM non-determinism, prompt sensitivity, and hallucination undermine reproducibility; that existing ground-truth labels from automation systems are often too generic to serve as evaluation targets; that current methods are tightly coupled to specific processes and sensor configurations; and that most available datasets are synthetic or from controlled settings. They confront limitations of the field directly rather than minimizing them. What they do not scrutinize is the completeness of their own decomposition or their collective conflict of interest as participants in (and authors of) much of the surveyed work. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - The seven gaps overlap heavily (Gaps 1, 3, and 5 all concern automation/evaluation/integration of the same pipeline), and no prioritization or dependency structure among them is offered beyond the time-horizon table, which limits the agenda's actionability. - The long-term vision — an LLM/JEPA-based "expert system" for automated abstraction — is asserted without any argument for why JEPA-style architectures fit this problem, reading more as aspiration than as a research thesis. - The paper does not engage with why industrial adoption has stalled despite a decade of frameworks (2017–2026): missing is any analysis of deployment barriers such as cost, integration with MES/ERP vendors, or organizational factors, even though recommendations target industrial partners. - Actuation and closed-loop process control, privacy/edge constraints on LLM use in factories, and quantitative evidence on how much of the end-to-end pipeline is currently automatable are all absent from the sub-challenge list without justification. - The claim that the six sub-challenges cover the "minimal and essential" pipeline is the paper's core structural assumption and is never tested against, e.g., the prior manifesto's challenge list or a formal coverage argument. Bottom Line: For a researcher, funder, or graduate student deciding where to invest in IoT-driven process mining, this is a genuinely useful and honestly scoped roadmap that consolidates the field's blocking problems better than any single prior survey — but it delivers a map, not a vehicle, and anyone seeking methods or evidence should go straight to the primary works it cites (e.g., the van Zelst et al. taxonomy and the CORE metamodel paper).

Problem & Motivation: Organizations that want to move beyond AI-assisted tools toward architectures where autonomous components hold real decision authority have no shared vocabulary, reference pattern, or evidence base for what this costs, how long it takes, or what it delivers — especially under dense regulation. Most enterprises sit at maturity Levels 1–2 (advisory AI), and Levels 4–5 are described as largely theoretical. The paper targets architects, engineering leaders, and banking transformation leads who have identified a specific expensive bottleneck (release velocity at Company A; loan cycle time, AML noise, and fraud detection at Bank B) and need to know under what conditions governed autonomy improves measurable outcomes — and where it does not apply. The comparison across opposite ends of the regulatory spectrum is the paper's stated analytical device for separating universal architectural patterns from domain-specific governance adaptations. Key Idea: The core construct is 'AI-Based Architecture' — AI components treated as first-class architectural elements (with explicit interfaces, failure modes, and audit obligations) that govern at least one lifecycle dimension (design, operation, optimization, recovery), crossing the boundary from 'machine suggests, human decides' to 'machine decides within governed boundaries.' The key analytical insight is that architectural patterns are largely domain-independent while governance mechanisms are domain-specific, with regulatory density acting as the moderator of adoption speed and automation depth. The five-layer reference stack (data/knowledge → AI model/agent → decision/policy → automation/execution → observability/governance) and the autonomy-based maturity model (Level 1 reactive to Level 5 autonomous) are the operational forms of this idea; neither involves a new algorithm — the contribution is the framing and its instantiation in two settings. Methodology: This is a qualitative-plus-descriptive-quantitative comparative case study, not a controlled experiment. For each organization, the paper documents before/after states across the SDLC (Company A) or four banking functions (Bank B: loan processing, risk assessment, compliance monitoring, fraud detection), team role evolution at three time points, and KPIs at baseline/mid/post (Months 0/6/12 for Company A; 0/9/18 for Bank B). Metrics were drawn from existing monitoring, CI/CD, issue-tracking, and core-banking systems, and Bank B's KPIs were reportedly audited by internal audit and reviewed by the Federal Reserve during examination. Conceptual artifacts include the five-layer architecture (bidirectional data/policy flows), five design principles (autonomy with oversight, decision transparency, continuous learning, resilience by design, governance at architecture level), and the maturity model. Critical design decisions: (1) single-case-per-domain selection at regulatory extremes — reasonable for illustration, but it cannot support the generalization the framework implies; (2) measuring KPIs from operational systems rather than self-report — a genuine credibility positive; (3) attributing KPI deltas to the AI architecture despite concurrent interventions — acknowledged but not analytically resolved. An objective function or algorithmic framework is not applicable; no formal model is derived. Key Results: Company A (18 engineers, SaaS): median cycle time 18 → 7 working days (−61%); defect rate 4.2 → 2.3 per KLOC (−45%); deployment frequency 2 → 9 per week (4.5×); lead time for changes 48 hours → 30 minutes; MTTR 4 hours → 45 minutes; code review turnaround 6 hours → 90 minutes; test suite per commit cut from 3,000 to 200–400 tests (45 → 8–12 minutes); auto-rollback within 5 minutes vs. 30-minute manual rollback. Bank B (~8,000 employees, $45B assets): loan time-to-decision 21 days → 48 hours (consumer), 35 → 5 days (commercial), 45 → 7 days (small business); processing cost per application $450 → $220 (−51%); credit model Gini 0.62 → 0.74; AML false-positive rate 95% → 65% with investigation yield 5% → 35%; regulatory reporting 3 person-weeks → 2 person-days per report; novel-fraud detection rate <20% → 85% (RNN + GNN approach) with fraud false positives 90% → 50% and detection latency 48 hours → 15 minutes. Scale is modest (one 120-person SaaS firm; one mid-size bank). Baselines are the organizations' own pre-transition states — no external benchmarks or competing approaches are compared. The paper's own observation that both organizations reached ~70% of target maturity within the first 6 months regardless of domain complexity is the most interesting (and least developed) finding, suggesting organizational learning, not technology, paces adoption. The provided text is truncated mid-Section 5.2, so the cross-domain KPI framework (Section 6), discussion (Section 7), and conclusions (Section 8) could not be evaluated. Novelty Classification: NEW FORMULATION (a defined construct — AI components as first-class architectural elements — plus a five-layer reference pattern and an autonomy-axis maturity model) combined with NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING (two documented cases with quantified pre/post deltas and the regulatory-density moderation claim). Genuinely novel relative to the related work surveyed: the maturity model's axis (autonomy/oversight rather than organizational readiness) and the explicit treatment of AI as architectural specification rather than bolt-on tooling. Standard or pre-existing: the individual technologies (LLM code generation, gradient-boosting credit scoring, RNN/GNN fraud detection, SHAP/LIME explainability, drift detection via PSI/AUC), the MRM three-lines-of-defense structure, and the general shape of maturity models (Gartner, Forrester, NIST AI RMF) — the contribution is their assembly into a new framing applied to two settings, not any new technical mechanism. Rigor & Reproducibility: Rigor is the paper's weakest dimension. There are no ablations isolating which AI components drove which KPI movement, no error bars, no confidence intervals, no significance tests, and no multiple-organization sampling — each domain has n=1. The authors honestly list attribution caveats (concurrent mentoring program shifts, legacy data migration, and a new core banking system at Bank B also contributed to gains), which is commendable, but no attempt is made to apportion effects. No code, data, model weights, or replication artifacts are released, and 'Not stated.' applies to any public repository. Both cases are the author's descriptive accounts of anonymized organizations; the single-author affiliation (e-Softworks, a consulting firm) and the absence of peer review place this firmly in vendor-self-report territory pending external verification. Bank B's KPIs being 'audited by internal audit and reviewed by the Federal Reserve' is the strongest verification signal offered, but no evidence of that review is provided. No Goodhart-style benchmark gaming is evident since the metrics are operational rather than benchmark-derived, though the KPIs are chosen by the same party claiming the improvement. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (with a SYSTEMS flavor — the paper describes deployed systems, but the artifact evaluated is the organizational transformation). - Practical: Yes in principle — all described technologies (LLM tooling, gradient boosting, OCR document AI, RNN/GNN detectors, drift monitors) run on commercially available cloud/GPU hardware; 'Not stated.' on specific hardware requirements. - Efficient: Not rigorously quantified — the paper notes GPU clusters, data pipelines, and new governance headcount (AI risk officer reaching 100% FTE; ~20% of Bank B's budget spent on data cleaning) partially offset savings, but no total-cost-of-ownership comparison to an alternative approach is given. - Effective: The KPI deltas are large and internally plausible, but they demonstrate improvement on the organizations' own metrics with acknowledged confounds, not causal attribution to the architectural paradigm; effectiveness of the reference pattern itself (vs. good tooling plus process change) is untested. - Scalable: Only claimed, not tested — the largest case is a single $45B bank; whether the pattern holds at larger institutions, across multi-jurisdiction deployments, or at 10× decision volumes is unexamined, and the authors themselves report that scaling governance headcount linearly (governance officer FTE growth) was necessary. The work delivers no software artifact, library, or dataset; its outputs are conceptual (reference architecture, maturity model, KPI framework, assessment questionnaire in appendices) plus a reusable case-study narrative. Strengths: - The comparative two-domain design is the right instrument for the question asked: it surfaces concrete asymmetries (12 vs. 18 month timelines; 40–60% vs. 25–35% automation depth; market-driven vs. compliance-driven transformation drivers) that a single-domain study structurally cannot produce. - The maturity model's choice of axis — degree of autonomous agency and corresponding oversight regime, from human-in-the-loop to human-out-of-the-loop with immutable AI-controlled guardrails — is a genuinely useful practitioner vocabulary, and the Level 4/5 governance requirements (guardrail enforcement, drift-vs-adaptation discrimination, optimization audit) are specified concretely rather than hand-waved. - The failure-mode documentation is unusually candid and specific for a self-affirming case study: the over-reliance incident (null-value bug accepted from AI output), the seven-to-four tool consolidation, the training-data quality feedback loop that starved poorly-documented modules, and the quantified cost of regulatory timelines (SR 11-7 validation adding 3–4 months per model) are actionable, not decorative. - The regulatory analysis (US patchwork vs. EU horizontal regime; the eight AI Act high-risk obligations mapped to design impact; 6–12 vs. 3–6 month compliance timelines) is a substantive synthesis that alone justifies the paper for banking transformation teams. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors explicitly concede: (1) single-organization measurements that may not generalize; (2) KPI improvements not solely attributable to AI-Based Architecture, with named concurrent changes (mentoring program at Company A; core banking replacement and data lake migration at Bank B); (3) measurement windows that ended while metrics were still trending positively; (4) at Company A, an over-reliance failure mode requiring mandatory human review reinstatement; (5) at Bank B, customer trust erosion addressed only partially (satisfaction at ~92% of the pre-transition human-only baseline — the authors do not treat the residual 8% gap as a finding). The paper confronts limitations more directly than is typical for consulting-affiliated case studies, which is a credibility positive, though the limitations section proper (Section 7) falls in the truncated portion of the provided text and could not be evaluated. Analyst-Identified Gaps: Beyond the acknowledged confounds: (1) no counterfactual or comparison organization — the deltas may largely reflect the effect of any serious process-improvement investment, AI-based or not; the paper never tests whether a non-AI automation program would have achieved similar KPI movement; (2) the two headline theoretical claims ('regulatory density slows adoption but not eventual value magnitude' and 'patterns are domain-independent, governance domain-specific') rest on exactly two data points and cannot support the generality asserted; (3) KPI selection and measurement were controlled by the improvement's sponsor with no independent verification described beyond the bank's routine examination cycle; (4) no adverse outcomes are quantified — AI-caused incidents, wrongful credit denials, model failures caught by rollback, or false-negative rates for fraud/AML (the paper reports false-positive improvements but is silent on whether detection of actual suspicious activity or fraud dropped, the metric regulators care most about); (5) the anonymization is unverifiable, and the author's consulting affiliation creates an incentive alignment problem the paper does not disclose or discuss; (6) some figures reference broken cross-references ('Section ??', 'Figure ??'), suggesting an unpolished preprint. I do not flag missing statistical tests as a manufactured weakness — with n=1 per domain they would be nearly meaningless — but the paper should not have drawn cross-domain conclusions it cannot support. Bottom Line: A practitioner leading AI adoption — particularly in a regulated financial institution — will extract real, usable value from the maturity model, governance checklists, and honest failure catalog, but the KPI numbers should be treated as illustrative self-report from an unreviewed consulting preprint rather than evidence, and researchers seeking rigorous comparative findings should look elsewhere.

Evidence-Bound Verification for Agentic SystemVerilog Workflows

JS Dinakar · openreview.net · specification to code with formal verifications - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper proposes an evidence-bound assurance architecture for LLM-agent-driven SystemVerilog development, in which completion claims are accepted only when deterministic tool evidence is cryptographically bound to the exact artifact versions it evaluated, and upstream changes automatically invalidate stale evidence. - Why it's important: LLM agents can present obsolete green test reports or approvals as completion evidence after specs or dependencies change — a 'stale-evidence escape' that snapshot-style RTL benchmarks (pass@k, one-shot testbench checks) structurally cannot detect. - How it does it: Versioned artifacts (requirements, SystemRDL, RTL, assertions, results, approvals) are connected in a typed dependency graph; a fail-closed completion predicate requires coverage, freshness, pass, and authority, with transitive invalidation and selective recertification computed over the graph rather than decided by the agent. - The good: The evaluation protocol is genuinely prespecified — 30 frozen artifacts, 36 change events, 3 conditions, 108 runs, pre-frozen ground-truth impact sets, an explicit NO-GO stop gate, and an honest admission that no results exist yet — an unusually rigorous anti-Goodhart discipline. - The missing: No empirical results are reported at all; the registered study is explicitly NO-GO at submission time, so every claim about invalidation recall, escape prevention, and recertification cost is a hypothesis, not a measurement. - Read it or not: Read it if you work on agent assurance, CI/CD-style verification for LLM-generated hardware, or evaluation methodology for lifecycle-aware agent benchmarks; skip it if you need measured evidence of effectiveness, because the paper deliberately contains none.
Why this rank
Scored using Systems profile. The composite is dragged down by Impact (25) and Resilience (45): no prototype is demonstrated, nothing is released, the registered study is explicitly NO-GO, and every effectiveness claim is a hypothesis — under a Systems weighting (30% Impact) this is fatal to the composite. Novelty (78) is real — 'stale-evidence escape' as a problem formulation and the correctness/integrity/freshness tripartite split are genuine conceptual contributions — and Rigor (50) credits the unusually strong pre-registration discipline while penalizing the absence of any executed evaluation. Completeness (52) reflects unimplemented machinery and the unexamined closest prior art in EDA impact analysis. Weighted composite: 0.15*78 + 0.15*50 + 0.10*68 + 0.15*52 + 0.15*45 + 0.30*25 = 48.

Problem & Motivation: Hardware engineering teams adopting LLM agents for RTL, assertion, testbench, and verification-plan generation face a lifecycle problem no current benchmark addresses: after an upstream artifact changes (a renamed register field, a revised reset value, a modified AXI-Lite timing requirement), previously accepted evidence — simulation reports, approvals, synthesis checks — may refer to a superseded state, yet still be presented as proof of completion. The paper calls this failure mode 'stale-evidence escape.' Static pass@k and repository-level benchmarks collapse engineering history into a single snapshot, so they cannot measure whether a completion decision remains justified across change events. The stakeholders are hardware verification teams and, ultimately, safety-relevant semiconductor flows where stale approvals carry real cost. Key Idea: Separate three properties usually conflated in agent systems — artifact correctness (does the RTL meet the spec), evidence integrity (does the report match the stated artifact/oracle/environment, enforced by content-addressed digests), and evidence freshness (do those bindings still match the current dependency state) — and make freshness a machine-enforced graph property: on any change, compute the transitive impact closure over typed dependency edges, mark all bound evidence stale in the same transaction, and re-admit completion only via a fail-closed predicate `Complete(x,s) = Covered ∧ Fresh ∧ Pass ∧ ¬Block` that the proposing agent cannot override. Methodology: The system models an artifact graph G=(V,D) where vertices are versioned engineering objects and edges encode dependency semantics. Each evidence record is an 8-tuple binding claim, artifact digest, oracle digest, tool/environment identity, policy decision, and result. Tasks are frozen with an eight-field completion contract (intent, expected artifact, authoritative sources, deterministic oracle, forbidden shortcuts, permitted actions, escalation triggers, mandatory audit events). The invalidation procedure is six steps: commit new digest, compute transitive impact closure I(u) over typed edges (unknown dependency types fail closed and escalate), mark stale every evidence record whose binding set intersects {u}∪I(u), expand target contracts into required claims and schedule only checks lacking fresh passing evidence, run checks in isolated workspaces with the agent barred from writing passing evidence, and re-evaluate the completion predicate. Tooling is standard open-source EDA: Verilator, cocotb, Yosys, SystemRDL. Three design decisions stand out: (1) SystemRDL as a single source for RTL-facing and firmware-facing register views — well justified, since it creates genuine cross-view dependencies; (2) evidence types kept separate (simulation, lint, synthesis, assertions) rather than collapsed into a 'tests passed' flag — well justified, directly serving freshness semantics; (3) reuse eligibility defined by the graph and policy, not the agent — justified in principle, but its quality depends entirely on dependency-edge precision, which the paper acknowledges is unvalidated. The evaluation design is a three-condition comparison (C0 human-only, C1 unconstrained RAG+tools agent, C2 full governed workflow) over 36 change events in six classes, with invalidation recall and stale-evidence escapes as primary outcomes and recertification effort, schedule variance, and human interventions as supporting outcomes. Key Results: None reported. The paper states explicitly that the registered study remains NO-GO at submission: 'this paper reports an architecture and evaluation protocol, not measured comparative performance.' All anticipated outcomes — invalidation recall, stale-evidence escapes, recertification cost relative to full reruns — are prespecified hypotheses. The scale of the planned evaluation is modest: one bounded RISC-V SoC with an AXI-Lite DSP accelerator, 30 artifacts, 36 change events, 108 runs, with event-level pairing explicitly used to prevent 30 artifacts from inflating sample size. Baselines C0 and C1 are designed to be fair (C1 gets identical tool access, not a deliberately weak agent), which is methodologically sound but untested. Novelty Classification: NEW PROBLEM (stale-evidence escape as a defined failure mode and evaluation unit — the controlled change event rather than the task snapshot) plus NEW FORMULATION (evidence freshness as a distinct assurance property governed by a fail-closed graph predicate). The mechanism itself is a competent combination of existing ideas: content-addressed attestations from software supply-chain systems (in-toto), standard transitive-closure invalidation from build systems, and bounded oracles from existing verification practice, applied to agentic hardware development. The framing and problem definition are the genuine novelty; the algorithms are not. Rigor & Reproducibility: No ablations, error bars, seeds, or significance tests exist because no results exist. What the paper offers instead is pre-registration discipline of unusual quality: ground-truth impact sets and withdrawal sets frozen before any run, adjudication independent of condition outputs, event-level pairing, class-stratified bootstrap intervals, paired permutation tests, forbidden optional stopping and outcome-driven transformations, and an immutable environment freeze (container digest, tool versions, protocol hash) with a hard NO-GO gate. The NeurIPS checklist answers are honest — experimental items are marked N/A. No code, data, or artifact is released; the checklist states this explicitly. Methodological concerns: (1) the entire contribution rests on a study that has not run, so the architecture's central claims are currently unfalsifiable in practice — only falsifiable in principle; (2) dependency ground truth is expert judgment, so 'invalidation recall' measures agreement with the authors' own frozen adjudication; (3) the three conditions are architecturally confounded, which the authors acknowledge, so even successful results would not isolate which component (contracts, gates, recertification) drives any effect. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: SYSTEMS (a specified workflow architecture with a planned deployment-style evaluation; no built-and-deployed artifact is released). Practical: Yes — the stack is commercially available open-source tooling (Verilator, cocotb, Yosys, SystemRDL) plus an artifact ledger; no exotic hardware is required. Efficient: Claimed, not measured — selective recertification is positioned against full reruns as an explicit comparator, but the efficiency delta is a prespecified outcome, not a result. Effective: Unknown — the primary outcomes (invalidation recall, escape count) are exactly the measures that would establish effectiveness, and they have not been collected. Scalable: Not evaluated and plausibly the weakest point — a 30-artifact, 36-event single SoC gives no evidence the dependency-graph modeling cost stays tractable or that edge-typo/maintainability risk is manageable on industrial designs with thousands of coupled artifacts. Deliverable form: paper only — no library, CLI, dataset, or reference implementation is released. Strengths: - The problem definition is real and crisp: 'stale-evidence escape' names a lifecycle failure that snapshot benchmarks genuinely cannot capture, and reframing the unit of evaluation as the controlled change event is a transferable methodological idea beyond hardware. - The tripartite decomposition (correctness / integrity / freshness), with the explicit observation that digests solve only integrity and that freshness requires dependency semantics, is a clean conceptual contribution that clarifies muddled practice in agent-assurance discussions. - The pre-registration discipline — frozen ground truth, NO-GO stop gate, preserved oracle failures, event-level pairing against pseudo-replication — exceeds the norm for agent-benchmark papers and models good evaluation hygiene. - The fail-closed authority separation (the proposing agent cannot author its own passing evidence) is a correctly-identified structural control, aligned with supply-chain attestation practice. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors confront limitations directly and at length (a credibility positive): synthetic rather than proprietary artifacts; no coverage of automotive safety or production semiconductor flows; dependency ground truth is expert judgment; a single bounded SoC limits external validity and 36 events may underrepresent coupled, long-latency industrial changes; the three-condition design confounds components; C0 is sensitive to engineer familiarity; LLM nondeterminism persists despite pinned prompts; 36 events bound statistical power; and simulation/synthesis are bounded, semantically incomplete oracles. This is candid, non-minimizing, and specific. Analyst-Identified Gaps: Beyond the acknowledged limits: (1) the paper never demonstrates a working prototype — there is no evidence the artifact ledger, digest binding, and gate machinery have been implemented at all, which makes the 108-run protocol's feasibility itself an unvalidated assumption (e.g., whether SystemRDL/Verilator/cocotb integration produces the fine-grained dependency types the graph requires); (2) no prior work is cited on change-aware regression selection or impact analysis in EDA (formal equivalence checking, incremental compile, regression triage), where related invalidation semantics have long existed industrially — the related-work comparison against software supply chains omits the closest hardware-domain prior art; (3) the recertification-efficiency claim is only testable if over-broad edges don't collapse it to full reruns, and the paper offers no analysis of how edge precision is engineered or audited on real designs — the acknowledged cost concern is deferred entirely to the future study; (4) the threat model excludes host compromise and trusted-binary tampering, which is stated, but the interaction between an LLM agent with tool access and the evidence ledger's write permissions (e.g., prompt-injection-induced tool misuse within isolated workspaces) is unexamined; (5) an earlier 'six-candidate completion-evaluation pilot' is mentioned in passing but never described, so prior exploratory results that shaped the design are invisible to the reader. Bottom Line: As a problem formulation and pre-registered protocol this is a genuinely useful contribution to agent-assurance methodology that hardware-verification and agent-evaluation researchers should read — but with zero implemented results, a NO-GO study, and no released artifact, it is a promise of evidence rather than evidence, and any practitioner seeking demonstrated effectiveness should wait for the follow-up paper that reports the registered outcomes.
