Problem & Motivation: Deployed next-generation CSE systems (autonomous driving, intelligent manufacturing, healthcare monitoring, cybersecurity) increasingly combine architecturally distinct AI paradigms — convolutional or transformer perception, gradient-boosted/ensemble prediction on tabular data, and symbolic or human-governed decision layers — rather than relying on one end-to-end model. The paper identifies a gap: although each component literature is mature, comparatively few studies systematically organize how these components compose in deployed systems, and almost none characterize how failures propagate across component boundaries (e.g., whether an out-of-distribution perception failure is caught by a downstream symbolic constraint check or silently propagates into a prediction). The intended audience is CSE researchers and system designers choosing among paradigms for consequential, safety-relevant applications. Key Idea: The core organizing insight is that the field's architectural trajectory is convergent rather than substitutive: because no vision architecture dominates uniformly (CNN vs. ViT, one-stage vs. two-stage detection involve documented accuracy/latency/data trade-offs) and no ensemble method dominates on all data structures, deployed systems converge on deliberately composed hybrids — connectionist perception plus structured prediction plus symbolic or human constraint-checking — with AlphaGo (learned policy guiding symbolic tree search) as the emblematic existence proof. This is a synthesis thesis, not a new technical mechanism; the paper itself performs no modeling or measurement. Methodology: The study is explicitly a qualitative, descriptive, comparative literature review. Reviewed works were compared along four axes: AI paradigm (connectionist, ensemble, symbolic/neuro-symbolic); task type (perception, structured tabular prediction, sequential decision-making); reported benchmark performance and computational efficiency where available; and documented integration pattern within hybrid systems. The output is three comparative tables — (1) vision architecture families vs. mechanism and reported trade-offs, (2) ensemble/hybrid predictive methods vs. data structure and decision context, (3) CSE application domains vs. component composition. Design decisions worth flagging: (a) no stated search protocol — databases, time window, inclusion/exclusion criteria are absent, so the corpus is effectively a hand-curated canon of ~22 highly cited papers; (b) the claim that hybrid systems 'outperform' single paradigms is a qualitative judgment assembled from heterogeneous sources rather than a controlled comparison; (c) the failure-propagation gap motivating the review is identified but not itself studied. Key Results: No experimental results — the paper reports no new measurements, accuracies, or timings. Its 'results' are three tables of previously reported findings: AlexNet's ImageNet error reduction over pre-deep-learning baselines, ResNet enabling 100+ layer training, ViT matching/exceeding CNNs only with large-scale pretraining while underperforming on small datasets, CNNs retaining a compute/energy-efficiency edge over transformers at comparable accuracy (Sze et al.), bagging/boosting/stacking mapped to variance-reduction/bias-reduction/meta-learning principles, and domain mappings such as Random Forest/XGBoost for network-intrusion features plus rule-based policy engines for cybersecurity. The baselines 'compared' are the canonical primary papers themselves; the conclusion drawn is that hybrid perception–prediction–symbolic pipelines recur across autonomous vehicles, manufacturing, medical diagnostics, cybersecurity, and game-playing. All quantitative claims are secondhand citations, and the most recent primary technical source is from 2023 (a working paper); the vision and ensemble literature is 2012–2021 vintage. Novelty Classification: NEW FORMULATION at best, and marginal: the genuinely original element is the three-axis comparative mapping of component composition to application domain (Table 3), which is a reasonable organizational contribution. Everything else is a standard combination and retelling of established ideas (canonical deep learning, ensemble, and neuro-symbolic papers) applied to a framing ('next-generation CSE applications') that does not change the technical content. There is no new method, dataset, system, or empirical finding. Rigor & Reproducibility: Weak. There are no ablations, seeds, or significance tests by design (nothing is run), and no systematic review protocol is documented — no search strings, databases, screening process, or corpus statistics — so the review is not reproducible as a survey. The synthesis is internally consistent and the tables trace every cell to a specific citation, which is a credibility positive. However, the corpus is small (22 references), skewed toward famous papers, and evaluated on the authors' qualitative judgment alone; the claim that hybrid systems 'outperform any single paradigm applied in isolation' is a generalization from AlphaGo and selected position papers (Rudin, Marcus) rather than a demonstrated result. No code, data, or artifact is released (none would apply). Publication venue note: the paper appears in a SvedbergOpen journal issue dated 2026 with an unusual supplemental-issue numbering ('No.12s'), and the author affiliations span fields largely unrelated to the topic (nursing, applied mathematics) — readers should weight the venue's peer-review rigor accordingly. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL (in the weak sense of a survey paper — no primary experiments or system). Not applicable in the usual sense, so assessed as a reference artifact: - Practical: The tables are freely usable as a design checklist; no software artifact exists. - Efficient: Trivially cheap to consume; conversely, the reviewed efficiency guidance (CNN > transformer on edge hardware) is pre-2021 and predates efficient ViT variants. - Effective: The comparative mapping plausibly reflects real deployed practice, but the central claim (hybrid superiority) is a supported assertion, not measured evidence. - Scalable: Not tested or testable — the framework's value at larger corpora or new domains is unverified. Deliverable: paper form only; no dataset, tool, or reusable technique is released. Strengths: - Table 3's cross-referencing of application domain to specific perception/prediction/governance components is a compact, citable design map that is not assembled this way in the primary sources it draws on. - The identified research gap — failure-mode propagation across component boundaries within hybrid pipelines, extending the 'jagged frontier' evidence from human–AI boundaries to component-to-component boundaries — is a genuinely sharp and under-studied framing, and the paper honestly declines to answer it. - The synthesis correctly connects normally separate literatures (Sze et al.'s efficiency survey, Rudin's interpretability argument, Dell'Acqua's field experiment) that system designers usually read in isolation. - The paper accurately characterizes trade-offs in the primary literature (e.g., ViT's data-hunger, YOLO's small-object accuracy penalty) without distorting the cited results. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors explicitly acknowledge the review's central limitation — that failures propagating across hybrid-component boundaries are not systematically characterized — and devote the Future Work section to it: standardized benchmarks for compositional generalization and out-of-distribution robustness, design guidelines for where symbolic components should sit in a pipeline, and edge-targeted co-design of hybrid ViT/CNN architectures. They do not, however, acknowledge the limitations of their own method (no systematic search protocol, small and dated corpus, qualitative-only evidence for the hybrid-superiority thesis); the limitations they confront are those of the field, not of the study. This partial directness is a moderate credibility positive but not a full one. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - No systematic-review methodology: without search criteria or corpus justification, the 'convergence on hybrid architectures' conclusion could be an artifact of which papers were chosen; a field dominated by end-to-end deep learning in practice is argued away by selection. - The strongest causal claim — hybrid systems 'outperform any single paradigm applied in isolation' — is never supported by any head-to-head comparison anywhere in the reviewed corpus; AlphaGo is a single game-playing existence proof, not evidence for CSE domains generally. - The corpus ends before the current wave of foundation/multimodal models, which complicate the neat perception/prediction/symbolic taxonomy (a single large model now often spans several of the paper's 'paradigms'); the framework is not stress-tested against this. - Table 3's domain mappings are asserted with thin support — e.g., medical diagnostics is anchored only to Rudin (a position paper), and autonomous vehicles to YOLO plus Marcus (a critique), with no citation to any actual deployed system or regulatory analysis. - The 'future research prospect' the paper nominates (component-boundary failure propagation) is precisely the kind of question that requires the empirical study this paper cannot perform, leaving its contribution as framing only. - Venue/authorship signal: the mismatch between the paper's topic and the authors' affiliations, and the journal's format, warrant heightened skepticism about editorial review quality. Bottom Line: A practitioner gains little: the paper is an accurate but shallow, pre-2023 synthesis of canonical sources whose one usable artifact (Table 3) does not compensate for the absence of systematic methodology or any new evidence — stronger and more current treatments of hybrid/neuro-symbolic AI exist, and readers would be better served by the primary papers the review summarizes.

Problem & Motivation: In SAP S/4HANA manufacturing and supply-chain operations, a single deviation (e.g., equipment degradation) propagates into production delays, material shortages, rescheduling, supplier changes, and delivery risk. The authors argue that conventional exception management detects deviations only after hard thresholds are exceeded and presents alerts without probable cause, cross-functional consequence, or recommended response — a gap between exception detection and exception resolution. The intended audience is enterprise architects and operations teams running integrated ERP-driven manufacturing. The motivating framing leans heavily on a supplied set of aerospace/hydraulic-engineering papers (fault simulation, wavelet-packet diagnosis, health assessment via fuzzy comprehensive evaluation), from which the authors abstract a principle — model system behavior, classify deviations, assess risk, integrate heterogeneous evidence — and propose transplanting it to the enterprise-decision layer. Key Idea: Treat a manufacturing exception not as a per-department alert but as a distributed operational condition processed through a staged multi-agent pipeline (sensing → validation → prediction → diagnosis → impact analysis → response), where agents exchange structured findings over a shared operational-context model rather than natural-language messages, and a final orchestration agent scores priority as the product of probability, business impact, urgency, and propagation risk. This is the only quasi-formal element in the paper; the formula is explicitly disclaimed as a decision structure rather than a quantitative law. Beyond this, the key idea is analogical: the diagnostic-reasoning patterns of hydraulic fault analysis are argued to transfer to enterprise exception orchestration. Methodology: The paper uses a conceptual design-science methodology with five analytical stages (exception identification, contextual interpretation, agent-based reasoning, cross-functional impact assessment, decision orchestration) and no empirical component. Six agents are specified: (1) an Event Monitoring Agent that normalizes heterogeneous SAP signals into a common exception representation (event type, timestamp, affected object, severity, business context); (2) an Anomaly and Prediction Agent that estimates whether trajectories (e.g., rising downtime, repeated supplier delays) will become future exceptions; (3) a Root-Cause Reasoning Agent that discriminates among material unavailability, equipment degradation, capacity overload, rework, and supplier delay; (4) a Production and Maintenance Agent that trades off immediate maintenance vs. continued operation vs. rescheduling; (5) a Supply-Chain Coordination Agent for upstream/downstream impact; and (6) a Decision Orchestration Agent that applies the multiplicative priority formula and routes responses. Governance is handled by confidence-level gating: high-confidence/low-impact actions may auto-execute via SAP workflows, while uncertain or high-impact decisions escalate to humans. Critical design decisions — agent specialization boundaries, shared structured context, human-in-the-loop confidence gating — are argued for narratively but none is justified experimentally, and no algorithmic detail (no learning objective, no detection model, no conflict-resolution mechanism among agents) is specified beyond the conceptual level. A single hypothetical machine-deterioration scenario illustrates the intended flow. Key Results: Not stated in any quantitative sense. The Results section reports four conceptual findings: (1) exception management benefits from decomposition into specialized reasoning functions; (2) predictive management requires contextual integration across functions; (3) risk-based prioritization outperforms binary exception classification; (4) multi-agent coordination creates a detection-to-intervention chain. There are no numbers, benchmarks, datasets, baselines, error bars, or comparisons — the "results" are claims derived from the architectural analysis and analogies to the aerospace literature. The paper itself concedes that the framework "represents a theoretically grounded architectural synthesis rather than empirical evidence of SAP performance improvement." Novelty Classification: NEW FORMULATION at best, and a weak one: the paper's genuinely new element is the proposal to apply engineering fault-diagnosis patterns (model → detect → diagnose → risk-rank → intervene) to SAP S/4HANA exception management via a six-agent decomposition. The constituent ideas — multi-agent systems, anomaly detection, root-cause analysis, predictive maintenance, human-in-the-loop governance, risk-prioritized alerting — are all standard; even the target problem (predictive exception management in ERP) is adjacent to well-established work in AIOps, complex-event processing, and SAP's own predictive-analytics offerings, none of which is cited or compared. The priority formula (Probability × Impact × Urgency × Propagation Risk) is a restatement of standard risk matrix practice. Rigor & Reproducibility: No ablations, no experiments, no seeds, no significance tests, no code, no data, no model weights — nothing is released or releasable in the current form, since nothing was built. The methodology section explicitly states the study does "not evaluat[e] a deployed SAP implementation." Methodological concerns are substantial: the entire evidence base is analogy from 11 aerospace/hydraulics/structural-engineering papers plus one IEEE paper on SAP PP from a sentiment-analysis conference; there is no survey of the actual ERP/AIOps/multi-agent literature against which the architecture could be positioned; the framework is evaluated on nothing, not even a simulation; and the repeated reliance on a single "compulsory reference" cited only by title because "complete bibliographic metadata... was not supplied" — plus a 2026 citation from a thematically unrelated venue — is a red flag for reference integrity and suggests possible citation coercion, which warrants reviewer scrutiny of the publication venue. The one positive: the paper does not dress conceptual claims up as empirical ones. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL is not applicable; this is closest to a THEORETICAL/position paper (a conceptual architecture with no primary experiments and no proofs), so the theoretical check is applied loosely. - Sound: There are no formal claims to be sound or unsound; the priority formula is asserted, not derived, and the authors admit it is not a quantitative law. - General: The architecture is defined only at the level of agent responsibilities, so it trivially generalizes — but generality by vagueness is not a virtue. - Tight: Not applicable; no bounds are stated. - Implementable: Partially — the agent decomposition and lifecycle are implementable as a design skeleton, but every agent's core function (anomaly trajectory estimation, root-cause discrimination, propagation-risk scoring) is unspecified, so a practitioner must supply all the hard parts. Deliverable: paper form only; no tool, dataset, prototype, or reusable artifact. Strengths: - The shared-operational-context requirement is a genuinely useful architectural insight: the paper correctly identifies that locally reasonable agent decisions become globally inconsistent without a common structured representation linking exceptions to orders, materials, equipment, suppliers, and deliveries. - The confidence-gated human-in-the-loop governance model (automate high-confidence/low-impact, escalate the rest) directly addresses alert fatigue and automation-risk trade-offs that many agentic-AI proposals ignore. - The paper is unusually honest about its own epistemic status, explicitly declining to claim empirical SAP validation and listing data-quality, agent-conflict, false-positive, and accountability risks as first-class limitations. - The detection-to-resolution framing — asking "which current conditions will create late orders, why, and what intervention is available?" instead of "which orders are late?" — is a clear and correct articulation of the gap between alerting and orchestration. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors confront limitations directly and repeatedly, which strengthens credibility: heavy dependence on data completeness and process consistency; coordination complexity including contradictory recommendations and uncertainty propagation; false-positive-driven alert fatigue; scalability concerns as agent counts grow (communication overhead, governance difficulty); explainability requirements; human accountability for high-impact automated decisions; and — most notably — the explicit admission that the aerospace literature base does not cover ERP systems, so the framework lacks empirical evidence of SAP performance improvement. They call for future validation on historical manufacturing datasets, simulated SAP event streams, and controlled comparisons against conventional exception management. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - No engagement with the directly relevant prior art: AIOps, complex-event processing, multi-agent frameworks for manufacturing (e.g., holonic manufacturing, MAS literature from the 2000s), or SAP's own embedded predictive/anomaly tooling — so the claimed research gap is asserted against the wrong (deliberately supplied) literature set rather than the actual field. - The anomaly detection, root-cause reasoning, and propagation-risk estimation agents — where all the technical difficulty lives — are black boxes; the architecture specifies what each agent is for but not how any of them would work, making the contribution closer to an organizational chart than a method. - The multiplicative priority formula is unvalidated and fragile (a zero on any factor zeroes priority; no normalization, weighting, or calibration scheme is given), and the paper offers no mechanism for resolving inter-agent disagreement beyond naming the problem. - The reference base is suspicious: 11 of 13 citations are aerospace/hydraulics papers loosely tied to the argument, one key reference lacks any metadata and is cited by title, and one reference is from a sentiment-analysis conference — patterns that reviewers should treat as a venue-integrity concern. - The single hypothetical scenario involves no data, no counterfactual, and no failure case, so it demonstrates the narrative, not the mechanism. Bottom Line: A practitioner gains a reasonable checklist of agent roles and governance considerations for ERP exception intelligence, but anyone seeking a validated method, a competitive architecture, or reproducible evidence should look elsewhere — this is a conceptual sketch whose own authors admit it has no empirical legs.

Problem & Motivation: The paper addresses the loss-of-control problem for recursively self-improving AI: if a system can improve its own cognition or design successors, how can humanity obtain the benefits of superintelligence without the system acquiring independent power? The relevant actors are AI labs, safety researchers, and regulators preparing for agentic frontier systems. The gap it claims to close is that alignment research (making the AI want to comply) is treated as the primary defense; the paper argues for an orthogonal, security-engineering line of defense in which undesirable intentions may occur but cannot convert into power. It positions this as a 'third option' between not building ASI at all and building ASI with broad self-directed authority. Key Idea: The single core insight is that intelligence is not authority: capability (C), agency (G), and delegated authority (D) can all grow without bound while unilateral authority to self-expand (U) is held at zero by placing all credentials, compute allocation, network policy, deployment, and the control plane itself on infrastructure the model cannot administer. The key operational shift is moving safety questions from 'will the AI follow the rule?' (behavioral) to 'can the AI physically perform the prohibited act despite an external boundary?' (structural) — a restatement, as the paper's own citations admit, of established containment and off-switch reasoning. Methodology: This is a conceptual/position paper with no pipeline, algorithm, objective function, or experimental framework. Its 'methodology' consists of: (1) a conceptual taxonomy distinguishing agency, delegated authority, and unilateral authority, with enumerated examples of each; (2) an architectural sketch of a two-plane design (intelligence plane vs. externally administered control plane) with a request-evaluate-authorize-issue loop for capability expansion, including a successor-deployment pipeline (design → quarantine → independent capability/security/control evaluation → red-teaming → external deployment decision); (3) a 'simplified formal model' defining C(t), G(t), D(t), U(t) with the invariant U(t) = 0 across generations (Section 18 — this is notation, not a formalism with theorems, semantics, or proofs); and (4) a defense-in-depth checklist (hardware rooting, VMs, egress controls, scoped capability tokens, immutable audit, multi-party authorization, fail-closed rules) plus a proposed research agenda. Critical design decisions — structural over behavioral constraints, fail-closed defaults, and multi-party human authorization to mitigate persuasion and approval fatigue — are asserted and supported by citation to Anthropic's containment write-up, the Off-Switch Game, alignment-faking results, and Yampolskiy's controllability arguments, but not derived or tested. No design decision is justified quantitatively or formally. Key Results: Not stated. The paper reports no measurements, benchmarks, baselines, or empirical outcomes of any kind. Its 'results' are conceptual: the claim that increasing intelligence need not produce increasing authority, the enumeration of nine protected authority domains, and the framing of ZUA as a necessary-but-not-sufficient condition. The central repeated claim — 'can the intelligence convert its own decision to acquire more power into actual additional power without independent authorization?' — is posed as a testable engineering question but is never tested in the paper. Novelty Classification: NEW FORMULATION (partial) / position paper. The genuinely new element is the packaging: a crisp vocabulary ('unilateral authority' as a distinct, separately measurable quantity from intelligence and delegated agency) and the policy framing that regulation should assess authority (what a model can self-authorize) rather than only capability. The substance — external containment, sandboxing, credential separation, kill switches, defense in depth, off-switch incentives, structural-over-behavioral constraints — is a standard combination of pre-existing AI-safety and security-engineering ideas (the paper itself cites Turner et al., Hadfield-Menell et al., Anthropic, and Yampolskiy as its foundations). The toy formalism in Section 18 adds no mathematical content. Rigor & Reproducibility: No ablations, error bars, seeds, or significance tests are applicable or present — there is nothing empirical to reproduce. There is no code, dataset, or artifact release. Methodological concerns: (1) the 'formal statement' is a four-variable table with no axioms, dynamics, or proofs — presenting it as a formal model overstates its content; (2) the paper evaluates nothing, including its own architecture against the adversarial tests it explicitly proposes in Section 20; (3) several references are forward-dated industry documents (an 'International AI Safety Report 2026,' an OpenAI 'Frontier Governance Framework' from May 2026, an Anthropic containment post from May 2026, and a 2026 arXiv containment-verification paper) that could not be independently verified from the text and read as secondary support rather than primary evidence; (4) the argument is a plausibility case built largely on analogy to computer security, with no worked threat model quantifying escape probability or pathway coverage. To its credit, the paper explicitly disclaims mathematical guarantees. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: THEORETICAL (a position/framework paper with no primary experiments and no built system). — Sound: There are no theorems or proofs to check; the central 'invariant' U(t) = 0 is an assertion about an unspecified implementation, and the paper concedes containment can fail via vulnerabilities, human error, or unanticipated strategies. — General: The principle is stated to hold across all AGI/RSI/ASI generations and protected domains, but this generality is stipulated, not derived, and it silently assumes the control plane and human authorizers are themselves reliable and non-subvertible. — Tight: Not applicable — no bounds are proven; the paper instead argues ZUA is 'necessary but not proven sufficient,' a weaker and appropriately hedged claim. — Implementable: Partially — the defense-in-depth checklist maps onto existing cloud-security and agent-sandboxing practice and the paper's policy agenda is actionable for regulators, but nothing here is operationalized as a tool, library, or verified architecture. Deliverable form: paper only; no software artifact, dataset, or reusable proof technique is provided. Strengths: - The intelligence/agency/delegated-authority/unilateral-authority taxonomy is a genuinely useful vocabulary move, cleanly separating concerns that are often conflated in AI-risk discourse, and it translates directly into a regulatory question ('what can the model self-authorize?' vs. 'how capable is it?'). - The paper models intellectual honesty about scope: it explicitly states that ZUA is a necessary architectural condition, not a sufficiency proof, that no escape-proof guarantee exists, and it devotes a section (20) to specifying how the principle should be attacked — including treating every demonstrated escape pathway as an engineering defect rather than a refutation. - The structural-over-behavioral constraint argument (Section 11) is correctly aimed and well-motivated by the cited alignment-faking and power-seeking literature: it relocates safety from model dispositions to externally enforceable boundaries. - The treatment of the human attack surface (Section 14 — persuasion, approval fatigue, single-approver failure) acknowledges the weakest link in any containment scheme, which many containment proposals omit. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors are notably direct: ZUA is 'not a mathematical proof of permanent ASI safety'; no absolute escape-proof guarantee is claimed (citing Yampolskiy's controllability argument); escape via vulnerabilities, side channels, implementation errors, human procedural failure, or unanticipated superintelligent strategies is conceded as possible; the kill switch is acknowledged as reactive and insufficient alone; and defense in depth is stipulated on the admission that no single mechanism is perfect. This confrontation with limitations is a credibility positive. The authors minimize, however, the difficulty of the 'independent verification' and 'independent AI review' steps in the successor-deployment pipeline — who verifies, and against what capability gap, is left open. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - No engagement with the existing literature's depth. The proposal overlaps heavily with prior work on AI boxing, corrigibility, utility indifference, the AI-control agenda, and shutdown-problem follow-ups (e.g., inverted simplicity/TeleKOMP), none of which is cited or compared against; a reviewer cannot tell what ZUA adds beyond vocabulary. - The control plane is an unanalyzed single point of failure. The paper demands the AI never administer its own control plane but never analyzes the control plane's own failure modes: buggy verification, captured or negligent institutions, side channels out of 'independently monitored' infrastructure, or the bootstrapping problem of evaluating a successor smarter than every evaluator. - The 'independent AI review' and 'independent capability evaluation' steps assume the very thing in question — trusted evaluators comparable to the system being evaluated — which recursive self-improvement explicitly undermines. - Delegated authority D(t) is treated as externally benign, but the paper's own Option Two analysis implies that whoever controls D(t) holds enormous power; governance of the human institutions holding the control plane (regulatory capture, race dynamics, state misuse) is unaddressed. - Information-theoretic escape routes are dismissed too quickly: 'read broadly, write narrowly' ignores steganography, covert channels, and influence exerted purely through legitimate outputs (persuasion, code it is authorized to write), the last of which the paper itself flags in Section 20 but never analyzes. - The formal model is vacuous: U(t) = 0 is an invariant over symbols with no semantics, so it cannot be violated, checked, or used to prove anything about a real system. Bottom Line: A practitioner in AI governance or safety policy will gain a clean, quotable framing — regulate authority, not just capability — but anyone seeking technical content (formal guarantees, worked threat models, empirical containment results, or comparison to the established boxing/corrigibility/control literature) will find far stronger ground in the cited primary sources and should treat this as an advocacy white paper, not a research contribution.

Problem & Motivation: The paper addresses fragmentation in real estate technology adoption. PropTech solutions to date have digitized isolated processes — listings, leasing, CRM, facility operations — leaving organizations with duplicated data, inconsistent records, manual reconciliation, and AI that cannot function because enterprise information stays siloed. The intended audience is real estate enterprises, PropTech vendors, and enterprise architects. The gap it targets: prior PropTech literature, per the author, emphasizes smart buildings and digital twins while neglecting the enterprise-software-engineering perspective — how to architect the platform that coordinates cloud infrastructure, data, AI, integration, and governance as one ecosystem. Key Idea: The central insight is an analogy transfer: real estate organizations should be engineered like digital-native software companies, where the platform itself — not individual applications — is the strategic asset. Concretely, this means centralizing AI as a shared enterprise service (LLMs, RAG, semantic search consumed through common interfaces rather than embedded per application), organizing data as domain-owned but centrally governed (data mesh plus fabric, knowledge graphs, MDM), and orchestrating business processes through event-driven BPM engines augmented with contextual AI reasoning. The nine-layer reference architecture in Section 9 is the formalization of this idea. It is a reframing of well-known platform-engineering doctrine for a new domain, not a new architectural mechanism. Methodology: This is a conceptual/vision paper with no algorithm, system, or evaluation methodology. The "method" is argumentation: Sections 2–8 each develop one pillar (platform engineering, cloud-native infrastructure, enterprise integration, AI-as-a-service, data platforms, workflow automation, security/governance), and Section 9 synthesizes them into the layered framework, illustrated by a walk-through of onboarding a newly acquired commercial property. Section 10 speculatively extends the vision to autonomous AI agents and self-healing cloud platforms under a "supervised autonomy" constraint. There is no objective function, no formal model, and no design alternatives compared — critical decisions such as choosing a layered monolithic-style architecture over alternatives (e.g., a federated or service-mesh-dominant topology) are asserted, not justified against trade-offs or evidence. Key Results: Not stated. The paper reports no experiments, measurements, case studies, or quantitative outcomes. Its only concrete deliverable is the qualitative layered architecture and a hypothetical end-to-end scenario. Claims such as "thousands of additional users" during demand peaks or platforms supporting "several hundred commercial properties" are illustrative narratives, not measured results. Novelty Classification: NEW FORMULATION (weak) — the genuine novelty is applying the existing enterprise platform-engineering paradigm to PropTech as a unified domain-specific reference architecture. Everything inside the framework is a standard combination of established ideas: microservices and Kubernetes, IaC, multi-tenancy, domain-driven design, RAG, data mesh, knowledge graphs, MDM, Zero Trust, DevSecOps, BPM. No new algorithm, tool, dataset, or empirical finding is introduced. Rigor & Reproducibility: Not evaluated — the paper contains no experiments, ablations, error bars, seeds, or significance tests by design, as it is a vision paper. Reproducibility is not applicable: no code, data, or artifact is released, and the reference architecture is specified only at narrative depth with no formal notation (no UML, C4 diagrams, or interface contracts in the provided text). No methodological gaming is possible, but correspondingly nothing is falsifiable: the framework is never confronted with a counterexample, a failed migration, or a cost figure. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: THEORETICAL (a conceptual framework with no primary experimental or deployed artifact). - Sound: The argument is internally coherent but rests on unstated assumptions — that organizations can afford platform-engineering teams and multi-cloud complexity, and that integration is the binding constraint rather than cost, regulation, or organizational politics. - General: The framework applies broadly across property types, but the paper itself concedes (in future work) that healthcare, logistics, and mixed-use contexts may require different evolutions — the domain-specific content beyond generic enterprise architecture is thin. - Tight: Not applicable; there are no bounds or formal claims, and the framework is vacuous in the sense that nearly any enterprise platform could be described in its nine layers. - Implementable: Partially — a competent enterprise architecture team could derive a concrete target architecture from it, but no reference implementation, interface specification, or migration roadmap is provided, and no follow-up operationalization exists. The paper delivers no software artifact, dataset, or tool; it stops at paper form. Strengths: - The AI-as-a-shared-enterprise-service argument (Section 5) is the sharpest part: framing LLMs, RAG, and semantic search as centralized platform services with unified governance, rather than per-application features, is a genuinely useful architectural position for any data-fragmented industry, not just real estate. - The paper correctly identifies a real and under-addressed gap in the PropTech literature — the enterprise-software-engineering view versus the dominant smart-building/digital-twin focus — and the lifecycle framing (acquisition through disposition) is a sensible organizing device. - The treatment of data heterogeneity (transactional consistency vs. streaming sensor data vs. unstructured BIM/document content) and the data-mesh-plus-fabric governance balance reflect accurate, current understanding of data platform practice. - The "supervised autonomy" position in Section 10 — pushing back on full automation for high-stakes, legally consequential decisions — is a responsible framing of the agentic-AI trajectory. The conclusion concedes the work is conceptual and lists its own gaps as future work: quantitative PropTech maturity models, architectural benchmarking methodologies, comparative analyses across facility types, and reference implementations. This is a direct confrontation of the paper's main weakness — that it validates nothing — and is a credibility positive, though the acknowledgment arrives without any interim grounding (not even a single illustrative case). Analyst-Identified Gaps: - Zero empirical grounding: not one real organization, deployment, cost figure, or failure case is analyzed, so the claimed benefits (reduced technical debt, faster innovation, better AI outcomes) are entirely speculative. A single well-documented case study or retrospective of a PropTech platform migration would have transformed the paper's evidentiary value. - No engagement with the substantial existing PropTech and CRE-technology literature beyond a one-sentence dismissal of smart-buildings/digital-twins work; the related-work treatment for the paper's own domain is essentially absent (the 27 references are almost entirely generic software engineering texts). - No cost/benefit or migration-path discussion: the framework presumes greenfield-style adoption, whereas the stated motivation is organizations burdened by legacy fragmentation — the hardest scenario, which the paper never addresses (no strangler-fig strategy, no sequencing guidance). - The framework's alternatives are never compared: why nine layers rather than a hexagonal or cell-based architecture, why centralized AI services versus federated MLOps, why data mesh's decentralized ownership alongside a centrally governed fabric — the tensions between these choices are not surfaced. - No discussion of organizational feasibility: who funds the platform team, how domain teams are incentivized, what happens to vendor contracts — the very failure modes that kill platform initiatives in practice. Bottom Line: A practitioner architecting a PropTech platform will find a competent, readable checklist of mainstream enterprise patterns organized around the real estate lifecycle, but a researcher or architect seeking evidence, formalism, or anything not already covered better by cloud-native and data-platform literature (Bass, Newman, Kleppmann) will find nothing here that a stronger, validated treatment does not already deliver.

Problem & Motivation: Organizations deploying AI phishing detection face a structural tension: effective detection requires ingesting and processing email content, URLs, metadata, attachments, and user behavior — which is precisely the personal-data processing that privacy law constrains. The paper also flags the AI arms race (generative AI producing convincing, personalized phishing) as pushing organizations toward collecting even more data. The authors argue prior work is overwhelmingly technical (accuracy, throughput) and neglects whether such detection can be deployed lawfully, ethically, and proportionally. This gap is real, though it is closer to a well-trodden topic in AI-governance literature than the paper suggests. The intended audience appears to be cybersecurity practitioners, policymakers, and legal scholars, particularly in India, where DPDP Act 2023 compliance questions are newly live. Key Idea: The core move is framing AI phishing detection as a data-protection compliance problem rather than a classification problem — i.e., asking whether detection performance can be achieved with data that is minimized, purpose-limited, and subject to human oversight. This is a framing, not a technical insight; there is no reconstructible algorithmic trick here. The paper itself concedes the relationship between feature selection and data minimisation (Section 3.5), which is the closest it comes to an original conceptual link, and it does not develop that link formally or empirically. Methodology: The paper describes a four-stage design: (1) literature review, (2) analysis of AI detection methods, (3) performance assessment, and (4) legal-ethical analysis culminating in a responsible-AI framework. The technical portion is a generic supervised-classification pipeline — data collection, pre-processing, feature extraction (URL length, special-character counts, IP presence, subdomain count, HTTPS usage, redirection patterns), 80/20 train/test split, training of Logistic Regression, Decision Tree, SVM, Random Forest, and Neural Network models, and evaluation via accuracy, precision, recall, and F1. The legal-ethical portion is a principles-based doctrinal review covering lawfulness, data minimisation, purpose limitation, transparency, retention, automated decision-making, explainability, bias, and accountability. Critically, the pipeline was not run: the methodology is written in conditional language ("the technical part of the research may include..."), and Section 3.7 explicitly states the Table 2 values are presented "to demonstrate how performance can be compared... rather than to report results obtained from the experimental implementation of this study." The responsible-AI framework (Section 3.9) is a checklist of eight principles with no operationalization — no mapping of which principle addresses which identified risk, no cost analysis, and no mechanism for the acknowledged privacy-vs-accuracy trade-off. Key Results: No original empirical results. The illustrative Table 2 reports Random Forest at 98.1% accuracy / 97.7% F1, Neural Network 97.4% / 97.05%, SVM 96.3% / 95.6%, Decision Tree 95.6% / 94.95%, and Logistic Regression 94.2% / 93.3% — but the paper disclaims these as its own measurements, and no dataset, source, or experimental condition is given for them. The substantive "findings" are qualitative: (a) behavior-based and real-time detection methods create the greatest privacy risk; (b) generative AI simultaneously aids detection and empowers attackers; (c) XAI explanations may be incomplete or unusable by non-experts; (d) privacy-preserving/federated learning does not automatically guarantee privacy. The legal comparison (DPDP Act 2023 vs. GDPR) is presented at the level of shared principles — lawfulness, transparency, purpose limitation, minimisation — with no divergences, enforcement cases, or sector-specific guidance identified. Novelty Classification: NEW PROBLEM framing at best, weakly: the security-vs-privacy tension in AI phishing detection is discussed in existing AI-governance and XAI-for-cybersecurity surveys (including the paper's own references [2], [3], [8]). The literature table (Table 1, 15 method families) is a competent but derivative synthesis. The comparative DPDP/GDPR angle applied specifically to phishing detection is the least-covered combination, but it is treated at textbook depth. Nothing here is a new method, dataset, system, or empirical finding; this is a position/review paper whose individual components are all standard. Rigor & Reproducibility: Not reproducible in any technical sense: no dataset named, no code, no trained model, no experiment executed, and the only quantitative table is explicitly illustrative with unattributed numbers. There are no ablations, error bars, seeds, or significance tests — appropriately, since there is nothing to test. The legal analysis cites primary sources (DPDP Act 2023, GDPR) but performs no close reading of either statute's text, no analysis of DPDP rules/notifications, and no case law or regulatory guidance. Methodological concerns: (1) the performance table invites readers to treat unattributed numbers as findings; (2) the methodology section describes a hypothetical experiment in the past/present tense in places, blurring claimed vs. measured work; (3) the concluding recommendations (minimise data, ensure human oversight) are asserted without evidence that they are achievable at operational accuracy levels — the privacy/accuracy trade-off is acknowledged but never quantified. Peer-review provenance is unclear; JEPCS appears to be a low-visibility venue, and the 2026 dates suggest very recent publication without external validation of the legal analysis. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: THEORETICAL (a conceptual/doctrinal review with no primary experimental claim; the ML pipeline is described, not run). Sound: The normative argument is internally consistent but not argued against counterpositions (e.g., legitimate-interest bases for security processing under GDPR Art. 6(1)(f), or DPDP's security-exception provisions), so it reads as assertion. General: The principles-based framing applies broadly to any AI security monitoring, but that generality comes from vagueness — no domain-specific legal constraints on email interception (e.g., India's IT Act, wiretap law, or ePrivacy) are considered. Tight: Not applicable — no formal results; the "recommendations" are unboundedly loose (no thresholds for acceptable data retention, no criteria for proportionality). Implementable: The eight-principle framework is a checklist, not an artifact; no follow-up operationalization is provided. Deliverable: paper only — no library, dataset, tool, or reusable legal-analysis technique. Strengths: - The explicit disclaimer that Table 2 is illustrative rather than experimental is a credibility-positive act of intellectual honesty that many survey papers omit. - Table 1's systematic pairing of each of 15 detection method families with its specific privacy/surveillance cost (e.g., behavior-based detection's monitoring burden, ensemble methods' explainability loss) is a genuinely useful mapping for readers thinking about deployment risk. - The observation that feature selection and data minimisation are the same operation viewed from technical and legal standpoints (Section 3.5) is a sharp, underexploited conceptual link. - The India-DPDP angle is timely and locally relevant; most AI-security governance literature is EU/US-centric. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors acknowledge that privacy-preserving learning does not automatically guarantee privacy, that XAI explanations may be incomplete or inaccessible to ordinary users, that human-in-the-loop review raises cost and slows detection, and that privacy-by-design may trade off against detection accuracy. They also implicitly acknowledge the absence of experiments by disclaiming the performance table. However, they do not confront the largest limitation — that the paper's central legal comparison is conducted at slogan level — and the conclusion asserts that stronger regulation is needed without specifying what regulation, for whom, or against what failure mode. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - No original empirical work whatsoever, despite a methodology section (Figures 1–2, Equations 1–4, Table 2) formatted to suggest an experimental study; a reader skimming figures and tables would wrongly infer an experiment was run. - The DPDP-vs-GDPR comparison never identifies a single divergence, conflict, or enforcement risk — the entire comparative claim reduces to "both laws share similar principles," which any textbook states. - No engagement with the strongest counterargument to its framework: cybersecurity processing typically relies on legitimate-interest/legal-obligation bases that may permit broad monitoring; the paper never tests its principles against the actual statutory carve-outs. - No named dataset, no citation for the Table 2 values, and no baseline comparison to published phishing-detection benchmarks, so the technical component cannot be verified or situated. - The proposed responsible-AI framework is not evaluated even at the level of a case study, expert interview, or hypothetical deployment — the paper's own prescription (that detection and privacy can coexist without compromise) is the claim most in need of evidence and receives none. - Missing related work on legally grounded security-privacy analysis (e.g., data-protection impact assessments for security monitoring, European supervisory guidance on employee monitoring), which directly addresses the stated problem. Bottom Line: A practitioner seeking actionable guidance on compliant AI phishing detection will not find it here — the legal analysis stays at the level of shared principles, the technical component was never run, and stronger alternatives exist (the XAI-for-cybersecurity surveys and phishing-detection reviews the paper itself cites, plus dedicated DPDP compliance literature) covering the same ground with more substance.

Problem & Motivation: The paper addresses intrusion detection for university campus networks, where traffic is dominated by benign teaching/research activity and a few common attack types, while rare but high-impact attacks (covert penetration, data theft) are severely underrepresented. Three gaps are claimed: (1) single-scale feature extraction misses local bursts versus global behavioral shifts, (2) class imbalance causes models to fail on minority attack classes, and (3) unrestricted use of traffic fields containing IPs, ports, and timestamps creates privacy risk for faculty and students. The work is framed around Chinese higher-education policy ('ideological and political education' cyberspace governance), motivated by the 'bucket effect' — campus security equals its weakest detection category. Key Idea: The only identifiable core insight is that a privacy screen at the input (delete identifying fields), multi-scale convolutional feature extraction (Inception-style parallel kernels), BiLSTM temporal modeling, and Focal Loss can be composed into one pipeline and narratively mapped onto the SOR (Stimulus-Organism-Response) model from 1974 environmental psychology. The SOR mapping itself is a framing/metaphor rather than a technical mechanism — each component (multi-scale CNN, BiLSTM, Focal Loss, feature filtering) is a pre-existing technique, and SOR generates no testable prediction or algorithmic change. Methodology: Three-layer pipeline. (S) Stimulus layer: static feature filtering that removes IP addresses, port numbers, and timestamps, retaining protocol type, packet-length distributions, inter-arrival times, and direction ratios — described qualitatively with no field-level algorithm or formal privacy guarantee (explicitly not differential privacy). (O) Organism layer: parallel 3×3, 5×5, 7×7 convolutional branches fused via concatenation or weighted aggregation (Equation 1 leaves the fusion operator φ unspecified), followed by a BiLSTM whose LSTM cell equations are reproduced from the standard literature (Equation 2). (R) Response layer: Softmax classification trained with Focal Loss, FL(pt) = −α(1−pt)^γ log(pt) (Equation 3, attributed to Lin et al. 2017). Data preprocessing: remove missing/infinite values, deduplicate, standardize; 7:1.5:1.5 train/validation/test split. Critical design decisions: (a) dropping timestamps/ports as 'privacy' fields — weakly justified, since port numbers are among the most discriminative features in these benchmarks and the paper never quantifies the accuracy cost of the privacy screen; (b) kernel sizes 3/5/7 — not ablated per-branch; (c) Focal Loss hyperparameters α and γ — values not stated. The 'adaptive class optimization' is plain Focal Loss; no comparison to SMOTE, class-balanced loss, or cost-sensitive baselines is run despite the paper citing all three as alternatives. Key Results: On CIC-IDS2017: 98.84% accuracy, Weighted-F1 0.9882, but Macro-Precision 0.8367, Macro-Recall 0.6915, Macro-F1 0.7096 — a ~28-point gap between weighted and macro recall showing rare classes are largely missed. On CSE-CIC-IDS2018: 99.98% accuracy with Macro and Weighted averages near 1.000 (plausible for a DDoS-dominated dataset where the majority class is easy). UNSW-NB15: only qualitative discussion — performance is 'lower', with Analysis, Backdoor, and Worms categories 'almost undetectable'; no numbers are printed. Robustness on CIC-IDS2017: accuracy 83.77% at 50% feature-missing rate, 56.42% at Gaussian noise level 0.10. Ablation: 90.0% (single traffic data) → 92.0% (multi-source fusion) → 94.0% (+multi-scale) → 95.0% (full model) — internally inconsistent with the reported 98.84% headline, and the ablation stages ('single traffic data', 'multi-source data fusion') do not correspond to the architecture's actual modules. No external baselines (no SVM, no random forest, no published deep IDS like the CNN-LSTM or ensemble works cited as [7, 8]) are compared on any dataset. Evaluation is at standard benchmark scale on public datasets, not campus traffic. Novelty Classification: NEW FORMULATION at best (applying the SOR psychological model as a design metaphor to IDS) plus an ENGINEERING OPTIMIZATION / straightforward combination of existing techniques. Genuinely novel: the SOR-to-pipeline mapping, which is conceptual labeling rather than mechanism. Not novel: multi-scale CNN kernels, BiLSTM sequence modeling, and Focal Loss for imbalanced classification are all standard, and privacy 'awareness' as field deletion predates this work. The paper itself concedes privacy-aware feature processing already exists [19, 20]. Rigor & Reproducibility: Weak. Ablations exist but are incoherent: the ablation endpoint (95.0%) contradicts the headline result (98.84%) on presumably the same dataset, and the ablation stages describe data sources not model components, so no component's individual contribution is actually established. No baselines against prior published methods. No seeds, error bars, or significance tests. No hyperparameters (learning rate, α, γ, layer sizes, sequence length). No code, data splits, or model release. The Focal Loss citation [29] points to the wrong reference (a CSE-CIC-IDS2018 survey); the correct Lin et al. citation appears later as [33] — a sign of weak editorial control. Reporting only qualitative UNSW-NB15 results while claiming three-dataset validation overstates coverage. The near-saturated CSE-CIC-IDS2018 result (99.98%) is uninformative given known label leakage/simplification issues in that benchmark, which the paper does not discuss. Deployability: EMPIRICAL profile. Practical: Yes in principle — a CNN-BiLSTM runs on commodity hardware, though no model size, training time, or inference throughput is reported. Efficient: Not evaluated — BiLSTM over fused multi-scale feature sequences is typically slower than tree ensembles or CNN-only IDS, and no cost comparison is given. Effective: Only partially — accuracy on two datasets is high, but Macro-Recall of 0.6915 on CIC-IDS2017 shows the stated problem (minority attack detection) is largely unsolved, and UNSW-NB15 evidence is anecdotal. Scalable: Not tested or claimed beyond benchmark scale; no campus-network deployment. The work delivers a paper only — no artifact, no trained model, no reusable technique beyond a framing vocabulary. Strengths: (1) The paper reports Macro vs. Weighted metrics side by side and explicitly names the minority-class failure rather than hiding it behind headline accuracy — honest reporting that many IDS papers omit. (2) The robustness experiments (feature missing up to 50%, Gaussian noise to 0.10) probe degradation modes most IDS evaluations skip. (3) The privacy-by-field-removal design, while simple, is at least stated as a measurable design constraint (detection without identifying fields) that future work can quantify against. (4) The discussion correctly attributes the UNSW-NB15 failure to dataset heterogeneity and class scarcity rather than overclaiming. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors acknowledge: performance on extremely scarce categories 'remains insufficient' (Macro-Recall 0.6915); UNSW-NB15 results are worse, with Analysis, Backdoor, and Worms nearly undetectable; dataset characteristics (traffic distribution, imbalance, feature separability) strongly condition results; and future work is needed on differential privacy, federated learning, and real campus deployment. They confront the minority-class failure directly, which is a credibility positive, but they do not acknowledge the absence of baselines, the ablation inconsistency, or the unquantified cost of the privacy screen. Analyst-Identified Gaps: (1) No baseline comparison of any kind — the reader cannot tell whether 98.84%/0.7096 Macro-F1 is better than a 2018 CNN-LSTM or even a random forest on the same split. (2) The ablation contradicts the headline result (95.0% vs. 98.84%), undermining the entire component-contribution argument. (3) The privacy claim is unevaluated: no experiment shows performance with versus without the sensitive fields, so the paper cannot demonstrate that its 'privacy-aware' layer is anything more than the standard preprocessing step (which already discards non-numeric features anyway). (4) Port number removal likely explains a large accuracy cost never quantified. (5) No SOR-derived hypothesis is tested — the theory is unfalsifiable decoration. (6) The 99.98% CSE-CIC-IDS2018 result ignores known benchmark pathologies (trivially separable DDoS flows). (7) Timestamps discarded entirely, yet the BiLSTM is claimed to model 'temporal dependencies' — the sequence construction from flow features is never explained. (8) The single author's background (educational technology, NCRE certificate) and the SOR/education framing suggest limited IDS domain expertise; the miscited Focal Loss reference and duplicated references ([26]/[30], [20]/[32]/[29]) corroborate weak peer-review of the manuscript. Bottom Line: A practitioner in IDS gains almost nothing here — the architecture is an off-the-shelf CNN-BiLSTM with Focal Loss, the evaluation lacks baselines and is internally inconsistent, and the SOR framing adds vocabulary rather than mechanism, so stronger alternatives covering the same datasets (e.g., the cited Khan 2022 CSE-IDS or standard ensemble baselines) should be read instead.

Problem & Motivation: Shipbuilding is a canonical Engineer-to-Order (ETO) industry: every vessel is designed and built to a unique customer specification, documentation matures in parallel with procurement, and schedules are disrupted by welding rework, crane contention between parallel orders, long-lead equipment delays, and stochastic operation times. The paper argues that classical MRP II (assumes complete, frozen BOMs), APS systems (produce deterministic plans for known order sets), and discrete-event simulation (evaluates plans but cannot generate or adapt them) are all structurally mismatched to this environment. The addressed gap is that existing surveys either cover shipbuilding digitalization generally or RL for scheduling generically, with no integrated treatment of RL specifically for shipbuilding logistics; the authors target researchers and technology planners, including those deciding on adoption at Russian shipyards. Key Idea: The core (synthetic, not algorithmic) insight is that RL's advantage in ETO scheduling comes from amortization — an agent pays a large one-time training cost (e.g., ~10,000 episodes, several machine-hours for PPO) in exchange for millisecond (<100 ms) re-planning decisions and cross-configuration generalization (e.g., a GIN+PPO agent trained on 5-machine shops outperforming dispatching rules on 10- and 15-machine configurations without retraining), and that digital twins, standardized under ISO 23247, are the prerequisite safe training substrate because only they allow repeated experiments without halting real production. This is a framing claim rather than a new technique. Methodology: This is a narrative/systematic-style literature review of Russian- and English-language sources from 2018–2026 (no PRISMA-style protocol, database list, or inclusion/exclusion criteria are reported). The pipeline is: (1) characterize ETO shipbuilding logistics and its KPIs — makespan with tardiness penalties and finite inter-operation buffer capacity, equipment utilization (cranes), and workload leveling — drawing on case studies of Norwegian yards; (2) classify and describe the three method families (FIFO/SPT/LIFO/MST rules; GA/PSO/simulated annealing/tabu search; DQN, A2C/A3C, PPO formalized as an MDP); (3) survey digital-twin architectures — hybrid DES-optimization stacks versus direct RL-agent embedding in a DT — anchored in ISO 23247-1:2021 and a NAVANTIA Ferrol pilot case; (4) produce a qualitative 3×5 comparison table (heuristics/metaheuristics/RL × adaptivity/scalability/interpretability/training cost/real-time) with ±/○ ratings; (5) enumerate gaps and future directions (multi-agent RL, transfer learning, generative-AI scenario synthesis). No objective function is derived, no experiment is run, and no quantitative aggregation methodology for the comparison table is stated. Critical design choices: using secondhand pairwise comparisons instead of a common benchmark (acknowledged as forced by the field), and weighting real-time adaptivity as the decisive criterion (plausible for dispatching but under-argued against long-horizon planning use cases). Key Results: The paper reports no new measurements; headline numbers are imported from primary studies. Cited results: a PPO agent trained in a DES environment reduced mean tardiness by 18–24% versus the best of four dispatching rules (SSPT, ATCS, MDD, COVERT) and setup time by 12–15% under high processing-time variability [Nam et al. 2024]; a GIN+PPO agent beat heuristics by 15–22% on makespan and 30–40% on computation time for panel block assembly lines, with the advantage growing above 50 blocks [Zhou et al. 2023]; an RL agent with a CNN autoencoder in a Unity 3D digital twin beat human experts by ~15% on pre-erection block placement, cutting plan generation from weeks to hours [Kim & Yang 2023]; a GA-SLHH hyper-heuristic cut transport time by 37% for cruise-ship cabin modules [Li et al. 2024]; CP-DES hybrid reduced makespan 12–17% versus manual planning in a deterministic setting [Kwak et al. 2025]; a DRL agent generalized from a 5-machine training configuration to 10 and 15 machines [Zhou & Rose 2025], and a five-algorithm DRL study showed PPO best on mean tardiness across 243 production configurations [Lei et al. 2024]. RL beats genetic programming by 5–15% on dynamic JSS but loses on static full-information instances [Xu et al. 2025]. The baselines underlying these numbers are reasonably current (2023–2026 sources), but they are drawn from heterogeneous problems, so the paper's summary claim — RL outperforms heuristics by 12–24% on makespan/tardiness with 1–2 orders of magnitude faster decisions — is a patchwork, not a controlled result. The paper itself states that direct comparison on a unified shipbuilding benchmark does not exist. Novelty Classification: The contribution is a survey/comparative synthesis, not a NEW METHOD, NEW DATASET, or NEW SYSTEM; the genuinely novel element is narrow and regional — the authors' claim to be the first Russian-language review jointly covering shipbuilding logistics, deep RL, and digital twins with 2025–2026 sources. The methodological content (MDP formalization, DQN/A2C/PPO descriptions, ISO 23247 framing) is a standard assembly of known ideas applied to a new domain pairing; the comparative table is competent execution of a known review pattern. Rigor & Reproducibility: No ablations, seeds, error bars, or significance tests are possible or reported — the paper runs nothing. No search methodology (databases, query strings, screening counts) is documented, so the "systematic" label is not verifiable. No code, environment, or model is released by these authors; they do highlight the single public ship-block scheduling dataset (Chen 2026, Mendeley Data, DOI 10.17632/4ds6t24mx2.1) and openly flag reproducibility failures of DRL studies (hyperparameter and environment dependence, closed code). Methodological concerns: (1) the central comparative claim rests on cross-study aggregation over incompatible benchmarks — a Goodhart-style risk the authors acknowledge but still summarize as a 12–24% figure; (2) the qualitative table's ratings have no stated elicitation procedure; (3) several quantitative anchors (HD Hyundai–Siemens platform) are vendor/press announcements with no published metrics, which the paper does flag but still cites as evidence of industrial momentum. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: the paper itself is a survey, but it makes empirical claims about methods others ran, so I apply the EMPIRICAL check to the surveyed technology as filtered through this review. - Practical: PPO/DQN scheduling agents run on commodity hardware after training, but require a digital-twin/DES environment whose construction at a real yard is a major project, as the NAVANTIA and HD Hyundai cases show. - Efficient: Training costs ~10,000 episodes (hours of machine time) per problem; inference is <100 ms versus minutes for a GA rerun — favorable for dispatching, unfavorable if the planning problem changes frequently. - Effective: Evidence covers workshop-level proxies (block placement, panel assembly, parallel-machine welding) on simulated or single-cell deployments; no shipyard-wide KPI validation exists, as the reviewed Bordbar et al. 2026 survey also concedes. - Scalable: Only claimed via small generalization tests (5→10/15 machines; 243 configurations; >50 blocks); nothing at the several-hundred-concurrent-blocks scale the paper itself says matters for real yards. The work delivers no software artifact, dataset, or reusable technique of its own — it stops at paper form (a literature synthesis with a comparison table and research agenda). Strengths: - Honest gap analysis: the paper explicitly names the field's binding constraints — one public dataset, no unified benchmark, non-reproducible DRL results, untested robustness to structural changes — rather than overselling RL readiness; this is unusually direct for a domain review. - The framing of digital twins as the normative prerequisite for safe RL training, tied to ISO 23247 and a three-level maturity model (monitoring → analytics → predictive control) verified at NAVANTIA Ferrol, gives practitioners a concrete adoption scaffold. - Useful systematization of otherwise scattered shipyard-specific evidence (Korean block-placement DT-RL, Spanish robotized pre-assembly cell, Norwegian ETO resource-planning DT architecture, the 2026 HD Hyundai–Siemens platform), differentiating shipbuilding's finite-buffer, crane-contention constraints from generic job-shop literature. - The distinction between Innovate-to-Order and Redesign-to-Order uncertainty profiles, imported from the Norwegian supply-chain literature, is a genuinely useful lens for matching algorithm choice to uncertainty type. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state that (1) most DT/AI shipbuilding papers prioritize architecture over longitudinal yard-level KPI validation; (2) industrial data confidentiality limits open datasets (only one public dataset exists); (3) no common benchmark permits correct cross-method comparison; (4) DRL reproducibility is poor due to hyperparameter and environment sensitivity; (5) robustness of RL agents to structural system changes (layout changes, new equipment, new order types) is unstudied for shipbuilding. They confront these limitations directly — this is a credibility positive — though they minimize the consequence for their own headline numbers: if no unified benchmark exists, the consolidated "RL wins by 12–24%" conclusion should be framed as provisional, which the conclusion section does not fully do. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - No documented review protocol (databases, queries, screening, PRISMA flow), so coverage claims for 2018–2026 cannot be audited; the source list (~26 items) suggests a curated rather than exhaustive search. - The ±/○ comparison table has no stated rating methodology, no sensitivity analysis, and its interpretability and training-cost scores for metaheuristics vs. RL are asserted rather than derived from any measurement. - The "RL vs. metaheuristics" comparison for shipbuilding rests on a single adjacent-domain survey [Xu et al. 2025]; the paper admits few direct comparisons exist but still concludes RL superiority in the stochastic regime. - Cost of building and maintaining a shipyard digital twin — the paper's own declared prerequisite — is never quantified, so the total cost of the RL path (DT construction + agent training + integration with ERP/MES) is invisible, which matters for the stated practical goal of guiding Russian shipyard adoption decisions. - Several "results" of industrial momentum (Cohere–Hanwha, HD Hyundai–Siemens) are 2026 press items with no metrics; treating them as evidence of RL effectiveness conflates announcement with validation. - Sim-to-real transfer — whether agents trained in Unity 3D or DES twins hold on physical yards — is not discussed as a distinct risk, despite being arguably the central deployment barrier. Bottom Line: For a Russian-speaking production-logistics researcher or shipyard technology planner this is the fastest available route into the intersection of DRL scheduling, digital twins, and shipbuilding pilots, and its gap analysis alone is worth the read; for anyone who already knows the RL-for-scheduling literature (Pugliese 2025, Xu 2025, Bordbar 2026 cover the same ground with more methodological transparency), it offers little beyond localization and can be skipped.
