Problem & Motivation: HR departments in Industry 4.0 conditions face rising automation pressure, expanding "people data" across the employee lifecycle, and competitive labor markets, yet AI adoption in HRM outpaces the field's understanding of when it works, when it fails, and under what governance conditions. The review addresses four research questions: (RQ1) the main AI applications in candidate attraction, selection, and performance evaluation; (RQ2) the main benefits; (RQ3) the challenges and risks; and (RQ4) the organizational conditions for successful integration. The intended audience is business administration practitioners and HR strategists; the review also flags a contextual gap concerning AI-HRM evidence from developing economies and includes a Greek-market observation (more than 7 in 10 Greek companies are poorly informed about AI-in-HR applications, per a cited PwB survey). Key Idea: There is no single novel technical idea. The organizing thesis is that AI in HRM is a socio-technical phenomenon whose value is realized only under a hybrid, human-in-the-loop governance model—the "automation–augmentation paradox" framing borrowed from Raisch & Krakowski (2021)—where AI handles high-volume, pattern-based tasks (screening, outlier detection, workflow analysis) while humans retain judgment over high-stakes, context-dependent decisions. This framing is imported from the existing literature, not developed by the author. Methodology: The paper is a narrative literature review. The pipeline is: keyword searches on Google Scholar, Scopus, and ScienceDirect (terms such as "artificial intelligence in HRM," "recruitment and artificial intelligence," "workplace surveillance," "ethical issues of AI in human resources"); a 2017–2025 date window with selective older theoretical sources; inclusion criteria of topical relevance, peer-reviewed or academically prestigious publication, and clear theoretical/research orientation; exclusion of non-HRM-relevant, undocumented, non-English/Greek, and non-academic sources. The body synthesizes findings thematically: a brief AI history and taxonomy (narrow/general/superintelligence; symbolic vs. connectionist paradigms), AI in recruitment (ATS/resume parsing, chatbots, predictive analytics, video-interview analysis), AI in performance management and continuous evaluation, then seven application areas (health and safety, employee comfort, productivity measurement, payroll automation, real-time feedback, HR digitization, organizational network analysis, organizational design), closing with a benefits-and-challenges synthesis, discussion, and conclusions answering the four RQs. No objective function, algorithm, or formal framework is proposed—by design, given the genre. Critical design decisions: (1) narrative rather than systematic review methodology is stated but not justified against alternatives, and no screening counts or corpus inventory are reported; (2) a 2017–2025 window chosen to capture recent developments is reasonable for a fast-moving field; (3) inclusion of Greek-language grey-market material (a Greek company survey) adds local relevance but sits uneasily with the academic-source exclusion criterion. Key Results: Not applicable in the quantitative sense—this is a review, not an experiment, so it reports no accuracy, F1, speedup, or benchmark numbers of its own. The headline secondary statistics it relays are: 86% of senior HR leaders expect predictive recruitment/retention models to significantly transform workforce strategy by 2030 (WEF 2025); top-quartile talent-productivity companies achieve more than 3× the revenue per employee, attributed partly to AI-based talent analytics (McKinsey 2025); Siemens/PwC projections of €420B+ annual contribution to the European economy and $15.7T globally from AI by 2030; and a Greek survey (People of Business) showing >70% of Greek firms poorly informed about AI in HR while >80% expect significant future impact. The qualitative "results" are the four RQ answers: AI applications concentrate where decisions are repetitive, metrics are measurable, and data volume is high (resume screening, chatbots, algorithmic matching, continuous monitoring); benefits cluster into efficiency, decision-quality, and strategic repositioning of HR; risks cluster into bias, opacity, privacy/surveillance, and employee acceptance; and integration success hinges on data governance, strategic alignment, infrastructure, managerial capability, and ethical/human oversight. These are claims synthesized from the literature, not measurements made by this paper. Novelty Classification: SURVEY (with substantive synthesis intent) — the contribution is a thematic consolidation, not a NEW METHOD, NEW DATASET, NEW FORMULATION, or NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING. Genuinely novel content is minimal: the topic (AI in recruitment and performance management) is saturated with prior reviews—several of which (Pan & Froese 2022, Vrontis et al. 2022, Hunkenschroer & Luetge 2022, Albassam 2023) are the review's own backbone sources. The only mildly distinctive element is the inclusion of Greek-market adoption data and a broad lifecycle sweep extending into safety, comfort, payroll, ONA, and organizational design, which is a standard breadth-over-depth combination of existing surveys. Rigor & Reproducibility: Weak by the standards of a systematic review, though typical for a narrative MBA dissertation. The search strategy is described (databases, keyword combinations, date range, inclusion/exclusion criteria), but there is no PRISMA-style flow, no count of identified/screened/included studies, no corpus table, and no quality-appraisal step, so the review is not reproducible. There are no ablations, error bars, seeds, or significance tests (none would apply), but also no systematic quality weighting of the evidence—vendor reports (McKinsey, PwC, Siemens, EY, IBM, Oracle/HR Research Institute), conference papers, LinkedIn posts (Schawbel 2023; van Niekerk 2023), a WIRED article, and bachelor's theses (Savola & Troqe 2019) are cited alongside peer-reviewed journals with equal narrative standing. No code, data, or artifacts exist or are released. A methodological concern: several cited statistics are self-reported by consultancies with a commercial interest in AI adoption, and the review passes them through without source-critical assessment. Some citation entries show errors (e.g., Tambe, Cappelli & Yakubovich 2019 and Cappelli et al. 2018 share the same DOI; "RąbKettler & Lehnervp" misspells the authors; an "Raghavan et al., 2019" in-text citation corresponds to a 2020 FAccT reference), which weakens confidence in citation handling. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL is not applicable in the experimental sense; this is a SURVEY/THEORETICAL-synthesis profile with no primary experiments, no built system, and no deployment. Applying the empirical check loosely: Practical: Not applicable—no artifact is produced; the recommended practices (bias audits, human-in-the-loop review, data governance) are implementable by organizations using commercial AI-HR tools. Efficient: Not evaluated—no cost or performance figures are generated by the paper itself; the implementation-cost concern for SMEs is noted qualitatively. Effective: The evidence that AI-HRM "works" is entirely secondhand and largely cross-sectional or conceptual, as the review itself concedes; the paper does not and cannot demonstrate effectiveness. Scalable: Not tested or testable at this paper's level; scalability claims come from the cited vendor literature. The work delivers no software artifact, dataset, or reusable technique—it stops at paper form. Strengths: - Balanced risk treatment: unlike many practitioner-facing AI-in-HR pieces, the review consistently pairs each claimed benefit (screening speed, consistency, real-time feedback) with its documented failure mode (bias inheritance from historical data, surveillance legitimation, procedural-justice backlash), and engages serious critical sources (He 2017 on AI's inability to handle moral ambiguity; Cappelli et al. 2018 on uncertain payback). - Broad lifecycle coverage: the sweep beyond the usual recruitment focus into payroll automation, occupational safety, ergonomic comfort, ONA, and organizational design gives a fuller map of the AI-HRM application space than recruitment-only reviews. - Honest gap identification: the conclusions explicitly name the field's weaknesses—preponderance of cross-sectional, conceptual, developed-country evidence; lack of longitudinal work on attitudes, fairness perceptions, and trust—which is an accurate self-assessment of the evidence base. - Local contextual contribution: the Greek-market data point (low awareness, high expected impact) is a small but genuinely useful addition for a regional audience otherwise absent from the Anglophone literature. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The author explicitly acknowledges: (1) the evidence base is dominated by short-term effects, cross-sectional, conceptual, or exploratory designs, making causal inference impossible; (2) geographic bias—most evidence comes from developed countries, with low- and middle-income contexts (Africa, South Asia) underrepresented; (3) implementation is contingent on data quality, infrastructure, digital maturity, leadership commitment, and change management, so benefits are not automatic; (4) risks of bias amplification, transparency deficits, privacy erosion, depersonalization, high costs for SMEs, and employee resistance. These are confronted directly rather than minimized—a credibility positive. Notably, the author does not acknowledge the methodological limits of the review itself (narrative, non-reproducible, uncritical sourcing of vendor statistics). Analyst-Identified Gaps: - No systematic-review protocol: without documented study counts, search-date logs, and a corpus inventory, selection bias in which studies were included cannot be assessed, and the review cannot be replicated or updated. - Unequal evidentiary sourcing: consultancy white papers, LinkedIn essays, a WIRED news piece, and bachelor's theses are synthesized at the same level as peer-reviewed journal articles, and the macroeconomic figures (€420B, $15.7T, 3× revenue per employee) are relayed uncritically from parties with commercial stakes—this is the single largest rigor deficit. - No critical appraisal of the technical claims underlying the reviewed tools: assertions that video-interview AI can "assess personality traits" from facial expressions are presented as application descriptions without noting that this line of technology is scientifically contested and has faced regulatory pushback (e.g., the EU AI Act's treatment of emotion recognition in employment); the review cites Raghavan et al. and Buolamwini & Gebru but does not connect their findings to the specific tool categories it endorses. - The Greek-market statistic is sourced to a single industry survey (People of Business) whose methodology is not described, yet it anchors the paper's only original regional claim. - Citation hygiene issues (duplicate DOIs, misspelled author names, in-text/reference mismatches) suggest the bibliography was not verified, which matters for a work whose entire contribution is the accuracy of its synthesis. - The "hybrid human-in-the-loop" recommendation—the paper's prescriptive centerpiece—is asserted as the solution without reviewing any evidence on whether such hybrid deployments actually reduce bias or improve outcomes in practice. Bottom Line: A practitioner seeking a rigorous or novel account of AI in HR will gain little—Pan & Froese (2022), Vrontis et al. (2022), and Hunkenschroer & Luetge (2022) cover the same terrain with systematic methods—though a Greek HR manager wanting an accessible, balanced first orientation to the topic, with a local adoption snapshot, could reasonably start here.

Problem & Motivation: University LMS platforms and MOOCs struggle to give students guidance matched to what they currently know. Existing recommender systems in education rely on collaborative filtering, content matching, or transcript-based prediction; they operate on surface metadata, never test a student's readiness immediately before recommending, cannot identify which specific prerequisite is missing, and offer no corrective action when a student is unprepared. The motivating audience is educational technology researchers and university learning-platform builders. The paper argues the literature has no unified framework linking real-time skill assessment, automatic flaw detection, and generative corrective instruction in one loop. Key Idea: The key insight is that course recommendation should be preceded by an AI-generated diagnostic assessment and followed by generative remediation — i.e., convert recommendation from a static prediction task into a closed diagnostic-remediate-replan loop, where every detected "flaw" is exposed in the UI as a clickable button that triggers on-demand generation of bridge micro-modules that restructure the pathway. This is a pipeline-architecture insight, not a new algorithm; the underlying components (adaptive quizzing, knowledge tracing, matrix factorization with attention, constrained prompting, PPO-based RLHF, differential privacy, SHAP-based explanation) are all standard techniques assembled in a new configuration. Methodology: The paper first presents a narrative literature review organized into three paradigms (traditional ML/heuristic recommenders; cognitive/context-aware adaptive systems; Gen AI/LLM diagnostic agents), then a gap analysis, then the proposed framework. The framework is a five-stage pipeline: (1) domain selection and competency-map initialization with prerequisite hierarchies; (2) an adaptive Gen AI-generated diagnostic mini-quiz producing a domain mastery score; (3) a recommendation engine combining hybrid matrix factorization, attention, and Hidden Markov Model sequential trajectory modeling to order courses; (4) flaw/backlog extraction from incorrect or delayed quiz responses to isolate missing sub-concepts; (5) a "Flaw Button" that invokes a constrained-prompt transformer to generate summaries and exercises and inserts bridge modules into the path. Governance layers include a reward model scoring remediation quality (positive reward when a student passes post-remediation re-diagnosis) updated via PPO, calibrated Laplacian/Gaussian noise on gradients for ε-differential privacy, and SHAP-based natural language explanations. Critical design decisions: replacing transcripts with live diagnostics (well-motivated by the gap analysis but unvalidated); using a scalar pass/fail re-diagnosis reward for RLHF (plausible but no reward-shaping or reward-hacking analysis); and differential privacy at the analytics-aggregation level (asserted, not analyzed — no privacy budget ε is specified). No objective function is stated mathematically. Key Results: The evaluation section reports simulated comparisons on two public datasets — OULAD (Scenario A: dropout prevention, 1,000 historical student profiles) and EdNet (Scenario B: MOOC skill adaptation, 1,500 user profiles) — against "traditional collaborative filtering and metadata-based recommenders." Reported numbers: Scenario A — prerequisite detection accuracy 92% (proposed) vs. 45% (traditional), pathway adaptability 88% vs. 30%, remediation success 85% vs. 20%; Scenario B — pathway adaptability 91% vs. 22%, remediation success 82%. These figures cannot be treated as measured results: the paper itself states real-world human trials are planned for the future, and the "simulation" methodology is never described — how profiles were constructed, what the baseline algorithms were, how prerequisite detection accuracy or remediation success was computed in simulation, or how a simulated student "overcomes" a gap. No confidence intervals, seeds, or statistical tests are reported. Baselines are weakly specified and likely outdated (collaborative filtering without knowledge-tracing or LLM-based comparators). No ablations. Novelty Classification: NEW FORMULATION (framing course recommendation as a closed diagnostic-remediate-replan loop) plus an unexecuted SYSTEM DESIGN; the genuine novelty is limited to the architectural integration and the "Flaw Button" interaction concept — the review itself, the RLHF/DP/XAI components, and the evaluation design are standard combinations of existing ideas applied to the education setting, and no implementation exists yet. Rigor & Reproducibility: Rigor is low. There are no ablations isolating which of the five stages matters, no error bars or multiple seeds, no significance testing, and no mathematical formalization of the objective. No code, data, or model weights are released (no repository URL is given). The evaluation is the paper's central methodological concern: the reported 92%/88%/85% and 91%/82% figures appear in a "simulated" setup whose construction is undocumented, making them effectively unverifiable projections — a Goodhart-style risk where the authors evaluate on an imagined setup tuned to favor the proposal, with unspecified baselines. The literature review cites 36 references but provides no systematic search methodology, inclusion criteria, or comparison table, so it is a narrative rather than a systematic review despite the "comprehensive review" title. The publication venue (International Journal of Computer Applications, Volume 187, No. 142, dated September 2026) is a low-tier outlet; treat all claims with reduced confidence. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: SYSTEMS-leaning conceptual design with an EMPIRICAL evaluation claim — but since no system is built, it is best classified as THEORETICAL/architectural with an unexecuted evaluation plan. - Practical: Cannot be assessed — nothing is implemented; the described stack (LLM generation, PPO fine-tuning, SHAP, DP-SGD) is buildable on commercial hardware but requires LLM serving infrastructure the paper does not cost or size. - Efficient: Not evaluated; the paper does not report generation latency, training cost, or inference overhead (it lists latency as a future measurement). - Effective: Evidence is only a proxy — the simulated numbers assert effectiveness but do not demonstrate that real students' outcomes improve. - Scalable: Not tested and not claimed beyond the 1,000–1,500 simulated profiles; per-student LLM quiz generation and remediation at university scale is unaddressed. The work delivers no software artifact — it stops at paper form (a conceptual architecture plus figures). Strengths: - The gap analysis is genuinely diagnostic: the four identified failures (no pre-enrollment assessment, black-box course lists without prerequisite identification, no remediation mechanism, rigid semester-locked curricula) are correct and actionable criticisms of the deployed-education-recommender literature. - The closed-loop formulation — requiring that a recommendation be preceded by live diagnosis and that every detected gap have a one-click generative remediation that re-plans the path — is a coherent and usable design pattern that goes beyond the sequential "predict next course" framing the paper critiques. - The paper is explicit that real-world trials are future work, which is honest positioning, and it correctly surfaces governance concerns (differential privacy, XAI-based explanations for student trust) that most educational-recommender proposals omit. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state that real-world human trials are planned for the future and that the current evidence is a simulated evaluation on historical datasets; future work is framed as turning the "theoretical architecture" into software and measuring recommendation accuracy, generation latency, and actual learning outcomes in real university settings. This is direct acknowledgment that the system is unimplemented — a credibility positive. However, the authors do not acknowledge that their reported simulation numbers lack a described methodology, and they present them with comparative figure (Fig 2) as if they were findings. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - The simulated results have no traceable provenance: no description of how student profiles were generated, what the "traditional" baselines exactly were, how prerequisite detection accuracy was ground-truthed, or how a simulated student completes remediation. The 92% vs. 45% and 20% → 85% figures should be read as illustrative targets, not evidence. - No LLM-based or knowledge-tracing baselines (e.g., BKT, DKT, existing Gen-AI tutor systems) are compared — only a strawman collaborative filter. - The RLHF loop (positive reward on passing re-diagnosis) invites reward hacking (students gaming quizzes to elicit positive rewards) and curriculum-quality drift; no mechanism or analysis is offered. - The differential privacy section names no ε value, threat model, or utility-cost measurement, so the privacy claim is decorative. - No discussion of hallucinated or pedagogically wrong generated remediation content, assessment validity (quiz items testing what the authors think they test), fairness/bias across student populations, or instructor-in-the-loop oversight. - The literature review has no systematic methodology (no search string, databases, or inclusion criteria) despite the title claiming a comprehensive review. - Self-citations [33, 36] by the first author are present but immaterial to the argument; the deeper issue is that the strongest related work on knowledge tracing and intelligent tutoring systems (item response theory, Bayesian knowledge tracing, cognitive tutors) is absent from the review. Bottom Line: A practitioner designing a personalized-learning recommender can use Sections 3–4 as a useful checklist of closed-loop capabilities missing from current systems, but the reported performance numbers are unsubstantiated simulations and the field has stronger, implemented alternatives — read this as an architecture sketch, not as evidence.

Problem & Motivation: Compound feed production involves four stages (reception/storage, dosing/mixing, pelleting, cooling/packaging) governed by strongly interacting physicochemical parameters — moisture, temperature, pressure, particle dispersion — that are hard to control with the semi-automatic systems many plants still run. The pelleting stage alone is a multidimensional optimization problem (moisture 14–16% cited as most critical at impact weight 0.85, temperature 75–85°C at 0.72). The stated gap is that comprehensive application of information-analytical systems to feed production remains insufficiently explored, particularly for Azerbaijan, where modernization is a national priority but no end-to-end IAS methodology exists. The audience is feed-industry engineers, enterprise managers, and Azerbaijani agricultural policymakers. Key Idea: The central synthesis claim is that no single modelling paradigm suffices: effective feed-production management requires hybridizing deterministic (thermodynamic/rheological) models for physical structure, statistical and ML models for short-term forecasting, and fuzzy logic for expert-knowledge formalization under uncertainty, all deployed on a four-level ISA-95-style architecture (field/PLC/SCADA-MES/ERP). This is a well-known integration thesis restated for the feed domain — the paper has no identifiable new technical trick. Methodology: The method is literature review, comparative analysis, and synthesis. The authors screened sources by relevance and thematic criteria, retaining 16 references. The comparative analysis classifies modelling approaches (deterministic, statistical, neural networks, fuzzy logic, hybrids) by advantages, limitations, and fit to production tasks; surveys a four-level IAS architecture with functional modules (data collection via OPC UA/Modbus/Profinet, time-series storage, ML analytics, visualization, decision support, cybersecurity via defense-in-depth); catalogs supervised, unsupervised, and deep learning applications; and reviews metaheuristics (GA, PSO, ACO, SA, DE, GWO) and decision-support techniques (MPC, robust optimization, stochastic programming, Monte Carlo). Design decisions: (1) the hybrid-modelling recommendation is justified by appeal to process-informed models generalizing better under limited data — plausible but asserted from secondary sources; (2) the four-level architecture follows standard ISA-95/automation practice, well-justified as an established pattern; (3) the Azerbaijani-context recommendations (regional raw materials, climate, phased rollout for small enterprises) are motivated but entirely unvalidated. Note: this is a narrative/synthesis review, not a PRISMA-compliant systematic review despite the "systematic" framing. Key Results: The paper reports no original experimental results. Its headline quantitative claims are synthesized literature ranges in Table 4: IAS adoption is said to reduce raw material loss by 28–35% (from 6.5–8.0% to 4.2–5.5%), cut energy consumption by 18–24% (45–55 to 35–42 kWh/ton), reduce product quality variation (CV) by 58–62% (8–12% to 3–5%), raise productivity 20–30% (8–10 to 10–13 t/h), reduce deviation from plan by 67–75%, cut downtime 30–40%, and cut quality-control labor 57–60%, with 2–3 year payback. Table 3 compiles ML accuracy ranges from the literature (e.g., XGBoost 90–94% for pellet mechanical-strength prediction, CNN 92–96% for visual inspection). Notably, the Polish abstract reports different ranges (automation increase 35–42%, raw-material loss reduction 18–23%) than the English abstract — an internal inconsistency. Baselines are the cited primary studies, many of which are recent (2019–2023) and reputable (Animal Feed Science and Technology, Biosystems Engineering, Journal of Manufacturing Systems), but the aggregation is unweighted, unverified, and lacks per-source attribution of each number. Novelty Classification: NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING is claimed (the efficiency ranges) but is not genuinely novel — it is a compilation of published pilot results. The genuine contribution, modest as it is, is a NEW FORMULATION at the domain-synthesis level: a domain-specific conceptual IAS architecture plus management principles (complexity, adaptability, intelligence, openness, security) tailored to feed production and the Azerbaijani context. Everything technical — hybrid neuro-fuzzy modelling, ISA-95 layering, metaheuristics, MPC, XGBoost quality prediction — is a standard combination of existing ideas applied to a new national/regional setting. Rigor & Reproducibility: No ablations, error bars, seeds, or significance tests are possible or reported — there is no experiment. The screening procedure is described only in two sentences (relevance and thematic criteria), with no database names, search strings, inclusion/exclusion operationalization, or PRISMA flow, so the review is not reproducible. No code, data, or system artifact is released. Methodological concerns: (1) Table 4's efficiency percentages are presented with source citations but the mapping from individual studies to each range is unverifiable; (2) the English and Polish abstracts cite inconsistent figures for the same indicators, undermining confidence in the synthesis; (3) Table 1's country automation levels (e.g., USA/Europe 70–90%, Azerbaijan 20–40%) and Table 2's impact weights (0.85, 0.72...) are described as averaged from literature but their derivation is opaque; (4) a narrative review of only 16 sources cannot support the breadth of conclusions drawn. The authors do transparently label the numbers as "synthesized literature ranges rather than single-source values." Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL (a literature-synthesis paper; no system is built or deployed, and no primary experiment is run). - Practical: Not demonstrated — the paper specifies commercially standard components (PLC/SCADA/MES/ERP, NIR sensors, OPC UA) but builds nothing that runs. - Efficient: Not evaluated — the only cost evidence is second-hand payback claims of 2–3 years from other countries' pilots. - Effective: Not shown for the paper's own proposal — the efficiency numbers concern systems others built, not the conceptual architecture recommended for Azerbaijan. - Scalable: Not tested and not claimable — the authors themselves note that adaptation of general models to specific plants and raw materials is a core open problem. The work delivers no software artifact, dataset, or reusable technique; it stops at paper form, offering a conceptual architecture and recommendations as its output. Strengths: - Genuinely candid limitation disclosure: the authors state that no practical experimental work was conducted and that Table 4 figures are synthesized ranges — a credibility positive. - Well-organized domain synthesis connecting feed-process physics (starch gelatinization, protein denaturation, Maillard reactions during pelleting) to the choice of modelling paradigm, which is more technically grounded than typical automation surveys. - Structured, actionable framing for a specific national context: Azerbaijan-specific constraints (climate, regional raw-material base, heterogeneous enterprise technical levels) are translated into phased-implementation and training recommendations, and concrete future-work directions (local model validation, pilot deployment, digital-twin adaptation, blockchain traceability) are enumerated. - The three-barrier diagnosis (sensor-data scarcity, model-to-plant adaptation, human/organizational factors) is an accurate and useful map of why feed-industry digitalization stalls in practice. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors explicitly state: (1) the literature analysis mainly covers the last ten years; (2) no practical experimental work was performed; (3) the Table 4 indicators are generalized ranges from pilots in various countries, not single-source values; and (4) future work must include experimental validation with Azerbaijani raw materials and a pilot IAS at a real enterprise. This is direct confrontation of limitations and is commendable; however, they minimize the implications of the small evidence base (16 sources) and do not address the internal inconsistency between the English and Polish abstracts. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - The screening methodology is not reproducible: no databases searched, no search strings, no PRISMA flow, no exclusion justification — "systematic review" is claimed but not delivered. - The English and Polish abstracts report materially different efficiency ranges for the same indicators (e.g., 28–35% vs 18–23% raw-material loss reduction), an unexplained inconsistency that casts doubt on the synthesis. - Table 4 aggregates numbers from heterogeneous pilots (different countries, feed types, baselines) into single ranges without stating which source supports which value, enabling attribution laundering of optimistic figures; the cited sources for some rows (e.g., quality-variation CV reduction attributed to [3, 6, 13]) are pellet-quality ML studies, not IAS deployment studies. - Table 1's country-by-country automation percentages and Table 2's impact weights lack derivable provenance and appear to be authors' estimates dressed as literature findings. - No cost model, TCO analysis, or sensitivity analysis accompanies the 2–3 year payback claim, which is central to the economic-justification argument. - The proposed Azerbaijani architecture recommendations are never stress-tested even against the cited literature (no reference pilot in a comparable post-Soviet feed plant is analyzed). Bottom Line: A serviceable entry-level survey for Azerbaijani/Caucasus feed-industry planners, but researchers and practitioners with access to the primary literature should read the underlying sources directly (You et al. 2022, Sun et al. 2023, Mancini et al. 2020, Verdouw et al. 2021), since this paper adds no original data, no validated architecture, and carries internal inconsistencies that make its synthesized numbers unreliable.

TL;DR - What it does: This paper combines a qualitative survey of NGFW/IDS-IPS technologies with a small regression experiment (linear, Ridge, Lasso, Random Forest on a 500-row dataset) in which a leakage-free modeling scenario and a log1p target transformation raise R² on predicting 'Lifetime Engaged Users' from ~0.02 to ~0.27–0.28, alongside a lab DDoS simulation against a Palo Alto NGFW. - Why it's important: The stated stake is that signature-based intrusion detection is losing effectiveness against sophisticated attacks and data exfiltration, so operators want ML-augmented behavioral detection. - How it does it: The core methodological move is excluding post-hoc/leaky variables from the feature set (leakage-free scenario) and applying a log1p transformation to the right-skewed, heavy-tailed target (skewness 4.52, kurtosis 34.11, ~8.8% IQR outliers) before fitting regularized linear models. - The good: The honest, explicitly leakage-free experimental design — where Ridge/Lasso/Random Forest all land within RMSE 626–632 and the authors report the low R² (~0.27) as the true difficulty of the problem rather than hiding it — is the most credible element. - The missing: The regression target is a social-media engagement metric, not any network-security outcome, so the paper never actually evaluates whether any model improves intrusion detection, anomaly detection, or data-leak prevention — the headline problem. - Read it or not: Skip it unless you are studying methodological hygiene (leakage, target transformation) in small-scale ML case studies; for actual AI-based IDS and anomaly detection there is a large, far stronger literature (e.g., the papers' own cited surveys by Liu & Lang 2019 and Thakkar & Lohiya 2021).

Empirical profile. The central flaw is a title–content mismatch the authors themselves concede: no model is ever evaluated on network traffic or any security outcome, so Novelty (20) and Rigor (25) both collapse — the regression experiment is a 500-row social-media dataset with textbook leakage and log1p handling. Resilience (30) is undermined by conclusion-level claims (SQL injection, phishing metrics) with no supporting results anywhere in the body. Honest reporting of weak R² (~0.27) and the leakage-free redesign keep Completeness (45) from being lower, but Practical Impact (20) is negligible — no artifact, no IDS evaluation. Problem & Motivation: The paper addresses the problem that traditional signature- and rule-based intrusion detection systems (IDS) are ineffective against atypical user behavior, hidden channels, and data exfiltration in corporate networks. The intended audience is corporate security teams choosing among next-generation firewalls (NGFWs) and IDS/IPS architectures. The stated gap is the integration of NGFW/IDS-IPS with machine learning for intelligent traffic analysis and detection of data-leakage channels. However, the actual experimental work addresses a different problem: predicting social-media user engagement from a small tabular dataset. The paper acknowledges this disconnect, stating the regression dataset 'is not treated as an IDS benchmark and its predictive performance is not interpreted as evidence of intrusion-detection effectiveness,' linking the two parts only at the 'methodological level.' Key Idea: The identifiable methodological idea is a leakage-free regression protocol: strip features that would not be available at prediction time (which had inflated a first-round model), impute missing values (median for numeric, mode for categorical), one-hot encode (19 → 56 variables), and apply log1p to the heavy-tailed target to stabilize linear-model generalization. There is no new algorithmic idea; the NGFW/IDS half is a comparative survey, and the ML half applies standard scikit-learn techniques. Methodology: Two loosely coupled pipelines. (1) Survey/comparative analysis: taxonomy of IDS vs. IPS (monitoring vs. intervention), NIDS/HIDS/hybrid trade-offs, and a vendor comparison (Palo Alto, pfSense, MikroTik; FortiGate/Firepower/Check Point mentioned in prose) across APT detection, TLS 1.3 support, sandboxing, ML support, DLP, and threat-intelligence integration. (2) Laboratory attack simulation: DDoS SYN-flood via hping3 in Kali Linux against a virtualized Palo Alto NGFW, with logs captured as training data; the conclusion also lists sqlmap, nmap, hydra, reverse-shell and phishing scenarios across three NGFW environments. (3) Regression experiment: 500 rows from open sources (attributed to Theodoridi & Gkikas 2025), 80/20 train/test split with fixed random seed, models = DummyRegressor(mean), linear regression, Ridge (L2), Lasso (L1), Random Forest (hyperparameters n_estimators, max_depth, min_samples_leaf tuned over several values), evaluated by MAE, RMSE, R². The target is 'Lifetime Engaged Users.' No explicit loss function beyond these metrics; no time-based split results are reported despite being claimed as validation. Key Results: In the leakage-free scenario: Dummy baseline RMSE ≈ 758.38, R² ≈ −0.057; Ridge on the raw target RMSE 731.34, R² 0.017; Ridge with log1p-back RMSE 629.66, R² 0.271 (MAE 357.05); Lasso log1p-back RMSE 626.10, R² 0.280 (best); Random Forest log1p-back RMSE 631.67, R² 0.267. Ridge raw → log1p therefore improves RMSE by ~14% and R² from ~0.02 to ~0.27. Random Forest showed no accuracy gain over Ridge even after hyperparameter tuning, attributed to the small sample and aggregated features. The initial leakage-containing model produced 'artificially inflated' results (no numbers given). Descriptive statistics: skewness 4.52, kurtosis 34.11, ~8.8% outliers. DDoS simulation: Palo Alto NGFW classified and blocked a TCP SYN flood and logged events — a qualitative vendor-platform observation, not a comparative benchmark. Baselines are trivial (a mean predictor) rather than competing IDS methods; all headline numbers are on a 500-row social-media dataset, i.e., toy scale. No numbers are reported for the SQL-injection, phishing, or other attack scenarios listed in the conclusion, nor for the time-based split. Novelty Classification: At most ENGINEERING OPTIMIZATION / NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING at textbook level: the finding that log1p transformation matters more than model choice for a skewed target, and that Random Forest underperforms regularized linear models on 500 rows, are well-known phenomena demonstrated on one small dataset. The leakage-free scenario applies Kapoor & Narayanan's published critique to a new dataset — a standard combination of existing ideas. The claimed 'scientific novelty' (an 'author's NGFW log analysis module' using behavioral analysis) is asserted but not specified, evaluated, or released, so it cannot be credited as a NEW SYSTEM/TOOL. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablation-like structure exists (raw vs. log1p target; leaky vs. leakage-free feature sets), and the fixed random seed aids reproducibility. However: no error bars, multiple seeds, or significance tests; no code, data, or model release ('DATA AVAILABILITY STATEMENT: Not applicable'); no time-based-split numbers despite claiming time-based validation; the leakage claim is self-diagnosed with no quantification of the inflation. Methodological concerns are severe: (a) the regression is run on a social-media engagement dataset while the paper is framed as IDS research — the central evaluation does not test the paper's stated problem; (b) the 'NGFW comparative analysis' mixes self-authored qualitative tables with no measured metrics; (c) conclusions about attack scenarios (SQL injection, phishing, etc.) appear only in the conclusion without any supporting results in the body. The internal contradiction between the body (AI tools used for structuring/translation) and the formal statement ('they did not use artificial intelligence (AI) tools in the preparation of this work') further weakens confidence in the write-up. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL (with a small SYSTEMS-style lab demonstration), evaluated as such. - Practical: Yes — scikit-learn on commodity hardware and commercial NGFW appliances (Palo Alto, pfSense, MikroTik) all run on widely available infrastructure. - Efficient: Training four small models on 500 rows is trivially cheap; no cost comparison to dedicated IDS tooling is given. - Effective: Not demonstrated for the stated problem — no experiment shows detection of intrusions, anomalies, or data leaks by the ML models; the R² of 0.28 engagement predictor solves a proxy unrelated to security. - Scalable: Not tested or claimed with evidence; the authors themselves note the small dataset prevented Random Forest from realizing its potential, so behavior at 10×–100× scale is unknown. The work delivers no released software artifact, dataset, or trained model — only paper-form code snippets and a lab setup description. Strengths: - Explicit confrontation of data leakage (Kapoor & Narayanan) with a concrete leakage-free redesign, which is methodologically correct and uncommon in applied-ML security papers of this type. - Honest reporting of weak absolute performance (R² ≈ 0.27) framed as 'the true difficulty of the forecasting problem' rather than oversold. - The demonstrated insight that target transformation (log1p) mattered more than model family — Ridge, Lasso, and Random Forest converged to RMSE 626–632 — is a legitimate, cleanly shown comparison. - The IDS/IPS taxonomy and NGFW comparison tables (Tables 1–3) are serviceable pedagogical syntheses for practitioners new to the domain. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors explicitly state: linear models at the original scale barely beat baseline; Random Forest gains nothing here due to limited data volume and aggregated features; low R² reflects genuine problem difficulty, not model weakness; model interpretability, false positives, and the need for continuous retraining remain open issues; and the regression task is disconnected from IDS evaluation ('not treated as an IDS benchmark'). This is a credibility positive — the authors confront the disconnect directly rather than hiding it. They minimize, however, the implication of that disconnect: with it acknowledged, most of the paper's framing (title, introduction, 'scientific novelty') is no longer supported by any experiment. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - Title–content mismatch: The paper is titled and motivated around AI-based anomaly detection in network traffic, yet no model is ever evaluated on network traffic, IDS data (KDD/NSL-KDD/CIC-IDS are absent), or any security outcome. The only security experiment is a single-vendor DDoS demonstration. - Missing security baselines: No comparison against signature-based IDS, any published ML-IDS method, or even non-trivial detection metrics (precision/recall/F1 on attacks) — the classification_report code snippet is shown but never executed with reported output. - Unreported validation: A time-based data split is claimed to 'confirm the methodological correctness' of conclusions, but no numbers, setup, or figures for it are presented. - Unsubstantiated claims in the conclusion: Testing across 'SQL injection, phishing, HTTP flooding, reverse shell, malicious binaries' with metrics ('proportion of blocked threats, inspection depth, response speed') is asserted for three NGFW platforms, but zero such results appear in the body — a serious reporting gap. - No threat model for the 'data leakage' contribution: The proposed 'intelligent approach based on event log analysis' is described only abstractly; the 500-row engagement dataset bears no relation to leakage detection. - Internal contradiction on AI use (used for translation/structuring per the body, denied in the formal statement), which undermines confidence in process rigor. - Table 3 inconsistencies (e.g., pfSense 'ML/AI support: Yes' is contestable; 'TCO: Short' for a 5-year cost column is likely a mistranslation of 'Low') suggest insufficient editorial care. Bottom Line: A practitioner in AI-driven intrusion detection gains essentially nothing here beyond a cautionary tale about data leakage and target transformation; the actual ML-IDS and anomaly-detection literature — including the surveys this paper itself cites — covers the same ground with real network-traffic benchmarks and far stronger evidence, making this paper skippable.

TL;DR - What it does: This paper proposes NeuroSymbolic-RLNet, a hybrid architecture that fuses 12 learned binary symbolic predicates with a 3-layer MLP via gated attention, claiming 23.7% better sample efficiency, 0.87 vs 0.15–0.21 interpretability scores, and 18.9% better adversarial robustness than deep RL baselines. - Why it's important: Black-box RL agents cannot be deployed in safety-critical domains (autonomous driving, trading, healthcare) where decisions must be auditable, so an architecture that is both performant and inherently interpretable would remove a major deployment barrier. - How it does it: Raw observations are mapped in parallel to (a) 12 threshold-style binary predicates whose linear weights are re-fit every 50 episodes under a semantic-anchoring regularizer, and (b) a 128-d neural embedding; the two are fused by softmax-gated attention and fed to a linear policy, trained with a three-term loss (policy gradient + symbolic consistency + cross-modal alignment). - The good: The paper is unusually explicit about the forward-pass derivation (all tensor dimensions given), provides a full seed-predicate table, reports 5-seed means with standard deviations, and includes ablations showing the symbolic layer drives interpretability (0.87 → 0.23 when removed). - The missing: The evaluation is internally incoherent — continuous MuJoCo control tasks are scored with accuracy/F1/confusion matrices/ROC-AUC instead of returns, the headline 'urban, rural, mixed' environments are never defined, and the interpretability and sample-efficiency metrics are unitless and formally undefined, so none of the headline numbers can be verified or trusted. - Read it or not: Skip it unless you are specifically studying red flags in neuro-symbolic RL evaluation or reviewing for a venue; rigorous readers should instead consult the cited surveys (Núñez-Molina et al., ACM Comput. Surv. 2024) and primary methods (BlendRL, Luo et al.) it compares against.

Problem & Motivation: Deep RL policies are opaque, generalize poorly to unseen conditions, and are vulnerable to adversarial state perturbations, which blocks deployment in domains where transparency is mandatory (autonomous vehicles, financial trading, healthcare decision support). Existing neuro-symbolic RL (NS-RL) approaches reportedly suffer from static, manually specified symbolic representations that cannot adapt to dynamics, post-hoc explanations that may not faithfully reflect the decision process, and poor scalability. The paper targets the intersection: adaptive symbolic representations, in-process (not post-hoc) transparency, and low overhead. Who has this problem: practitioners deploying RL in regulated, safety-critical settings. The gap claimed is real and well-documented in the XAI/NS-RL literature; the paper's framing of it is standard. Key Idea: The core move is a 'semantic anchoring' mechanism: 12 human-readable seed predicates (e.g., 'RSI > 70', 'joint velocity > v_thresh') are manually initialized per domain, then their linear weights are re-optimized every 50 episodes via a symbolic consistency loss while a regularizer penalizes angular drift from the seed weight vectors — the intent being that predicates adapt their decision boundaries to the environment without losing their original human-assigned meaning. These adaptive predicates are fused with a neural embedding by learned gated attention so that every action remains traceable to active symbolic rules. This is a plausible idea, but it is an incremental combination of threshold-feature engineering, auxiliary consistency losses, and attention fusion rather than a fundamentally new mechanism. Methodology: The framework is an MDP agent with a four-component pipeline: (1) a Symbolic State Abstractor computing 12 binary predicates p_k = 1[w_k·s + b_k > 0] from the raw observation; (2) a Neural Feature Encoder (Linear(n,256) → ReLU → Linear(256,256) → ReLU → Linear(256,128)); (3) a Neuro-Symbolic Fusion Module that projects both representations to d′=128 and combines them via softmax attention weights; (4) a linear Interpretable Policy Generator with softmax output. Training minimizes L = L_RL + λ·L_symbolic + γ_c·L_consistency, where L_RL is a policy-gradient loss with value bootstrap, L_symbolic penalizes weighted rule violations, and L_consistency aligns projected symbolic and neural representations. A convergence 'theorem' is sketched in three steps (Banach fixed-point for the symbolic Bellman operator under a Lipschitz condition, bounded-gradient stability for the neural component, Lyapunov decrease for the joint loss), but the proof is a sketch with 'full derivations… available upon reasonable request', and the final step's leap from convergence to a stationary point of a non-convex loss to 'the optimal neuro-symbolic policy π*' is not established. Critical design decisions: (a) 12 fixed-count predicates per domain (justified only by listing them, not by any capacity analysis); (b) update frequency of 50 episodes (chosen by sensitivity sweep, but the sweep itself is suspiciously tidy); (c) bounded drift via the semantic regularizer μ_k = 0.1 (motivated by the theorem's Lipschitz condition, though the theorem is not validated empirically). The paper is explicit that predicate seeds are manually defined — contradicting the abstract's claim of fully adaptive symbolic representations — a credibility-relevant inconsistency. Key Results: The paper reports accuracy 93.1% ± 2.6 (mixed environment), sample efficiency 0.78, interpretability 0.87, robustness 0.82, latency 11.2 ms, and 298 MB GPU memory, versus DQN (76.3% accuracy, 0.15 interpretability), PPO (81.7%, 0.18), SAC (84.2%, 0.21), and recent NS-RL methods (Luo et al. 87.9%, SymDQN 85.4%, BlendRL 86.1%, LogiCity 87.4%). Ablations: removing the symbolic layer drops accuracy to 78.5% and interpretability to 0.23; removing neural features drops accuracy to 72.3%. Adversarial degradation is 12.7% vs 34.2% for baselines under PGD (ε=0.05, 20 iterations). Claimed real-world deployment: 96.2% navigation completion. However, the evidentiary basis is compromised: (i) 'accuracy', 'F1', 'confusion matrices', and 'ROC-AUC' are reported for HalfCheetah-v4/Ant-v4/Hopper-v4 continuous-control tasks, where the standard metrics are cumulative return — no return figures appear anywhere; (ii) DQN cannot natively act in continuous action spaces as configured; (iii) the 'urban, rural, mixed' scenarios receiving the headline accuracy table are never defined as environments and do not map onto the three stated benchmark categories; (iv) 'sample efficiency 0.78' and 'interpretability 0.87' are unitless with no stated definition or normalization. Baselines are recent (2024–2025 NS-RL methods) but all cross-method numbers have the character of self-reported summaries rather than a shared, controlled evaluation. Scale is standard (MuJoCo, n ≤ 111, plus synthetic scaling to n = 1024); nothing is stress-scale. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD (modest) plus claimed NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING. The genuinely new element is the semantic-anchored adaptive predicate mechanism (learned threshold predicates constrained to stay near human-seeded semantics, with post-hoc expert validation, κ = 0.81). The rest — attention fusion of symbolic and neural streams, auxiliary consistency losses, standard policy gradients, SHAP-based attribution — is a competent combination of existing ideas; the convergence theorem is a standard stochastic-approximation argument (citing Achiam et al. and Borkar) and provides no new theory. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations exist (Table 4) and are the paper's strongest experimental element; 5 fixed seeds with mean ± SD are reported; hyperparameter sensitivity (Table 6) is included. However: the interpretability and sample-efficiency metrics are never operationally defined, making the central claims unverifiable; the 'theorem' proof is sketch-only; the Zenodo DOI in the experimental setup is an explicit placeholder ('to be activated upon acceptance') while the Data Availability statement says code is available 'on reasonable request' — contradicting the Code Availability section's GitHub URL — so at the time of publication no verifiable artifact exists; baseline hyperparameters are 'default except matching lr/batch', a non-trivial choice for fair comparison; and the evaluation metrics are misapplied to the task domain (classification metrics on continuous control), which is a disqualifying methodological flaw for the robotics results. The three-expert interpretability study (κ = 0.81) is a genuine but very small (n=3) validation. The paper does not develop its method on the benchmark it evaluates on, but the undefined metrics and incoherent environment naming ('urban/rural' vs MuJoCo/finance/adversarial) create a Goodhart-style risk that the evaluation was constructed to produce the reported numbers. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (with a THEORETICAL component). Practical: Yes in principle — 4.7M parameters, 298 MB training memory, runs on consumer GPUs per the paper's own measurements (though experiments used an A100). Efficient: 11.2 ms inference and ~64 MB memory overhead over DQN is acceptable, and the symbolic layer adds only ~1.3 ms — the cost analysis is one of the better-executed sections. Effective: Not demonstrated for the stated problem: no return-based RL evidence, undefined interpretability metric, and an undocumented 'real-world deployment' make the central effectiveness claims unverified. Scalable: Only a synthetic observation-dimension scaling test (n = 512, 1024; training time 14.1 → 18.3 h, memory 341 → 412 MB) supports sub-quadratic scaling; nothing tests scaling in task complexity, environment count, or multi-agent settings, and the paper only claims (does not test) applicability to real autonomous systems. Delivers a claimed software artifact (GitHub repo, Docker, checkpoints) that is not independently verifiable at publication time due to placeholder/contradictory availability statements. Strengths: - The semantic-anchoring design (seed predicates + angular-drift regularization + post-hoc top-5 feature annotation) is a concrete, well-specified answer to the real problem of learned predicates becoming semantically vacuous, and the small expert study (3 annotators, Cohen's κ = 0.81) is the right kind of validation to attempt. - The end-to-end derivation with fully specified dimensions (Eq. 1–6, all matrices sized) and the component-level latency/memory breakdown (1.3 ms symbolic, 6.4 ms encoder, 2.1 ms fusion) are more transparent than typical for this literature. - The ablation table isolates component contributions cleanly (e.g., symbolic layer: interpretability 0.87 → 0.23; consistency loss removal: accuracy 93.1 → 88.9), which is the correct experimental question to ask of a hybrid architecture. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state that the framework requires domain expertise for initial rule specification; that a performance/interpretability trade-off may not suit all applications; that human comprehension of explanations can improve; that comprehensive field testing 'is still needed'; and that the rule update frequency (50 episodes) is manually set, with fully automated rule discovery left to future work. These are acknowledged directly, which is a credibility positive, but the acknowledgments are superficial relative to the severity of the evaluation problems (they never address the metric/environment mismatch or the undefined interpretability score). Analyst-Identified Gaps: A reviewer should flag the following, none acknowledged by the authors: - Category error in evaluation: classification metrics (accuracy, F1, ROC-AUC, confusion matrices) applied to continuous-control MuJoCo tasks, with no episodic returns reported — the primary evidence for the robotics claims is therefore not interpretable as RL performance. - The 'urban, rural, mixed' operational environments that carry the headline accuracy/latency/generalization results are never defined (observation space, dynamics, reward, or relation to the MuJoCo/financial/adversarial benchmarks), and Figs. 1, 5–7 reference them without any experimental-setup description. - The interpretability score (0.87) and sample efficiency (0.78) are undefined scalars; 'interpretability' for DQN (0.15) vs this method (0.87) is not reproducible from the text. - The convergence theorem claims convergence to the optimal policy π*, but the sketched argument only supports convergence to a stationary point of a non-convex composite loss; no formal statement reconciles this, and proofs are 'on request'. - The abstract claims symbolic representations are 'adaptive' and learned, while the methodology states predicates are manually seeded with bounded drift — the headline novelty claim overstates what the mechanism does. - Contradictory and placeholder artifact availability (Zenodo DOI 'to be activated', 'on reasonable request' vs public GitHub) prevents independent verification; the paper was evaluated as an Article in Press, and the listed acceptance date (11 September 2026) precedes this analysis. - The financial environment is a single-asset (S&P 500 index proxy) buy/hold/sell task with no comparison to standard portfolio baselines, and the 96.2% 'real-world deployment' result has no platform, duration, or protocol description. - Suspiciously uniform results: the proposed method leads every column of Table 5 and every scenario of Table 2, with no failure case reported anywhere — a pattern more consistent with favorable metric construction than with genuine multi-domain dominance. Bottom Line: A practitioner should not rely on this paper: the core empirical claims rest on undefined metrics, category-error evaluation of continuous-control tasks, and an unverifiable artifact, so the well-executed components (semantic anchoring, cost analysis) are better sourced from the stronger prior work the paper itself cites (BlendRL, Luo et al., Núñez-Molina et al.'s survey).

TL;DR - What it does: This paper builds a lightweight CNN-based deepfake image detector that combines a standard backbone, a Squeeze-and-Excitation (SE) channel-attention module, and an F1-driven adaptive classification threshold, evaluated on a small FaceForensics++-derived dataset. - Why it's important: Deployed deepfake detectors in social-media pipelines need reliable real/fake decisions under distribution shift, and the paper argues the near-universal fixed 0.5 decision threshold is a silent source of error that costs almost nothing to fix. - How it does it: The trick is selecting the decision threshold on a validation set to maximize F1 (yielding an optimal threshold around 0.326 rather than 0.5), paired with SE channel recalibration and a video-group-level train/val/test split to prevent leakage. - The good: The ablation cleanly isolates the mechanism: threshold tuning lifts ResNet18 accuracy from 0.8835 to 0.9016 and F1 from 0.8773 to 0.9042 while ROC-AUC stays flat (0.9655 vs 0.9654), correctly showing the gain is a decision-boundary effect, not a ranking effect. - The missing: The paper's own ablation shows SE attention adds no measurable benefit (accuracy actually drops from 0.9016 to 0.9006 when added), and the headline 0.9960 'hard-test' accuracy contradicts the 0.9061 cross-validation accuracy with no explanation — the two results cannot both describe the same evaluation regime. - Read it or not: Skip it unless you specifically need a worked example of F1-optimal thresholding applied to deepfake detection; the core technique is a 2014-era standard practice (Lipton et al., which the paper cites) and stronger coverage exists in the robustness-focused deepfake literature (Face X-Ray, SBI, DeeperForensics).

Problem & Motivation: CNN-based deepfake image detectors are typically deployed with a fixed 0.5 probability threshold, which the paper argues becomes unstable when social-media images arrive compressed, resized, cropped, or otherwise degraded. Practitioners in content moderation and multimedia forensics need detectors that are reliable under such shifts, computationally cheap, and evaluated without video-level or identity-level leakage between train and test splits. The paper identifies three gaps in prior work: fixed thresholds, uniform treatment of feature channels, and optimistic frame-level random splits. This framing is reasonable but each gap is addressed with a known or trivial remedy rather than a new technique. Key Idea: The core idea is that the decision threshold — not just the backbone — is a tunable hyperparameter: select the threshold maximizing validation F1 after training, so the operating point adapts to the score distribution of the actual data rather than defaulting to 0.5. This is paired with SE channel attention for feature recalibration and a group-level (video-exclusivity) data split. The key idea is essentially standard threshold calibration; the paper's framing of this as 'jointly improving representation and decision mechanism' overstates what is a conventional combination. Methodology: The pipeline is: face detection and cropping, resize to 224x224, CNN feature extraction (backbones tested: Xception, EfficientNet-B0, MobileNetV3-Large, ResNet50), a linear classifier with sigmoid output trained with binary cross-entropy, then threshold selection on the validation set maximizing F1. The SE module applies standard squeeze-and-excitation channel gating between backbone stages. The data protocol groups all frames from one source video into exactly one of train/val/test, using 480 real and 480 fake source videos filtered from 998 FaceForensics++ folders, yielding 5,150 face images split 3619/533/998 (test: 510 fake, 488 real). Critical design decisions: (1) the F1-optimal threshold — well-motivated for imbalanced operating points and explicitly credited to Lipton et al. (2014); (2) the SE module — a 2018 technique applied off-the-shelf, and the ablation provides no evidence it helps; (3) the group-level split — good hygiene, but a known best practice in this literature, not a contribution. No explicit objective beyond binary cross-entropy is introduced. Key Results: Under five-fold cross-validation, ResNet50 achieves the best backbone results: accuracy 0.9061±0.0161, F1 0.9065±0.0185, ROC-AUC 0.9680±0.0075, PR-AUC 0.9677±0.0073, on the 5,150-image derived dataset. Threshold tuning improves ResNet18 accuracy from 0.8835±0.0186 to 0.9016±0.0151 and F1 from 0.8773±0.0253 to 0.9042±0.0138 with ROC-AUC unchanged; the selected threshold is 0.326±0.251 across folds, a very large variance that itself signals instability of the 'adaptive' threshold. Adding SE attention to the threshold-tuned model slightly hurts accuracy (0.9006 vs 0.9016). Under the 'strict group-level hard test,' ResNet50 reports 0.9960 accuracy, 0.9959 F1, and 0.9999 ROC-AUC/PR-AUC (508/510 fake and 486/488 real correct) — roughly 9 accuracy points above cross-validation and near-perfect, which is internally inconsistent with the CV numbers and with the paper's own argument that group-level splitting is the harder setting. Table 3 compares against Face X-Ray (0.94 acc), SBI (0.95), and multi-attention (0.96) using numbers 'taken directly from the original papers' on different data and protocols — not a controlled comparison — while declaring 'This Work' at 0.996 with 'Low' complexity. No robustness-to-compression experiment, the stated core motivation, is actually run. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD is not credible here; the contribution is best classified as ENGINEERING OPTIMIZATION (threshold tuning applied to deepfake detection) with a competent evaluation-protocol choice (group split). The genuinely novel content is minimal: F1-optimal thresholding (Lipton et al. 2014), SE attention (Hu et al. 2018), and group-level splitting are all standard techniques combined in a new application setting; the paper's own related-work citations acknowledge each ingredient exists. Rigor & Reproducibility: Five-fold cross-validation with mean±std is reported for main results, and a targeted ablation (baseline vs +threshold vs +threshold+SE) exists and is informative — the threshold effect is real but modest, and it honestly shows SE contributes nothing measurable. However: (1) the optimal threshold's cross-fold std of ±0.251 is not discussed and undermines the stability claim; (2) the 0.9960 hard-test result is reported as a single number with no cross-validation, no seeds, no significance testing, and no explanation of the 9-point gap to CV; (3) Table 3 comparisons are imported from other papers under different protocols and datasets — a methodological flaw presented as evidence of generalization; (4) citations appear garbled (SBI is attributed to reference [33], which is actually an image-montage paper, and multi-attention to [34], an image-hashing paper); (5) the dataset is a small, non-standard subset of FaceForensics++ (5,150 images from 960 videos) with no public release, code, or model weights; (6) evaluation is entirely on the authors' own derived split — a Goodhart risk since the threshold and all model selection occur on the same distribution being scored. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (the paper runs experiments; no formal results). - Practical: Yes — ResNet18/50 and MobileNetV3 backbones at 224x224 run on commodity hardware, and the threshold step is a post-hoc scalar selection costing essentially nothing. - Efficient: The paper claims low complexity and this is plausible (no temporal modeling or fusion), though no inference-latency, parameter-count, or FLOP measurements are reported; 'Low' complexity in Table 3 is asserted, not measured. - Effective: The evidence shows the method solves a proxy — in-domain binary classification on a small derived dataset — not the stated problem of robust detection under compression, noise, and distribution shift, for which no degradation experiments exist. - Scalable: Not tested and not claimed with evidence; the authors defer full FaceForensics++, Celeb-DF, and DeeperForensics evaluation to future work, so behavior at standard benchmark scale is unknown. The work delivers a paper only: no code, dataset, or trained model is released. Strengths: - The threshold-tuning ablation is cleanly designed and interpretable: accuracy and F1 improve while ROC-AUC/PR-AUC stay flat, precisely localizing the effect to the decision boundary rather than ranking quality — an honest mechanistic finding. - The group-level (video-exclusivity) split is correctly applied and explicitly motivated, avoiding the frame-level leakage that inflates many deepfake results. - The paper is transparent that threshold tuning improves decision-making rather than representation, which correctly tempers the interpretation of its own gains. - Multi-backbone comparison (four architectures under identical protocol) gives a useful, if small, relative picture. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The conclusion explicitly concedes the evaluation used only a derived subset: future work will evaluate on the full FaceForensics++ and external benchmarks (Celeb-DF, DeeperForensics) for cross-dataset generalization, test robustness under real social-media degradations (recompression, resolution change, cropping, filtering, unseen manipulations), and extend to temporal/multimodal cues. This is a direct and honest acknowledgment that none of the motivating robustness conditions were actually tested — a credibility positive, though it substantially narrows what the current results support. The authors do not acknowledge the null result for SE attention as a limitation; they describe it as 'stable feature-representation support' and 'limited' gain, which minimizes evidence contradicting their own headline contribution. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - The central unexplained anomaly: the 'hard test' accuracy (0.9960, AUC 0.9999) far exceeds five-fold cross-validation (0.9061, AUC 0.9680). A genuinely harder held-out split producing near-perfect scores while CV struggles suggests the test split is easier, or that residual video/identity correlation remains; the authors present this as evidence of generalization with no comment on the inconsistency. - The paper claims robustness to compression/cropping/noise as its motivation but runs zero degradation experiments; the word 'robust' in the abstract and Table 3 is unsupported by any measurement. - The SE module — half of the title and claimed novelty — is shown by the paper's own ablation to provide no benefit (accuracy 0.9016→0.9006, all metrics flat or worse), yet the framing does not change. - Table 3 is an apples-to-oranges comparison: numbers for Face X-Ray, SBI, and multi-attention are imported from papers evaluated on full FaceForensics++ under standard protocols, then placed alongside the authors' number on a private 5,150-image subset, with a subjective 'Complexity: Low vs High' column. - The reference list appears corrupted: SBI and the multi-attention method are cited via [33] and [34], which are Steinebach et al. papers on image montage recognition and robust image hashing — unrelated to the methods compared. - Threshold 0.326±0.251 across folds means in some folds the 'optimal' threshold is near 0.075 or 0.577 — the adaptive threshold is itself unstable on this data, which directly undercuts the motivation that it stabilizes decisions. - Keywords include 'cross-modal semantic consistency,' a concept absent from the paper; Figure 1 appears to describe a watermarking/knowledge-distillation system unrelated to the proposed pipeline, suggesting template reuse and weak quality control. - Single author from a vocational university with a background in film/design studies and no code/data release limits independent verification. Bottom Line: A practitioner gains only the reminder that F1-optimal thresholding is a free, worthwhile default over 0.5 — the rest (SE attention, the 0.996 hard-test claim, the SOTA table) is either contradicted by the paper's own ablation or unsupported by its evaluation, and far stronger, properly benchmarked alternatives (SBI, Face X-Ray, DeeperForensics line of work) cover the same ground with public code and real robustness testing.

Problem & Motivation: The paper addresses the problem that modern high-tech product lifecycle management requires integrating design, production, and market intelligence into a single adaptive system, whereas traditional (linear, non-cognitive) approaches cannot self-organize, automatically optimize processes, or adapt to changing external conditions. The intended audience is industrial enterprises undergoing digital transformation, framed explicitly against Russian policy documents (the Ministry of Science and Technology's 2030 technological development concept) and Industry 4.0 adoption. The gap claimed against prior work is the absence of a unified cognitive management platform: prior treatments cover individual tools (digital twins, predictive analytics, adaptive management) but not a system of interconnected models spanning the whole lifecycle. Key Idea: The identifiable organizing idea is the decomposition of lifecycle management into three interconnected digital control loops — cognitive marketing (demand monitoring/forecasting), technological (digital design and virtual testing), and production (intelligent planning) — coordinated through a platform whose models are continuously retrained on data from production lines, product sensors, and market indicators. The sustainability analysis reframed around a "resource triangle" (scientific-technical potential, production capability, market intelligence) and a cognitive reworking of the break-even point (incorporating competitive-advantage costs, commercialization dynamics, imitation risk, and obsolescence rate) is the second conceptual move. Neither idea is mathematically formalized in the text. Methodology: The paper is a conceptual architecture study, not an algorithmic one. Methodologically it synthesizes literature and presents: (1) a stage-technology-effect mapping (Table 1); (2) a prose specification of a hybrid model suite — neural network demand forecasting, stochastic optimization of production parameters, agent-based competitiveness models, big-data cognitive analytics, and discounted cash flow evaluation augmented with strategic-value and synergistic-effect indicators; (3) two architecture diagrams (a full cognitive digital manufacturing ecosystem, Figure 1, and a local production circuit fragment, Figure 2) showing automated workplaces, a central intelligent management system, blockchain for operation transparency, and connections to global data sources. The adaptive mechanism is described as dynamic recalculation of objective functions depending on lifecycle phase and market conditions. Critical design decisions — the three-loop decomposition, blockchain integration, and the autonomous end-state — are asserted rather than justified against alternatives; no formal model is derived, no loss function or equation is stated, and no implementation path is given. Key Results: The paper reports no empirical results, no experiments, no case studies, and no quantitative measurements of its own. Table 1 presents ranges of claimed economic effects by lifecycle stage — design: 25–40% R&D cost reduction, 30–50% faster market launch; production: 15–25% cost reduction, 40–60% defect ("marriage") reduction; operation: 20–35% service-life increase, 30–45% maintenance cost reduction; modernization/disposal: 15–30% residual value increase, 25–40% environmental cost reduction — but these are unsourced, and the paper does not measure anything. No baselines, datasets, or deployment scale exist. The headline deliverables are the Table 1 mapping and the two architecture diagrams (Figures 1–2). Novelty Classification: At most a NEW FORMULATION (a three-loop conceptual decomposition of cognitive lifecycle management) plus a vision/architecture synthesis; it is not a NEW METHOD, DATASET, SYSTEM, or EMPIRICAL FINDING. Genuinely novel content is minimal: the constituent elements — cognitive digital twins, multi-agent modeling, stochastic optimization, adaptive production management — are all established in the cited literature (including the authors' own prior work), and the contribution is their assembly into a conceptual framework. The claimed "economic-mathematical apparatus" is asserted in prose but never actually presented as mathematics. Rigor & Reproducibility: Not reproducible in any meaningful sense: there is no formal model to implement, no data, no code, no algorithm, and no protocol. No ablations, seeds, or significance tests exist because no experiments were run. The Table 1 effect ranges carry no citations or methodology, which is the paper's most serious rigor defect — unsourced quantitative claims presented as findings. The literature review is current (2022–2025 sources) and reasonably broad for a conceptual paper, but the evaluation is entirely absent; the framework is developed and "validated" only by internal narrative coherence. Peer-reviewed in RUDN Journal of Economics (a Russian-language economics journal), but the review standards clearly did not demand formalization consistent with the title. Deployability: Profile: THEORETICAL (a conceptual framework and architecture with no primary experimental or deployed claim), with aspirational SYSTEMS elements. — Sound: No assumptions are stated and no formalism is given, so soundness cannot be assessed; the mathematical claims are empty placeholders. — General: The framework is pitched at the level of any high-tech enterprise, but with no boundary conditions, applicability criteria, or cost model, its scope is undefined. — Tight: Not applicable — there are no bounds or quantitative propositions. — Implementable: The architecture diagrams suggest a system blueprint, but no interface, data schema, or engineering specification is provided; nothing here could be built without enormous additional design work. The work delivers a paper and two diagrams only — no software artifact, dataset, or reusable technique. Strengths: - The three-loop decomposition (cognitive marketing / technological / production circuits) is a clean organizational lens that could structure a research program or an enterprise transformation roadmap, even if not formalized here. - The extension of break-even analysis to include competitive-advantage creation costs, imitation risk, and technology obsolescence rates is a genuinely interesting conceptual proposal that mainstream cognitive-manufacturing literature largely ignores. - The literature grounding is current and international (Zheng & Kiritsis on cognitive digital twins; Singh & Sharma 2025 on multi-agent quality analysis), connecting the Russian policy context to mainstream research. - Table 1, whatever its evidentiary basis, usefully consolidates the claimed value proposition of cognitive technologies per lifecycle stage in one place. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The paper acknowledges no specific limitations. It does not address data requirements, integration costs, organizational barriers, failure modes, or the gap between its proposed autonomous end-state and present-day capabilities. The concluding section frames the path toward "fully autonomous" production approaching "strong artificial intelligence" cognition without qualification — a credibility negative, as limitations are neither confronted nor listed. Analyst-Identified Gaps: A critical reviewer would flag: (1) the title promises an economic-mathematical framework but the paper contains no equations, no model specification, no parameterization, and no worked example — the central deliverable is missing; (2) Table 1's effect ranges are unsourced and indistinguishable from estimates or literature transcriptions, presented without provenance; (3) no cost side is analyzed anywhere — the claimed benefits are never weighed against the substantial investment cognitive platforms require; (4) the blockchain component appears without motivation, a security analysis, or a use case where its cost is justified; (5) the framework is never instantiated on even one real or hypothetical product, so internal consistency of the three loops is untested; (6) "cognitive" is used as an umbrella label without a definition distinguishing it from ordinary ML-based automation; and (7) the transition logic from today's technology to autonomous, goal-forming production systems is asserted, not argued. Bottom Line: A practitioner gains a readable Russian-language conceptual scaffold for thinking about cognitive lifecycle management, but the paper fails to deliver its titular mathematical framework or any evidence, and stronger alternatives (e.g., Zheng, Lu & Kiritsis 2022 on cognitive digital twins; Zhou et al. 2022 on production and operations management for intelligent manufacturing) cover the same ground with substantially more substance.
